The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* of Vasubandhu Chapter One: Elements (*Dhātunirdeśa*) Homage to the Buddha. 1. The [five] aggregates (*skandha*), the [twelve] bases (*āyatana*), and the [eighteen] elements (*dhātu*) are taught. What are they? Form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these are the five aggregates. The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—these are the twelve bases. The eye element, the visible-form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element—these are the eighteen elements. 2. Form consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements. 3. The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and air. Their characteristics are respectively solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. 4. Derived form consists of the faculties, their objects, the unmanifest, and the non-obstructive. 5. The faculties are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the faculties of femininity, masculinity, and life. The objects are visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibles. Unmanifest form is that which is not manifest. Non-obstructive form is space. 6. Visible form is color and shape. Color is blue, yellow, red, white, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness. Shape is long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, fine, coarse, smooth, and rough. 7. Sound is of eight kinds: pleasant and unpleasant, caused by living beings and not caused by living beings, and each being either defiled or undefiled. 8. Odor is of four kinds: pleasant, unpleasant, equal, and unequal. 9. Taste is of six kinds: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. 10. Tangibles are of eleven kinds: the four great elements, smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst. 11. The eye sees visible forms; it does not see them as near or far, nor does it see them as obstructed. It sees those forms that are within its range. 12. The ear hears sounds; it hears those sounds that are within its range. 13. The nose smells odors; it smells those odors that are within its range. 14. The tongue tastes flavors; it tastes those flavors that are within its range. 15. The body feels tangibles; it feels those tangibles that are within its range. 16. The mind knows mental objects; it knows those mental objects that are within its range. 17. The eye and the ear are both past, present, and future. The nose, tongue, and body are present and future. The mind is past, present, and future. 18. Visible form is past, present, and future. Sound is the same. Odor, taste, and tangibles are present and future. Mental objects are past, present, and future. 19. The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are internal elements. Visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental object are external elements. 20. Eight elements are material: the five sense-faculties, visible form, odor, taste, and tangible. The remaining ten are immaterial. 21. Nine elements are non-defiled: the seven consciousness-elements and the two mental-object elements. The remaining nine are both defiled and undefiled. 22. Eight elements are non-appropriated: the seven consciousness-elements and the mental-object element. The remaining ten are both appropriated and non-appropriated. 23. Eight elements are neutral: the seven consciousness-elements and the mental-object element. The remaining ten are both wholesome and unwholesome. 24. Eight elements are non-sensuous: the seven consciousness-elements and the mental-object element. The remaining ten are both sensuous and non-sensuous. 25. [Śrīḥ Bṛhaspatismṛtiḥ] [1. Vyavahārakāṇḍam])
[1.1.0] In former times, persons were devoted to the Dharma and were non-violent.
The legal procedure was instituted for those overcome by greed and hatred.
If the master does not pay wages to servants who are performing their work,
and the servants do not perform it, then a legal dispute arises in that matter.
For someone may commit violence, or fail to pay what is due;
these two are indeed the grounds for dispute, and between them, the latter has more numerous outcomes.
When a commodity is sold and money is received for the purpose of discharging a debt,
that transaction involving the principal amount and the highest interest is known as *vyavahāra*.
[1.1.1 Qualities of a King] Therefore, I shall describe in due order the qualities and duties of a king:
creditors, debtors, and those in dispute; sureties, documents, and witnesses.
Listen now to the origin of him who correctly investigates [the self]:
it is from Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vitta, Āpatti, and Yama.
Having extracted the mere essence of fire, the form of the King was indeed fashioned;
all beings, both moving and stationary, are composed of that.

Out of fear [of punishment], they become capable of providing enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties; in a state of anarchy, however, there is no cultivation, trade, lending at interest, or protection of subjects.
Therefore, he was created of old as the leader of the social classes and stages of life;
legal procedure (vyavahāra) consists of two parts, arising from property and injury.
The root of wealth consists of fourteen [factors], while the root of violence is fourfold:
two types of harshness, killing, and likewise the abduction of another's wife.
Lending at interest, finding hidden treasure, and joint undertakings;
non-payment of wages, failure to serve, disputes over land, and selling what one does not own.
Rescission of purchase and sale, breach of contract,
matters concerning men and women, theft, partition of inheritance, and gambling with dice.
These fourteen words, which arise from [the pursuit of] wealth,
are further divided in this way into many hundreds through the distinctions of action.

Bṛhaspati has stated that there are four categories arising from violence (*hiṃsā*): the two types of verbal abuse (*pāruṣya*), assault (*sāhasa*), and the abduction of another's wife (*parastrīsaṅgraha*).
They are distinguished individually according to whether they are inferior, middling, or superior; the specific distinction among these four is likewise set forth in their proper order.
These eighteen topics declared in the Dharmaśāstras are the foundation of all disputes; those who know them are the true investigators.

The first quarter is known as the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*); the second is likewise the rejoinder (*uttara*); the third quarter is to be stated as the application (*kriyāpāda*), and the fourth is the final decision (*nirṇaya*).
[1.1.3 The Strength and Weakness of the Fourfold Authority,
beginning with Dharma] Through *dharma*, through legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), through conduct (*cāritra*), and by the command of the king—
thus is the decision regarding a doubtful matter declared to be fourfold.
Where a legal decision is made by relying solely upon the sacred scriptures, that is to be known as a formal judicial proceeding (*vyavahāra*); through it, *dharma* also increases.
A decision may be made there based on local custom, inference, and the consensus of merchants; however, in such a case, the formal legal procedure is subverted.
Where a king, having set aside established conduct and custom, issues a decision, that is a royal decree; by it, established conduct is superseded.

In accordance with the treatises on Dharma, the king— accompanied by his ministers and his domestic priest, free from anger and greed, truthful, and having conquered his senses— should examine legal cases for the sake of protecting his subjects.
[1.1.4 The Topic of Dharma] That which consists of seven constituent elements for both the seeker of victory and his enemy—
this very circle of fourteen is what they call the *maṇḍala*.
There are four protectors of the earth; together with their separate allies, they constitute a group of eight.
And these, along with ministers and others, are imperishably united in this world.
Having risen in the morning and performed purification according to the prescribed rules,
the king [should honor] his gurus, astrologers, physicians, gods, Brahmins, and domestic priests.
Having honored these [elders] as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having greeted his teachers and others with a cheerful countenance, he should enter the assembly hall.
The king, surrounded by exactly three virtuous men, should examine legal cases after entering the preeminent assembly hall, either seated or standing.

[1.1.5 Characteristics of a Fortress] For the protection of his own person, his wives, his wealth, and his subjects— once these have been accumulated— the king should cause a fortress to be built, provided with two types of ramparts.
It is provided for kings with fuel and liquids, cane, young grass, food, and vehicles;
and with various machines and weapons, as well as with smooth and brave men.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas and Kṣatriyas who maintain the sacred fire-offerings,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
Taxes shall not be levied upon them; they should be granted house-sites and made exempt from royal dues by recording this in a royal edict.

They shall perform the daily rites (*nitya*), the occasional rites (*naimittika*), the rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), as well as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*); likewise, they shall carry out the ancient rituals (*paurāṇa-karma*) and the administration of justice in doubtful cases.
Wherever the ground is level, or even low-lying or elevated according to its nature,
the halls, towers, moats, and so forth should be constructed in that same manner.
Thereafter, the subjects— including the twice-born, Vaiśyas, merchants, artisans, craftsmen, and guards— should construct their dwellings all around that area.
He shall establish barracks, watch-stations, outposts, crossroads, assembly places, marketplaces, and pasture lands for cattle.
How can one who has been proclaimed as "virtuous" in the assembly of people be described by that very same mouth as being "devoid of virtue"?
Therefore, one should not deprive an innocent person of his authority or livelihood;
for otherwise, there would be the consequence of endless instability, and royal favor would perish.
[1.1.6 The Characteristics of Protecting the Subjects] But a territory that has been properly settled and fortified according to the treatises,
he should constantly apply his supreme strength toward the removal of thorns (the suppression of criminals).
That protection of the subjects is declared by those who know the law to be threefold:
[protection] from foreign armies, from the fear of thieves, and from the strong who act unjustly.
The king should pacify the fear of thieves from enemy armies through strategic means,
and he should provide daily judicial review for those oppressed by the powerful.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one offers oblations, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes entitled to a sixth part of that, provided he protects [his subjects] properly.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees.
The cultivator shall pay a tenth, an eighth, or a sixth part as the king’s share from fallow land,
from land sown in the rainy season, and from land sown in the spring, respectively.
According to local custom, they shall pay the tax—whether monthly, six-monthly, or annual;
this is declared to be the ancient law for tillers of the soil.

[1.1.7 The Manner of Constructing the Assembly Hall] One should construct the assembly hall within the fortification— whether it be a water-fort, a mountain-fort, a forest-fort, an earth-fort, or a desert-fort— as a separate building surrounded by water and trees.
To the east of that [hall], he should cause a distinguished assembly hall to be constructed facing the east,
provided with garlands, incense, and seats, and furnished with seeds and gems.

[The house] should be provided with images, paintings, and deities, as well as fire and water; it should be auspiciously marked and endowed with the characteristics prescribed in the treatises on architecture (vāstu-śāstra).
Having occupied the auspicious throne, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should pay homage to the world-protectors and then begin the inspection of affairs.
The Brahmin is the root of the tree of Dharma; the king is its trunk and branches; the ministers are its leaves and flowers; and protection through justice is its fruit.
Fame, wealth, the essence of fruits, enjoyment, acquisition, and honor;
invincibility, inclusion in the ranks of the world, and an eternal station in heaven.
Having drunk in these essences of justice and having become impartial,
the king, having abandoned greed and other such vices, shall carry out the decision of the law.
The king himself shall preside over disputes concerning means of subsistence;
he is served by the learned according to the path seen in the scriptures.
Therefore, a king should protect [his subjects] properly and with diligent effort according to justice;
from that, he shall obtain wealth, sovereignty, and vast fame.
The gods, in brief, know truth; but men know falsehood.
He whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
The sacrifice arises from the conjunction of the animal, the clarified butter, the officiating priests, and so forth;
just as it is connected with these, so is its conventional designation explained.
But he who, relying on the opinions of the presiding judge and the members of the court,
reaches a decision on matters through the application of their reasoning, does not deserve punishment.
[1.1.8 Varieties of Assemblies] The assembly is declared to be fourfold: established, unestablished, sealed, and likewise disciplined; and the members of the assembly are of the same kinds.
In a city or a village, it is established; that which is not established is called "mobile.
It is sealed, associated with a superintendent, appointed by the king, and governed.
One who, having formed a firm resolve, examines legal cases— that assembly is equal to a sacrificial rite.
Its members should be seven, five, or even three, being knowers of the world, the Vedas, their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma.
That assembly hall where the foremost of Brahmins are seated is like a sacrificial ground.
The king should always keep the plaintiff and the defendant under guard without requiring sureties;
that court which the monarch occupies is said to possess these ten constituent parts.
Having set aside one-eighth of the day, he should go to sleep;
that time is recorded in the scriptures as the supreme period for legal proceedings.
The king should appoint as members of the court those who are engaged in performing virtuous deeds, devoted to truth and righteousness, free from anger and greed, and learned in the scriptures.
There should be seven, five, or three members of the court assembly;
those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, or devoid of scriptural knowledge [should not be included].
Those who are insane, angry, greedy, or afflicted by pain should not be questioned in a legal determination.

The king, or else a learned Brahmin acting as the presiding judge, shall examine the legal cases, having placed at the forefront the constituent elements of justice and remaining steadfast in the opinions of the court members and the scriptures.
Because he delights the subjects through his fourfold power (*caturaṅgabala*),
and because he shines with his own body, he is therefore called a "king" (*rājā*). However,
this single term has been declared by the wise to have many applications in common usage.
The king and a learned Brāhmaṇa are the final authorities for its determination.
The Vedic revelation states that he asks the question concerning the legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*); he who disputes therein is known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
In a legal dispute, he asks the question as well as the counter-question;
because he speaks first with kind words, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
The king who presides over the court together with his judges, his ministers, his Brahmin domestic priest, and the members of the assembly,
remains in heaven by virtue of his righteousness as an impartial observer.

He should appoint as a minister a twice-born Brāhmaṇa who understands the meaning of all the scriptures, is free from greed, speaks with justice, is wise, and has attained his position through successive succession.
He who, setting aside the twice-born, should look after affairs together with the Śūdras,
his kingdom will waste away, and his army and treasury will perish.
And for those who roam the forest, their trial shall take place in the forest;
likewise, for soldiers it shall be in the army, and for merchants in the caravans.
Plowmen, artisans, wrestlers, those who live by usury, guildspeople,
ascetics, and thieves— these are to be judged according to their own specific laws.
Families, guilds, and assemblies—the king is the authority over these; they are the foundation of legal proceedings, each succeeding one being more authoritative than the preceding.
The affairs of ascetics, however, he should have carried out by those learned in the three Vedas alone,
as well as by those skilled in the application of *māyā*, and never by himself for fear of provoking anger.
A king who punishes those who should not be punished, and fails to punish those who deserve punishment,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
Whether it be a brother, a son, a worthy guest, a father-in-law, or even one's maternal uncle—
if he has deviated from his own duty, there is no one who is not subject to punishment by the king.
Where there is no learned Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya there, or a Vaiśya who knows the Dharmaśāstras; one should avoid a Śūdra with every effort.
But one who is devoid of righteous conduct and actions, though lacking the external marks of a Brahmin,
yet says "I am a Brahmin"— him they call a "Brahmin-claimer" (*brāhmaṇabruva*).
The king should appoint as accountant and scribe those who know the true nature of words and their designations, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and not ignorant of scripts.
When witnesses, the plaintiff, or the defendant fail to appear without a valid reason, that man who speaks the truth must be appointed by the members of the court as the guardian of the case.
That assembly in which a king, having seated himself upon this ten-limbed judicial procedure, perceives justice with a disciplined mind, is equal to a sacrificial rite.

Of these limbs, the king is remembered as the head and the presiding judge as the mouth; the members of the court are the arms, the legal codes are the hands, and the accountant and the scribe are the shanks.
Gold, fire, water, and the eyes; the heart and the feet; likewise, one's own men.
The king should place gold, fire, water, the treatises on Dharma, as well as sacred objects and things that are beneficial, in their midst.
One should visualize the Sun, the Moon, the gods, and so forth, as well as the guardians of the directions there;
indeed, gold, fire, water, and one's own person are the ten constituent means.
The duties of all these ten [officers] have been declared separately:
the speaker, the supervisor, the king, the punisher, and the court member who examines the case.

Smṛti declares that the decision [of a case] consists of the awarding of victory and the imposition of punishment; furthermore, for the purpose of an oath, gold, fire, and water are used when living beings are thirsty.
The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal reasoning;
the king’s own officers shall summon the parties, the plaintiff, the members of the court, and the witnesses.
The punishment of speech and the punishment of censure depend entirely upon the Brahmin;
however, the punishment of fines and corporal punishment are both said to be under the authority of the king.
Those families, guilds, corporations, and so forth, who are properly known by the king, shall carry out the legal affairs of men, excluding cases involving violence or injustice.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies are declared to be the makers of legal decisions;
a case that has not been deliberated upon by families should be deliberated upon by guilds.
What is not known by the guilds (gaṇa) is known by the corporations (śreṇī); what is not known by the corporations is known by the appointed officials (niyuktaka).
The members of the court (sabhyāḥ) have authority over families and the like; the presiding officer (adhyakṣa) is declared to have authority over them.
The king is superior to all because he diligently upholds the determined Dharma through the adjudication of disputes among the highest, lowest, and middle classes.
The cognitions of the Lord move ever higher above all other cognitions,
[directed toward those] who are afflicted by the darkness of ignorance and covered by the film of doubt.
He who renders the scriptures free from defects by means of the probe of scriptural collyrium attains fame in this world, honor from kings, and a destination in heaven.

He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, should carry out the determination of legal matters according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
The members of the court must not overlook a proceeding that has been conducted unjustly; by overlooking it, those kings go headlong to hell.
"But having recognized that the mind of the king has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is unpleasant there; a member of the assembly does not thereby become a sinner."
First, the member of the court must speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the court is blameless.
If the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding a matter that has not been determined,
he shall be punished, as shall the members of the court, especially so.
Whether through ignorance, delusion, greed,
or even malice, where a member of the court speaks falsely, he is declared by tradition to be an unworthy member and shall be punished.
Where there is no written document, no witness, and no possession, and where no means of proof exist, the king alone is the sole authority in that case.
Those doctrines which cannot be determined and whose nature remains doubtful—
of these, the king shall be the authority, since he is the lord of all.
Every day, surrounded by his councilors, he should personally oversee legal proceedings. Those councilors who speak unjustly,
as well as those who live on bribes and those who deceive the trustful— all of them must be banished.
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the treatises is entitled to speak;
whatever he declares in that assembly is the Dharma—of this there is no doubt.
The king should sit facing the east, while the members of the court face the north;
the calculator faces the west, and the scribe faces the south.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when the time has come, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
In accordance with the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*, the king,
examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, should guide them.
If the members of the court, disregarding the principles of the science of logic, reach a decision here [on their own], then dharma is destroyed therein; it destroys everyone without a doubt.
The treatises of Manu and others are to be upheld, and never the treatises on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*).
When there is a conflict between the two, the word proclaimed in the *dharmaśāstra* must be followed.
A definitive conclusion should not be reached by relying on the scripture alone;
for if an inquiry is devoid of reasoning, the loss of Dharma arises.
Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon, he should look upon [his affairs] with aged ministers and dependents,
and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on Dharma and Artha.
"Through worldly convention, a thief may become a non-thief, and a virtuous man an unvirtuous one;
without logical inquiry, Māṇḍavya was reduced to the status of a thief."
Unreal things appear like the real, and real things appear like the unreal;
they are seen as producers of delusion, therefore one should investigate them through reasoning.
In a sacrifice, Viṣṇu is worshipped; in legal proceedings, the king is worshipped. Here, the victor is the sacrificer, while the defeated one is declared to be the sacrificial animal.
The first part is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the reply (uttara); the initial [statement] is known as the proposition (pratijñā) and the oblation (havis).
The three Vedas are the scriptures, the members of the assembly are the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and self-restraint is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In the same way, the calculator and the scribe should be understood as the two witnesses;
this judicial procedure has been declared to be equal to a sacrifice.

When one, unassailed by others, brings a matter before the king by a path that deviates from the traditional law (*smṛti*) and established custom (*ācāra*), that indeed constitutes a subject of legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*).
A plaint brought by one who is an outcast or similar person, by one who has not returned to his natural state,
or by one who acts without independence, is not established.
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, suffering from a calamity, a child, or an elderly person,
as well as one conducted by an unrelated party, is not valid.
Teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, master and servant: legal transactions among these when they are united as a group do not stand valid.
In this manner, the judge should have the plaint, as examined by the members of the court, committed to writing;
however, he shall not investigate a lawsuit that is unestablished or one that is prejudiced against the city.

[1.1.10 The laws of place and caste must likewise be protected: The laws that have been established for those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), as well as for those dwelling in difficult terrains, and for the customs of regions, castes, families, and so forth— these must be maintained.
In that very same way, those subjects must be protected; otherwise, they become agitated. When the people are alienated, the army and the treasury perish.
In the South, the twice-born marry the daughters of their maternal uncles;
in the Middle Country, laborers and artisans eat beef.
In the east, men are fish-eaters and women are devoted to adultery;
in the north, women drink liquor and menstruating women are touchable by men.
Those born of the same womb take the wife of their brother who is without a husband;
by this act, they do not become liable to penance or punishment.
Because they constantly fail to perform what is enjoined and practice what is forbidden,
the king, having provided them with food and clothing, shall take their surplus.

[For those born of inverse unions and likewise for those dwelling in difficult regions, they must be protected with effort according to the scriptures; however, when there is doubt, that [scriptural authority] is the means of proof.]
Having observed that [evidence], he should reach a decision according to the established rules previously laid down regarding the court,
the customary fees, fines, and the monthly, half-monthly, or annual taxes.
A boundary should always be established in writing and supervised by merchants;
the words of the plaintiff must be acted upon, and likewise the words of the defendant.
Having investigated thoroughly, one should take action; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
A lawsuit filed by a single person against many, or against women, or against spectators,
is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.

[1.1.11 Those who are not to be obstructed] One engaged in a sacrificial session (*sattra*) or a wedding, one who is ill, one afflicted by grief, one who is insane, a child, one intoxicated, an elderly person, one who has been summoned for trial, one engaged in royal business, and one observing a vow— these are not to be obstructed.
A soldier on the battlefield, a farmer during the harvest season, those in a precarious situation, and likewise women accompanied by a protector, must not be obstructed.

A minor who has not yet attained legal capacity, an envoy, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, those in distress, and likewise women who have a protector— these are not to be obstructed.
But when grain has grown, the merchant who has sold his merchandise, as well as the cultivator and those engaged in a sacrificial session,
shall be made to pay [the tax] once their transactions are completed.
When the mind is unable to resolve a dispute, yet one desires to engage in litigation, time for deliberation should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
Whomever one brings a charge against, whether on the basis of truth or even out of suspicion,
the king shall have that very person summoned by means of a female messenger or a male servant.

In the case of those who are timid, dull-witted, insane, aged, female, minor, or diseased, a kinsman— or another person appointed for the purpose— shall state both the preceding and the subsequent [facts].
In the case of a sacrificial priest and one who is appointed [as an advocate], they are declared to be equal;
at a sacrifice, the patron obtains merit, whereas in a legal dispute, he obtains either loss or victory.
[1.1.12 Summoning] BP1.1.144a:

But if one who has been summoned does not come out of arrogance, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen; BP1.1.144b: the judge shall determine a fine for him in accordance with the nature of the legal claim.
At the appropriate time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your distress? Do not fear; speak, O man!"

When he has been questioned in this manner, whatever he may say, the members of the court, together with the Brahmins, should deliberate upon it; if the matter is found to be just, then further steps shall be taken for the purpose of summoning him.

He should provide a seal [on the document], or he may direct a person [as a witness]. But if one who is summoned disregards the royal command while being capable [of obeying it], the king shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the charge.
One who is incapable, a child, an elderly person, one in a precarious state, or one overwhelmed by illness; for such persons,
the fine shall be fifty *paṇas* for a minor offense, at least one hundred for middling offenses, and for serious matters, they shall always be fined at least five hundred *paṇas*.
In a region destroyed by an enemy army, or afflicted by famine or disease,
one should issue a call for a general amnesty and should not impose punishment.
Those who have neglected their duties, those afflicted by calamities, those occupied with the king's business, and those distracted by festivals.

The king should not summon servants who are aged, those who have risen up in rebellion, those who are dependent on others, those of deceitful character, or those who are intoxicated, insane, or negligent.
Neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a legal mandate,
shall be exempt from punishment when speaking falsely for the sake of another in judicial proceedings.
A young woman born of a noble family who has not been defiled by another, who is about to give birth,
and who is the most excellent among all classes— such a maiden is declared to have been enjoyed by her paternal kinsmen.
Having ascertained the time and place, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the cases,
the king should gradually cause even those who are incapable of appearing in court to be summoned by means of vehicles.
The summoning of those who are dependent on their families, wanton women, courtesans, those who have lost their caste, and those who are outcastes is prescribed.
A surety capable of resolving the matter should be accepted for both parties.
Even those who have retired to the forest as ascetics and the like, once their intent is known,
the king should cause them to be summoned for important matters, provided he does not provoke their anger.
While the matter is yet to be stated, the plaintiff shall not restrain one who is standing still or departing;
he may do so only until the appearance of the defendant at the summons.
Restriction from place, restriction by time, restriction from travel, and likewise restriction from occupation—restriction is of these four kinds; one who is under restriction must not violate it.
Fields, gardens, houses, and the like, as well as wealth, grain, and so forth—
these are to be subject to legal restraint for litigants who speak unjustly.
But if one who has been placed under restraint should himself voluntarily relinquish that restraint,
there is no fault on account of his transgression, nor shall a fine be imposed upon him.
After reporting to the king, the one who has placed a blockade shall not release [the person] on his own;
if he should release him, he must be made to pay a fine, and the blocked person shall not escape.
In cases such as crossing rivers, traversing deserts, or encountering dangers in difficult terrain,
one who departs while still unaccomplished in his task does not incur guilt for violating a prohibition.

One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in the king's business— [these may be exempted].
Cowherds [should be exempt] during the grazing of cattle; farmers at the commencement of cultivation; artisans at the time of their work; and those who bear arms during times of war.

Those who have climbed a tree or a mountain, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats, and all those in precarious positions— these must not be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their business.
But he who, by restraining his senses and through fasting, holding his breath, and so forth,
should cause [the debtor] to be pressured— not by physical force— is not to be punished, for he has not transgressed.
One who is subject to restraint incurs punishment for evading it;
however, one who restrains a person not subject to restraint is to be punished by the king—this is the established rule.
The king shall examine the legal cases brought before him by litigants who have arrived for dispute, but he shall not consider cases initiated by himself nor those merely reported by his officials.
[1.1.13 The Sequence of Statements by the Plaintiff and the Defendant] When one is oppressed, has come of his own accord, or seeks [redress] through legal weaponry,
the judge— or a person acting on his behalf— should question him slowly and steadily.
The testimony of one who acts without being appointed— because he is not entitled to engage in legal proceedings—
shall not be accepted, except for what is written or sent by him.
When two litigants arrive by claiming "I came first," the trial should be conducted according to the order of their castes, or else by considering whose suffering is greater.

Those who are insane, intoxicated, or driven by madness; those defiled by a mortal sin; and those who are mentally deficient, very old, or children—these should be understood as being without recourse.

"A position that has been stated but is unacceptable, as well as a proponent who fails to provide a reply—such a proponent and such a position shall not be accepted; I shall now explain what kind of proponent and what kind of position are to be accepted."

When a proponent, intent on establishing his own position, speaks with the intention of expressing something by resorting to an exaggeration of suffering, that is called the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument).
[1.2. The Introduction to the Fourfold Legal Procedure] [1.2.0] The section on the plaint (*bhāṣāpāda*),
the section on the reply (*uttarapada*), and likewise the section on the proof (*kriyāpāda*).
And the stage of the rejoinder (pratyākalita) constitutes the fourth limb; thus, the judicial proceeding consists of four limbs.

"False confession (*mithyā-sampratipatti*), as well as counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*), prior plea (*prāṅnyāya*)—these four replies have been declared by those learned in the treatises. In the case of a false reply (*mithyā*), there are four legs (*catuṣpāda*); likewise in the case of a counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*)."

In a case where the plaintiff has already stated his claim, that [defendant] is to be understood as having failed in his defense when he does not provide an answer, even though he is being urged by various means during the two stages of the proceedings. If seven nights have passed and he still does not give an answer, he is defeated and deserves punishment.

[1.2.1 Definition of the Thesis] Once that [assembly] has been convened, the proponent should formulate a thesis that is faultless, accompanied by a proposition, and consistent with valid means of knowledge and authoritative tradition.
One should record the place, location, year, month, fortnight, day, name, and caste; as well as the substance, number, profit, loss, and the signs of emaciation.
Furthermore, one should not alter the meaning of the claim that one brings forward.
And one should not go to another side; by going from the former [side], one is defeated.
[1.2.2 Faults of the Thesis] The king should avoid a thesis that is unestablished, faulty, meaningless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory.
That which has not been composed by anyone is declared to be "unestablished" (aprasiddha).
That which has a different meaning and is devoid of its own intended meaning is proclaimed to be "faulty" (sadoṣa).
One who has committed a minor offense and seeks a small amount of wealth is known as "insignificant" (*nirarthaka*);
however, one who is devoid of any obstruction to his purpose should be understood as "useless" (*niṣprayojana*).
A legal proceeding that lacks [proper] terms such as "kusīda" and so forth is considered meaningless;
likewise, it should be understood as purposeless when it involves verbal abuse, physical assault, and the like.
"‘This bow made of hare-horn must be given by him to me’—
the wise call such a claim an impossible and unachievable plea.
When such a plea has been presented before the judge and the king,"
When there is opposition within one's own kingdom, it is called "internal conflict" (*viruddha*).
Those who know the subject (*pakṣa*) recognize it as being free from defects of the proposition, endowed with a valid proof, established, and proven by common worldly consensus.
It consists of very few syllables yet conveys abundant meaning; it is free from doubt and free from confusion;
it is devoid of contradictory causes and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
The statement itself constitutes the proposition (*pratijñā*),
for its meaning is the subject (*pakṣa*) in legal proceedings that must be articulated by the disputants without confusion.
Whether due to delusion or through deceit, that which was not stated by the proponent—
whether it be included within the rejoinder or otherwise— should be accepted by both parties.

Having thoroughly examined such qualities as these and being well-ascertained, a *pakṣa* (proposition) thus established is acceptable; otherwise, it is a mere semblance of a *pakṣa*. Furthermore, one that is devoid of place and time, and lacking in substance and number, is likewise unacceptable.
And a thesis that is devoid of both the probandum and the means of proof is held to be unacceptable.
If a plaintiff records a claim that is based on false reasoning, devoid of legal action, concerning an impossible matter, or is confused,
he suffers a loss of his suit (*vādahāni*).
If a litigant, having stated his charge, should overstep it and state another,
or having set forth a line of action, should speak otherwise, that plaintiff shall suffer defeat.
In the first half of the trial, the plaintiff shall rectify whatever is deficient or excessive, until the defendant, in the presence of the assessors, has provided his answer.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the teacher's wife,
as well as in other instances of indecent speech, no counter-argument is permitted.
In the case of killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden;

In cases of verbal or physical assault, the fabrication of false evidence, and likewise in acts of treason against the king, the informant shall not be made to pay; rather, the perpetrator himself shall litigate the matter.
The legal dispute, having been presented for deliberation, consists of eighteen points. There are other points within this [list] which the King himself should investigate:
the seizure of a sixth part [of property], purification, violation of agreements, and treasure-troves.
Killing, seizure, theft, and the violation of prohibitions and royal edicts; these are the [offenses].
Neither the king nor his official should personally initiate a legal case;
he should reduce excessive claims and fulfill those that are deficient.
One should cause it to be recorded on the ground for as long as the matter remains undecided;
once it has been heard, written down, corrected, and deliberated upon, [it shall be finalized].
Then the presiding judge shall cause the plaintiff's case, as stated by himself, to be written on a wooden board with chalk; thereafter, it shall be refined and written upon a leaf.
But for those who, having had their case stated and the matter established, settle the dispute among themselves,
one should determine a fine for them in accordance with the nature of the accusation.
Or others who create discord within cities, villages, great royal assemblies, or among the people—
all such legal proceedings are declared to be inadmissible.
One should first draft the document on a wooden board or on the ground using chalk;
after correcting what is deficient or excessive, one should subsequently inscribe it on the final leaf.
When the plaintiff, due to lack of confidence, is unable to speak,
time should be granted to him in accordance with his capacity and the nature of the case.
If [the judge] is unable to settle the dispute between the two who wish to litigate,
then a period of time must be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is of four kinds, and likewise the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).
Decision (*nirṇaya*) is said to be fourfold, though some maintain it is eightfold.
Place, time, as well as location and likewise the settlement; the name of the knower, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: the father's name, the grandfather's name, and the mention of previous kings.
Or he may obtain a postponement for three days or even seven days,
until such time as insight arises in him who desires to speak in the dispute.
Even if a case in legal proceedings has been settled with many assertions, the king may, if he desires to ascertain the truth, take up that matter as well.

Accusation based on suspicion, the truth, a request regarding a matter to be examined, and a renewed legal proceeding after a case has been concluded: these are to be known as the four kinds of plaints.

Delusion is defined as doubt, which is necessarily the perception of a lost object; likewise, infatuation is the solicitation for an object already obtained, as well as the repeated performance of actions regarding what has already been accomplished.

He who does not wish to act justly, or who acts unjustly,
or likewise he who does not cause [the matter] to be recorded in writing— his case shall not succeed.
When both contradictory and non-contradictory meanings are established within a single [statement],
one should avoid that position from afar.
The Reply] [1.3.0] But when such a thesis has been formulated by the proponent (pūrvavādin),...
The defendant shall then provide a reply connected with that same side of the issue.
When the plaintiff's case has been determined, distinguished as to what is admissible and inadmissible,
and when it has been formally stated and stabilized, one should then cause the defendant's reply to be recorded in writing.
[1.3.1 Time should be granted to one who requests it: Where a defendant requests time due to timidity, fear, or likewise due to a lapse of memory, he deserves to obtain that time.
For one day, three days, five days, seven days, or even a fortnight;
for a month, three months, four months, or a year—he obtains [the fruit] according to his capacity.

Those who know it declare that a reply is one which pervades the entire position (*pakṣa*), is essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation to be understood. (BP 1.3.005)

The reply is of four kinds: the direct reply (*sampratipatti*), the false reply (*mithyottara*), the reply based on prior judgment (*prāṅnyāyottara*), and the reply based on a special cause (*kāraṇottara*).
However, he who does not provide a reply that corresponds to the facts of the plaintiff's case...
One who has witnessed [the transaction] should be made to pay [the debt] through means such as conciliation and the rest.
Conciliation is speech preceded by pleasant words; sowing dissension is the pointing out of danger; punishment consists of the deprivation of wealth, as well as beating and imprisonment.

Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations regarding cattle, and likewise in matters of urgency, one may litigate on the spot even outside of the prescribed time.

One who speaks inconsistently, one who evades the legal procedure, one who fails to appear, one who offers no reply, and one who flees when summoned— these are declared to be the five kinds of defeated litigants.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, and acts of violence, [the defendant is defeated] even if he does not appear.
In cases of forgery and false testimony, one should initiate legal proceedings immediately.
In the case of a milch cow, a draft ox, a field, women, and likewise in procreation;
in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and likewise in buying and selling.
In a case of prior plea (*prāṅnyāya*) and in the statement of a reason (*kāraṇa*), the defendant (*pratyarthī*) shall point out the means of proof (*kriyā*);
but in a case of denial (*mithyā-ukti*), the plaintiff (*pūrvavādī*) shall do so; however, it cannot be so in a case of admission (*pratyavaskandana*).
When a proponent advances a position without stating a reason, that should be known as a *pratipatti* (admission); however, the *kāraṇa* (reason) is a distinct form of reply (*uttara*).
But he who, having engaged in all manner of conversation, should converse with another even in private— even if it be but a little—
Bṛhaspati says that such a person, when accused, shall be made to pay the entire amount.

In cases of verbal assault, in disputes over land, and when one is unwilling to undergo the formal legal procedure, one should avoid the ordeal; likewise, in matters concerning the sale or receipt of property.
[1.3.2 The Fourfold Reply] If a defendant,
when being accused, should practice concealment of the charge, one should recognize that reply as false according to legal procedure.
If, upon hearing the charge, the defendant admits it,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "admission" (*sampratipatti*).
If the defendant, having been confronted with the matter asserted by the plaintiff,
admits it as such but then states a legal justification for it, that is indeed a plea of "counter-attack" (*pratyavaskandana*).
If the defendant admits the very claim asserted by the plaintiff and states the grounds for it accordingly, Manu has declared that he is defeated.
If one who has been defeated by conduct is made to write [an admission] again, he is to be punished as previously defeated; that is called *prāṅnyāya* (judgment on the basis of prior proof).
One should employ the truth in the case of truth, and one should record the falsehood in the case of falsehood;
likewise, one should state the reason in a matter supported by reasons, and victory in the case of victory.
A confession arising from fear or delusion is considered false and is censured by those who know the scriptures; however, a confession made with truth is declared to be righteous.
When a case is decided according to the prior plea, the truth is praised by the virtuous;
conversely, that which is contrary to it is unrighteous, and the defendant shall suffer defeat.
When the plaintiff and the defendant have both arrived through mutual rivalry for precedence,
the trial should be conducted according to the order of the social classes and by considering the relative suffering involved.
When the defendant has been brought at the same time as the plaintiff into the presence of the court members,
he shall then write his reply corresponding to the words of the plaint.
The rule regarding the meaning of the suffixes has been explained in the presentation of the connected sense;
now, that which is to be grasped among the fourfold types [of verbal roots] is being stated.

One should not characterize that which is other than the subject at hand, that which is neutral, that which is deficient or excessive, that which is irrelevant, that which lacks the essence of what is to be said, that which is doubtful, or that which is contrary to the position.
He who creates fear, or causes dissension, or intimidation, or obstruction—
such a litigant loses his case in legal proceedings.
But when an officiating priest or the like has been appointed, both are declared to be equal;
in the sacrifice, the patron obtains merit, while in the debate, he may incur loss or victory.
Where the plaintiff or the defendant dies after the plaint and the reply have been written down, their son shall clear up the legal dispute on their behalf.
If a legal dispute remains undecided, the king would be deceived;
the granting of victory would not be impartial. Therefore, he should resolve all cases.
But if one, having designated witnesses, does not proceed to a legal dispute with them after thirty nights or three fortnights, his case suffers defeat.
One who flees after being summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the testimony of witnesses,
and one who admits the claim by his own statement— these are the four types of a defeated litigant.
One who flees is defeated after three fortnights; one who remains silent, after seven days;
one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and likewise, one who admits the claim.
Not stating what has been presented, failing to appear in court,
silence, and [admitting] the defects of one's own position are the characteristics of one who is losing the case.
Those people know him to be joined with sin who, in an assembly, endures being accused of a great crime, a minor crime, or a transgression.
Therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the purification of the self;
whatever task is more important, that one should first purify.
He who is accused of a great sin and desires to escape from that transgression must first acknowledge it; having been defeated [by his own admission], he deserves punishment.
When a trial by ordeal has been conducted according to established custom, and a formal appearance has been determined,
one must not allow any deception if someone fails to appear.
If, at that time, a calamity caused by fate or the king should occur,
he shall not be defeated merely by the abandonment of the boundary.
When a dispute has been initiated between two parties who have taken their respective positions as plaintiff and defendant,
those who settle it between themselves shall be made to pay a fine double the amount [in contention].
When the claims of the plaintiff and the defendant have been set forth and the determination of the case has begun,
a settlement between the two heated parties may occur like that of two pieces of iron.
[1.3.3 Examination of the Treaty] However,
if there is a disagreement between the witnesses and the members of the assembly regarding both parties,
those who are discerning should conclude a treaty while the two sides remain in a state of suspense.
Where there is equality of power but a difference in either the scriptural tradition or the conduct of the two parties,
a peace treaty with the king is recommended for both.
Where a matter is subject to doubt and the legal proceeding before the king is likewise uncertain,
a settlement should be made there, just as one joins two pieces of heated iron together.
In that case, a peace treaty on equal terms should be made, for an unequal one will fail.
Through equality, the king secures dharma, wealth, support, and fame;
the witnesses and court members suffer no distress, and enmity ceases.
Punishment involving restraint and favor, as well as dharma, fame, and infamy, arises for men from conflict; likewise, further fault is born from it.

Therefore, what those presiding over the family and the guild— who know the law, who are impartial in view, and who are free from hatred and greed— may declare, that should be done by one who understands.
[1.4. Section on Procedure] [1.4.0] BP1.4.001a:
When it has been properly examined and written down, and the reply is faultless;
In the case of either the defendant or the plaintiff, legal action is held to depend upon proof.
But for those who remain in the court, their case must be investigated by the members of the assembly;
after the defendant has properly stated his reply, it must be presented to one of the litigants.

[1.4.1 The Strength and Weakness of Means of Proof] The proponent shall establish his claim, and likewise the opponent shall establish the grounds for his defense; the proponent of the prior facts shall establish victory by means of a certificate of victory.
In the first quarter [of the verse], he should write down [the claim] exactly as it was stated, without omission;
however, in the third quarter, the plaintiff should substantiate it with evidence.
After hearing both the prior and subsequent statements, once the members of the court have determined whose proof (*bhāvanā*) is required,
that party shall substantiate their entire claim by means of written documents and other evidence.
Action is declared to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine. Each of these is divided into many varieties by the seers who know the truth.
Human action is recorded in tradition as being threefold: witnesses, written documents, and possession.
The divine means of proof (*daivī kriyā*) is ninefold, beginning with the balance (*dhaṭa*) and ending with that born of *dharma*;
the human means of proof (*mānuṣī kriyā*) is threefold: witnesses, documents, and inference.
Witnesses are recorded as being of twelve types, while documents are traditionally held to be of eight kinds.
Inference is declared to be threefold, and judicial procedure based on divine means is ninefold.
In the first or the third stage, both human and divine means of proof are authoritative;
in the subsequent fourth stage, however, there shall be witnesses and a written document of victory.
In matters such as debts and the like, one should employ human means of proof;
in a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a counter-plea (*pratyavaskanda*), the defendant himself must establish his case.

For the sake of the subsequent [reply] and for the sake of the claim, the plaintiff may state a false reply; however, when witnesses are available, no divine ordeal is prescribed. Furthermore, when there is a written document in legal disputes, there should be neither an ordeal nor witnesses.

In cases of verbal assault, disputes over land, and indeed in all four types of violent crimes, divine means of proof (*daivikī kriyā*) are prohibited; rather, such evidence must be diligently administered.
In cases of treason against the king and in acts of violence, one should employ divine proof (*daivikī kriyā*).
One who steals or conceals gems, pearls, and corals by means of deception, as well as an assailant or one who consorts with another's wife, must always be examined through oaths.
In cases of accusations of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), in the misappropriation of a deposit, and likewise in cases of theft,
the king should administer ordeals (*divya*) even when witnesses are present. If doubt should arise regarding a written document or the testimony of witnesses, [he should resort to ordeals].
And when there is confusion regarding inference, divine proof is the means of purification in that case.

When a dispute concerning gambling or betting has arisen, witnesses are declared to be the means of proof, not ordeals nor written documents. The king should cause a decision to be made by those who appear according to their availability.
In cases of assault, verbal abuse, and physical injury,
as well as in matters arising from the use of force, witnesses and even divine proof (ordeal) are admissible.
In a dispute over debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even a trace of circumstantial reasoning may be employed.
Or, out of a desire for the welfare of the subjects, a divine procedure has been prescribed:
when witnesses have long since perished or have become silent,
and when inferential evidence is corrupted, one should settle the case by means of ordeals.
[1.5. Witnesses] [1.5.0] There should be nine, seven, five, four, or even three witnesses.
Or he may consult two who are both learned in the Vedas and renowned; he should never consult only one.
The keeper of the gambling hall, the receiver of the stakes, and likewise one who is present within the proceedings—
each of these alone may be authoritative, as may the king or his superintendent.
Thieves, violent criminals, eunuchs, gamblers, and informers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; witness-status does not exist among them. [1.5.1 Witnesses: Varieties]
The written, the secret, the reminded, the one by relatives and messengers,
the incidental, the subsequent, and another which occurs in the midst of a legal proceeding.
The king, the official, and likewise the village headman—these are recorded as the twelve kinds of witnesses.
I shall explain their distinctions properly and in due order.
He by whom one's own [name], that of one's father, the caste, and the place of residence have been recorded should be known as a witness designated as "written" (*likhitasākṣin*).
When a creditor, having performed various transactions such as the lending of money and so forth,
causes [the debtor] to write [a document] in his presence, that is declared to be a *lekhita* (written) document.
But he who is made to hear the statement regarding a debt while separated by a wall,
and who denies it as it truly is, is called a concealed witness.
One who has been summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, or transactions, and who is repeatedly reminded of his duty, is declared to be a "reminded witness" (*smārita*).
In matters of partitioning an inheritance or in trade, a kinsman who is employed by both parties— one who knows the law and belongs to the same lineage— is proclaimed as a *kulya*.
He who, being sent by the plaintiff and the defendant, listens to their statements and is approved by both as a virtuous person, is declared to be a *dūtaka* (messenger/witness).
But when a matter is being transacted, whoever comes of his own accord and says,
"You are our witness here," he is called an incidental witness.

Where a witness departs for another region, or is about to die, in due order, he should cause another to hear the testimony; one should know that person to be the "subsequent witness" (uttara-sākṣin).
Among witnesses who are giving testimony repeatedly, one who hears it again and again is designated as the "respondent witness" (uttara-sākṣin).
He whose confidence is placed in both [parties] and who is informed of their business should be known as a "secret-bearer" when he has entered into the midst of the matter.
Whatever statement of the plaintiff and the defendant is heard by the king himself,
he alone shall be the witness in that case, even in the event of a disagreement between the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a retrial occurs, the presiding officer together with the members of the court shall be the witnesses there; it cannot be otherwise.
Where a dwelling has been occupied and covered on all sides up to the boundary,
that village is undoubtedly a witness even if it has been cut down.
Two written witnesses, as well as three, four, or five secret witnesses;
those who appear spontaneously, those reminded of their testimony, kinsmen, and likewise superior witnesses.
The messenger, the bearer of his own seal, and one who is present within the matter itself—
each of these alone may be authoritative, as may the king or the official supervisor.
[1.5.2 Discussion of the Faults of Witnesses and Punishment for the Corrupt] If a litigant should impugn with a fault a witness who has been designated by the parties as honest,
yet who is actually faultless, that litigant deserves a punishment equal to the value of the claim.
Whatever defects of the document may exist, as well as those attributed to the witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; once they have been stated, one should not raise them later.
The defendant in court must state all the defects of the witnesses in writing on the document; thereafter, the reply should be delivered.
Those who have already performed their duty are never fit to be witnesses;
therefore, they should be treated otherwise by the defendant in the course of the legal proceeding.
If the defendant clearly fails to prove his case through witnesses, he shall be compelled to pay a fine;
likewise, all witnesses who have been proven false shall be deprived of their witness-status according to the law of witnesses.
Whether it be the defendant or the plaintiff, when proving the defects of witnesses,
there shall be no separate legal proceeding, provided it is relevant to the matter at hand.

If the plaintiff has no further desire for more and the witness remains established in the truth, then that defeated party shall be made to pay a fine according to the disciplinary procedure prescribed by the scriptures.
But he who, when the matter has been stated, impeaches witnesses who were previously unimpeachable and does not state the grounds for doing so, shall incur the first amercement.
In a legal dispute, if either the document or the witnesses of a party are found to be tainted,
that party's case shall not be adjudicated until those [taints] have been cleared away.
When the decision has been reached through the testimony of witnesses and the members of the court, if a party initiates a renewed lawsuit, the king shall investigate that case himself.
When witnesses are suspected of corruption, the purification of the witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been cleared, one should subsequently purify the legal matter itself.
The members of the court, who are learned in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, should address [the witness] with words praising truth and rejecting falsehood:
"Whatever merit you have acquired from birth until death— "
All that goes to ruin through the false accusation of one who is innocent.
A false witness, a false judge, and a slayer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
among these, a killer of an embryo or a betrayer of a friend is said to be no greater [in sin].
Having understood this, the witness who speaks the truth thereby attains fame in this world and a blessed state in the next.
There are men who, out of greed, might declare a matter otherwise;
and there are other evil-minded men who forge false documents.
I shall now describe those witnesses who are to be questioned, as well as those lowest of men who must be excluded, as prescribed by the scriptures.
Those engaged in the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites, free from greed and hatred,
of noble birth, irreproachable, and endowed with austerity, charity, and compassion, are fit to be witnesses.
[1.5.3 Non-Witnesses] The father of a mother, a paternal uncle, the brother and mother of a wife,
a brother, a friend, and a son-in-law are non-witnesses in legal disputes concerning debts.
Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those previously discredited,
the insane, the afflicted, the violent, and atheists are not to be witnesses.
Even those who are virtuous do not constitute valid witnesses after the death of the owner of the property;
however, those who were informed by the owner himself when he was near death may serve as witnesses.
Having removed his sandals and turban, he should raise his right hand;
taking gold, cow dung, and *darbha* grass, he should speak the truth.
Those who have presented themselves should be examined by means of their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth.
Even if one must speak falsehoods, one should protect a Brahmin who has committed an offense through negligence once, who is afflicted by calamity, or who is being beaten by soldiers and the like.
If the entire subject matter of the plaintiff's claim is corroborated by the witnesses, he shall be the victor; otherwise, however, he shall not obtain the object of his suit.
If a witness who is free from illness does not come when summoned,
he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed.
[1.5.4 Examination of the Strength and Weakness of Witness Statements] When witnesses are divided, the majority should be accepted; when they are equal in number, those endowed with good qualities;
when those with good qualities are divided, those who possess corroborating evidence; and when even those are equal, those who are more pure.
Witnesses who, when not questioned, speak the truth, or likewise fail to answer a question, shall be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
If it is stated without deficiency in terms of place, time, age, substance, name, caste, and measure, one should point out that which is to be proven as established.
In cases where there may be disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or species,
even that testimony must not be considered otherwise [than false].
When the categories of the matter have been specified and the witness has arrived for testimony, if he does not speak, it is as if he were blind; that [testimony] shall not be declared [valid].
In the first half [of the trial], one should present the entire claim as it was asserted;
however, that which was stated as deficient or excessive shall not be considered as having been formally declared.
Where witnesses state a matter either less than or more than it actually is, that matter should be understood as not having been stated; this is the rule for witnesses as recorded in the Smṛti.
When the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by the witnesses, the entire case shall be considered established.
In cases of sexual intercourse with women, acts of violence, and theft, that which is to be proven is determined [by the evidence].
But where testimony is either deficient or excessive, one should reject it; in such a case, the witness should not be punished, whereas one who fails to speak deserves punishment.
[1.6. Written] [1.6.0] This determination regarding the number and characteristics of witnesses has been set forth.
Now I shall describe the procedure for written documents in their proper sequence.
Since confusion may arise even regarding matters such as debts at the time of their settlement,
the Creator created letters and placed them upon paper in ancient times.
[1.6.1 Characteristics of a Written Document] A document is said to be that which is consistent with local custom, which records the increase in years, months, fortnights, and so forth,
and which bears the signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
[1.6.2 Varieties of Documents] A royal document, one executed at a specific place, and likewise one written in one's own hand—
document is said to be of these three kinds; furthermore, it is divided into many types.
Documentary evidence in common worldly practice is sevenfold, consisting of [deeds concerning] shares, gifts, purchase, pledges, agreements, slaves, and debts; royal edicts are of three kinds.

The document known as the *vibhāgapatra* is established for the determination of shares; when a boundary dispute has been settled, the document concerning that boundary is traditionally called the *sīmāpatra*.
A deed of gift, a deed of partition, and likewise a deed concerning boundaries; a deed of purchase, a deed of slavery, and thereafter a deed of mortgage.
A written agreement, a document of victory,
and likewise a treaty— these are of many kinds according to the differences in their legal transactions.
A document for a pledge should be executed for the purpose of a loan, and a document for a slave should be executed for the purpose of a slave.
For the sake of accomplishing their desired objectives, villages, guilds, corporations,
and other such groups may establish a charter of agreement for the purpose of dharma, provided it does not conflict with the sacred scriptures.
When brothers who have already divided their inheritance execute a mutual deed among themselves by their own consent,
that is called a *bhāgalekhya* (a deed of partition).
But when one, having given land, should execute a document for its duration as long as the moon and sun,
that deed of gift is known as an *anācchedyam* (inalienable) and *anāhāryam* (non-confiscable).
Having purchased a house, field, or other property, that document which one causes to be executed, containing the price and the names [of the parties],
is called a *kraya-lekhya* (purchase deed).
When one executes a document after providing movable or immovable property as a pledge,
that document— characterized by the functions of being kept in custody or being used— is known as a *ādhi-lekhya* (mortgage deed).
When a village or a district should mutually execute a document while intoxicated,
provided it does not conflict with the king and concerns matters of dharma or wealth, they call that a *saṃvitpatra* (contractual document).
"If a man, destitute of clothing and food in the wilderness, writes that 'I shall perform whatever work you command,' that is recognized as a document of slavery."
Having received money at interest, one may either perform the work oneself or cause it to be done by another;
this is declared by the wise to be an *uddhāra-patra*, a document for a debt.
Regarding the established rule for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, the proof thereof is documentary evidence; neither divine ordeal nor witnesses are required.
But that which is made for the maintenance of the agreement of guilds, corporations,
and the like, is declared by those who know the Smṛtis of Manu and others to be a *sthitipatra* (a document of established rule).

[1.6.3 The King’s Edict on Giving] Having bestowed land and other gifts, the king should cause an edict to be made— whether on a copper plate or on cloth— recording the gift according to the Dharma, together with the location, the lineage, and other details.
"For the merit of my mother, father, and myself, this gift is given by me today to such-and-such a person, the son of so-and-so, who is a fellow student of the holy life."
It is unseizable, unremovable, free from all future liabilities, coeval with the moon and sun, and transmitted through the lineage of sons and grandsons.
He who severs the grant of land shall write down this as the fruit of his act: for sixty thousand years, heaven awaits the giver and protector, while hell awaits the one who takes it away.
The year, month, and so forth, including the rainfall from the ocean, accompanied by the signature of the Superintendent of Revenue,
and written by the secretaries of peace and war with the words "This was known by me."
Such a royal edict is declared to be a "grant by favor" (*prasādalikhita*),
which the king issues when he grants land or other property to someone in writing.
But that which is written by one who is pleased by service, valor, or the like, is indeed a document of favor (*prasāda-likhita*).

[1.6.5 The Document of Victory] When, at the conclusion of the determination following the arguments and counter-arguments of the plaintiff and defendant, the king grants a written document to the victor, that is called a *jayapatra* (document of victory).
Whatever has occurred in the legal proceeding— the plaint, the reply, and so forth—
along with the evidence and the determination of the case, he shall write all of this in the document of victory (*jayapatra*).
He shall establish the matter to be proven (*sādhya*) in accordance with the victory, provided it is endowed with its four constituent parts.
And the document of victory is required to be provided with the royal seal.
To those other than those who have failed in their arguments and so forth, [the judgment] is granted;
and that, being established by a recital of the proceedings, shall be the document of victory (*jayapatra*).
[1.6.6 Defects in Documents] A document executed by one who is about to die,
by one whose capacity is impaired or whose purpose is lost, by one who is insane,
afflicted by calamity, or produced through the force of poison or fraud, is not valid.
Where a single witness who is tainted or censurable is appointed, that document is a forged one;
so too is it when the scribe is of such a character.
A document that is bright [in color], made long ago, yet soiled and of recent date;
or one that is broken and contains indistinct letters—such a document shall be considered forged.
Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears to exist though it is non-existent,
so too do skillful people create paintings that possess the likeness of forms.
For proof is established by truth, while refutation is established by fault;
that in which such a fault exists is indeed what is investigated in the king's court.
Having deliberated together with the Brahmins, he should examine the fault of the speaker.
By that [corruption] through which the witnesses, the scribe, and the author fall into falsehood, by that the document becomes tainted; one should declare it pure when they are pure.
If a debtor denies a debt that has been recorded in writing with his own hand,
he may be compelled to pay by means of witnesses present in the document, by oral testimony, and with the consent of the scribe.
"But where letters are displaced from their positions, lack clarity, are indistinct, or have deviated from their proper forms— there, Bhṛgu says, the document is defective."
The claimant shall produce the document; however, his son shall produce only the possession.
If the one who was sued has died, his son shall produce that [document].
Having ascertained the matter, forgers who are skilled in place and time produce a document resembling it; one should examine that with great care.
Some skillful people write a document like a painting;
therefore, it is held that the validity [of a claim] is not established solely by the power of the document.

Relatives deceive women, children, the afflicted, and those ignorant of writing by having them sign a document marked with their own names; that [deed] should be recognized as such through reasoning and evidence of its origin.
When an error arises in this threefold document,
one should then correct it by the written declaration of the hand of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.

An *upadhi* (fraudulent inducement) should be recognized as existing where there is an exertion [of effort] because of the taking of profit, an undertaking because of the accumulation of results, and a state of being rich in wealth because of the presence of a counter-claimant. (p. 67) BP1.6.044ab.

A document is established as valid in all cases— indeed, even when the witnesses have died— if it was presented at the proper time, and if its contents were both heard and reminded [of by the parties].
Where the capacity of syllables as signifiers is obstructed,
there would be the total destruction of actions and an infinite regress would arise.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be living.
But when a loan has been settled and the profit realized, if the debtor does not produce the written document nor does the creditor demand it, he shall incur suspicion regarding that matter.

When the assemblies of families, guilds, corporations, and so forth are convened at the appropriate time, one should cause them to hear [the matter] and remind them of it; in this way, the decision shall be most authoritative.
If something has been obtained, or if there is a formal designation [of the debt] in that manner,
the document itself is indeed the proof, even if the witnesses have died.
When a wealthy person standing nearby has not been requested by one who is capable [of asking],
that document will be rendered weak due to the suspicion that it is a simple debt (*śuddharṇa*).
A document executed by those who are insane, idiotic, or weak; by those living abroad out of fear of the king; or by those who are timid, fearful, or afflicted, shall not be subject to loss.
Now, if the scribe together with the witnesses has met his death, that [document] is purified by their own handwriting and so forth; of this there is no doubt.
In case of doubt regarding a debt, whether the debtor is living or dead,
the determination of that document is made by other papers written in his own hand.
When a doubt arises regarding a document, it should be resolved by means of the witnesses, the scribe, and the maker;
and if they are found to be corrupt, by means of previous letters written by their own hands and other such evidence.
A written document is never superseded by witnesses or by an oath.
One incurs loss through neglect by virtue of both non-appearance and non-announcement.
Therefore, both of these must be examined especially by the king;
there should be only one document for the sake of establishing a single matter.
However, among many documents, one may find defects:
that which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which was executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is deficient in its subject matter— all such are defective.
[1.7. Enjoyment] [1.7.0] All activities have wealth as their root; all efforts are considered to be for the sake of accomplishing it.
