"Increasing, protecting, and enjoying—this is the sequence of its management."
Furthermore, that [wealth] is to be known as threefold: white, variegated, and black; therein, the classification is further to be understood as sevenfold.

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a pupil, a sacrificial patron, or inheritance—this is the sevenfold wealth; for both [the giver and the receiver] are of that same nature regarding it.
That which is acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, tolls, the practice of crafts,
or from one who has received a favor, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling with dice and the like, by means of messengers, by fraud, by violence, or by deceit, is declared to be "black" wealth.
By means of that [coin], buying, selling, giving, and receiving,
as well as various transactions and the enjoyment of goods, are carried out.
Whatever a man performs with a particular kind of substance, he obtains a corresponding result for that both after death and in this world.
That [dharma], moreover, is traditionally held to be twelvefold, based on the respective castes;
it is threefold as common [to all], while the remainder is traditionally held to be ninefold.
That which has come down by succession, that which is given out of affection, and that which is acquired together with the wife—
these three kinds of property are declared to belong to all social classes without distinction.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics:
that which is obtained through acceptance of gifts, that which is received from a patron for officiating at sacrifices, and likewise that which is received from a pupil.
They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific kinds of wealth: that acquired in battle, from taxes, and from fines in legal proceedings.
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics:
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; and for a Śūdra, [the means of livelihood] consists of service to these [other castes].
For all social classes alike, the acquisition of wealth in this manner is righteous;
through the opposite method it would be unrighteous, unless there is a grave emergency.

In times of distress, the practice of the next lower order is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa; however, the occupation of a Vaiśya is also declared for him, but never that of a Śūdra under any circumstances.
Under no circumstances should a Brāhmaṇa perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brāhmaṇa; for those two acts lead to their respective fall.
Neither superior nor inferior action exists for those two;
for, setting aside intermediate actions, they are indeed common to all.

Having crossed over a time of distress while supporting his dependents through the occupation of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation after performing a purificatory rite for himself.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, out of passion, delights in that very same mode of livelihood—
he is fallen from the path, a mere bowman (kāṇḍapṛṣṭha), and is proclaimed to be "marked" (aṅkita).
"He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to another's family—
by that misconduct he is known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*."
When a legal procedure has been initiated during the daytime in villages and cities,
and when witnesses are available, the ordeal is not to be employed.
In the case of doors, paths, works, enjoyment, water-conduits, and the like, possession alone shall be the superior proof; neither a written document nor witnesses are required.
This rule has been declared regarding witnesses and written documents;
now the procedure for the acquisition of immovable property and for possession is being stated.
Through learning, by means of a purchase agreement, through valor, as an inherited share, or as property obtained from a relative—
immovable property acquired in these ways belongs to a sapinda who is childless, and it is divided into nine parts.
[1.7.2 Sevenfold Possession] Regarding paternal inheritance, what is obtained, purchased, or received as a gift, as well as through partition, by valor, or by discovery—
when possession has been acquired in these seven ways, it attains validity provided it is accompanied by a legal title (*sāgama*).
That possession which has been inherited in due order, or obtained by royal decree, or accompanied by purchase or formal grant—
such possession shall attain legal validity.
Immovable property obtained through partition, purchase, inheritance from a father, or received from the king, attains legal validity by being enjoyed; it is lost through neglect.
When someone has taken possession and enjoyed what was obtained—having accepted it without opposition—he acquires ownership of it; yet he suffers loss through neglect. Thus it is.
If one's possession has been uninterrupted for thirty years, beginning from the time it was first occupied, one shall not displace that person from it.
There shall be no enjoyment of women by any means whatsoever without a written document;
nor [shall there be enjoyment] of the property of the king, of a Śrotriya, or of the wealth of the mentally disabled or of minors.
Ownership is never established by mere possession alone;
it is established by both clear title and possession, and not otherwise.
And when the property of a child or a Vedic scholar has been obtained from the father in due order,
neither the one who took it nor his son should use force to recover it during its enjoyment.
The law regarding cattle, women, men, and so forth is established [as follows]:
if, under a single title deed, villages, fields, and gardens are recorded.
Even when only a portion has been enjoyed, all [the properties] are considered to have been enjoyed;
for where there is no possession, even a small amount, title alone possesses no strength at all.
An eyewitness is superior to inference; a written document is more authoritative than eyewitnesses;
and possession by three successive generations, being unopposed, is weightier than these.
Inference [is established when] there is a witness residing there until death; however, possession based on an uncontradicted document is authoritative for three generations.
If one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living,
yet land has been enjoyed for thirty years without being obstructed by others;

That possession is known as *pauruṣī* (belonging to one person); it is doubled for two persons (*dvipuruṣī*), and tripled for three persons (*tripūruṣī*); beyond that, it becomes *cirantanā* (of long standing).
Where the one who brings forward the claim is challenged, then the document and the witness are authoritative;
but in their absence, possession alone is the most weighty proof among the sons.
The person who brings forward the title shall establish possession or the legal title in court;
his son may establish possession alone; but a grandson or later descendant need establish nothing at all.
If property is given openly by others to one who is not the heir,
while another person is already enjoying it, that [first] person does not deserve to obtain it.
He who, while watching another give away land, does not prevent it,
shall not regain that land even by means of a valid document.
Bhṛgu says that whether given by the heirs or by others, that [gift] belongs to him alone;
possession for three generations is established for others, there is no doubt in this matter.
However, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for the sakulyas.
But that which has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner— such as a house, field, or shop—
does not become lost to the friend, kinsman, or relative through such enjoyment.
For one learned in the Vedas, merit is inexhaustible; from a king's servant, he receives fearlessness;
and toward kinsmen and friends, he maintains affection; what has been eaten by these is never lost.
Food consumed at a wedding by those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), as well as by the king and his ministers,
does not become effective for them even after a very long period of time.
In the case of those who are incapacitated, lazy, afflicted by disease, children, fearful, or traveling abroad,
a document executed by another does not lose its validity through mere possession.
When a doubt arises regarding a house or field whose enjoyment has been interrupted,
one should establish its purity through a written document, those who know the facts of possession, or witnesses.

Those who know the names of the parties, the arrival at the boundary markers, the number, the time, the specific direction, and the cause for the interruption of possession are witnesses in that case.

Those who have arisen [as witnesses] and are very close at hand, as well as those residing in another country, are designated as primary; they should be questioned for the determination of the legal matter.
Whatever those who are uncorrupted and impartial may say regarding a doubtful matter, that must be made authoritative; in this way, the Dharma is not lost.
This has been declared concerning immovable property as the means of establishing ownership and enjoyment.
But in a case where the statement lacks supporting evidence, the divine ordeal must be prescribed.
Even if it has been enjoyed by three other kings without formal title,
a royal grant to a Brahmin must never be confiscated by a king.
Where possession has been exercised by three generations and continues into the fourth, that enjoyment attains stability; one need not inquire about the title in such a case.
When a property has been enjoyed by three generations of persons without being prohibited, no legal title need be produced there; in that case, possession is more weighty.
In disputes concerning immovable property, possession extending over three generations is to be known as independent; it is indeed the authoritative means for determining the matter to be proven.
If a grant has been enjoyed by [an ancestor] for three generations and is accompanied by a valid document,
such a gift to a Brahmin (*brahmadeya*) cannot be taken away from him.
If possession has continued for three generations, transmitted through a succession of ancestors,
it cannot be overturned except by a prior royal edict.
If land has been enjoyed for three generations in the presence of the owner without being forbidden,
it must not be taken away from him, unless he declares that there was a title of ownership.
In the treatise, possession that is long-standing and uninterrupted is powerful;
for even if it has been interrupted, it should be understood as such if it was previously established.

If property has been enjoyed by the father in accordance with custom and according to dharma, even after he has died, that property is acquired by the [son] through such enjoyment; it belongs to him by virtue of that possession.
But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law,
in the absence of a written document, a fourth person may acquire it there.

If property has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, relatives, or likewise by one's own people, there can be no legal proof of ownership based on that enjoyment; in such cases, one should consider the enjoyment as belonging to others.
Possession with title, long duration,
uninterrupted and undisputed, along with the presence of the opponent and actual enjoyment— possession is thus fivefold.
Quadrupeds, wealth, grain, and so forth, suffer loss after one year. Non-enjoyment of land, the failure to produce a document at the proper time,
and the failure to recall witnesses— these indeed cause the loss of one's own right.
Therefore, one should diligently maintain the authority of the means of proof;
by that, both immovable and movable legal matters are successfully accomplished.
In a case where there are no witnesses and the matter has been long since committed, one should question the witnesses of the subsequent event,
or subject the defendant to oaths, or employ an ordeal.
And there is the non-obstruction of teaching, as well as a summary of the logical reasoning.
Property stolen by thieves must be recovered from all [suspects] and restored;
if it cannot be recovered, it shall be paid from the king's own treasury, otherwise the king would incur the guilt of the thief.
Divine Matters] [1.8.0] Thus has been explained the means for achieving gain and enjoyment for an immovable property.
But in a lawsuit lacking evidence, the divine ordeal is faultless.
When the methods of inference have proven defective, one should settle the case by means of divine ordeals (*divya*).
The divine ordeal is recorded as being of nine kinds, beginning with the balance (*dhaṭa*) and ending with *dharmaja*.
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth is the oath (*kośa*).
The sixth is said to be rice-grains, and the seventh is that *māṣaka*.
The eighth is called the time-period (*kāla*), and likewise the ninth is the dharma-period;
all these have been declared by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*) through divine [vision].
[1.8.1 Divine Arrangement] Since these [teachings] were employed by the great-souled gods for the sake of what is difficult to accomplish,
I shall state them in summary for the sake of purifying doubtful meanings.
These are employed in their proper sequence according to place, time, purpose, and number.
According to the sequence of offenses and with the intent to distinguish between the virtuous and the non-virtuous,
punishments should be administered according to the procedure prescribed in the treatises, and not otherwise.
In matters such as debts and the like, when there is mutual disagreement,
[the judge] should issue a decision endowed with the details of the property and its quantity, taking likewise into account the status of the individuals involved.
For the purpose of worldly transactions, this designation has been declared on earth:
a coin struck from a karṣa of copper is to be known as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*; a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is known as a *paṇa*. A stamped coin made from a *karṣa* of copper should be understood as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
That same [unit] is called an *cāndrikā*; four of those are a *dhānakā*.
Twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*, which is also known as a *dīnāra*.
A fine of one thousand kārṣāpaṇas is the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that again is remembered as the lowest.
A balance should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya,
water should be given to a Vaiśya, and poison indeed to a Śūdra.
The treasury is declared by the wise to be common to all [the members of the assembly].
"Witnesses may fall into disagreement due to affection, anger, or greed;
however, no disagreement ever arises regarding a divine ordeal administered according to the prescribed rule."
The ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rule by those expert in ordeals; if it is administered contrary to the rule, then neither the proof nor the disproof is valid.
Evidence presented at an improper place or time, and that which has been fabricated by outsiders, always leads to error regarding the facts; of this there is no doubt.
Those expert in divine ordeals should administer the ordeal to one who is accused;
or, by mutual consent, either party may undergo it, while the other shall bear the head [of the animal used in the ordeal].
Even without a formal charge, one may administer an ordeal in cases of treason against the king or for mortal sins;
such administration of divine tests is declared to be permissible except by royal command. No one should thus compel the accuser himself to undergo the ordeals.
[1.8.2 Divine Deities] Dharodhrava, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa— these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas;
they are Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who is not the youngest, though born last.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names.
To the western part of Agni, they know to be the abode of the Rudras:
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Girīśa, and Mahāyaśas.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the unconquered Apratijita;
The lords of the worlds, Kapālī the lord of the people,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhaga— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
One should designate the station of the Mothers between Preteśa and Rakṣasa:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā accompanied by her Gaṇas—
[they] know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti.
To the north of Varuṇa’s region, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located. [The names of Vāyu are: Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.

[1.8.3 Divine Ordeals by Number] Manu has declared that the number [of coins] for divine ordeals begins with a *raśmi* and ends with a *kārṣāpaṇa*; one should employ it accordingly in the administration of justice.
When a thousand [paṇas] have been stolen, or when it is less by one-quarter, poison is used;
when it is less by three-quarters, water; and when it is half, the balance (dhaṭa) should always be administered.
In a case involving a claim of four hundred [paṇas], a heated māṣaka coin must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains are to be given, and for half of that amount, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) is prescribed.
When a hundred [pieces of gold] have been lost or stolen, the purification by ordeal must be administered.
In the case of a cow-thief, the members of the court should diligently administer the ploughshare ordeal.
Or, in the event of the loss of half a *yava*, rice grains corresponding to that same value shall be used.
Then, upon the destruction of half, a quarter, and an eighth [of the debt], both the legal process and worldly practice are considered applicable.
[1.8.4 The Procedure for Oaths] The mounts and weapons of the virtuous, as well as cattle, seeds, and gold;
the feet of gods and Brahmins, and the heads of one's sons and wife.
These oaths have been declared as always easy to perform in matters of small value; however, for violent crimes and serious accusations, they say that divine ordeals are the means of purification.
One should say "Speak" to a Brāhmaṇa, "Speak the truth" to a Pārthiva (Kṣatriya),
[threaten] a Vaiśya with [the loss of] cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra with all [possible] sins.
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by the truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons;
likewise cowherds, merchants, artisans, and actors;
as well as servants and usurers. One should not treat Brāhmaṇas in the same manner as Śūdras.
Those who have fallen away from their own duties, who subsist on the food of others, yet desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them as one treats Śūdras.
Each person should be made to swear separately by means of oaths appropriate to their respective social classes.
In matters concerning women, in marriages, regarding cows, fuel, and food,
and in the case of a Brahmin’s misfortune, there is no sin in taking an oath.
Witnesses must give their testimony while standing within the court, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.

If there is a dispute regarding the killing of living beings, one should state the testimony in the presence of the corpse; but in its absence, one should state it in the presence of a distinctive mark, and not otherwise.
Witnesses who have arrived at the place of dispute must not, unless they are questioned or appointed, deliberately give testimony that is inconsistent with the truth.

The testimony of those witnesses, which is stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted; once they have spoken, however, the witnesses should not be questioned again and again by the king.
For those who have settled in the presence of witnesses, there is no rule for remarriage at all.
Likewise, the Seven Sages, Indra and the others, whose wealth is their asceticism,
remained composed and uttered an oath at Puṣkara for the sake of mutual purification.
Within seven days, or within fourteen days, no misfortune caused by the king or by fate shall occur;
regarding wealth held by kinsmen and sapinda relatives, one becomes pure through oaths.
When there is no human evidence whatsoever, a decision must be reached by divine means alone;
however, when witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid recourse to divine ordeals.

Thus, this number is prescribed for those of inferior status; for those of middling status, it is remembered as double that amount; and for those of superior status, it should be calculated as fourfold by the investigators.
[1.8.5 The Procedure for the Balance] In the case of the balance (*dhaṭa*), if the accused, when weighed, is lighter, he shall suffer loss;
but if he is equal, and when weighed again he is heavier, he shall be the victor.
In the event of a sling breaking or an axle snapping, the king shall provide a new sling;
the witnesses, preferably Brahmins, must speak according to what they have actually seen.
The king should appoint kinsmen who are pure yet free from greed;
the determination of purity or impurity is to be understood from their testimony.
In the case of the cutting of the side-posts, the breaking of the balance-beam, or likewise the breaking of the *dhaṭa* or the *karkaṭa*,
as well as the snapping of the cord or the failure of the pivot, one shall incur impurity in exactly the same way.
[1.8.6 The Ritual of Fire] I shall proclaim the ritual of the fire exactly as it is enjoined by the rules:
one should cause eight mandalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth.
The first mandala belongs to Agni; the second is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity, and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity, and the eighth has all the gods as its deity.
That which is the ninth from the front is known as the great earthen vessel;
it should be made of cow-dung and soaked overnight in water.
They say that the distance from one mandala to the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
however, the mandala should be made according to the measure of the performer's own even footstep.
[1.8.7 The Procedure for Water] From the point where an arrow was discharged, a youth endowed with speed should go with his utmost strength to where that middle arrow has fallen.
Taking up a middle-range arrow, another man of similar build should return with speed from the direction where that first man has gone.
"But when the one who has come to take the arrow does not clearly see [the object] within the water, then one should declare purification."
When the middle arrow has been drawn back, one whose body is submerged [in water] attains purity;
otherwise, one is not purified even if only a single limb is seen [above the water].
Or, from the place where one first placed it, by moving elsewhere, [one becomes pure].
Having caused the man to enter the water, one should discharge three arrows;
a wise man should not release the arrows while the wind is blowing violently.
And on uneven ground, crowded with trees and stumps,
and filled with grass, shrubs, creepers, vines, mud, and stones.

He by whom the poison administered according to the prescribed rite is digested without the use of mantras or medicinal herbs shall be deemed innocent; otherwise, however, he is to be punished and made to pay that wealth.
If, within seven days or even fourteen days, there is no loss of his sons, wife, or wealth, he shall be pure; of this there is no doubt.
[1.8.8 The Procedure for the Vessel] Whatever food the accused has eaten, that very same circle of weapons should be washed and made him drink three handfuls of that water.
The king should cause the goods to be moved there under the supervision of his own men for three or five nights, keeping them confined due to the suspicion of trickery.

In cases of a grave accusation, against one who is devoid of dharma, an ungrateful person, a eunuch, a contemptible person, an atheist, or one whose guilt has been previously observed, one should administer the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna).
One should always avoid divine ordeals for men afflicted by diseases; however,
one may employ rice in the case of people suffering from diseases of the mouth.
During a solar eclipse, one who is fasting and pure should eat rice grains; he shall become purified after vomiting white [rice], but if the opposite occurs, he incurs guilt.
Where blood is seen, and where the jaw and palate are shattered,
and whose body trembles— one should declare such a person impure.
[1.8.10 The Procedure for the Heated Māṣa Coin] He should extract a heated māṣa coin from well-heated oil or clarified butter,
while summoning the truth with his thumb and finger joined, being free from fear.
Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
One should cast into it a very beautiful ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron,
which has been washed once with water.
In a place rich with whirling whirlpools and waves, and beyond the reach of the touch of a fingernail,
one should test for the presence of a *caruka* (a sacrificial vessel) by means of a moist leaf, listening for its sound.
Then, one should consecrate that [clarified butter] once with this mantra:
"O clarified butter, you are the supreme purifier, the nectar in sacrificial rites."

"O Purifier, burn away his sin; O Cool as Snow, become pure! Having thus addressed [the fire], he should then cause the accused—who has fasted, bathed, and arrived wearing wet clothes—to grasp that ring while it is submerged in clarified butter.
Then the examiners should also examine his index finger;
if he can shake the tip of his hand without a blister or swelling arising,
he is proven pure by the law, according to the word of Pitāmaha.
[1.8.11 The Procedure for the Ploughshare Test] A forged iron ploughshare weighing twelve palas is prescribed;
if it remains unburnt, one attains purification, but otherwise, one is defeated.
It should be eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide;
heated until it is the color of fire, the thief shall lick it once with his tongue.
If he is not burned, he attains purification; otherwise, he is defeated.
In cases involving serious charges, when the accuser has placed his head upon the stake,
the members of the court must diligently provide a ploughshare as the ordeal for one whose conduct is under suspicion.
[1.8.12 The Ritual for the Dharmaka] On two leaves, one should write *dharma* and *adharma* in white and black [ink].
[This is done] with mantras such as the *jīvadāna*, and with the *sāman* chants beginning with the *gāyatrī*.
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the two [images] should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made those two equal and placed them in the jar unobserved,
he should then take one ball from the jar without delay.
If *dharma* is upheld, he shall be pure and honored by the examiners;
but if *adharma* is upheld, he should be punished or even banished.
One should write *dharma* and *adharma* as white and black upon a birch-bark sheet.
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship it with perfumes and garlands.
Dharma is white-flowered, while adharma is that which bears black flowers;
having thus prepared and anointed them, one should cause those [offerings] to be placed upon the two balls.
Then, two equal lumps should be made either from cow-dung or from clay;
these should be placed in an undamaged clay vessel, remaining unobserved.
On a clean spot that has been smeared with cow-dung, in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he should then worship the gods and the guardians of the world as before.
But preceded by the invocation of Dharma, one should write the document of the claim:
"If I am free from sin, may Dharma come into my hand."
Of those two [the scales], the accused shall seize one without delay;
if he seizes the scale of *dharma*, he shall be purified, but if he seizes the scale of *adharma*, he shall be defeated.
Reflecting in this manner, the king does not fall away from righteousness or worldly prosperity.
[1.9. The Manner of Determination] [1.9.0] By means of dharma, by judicial procedure, by customary conduct, and by the king’s command.
The determination of a doubtful matter has been declared to be of four kinds.
Each one is declared by the wise to be of two kinds according to the distinction of action;
and he shall determine the punishment in accordance with the offense.
Having thoroughly deliberated upon the matter and determined it through reasoning,
and having further examined it by means of oaths— that is to be known as the judicial determination of Dharma.
Where the defendant admits [the claim], that is a legal decision;
when it has been properly cleared by ordeals, it is declared a correct decision.
A legal proceeding that is determined by means of valid evidence is called the first [type]; the second is proclaimed as that which lacks a reply due to quibbling over words (*vākchala*).
Conduct determined by inference is so described;
however, the third [type] is cited by those learned in the scriptures as being established by local custom.

But when there is equality of evidence, the king’s command is declared to be the final decision; this fourth method is proclaimed as that which does not contradict the scriptures or the members of the court.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, a rule that is supported by reason is declared [authoritative].
Except for execution, there is never a punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Vedic tradition holds that in this world, Brāhmaṇas and cows are not to be slain.
Even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a Brahmin does not deserve corporal punishment; rather, the king should impose banishment, branding, and shaving of the head upon him.
And those guilty of great crimes he shall punish with the death penalty.
For a very minor offense, there shall be punishment by word or the "fie" (dhik) punishment; for the first degree of violence, the same;
but for the middle and highest degrees, half the penalty applies, as does imprisonment for treason against the king.

One who desires his own welfare should carry out either banishment or even execution for a perpetrator of a mortal sin— whether these measures are applied individually or collectively against that single offender.
One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on these wretched men!
And one should punish with fines those men who are litigious as well as those who are hostile.
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—
none who has deviated from his own duty is exempt from punishment by the king.
Sacrificial priests, domestic chaplains, ministers, sons, kinsmen,
and relatives who deviate from the Dharma shall be punished by kings and banished from the city.
One should punish teachers, domestic priests, and those worthy of honor with a verbal reprimand alone;
other litigants, however, one should punish with a reproach, a fine, or both.
Likewise, those born in the inverse order of castes and the outcastes are declared to be the dregs of men;
when they commit an offense against a Brāhmaṇa, they are to be executed, and no fine is to be imposed upon them at any time.
A man deserving of death shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
one deserving of the amputation of a limb shall pay half of that, and one deserving of a cut on the ear shall pay half of that again.
"Beating, imprisonment, and likewise the giving of food as wages—this indeed is the punishment for a Śūdra; there is no monetary fine, says Bṛhaspati."
One is declared a victor in the world by virtue of establishing one's proposition through proof, by honoring the judge and other officials,
and by the issuance of the certificate of victory.

The defeat of an inferior party is recognized through fleeing, through failing to offer a reply, or through relying on the side of another; it is not [recognized] for one who has been defeated by their own statements.
Even when the facts have been determined by the family and others, if the defendant does not accept them with satisfaction,
the king, having investigated the matter, should set aside that wrongful act and rectify it.
Having reached a decision together with many Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the scriptures,
he should punish the former members of the court along with the victorious party if they are found guilty.
And in this matter, a punishment corresponding to the offense has been prescribed;
one is declared defeated through witnesses, documents, inference, or properly by means of an ordeal.
He who does not pay the prescribed fine for what is to be given shall be banished from that city.
A branded mark on the forehead is the only punishment prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve the death penalty. The king should instead carry out banishment, branding, and shaving the head.
Whatever authority has been granted by him regarding all matters of profit, loss, expenditure, and income—
whether in his own country or abroad— that independence shall not be contradicted.
He who, having been appointed by his master to manage wealth, is entrusted with the authority to engage in lending at interest, agriculture, or trade, is known as one whose means have been delegated.
The king must diligently investigate matters that are doubtful;
in doing so, three parties are benefited, while the loss falls upon only one.
The victor obtains wealth and honor; the defeated receives discipline and restraint.
The king attains victory, charity, and self-control, while the members of the court acquire merit.
Thus, by performing the adjudication and protection ordained in the scriptures, a king,
having spread his fame throughout this world, shall become equal to Mahendra.
By resolving legal cases through witnesses, written documents, and inference,
a king spreads his fame here on earth and attains the realm of the Sun.
Wherever a king thus understands the determination of the sacrificial rite,
he attains glory in this world and goes to the same realm as Śakra.
[1.10 Non-payment of Debt] [1.10.0] This legal procedure has been proclaimed as consisting of eight parts.
Now hear the other categories that serve as causes for litigation.

I shall explain in due order, according to their true nature, the principal matters concerning the non-payment of debt, as well as gambling and betting, along with the various types of legal procedures.
That which is debt to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner,
as well as the rules for giving and receiving— this is recorded in the Smṛti as "the non-payment of debt."
[1.10.1 Consideration of Interest] The interest shall be one-eightieth part [per month] when there is security;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month.
Having received the pledge or the mortgage in its entirety along with reliable witnesses,
the creditor shall always deliver the debt, whether it has been recorded in writing or witnessed by others.
From one who is contemptible and from one who is in distress, [money] is taken by those free from hesitation;
therefore, that which is called usury is recorded as being fourfold or eightfold [of the principal].
In the Purāṇa, it is one paṇa;
interest is said to be fourfold by some, and proclaimed as fivefold by others.
These sixfold [categories] have been proclaimed by others; understand them according to their true nature.
Interest on the body, periodical interest, and the wheel-interest which follows from it; stipulated interest, crest-interest, as well as interest on enjoyment and interest on profit.
Interest connected with bodily labor may be collected after one month;
likewise, interest paid periodically, compound interest, and interest stipulated by the debtor himself.
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi*.
Like a topknot, it grows constantly; it ceases only upon the severing of the head.
But that interest which has been stipulated by the debtor himself as being excessive,
having been agreed upon during a time of distress, must always be paid as contracted.
Interest that has been stipulated otherwise must not be paid under any circumstances whatsoever.
Like a crest-lock, it grows constantly and ceases only upon the severing of the head;
likewise, when the root is provided, this growth of the crest-lock continues—thus it is remembered.
The share of grain from a field is proclaimed as the *stoma*, while the share of produce is called the *bhoga-lābha*.
They say that interest is fourfold: corporeal, interest on use, stipulated interest, and that which consists of the crest-lock; with compound interest, there is a fifth.
The creditor may collect interest, bodily labor, and likewise the profit from the use of the property,
only so long as the principal has not been repaid.
[1.10.3 Interest on Gold, Grain, and Other Goods] Interest on gold is said to be double; on clothing and household goods, triple;
and on grain, as well as on fodder, beasts of burden, and wool, it is declared to be fourfold.
In the case of potherbs, the five qualities mentioned are prescribed; for seeds and grain, they are traditionally held to be sixfold.
For salt, sweat-products, and fresh foods, an eightfold increase is considered appropriate.
This same rule is stated for molasses and honey when they have been kept for a long time.
For all types of oils, as well as for liquors, honey, and clarified butter, an eightfold increase is declared; the same applies to molasses and salt.
The interest on precious metals shall be fivefold; that on cotton cloth shall be fourfold;
and the increase on wood, such as sandalwood and the like, shall be eightfold.
If a share [of interest] is taken that exceeds double the principal, or if compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) is charged,
or if the entire debt with interest is collected at once and thereafter usury is practiced— that is censured.
The eightieth part [of the principal] shall increase until the profit reaches double the amount;
there is no doubt that a loan so invested will do so within seven years and three quarters.
In the case of grass, wood, bricks, thread, fermenting agents, skins, bones, armor, weapons,
flowers, and fruits, interest does not cease.
The interest on gold, grain, and cloth is two, three, and four times the principal respectively;
the interest on ghee is eightfold, and that on copper and similar metals is fourfold.
The creditor may collect interest on the head, bodily interest, and likewise profit from the use [of the property],
only so long as the principal has not been repaid.
For the others, [the punishment] increases by one quarter in succession.
In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail through verbal quibbling;
even if he is to be punished in cases involving another's wife, land, or the non-payment of debt, he does not lose his case.
One should always ensure that the interest is equal; however, if it is unequal, it shall cease.
[1.10.4 Interest on Wealth] Listen to the interest rates for a moneylender as declared by the words of Vasiṣṭha:
five māṣas for every twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; in this way, dharma is not violated.
A māṣa is proclaimed to be one-twentieth part of a pala.
But in that case, whatever man shows indifference toward this [duty],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is prescribed for him.
Whatever one may obtain for the sake of accomplishing the business of a corporation, or upon appearing before the king and other authorities, that shall be shared equally among all members.
In the case of those who have inherited property and so forth, this is their eternal law:
a debt that was acquired through efforts, or preserved, or contracted for the sake of the community.

[1.10.5 Interest Not Contracted] Even if he resides in his own country, he who does not pay when repeatedly requested shall, even against his will, pay the interest as it has been determined by the court.
A debt of six months' duration or even one of a month's duration should be divided according to their respective shares;
or it may be paid to those who are destitute, the elderly, the afflicted, women, children, the infirm, and the sick.
After three seasons, one may recover the principal along with interest;
in such cases as these, an eightieth part [of the principal] is intended as the rate of interest.
That which does not flow out [as interest] shall be the principal portion for the creditor;
even when doubled, it remains so, as does that which is designated as *kālika* from the outset.
Then the king should decide the case with the help of those who know the principles and the true nature of legal disputes.
[1.10.6 Pledge] But a pledge is used only so long as it has not been returned.
A pledge (ādhi) is defined as a "bond" (bandha), and it is said to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as to be kept (gopya) or to be enjoyed (bhogya).

A debt that is voluntary, has a fixed term, is recorded in writing, and is witnessed by others— likewise, when the interest on such a debt has ceased or the term has expired, the creditor may recover it.
He who, out of greed, consumes a pledge shall not receive the interest again;
it must be preserved like a deposit, for the interest perishes if it is lost through such use.
In the event of damage caused by fate or the king, if the pledge should be destroyed, the debtor shall cause another pledge to be given; otherwise, he must pay the debt along with the interest.
Whatever may be due from one whose hands are bound, whether by a painting or by a performance,
if the object has not been delivered, he shall not be made to pay the full amount against his will at any time.
When the pledged object has been used and has reached a state of worthlessness, a loss of the principal occurs;
whatever was of great value therein is lost, and the debtor should satisfy the creditor in that matter.
When a single field has been given as a pledge to two parties at the same time,
whoever possesses it first shall obtain its established ownership.
When two [items] are presented at the same time, the distribution shall be equal;
this very rule is proclaimed for both gifting and sale.
When a mortgage, sale, or gift has been executed with a sealed document,
that document is considered a means of proof in that matter through its connection to a single legal act.
Kātyāyana declared that an unspecified [document], one that has been specified, and one that is qualified in a single respect— among these, the one written with specific qualifications is superior.
When the interest on gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for twelve days.
By paying the debt within that interval, the debtor may recover the pledge;
when the term is fulfilled and the interest has been realized, he shall then become the owner of the pledge.
However, if ten days have not yet elapsed, the debtor is entitled to redeem it.
When a pledge for custody has reached double its value, or when the stipulated time has expired according to the rule,
it shall immediately be announced in the debtor's family and then enjoyed [by the creditor].
When the gold has doubled in interest and the debtor is still unable to pay,
the creditor shall take possession of the debtor's property and sell it in the presence of witnesses.
Or, having fixed a price, he should keep it for ten days in the presence of a public assembly;
thereafter, having received a deposit proportional to the debt, he should relinquish the other [item].
If a debtor does not enjoy his own pledge, nor deliver it, nor announce it [to others],
and if the witness has died, the creditor's written document is rendered useless.
A house, a field, a shop, grain, livestock, women, and vehicles— these perish through neglect, or likewise fall into a state of worthlessness.
Having secured his own wealth with men skilled in accounting, he may take possession of it while it is known to its kinsmen and relatives; thus he would not commit an offense.
The eighteen-fold litigation, distinguished by its plaints and rejoinders, has been explained; now, learn correctly the various types of legal procedures.
An action that was previously performed must be maintained exactly as it was;
where it is performed otherwise, then there would be a deviation from the action.
Having first abandoned the instrument [of proof], whether the creditor or the debtor should make it less,
more, or equal [to the original claim], that is called a "variation of the transaction" (*kriyābheda*).
He who, having undertaken a loan at two per cent interest, subsequently agrees to five per cent—
the latter rate shall be the authority regarding the profit, for it is the one finally settled.
But a gift or a sale that has been made by one who is not the owner is to be understood as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
By each successive bond, the preceding bond becomes loosened;
whatever action is performed last is more powerful than the one before it.
Whether one has made a deposit elsewhere or has already established a pledge,
if he subsequently establishes another pledge or performs a sale, the latter transaction therein is the more authoritative.
If a sale, a mortgage, and a gift are all performed on the same day,
and it is doubtful among these three [which belongs to whom], how should the investigation proceed in that case?
In this case, there are only three authorities; they should divide [the property] according to their respective shares.
Both [the father and the mother] shall do so according to the purpose, while the recipient shall take one-third.
If the debt has been paid in full and the land has been cultivated, then the owner of the wealth shall not receive his share,
nor shall the debtor recover his pledge, except by mutual agreement.
When a debtor, having paid the principal amount of money, requests the release of the pledge, it must be released at that very moment; otherwise, the creditor becomes liable for the offense.
When land or other property has been enjoyed [by the creditor] such that the profit derived from it exceeds the principal,
and the interest has entered into the principal, then the debtor shall recover the pledge.

If the creditor is absent, the debtor shall deposit the money with the owner of the pledge and take possession of the pledge itself. When the debtor, having made a formal agreement, gives the field to the creditor,
it is settled that the pledge must be released once the profit derived from it has been exhausted.
"But the pledge must be returned to me when the principal has yielded its interest;
this is declared to be the righteous rule for the procedure regarding loans and pledges."
Where there is an additional house or field that has been long possessed,
in that case the debtor shall recover his pledge and the creditor likewise his debt.
When the excellence is complete, that equality of both is proclaimed;
but when it is incomplete, the two should act according to each other's consent.
If that [debt] has been fully discharged, then the creditor no longer holds a share of the wealth;
the debtor does not forfeit his property without the mutual consent of both parties.
Surety] In the treatises, wise men have observed that a surety is of four kinds: for appearance, for trust, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of the debtor's property.
One says, "I shall show it," while another good man says, "I am the giver"; yet another might say, "I will pay this wealth."
But a surety for appearance who produces the person at the proper place and time,
or brings forward the security, shall not be liable, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
The creditor shall grant time for the recovery of lost property to the surety;
depending on the distance, the route, and the nature of the object, this period may be one fortnight, one month, or even half a month.
If a man stands as a surety for another's appearance here,
he shall pay that debt from his own property to the creditor if he fails to produce him.

If the first two [witnesses] prove to be false, they shall be made to pay the wealth as it was known at that time; however, if the latter two disagree, those two shall be made to pay, or likewise their sons in their absence.

The owner, one imprisoned by an enemy, an official, one punished, those under suspicion, an heir, a friend, an outcaste, a resident pupil, one following the conduct of a king, one free from passion, an ascetic, a pauper, a child, an elderly person, a woman, and a sick person are not eligible as sureties.
If the person for whom bail was posted fails to appear, the guarantor must again be made to pay for the one who failed to appear.
The entire paternal debt must be paid even by a son. However, if a person who had been pressured to stand as a guarantor pays the amount for which he was guaranteed, [he may seek reimbursement].
After three fortnights, he is entitled to recover his property along with double the interest.
If, because they are of dull intellect, those who have not been educated should pay a debt out of a sense of propriety,
they shall by no means recover from that person the very object for which they were made to pay.
They should not be excessively harassed; rather, they should be made to pay the debt gradually.
They should not be compelled to serve as witnesses for themselves; this is the rule regarding sureties.
When the debtor has disappeared or died, the creditor shall present the document and cause a new deed of location to be executed, specifying the time limit for its validity.
But when money has been paid by a surety to the creditor without being authorized by the debtor,
the debtor shall not have to pay double that amount back to the surety.
A debtor who has admitted the debt should be made to pay it through conciliation and other such means, as well as by means of religious pressure, deception, force, or confinement in his own home.
By means of religious pressure, deception, force, or confinement in his own home, he should be made to pay the debt he has acknowledged.

Through the mediation of friends and relatives, by means of conciliatory speech, and by following [the debtor], the creditor should generally be made to pay; this is declared to be the righteous course.
But a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income. Where a creditor, having brought back from the debtor money that was borrowed under a pretext,
or having recovered a deposit or the like, forces payment, that is a fraudulent transaction (*sa-upadhi*).
When a debtor is brought to his own house and compelled by force through methods such as beating and the like to pay, that is declared to be *balāt-kāra* (coercion).
Even by means of labor, the debtor may make himself equal to the creditor;
likewise, one of equal or lower caste shall pay the remainder gradually.
One may compel a man of low caste who has become destitute to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is destitute should be made to pay gradually, according to his income.
Having bound his wife, sons, and cattle, and having sat at the very threshold,
where a debtor is made to pay his own debt— that is called *ācarita* (customary practice).
This law applies to one who has admitted his debt; however, if he denies it in court, he is made to pay after being compelled to prove his denial by means of a document or witnesses.
"I am giving that which is rightfully to be given"—
where a debtor speaks thus, he is called one who asserts his legal claim (*kriyāvādī*).
One who asserts a legal claim regarding a doubtful matter must not be obstructed in any way whatsoever;
however, one who improperly restrains a person who should not be restrained is liable to punishment according to the law.
When there is a confusion between two parties regarding form, number, and so forth, or concerning gains,
or even when the matter of what is to be given and what is not to be given is doubtful— that is declared to be a "disputed case."
When the stipulated period has expired and the interest has ceased to accrue, the creditor may recover the debt,
or the debtor may retain the document under an arrangement for compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
When compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*) on a doubled debt is no longer accepted,
then the profit from the use of the property (*bhogalābha*) shall constitute the principal with interest for the creditors.
But he who proceeds with a doubtful matter without having informed the king shall be punished by force, and that legal matter shall not be established.
Now it is stated what debt, having been received from the hand of another according to the rules of usury,
must be repaid by whom, where, and how, and what need not be repaid.
A debt contracted for a short period must be paid upon request;
when the term has expired, it must be paid with interest ceased, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still indebted,
both his ascetic merit and his fire-sacrifice shall belong entirely to the owner of the wealth.
A debtor who has no wealth, having been brought to the house, should be made to work;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is a drunkard or of similar character should be made to pay the debt gradually.
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son [of a deceased person], the liability for debt follows in order according to their precedence.
In their absence, the inheritance shall go to the others who are entitled to share the estate, in their respective order.

Debts to be Paid] A debt must be acknowledged from the outset according to the law; however, if one does not record it in writing, nor indeed pay what has been admitted, he shall incur interest on that amount.
In the case of those who are diseased, insane, aged, or likewise living abroad for a long time,
one should cause such debts to be paid by their sons, even while they are still alive.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
however, this does not apply to those who are born blind, outcastes, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases.
Among those who have entered under a single title of ownership, he who is seen there shall be made to pay;
however, the son of one who has gone abroad shall receive the entire paternal share upon that father's death.
When the father has died, the son shall pay all debts contracted under a single liability; however, he shall never pay another's debt, except for that portion which was his father's share.
The debt of the father must first be paid, and then one's own;
of those two, the grandfather’s debt must be paid first—thus is a debt always to be settled.

A debt contracted by one's father must be paid by the sons once it has been proven, just as if it were their own; a debt of a grandfather is to be paid equally [by the grandsons], but that of a great-grandfather is not to be paid by his son.
Even one who is dependent may conduct legal business for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad; a learned man shall not obstruct him.
Therefore, once a son is born, the father must strive with effort to liberate himself from his debt by means of that son, so that he does not fall into hell.
When the father has died, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares, whether they are divided or undivided; or whoever shall take up that burden [of the wife].

One should not compel a son to pay a gift made for the sake of the sun or for the sake of a guest, a gift given in vain, a promise made under the influence of lust or anger, a suretyship obligation, or the remainder of a fine or a tax.
The person who acts as a supervisor for the wives of liquor-sellers, hunters, washermen, cowherds, barbers,
and boatmen shall be made to pay their debts incurred in the business activities of those husbands.
If a son who inherits the property and the debts is also a source of trouble, he shall likewise be the one to take the wife; this applies in the absence of an heir to the wealth.
What has been borrowed for the sake of the family by a paternal uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent, that the householder ought to repay.
He who, having been appointed by his master to manage income and expenditure,
or to engage in lending at interest, agriculture, or trade, is known as one "entrusted with funds" (nisṛṣṭārtha).
"He who, having taken items such as a loan or a deposit, does not return them to the owner,
is born as that person's slave, son, wife, or livestock in his household."
A father must discharge a debt contracted by his son if it was approved by him; or, out of affection for his son, he may pay it himself, but he is not otherwise obligated to pay it.

The debtor shall recover his pledge after having paid the debt, provided it is a pledge for the enjoyment of its fruit, once the full term has elapsed; however, if it is a pledge for a fixed sum, he shall recover it upon paying the principal amount.
If that [transaction] were excessive, then the creditor shall not receive his share of the wealth,
nor shall the debtor recover his pledge, without the mutual consent of both parties.
When a debtor who is being sued by a creditor for the recovery of a debt is summoned by another creditor for the purpose of settling his own lower debt,
the judge shall cause him to pay the amount of the creditor's claim as proven by the debtor himself.
But one who denies a debt, yet is proven by evidence,
shall be made to pay the creditor's claim and a fine according to his ability.
If one conceals an object to whatever extent, or if one should falsely claim it for whatever amount,
both of those, being ignorant of dharma, shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
If one has received money on account of a lawful debt and the like, but does not record it in writing,
nor indeed pays back the principal when it is due, that sum shall accrue interest for him.
[1.11 Nikṣepaḥ] [1.11.0] (p.120) The taking of loans is proclaimed to begin with the lending and end with the causing of repayment.
Now, let the correct procedure for deposits be heard.
[1.11.1 Aupaniḍhikam] (p.
120) That which is given unannounced, kept apart, uncounted, and not shown,
and which is marked with a seal, is known as *aupaniḍhika*.

[1.11.2 The Nature of Deposit (*nyāsa*)] When property is placed in another's house out of fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or due to deception regarding the receipt of an inheritance— that is proclaimed to be a deposit (*nyāsa*).
[1.11.3 The Method of Concealment] Having examined the location,
the house, the ground itself, as well as that debt from various perspectives,
and having considered truthfulness, purity, and kinsmen, one should conceal the treasure.

[1.11.4 Its Two-fold Nature] Furthermore, that [non-perception] is said to be of two kinds: that which possesses a witness and the other [which does not]. Likewise, in the case of its reversal, there should be a counter-delivery or a counter-proof.
It is declared to be of two kinds: that given in the presence of witnesses and that given in secret.
It must be protected like a son; otherwise, it perishes through neglect.
Whatever merit may arise from giving gold, base metals, clothing, and so forth, that same merit belongs to one who protects a deposit,
as well as one who has come for refuge.
Just as there is no fault for a noble woman in betraying her husband, nor for a man in killing his son or friend,
so too there is no fault for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit [entrusted to them].
One should not take possession of property left in deposit; its loss, however, brings ill repute.
What has been accepted should be guarded with care, and it should be returned when requested once.

Whatever has been deposited according to which procedure and by whom, and whatever has been proven [to belong to him], that must be returned to him exactly as it was; what is not to be returned is that which is immediately subsequent [in the sequence].
[1.11.6 Rules regarding the Loss of a Deposit] If that [deposit] should be destroyed due to an act of God or the king,
there is no fault in that case, provided it is returned together with the property of the depositary.
If the borrower, having received a deposit with its specific characteristics and with the understanding that it may be neglected, should lose it,
or if he should not return it when asked for it, he shall be compelled to pay it back along with interest.

[1.11.7 Punishment for Misuse of Deposits] Whoever should accomplish his own business by means of a deposited object shall be punished by the king and compelled to pay that object back along with interest.
[1.11.8 Decision in cases of denial: If a person, having received a deposit, denies it, he should be made to produce the deposit through witnesses or by means of an oath;
and he should be made to pay the deposit along with an equal fine as a penalty.
Where a dispute arises regarding a secret deposit,
it is ordained that an ordeal shall serve as the means of proof for both parties.
If a gift has been made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
One shall not recover anything from the sea if it has not been taken from there.
This same rule applies to what has been placed for safekeeping, what has been borrowed, what has been entrusted to an artisan, a deposit, and a pledge, as well as to one who has come for refuge.
If a deposit is being refined over a fixed number of days,
and the artisan keeps it beyond that period, he must pay for it even if it has been destroyed by an act of God.
One who gives away what has been requested with the owner's permission shall not be at fault. [Non-delivery by one who is not the owner] (p.
Immediately after the topic of deposits, Bhṛgu has declared the sale by one who is not the owner;
listen to that with diligence, for I shall explain it to you in detail.
[1.12.1 Definition of One Who Is Not the Owner] He who takes a deposit, a loan for use, a pledge, what has been stolen, what has been asked for,
or what has been sold in secret or before a crowd, is declared to be one who is not the owner.
[1.12.2 Fault in a Purchase Reported to the Superintendent] But for one who has purchased [an item] at a price after it was previously reported to the superintendent,
there is no fault; for the thief would be one who purchases by fraud (*upadhikrayāt*).
[1.12.3 The Definition of Upavikraya (Selling at a Loss)] That which is purchased within the house, outside the village, at night, from an unknown person,
or for a low price— this is to be known as *upavikraya*.
[1.12.4 Determination of the Purity of the Purchaser] But if the former owner, having arrived, should investigate that property,
then the price must be shown; from that, the purity of the purchaser shall be established.
If the original price has been recovered, the purchaser may not be prosecuted in any way;
however, a dispute regarding the price does not cause the eightfold interest to be lost.
Where the seller has been produced [in court], he loses the legal proceeding;
he shall pay the purchase price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner.
He who, being devoid of ownership, desires another's property out of greed,
and subsequently fails to relinquish it, shall be made to pay a fine double the value of that property.
But in a lawsuit where the evidence is deficient,
the king himself should make a decision based on the status of the individuals involved, according to whether they are equal, inferior, or superior.

When an item has passed through a merchant's row and is recognized by royal officials, or when it is purchased from an unknown source, or where the seller is dead; [in these cases, the purchaser shall be held liable].
The owner, having paid half the value, shall take back his own property; in that case, half of the stolen goods shall belong to both parties according to legal procedure.
Purchasing without proper knowledge and likewise failing to provide protection—
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of property.
If an article found in a merchant's shop has been recognized by royal officers,
and it was seized during the day, the purchaser of good standing recovers his wealth.
But he who, having sold land, does not provide the purchaser with possession, shall restore that wealth to him; otherwise, he incurs the punishment for theft.
These two have been declared by the wise to be causes of loss of value for goods,
because their specific qualities are unknown and thus no price can be obtained for them.
In that case, the loss shall be considered equal for both the buyer and the one who denies the debt.
[1.13 Collective Undertaking] [1.13.1 Those Authorized to Act Collectively] (p.
129) BP1.13.001a/ By those who are of noble birth, capable, diligent, wise, and conversant with coinage;
One should carry out undertakings together with those who know income and expenditure, who are pure, and who are brave.
Wherever a share is equal, greater, or less than another's,
its loss, expenditure, and increase shall likewise be of that same proportion.
[1.13.2 Those Who Are Unqualified] Wise men should not engage in activities such as trade and the like with those who are incapable, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support.
[1.13.3 Gain according to the nature of the commodity] But for those who carry out an investment with gold, grain, liquids,
and so forth, their gain shall be of a corresponding kind, according to whether the shares are equal, less, or more.
Whether a share is equal, smaller, or larger than that which was assigned, it shall be exactly so;
one must pay the expenses, perform the work, and indeed receive the profit accordingly.

[1.13.4 Decision in those debates: Those very same individuals are declared to be both examiners and witnesses for one another in a doubtful matter, provided they are free from deception and not possessed by mutual hatred.
Anyone among them who is known to be a fraud in buying or selling must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies in all disputes concerning transactions.
[1.13.5 Decision regarding Loss of Property] When a loss occurs there due to acts of fate or the king,
it is declared that this loss shall be apportioned among all [the partners] according to their respective shares.

If, however, one who was not specifically assigned the task loses [the property] through negligence while it is being sought, he alone must provide that which is due; this applies to all those who were partners in the undertaking.
Having given a sixth part to the king, they shall receive their shares according to their respective portions.
[1.13.6 The Protector’s Tenth Share] Out of fear of divine or royal calamity, he should protect [the community] to the best of his ability;
having given him a tenth share, they may take the remainder from that portion.
[1.13.7 Customs Duties] When a merchant arrives at a customs station, he shall pay the duty as is appropriate. He must not deviate from that; this is proclaimed as the tribute due to kings.
This is not the case when a calamity involving thieves, kings, or fire has arisen;
however, for one who protects [the property] according to his own ability, a tenth part is prescribed as his share.
[1.13.8 Decision regarding the loss of one among those performing joint labor: When a certain merchant there should die through negligence,
his merchandise must be displayed by the appointed royal officers.
When someone arrives, that man who is an heir to the estate may establish his ownership through other means; he is then entitled to receive it.
The king should take a sixth, a ninth, or likewise a tenth part from the Śūdra, Vaiśya, and Kṣatriya castes; however, he should take a twentieth part from the Brāhmaṇa.
But if the owner does not come forward by any means after three years, then the king may take that property; however, he should bestow the property of a Brāhmaṇa upon other Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, when anyone among those engaged in a ritual action passes away,
that rite must be performed by his kinsman together with all the other participants.
[1.13.9 The Priests] The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the establishment of the sacred fires;
the Hotṛ shall take the horse that chooses the *nivid* verses, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Of all [the sons], the primary ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third share, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth share.

Those who are newcomers, those who have arrived by succession, and likewise those who have established themselves on their own—these are declared to be of three kinds; one should conduct oneself toward them accordingly.
[1.13.10 Types of Joint Undertakings] If a man, being approved by many, should give wealth or cause a legal act to be performed, it shall be considered as having been done by all of them.
A debt contracted with kinsmen, relatives, or friends may be paid even when secured by a pledge;
however, for others, it must likewise be accompanied by a mortgage, a written document, or witnesses.
Gold may be taken at one's own will; however, liquids and grain must be given with a time-limit. They should be given and likewise received in accordance with local custom.
But that which is given by those assembled together must likewise be requested back;
whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain.
[1.13.11 Joint Agricultural Work] Listen; this rule concerning farmers and others is now being stated.
A wise man should engage in agriculture together with those who are equal to him in terms of draft animals, laborers, seed, and other implements for the field.
Where the loss of a field occurs due to the destruction of external seeds,
that [loss] must be made good by that very person for all those who live by agriculture.
One should carefully avoid a field that is on a mountain, near a city, or along a royal road, as well as one that is saline or infested with rats.
One who sows at the proper time in land that has pits filled, is situated near water, is well-irrigated, is surrounded by fields, and has been thoroughly plowed, enjoys the fruit.
A wise farmer should not take as his draft animal one that is emaciated, overgrown, lowly, diseased, or fleeing; nor one that is one-eyed or lame.
This ancient law has been fully declared for the *kīnāśas* (plowmen/artisans).
[1.13.12 Artisans] It concerns those who work with gold, base metals, and thread, as well as wood, stone, and leather.
But the one who performs the refinement, being skilled in the arts, is called an artisan by the wise.
Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively,
they shall receive wages corresponding to their work in proportion to their respective shares.
Instructors, masters, and experts are the artisans;
they shall receive one, two, three, or four shares, respectively, according to their superior skill.
Of those who, acting together, construct a mansion, a temple, or even the furnishings of a righteous person,
the leader deserves two shares.
This same rule has been declared by the virtuous as the law for dancers:
one who knows the rhythmic beats (*tāla*) receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares.
[1.13.13 Division of the Gain of Thieves] But that which has been brought from a foreign land by thieves at the command of their master,
they shall divide among themselves according to their respective shares after giving one-sixth to the king.

Then the eldest son shall receive four shares; a heroic son shall obtain one share [in addition to his own]; but a capable son may take two shares, while all the remaining sons shall have equal shares.
Thus has been declared in its entirety the settlement for those who have risen together; now the rules concerning what should not be given,
what may be given, what has been given, and what has not been given are being stated.
Common property, such as sons and wives; all one's own wealth; a deposit;
that which has been requested; and likewise that which has been promised to another—these eight kinds of things are traditionally held to be not subject to gift.
That which remains after providing for the food and clothing of one's family must be given away;
otherwise, like the taste of honey followed by poison, the fate of the giver shall be otherwise.
Whatever field is acquired from a garden or a house-site,
whether inherited from a father or obtained by oneself— that which is intended for distribution must be given.

That which is given by one's own will, that which is acquired by oneself, and collateral given according to the custom of pledging—these may be freely disposed of; however, in the case of property received through marriage or inherited in succession, there is no such right to give away everything.
That which is received as a dowry, inherited in due order, or acquired through valor,
as well as that which is given with the permission of the wife, her kinsmen, or the owner, shall attain validity.

Except for his entire estate and his home, whatever property remains for the maintenance of his family and other such purposes—that is his own property which may be given; otherwise, it shall not be given.
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights over immovable property;
for in all matters of giving, causing to be given, or selling, a single person has no power.
Wages, the price for goods, a bride-price, a gift to one who has rendered assistance,
and that which is given out of faith, favor, or affection— this is recorded as the eightfold [classification of] gifts.
A gift given to a Śūdra is said to yield an equal reward; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as yielding twice that;
to a Kṣatriya, the gift yields three times that; and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as yielding six times that.
For a *śrotriya*, the fine is one thousand; for a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), it is twice that;
for a teacher (*ācārya*), it should be known as threefold; and for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it is twice that.
If the offense is committed against one's own kin, the fine is one thousand; but against an Agnihotrin, it is infinite.
Against a Soma-drinker, it is one hundred thousand; against a teacher of the Veda, it is infinite.
A woman should bestow her own property upon the women of her own family, avoiding men; in the absence of such women, she should give it to her kinsmen; and in their absence, to the twice-born.
That which is given with the thought "after my death" does not bring about merit for a living being;
because it has not been given at that time, it shall fall to the heir upon his death.
With those who are angry, joyful, intoxicated, afflicted, childish, insane, or tormented by fear;
with those who are drunk, very old, dismissed, overwhelmed, or seized by the force of grief.
Likewise, that which is given by Nandas and Dattas is proclaimed as "given improperly" (adatta);
it is what is given with the desire for personal gain to one who is unworthy, under the mistaken impression that he is worthy.

Or, if the work is connected with unrighteousness, the owner shall recover that [payment]; the one who enjoys what was not given, as well as the one who gives what should not be given, shall be punished.
[1.15 Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā]
[1.15.0] The rules for those who have entered service regarding what may not be taken and so forth have been declared;
having undertaken service, this first point is now being stated.
But when one has agreed to service yet does not perform it—
this agreement to service that is not fulfilled is called the legal head of dispute known as "non-performance after agreement."
The non-payment of wages, and for that purpose the disputes between the owner and the herdsman, are dealt with in due order; this constitutes the threefold classification of hired laborers.
However, it is described in many ways according to birth and action;
it is fourfold by reason of knowledge, realization, desire, and wealth.
Furthermore, each one of these is divided according to the differences in its ritual application.
The triple knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) is declared to be characterized by the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas].
For the sake of that, one should perform the service to the teacher as enjoined.
Skill is said to be proficiency in the arts, such as the refinement of gold and silver, as well as dancing and so forth; having acquired that, one should perform work in the teacher's house.
He who enjoys another's female slave should be known as one hired by a mare;
he must perform that work for her master just as a man hired for food would do.
It is taught that there are many kinds of those who provide wealth, as well as others who provide a share;
furthermore, the classification of all of them into inferior, middling, and superior has been declared.
One who has been made to work for a day, a month, half a month, three months, or a year,
shall perform the labor as promised and receive the wages stipulated.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior;
their wages shall depend upon their work and be determined according to their ability and devotion.
In this regard, the highest wage is for a soldier, the middle for a cultivator, and the lowest for a porter; such is the threefold classification of hired laborers.
The soldier is declared the highest; the farmer is the middlemost;
the burden-carrier is declared the lowest, as is the one who performs domestic labor.
The sharecropper is recorded as being of two kinds among those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing;
he shall receive [a portion] from the harvested grain as well as from the milk, without a doubt.
For these four are declared to be performers of auspicious work:
the student (*śiṣya*), the resident pupil (*antevāsī*), the hired servant (*bhṛtaka*), and the laborer (*karmakara*).
However, the remaining fifteen types of slaves are entitled only to the lowest form of labor.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: auspicious and indeed inauspicious.
Unpleasant work is prescribed for a slave, while pleasant work is traditionally assigned to a laborer;
this includes cleaning the house, the door, unclean places, the streets, and the refuse heaps.
Touching the limbs of one who has been grasped, touching the limbs of one who is impure from eating, receiving or discarding feces and urine,
and finally, attending upon a departing master with one's own body.
Inauspicious action is to be understood as that which precedes this; other than that, it is auspicious.
