From that point forward, he is to be called one protected by the favor of his master;
he becomes one whose food may be eaten and from whom gifts may be accepted, and is esteemed by the virtuous.
Until he has grasped the [teaching on] ignorance, the student should serve his teacher with diligence;
his conduct toward the teacher’s wives and likewise toward the teacher’s son should be the same.
Having returned from his studies and having presented the teacher’s fee (*guru-dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher, he returns home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student (*śiṣya-vṛtti*).
In this regard, the first group of four is not released from servitude except by the favor of their master; for them, slavery is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself as a slave—
he is the most contemptible of all these, and he is not released even from slavery.
A female slave who has been married by a slave shall also attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, since his own authority is dependent upon his master.
And those sons born of a female slave, whether by her husband or by another,
if the progenitor is their master, the lord shall not compel the female slave to work.
[1.16 Non-payment of Wages] [1.16.0] A plowman shall take one-third or one-fifth [of the crop].
From the grain, from the grass for fodder, and from the ploughing, let them take a fifth part as their share.
If he is not maintained by wages, he may take a third part from the harvested crop.
A hired servant must not practice even the slightest deception toward his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a legal dispute arises.
[1.16.1 Determination regarding the non-performance of work by a hired laborer] If a hired laborer,
being free from illness, should out of pride fail to perform the work as stipulated,
he shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid.
[1.16.2 Punishment for One Who Has Received Wages] When a hired laborer who has received wages does not perform the work,
if he is capable, he shall be made to pay a fine of double those wages.
One who has received wages and abandons his work shall pay double the amount.
[1.16.3 Punishment for one who has not received wages:
If wages have not been received, the employer shall cause the worker to be paid an equal amount; furthermore, the tools must be protected by those who have been hired.
[1.16.4 Punishment for Failing to Fulfill a Promise] He who, having given his word, does not act upon it, should be compelled to do so even by force;
if he still does not perform that task, he shall incur a fine of twenty [paṇas].
He shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid.
[1.16.5 Absence of Liability for Wages] When a hired servant performs an act that is harmful to the purpose for which he was appointed by his master, the master shall not be held liable for it.
[1.16.6 Times when the herdsman is free from fault] In the event of an act of God, or by the king's decree, or likewise during a calamity of the kingdom,
if cattle are lost or killed, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
[1.16.7 The Rule of Punishment for the Master] If a master, after the work has been performed, does not pay the wages to the laborer,
he shall be compelled by the king to pay them, as well as a proportionate fine.
[1.16.8 Punishment for the Fault of the Herdsman] But if there is destruction [of the cattle] without fault on the part of the herdsman,
a fine of twelve and a half paṇas is prescribed for the herdsman, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner.
If she is ill, exhausted, distracted, or occupied with royal duties,
and yet does not come when invited, she is considered a "barren mare" (baḍabā) and is beyond reproach.
[1.16.9 Duties of the Owner and the Herdsman] Likewise, one who has been hired for the milk of a cow shall receive all of it on the eighth day;
he shall deliver all of this back to the owner... [as before].
If a cowherd fails to exert himself, fails to raise an alarm, and fails to inform the owner,
he must bear the cost of the loss and pay a fine to the king.
He shall protect [the pasture] from the danger of worms, thieves, tigers, caves, and dogs;
he shall drive them away to the best of his ability, or report it to the owner within the distance of one *krośa*.
One should drive the cattle away from the standing crops; however, if they have fed upon them, two faults arise:
the owner shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], and the keeper deserves corporal punishment.
Furthermore, if the crop has been consumed along with its roots, the fine shall be equal to the value of the damage.
[1.17 Transgression of Agreements] [1.17.0] For this indeed is proclaimed as the conduct between masters and servants.
Now, learn in brief the rules concerning agreements (saṃvid).
[1.17.1 Establishing the True Brāhmaṇas and Their Duties] Having summoned learned brāhmaṇas who are knowers of the Vedic sciences, śrotriyas, and maintainers of the sacred fire-offering,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
The king should grant them house-sites with the right to tax-free cultivation;
having recorded this in his own edicts, he should ensure they are held as freehold.

They should perform the daily rites (*nitya*), the occasional rites (*naimittika*), the rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), as well as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*); likewise, they should provide a definitive resolution in matters of doubt regarding ancient rituals (*paurāṇa-karma*).
[1.17.2 Performing Dharma-deeds Collectively] However, for the sake of the village, guild, or corporation, an agreement and the establishment of rules should be made;
that [agreement] must be carried out in times of distress, and likewise in matters concerning dharma.
Fear of robbers and thieves, as well as general oppression, is declared to be common to all; in such cases, a remedy must be sought by everyone collectively, not by any single individual alone.
[1.17.3 Establishing Trust] Having first established mutual trust through a deposit, a written contract, or mediators, they should thereafter carry out their business affairs.
Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, as timid as rice stalks,
those who are neither authorized nor unauthorized, and those who are greedy, very old, or children, should not be appointed as deliberators on affairs of state.
Those who are pure, knowers of the Veda and the Dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all matters— such men of great excellence should be appointed.
Two, three, or five persons should be appointed who speak for the welfare of the community;
their word must be carried out by the village, guilds, corporations, and so forth.

[1.17.5 Samayakriyā] The restoration of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, ponds, and parks; likewise, the performance of funeral rites for the destitute and the poor, and the act of joining them in marriage.
"The lineage and its cessation must be maintained by us according to our respective shares;
as for this document that has been thus written, it is a righteous formal agreement."

Those who are capable must protect [the children]; however, for one who is capable but fails to provide support, the punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
In that case, whatever man creates a breach or shows indifference toward it,
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
But he who injures common property, or reviles one learned in the three Vedas, or obstructs a formal agreement or a ritual act, shall be banished from that city.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who commits violence,
and one who hates a guild, a corporation, or the king, shall be swiftly banished from there.
The heads of families, guilds, and corporations, as well as those residing in cities and fortresses,
shall impose verbal censure, fines, corporal punishment, or banishment upon evildoers.

The punishment and favor toward men carried out by them according to their own duty must also be approved by the king, for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated with full authority.
When those who have become filled with hatred cause harm to one another,
or when a dispute arises among the assemblies concerning their leaders,
the king should then investigate the matter and establish them upon the proper path.
He who, being capable [of fulfilling his duty], should fail to do so,
shall be punished with the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
Those who, having formed a partnership, appropriate for themselves the king’s share by acting as one,
and those merchants who flee, shall be made to pay eight times that amount.
Then, whatever he may obtain, that shall be shared equally among all;
it should be divided according to their respective shares, whether it be a monthly or a six-monthly portion.
Or it may be given to those who are destitute, aged, blind, women, children, the infirm, or the diseased; likewise to those seeking to establish a lineage and so forth—this is the eternal law.
Whatever is acquired through exertion, or preserved, or staked for the sake of the community,
or obtained as a royal favor— that belongs equally to all.
[1.18 Residual Doubts Concerning Purchase and Sale] [1.18.0] This determination of conventional practice has been stated in brief.
Let this dispute arising from buying and selling be heard.
[1.18.1 Commodity] Two types of property are declared: movable and immovable.
At the time of purchase, the term "commodity" (paṇya) is traditionally applied to both.
[1.18.2 Punishment for Buying Defective Goods] If an unwise man, knowing that a commodity is defective, sells it,
he shall be made to pay double that very amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty.
[1.18.3 Things to be Rescinded] That which was sold by one intoxicated or insane, for a low price, or out of fear;
or that which was abandoned by one who is not independent or is deluded— this must be returned to him.
But he who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another,
shall be made to pay double that value as a fine, and an equal amount as a penalty.

[1.18.4 Times for Inspection] The inspection of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, or half a month respectively.
If, however, a defect in the commodity should arise before that time,
it must be returned by the seller, and the buyer shall recover the purchase price.
But if something is purchased without being examined and is later found to be defective, that merchandise must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
One should personally examine the merchandise and show it to others; having purchased what has been examined and approved by many, one should not later reject it.
For horses, silver, gold, grain, iron, goats, and clothing,
as well as for products made of leather and wood, the period of examination shall be one day.
The valuation of pearls, shells, horses, and female horses shall be determined by experts;
for goods situated in the marketplace, it shall be by the king’s command; and for cattle and land, it shall be by the mutual agreement of both parties.
In the case of sharing or exchange between both fields,
success in the undertaking shall be achieved by those two through mutual recollection.
If those standing nearby— the buyer's kinsmen and others— are traditionally considered to be questioned,
then, if the transaction was otherwise conducted, one should subsequently demonstrate the will of the kinsmen.
The purchase of immovable property is required to be based precisely on the testimony of kinsmen and others;
otherwise, if there should be a sale, [the matter] shall be investigated for three fortnights in another village.

Those born of the same womb, those connected by the piṇḍa offering, those connected by the water libation, those of the same lineage, neighbors, and creditors— these seven are considered sources from whom [the property] may be seized.
If one pays more or less than the price, it is considered improper for the price;
however, once the purchase is finalized, it shall not be so, even after hundreds of years.

[1.18.5 Special Rules Regarding the Purchase of Land] Bṛhaspati states that in all sales, one should have recorded the wells, trees, and so forth, as well as water channels and whatever else exists, by other parties as well.
They say that a field and so forth endowed with [favorable] qualities, ripened crops, a tree, or even fruit fit for enjoyment;
likewise a well, a pond, a house, and high ground—these belong to the buyer and the seller alike.
If an exchange has been made with those who are intoxicated, deluded, ignorant, afflicted, or confused,
or if anything should be given at an improper price, all of that shall be rescinded.
Relatives, neighbors, and creditors who have gone outside the village for the purpose of a purchase do not deserve to object to a sale completed after three fortnights have passed in succession.
Or else, after three fortnights or three months, he shall obtain that [result].
[1.19 Sīmāvādaḥ] [1.19.0] This rule has been set forth regarding disputes concerning purchase and sale.
Learn now the legal procedure regarding boundary disputes concerning villages, fields, houses, and so forth.
[1.19.1 Boundary Junctions: Trees and Other Markers to be Established] They should establish boundary trees— *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka*— as well as *śālmalī*,
*śāla*, *tāla*, and milky-sap trees.
Thickets, various kinds of bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and mounds, as well as reeds and thickets of *kubjaka*— by these, the boundary does not perish.
Reservoirs, wells, ...
and springs should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries, as well as temples for deities.

The king, having granted a field, should demarcate it as being supervised by the fourfold assembly of experts, the village headman, the village officials, all the villagers, and the officers of the great lord of that district.

If a Śūdra should be the leader, one should mark him with the insignia of impotence, smear his face with the ashes of a corpse, make five finger-marks on his chest with the blood of a victim sacred to Agni, fasten intestines around his neck, and have him hold a clod of earth from the boundary line upon his head with his right hand.
At the time of settling a new dwelling, the determination of the boundary must be made;
it should be marked with both public and secret signs to remove all doubt.
By their very nature, without conflict, imperishable substances consist of ponds,
wells, tanks, sacred mounds, groves, and temples.
He should always cause these visible markers to be made at the boundary: high ground, depressions, river currents, reeds, thickets, mountains, and so forth.
[1.19.3 Witnesses in a Boundary Dispute] If there should be doubt even when signs are observed,
the determination of the boundary in a dispute must depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses.
In the absence of witnesses, four inhabitants living near the village boundaries shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.

Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
When they have been questioned, whatever mark for the boundary junctions they may declare,
that the king shall establish accordingly between the two villages in accordance with the law.
Having grasped the earth with their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and being sworn by their respective meritorious deeds, they shall speak the truth.
He should thus fix the boundary and record all those [markers] by name;
he should always cause these visible signs to be established at the boundary.
Likewise, he should establish other hidden marks which the earth would not consume,
and he should cause other boundary markers to be made that serve as protective covers.
Having observed the constant flux in the world regarding the knowledge of boundaries—
such as the bones in cemeteries, cow-hair ropes, ashes, and skull-fragments— [one should remain detached].
He should cause dry cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel,
and sand to be placed in the junctions of the boundary so that they remain hidden from view.
Cow-dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, pebbles,
potsherds, sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton seeds, and ashes.
Having placed these items in jars, he should have them deposited at the boundaries; these marks,
which must be shown with great care, he should then diligently display to children of tender age.
In old age, they should likewise show those children [the boundary];
in this way, when there is mutual knowledge [of the boundary], no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
By the power of fortune or misfortune, it effects the taking away or the bestowing of gifts upon men;
in one place there is the collapse of the earth’s banks, while in another there is stability.
One should not displace a boundary that has been established along a riverbank;
likewise, when a field with standing crops is overstepped and the ground becomes desired by another, [the boundary shall remain].
The owner of a field shall recover that land which has been taken away by the king through anger or greed, or by force, or unjustly, by means of the current of a river's flow.
[1.19.6 Decision on Disputes Concerning Houses and Fields] In disputes concerning houses and fields, the decision is reached based on the testimony of the neighbors,
as well as those who are the heads of city or village guilds and those men who are the eldest.
Plowmen, artisans, and laborers; cowherds, hunters, and those who live by gleaning;
root-diggers, fishermen, and those who breach or obstruct irrigation channels.
Those who know the title-deed, the legal proof, the possession, the desire, the name,
as well as the characteristics of the portion of land, are the witnesses in this matter.
But that land which was given to another by one who was pleased,

yet later taken away by the king through anger, greed, fraud, or even by legal means, shall not attain validity. For one who enjoys land that lacks legal proof, that land which was taken from him [is lost].
Or if she has been given to one superior in qualities, one must never cause her to depart from him.
Bound by oaths taken according to their respective classes, they shall declare the decision regarding the boundary;
they shall point out hidden deposits, for that is the established rule of evidence.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by the truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons.
Even a single honest man, recognized by both parties, who is devoid of personal marks,
wearing red garlands and garments and holding earth upon his head, [may administer the oath].
A man who has taken a vow of truth and observed a fast should point out the boundary.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary marker,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
Those who lead the case according to what has been stated are purified as truthful witnesses;
but those who lead it otherwise shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
This rule is proclaimed for every dispute concerning immovable property.
Those born there who reside in neighboring regions or in other countries are designated as "original" (maula) witnesses; they should be questioned for the determination of the case.
Whatever those who are faultless, impartial, and of equal conduct may say when there is doubt, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
When land is brought from another village and given to someone else, it becomes the property of those men;
otherwise, the acquisition would be due to the king or fate.
Now, how should the legal determination be made regarding a great river or by a king?
That land which is abandoned by a river or granted by a king belongs to that very person [who possesses it];
otherwise, the acquisition of land by men would depend solely on fate or royal whim.
The decline, prosperity, and livelihood of men are under the power of fate and the king;
therefore, at all times, one should not subvert what has been ordained by them.

Wherever a river has been established as the boundary between two villages, it may, by the fortune or misfortune of men, effect the transfer of gifts; and when it diminishes or rises, even slightly, causing the boundary to shift, the king deserves to impose a fine.
The king should establish clearly defined boundaries for villages consisting of ten, a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand households, using various distinctive marks.
Starting from the time of settlement, one should not displace the house, field, shop, or other property of anyone,
in whatever quantity and in whatever manner it was enjoyed by them.
One should not disturb the windows, the drainage channels, the turrets, the balconies, or the water-channels of the four-winged palace, provided they have been established facing the east.
One should not obstruct the girdle, the drainage channel, the eaves, or the windows; one who obstructs a water-conduit or the site of a house shall be liable to a fine.

After the time of settling into a residence, these [prohibitions] should not be applied in any way whatsoever. One should not construct a drainage channel that falls within the sight of another's house.
A latrine, a fire-pit,
a pit, or the place for pouring away water from food remnants should never be made too close to the wall of another's property.
One should construct the receptacles for excrement, urine, and water, as well as the fire-place and the pit,
leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the outer wall.
That by which people and animals go and come without restraint is called *saṃsaraṇa*; it must not be obstructed by anyone.
Whoever there intentionally creates a mixture of castes, digs a pit, plants a tree,
or voids excrement, his fine shall be one māṣaka.
Having taken [the grain], he should cause it to be sown, guarded, and harvested at the proper time;
if he fails to do so, he shall be made to pay the owner half of the crop from the cultivated field.
If anyone, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
he shall be made to pay the crop-rent to the owner and a fine equal to that amount to the king.
If the field has been neglected for a long time, one-tenth [of the produce] shall be given; likewise, if it is being cultivated, one-eighth.
But if it is well-prepared, one-sixth shall be given, having calculated it according to the rule.
[1.20 Harsh Speech] [1.20.0] Harsh speech is traditionally held to be of two kinds: unpleasant verbal expression and physical assault.
Each of these three, moreover, is divided into three kinds; thus, self-control (dama) is said to have three characteristics.
[1.20.1 Regarding the threefold nature of verbal abuse: The reviling of local customs, family lineages, and so forth, by associating them with evil—
without, however, involving material wealth— is called the first form of verbal abuse.
The disclosure of a minor offense (upapātaka) concerning a sister or a brother,
as well as verbal cruelty, is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "middling" verbal [offense].
The discourse on forbidden foods and drinks is a defilement equal to a great sin;
it is declared to be the highest form of harshness, involving the infliction of severe injury.
[1.20.2 Punishment] But for mutual verbal abuse between those of equal caste and quality,
the discipline prescribed in the treatise is a fine of twelve and a half paṇas.
A fine of two *kārṣāpaṇas* shall be imposed on those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly disabled.
For insulting someone of equal caste, the fine is twelve *paṇas* and a half;
for insulting someone of lower caste, the fine is six *paṇas* and one *kākiṇī*.
The same applies to those who are one-eyed, lame, and so forth.
When two persons are of equal status, the punishment is equal; for the inferior, it is double;
and for the superior, it is declared to be greater, in the case of mutual verbal abuse.
One who insults a sister or other such relatives shall pay a fine of fifty paṇas;
however, in the case of verbal abuse, a Brāhmaṇa shall not be held liable for an offense against one inferior in qualities.
By saying "he is fallen" regarding one who is fallen, or again "he is a thief" regarding a thief,
one incurs an equal fault through such speech.
[1.20.3 Differentiation of Punishment according to Caste] When this king imparts instruction on dharma to Brahmins in accordance with dharma,
the king shall cause heated oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
The fine for a Kṣatriya who brings false accusations against a Brāhmaṇa is fifty [paṇas];
likewise, for a Vaiśya it is twenty-five, and for a Śūdra it is twelve and a half.
This discipline has been prescribed for a Śūdra who is truthful and free from fault;
however, a Brāhmaṇa shall not incur guilt even if he speaks harshly to one who is devoid of merit.
A Vaiśya who reviles a Kṣatriya should be fined one hundred;
a Kṣatriya who insults a Vaiśya deserves half of that fine as a disciplinary measure.
For a Kṣatriya who reviles a Śūdra, the fine is twenty-five paṇas;
for such an act involving a person of high status, double that amount has been declared by those learned in the scriptures.
A Śūdra who insults a Vaiśya shall be made to pay the first amercement;
one who insults a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; and one who insults a Brāhmaṇa, the highest amercement.
One who defames another by means of [false accusations regarding] their country and so forth shall be made to pay twelve and a half paṇas;
one who, out of arrogance, joins another with a sin shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who imparts instruction in Dharma supported by Vedic citations,
and one who reviles Brahmins, shall be punished by the cutting off of the tongue.
This punishment has been fully declared by me with reference to the status of the individual;
it should be determined by the wise according to whether the offense is equal, lesser, or greater.
[1.21 Cruelty with a Staff] [1.21.0] With hands, stones, or clubs; with ashes, mud, or dust;
Assault with weapons and instruments of striking is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (physical violence).
When verbal abuse has been committed, whatever punishment is prescribed for the one who initiated it,
the king shall cause that very same person to pay double that fine, except in cases involving death.
When two persons strike each other, the punishment is declared to be equal for both;
however, the one who initiated the attack and the one who persisted in it shall be made to pay a higher fine.
A man who returns an insult for a previous insult, or strikes back when struck,
or even kills an assailant, incurs no guilt.
If a low-born person should insult a noble man with verbal abuse or other such means, the king need not investigate that very person when he strikes back in self-defense.
[1.21.1 First: Verbal Assault] The throwing of ashes and the like, as well as striking with the hand or other means, constitutes the first form of physical assault;
in this case, a fine of one *māṣa* should be imposed.
This punishment has been declared for cases involving women of equal status and those who are superior;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, depending on the relative preeminence [of the woman].
For throwing stones, rocks, or wood, the first fine shall be imposed;
likewise, for [striking] each other with hands or feet, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively.
[1.21.2 Middle] The middle [fine] should be applied when two [parties] have become agitated during the employment of weapons; however,
the wise should impose a fine corresponding to the injury inflicted at the moment of the attack.
For striking with a clod of earth, a stone, or a piece of wood, the fine shall be two māṣas;
for drawing blood, the punishment prescribed by the wise should be double that amount.
For piercing the skin, the first amercement is the punishment; for piercing the flesh, however, the middle amercement;
but for piercing a bone, the highest amercement shall be imposed, while for destroying [the bone], there shall be the death penalty.
For cutting off the ears, nose, or hands; for breaking teeth;
or for piercing bones, the middle amercement shall be imposed; however, it shall be double in the case of those who have committed mortal offenses.
For the cutting off of the ear, lip, nose, foot, eye, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine shall be imposed; for the piercing or breaking [of these], the middle fine is prescribed by the teacher.
The punishment for one who merely threatens is that prescribed for verbal assault;
if [the object] is actually taken, it is double that, and the royal fine is even greater than that.
In cases of piercing a limb, causing pain, or likewise amputation,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery and whatever was seized during the quarrel.
But when one who was beaten in a secluded place is seen dead or [is presumed] to have been killed,
the killer should be identified either by inference or by an oath.
If blood is seen where one was beaten— whether inside a house or in the forest— at night, one should not question witnesses in that case.
If someone, having marked himself with a sign, should attack another out of malice for the sake of a pretext using excessive force, an investigation is appropriate in that case.
A man who, when reviled, reviles in return; or when struck, strikes back;
or who kills one who has committed an offense against him, shall not be considered guilty.
Those born in the inverse order (prātilomya) as well as those of the lowest castes (antyāḥ) are recorded as the impurities of men;
they are to be executed for violating a Brāhmaṇa, and their property must never be confiscated.
He who causes oxen that are exhausted, afflicted by hunger, or thirsty to work at an improper time must perform the expiation for killing a cow, or else be made to pay a fine.
He shall be made to pay the costs of recovery and whatever was spent for the sake of the quarrel.
If a Śūdra strikes members of the twice-born in anger with any limb, that very limb of his must be cut off; so it has been declared by Manu.
[1.22 Theft] [1.22.0] It is recorded that thieves are of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret.
Through these powers, those [faculties] are divided a thousandfold by the capacity of wisdom.

[1.22.1 Thieves in the Light and in the Dark] Traders, physicians, gamblers, members of an assembly who take bribes, deceivers, those who predict omens and portents, auspicious men, artisans, and counterfeiters;
Those who fail to perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, and false witnesses— these are indeed open thieves, as are those who live by deception.
Those who break into houses, those who rob travelers, those who steal bipeds or quadrupeds, those who dig up crops, and those who steal grain are to be known as concealed thieves.

[1.22.2 Punishment for them: Those identified by royal officers through their associations, signs, or appearances shall be made to restore what was stolen and be punished with the penalties prescribed by the scriptures.
The one who commits highway robbery shall be torn apart with pincers by the king's officers;
the stealer of grain shall be made to pay ten times the value, along with double the fine as punishment.
When the death of a single evildoer brings security to many, his execution bestows merit.
Likewise, having tied a traveler to a tree by the neck at dawn, one should cause him to hang there.
For one who breaks a finger-joint, [the king] shall cause [the offending joint] to be cut off upon the first apprehension;
on the second, both hands and feet; on the third, he deserves the death penalty.
A physician who is ignorant of medicinal herbs and mantras, and who does not understand the true nature of diseases,
yet takes wealth from the sick, shall be punished like a thief.
The stake must be made public; those who play with fraudulent dice shall be banished.
Those who play with false dice, the base, those who seize the wives of kings, as well as accountants and deceivers— these gamblers are declared to be punishable by law.
Furthermore, one who sells refined goods that are mixed with or concealed by defects shall be made to pay twice the value of those goods, as well as a merchant's fine equal to that amount.
Those members of the court who speak unjustly, as well as those who live by bribery and those who deceive the trusting—
all of them shall be banished.
Those who, out of greed for wealth, preach to people regarding astrology and portents without actually knowing them, should be restrained with great effort.
Those who display themselves as being endowed with staffs, antelope skins, and other such emblems,
while secretly harming men, are to be executed by the king's officers.
Those who, by refining items of little value, bring them to a state of high value,
and those who deceive women and children, shall be punished in accordance with the nature of the offense.
Those who manufacture artificial gold, pearls, coral, and so forth,
shall be made by the king to pay the value to the purchaser and a fine double that amount.
When neutral witnesses deceive one party through affection, greed, or other motives,
and testify falsely, they shall be made to pay a fine double the amount in dispute.
Those who, by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, display some form of delusion or perform the rite of the roots (*mūlakarman*), shall be banished by the king.
Those who break a boundary-mark, steal property, or abandon their kin should be impaled on a stake;
likewise, one who steals a traveler’s goods should be bound by the neck to a tree at dawn and suspended there.
Those who carry off human beings should be burned by the king with a fire of straw; the stealer of a cow should have his nose cut off, or, having been bound, he should be submerged in water.
For stealing more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for lesser amounts, the thief shall be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property shall be returned to its owner.
One who steals grain should be made to pay ten times its value as a fine, and double that amount as a penalty.
Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—
one who takes these without having asked permission deserves the amputation of the hand.
One who has been well-conducted and devoted to Vedic study, even if he is a thief, shall suffer long in prison;
he must be made to restore that wealth to its owner, but no penance is to be performed for him.
[1.23 Sāhasa] [1.23.0 Sāhasa] This has been declared as the suppression of punishment for all types of thieves.
Now, let the proper legal procedure for the punishment of violent crimes be heard correctly.
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and both forms of harshness constitute the fourfold category of *sāhasa* (violent crime).
That [fine] is proclaimed to be of three kinds—low, middling, and high—depending on the nature of the object;
among these, the lowest, highest, and middling fines are determined in relation to the value of the property.
The wise declare that these following duties are to be avoided in the Kali age: the killing of an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) or of the foremost of the twice-born in accordance with righteous warfare.
One who destroys or steals the implements of a field, an irrigation embankment, or the roots, flowers, and fruits [of that field] shall be fined one hundred panas, proportionate to the damage.
One who destroys livestock, clothing, food, drink, or household utensils shall be made to pay for them as if he were a thief, and shall likewise be fined two hundred panas.
In cases involving women and men, gold and gems, as well as the property of gods and Brahmins, silk garments, and other articles of superior value, the fine shall be equal to their market price.
Or, the king should determine a double fine in consideration of the status of the person;
or else, the killer should be executed in order to prevent a recurrence of the offense.
Sāhasa (violent crime) is declared to be of five kinds; among these, the death penalty is recorded as the most severe.
Those who commit such acts are not to be punished with fines for wealth, but must be executed with diligence.
Those who are open murderers, as well as those who are assassins by stealth,
having been properly identified and having seized wealth, shall be executed by various means of death.

[1.23.1 Punishment for the Violent] Whether for the sake of gaining allies, wealth, or profit, a king who seeks the welfare of the world must not release violent offenders, who bring fear to all people.
If a king, out of greed or fear, does not punish those who act unjustly,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is deprived of his sovereignty.
But that man who causes others to perish by means of confinement, fire, poison, or a weapon,
motivated by anger or other such causes, is a perpetrator of violence (*sāhasika*).
[1.23.2 Determination of Joint Assault] When many people, filled with rage, strike at one person,
he who inflicts the blow upon the vital organ is declared to be the killer.
But he who strikes a vital organ among them, one shall cause to pay the fine as previously stated;
likewise the instigator, the accomplice, the guide to the way, the shelterer, the provider of weapons, and the provider of food for those engaged in illegal acts.
The instructor of war, the one who demonstrates its destruction, the one who remains indifferent, the one engaged in the task, the one who speaks of faults, and the one who approves.
[1.23.3 Killing an Assassin] One who kills an assassin shall never incur sin;
by slaying one who comes seeking his destruction, he does not commit an offense.

He who does not kill an *ātatāyin*— even one of superior status— who is endowed with good conduct and Vedic study, when that person has reached the point of being liable to death, shall obtain the fruit of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice.
If one kills an assailant who is born of a noble family and devoted to Vedic study, by not killing him he becomes a killer of an embryo;
by killing him, he does not become a killer of an embryo.
Now, let the nature of violence and theft arising from anger and greed be heard;
[this concerns] the determination when the perpetrator is not seen: the smallness of the wound, the fact that it was not fatal, and the careful examination of the vital spot.
Having ascertained both his capability and his motive through various signs, one should win him over.
But where a person is seen killed and the killer is not seen,
he should be identified by the king through the pursuit of prior enmity.
But he among them who strikes a blow shall be made to pay the fine as prescribed;
the one who initiates the act and the one who assists share the guilt, each being liable for half of that.
The neighbors living next door and those living beyond them, as well as his friends,
enemies, and kinsmen, should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
He should be identified by men through association with the wicked or through the discovery of stolen goods;
this has been declared as the method for apprehending murderers and thieves.
But he who, having been apprehended on suspicion, does not undergo that legal proceeding, must be cleared by means of an oath; this rule applies to all types of disputes.
One who is purified by ordeals is pure; one who is not pure deserves execution.
Through such restraint and favor, the king's fame and merit increase.
[1.24 Adultery with Women] [1.24.0] Harshness is said to be of two kinds, and violence is characterized by two types.
Understand that adultery, the root of evil, is of three kinds.
Two types [of love] are produced through the influence of power, while the third arises from passion;
that, moreover, is said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is done by force in secret with a woman who is unwilling, or who is asleep, insane, intoxicated, or talking in her sleep, is known as an act committed through compulsion (*balātkāra*).
They know that union which is brought about through deception— by bringing a woman to one's house under false pretenses or by administering intoxicants or aphrodisiacs— is "contracted under duress."
That which arises from mutual passion for one's eyes, through the dispatching of female messengers,
and by reason of greed for beauty or wealth, should be known as born of mutual affection.
Furthermore, that is said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
Glancing with a sidelong look, smiling, and likewise sending a female messenger;
The first [stage] is traditionally taught as the accumulation of ornaments and garments for touch.
The sending of perfumes and garlands, incense on the road, garments,
and private conversation— these they know as the intermediate form of seduction (*saṅgraha*).
Sharing a bed and a seat, as well as playing, kissing, and embracing—
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is declared to be the middling form of seduction.
The sending of perfumes, garlands, fruits, wine, food, and clothing,
as well as private conversation, they know to be the middling form of seduction (*saṅgraha*).

For each of these three [categories of offenses], the first, middle, and highest forms of discipline should be prescribed; furthermore, the punishment should be increased for one who possesses greater wealth.
But a man who engages in secret conversation with another's wife,
having previously been accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
If one desires the entire wealth of another,
he should cut off that man's penis and testicles and cause him to be paraded around on a donkey.
But he who should desire her by means of deception shall suffer the forfeiture of all his property as punishment;
having been branded with the mark of a female organ, he shall then be banished from the city.
A man who is led by force into an assembly that is inferior to his own shall be fined; however, if he enters an assembly that is superior to his own, he shall be put to death.
If a woman, having come to a man's house, entices him with touching and other such acts and desires him there, she shall be punished; for the man, half the fine is prescribed.
Those whose noses, lips, or ears have been severed should be submerged in water after being whirled around,
or they should be devoured by dogs in a place where many people are assembled.
But she who has been enjoyed against her will should be kept in the house under guard;
with soiled limbs, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on a mere morsel of food.
If she has had intercourse with an equal, he should cause her to perform an expiation consisting of either a *kṛcchra* or a *parāka*.
However, if she has been enjoyed by one of a lower caste, she should be abandoned or else put to death.
[1.25 Means of Conduct for Women and Men] [1.25.0] This rule regarding adultery has been declared, as well as the nature of adultery itself.
Listen as I speak of the means for the conduct of women and men.
A woman should be kept away from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct by her own kinsmen;
she must be protected day and night by her mother-in-law and other elder women.
But she who, while indulging her own desires, was not restrained out of affection,
will inevitably come to grief later, just like a disease that has been neglected.
[1.25.1 Duties of Fathers, Husbands,
and Sons] A father who does not give [his daughter in marriage] at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her season,
and a son who does not provide for his mother— these are subject to punishment according to dharma, even if they are householders.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice; there prosperity, progeny, and purity abound, and every ritual action becomes fruitful.

Women should be employed in the management of income and expenditure, the preparation of food, the maintenance of household utensils, cleanliness, and the performance of fire-rituals; this is declared to be the proper conduct for women.
A wife should be honored by her husband with clothing, ornaments, and food,
especially during festivals, as well as by her father, brothers, fathers-in-law, and other kinsmen.
She who does not transgress against her husband through thought, word, or deed, being fully restrained,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous.
[1.25.2 Faults of Women] A woman should not live in another's house separated from her husband, father, or sons; especially by associating with the wicked, she certainly incurs reproach.
Rising before one's elders, eating and serving food and condiments after them,
and occupying a lower seat and bed— this is declared to be the duty of women.
Drinking, wandering about, sleeping during the day, idleness, and defaming women; these are [the faults].
When her husband is distressed, she is distressed; when he is joyful, she is glad; when he has gone abroad, she is soiled and emaciated;
and when he dies, she follows him in death—such a woman is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).

When her husband is away on a journey, she should not engage in personal adornment, nor attend performances of dance and song, social gatherings, or festivals; nor should she indulge in meat or liquor.
A wife is declared to be half of one's own body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit;
following her husband in life and in death, that virtuous woman exists for his welfare.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, firmly established in celibacy,
and constantly intent on the gift of Dharma, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
[1.25.3 Prohibition of Niyoga] Having prescribed *niyoga*, Manu himself prohibited it;
due to the decline of the age (*yuga-hrāsa*), this cannot be performed by anyone according to the rules.
In the Kṛta and Tretā ages, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali ages, a decline in the power of men has been ordained.
[1.26 Partition of the Inheritance] [1.26.0] That property which is given (or is being given) by the father to his sons is called *dāya*.
That [is] the inheritance... [rest of the verse omitted].
One woman should be made to perform work in each house according to her share; many women may be assigned [work] with equal shares. This same rule applies even to male slaves.
Having drawn water from a well or a tank, it is taken according to the [established] order;
likewise, a field is divided by means of a boundary embankment according to the proportion of shares.
That [property] should be divided according to reason; otherwise, it would be useless.
[1.26.1 Distinct Characteristics] For those living together under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods,
and the twice-born should be performed as one; even if they eat separately, that same ritual should take place in every house.
Witnessing, acting as a guarantor, giving, and receiving—
these brothers who have divided their property may perform among themselves, but not those who have not divided.
Those among whom these transactions proceed in the world regarding their own inheritance—
them one should recognize as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
The obstruction of family continuity, the discovery of violence,
and separate wealth from the division of immovable property belonging to each individual's own enjoyment.
[1.26.2 The Time of Partition] Partition among brothers has been demonstrated to take place upon the death of both parents,
when the mother’s menses have ceased and her sisters have been given away in marriage.
[1.26.3 Order of Partition] When ancestral houses or fields have come down by succession, the father and sons share them equally; however,
they are not entitled to a partition of paternal property against the father's will.
Sons born of wives of equal caste for twice-born men shall all divide the inheritance equally after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest.
Indeed, by virtue of age, learning, and austerity, one receives two shares of the wealth;
for in such a way that the wealth obtained through partition may serve the purpose of sacrifice,
so should the learned arrange for the preeminence of the share.
Their sons, whether equal or unequal [in number], are declared to be entitled to their father's share.
Regarding property acquired by the grandfather, whether it be immovable or movable,
an equal share is declared for both the father and the son.
Those portions which have been assigned by the father as equal, less, or more, must be maintained exactly in that manner; otherwise, they should be disciplined.
But in the case of a division during the father's lifetime, the father shall take two shares for himself.
The division of inheritance for heirs is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
one according to the order of seniority by age, and the other an equal distribution of shares.
But when property is acquired by those who have assembled together, all of them are entitled to equal shares;
it is recorded that their sons, whether unequal or equal [in number], shall take the paternal shares.
All sons who inherit their father's estate are entitled to equal shares;
however, among them, one who is devoted to learning and virtuous conduct deserves to receive more.
He whose fame is celebrated here for the sake of sacred learning, practical knowledge, and heroism, and for acts of imparting wisdom, by him his ancestors are truly made fathers of sons.
The eldest, by virtue of birth, learning, and qualities, shall receive two shares of the inheritance;
the others, however, shall share equal portions, but he who is equal to his father [in merit] shall likewise receive two shares.
In the absence of that [father], however, the mother shall receive a share equal to her son's;
their other mothers shall receive equal shares, and the unmarried daughter shall receive a fourth part of a share.
For unmarried daughters, however, one-fourth share is prescribed;
for sons, there are three shares. But equality is ordained when the property is small.
If there are many sons born of one [mother] who are equal in number according to their caste,
they shall divide their own wealth according to the mother's share, in accordance with the law.
When there are [paternal] uncles of the same caste but of different numbers, the share of the male portion is recommended for them;
however, all those paternal grandmothers are declared to be equal to mothers.

But those among them who have not been consecrated with sacraments should be consecrated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth alone, just as the unmarried daughters are, according to the rule.
But those younger brothers who may be unconsecrated,
they should indeed be consecrated by the elder brothers from the paternal wealth held in common.
And he should give him sufficient wealth or a share of the field, whichever he desires.
That which is received by a married woman or even by an unmarried girl from her husband, from her father's house,
from her brother, or from her parents, is known as *saudāyika* (gift of affection).
Upon receiving dowry property, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by their [relatives] as a means of subsistence out of compassion.
In the sale or even the gift of immovable property, she may act as she pleases;

however, the woman's property shall belong to her offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share of it. If she is unmarried, she receives that share; but if she is married, she receives only honor.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife,
a father’s sister, a mother-in-law, and the wife of an elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to one’s own mother.
If these [women] have neither a biological son nor a daughter’s son,
their wealth shall go to their sister’s sons, or those [nephews] who may have received their maternal aunts’ property.
[1.26.4 Characteristics of a Son] Even one born of a wife of the same caste is unworthy of the paternal wealth if he lacks good qualities; rather,
that [wealth] is ordained for those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for him.
A son protects his father from those who owe him the highest debts and those who owe him the lowest debts; therefore, there is no purpose served by one who acts in the opposite manner.
"What is the use of that cow which neither yields milk nor bears calves?
What is the purpose of a son who is born but is neither learned nor righteous?"
A son who is devoid of learning, heroism, and wealth, lacking in austerity and wisdom, and bereft of proper conduct, is declared to be equal to urine and excrement.
[1.26.5 Partition of Sons] Even immovable property and bipeds, though acquired by oneself,
cannot be given away nor sold without having assembled all the sons.

Those humans who are born, those yet to be born, those dwelling in the womb, and those residing in the world of the ancestors—all of them desire that mode of livelihood; therefore, it must not be interrupted.
Household utensils, vehicles, and so forth; food, ornaments, and laborers—when these are visible, they are divided [equally], but in the case of hidden property, a portion for hair is ordained.
Those born of the Kṣatriya [caste] receive three, two, or one shares; those born of the Vaiśya [caste] receive two or one share.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras born from a Brāhmaṇa [father] in successive order shall possess four, three, two, and one shares respectively.
One born of a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of land; the twice-born man shall receive everything—thus is the law established.
Among them, those sons who are of the same caste as their father shall receive a third share of the inheritance;
those of lower caste shall live with him, provided with food and clothing.
For all these sons of one who has no son of the body are declared to be heirs; however, when a son of the body is subsequently born, their status as the eldest ceases.

That which has been given by the grandfather, by the father, and that which may have been given by the mother—none of that should be taken away from him; likewise, the wealth acquired through valor and the husband's property [should not be seized].
Those who stated that clothing and such items are indivisible have not considered that wealth belonging to the affluent may consist of clothes and ornaments.
A debt that has been recorded in writing after being contracted... [and so forth].
Indeed, when a debt is recorded on a document, it should be understood according to the manner described above;
it must be divided by means of that statement, for otherwise it would be meaningless.
If an object situated in the middle cannot support life and cannot be given to a single person, it must be divided by means of a skillful method; otherwise, it would be useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, having received money for which a document was written,
and having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, [the property] is divided.
The profit from property held for the sake of security and protection shall be divided equally; and the heirs must always manage its use according to their respective shares.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take the land that has become a religious endowment (*brahmadāya*);
likewise, all twice-born men shall take the house and the field inherited through succession.
[1.26.6 The Arrangement for Those Divided with the Father] Those who were divided from their father— whether stepbrothers or uterine brothers—
and those who are junior to them, they are the ones entitled to receive the father's share.
The elder brother born before partition has no authority over his paternal share; the brother born after partition has no authority over the share of his brothers.

Whatever has been acquired by a father himself after he has divided his property with his sons, all that belongs to the son born after the partition; it is declared that the earlier-born sons have no right to it.
Just as with wealth, so it is with debt, in matters of giving, not giving, and buying;
they have no mutual authority over one another, except regarding impurity and the water-libation rites.
Regarding property inherited from the grandfather that was acquired by the father through his own power—
attained by means of learning, valor, or other such means— it is traditionally held that the father has ownership over it.
One may, according to one's own will, make a gift [of property] and likewise enjoy it from that wealth;
even in the absence of such [a gift], the sons are declared to have equal shares.
Having honored with perfumes and garlands the father’s clothes, ornaments, bed, vehicle, and so forth, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha feast.
If ornaments have been worn by women while their husband is still living, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their caste.

By the father’s favor, garments and ornaments may be enjoyed [by the sons]. Where an heir comes forward, whether the partition has been made or not, if he provides for what is common, he shall indeed receive a share.
If a man possesses a debt, a document, a house, or a field that belonged to his grandfather,
he shall receive his share even if he has been absent for a long time, provided he returns.
If one who shared in the ancestral property abandons it and takes refuge in another land,
a share must undoubtedly be given to him when he returns from that place.
If the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [ancestor] is unknown by birth, one shall receive the share according to the order of succession.
If all the hereditary tenants know a person, through a continuous succession, to be their master,
then the land must be given to one who has come from that lineage by the kinsmen of the original owner.
For kinsmen who live together, whether they have previously divided their inheritance or not, a further division of the estate shall take place up to the fourth generation; such is the settled rule.
[1.26.7 Varieties of Sons] Sons have been categorized in many ways by the ancient seers;
they cannot be established now by those who lack such power and are modern.
The legitimate son of the body alone is proclaimed the sole owner of the paternal estate;
the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him, while all others are declared to be merely entitled to maintenance.
But the other sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, are entitled to five, six, or seven shares.
The *datta* (given), the *apaviddha* (cast off), the *krīta* (bought), the *kṛta* (made), and likewise the *śaudra* (slave-born)—
these are all considered middle-class sons who are pure by birth and entitled to inherit property.

The son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), the secretly born son (gūḍhaja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-suta) are all censured by the virtuous.
The son of a Śūdra woman, one who has given himself, and those who are known as "purchased"—all these are declared to be Maitras; they are undoubtedly Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, indeed goes to another's family— by that misconduct he becomes a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, without a doubt.
Having sacrificed to Agni and Prajāpati, Gautama declared that [the practice] is performed;
others, however, say that for one who has no son, a daughter may be considered as a son.
Thirteen types of sons were previously declared by Manu;
among them, the son of the body (aurasa) and the appointed daughter (putrikā) are the causes for the continuation of the lineage.
Just as oil is remembered by the virtuous as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons considered substitutes for the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*).
If there are many uterine brothers born of the same father,
then when a son is born to even one of them, they are all considered to have sons.
This same rule is prescribed for many wives who have one husband;
if even one among them has a son, he is the giver of the rice-balls for all of them.
Since a son protects his father from the hell named Put,
he should strive for the birth of such a son even by merely looking upon his face.
Both the grandson and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) cause one to attain heaven;
they are declared to be equal in regard to both the inheritance of property and the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa).
And if the son born of a Śūdra woman from a marriage out of desire remains devoted to service, his brothers should,
upon the death of the father, give him a share merely for the sake of honor.
For the sake of food, one prastha of rice with fuel should be given in the afternoon;
and a garment purchased for three paṇas should be given once every three months.
[1.26.8 The Widow's Share] Only this much has been prescribed as the property of a widow for virtuous women.
Having set aside the value of the clothing, the food, and likewise that of the washerman, one should assign the remainder to those entitled to the inheritance.
Now, for one who has no son, the wife born of a family of equal status, or the daughters, are [the heirs];
in their absence, it is declared that the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons [succeed].
A man without a son should, with great effort, adopt a son of whatever kind may be available,
for the sake of performing the rites of funeral cakes and water-libations, and for the proclamation of his religious merit.
The ancestors, fearing the descent into hell, long for sons, thinking: "Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us."
Just as a man drowning while crossing water with a leaky boat sinks down,
even so a father sinks into blind darkness because of a bad son.
"He will perform the ritual release of a bull, as well as sacrifices and works of public utility;
he will protect the kingdom in his regency and offer ancestral oblations every day."
[1.26.9 Wife as a Share] According to the Vedas, the treatises on tradition (smṛti), and the conduct of the world,
the wise have declared that the wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit.
He whose wife has not passed away lives with half of his own body;
while that half-body still lives, how could another take possession of its wealth?
But when there are kinsmen (sakulyas)— namely, paternal uncles and blood relations—
the wife of a deceased man who leaves no son shall take that inheritance.
When the husband has died, the wife devoted to her husband shall take the wealth of that deceased Agnihotra-sacrificer;
this is the eternal law.

A woman who dies while her husband is still alive shall take [his] fire; one who has ascended after him shall take [his] sin. In the absence of a son, the wife shall be the heir; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the heir; and after that, the daughter's son shall take the wealth.
Having taken moving property, immovable property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the Śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other occasions to be performed.

One should honor with offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) and to the gods (*pūrta*) the paternal uncle, the teacher, the daughter's son, the sister’s husband, the maternal uncle, the aged, guests, and women.
Whatever rules regarding mortgages and the like are prescribed concerning divided property,
a wife whose husband has passed away may receive that, with the exception of immovable property.
Even if she has remained faithful to her conduct, a woman does not have a right to immovable property even when a share [of other assets] has been granted to her.
If a widow, being in the prime of youth, becomes harsh,
then only a maintenance sufficient for the remainder of her life should be given.
When her husband has died, a woman who protects the family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, she possesses no ownership over it regarding giving, mortgaging, or selling.
A woman who has been purchased by purchase, or one taken for the purpose of sexual enjoyment by a man seeking offspring, or even one belonging to another— she alone is designated as a wife.
Or he may, at his own will, give either a funeral cake or a share of the field.
Whatever property for her maintenance was given by the father-in-law to women from immovable assets,
that cannot be taken away by others after the father-in-law has died.
Those sapinda relatives who act as obstacles to her and would seize her property,
the king shall have them executed with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
[1.26.10 Division of Reunited Property] Furthermore, two who have reunited out of affection shall share with one another;
likewise, those brothers who, having been divided, live together again in one place out of mutual affection.
If there is a subsequent partition [of the estate], their seniority no longer exists.
If, however, he should die or somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
Whether she has been given away or not, if a uterine brother dies, she alone shall take his share;
for this is clearly the reason for both cases.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda relative.
If a man has died without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all his *sapiṇḍa* relatives shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.

But among those who have reunited, whoever acquires wealth through learning, valor, or other such means, two shares of that wealth must be given to him; the remaining co-heirs shall receive equal shares.
Furthermore, one who, having been divided from his father or brother, resides together with them again—
whether with his paternal uncle or another— out of affection, is called "reunited" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
The uterine brothers, having assembled together, shall divide it equally,
as well as those brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If among them the eldest or the youngest is deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them dies, his share is not lost.
But a uterine brother shall give and take the share of a uterine brother, whether he be born or deceased.
But a half-brother who is a co-resident shall not take the wealth from one born of a different mother;
and even if he is not a co-resident, a full brother born of the same mother shall receive it, not one born of a different mother.
But for those whose fathers have died, the allotment of shares is calculated from the side of the fathers.
Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are childless and devoid of wives or brothers—
the king shall take their wealth, for he is the sovereign lord of all.
[1.26.11 The distinction among sons according to their caste] A son born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa, being the eldest by birth and endowed with good qualities,
shall receive an equal share with the Kṣatriya son; and likewise a son born of a Vaiśya woman.
Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if their father should give it, once he is dead, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take it back.
A son born of a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of land;
he shall receive everything from his own paternal kin—thus the law is settled.
If there is an only son who is a Niṣāda, he shall take the third share of the Brāhmaṇa’s estate;
then two kinsmen (sakulyas) or sapinda relatives, or the giver of the funeral oblation (svadhādātṛ), shall take the remainder.
In the absence of a kinsman, the giver of the *svadhā*— whether it be the teacher or even the pupil—
should likewise provide for those castes in all calamities.
A virtuous son born of a Śūdra mother who serves a childless man shall receive enough for his livelihood; the remainder of the estate, the sapinda relatives shall obtain.
[1.26.12 The Daughter’s Right to Inherit]: The wife is the heir to the husband's wealth; in her absence, the daughter is declared to be so.
"A daughter arises from every limb of men, just like a son;
therefore, how could any other man take the father's wealth?"
In the absence of those, however, if there is an unmarried daughter, then, in the absence of sons and grandsons, the daughters' sons shall obtain the wealth.
For as one's own self, so is a son; and by a son, a daughter is equal.
Since they reside within that very self, how could another take away the wealth?
"In this world, according to the law, there is no distinction between a grandson and a daughter's son;
it was by this very rule that he then made his daughter a *putrikā*."
A male is born when the semen is in excess; a female is born when the female seed is in excess.
A wife who is suitable, wedded by a suitable man, virtuous, and devoted to service—
whether she has borne sons or not, she shall indeed inherit her father's wealth.
Just as she has ownership over her father’s wealth even while her kinsmen are alive,
so too does her son have a right to his mother’s and maternal grandfather’s desired wealth.
In the absence of those, the brothers, the sons of brothers,
the uterine kinsmen (sanābhayaḥ), the family members (sakulyāḥ), the relatives (bāndhavāḥ), the pupils, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyāḥ) are entitled to the wealth.
[1.26.13 Division of the Estate of One Without Sons] The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies childless; indeed,
she shall take the estate of a deceased son who is himself bereft of both wife and children.
The mother should be known as the inheritor of the estate, or the brother with her permission.
In the absence of a son, however, the wife [shall inherit]; in the absence of the wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the heir; and after that, the daughter's son shall take the wealth.
From the wealth that has been acquired, one should diligently set aside half for the sake of that [ancestors],
specifically for the monthly, six-monthly, or annual Śrāddha ceremonies.
Where there are many kinsmen, such as those belonging to the same lineage (*sakulya*) or other relatives (*bāndhava*),
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who leaves no offspring.
A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the rite of the rice-balls together, should thereafter perform the rite for prosperity.

If one who has made a partition by his own free will should again act inconsistently with it, he shall be compelled by the king to remain within his own share and punished according to the circumstances.
In cases of denial of a common debt or deposit,
or when one has employed fraudulent means or caused loss to a partner, the judge shall not compel payment by force.
Those men who are deceitful, possessors of wealth, cruel,
and greedy should be won over through affection, or by the loss of their own interests, or through guile.
Violence, ownership of immovable property, and the prior partition of inheritance among heirs are to be determined by inference when there are no witnesses present.
These transactions proceed among them in the world regarding their own inherited property;
one may recognize those who have been divided even without a written document.
Those who have not yet divided their inheritance must perform the Vaiśvadeva and other such rites together.

The obstruction of force and its persistence, the seizure of property, and the intent for violence; the enjoyment of one's own immovable property, and the separate wealth of a partitioned inheritance.
Those who maintain separate income, expenditure, and assets, engage in lending money to one another,
and conduct trade on their own account, have undoubtedly divided their property.
When brothers who have divided their inheritance are at variance with one another, they should mutually cause a formal declaration and a written record to be made,
or else appoint blameless witnesses for the purpose of settling their dispute.
One should not dispossess a person of that very share, of whatever kind it may be, which has been enjoyed by them.
[1.27 Gambling] [1.27.0] Gambling has been forbidden by Manu, as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth.
But that [system] was set in motion by others, however, accompanied by the king's share.
The affairs presided over by the master of the gaming house are for the purpose of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applying to animal-betting and gambling with dice.

[1.27.1 The Duties of the Master of the Gaming Hall] The master of the gaming hall shall, in that case, pay [the stakes] to the winner and to the king. From the gambling proceeds, the royal tax shall be ten percent from the master of the gaming hall.
Or it may be according to the agreed time... [and so forth].
[1.27.2 Victory and Defeat of the Master] If anyone should suffer exhaustion in a duel,
the master must pay the stake that was agreed upon therein.

One who has won in secret, one who is ignorant of the game, or one who uses false dice or deceit, shall be released; even one who is knowledgeable [of the rules] shall not be made to pay the entire stake if it was won through fraud.

[1.27.3 Punishment for Fraudulent Gambling] Those wicked gamblers who play with false dice, those who steal the king’s share, and those who practice deception in counting— the law codes declare that such gamblers are to be punished.
Public exposure must be carried out for those who practice fraudulent gambling;
however, those who commit murder shall receive various forms of capital punishment.
[1.27.4 Determining Victory and Defeat when Doubtful] That same witness, surrounded by three other members of the court, shall determine the doubt between the two parties; however,
the gamblers themselves are the judges of the doubtful matter.
But when they become hostile, then the king should investigate the matter.
In this manner, the king should daily examine the legal disputes brought by litigants,
as well as other matters related to the state, together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
[1.28 Samāhvaya (Combat)] [1.28.0] Birds, rams, bulls, and so forth, when seized by one another, [engage in combat].
Those who strike at one another after having made a wager call that a *samāhvaya* (a formal challenge).
If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel,
his master must pay the wager that was stipulated for that occasion.
[1.29 Miscellaneous] [1.29.0] This legal procedure (vyavahāra) performed by the litigants has thus been declared in brief.
I shall now declare the miscellaneous legal proceedings (prakīrṇaka) that depend upon the king.
Having ascertained the nature and extent of the offender's fault, the king should duly impose one of the fourfold punishments: verbal reprimand, fine, censure, or corporal punishment.
One who deserves the death penalty shall pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
for one deserving mutilation of a limb, half of that; and for one deserving exile, twenty-five.
The hands, feet, sexual organ, eyes, tongue, ears, and nose;
the tongue, half-foot, sandaṃśa, forehead, lips, anus, and hips.
These fourteen places for punishment have been specified;
for a Brāhmaṇa, branding on the forehead is ordained, and no other punishment is prescribed.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of intimidation.
But when one is unable to restrain these [enemies] even by means of piercing [them with weapons],
then one should employ all four of these [strategic means] against them.
One should first apply the punishment of verbal censure, immediately after that the punishment of reprimand,
thirdly the punishment of a fine, and after that the punishment of corporal death.
And he should place all prisons along the royal highway,
where those who have committed evil deeds may be seen suffering and disfigured.
He who burns the corpse of one who has no relatives shall take a tenth part of the wealth, or a fifth, or even the whole of it.
Tenth of the produce belongs to one who has many dependents to protect, and fifth to one who has few;
Śaunaka says that for one whose father is childless and whose wife is barren, the entire share belongs to him.
A sixth part [of the value] and a ferry-toll must likewise be paid when [the goods] have been transported;
so too must those who cause dissension in battle, thieves, spies, and those who destroy crops.

The failure to perform expiations, the transgression of commands and prohibitions, the neglect of the duties of the castes and stages of life, and the neglect of the prevention of the intermixture of castes.
A treasure-trove, the wealth of a family-less person, the arrival of riches for a pauper,
unrecorded legal matters, and the ritualistic arguments of disputants.
The provocation of the constituent elements, mutual conspiracy, and whatever among the subjects is proclaimed that is not ordained by the scriptures; [these are the signs of decline].
If witnesses, members of the court, or the parties themselves are found to be corrupt, there shall be a retrial;
however, for those who have been defeated by their own testimony, no rule for a second trial has been prescribed.
End of BP1] Because it is based upon the meaning of the Vedas, the authority of Manu’s work is considered preeminent;
any Smṛti that contradicts the meaning of Manu is not praised.
