www.sub.uni-goettingen.de/ebene_1/fiindolo/gretil/gretdias.pdf [The Śrī Bṛhaspati Smṛti] [Bṛh 1, Vyavahārakāṇḍa]
In former times, men were devoted to righteousness and practiced non-violence.
The worldly transaction was set in motion by those overcome by greed and hatred.
If the master does not provide wages to servants performing their work,
and the servants do not perform it, a dispute arises thereon.
Someone may commit violence, or someone may fail to give what is due;
these two are indeed the grounds for dispute, and between them, the latter has more extensive consequences.
When a substance is sold and taken for the purpose of repaying a debt, that price paid by the creditor is known as *vyavahāra* (legal transaction). // Brh_1.1.4 //
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1: Qualities of a King] Therefore, I shall describe the duties and qualities of a king in their proper order:
the creditor, the debtor, the one in doubt, the surety, the document, and the witnesses.
Listen to the origin of him who reflects correctly upon Soma,
Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Apati, and Yama.
Having extracted the mere essence of fire, the form of the King was indeed fashioned;
all beings, both moving and stationary, are composed of that.
Out of fear, people are able to enjoy their wealth and do not deviate from their own duties;
for there can be no agriculture, trade, lending at interest, or protection of property in a kingless state.
Therefore, he was created in the past as the leader of the social classes and stages of life; legal procedure consists of two parts, arising from property and injury.
The root of wealth consists of fourteen [factors], while that of violence is fourfold:
two types of harsh speech, killing, and likewise the abduction of another's wife.
One should avoid laziness, hoarding wealth, and rising up [only] after a collective effort;
as well as failing to support dependents, lack of service, false claims regarding land, and selling what one does not own.
Regret regarding purchase and sale, breach of contract,
the union of man and woman, theft, partition of inheritance, and gambling with dice.
These fourteen words, which originate from their respective meanings,
are further divided in this way into many tens through the differentiation of actions.
Harsh speech, violence, and likewise the abduction of another’s wife— Bṛhaspati has thus declared these four to be the sources from which injury arises.
Distinguished individually as inferior, middling, and superior,
the specific distinction of these four has been set forth in their proper sequence.
These eighteen points proclaimed in the treatises on Dharma are indeed the root of all disputes; those who know them are the true judges.
The first quarter is known as the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), and likewise the second is the reply (uttara);
the third is to be stated as the section on action (kriyāpāda), and the fourth is the final determination (nirṇaya).
The determination of a doubtful matter is declared to be of four kinds: by means of dharma, by legal procedure, by conduct, and by the king’s command. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.18)
That legal proceeding in which a decision is made by relying solely upon the treatises (śāstra) should be known as *vyavahāra*; through it, Dharma also increases.
A definitive conclusion is reached there through the customs of the region, by inference, and by what is accepted by the people; however, in such a case, the formal legal procedure is set aside.
If a king should issue a legal decision setting aside established custom,
that royal decree prevails, for it overrides the customary practice.

In accordance with the Dharmaśāstras, the king— free from anger and greed, truthful, and having his senses subdued— should, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, examine legal cases for the sake of protecting his subjects. (Br̥haspati Smṛti 1.1.22)
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4, Section on Dharma] That which belongs to the seeker of victory and that which belongs to the enemy, consisting of seven constituent elements each—
this is what they call the fourteen-fold circle (maṇḍala).
The four guardians of the earth, together with their respective eightfold groups of ministers and others, are thus composed of imperishable syllables in this world.
Having risen in the morning and performed purification according to the rules,
the king [should honor] his gurus, astrologers, physicians, gods, Brahmins, and domestic priests.
Having honored these people as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having greeted his teachers and elders, he should enter the assembly hall with a cheerful countenance.
The king, having entered the foremost assembly hall, should examine the affairs of state while surrounded by three virtuous men, either seated or standing.

[The characteristics of a fortress: For the protection of his person, wife, wealth, and subjects already accumulated, the king should cause a fortress to be built, provided with two types of enclosures.
It was provided for kings with fuels and liquids, with cane, grass, food, and vehicles,
as well as with various machines and weapons, and with affectionate, heroic men.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas and Kṣatriyas who maintain the sacred fire-offerings,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
Incomparable taxes should be granted to them, and houses and lands should be bestowed;
having recorded this in their own edicts, they should be made exempt from the king's authority.

They should perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, as well as those for pacification (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika), and likewise the ancient rituals (paurāṇa-karma) and the penance for doubtful offenses (saṃdigdha-vinaya).
Wherever the ground is even or uneven, or of whatever nature it may be,
the halls, towers, moats, and other such structures must be constructed accordingly.
Then the subjects should construct houses there on all sides;
likewise, the twice-born, Vaiśyas, merchants, artisans, craftsmen, and guards [should do so].
One should likewise provide for the placement of gates, exits, roundabouts, wells, crossroads, assembly halls, marketplaces, and cow-pens.
How can he who was proclaimed "virtuous" and made famous in the assembly of people be described as "devoid of virtue" with that very same mouth?
Therefore, one should not disturb the authority or the livelihood of one who is faultless;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of infinite regress, and likewise, the support [of the community] would perish.
But having properly settled his territory and constructed fortifications according to the treatises,
he should constantly apply his supreme effort to the removal of thorns (the suppression of criminals).
That protection of the subjects is declared by those who know the law to be threefold:
[protection] from the enemy's army, from the fear of thieves, and from the powerful who act unjustly.
The king should pacify the fear caused by the enemy's army through strategic means,
and he should daily provide the administration of justice for those who have been oppressed by the powerful.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one offers as oblation, and whatever one recites— of that,
the king receives a sixth part by virtue of protecting [the people] properly.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices day after day with hundreds and thousands of sacrificial fees.
A cultivator shall give one-sixtieth as the king’s share from fallow land,
and one-eighth from land ploughed during the rainy season and spring, respectively.
They should offer oblations to the spirits (*bhūta*) every six months and annually according to the customs of their region;
this is declared to be the ancient duty of farmers.
[The manner of constructing the assembly hall: Within the fortification, one should build separate houses— whether made of water, mountain, wood, earth, or desert— surrounded by water and trees.
To the east of that [fire], he should construct an auspicious assembly hall facing the east,
provided with garlands, incense, and seats, and furnished with seeds and gems.
It should be provided with images, paintings, and deities, as well as fire and water;
it must be auspicious and marked by the characteristics prescribed in the treatises on architecture (vāstuśāstra).
Having occupied the auspicious seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should pay homage to the world-protectors and begin the examination of legal cases.
The Brahmin is the root of the tree of Dharma; the king is its trunk and branches;
the ministers are its leaves and flowers; and protection through justice is its fruit.
Fame, wealth, the essence of fruits, enjoyment, acquisition, and honor;
invincibility, standing in the ranks of the world, and an eternal station in heaven.
Having become impartial toward these juices of justice, the king, having abandoned greed and other such passions, should carry out the legal determination by means of debate.
The king himself shall preside over disputes concerning livelihoods according to the path seen in the scriptures; he is to be served by the learned.
Therefore, the king should protect [his subjects] properly and with diligent effort according to justice;
thereby he shall obtain wealth, sovereignty, and vast fame.
In brief, the gods know truth, while human beings know falsehood.
He whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
The sacrifice arises from the conjunction of the animal, the clarified butter, the officiating priests, and so forth;
just as it is connected with these, so too is its conventional usage described.
However, one who reaches a decision on matters by relying upon the opinions of the judge and the members of the court through the application of logical reasoning does not incur punishment.
The assembly is declared to be of four kinds: the established, the unestablished, the sealed, and likewise the disciplined; and the members of the assembly are of the same types.
Established in the city and village, she is called "the Moving" (calā) and "the Unestablished" (apratiṣṭhitā);
she is sealed, conjoined with the overseer, joined with the king, and is the ruler.
A person of refined intellect should observe the principles of logic; that assembly is equal to a sacrificial rite.
The members of the assembly (sabhyas) should be knowers of the worlds, the Vedas, their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma—whether there be seven, five, or even three.
That assembly hall, where the foremost of Brahmins were seated, was like a sacrificial ground.
The king should always ensure that the plaintiff and the defendant are protected by guarantors;
this is the tenfold administration of justice (karaṇa) upon which the monarch should preside.
Having set aside one-eighth part of the day, one should go to bed;
that time is declared in the scriptures to be the supreme period for legal transactions.
The king should appoint as members of the assembly those who are engaged in performing virtuous deeds, devoted to truth and righteousness, free from anger and greed, and learned in the scriptures.
There shall be seven, five, or three members of the assembly.
Those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
and those who are insane, angry, greedy, or afflicted by distress— these should not be questioned in reaching a definitive conclusion.
The king, or else a Brahmin acting as the presiding judge, shall examine the cases,
having placed at the forefront the constituent elements of justice and remaining steadfast in the opinion of the legal treatises and the court members.
Because he delights the subjects through his fourfold army and shines with his own physical form, he is therefore called a "rājā" (king).
However, worldly affairs, though manifold, have been declared by the wise to be of one kind;
the king and the learned Brahmin are the arbiters of their decision.
The Śruti declares that he who asks the question concerning matters based on legal procedure is called *prāṭ*;
and he who would deliberate upon that matter therein is traditionally known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
In a legal dispute, he asks the question and likewise the counter-question;
because he speaks first with words of kindness, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka* (the judge).
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven as a witness through his adherence to dharma.

He should appoint as a minister a twice-born Brahmin who understands the meaning of all treatises, is free from greed, speaks with justice, is wise, and has been passed down through hereditary succession.
He who, setting aside the twice-born, should attend to affairs together with the Śūdras,
his kingdom flows away and his army and treasury perish.
For those who wander in the forest, their practice should take place in the forest;
likewise, for soldiers it should be in the army, and for merchants in caravans.
For plowmen, artisans, wrestlers, moneylenders,
guilds, ascetics, and thieves, legal decisions shall be made according to their own specific laws.
Families, guilds, assemblies, and the authorized king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
One should have the affairs of ascetics conducted by those learned in the three Vedas,
and likewise by those who know the application of illusion (māyā-yoga), but not personally, for fear of provoking anger.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
Whether it be a brother, a son worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even one's maternal uncle, there is no one who,
having deviated from his own duty, is not subject to punishment by the king.
Where there is no learned Brahmin, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should carefully avoid a Śūdra.
But one who is devoid of righteous conduct and destitute of the marks of a Brahmin,
yet says "I am a Brahmin," him they call a "Brahmin-in-name-only" (brāhmaṇabruva).
The king should appoint as astrologer and scribe those who know the true nature of words and their designations, who are skilled in calculation, pure, and proficient in various scripts.
In matters where there is no [other] means of protection, and regarding the testimony of witnesses, claimants, and defendants,
that man who speaks the truth must be appointed as dependent upon the members of the court.
That assembly hall, presided over by a king who, having fixed his mind upon it, examines legal cases according to this tenfold procedure, is equal to a sacrificial rite.
Among these, the king is remembered as the head; the presiding judge is the mouth;
the members of the court are the arms; the legal code (Smṛti) is the hands; and the astrologer and the scribe are the two shanks.
The eyes are like gold, fire, and water; the heart and the feet are likewise the self-manifest person (svapuruṣa).
Indeed, the king should place gold, fire, water, and the treatises on Dharma— things that are meritorious and beneficial— in the midst of them.
One should visualize the Sun, the Moon, the gods, and so forth, as well as the guardians of the directions there;
indeed, gold, fire, water, and one's own person are the ten constituent elements of the practice.
Furthermore, the specific function of each of these ten has been declared individually:
the king is the presiding authority over speech, the ruler, the instructor, the member of the assembly, and the examiner of legal cases.
Smṛti declares the determination of victory, as well as the granting of rewards and punishments;
for the purpose of oaths, gold, fire, and water are used when living beings are thirsty.
The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal procedure;
his own attendants shall summon the parties, the litigants, the members of the court, and the witnesses.
The punishment of speech and the punishment of reproach both depend upon the Brahmins;
however, the punishment of fines and corporal punishment are both said to reside with the king.
Those families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth, who have been properly recognized by the king,
shall carry out the legal affairs of men, excluding cases involving violence or injustice.
The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies are declared to be the makers of final decisions;
a matter that has not been deliberated upon by the families must be decided by the guilds.
That which is unknown to the guilds and the corporations is known by the officials;
the members of the court are superior to the families and other such groups, and the presiding officer is declared to be superior even to them.
The king is superior to all because he diligently adjudicates disputes among the highest, lowest, and middle classes according to the determined Dharma.
The cognitions of the Lord, moving higher and higher above all other cognitions,
[perceive those] possessed by the darkness of ignorance and covered by the film of doubt.
He who renders the scriptures free from defects by means of the probe of the collyrium of learning attains fame in this world, honor from kings, and a destination in heaven.

He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, should carry out the determination of legal matters according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded contrary to dharma;
by overlooking it, those kings go headlong to hell.
But having recognized that the king's mind has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is unpleasant; a member of the assembly does not thereby become a sinner.
First, a member of the assembly should speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the assembly becomes sinless.
If the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding matters that have not yet been decided,
he too shall be punished, and the members of the court especially so.
Whether through negligence, ignorance, delusion, or even greed,
wherever a member of the assembly speaks falsely, he is considered by tradition to be a non-member and should be punished.
Where there is no document, no witness, and no possession—
where no means of proof exist— the king alone is the sole authority in that case.
Those doctrines which are of a doubtful nature and cannot be definitively determined—
of these, the king shall be the authority, since he is the lord of all.
Every day, surrounded by his courtiers, he should personally preside over legal cases.
Those members of the assembly who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes,
and those who deceive the person of confidence— all of them must be banished.
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the scriptures is qualified to speak; whatever he declares in the assembly is the Dharma—of this there is no doubt.
The king should sit facing the east, the members of the court facing the north;
the calculator should face the west, while the scribe faces the south.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must the subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Without contradicting the Dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstras, the king, examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, should guide them.
But when the members of the court here deviate from the science of logic (nyāyaśāstra) and reach a decision, then dharma, being violated, destroys everyone; of this there is no doubt.
The treatises of Manu and others are to be upheld, but never the treatises on worldly affairs (artha-śāstra).
When there is a conflict between the two, one must act according to the words proclaimed in the treatises on Dharma.
A definitive conclusion should not be reached by relying on the scriptures alone;
for if an investigation is devoid of reasoning, the loss of dharma arises.
Having occupied that [throne] in the forenoon, he should look upon [his affairs] with his aged ministers and dependents,
and likewise listen to the ancient treatises on dharma and artha.
A thief may become a non-thief, and a virtuous man an unvirtuous one, through worldly convention;
without investigation based on reason, Māṇḍavya was treated as a thief.
The unreal appears like the real, and the real appears like the unreal;
they are seen as producers of delusion. Therefore, one should investigate by means of reasoning.
In sacrifice Viṣṇu is fully worshipped; in worldly affairs the lord of the earth is worshipped.
Here, the victor is the sacrificer, while the defeated one is declared to be the sacrificial victim.
The prima facie argument and the rejoinder are known as the opening [elements], while the proposition is considered the oblation;
the three Vedas and the scriptures are the members of the assembly, and self-restraint is the sacrificial fee for the officiating priests.
In the same way, the calculator and the scribe should be understood as the two witnesses;
this judicial procedure has been declared to be equal to a sacrificial rite.
When one, unassailable by others because he follows a path consistent with mindfulness and proper conduct,
brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a subject for legal dispute.
A plaint made by one who is an outcaste or the like, one who has not returned to his natural state,
or one made by someone who is not independent, is not established.

A legal transaction initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, or driven by passion, as well as one entered into by a child, an elderly person, or one who is unrelated, is not valid.
Between teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, or master and servant—
among these who are joined together in such relations, a legal dispute is not valid.
Once the plaintiff's case has been thus examined by the members of the court, he should have it committed to writing;
however, one should not adjudicate a dispute that is unestablished or one that is detested by the city.
Likewise, the duties pertaining to regions,

castes, and families— those established for those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) as well as for those dwelling in difficult terrains, and for their respective regions, castes, lineages, and so forth— must be maintained in that very same way.
In that very same way, those subjects must be protected; otherwise, they become agitated.
When the people turn hostile, the army and the treasury perish.
In the South, the daughters of maternal uncles are married by the twice-born;
in the Middle Country, manual laborers and artisans eat beef.
In the east, men were eaters of fish and women were devoted to adultery;
in the north, women were drinkers of liquor and were to be touched by men even during their menstrual periods.
Those born together [as twins] take as their wife the brother's wife who is without a husband;
by this act, they are not worthy of being given penance.
Because they constantly fail to perform what is enjoined and indulge in what is forbidden,
the king should provide them with food and clothing and take the remainder for himself.
Those born of inverse unions as well as those dwelling in outcaste settlements must be protected with effort according to the scriptures; for she is the very means of proof when matters are doubtful.
Having seen that [case], the court should reach a decision according to the established rules previously settled regarding the fine appropriate for the toll,
or the monthly and six-monthly taxes.
A boundary must always be established in writing and supervised by merchants;
the words of the plaintiff must be recorded, as well as the words of the defendant.
Having investigated thoroughly, one should take action; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
When one person engages in debate with many people, including women and spectators,
his argument is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.
Those who should not be obstructed:

one intent on a sacrificial session or a wedding, a sick person, those afflicted by grief, the insane, children, the intoxicated, the elderly, one who is being interrogated, one engaged in royal business, and one observing a vow.
A soldier in the midst of battle, a farmer during the harvest, those in a state of distress, and likewise women accompanied by their protectors, must not be obstructed.

A messenger, one who has not yet attained legal majority, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, those in a precarious situation, and likewise women accompanied by a protector, shall not be obstructed.
But when the grain has grown, the merchant who sold the goods, the farmer, and those who were striving for the harvest,
having completed their transactions, must likewise be made to pay.
When the mind is unable to decide while one wishes to engage in a dispute,
time for deliberation should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The king shall cause that very person against whom one brings a charge— whether based on truth or even out of suspicion— to be summoned by means of a female messenger or a male servant.
For those who are lacking in confidence, the dull-witted, the insane, the elderly, women, children, and the sick, a kinsman,
an appointed official, or another person may state the preceding and subsequent [statements].
When appointed as a priest in a debate, both [the priest and the opponent] are proclaimed to be equal;
in the sacrifice, the patron obtains merit, while in the debate, he obtains either loss or victory.
If one who has been summoned does not come out of arrogance, even though supported by the strength of his kinsmen,
the judge shall determine a punishment for him in accordance with the nature of the legal charge.
At the appropriate time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your affliction? Do not fear; speak, O man!"

When he has been questioned in this manner, the members of the assembly, together with the Brahmins, should deliberate upon what he says; if the matter is found to be just, then after this, he should be summoned for further proceedings.
He should provide a seal such that it may designate either a document or a person.
If one who is summoned, being capable [of obeying], should disregard the king's command,
the judge shall determine his punishment in accordance with the nature of the legal charge.

In cases involving the incompetent, children, the elderly, those in distress, or those confused by improper actions, the fine for a minor offense shall be fifty; for middling offenses, it shall be at least one hundred;
and for grave matters, he shall always be subject to a fine of at least five hundred.
In a region struck by an enemy army, or afflicted by famine or disease,
one should issue a general amnesty and should not inflict punishment.
Those who are addicted to the neglect of their duties, and those who are preoccupied with the festivals and affairs of the king.
A king should not summon servants who are striving for other gains, those who are deceitful in appearance toward their master, or those who are intoxicated, insane, or negligent.
Neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor one acting under a legal mandate,
shall be exempt from punishment when speaking falsely in judicial proceedings while testifying on behalf of another.
A young woman born of noble family who has not yet had offspring,
even if she is the best among all castes, is considered by them [the relatives] as a maiden already enjoyed by her kin.
Having understood the time and place, as well as the strength and weakness of the matters at hand,
the king should gradually cause even those who are incapable of legal proceedings to appear before him by means of messengers.
The invitation of those who are dependent on their families, of wanton women, of courtesans, of those from broken families, and of those who have fallen from their caste is prescribed.
A guarantor capable of resolving the matter should be taken from both parties.
Having ascertained their intent, even those who have gone forth into the forest as renunciants and the like,
the king should summon them for important matters, provided he does not provoke their anger.
The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated and who departs from that speech,
until the appearance for the summons.

Restriction may be of four kinds: restriction to a place, restriction by time, restriction from travel, and likewise restriction from occupation; one who is under such restriction must not violate it.
Fields, gardens, houses, and so forth, as well as wealth, grain, and the like—
these must be restrained from litigants who speak unjustly.
But if one who has been placed under restraint should himself voluntarily relinquish that restraint,
there is no fault arising from his transgression, nor shall a fine be imposed upon him.
After reporting [the matter] to the king, one who has been placed under restraint shall not release himself on his own accord;
if he should release himself, he must be made to pay a fine, and one who is under restraint shall not break his confinement.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering a calamity in a difficult region,
one who has not yet completed his studies does not commit an offense by departing before the formal dismissal.
One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one engaged in royal business [should not study].
Cowherds [should be honored] at the time of grazing the cattle, farmers at the commencement of the crops,
artisans at their respective times, and those who bear arms during a conflict.
Those who have climbed a tree or a mountain, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those in difficult positions— none of these should be obstructed by those intent on accomplishing their purpose.

But he who, by means of restraining the senses, as well as by fasting, holding his breath, and so forth, should cause [the debtor] to be constrained when he is not otherwise constrained, shall be punished; he is not merely one who has transgressed.
One who is subject to restraint and yet violates that restraint deserves punishment;
however, one who restrains someone who is not subject to restraint must be punished by the king—this is the established rule.

The king should examine the arguments of litigants who have come before him and are disputing repeatedly; he should not consider arguments fabricated by himself, nor those merely reported by his officials.
When one who has been oppressed comes of his own accord seeking redress by means of the legal instrument, the judge,
or a representative, shall question him slowly and gradually.
The testimony of one who acts without being appointed because he was not included in the legal proceedings shall not be accepted,
except for what is written or sent by messenger.
When the plaintiff and the defendant arrive one after the other,
the trial should be conducted according to the order of their castes, or else by considering whose suffering is greater.
Those who are insane or intoxicated, those defiled by mortal sins,
as well as the mentally dull, the very elderly, and children, should be known as those who are exempt from being defeated in debate.
A position that has been stated is declared unacceptable, as is a disputant who lacks a reply; I shall now explain what kind of disputant and what kind of position are to be accepted.
When a proponent, intent on establishing his own position, speaks what he intends to say by resorting to an excess of argumentation, that is called the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie view).
[The Beginning of the Fourfold Discourse] (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2):
The section on speech, the subsequent section, and likewise the section on action.
And the legal proceeding (vyavahāra) has four stages, including the final determination (pratyākalita).
"False rejoinder," "counter-attack," and likewise "prior plea"—
these four types of replies have been declared by those who know the treatises."
It should be known that the trial consists of four legs in cases of falsehood, as well as in counter-pleads and pleas of prior judgment; it consists of two legs in cases of admission.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer when seven nights have passed, is defeated and deserves punishment.

[Brh_1.2.1 Definition of the Thesis] Then, when that [opponent] has presented himself, the proponent should formulate a thesis that is faultless, accompanied by a proposition, and endowed with means of valid cognition and authoritative tradition. // Brh_1.2.5 //
One should record the location, place, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, the quantity of substances, the number, the time of occurrence, the affliction, and the symptoms of emaciation.
Whatever point one may advance, one should not lead it into a state of contradiction, nor should one shift to another position; for by shifting from the original position, one is defeated.
The king should avoid a thesis that is unestablished, faulty, useless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.2; 1.2.8)
That which has not been created by anyone is declared to be "unestablished" (aprasiddha);
it is proclaimed as faulty because its meaning is other than intended and it is devoid of its own proper meaning.
An action involving a minor offense and a minor benefit is known as "insignificant" (nirarthaka);
however, that which is devoid of any obstruction to its purpose should be understood as "useless" (niṣprayojana).
A legal proceeding devoid of such elements as diligence is meaningless;
likewise, it should be understood as useless when characterized by verbal abuse, physical assault, and the like.
"He must give me a bow made of hare's horn"—
the wise say that such a position is impossible and unachievable.
That case in which, once it has been presented, there would be opposition toward the judge, the king, the city, or the kingdom, is declared to be "contradictory" (viruddha).

Those who know the subject matter of a thesis recognize the *pakṣa* as that which is free from defects of the proposition, is yet to be proven, is endowed with valid reasons, is well-defined, and is established by common worldly consensus.
It consists of very few syllables yet contains abundant meaning; it is free from ambiguity and confusion;
it is devoid of contradictory causes and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
For in formal debates, when disputants must speak without confusion, it is the statement that constitutes the proposition (pratijñā), while its meaning constitutes the subject of debate (pakṣa).
Whether out of delusion or through deceit, that which was not stated by the proponent— whether it be included within the reply or otherwise— that too shall be taken into account for both parties.
Having correctly reflected upon such qualities and reached a firm conclusion, a position that is acceptable has been established; a fallacious position (pakṣābhāsa) is otherwise.
A thesis that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number,
and deficient in the proof of the probandum, is considered unacceptable.
If the initial plea is written down as being based on false reasoning, devoid of action, concerning an impossible matter, or confused,
the defeat of the litigant occurs.
The plaintiff who, having stated his charge, passes over it and speaks of another,
or who, having stated his proof, should speak otherwise, shall suffer defeat.
In the first stage, the plaintiff shall clear up any deficiency or excess,
until the defendant has presented his reply in the presence of the members of the court.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and other such indecent accusations, no counter-accusation is permitted.
In the case of killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife, eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden; ||| Brh_1.2.24 |||
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the informant shall not be made to pay; rather, the perpetrator himself shall plead the case.
The debate consisting of eighteen points has been presented for deliberation; there are other points here as well, which the King may investigate himself.
Taking one-sixth [of the produce] as tribute, purity, non-transgression of agreements, treasure-troves, execution, seizure, theft, and the violation of prohibitions and royal edicts; // Brh_1.2.27 //
Neither the king nor his official should initiate a legal case on their own;
they should reduce excessive claims and fulfill those that are deficient.
One should record it on the ground as long as the matter has not been fully determined;
once it has been heard, written down, verified, and deliberated upon, [it is finalized].
Then the judge shall cause the plaintiff's case, as stated in its own nature, to be written on a wooden board with chalk;
thereafter, once it has been refined, he shall write it down on the official document.
But for those who, after the matter has been presented and accepted, settle their dispute among themselves,
one should determine a fine for them in accordance with the nature of the legal claim.
Furthermore, those legal cases involving those who oppose cities, villages, or great kings,
as well as all matters that are not to be granted, are declared to be inadmissible.
One should first write on a wooden board or on the ground using chalk;
having corrected what is deficient or excessive, one should subsequently inscribe it on the formal document.
When the plaintiff, due to lack of confidence, does not dare to speak,
time should be granted to him, in accordance with his capacity and the nature of the case.
If he is unable to decide where two parties wish to engage in a dispute,
then a period of time must be granted there to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is fourfold, and likewise the counter-argument (pratipakṣa);
the final determination (nirṇaya) is said to be fourfold, though some maintain it is eightfold.
The country, the time, as well as the place and the layout, the designation of the knower, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: the names of the ancestors and grandfathers, and the eulogy of former kings.
Or he may obtain a postponement for three days or even seven days,
as long as it takes for the thought to arise in him who wishes to speak in the dispute.
Even a case involving many assertions that has been settled in legal proceedings,
the king may, if he desires to ascertain the truth, take it up again at his pleasure.
Accusation based on suspicion, the truth, a request regarding the matter at hand,
and a renewed legal proceeding once a case has been concluded— these are to be known as the fourfold types of plaints.
Delusion is defined as doubt; it is the certain perception of something lost.
Delusion is also the solicitation for what has already been obtained, as well as the repeated performance of actions regarding what has already been accomplished.
But he who is disapproved by the king, or who causes opposition among the citizens, or likewise among the whole kingdom and its constituent subjects; // Brh_1.2.43 //
He who does not wish to act justly, or who acts unjustly,
or likewise he who does not cause [the record] to be written— his case is not established.
One should avoid from afar that position in which both contradictory and non-contradictory meanings are seen to be established within a single [subject]. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.45)
[Br̥h 1.3.2] But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent, [the following is said: [Br̥h 1.3. "But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent..."
Then the opponent should offer a reply connected to that very position.
Once the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) has been determined, distinguished by what is to be accepted and what is not to be accepted,
and once it has been formally stated and stabilized, one should then cause the rejoinder (uttara) to be written down.
Whether due to timidity, fear, an adversary, or a lapse of memory, wherever one requests time,
there one deserves to obtain it.
Depending on one's capacity, one may receive [the gift] for one day, three days, five days, seven days, or even a fortnight, a month, three months, four months, or a year.

Those who know it recognize this answer as being pervasive of the side [of the argument], essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation to be understood. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.5)
The reply is of four kinds:
the direct reply (sāmpratam), the false reply (mithyottaram), the reply based on a prior judgment (prāṅnyāyottaram), and the reply based on a legal reason (kāraṇottaram).
But he who does not give a reply according to the facts during the plaintiff's case must be compelled to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods, even while being a witness.
Kindly speech preceded by affection, sowing dissension, displaying fear, the deprivation of wealth, as well as beating and imprisonment— these constitute punishment (daṇḍa).
Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations regarding cattle, or an emergency, one may litigate over land immediately, even outside of the prescribed season.

One who speaks falsely, one who hates the performance of legal acts, one who does not present himself, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these five are declared to be defeated.
In cases of violating a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence,
fraud, and perjury, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.
In the case of cows, oxen, a field, women, and offspring;
likewise in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and in buying and selling.
In a plea of prior judgment and in a plea of justification, the defendant shall point out the means of proof;
but in a plea of denial, the plaintiff shall do so, while in a plea of admission, it is not possible [for either party to produce evidence].
When a proponent advances a position without stating a reason, that should be known as a mere assertion (*pratipatti*); the reason, however, is a distinct matter, namely the reply (*uttara*).
But Bṛhaspati states that if one, having engaged in all manner of conversation, should converse even slightly with the other party in secret, he shall be made to pay the entire amount when accused.
In cases of verbal abuse, disputes over land, and transactions involving sale or gift, one should avoid divine ordeals when the party is unwilling to undergo the legal proceeding.
If one who is accused should deny the accusation, one should know that the defense is false according to the principles of legal procedure. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2; 1.3.17)
If, upon hearing the charge, the defendant admits it,
that is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "admission" (saṃpratipatti).
If the defendant, when confronted with the matter asserted by the plaintiff,
admits it as such but states a legal justification for it, that is indeed a plea of "counter-attack" (pratyavaskandana).
If the defendant admits the very point that has been stated by the plaintiff and states the grounds for it accordingly, Manu has declared that he is not liable to punishment.
If one who has fallen away from proper conduct is made to write again, that litigant,
having been previously defeated, is said to be a *prāṅnyāya* case.
One should employ the true against the true, and one should record the false against the false;
likewise, one should apply reason to that which is supported by reason, and victory to that which has already been victorious.
That which arises from a false perception of danger is considered false and is censured by those who know the scriptures;
however, that which is a correct apprehension is declared to be true and righteous.
When a legal proceeding has been initiated, the truth is declared by the virtuous as praiseworthy;
the opposite would be unrighteous, and the defendant shall suffer loss.
When both the plaintiff and the defendant arrive simultaneously in a spirit of rivalry,
the trial should be conducted according to the order of their social classes and by considering the relative severity of their suffering.
When the defendant has been brought at the same time into the presence of the court members,
he shall then write his reply corresponding to the words of the plaintiff's case.
The rule regarding each respective subject has been declared for the purpose of conveying the coherent meaning;
now, that which is to be grasped among the fourfold [means] is being stated.

One should not characterize that which is other than the subject at hand, that which is neutral, that which is inferior or superior, that which is irrelevant, that which lacks essential meaning, that which is doubtful, or that which is contrary.
If he causes fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction,
he loses his case in the legal proceeding.
But when appointed as a priest or the like, the two are declared to be equal;
in a sacrifice, the patron obtains merit, while in a debate, he obtains either loss or victory.
If the plaintiff or the defendant dies after the statements have been recorded in the north-eastern corner,
their son shall clear up the legal proceedings on their behalf.
If a legal dispute remains undecided, the king would be deceived; the awarding of victory would not be impartial. Therefore, he should decide the cases.
If, however, one points out witnesses but does not bring them to trial within thirty nights or three fortnights, a loss of the case occurs for him.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses,
and one who admits his own case— all these are of four kinds of defeated litigants.
One who flees is defeated after three fortnights; one who remains silent, after seven days;
one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and one who admits his claim, likewise loses the case.
Not stating what has been presented, failing to appear,
silence, and the defects of one seeking a position— these are the characteristics of one who is losing the case.
People know him to be endowed with patience who forgives when he is accused in an assembly of a great sin, a minor sin, or a transgression.
Therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the purification of the self;
whatever task is most important, that one should first purify.
He who, accused of a great sin, desires to escape from that transgression, deserves punishment for having previously admitted it; he is defeated.
When a divine ordeal has been performed for the purpose of establishing conduct,
and no one has appeared to undergo it, one must not employ any deception therein.
If, however, a fault caused by fate or the king should occur at that time,
he shall not be defeated merely for abandoning his place of confinement.
When a dispute has arisen and an investigation has been conducted,
those who reach a settlement among themselves must be made to pay double the fine.
When the former and latter points have been written down and the determination of the case has begun,
a reconciliation may occur between the two heated parties, like that of two pieces of iron.
In that case, there may be a conflict between the witness and the judge;
the wise should then effect a reconciliation between the two as they waver.
Where there is equality of power but a difference in the scriptures and conduct, a peace treaty between both parties is recommended by me for the king.
In a case where the legal matter before a king is subject to doubt,
a settlement should be made there, just as two pieces of heated iron are joined together.
Then a peace treaty should be concluded on equal terms, for an unequal one leads to withdrawal.
Through equality, the king secures dharma, wealth, support, and fame;
neither the witnesses nor the members of the court suffer, and the enemy retreats.
From conflict arise for men the power to punish and favor, the administration of justice, fame and infamy, and likewise the occurrence of further faults.
Therefore, whatever those presiding over the family and the assembly— who know the Dharma, who possess impartial vision,
and who are free from hatred and greed— should declare, that must be carried out by one who understands.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4. Kriyāpāda] [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.
When it has been properly purified and written, such that the answer is flawless;
Whether it be a defendant or a plaintiff, legal action is held to depend upon a cause.
But for those who persist in their claim, the members of the court shall,
after having properly stated the defendant's reply, cause the judgment to be given against one of the litigants.
The proponent shall establish his thesis, and likewise the opponent shall establish his grounds;
the proponent who has spoken first shall establish his victory by means of the certificate of victory.
Just as it was written in the first quarter, letter by letter and without exception,
the seeker should establish that meaning through practice in the third quarter.
Having heard the plaintiff's initial statement,
that party whose case has been determined by the members of the court shall substantiate his entire claim through written documents and other means.
Action is said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine;
each of these is divided into many varieties by the seers who know the truth.
Witnesses, documentary evidence, and possession are recorded as the threefold human means of proof;
while the divine means of proof consists of nine kinds, beginning with the balance and ending with that born of dharma.
Human proof consists of three kinds: witnesses, documents, and inference.
Witnesses are recorded as being of twelve types, while documents are traditionally said to be of eight kinds.
Inference is declared to be threefold, and divine action is ninefold;
in the first or in the third [stage], both divine and human means of proof are authoritative.
In the fourth stage, however, there should be the document of victory along with witnesses;
in matters such as debts and the like, one should employ human means of proof.
In the case of a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or a plea of denial (*pratyavaskanda*), the defendant himself must prove his case;
however, in the case of a plea of denial (*mithyottara*), the plaintiff must prove both the meaning of the reply and the meaning of the original claim.
When witnesses are available, an ordeal is not prescribed;
and when there is a written document in legal disputes, neither an ordeal nor witnesses should be employed. (Br̥haspati 1.4.12)
In cases of verbal abuse, disputes over land, and in all four types of violent offenses, divine means of proof are forbidden; they must be diligently avoided.
In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, one should employ divine proof (ordeals).
One who steals heaps of gems, pearls, corals, or heart-shaped necklaces,
as well as one who is violent and consorts with other men's wives, must always be examined by means of oaths.
In cases of grave accusations of sin, as well as in matters of deposits and theft,
the king should investigate by means of divine ordeals, even when witnesses are present.
If doubt arises regarding a written document, oral testimony,
or confused inference, then an ordeal is the means of purification in that case.
In matters of gambling, dueling, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared the means of proof; neither an ordeal nor a written document is required.
The king should cause a decision to be made by those witnesses who have appeared according to their availability; however, in cases of violent acts, verbal disputes, verbal abuse,
and matters arising from force, he should rely on witnesses and divine ordeals alone.
In matters of debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even fragments of reasoning,
as well as divine means of proof, have been declared for the benefit of subjects.
When witnesses have long since disappeared, when they were previously kept silent, or when inferential signs have become corrupted,
one should clear the matter by means of ordeals.
There may be nine, seven, five, four, or even three witnesses.
Or both [should be] learned in the Vedas and renowned; one should never question only one.
The keeper of the gambling hall, the receiver of the stakes, and likewise one who is involved in the business,
as well as the king and his superintendent— each of these alone shall be an authority.
Thieves, violent criminals, eunuchs, gamblers, and informers are not witnesses because of their wickedness; witness-status does not exist among them.

The types of witnesses are: the written witness (*likhita*), the secret witness (*gūḍha*), the reminded witness (*smārita*), the family witness (*kulya*), the messenger witness (*dūtaka*), the incidental witness (*yadṛccha*), the responding witness (*uttara*), and another who is present in the midst of the transaction (*kāryamadhyagata*).
The king, the official, and likewise the village headman are recorded as the twelve kinds of witnesses;
I shall describe their distinctions correctly and in due order.
One by whom his own [name], that of his father, and so forth,
as well as his place of residence, have been recorded, should be known as a witness designated as "written" (likhitasaṃjñaka).
When a creditor, having performed transactions such as lending money and so forth with various formalities,
causes [the debt] to be written down in his presence, that is declared to be a *lekhita* document.
But he who is made to hear the statement regarding a debt while separated by a wall,
and who denies it as it truly is, is called a hidden witness.
He who is summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, and transactions,
and who is repeatedly reminded of his duty, is declared to be a "reminded witness" (smārita).
One who is employed in the distribution of shares, in trade, or as a kinsman,
and who is impartial toward both parties, is proclaimed by those who know the Dharma to be a *kulya*.
But he who, being sent by both parties, listens to the statements of the plaintiff and the defendant—
being virtuous and approved by both— is declared to be a witness (*dūtaka*).
But when a duty is being performed, whoever happens to arrive of his own accord and says,
"You are our witness here," he is called an incidental witness.
Where a witness departs for another direction, or where one who is about to die speaks in due order,
one should know that person whom he causes to hear it as the subsequent witness.
When witnesses are giving testimony repeatedly, he who hears it again and again is known as the "subsequent witness" (uttara-sākṣin).
He in whom both [parties] have placed their trust and who has been informed of the matter should be known as a secret keeper; likewise, he who enters into the midst of the business [is also such].
Whatever statement of the plaintiff and the defendant has been heard directly by the king himself,
that alone shall be the witness there in case of a disagreement between the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a new trial should take place, the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, shall be the witness therein; it cannot be otherwise.
Where it has been inhabited and covered on all sides by the boundary, that village is undoubtedly a witness, even if it has been cut away. // Brh_1.5.18 //
Two who are written down and likewise secret witnesses, those written as three, four, or five,
those recalled by chance, kinsmen, and likewise secondary witnesses (uttara-sākṣins).
The messenger who holds his own seal, as well as one who is involved in the internal affairs of the matter—
each of these alone may be authoritative, just like the king and the official supervisor.
But the plaintiff who, by means of a fault, seeks to corrupt witnesses who have been duly designated for the case—
corrupting those who are not corrupt— is liable to a fine equal to the value of the claim. (Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21)
Whatever defects of the document or of the witnesses are recorded, they must be stated at the time of the trial; one may not raise them after they have already been spoken.
The defendant must set forth the defects of the witnesses in court;
having written all of them down on the document, he must then state his rebuttal.
However, they are never entitled to act as witnesses regarding the performance [of a rite];
otherwise, they must be meditated upon by the defendant during the ritual action.
If the defendant fails to prove his case, he must clearly be compelled to pay by means of witnesses;
all witnesses who have been examined must be excluded from the status of witnesses if they violate the rules governing testimony.
Whether it be the defendant or the plaintiff, when proving a defect in the witness,
there is no separate legal proceeding provided it is relevant to the matter at hand.

If the plaintiff is free from further desire and the witness remains established in the truth, he who has been defeated shall be made to pay a fine according to the disciplinary procedure prescribed by the scriptures.
But he who, after witnesses have been declared, disparages those previously unimpeached and does not state the grounds for that [disparagement], shall incur the first amercement.
In a legal dispute, if either the documents or the witnesses are found to be tainted,
the case of that party shall not be adjudicated until those [tainted elements] have been cleared.
But when a verdict has been reached by the members of the court based on the testimony of witnesses, if anyone initiates a lawsuit again, the king shall investigate that matter.
When witnesses are suspected of corruption, the purification of the witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been cleared, one may thereafter purify the case itself.
The members of the assembly, who are conversant with the meaning of the treatises on Dharma, must admonish [the litigants] with words praising truth and rejecting falsehood.
Whatever merit you have earned from birth until death—
all that goes to ruin through the false accusation of one who has failed in his vows.
A perjuror, a false witness, and a slayer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
a destroyer of an embryo and a betrayer of a friend are said to be no greater than these.
Having understood this, the witness who speaks according to the truth thereby attains fame in this world and an auspicious state in the hereafter.
There are men who, out of greed, would state a case otherwise;
and there are other evil-minded men who forge false documents.
I shall now describe those witnesses who are to be questioned and those lowest of men who are to be excluded, as prescribed by the scriptures.
Those who are engaged in the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, who are free from greed and hatred,
who are of noble birth, blameless, and endowed with austerity, charity, and compassion— such persons are to be witnesses.
The father of the mother, the paternal uncle, the brother-in-law, the mother of the wife,
the brother, the friend, and the son-in-law are not witnesses in any legal disputes.
Those addicted to other men's wives or to drinking, gamblers, those previously convicted,
the insane, the afflicted, the rash, and atheists are not to be witnesses.
Even virtuous persons would not be valid witnesses after the death of the wealthy man,
unless they had been informed by the man himself when he was near death that his son was the heir.
Having removed his sandals and turban, he should raise his right hand;
taking gold, cow dung, and darbha grass, he should speak the truth.
Those who present themselves should be examined by means of their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth.
One should protect even a Brahmin who has committed an offense through a single lapse, who is afflicted by calamity,
or who is being beaten by soldiers and others, even by speaking untruths.
He whose entire claim has been corroborated by witnesses shall be the victor; otherwise, however, he shall not attain his objective.
If a witness who is free from disease does not come when summoned,
he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed.
In a conflict between witnesses, those who are more numerous should be accepted; if they are equal in number, those endowed with superior qualities;
if there is a conflict between those of superior qualities, those who possess corroborating evidence; and if they too are equal, those who are more pure.
Witnesses who, when not questioned, do not speak the truth, or likewise fail to answer a question, shall be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
If that which is uttered is not deficient in terms of place, time, age, substance, name, caste, and measure, one should declare the object to be accomplished as successful.
In matters concerning place, time, age, substance, quantity, form, and caste,
wherever there may be a dispute, even that testimony must not be otherwise [i.e., it must be accepted as valid].
When the various matters have been set forth and the witness has been brought to testify, if he does not speak, that testimony is as good as lost; it shall not be considered properly declared.
One should contemplate the entirety of what was proposed in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa);
however, that which was stated there as deficient or excessive shall not be considered as having been truly declared.
Where witnesses state a matter either deficiently or in excess, that matter should be understood as not having been stated; this is recorded as the rule regarding witnesses.
When the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by the witnesses, it shall be considered complete;
for in cases of sexual intercourse, violence, and theft, whatever is to be proven is determined by the testimony.
But where the testimony should be deficient or excessive, one should reject it;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
This determination regarding the number and characteristics of witnesses has thus been set forth.
Now I shall explain, in due order, the procedure for the written [charter].
Since confusion may arise even regarding matters such as debts,
the Creator created letters and placed them upon paper in ancient times.

[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.1: Characteristics of a Document] A document is said to be that which records the local custom, the amount lent, and the interest accrued over years, months, fortnights, and so forth;
it must bear the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe. Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.3.

[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.2: Varieties of Documents] A royal document, one executed by a local official, and likewise one written in one's own hand—document is said to be of these three kinds; furthermore, it is divided into many varieties.
Documentary evidence in worldly affairs is sevenfold, consisting of [deeds concerning] shares, gifts, sales, pledges, agreements, slaves, and debts; royal edicts are of three kinds.
This document known as the *vibhāgapatra* (partition deed) is executed for the determination of shares;
when a boundary dispute has been settled, it is traditionally called a *sīmāpatra* (boundary deed).
A deed of gift, a deed of partition, and likewise a deed concerning boundaries;
a deed of purchase, a deed concerning slaves, and thereafter a deed of mortgage.
A document of agreement, a deed of victory,
and likewise a treaty— these are of many kinds according to the diversity of legal transactions.
A pledge-deed shall be for the purpose of a pledge; a slave-document shall be for the purpose of a slave.
For the sake of accomplishing their desired aims, the village councils, guilds,
and assemblies have drawn up a document of agreement for the purpose of dharma, in accordance with the scriptures.
When brothers who have divided their inheritance among themselves by mutual consent execute a deed of partition,
that is called a *bhāgalekhya* (a document of division).
But that which one should have made as a document after giving land, valid for as long as the moon and sun endure—
an unseizable and irremovable deed of gift— that they know to be a *dānalekhya*.
Having purchased a house, field, or the like, that document which one causes to be made, accompanied by the letters [indicating] the equivalent value,
is called a deed of purchase (krayalekhya).
When one, having given movable or immovable property as a pledge,
executes a document specifying it as being subject to the conditions of "custody" (gopya) or "enjoyment" (bhogya), that is known as a *ādhi-lekhya* (mortgage deed).
Whatever a village or a district may execute among themselves in a state of mutual intoxication,
provided it does not conflict with the king and is for the sake of dharma or wealth, they call that a *saṃvitpatra* (contractual document).
Whatever deed one who is destitute of clothing and food performs in the wilderness, I shall perform that work for you; that is known as a "slave-deed" (dāsapatra).
Having received wealth through interest, one may either perform the transaction oneself or cause it to be done;
this is called a *uddhāra-patra* (a deed of withdrawal) by the wise, as well as a *ṛṇa-lekhya* (a debt document).
Regarding the established status of guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, which has been fully proclaimed, its proof is documentary evidence; neither ordeal nor witnesses are required.
However, that which is established for the sake of maintaining the agreement of guilds, corporations, and the like,
is called a *sthitipatra* (deed of settlement) by those who know the Smṛtis of Manu and others.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.3: The King’s Edict on Gifts] Having bestowed land and other gifts, the king shall cause a charter to be made upon a copper plate or a cloth, containing the Dharma and joined with the description of the location, lineage, and so forth.
For the merit of my parents and myself, I have today given this gift to such-and-such a person, a fellow practitioner of the holy life, for the sake of such-and-such a son.
Inviolable and unassailable, entirely free from all that is subject to transformation,
it endures as long as the moon and sun, and is transmitted through the lineage of sons and grandsons.

He who severs the practice of giving shall write down the fruit of that act as follows: for sixty thousand years, he will dwell in heaven as one who gives and protects, and likewise in hell as one who takes away.
"The ocean, the rains, the months, and so forth, along with the figures of the treasurer—
'this has been ascertained by me,' thus it was written by the scribes of peace and war."
Such is the royal edict described as being "written by favor" (prasādalikhita),
which the king issues when he grants a document concerning a region and so forth.
Indeed, that document written as a favor, granted by the king when he is pleased by service, valor, or other such qualities, is a *jayapatra* (decree of victory);
it is issued at the conclusion of the determination of the plaintiff's and defendant's claims and defenses.
One should grant a document to the victor; that is called a *jayapatra* (a decree of victory).
Whatever occurred in the legal proceeding— the plaint, the reply, and so forth— along with the evidence and the final determination, he shall write all of that in the document of victory (jayapatra).
One should establish the matter to be proven in a victory that is endowed with its four components;
indeed, a document of victory (jayapatra) is required to be accompanied by the royal seal.
To others who are devoid of other means of proof and the like, [a document] is granted;
that, being established through the recounting of the proceedings, shall be the *jayapatra* (document of victory).

A document executed under the influence of poison or drugs, or by one who is about to die, by one whose property has been diminished or lost, or by one afflicted by madness or calamity, is not valid. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.6.30)
Where a single witness who is tainted and censured is appointed, that is called a forged document;
or likewise, so is one written by such a scribe.

A document that is brilliant [in appearance], though long ago executed; or one that is stained, though recent; or one that is broken, or contains indistinct syllables—such a document shall be considered forged.
Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears to exist though it is non-existent,
so too do skillful people create painted images that possess the likeness of forms.
For a judgment is indeed based on truth, while a refutation is based solely on fault;
that in which such a flawed matter is deliberated is the royal court.
Having deliberated together with the Brahmins, one should examine the fault of the speaker.
By that [evidence] through which witnesses, scribes, and authors fall into falsehood, by that the document shall be deemed corrupt; one should declare it pure when [these parties] are pure.

If a debtor denies a debt that has been entered in writing with his own hand, he may be compelled to pay by means of witnesses recorded on the document, or by the oral testimony of the scribe, with the latter's consent.

But when letters are displaced from their positions, lack beauty, are indistinct, or have fallen away from their proper characteristics— if they remain thus, Bhṛgu declares that the writing is defective.
The plaintiff shall recover the document, but the son shall recover possession alone;
if the defendant has died while being sued, his son shall recover that [document].
Having ascertained the matter, those skilled in place and time who fabricate forgeries produce a document that appears similar; therefore, one should examine such a document with great care.
Some skillful people write [the letters] like a painting;
therefore, it is held that success is not achieved solely through the power of writing.

One's own kinsmen may deceive women, children, the afflicted, and those ignorant of writing by having a document prepared marked with their own names; such a deed must be scrutinized through reasoning and legal precedents.
When an error arises in this threefold document,
one should then correct it by the verbal testimony of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.

One should recognize that where a fraudulent condition (*upadhi*) has been made, there is "exertion" because of the undertaking of the enterprise, "possession" because of the acquisition of the fruit, and "wealth" because of the possession of the rival's property. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.44)
A document is established as valid in all cases— provided it was presented at the proper time, read aloud, and made known— if even the witnesses have died.
Where the expressive power of syllables is obstructed by their denotators,
there would be the total destruction of actions and an infinite regress would arise.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be living.
But when the profit from the pledge has been realized, if the debtor does not produce the document nor does the creditor demand it, he shall fall into doubt regarding that matter.
One should cause the members of families, guilds, assemblies, and so forth to hear and remember what has been presented at the appropriate time; in this way, it shall become even more powerful.
If anything has been received, or if there is a formal designation [of the debt],
that document itself shall serve as proof, even if the witnesses have died.
If a person who is capable does not request a debt from a wealthy person standing nearby,
that document may be rendered weak on account of the suspicion that it is merely for the sake of clearing the debt.
A document executed by those who are insane, dull-witted, or women; by those fleeing due to fear of the king; or by those who are timid or afflicted by fear, shall not be held valid as evidence.
Then, if the scribe together with the witnesses has met his death,
there is no doubt that [the matter] is cleared for them by means of their own handwriting and other such evidence.
When there is doubt regarding a debt, whether the debtor is living or deceased,
the determination of that document is made by other documents written in his own hand.

When doubt arises regarding a document, it may be resolved by the witnesses, the scribe, and the author; and if they are found to be corrupt, [the authenticity is determined] by means of the previous characters and other marks written by their own hands.
A written document is never invalidated by witnesses or by an oath; however, one suffers loss through neglect by failing to present it or by failing to have it read aloud.
Therefore, both of these must be examined especially by the king;
there should be only one document for the sake of establishing a single matter.
However, among many types of documents, one may produce a defect:
that which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which was executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is devoid of a matter to be proved— all such are defective.
All ritual actions have wealth as their root; all efforts are considered to be for the sake of accomplishing that.
Its sequential method consists of increasing, protecting, and enjoying.
Furthermore, that is to be known as threefold: the white, the variegated, and the black;
therein, the classification is further to be understood as sevenfold.

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a pupil, a sacrificer, or inheritance—these are the seven kinds of wealth; for both [the teacher and the pupil] are of such a nature regarding it.
That which is obtained through idleness, agriculture, trade, tolls, the practice of crafts,
or from one who has received a favor, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling with dice and the like, by means of messengers, by deception, by violence, or under some pretext, is declared to be "black" wealth.
By means of that, buying and selling, giving and taking,
as well as various activities and the enjoyment of their fruits, are carried out.
Whatever a person performs with whatever kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit for that, both in this world and after death.
Furthermore, that [meditation] is known to be twelvefold, based on the individual castes;
it is threefold as common, and the remainder is known to be ninefold.
That which is inherited by succession, that which is received as a gift of affection, and that which is acquired together with one's wife—
these three types of property are declared to belong to all social classes without distinction.

The specific wealth of a Brahmin should be known as having three characteristics: that which is obtained through acceptance of gifts, that which is earned from officiating at sacrifices, and likewise that which is received from a pupil. // Brh_1.7.10 //
They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific kinds of wealth:
that acquired through battle, from taxes, and from fines levied in legal disputes.
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics:
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; while for a Śūdra, it consists of service to these [other classes].
For all social classes alike, the acquisition of wealth in this manner is righteous;
by the opposite method it would be unrighteous, unless there is a grave emergency.
In times of distress, the practice of the Vaiśya is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as his immediate recourse;
however, no inferior occupation is ever permitted for him.
A Brahmin should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brahmin; for those two [tasks] lead to their downfall.
Between those two, neither superior nor inferior action exists;
for, having abandoned intermediate actions, they are indeed common to all.

Having crossed over a time of distress while supporting his dependents through the occupation of a Kshatriya, a Brahmin should relinquish that Kshatriya occupation once he has performed purification for himself.
But that Brahmin who, out of sensual passion, delights in that very act of eating is fallen from the path; he is proclaimed as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* and is marked [as such].
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to the family of another,
is known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* because of that misconduct.
When the performance of legal business has been conducted during the day in villages and cities,
and when witnesses are available, the procedure of divine ordeals does not take place.
Likewise, in matters concerning doors, paths, works, enjoyment, water-conduits, and so forth, possession alone shall be the proof for the superior [title];
there is neither need for a document nor witnesses.
This rule has been declared regarding witnesses and written documents;
now the procedure for the acquisition of immovable property and for possession is being stated.

Immovable property acquired through learning, purchase, alliance, valor, inheritance, or family succession, as well as a share belonging to a sapinda who is childless, may be alienated by means of a written deed.
Regarding the sevenfold enjoyment: whether obtained from a father, through purchase, through a gift, through inheritance, through valor, or through discovery;
when such sevenfold enjoyment is acquired, it attains validity only when accompanied by a legal title (*sāgama*).
That possession which has come down by succession, is documented by royal edicts, and is accompanied by purchase or formal grant—
such possession shall attain legal validity.
Immovable property obtained through partition, by purchase, inherited from a father, or received from a king attains validity through possession; it is lost through neglect.
Whatever has been obtained and consumed by one who has accepted it without opposition, that [result] reaches fulfillment for him; yet through neglect, it leads to loss.
If a person’s possession has begun with actual occupation and has been enjoyed for thirty years without interruption and without opposition, one shall not displace him from that possession.
There shall be no enjoyment of women by any means without a written document,
nor in the case of the wealth of the king, of a Vedic scholar, or of the property of the mentally disabled or minors.
One cannot attain perfection through experience alone, nor even through pure scripture; it is accomplished by both, and not otherwise.
When the wealth of a learned child of the Veda is obtained, whether from a father or acquired through succession,
neither the one who took it nor his son should exert force in its enjoyment.
