||| Brh_1.7.32 ||| If, within a single legal document, cattle, women, men, and so forth
Even when only a portion is enjoyed, all [the owners] are considered to have been deprived of their possession;
for where there is no title whatsoever, even a slight enjoyment carries no weight.
An eyewitness is superior to inference; a written document is weightier than witnesses;
and possession by three successive generations, being unopposed, is more authoritative than these.
In this matter, inference resides, and it shall be a witness until death;
however, a document and possession that are uncontradicted are authoritative for three generations.
If one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living, yet land has been enjoyed for thirty years without being obstructed by others; [that possession is valid].

That enjoyment lasting for one generation is to be known as *pauruṣī*; that lasting for two generations is *dvipuruṣī*, which is double; that lasting for three generations is *tripūruṣī*, which is triple; and beyond that, it is *cirantanā* (of long duration).
Where the claimant is accused, then the documentary evidence is more authoritative than witnesses;
in the absence of those, possession alone is the weightiest proof for sons.
The original acquirer shall establish possession or title in an assembly;
his son may establish possession alone; but a grandson or later descendant need establish nothing at all.
If property is openly given by others to one who is the heir,
yet another person subsequently enjoys it, the former is not entitled to recover that property.
He who, seeing another giving away land, does not restrain him,
shall not regain that land even by means of a valid document.
Bhṛgu says that what is given by the heirs or by others belongs to that very person [who gave it].
The enjoyment [of the property] by three generations shall be established for others; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established for the sakulyas.
But property such as a house, field, or shop that has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner does not lapse through that enjoyment in favor of a friend, kinsman, or relative.
The Vedic scholar possesses inexhaustible merit; he has fearlessness from the king’s officers;
he has affection for his friends and kinsmen; and what is eaten by these is never lost.
That which has been eaten by those related by marriage, by Vedic scholars, and likewise by kings and ministers,
does not succeed for them even after a very long time.
The property of those who are incapacitated, lazy, diseased, afflicted, children, afraid,
or traveling abroad does not lapse by being enjoyed by another who holds a royal edict, nor is it lost through such enjoyment.
When a house or field has been deprived of its enjoyment, and doubt arises therein,
one should establish its purity through a document, those who know of the possession, or witnesses.

Those who know the names of the parties, their lineage, the number [of items], the time, the direction and location, as well as the cause for the enjoyment or the termination [of the right], are the witnesses in that case.
Those who have been born very recently, as well as those residing in other lands, are designated as "primary" witnesses; they should be questioned when determining the facts of a case.
But what those who are free from malice and impartial in their vision should say regarding a doubtful matter, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
That has been declared regarding immovable property as the means for establishing gain and enjoyment;
however, in a dispute concerning a claim lacking proof, divine proof (ordeals) should be prescribed.
Even if it was enjoyed by three preceding kings without formal legal title,
a gift to a Brahmin must never be confiscated from him by a king at any time.
Where possession has been established for three generations and is extended into the fourth, that enjoyment attains stability; one need not inquire about the title deeds anywhere.
When something has been enjoyed by exactly three persons without being prohibited, no legal title (āgama) need be produced; in that case, possession (bhukti) is more weighty.
In disputes concerning immovable property, possession extending over three generations is to be known as independent; it is the authoritative means for determining the matter to be proved.
The gift of a Brahmin (brahmadeya), for which possession has continued through three generations and which is accompanied by a formal document— such a grant cannot be taken away.
Possession that has been enjoyed by three generations, transmitted through a continuous succession,
cannot be overturned except by a prior royal edict.
If land has been enjoyed for three generations in the presence of [the owner] without being contested,
it must not be taken away from him, unless he declares a title of ownership.
In the scriptures, possession that is long-standing and uninterrupted is indeed powerful;
however, even that which has been interrupted should be understood as valid if it was previously established.

Whatever property was enjoyed by the father through the practice of enjoyment in accordance with dharma, even when he has passed away, that is acquired by the son; for that which was acquired through enjoyment belongs to him.
However, when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law,
in the absence of documentary evidence, a fourth person may acquire it there.
Whatever has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, and likewise by one's own kin—there is no success through enjoyment in that case; one should arrange for enjoyment with others.
Possession is fivefold: it consists of title, long duration, absence of interruption or opposition, the presence of an adversary, and actual enjoyment. (Br̥haspati Smr̥ti 1.7.64)
Quadrupeds, wealth, grain, and so forth will suffer loss after the year.
Non-enjoyment of land, failure to present a document at the proper time,
and the failure to recall witnesses— all these indeed cause the loss of one’s own right.
Therefore, one must diligently maintain the authority of the means of valid cognition;
by that, all affairs, both stationary and moving, are accomplished.
In a case that occurred long ago and for which there are no witnesses, one should question subsequent witnesses,
or subject the defendant to oaths, or employ an ordeal.
And the absence of obstruction in teaching, as well as a portion of the logical method.
That which has been stolen by thieves must be recovered from all [suspects] and restored;
or, if it cannot be found, it must be paid from his own treasury. Otherwise, he would incur the guilt of a thief.
Likewise, it has been declared that the means for attaining gain and enjoyment consist of divine things belonging to the stationary realm.
But in a debate lacking valid means of knowledge, a divine ordeal is faultless.
When the methods of inference have failed, one should clear the matter by means of divine ordeals;
the divine ordeal is recorded as being ninefold, beginning with the balance (dhaṭa) and ending with the sacred law (dharmaja).
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation (kośa);
the sixth is said to be rice grains, and the seventh is the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka).
The eighth is called Kāla, and likewise the ninth is Dharmaka;
all these have been declared by the Self-Existent One as being attained through divine means.
[The Divine Arrangement] Since these [rules] were established by the high-souled gods for the sake of difficult matters,
I shall state them in their general outline for the purification of doubtful points.
These are applied in their proper sequence according to place, time, purpose, and number.
According to the sequence of offenses and with the intention of declaring what is right or wrong,
these should be administered according to the rule declared in the scriptures, and not otherwise.
In matters such as debts and the like, when there is a mutual disagreement,
a surety endowed with the value of the property should be provided, taking into account the status of the person involved.
For the sake of worldly transaction, this designation has been declared on earth:
a coin made from a karṣa of copper is to be known as a kārṣika paṇa.
Four *niṣkas* of gold are one *kārṣika*; a *paṇa* is made of copper.
A coin (*mudrā*) struck from a *karṣa* of copper should be known as a *kārṣika-paṇa*.
That very [unit] is called an *āndrikā*; four of those are a *dhānakā*.
Twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*, which is indeed what is known as a *dīnāra*.
A fine of one thousand kārṣāpaṇas is the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that again is recorded as the lowest.
The balance is to be administered to the Brāhmaṇa, fire to the Kṣatriya;
water is to be administered to the Vaiśya, and poison indeed to the Śūdra.
The treasury of all [the Vedas] is declared by the wise to be common to them all.
Witnesses may fall into discord due to affection, anger, or greed;
however, no such discord ever arises regarding a divine ordeal administered according to the prescribed rule.
The divine ordeal should be administered according to the prescribed rule by those expert in divine trials;
if it is administered contrary to what has been prescribed, it is as if not administered at all regarding the proof of the matter to be established.
Those gifts given at an improper place or time, or those made by outsiders, undoubtedly cause deviation from the true goals in this world; of this there is no doubt.
The ordeal should be administered to the accused by those experts in ordeals;
one party may choose the ordeal according to their preference, while the other must submit his head to it.
One may administer the ordeal even without a formal charge in cases of treason against the king or other grave sins;
the administration of ordeals is declared [to be permissible] elsewhere than by the king's command.
No one should thus subject an accuser to ordeals.

Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.2) p.83 [Celestial Deities] Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.19: Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Between Deveśa and Īśāna is the path of the Ādityas:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga.
Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth;
after him Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, who, though born last, is not the least.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed by their names.
To the western part of Agni, they know to be the abode of the Rudras:
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, and the highly illustrious Girīśa.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and Aprajita.
Bhuvanādhiśvara, Kapālī the lord of the people,
Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhaga— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
Between the lord of the pretas and the rākṣasa, one should arrange the station of the Mothers:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā together with her attendants;
they know the abode of Gaṇeśa to be in the northern part of Nirṛti.
To the north of Varuṇa’s region, the abode of the Maruts is said to be located.
[There dwell] Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and likewise Māruta.
Regarding the number of divine substances:
"The number of rays, rooted in goats, was proclaimed by Manu;
that [scale] ending with the *kārṣāpaṇa* should be employed in divine ordeals, and one should administer it accordingly. (Br̥h. 1.8.28)
When a thousand *paṇas* have been stolen, poison is the ordeal;

when three-quarters [of a thousand] have been stolen, fire; when two-quarters [of a thousand] have been stolen, water; and when half [of a thousand] have been stolen, the balance should always be administered.
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], a heated māṣaka coin must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains are to be given, and for half of that (one hundred and fifty), the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) is prescribed.
When a hundred [coins] have been lost or stolen, a purification by means of dharma must be administered;
the members of the court must diligently provide a ploughshare for the thief of the cow.
Or, upon the destruction of half a *yava*, there is the destruction of its half-measure of rice;
and when half of that, and then half of that again, have been destroyed, the worldly practice is considered to apply.
The vehicles and weapons of the virtuous, as well as cattle, seeds, and gold; the feet of the gods and Brahmins, and the heads of one’s sons and wife. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.4, Śapathavidhi)
These oaths have been declared as always easy to perform for minor matters;
however, in cases of violent crimes and grave accusations, they say that divine ordeals are the means of purification.
One should say "Speak! to a Brahmin; "Speak the truth! to a Kshatriya;
with [the threat of] cows, grain, and gold to a Vaishya; and with all [possible] sins to a Shudra.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by [the truth of] the Vedas; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons;
cowherds, merchants, artisans, and bards, as well as servants and usurers, one should treat like Śūdras. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.8.36)
Those who have strayed from their own duties and subsist on the alms of others,
yet still desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them as one would a Śūdra.
Each person should be made to swear separately by oaths corresponding to their respective social classes.
In matters concerning women, at weddings, regarding cattle, fuel,
and the protection of Brahmins, there is no sin in taking an oath.
Witnesses must give their testimony within the assembly and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in matters concerning immovable property.
If there is a killing of living beings, one should cause the testimony to be declared in the presence of the corpse;
in its absence, however, in the presence of a identifying mark, but one should not cause it to be contested otherwise.
Witnesses who have arrived at the place of dispute must not, unless asked or appointed, speak the truth with effort regarding the testimony.
The testimony of those witnesses, which is free from defects, should be accepted as it was spontaneously spoken;
once the witnesses have been questioned by the king, they should not be interrogated again and again.
For witnesses, members of the court, and those who have fallen from their status, there is no rule for returning to their former state.
Likewise, the seven ṛṣis, Indra, and others whose wealth is their austerity,
remained unperturbed and swore an oath for the sake of Puṣkara and for mutual purification.
Within seven days, or within two weeks, no misfortune caused by kings or fate shall occur;
one becomes pure through oaths regarding kinsmen, sapindas, and wealth.
In the absence of any human evidence whatsoever, a decision must be reached through divine means alone;
however, when witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid recourse to divine ordeals.
Thus, the number for those of inferior status is prescribed; for those of middling status, it is remembered as double that;
and for those of superior status, it should be calculated by the examiners as fourfold.
[The Procedure for the Balance (Dhaṭa)] [p.87] If the accused, when weighed on the balance, is found to have decreased in weight, he shall suffer loss;
but if he is equal to his previous weight, or if he has increased in weight, he shall be the victor. // Brh_1,8.49 //
In the event of the breaking of the sling or the snapping of the axle, the king shall provide a new sling;
the witnesses should be eminent Brahmins who speak according to what they have actually seen.
The king, however, should appoint kinsmen who are pure and free from greed;
the determination of purity or impurity is to be understood according to their testimony.
In the case of the breaking of the armpit-strap, the failure of the balance-beam, or likewise of the *dhaṭa* and *karkaṭa*,
as well as upon the snapping of the cord or the breaking of the axle, one shall incur impurity in the same manner.
[The Procedure for the Fire Sacrifice] I shall proclaim the procedure for the fire sacrifice exactly as it is enjoined by the rules.
One should cause eight mandalas to be made in front, and likewise a ninth.
The first mandala belongs to Agni; the second is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity; and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth is dedicated to Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity; and the eighth has all the suns as its deity.
That which is the ninth, situated in front, they know to be the great earthly [element];
it should be made with cow-dung and saturated with water overnight.
They say that the distance between one mandala and the next is thirty-two finger-breadths;
however, the mandala should be made by the practitioner according to the measure of his own even footstep.
[The Procedure for Water] From the point where an arrow was shot, a youth endowed with speed should go with his utmost power to where that middle arrow has fallen. // Brh_1,8.58 //
Then another man of similar appearance, taking up a middle-sized arrow,
should return with speed from the direction where that first man had gone.
But when the arrow-retriever, having entered the water, does not see [the arrow] clearly while it is submerged within the water, then one should declare him pure.
When the middle arrow has been brought back and his body is found submerged [in water], he attains purity;
otherwise, he would not be purified even if only one limb were seen,
whether it remains in its original place or has moved elsewhere, provided that he was previously placed [there].
Having cast the man into the waters, one should discharge three arrows;
however, a wise man should not shoot them when a strong wind is blowing violently.
And on uneven ground, crowded with trees and stumps, and filled with grass, shrubs, creepers, vines, mud, and stones. // Brh_1.8.63 //

He by whom poison administered according to the prescribed rite has been digested without the use of mantras or medicines shall be considered pure; otherwise, however, he shall be punished and made to pay that wealth.
He whose loss of sons, wife, and wealth does not occur within seven days or fourteen days shall be pure; of this there is no doubt.
[The Procedure for the Vessel (Kośavidhi):
Whatever food the accused person has eaten, that very same quantity should be washed and made to drink from three handfuls of that water. Brh_1.8.66.
The king should cause the goods to be moved through that place while guarded by his own men for three or five nights, out of suspicion of trickery.

In cases of a great accusation, in matters lacking righteousness, against an ungrateful person, a contemptible eunuch, an atheist, or one whose guilt has been witnessed, one should reject the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna).
One should always avoid divine [medicines] for men afflicted by diseases; however,
one should not employ rice-grains for those among the people suffering from diseases of the mouth.
Fasting during a solar eclipse, one who is pure should eat rice grains;
he becomes purified by spitting out white [grains], but if the opposite occurs, he incurs sin.
Where blood is seen, and the jaw and palate waste away,
and whose body trembles— that one should be designated as impure.
Free from fear, he should draw out a heated bean from the well-heated oil or ghee by joining his thumb and finger, having called upon Truth.
Having taken cow's ghee in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even clay, one who is pure should heat it over a fire.
One should cast into it a very beautiful ring made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, which has been washed once with water.
In water abounding with whirling whirlpools and waves, which is beyond the reach of the touch of the nails,
one should test for the presence of a *caruka* (a small fish) by means of a moist leaf, noting whether it makes a sound.
Then, one should consecrate that [ghee] once with this mantra:
"O ghee, you are the supreme purifier and nectar in sacrificial rites."
"O purifier, burn away his evil; O cool one as snow, become pure!
Then, when he has fasted, bathed, and approached wearing wet clothes, one should have him take that ring, likewise placed within clarified butter."
Then the examiners should examine his ring finger;
he who can shake the tip of the hand without a blister arising becomes pure according to dharma, just as the word of the Grandfather [Brahmā] declares.
[A rule concerning the ordeal of the plowshare:
An iron plowshare weighing twelve palas, when heated, is called a *phāla*.
If it remains unburnt, one attains purification; otherwise, however, one is defeated.
It should be eight finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide;
if it becomes the color of fire and the thief licks it once with his tongue and is not burned, he attains purification, but otherwise he fails.
The members of the court must diligently provide the ploughshare for the object of the investigation;
these [ordeals] are to be used in major charges when the accuser has placed his head [as a stake].

[The Ritual for Distinguishing Dharma and Adharma] Dharma and adharma, white and black respectively, should be written upon two leaves with mantras such as those for the gift of life, and with Sāman chants beginning with the Gāyatrī. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.8.12)
Having addressed [the image], one should worship it with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the two [images] should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made those two equal, they should be placed in the vessel unobserved;
then, one should take a single lump from the vessel without delay.
When the law is upheld, he shall be pure and worthy of honor by the examiners;
but when unrighteousness is upheld, he is to be punished or even banished.
One should draw both dharma and adharma, white and black respectively, upon a birch-bark scroll;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship them with perfumes and garlands.
Dharma is white-flowered, while adharma is the wearer of black flowers;
having prepared them in this manner and smeared them, one should place those [flowers] upon the two balls.
Then, two equal-sized balls should be made either from cow-dung or from clay;
they should be placed in an undamaged earthen vessel and remain unobserved.
In a clean place that has been smeared [with cow dung], in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he should then worship the gods and the world-protectors (lokapālas) as before.
Preceded by the invocation of Dharma, one should write a written pledge as follows:
"If I am free from sin, may Dharma come into my hand."
When accused, he should take one of the two without delay;
if he takes the dharma, there shall be purification, but if he takes the adharma, he is defeated.
Reflecting in this manner, the king does not fall away from dharma or artha.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.9. The Method of Determination] By means of dharma, by legal procedure, by conduct, and by the king's command.
The determination of a doubtful matter has been declared to be of four kinds.
Each one of these has been declared by the wise to be of two kinds according to the distinction of their actions;
and one should determine the punishment in accordance with the offense.
Having properly deliberated upon the matter and determined it through reasoning,
and having examined it by means of oaths— that is to be known as the judicial determination of dharma.
Where the defendant admits [the claim], that is a legal decision;
a decision thoroughly purified by ordeals is declared to be a correct one.
That discourse which is determined by valid means of knowledge is called the first; the second is proclaimed as that which lacks a reply due to quibbling over words.
Conduct determined by inference is so described;
however, the third type is cited by those learned in the scriptures as being based on local custom.
But when there is equality of the means of proof, the king’s command is recorded as the final decision;
this is proclaimed as the fourth case, provided it does not conflict with the scriptures or the members of the court.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, a rule that is supported by reason is considered authoritative.
Except for killing, there is never any punishment for a Brahmin;
Brahmins and cows are not to be slain—this is the Vedic tradition in this world.
Even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), a Brahmin does not deserve corporal punishment;
the king should instead impose banishment, branding, and shaving his head.
And those who have committed great offenses, he should punish with the penalty of death.

For a very slight offense, there shall be punishment by word or the "fie" reprimand; for the first degree of violence, the same; but for the middle and highest degrees, half the penalty is prescribed, as well as imprisonment for treason against the king.

One who desires his own welfare should either banish or even execute a person who has committed a great sin (mahāpātaka), whether the offense was committed individually or collectively against a single person.
One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on these wretched men!
And one should punish with fines those men who are litigious or hostile.
Father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, or domestic priest— there is no one who,
having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king.
Sacrificial priests, domestic chaplains, ministers, sons, kinsmen,
and relatives who have deviated from dharma should be punished by kings or banished from the city.
One should punish gurus, domestic priests, and those worthy of honor solely with the rod of speech;
other disputants, however, one should punish with reproach and fines.
Likewise, those born in the inverse order and the lowest castes are remembered as the impurities among men;
they are to be executed for the offense of violating a Brahmin, but never shall a fine be imposed upon them.
A man deserving of death shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
but one deserving of mutilation of a limb shall pay half that amount, while one deserving of a bite [from a dog] shall pay half of that again.
"Beating, binding, and likewise the provision of coarse food—this indeed is the punishment for a Śūdra; there is no monetary fine, says Bṛhaspati. (Br̥haspati Smr̥ti 1.9.20)
One is declared a victor in the world by virtue of maintaining one's proposition, through devotion, by honoring the judge and others,
and by the issuance of the document of victory.

A debate is considered lost by one who flees, by one who fails to reach a conclusion, by one who relies on the support of another's position, or by one who is inferior; it is not lost for one who has been defeated solely by his own words.
But if one does not find satisfaction even when the facts have been determined by the family and others,
the king, having investigated that person's actions, should overturn a wrongful decision.
Having reached a decision together with many Brahmins who have mastered the scriptures,
he should punish the members of the previous court along with the victorious party if they are found guilty.
And a punishment corresponding to the offense has been prescribed here;
one who is defeated by means of witnesses, documents, inference, or properly by ordeal [is to be punished].
He who does not give the prescribed gift shall be banished from that city.
For a Brahmin, no other punishment than branding on the forehead is ordained;
even if he is guilty of a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), a Brahmin does not deserve corporal death. The king should instead impose banishment, branding, and the shaving of the head.
Everything he does—whether gain or loss, decline or rise—is authoritative;
whether in his own country or abroad, no independence shall contradict it.

But he who is appointed by his master to deny the receipt of wealth for the purposes of lending at interest, agriculture, or trade, is known as one to whom the matter has been entrusted (nisṛṣṭārtha).
A king must diligently investigate matters that are subject to doubt;
in such cases, three parties are benefited while the loss falls upon one alone.
The victor obtains wealth and honor; the defeated one receives discipline and restraint.
Through victory, the king, the donor, the self-controlled man, and the court members all attain merit.
Thus, by carrying out the decisions and protections ordained by the scriptures, a king,
having spread his fame throughout the world, shall become equal to Mahendra.
By determining legal cases through witnesses, documents, and inference,
a king spreads his fame here on earth and attains the world of the Sun.
When a king thus understands the definitive conclusion regarding the sacrifice,
he attains glory in this world and goes to the same realm as Śakra.
This legal procedure is proclaimed as being accompanied by the division of the subject matter.
Now hear the words that are the causes of dispute for him.

I shall explain in due order, according to their true nature, the matters concerning the non-payment of debts, those primarily involving deposits, and those ending with gambling and challenges, as well as the various types of legal procedures.

That which is to be given and that which is not to be given, by whom, where, and in what manner, as well as the rules for giving and receiving— this is known as the legal title of "Recovery of Debt" (ṛṇādāna).
The interest shall be one-eightieth part each month when there is a pledge;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred.
The creditor shall always repay the debt, whether it was taken as a pledge, a mortgage, or a collateral deposit, provided it is recorded in writing or witnessed by others.
Because it is taken from one who is despised and in distress by those who are free from hesitation,
it is therefore remembered as "kusīda" (usury), being fourfold or eightfold [in its interest].
In the Purāṇa, the offering... // Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.7 //
Growth is said to be fourfold, proclaimed as fivefold by others,
and described as sixfold by yet others; understand them according to their true nature.
There is bodily interest, periodic interest, and another known as compound interest;
likewise, there is interest on a loan for a specific purpose and interest on the use of collateral.
Interest is of four kinds: bodily (kāyikā), that which is connected to the labor (karmasaṃyuktā), that which is to be taken monthly (māsagrāhyā), and that which is periodic (kālikā);
furthermore, there is compound interest (vṛddher vṛddhiḥ), interest at a fixed rate (cakravṛddhiḥ), and that which is stipulated by the debtor himself (kāritā).
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (topknot interest);
it grows constantly like a topknot and ceases only upon the cutting off of the head.
However, whatever interest exceeding [the legal rate] has been stipulated by the debtor,
being contracted during a time of distress, that must always be paid as agreed;
otherwise, interest contracted in any other manner must never be paid under any circumstances.
It grows constantly like a crest, yet it ceases upon the cutting off of the head; likewise, when the root is struck, this growth of the crest is said to stop. Thus it is remembered.
For a householder, the acquisition of enjoyment from a field is proclaimed as *stoma* and *śada*.
They say there are four kinds of increase: bodily, the increase of enjoyments, that which is produced, and that which consists of the crest; while the fifth is the wheel-like increase.
The creditor may collect interest on the principal, as well as physical labor and the acquisition of property;
he may do so only until the principal has been cleared.
Interest on gold is said to be twofold; on cloth and base metals, threefold;
and on grain, as well as on beasts of burden and wool, it is declared to be fourfold.
The fivefold increase mentioned applies to vegetables; for seeds and wood-apples, it is recorded as sixfold;
for salt, sweat, and fresh meat, an eightfold increase is considered appropriate;
and for molasses and honey, when used over a long period, the same is declared.
The increase for all types of oils, liquors, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as for molasses and salt, is declared to be eightfold.
The profit on precious stones is fivefold; that on cotton is fourfold;
and the increase on woods such as sandalwood and the like shall be eightfold.
That interest which is taken as double the principal, or interest that continues to accumulate beyond that,
or interest upon interest once the debt is fully matured— such usury is censured.
The interest shall increase by one-eightieth part until the principal has doubled;
lent for seven years, it will reach this state without a doubt.
The growth of grass, wood, bricks, thread, leaven, leather, bone, armor,
weapons, flowers, and fruits does not cease.
The interest on gold, grain, and clothing is two, three, and four times the principal respectively;
that on ghee is eightfold, and on copper and other metals it is fourfold.
The creditor may collect the increase on the principal, as well as the bodily labor and the profit from the enjoyment [of the collateral],
only so long as the principal has not been cleared.
The others [the qualities] increase gradually by increments of one quarter.
In all disputes concerning property, one does not fail through verbal deception;
even if punished for seizing another's wife, land, or a deposit, one does not lose the property itself.
One should always act with equal interest, but that which is unequal ceases.
[The Increase of Wealth] Listen to the interest declared by Vasiṣṭha for a moneylender: five māṣas on twenty; thus the law is not violated. (Br̥had-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.4) 28.
Listen to the interest proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha regarding a usurer:
it is five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; in this way, the dharma is not lost.
A māṣa is proclaimed to be one-twentieth of a pala.
In that case, however, whatever man shows indifference toward this [matter],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
Whatever one may obtain for the sake of accomplishing the business of the community, or upon being presented by kings and others, that shall be shared equally among all.
Likewise, among those related by lineage and others, this is their eternal law:
[to pay] a debt acquired through efforts, or one protected [from creditors], or one contracted for the sake of the community.
Even if he remains in his own country, he who does not pay when asked repeatedly shall,
even against his will, pay the interest stipulated by the court.
Whether it be for six months or for a month, the property should be divided according to their respective shares;
or it should be given away to those who are destitute, the elderly, the distressed, women, children, the sick, and the diseased.
After three seasons, one may recover the principal along with interest;
in such cases as these, an eightieth part [of the principal] is intended as the rate of interest.
That which does not flow out [as interest] would be like a creditor who remains with only his principal;
even when there is an increase beyond double, the king should settle the case regarding those whose debts are time-bound, by means of those who know the true principles of legal procedure.
But a pledge is enjoyed only so long as it is not returned.
A pledge (ādhi) is defined as a bond, and it is said to be of four kinds:
movable and immovable, as well as that which is to be guarded (gopya) and that which is to be enjoyed (bhogya).

Whether it be spontaneous, for a fixed period, recorded in writing, or witnessed by others—in such cases of debt where no interest has been settled, the creditor may act when the stipulated time limit has expired. // Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.10.39 //
If one consumes a pledge out of greed, that profit shall not be recovered;
it must be protected like a deposit, for interest is lost if it is squandered.
And in the event of damage caused by the king or fate, just as the pledge may be lost, so too the creditor shall cause the pledge to be returned; otherwise, he shall pay the debt along with interest.
Whatever is to be given by one who has been placed under arrest may be recovered through a painting or by means of a written document;
however, when the object is not in hand, the entire amount of the bond shall not be made to be paid against his will.
And when the enjoyment has ended and the property has become worthless, a loss of the principal occurs;
in that case, the high value is lost, and one should satisfy the debtor.
When a single field is given as a pledge to two parties at the same time,
it shall belong to the one who first takes possession of it.
When two [items] are presented at the same time, the procedure for giving and selling should be equal; that is the rule proclaimed.
When a mortgage, sale,
or gift is executed through a single deed involving witnesses and a written instrument, that document is the means of proof in such a case.
Kātyāyana declared that what is not specified, what is specified, and what is distinguished in one place— among these, that which is written with specific detail is superior.
When gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge, provided he has waited for two weeks.
If the debtor provides collateral during that interval, he may obtain the pledge;
once the full term has elapsed along with the accrued interest, he shall become the owner of the pledge.
However, if ten days have not yet passed, the debtor is entitled to redeem it.
When the value of a pledge for use has doubled, or when the stipulated time has expired according to the rule,
it should be announced to the debtor's family and may immediately thereafter be enjoyed [by the creditor].
When gold has doubled [in interest] or when the debtor has disappeared, the creditor,
having seized that man's property, may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
Or he may keep it for ten days in the presence of the public after its price has been paid;
thereafter, having received a deposit corresponding to the debt, he should relinquish it.
If a debtor does not enjoy his own property, nor take it back, nor present it as evidence,
and if the witness has died, the creditor's document is rendered useless.
House, cattle, shops, grain, livestock, women,
and vehicles likewise perish through neglect and fall into a state of worthlessness.
Having secured his own property with men skilled in accounting, he should take possession of it only after it has been made known to its kinsmen and relatives; thus he would not commit an offense.
The eighteen-fold dispute, distinguished by its prior and subsequent stages, has been explained; now, understand correctly the various types of legal proceedings.
An action that was previously performed must be maintained in exactly that same way;
where it is performed otherwise, then there is a deviation of the action.
Having first abandoned the instrument [of proof], the creditor or the debtor may alter it by making it less or more; that is called a "variation in the action" (kriyābheda). // Brh_1.10.58 //
If one who has undertaken a fivefold vow accepts a gift consisting of two items, the latter— the fivefold vow—
is the authority regarding that gain, for it is the more firmly established.
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner,
that is to be understood as invalid according to the established rule in legal proceedings.
By means of each subsequent bond, the preceding bond becomes loosened;
whatever agreement is made later is more powerful than the one before.
When one has made a formal deposit or a pledge,
and then subsequently creates another pledge or sells it, the latter transaction therein is the stronger.
If a sale, a pledge, and a purchase were all performed on the same day,
and the ownership of all three is in doubt, how can there be a legal determination in that case?
In this matter, they should divide the three [shares] according to their respective portions;
both [the father and the mother] shall receive their shares in accordance with the purpose, and the recipient shall take one-third.
If that debt has been settled through equalization, then the creditor shall no longer share in the debtor's wealth,
nor shall the debtor be liable for the seizure of property, except by mutual agreement.
If a debtor, having paid the principal amount, should demand the release of the pledge, it must be released to him at that very moment; otherwise, the creditor becomes liable for a penalty.
When a field or other property has been enjoyed and the profit derived from it exceeds the principal,
and if that profit has entered into the principal, then the debtor shall recover the pledge.
If the creditor is absent, the debtor should deposit the money with the owner of the pledge and recover the pledge;
when the debtor has verbally agreed to give the field to the creditor, it is settled that the pledge must be released once the debt, together with interest, has been extinguished. // Brh_1.10.68 //
"But the pledge must be returned to me along with interest on the principal;
this is declared to be the righteous rule regarding the procedure for usury and pledges."
Where there is additional property, such as a house or field, which possesses excellence through its enjoyment,
there the debtor shall obtain a pledge and the creditor likewise [obtains] the debt.
When the excellence is complete, the equality of both is proclaimed;
however, when it is incomplete, the two should act toward each other according to their respective intentions.
If that [debt] were outstanding, then the creditor would not be entitled to his wealth,
and the debtor would not be liable for seizure, without the mutual consent of both parties.

In the treatises, the wise have observed four types of surety (*pratibhū*): for appearance, for trust, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of a debt or property. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.7)
One said, "I shall show it"; another spoke, "I am the giver of this wealth"; yet another said, "I shall obtain it. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.10.74)
But a surety for appearance who produces the person at the proper place and time,
or causes the debt to be paid there, shall not be liable, except in the case of loss caused by fate or the king.
The creditor shall grant time to the surety for the recovery of what is lost;
this period may be one fortnight, one month, or even one and a half months, depending on the location, the nature of the journey, or the form of the object.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
he shall pay that debt from his own property to the creditor if he fails to produce him.
The first two [types of witnesses], if they give false testimony, shall be made to pay the wealth claimed at that time;
however, in case of discrepancy, the latter two are liable for it, as are their sons in their absence.
A master, one obstructed by enemies, an official, one punished, those under suspicion, an heir, a mere friend, an outcaste, a resident pupil, one following the conduct of a king,
one free from passion, an ascetic, a pauper, a child, an elderly person, a woman, and a sick person are not eligible to be sureties.
In the event of the failure of the person for whom bail was posted, the guarantor must be made to pay again.
Indeed, the entire paternal debt must be paid even by the son together with [the father].
But he who, being pressed by the debtor, gives a surety, shall,
after three fortnights have passed, be entitled to receive double the amount of that debt.
If, out of a sense of propriety, those of dull intellect who have not been educated should pay a debt,
they shall by no means recover from that person the very purpose for which they were made to pay it.
They should not be excessively oppressed; the debt should be made to be paid little by little.
They should not be compelled to act as witnesses against themselves; this is the rule regarding sureties.
If the debtor has disappeared or died, the creditor shall present the document and cause a new deed of location to be executed,
specifying the time limit for its validity.
But the money that has been paid by a surety to the debtor without being requested shall not be made double and returned to the surety by the debtor.
A debtor who has acknowledged the debt should be made to pay it through conciliatory means such as persuasion,
or by means of legal pressure, threats, force, and the confinement of his residence. (Br̥haspati 1.10.87)
By means of messages from friends and relatives, and by following through with conciliatory speech, one should generally cause the debtor to pay; this is declared to be the righteous course.
But a Brahmin who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.

When a creditor, having brought back wealth requested under a pretext from a debtor, or having recovered items such as those held in trust, causes the debtor to pay, that is a fraudulent transaction (*sopadhi*).
When a debtor is brought to his own home and compelled to pay by means such as beating and other forceful measures, that is declared to be *balātkāra* (coercion).
A debtor should settle his account with a creditor even by means of labor;
one of equal or lower caste should pay immediately, but one of superior caste should pay it gradually.
One may compel a person of low birth who has fallen into ruin to perform labor for the sake of repaying a debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into ruin should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.
Having bound his wife, sons, and cattle, and having made them sit at the door,
where the debtor is forced to pay his own debt— that is called *ācarita*.
This law applies to one who has admitted the debt; however, if he denies it in court, he must be made to pay after proving his obligation by means of a document or witnesses.
"I shall give that which is rightfully to be given"—
when a debtor speaks thus, he is called a *kriyāvādī* (one who asserts the validity of the legal action).
One should never obstruct a proponent of action (kriyāvādī) regarding a doubtful matter;
however, one who restrains that which should not be restrained becomes liable to punishment according to the law.
That matter is declared to be "doubtful" in which both parties may have an error regarding the form, number, and so forth, or even regarding what should be given and what should not be given.
When the stipulated period has expired and the debt remains unpaid, the creditor may demand payment from the debtor;
or the debtor may retain the document under an agreement regarding compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
When compound interest (cakravṛddhi) is stipulated at more than double [the principal],
then the profit from the use of the property (bhogalābha) shall constitute the principal with interest for the creditors.
But he who proceeds with regard to a doubtful matter without having informed the king should be forcibly punished, and that legal matter shall not be settled.
Now it is stated by whom, where, and in what manner a debt— taken from the hand of another according to the rules of usury— is to be repaid, and when it is not to be repaid.
A debt contracted for a short period must be paid when requested;
once the term has expired, it must be repaid with interest, and in the absence of the father, it must be paid by the sons.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still burdened by debts,
then both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifices shall all belong to the owner of that wealth.
One should bring an indigent debtor to one's house and compel him to perform labor;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who owes money to a vintner or similar person should be made to pay back gradually.
Among those who take away wealth, a wife, or a son, the degree of debt increases in the order mentioned.
In their absence, the inheritance shall pass in due order to the other heirs entitled to the estate.
Debts to be paid:

A debt that has been received from a creditor on account of a religious duty (*dharma*) or other such grounds, but which the debtor does not record in writing, nor does he pay when it has come due—that debt shall accrue interest for him. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.10.108)
In such cases, one should cause even the sons to pay the debt of those who are diseased, insane, aged, or long absent from home, even while they are still living.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
this applies even if he is blind from birth, an outcast, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, or similar diseases.
Among those who have entered under a single roof, whoever is seen there shall be made to pay;
but for one who has gone abroad and died, the son shall receive the entire paternal share.
When the father has died, the son, being sent forth, shall provide everything under a single charge;
he shall never pay his father's share of the debt to others.
First, that which belongs to the father must be given, and afterwards that which belongs to oneself;
of these two, the paternal debt must always be paid first—thus is the law regarding debt.
A debt contracted by one's father must be paid by the sons once it has been proven; a debt of a grandfather must be paid equally [by all descendants], but that debt is not to be paid by the grandson.
Even one who is dependent for the sake of his family may conduct legal business, whether in his own country or abroad; a learned man shall not obstruct such a transaction.
Therefore, once a son is born, he should diligently strive to liberate his father from debt by renouncing his own self-interest, so that the father does not go to hell.
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, or whoever may have undertaken that burden.
One should not compel a son to pay a gift made under duress, a gift given in vain, a promise made out of lust or anger, a surety's obligation, or the remainder of a fine or a tax.
The husband of women belonging to the classes of vintners, hunters, washermen, cowherds, barbers,
and boatmen must be made to pay their debts incurred in the course of their husbands' business.
If a son who incurs debts or misappropriates property is also troublesome,
he shall likewise be the one to take the wife in the absence of an heir who takes the wealth.
Whatever has been borrowed for the sake of the family by an uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent,
the householder ought to repay that.
He who is appointed by his master to the management of income and expenditure,
as well as for money-lending, agriculture, and trade, is known as one to whom the funds have been entrusted (nisṛṣṭārtha).
He who, having taken goods such as a goat or other property, does not give them back to the owner,
is born in that person's house as a slave, a son, a wife, or a beast.
A debt incurred by a son must be cleared by the father if it was approved by him;
or he may pay it out of affection for his son, but otherwise he is not required to pay it.
... the debtor shall incur bondage;
however, having paid the principal amount together with the fruit-enjoyment for the full term, he shall be released.
If that [debt] were outstanding, then the creditor would not be entitled to his wealth,
nor would the debtor incur bondage, without the mutual consent of both parties.
When a debtor is summoned by a creditor for the purpose of recovering the debt,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount to the creditor that has been proven by the debtor.
But if a debtor denies the debt, yet it is proven by evidence,
the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor's due and a fine according to his capacity.
Those two who conceal an object to whatever extent, or who falsely claim it to be of whatever value,
being ignorant of the Dharma, must be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
If one who has received money through a legal agreement or other means does not record it in writing,
nor pays back what was advanced, that debt shall continue to accrue interest.
The non-payment of debts, beginning with the lending of money and ending with the methods of compelling payment, has been fully proclaimed.
Now, let the proper procedure for the deposit be heard. // Brh_1,11.1 //
[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.1 (Aupanidhika)] p.120) That which is given unannounced, kept apart, uncounted, not shown,
and marked with a seal, is known as *upanidhi* (a deposit). Br̥h 1.11.2.
[The Nature of Deposit (Nyāsa):
When property is placed in another's house out of fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or due to deception by heirs, that is proclaimed as a deposit (nyāsa). Brh_1,11.3.

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.3–4: The Method of Establishing] Having examined the location, the house, and the site itself, as well as the various qualities, truthfulness, purity, and the people of the vicinity, one should establish the treasure.

Furthermore, that [debt] is said to be of two kinds: one with a witness and the other otherwise. Likewise, in the case of its reversal, there should be a counter-transaction or a formal acknowledgment.
That [debt] is declared to be of two kinds: that given in public and that given in secret;
it must be protected like a son, for it perishes through neglect.
Whatever merit may come from giving gold, base metals, garments, and so forth, that same merit shall belong to one who protects a deposit,
as well as one who provides refuge to those who have sought it.
Just as there is guilt for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend,
so too is there guilt for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit.
One should not accept property placed in trust; its loss brings dishonor.
What has been accepted should be protected with effort, and what was requested only once should be returned.
Whatever has been established by which procedure, and whatever has been manifested by whom, that very thing must be given to him; it is not to be withheld, provided there is no subsequent obstacle.
[The legal settlement regarding the loss of a deposit:
If that [deposit] should be destroyed due to an act of God or the king,
then no fault is found in the case where it is [returned] together with the property of the receiver.
If the borrower, having taken a deposit with a specific distinction and through negligence,
should lose it, or if he should not return it when asked for it, he shall be made to pay it along with interest.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.7: His punishment for enjoyment:
Whoever accomplishes his own business by means of a deposited object shall be punished by the king and shall be made to pay that [object] along with interest. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.11.13)
If a person, having received a deposit, denies it— whether by means of witnesses or by oath— the judge,
having established the truth, shall cause him to pay back the deposit along with an equal amount as a fine.
Where a dispute arises regarding a secret deposit,
it is ordained that an ordeal is the means of proof for both parties.
If a gift was made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so too must be the taking back.
One would obtain nothing from the ocean if one were not to draw from it.
This same rule is declared to apply to property that has been deposited, borrowed, handed over by an artisan, pledged, as well as to one who has come for refuge.
But if a deposit is being refined over completed days,
the artisan, having kept it beyond that period, must pay for it even if it was destroyed by an act of God.
One who gives what has been requested and authorized by the owner does not commit an offense.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.12: Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner] Following the section on deposits, the sale by one who is not the owner was proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
Listen; I shall speak of that with particular care and detail.
One who takes possession of a deposit, a pledge, a bailment, what has been taken away,
what was borrowed, a security, or what was sold in secret or by a crowd, is declared to be a non-owner.
But for one who has purchased [an item] at a price after it was previously reported to the official,
no fault exists; however, there would be a thief due to fraudulent purchase.

[The definition of selling at a loss: That which is purchased inside the house, outside the village, at night, from an untrustworthy person, or for a low price— this should be known as selling at a loss (*upavikraya*).

[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.12.4–5: Determination of the Purity of the Purchaser] But if the former owner comes and claims that property, the price must be shown; from that, the purity of the purchaser shall be established.
Once the original price has been recovered, the purchaser can by no means be prosecuted;
for the dispute concerning the non-delivery of the goods ceases along with the recovery of the price.
Where the seller is produced [as a witness] and thus loses the legal case,
he shall pay the purchase price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner.
If one who is not the owner, being possessed by greed, covets another's property and subsequently fails to abandon it, he shall be compelled to pay a fine double the value of that property.

But in a debate lacking formal means of proof, O King, the monarch himself should make the decision based on the relative status of the individuals involved— whether they are equal, inferior, or superior.
Where a stolen item is found in a marketplace, having been recognized by royal officers, yet purchased from one whose source is unknown, or where the seller has died; ||| Brh_1,12.10 |||
The owner, having paid half the value, may take back his own property;
in that case, by legal proceeding, half of both [the value and the stolen goods] shall be forfeited.
Unrecognized purchase and likewise failure to protect—these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of wealth. // Brh_1,12.12 //
If it is discovered by royal officers that the object was obtained from a marketplace and seized during the day,
the wealthy purchaser incurs a fine.
But if one who has sold land does not establish the purchaser's possession, he shall restore that property to him;
otherwise, he incurs the punishment of a thief.
These two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of one's wealth:
that which, because its specific qualities are unknown, no price can be obtained for it.
In that case, the loss should be considered equal for both the purchaser and the one who denies ownership.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13] [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.1: Those Eligible for Joint Undertaking] (p.129) By those who are of noble birth, skillful, untiring, wise, and knowledgeable in coinage;
One should carry out affairs together with those who are pure, brave, and knowledgeable regarding income and expenditure.
Whatever portion of a thing is equal, excessive, or deficient, its decrease, expenditure, or increase will be of that same kind in that same place.
[Those who are ineligible:
Wise men should not perform activities such as trade together with those who are incapable, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.2–3)
But for those who carry out an investment with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to equal, deficient, or excessive shares.
If a partner has contributed a share that is equal, less, or more [than the others], he shall likewise bear the loss, perform the work, and receive the profit accordingly. // Brh_1,13.5 //
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.4–6: The Decision on Those Arguments] Those very same individuals are declared to be both the examiners and the witnesses for one another regarding a doubtful matter,
provided they are not subject to deception and are free from the influence of passion or hatred.
Whosoever among them is known to be a cheat in buying or selling must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies in every legal dispute.
[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.5; Decision regarding loss of goods:

When a loss or destruction occurs there due to acts of fate or the king, it is declared that this applies to all [the partners]; likewise, it should be apportioned according to their respective shares.
If, however, one who has not been specifically designated should, through negligence, cause the property to be lost while it is being withheld,
he alone must provide that which is to be given to all the partners.
Having given a sixth part to the king, they shall receive their own respective shares.
[The protector’s tenth part: Out of fear of gods and kings, let him protect [the people] according to his own ability;
having given him a tenth part, they may take another portion from that share. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.6, 11)
When a merchant arrives at a customs station, he should pay the toll as is appropriate;
he must not deviate from that, for this is proclaimed to be the tribute due to kings.
It is not so when a calamity from thieves, kings, or fire has arisen;
however, for one who protects [the goods] according to his own ability, a tenth part is prescribed as his share.
[The decision regarding the loss of one among those performing joint labor: When a certain merchant there should die through negligence,
his goods must be displayed by the appointed royal officers.
When someone arrives, that man who is the heir to the inheritance must demonstrate his ownership before others; only then does he deserve to receive it.
The king shall take a sixth part, as well as a ninth or a tenth;
from those of the Śūdra and Vaiśya castes, he may take a twentieth part from the Brāhmaṇa.

If, however, after three years, the owner does not come for it by any means whatsoever, then the king shall take that property; yet he should entrust the property belonging to a Brahmin to other Brahmins.
Thus, when anyone among those engaged in the performance of rites passes away,
his kinsman must perform the rite for him together with all the assistants.
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the consecration;
the Hotṛ the horse that chooses the *nivid*, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase.
Among all [the priests], the chief ones are entitled to half; others entitled to a half are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part.
They are declared to be of three kinds: those who are newcomers, those who have come down by succession, and likewise those who are self-appointed; one should conduct oneself toward them accordingly.
[The manner of joint action: If a single man, approved by many, should give wealth or cause a legal instrument (*karaṇa*) to be executed, it shall be considered as performed by all.
A debt to kinsmen, relatives, and friends may be paid even with collateral;
for others, it must likewise be accompanied by a guarantor, as well as a written document and witnesses.
Gold may be given at one's own will, but liquids and grain must be given with a time limit;
they should be given according to local custom, and likewise, they should be received in that same manner.
But that which is given by those assembled together must likewise be requested;
whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain.
[Regarding the collective performance of agricultural work: Listen; this procedure for farmers and others is now being stated. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.26)
A wise man should engage in agriculture together with those who are equal to him in terms of draft animals, drivers, seeds, and other agricultural implements and equipment.
Where a loss of the field occurs due to the failure of external seeds,
that [loss] must be borne by all those who live by agriculture.
One should carefully avoid a field that is on a mountain, near a city, or along a royal road, as well as one that is saline or infested with mice.

One who sows at the proper time in a field that is provided with ditches, situated near water, well-irrigated, and surrounded on all sides by other fields, enjoys the fruit of that excellent cultivation.
A wise farmer should not employ one who is emaciated, excessively old, low-born, diseased, a fugitive, one-eyed, or lame; he should instead employ an outsider.
This ancient law of the plowmen has thus been fully declared.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.12 Śilpins]:
"The wise have declared that a *śilpin* is one skilled in the arts who refines gold, base metals, thread, wood, stone, and leather. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.33)
Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively,
they shall receive wages according to their respective shares in accordance with the work performed.
Teachers who are skilled in training and masters of the arts shall receive one,
two, three, or four shares, respectively, in ascending order.
For those who, having joined together, construct a mansion, a temple, or even the furnishings for a righteous purpose,
the leader among them deserves two shares.
This indeed is the duty of dancers proclaimed by the virtuous:
one who knows the rhythm receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares.
[The Division of the Gain of Thieves] But that which has been recovered by thieves from a foreign land by the king’s command,
they shall divide among themselves according to their respective shares after giving one-sixth to the king. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.13.38)
Then, the chief shall receive four shares, the hero three shares, and the capable one shall take two shares; all the remaining sons shall have equal shares.
Thus has been declared in its entirety the expiation for collective offenses. Now,
the rules concerning what should not be given, what may be given, what has been given, and what has not been given shall be stated.
Common property, sons, wives, and so forth, one's entire estate, a deposit, what has been requested,
and likewise what has been promised to another— these eight kinds of things are traditionally held to be not to be given away.
That which remains after providing for one's family and the necessities of food and clothing should be given away;
otherwise, the gift of the donor becomes like poison following the taste of honey, and his merit is lost.
Whatever field is acquired from a garden or a house-site,
whether inherited from a father or obtained by oneself, that which is intended for distribution must be given away.

That which is given at one's own will, that which is acquired by oneself, a pledge according to the practice of pledging, and property obtained through marriage or inherited in succession— there is no restriction on giving any of these away.
That which is obtained as a dowry, inherited through succession, or acquired by valor,
when given with the permission of the wife, kinsmen, and the owner, attains validity.
Except for his entire estate and his home, whatever property he possesses for the maintenance of his family and other such purposes is his own to give; otherwise, it shall not be given.
Whether partitioned or unpartitioned, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for a single person has no power over it in regard to giving, mortgaging, or selling.
Wages, that which is given out of satisfaction, the price for goods, the bride-price, and that given to a benefactor;
what is given through faith, favor, or affection—this is remembered as the eightfold gift.
A gift given to a Śūdra is said to yield equal merit; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as yielding twice that;
to a Kṣatriya, the gift yields three times that; and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as yielding six times that.
For a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), the fine is one thousand; for a sub-teacher (upādhyāya), it is twice that;
for a teacher (ācārya), it should be known as threefold; and for those who have maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), it is twice that.
A thousandfold [merit] accrues for one who knows the Ātmika; it is infinite for a maintainer of the sacred fire (agnihotrin);
a hundred-thousandfold for a Soma-sacrificer; and it is infinite for a teacher of Brahman.
A woman should bestow her property upon her own kinsmen, avoiding a husband;
in the absence of kinsmen, however, it goes to her relatives, and in their absence, to the twice-born.
That which is given after my death shall not bring about [the status of] a true son;
because it has not been given by me now, it shall fall to the heir upon my death.

By those who are angry, elated, intoxicated, or afflicted; by children, the insane, or those tormented by fear; by the intoxicated, the very old, the arrogant, the deluded, or those overwhelmed by the force of grief.
Likewise, that which was given by Nandadatta is proclaimed by them as what was not given.
If a gift is given with the desire for personal gain, to an unworthy recipient while suspecting them to be worthy,
or for a purpose associated with unrighteousness, the owner shall recover it.
One who consumes what has not been given and likewise one who gives what should not be given shall be punished.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.15] Having explained what is not to be given and so forth, the rule concerning those who have been hired is now stated.
Having undertaken service, this state is declared first.
But when one, having undertaken service, does not perform it;
this is called the legal dispute concerning the failure to perform service after having undertaken it.
The non-payment of wages and the dispute between the owner and the keeper for that purpose are to be settled in due order; this, however, constitutes the threefold division of hired laborers.
However, she is described in many ways according to her birth and actions;
she is fourfold by way of knowledge, realization, desire, and wealth.
Furthermore, each one of these is further divided according to the difference in their functions.
The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
for the sake of that, one should perform service to the teacher as enjoined.
Craftsmanship is said to be the working of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as dancing and the like; having acquired that, he should perform work in the house of his guru.
He who enjoys another's wife should be known as one supported by a mare;
he should perform work for her husband, just as a man supported by food [performs service] for its provider.
One is said to be a bearer of many meanings, while another is a bearer of parts;
furthermore, the states of inferior, middling, and superior have been declared for all of them indeed.
Likewise, one who maintains [the practice] for a day, half a month, six months, three months,
or a year shall perform the prescribed action and obtain what has been declared.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages shall depend upon their work and be commensurate with their ability and devotion.
Among these, the soldier is the highest, the farmer is middling, and the porter is the lowest; such is the threefold classification of the hired laborer.
The warrior is declared the highest; the farmer is middling;
the burden-bearer is declared the lowest, as is the one who performs domestic labor.
The livelihood of those who subsist by agriculture and cattle-rearing is traditionally held to be of two kinds;
from the grain produced and likewise from milk, he shall obtain [his sustenance], of this there is no doubt.
For these four are declared to be performers of auspicious work:
the disciple, the resident pupil, the hired servant, and the laborer.
However, the remaining fifteen types of slaves are partakers of the lowest kind of work.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: indeed, the inauspicious and the auspicious.
The inauspicious is called the work of a slave; the auspicious is remembered as the work of a laborer.

The cleaning of the house door, impure places, the road, and the refuse heap; the touching of the limbs of those belonging to the household, and the taking up and discarding of food remnants, feces, and urine. // Brh_1,15.17 //
Furthermore, attending upon one's master while he is walking by using one's own limbs should be understood as impure action; other than that, it is pure.
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
his food may be eaten and gifts accepted from him, and he becomes esteemed by the virtuous.
Until the acquisition of ignorance [is dispelled], the disciple should serve his teacher with diligence;
his conduct toward the teacher’s wife and likewise toward the teacher’s son should be the same.
Having completed his studies and having presented the teacher’s fee to the guru, he returns home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
In this matter, the first four classes are not released from servitude except through the favor of their master; for them, slavery is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most contemptible of all these, and even he is not released from servitude.
A female slave who is married by a slave shall herself attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, since his own authority is dependent upon his master.
And those sons born of her who are the offspring of her husband or of another man—
if the progenitor is not the master, the lord shall not compel the female slave to work.
A plowman shall take a third or a fifth part as his wages for the work.
From the sharecropper, from the laborer, and from the plowman, you shall receive a fifth part as your share.
Furthermore, from a field where the crop has grown, he may take a third part, provided he has not been supported by them.
A servant should not commit even the slightest act of deceit against his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a dispute arises.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.1: Determination regarding the non-performance of work by one who has been hired.
If one who has been hired, being not ill, should out of pride fail to perform the work as directed, he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid. Br̥h 1.16.4.
When a hired laborer who has received wages does not perform the work,
if he is capable, he shall be made to pay a fine and twice that amount as wages.

One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double; for one who has not received wages, the punishment is equal [to the wages]. If wages have not been received, he should be made to pay the full amount, and the tools must be protected by the workers.
[The Punishment for Failing to Act on a Promise] He who, having made a promise, does not fulfill it, should be compelled by force to do so;
if he still does not perform that action, he shall incur a fine of twenty [paṇas]. (Br̥had-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.4) (Br̥had-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.7)
He shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid to him.
Whatever unwholesome action a servant performs while being directed by his master, the master incurs the fault for that purpose. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.5) (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.9)
[The occasions when the herdsman is free from fault:

Likewise, in the case of an act of God or the king, or when there is a general upheaval in the kingdom, if cattle are lost or killed, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.10)
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.7: The Master’s Rule on Punishment] If a master, once the work has been performed, does not pay the wages to the laborer,
he shall be compelled by the king to pay it, along with a proportionate fine.

[Br̥hadaranyaka Upaniṣad 1.16.8: Punishment for the Fault of the Herdsman] But if there is destruction [of the cattle] without fault on the part of the herdsman, punishment is ordained for the herdsman:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner.
If she is ill, exhausted, distracted, or occupied with royal business,
and yet does not come when invited, she is declared to be an unpraiseworthy "barren mare."
Likewise, one who is maintained by milk shall receive all of it on the eighth day;
he shall offer everything back in the evening. ... ... // Brh_1,16.14 //
Without making an effort to recover it, without raising a cry for help, and without informing his master,
the cowherd must bear the loss and pay a fine to the king.
One should protect [the property] from fear of worms, thieves, and tigers, as well as from caves and pits;
one should recover it by all possible means within the distance of a *krośa*, or report it to the owner.
One should turn cattle away from standing crops; however, if damage is done, two faults arise:

the owner shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], and the keeper deserves corporal punishment. Furthermore, for damage to a field with its roots consumed, the fine is one hundred paṇas along with the value of the crop.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.17] This indeed is proclaimed as the conduct for masters and servants. [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.17. For this is the duty well-expounded for masters and servants.
Now, learn in brief the exposition of consciousness.
Having summoned Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures, and maintainers of the sacred fire,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
The king should grant them house-sites with non-confiscable taxes,
and having recorded it in his own edicts, he should ensure they are made exempt.

They should perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), pacificatory (śāntika), and nourishing (pauṣṭika) rites according to the Purāṇas, as well as provide a definitive decision in cases of doubt.
For the sake of the village, the guild, or the corporation, an agreement and the performance of its terms shall be made;
it must be carried out in times of distress as well as in matters of dharma.
Fear of deceitful thieves and affliction are known to be common to all;
therefore, their pacification must be undertaken by everyone collectively, not by any single individual alone.
Having first established mutual trust through a deposit, a written contract, or neutral mediators, they should thereafter carry out their business affairs.
Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, modest, lazy, or timid;
those who are unfit for employment, as well as the greedy, the very old, and children— these should not be appointed as counselors in matters of state.
Those who are pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all tasks— these most excellent men should be appointed.
Two, three, or five persons who speak for the welfare of the community should be appointed;
their word must be carried out by the village, guilds, assemblies, and so forth.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.17.5: A Compact] The construction of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, ponds, and gardens;
