likewise, the rehabilitation of the destitute and the poor, and the performance of works of public utility.
"The building of a nest and its destruction must be performed by us in our respective portions;
as for this document that has been written, it is a righteous formal agreement."
Those who are capable must protect [the weak]; however, for one who is capable but violates [this duty], the punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
In that regard, whatever man creates a division or displays indifference [toward the teacher],
a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him.
But he who should injure common property, or insult one learned in the three Vedas, or obstruct a formal agreement or a ritual act, must be banished from that city.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as an assailant,
and one who hates a guild, a corporation, or the king, shall be swiftly banished from there.
The heads of families, guilds, and corporations residing in cities and fortresses shall impose verbal censure, fines, or banishment upon those who commit evil deeds.
The punishment and favor toward men performed by them according to their own duty must also be approved by the king, for they are traditionally regarded as his delegated agents.
For those who have become possessed by hatred might cause harm to even a single person.
Whenever a conflict arises between the assemblies and their leaders,
the king should investigate the matter and establish them upon his own path.
... whoever is capable of violating [this rule], his punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
Those who, having come together and made a single unit, seize what is due to the king,
as well as merchants who flee, shall be made to pay eightfold.
Whatever may be obtained from that, it shall be shared equally among all;
whether it be for six months or for one month, it must be divided according to their respective shares.
Or it should be given to those who are destitute, the aged, the blind, women, children, the afflicted, and the sick, as well as to those seeking offspring; this is the eternal law.
Whether acquired through exertion, protected, staked for the sake of the community,
or obtained through the favor of the king— it is equal for all.
Thus, this determination of customary conduct has been stated in brief regarding the rescission of purchase and sale.
Let this dispute arising from buying and selling be heard.
Two types of goods are declared: the movable and the immovable. At the time of purchase, the term "merchandise" (paṇya) is traditionally applied to both of them.
[The punishment for selling defective goods:
An unwise man who, knowing a commodity to be defective, sells it,
shall be made to pay double that very amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.18.3–4: Things to be Avoided] What has been sold by one who is intoxicated or insane, for a low price, or out of fear;
or what has been relinquished by one who is not independent or is deluded—this must be returned to him.
But he who, having sold an item into the hand of one person, delivers it to another,
shall be made to pay double that amount as a fine, and an equal amount as a penalty.
The periods for examination are ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month;
these apply respectively to seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.18.4–6)
Therefore, if any defect or flaw should arise in the goods prior to this [time],
it must be returned to the seller, and the buyer shall recover his purchase price.
But that which was purchased without being examined, and later discovered to be defective, must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
One should personally examine the merchandise and show it to others;
having accepted what has been examined and approved by many, one should not reject it again.
The examination of horses, silver, gold, grain, iron, goats, clothing, and products made of leather and wood shall last for one day.
The valuation of horses, mares, and mules shall be determined according to the authoritative texts;
for goods situated in the marketplace, it shall be by the king's command; and for cattle and land, it shall be by the mutual consent of both parties.
In the distribution and exchange of both fields,
the accomplishment of their purpose will come about through the mindfulness cultivated by those two.
If they are present, those who are designated as relatives by the purchaser should be questioned;
otherwise, if the rite has been performed, one should then show the consent of the relatives.
The purchase of immovable property is accepted only when based on the testimony of relatives and others;
otherwise, if there should be a purchase, [the validity] depends on a period of three fortnights in another village.
Full brothers, sapindas, those related by water (sodakas), and those of the same lineage (gotra); neighbors and creditors—these seven are considered the sources from whom [the heirs] are to be taken.
If a price is paid that is either excessive or deficient, it is considered improper for the price; however, once the purchase is finalized, it cannot be annulled even after hundreds of years.
Bṛhaspati states that in all sales, one should record the wells, trees, and so forth, as well as water channels and whatever else exists, including other features.

They say that a field endowed with such qualities, ripened crops, a tree or fruit fit for enjoyment, a well, a pond, or an elevated house belong to the buyer, and not to the seller. (Br̥had-yogiyājñavalkya Smr̥ti 1.18.18)
An exchange has been made with those who are intoxicated, deluded, ignorant, distressed, or confused;
whatever was given at an improper price, all of that shall be rescinded.
Relatives, neighbors, and creditors who have gone outside the village at the time of purchase do not deserve to object to the sale once three fortnights have passed in succession.
Or else, one may obtain that [result] after three fortnights or after three months.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.19, the Discourse on Boundaries] This rule has been set forth regarding disputes over purchase and sale.
Learn now the rules regarding the boundaries of villages, fields, houses, and so forth.
And they should establish boundary trees, such as the *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka*;
as well as the *śālmalī*, *śāla*, and *tāla* trees, and other trees that produce milky sap.
By means of thickets, various bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and level ground,
as well as reeds and clusters of *kubjaka* shrubs, the boundary is not lost.
Ponds, wells, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
Having granted a field, the king shall demarcate it as being supervised by the four classes of physicians, merchants, village officials, the village headman, and the proprietor’s men.

If a Śūdra should be the leader, one should adorn him with the ornament of impotence, smear his face with the ashes of a corpse, make five finger-marks on his chest with the blood of a sacrificial animal, fasten intestines around his neck, and with his own hand, he should place a clod of earth from a boundary upon his head.
At the time of settling [the village], the determination of the boundary must be made;
it should be marked by both public and secret signs to remove all doubt.
By their very nature, without contradiction, these substances are imperishable:
ponds, wells, tanks, sacred shrines, groves, and temples.
High ground, low ground, the course of a river, reeds, thickets, mountains, and so forth—
these visible markers one should always cause to be established at the boundary.
If there should be doubt even when signs are observed,
the determination of the boundary in a dispute must depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses. (Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.19.10)
And in the absence of witnesses, four inhabitants living on the outskirts of the village boundary,
being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
But in the absence of neighboring villagers who are witnesses to the boundary,
he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forest.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest.
The king shall establish according to dharma whatever boundary markers those [witnesses] declare when questioned regarding the junctions of the borders between two villages.
Placing their heads upon the earth, wearing garlands and red garments,
and being sworn by their respective meritorious deeds, they shall speak the truth.
One should thus establish the boundary and record all those [markers] by name;
one should always cause these visible signs to be made at the boundary.
Likewise, he should establish other concealed signs which the earth shall not consume;
he should also cause other boundary markers to be made that serve as parasols.
Seeing the constant reversals in the world regarding the knowledge of boundaries—
such as bones in a cemetery, cow-hair, ashes, and skull fragments— [one should realize the nature of existence].
He should cause cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel,
and sand to be placed in the junctions of the boundary so that they remain hidden from view.
Dried cow dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones, potsherds,
sand, bricks, cow hair, cotton seeds, bones, and ashes.
Having cast these into jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries of the boundary-line, with their identifying marks clearly displayed with great care;
thereafter, one should diligently show them to children of tender age.
And likewise, they should show those children [the boundary] when they have reached old age;
in this way, through knowledge passed down in succession, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
By the power of fortune or misfortune, it effects the taking away or the giving of gifts to men;
just as on one side there is the collapse of the earth's slope, while on the other there is its stability.
One should not displace the boundary that has been established along the riverbank;
when the land is cut off after crossing a field containing crops, it becomes [the property of] the earth.

The owner of the field shall recover that [land] which was seized by the king through anger or greed, either by force or by legal means, just as water flows back into its course from a river's current.
In disputes concerning houses and fields, the decision is reached based on the testimony of neighbors,
as well as those who are the heads of city or village corporations and the most venerable men.
Plowmen, artisans, laborers, cowherds, hunters, those who live by gathering gleanings, root-diggers, fishermen, those who breach irrigation channels, and those who cause harm; // Brh_1,19.27 //
Those who know the title deed, the means of proof, the possession, the desire, the name,
and the characteristics of the portion of land— they are the witnesses in this matter.
But that gift which has been taken away by a king through anger, greed, deceit, or even by legal means, shall not attain success even if given by him with satisfaction.

If land that was seized from someone is given to another who possesses superior virtues, one must never displace that person while he enjoys the land, even if it was originally held without legal title.
Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination regarding the boundary;
they shall point out hidden deposits, for that is the established rule as the authoritative proof.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons.
Even a single virtuous person, though lacking the outward marks of a knower, is honored by both [laypeople and renunciants] when he wears red garlands and garments and carries earth upon his head.
A man who is devoted to truth and observes a fast should point out the boundary.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
Those witnesses of truth who lead the case according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
This rule has been proclaimed for every stationary legal proceeding.
And those neighbors who have arisen from them and are situated in other regions are designated as the primary ones; they should be questioned in the determination of legal matters.
Whatever those who are free from malice, impartial, and of equal conduct may declare regarding a doubtful matter, that must be accepted as authoritative; in this way, dharma is not lost.
When land is acquired from another village and given to someone else,
the acquisition by men shall otherwise be considered as resulting from royal or divine causes.
Or in the case of a great river, how can there be deliberation by the king? That land which is abandoned by a river or granted by a king belongs to him alone;
otherwise, the acquisition of land by men arises from human effort or divine providence.
The decline, rise, and life of men are subject to the power of fate and the king;
therefore, at all times, one should not subvert what has been ordained by them.
Wherever a river is established as the boundary between two villages,
it effects the taking away or the giving [of land] to men according to their fortune or misfortune;
and by its fluctuation through decrease or increase, even if it is small, it deserves punishment for causing displacement.
The king shall establish clearly defined boundaries for a district of ten villages, a hundred villages, a thousand villages, or a hundred thousand villages, using various marks.
From the time of its construction, whatever house, shop, or other property was enjoyed by whomsoever, and to whatever extent and in whatever manner, that should not be altered for him.
Furthermore, one should not disturb the windows, the drainage channels, the turrets, the altars, or the courtyards and carriage-ways already established in a four-winged house.
One should not obstruct the girdle-closet, the window, the drain-pipe, or the site of the house; one who causes such damage shall be liable to pay a fine.
After the time of settling [the house], these [rites] should not be performed under any circumstances.
One should not construct a water-channel or a drainage ditch that extends into another person's house.
One should never, under any circumstances, construct a place for fire, a pit, or a receptacle for pouring out leftover water too close to another person's wall.
One should construct embankments for excrement, urine, and water, as well as fireplaces and pits,
leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the neighbor's wall.
That by which people and animals go and come without restraint is called the path of transmigration; it must not be obstructed by anyone.
He who, out of desire, creates a mixture [of castes], digs a pit, plants trees, or voids excrement there, shall be fined one *māṣaka*.
Having taken [the grain], he should transport it at the proper time for the purposes of protection and storage;
if he fails to do so, he must pay the owner half of the harvested yield.
If anyone, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
he shall be made to pay the rent to the owner and a fine equal to that amount to the king.
When [the fire] has long been extinguished, one should perform the tenth [offering]; likewise, when it is being drawn out, the eighth;
but when it is well-consecrated, the sixth should be performed, having prepared it according to the rule.
[Harshness of Speech] Harshness is traditionally held to be of two kinds: unpleasant speech and physical assault.
Each of these, moreover, is divided into three kinds; thus, self-restraint (dama) is said to possess three characteristics.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.20.1; Vākpāruṣya, threefold:
Insulting the laws of a region, family traditions, and so forth, or associating someone with sin without using material wealth—that is called the first type of verbal abuse.
Speaking of a minor offense related to sisters or brothers,
as well as harshness of speech, is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the middling verbal [sin].
The discourse on what is unfit to be eaten or drunk, the defilement by mortal sins,
harshness, and the intense act of causing a wound— these are declared to be the highest [forms of verbal abuse].
But when those of equal caste and qualities engage in verbal abuse with one another,
the prescribed punishment in the legal treatise is a fine of twelve and a half panas.
For those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly disabled, the punishment shall likewise be two kārṣāpaṇas.
For insulting someone of the same caste, the fine is twelve and a half paṇas;
for insulting someone of a lower caste, the fine is six paṇas and one kākiṇī.

In cases of mutual verbal abuse, the punishment for those who are equal is the same; however, for one who is inferior, it is double, and for one who is superior, it is declared to be greater— just as in the case of the blind or the lame.
One who insults a sister or other such relatives shall be fined fifty paṇas;
however, a Brāhmaṇa does not incur guilt for using harsh words against one who is deficient in merit.
By calling one who has fallen a "fallen person," or likewise by calling a thief a "thief," one incurs an equal fault through that speech. ... // Bṛhad-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.20.10 //
If a king unjustly administers instruction on dharma to Brahmins according to his own whims,
he should have boiling oil poured into his mouth and his ears.
If a Kṣatriya brings false accusations against a Brahmin, his fine shall be fifty;
likewise, for a Vaiśya it is twenty-five, and for a Śūdra it is twelve and a half.
This discipline has been prescribed for a Śūdra who is truthful and innocent;
however, even when one devoid of merit is harsh, a Brāhmaṇa should not commit an offense against him.
A Vaiśya who reviles a Kṣatriya should be made to pay a fine;
a Kṣatriya who insults a Vaiśya deserves half that amount as a disciplinary measure.
For a Kṣatriya who reviles a Śūdra, the fine is twenty-five [paṇas];
for one of high status, double that amount has been declared there by those learned in the scriptures.
A Śūdra who slanders a Vaiśya shall be made to pay the first fine;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle fine; and for a Brāhmaṇa, the highest amercement.
One who defames another by means of [false] accusations regarding country and so forth shall be made to pay twelve and a half paṇas;
one who, out of arrogance, joins another with a crime shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who imparts instruction in the Dharma should be accompanied by citations from the Vedas;
however, one who reviles Brahmins is to be punished by the cutting off of his tongue.
This punishment has been fully declared by me with respect to men;
it should be determined by the wise according to whether it is equal, less, or more [than the offense].
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.21] [Assault with a staff:
With hands, stones, or clubs; with ashes, mud, or dust.
And the use of weapons and implements of violence is called physical assault.
Whatever punishment is prescribed for one who has committed verbal abuse,
he shall be made to pay double that fine, except in the case of death.
When two persons strike each other with a staff, the punishment is declared to be equal;
however, the initiator and the one who persists in the assault shall be made to pay a higher fine.
If one who was previously insulted returns the insult, or one who was struck strikes back,
or a man kills an assassin, he incurs no guilt.
If a base person should insult a virtuous man through verbal abuse and the like, it is that very person whom the king should strike; he must not seek out the fault of the victim.
[First:
Assault] Throwing ashes and the like, as well as striking with the hand or other means, constitutes the first degree of assault; in this case, a fine of one *māṣa* shall be imposed.
This punishment has been declared for [violating] women of equal status and those who are superior;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, depending on the relative preeminence [of the woman].
When a stone, a brick, or a piece of wood is raised [to strike another], the first amercement shall be imposed;
likewise, for mutual striking with hands or feet, the fine shall be ten and twenty paṇas respectively.
In the case of two agitated parties engaged in a conflict of arms, a middling fine should be imposed; however,
when a blow has actually fallen at the appointed time, the wise should inflict a punishment proportionate to the act committed.
For striking with bricks, stones, or wood, the fine shall be two māṣas;
for drawing blood, the wise should impose double that penalty.
For piercing the skin, the first amercement is the punishment; for piercing the flesh, however, the middle;
for piercing the bone, it shall be the highest; but for killing with a blow, there is execution.

For cutting off the ears, nose, or hands, for breaking the teeth, or for piercing the bones, a middle fine shall be imposed; however, it shall be double in the case of those who have fallen from their caste.
For the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine shall be imposed; for their piercing, the middle fine is prescribed.
But the punishment for one who merely threatens has been prescribed according to the rules for physical assault;
if [the object] is actually taken, the fine is double that, and the royal penalty is even greater than that.
In cases of breaking a limb, causing pain, or likewise cutting off a part,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery and whatever was seized during the quarrel.
If one who has been struck in a secluded place is seen or heard to have been killed,
the killer should be identified either by inference or by an oath.
Whether inside a house or in a forest, wherever blood is seen at night where [a person] was beaten, one should not question witnesses there.
Someone, having made a mark upon himself, might attack another out of malice;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of excessive powers for the sake of determining the cause.
A man who, when reviled, reviles in return; when struck, strikes back;
or who kills one who has committed an offense, does not become innocent himself.
Likewise, those born in the inverse order and the lowest castes are remembered as the impurities of men;
they are to be executed for the offense of violating a Brahmin, and their wealth must never be confiscated.
He who causes oxen to work when they are exhausted, afflicted by hunger, or thirsty, or at an improper time,
shall be made to perform the expiation for killing a cow, or else be made to pay a fine.
He who initiates a quarrel shall be made to pay the expenses incurred and whatever was done for the sake of the dispute.
It has been declared by Manu that whichever limb of the twice-born a Śūdra strikes out in anger, that very limb of his shall be cut off.
Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret.
Through these [powers], they have been split asunder a thousandfold by the force of wisdom.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.22.1–2] Those who deal in light and darkness, thieves; those learned in the Vedas, physicians, and gamblers; members of an assembly, bribe-takers, and deceivers;
those who know the omens of fate, fortune-tellers, artisans, and forgers.
Those who do not perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, false witnesses, open thieves, and likewise those who live by deceit— these indeed are public thieves.
Those who break into houses at night, those who rob travelers, those who steal bipeds or quadrupeds,
those who lift up [goods from storage], and those who steal crops— these should be known as secret thieves.
[The Punishment for Them:

Those who are identified by royal officers through their associations and outward signs shall be made to restore what was stolen and be punished with penalties prescribed by the scriptures. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.22.2; 1.22.5)
The one who steals a pickpocket should be torn apart by the king’s men with pincers;
a stealer of grain should be made to pay ten times its value as a fine, and twice that amount as a penalty.
When the death of a single evildoer brings security to many, his killing bestows merit.
Likewise, O Dawn, one should hang a traveler from a tree by tying him around the neck.
For one who breaks a knuckle-joint, the king should have the offending finger cut off at the first offense;
at the second, both hands and feet; and at the third, he deserves the death penalty.
But that physician who, being ignorant of medicines and mantras and lacking knowledge of the true nature of disease,
takes wealth from the sick, should be punished like a thief.
The gambling must be conducted openly, and those who cheat at play shall be banished.
Those who play with false dice, the base, those who seize the wives of kings, astrologers, and deceivers— these gamblers are declared to be punishable by law.
Furthermore, a merchant who sells refined goods that are mixed with concealed defects shall be made to pay double the value of those goods, as well as a fine for the merchant equal to that amount.
Those members of the assembly who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes and those who deceive the person who trusts them— all of these must be banished.
Those who, out of greed for wealth, proclaim to people knowledge of astrology and portents without actually understanding them, should be restrained with great effort.
Those who display themselves as being endowed with the staff, deerskin, and other such emblems,
yet secretly injure men, are to be executed by the king's officers.
Those who, by means of refinement, bring an article of small value to a state of high value,
and who deceive women and children, shall be punished in proportion to the value of the object.
Those who manufacture artificial gold, pearls, coral, and the like,
shall be made by the king to pay the purchaser the value of the goods and a fine double that amount.
When neutral witnesses deceive one party out of affection, greed,
or other such motives, and when witnesses speak falsely, they shall be made to pay a fine double the amount in dispute.
Those who, through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, display some form of delusion or perform root-rites (mūlakarma) should be banished by the king.
One who breaks a joint, one who steals, and those who must be abandoned should then be impaled upon a stake;
likewise, a traveler caught at dawn should be bound by the neck and suspended from a tree.
Those who abduct human beings should be burned by the king with a fire of straw;
one who steals a cow should have his nose cut off, or, having been bound, he should be submerged in water.
For stealing more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for lesser amounts, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property must be returned to its owner.
One who steals grain shall be made to pay ten times its value as a fine, and double that amount as a penalty.
Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—
one who takes these without having asked permission deserves the amputation of the hand.
One who has committed theft, even if he possesses good conduct and Vedic study, shall suffer long in prison;
he must restore that wealth to its owner, and no penance is to be performed for him.
This has been declared for all thieves regarding the application of punishment.
Now, let the proper punishment for violence be heard.
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and both forms of harshness— these constitute the fourfold category of violence (sāhasa).
That [gift] is proclaimed to be of three kinds—inferior, middling, and superior.
In that regard, based on the material substance, the first, the best, and the middling [qualities] consist of self-restraint (dama).
The wise declare that these practices are to be avoided in the Kali age: the killing of foremost Brahmins who are aggressors by means of a righteous war.
One who destroys or steals the implements of a field, a boundary marker, or the roots, flowers, and fruits [of that field] shall be fined one hundred panas according to the gravity of the offense.
One who destroys livestock, clothing, food, drink,
or household utensils should be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas, as well as a penalty for theft.
For women, men, gold, gems, the property of gods or Brahmins,
silk, and other such superior articles, the fine shall be equal to their value.
Or rather, kings should impose double the fine in consideration of the person;
or the killer should be executed to prevent a recurrence of such incidents.
Violence is said to be of five kinds, among which killing is considered the most serious. Those who commit such acts should not be punished with fines; they must be executed with diligent effort.
Those who are open assassins as well as those who are assassins by stealth—
having identified them and having confiscated their wealth— they should be executed by various means of capital punishment.
Whether for the sake of gaining a friend or for the acquisition of wealth, a king who desires the welfare of the world must not release perpetrators of violence,
for they bring fear to all people.
If a king, out of greed or fear, does not punish those who act unjustly,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is deprived of his sovereignty.
That man who causes the death of others by means of confinement, fire, poison, or weapons,
motivated by anger or other such causes, is a perpetrator of violence (sāhasika).
[The Determination of the Lethal Blow in a Group Assault] Where many people, filled with rage, strike at one person,
he who delivers the blow to a vital organ (marmaprahāra) is declared to be the killer.
But he who strikes their vital points shall be made to pay the penalty as previously stated;
likewise the instigator, the accomplice, the one who points out the way,
the shelterer, the giver of weapons, and the giver of food to those who act unlawfully.
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction, one who is indifferent, one who is engaged in the task, one who speaks of faults, and one who approves [of them]. // Brh_1.23.16 //
In the slaying of an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor), the killer shall never incur sin;
one who causes the death of one approaching with the intent to destroy does not commit an offense. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.23.17)

He who does not kill an assassin— even one who is superior and endowed with good conduct and Vedic study when that assassin has reached the point of being slain— shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.

If one kills an assailant who has come with intent to harm, even if that assailant is born of a noble family and is devoted to Vedic study, he does not become a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan) by not killing him; by not killing him, he would indeed become a killer of an embryo.
Now, hear about the crime of robbery committed through rashness, born of anger and greed;
as well as the determination of the case when the perpetrator is not seen, based on the slight nature of the wound, the absence of a fatal injury, and the location of the vital spot with great care.
Having ascertained both his capability and his disposition through various signs, one should win him over.
But where a person is seen killed while the killer is not seen,
that [offender] should be identified by the king through the pursuit of past enmity.
But he who actually strikes them down shall be made to pay the penalty as previously stated;
the one who initiates the act and the one who assists him share the guilt, each receiving half of that penalty.
His neighbors, both those living next door and those further away, as well as his friends, enemies, and kinsmen,
should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
He may be identified by men through association with the wicked or by means of stolen goods and signs;
thus has been declared the method for discerning murderers and thieves.
But he who, having been apprehended on suspicion, does not proceed to fulfill that task, must be cleared by an oath;
this is the rule in all legal disputes.
One who is purified by divine means becomes pure and worthy; one who is impure deserves execution.
Through punishment and favor, the king’s fame and righteousness increase.
Harshness is said to be of two kinds, and violence (sāhasa) likewise has two characteristics.
Understand that the gathering of the roots of evil is threefold.
Two types [of union] are produced by the condition of physical strength, while the third is born of passion;
that, moreover, is said to be threefold: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is done against her will by one who is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted,
or by one who is speaking incoherently in private— that is considered an act committed by force.
When a union is brought about by bringing a woman to one's house under false pretenses or by administering intoxicants or magical charms, they know that to be a marriage contracted through fraud.
That which is produced by mutual passion for each other's eyes, by the dispatching of female messengers,
and by greed for beauty and wealth, should be known as arising from passion.
That [union] is further said to be threefold: the first, the middling, and the highest.
Gazing with a sidelong glance, laughter, and likewise the dispatching of a female messenger;
touching and the gathering of ornaments and garments—this is recorded as the first.
The sending of perfumes and garlands, incense on the road, clothing,
and private conversation— these they know as the middling means of winning over.
Sharing a bed and a seat, as well as playing, kissing, and embracing—
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is recorded as the middling means of winning over.
The sending of perfumes, garlands, fruits, food, drink, and clothing,
as well as conversing in private, they know to be the middling form of seduction.
And among these three types of punishment, the first, the middle, and the highest should be prescribed;
a more severe penalty should be applied to one who possesses greater wealth.
But a man who engages in conversation with another's wife in secret,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
One who desires the wealth of a co-wife shall take all of it;
moreover, having cut off her penis and testicles, he shall cause her to be paraded on a donkey.
But he who desires [another man's wife] through deception shall suffer a fine that takes away all his property;
having branded him with the mark of a female organ, he shall then be banished from the city.
A man who approaches a woman of lower caste in an assembly where he is superior to her should be disciplined; however, if he approaches a woman of higher caste, his execution must be carried out.

If a woman, having come to his house, should entice him with touching and other such acts and desire him there, she is to be punished; for the man, a fine equal to half that [of the woman] is prescribed.
One whose nose, lips, and ears have been cut off should be made to wander and be submerged in water,
or should be devoured by dogs in a place where many people are assembled.
But she who was enjoyed against her will, he should keep in his house under protection,
with soiled limbs, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on a mere morsel of food.
If she has had intercourse with an equal, he should cause her to perform an expiation consisting of either a Kṛcchra or a Parāka penance;
however, if she has been enjoyed by one of a lower caste, she should be abandoned or even put to death.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5] This is the rule for sexual union that has been declared, as well as the act of union itself.
Listen as I speak of the means for the conduct of women and men.
A woman must be kept away from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct by her own kinsmen;
she must be guarded day and night by her mother-in-law and other elderly female elders.
But she who, while indulging her own desires, is not restrained out of affection,
will inevitably come to grief later on, just like a disease that has been neglected.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time, a husband who does not approach his wife during her season,
and a son who does not provide food for his mother, are all subject to public reproach and punishment according to the law.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
there prosperity, progeny, and purity prevail, and every action becomes fruitful.

Women should be engaged in income and expenditure, the preparation of food, the maintenance of household utensils, cleanliness, and the performance of fire-rituals; this is declared to be the purification for women.
A wife should be honored by her husband with clothing, ornaments, and food,
as well as by her father, brothers, fathers-in-law, and other kinsmen during festive occasions.
She who does not transgress against her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous.
A woman should not live apart from her husband, father, or sons in another's house;
especially by associating with the wicked, she certainly incurs reproach. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.25.2, 9)
Rising before [the elders], serving food and condiments,
and occupying a lower seat or bed— this is declared to be the duty of women toward their elders.
Excessive drinking, wandering about, sleeping during the day, inactivity, and the corruption of women [are the causes of decline].
She who is distressed when her husband is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey,
and who dies when her husband dies— she is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
When the master has gone abroad, one should not engage in personal adornment, nor witness dances, songs, social gatherings, or festivals, nor indulge in meat or liquor.
A wife is considered half of the body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit;
as long as she lives following her husband, that virtuous woman acts for his welfare.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, firmly established in celibacy,
and constantly intent on the gift of Dharma, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
[The Prohibition of Niyoga] Having prescribed *niyoga*, Manu himself prohibited it;
because of the decline of the age (*yugahrāsa*), this cannot be performed by anyone according to the rules.
In the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has been ordained.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.6] [The Division of the Inheritance] That wealth which belongs to the father is given by him to his sons.
That inheritance... // Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.1 //
One woman should be assigned work in each house according to her share; many women should be given equal shares. This same rule applies even to male slaves.
Just as water from a well or a pond is drawn out according to its depth,
so too is a field divided by a boundary according to the proportion of shares.
That must be analyzed through reasoning; otherwise, it would be meaningless.
For those living together with a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods,
and the twice-born shall be one; for those who have divided into separate households, that same worship shall be performed in each individual house.
Witnessing, acting as a guarantor, giving, and receiving—
these brothers who have divided their inheritance may perform among themselves, but not those who have not divided.
Those among whom these customary practices prevail regarding their own inheritance,
one should recognize them as divided even in the absence of a written document.
The obstruction of family lineage is known as *bodha*, which accomplishes rash acts;
it consists of separate wealth for the division of one's own stationary property and enjoyments.
[The Time for Partition] The partition among brothers has been demonstrated to take place upon the death of the parents,
when the mother’s menses have ceased and the sisters have been given away in marriage. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.2–9.
[The Order of Partition] (Br̥h 1.26.3):
Sons share equally in the house and field inherited in due order; sons are not entitled to a partition of paternal property without the father's consent. (Br̥h 1.26.10)
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of wives of equal caste shall,
after giving a preferential share to the eldest, divide the remainder equally.
Indeed, one obtains a double share of the wealth by virtue of age, learning, and austerity;
however, the learned should ensure that the relative weight of each share is such that the wealth thus distributed may be employed for the purpose of sacrifice.
Their sons, whether equal or unequal [in number], are traditionally declared to be the heirs to their father's share.
Regarding property acquired by the grandfather, whether it be immovable or movable,
an equal share is declared for both the father and the son.
If portions that are equal, deficient, or excessive have been assigned by the father to his sons, they must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, they would be liable to punishment.
But in the division of property while the father is still living, the father shall take two shares for himself.
The division of inheritance for heirs is proclaimed to be of two kinds:
one according to the order of seniority by age, and the other an equal distribution of shares.
But whatever is acquired by those who are united, all of them shall have equal shares therein; their sons, whether of unequal or equal status, are declared to be entitled to the paternal share.
All sons who inherit their father's estate are entitled to equal shares;
however, among them, one who is devoted to learning and virtuous action deserves to receive more.
He whose fame in this world is celebrated for the sake of sacred knowledge, discernment, and heroism, and for acts of bestowing wisdom— by him his ancestors have truly found a son.
The eldest by birth, learning, and virtues shall receive two shares from the inheritance;
the others, however, shall share equal portions, for he is equal to a father to them.
In the absence of that [father], however, the mother shall share an equal portion with her son;
the other mothers shall have equal shares, and the daughter shall receive a fourth part.
For unmarried daughters, however, a fourth part is prescribed;
for sons, three parts are prescribed, while equality is ordained when the property is small.
If many [sons] are born of one [mother] and are equal in the number of their caste,
they shall divide the mother’s own property according to her share, in accordance with the law.
Among those who are of the same caste but differ in number, the paternal share is recommended;
however, all grandmothers on the father’s side are declared to be equal to mothers.

But those among them who have not undergone the sacramental rites are to be consecrated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth alone, as well as the unmarried girls, according to the prescribed rule.
But those brothers who remain uninitiated and are younger than others should indeed be initiated by their elder brothers from the paternal wealth held in common.
And he should give him sufficient wealth, or a portion of land, according to his wish.
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried girl, that which is received from the husband, from the father's house,
or from a brother or parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman’s separate property).
Upon receiving the wealth given as a dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was granted by them for the sake of compassion as a means of subsistence.

In the sale or gift of even immovable property, the woman's wealth (strīdhana) may be used as she desires; it shall belong to her children, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof. If she is unmarried, she receives it; but if she is married, she receives only a token honorarium.
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal uncle’s wife,
a father’s sister, a mother-in-law, and the wife of an elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to one’s own mother.
If these women have neither a biological son nor a daughter's son,
their wealth shall go to their sister's son, or to those [nephews] who may inherit from them.
Even a son born of a woman of the same caste, if he lacks good qualities, is not entitled to his father’s wealth; rather,
that property is ordained for those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) for him.
A son protects his father from creditors and those to whom he owes a debt;
therefore, there is no purpose served by one who acts in the opposite manner.
What is done with that cow which neither gives milk nor is pregnant?
What is the purpose of a son who is born but is neither learned nor righteous?
A son who lacks the strength of learning and wealth, is devoid of austerity and wisdom,
and is bereft of proper conduct, is considered equal to urine and excrement.
Even with regard to immovable property and bipeds, though they may have been acquired by oneself,
there can be neither gift nor sale without having assembled all the sons.
Those humans who are born, those yet to be born, those dwelling in the womb, and those residing in the world of the ancestors—all of them desire that livelihood; therefore, it must not be cut off.

Household utensils, vehicles, and the like, as well as food, ornaments, and servants, are divided when they are visible; however, when hidden, a portion of hair is prescribed [as the means of division].
Those born of the Kṣatriya [caste] receive three, two, or one shares; those born of the Vaiśya [caste], however, receive two and one shares respectively.
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are produced from the Brahmin in due order;
they shall possess four, three, two, and one parts respectively, according to their sequence.
One born of a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of the land;
that a twice-born man may receive everything is the established law.
Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a third part of the inheritance;
those of lower caste shall live with him, provided with food and clothing.
For all these sons of one who has no legitimate son (aurasa) are declared to be heirs;
however, once a legitimate son is born, seniority among them ceases to exist.

That which has been given by the grandfather and the father, as well as that which may have been given by the mother, must not be taken away from him; likewise, so too is the property acquired through valor and the wealth of a wife.

Those who declared that garments and such items are indivisible have not reflected upon the fact that for the wealthy, wealth consists primarily of clothing and ornaments. (Br̥hadāranyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.47)
Having paid off a debt that was recorded in writing... // Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.48 //
This aforementioned method is indeed to be understood in the case of a debt recorded on a document;
it must be divided by means of a statement, for otherwise it would be meaningless. // Brh_1.26.49 //
That which stands in the middle and cannot sustain life cannot be given to a single person;
it must be distributed with skill, otherwise it would become useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, having collected wealth through a written contract,
and having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, [the property] is then divided.
The acquisition of property that ensures security and well-being shall be divided equally;
the heirs must always manage its use according to their respective shares.
If a son of a Brahmin woman takes land that has become a gift of Brahmā,
all the twice-born may take his house, as well as his field inherited through succession.
[The arrangement for those divided from the father:
Those who are divided from the father—whether they be stepbrothers or uterine brothers, and even those who are junior—they alone shall take the paternal share. *Bṛhaspati Smṛti* 1.26.54.
The first-born son has no independent power over his paternal inheritance; one born after partition has no claim on the share of his brothers.

Whatever was acquired by the father himself after he had divided his property with his sons, all that belongs to the son born after the partition; the sons born previously are declared to have no right to it.

Just as they have no authority over wealth, so too they have no authority over debt, giving, receiving, or buying and selling; they are mutually powerless, except regarding the period of impurity and the water-libation rites.
Regarding that which was seized from the grandfather, that which was acquired by the father through his own power,
and that which was obtained through learning, valor, and so forth— the father's ownership over these is declared in the Smṛti.
One may make gifts at one's own will and likewise enjoy wealth from that [estate];
in the absence of such [a male heir], daughters are declared to be entitled to equal shares.
Having honored with perfumes and garlands the father’s clothes, ornaments, bed, vehicle, and so forth, one should present them to the recipient of the śrāddha feast.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do so fall from their status.
By the grace of their father, they enjoy garments and ornaments.
Whether the partition has been made or not, if an heir who is entitled to inherit claims that a common property exists,
he shall indeed receive a share of it.
If a debt, a document, a house, or a field belongs to one's paternal grandfather,
he shall receive his share even if he has been away for a long time, provided he returns.
Having abandoned the common ancestral estate, he who has resorted to another region must, upon his return, be given a share of half [the property]; of this there is no doubt.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [birth],
if the births are not fully known, one shall receive the share according to the sequence of succession.
When the primary heirs, all of them acting in succession, recognize a person as their master,
then the land must be given to that descendant who has come through the lineage by the kinsmen of the same clan.
When undivided kinsmen who were previously divided live together again, a further partition of the inheritance shall take place up to the fourth generation; such is the settled rule.
Sons have been created in many ways by the ancient seers;
they cannot be created now by those who are long-lived but lack such power.
The biological son alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal wealth;
the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him, while all others are remembered as those who must be maintained.
But other sons, such as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the rest, are entitled to five, six, or seven shares.

The *datta* (given), the *apaviddha* (cast off), the *krīta* (bought), the *kṛta* (made), and likewise the *śaudra*—these are considered pure by birth; they are all remembered as sons who share in the inheritance.

The son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), the son secretly born (gūḍhaja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta) are all censured by the virtuous.
The son of a Śūdra woman who has been self-given, and those who are recorded as being purchased—all these are declared to be Maitrins; they are undoubtedly Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to the family of another, becomes by that evil conduct a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*; of this there is no doubt.
Gautama said that [the rite] is performed after sacrificing to Agni and Prajāpati;
however, others say that for one who has no son, a daughter may be designated as a son through formal intention (*cintitā*).
Thirteen types of sons were previously declared by Manu;
among them, the son of the body (aurasa) and the appointed daughter (putrikā) are the causes for the continuation of the lineage.
Just as oil is remembered by the wise as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons considered substitutes in the absence of the appointed daughter (putrikā) and the legitimate son of the body (aurasa).
If there are many uterine brothers born of one father,
then when a son is born to even one of them, they are all considered to have sons.
This same rule is recorded for many wives who have one husband:
if even one among them has a son, he is the giver of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) for all of them.
Since a son protects his father from the hell named Put,
he should strive for his birth even by merely looking upon his father's face.
Now, both the grandson and the son of an appointed daughter bring about the attainment of heaven;
they are declared to be equal in regard to the inheritance and the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
And if the father has died, those who are born of a Śūdra wife through lust should give to their brother only a share for the sake of honor, provided that he is intent on service.
For the sake of food, one *prastha* of rice with fuel should be given in the afternoon;
and a garment purchased for three *paṇas* should be given once every three months.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.26.8: The Widow’s Share] This much alone is prescribed as the property of widows for virtuous women.
Having set aside the wealth for clothing, food, and likewise for the washerman,
he should allot what remains to the heirs.
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters are designated;
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be the heirs].
A man without a son should, with great effort, adopt a son of whatever kind may be available,
for the sake of performing the rites of offering funeral cakes and water, and for the proclamation of his religious merit.
The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking:
"Whoever shall go to Gayā will deliver us."
Just as a man drowning while crossing water with a leaky boat sinks down,
even so does a father sink into blind darkness because of a wicked son.
He will perform the rite of releasing a bull, as well as sacrifices and works of public utility;
in his old age, he will protect [the lineage] and offer ancestral oblations every day.
In the Vedas, in the Smṛti scriptures, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of both merit and demerit.
He whose wife has not passed away lives with half of his body;
while half of one's body is still living, how could another take possession of that wealth?
But when there are kinsmen (sakulyas)— namely, paternal uncles and uterine brothers—
of one who has died without a son, the wife shall take that inheritance.
When her husband has died, a devoted wife shall inherit the wealth of that deceased Agnihotra-sacrificer;
this is the eternal law.
The *mūrva* plant removes the fire of death, while the *anvārūḍhā* (a woman who has ascended the funeral pyre) removes sin.
In the absence of sons, the wife shall inherit; in the absence of the wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the heir; and after that, the daughter's son shall take the wealth.
Having taken moving and stationary property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing,
one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other periods to be performed.

One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, and daughters' sons, as well as sisters, the wives of brothers-in-law, maternal uncles, elders, guests, and women, by means of offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and charitable works (pūrta).
Whatever was previously ordained by rule regarding ancestral property and so forth when the wealth had been divided,
that the wife shall receive upon her husband’s death, with the exception of immovable property.
Even if she has been established in her duties and even if a portion [of the estate] has been assigned, a woman does not deserve immovable property.
If a widow becomes harsh while in the prime of youth,
then a livelihood must be provided for the sake of sustaining her life.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman who protects her family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, she has no ownership over it regarding giving, mortgaging, or selling.
A woman who has been purchased for the sake of sexual enjoyment by one desiring offspring,
or who has been taken from another, is declared to be a *strī* (wife).
One should indeed give either a funeral cake (piṇḍa) or a portion of land according to one's inclination.
That means of subsistence given by a father-in-law to women from immovable property cannot be taken away by others once the father-in-law has died.
Those sapindas and kinsmen who act as obstacles to her [the widow] and would seize her wealth, the king shall have them executed with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
[The Division of Reunited Co-heirs:
Furthermore, those who have reunited out of affection shall share in each other's portions.
As for brothers who, having been divided, reside together again in one place out of mutual affection;
Furthermore, when a division [of property] is made, no seniority exists among them.
Should he ever die or somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and destitute of both wife and father.
Whether she has been given away or not, if a uterine brother dies, she alone shall take his share;
for this is clearly the reason for both cases.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda relative.
If one has died without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all the sapinda relatives shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.
But among those who have lived together, whoever acquires wealth through learning, valor, or other such means,
two shares of that wealth must be given to him, while the remainder shall share equally.
Furthermore, one who, though previously divided by his father or brother,
or by his paternal uncle, resides together with him out of affection, is called "reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭa).
The uterine brothers and the uterine sisters, having come together and assembled, shall divide that property equally; as shall those brothers who are reunited.
If among these the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them should die, his share is not lost.
But a uterine brother shall give and take the share for both one who is born and one who has died.
But a uterine brother who is a reunited coparcener shall not take the wealth from one who is not uterine;
likewise, even if he is not a reunited coparcener, a uterine brother shall take it, and not one born of a different mother.
But for those whose father has died, the allotment of shares is calculated from the father's side.
Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are childless and deprived of wives and brothers—
the king shall take their property, for he is the sovereign lord of all.
A son born to a Brahmin from a Kṣatriya woman, though senior by birth, shall share equally with the Kṣatriya if he is endowed with good qualities;
likewise, a son born to a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya woman shall share equally with that Kṣatriya.
Land acquired as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if their father should give it, once he is dead, the son of the Brāhmaṇa shall take it.
One born to a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of the land;
he shall receive everything [only] from one of his own caste—thus the law is established.
If there is a Niṣāda who is the only son of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall receive the third share;
then two kinsmen (sakulyas) or sapindas, being the givers of the svadhā offering, shall take [the remainder].
In the absence of a kinsman, the teacher or even the pupil who offers the *svadhā* should likewise provide for those castes in all calamities.
A virtuous son born of a Śūdra womb who serves a childless man shall receive his livelihood;
the remainder of the estate the sapinda relatives shall obtain.
The wife is the heir to the husband's wealth; in her absence, it is recorded that the daughter is the heir.
A daughter is born from every limb of men, just like a son;
therefore, how could another man take the father’s wealth?
But in the absence of him, if there should be an unmarried daughter, then,
in the absence of a lineage of sons and grandsons, the daughters' sons (dauhitrāḥ) shall obtain the wealth.
Just as one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
Since they both abide within that very self, how could anyone else take away the wealth?
"In this world, according to the law, there is no difference between a son's son and a daughter's son;
by this very ordinance, he then made his daughter a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter)."
A male is born when the semen is in excess; a female comes into being when the female element is in excess.
A virtuous wife, wedded to a man of equal status and devoted to service—
whether she has borne sons or not— is the heir to her father's wealth.
Just as she has ownership over her father’s wealth even while her kinsmen exist,
so too does her son have a claim to the wealth of his mother and maternal grandfather.
In their absence, however, the brothers, the sons of brothers, the uterine kin (sanābhayaḥ),
the distant relatives (sakulyāḥ), the kinsmen (bāndhavāḥ), the disciples, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyāḥ) are entitled to the wealth.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies childless; likewise,
she shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without a wife or children.
The mother should be known as the heir to the inheritance, or the brother with her permission.
In the absence of a son, the wife shall inherit; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother;
in his absence, the heir; and after that, the daughter’s son shall receive the wealth.
From the wealth that has been acquired, one should diligently set aside half of it for the monthly,
six-monthly, or annual *śrāddha* ceremonies.
Where there are many kinsmen, such as those of the same lineage and relatives,
he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who has no offspring.
A brother, or a brother’s son, a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the rite of the rice-balls together, should thereafter perform the rite for prosperity.
Furthermore, he who makes a division according to his own will and then acts in contradiction to it,
shall be made to pay the king’s share and be punished for the offense committed.
In the case of denying a joint debt or concealing a transaction through fraud,
one should not force the debtor to pay by means that cause loss to their dependents.
Those men who are deceitful, wealthy, cruel,
and greedy should be won over through affection, or by the sacrifice of one's own interests and through guile.
An act of violence, ownership of immovable property, and the prior partition of inheritance among heirs are to be known by inference when there are no witnesses present.
These transactions of theirs proceed in the world among their own heirs;
they should recognize those who have been divided even without a written document.
And the rites beginning with the Vaiśvadeva should be performed by those who have not divided their property.
The obstruction of the continuity of power, theft characterized by violence,
the enjoyment of one's own immovable property, and wealth held separately from the partition.
Those who maintain separate income, expenditure, and assets, and engage with one another in lending,
trade, and commerce, are undoubtedly divided.
When brothers who have divided their inheritance record the division among themselves,
or when they divide it in the presence of blameless witnesses, that document of the division shall be proclaimed as the legal act.
One should not displace that portion of a share which has been enjoyed by someone in such a manner.
Gambling, which destroys truth, purity, and wealth, has been forbidden by Manu.
But that [system] was set in motion by others, however, together with the king's share.
An activity presided over by a master of the assembly for the purpose of identifying thieves—
this very same rule is to be understood as applying to gambling with living creatures and to betting matches.
[The Conduct of the Master of the Gaming Hall] The master of the gaming hall is the collector; he shall pay the winnings to the victor and to the king.
The king’s share from the gambling proceeds is ten percent from the master of the hall.
Or it may occur at the appropriate time. ... ... // Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.27.4 //
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.27.2: Victory and Defeat of the Masters] Whosoever should suffer defeat in a duel,
the master must pay the stake that was stipulated therein.

One who has been defeated in private, or who was unaware of fraudulent dice or deceit, must be released; even one who is aware [of the trickery] shall not be made to pay his entire wealth, nor shall he be made to pay everything won.
[The Punishment for Cheating at Dice:

Those wicked gamblers who play with loaded dice, those who misappropriate the king's share, and those who deceive in counting—these gamblers are declared to be subject to punishment. (Br̥had-āranyaka Upaniṣad 1.27.3; 1.27.7)
Public exposure must be made, and those who practice fraudulent gambling shall be banished;
however, one who commits murder shall suffer a diverse form of capital punishment.
He alone is the witness when the victory or defeat is in doubt, provided he is accompanied by three other members of the court;
for the gamblers are the judges regarding the doubt concerning both parties.
But when they become hostile, then the king should investigate.
In this manner, the king should daily oversee the legal disputes brought by litigants,
as well as other matters concerning the king's dependents, together with learned Brahmins.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.28] [Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.28.
Birds, rams, bulls, and so forth, are held in mutual embrace.
When those who have made a wager strike one another, they call that a *samāhvaya*.
If anyone should suffer defeat in a duel,
the wager that had been stipulated therein must be paid by his master.
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.29,
Miscellaneous] This judicial procedure composed by Vādi has been declared in brief.
I shall now declare the judicial procedure concerning the king, known as the miscellaneous category (prakīrṇaka).
Having ascertained the nature of the person's fault and their capacity, one should duly impose the fourfold punishment consisting of verbal reprimand, fine, and even corporal punishment.
One who deserves death shall be fined one hundred gold pieces;
for one whose limb is to be severed, half of that; and for one to be banished, twenty-five.
The hands, feet, genitals, eyes, tongue, ears, and nose;
the tongue, half of the foot, the claspers, the forehead, the lips, the anus, and the hips.
These fourteen places for punishment have been specified;
however, for a Brahmin, the forehead mark is ordained, and no other punishment is prescribed.
One should diligently restrain those who act contrary to dharma by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of intimidation.
But when one is unable to restrain these even by piercing,
then one should employ all four of these [remedies] against them.
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of physical violence.
And he should place all prisoners along the royal highway,
where those miserable, deformed evildoers may be seen.
One who cremates the corpse of a deceased person who has no relatives shall take a tenth part of the wealth, or a fifth, or even the whole of it.
The tenth [part] for one with many protectors, the fifth for one with few protectors;
Śaunaka says that for one whose father is childless, it is the whole [of the inheritance].
Likewise, one who has fled [from the army] must pay a sixth part as a fee for crossing;
so too must one who causes dissension in battle, a thief, and one who destroys crops.

The failure to perform expiatory rites, the transgression of prohibitions and injunctions, the neglect of the duties of the social classes and stages of life, and the neglect of the prevention of the intermixture of castes; // Brh_1,29.13 //
A treasure-trove and the wealth of a familyless man, the arrival of riches for the poor,
actions not prescribed by scripture, and the ritualistic doctrines of disputants.
The provocation of the constituent elements (prakṛtis), mutual conspiracy, and whatever is proclaimed among the subjects that is not ordained by the scriptures; // Brh_1,29.15 //
In the case of the disqualification of witnesses, assessors, or litigants, there is a requirement for a renewed examination;
however, for those who have been defeated by their own words alone, the rule for a retrial has not been stated.
Because it is based upon the meaning of the Vedas, the Smṛti of Manu is considered preeminent;
any Smṛti that contradicts the meaning of Manu is not praised.

The *Kātyāyanasmṛtisāroddhāra*: [Qualities of a King] (p.1) K.001a.
One who is disciplined, perfected in the sciences, and endowed with both treasury and valor;
A king should be devoted to the Brahmins, virtuous in giving, and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Free from arrogance, malice, backbiting, fickleness, and anger; confident yet humble, exalted yet approachable, eloquent, and pleasant to behold.

Prosperity attends to the utmost degree that king who has his senses under control, who has conquered himself, who wields the rod of punishment against those who deserve it, who acts only after careful deliberation, and who is steadfast.
[The Duties of Kings: Due to an abundance of valor, learning, and wealth, and especially because of their sovereign power,
the minds of kings constantly fall into delusion for this reason.
Therefore, the mind should always be awakened by the twice-born regarding the duties of kings;
one should not transgress the words of the Smṛtis, which are supremely purifying and meritorious.
By the power of the sound of the Vedas, even the gods who dwell in heaven rejoice there,
being satisfied by the worship of the twice-born.
Therefore, kings should always perform the worship of the twice-born with great effort;
by that, they shall repeatedly attain the status of Śakra as well as the sovereignty of men again and again.
The superintendent of liquor, having fallen from heaven, dwells in the form of a king;
he must constantly perform that by which he may attain the ultimate truth.
Kings who remain established in their own duty shall attain the state of Śakra;
however, those who are constantly devoid of proper conduct shall dwell in the Avīci hell.
That king who, failing to understand correctly, falls under the sway of anger, shall dwell for half a *kalpa* in a terrible hell; of this there is no doubt.
A minister who contemplates the affairs of state should be endowed with these very same qualities.
But he should appoint a Brahmin who is devoted to the king and of noble lineage.
Where the ministers, court members, and physicians are merely pleasant-spoken,
there the king will quickly fall away from his kingdom, his merit, and his happiness.
One should not give way to anger at his words, for these [ministers] must always speak what is just and well-established.
Where the king personally oversees legal cases according to dharma,
there the subjects, practicing virtuous conduct, shall dwell in happiness.
The constant protection of the subjects, the removal of thorns,
and the honoring of the twice-born— for this purpose the king was created.
The king is always considered the owner of the land, but never of other property;
for he receives a sixth part of its produce, and not otherwise.
Because the beings dwell within it, its lordship is proclaimed by that [wind];
its activity consists of the offering of the sixth part [of produce] arising from auspicious and inauspicious omens.
O lord of men, for that ruler who proceeds in this manner and abandons greed,
sons are born to him, and his kingdom and treasury increase.
For that king who, by unjust means, takes taxes, fines, a share of the grain, and tolls from his kingdom, shall partake of the guilt.

Abandoning what is stated in the *Arthaśāstra*, one should follow what is stated in the *Dharmaśāstra*. Even if a king is wicked, one should not destroy his kingdom, because he does not engage in unjust acts without the consent of his subjects.
But that king who, without distress, properly grants what is requested by one in need, saves him from an infinite [debt]; such is a gift for the sake of Dharma.
That which is obtained by kings through justice, having conquered their enemy, is pure; that should be given back, for it has never been acquired otherwise.
The king should appoint as his domestic priest a Brahmin who is renowned,
well-disposed, accomplished in sacred study, free from greed, and truthful in speech.
[The Characteristics of Legal Procedure,
etc. In the extensive treatise on justice known as *dharma*, which is accomplished through effort and involves interruption,
that dispute which is rooted in what is to be proven is called *vyavahāra* (legal procedure).
The removal (*haraṇa*) of various meanings and doubts is called *hāra*; because it removes various doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*.
But a king, out of a desire for power or greed for wealth, should not personally investigate legal cases among men who are not disputing.
"He who incites violence or refuses to give what is due, or who, out of misconduct, does not grant a request— such a person may be dragged away by the king's command."
When the eighteen steps are reached through the differentiation of the subject matter in the two-footed [verse],
they become eighteen thousandfold through the differentiation of the legal actions.
The root of the plaintiff's claim is that which has been presented by the litigant;
"non-payment of what is due" and "injury" are said to be the two grounds for legal action.
The plaint, the reply, the rejoinder, and the stage of proof— by these it is declared to have four feet.
In the Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra, however, two branches are proclaimed;
victory and decisive settlement are declared to be the two fruits.
But he who, though urged by the king, first reports a matter that is censured by the treatise because it is contrary to his primary interest,
is declared to be a "stobhaka" (an obstructer).
He who, appointed by the king himself to examine the faults of the administration,
informs the king of them once he has learned of them, is called an informant (*sūcaka*).
[Consideration of the relative strength and weakness of legal procedures, customary practice, conduct, royal edicts,

and so forth: But where, in a dispute, the one who committed the offense establishes his authorship and the owner of the property recovers his own wealth, that alone shall be the decision according to *dharma*.
Whatever treatise on law (smṛti-śāstra) has been proclaimed by those who seek to establish dharma,
that indeed is known as legal procedure (vyavahāra), intended for the purpose of deciding lawsuits.
Whatever is constantly practiced by a region, whether it be righteous or even unrighteous, that is proclaimed as *caritra* (customary law) because of its local practice.
Whatever law the king shall establish, in accordance with the treatises on logic (*nyāya-śāstra*) and likewise according to local custom, that is the righteous royal edict (*rājaśāsana*).
But when a legal matter is consistent with reason and free from the need for divine ordeals, then the Dharma is sublated by the judicial proceeding, and not otherwise.
Regarding those born of inverse unions and those dwelling in difficult terrains, they say that the established custom is authoritative; one should not subvert that dharma.
But when the king shall issue a final decision according to that law, then the legal proceeding by custom is superseded by that very [decision].
But when a customary practice (*caritra*) is found to be contrary to logic (*nyāya*), it should be set aside by the king's command; thus is custom rejected in such cases.
Whatever rebuttal is employed according to this rule constitutes a valid sublation;
however, where there is sublation in any other manner, there the Dharma is violated.

When a king acts on his own authority despite having a [counselor’s] word, that action leads away from heaven, causes the destruction of the world, brings fear from enemy armies, and robs kings of their life-span and seed.
Therefore, the king should settle legal cases in accordance with the treatises; however, in the absence of such texts, he should decide them according to local custom.
Whatever custom has been established in a particular region and persists for all time,
provided it does not conflict with the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called a "local custom" (deśadṛṣṭa).

For those residing in districts, ports, cattle-pens, cities, or villages, [the king shall decide] according to their own customary laws; for others, he shall decide together with them in accordance with the *dharmaśāstra*.
The settlement that has been determined solely with the consent of the region must always be recorded in writing and kept under seal by the king's authority.
Having examined her, one should decide [the case] after guarding her with care as prescribed by the treatises;
however, whatever matter has been committed to writing and established by those who abide by the rules of the guilds (naigama).
Therefore, that [scripture] should proceed accordingly and not otherwise;
for that which is seen in the regions of authoritative tradition is thus determined to be so.
Where an act previously unperformed has been done in accordance with the approval of the Śruti and Smṛti, it should not be done otherwise; one should avoid what is contrary to justice.
The judicial court (*dharmādhikaraṇa*) is that place where, through an investigation into the treatises on Dharma, there is a discernment of the root and the essence.

Having risen in the morning and performed his purification with a concentrated mind, the king [should honor] his teacher, the astrologer, the physicians, the gods, the Brahmins, and the domestic priests.
Having honored these [deities] as is fitting with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
