and having paid homage to his teachers and elders, he should enter the assembly hall with a cheerful countenance.
Having entered the assembly hall with a modest appearance and a composed mind, the king,
seated and facing the east, shall attend to the legal cases of the litigants together with those learned in the three Vedas, the elders, and ministers skilled in counsel.
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic chaplain, and the members of the court, the king remains in heaven as a witness through his adherence to dharma.

Together with the members of the court— who are steadfast, disciplined, wise, hereditary, and the best among the twice-born— and who are skilled in the meaning of the *Dharmaśāstras* and proficient in the *Arthaśāstra*.
It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good character, youth, proper conduct, and wealth, who are free from envy, and who are like true members of a family.
In that regard, merchants who perceive what is right should be appointed as witnesses. (K.059a) [The time for the examination of cases:
In the morning, in the assembly halls, the king should reach a decision on the cases. (K.060a)
One who draws out his enemies should act according to the path prescribed by the treatises.
Except for the eighth part of the day, the three periods of time that remain are declared in the scriptures to be the supreme time for legal proceedings.
That period which follows the third of the eight parts of the first day is seen by the wise in the legal treatises as the time for judicial proceedings.
[The King as Judge]: When the king does not personally carry out the decision of a legal case, then he should appoint there a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the scriptures.
One who is skillful, of noble birth, impartial, free from causing agitation, steadfast, fearful of the next world, most righteous, diligent, and devoid of anger.
One who is not cruel, sweet-spoken, affectionate, patient, discerning,
energetic, and free from greed should be employed by the king in legal disputes.
One who studies only a single treatise cannot know how to reach a definitive conclusion regarding legal matters;
therefore, kings should ensure that in disputes there is recourse to many authoritative scriptures as the highest standard.
Where there is no Brāhmaṇa, one should appoint a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.

Therefore, whatever business has been performed by others in an unjust manner should be recognized as invalid— even if it was carried out by those appointed [to the task], whether by chance or according to the scriptures.
It is established that he asks the question concerning the legal dispute as "prāṭ";
he who investigates (vivecayati) that matter is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
But if the judge should converse in secret with the plaintiff regarding a matter that has not yet been decided,
he shall be punished, and the members of the court all the more so.
[The members of the assembly] should be the best of the twice-born, free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all the Śāstras.
Where the members of the court have reached a decision by overstepping the science of logic (*nyāya-śāstra*),
there dharma, being struck down by adharma, destroys [the wrongdoer]— of this there is no doubt.
Where dharma is struck down by adharma, and truth by falsehood,
while those present look on, there the members of the court are themselves slain.
But the members of the court must not overlook a case that has proceeded contrary to the law;
by overlooking it, they, along with the king, go headlong into hell.
Those members of the court who follow him even as he proceeds unjustly shall also share in that guilt; therefore, they must awaken the king to the truth.
But having recognized that the king’s mind has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is pleasing to him in that situation; the member of the assembly shall not thereby incur guilt.
A member of the court must necessarily speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the court is blameless.
When the king should employ the litigants for an unlawful purpose, the member of the court,
having informed the monarch, should then set aside that matter.
Whether out of affection, ignorance, greed, or even delusion,
if a member of the assembly speaks otherwise than the truth therein, he is considered an unseemly person and shall be punished.
Having correctly understood the determination of the case, the member of the court should then speak;
otherwise, he must not speak at all, for the speaker shall be liable to double the fine.
But that which is lost due to the fault of the court members must then be paid by those members;
however, once a legal matter has been decided for the litigants, one should not overturn it.

[The relative weight of the judges of legal cases: Families, guilds, assemblies, authorized officials, and the king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
But the affairs of ascetics he should have carried out by those learned in the three Vedas alone,
and likewise by those skilled in the application of magic, and never by himself, for fear of provoking their anger.
One endowed with perfect knowledge should not offer instruction to those of superior birth, character, or conduct, nor to gurus, teachers, or ascetics.
But that which is the stability of their lineage, which comes about through the natural order of things, they call the "family dharma"; one should indeed preserve it in that very same way.
[The Manner of Inquiry] At the proper time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your grievance? Do not fear; speak, O man!"
"By whom, in what place, when, and for what reason?"—thus should one who has entered the assembly ask.
Whatever he may say when questioned in this manner, that should be accepted by the members of the court together with the Brahmins.
Having deliberated on the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter issue a summons;
otherwise, he should deposit a seal upon it or appoint an official.

One who is presented by the plaintiff as another person acting on his behalf before the judicial authority is to be known as a representative (*pratinidhi*); so too is one who has personally entered into the defense.

The right to sue belongs to the one who is formally accused, not to another, because there is no connection [between them and the case]. Even the other party is considered to have been made a defendant by the one who has brought the suit against him.
Whether appointed by the plaintiff or sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
Slaves, laborers, pupils, those appointed to service, and likewise kinsmen—these litigants shall not be subject to punishment; however, anyone other than these is liable to punishment.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and other such heinous crimes, no defendant is permitted.
In the case of killing a human, theft, violating another's wife, eating forbidden food, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden;
In cases of verbal abuse, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, no defendant shall be granted time; the perpetrator must plead his case himself.

The king should summon those who are eager for justice and those seeking prosperity; however, he should not summon the sick, the dull-witted, nor women who are unwell, intoxicated, insane, or afflicted.

A young woman of noble birth who has not yet reached her menses, even if she has given birth, and a maiden who is the most excellent among all castes— these are declared to be under the authority of their paternal kinsmen.
The summons of those women who are dependent on others for their livelihood, wanton women, courtesans, those of no family, and those who have fallen from their caste is prescribed.
One who speaks while bearing a weapon, or without an upper garment, or with disheveled hair, or seated upon a throne,
or using the left hand, shall incur punishment.
But if one who is capable should disregard the king's command when summoned,
the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law.
In minor matters, the fine shall be at least fifty; in middling matters, it shall be at least two hundred;
and in serious matters, the punishment shall always be at least five hundred.
Whatever punishment has been specifically prescribed for a particular offense must, with diligence,
result in the collection of fines in paṇas or their equivalent value from the offender by the king.
[Seizure]: "Indeed, he who causes injury or does not pay what is due, when summoned for his misconduct, may be dragged forth by the king's command."
But having reported the matter to the king, when it is certain and he has given his assent,
one should apply the injunction of restraint until the appearance for summons.
One who is subject to arrest but evades arrest while being arrested deserves punishment.
[Those who are not to be arrested: But one who, by restraining his senses, remains silent and stops breathing and so forth—
If he should detain one who ought not to be detained, he shall be punished, but [the other] shall not be liable for transgression.
Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those standing in difficult terrain— none of these should be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their business.
Those afflicted by disease, those in distress, as well as sacrificers,
those who have not yet crossed over [to the other side], and likewise those who are intoxicated, insane, or mentally deficient, are not to be arrested.
A farmer does not fail at the time for sowing, nor a soldier at the time for battle;
and one who has set out after making a vow does not turn back before the appointed time.

A farmer who is diligently engaged with his crops, from the commencement of the work until the arrival of water, shall not be subjected to a lawsuit during that time; however, it is the established rule that one who restrains a person who should not be restrained shall be punished by the king.
One who is accused, one who is imprisoned, or one who remains under the king's command—
wise men know that no other legal action should be taken against him while he is thus accused.
Depending on whether the mission took one day, two days, or more, and depending on the place, time, and other circumstances,
once the business has been accomplished by the messenger, the king should cause him to be provided with food.
Those who know the truth understand that eating is prescribed as dependent upon place, time, age, strength, and so forth; this applies everywhere to the agent.
[As witnesses, they are not to be accepted:
neither an owner nor an enemy, nor one appointed by an owner; likewise, one who has been imprisoned, one who has been fined, and those in a state of legal uncertainty are never [to be accepted].
Neither an heir nor one who has been disinherited, nor those who reside permanently [elsewhere], nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants.
One who is unable to pay the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king,
or one whose father is still living and acts according to his own will,
should not be accepted as a surety for the performance of the obligation when he is unknown [to the parties].
Now, if there is no surety for a litigant who is fit to plead,
he shall, being protected, pay a fee to the messenger at the end of the day.
A member of the twice-born classes who lacks a surety should be guarded by the city guards;
however, Śūdras and others who lack a surety should be bound with fetters.
If he transgresses or departs, the king should fine him eight *paṇas*;
furthermore, the performance of daily duties must be ensured for all social classes.
One who has already been convicted of an offense should not be subjected to legal proceedings by the king;
rather, the king should either hand him over to that person or consign him to another.
[The Order of Speaking for the Plaintiff and Others:
In that regard, the plaintiff (abhiyoktṛ) should speak first, and the defendant (abhiyukta) immediately thereafter;
at the conclusion of those two, the member of the assembly (sadasya) shall speak, and after that, the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka).
He who suffers greater hardship, or whose legal claim is more substantial, shall be the plaintiff;
he who does not present his case first shall not be so.
Or, to whichever party there may be financial loss or excessive physical suffering, to him the right of pleading first shall be granted; not to one who fails to present his case beforehand.
[The Nature of the Declaration] Having established the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, as well as the day,
the hour, the location, the subject matter, the place, the caste, the appearance, and the age;
He should record the matter to be proved, the evidence, the number [of witnesses], his own name,
the names of the kings in their proper order, the place of residence, and the name of the party to be proved.
Having announced the names of the ancestors in order, as well as the claimant and the defendant,
the afflictions, other signs of forbearance, and the side [of the case], he should frame the plea.
Likewise, the region, the location, the configuration,
the genus, the designation, the dwelling, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: [the names of] the father and grandfather, and the proclamation of former kings.
If one is provoked by any one of passion or the other [defilements] during the procedure,
he should write "om" for everything on the board or other surfaces for the proponent.
One should rectify excessive items and fill in those that are deficient;
one should record them on the ground for as long as the case remains established.
The judge shall cause the plaintiff’s case, as stated in its own nature, to be recorded on a wooden board with chalk; thereafter, it shall be refined upon a leaf.
If one writes down something other than what was stated by the plaintiff or the defendant,
a righteous king should punish him like a thief.
Or he may obtain a period of three days or even seven days for deliberation,
until such time as the thought arises in him who wishes to speak in the dispute.
Since a determination [of the truth] occurs only after a long time from the commencement of the legal action,
one who is diligent does not suffer the lapse of time, even though he is subject to it.
In a dispute where the minds of two parties seeking a legal outcome are unable to reach a decision,
a period of time should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
[A Faults of the Proposition (Faults of the Plaint):
A plaint that is contrary to the interests of the state, one that has been rejected by the king,
or one that is confused by multiple points does not succeed.
Even a matter in legal proceedings that has been determined to involve many counter-claims,
the king may certainly take up at his pleasure, out of a desire to discover the truth.
It is devoid of place and time, and free from substance and number.
And a thesis that lacks both the probandum and the means of proof is held to be unacceptable.
If he does not wish to act according to justice, or acts unjustly,
or likewise fails to have it recorded in writing, his case shall not succeed.
One should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is unestablished, unassailable, purposeless, useless,
impossible to prove, or contradictory.
Those who know the subject of a thesis understand the *pakṣa* to be that which is free from defects of the proposition, endowed with valid reasons, certain, and established in the world.
Containing few syllables yet abundant in meaning, free from ambiguity and confusion,
it is devoid of contradictory reasons and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
But when such a plaint has been formulated by the proponent, the defendant should then provide a reply connected to that very position.
When a matter is being announced by the plaintiff and is not contested,
or when one remains silent at the time of the payment, that matter is deemed consented to.

[The reply must be given either immediately or after a lapse of time. If, having heard the matter set forth in the written document, the defendant requests a delay in the lawsuit for a valid reason, a period of time must be granted to him; of this there is no doubt.

In matters such as debts and the like, he may obtain [the result] immediately, or after one day, five days, or three days, depending on the gravity or lightness of the case; or after three fortnights, or even seven days.
Having ascertained the time, the capacity [of the parties], and the strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the lord may grant a period— whether short or long— to the defendant.
Whether it be a day, a month, a fortnight, a season, or even a year—
the time for repayment must be fixed by the other party in accordance with the nature of the transaction.
Where respect disappears, whether through destruction or abandonment, one should not wait for time; for that matter is urgent.
In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, or offspring;
likewise in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, or in buying and selling.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, violence, embezzlement of a deposit, fraud, and perjury, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.

Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations regarding cattle, and likewise in matters of urgency, one may litigate over land even at an improper time.
In cases where the matters have been recently committed, the master [the judge] should allow a lawsuit to proceed immediately;
or, in cases where time has elapsed, he should grant a period of time to the defendant.
In the case of a death occurring immediately, the impurity lasts for that very day; if it occurs after one month has passed, it lasts for one day;
if after six years, it shall be three nights; and if after twelve years, it lasts for seven days.
If [the period] is twenty years, he shall receive ten days or half a month;
if thirty years have passed, it shall be one month; and beyond that, it shall be three fortnights.
Within a year, one may [revoke the gift] at one's own will as desired;
however, in the case of one who is dull-witted, insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by disease, the period is one year.
Or when the matter has reached another region, or when the facts are unknown;
or when the original source or the witnesses are situated in a foreign land.
In that case, the time for men [to pay] shall be until they return to their own country;
even if the time has been fixed, the payment may still be deferred due to the gravity of the matter.
But immediately thereafter, the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case,
shall present his counter-argument connected to the subject matter of that initial claim.
In matters concerning conduct, the giving of goods, sacrifices, or the performance of duties,
if no one is present, one should not cause a formal assembly to be convened there.
If at that time there should be a calamity caused by fate or the king,
he does not become defeated merely by abandoning the suit due to that distress.
One should establish a fault caused by fate or the king through witnesses; however, for one who acts with deceit, the fine shall be made to pay that wealth as a penalty.
One who is being prosecuted shall never prosecute the prosecutor in return,
except in cases of assault, theft, adultery, and heinous crimes.
Whatever established practice has come down through a traditional succession in a particular case,
the king, having considered that according to what is right, shall cause a reply to be given.
[The fourfold reply: Truth, a false reply, as well as a counter-attack,
and likewise the plea of prior judgment— thus the reply (uttara) is of four kinds.
But when another, having heard the meaning of what was spoken, refutes it either in substance or in its verbal expression, that reply should be known as false.
If a defendant, when being prosecuted,
should deny the charge, one should recognize that as a false answer according to the principles of legal procedure.
The truthful declaration of the defendant is declared to be an act of admission.
"This is false; I do not recognize it, for I was not present there at that time, and I had not yet been born then"—thus is the fourfold denial.
If the defendant admits the very claim set forth by the plaintiff,
the Teacher has declared that he may state his defense, provided it is not frivolous.
If one who has been defeated by conduct is made to write again, he is to be declared as previously defeated; that is called a *prāṅnyāya* (a case of prior judgment).
"I shall establish [my claim] through witnesses, documents, or by means of a family record;
furthermore, this threefold judicial proceeding has already been won by me."
[These are pseudo-answers or faults of the answer: That which is unestablished, contradictory, too little, or excessive;
that which is doubtful, impossible, unclear, or has a different meaning—these are highly defective.
An answer that is non-comprehensive, contains disjointed words, has a hidden meaning, is inconsistent,
requires interpretation, or is devoid of substance is not praised by the wise.

An answer that has disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is improper, requires interpretation to be understood, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the establishment of one's own position.
However, that which is stated by one who does not know the thousandfold forms of signs and the convention,
or which is expressed in a different dialect, is an unestablished answer.
"I returned it in my childhood; I did not return it"—when one says this, that contradictory reply should be understood here as a *viruddha* (contradictory) rejoinder.
"To say, 'This was previously defeated by me in this matter,' yet to state 'previously by me'— that which is deficient [in its application] is known as *ūnam* (the deficient rejoinder)."
When it should have been stated, "It was taken," he instead says, "The task was performed by me";
or when he says, "That which was previously taken as property was exceedingly great."
When one ought to say, "It must be given by me," if instead one says, "It must not be taken by me," the wise should then recognize such an answer as ambiguous in a legal proceeding.
Furthermore, whatever act of violence was previously committed by this man through weakness,
they consider that unspoken matter to have been stated for the sake of another purpose.
When it is stated, "I have given a thousand together with him," that which is returned as half of that is known here as non-comprehensive (*avyāpaka*).
The proponent shall not properly set forth his case until the legal procedure has been concluded; if he says, "I previously took it," that is called a confused statement.
"Will anyone give a lotus that has not been taken?
That answer was stated with a hidden meaning according to legal procedure."
"Should he always give with that very [person], or should it be given by me?"—
those who know the truth recognize this as the reply stated when [the situation] is improper.
The reply, "A crow has no teeth," and so forth,
is not considered a correct answer in reality, for it is essentially without substance.
One should not overstep what is irrelevant, insignificant, indistinct, deficient or excessive, inconsistent, lacking in pervasive essence, doubtful, or contrary to the opponent's position.
That which is ambiguous, different from the subject matter, too little, or too much—
like that which pervades only a portion of the thesis— is not a valid rejoinder at all.
That which is true regarding one part of the claim, provides a reason regarding another part,
and is false regarding yet another part, is not a valid reply because of its internal inconsistency.
In a single lawsuit, there should not be legal proof for both of the two litigants;
there can be no establishment of the case for both, nor can there be two proofs in one proceeding.
If,
having first accepted a reason, one should later state another, more weighty reason contained within the opponent's reply, then that [latter] is established, and not the other.
One should give a reply according to the facts, and cause even one who does not wish to pay to pay it by means of conciliation,
sowing dissension, and other such methods, until that matter has been fully resolved.
Whether spoken out of delusion or through guile, whatever was not stated by the proponent but is included within the reply shall be accepted from both parties as well.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer when seven nights have elapsed, is defeated and is liable to pay.
Having caused [the claim] to be heard, if he abandons what ought to be done or says something else,
and thereby takes recourse in another position, that proponent is defeated.
One should not say, "The case was not stated by me," after having brought another forward;
and one who speaks falsely in this manner should likewise be declared defeated.
But if a litigant, having had a statement written down, should then speak of it as deficient or excessive, he shall suffer defeat; he does not deserve to maintain his original claim.
The wise should understand that the members of the court and the witnesses constitute the "action" (*kriyā*).
He who, out of delusion, hates that action is called a "hater of the action."
By failing to appear when summoned, one is immediately excluded.
Even if he is prepared, one should not speak; he deserves immediate imprisonment.
On the second day, one should know that the defeat of that evil-minded person has occurred.
But where one seeks to prolong the matter for a long time through mere pretext,
one should recognize that as a "pretext" (*sapadeśa*), which is recorded as causing a loss of the legal argument.
One who speaks otherwise shall pay five *paṇas*; one who hates the performance of the legal act, ten *paṇas*;
one who does not appear, twelve *paṇas*; one who remains without an answer, sixteen *paṇas*; and one who flees after being summoned shall be made to pay twenty *paṇas*.
The lord of the earth shall punish one who does not come when summoned three times, one who flees after being summoned, or one who has exceeded a period of five nights.
If one should divide a lawsuit that has already been formally announced,
or if one should entice the plaintiff with greed, one should designate him as the defeated party.
If one creates fear, or causes a split, or employs intimidation or confinement,
he loses his case in the legal proceeding regarding the matter between the two litigants.
Having taken account of the fault, he should be subjected to a retrial; there is no further appeal.
When both parties have committed their statements to writing and the determination of the case has begun, whoever speaks what is improper therein is defeated on that point.
But the plaintiff who, having designated witnesses, does not litigate out of his own will—
he loses that case after thirty nights have passed.
A defeated party's plea is accepted when it is due to flight or taking refuge with another faction; however, this does not apply to one who has been defeated by his own statements.
The wise know that for one who has been defeated by an inferior statement, there is a means of reversal;
however, for one who is himself devoid of a statement, no reversal exists.
Those who, having presented their case and accepted the matter, reach a settlement between themselves,
shall all be fined double, as they have deceived the king.
[Kriyāpāda] (p. 30):
For even the plaintiff's case (*pūrvapakṣa*) attains the status of a "reply" (*uttara*) because of a specific cause;
therefore, the legal action (*kriyā*) is said at that time to be that which establishes the plaintiff's case.
When the case has been properly examined and recorded, and the defendant's reply is found to be faultless,
it is then desired that the plaintiff or the defendant proceed with the proof of the matter.
That which is intended by the proponent himself to be clearly established is the *sādhya* (the probandum); that by which it is entirely established is the *sādhana* (the means of proof).

[The Means of Proof and the Investigation of Their Strength and Weakness] They know that the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) are threefold: written documents, witnesses, and possession (*bhukti*). Logical reasoning (*yukti*) consists of circumstantial evidence and summary indications; here, the ordeals (*divya*) include poison and the like.
Even when the plaintiff's prior claim has been written down in its entirety, letter by letter,
he must establish it in the third stage by means of evidence.
For it has been stated that the "task" (kārya) is that which is to be accomplished, while the "means of accomplishment" (sādhana) is called action (kriyā).

Furthermore, that [action] should be known as being of two kinds: divine (daivikī) and likewise human (mānuṣī). Human action consists of documents, witnesses, and so forth; divine action is considered to consist of ordeals such as execution and the like.
When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof; for by employing divine means when witnesses are available, he is defeated thereby.
If one party should propose human evidence and the other should propose divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure.
If human action exists even when it pervades only a single part [of the case], that is to be accepted by men who speak; however, divine action is not to be accepted even if it is complete.
Divine action is said to be of five kinds, while human action is traditionally held to be of three kinds.
If one abandons a strong means of proof and resorts to a weak one,
he shall not regain that means of proof once his defeat has been determined by the members of the court.
Setting aside even many insubstantial points, one should accomplish that action which possesses essence; one should abandon an action devoid of essence.
One should abandon from afar that legal procedure which attempts to establish both sides of a dispute.
When witnesses are available, it is declared that no divine means of proof shall be employed;
and when there is a written document in legal disputes, neither divine proof nor witnesses are required.
A document loses its validity over time, as does one that is legally defective. In a legal dispute lacking documentary evidence or witnesses, one should resort to divine proof;
however, in a matter to be settled by human effort, one should not employ divine proof, nor should one rely on a document [if it is otherwise flawed].
Regarding the established custom of guilds, trade associations, corporations, and the like, which has been fully proclaimed:
its proof is documentary evidence, not divine ordeals nor witnesses.
Likewise, in the case of gates, paths, works, enjoyment, watercourses, and so forth, possession alone is indeed weighty;
neither a document nor witnesses [are required].
Now, when there is a dispute between a master and his servants regarding what has been given or not given,
or in connection with the taking of goods for sale, [the case arises] when one, having purchased wealth, does not pay for it.
In the case of gambling, betting, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared to be the means of proof; neither ordeal nor documentary evidence is required.
When a case involving violence, verbal abuse, or threats with a staff has been brought forward,
or in matters arising from the use of force, witnesses or even divine ordeal shall be employed.
But for those who have committed secret acts of violence, examination by ordeals is appropriate;
for among men, [guilt] is revealed through reasoning, signs, gestures, facial expressions, speech, the eyes, and physical movements.
Bhṛgu says that in all cases of the highest violence, one should investigate the true state of affairs through divine ordeals when there are no witnesses present.
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should even then verify it by means of ordeals.
In disputes concerning life-and-death matters, if witnesses are available,
the litigant who resorts to an ordeal shall not be questioned regarding those witnesses.
In matters of debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even slight circumstantial proof,
as well as divine ordeals, have been prescribed for the subjects out of a desire for their welfare.
A formal demand at the appropriate time, a slight application of reasoning, and likewise,
thirdly, an oath— by these means one should recover a debt in due order.
Even if he is repeatedly exhorted, if he should reject those words, one may perform the matter for him three, four, or five times; beyond that, one should cease.
But when there is an opposition to an injunction, one should provide support with fragments of reasoning based on place, time, purpose, connection, quantity, action, and so forth.

Even when logical arguments are insufficient, one should determine the truth by means of oaths— such as those involving fire, water, or meritorious deeds— which are applied with due regard for the matter at hand, the time, and the strength of the parties involved.
Where there may be a document involving fraud, if it has been presented to the king,
the king, seated upon the throne of justice, shall have it cleared by means of an ordeal.
In cases of verbal abuse and regarding land, one should not employ divine ordeals.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should administer ordeals;
one should establish the matter through witnesses, written documents, and possession.
One may reach a definitive conclusion by means of evidence, reasoning, or indeed by ordeal.
In all disputes whatsoever, the lord of men should always act [in this manner].
A written document, witnesses, and possession are recorded as the threefold means of proof;
the wise know that inference is the logical reason, as well as reasoning itself.
In the absence of the prior [title], one may establish ownership only by the subsequent [possession], and never otherwise—
neither by the means of proof (pramāṇa) cited by the plaintiff, nor by possession alone, nor by documents and witnesses.
No one should cause the plaintiff to undergo ordeals;
those expert in ordeals must administer the ordeal to the defendant.
In cases of false testimony, as well as in a counter-attack, that [proceeding] shall consist of four stages;
it should be understood as having two stages in the case of a prior judgment and in cases of admission.

Defeat is said to be of two kinds: that based on what is stated by the opponent and that based on what is stated by oneself. That based on the opponent's statement is of ten types, while that based on one's own statement is recorded as being of one type.
The shifting of the dispute to another matter, contradiction between the preceding and the subsequent,
the emergence of one's own action as a point of refutation, and the production of another's statement [as a pretext].
The non-specification of the place, the specification of the wrong place or time, the instigation of witnesses, and the suborning of testimony; K.248b.
[The document: A document is said to be of two kinds: that written by one's own hand and that written by another;
it may be without witnesses or with witnesses, and its validity depends on the established customs of the region.
A document written by the debtor's own hand, even if devoid of witnesses, should be known as a "handwritten document" (*svahasta-lekhya*); it is considered valid evidence by the wise.
One should cause [the document] to record the origin, the caste, the name, and the amount of the debt.
If one who has made such a claim merely remembers it, the matter shall perish if it was not recorded in writing.
A document, however, should be executed with witnesses, with the sequence of its letters uncorrupted,
consistent with the customs and laws of the region, and complete in all its matters.

A document that is endowed with proper color, phrasing, and action; which is free from doubt and possesses clear syllables; and which has no deficiency in its sequence or marks—such a document shall attain validity.
The established order of the four classes of knowledge, cities, guilds, corporations, citizens, and so forth,
as well as the document written for the sake of its formalization, is called a *sthiti-patra*.
When a formal accusation has been resolved and the penance has been performed by the people,
a certificate of purification should be obtained from them, accompanied by witnesses.
When all the highest [offenses] have been collectively brought together as a formal accusation,
that written record of the proceedings and the recital thereof is to be known as a *sandhipatra* (treaty or agreement).
When a dispute regarding boundaries has been settled, a boundary-deed is prescribed.
A document bearing the king's own hand, likewise marked with his seal,
and containing witnesses, is declared to be a royal edict in all matters.
The statements of the plaintiff and the defendant, the testimony of witnesses, the decision regarding the case, and how it was determined by himself; these are the matters to be recorded.
One should record this exactly as it was stated in writing, just as before;
first, one should set down the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant.

Thereafter, he should cause the decision regarding the doctrine of the Smṛti-śāstra to be recorded right there by the members of the court, the presiding judge, or the representatives of the families.
The king should first honor the plaintiff and, having joined him with the proven matter,
should give him a written document bearing his own signature.
And those members of the court who are present there, being experts in the treatises on law (*smṛti-śāstra*),
shall likewise cause their own signatures to be affixed there according to the rules for drawing up documents.
The wise know that a document executed according to this procedure is a *paścāt-kāra* (a subsequent confession).
However, where a legal action has been refuted by the plaintiff himself through evidence, there a *paścāt-kāra* may occur; it is not prescribed in all cases.

To those other than the inferior types, such as the false accuser and so forth, a document is granted; and that, being established by a summary of the proceedings, shall be the certificate of victory (*jaya-patraka*).
[Examination of Documents]
Having summoned them by the king's command, he should investigate the case according to the law:
a written document by means of the procedure for writing, and witnesses by means of the procedure for witnesses.

A document that is endowed with correct color, phrasing, and action; which is unambiguous and has clear syllables; and which possesses no deficiency in its sequence or formal marks—such a document shall attain validity.
A document that includes the place of transaction, the year, the month, the fortnight, and so forth,
and which bears the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe, is called a written instrument (*lekhyam*).
But when letters are displaced from their positions, out of order, doubtful,
or deviate from their proper forms, then that document is considered a forged writing.
That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which has been executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is deficient in its subject matter— such [legal documents] are defective.
A document executed by one who is intoxicated, one who fears for his property, one who is insane, or those who are afflicted; or by women, children, or those who are not independent, is not valid.
If it has been proclaimed and no one reverses it on the second day,
then that shall be authoritative, except in cases involving those who are intoxicated or insane.
A document may be rendered invalid due to the fault of the witnesses or the scribe; likewise, it may be invalidated by the fraudulent deception of the creditor or the debtor.
A written instrument is declared invalid if it is produced by corrupt persons, but it should be recognized as pure if produced by honest ones.
That document [is invalidated] by witnesses, scribes, and executors who are corrupted by bribery.
Indeed, whatever defects there may be in the means of proof must be stated by the disputant;
however, those that are concealed must be brought to light by the members of the court at the appropriate time through the citation of the scriptures.
Just as the witnesses, the scribe, and the author of the document incur guilt for their forgery, so too should the faults be attributed to those who corrupt the document through wickedness.
"If it was not written by the scribe, nor witnessed by the witnesses," when the defendant has stated this, the document is declared to be forged.
One should not invalidate a means of proof with a groundless defect; rather, one should invalidate it only through a genuine fault.
In the case of a false accusation, the accuser shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
In this manner, when a case involving a wicked person is being investigated in the king's court,
he should deliberate together with the Brahmins and determine the defects of the written document.
By that [same criterion] by which witnesses, scribes, and executors fall into the state of being fraudulent, the document becomes tainted; one should declare it to be pure when the parties are pure.
A document written by the creditor’s own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall be considered forged unless the maker can prove that it was indeed executed by him.
If a debtor denies a debt that has been recorded in writing with his own hand,
he shall be questioned by the witnesses present in the document or according to the testimony of the scribe.

In disputes concerning what has been done or not done, the determination of the case is made by witnesses through the written document; if the document is challenged, the plaintiff must point out those who were present when it was recorded.
Confusion regarding even the three types of written documents may arise among men;
therefore, one should establish the truth through the testimony of the debtor, witnesses, and the scribe, as well as by means of their handwriting.
Now, if the scribe and the witnesses have met their death,
they shall undoubtedly be cleared by means of their own handwriting and other such evidence.
When there is doubt regarding a debt-holder's own handwriting— whether he is living or deceased—
the determination of that document is made by means of other documents written in his own hand.
Even in the case of a document concerning the ocean, all those [deceased] remain recorded therein;
for that written record remains authoritative even when they have passed away.
Perception is never sublated by inference;
therefore, when a document is defective, its validity must be established by the testimony of witnesses.
For one who, for the sake of his own property, personally defaces a document,
that written deed must be countered by another written deed, or it may be set aside by means of witnesses where there were witnesses.
When a document is proven false by the testimony of witnesses or the scribe,
he who does not restore it to its original state shall be made to pay the highest fine.
When a wealthy person standing nearby is not requested for a loan by one who is capable,
that document— due to the suspicion that it is a pure debt— will reach a state of weakness.
A document that has remained unviewed and unheard for thirty years does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be living.
But when the recovery of the debt has been settled, he who does not produce the written document, nor even ask the debtor for it, shall not attain success in that matter.
One should carefully examine that which is recorded as a subsequent transaction;
if it is indeed consistent with reason, then that written document shall be accepted as valid evidence.
Otherwise, the matter must be decided again from the beginning,
for what was untrue has been established as true due to a failure of discernment.
That which is established by them should be set aside, even if it was executed with great effort by kings.
A royal edict that is pure in its seal, pure in its execution, pure in its enjoyment, and marked with the insignia,
and which is certified by the king’s own hand, attains validity.
But a document that is proven to be faultless shall attain validity.
If, when the document has been inspected, the debtor does not state the manifest defects therein,
then the document, having remained for twenty years, shall be considered valid.
When property is enjoyed by means of a document in the presence of one who is capable [to object], [it is valid].
For as long as twenty years, that document shall be free from defects.
Now, if a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years with absolute certainty,
its validity is established by that document, provided it is free from defects in the writing.
When a dispute over a boundary has been decided, a formal document regarding the boundary is to be prepared;
its defects must be declared for a period of twenty years.
Where a debt, together with the pledge, is recorded in writing,
they know that— even if witnesses have died— that document is the authority in cases of small transactions.
If something has been received by him, or even a gift that was not formally specified,
a document— even without a seal— is valid evidence when the witnesses are deceased.
If something has been received, or if a formal designation has been made,
or if a document has been written as proof— even if the witnesses have died.
A document is established as valid in all cases— provided it was presented at the proper time, and was accepted and likewise reminded of— even when the witnesses have died.
A written document is never invalidated even by divine witnesses;
for the rule of the written document is always superior, and thus it is not set aside by anything else.
The execution of a document should always be set aside by means of a counter-document associated with it or one that is superior to it; it should never be set aside by any other means.
Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears as if it were both non-existent and existent,
so too do skilled people create the likenesses of paintings.
A document that, having received property, is delivered to another;
or one that is concealed, or entered into by another, or executed in the house of someone else.
Whether the property has been delivered or not, or in some cases when it was previously recorded in writing,
this same rule is to be understood as the determination for the validation of a document.
He who forges a document regarding the sale or mortgage of immovable property shall be properly punished by having his tongue, hands, and feet cut off.
If a document is marred by stains, burnt, torn, or even worn out,
or likewise rubbed away by perspiration, one should have another document prepared.
Written documents, witnesses, and possession— these three are accepted as means of proof. Among these proofs, for men, possession is considered by tradition to be equal to a written document.
In cases of doubt regarding a carriage road, an exit gate, a watercourse, and so forth, possession alone is the weightier factor; such is the settled conclusion among the means of proof.
An inference is superior to a witness; a written document is superior to witnesses;
and possession by three generations, being unopposed, is more authoritative than these.
Neither the seizer nor his son shall employ force regarding the enjoyment of cattle, women, men, and so forth; such is the established law.
Possession is said to be of two kinds: with title and likewise without title;
that which has continued through three generations by itself is independent, but if it is of short duration, it must be with title.
Possession inherited from a grandfather is considered primary, as is that inherited from a father;
when uninterrupted by these three, it is deemed stable and valid for sixty years.
But when possession has been accompanied by documentary evidence, and that which was properly possessed is thus established, the claimant recovers it; indeed, it may never be taken away from him.
When a plaintiff brings a claim for lost property or for possession based on documentary evidence,
he must declare in court the time, the proof, and the circumstances of the gift.
In the period governed by the Smṛtis, possession of land is held to be valid only when accompanied by a title;
however, in the period beyond the reach of memory, due to the absence of such a title, possession acquired through succession over three generations is valid.
In the first case, possession must be accompanied by title; in the middle case, possession must likewise be accompanied by title.
But where possession has continued uninterruptedly for three generations, that possession alone is the sufficient title.
The acquirer, even if his possession is accompanied by documentary evidence, must clear it of defects in that document;
however, his son need only clear it of defects in possession and shall not be liable for defects in the document.
For whatever property has been taken up by someone, that person alone shall recover it when sued;
even if there has been enjoyment for a long period of time, possession is not held to belong to anyone other than him.
One should not, out of greed, disturb long-standing possession that has been unclaimed.

But regarding property that was enjoyed by the father in accordance with legal custom and practice, when he has died, no objection can be raised; for that property was acquired by him through such enjoyment.
But when land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the rule,
even in the absence of a written document, the fourth person shall obtain it there.
Just as milk produces curd endowed with flavor after a period of time,
so too does the cause of a gift produce enjoyment that has descended through three generations after a period of time.
In the treatises, possession is powerful when it is continuous and long-standing;
however, that which was previously established is to be understood as valid even if it has been interrupted.

One should not claim ownership over women, nor over the property of a king or a deity; likewise, one should not claim it over the wealth of a child or a Vedic scholar, as these belong respectively to their mothers and fathers.
A certain man, seeking wealth, might live for thirty-six years as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) without having fulfilled his vows; or he might dwell for a long time in another kingdom.
A student who has returned home but remains without vows should thereafter seek out his own property;
possession for fifty years constitutes one who has appropriated that wealth.
It is traditionally taught that twelve years is the period for those seeking knowledge;
likewise, for those seeking the knowledge of arts and crafts, it is proclaimed that the period lasts until they have mastered them.
Whatever property of theirs has been enjoyed by friends or kinsmen while they were unaware of it,
and likewise by those who are not dependent on the king, that is not lost by the lapse of time.

When property has been enjoyed by paternal kinsmen, relatives, or one's own people, there can be no legal proof of ownership based on that enjoyment alone; one must consider the enjoyment as having occurred elsewhere.
[The Principle: But he who, being requested by a creditor, does not provide the means of payment three, four, or five times, shall become a debtor to the other.
Giving, instigation, sowing dissension, the act of enticing,
and the removal of the mind— these are indeed the causes that bring about division.

Whichever of these [grounds for defeat] is established by the proponent in that case, there the primary action shall apply; however, when the proponent's denial has been established, the primary action shall apply to that denial.
The king must not cause a delay in the testimony of witnesses;
for through time, a great evil arises characterized by the subversion of Dharma.
The king himself should examine the witnesses who have been presented;
together with the members of the court, he should scrutinize the statement spoken by the witnesses.
The time for witnesses to be summoned is when there is a need for a full understanding of the correct course of action;
however, where the testimony is doubtful, one should litigate the matter immediately once it becomes clear.
Within the assembly, the judge shall, while the plaintiff and the defendant are present, formally appoint all the witnesses according to this procedure, addressing them with conciliatory words.
"Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter, speak all of that with truth; for your role here is that of witnesses."
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, he, being pure himself, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either north or east.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are known for their conduct and who understand the matter— the judge shall question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths.

But when that which was personally experienced occurs due to the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, the testimony of the witnesses must be accepted; otherwise, it is not so, according to Bṛhaspati.
Those who are of renowned family and character, free from greed and delusion,
trustworthy, pure, and distinguished— their testimony is undoubtedly valid.
The witness should be examined by the litigant as he is; one should have him examined by witnesses who are exactly like him.
One should never have a superior or an inferior person examined by witnesses.
Bhṛgu spoke to the wearers of sectarian marks, the guilds and associations, the merchant corporations, and others who exist as collectives, as well as whatever other groups there may be.
For groups of slaves, wandering performers, wrestlers, and those who live by elephants, horses, or weapons—
each of these associations has its leaders and members;
their disputes within their own groups are settled by those members, who serve as witnesses for them.
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes.
Where it is impossible for residents of foreign lands to appear, one should admit documentary evidence and witnesses sent by those learned in the three Vedas.
In the case of a deposit, however, even a single person may be declared as a witness if he is an insider;
even a single messenger sent by the plaintiff becomes a witness.
Whatever commodity has been processed by whomsoever, that person alone shall establish its value;
in a dispute concerning it, he alone is declared to be the authority.
The scribe, the presiding judge, and the members of the court, in their respective order,
are declared to be witnesses when the king observes the legal proceeding.
Furthermore, others who have not been specifically designated are declared to be witnesses for litigants:
the village headman, the presiding judge, and the king.
One who is an insider in the affairs [of the family], one who has been sent by the plaintiff,
and those of the same lineage in disputes between families— these too may serve as witnesses.
But when a dispute over the division of inheritance arises and doubt is present, the testimony of the kinsmen is the authority in that case; in their absence, [the testimony of] others.
Among witnesses who have been recorded in writing or specified by the plaintiff,
if even one of them gives testimony otherwise, then all are not valid witnesses due to that discrepancy.
For a witness appointed by one person may not indeed dispute the case for another;
in his absence, however, either a representative or a relative may dispute it.
Those who live by his occupation, those who perform services for him, his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates— these, however, are not to be witnesses.
The sons of a maternal aunt, as well as the sons of a uterine brother and a maternal uncle—these are declared to be "sapindas" (blood relations); one should not employ them as witnesses.
Kinsmen, relatives by marriage, the husband of one's sister,
the father, a kinsman, a paternal uncle, a father-in-law, and likewise spiritual teachers;
Those appointed to positions in cities, villages, and districts, as well as royal favorites, do not inquire [into the truth]; such royal servants are merely devoted to their own interests.

In cases concerning debts and the like, as well as in stable legal matters, one should examine the witnesses; however, in cases of violence and urgent offenses, examination is prescribed only in certain instances.
In cases of contradiction with the king's command, in matters of seizure and acts of violence,
and likewise in theft and verbal assault, one should not examine witnesses.
If the legal action concerns what occurred inside a house at night, or outside a village,
one should not examine witnesses in these very cases.
Witnesses should never state their testimony unless they are questioned by the plaintiff;
there should be no testimony among them where one would offer it of one's own accord.
A witness who has been recorded in writing and one who is present at the trial follows two paths.
Now, if he alone has ascended by his own hand and remains there,
but does not recognize [the debtor], then one should establish the claim by means of his own handwriting.
One who is brought by the plaintiff himself and recorded in the document is called a "written witness" (*likhita-sākṣin*); such a witness exists even without a formal written record.
But that witness who, having seen the matter repeatedly for the sake of accomplishing the business,
is reminded by the plaintiff— that one is called "reminded" in this context.
One who has been brought for a specific purpose and one who has arrived incidentally— these two, though not recorded as witnesses, are effective in proving the plaintiff's case.
He who, remaining hidden, has been clearly informed by the plaintiff for the sake of establishing his own case regarding the statement of the defendant,
is called a hidden witness.
He who, among witnesses, repeatedly states his testimony— whether by hearing it from others or by making it heard himself— is designated as a "subsequent witness" (*sākṣy-uttara*).
One who, through trust, has been addressed with secret counsel or informed of a task,
and likewise one who has gained access to that task, should be known as a "secret agent" (gūḍhacārī).
Where the plaintiff has perished, there a witness who has died in the interval [is considered as such];
and where the defendant has perished, it is likewise ordained in that case.

[The disclosure of defects in witnesses: Whatever defects of the document there may be, as well as those attributed to the witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been stated.
But he who, regarding the meaning of what has been stated, should revile witnesses who were previously examined and fail to state the reason for that [reviling], shall incur the first amercement.

One should not invalidate the evidence through a pretext, but rather through a genuine defect; for in the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
When the defendant or the plaintiff proves the defects of a witness,
there is no separate legal proceeding, because it serves the purpose of the matter at hand.
The defects of the witnesses must be declared by the defendant in the assembly;
having written all of them down on a document, he should then state his rebuttal.
But they are never eligible to serve as witnesses in the defense;
therefore, they must be treated otherwise by the defendant through legal action.
If the defendant fails to prove his wealth, he shall be compelled to pay it;
all witnesses who have been proven [to be false] are excluded from the status of witnesses.
One should discern his internal state through facial expressions, gestures, and movements;
the opponent is considered defeated when he is identified by such inference.
Trembling, perspiration, then agitation, dryness of the lips, touching [the body], scratching the ground, leaving one's place, looking sideways or upwards,
and a change in voice— these the wise declare to be the signs of a wicked person.
Witnesses must give their testimony while remaining within the assembly hall, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.
In the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, and in the presence of the matter to be proved, one should give testimony directly; never under any circumstances should one do so in absentia.
In some cases, it may be stated even without those two;
this rule applies to four-footed animals as well as to bipeds and immovable things.
Even in the absence of weights, articles to be counted, or measures, one may dispute;
in all formal transactions, witness-status is not otherwise than that.

If one must testify regarding the killing of living beings, let him declare it in the presence of Śiva; but in the absence of such a witness, he should not declare it otherwise than by means of a mark.
The testimony of those witnesses, which is stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted; once the witnesses have spoken, they should not be questioned again by the king.
Whatever they may state according to its very nature should be accepted as the legal proceeding; whatever else they might state regarding dharma and artha is meaningless.
But what is seen by those assembled together must be stated exactly as it was;
however, what concerns individual or separate tasks must be stated individually.
But when a matter is discovered at a different time, one should have each witness questioned regarding it separately; for Bhṛgu says that such is a "separated" (bhinna-kāla) case.
In disputes concerning debts and the like, which are generally of a fixed nature, once a decision has been reached,
the matter to be proven is not established if the amount stated is either less or more than the actual sum.
Even when only a portion of the matter to be proven has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established;
this applies to matters involving sexual intercourse with women, acts of violence, and theft, as well as whatever else has been specifically defined as the matter to be proven.
But where there may be a deficiency or an excess [in the testimony], one should exclude that witness from the case;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, whereas one who fails to speak [the truth] deserves punishment.
Where one contradicts [the truth regarding] the place, time, wealth, number, form, caste, appearance,
or age in testimony, the wise know that as unspoken [though it has been spoken].

When the categories of the matter have been specified and the witness has been brought to testify, if he does not speak in accordance with the facts, that testimony is not considered properly delivered.
Where witnesses state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too should be known as improper; this is the determination regarding witnesses.
[The Faults and Punishments of Witnesses] If they speak everything without being questioned, or likewise fail to speak when questioned,
witnesses shall be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
In cases of verbal abuse, fraud, or litigation, they should be fined three hundred [paṇas].
In disputes concerning debts and the like, they shall likewise be made to pay the money and the debt itself.
A witness who has not been designated, nor summoned, nor even produced—
whoever should speak falsely or even the truth— is to be punished as the lowest of men.
If a witness does not testify to the matter for which he was summoned, he shall pay the debt and receive an equal fine;
in other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred [paṇas].
And those who, having spoken one way, speak otherwise, are to be punished as being guilty of quibbling with words (*vākchala*).
Having seized all the property of one who, out of greed for a legal matter, has designated false witnesses, the king should thereafter banish him from the realm.
When the case has indeed been established by the witnesses for the plaintiff,
but the defendant then establishes the case otherwise,
or when there are many or noble men [acting as witnesses], they shall be considered false witnesses.
When the legal procedure has been purified according to the rule, then there is the purification of that statement;
and he who is proven from a purified statement is proven as to the matter—this is the established principle.
One should recognize that within seven days, where a witness speaks falsely,
there shall be disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman, occurring after two weeks, three weeks, or even forty-six days, depending on the specific nature of the object and other factors.
[The divine ordeals and the rules concerning the subject matter of their disputes:
No one shall cause the accuser to undergo the divine ordeals; those skilled in the administration of ordeals shall administer the ordeal to the accused.
But for those suspected by kings, one should employ the balance and other such ordeals;
and in the procedure for self-purification, one should not require the oath by the head.
For those who are tainted by public scandal or suspected of being thieves, weights and the like should be employed;
in such cases, indeed, Bhṛgu says that the head ordeal must not be used.
One should never employ the ordeal of the head in cases of suspicion;
rather, one should cause headless ordeals to be administered to the king's servants.
In cases of suspicion, the establishment of trust, the division of inheritance among heirs, and the performance of collective undertakings, one should always cause a deposit to be made.
Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should determine the proof;
however, in cases of theft or violence, one should administer an ordeal even when the matter is of small value.
Having ascertained the total value of all the goods, one should determine the amount of gold; then, one should administer the ordeal corresponding to that amount of gold.
Having determined the number of gold pieces, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
however, upon the loss of eighty, one should indeed offer oneself into the fire.
In the event of a loss of sixty [paṇas], water should be administered; for a loss of forty, indeed a jar [of water];
and for a loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of the ordeal from the royal treasury (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, upon the loss of more than five [māṣakas], rice [should be given] for half of that half;
but upon the loss of half of that half, one should touch the eighth [relative], such as a son or the like.
But when even half of that half is lost, worldly transactions are prescribed;
by investigating in this manner, the king does not fall away from dharma and artha.
[The regulations for divine ordeals according to the status of the plaintiff, the defendant, their caste, and their craft:

One should employ fire in the case of a Kṣatriya, a water-pot in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, and water in the case of a Vaiśya; or one may employ any divine ordeal for all castes, except poison, which is forbidden for those of the highest twice-born caste.
Cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors,
servants, and usurers— one should cause these twice-born men to be treated like Śūdras.
One should never administer fire to metalworkers, water to those who subsist on water,
nor poison to those who know the application of mantras.
One should not appoint a person observing a vow who suffers from diseases of the mouth to consume rice.
One should avoid fire for those suffering from leprosy, water for those with asthma and coughing,
and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with disorders of bile and phlegm.
The treasury should not be given by the wise to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the conduct of nihilists.
For those who have killed their mother, father, a twice-born, a teacher, a child, a woman, or a king;
for those burdened with mortal sins (mahāpātaka); and especially for atheists—

But those who bear the marks of religious orders yet are licentious, who know the practices of spells and yoga, who are born from the mixture of castes, and who persist in the practice of evil— K.428a/ liṅgināṃ praśaṭhānāṃ tu mantra.yoga.kriyā.vidām / K.428b/ varṇa.saṃkara.jātānāṃ pāpa.abhyāsa.pravartinām //
In these very cases of accusation, and especially in those that are blameworthy, a king devoted to righteousness should never, even with effort, ordain an ordeal.
An ordeal by divine test is fit for virtuous men appointed by these very [authorities];
where virtuous men do not desire it, those to be cleared must be tested by their own people.
Divine ordeals must not be administered to those guilty of mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), especially to atheists, nor to those who are habitually engaged in sinful practices.
In these types of disputes, divine ordeals are strictly prohibited;
Manu states that one should have them performed by virtuous men and should not abandon one who has been falsely accused.
For those who are untouchable, the lowest of slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions (prātilomya), there is no legal standing before the king.
One should prescribe those well-known divine ordeals when there is doubt regarding them.
[Divine Locations]:
One should employ those men who have been accused of great crimes (*mahāpātakin*) in the abode of Indra;
and those who have engaged in treason against the king, at the royal gate.
For those born of inverse unions (prātilomya), the ordeal must be administered at a crossroads;
for others besides these, the wise know that the ordeal should be administered in the midst of the assembly.

But when there is a conflict regarding time or place, one should determine what is appropriate; in such a case, one should have the ordeal performed by another person—this is the rule for the reverse situation.
Those gifts given at an improper place or time, or those made while one is living abroad, always lead to deviation from one's goals in this world; of this there is no doubt.
If there is a contradiction in the means of proof, he should establish that which is to be proven;
for even if the divine ordeals have been administered as prescribed, the king should reject them.
Indeed, those [deposits] must be returned again by [those who are] foolish, greedy, and wicked.
Therefore, the ordeal should be administered by experts according to the prescribed rule;
however, when applied contrary to the rule, it is not capable of proving the case.
If the sling breaks, the balance beam snaps, or likewise the cord,
or if there is doubt regarding the purity [of the ordeal], one should test the man again.
[The Procedure for the Fire Ordeal] If the accused stumbles or is burned in a place other than the designated spot,
the gods consider him not burnt; one should therefore cause him to undergo the ordeal again.
[The Procedure for the Water Ordeal] For the sake of purification, one should prepare arrows with tips not made of iron,
as well as those made of bamboo; and the thrower should discharge them with great firmness.
Once it has been thrown, the sinking must be observed; the time for the descent and the emergence must be simultaneous.
Upon the descent, however, the emergence must be observed; another man shall enter the water.
If, however, only the head is seen [floating] while neither the ears nor the nose are visible when he enters the water, one should declare even such a person to be pure.
If a man who has submerged himself is seen by living beings as he emerges,
he shall dive again in that very place, once it has been identified by local landmarks.

[The Procedure for the Poison and Divine Ordeals] That which resembles a goat's horn, dark green, and very thick, produced from a horn; and which, when broken, has the appearance of *verā*— this is known as the poison of horned animals.
One should make that red and black, and likewise hard according to its characteristics; by this method, it should be known as divine by those skilled in the divine.
That which resembles the vatsanābha [poison] is yellow; this is the certainty through the knowledge of its color.
One should recognize that as vatsanābha which has the shape of a pearl-oyster shell or a conch shell when it is broken.
One should make it clear by mixing it with honey and milk;
thus has the external characteristic been described by those who accomplish the Dharma.
In the forenoon, in a cool place, one should administer poison to living beings,
having ground it finely and mixed with thirty times its amount of clarified butter.
From a pala of poison, that portion which is one-twentieth should be taken;
this, reduced by one-eighth and saturated with clarified butter, is to be administered to the person undergoing purification.

[The Procedure for the Divine Ordeal by the Balance] When the offense against the gods is slight, one should have them bathe in water consecrated with weapons; they must be made to drink it. If a change [of color] occurs, they are impure; otherwise, being pure, they are to be restrained [and released].

[The Procedure for Rice] K.453a: In the ordeal of drinking the water used for bathing a deity, or in the ordeal of eating rice, K.453b: one who spits out pure rice is declared pure; otherwise, he is to be restrained as impure.
In the case of one who has been subjected to detention but is proven pure by means of the treasury,
the judge shall compel the accuser to pay both the fine and the legal costs of the accusation.
A righteous king should honor a man who has been proven innocent by the ordeal of divine proof.
Where blood is seen, and the jaw-hair withers,
and whose body trembles— one should declare such a person to be impure.
Then, if there is a failure of fate, after twenty-one days, he should cause the defendant to pay that matter with effort, as well as the fine.

If that [debt] were to belong to that one person alone and not to all the people [of the guild], then he shall be liable for the disease, fire, death of a kinsman, and the debt; and he shall be made to pay a fine.
Consumption, dysentery, and eruptions; pain in the palate and bones;
eye disease, throat ailments, as well as insanity;
headache and paralysis of the arms—these are the diseases of men caused by fate.
One who is pure shall be made to pay fifty [paṇas]; one who is impure shall become liable to punishment.
In cases of poison, water, fire, the balance, the holy water-vessel, rice,
and the ordeal of the heated gold bean, one should prescribe punishment in the respective order.
One thousand and six hundred, as well as five hundred,
four, three, two, and one— likewise, one should determine a reduction according to the degree of degradation among those who are degraded.
[The Rule for Oaths] K.462a: Where a ritual act is prescribed but the specific limb of the performer is not mentioned, K.462b:
it should be understood that in such cases, the right hand is the means for reaching the completion of those acts.
He for whom no terrible misfortune caused by kings or fate occurs within fourteen days shall be known as pure regarding the oath.

[Consideration of acts performed by those who are insane, lacking independence, and so forth: Whatever is given or whatever is done by one who is insane, intoxicated, or likewise in another state of mind— that shall have no legal validity whatsoever.
The master should rescind any transaction performed by one who is not independent;
no one other than the master may dispute it, except in cases involving transactions made by one who is terrified or insane.
A father who lacks independence, a son, a brother, or even a nephew;
or one who is younger, whose property is undivided, as well as a slave or a laborer.
Transactions involving fields, houses, or slaves— whether gifts, mortgages, or sales—
performed by those who are not independent do not attain validity, unless they have been subsequently ratified.
All these [weights and measures] are authoritative for the purchase and sale of commodities,
provided that they are approved while being used in commercial transactions.

In the same manner, the brother, the brother's son, or the son may [dispose of] fields and other property, provided they have been authorized by the elder to perform the necessary duties when he is departing.
But he to whom authority has been delegated regarding a particular matter is the master in that matter; his employer cannot undo the business transacted by him otherwise.
A father has authority over his son's offspring and wife regarding their instruction, as well as regarding their sale or gift; however, he has no authority over the son himself.
[The Function of Determination] K.472a: Purification has been declared by those who know the true principles of the scriptures to be medical treatment;
K.472b: and it is recorded as being of two kinds, consisting of expiation and punishment.
Even when multiple claims are brought forward, the creditor recovers only as much wealth as he can prove by means of witnesses; that much alone is the recovered debt.
Bṛhaspati states that if a person, having made a total denial, should later admit even a small portion of it in private, he must be made to pay the entire amount for which he was sued.
Thus, seated upon the seat of justice and remaining impartial, the adjudication of legal cases should be observed by him together with Brahmins, and not otherwise.
Having personally observed or heard the legal proceedings from the presiding judge,
the king should then issue a certificate of victory for the sake of official recognition.

[The Procedure for Punishment] K.477a: But the king should cause a Brahmin to pay [the debt] to the owner by means of conciliation alone; K.477b: but others who are wicked, he should cause to pay by afflicting them according to the local custom.
Bhṛgu declared that one may cause even an heir or a friend to pay [the debt] through deception; he spoke thus regarding merchants, farmers, and artisans as well.
Having ascertained that he is unable to pay the fine, the king should make him perform labor under his own supervision;
if he is incapable of even that, he should be cast into prison—with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
But he should cause cultivators who belong to the kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra castes to pay [the tax] when they are making efforts [to cultivate].
