In the case of offenses against the teacher, the father, the mother, and likewise against kinsmen— for these, no punishment whatsoever is ordained.
But where an improper act has been committed in order to save one's life, there shall indeed be no punishment; this is the law remembered by Bhṛgu.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in every kind of sin;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth intact and unhurt.
For those of all four castes who do not perform penance,
he shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both their bodies and their wealth.
By whatever fault a Śūdra incurs a punishment according to the law, if that same fault occurs for a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be double, double [the penalty].
A Śūdra who has renounced the world and devoted himself to the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings—
if he commits a crime, he should be punished with death, or else fined double the usual amount.
In all offenses, whatever fine in money is prescribed for a man, half of that shall be paid by women; in the case of killing, however, there shall be the amputation of a limb for the man.
Women are not to be held accountable when they lack independence; in such a case, the man is the one at fault.
They are to be disciplined by their master, but the king shall bring the man to justice.
If a woman whose husband is away has been seized,
she shall be kept in confinement for as long as it takes for her master to return.
Whatever punishment has been diligently prescribed for a particular offense,
the king shall receive either the payment in paṇas or its equivalent value.
Where a fine of one māṣa or two pādas is prescribed,
it should be understood that if no specific coin is mentioned, a māṣaka is to be calculated as the unit.
Where a fine is stated in terms of *māṣakas*, one should specify there the corresponding amount in silver;
where it is stated in terms of *kṛṣṇalas*, that indeed shall be the determination of the stated fine.
A *māṣa* should be known as the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, however, is a fourth part of a *māṣaka* or a *paṇa*.
In the region of the Five Rivers, this is the conventional designation:
four *kārṣāpaṇa-uṇḍikās* are to be known as one *dhānaka*;
twelve of those *dhānakas* are a *suvarṇa*, and a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
[The Re-examination of the Legal Process:
When the members of the court have determined that a claim which was previously non-existent is indeed existent,
that case is declared "adjudicated" (tīrita) and is said to be "instructed" (anuśiṣṭa) based on the testimony of witnesses.
But if one who has not attained satisfaction, even though his family and other circumstances have been determined,
should reconsider that which was done, the king shall rescind that ill-deed.
[Consideration of Interest on Loans] K.497a: One should never grant an advance to women, slaves, or children;
the giver shall not recover it from them, though he may give whatever wealth he possesses to them.

But whatever interest has been stipulated by the debtor as excessive, it must always be paid if it was agreed upon during a time of distress; however, that which was voluntarily contracted [at other times] shall not be paid.
Interest stipulated otherwise must not be paid under any circumstances.
When one clears a debt where the interest increases exclusively and continuously,
and the debtor pays it back at every fixed time, that is known as *śikhā-vṛddhi* (topknot interest).
Satisfaction is proclaimed as the fruit of the home, and the acquisition of enjoyments as the fruit of the field.
But that which is used up entirely, while interest is still being calculated,
and where the loan is employed in such a manner— that is called *ādhibhoga*.
[Ākṛtavṛddhiḥ]:
If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without returning it,
after the lapse of one year, that creditor may recover interest on that debt.
If one who has been requested for a loan departs for another region after having made an advance but without giving the principal,
his debt shall begin to accrue interest after three months have passed.
But if one who resides even in his own country does not pay when requested at any time,
the judge shall compel him to pay interest that has accrued without his having caused it, even if he is unwilling.
A gift given out of affection shall not increase until it has been asked for;
if it is asked for and not given, it increases by five percent per month.
Interest on a deposit, the remainder of interest, and likewise profits from buying and selling—
if these are not paid when requested, they increase by five percent per month.
If one who has taken merchandise should depart for another region without paying the price,
the creditor shall recover that wealth with interest after three seasons have passed.
Interest shall never accrue on hides, grain, liquor, gambling debts, the price of merchandise,
bride-price, or amounts received as surety.
The maximum limit of interest should be understood as follows:
the property lent by creditors shall always be doubled;
if it does not reach double, one may calculate further interest.
Interest on jewels, pearls, corals, gold, and silver, as well as on iron,
tin, lead, and wool, remains at double the principal;
and likewise for all oils, liquors, and clarified butter.
The interest on molasses and salt should be known to be eightfold.
Base metals are considered to yield a fivefold return, and land likewise an eightfold return;
because of the statement "immediately," it is paid immediately.
[Discharge of Debt] [The Rule for When Multiple Debts Are Combined]:
That which has been recorded on the same day, however, one should discharge as an equal debt.
Seizure, protection, and profit [are the results] in that order; otherwise, however, they follow the sequence [of the offenses].
But when there is a concurrence of various debts, whichever was contracted first must be paid first; after that, one may pay the king, and then the debt to a *śrotriya*.
If it can be proven that a certain commodity was acquired by means of another's property,
that property must be returned by the debtor to its owner alone, and not otherwise.
[The pledge for use]: If, having received property for the sake of interest, one gives it over as something fit for enjoyment—
whether it be movable or immovable— that is called a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*).
Having paid a price exceeding that [original value], one may acquire one's own field or other property.

If one person should provide a pledge to two people, what should be the course of action? Of those two, the prior claim shall be accepted; the one who made it later is liable for the punishment of a thief.
When a document concerning a pledge, sale,
or gift is contradicted by a single act, that document is considered fraudulent.

Kātyāyana declared that an unspecified [document], one that has been specified, and one that has been written down in a single place are all superseded by a document written with specific details; such a document is superior.
If one were to first posit something non-existent whose nature has not been specified,
it would be like space, and that [posited entity] would remain unspecified.
Whatever he may possess at that time, he shall point out as the prescribed amount.
But when one has first assigned all one's property and subsequently deposits it marked with one's name, how could that not be the more powerful evidence?
When a field or even a village is marked by boundary signs,
and when the villages and so forth are recorded in writing, then one shall obtain success.
But whatever has been pledged as a deposit (ādhīkṛta) and is destroyed through an act of God or by the king,
in that case the debtor must pay the debt to the creditors along with interest.
If [the debtor] should fall ill or die due to a fault of the creditor,
the creditor shall be made to provide another pledge, and the debtor shall be released from the debt.
If one causes a debtor to perform work against his will and without his consent, he shall be made to enjoy the fruit of that labor; alternatively, he does not receive interest on the loan.
But he who, while another is performing work as a pledge, harasses or threatens him with words, punishment, or physical acts, shall incur the first amercement.
If one should forcibly enter a pledge that has not been released and which was not intended for such use, he shall incur the first amercement;
and the pledgor shall likewise incur [the same penalty].
If a creditor enjoys a pledge on the basis of a fraudulent document from a debtor,
the king, having caused him to pay a fine, shall cause that document regarding the pledge to be destroyed.
But where the depositor is not present, the creditor shall report the pledge [to the king]; it is the established rule that such a pledge, once publicly proclaimed by the king, may then be sold.
But having received the amount with interest, O King, he should return the remainder as it is due.

[The Procedure for Sureties] K.530a: In matters of gifts, attendance, and verbal agreements, and for the purpose of a pledge based on trust, one should cause a surety to be taken; likewise, in the opposite case, as appropriate. K.530b: One should cause a surety to be taken accordingly in the reverse situation.
If a guarantor for appearance does not produce the person at the proper place and time,
he shall pay the debt, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
For the purpose of searching for what has been lost, however, a period of up to three fortnights should be granted;
if he can produce it there, the surety shall be released.
If, when the time has elapsed, the surety does not produce that person, he shall be made to pay that amount; this same rule is ordained even in the case of the debtor's death.
Where a pledge has been taken and the debtor is present to show it,
the son shall be made to pay that debt from his own wealth, even without his father's consent.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
failing to produce him, he shall pay the debt from his own property to that person.

If the first two [witnesses] give false testimony, they shall be made to pay the wealth [in dispute] as it was known at that time; but if the latter two disagree, they shall be punished along with their sons, even in their absence.
If all the sons are living under one roof, they should pay the debt together; however, if the father has gone abroad, the son should pay it.
But if the father has died, Bṛhaspati says that the son shall pay only his own paternal share, not the debts of others.
Among those who have entered under a single roof, he who is seen there [at the time of the debt] shall be made to pay;
if the debtor has gone abroad, his son shall pay everything; but if he is dead, the son shall pay his father's share.
But he who, being pressured, gives a surety for another while himself being pressed for debt,
shall be entitled to receive double that amount after three fortnights have passed.
If a person for whose sake a thing was given by another who had been requested according to the prescribed rule,
that surety shall receive it once he has been proven [guilty] by witnesses.
In the event of a breach of a solemn agreement, one should cause double the amount to be paid;
however, for one who fails to fulfill it, there shall be a forfeiture of that sum—this is the purpose of the solemn agreement.

[By whom should a debt incurred by the father and others be repaid? K.542a: One should know that what was borrowed for the sake of the family by one who was incapable, or by one who was ill, or on account of a calamity, is a debt incurred in times of distress. K.542b: One should know that as being contracted in times of distress.
Whatever was spent on the marriage of a daughter and whatever was performed for funeral rites—
all this, if done by the family, must be paid to the master.
According to the law, a debt incurred by a son need not be paid by the father;
however, that which has been promised or that which has been approved must be paid.
Bhṛgu declares that a debt contracted for the sake of the family by a slave, a wife, a mother, a pupil, or even by a son, must be paid, even if the absent husband has not given his consent.
A debt contracted with the husband or the son, or by the woman alone—such a debt must be paid; otherwise, that which was contracted by her [alone] need not be paid.
If a woman has been told by her husband who intends to die, "You must pay this debt," she shall be compelled to pay it even if she does not consent, provided that wealth was entrusted to her.
Even if the father is afflicted by disease or has departed from his own country,
the sons must pay the debt contracted by the father after twenty years have passed.
In such cases, one should cause the sons to pay the debt even while their fathers are still living— namely, when the fathers are diseased, insane, aged, or have been away on a long journey.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
this applies even if [the father] is born blind, an outcast, insane, suffering from consumption, leprosy, or other such diseases.
Since sons who have been born deliver their fathers from the lowest debt through the very act of giving, for that reason fathers desire sons.
When the father has died, the inheritance must never be given at any time by one who has not yet attained legal capacity;
however, it should be given at the proper time according to the prescribed rule. Otherwise, they shall dwell in hell.
If he has not yet attained legal capacity, even though he is independent, he remains liable for debt in this world;
for independence is traditionally held to belong to the eldest, based on qualities and age.
That debt which was witnessed or remains after what was paid, being ancestral, must be repaid;
however, a debt that is defective or was opposed by the father should never be paid under any circumstances.
But that debt which was seen by the father, inherited in due order from the grandfather, and which remains undisputed and unpaid by the sons—that must be paid by the grandsons; so says Bhṛgu.
But that which belonged to the grandfather and was not given away by his sons while they were living in sickness—
it is from such property that the grandsons must give an equal share to their grandfather's heirs.
But one should compel the son to pay the debt if he is free from affliction, capable of possessing wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not compel the son to pay.
Whatever must be given constantly by fathers, in their absence it should be paid from that wealth;
or rather, that wealth should be given to the owner at that time by the sons or the grandsons.
While the father’s debt still exists, the son shall not take the inheritance; that wealth must be given to the creditor, but if he takes it after the father has died, he shall be made to pay it back.
In the absence of a son, however, the debt must be paid by the grandson with diligence;
it should not be paid by the fourth descendant, for from that point it ceases.
A grandson must never pay a debt incurred as a surety;
however, a father’s debt must always be paid by his son in its entirety.
The debt must be paid by the heir to the estate; in his absence, by the wife;
and in her absence, by the sons; and in their absence, by other heirs to the estate, in due order.
As long as a son does not receive his existing paternal property,
the creditor shall not be made to pay, even if the debtor is very wealthy.

Whatever has been promised, whether recorded in writing or given as a verbal gift, and whatever men know to have been given out of lust to a woman who previously belonged to another; [all such gifts may be recovered].
For where, having caused injury or having destroyed property out of anger,
one says something intended to cause satisfaction, one should know that to be an act committed out of anger.
Whether healthy or afflicted by illness, one who has made a promise for a religious purpose must pay it;
if he dies without having paid, his son shall be compelled to pay—of this there is no doubt.
But whatever debt has been contracted by those who are penniless and childless, such as vintners and others,
the one who enjoys their wives must indeed pay that debt.
The manager of the debts of female liquor-sellers, hunters, washermen, cowherds,
and boatmen shall be made to pay those debts, as he is responsible for their husbands' affairs.
And a debt contracted by a wife shall not in any way bind her husband, except for what was incurred during times of distress; for men have extensive obligations toward the maintenance of the family.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and vintners;
for their livelihood is centered on those [occupations] and their families depend upon them.
If a woman,
while her husband is still alive, resorts to another man, that property must be taken away by the son alone, excluding the daughters.
One should take up the thread for the sake of the debt, never for the sake of pleasure;
for one should not cause the parents to give it when there is no valid reason.

If a woman who has sons, even though she possesses capable male offspring, should abandon her own son after taking his mother’s property, Manu says that in that case the father’s debt shall be cleared from that property.

If a woman, for the sake of her young son or for excessive wealth, has resorted to another man, that man who she has resorted to shall pay her debt; this is declared to be the rule regarding women with young sons.
For those who have lived abroad for a long time, those who are without kin, the dull-witted, the insane, the afflicted, and those wearing the marks of ascetics—
even while they are still alive, their property must be given by those dependent upon their wives' wealth.
When a son is overwhelmed by calamity, or when a child is seen making an effort [to pay], he who takes the property shall be made to pay; in his absence, she who takes the household goods shall pay.
First, the one who takes the property shall give;
after him, the one who takes the wife; in the absence of a daughter, or if the son is utterly destitute, [the husband shall give].

A debt contracted by a wife must be paid by the husband, and a debt belonging to the mother must be paid by the son; likewise, that which was contracted for the sake of the husband must be paid when he has departed for another land after having made the agreement.
That which was done by a son shall be paid;
likewise that which has been formally acknowledged, that which was done without being contested, and that which was heard of and not subsequently called into question.

[A debtor's confinement and the consideration for recovering the debt: A debtor who is to be detained shall be held in public view within an assembly of people, until he has paid what is due, in accordance with the established customs of the region.
If a person being carried should feel the urge to void excrement or urine,
he should either be followed behind or released while still tied up.
He who has provided a surety must be released day by day;
at mealtime and at night, the surety remains standing for the bond.
He who cannot find a surety for his appearance nor provide one for it shall be confined in prison or kept under guard, having informed the guards.
A noble person who is reliable and pure should not be imprisoned;
he should be released unconditionally, or if already bound, only upon taking an oath.
A creditor may recover his debt from a debtor through pressure, confinement, forced labor, legal action, or first of all, by means of conciliation, as the case may warrant.
In this manner, however, he may take wealth through interest and customary practice;
likewise, by means of labor, he should cause the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—who are equal or inferior—to pay it.
One should cause a king, a master, or a Brahmin to pay by means of conciliation alone;
however, one may settle the matter with a kinsman or a friend even through deception.
Bhṛgu said to merchants, farmers, and artisans:
"They should be made to pay according to local custom; one should cause those who are wicked to pay by means of pressure."
But where a creditor harasses a debtor who speaks the truth,
he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to it.
For if he should first cause [the debtor] to perform an unapproved act that is harmful,
the debtor shall first incur a fine for violence and then be released from the debt.
"He who, having taken an advance payment or other such items, does not give them back to the owner,
is born as his slave, servant, wife, or animal in the household."
[Deposits: That which is entrusted by one who has gone abroad, that which is deposited, that which is handed over for delivery,
that which is borrowed, and that which is placed with a Vaiśya for his livelihood— this is known as an *upanidhi*.
Whatever has been deposited with someone, that person should protect it with great care;
any destruction of it other than caused by fate or the king is declared to be [the fault] of that [depositor].
If anything whatsoever is destroyed or stolen through the fault of someone,
that person shall be made to pay for the goods along with interest, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
If the object is lost immediately after being requested, even if the loss was caused by fate or the king, the borrower must be made to repay the mere value; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever property belonging to another— such as a deposit or the like— has been consumed, neglected,
or destroyed through negligence, that very person shall be made to pay for it.
If [the deposit] has been consumed, he shall be made to pay it with interest; if it has been neglected, he shall be made to pay the same amount;
if it has been destroyed through negligence, he shall be made to pay a small portion less.
If a deposit is destroyed even by one who is neither a king nor an act of fate,
it is said that the loss falls upon the receiver along with the goods, while the giver remains unharmed.
But if the depositor, having learned of the loss of the property, deposits it elsewhere,
the receiver is not at all made to pay for it, even if it is destroyed by every possible means.
For whatever is lost due to the fault of the purchaser belongs to the purchaser;
when that [item] is lost or even stolen, the purchaser shall pay its value.
A deposit may be reclaimed at the proper time, but one should avoid reclaiming it when the time has passed.
If one returns it after the time has elapsed, they shall be fined and made to pay double the value.
In all cases of deposits, these rules have been proclaimed.
If a deposit is being restored over a fixed number of days, the artisan shall set it aside after that period; he must deliver it even if it has been damaged by fate.
If destruction occurs due to a defect in the deposit itself, the artisan shall not be made to pay for it;
however, if it was damaged due to a defect in the artisan's work, he shall be made to pay for the purpose of restoring it to its original condition.
Furthermore, if even a small amount of work is lost by a hired servant,
it shall be lost for him even if he intends to pay the full wage, provided he does not actually pay it.

If a person has been solicited for a specific purpose or for a fixed period of time, and that purpose is only half-accomplished and the time limit has not yet expired, he shall not be compelled to pay.
If a transaction is performed when the time for it has arrived, one shall not pay even if requested;
however, if that [transaction] is lost, the receiver shall recover the value.
If, when requested, he does not pay, he shall be compelled to pay it along with interest.
Now, if there is a failure of the task, that loss shall belong to the master himself;
however, if the time has not yet arrived, he must be made to pay it even if the work is only half-finished.
He who, having taken something on loan, does not return it when asked for, shall be seized by force and compelled to give it; and he who does not return it shall be fined.
When one says, "You should give this to another person in accordance with my word regarding the matters at hand," that which is given is called here an *anvādhi* (a secondary pledge).
[On Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner]:
He shall annul a sale, a gift, or a pledge made by one who is not the owner.
The plaintiff shall first provide his own wealth through his kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of self-purification, the purchaser shall provide it through his own relatives.
But the owner who has lost his property should have that wealth restored by his relatives;
having established that it was not given, abandoned, or sold, he recovers his own wealth.
He may either make a public purchase or produce the source [of the goods];
however, the time for producing the source must be granted in proportion to the number of *yojanas* [from which it was obtained].
One should effect the purchase openly with trustworthy kinsmen and one's own people;
in that case, no other means of proof—neither divine nor human—is prescribed.
When a litigant, having presented the original source, subsequently speaks of a purchase, he should indeed produce that original source;
there is no need for the purchase itself.
But one whose title is not subject to challenge must simply prove the purchase;
once the purchase has been proven, he should not be made to say anything further by the king.
If he does not produce the original document or fail to clear his purchase,
he shall be made to pay the money to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine.
If one who has lost his wealth does not restore it to his kinsmen,
he deserves punishment like that of a thief, in order to prevent the recurrence of such incidents.

Property that has passed through the market stalls and been recognized by the king's officers, or which was purchased from an unknown source, or where the seller is dead; [in these cases, the purchaser is liable].
But the owner, having paid half the value, may take back his own property; in that case, by legal decision, half of the stolen goods shall belong to both parties.
Purchasing without proper knowledge and likewise failing to protect [the property]—
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes for the loss of wealth.
[Joint Undertaking] Whatever physicians or merchants may be united together,
the profit obtained therein shall be shared equally by those who have not separated from one another.
Established by a formal agreement, they shall without deviation oversee the merchandise, the bundles, the expenses, the deductions, the loads, the quality, and the value.
But for those who engage in trade using gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to shares that are equal, less, or more.
If a man, being approved by many, gives wealth or even incurs a debt on his own, it shall be considered as having been done by all of them.

A debt contracted by kinsmen, relatives, or friends must be paid along with its security; likewise, the debts of others must be paid when they are accompanied by a pledge, a written document, or witnesses.
Gold may be given at one's own will, but liquids, grain, and the like must be given according to established rule; they should be given and likewise received in accordance with local custom.
But that which is given by those assembled together must likewise be requested [back] by them collectively;
whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his share of the profit.
But he who recovers property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of that shall be given to him; this is the rule in all such disputes.
The apprentices, those proficient in the specialized skills, and the master artisan shall take one,
two, three, or four shares respectively, according to their seniority.
Whatever wealth may have been brought from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the king's command,
they shall divide it according to the rule, having set aside a tenth part for the king.
But the one who acts as the leader of the thieves shall take four shares from that;
the brave man, three shares; the capable man, two; and each of the others who merely emaciate [the prey], one share each.
If, among those who have fled, someone should be captured, they shall bear, according to their respective shares, whatever was given for the purpose of his ransom.
This very rule has been declared by the virtuous as the law for dancers:
one who knows the rhythm (*tāla*) receives half [the share], while the singers receive equal shares;
those who are the leaders deserve two shares—this is the rule for those performing in concert.
This is the decision for all merchants, farmers, thieves, and artisans who have failed to fix their shares.

[The non-payment of what has been given, or the refusal to give what has been promised: Neither the sale nor the gift [of property] should be carried out against the will [of the owner]; however, one may personally bestow one's wife, sons, and all one's possessions.
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the property] must be performed;
otherwise it shall not be carried out—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Except for one's entire property and house, whatever wealth remains after what is necessary for the maintenance of the family is one's own to give; otherwise, it shall not be given.
Therefore, while a father has authority over his children and wife regarding their instruction,
he has no authority over his son regarding sale or gift.
He who, having promised a gift to a Brahmin of his own accord,
does not give it, shall be made to pay like a debtor and incur the first amercement.
By failing to take up what was promised and by misappropriating what has been given,
a mortal is born in the womb of an animal for hundreds of millions of eons.
Where a gift is prescribed for the purpose of obtaining something not yet known,
that which is obtained through the act of acquisition is proclaimed as *bhṛti* (wages).

That which is obtained through this method for the sake of protection from fear, for the purpose of guarding, or for the accomplishment of a task, one should know as being acquired through reciprocal service (*pratyupakāra*).
"Even if it were said, 'I shall give my entire wealth to whoever rescues me from this life-threatening danger,' it would not necessarily come to pass."
That which is given by one who is under the sway of lust or anger, one who is distressed, impotent, insane, or deluded,
as well as that which is given through a mistake or in jest, may be taken back.
But as for a bribe that has been promised for the sake of accomplishing a task,
it must not be given under any circumstances even if that purpose has been achieved.
Now, if she has already been given away previously, he should be made to give her back by force; so say Gārgya and the followers of Mānava, that the fine shall be eleven times [the value].
By reporting thieves, violent criminals, the depraved, and adulterers;
by revealing those who have lost their moral conduct; and likewise by promoting truthfulness.
Whatever has been obtained by these [officers] is called a bribe;
in such a case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall bear the guilt.
But if one who has been appointed to official duties should receive a bribe,
he shall be made to pay that entire sum as well as a fine eleven times its value.
But if one who is not appointed should receive a bribe for the sake of a legal matter,
there is no offense for him if it is for the purpose of providing a reciprocal service.

Whether given by one who is healthy or by one who is afflicted, provided it was promised for the sake of a religious duty—if he dies without having given it, his son must be made to pay; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given as a gift, or received as a gift through fraud,
or whatever one may perceive to have been obtained by means of deception— all that he shall annul.
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall each receive a tenth part of the profit, the milk, and the crops, respectively.
[Non-payment of wages: But he who, having undertaken the commencement of work, does not have it completed, must be forced to do so by compulsion; if he does not do it, he deserves punishment.
Or, if the carrier causes an obstruction, he shall be made to pay double the wage for the journey.
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or destroyed by fire, or swept away by water.

He who abandons a companion on the road who is exhausted or afflicted by disease shall incur the first amercement; likewise, one who fails to provide protection for three days in a village shall incur the same.
But when that merchandise is lost or stolen on the road,
he shall receive wages proportional to the distance already traveled.
He who, having taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and so forth on lease,
does not return them after having accomplished his purpose, shall be made to pay the lease along with a fine.
If someone, having taken a house, a water source, a shop, or the like on lease,
does not return them to the owner, he shall be made to pay [the value] together with the rent for as long as he has withheld them.
[Disputes between Owner and Herdsman] Bṛhaspati states that for those who enter fields, groves, pasture lands, houses, or cattle pens, there shall be either seizure or corporal punishment.
In cases where the owner disputes the beating of animals— whether they be low, superior, or middling—
the judge shall determine the appropriate punishment.
One should erect a great barrier while the crops are still unripe;
for deer, having once tasted their sweet flavor, are driven away here with difficulty.
One should cause a quarter-pana to be paid for a cow, two quarters for a buffalo,
and likewise, a quarter is declared as the fine for goats, sheep, and calves.
[The non-fulfillment of an agreement or the violation of a convention.
But whatever is the law of those who live in groups, by that law they should always perform all their duties, remaining established in their own specific obligations.
The royal edict has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, its practice must first be carried out by the command of the king.
That man who does not observe the laws promulgated by the king is blameworthy and sinful; he deserves punishment for violating the royal decree.
He who destroys what is logically consistent, he who provides no opportunity for the speaker,
and he who speaks what is illogical, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who commits violence, one who causes dissension, and one who destroys the property of a corporation—all these must be executed after being publicly proclaimed as such by the king; so said Bhṛgu.
If someone who has eaten from the same vessel or in the same row fails to report the fault of another, he shall be punished in the same manner as that offender.
Whatever debt may have been incurred for the sake of the community, or consumed,
or expended for one's own personal use, that must be repaid by those very individuals themselves.
Those who have entered into the midst of guilds, trade associations,
or corporations shall all share equally in the debts and assets of their predecessors.

Likewise, in matters of food, distribution of property, gifts, and religious acts, one who remains in the group shall share in the portion; however, one who has departed does not share in the portion.
Whatever has been acquired or preserved by them for the sake of the community, whatever debt has been incurred,
and whatever has been obtained through the favor of the king— all that belongs equally to everyone.
[The definitions of the designations such as *naigama* and others:
A multitude of various citizens is proclaimed to be a *naigama*; groups of people who have assembled while bearing various weapons are proclaimed to be *vrātas*.
A corporation of merchants and the like is proclaimed to be a *pūga*;
those who have settled into the life of renunciation are proclaimed to be *pāṣaṇḍas*.
A collection of Brāhmaṇas is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*;
those who subsist by means of crafts are proclaimed to be artisans (*śilpins*).
The assembly of the Arhats and the followers of Sugata is called a *saṅgha*;
the assembly of Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others is called a *gulma*.

Bṛhaspati states that *gaṇas*, heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), corporations (*pūgas*), guilds (*vrātas*), as well as trade associations (*śreṇis*), and whatever other groups exist that are designated as "classes" (*vargas*), are all [subject to the same rules].
[The remorse regarding buying and selling; the remorse after having bought or having sold.

If one has purchased something and obtained it, yet does not accept it, or if one has sold it and does not deliver it while it remains undamaged, that person shall recover their own property by paying one-tenth of the price.

If the time for performing the purposeful act has not yet arrived, one should certainly not cause [the debt] to be paid; such is the law. However, after ten days have passed, there can be no further objection.
In the case of land, the impurity lasts ten days for both the seller and the buyer;
it lasts twelve days for the sapinda relatives, and after that, it is minimal.
If a man, having purchased an article such as a milch cow or the like,
later regrets his purchase while it remains unspoiled and within the [legal] time period, he shall forfeit one-tenth of the price.
If, after having purchased [an item], the buyer develops regret once it has come into his hand,
the wise man should abandon that purchase by paying one-sixth of the price.
But if something is purchased without being examined and is later discovered to be defective, it must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, delivers it as faulty,
shall be made to pay double its value and an equal fine for the offense.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss falls upon the seller alone for having sold it without delivering it.
If a buyer does not accept the goods being offered for sale,
or if a seller sells what has already been sold elsewhere, neither of them shall be held at fault.
If a sale is made by one who is intoxicated or insane, or for a low price out of fear, or by one who is not independent or deluded, it must be relinquished; it shall belong to him once again.
One should test a milch cow for three days, but a draft animal for five days.
For diamonds and corals that have been released from their settings, the period of observation shall be seven days.
For bipeds, however, the impurity lasts for half a month; for males it is that same period, but for females it is double.
For all seeds, it lasts ten days; for metals and clothes, one day.
If, however, a defect in the merchandise should arise at any time after this [period],
it must be returned by the seller, and the buyer shall recover the purchase price.
But a garment that has been worn, which is discolored and soiled—
even if it is defective— that which has been purchased shall not be returned by the seller.
But that which has been purchased as joint property, the lowest of men should not give it away alone;
he should not take it, nor should he accept it, nor indeed should he sell it.
If, after purchasing goods for a price, the buyer considers them a bad purchase,
they must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided they have not been inspected [for defects].
If the purchaser delivers [the animal] on the second day, he shall pay one-third of the price as a fine;
on the third day, it shall be double that amount; beyond that, it belongs to the purchaser alone.
Having divided the value of the goods into five parts, three parts are called the price;
the fourth part shall be the profit, and the fifth is called the true remainder.
A joint, an exchange, or an unequal transaction regarding the three types of enjoyment—
even by means of a command or a purchase— may be rescinded within ten years.
It is the settled legal conclusion that there is no right of sale or purchase even for land if one has not obtained the consent of kinsmen and others who reside nearby and are not blameworthy.
In one's own village, the period shall be ten nights; in another village, three fortnights;
in other kingdoms, six months; but when there is a difference in dialect, it shall be one year.
But if a taxpayer has fled,
the members of the assembly shall sell the taxpayer's land for the sake of the tax, together with the surety for the tax.
But by neighboring landowners who are assembled together, who are knowledgeable, and who fear wrongdoing,
[the boundaries] of fields, groves, houses, and so forth, as well as of bipeds and quadrupeds, [should be determined].
They say that the "appraised value" is determined by dividing that [price] into eight parts;
a value exceeding one part or falling short of it is considered improper.
Even after a hundred years have passed, all of that is rescinded;
in the case of buying and selling, whatever price an article rightfully deserves is the basis for its validity.
If, when the purchase or sale has been concluded, [the price] is deficient by one-fourth, one-fifth, one-sixth, one-seventh, or even one-eighth;
All that which is of inferior value, even if completed, shall be considered as uncompleted; if the purchase price is lower than what was stated, there is no offense at all.
"By that very portion [of the price], the transaction—whether purchase or sale—is diminished in value;
others who know the law declare such a transaction to be as good as unmade."
If the price is half more, the purchase is valid; if it exceeds ten percent, the profit is as stated [twofold].
A lease may be terminated by one-third [of the term], while a consensual sale takes effect immediately.
Even if only a small amount has been paid toward the price, the sale is considered completed;
however, in the case of interest on capital (cakravṛddhi), the full amount must be paid, except as otherwise agreed upon by contract.

[Failure to serve after having agreed: But he who, having accepted [the pupil], does not cause him to learn the craft and instead causes him to perform other tasks, shall incur the first amercement; from him the pupil may withdraw.
Even if he has been trained, a pupil may perform his desired service;
whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone.
Bhṛgu declares that through the gift of an independent self, one enters a state of servitude like that of a wife;
however, such slavery for a Brāhmaṇa is to be understood as never occurring among the three [lower] castes.
Slavery occurs according to the natural order of the castes, not against it;
for when members of the *rājanya*, *vaiśya*, and *śūdra* castes abandon their independence, they enter into servitude.
Even one of equal caste must never compel a Brāhmaṇa to servitude;
for by the servitude of a Brāhmaṇa, O King, the royal splendor is destroyed.

But Bṛhaspati has stated that a Brāhmaṇa should never, under any circumstances, be made to perform the duties of a slave or manual labor by those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, even if they are of the same varṇa.
Even toward one who is endowed with virtue and Vedic study, a twice-born man should not intentionally perform any action that falls short of his status, nor should he do anything unwholesome.
The cleaning of feces and urine, as well as massaging while naked— these tasks,
as well as the herding of cattle and similar duties, are generally performed by the sons of female slaves.
Where the three castes, beginning with the twice-born, have attained mastery over the life of renunciation,
the king should cause the Brāhmaṇa to be banished and the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya to enter into slavery.
But a Śūdra, whether bought or even unbought, one should cause to perform service as a slave; for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for servitude.
If a man should have intercourse with his own female slave and she subsequently gives birth,
she and her offspring shall not be considered slaves, provided that the seed [of the father] has been taken into account.
Whatever wealth a slave may possess, it is traditionally held that the master is its lord; however, as for that which was sold openly, the master has no right to that wealth.
A female slave who is married by a slave shall also attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, and since the master is dependent upon the owner.
If anyone should take a Brāhmaṇa woman as a wife, or likewise purchase her,
that act shall be declared invalid by the king, and all of them shall be punished.
But he who, out of lust, makes a woman of good family who has sought refuge a slave, or transfers her to another, shall be punished; and that [act] shall be as if it were never done.
He who treats a nurse for children or a non-slave woman as if she were a slave,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a female slave who is devoted to him and crying out in protest, shall incur a fine of two hundred panas.
If one who is not his own master offers himself, saying "I am yours," he shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall recover him.
A slave who has entered the religious life must not be released by anyone;
one who has been maintained [as a slave] during times of distress is freed from slavery by giving a pair of cattle.
[Disputes concerning boundaries]:
Excess, deficiency, and the existence or non-existence of a share;
possession through enjoyment, and the boundary—these six are the grounds for a dispute over land.
In that case, the enjoyment [of the property] should be established before all witnesses;
for both the witness recorded in writing and the other kind of witness follow two paths.
In disputes between two parties concerning fields, buildings, tanks, wells, groves, or embankments— in all such matters, the neighbors are the authority.
In the absence of neighbors, those who are not neighbors shall determine the boundaries of fields and other such matters;
and likewise for village boundaries, as well as for cities and districts.
A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village, and a field of a field; likewise, a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, for it surrounds it on all sides.
In their absence, the neighbors, the original founders, the elders, the emancipated, and so forth [shall decide];
even in the case of the six types of immovable property, there should be no hesitation in this matter.
When the neighbors are contiguous, and those beyond them are likewise contiguous to them,
and those further beyond are contiguous to those who are contiguous to the neighbors, they are proclaimed to have the shape of a lotus.
When neighboring kings have become hostile in the pursuit of their own interests due to the weight of [political] gain, a rescue must be carried out by those allied with them;
there is no doubt in this matter.
But when there is a fault regarding those who are attached or closely connected, those who are themselves attached to them are declared [guilty];
however, those who are not corrupted should not be punished by the king who knows the Dharma.
Neighbors are not released from liability regarding the decision simply by claiming ignorance;
if they declare ignorance, the king should fine them and then investigate the boundary again.
If a dispute arises after the boundary has been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest fine.
Having set aside wicked neighbors, one should cause the boundary to be established by mixing them with others such as the original inhabitants; thus do those who know the law understand it.
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the seers as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that very place.
Those endowed with human virtues who have witnessed a task being accomplished are proclaimed as "elders," whether they are actually old or not.
Because they extract [the truth] from there— being characterized by eavesdropping, shared enjoyment, the narration of events, and signs— they are therefore known as *uddhṛtas*.
The neighbors are the first means of proof when they are endowed with good qualities and have not previously been enemies;
those beyond them are known as twice as many, and others beyond them are considered three times as many.
Just as one person, desired by both parties, might in some cases mark the boundary—
having placed earth upon his head, dressed in red garments, and composed in mind.
In the absence of all [other means], it was made by the king himself, who was free from fear.
Regarding fields, wells, and tanks, as well as arable lands and pleasure groves,
and also houses, palaces, dwellings, and temples dedicated to kings and deities.
But if, among many who have been summoned as witnesses, they do not reach a verdict because of fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
In cases of crossing a boundary, [theft from] a treasury, and likewise touching the feet [of a superior],
a trial by divine or royal ordeal is prescribed for three fortnights, one fortnight, and seven days respectively.
One should not obstruct the girdle-closet, the drainage outlet, or the window;
nor should one who causes damage to a water-conduit or the site of a house be liable to a fine.
After the time of settling into the house, these [rules] should never be applied;
one should not construct a drainage channel that falls within the sight of another's house.
One should construct a moat filled with feces, urine, and water, and a dwelling provided with fire-pits and pits,
leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the neighboring wall.
That by which all people always travel is a crossroads;
that which remains unobstructed at the proper time is called a royal road.
One should not plant anything there, nor should one damage it in any way;
however, one incurs punishment for obstructing the path of gurus, teachers, kings, and others.
If anyone there should out of desire void excrement in pits, chasms, or even plant trees, his fine shall be one māṣaka.
He who defiles tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing places with impure matter shall,
after having the impurity cleared away, be fined the first amercement.
He who defiles established sacred sites and holy places of pilgrimage founded by great souls shall incur the punishment for the first degree of violence.
But for trees grown within a boundary line between two fields,
one should declare that the fruits and flowers belong in common to the owners of both fields.
But for those born in another's field whose branches are supported by another,
one should know him to be the owner in whose fields they are supported.
But he who performs repairs on a house, garden, or tank without the permission of the owner does not obtain [ownership] of those repaired structures.
If expenses have been incurred when the owner has arrived and they were not reported to the king,
yet the expenditure was authorized without such reporting, the owner shall recover those expenses.
If, due to incapacity, he does not pay [the share],
then the cultivator shall receive the produce minus one-eighth of the expenses incurred for the fallow land.
He shall be the enjoyer for eight years; thereafter, however, it belongs to the owner.
If the owner of the field is unable, deceased, or lost, and no one else prevents it,
if someone should cultivate the field, he shall enjoy its fruit.
If a field is being ploughed and the owner returns, he shall recover the entire field by providing for its cultivation and maintenance, including the clearing of fallow ground.
By reducing that [share] by one-eighth each year for seven years,
when the eighth year is completed, he shall obtain the cultivated field.
[Harsh speech: Uttering the sound "huṃ," coughing, and whatever else is censured in the world—
if one should imitate or speak such things, that is called harsh speech.
Because of its harshness, vulgarity, and intensity, that [abuse] is also recorded as being threefold:

abuse (*ākṣepa*) is to be known as harsh (*niṣṭhura*); vulgarity (*aślīla*) is designated as a blemish (*nyaṅga*); and the wise say that intensity (*tīvra*) consists of insults involving grounds for expulsion (*patanīya*).
But when one, by means of limbs [of speech] perceived as untrue,
or whether they be unreal or real, reviles another, that is declared by the wise to be harsh speech.
When one, out of anger, uses speech to cause the humiliation of another's conduct,
country, family, and so forth, that is considered by the wise to be "obscene" (aślīlā).
That speech which binds one with the fetters of the great sins, which produces passion and hatred, or which causes the loss of caste— that indeed is known as intense speech.

Those who, out of anger, proclaim the faults of one who is faultless, or who, being devoid of merit, pretend to recognize merit, or who pursues a different intention— such a man they know to be corrupt in speech.
One who proclaims the faults of an innocent person for the sake of causing harm,
and one who speaks with pretexts, they know such a man to be corrupt in speech.
If one says, "I spoke thus out of delusion, negligence, rivalry, or affection," he shall not speak so again; for such a person, the judge should prescribe half the fine.
Where there is a mention of one's own fallen status for the purpose of providing a defense,
there shall be no fault on account of that statement, provided one can substantiate it.
Otherwise, the fault would be equal; however, in the case of a false statement, the highest fine is prescribed.
By means of a great solemn oath, one may convict a man who is corrupt in speech;
however, the king should carefully investigate a case where something untrue has been reported.
For those habitually inclined toward speaking falsehoods, the purification is the cutting off of the tongue.
[Assault] K.779a: If one does not perceive the cause of assault through the evidence of motive and other such factors, K.779b:
then one should employ witnesses or an ordeal in that case.
If a man strikes with a terrifying weapon,
whether he was previously unharmed or not, he is declared to be liable for punishment.
According to Bhṛgu, for the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine shall be imposed; for the piercing or mutilating of these, the middle fine.
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain,
the punishment shall be inflicted in exact proportion to the suffering that has been caused.
For those who are untouchable, rogues, slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), corporal punishment is not intended to be a monetary fine.
When defiled by vomit, urine, feces, and the like, the water becomes fourfold [impure];
it is sixfold [impure] in the middle of the body, but is traditionally held to be eightfold [impure] on the head.
For raising a hand [in a threatening manner], a fine of twelve [paṇas] shall be imposed;
for striking those of one's own caste, that same fine is declared to be double.
Just as the punishments for verbal abuse have been declared according to the inverse and direct order of castes,
so too shall the punishments be inflicted in the same sequence for physical assault.
But when the body or the sense organs are destroyed, the wise should inflict a punishment such that it causes satisfaction and ensures the restoration of the means of livelihood.
He shall also pay the expenses for the treatment, until the wound has healed.

Those offenders against whom verbal censure and corporal punishment have been prescribed shall be made to restore what was stolen or broken; however, those who possess no wealth shall be purified by labor.
If a man makes exhausted, thirsty, or hungry donkeys,
oxen, buffaloes, camels, and other such animals work at an improper time, he shall incur the first amercement.
For the killing of wild animals or birds, the fine is twelve paṇas;
for the killing of humans by means of snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, or pigs, the fine is two paṇas.
One who makes a young cow, a divine animal, a bull, or a breeding bull work shall incur the first amercement;
for making them work, the highest amercement or even death shall be the penalty.
"In the case of killing living beings, one should provide a substitute for them, or pay a corresponding price; thus spoke Manu."
The established rule is that for the destruction of any forest trees, a fine shall be imposed in proportion to their utility.
If a teacher should strike a disciple out of anger with anything other than a cane—
by which excessive pain would be caused— the dispute would be between the disciple and his father.
[Violence: An act that is performed impulsively is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence).
Theft with kin involved, as well as that which is carried out by force and acts of violence—these constitute *sāhasa* (outrageous crime); likewise, theft is defined as the act of denial.
But when an act known as *sāhasa* (violence) proceeds without physical marks [of the crime], it must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies in all such cases.
If many men, acting with fury, should kill one person,
he among them who strikes a vital organ is traditionally considered the slayer.
One who commits such an act through the intent to kill shall suffer various forms of execution;
however, one should indeed slay without hesitation anyone who approaches as a cause of destruction.
But for those who have raised their weapons against evildoers, there is no fault for the slayer;
however, when they have desisted from their undertaking, their capture—not their killing—is prescribed by tradition.
Even against an assassin who is superior in asceticism, Vedic study, or birth, there shall be no execution; however, Bhṛgu maintains that execution is appropriate for one who is inferior in merit.
One who brandishes a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who holds a bow raised in hand;
one who kills by means of the Atharvaveda; and a slanderer against the king—[these are all equal to a killer of a Brahmin].
One who violates his wife, one who is intent on seeking out his vulnerabilities—
one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin*s (assassins).
They say that those wicked men who steal one's reputation and conduct are thieves of both dharma and wealth;
yet, he who commits an offense without having been previously accused is [not so considered].
And one should know that person who seizes one's life or property to be an *ātatāyin*.
In the case of killing those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins (ātatāyins),
as well as elephants, horses, and other such creatures, the killer incurs no guilt.
One who causes an abortion by the use of a weapon is a thief;
for even a Brāhmaṇa, having killed an innocent woman, must be put to death.
The man who causes injury, breakage, or crushing of goods shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; the owner of the goods is declared to be the one who receives the compensation.
If one should steal, break, or burn an image of the gods,
or likewise break down its temple, he shall incur the first amercement.
He who should breach a wall, or cause it to fall, or likewise demolish it,
or block the course of water, shall incur the first amercement.
[Theft:
Whether it be concealed or open, by night or by day,
the taking of another's property is proclaimed to be theft.
One should carefully examine an object that has fallen from another's hand, been picked up on the ground unintentionally, or dropped by a thief.
One who deals with counterfeit weights, measures, and counterweights,
whether they are marked or unmarked, shall incur the first amercement.
If something is stolen from a house, however, the king shall cause the catchers of thieves,
the guards, and the guardians of the quarters to pay for it, provided that the thief is not apprehended.
Property stolen within a village shall be made good by the village headman;
in a pasture, it shall be given by the owner, and in a forest preserve, by the forest-guardian.
Whatever has been deposited by anyone in his own country must be returned by the king;
if it is lost, the monarch, having searched for it, shall take possession of it himself once it is recovered.
He should diligently restore the stolen object in its original form when it has been carried off by thieves;
in its absence, however, the value [must be paid], otherwise the king becomes guilty of a crime.
But even if the thief has been apprehended, if the stolen property cannot be recovered from him,
then he shall pay that amount, or he shall cause the thief to be handed over at the owner's discretion.
If, while they are being made to pay, there should be doubt regarding the guilt,
the person accused of theft shall be made to swear an oath, or he may clear himself through his kinsmen.
If the owner recovers even a small portion of the property from that which was stolen,
he shall receive the remainder once the owner has made his claim.
Those who kill people in their own country, as well as those who obstruct the royal highway— the king shall confiscate all their property and impale them upon a stake.

When property has been recovered from someone other than the thief by those intent on searching for the thief, they shall receive it; in that case, the king shall cause them to be paid double its value.
With whichever limb a thief commits an injury against another,
the king shall cut off that very limb so that he does not do it again.
One who takes two fruits each of cucumber and gourd, five mangoes and five pomegranates,
or a handful of dates, jujubes, and the like, does not incur guilt.
The Mānavas declare that the immediate banishment of those caught in adultery (sahoḍha) is what Gautama finds undesirable, as it involves the destruction of living beings and is therefore censurable.
Whether he was caught in the act (*sahoḍha*) or not caught in the act (*asahoḍha*), once his violent crime has been established by evidence,
the king should seize him, have his nose and ears cut off, announce the punishment, and deprive him of all his property.
"However, those guarded by iron chains, who are frugal in food yet endowed with strength, may perform services for the king until death; so says Kauśika."
When property has been seized from a foreign land by a foreigner, the king,
having recovered that property, should release him without punishment.
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who supply fire and water,
those who purchase their goods, and those who receive them;
For these, as well as those who conceal them, are declared to deserve equal punishment.
One who is ignorant should not be a sacrificer, nor should one who is unstable be a teacher;
having punished both of them with the penalty for a thief, he should establish them on the right path.
[On Sexual Intercourse with a Woman: If he employs a female messenger, stays at an improper time or place,
seizes her by the throat or hair, or grasps her ears, nose, hands, and so forth;
Sharing the same place, seat, and food—this is known as the ninefold means of winning over others.
When a man forcibly enjoys a woman who has been violated by another, he should proceed with her execution; for that constitutes a transgression of the law.
But a wanton woman who, afflicted by passion, seeks [a lover] of her own accord,
shall be released by the king's command after being publicly proclaimed in the presence of the people.

The one who initiates the act, the accomplice, as well as the one who points out the way, the one who provides shelter, the one who gives weapons, and the one who provides food for those committing forbidden acts;
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction, one who is intent on indifference toward what ought to be done, and one who speaks of faults while acquiescing to them.
If there should be one who is unable to prevent [the offense], all those who fail to do so shall be held responsible for that act;
one should impose upon them a punishment according to their capacity and the nature of the offense.
[The Duties of Wife and Husband] K.835a: A wife who is not separated from her husband should serve the sacred fire with humility;
K.835b: out of devotion to her husband and desiring good fortune and freedom from widowhood.
By means of service with a devoted mind alone, a woman enjoys all desires;
having returned here from heaven, she shall become a treasure-house of happiness.
When her husband has died, the virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy and conducts herself like Arundhatī is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[The Division of Inheritance] K.838a:

When the fathers and the brothers take the entire collection of property in equal shares, that division is declared to be lawful (dharmya). K.838b: That division of inheritance is called righteous when they take the whole mass of goods in equal portions.
Property inherited from a grandfather is common to both father and son;
however, regarding property acquired by the father himself, the son does not possess ownership.
In the division among heirs, all of this— the property of the grandfather, that of the father, and whatever else was acquired by oneself— is divided.
If a house, field, or quadruped is being divided while still visible, it should be partitioned; in cases where there is suspicion of hidden property, the means of proof therein has been declared.
Household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and laborers are divided while being visible; regarding hidden property, Bhṛgu declared that it goes to the treasury.
When dividing the estate during one's lifetime, a father must not treat one son differently;
nor should he exclude one from his share without a sudden cause or reason.
The division [of property] is prescribed for those who have attained legal capacity;
and for men, the status of being legally capable arises at the sixteenth year.
And the wealth of those who have not yet reached legal majority,
as well as that of those who are away on travel, shall be deposited with kinsmen and friends, free from any expenditure.
But the share belonging to one who has gone abroad, all [the heirs] together shall protect;

when he dies with a minor son, that inheritance must be protected by the kinsmen of the lineage. Once he has reached the age of *paugaṇḍa*, however, they shall divide it according to their respective shares.
A debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a mother for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition.
That debt must be paid to the creditor; one should not cause it to be paid otherwise, provided that when [the defendant] is proven by evidence, [the claim] is subsequently contradicted.

A debt contracted for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*), or one given out of affection (*prītidatta*), or one that has been formally assigned—when such a debt is visible, it shall be divided; it is not to be paid from the paternal estate.
A debt of this kind— namely, that inherited from a father which has been cleared of the father's own debts, and that which was contracted by oneself—
must be settled by the kinsmen together during the partition of the estate.
Having paid off debts and gifts made out of affection, one should divide the remainder.
A father, by virtue of acquiring property through his sons, shall take two shares or half a share;
likewise, when the father has died, the mother shall also receive a share equal to that of a son.
In whatever manner the wealth obtained through partition should be applied to the purpose of sacrifice, in that same manner the learned should determine the relative weight of the shares.
Even in the world, when there is a division of inheritance, no one shall exercise ownership;
rather, only enjoyment may be exercised, but neither giving nor selling is permitted.
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights over immovable property;
for no single person has authority anywhere to give, mortgage, or sell it.

When a younger brother has died while the estate remains undivided, one should make his son an heir to the inheritance by providing him with a means of livelihood that he did not receive from his grandfather.
He shall receive his paternal share from his uncle or from that uncle's son;
for according to justice, that very same share belongs to all the brothers.
His son, or even his grandson, may obtain it; beyond that, there shall be cessation.
When a legitimate son of the body has been born, the sons—whether of equal or unequal caste—shall receive a fourth part; however, those of unequal caste are entitled only to food and clothing.
For unmarried daughters, however, a fourth part is prescribed;
for sons, there are three parts, while equality is ordained when the wealth is small.
If one should produce fruit even with the consent of the landowner, both of them are indeed sharers of that fruit here; for there is no fruit without the other.
If a woman, having abandoned a husband who is impotent or outcast, takes another husband,
a son born of her from that second marriage is clearly the offspring of the biological father.
He whose urine is not frothy and whose feces sink in water,
and who lacks both testicles and semen, is called a *klība* (eunuch).
Furthermore, the son of a woman married out of order, one born from a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*),
and one who has abandoned the religious life— none of these are entitled to inherit property.
But the son of a woman married out of order inherits the estate if he is of the same caste as his father;
so too does the son born of a woman of a different caste who was married in the proper order.
The son born of a woman produced in the inverse order of castes does not inherit property;
it is held that his kinsmen should provide him with food and clothing for as long as he lives.
But in the absence even of kinsmen, he shall obtain that paternal property;
however, kinsmen are not to be compelled to pay back wealth acquired that was not ancestral.
[Indivisible items:
That which was lost after being taken by one's own power, that which was lost on its own, and that which was acquired by oneself—
all this is not to be divided by the sons with their father at the time of partition.
Whatever wealth is obtained through that knowledge which was acquired by means of utilizing the food provided by another, that is called "wealth acquired through learning" (vidyā-prāpta).
But that which is obtained through learning after it has been offered as a wager is known as "wealth acquired by learning" (*vidyādhana*); it is not to be divided during a partition of inheritance.

That which is obtained from a pupil, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubts raised by others, from proclaiming one's own knowledge, from debate, and from recitation—
this they call "wealth of learning" (*vidyā-dhana*), and it is not to be divided at the time of partition.
For this same rule applies even among craftsmen regarding whatever may be in excess of the price.

That which is obtained by surpassing another through learning, whether by means of debate or gambling, is known as "wealth from learning" (*vidyādhanam*); Bṛhaspati declares that it is not to be divided.

Bhṛgu declares that wealth obtained through a promise of instruction, received from a pupil, or acquired according to the rule of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), constitutes "wealth acquired through learning" (*vidyādhana*).
That which is acquired through the power of learning from a patron or from a pupil is called "wealth of learning"; anything other than this is considered common property.
Bṛhaspati states that wealth acquired through valor must be divided among brothers who have been educated in their family or even by their father.
A physician shall never give any portion of his medical knowledge or wealth to those who are ignorant; however, he may give that wealth to those whose knowledge is equal to or superior to his own.
When they perform a task by force, having entered into a state of uncertainty,
if the master, being pleased with that work, grants his favor;
Whatever wealth is obtained there through valor shall belong to him.
That which is acquired through valor, that which is obtained through learning, and that which is traditionally declared to be a woman’s property—
all this must not be divided by the heirs during a partition.
That which is acquired under a banner is declared by the sages to be non-partible.
That which is acquired in battle after routing the enemy force,
having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, is called "acquired under a banner."
Whatever is obtained at the time of giving along with a maiden of one's own caste,
that wealth acquired through a maiden is declared to be pure and productive of growth.
One should know that which was brought by the wife at the time of marriage as *vaivāhika*;
all such wealth should be understood as conducive to the fulfillment of *dharma*.
Whatever is given to the groom at the time of marriage, having been designated for the bride— that entire property is not to be divided by her kinsmen.
But wealth recorded in a document, that which was designated for religious purposes, water, a slave, and any hereditary pledge; these are [not lost by adverse possession].
Clothing and ornaments that have been worn, provided they are not unsuitable,
should be applied by the kinsmen in a manner appropriate to the occasion.
Bṛhaspati states that pasture land for cattle, protection, clothing, and whatever is attached to the body should not be divided; rather, it should be used for the sake of dharma.
Whatever law has been declared for a region, a caste, a guild, or a village by Bhṛgu,
one should determine the distribution of inheritance according to that very law.
[The re-division of concealed property: If concealed wealth is discovered again, it shall be divided equally with the brothers; indeed, in the absence of the father, the sons [shall divide it].
Whatever property may have been stolen from one another or improperly divided, if it is discovered later, Bhṛgu says that it should be divided equally.

Whatever property was acquired by one who had already been partitioned belongs to him alone; however, what was lost and recovered, or what was found, or what was previously mentioned, shall be shared again.
One must certainly not cause property seized by a kinsman to be returned by force;
nor should one cause the enjoyment of property belonging to undivided kinsmen to be restored [to an outsider].
If one has abandoned common property and settled in another country,
a share must undoubtedly be given to his descendant when he returns.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [in descent],
if the lineage of births cannot be fully ascertained, he shall receive the share that has come down by order of succession.
The land acquired through the lineage of those who have come down from the original ancestors and neighboring landowners, whom they know to be the owner,
must be given to the one who has arrived as a member of that lineage, along with the produce of the soil.

If those who were previously divided from their father's estate are living together again, they should divide [the property] once more; he shall receive two shares from whatever source the increase originated.
They may live for ten years with distinct emblems and so forth, following separate religious duties and separate activities;
those brothers should also be known as "divided" from the paternal estate.

[The definition and types of woman's property: That which is received at the nuptial fire, that which is received with the bridal procession, that which is given out of affection by her [relatives], and that which is obtained from her brothers, mother, and father— this sixfold kind is declared to be woman's property.
Whatever is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *strīdhana* (woman's property) known as *adhyagni-kṛta*.
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives while being led away from her father’s house,
as well as the *adhyāvahanika*, is declared to be her *strīdhana* (woman's property).
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given for the purpose of honoring one's feet— that is called "given out of affection."
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, or laborers, that is declared to be the *śulka* (toll or duty).
That which is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage is called *anvādheya*; likewise, that which is obtained from her own kinsmen is also so termed.
Whatever a woman receives after marriage,
whether from her husband, her parents, or through refinement and affection, that is called *anvādheya* according to Bhṛgu.
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried maiden, that which is received from her husband, from her father’s house,
from her brother, or from her parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (gift of affection).
[Consideration of Ownership and Other Matters Regarding Women's Property] K.902a–b: Women's property should be given to a woman by her father, mother, husband, brothers, or kinsmen,
according to their ability, up to a maximum of two thousand [paṇas], with the exception of immovable property.
However, that which is given with a specific condition, or by reason of a particular connection, by a father, brother, or husband— that is not considered woman's property.

Whatever wealth has been acquired through crafts, or whatever else has been obtained through affection from others—the husband has ownership over that; the remainder, however, is declared to be the woman's property.
Upon receiving dowry property, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by their [relatives] as a means of subsistence out of compassion.
It is declared that women always possess independence regarding property received as a dowry;
they may dispose of it as they wish, even in the case of immovable property, whether by sale or by gift.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman may dispose of her husband’s inheritance as she pleases;
however, while he is still living, she must preserve it, otherwise it shall be lost to her family.
But if he has two wives and does not treat her with affection again,
even if she had been released by him out of love, he must be compelled by force to give her back.
Wherever a woman is deprived of food, clothing,
and shelter, she may take for herself her own property as well as a share from the heirs.

This is the law for one who has been formally recorded [as a wife]: she shall reside in the husband's family when the time arrives; however, if she is ill, she may go to her kinsmen during the period of mourning for the deceased.
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over the woman's property, whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
For if even one among them should forcibly consume the woman's property,
