he should be made to pay it back with interest and shall also incur a fine.
If he should eat that very same thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay its price, provided that he is wealthy.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, beset by calamity, or oppressed by creditors, he may— out of affection and according to his own will— give what has been released [as a gift].

While she is alive, the husband's brothers, sons, paternal kinsmen, and maternal relatives are declared to have no authority over a woman’s property; those who seize it, however, are liable to punishment.
The sons must repay the woman’s property as a debt, just as they would a loan promised by their father;
however, she who remains in her husband’s family shall not live in her father’s family.
[The heirs to the wealth of a deceased woman: "Sisters, together with their kinsmen and accompanied by their husbands, shall divide [the inheritance];
this is the law regarding a woman's property, and this division has been ordained."
In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall go to the sons;
but property given by kinsmen goes to the kinsmen, and in their absence, it goes to the husband.
Whatever immovable property has been given by both parents to a daughter always goes to her brothers when she dies without offspring and while her father is still living.
Whatever paternal wealth a woman has obtained from her father in marriages such as the Āsura and others,
that is declared to belong to her mother and father in the absence of offspring.

When the husband has passed away, however, the wife is entitled to food and clothing;
but if the share of the wealth has not been divided, she receives it until her death.
She who is devoted to serving her teacher deserves to enjoy her allotted share;
if she does not perform service, she should be assigned to the work of weaving cloth and making food-balls.
When her husband has died, a woman who protects the family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, she has no ownership over it regarding giving, mortgaging, or selling.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, firmly established in celibacy,
and constantly delighted in self-restraint and charity, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
The wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall take his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall go to the daughter, provided she be unmarried.
Now, for one who has no son, the wife born of a family of equal status, or even the daughters, are [the heirs];
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be so].
When the property has been divided and the estate is settled, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the wealth;
or else the brother, or the mother, or the paternal grandmother, in that order.
One who is engaged in improper conduct, shameless, or a destroyer of wealth [is unfit].
And a woman who is devoted to adultery does not deserve that property.
Indeed, if a woman performs funeral rites for a deceased relative without being authorized by her father, husband, or son,
that act shall be fruitless for her.
Property that has no heir goes to the king, as do the belongings of women and servants, and the estate for funeral rites;
however, setting aside the property of a *śrotriya*, he shall bestow it upon other *śrotriyas*.
But among those who have reunited, it is those who have reunited who inherit; among those who remain separate, it is those who remain separate.
In the absence of a primary heir, they should be known as the takers of the property; those without seed share with one another.
[Gambling and Betting] One should certainly not indulge in gambling, for it increases anger and greed;
it is cruel, produces wicked people, and destroys the wealth of men.
Since strife is certain to arise from gambling, just as poison from the mouth of a serpent,
therefore a king should abstain from it, for it is a vice within his realm.
If, however, it should be visible, he should have a hand-sign made at the gate and archway for the sake of the noble ones' non-confusion.
The keeper of the gambling hall shall cause the game to be conducted and shall personally pay the debt to the king;
he may take a ten percent interest on the amount lost.
The winner shall pay his own wealth; from the loser, the stake should be recovered within three fortnights, or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house itself—of this there is no doubt.
Whether appearing as one form or two forms, victory is seen for that gambler at dice upon whom protection is established.
Alternatively, a gambler, having paid the king the share as prescribed, may engage in gambling openly; in this way, no offense exists.

One should cause that which is due to be paid by force in that very place, and not otherwise; for in such a case, the assembly master has won, and the legal proceeding depends upon the authority of the assembly master.

One who is defeated without knowledge should be released, while one who is defeated with knowledge should not be released; even when all one's property has been won, one who possesses knowledge should not be made to surrender his entire possessions.
In disputes concerning victory, gain, or fraudulent gambling, the keeper of the gaming house is the authority,
provided that the keeper of the gaming house is honest.

For Mlecchas, Śvapākas, rogues, gamblers, and those who practice penance for such [deeds], there is no settled rule regarding their conduct other than that which they themselves have established; it does not depend on the king.

[The Miscellaneous Section] Whatever remains unsaid from what was previously stated, and whatever has fallen away from its proper context, having been extracted and joined with the meaning of another treatise, is considered inconsistent (*asamañjasa*).
That which is stated at the end of the treatise by way of illustration, established as a repeated action,
and whatever sentence follows this rule— that shall be the *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous).
The duties of kings, one's own specific duties, the statements of those who are under suspicion,
and everything remaining unsaid from what was previously mentioned— all that constitutes *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters).
A sixth part of the produce, taxes, and customs duties must likewise be paid into the treasury;
as well as those who incite discord in battle, thieves, traitors, and those who violate the wives of others.
The desire to kill cows or Brahmins, as well as acts that destroy crops—
the king himself should investigate these ten offenses.

The failure to perform expiations, the transgression of commands and prohibitions, the destruction of the castes and stages of life, and the neglect of the rules for marriage and the mixing of castes;
A hidden treasure, wealth that yields no fruit, and the arrival of riches for a pauper—
the king himself, having thoroughly ascertained these through spies, should prevent them.
Those matters not recorded in the legal codes, the ritual disputes of litigants,
the provocation of the subjects, and secret conspiracies between one another;
Whatever among his subjects proceeds that is not ordained by the treatises,
the king should pacify those matters through strategic means such as conciliation and sowing dissension.

One should employ verbal punishment against friends and others, saying, "Shame on you, wretched woman! He should do for him what was explicitly stated, and what was not stated should be properly devised.
But he who should accomplish a legal transaction by means of a false measure, or with a forged seal, must be made to pay the highest fine.
Those who are addicted to the king's amusements, those who subsist on the king's means of livelihood,
and those who speak what is unpleasant to him— against them he should carry out the death penalty.
Those who manufacture counterfeit coins, those who inspect them,
those who distribute them, and those who steal the king’s wealth shall receive various forms of capital punishment.
A Śūdra who has abandoned the life of a renunciant, even if he is devoted to the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings,
should be punished for his sin by execution, or else fined double the usual penalty.
Even if the crime is accompanied by physical evidence, he should question the perpetrator regarding the cause of the offense;
then, having carefully established the fault, he should determine the punishment.
But when all those of good conduct should commit an offense,
even though it occurred involuntarily through fate, one should not impose punishment in that case.
Kings who administer justice correctly are worthy of worship even by the gods.
At the commencement [of an offense], one should impose the first [fine]; in its actual commission, the middle [fine] is prescribed.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for someone, that indeed shall apply when he is capable [of paying it].
Kings and ministers especially shall attain such [merit] by failing to punish the wicked and by inflicting punishment upon those who submit.
Those who are dependent on others, those who exist in a state of slavery, and those who are destitute are designated as "helpless"; for them, the punishment is a flogging.
Beating, imprisonment, and likewise humiliation—this indeed is the punishment for a slave; a monetary fine is not prescribed.
One who deserves the death penalty shall pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
for one deserving the amputation of a limb, half of that; and for one deserving exile, twenty-five.
In the case of those who are of noble birth, of the Ārya class, or distinguished, as well as those who are low-born,
he should seize their entire property according to the circumstances and quickly banish them from the city.
Those who are destitute should be placed in confinement, but one must never carry out the death penalty;
this applies to all those guilty of crimes, according to the specific provisions of the treatises.
A Brahmin deserving of corporal punishment or the amputation of limbs shall enter a prison without shackles;
for when he is released from that state, his conduct having been restored, that indeed is his punishment.
A false witness should be banished after being publicly proclaimed; one who accepts gifts from the wicked should have his limbs severed;
and one who violates his own duty should be separated by means of imprisonment.

In the case of those who have committed equal offenses, one should apply the same rule even there; however, for children, the elderly, the sick, and women, there shall be no corporal punishment—their penalty shall be a fine.
A righteous lord of the earth shall cause the woman's property to be paid as a fine;
however, a woman who has committed an offense but possesses no wealth deserves the punishment of being beaten.

One should deposit into the treasury any wealth acquired through unjust means that has been placed there; for the sake of the state's business, one should not cause the ruin of the treasury, nor should a wise man allow it to be depleted.
Having bestowed all that wealth arising from fines upon the Brahmins,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should retire to the forest for the final stage of life.
Thus, a king, a ruler of the earth, should always act with diligence in accordance with the laws that are for the welfare of the world, and he should employ all his servants in those same tasks.

The *Kātyāyanasmṛtisāroddhāra*: (The Qualities of a King) Disciplined, perfected in the sciences, and endowed with both treasury and valor;
A king should be devoted to Brahmins, habituated to giving, and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Free from arrogance, malice, slander, fickleness, and anger; confident yet humble, eminent, eloquent, and pleasant to behold.

Prosperity attends to the utmost degree that wise man who has his senses under control, who has conquered himself, who wields the rod of punishment against those who deserve it, and who acts only after careful deliberation.
[The Duties of Kings]: Because of their abundance of heroism, learning, and wealth, and especially because of their sovereignty,
the minds of kings constantly fall into delusion due to these causes.
Therefore, the mind must always be awakened by the twice-born toward the duty of a king;
one must not transgress the words of the Smṛtis, which are supremely purifying and meritorious.
By the power of the sound of the Vedas, even the gods dwelling in heaven rejoice there, being satisfied by the worship of the twice-born.
Therefore, kings should always perform the worship of the twice-born with great effort;
by that, they shall attain the state of Śakra again and again, as well as the status of a lord of men repeatedly.
The superintendent of liquor, fallen from heaven, remains in the form of a king;
he must constantly perform that by which he may attain the ultimate truth.
Kings who remain established in their own duty shall attain the state of Śakra;
but those who always behave contrary to their conduct shall dwell in the Avīci hell.
That king who, failing to understand correctly, goes under the sway of anger, will dwell in a terrible hell for half a kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
One should appoint as a minister who deliberates on affairs a Brahmin endowed with these very same qualities— one who is devoted to the king and born of a noble lineage.
Where the ministers, courtiers, and physicians speak only pleasant words,
the king there will swiftly fall away from his kingdom, from righteousness, and from happiness.
One should not direct anger toward his words, but rather toward these [faults],
because it is by means of these that what is right and well-established must always be spoken.
Where the king personally oversees legal affairs in accordance with dharma,
there the subjects, practicing virtuous conduct, shall dwell in happiness.
The constant protection of the subjects, the clearing away of thorns, and the honoring of the twice-born—for this purpose was the king created. // K_015 //
The king is traditionally remembered as the lord of the earth, but never of other property;
for he receives a sixth part of its fruit, and not otherwise.
Because the spirits dwell therein, their lordship is proclaimed;
their activity consists of the offering of the sixth part [of produce], arising from the causes of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
But for that lord of men who acts in this way, having abandoned greed,
sons are born to him, and his kingdom and treasury increase.
For that king who, by unjust means, takes taxes, fines, a share of the crops, and tolls from his kingdom, shall partake of the guilt.
Having abandoned what is taught in the treatises on worldly affairs (artha-śāstra), one should follow what is taught in the treatises on righteousness (dharma-śāstra).
Even if a king is wicked, his kingdom should not be destroyed;
for he does not proceed toward unrighteous acts without the consent of his subjects.

But when a king properly presents [an object] to one who does not seek it and is free from affliction, such a gift for the sake of Dharma saves an infinite number of beings. This is a gift for the sake of Dharma.
That which is obtained by kings through lawful conquest after defeating their enemy is pure; that alone should be given as tribute, for anything taken otherwise is never [pure].
A king should appoint as his domestic priest a Brahmin who is learned, well-spoken, beneficial, accomplished in sacred study, free from greed, and truthful.

In the extensive treatise on logic known as Dharma, which is to be accomplished through effort and is subject to interruption, that debate which has the matter to be proven as its basis is called *vyavahāra* (legal procedure).
Just as in the case of various objects, when there is doubt, "taking away" (haraṇa) is called *hāra*;
because it removes various doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*.
But a king, whether out of a desire for power or again out of greed for wealth, should not personally adjudicate the legal cases of men who have not yet reached a settlement.
For he who commits violence, or who does not give what is to be given, or who, out of misconduct, refuses one who asks— such a person may be dragged away by the king's command.

When the two lines reach eighteen words due to the variety of things to be accomplished (sādhya), they become eighteenfold; and through the variety of ritual actions (kriyā), they are divided into eight thousand types.
The root of the thesis (sādhya) is that which has been presented by the proponent; "giving what should not be given" and "violence" are said to be the two grounds for defeat (utthāna).
The plaint, the reply, the rejoinder, and the stage of legal action: by these it is declared to have four quarters.
In the treatises on Dharma and Artha, however, two branches are proclaimed;
victory and final resolution are declared to be their two fruits.
But he who, though urged by the king, first reports a matter that is censured by the treatise, is declared to be a *stobhaka*.
One who is appointed by the king himself to observe faults in conduct,
and having discovered them, reports them to the king, is designated as a "reporter" (sūcaka).
[The consideration of the relative strength and weakness of legal procedures, customary conduct, and royal edicts:

But where, in a dispute, the one who committed the offense is the perpetrator and the owner of the wealth is the rightful owner of his own property, that decision shall be made by the Dharma alone. // K_035 //

Whatever treatise on traditional law (smṛti-śāstra) has been proclaimed by those who establish the Dharma for the purpose of deciding legal cases— that indeed is known as judicial procedure (vyavahāra).
Whatever is constantly practiced by someone, whether it be righteous or even unrighteous, because it is the habitual practice of a region, that is proclaimed as *caritra*.
Whatever law the king shall establish, in accordance with the treatises on logic and likewise according to local custom, that is the just royal edict.
But an action that is consistent with reason, even if devoid of divine proof, prevails; for in legal proceedings, the Dharma is established by the verdict, and not otherwise.
Regarding those born of inverse unions and likewise those dwelling in difficult terrains, they say that the established custom is contrary [to the norm]; one should not unsettle that dharma.
But when the king makes a final decision according to that dharma, then the legal proceeding by way of custom is superseded by that very [dharma].
But when a legal custom is established by kings that is contrary to reason,
such a custom should be set aside by the king's command.
When a subsequent sublation is joined with this method,
and where there is a sublation by means of the contrary, there the Dharma is destroyed.

When one's own word exists, for kings to act by their own will leads to the loss of heaven, brings about the destruction of the world, invites fear from enemy armies, and robs them of their life-span and progeny.
Therefore, the king should accomplish his duties in accordance with the treatises;
however, in the absence of such texts, he should settle them according to local custom.
Whatever law has been established for a particular region and has persisted throughout all time, provided it does not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called "local custom" (deśadṛṣṭa).
In regions, ports, and cattle-stations, among those dwelling in cities and villages,
[the king shall act] according to their own conventions and the treatises on Dharma, and with others, together with them.
The legal settlement that has been determined according to the approval of the country shall always be recorded in writing and kept sealed with the royal seal.
She must be protected with diligence according to the scriptures; having examined her, one should reach a decision.
Whatever task is performed by those established in the Vedic tradition, and whatever has been recorded as settled law, [that shall prevail].
Therefore, that [cognition] should proceed accordingly; it should not proceed otherwise.
For that which is determined as "thus" is what has been observed in its proper place by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
That which has been performed where it was not previously practiced, yet is approved by the Śruti and Smṛti, should not be done otherwise; one should avoid that which is devoid of justice.
That department where the investigation of the Dharma-śāstras is conducted for the purpose of discerning the fundamental essence is indeed the Dharmādhikaraṇa (the Department of Justice).
Having risen in the morning, the king, having performed his purification with a concentrated mind,
[should honor] the teacher, the astrologer, the physicians, the gods, the Brahmins, and the domestic priests.
Having honored these as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having paid homage to his teachers and others, he should enter the well-proportioned assembly hall.
Having dressed in modest attire and entered the assembly hall with a composed mind,
the king should sit facing the east; standing there, he should attend to the legal cases of the litigants together with elders learned in the three Vedas and with ministers skilled in counsel.
Accompanied by the chief justice, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven as a witness through his adherence to dharma.
Together with his councilors—steadfast, disciplined, wise, hereditary, and most excellent among the twice-born;
skilled in the meaning of the treatises on dharma and proficient in the treatises on statecraft.
It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good conduct, youth, virtuous behavior, and wealth, and who are free from envy, acting as true members of the community.
In that case, the listeners should be like merchants who perceive what is right.

[The time for seeing legal cases: In the forenoon, in the assembly halls, the king— the subduer of enemies— should carry out the adjudication of legal cases according to the path prescribed by the scriptures.
Except for the eighth part of the day and the three specific times,
that time is declared by the scriptures to be the supreme period for legal transactions.
The three periods of time that follow the eighth division of the day have been observed by the wise in the treatises as the proper time for legal proceedings.
[The Judge]: When the king himself does not carry out the decision of a legal case, then he should appoint therein a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the scriptures.
One who is capable, born of a noble family, impartial, free from causing agitation,
steadfast, fearful of the next world, most virtuous, diligent, and devoid of anger.
One who is gentle, sweet-natured, affectionate, patient, discerning,
energetic, and free from greed should be appointed by the king to matters of debate.
One who studies only a single treatise cannot know the certain conclusion regarding what ought to be done;
therefore, kings should rely on many traditional authorities when settling disputes.
Where, however, there is no Brāhmaṇa, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should carefully avoid a Śūdra.
Therefore, whatever task has been performed by others, even if they were appointed [to the office], it should be understood as having been done unjustly,
even if it appears to be in accordance with the scriptures through the power of fate.
It is the established rule that he asks the question concerning the legal dispute as "praṭ";
therefore, he who investigates that matter is traditionally known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
But if the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding a matter that has not yet been decided,
he shall be punished, and the members of the court even more so.
[The members of the assembly] should be the best of the twice-born, free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all the scriptures. // K_071 //
Where the members of the court have reached a decision by overstepping the treatises on logic (*nyāya-śāstra*),
there dharma, struck down by adharma, destroys— of this there is no doubt.
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the assembly look on, they too are slain there.
But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded contrary to dharma;
by overlooking it, they, along with the king, go headlong to hell.
Even if he proceeds by unjust means, those members of the assembly who follow him share in that same guilt; therefore, the king must be enlightened by them.
But having recognized that the king’s mind has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is pleasing to him; in doing so, the courtier shall not incur guilt.
A member of the assembly must necessarily speak words consistent with Dharma and Artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the assembly would be blameless.
When the king should direct the litigants toward unrighteousness, the court member,
having informed the monarch, should then set aside that matter.
Whether out of affection, ignorance, greed, or even delusion,
if a member of the assembly speaks falsely therein, he is considered non-assembly-member and is subject to punishment.
Having correctly understood the determination of the case, the member of the court should then speak;
otherwise, he must not speak at all, for the speaker shall be subject to a double fine.
But that which has been lost due to the fault of the court members must then be paid by those members;
however, once the decision regarding the litigants' case has been finalized, one must not overturn it.
[The relative weight of those who decide legal cases:
Families, guilds, assemblies, authorized officials, and the king are the foundations of legal proceedings; among these, each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
One should have the affairs of ascetics carried out by those learned in the three Vedas,
and likewise by those who know the application of illusion, but never by oneself out of anger.
One endowed with perfect knowledge should not offer instruction to those of superior birth and character, nor to gurus, teachers, and ascetics.
But that which is their established lineage, which comes forth in due order according to the nature of things (dharmatā), they call the family dharma; one should protect it in that very same way.
[The Manner of Inquiry:
At the appropriate time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your affliction? Do not fear; speak, O man."
"By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason?"—one who has entered the assembly should ask in this manner;
and whatever he says when thus questioned, that the members of the assembly, together with the Brahmins, should accept.
Having reflected upon the matter, if it is just, he should thereafter summon [the defendant] for that purpose,
or else deposit a seal there, or appoint a person [as a representative].

One who is appointed by the plaintiff as another representative before the judge, being a different person, should be known as the *pratinidhi*; likewise, one who has himself accepted the role of the defendant (*prativādī*) is also such.
The right of legal standing belongs to the plaintiff; it does not belong to anyone else, as there would be no logical connection.
Furthermore, even the other party is considered to have been made a defendant by the plaintiff's opposition.
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two.
Slaves, laborers, disciples, appointed officials, and likewise kinsmen shall not be punished as litigants; however, anyone other than these is subject to punishment.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and other such extreme sins, no opposing witness is permitted.
In the killing of a human being, in theft, in violating another's wife,
in eating what is unfit to be eaten, and likewise in the abduction or defilement of a maiden.
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, no opposing witness shall be admitted; rather, the perpetrator himself shall litigate.

The king should not summon those who are eager for religious merit, nor those seeking prosperity, nor the sick, nor even the dull-witted; nor should he summon women who are unwell, intoxicated, insane, or afflicted by pain.
A young woman of noble birth who has recently given birth, even if she is the most excellent of all castes— her kinsmen are traditionally considered her masters.
The invitation of those women who are dependent on their families, those who are wanton, those who are courtesans, those who have lost their family status, and those who are outcasts is prescribed.
One who speaks in debate while armed with a weapon, without an upper garment, with disheveled hair, seated upon a throne,
or with the left hand [holding a staff], shall incur punishment.
But if one who is capable should, when summoned, disregard the king's command,
the king shall inflict punishment upon him according to the procedure prescribed by law.
For minor offenses, the punishment shall be fifty; for middling offenses, it shall be no less than two hundred;
and for serious matters, the fine shall always be no less than five hundred.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense with due effort,
there shall be the collection of fines in paṇas, or its equivalent value, to be paid to the king.
He who commits violence, or who does not give what is due when asked for, being of bad character— such a person may be seized by the king's command.

But having reported the matter to the king and having received his unambiguous promise [to act], one should apply an injunction (*āsedha*) against the defendant until the time of the summons for trial.
One who is fit for arrest but has not been arrested, if he escapes, deserves punishment. (K.105)
[Those who are not to be obstructed: But he who, by restraining the senses through speech, breathing, and so forth,
should obstruct one who is not to be obstructed— he is to be punished, but he does not transgress.
Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those situated on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those in difficult positions— none of them are to be obstructed by those who seek to accomplish their purpose.

Those afflicted by disease, those in distress, as well as those performing sacrifices, those who have not yet crossed over [the flood of existence], and likewise those intoxicated, insane, or mentally dull, should not be obstructed.
A farmer does not [reap] at the time of sowing; a soldier does not [act] at the time of the army's mobilization;
and one who has set out after making a vow does not turn back before the appointed time.

A farmer diligently engaged in his crops, from the commencement of the work until the harvest, shall not be sued during that time— even if he has obstructed one who should not be obstructed; such is the settled rule, and he should be punished by the king.
One who is accused, one who is imprisoned, and those who abide by the king's command—these others must not act on his behalf; the wise know him as "one who is accused."

When the mission for the messenger has been accomplished in dependence upon a one-day or two-day journey, and in consideration of the place, time, and other factors, one should cause him to be provided with food.
Those who know the truth understand that eating is prescribed as being dependent on place, time, age, capacity, and so forth; for there is no agent [of action] anywhere.
They are not to be accepted as witnesses;
they are neither a master nor an enemy, nor one appointed by a master,
nor one who has been imprisoned or fined, nor anyone under a legal dispute at any time.
Neither an heir nor one who is destitute, nor those who dwell in permanent residence, nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have gone forth as renunciants.
One who is unable to pay the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king,
or whose father is still living and acts according to his own will— such a person should not be accepted as a guarantor for the act of suretyship without being fully investigated.
Now, if there is no surety for a litigant who is fit for trial,
he, being protected, shall at the end of the day pay a fee to the messenger.
A twice-born man who lacks a surety should be protected by those who move outside [the city];
however, Śūdras and others who lack a surety should be bound with fetters.
If he transgresses or departs, he should be fined eight paṇas;
however, the non-obstruction of the daily duties of all social classes must be ensured.
A king should not employ one who has already accepted a commission according to the rule;
rather, he should either hand over that task to him or entrust it to another.
[The Sequence of Speech for the Plaintiff and Others: In that regard, the plaintiff (abhiyoktṛ) should speak first, and the defendant (abhiyukta) immediately thereafter;
at the conclusion of those two, the members of the assembly (sadasya) should speak, and after that, the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka).
He for whom there is greater suffering or who has more business to attend to shall be the first party;
he who does not report his case first shall not be so.
Or, if a person suffers a loss regarding their property or experiences some bodily affliction,
a claim for that property must be granted to them, provided they do not fail to report it beforehand.
Having established the nature of the claim, one should likewise specify the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, the lunar day,
the hour, the location, the region, the place, the caste, the appearance, and the age.
He should state the charge, the evidence, the substance, the number, his own name,
the names of the kings in their proper order, the place of residence, and the name of the person against whom the charge is brought.
Having announced the fortnight, one should determine, in due order, the names of the ancestors, the pain, the one who took [the property] and the one who gave it,
and other signs of forgiveness.
The country, as well as the location, the settlement, the caste, the name, the residence, the measurement, and the field-name.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: the names of the ancestors and grandfathers, and a recitation of former kings.
Whatever one of the [defendants], such as Rāga, might state when provoked during the proceedings,
all of that should be written as "om" by the proponent on the writing board and other surfaces.
One should rectify matters that are excessive and fulfill those that are deficient;
one should establish them upon the ground for as long as the faction remains firm.
The judge shall cause the plaintiff's statement of his own case to be recorded on a wooden board with chalk;
thereafter, it shall be refined and written upon the formal document.
A righteous lord of the earth should punish like a thief that litigant who writes down one thing while stating something else in the words of the plaintiff and the defendant.
He obtains either a reduction of his offense for three days or seven days,
until such time as the thought arises in him who wishes to speak in the dispute.
Since a firm conviction [arises] only after a long time from the undertaking of an action, one who is diligent does not waste time, but rather becomes a master of time.
When the minds of two parties desiring to settle a legal matter do not succeed in reaching an agreement,
time for deliberation should be granted to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
A prima facie argument (*pūrva-pakṣa*) that is contrary to the state, rejected by the king, or confused by multiple points does not succeed.
Even a case involving many claims that has been settled in legal proceedings,
a king may, if he desires to ascertain the truth, take it up again at his pleasure.
A thesis that lacks place and time, is devoid of substance and number, and is deficient in its objective and measure, is considered unacceptable.
He does not wish to do what is consistent with justice, nor does he perform what is unjust;
yet, because he does not cause it to be recorded in writing, his case is not proven.
One should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is unestablished, unobjectionable [in its formulation], devoid of meaning, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory.

Those who know the thesis understand the *pakṣa* to be that which is free from faults of the proposition, is yet to be proven, is endowed with valid reasons, is certain, and is established in the world.
It consists of very few syllables yet possesses abundant meaning; it is free from doubt and free from confusion;
it is devoid of contradictory causes and serves as a refutation of contradictions.
But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent,
the opponent should then offer a response connected to that very position.
When a petitioner states a request and that request is not obstructed,
or when one remains silent at the time of giving, that request is considered approved.

[The reply must be given either immediately or after a period of time: Having heard the matter set forth in writing, if the defendant requests a delay in the lawsuit for a valid reason, it should undoubtedly be granted to him.
Depending on the gravity or lightness of the offense, he shall pay off debts and the like either immediately, or within one day, three days, five days, three fortnights, or seven days.
Having understood the time, the capacity [of the litigants], and the strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the sovereign should grant the defendant a period of time, whether it be short or long.
Whether it be a day, a month, half a month, a season, or even a year—
the time for giving must be determined by the other party according to the nature of the action and its duration.
Where respect disappears, or where there is destruction or abandonment, one should not delay; for that matter is urgent.
In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and offspring; likewise in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, as well as in buying and selling.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, embezzlement of a deposit,
fraud, and perjury, one should initiate legal proceedings immediately.

Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations regarding cattle, or a life-threatening emergency, one may dispute over land immediately, even outside of the prescribed season.
In matters that have been recently committed, the lord should immediately institute a lawsuit;
or, in cases where time has elapsed, he should grant a period of time to the defendant.
If [the death] occurred today, the impurity lasts for that very day; if it was one month ago, it becomes one day;
if six years have passed, it should be three nights; and if twelve years have passed, it is seven days.
In the twentieth year, he shall receive ten days' wages, or half a month;
after thirty years have passed, it shall be one month; beyond that, it shall be three fortnights.
Within a year, or even sooner, according to one's own desire; [one should perform this] for one who is dull-witted, insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by disease. // K_156 //
Or when the matter has reached another region, or when the object is unknown,
or when the root witnesses or the witnesses themselves are situated in a foreign land.
In that case, the time for men [to give] should be until their reunion with their own country;
even when the time has been granted, it may still be given later due to the importance of the task.
But immediately thereafter, the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case,
should present his counter-position connected to the matter of that initial claim.
When someone is not present for the determination of conduct, the giving of requisites, desired duties, or attendance, one should not take advantage of that situation to cause him harm.
If at that time there should be a fault caused by fate or the king,
he would not be defeated merely by abandoning his position without having been forced out.
One should establish a fault committed by fate or the king through witnesses; however, for one who acts with deceit, the fine shall be the forfeiture of that wealth.
One who is being prosecuted should never prosecute the prosecutor in return, except in cases of physical assault, theft, adultery, or crimes involving mortal danger.
Whatever custom has been handed down through a continuous succession in a particular place,
the king, having considered that, should cause a legal decision to be given according to what is right.
The reply is fourfold:
the true reply, the false reply, the counter-attack, and likewise the plea of prior judgment; thus the reply shall be of four kinds.
But when another, having heard the meaning of what was spoken, refutes it either in terms of its meaning or its words, that reply should be known as false.
If a defendant, when being prosecuted,
should attempt to conceal the charge, one should know that his plea is false according to the principles of legal procedure.
The truthful speech of one who is to be accomplished is declared to be "practice" (pratipatti).
"I was not aware of this; I was not present there at that time;
I was not born at that time"—thus, falsehood is of four kinds.
If the defendant, when the claimant has stated his case,
admits it as such and states the grounds for it, the Teacher has declared that the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff.
If one who has already lost by conduct is made to write again, he is said to have been previously defeated; this is called a "decision on the basis of prior judgment" (prāṅ-nyāya).
I shall demonstrate [the truth] by means of witnesses, family elders, or written documents;
for this threefold judicial proceeding has already been won by me.
[The fallacies of the rejoinder (uttarābhāsa) or the faults of the rejoinder (uttaradoṣa) are:
that which is unestablished, contradictory, too little, or excessive; that which is doubtful, impossible, or unclear; and that which has a different meaning—these are the many faults.
An answer that is non-comprehensive, with disjointed words, whose meaning is concealed,
improper, requiring interpretation, or lacking substance is not praised by the wise.
An answer that has disjointed words, is incomplete, has a hidden meaning, is improper,
requires interpretation, or is substanceless, does not lead to the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
If, however, one who does not understand the convention speaks a thousand signs or uses another language, that answer is unestablished.
"It was returned by me in my youth; it was certainly not returned by me"—when one says this, it should be understood that the subsequent [statement] is contradictory in this context.
To say, "This was conquered by me long ago for this purpose," and to say,
"This was [conquered] by me in the past"— that which is said is known as the *ūna* and the *uttara*.
When it should have been said, "It was taken," he instead said, "The task was performed by me;
as for that vast amount of property which was previously taken, [it has been spent]."
When one ought to say "I must give," saying instead "I am not to give" is to be understood by the wise as a doubtful response in legal proceedings.
In the past, he established this doctrine of force and lack of force through sheer audacity; others consider this unspoken [teaching] to have been uttered for some other purpose.
When it is said, "I have given this thousand along with myself," and only half of that is returned,
that is considered here to be non-comprehensive (avyāpaka).
The proponent should not properly establish his case until the end of the action; what was previously accepted by me is now called a "disordered step."
"Will anyone give a lotus that has not been taken?"—
this answer, though its meaning was concealed, was spoken according to the context of the legal proceeding.
"Should he himself always give, or should it be given by me?"—
those who know the truth understand that this answer is improper.
The reply that "crows have no teeth" or "they do have them," and so forth,
is not accepted as a correct answer in reality, because it is essentially devoid of substance.
One should not overstep what is presented if it is meager, indistinct, deficient or excessive, inconsistent, lacking in pervasive essence, doubtful, or subject to opposition.
Anything other than that which is doubtful, as well as what is too little or too much,
and that which pervades only a portion of one side— this would certainly not constitute a valid response.
That which is true in one part of the thesis, but is a reason in another part,
and is likewise false in yet another part, is not a valid response because of its internal inconsistency.
In a single dispute, there should not be a formal proof for both disputants;
nor can there be the establishment of the object for both, nor can there be two proofs in one place.

If, after having first accepted a reason that causes the defeat of one's argument, one should state another, even more weighty, reason found in the opponent's reply, then indeed that [latter] is established, and not the other.
One should give a reply according to the facts and cause even one who does not wish to pay to pay,
by means of methods such as conciliation and sowing dissension, until that matter has been settled.
Whether out of delusion or through deceit, whatever was not stated by the proponent, even if it pertains to the subsequent part [of the argument], that should be accepted by both parties.
But if one, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer,
then after seven nights have passed, he is defeated and must pay.
Having caused [the opponent] to hear [his position], he may abandon what ought to be done and say something else;
by resorting to another's side in that manner, the proponent is defeated.
One should not speak of another's case after having been appointed to it;
if one speaks falsely in this manner, one should likewise designate that person as defeated.
But the litigant who, having caused a statement to be written, subsequently asserts it to be either deficient or excessive, shall suffer defeat; he does not deserve to maintain his legal action.
The wise should understand that the members of the court and the witnesses constitute the legal procedure (*kriyā*).
He who, out of delusion, hates that procedure is called a hater of the procedure (*kriyā-dveṣin*).
Through failing to attend when summoned, one is immediately cast out.
"Speak! Even if he is prepared, he should not speak; he deserves immediate imprisonment. On the second day, one should know that the defeat of that evil-minded man is certain."
But when one seeks to prolong the debate under some pretext, one should know that as *sāpadeśa*; it is recorded as causing defeat in the discussion.
One who speaks otherwise shall pay five *paṇas*; one who hates the legal proceeding ten *paṇas*;
one who does not appear for trial twenty-two *paṇas*; one who remains silent when questioned sixteen *paṇas*; and one who flees after being summoned shall be made to pay twenty *paṇas*.
The lord of the earth should discipline that man who does not come when summoned three times, who flees when called, or who has exceeded the limit of five nights.
If one should divide a single witness among those who have been made to hear the legal proceedings,
or should entice the plaintiff with bribes, one should declare him to be defeated.
If he causes fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction,
he loses his case in legal proceedings regarding the matter at hand.
When a case has been properly taken up according to the faults, there is no further appeal; once both sides have been committed to writing and the decision on the matter has begun,
he who speaks what is improper regarding that point loses his case.
But a plaintiff who, having designated witnesses, does not proceed to litigate out of his own will,
loses that case after thirty nights have passed.
Because fleeing is not the ultimate [response] and because of resorting to another's position,
a debate is attributed to the inferior one, but not to one who has conquered by means of his own words.
The wise know that one who has been defeated by inferior speech can be rescued;
however, for one who is himself devoid of his own speech, no rescue exists.
Those who, having presented their case, reach a settlement with one another after the matter has been taken up,
shall all be fined double, as they have deceived the king.

Because even the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) attains the status of a conclusion (uttara) by virtue of its cause, it is therefore called "action" (kriyā) when it establishes that prima facie position. (K_211)
When the answer has been properly examined and written down, being thus free from defects,
it is prescribed that the plaintiff or the defendant may proceed to present their evidence.

That which is intended by the proponent to be clearly established for himself is the *sādhya* (the thesis); that by means of which it is established is the *sādhana* (the proof), by which the entire *sādhya* is proven.

[The Means of Proof, and the Consideration of Their Strength and Weakness: They know that the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) are threefold: written documents, witnesses, and possession (*bhukti*). Logical reasoning (*yukti*) consists of circumstantial evidence (*leśa*) and indication (*uddeśa*), while in this world, the ordeals (*divya*) include poison and so forth.
Even when the plaint has been written down in its entirety, letter by letter,
the plaintiff shall establish his case through evidence in the third stage of the trial.

For it has been stated that the "task" (kārya) is that which is to be accomplished; however, the "means" (sādhana) is said to be action (kriyā). That [action], moreover, should be known as twofold: divine (daivikī) and likewise human (mānuṣī).
Human means include documents, witnesses, and so forth; divine means are considered to be lightning strikes, death, and the like.
When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof;
for by employing divine means when witnesses are available, he is defeated thereby.
If one person should speak of human evidence and another should speak of divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure.
If a human action, even if it pervades only a single part [of the rite], should exist, that is to be accepted by men who speak; however, a divine action, even if complete, is not.
The divine [means] are of five kinds; the human [means] are traditionally held to be threefold.
If one abandons a strong plea and resorts to a weak one,
once the victory has been determined by the members of the court, he shall not obtain that plea again.
Setting aside the essential word, one should accomplish even many non-essential actions; yet one should abandon that action which is devoid of essence.
One should abandon from afar that action which accomplishes both sides [of a conflict].
When witnesses are available and when there is a written document, no action based on fate is prescribed;
in such disputes, there is neither an ordeal nor [the need for] witnesses.

A document loses its validity through the passage of time, as does one that is vitiated by legal irregularities. In a lawsuit lacking documentary evidence or witnesses, one should resort to divine proof (oratory).
One should not employ human effort or documentary evidence in a matter that is to be resolved by divine means.
Regarding the status that has been proclaimed for guilds, corporations, assemblies, and so forth, their proof shall be documentary evidence; neither ordeal nor witnesses are required.

In the case of gates, paths, waterworks, enjoyment, and the like, as well as the carrying of water and so forth, possession alone shall indeed be the weighty proof; neither a document nor witnesses are required.
When a master has reached a decision regarding what has been given or not given to his servants, he may,
in connection with a sale or gift, purchase goods and yet fail to pay the money.
In matters of gambling, betting, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared the means of proof; neither divine ordeal nor documentary evidence is required.
In cases involving flight, in disputes over violence, in verbal assault,
and in matters arising from the use of force, witnesses or even divine proof may be employed.
But for those who commit secret crimes, divine ordeals are prescribed;
for men, [the truth] is to be discerned through reasoning, signs, gestures, facial expressions, speech, eyes, and physical movements.
And in all cases involving the highest forms of violence,
Bhṛgu says that one should determine the truth by means of divine ordeals when there are no witnesses present.
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should purify [the matter] even by means of ordeals;
but in cases of dispute involving the loss of life, if witnesses are available and yet the litigant resorts to an ordeal,
one should not question the witnesses in that case.
For a debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even slight circumstantial proof,
or divine means of proof have been declared for the subjects out of a desire for their welfare.
A formal demand at the proper time, a slight application of reasoning, and likewise a third means, an oath— by these he should recover the debt in due order.
Even if he is repeatedly exhorted, he may reject those words;
after three, four, or five times, he should act for the sake of the other's welfare.
But when there is an objection or contradiction, one should apply a modicum of reasoning based on place,
time, object, relation, measure, action, and so forth.
Even when logical arguments are insufficient, one should resolve the matter by means of oaths alone—
such as those involving fire, water, or meritorious deeds— taking into account the nature of the case, the time, and the strength of the parties involved.
Where there may be a document involving fraud, if it has been presented to the king, the king,
seated upon the throne of justice, shall have it cleared by means of an ordeal.
In cases of verbal abuse and regarding land, one should not employ divine proof (ordeals).
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should employ ordeals;
otherwise, one should establish the matter by means of witnesses, written documents, and possession.
In all disputes whatsoever, the lord of men should always reach a definitive conclusion by means of authoritative proofs, or by reasoning, or even by divine evidence.
A written document, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the threefold means of proof;
the wise know inference to be the logical reason, and likewise reasoning itself.
In the absence of prior [evidence], one should act only by means of subsequent [proof]— never otherwise—
by means of the authorities (pramāṇas) specified by the proponent, namely possession, documents, and witnesses.
No one at all should subject the accuser to the ordeals;
those skilled in ordeals should administer the ordeal only to the accused.
In a case of false testimony, it shall consist of four parts; likewise in a counter-attack and in a plea of prior judgment. It is to be understood as having two parts in cases of admission.
Defeat is of two kinds: that stated by another and that stated by oneself. That stated by another is of ten types; that stated by oneself is recorded as being of one type.
The shifting to another dispute, contradiction between what precedes and what follows,
the refutation of the production of one's own action, and the justification of another's statement.
The non-indication of the place, the indication of the wrong place and time,
the instigation of witnesses, and the subversion of the testimony.
A written document is said to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another;
it may be without witnesses or with witnesses. The validity of both depends upon their established usage in the region.
That which is written by the debtor's own hand, even without witnesses, is to be known as a "document in one's own hand"; it is considered authoritative by the wise.
One should record the date of birth, the caste, the wealth, and the number;
for one who applies himself in this way, even if the matter is not recorded, it will be remembered. However, if it is not written down, the purpose may be lost.
A document, however, must be executed with witnesses, with the sequence of its syllables uncorrupted,
conforming to the established customs of the region, and complete in all its matters.

That which is endowed with correct phonemes, syntax, and action; which is unambiguous, with clear syllables, and possesses an undiminished sequence and signs—such a written document shall attain validity.
The established order of the four classes of knowledge, the guilds, the city-districts, the assemblies, the citizens, and so forth—
any document written for the purpose of securing that [order] shall be a *sthiti-patra* (a deed of settlement).
When the curse has been lifted and the penance has been performed by the people,
a certificate of purification should be obtained from them, accompanied by witnesses.
When all the most excellent [witnesses] have assembled and a formal accusation has been brought forward,
that written record which recounts the facts of the case is to be known as a *sandhipatra* (a treaty or settlement document).
When a dispute over a boundary has been settled, a formal document concerning the boundary is to be prepared.
A royal document is defined as one bearing the king’s own hand, marked with his seal, and containing witnesses for all matters.
The statements of the plaintiff and the defendant, the formal claim, the testimony of witnesses,
the verdict, and how it was determined by himself.
One should record this according to the syllables as they appear in writing, setting it down exactly as before; first, one should set down the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant.
Thereafter, he should cause the decision of the legal experts, the judge, or the families to be recorded right there, in accordance with the doctrine of the Smṛti scriptures.
Once the matter has been settled, the king, having first shown honor to the disputant, should join him with the successful result and give him a written document bearing his own signature.
And those members of the assembly present there who are experts in the treatises on law (smṛti-śāstra),
he should likewise cause them to affix their own signatures there according to the procedure for drawing up a document.
The wise know that a document written according to this procedure is a *paścāt-kāra*.
However, where a legal action has been refuted by the plaintiff himself through some means of proof, there a *paścāt-kāra* may occur; it is not prescribed in all cases.

When [the defendant] is inferior to others such as those who offer different arguments, the other [party] is granted a document of victory; that document is established by the restatement of the facts. (K_265)

[Examination of Documents: Having summoned them by the king's command, he should investigate according to the law: a document by the procedure for documents, and witnesses by the procedure for witnesses.

A document that is endowed with correct phonemes, phrases, and actions; that is free from doubt, possesses clear syllables, and lacks no sequential order or marks—such a document shall attain validity.
A document is said to be that which is endowed with local custom, increased by years, fortnights, and so forth, and bears the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
But when the letters are displaced from their proper positions, out of order, ambiguous, or deviate from their defining characteristics,
then it constitutes forged writing.

That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence, that which has been executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is devoid of a claim— such a document is defective.
A document executed by one who is intoxicated, one who fears for his life, one who is insane, those who are afflicted, women, children, or those who are not independent, is not valid.
If it has been proclaimed on the second day and no one can overturn it,
then that shall be authoritative, except for what is done by one who is insane or intoxicated.
A document may indeed become invalid due to the fault of witnesses, or that of the scribe, or due to the fault of fraud by the creditor, or likewise by the debtor. (p.37)

A document written by the wicked shall be deemed wicked; one written by the pure, one should declare to be pure. Such a document [is invalidated] by witnesses, scribes, and executors who are corrupted by fraud.
For whatever faults there may be in the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be stated by the disputant;
however, those that are hidden [faults] are made manifest by the members of the assembly at the appropriate time through the citation of authoritative scriptures (śāstra).
Just as witnesses, scribes, and the author of the document fall into falsehood,
so too should faults be attributed [to them] by the wicked, for thus is the document corrupted.
When it is stated by the defendant that "this was not written by the scribe, nor was it seen by the witnesses," such a document is declared to be a forged one.
One should not invalidate a means of valid cognition through what is untrue, but rather through a defect;
for in the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
Thus, when a case involving a wrongdoer is brought before the king's seat,
he should deliberate upon it together with the brahmins and, after careful consideration, determine the faults of the written document.
By that same means by which witnesses, scribes, and executors fall into falsehood, the document becomes tainted; one should declare it pure when the parties are pure.
A document written by the creditor’s own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall be considered forged unless the maker proves that it was indeed executed by him.
If a debtor denies a debt that has been entered in writing with his own hand,
he shall be questioned by the witnesses recorded in the document or according to the testimony of the scribe.

In disputes concerning what has been done or not done, the determination of the case is made by witnesses through written documents; if the document is challenged, the plaintiff must point out those who are recorded therein.
In all three types of written documents, confusion may arise among men;
therefore, one should establish the truth by means of the signatures (handwriting) of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
Then, even if the scribe along with the witnesses has met his death, he shall be purified by their own handwriting and other such evidence; of this there is no doubt.
In case of doubt regarding a debtor's own handwriting— whether he is living or dead—
the determination of that document is made by other leaves written in his own hand.
Even those who have died are recorded in the register of the ocean;
indeed, that written record remains authoritative even when they have passed away.
Direct perception is never subverted by inference;
therefore, the testimony of witnesses should prevail over the statements of a corrupt document.

For a legal decision made for the sake of one's own wealth indeed invalidates the document itself; what is written [as evidence] must be countered by writing alone, and that which is supported by witnesses must be refuted by witnesses.

If a witness declares a falsehood, one should establish the truth through their testimony; and if a scribe does not purify the document by admitting it is forged, he shall be made to pay the highest fine.
When one who is capable does not request [repayment] from a wealthy person standing nearby,
out of fear that he might be considered a pure debtor, that document will suffer a loss of its legal force.
A document that has been more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard of,
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be living.
But when the attainment of peace has been applied, he who does not show the written document,
nor even asks the debtor for it, shall not obtain success.
Thereafter, one should carefully examine whatever is recorded as a subsequent action;
if it is indeed consistent with reason, then that written document shall be authoritative.
Otherwise, a legal matter decided from afar might have to be re-examined; for what was established as true through a delusion of knowledge, though it be untrue, must be overturned—
even if it was executed with great effort by kings— once its invalidity is proven.
A royal edict attains purity when it is pure in its seal, pure in its execution, pure in its distribution, marked with the insignia,
and authenticated by the king's own hand.
But that document which is proclaimed to be free from defects shall attain validity.
If, upon seeing the document, the debtor does not point out manifest defects,
then the document, having remained for twenty years, shall be considered valid.
A document by which property is enjoyed for twenty years in the presence of a capable person is free from defect.
Now, if a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years with absolute certainty,
its validity is established by that document, provided it is free from defects of the writing.
When a dispute over a boundary has been settled, a boundary document is prescribed;
its defects must be declared for as long as twenty years.
Where a debt is recorded in a document along with the deposit of collateral,
they who know the law consider that to be valid evidence even when the witnesses are deceased, provided the amount involved is small.
If something has been received by him, or even if a gift has not been formally specified,
a document— even without a seal— is authoritative when there are deceased witnesses.
If something has been received, or if a designation has been made,
or if a formal document has been written as proof— even if the witnesses have died.

A document is established as valid in all cases—whether witnesses are deceased or not—if it was presented at the proper time, and likewise if it was accepted and made known [to the parties]. // K_305 //
A written document is never superseded even by divine witnesses;
for the law of writing is always supreme, and thus it is not set aside by anything else.
The act of writing should always be avoided by means of a document that is either consistent with that [fact] or superior to it; it should never be avoided by any other means.
Just as a reflection situated in a mirror appears as if it were both non-existent and existent,
so too do skilled people create images from what is inscribed.
A document that, having received property, is delivered to another;
one that is concealed, or one that is not acknowledged by another, or one executed in the house of a third party.
Whether the object has been delivered or not, or in some cases where there is a prior written document,
this very same rule is to be understood for determining the validity of the document.
He who forges a document concerning the sale or mortgage of immovable property shall be thoroughly interrogated and then deprived of his tongue,
hands, and feet.
If it is marred by stains, burnt, perforated, or even worn out, one should have another painting made; likewise, if it is rubbed away by sweat.
Written documents, witnesses, and possession— these three are accepted as means of proof. Among these proofs, for men, possession is traditionally held to be equal to a written document.
In cases where there is doubt regarding the exit from a street, a gate, a watercourse, and so forth,
it is the settled conclusion among the means of valid cognition that possession alone is weighty.
An inference is superior to a witness; a written document is superior to witnesses;
and unopposed possession for three generations is more authoritative than these.
The one who takes [the property], or his son, must exert effort regarding its enjoyment;
thus is the law established for animals, women, men, and so forth.
Possession is said to be of two kinds: with title and without title;
that which has been held by three generations and is independent is [possession] with title, provided it is not insignificant.
Possession inherited from a grandfather is primary, and that from a father is also considered valid;
when uninterrupted by these three, it is regarded as stable for sixty years.
But when that which was eaten improperly becomes properly digested through the consumption of medicinal ghee, the one who brought it receives its reward; it shall never be confiscated from him.
When a plaintiff has lost the written document of title or when his possession is not firmly established,
he must declare the time, the evidence, and the gift in the assembly.
In the period of memory (smārta-kāla), possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by documentary evidence;
in the period beyond memory (asmārta), however, due to the absence of such records, it is established through succession over three generations.
In the beginning, however, there is the title-deed; in the middle, possession accompanied by [title];
but that continuous possession extending through three generations is the sole cause.
The acquirer, even if possessed of possession, must clear the defects of the document;
his son, however, must clear the defects of possession, but shall not incur the defects of the document.
For whatever property has been taken by someone, he alone, being the rightful claimant, shall recover it;
even if it has been enjoyed for a long time, possession is not admitted as belonging to anyone other than him.
Out of greed, one should not disturb long-standing wealth that has been unclaimed.
But whatever property was enjoyed by the father in accordance with the practice of enjoyment and according to dharma—
when he has passed away, that [property] need not be contested, for it was acquired by him through enjoyment.
But if land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law,
even in the absence of a written document, a fourth person may acquire it there.
Just as milk, over time, produces curd endowed with flavor,
so too does the cause of giving, over time, result in enjoyment that extends through three generations.

In the scriptures, possession (*bhukti*) is powerful when it is continuous and long-standing; however, that which was established previously should be understood as prevailing even if it has been interrupted.
One should not conceive of [ownership] over women, nor over the wealth of gods or kings;
and those [who possess such wealth] are merely ignorant Vedic scholars, inherited through the lineages of their mothers and fathers.
A man might practice the life of a celibate student for thirty-six years without observing the vows,
or he might dwell for a long time in another land seeking wealth.
Once he has returned from his studies but remains uninitiated into the vows, he may then seek out his own wealth;
for one who is fifty years of age, the enjoyment of that property is considered its rightful seizure.
It is traditionally taught that twelve years is the period for those seeking knowledge;
likewise, for those seeking the knowledge of crafts, it is proclaimed that the time lasts until they have mastered them.

That which was enjoyed by their friends and kinsmen while they themselves were unaware, and that which was taken from kings who had committed offenses— none of that is lost through the passage of time.

That which has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, and likewise by one's own people—there is no accomplishment through such enjoyment; one should instead direct that enjoyment elsewhere.
[The Principle: But he who, being requested by a petitioner, does not cause an obstacle for three, four, or five times, that other person becomes a debtor.
Giving gifts, causing dissension, acts of seduction,
and the removal of the mind [from its object]— these are indeed the causes that lead to separation.
Whichever among these has been established by the proponent, that shall constitute the fundamental proof; however, if the proponent retracts what he has established, the defeat occurs there.
The king must not cause a delay in the testimony of witnesses;
for through time, a great evil arises, characterized by the subversion of Dharma.
The king himself should examine the witnesses who have been presented;
together with the members of the court, he should scrutinize the statement spoken by those witnesses.
The time for witnesses to be summoned is when there is a need for a full understanding of the correct course of action;
however, where the testimony is doubtful, one should litigate the matter immediately and clearly.
In the midst of the assembly, the presiding judge, consoling them, shall appoint all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this procedure.
Whatever you know of each other’s conduct regarding this matter, speak it all in truth; for you two are the witnesses here.

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, he should question the twice-born regarding the truth; they should face either north or east, being pure themselves, at the time of the morning, while questioning those who are pure.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are well-known for their conduct and who understand the matter— one should question them individually, having bound them firmly with oaths.
When a matter has been experienced due to the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, the testimony of witnesses should be accepted; otherwise, so Bṛhaspati says, it is not valid.
Those who are of renowned family and character, free from greed and delusion,
trustworthy, pure, and distinguished— their testimony is beyond doubt.
A witness should be examined by the litigant exactly as they appear; one who is superior or inferior should never be made to testify by the witnesses.

Bhṛgu spoke to the wearers of sectarian marks, the guilds and associations, the merchant corporations, and others who were likewise organized in groups, as well as to whatever other classes existed in collective bodies.
Among the slaves, wandering minstrels, and wrestlers, as well as those who live by elephants, horses, and weapons—
each of these groups has its leaders and members;
their disputes within their own groups are settled by those members acting as witnesses.
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of equal status for twice-born men;
virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes.
Where it is impossible for residents of foreign lands to appear in person, one should admit documentary evidence sent by those learned in the three Vedas as proof.
However, in the case of a deposit, even a single witness may be declared;
even a single messenger sent by the plaintiff becomes a witness.
Whatever commodity has been refined by whom, that he alone shall demonstrate;
he alone is declared to be the authority in a dispute concerning it.
The scribe, the presiding judge, and the members of the court, in their respective order,
are declared to be witnesses when they observe the case while the king is looking on.
Furthermore, others who have not been specifically designated are declared to be witnesses:
the village community, the presiding judge, and the king for those engaged in legal proceedings.
One who is an insider in legal affairs, one who has been sent by a litigant, and those from the same lineage in family disputes— these also may serve as witnesses.
But when a dispute over the division of inheritance arises and doubt is present, the testimony of the kinsmen is the authority in that case; in their absence, [the testimony of] others.
But among witnesses who have been recorded in writing and designated by the plaintiff,
if even one of them speaks otherwise, they are all not valid witnesses due to that discrepancy.
For a witness appointed by one party may not contest the claim of the other;
in his absence, however, either a person authorized by the court or a relative may contest it.
Furthermore, those who live off his wealth, those who perform services for him,
his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates are not to be witnesses.
The sons of a maternal aunt, as well as the sons of a uterine brother and a maternal uncle—these are declared to be sapindas; one should not employ them as witnesses.
Kinsmen, relatives by marriage, the husband of one’s sister, the father, a blood relative, a paternal uncle, a father-in-law, and likewise spiritual teachers; // K_363 //
Those royal officials who are appointed to positions in cities, villages, and districts,
and who are favorites and devoted, would not inquire [into such matters].

One should examine witnesses in cases concerning debts and the like, as well as in matters of long-standing practice, in cases of violence, and in urgent matters; such examination is prescribed in these instances.
In cases of obstruction of the king’s command, in matters of seizure and acts of violence,
as well as in theft and verbal assault, one should not examine the witnesses.
If a case occurs within a house at night, or outside a village,
and the legal action concerns these very matters, one should not examine the witnesses.
Testimony should never be spoken by witnesses unless they are questioned by the plaintiff;
no testimony exists among them that they could apply to themselves of their own accord.
The defendant's reply, as well as the witness, are each associated with two paths.
Then, if he who was previously mounted by his own hand remains there alone, and if he does not recognize [the person], one should establish [his identity] by means of his own hands.

One who is brought by the plaintiff himself and recorded in the document is called a "written witness" (likhita-sākṣin); one who is reminded [of his testimony] without a document is [a witness] other than that.

But that witness who, for the sake of accomplishing the matter, is reminded again and again by the plaintiff after having seen the matter, is called "one who has been reminded" (smārita) in this context.
One who has been brought for the sake of a specific purpose, and one who has arrived incidentally—
these two witnesses, though not recorded in writing, are effective in proving the plaintiff's case.
One who, for the sake of establishing his own case, has been clearly informed of the opponent's statement by the plaintiff,
and remains hidden, is called a secret witness.
That witness who gives testimony again and again,
whether by hearing or by causing others to hear, is designated as a "subsequent witness" (sākṣy-uttara).
He from whom secrets may be whispered in confidence, or to whom a task may be entrusted,
should be known as a secret agent who has mastered his mission.
Where the plaintiff has perished, there the witness is considered as if dead;
and where the defendant has perished, it is likewise determined in that case.
