[The exposure of defects in witnesses:
Whatever defects of the document there may be, as well as those attributed to the witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have been stated.
But he who, regarding the meaning of what has been said, should maliciously attack witnesses who have already been cleared,
and cannot state the reason for his objection, shall incur the first amercement.
One should not invalidate a means of valid cognition through falsehood, but rather through a fault;
for in the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
Furthermore, when the defendant or the plaintiff establishes the disqualification of a witness,
this does not constitute a separate legal proceeding, because it is relevant to the matter at hand.
The defects of the witnesses must be stated by the defendant in court;
having written all of them down on a document, he should then be made to state his reply.
But they can never serve as witnesses regarding the performance [of the act];
therefore, they must be treated otherwise by the defendant through his own action.
If the defendant fails to substantiate his claim, he shall be compelled to pay the debt;
likewise, all witnesses who have been clearly established must testify, unless they are disqualified by the rules governing witness conduct.
One should discern the internal state of that person through their facial expressions, gestures, and movements;
thus the opponent is seen to be defeated by means of inference.
Trembling, perspiration, and then agitation; dryness of the lips upon touching them;
scratching the ground, leaving one's place, looking sideways or upwards, and a change in the voice—these the wise declare to be the signs of a corrupt person.
Witnesses must give their testimony while remaining within the assembly hall, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.
In the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, and in the presence of the matter to be proven, one should give testimony directly; never under any circumstances should one do so in absentia.
One should speak regarding the meaning; even in the absence of those two, this law applies in some cases to quadrupeds and to bipedal beings as well as to stationary things.
Even in the absence of weights, articles to be counted, or measures, one may dispute;
in all formal transactions, witness-hood is not otherwise than that.
If there is testimony regarding the killing of living beings, one should cause it to be proclaimed in the presence of Śiva;
but in the absence of that, [one should do so] by means of a sign, and one should not proclaim it otherwise.
The testimony of those [witnesses] should be accepted as their own inherent statement when it is free from defects;
once they have spoken, however, the witnesses must not be questioned again and again by the king.
Whatever they might say by its very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak regarding the Dharma is meaningless.
But that which is seen by those assembled together must be stated exactly as it was;
however, that which is the individual task of each distinct person must be stated separately for each.
But when a matter is discovered by witnesses at a different time, Bhṛgu says that one should examine each witness there separately; for that is a "separate-time" case.
In disputes concerning debts and the like, where the matter is generally stable,
if the amount stated is either less or more than what is certain, the case to be proven is not established.
Even when only a portion of the matter to be proven has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established—
provided that in matters involving sexual intercourse, violence, or theft, that which was intended to be proven is indeed addressed.
But where there may be deficiency or excess, one should avoid giving testimony there;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
Where one contradicts [the truth] regarding place, time, wealth, number, form, caste, appearance, or age in testimony, the wise know that as unspoken.
When the various matters have been set forth and the witness has been called upon to testify,
if he does not speak in accordance with the facts, that testimony is not considered properly delivered.
Where witnesses state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too should be known as improper; such is the determination regarding witnesses.

[The Faults and Punishments of Witnesses: Witnesses who speak everything when not questioned, as well as those who fail to speak when questioned, should be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
In cases of verbal abuse, fraud, or contentious debate, they shall be fined three hundred panas;
in disputes concerning debts and the like, they shall likewise be made to pay the debt as well as the fine.
That lowest of men who, though neither designated as a witness, nor summoned, nor even presented, should speak whether falsely or truthfully, he too is to be punished.
If a witness does not state the testimony, he shall bear the debt and an equal fine;
in other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred.
And those who, having spoken one way, speak otherwise, being possessed of verbal equivocation, should be punished.
Having confiscated all the property of one who, out of greed for a particular matter, has given false testimony, the king should thereafter banish him from the realm.
When a case has indeed been established by witnesses for the plaintiff,
if the defendant should then prove the matter otherwise,
or if there be many witnesses of noble birth, the former witnesses shall be considered false witnesses.
When an action is pure according to the rule, then its verbal expression is purified;
and he who is pure from that pure verbal expression is established as being pure in meaning.
One should recognize within seven days where a witness speaks falsely;

[the consequences may be] illness, fire, or the death of a kinsman, occurring after two weeks, three weeks, or even forty-six days, depending on the distinctions of the object, its class, and so forth.
[The procedure regarding the divine ordeals pertaining to the subject matter of their disputes:
No one at all should employ the accuser in the divine ordeals;
those expert in divine ordeals should administer the ordeal to the accused.
For those who are suspected by kings, one should employ the ordeal of the balance and so forth;
and in the performance of the rite for self-purification, one should not prescribe the [ordeal of] the head.

For those who are defiled by public scandal and those suspected by bandits, the balance and other such ordeals should be employed; however, Bhṛgu says that the head-weighing ordeal must never be used in those cases.
One should never fashion a head-enclosure for those in states of suspicion;
rather, one should cause headless divine images to be presented to the king’s servants.

In matters of suspicion or establishing trust, in the division of inheritance among heirs, and in the execution of a collective undertaking, one should always cause the treasury alone to be the party involved.
Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should determine the proof; in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value.
Having ascertained the measure of all the substances, one should fashion the gold;
once it is joined with the proper measure of gold, one should then employ that divine [image].
Having ascertained the number of gold pieces, it is traditionally taught that for the loss of one hundred, one should take poison;
and for the loss of eighty, one should indeed offer oneself to the fire.
If sixty [coins] are lost, water should be administered; for forty, indeed, a jar [of water];
and for the loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of a vessel of wine (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, upon the loss of more than five [grains],
one should touch the head of a son or another relative when half of that half (one grain) or half of that half again (half a grain) has been lost.
But when even half of that half has perished, worldly activities are prescribed;
reflecting thus, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha.
[The rules for divine ordeals according to the status of the plaintiff, the defendant, their caste, and their craft:
One should administer fire to a Kṣatriya, a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa, and water to a Vaiśya;
or one may employ any divine ordeal for all castes, except poison, which is to be avoided for the twice-born.
He should cause the twice-born to be treated like Śūdras— namely, cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, and usurers.

One should never give fire to metal-workers, nor water to those who subsist on water; likewise, one should never administer poison to those who know the application of mantras. One should not employ a person observing a vow or one suffering from mouth diseases for the preparation of rice-offerings.
One should avoid fire for those suffering from skin diseases, water for those with asthma and coughing,
and one must always strictly avoid poison for those with disorders of bile and phlegm.
The treasury should not be given by the wise to those addicted to liquor, women, or gambling, nor to gamblers, nor to those who follow the ways of nihilism.
For those who have committed the great sins of killing their mother, father, a twice-born, a guru, a child, a woman, or a king, and especially for those who are nihilists (nāstika).
But as for those who bear the marks [of asceticism], yet are utterly corrupt, who know the rituals of mantras and yoga,
who are born of mixed castes, and who persist in the practice of evil—
In these very cases of legal dispute, and especially with regard to those that are blameworthy, a king devoted to righteousness should not, even with effort, employ divine ordeals.
Those who are appointed by these very [means] deserve a divine ordeal;
however, where the virtuous do not accept it, there those to be cleared should be tested by their own people.
The ordeal should not be administered to those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātaka), especially to atheists,
nor to those who are habitually devoted to sinful acts.
In these legal proceedings, divine ordeals have been strictly prohibited;
one should have them performed by virtuous men, for Manu says that one who is accused should not be abandoned [to such tests].
For those who are untouchable, low-caste slaves, barbarians, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions, there is no fixed rule regarding the king;
however, in cases of doubt concerning them, one should prescribe the ordeals well-known among them.
[The divine places:
One should employ [these mantras] at the king’s gate for those men who have been accused in the abode of Indra, who are great sinners, and who have engaged in treason against the king.
For those born of inverse unions, the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for others, the wise know that the ordeal should be administered in the midst of an assembly.
But when there is a conflict regarding time or place, one should arrange it as is appropriate;
one should have another person undergo the ordeal—this is the rule in case of such a reversal.
Those gifts given at an improper place or time, and those made while residing abroad, always lead to deviation from one's true purposes in this world; of this there is no doubt.

Furthermore, one should re-examine that matter to be proven; for when there is a contradiction in the proof, the king should avoid the aforementioned divine ordeals even if they have been administered. Indeed, those same ordeals must be administered again by fools, the greedy, and the wicked.
Therefore, the experts should administer the divine ordeal according to the prescribed method;
however, when applied incorrectly, it is not capable of establishing the truth.
If the sling breaks, or the balance beam, or likewise the cord,
or if there is doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man again.
[The Procedure for the Fire Ordeal: If the accused stumbles or is burned in a place other than the designated spot, the gods do not consider him burnt; one should make him undergo it once again.
[The Procedure for the Water Divinity]:
For the sake of purity, one should prepare arrows with tips not made of iron, or even those made of bamboo stalks; and the shooter should discharge them with great firmness.
When [the vessel] has been thrown, one should perform the immersion; the departure and the arrival are simultaneous.
However, upon the departure, the arrival must be performed; another man shall enter the water.
If, upon entering the water, only the head is seen and neither the ears nor the nose, one should designate that person as pure.
If a man who has submerged himself and then emerges is seen by living beings,
he should submerge once more in that very spot, which is identified by local landmarks.

[The Procedure for the Poison and Divine Ordeals: That poison of horned creatures is known to resemble the horn of a goat, dark in color, very thick, originating from a horn, and appearing like aloe-wood (verā) when broken.
One should make that red [pigment] black and likewise hard according to its characteristics;
by this method, the divine [substance] is to be known by those skilled in the divine.
Yellow and resembling the vatsanābha [poison], this is the certainty through the knowledge of its color;
one should know that which has the shape of a pearl or a conch shell when broken to be vatsanābhaka.
By mixing honey and milk, one should make it clear at that very moment;
thus has the external characteristic been described by those who accomplish the Dharma.
In the forenoon, in a cool place, one should administer poison to embodied beings,
having ground it finely and mixed with thirty times its amount of clarified butter.
From six palas of poison, take that portion which is one-twentieth;
this should be given to the person to be cleared of suspicion, reduced by one-eighth and saturated with clarified butter.

[The Procedure for the Divine Ordeal in a Case-Involving a Casket: For a minor offense against the gods, having bathed the person with water from the weapon[-casket], he shall be made to drink it; if he is altered [by the ordeal], he is impure; otherwise, being pure, he shall be released.
[The Procedure for the Rice Offering:
When the water used for bathing and drinking the deity has been consumed as divine rice, one becomes pure by spitting it out cleanly; otherwise, one is impure and must be restrained.
If a defendant has been subjected to an assault and is proven pure by means of an ordeal,
the righteous king shall compel the accuser to pay both a fine and the costs of the lawsuit; however,
he should honor a person who has been cleared by an ordeal.
Where blood is seen, where the jaw drops,
and whose body trembles— one should designate that person as impure.
Then, if there is a discrepancy with fate, after twenty-one days,
one should cause the accused to pay that matter [in dispute] with effort, as well as the fine.
If that disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should happen to only one person and not to all people, he shall be made to pay the debt and be subject to a fine.
Consumption, dysentery, and eruptive boils; pain in the palate and bones;
eye disease, throat ailments, as well as insanity;
headache and the breaking of the arms—these are the divine diseases that arise for men.
One who is pure should be made to pay half of a hundred; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment.
One should prescribe punishment in due order for poison, water, fire, the balance, the sacred vessel, rice grains, and the ordeal of the heated gold coin.
One should calculate one thousand and six hundred, as well as five hundred, and likewise four, three, two, and one; thus should one arrange the lower [levels] among those who are lower.
[The Rule for Oaths: Where a ritual action is taught but the specific limb of the performer is not mentioned,
it should be understood that in those rites, the right hand is the one that brings them to completion.
If no terrible calamity, whether caused by the king or by fate, befalls anyone within fourteen days, he should be known as pure in his oath.

[The Examination of What Is Done by the Insane, the Independent, and Others: Whatever is given or whatever is done by one who is insane, or likewise by one who is intoxicated, or even by another state of being— that shall have no legal validity whatsoever.
An act performed by one who is not independent, its master may annul;
no other person shall dispute it, except for what is done out of fear or by one who is insane.
A father who lacks independence, a son whose father is still living, a brother or even a nephew,
a younger sibling who has not yet divided the property, as well as a slave or a laborer.
Transactions involving fields, houses, or slaves— whether gifts, mortgages, or sales— performed by one who lacks independence shall not be valid, nor have they been so described.
All of these are authoritative in the buying and selling of merchandise, provided that they are approved even as they carry out their transactions.
In the same way, the fields and so forth would belong [to the heirs] if the brother, the brother’s son,
or the son were authorized by the elder when he was departing to perform his duties.
But he to whom authority has been delegated in a particular matter is the master in that matter;
as its lord, he ought not to undo what has been done by him.
A father has authority over his son's wealth, his wife, and his instruction;
however, he has no authority over his son regarding the sale or the gift [of that son].
[The function of determination:
Purification has been declared by those who know the true principles of the scriptures to be medical treatment;
it is recorded as being twofold, consisting of expiation and punishment.
Even when multiple claims are brought forward, the creditor recovers only as much wealth as he can prove by means of witnesses; that much alone is the recovered debt.
If one, having made a total denial, should later confess even a small portion of it in private,
Bṛhaspati says that the defendant must be made to pay the entire amount.
Thus, seated upon the Dharma-throne, impartial and free from dispute, the adjudication of legal cases should be observed by him together with Brahmins, and not otherwise.
Having personally examined the legal proceedings, or having heard them from the presiding judge,
the king should then issue a certificate of victory for the sake of official recognition.
[The Procedure for Punishment:
But the king should cause a Brahmin to pay his debt to the owner by means of peaceful persuasion alone;
however, he should cause others who are wicked to pay by afflicting them according to the local custom.
Bhṛgu declared that one should cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of a pretext; this applies likewise to merchants, farmers, and artisans.
Having ascertained that [the debtor] is unable to pay the debt, one should compel him to perform labor under one's own direction;
if he is incapable even of that, he should be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
But he should cause those striving [to pay], whether they be farmers, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, to give [the tax].
In the case of offenses against the teacher, the father, the mother, and likewise one's kinsmen, no punishment whatsoever is prescribed for these.
But where an improper act has been committed to save one's life, there shall be no punishment at all; this is the law remembered by Bhṛgu.
One should never kill a brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of evil;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with his entire wealth intact and unhurt.
For all four castes who fail to perform penance,
he shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both their bodies and their wealth.
If, according to the law, the punishment for a Śūdra for a certain offense is such,
then for a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be double, double that amount.
A Śūdra who has settled in the life of a renunciant and is devoted to the recitation of prayers and burnt offerings,
if he commits a sin, should be punished by execution or else fined with double the usual fine.
In all offenses, whatever fine for wealth is prescribed for a man, half of that shall be given by women; in the case of killing, the man's limb shall be cut off.
Women who are not independent should not be held accountable; it is the man therein who commits the offense.
They are to be disciplined by their master, but the king shall deal with the man.
If a woman whose husband is away is captured by force, she should be kept in confinement for as long as her lord has not returned.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense with due care,
there shall be the collection of fines in paṇas, or else its equivalent value must be paid to the king.
Wherever a fine of one māṣa or two pādas is prescribed, it should be understood as unspecified; however, one should calculate it as one māṣaka.
Where a fine is stated in *māṣakas*, silver should be specified there;
likewise, where it is stated in *kṛṣṇalas*, that indeed shall be the determination of the stated fine.
A māṣa should be known as one-twentieth of a kārṣāpaṇa;
a kākaṇī, however, is one-fourth of a māṣaka and of a paṇa.
In the region of the Five Rivers, this is the conventional designation:
a kārṣāpaṇa is known as one ṇḍikā; four of those are a dhānaka;
twelve of those are a suvarṇa; and a dīnāra is recorded as being equal to a citraka.
[Furthermore, the principle:
That position which states "the non-existent is existent" is determined by the members of the assembly themselves;
once it has been adjudicated, it is declared to be a formal instruction based on the testimony of witnesses.
But that king who, even when the matter has been determined by his family and others, does not remain satisfied,
should reconsider what was done and rectify any wrong action.
[Consideration of Interest in the Non-payment of Debt: One should never grant a loan to women, slaves, or children;
the lender shall not recover that [interest], though he may give them whatever wealth he possesses.
But whatever interest has been stipulated by the debtor as excessive,
if it was agreed upon during a time of distress, that which was so contracted must always be paid;
otherwise, interest that was not so contracted must never be paid under any circumstances.
But where one purifies the interest by increasing it exclusively and at every period of time, that is known as *śikhā-vṛddhi*.
Satisfaction is proclaimed as the fruit of the house, and the acquisition of enjoyments as that of the field.
But that which is enjoyed in its entirety is the pledge for use (ādhibhoga); however, interest is considered to be the "imagined" (parikalpita) portion.
Where there is such an application [of capital], that is called a pledge for use.
[Ākṛtavṛddhiḥ]:
If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without having returned it,
that debt shall accrue interest after the lapse of one year.
If one who has been asked for a loan departs for another region without having made an agreement on repayment,
that debt shall accrue interest after the lapse of three months.
But even if he resides in his own country, if he should not pay when asked at any time,
the king shall compel him to pay that interest which has accrued, even against his will.
A gift given out of affection does not increase so long as it has not been asked for;
but if it is not given when asked for, it increases by five percent per month.
Interest on a deposit, the remainder of interest, and likewise profit from buying and selling—
if these are not returned when requested, they increase by five percent per hundred.
If one who has taken merchandise should depart for another region without paying the price,
that debt shall accrue interest after three seasons have passed.
Interest shall never accrue on hides, grain, liquor, gambling, the price of merchandise, bride-price, or amounts received as surety.
The maximum limit of interest that may be taken on goods lent by creditors should always be double the principal;
if it does not reach double, one may calculate further interest.
The price of gems, pearls, corals, gold,
and silver increases twofold, as does that of ploughshares and woollen blankets.
The increase for all types of oils, as well as for liquors, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt, should be known as eightfold.
Base metals are considered to be fivefold [the value of the land], and land likewise eightfold;
because of the statement "immediately," it is given immediately.
[The Settlement of Debt] [The Rule for When Multiple Debts Are Combined]:
That which was written down on a single day, one should discharge that debt equally.
Grasping, protecting, and obtaining; otherwise, however, it is in due order.
But when there is a combination of various debts, whichever was contracted first must be paid first;
after that, the king's debt must be paid, followed by that of a Śrotriya.
If one should prove that a commodity was acquired by means of another's property, that property must be returned by the debtor alone; it cannot be otherwise.
If, having taken a substance for the sake of interest, one gives it back as something fit for use—
whether movable or immovable— that is called a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*).
Having paid a price exceeding that, one may acquire one's own field and so forth.
If one should make a claim against two [parties], what course of action should there be?
Of those two, the prior claim should be accepted; the one who made it later incurs the punishment of a thief.
When a document concerning a mortgage, sale,
or gift is contradicted by a single act, that document is considered fraudulent.
"An unindicated [gift] and an indicated one, as well as one drawn in a single place and one specially drawn— of these, the latter is superior," so said Kātyāyana.
If one were to first assume that which does not exist, whose essential nature is unindicated,
and which is like space, then it would remain unindicated.
Whatever might then belong to it, that one should point out as indicated.
But if one were to designate all one's property and then deposit it, marked with one's name both before and after,
how could that not be a more powerful form of identification?
When a field or even a village is marked by boundary markers,
and the villages and so forth are recorded in writing, then one shall attain success.
But whatever has been pledged as security that is destroyed through an act of God or by the king,
the debtor shall be made to pay that debt to the creditors along with interest.
If, however, [the debtor] should fall or die through no fault of the creditor,
that debtor shall be made to pay another pledge, and the creditor shall be released from the debt.
If one should force a person to perform work against their will and without their consent,
he shall be made to pay the fruit of that labor, or else he receives no interest on his capital.
But he who, while another is performing work as a pledge, should oppress or threaten him with words, with a staff, or with physical acts, shall incur the first amercement.
If one should forcibly enter a pledge that has not been relinquished,
he shall incur the first fine for violence, and the depositor shall recover his pledge.
If a creditor enjoys a pledge by means of a fraudulent document from a debtor,
the king, having caused him to pay a fine, shall cause that fraudulent document to be destroyed.

But where the depositor is not present, the creditor shall report the pledge to the king; it is the settled rule that he may then sell it publicly. Having recovered the principal along with interest, he should hand over the remainder to the king.

[The Procedure for Sureties: In matters of gifts, attendance, and disputes, as well as for the sake of confidence and oaths, one should certainly cause a surety to be taken; in cases of the opposite, it should be done accordingly.
If a surety for appearance does not produce the defendant at the proper place and time,
he shall be liable for the debt therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
For the purpose of searching for what has been lost, however, a maximum of three fortnights should be granted;
if he can produce it there, the surety shall be released.
If, after the time has elapsed, the surety does not produce that person at all, he shall be made to pay that debt; this same rule is ordained even in the case of his death.
Wherever a son might remain after taking a pledge under a certain legal doctrine,
he should be made to pay that debt from his own wealth, even in the absence of his father.
Whatever man stands here as a guarantor for another's appearance,
failing to produce that person, he shall pay the debt from his own property.

But the first two [witnesses] shall be made to pay that wealth which was reported at the time [of the transaction] if it is found to be false; as for the latter two, they must pay in case of contradiction, and likewise their sons in their absence.
While the father is away on a journey, the son should pay all debts incurred under their common roof;
however, Bṛhaspati maintains that when the father has died, the son shall pay only his own paternal share, not the father's other debts.
When those who have entered under a single legal title (ekacchāyā) are seen there, he should be made to pay;
if the debtor has gone abroad, his son must pay the whole; but if the father is dead, the son [pays] the father’s share.
But he who, being pressured, gives a surety for another, shall,
after three fortnights have passed, be entitled to receive double that amount.
For whose sake, by whom, and for what purpose a gift was given according to the prescribed rule and at the request [of the recipient],
the guarantor shall receive that very thing when it has been proven by witnesses.
In the case of a breach of a solemn promise, one should cause double the amount to be paid;
however, for one who does not fulfill it, there is a loss of that very purpose for which the solemn promise was made.

One should know that a debt incurred by a father or others for the sake of the family, or taken out by one who is incapable or afflicted by illness, or on account of a calamity, is considered a debt contracted in times of distress.
Whatever was done for the marriage of a daughter and whatever was performed for funeral rites—
all this that was done by the family must be given to the master, O Lord.
According to the law, a debt incurred by a son need not be paid by the father;
however, that which has been promised must be paid, as must that which has been approved.
Bhṛgu says that even if he is away from home and has not given his consent, a debt contracted for the sake of the family by a slave,
a wife, a mother, a pupil, or a son must be paid.
A debt incurred in this manner must be paid by the husband together with the son, or by the individual himself; it is not otherwise payable by the wife for what was done by him.
If a woman is told by her husband who intends to die, "You must pay this debt," she shall be compelled to pay it even if she did not consent, provided that wealth was entrusted to her.
Even if he is afflicted by disease or residing abroad from his own country,
sons must pay a debt contracted by their father within twenty years.
In such cases as those of the diseased, the insane, the elderly, or those who have been away on long journeys,
one should cause even living sons to pay such a debt.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
however, this does not apply to those who are blind from birth, outcasts, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases.
Since fathers are liberated from the lowest debt through the giving of gifts by the sons who have been born to them, for that reason fathers desire sons.

When the father has passed away, the inheritance must never be given by one who has not yet attained legal capacity; rather, it should be given at the proper time according to the prescribed rule, for otherwise they shall dwell in hell.
If one is of an age not yet subject to legal capacity, even if independent, he is liable for debt here;
for independence is traditionally held to reside in the eldest, where seniority is determined by both qualities and age.
That which was seen [by the father], or that which remains after being given, is what should be paid as a paternal debt;
however, a debt that is defective, contested by the father, or not at all due, should never be paid.
Bhṛgu has declared that a debt which was incurred by the father, passed down in succession from the grandfather,
and remains unpaid and undisputed by the sons, must be paid by the grandsons.
But that which was ancestral and not given by the sons while they were living in a state of illness—
such ancestral property must likewise be given equally by the grandsons.
One should compel the son to pay the debt if he is free from misfortune, capable of wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not compel the son to pay.
Whatever must always be given by the fathers, in their absence it should be given from that wealth;
or else that wealth, along with the sons and grandsons, should then be given to the owner thereof.
But while the debt to the ancestors remains unpaid, a son shall not take the wealth;
that property must be given to the creditor, for he who takes it after [the father] has died is made liable for the debt.
In the absence of a son, however, the debt must be paid diligently by the grandson;
it need not be paid by the fourth descendant, for from that point it ceases.
A grandson must never pay a debt incurred through suretyship;
however, a father’s debt must always be paid by his son, even if he is still alive.
The debt must be paid by the inheritor of the estate; in his absence, by the wife;
in her absence, by the sons; and in their absence, by others entitled to inherit the property, in that order.
As long as a son does not obtain his paternal property that is available,
the debtor shall not be made to pay, even if he is very wealthy.
Whether it be a written document or one given orally,
that which has been promised to a woman who previously belonged to another, men should know to be the result of lust.
For when one has caused injury or destroyed property out of anger,
whatever is said that brings satisfaction, one should know that to be the result of anger.

Whether in good health or afflicted by illness, one should give what has been prepared for the sake of the Dharma; but if he dies without having given it, his son must be made to pay it—of this there is no doubt.
But whatever debt has been contracted by those who are penniless and childless, such as vintners and others,
the one who enjoys their wives must indeed pay that debt.
The supervisor of those who are wine-sellers, hunters, potters, cowherds, boatmen,
and women shall be made to pay their debts in place of them, provided he was authorized for their business affairs.

And a debt incurred by a wife shall in no way become the husband's obligation, except for what was contracted by men in times of distress; for such extensive expenditure is for the sake of the family.
Except for washermen, hunters, cowherds, and the wives of liquor-sellers;
for their livelihood is centered on those [crafts], and their families depend upon them.
A woman who has no son should resort to another only for the sake of amṛta;
that wealth must be taken away by the son alone, without the daughters.
One should take up the thread [of the lineage] for the sake of the debt, never for the sake of pleasure;
for one should not cause one's parents to give when there is no valid reason.
If a woman who has sons should abandon her own son even though he is capable, she shall forfeit her woman’s property; in that case, Manu says one should discharge the father’s debt from it.

And for a woman with young children who has resorted to another man for the sake of her livelihood, the one she has resorted to shall pay that debt; this is the rule recorded for women with young children.
To those who have been away on a long journey, to those without kin, to the dull-witted, the insane, the afflicted, and those wearing the marks of religious orders—
even while they are still alive— those who depend upon their wives' property must provide support.
If a son is seen to be overwhelmed by calamity or is a minor, then the one who took the property shall be made to pay; in his absence, the wife who took it shall pay.
First, the one who takes the wealth shall give; after him, the son;
in the absence of a son, the one who takes the wife; or, if there is no son at all, the one who is utterly destitute.
A debt contracted by a wife must be paid by her husband; likewise, a debt incurred by a mother must be paid by her son.
This also applies to a debt contracted for the sake of the husband, even if he has departed to another land after having made his intention known.
That which is done by a son shall be considered as given; likewise that which has been described, that which was done without being confirmed, and that which was not urged upon hearing it.
A debtor who is detained shall be held in public assembly before the people until he has paid what is due,
in accordance with the established customs of the region.
If a person carrying [the body] should feel the urge to void excrement or urine,
he should either follow behind [the deceased] or leave the body securely tied up.
Having provided a guarantor, he should be released day by day;
at the time of meals and at night, the guarantor remains bound.
He who cannot find a guarantor for his appearance, nor one upon whom he may rely,
should be confined in prison or kept under guard until he is brought back.
A noble man who is trustworthy and pure should not be confined in prison;
he should be released unbound, or at least released upon the taking of an oath.
A creditor should recover his debt from the debtor by means of pressure and restraint,
through manual labor or legal proceedings, and by conciliation at the outset, as is well known.
In this manner, he should indeed take wealth; through pretext and by means of conduct, he should cause the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—whether they be of equal or inferior status—to pay tribute.
One should cause a king, a master, or a Brahmin to pay by means of conciliation alone;
however, one should settle the matter with an heir or a friend even through artifice.
Bhṛgu declared that merchants, farmers, and artisans shall be made to pay according to the local custom; having oppressed the wicked, he should compel them to pay.
But where a creditor harasses a debtor who speaks rightly,
he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to it.
For if one were to cause an unwholesome deed to be performed that was not previously commanded,
one would first incur the penalty for violence, just as a debtor is released from his debt.
He who, having taken a loan or other such property, does not return it to the owner,
is born in that owner's house as a slave, a servant, a woman, or a beast.

A deposit (*upanidhi*) is that which is entrusted by three types of persons—those who have gone abroad, those who have been separated from their kin, or those who are bound—and includes what is handed over as a pledge, what is brought for carriage, and what is borrowed; furthermore, it is that which is delivered for the purpose of a merchant's trade; such is the object known as a deposit.
Whatever has been entrusted to one should be protected by that person with great effort;
any destruction of it other than through acts of God or the king is declared to be [the fault] of that person.
If anything whatsoever is destroyed or stolen through someone's fault,
that person shall be made to pay for the goods along with interest, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
If the object perishes immediately after being requested—even if caused by fate or the king—the borrower shall be made to repay the value alone; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever property belonging to another was consumed, neglected,
or destroyed through ignorance by someone, that person alone shall be made to pay for it.
If [the deposit] has been consumed, he should be made to pay it back with interest; if it was neglected, he should be made to pay the equivalent amount;
if it was lost through ignorance, he should be made to pay a small portion less.
Even when a deposit has been lost due to causes other than royal interference,
it is said that the loss falls upon the depositor along with the goods, provided it was destroyed while in the possession of the recipient.
But if the giver, having learned of the loss of the property, deposits it elsewhere,
then even if every means of recovery fails, the recipient shall by no means be made to pay.
For that which is lost due to the fault of the purchaser belongs to the purchaser;
when it is lost or stolen, the buyer must pay its value.
But a deposit should be reclaimed at the proper time; one should avoid reclaiming it when the time has passed.
One who returns it after the time has elapsed shall be punished with a fine and made to pay double the value.
These rules have been proclaimed to apply to all types of deposits.
If the deposit is being processed by the artisan over a fixed number of days, he may set it aside after that period; even if it is destroyed by fate, the artisan must still pay for it.
If destruction occurs due to a fault in the placement [of the image], he should not make the artisan pay for it;
however, if it is destroyed due to a fault in the craftsmanship, he should make him pay for the purpose of restoring what was entrusted to him.
If even a very small amount of work is lost by a hired servant,
it will suffice to ruin that master who wishes to give [wages] but does not take [the work].

If one has been asked for something with a specific purpose in mind, or for a fixed period of time, and that object is not returned when half of it has been used or the time has elapsed, then he must not be made to pay.
If a work has been performed when it was due, one should not pay even when requested;
but once that work has perished, the recipient shall recover the value.
If he does not give when being asked, he shall be compelled to pay it with interest.
But if there is a failure of the work, that loss shall belong to the master himself;
however, even if the time has not yet arrived, he must be made to pay for half the work completed.
He who, having taken something on loan, does not return it when asked for, should be seized by force and compelled to give it back; and he who does not give it shall be fined.
That which is given with the instruction, "You should deliver this to another in the course of your business," is called a *anvādhi* (sub-mortgage) here.
[On Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner:
He shall rescind a sale by one who is not the owner, a gift, and a pledge.
The plaintiff shall first provide the wealth from his own kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the purchaser shall provide it through his own relatives.
But the owner who has lost [the property] should have that wealth restored by his relatives;
having established that it was not given, abandoned, or sold, he recovers his own wealth.
One should either make a public purchase or present the original source;
however, the time for producing the original source must be granted according to the number of *yojanas* [between the locations].
One should perform the purchase openly with virtuous kinsmen and one's own people;
no other procedure is prescribed there, whether divine or human.
When a litigant, having first presented the original source, subsequently speaks of a purchase, he must produce that very source;
there is no need for the purchase.
But one who cannot be brought to admit the root cause [of his possession] must clear the purchase itself;
once the purchase has been cleared by the king, he should not be questioned about anything further.
If he does not produce the original document, or if he does not clear his purchase,
he shall be compelled to pay the debt to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine.
If one does not restore the wealth to his own kinsmen, he is a destroyer of inheritance; for the sake of putting an end to such attachment, he deserves punishment like that of a thief.
Where [the goods] were acquired from a market stall, or where they were purchased from royal officials, or where the seller’s identity was unknown, or where the seller has died; ||| K_621 |||
The owner, having paid half the value, shall take back his own property;
for in that case, according to legal procedure, half of what was stolen shall belong to both parties.
Purchasing without prior inspection is a fault, as is failing to protect [the goods] thereafter;
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes for the loss of wealth.
But whatever individuals have come together— whether they be physicians or merchants—
the fruit obtained therein by those who remain undivided shall be shared equally.
Established by agreement, they should perform the inspection of merchandise, provisions, expenditures, profits, loads, and the value of goods without deviation.
But for those who carry out the transaction by means of gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit is of a corresponding kind, according to whether their shares are equal, less, or more.
If a single man, who is approved by many, should give wealth or even cause a debt to be incurred, it shall be considered as having been done by all of them.
A debt secured by a pledge must be paid by kinsmen, relatives, and friends; for others, it must likewise be accompanied by a formal agreement, witnesses, or a written document.
Gold may be given at one's own will, as well as liquids and grain according to the prescribed rule;
it should be given in accordance with local custom, and likewise received.
But that which is given by those who have come together must likewise be requested;
yet whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain.
But whoever recovers property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of it must be given to him; this is the rule in all such cases.
Those skilled in training, those proficient in the superknowledges, and the preceptor— these artisans shall receive one,
two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order.
Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves at the king’s command,
they shall divide it according to the prescribed rule after setting aside one-tenth for the king.
But the leader among the thieves shall take four shares from that;
the brave one, three shares; the capable one, two; and each of the scouts, only one.
If, among those who have gone forth, someone should incur a seizure [of property], they shall bear,
according to their respective shares, whatever has been given for the purpose of his liberation.
This very rule has been proclaimed by the virtuous for dancers:
for one who knows the rhythm (tāla) receives half, while the singers share equally;
those who are the leaders deserve two shares—this is the law for those performing in concert.
This is the decision for all: for merchants and farmers, as well as for thieves and artisans who act without being restrained by their allotted shares.
In matters concerning the non-payment of what has been given, or the refusal to give what has been promised, as well as sales and gifts, those who are unwilling should not be coerced;
however, one may personally apply one’s own wife, sons, and all property to the cause.
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the property] must be done;
otherwise one should not proceed—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Except for one's entire estate and home, whatever wealth remains after what is necessary for the maintenance of the family is one's own to give; otherwise, it would be improper to give.
Therefore, while a father has authority over his children and wife regarding their instruction, sale, and giving, he does not have such authority over his son.
He who, having voluntarily promised a gift to a Brahmin,
does not give it, shall be made to pay it like a debt and shall incur the first amercement.
By failing to give what was promised and by misappropriating what has been given,
a mortal is born for a hundred million eons in the animal realm.
Where a gift is designated for the purpose of obtaining something not yet known,
and which is acquired through the act of acquisition, that is proclaimed as "wages" (bhṛti).
Because it provides protection from fear, guards against harm, and likewise accomplishes one's purpose,
one should understand that what has been obtained through this method is [the result] of a reciprocal service.
"Even if it were said, 'I shall give my entire possessions to whoever rescues me from this life-threatening danger,' it would not necessarily come to pass."

That which is given by those who are not masters of themselves due to lust or anger, by the distressed, by the impotent, by the insane, or by the deluded, as well as that which is given through error or in jest, may be taken back.
However, a bribe that may have been promised for the sake of accomplishing a task must,
under no circumstances, be given even if that purpose has already been achieved.
If, however, she had already been given away previously, he should be compelled to return her by force; so say the followers of Gārgya and Mānava, that the fine shall be eleven times [the value].
Because he denounced the thief, the violent, the immoral, and the adulterer; because he saw one who had lost his conduct and likewise established him in truth.
Whatever has been obtained by these [mediators] is called a "bribe";
in that case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall be liable for the offense.
But if one who has been appointed to official duties should receive a bribe,
he shall be made to pay that entire sum as well as a fine eleven times its value.
But if one who has not been appointed should receive a bribe for the sake of a legal matter,
there is no fault in him if it is for the purpose of providing a reciprocal service.
Whether given by one who is healthy or ill, provided it was promised for the sake of dharma—if he dies without having delivered it, his son must be made to pay; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever has been mortgaged or sold through trickery, whatever gift or acceptance [of a gift] is performed through trickery,
or whatever one perceives to be a deceptive artifice— let him annul all of that.
But when the wages have not been settled, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall receive a tenth part of the profit,
the cattle, and the crops, respectively.
But he who, having undertaken the commencement of work, does not have it completed,
must be made to perform it by force; if he does not do so, he deserves punishment.
If the driver causes an obstruction, he shall be made to pay double the wage for the journey.
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or destroyed by fire, or swept away by water.

He who abandons a companion on the road— whether he be exhausted or afflicted by disease— shall first incur a fine for violence, and if he fails to provide care in a village, he shall pay for three days.
But if that merchandise should be lost or stolen on the road,
he shall receive wages proportionate to the distance already traveled by him.
He who, having taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and so forth on lease,
does not return them once his business is accomplished, must be made to pay the rental fee together with interest.
He who, having taken houses, shops, and so forth on lease,
does not return them to the owner, shall be made to pay [the value] together with the rent for as long as he has withheld them.
[The Dispute between Owner and Herdsman]:
Bṛhaspati states that for animals entering fields, gardens, pasture lands, houses, or pens, there shall be their seizure or beating.
In cases where a master disputes the beating of animals— whether they be of low, high, or middle quality—
he shall determine the punishment accordingly.
One should erect a great enclosure even while the crops have not yet grown;
for here, deer that have tasted their sweet flavor are driven away with difficulty.
One should cause a quarter-pana to be paid for a cow, two quarters for a buffalo,
and likewise, a quarter is proclaimed as the fine for goats, sheep, and calves.
[The non-fulfillment of the agreement or the transgression of the compact:
But whatever is the law of the community, by that law they should always perform all their duties, remaining established in their own respective duties.
The royal edict has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, by the king’s command, one must first practice that very [Dharma].
That man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king is blameworthy,
wicked, and deserves punishment for violating the royal decree.
He who destroys what is consistent with reason, he who provides no opportunity for the speaker,
and he who speaks what is unreasonable— such a person shall be made to pay the first amercement.
The impetuous, the sower of dissension, and the destroyer of the community's property—all these must be executed; thus Bhṛgu declared to the king that they should be proclaimed as such.
And whoever should eat from the same vessel or in the same row as another,
if he does not report that person's fault, he shall be punished accordingly.
Whatever debt may have been incurred or consumed on behalf of the community,
or whatever has been diverted for one's own personal use, that must be repaid by those very individuals.
Those who have entered into the status of mediators among guilds, trade associations,
or groups shall all receive equal shares of the previous wealth and debts.

In the same way, regarding the distribution of food and drink, and in the performance of acts of giving and merit, one who remains in the group shall share in the portion; however, one who has departed does not share in the portion.
Whatever has been acquired or protected by them, or whatever debt has been incurred for the sake of the community,
as well as whatever has been obtained through royal favor— all that belongs equally to everyone.
[The definition of the designations beginning with *naigama*: A multitude of various citizens is proclaimed to be a *naigama*;
groups of people who bear various weapons assembled together are proclaimed to be *vrātas*.
A corporation of merchants and the like is proclaimed to be a *pūga*;
whereas those who have entered the life of renunciation are proclaimed to be *pāṣaṇḍas*.
A collection of Brāhmaṇas is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*;
those who subsist by means of a craft are proclaimed to be artisans (*śilpinaḥ*).
But for the Ārhatas and the followers of Sugata, a collection is called a *saṅgha*;
a collection of Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others is called a *gulma*.

Bṛhaspati says that *gaṇas*, heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), corporations (*pūgas*), guilds (*vrātas*), as well as trade associations (*śreṇis*), and whatever other groups exist that are designated as "classes" (*vargas*), are [to be understood in this context]. // K_682 //
[Regarding disputes over buying and selling, whether after purchasing or after selling:
If one who has purchased something does not accept it once obtained, or if one who has sold it does not deliver it while it remains undamaged,
that person shall receive their own property by paying a tenth part of the price.
If the time for performing the purposeful act has not yet arrived, one should certainly not cause it to be performed;
such is the rule within ten days, but beyond that, there is no further obligation.
In the case of land, impurity lasts ten days for the seller and likewise for the buyer;
for the sapinda relatives, it lasts twelve days, and after that, it is even less.
If a person, having purchased a commodity such as a milch cow or the like,
should later regret the purchase and abandon it while it is still unblemished and within the [stipulated] time, he shall pay one-tenth of the price.
If a buyer, having purchased [an object], feels regret as it reaches his hand,
the wise man should abandon the purchase by paying one-sixth of the price.
But that which was purchased without being recognized, and later discovered to be defective, must be returned to its owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, provides one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its value and undergo disciplinary action to that same extent.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss falls upon the seller alone, who sold it but does not deliver it.
If a buyer does not accept goods being offered for sale,
or if a seller sells what has already been sold elsewhere, neither of them shall be held at fault.
If [an item] has been sold by one who is intoxicated to another who is intoxicated, for a low price or out of fear,
or by one who is not his own master or is deluded, it must be relinquished and returned to him.
One should examine milked products for three days;
however, goods for transport should be examined for five days, while pearls, diamonds, and corals should be scrutinized for seven days.
For bipeds, however, it is half a month for males, but double that for females;
for all seeds, it is ten days, and for metals and clothes, one day.
If, however, a defect in the commodity should arise before that time,
it must be returned to the seller, and the buyer shall recover the purchase price.
But a garment that has been worn, which is soiled, stained,
and even defective, once purchased, would not be returned by the seller.
But that which has been purchased as common property, the lowest of men should not give away alone;
he should neither give it, nor take it, nor indeed sell it.
If, after purchasing goods for a price, the buyer considers them a bad purchase,
they must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided they have not been examined.
If the buyer delivers [the animal] on the second day, he shall pay a third part of the price as a fine;
on the third day, double that amount; after that, the loss falls upon the buyer alone.
Having divided the value of the goods into five parts, one-third is called the price;
the fourth part shall be the profit, and the fifth is called the truth.
A joint, a reversal, or an irregularity arising from the three enjoyments,
as well as a sale by command or even a purchase, shall be rescinded within ten years.

It is the settled conclusion that even the practice of buying and selling land is not permitted if one has not first obtained the consent of kinsmen and others who reside nearby or are otherwise censured.
In one's own village, it shall be ten nights; in another village, three fortnights;
in other kingdoms, six months; but when there is a difference in language, it shall be a year.
But when the taxpayer has fled,
the members of the assembly shall sell the taxable land for the sake of the tax, together with the guarantor for the tax.
But by neighboring lords who are assembled together, who are knowledgeable, and who fear wrongdoing,
[the boundaries] of fields, groves, houses, and so forth, as well as of bipeds and quadrupeds, [should be determined].
They say that the price is determined by dividing the object into eight parts;
a price exceeding one part or less than one part is considered improper.
Even after a hundred years have passed, all of that is withdrawn;
for in buying and selling, whatever price a commodity rightfully deserves must be paid.
If, when the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, or even the eighth part has elapsed, the purchase or sale has been concluded in a deficient manner; // K_708 //

But all that which is of low value, even if performed, shall be as if unperformed; when the purchase is deficient by even a small amount less than what was stated, one does not incur any fault at all.
If, by that same portion, there is a loss in value during purchase or sale,
other people who know the Dharma say that such a transaction is as good as unmade.
A purchase is valid when the price is half or more; the aforementioned profit is tenfold (or twofold);
a lease is by one-third (or by enjoyment); and an immediate sale is by mutual consent.
Even if only a small amount is given in addition to the price, the purchase shall be considered completed;
it must be paid with interest at the rate of one per cent per day, except as otherwise agreed upon by contract.

[Non-fulfillment of the agreement: But he who, having accepted [the pupil], does not cause him to learn the craft but instead makes him perform other tasks, shall incur the first amercement; from that, the pupil may withdraw.
Even if he has been trained, a pupil may practice according to his own desire;
whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone.
Bhṛgu maintains that by giving away one's own independent self, one enters a state of servitude similar to that of a wife;
thus, servitude for a Brahmin should be understood as permissible among the three [lower] castes, but never for a Brahmin himself.
For the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have abandoned their independence, servitude is permitted according to the direct order of the castes, but never in the inverse order.
Even if he is of the same caste, one must never compel a Brahmin to servitude;
for by the servitude of a Brahmin, O King, the royal splendor is destroyed.
But Bṛhaspati has declared that one should never cause a Brāhmaṇa to perform the duties of a slave, even if he belongs to the same caste as a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra.
Even toward one endowed with the study of the precepts, a superior twice-born man should not intentionally perform even a minor act that is unwholesome.
The cleansing of feces and urine, as well as the removal of dirt while naked,
and the tending of cattle and similar tasks— these are generally performed by the sons of slave-girls.
In that place where the three castes, beginning with the twice-born, have attained mastery over the life of renunciation,
the king may impose exile upon a Brahmin, but he shall reduce a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya to the status of a slave.
But a Śūdra one may employ as a slave, whether purchased or even unpurchased; for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for the purpose of servitude.
But if one should have sexual intercourse with his own female slave and she should subsequently give birth,
then, having considered the seed, she and her offspring shall not be a slave.
Whatever wealth a slave may possess, it is traditionally held that the master is its lord;
however, as for property acquired through open sale, the master does not have a right to that wealth.
A wife brought as a slave by her husband shall also attain the status of a slave,
because he is her master, and since a master is dependent upon his owner.
If anyone should take a Brāhmaṇī woman as a wife, or likewise purchase her, that act is not performed by the king; all such persons shall be punished.

But he who, out of lust, makes a woman of good family who has sought refuge his slave, or transfers her to another, shall be punished; and that [marriage] shall be considered as never having been performed.
He who enjoys a nurse for a child or a non-slave woman as if she were a slave,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a devoted female slave who is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
And he who, being without autonomy, offers himself up saying "I am yours," shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall regain him.
A slave who has reached the state of renunciation must not be released by anyone;
however, one who has been maintained [as a slave] for an improper period is freed from slavery by giving a pair of oxen.
[Disputes over boundaries: Excess and deficiency regarding the portion, existence and non-existence,
enjoyment through possession, and the boundary— these six are the causes for disputes over land.
In that case, the enjoyment [of the property] should be applied; it rests upon all witnesses—both that which is not recorded in writing and the other witness who follows the two paths.
In disputes between two parties concerning fields, buildings, ponds, wells, groves, or embankments, as well as in all other matters, the neighbors are the authoritative witnesses.
In cases concerning neighboring lands, one should determine the boundaries of fields and so forth by means of non-neighbors;
likewise, this applies to village boundaries, as well as to cities and districts.
A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village; a field is proclaimed to be the neighbor of a field;
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, for they embrace one another on all sides.

In their absence, the neighboring king, the hereditary ruler, the elder, and the one who has rescued [the property]—these shall take [charge] even in the case of the six types of immovable property; there should be no hesitation in this matter.
When the neighboring kings are engaged in battle, and those further beyond them are likewise engaged,
and those engaged with the engaged are themselves engaged, it is proclaimed as the "lotus" (padmākāra) array.
When one's own objectives have failed due to corrupt vassals because of their greed for wealth, a rescue must be carried out by those associated with them;
of this there is no doubt.
But regarding those who are attached to the faults of the addicted, they are declared to be "addicted to that";
however, a king who understands the Dharma should not treat them as corrupt.
For neighbors are not released from liability regarding a legal decision simply by claiming ignorance; if they speak out of ignorance, the king should fine them and then re-examine the boundary.
But if a dispute should arise after the boundary has been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest amercement.
Having abandoned wicked vassal lords and having associated with others who are hereditary and so forth, he should have the boundary established; thus do those who know the Dharma understand.
Those who were formerly the border-dwellers there, but later went to other lands—
they are proclaimed by the seers as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that [place].
Those endowed with human virtues who have witnessed the work being accomplished—
whether they be old or not old— are proclaimed to be the truly aged.
Because they rescue [beings] from that [suffering], being characterized by listening, enjoyment, and the proclamation of what is to be done,
they are therefore known as "Uddhṛtas" (the Rescuers).

The neighboring kings are considered to possess one unit of power; those endowed with virtues are twice as strong when they speak what is undesirable; others beyond them are held to be three times as strong.
Just as one person, clad in red garments and composed in mind, might lead both parties to a boundary somewhere, placing the earth upon his head, so too [should the king act].
By the king who was free from fear, this was personally composed in the absence of all [other teachers].
Of fields, wells, and tanks, as well as of rice-fields and pleasure-gardens,
and of houses, palaces, dwellings, royal residences, and temples of the gods.
But if, among many who have been summoned as witnesses, they all fail to reach a conclusion due to fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
In the case of crossing a boundary, entering a treasury, or likewise touching a foot [with impurity],
a period of three fortnights, one fortnight, or seven days is prescribed according to whether the offense was committed through divine power or royal command.

One should not obstruct the girdles, the decorative medallions, or the windows; nor should one block the drainage channel or the site of the house, for by causing such damage, one becomes liable to pay a fine.
After the time of settling [the house], these [rules] should never be applied;
one should not cast a glance or create a drainage channel toward another's house.
One should construct a wall for excrement, urine, and water, as well as a place for the fire and a pit,
leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the neighboring wall.
That path upon which all people always travel is called a crossroads;
that royal highway which remains unobstructed according to the season is called a main road.
One should not plant anything there, nor should one destroy anything by any means;
however, for failing to give way to one's preceptor, teacher, king, and others, one shall be subject to punishment.
Whoever there should void excrement out of desire in a place for refuse or in a pit, or even plant trees [in such a spot], his fine shall be one māṣaka.
He who destroys tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing places with impure matter shall be made to clean away that impurity and then be fined the first amercement.
One who defiles established holy sites and shrines founded by great souls— sites that are meritorious and purifying— shall incur the same punishment as a previous perpetrator of violence.
But for trees grown within the boundary of two fields,
one should declare that their fruit and flowers belong in common to the owners of those fields.
But for those born in another field, where their branches take refuge in yet another,
one should know him to be the owner in whose fields they are supported.
But he who performs repairs on a house, a garden, or a pond without the consent of the owner does not obtain ownership of those improvements.
If an expenditure has been incurred when the master has arrived, but it was not reported to the king,
then if it is subsequently reported, the one who employed the expense shall recover that expenditure.
If he does not pay due to incapacity,
the cultivator shall receive the fruit of the crop diminished by one-eighth of the expenses incurred for the purpose of clearing the land;
he shall be the enjoyer for eight years, after which it belongs to the owner.
If someone should cultivate a field when its owners are incapacitated, deceased, or lost, he shall enjoy the fruit thereof without being hindered.
If a field is being ploughed and the owner returns,
he shall obtain that field by paying for all the labor performed on it.
By reducing that [period] by one-eighth each year until seven years have passed,
at the completion of the eighth year, he shall obtain the field already enjoyed.
[Harsh speech: Uttering "huṃ," coughing, and whatever is censured in the world—
if one imitates or repeats such things, that is called harsh speech.
Because of its harshness, vulgarity, and intensity, that [abusive speech] is also recorded as being threefold:
insult is to be known as harsh, vulgarity is designated as the mention of private parts, and the wise say that intensity consists of reproaches involving grounds for expulsion.
When one, by means of parts characterized as unreal— whether they be non-existent or even existent— insults another,
that is known by the wise as harsh speech.
When one, out of anger, uses speech to bring about the humiliation of another's conduct,
country, family, and so forth, that is considered by the wise to be vulgar speech.
That speech which binds one with the fetters of the great sins (mahāpātaka), which produces passion and hatred, or which causes the loss of caste, is known as "intense" (tīvra).

Those who, out of anger, proclaim the faults of others— whether they themselves lack virtues or falsely claim to recognize virtue, or are preoccupied with false notions— they know such a person to be defiled in speech.
One who proclaims the faults of one who is actually faultless for the sake of creating offense,
and who speaks with pretexts, is known as a man of corrupt speech.
Whatever has been spoken by me out of delusion, negligence, rivalry, or even out of affection—I shall not speak thus again; for that offense, one should impose half a staff-punishment.
Where there might be a need for a defense, the declaration of one's fallen status by that person should not be considered a fault, provided that he can substantiate it through his own testimony.
Otherwise, the fault would be equal; however, in the case of speaking falsely, it is recorded as the highest. Through great resolve, one may bring a man of corrupt speech to success.
The king should investigate with diligence what has been reported as untrue;
for those whose habit is to speak falsehoods, the cutting off of the tongue is the purification.
[Regarding physical assault:
If one cannot perceive the grounds for physical assault through witnesses and other means,
one should employ evidence provided by witnesses in that case, or else administer an ordeal.
That man who strikes with a terrifying punishment,
whether he himself was previously unharmed or not, is declared to be one who deserves punishment.
According to Bhṛgu, for the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for their piercing, the middle fine.
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the sake of causing pain,
one should inflict a punishment in exact proportion to the suffering that has been caused.
For those who are untouchable, rogues, slaves, barbarians, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions, physical punishment is not a means of discipline for their reform.
That [wind], having been brought forth by vomit, urine, feces, and so forth, is said to possess four qualities at the feet,
six qualities in the middle of the body, and eight qualities in the head.
For raising a hand [in threat], a fine of twelve [paṇas] shall be imposed;
for striking those of one's own caste, that same fine is declared to be double.
Just as [the fines] were stated for verbal abuse according to the inverse and direct order [of castes],
in the same way, the fines for physical assault are to be imposed in their respective order.
But when the body or the sense organs are destroyed,
the wise should provide a means of livelihood and a reward that brings satisfaction; furthermore,
he should pay for the expenses of recovery until the wound has healed.

Those against whom verbal punishment or physical striking has been prescribed for their offenses shall be made to restore what was stolen or broken; however, those who possess no wealth shall be purified [of their debt] through labor.
If a man yokes animals such as donkeys, oxen, buffaloes, or camels when they are exhausted, afflicted by thirst, or hungry at an improper time, he shall incur the first amercement.
For the killing of deer and birds, the fine is two paṇas or twelve paṇas;
for the killing of men by means of snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, or pigs, the same applies.
One who previously drove away a cow, a young girl, a deity, a domestic animal, a castrated bull, or likewise a breeding bull,
shall first incur a fine of one thousand [paṇas] and then suffer the ultimate punishment of death.
In the case of killing living beings,
Manu declared that one should give an equivalent [animal] in return, or its corresponding value in money.
To whatever extent there is use of all forest trees, to that same extent self-restraint must be practiced; this is the established rule regarding injury.
If a teacher should strike a disciple out of anger without using a cane,
such that excessive pain is caused, there would be a dispute between the disciple and his father.
[Regarding *sāhasa*:
An action that is performed impulsively is declared to be *sāhasa*.
Theft (steya) is said to be that which involves concealment, as well as taking by force, and likewise any act of violence accompanied by denial.
But when a legal matter proceeds on the basis of what is termed "rash action" (sāhasa) without supporting evidence, it must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies to all types of disputes.
If many enraged men should together kill a single person,
he among them who strikes a vital organ is considered the slayer.
One who commits such an act through malice shall incur various forms of execution;
however, one should indeed strike down an approaching cause of destruction without hesitation.
There is no fault for one who slays evildoers who have raised their weapons;
however, when they have desisted from their undertaking, taking them captive is not considered killing.

Even against an assassin who is superior by virtue of asceticism, Vedic study, or birth, there should be no execution; however, Bhṛgu says that execution is permissible for one who is inferior in merit.
One who brandishes a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who holds a raised bow;
one who slays by means of the Atharvaveda; and one who is treacherous toward the king.
One who violates his wife and one who is intent on seeking out his vulnerabilities— one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin* (assassins).
They say that those who steal one's reputation and conduct are evil, as are those who seize one's dharma and wealth.
But one who commits an offense against someone who has never previously accused him, or who robs him of his life or property— one should know such a person to be an *ātatāyin* (an assailant).
In the case of killing those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins,
as well as elephants, horses, and other such beings, the killer incurs no fault.
One who causes an abortion is a thief; likewise, one who kills a Brāhmaṇa woman with a weapon—even if she is innocent—deserves to be put to death, for even a Brāhmaṇa may be slain.
A man who causes injury, breakage, or crushing of goods shall incur the first amercement; he is declared to be the owner who possesses the goods.
If one should steal, break, or burn an image of the gods,
or likewise destroy its temple, he shall incur the first amercement.
Whoever should breach a wall, cause it to fall, or destroy it,
or block the course of water, shall incur the first amercement.
Whether it be in secret or in public, by night or by day,
the taking of another's property is proclaimed to be theft.
One should carefully examine a stolen object that has fallen from another's hand, been picked up on the ground unintentionally, or been dropped by a thief.
One who acts by means of false weights, measures, or counter-measures, whether they are clearly marked or unmarked,
shall incur the first amercement.
If something is stolen from a house, however, the king shall cause the thieves to be seized; he shall also punish the guards and the guardians of the quarters if the thief cannot be found.
Property stolen within a village shall be made good by the village headman;
in a pasture, it must be paid by the owner; and in a forest, by the forest-guardian.
Whatever has been held by anyone in his own country must be given back by the king;
the king himself should take what was lost and found, after having searched for it.
If property has been stolen by thieves, he should diligently restore its original form; in the absence of that, however, there should be its value. Otherwise, the king becomes a sinner.
