Even if the thief has been caught, if the stolen property is not recovered from him,
one should either hand over that thief oneself or cause him to be handed over as desired.
If, however, there should be doubt regarding the guilt of those being made to pay,
the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to swear an oath, or he may clear himself through his kinsmen.
Since the owner has recovered only a small portion of the property taken away,
he shall receive that remainder once the owner has made his claim.
Those who would strike at their own country, as well as those who obstruct the royal highway— the king, having confiscated all their property, shall impale them upon a stake.
Property recovered by those intent on searching for thieves shall be made over to them;
in that case, he should cause double the amount to be paid as a reward.
With whichever limb a thief commits an injury against another,
the king should cut off that very limb, so that he does not do it again.
Taking two each of cucumber and gourd, five mangoes, five pomegranates, and a handful of dates, jujubes, and so forth, one does not incur fault.
The Mānavas declared immediately that the banishment of those caught in adultery was detested by the Gautamas, as it was censurable because it resulted in the destruction of living beings.
Whether he was caught in the act or not, once his violent crime has been established according to the facts,
the king should seize him, cut off [his offending limb], announce the punishment, and deprive him of all his property.
But those who are bound with iron chains, though they may have little devotion, if they are endowed with strength, will perform the king's tasks until death; so says Kauśika.
When property has been seized from a foreign land by a foreigner,
having taken that property back from him, one should release him without punishment.
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who provide fire and water,
those who purchase their goods, those who receive them,
and those who conceal them— all these are declared by the law to be subject to the same punishment.
One who is ignorant should not be a sacrificer, nor should one who is unstable be a teacher;
having punished both of them with the penalty for a thief, he should establish them on the right path.
[On Sexual Intercourse with a Woman: If there is the employment of a messenger, staying at an improper time or place, seizing by the throat or hair, or grasping the ears, nose, hands, and so forth;
Sharing a single place, a single seat, and a single meal—this is known as the ninefold gathering.
When a man, having indulged in the enjoyment of women,
proceeds to kill them by force, that indeed constitutes a transgression of his duty.
But she who, afflicted by passion, acts according to her own will and desires [another] of her own accord,
shall be released at the king's command after being publicly proclaimed in the presence of the people.
The initiator, the accomplice, likewise the one who points out the path, the refuge, the provider of weapons, and the giver of food to those who perform evil deeds.
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction,
one who is intent on the duty of indifference, and one who approves of the speaker of faults.
If there should be those who are unable to prevent [an offense], all of them shall perform the task;
however, one should impose a punishment upon them according to their respective capacities.
And a woman,
never separated from her husband, being humble, desiring good fortune and non-widowhood, and devoted to her husband, must serve the sacred fire.
By serving with her intellect alone, a woman enjoys all desires;
having returned here from heaven once more, she becomes a treasure-house of happiness.
The virtuous woman who, upon the death of her husband, remains established in celibacy and conducts herself like Arundhatī, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[The Division of Inheritance] When the ancestors and the brothers take the entire collection of property in equal shares, that is called the righteous division.
The paternal inheritance shall be common to both the father and the son;
however, regarding property acquired by the father himself, the son does not possess ownership.
That which was inherited from the grandfather, that which was inherited from the father, and whatever else was acquired by oneself—
all this is divided when there is a partition among the heirs.
Whatever is visible may be divided—houses, fields, and quadrupeds;
in cases of suspicion regarding hidden property, this is declared to be the means of proof therein.
Household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and servants are divided while being visible; regarding hidden property, Bhṛgu declared it belongs to the treasury.
When the estate is divided between two sons, the father should not treat one son differently;
he must not exclude one from his share without cause or reason.
The division of property is ordained for those who have attained legal capacity;
and for men, such capacity arises at the sixteenth year.

And they should deposit the wealth of those who have not yet attained legal majority, as well as that of those who are away on a journey, with their kinsmen and friends, provided it is free from expenditure.
But whatever share belongs to one who has gone abroad, all [the heirs] together shall protect it;
when a son dies while still a child, his inheritance must be protected by his maternal and paternal kinsmen.
But after they have reached the stage of paugaṇḍa, they shall divide that [property] according to their respective shares.
A debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a mother for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition.
That debt must be paid to the creditor; one should not cause it to be paid otherwise, provided that it has been proven by evidence and is not contested thereafter.

Any debt that may have been contracted for the sake of religious duty (dharma), for the sake of wealth (artha), or given out of affection, or any obligation incurred through employment—that should be divided while it is still visible; however, no portion of the paternal estate shall be taken away for the purpose of such a gift.
A debt inherited from one's father, cleared by means of paternal wealth, as well as a personal debt contracted by oneself—
such debts must be settled during a partition together with the kinsmen.
Having paid off debts and bestowed gifts of affection, one should divide the remainder.
Before the father acquires sons or wealth, he shall take two shares or half;
likewise, once the father has died, the mother shall also receive a share equal to that of a son.
In whatever manner the wealth obtained through partition may be made to serve the purpose of sacrifice,
in that same manner the learned should ordain the respect due to the shares.
Even in the division of inheritance in the world, no one should exercise authority;
rather, only the enjoyment [of the property] should be permitted, neither its giving away nor its sale.
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for in all matters of giving, mortgaging, or selling, a single heir has no authority.
If a younger brother dies before the property has been divided, one should provide for his son with that share which he would have received from his grandfather.
He shall receive that paternal share from his uncle or from the uncle's son;
for that same share rightfully belongs to all brothers.
Or his son may also receive it, but beyond that there should be cessation [of the claim].
When a legitimate son has been born, sons who are of the same caste as the father shall receive a fourth part [of the estate];
those of a different caste, however, are entitled only to food and clothing.
For unmarried daughters, however, a fourth part is prescribed;
for sons, there are three parts. But equality is ordained when the wealth is small.
Even if one should produce a fruit with the consent of the field-owner, both of them are sharers in that fruit here; for indeed, no fruit arises without the one [the field].
If a woman abandons a eunuch or an outcast and takes another husband,
the son born of her is clearly the offspring of the one who begat him.
He whose urine is not frothy and whose excrement sinks in water,
and whose penis is devoid of madness and semen— he is called a *klība*.
One who is born of a woman married out of order, one born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra),
and one who has abandoned the life of renunciation— none of these are entitled to the inheritance.
But the son of a wife married in the regular order is the heir when he is of the same caste as his father;
so too is the son born of a wife of a different caste who was married in the reverse order.
The son born of a woman through an inverse marriage (pratiloma) does not inherit property;
it is held that his kinsmen should provide him with food and clothing for as long as he lives.
But in the absence even of kinsmen, he shall obtain that paternal property;
however, kinsmen must not be compelled to pay wealth that is not ancestral.
[Inalienable assets:
That which was taken away by one's own power, that which was lost, and whatever may have been acquired by oneself—
all this is not to be given by the father to his sons at the time of partition.
Whatever wealth has been acquired through the use of knowledge obtained from one who is devoted to another— that is said to be "wealth acquired through knowledge."
But that which is obtained through learning after it has been offered as a wager—know that to be "wealth acquired by learning" (vidyādhana); it is not to be divided in a partition of inheritance.
That which is obtained from a pupil, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubts raised by others, from debating, and from recitation—
this they call the "wealth of knowledge," and it is not to be divided during a partition.
For this same rule applies even to craftsmen, as well as to whatever may be in excess of the agreed price.
Whatever is obtained through learning after having repelled an opponent in a gambling match,
Bṛhaspati declares that to be "wealth acquired through learning" (vidyādhana) and it is not to be divided.

That which is obtained through the promise of knowledge, that which is received from a disciple, and that which is acquired according to the rule of the officiating priest— Bhṛgu declares this to be the wealth of learning.

That which is acquired through the power of learning—whether from a patron for officiating at a sacrifice or from a disciple as a teacher—is called the wealth of learning; anything other than this is common property.
Bṛhaspati says that wealth acquired through valor by brothers who have been trained in the sciences within the family, or even by their father, must be divided.

A physician should never give away wealth acquired through medical knowledge to those who are ignorant of it; however, that wealth should be given by the physician to those whose knowledge is equal to or superior to his own.
When one has boldly undertaken a risky venture and performs the task with vigor,
if the master is pleased and bestows his favor upon that very deed,
whatever wealth is thereby obtained through such valor shall belong to him.
That which is acquired through valor, that which is obtained through learning, and that which is traditionally declared to be a woman's property—
all this must not be divided by the heirs during a partition.
That which is brought back under a banner is not considered to be divisible; rather,
that which is brought from battle after putting to flight the enemy force,
having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, is called "brought under a banner."
Whatever wealth was obtained at the time of giving along with one's own daughter is known as "wealth pertaining to a daughter" (kanyāgata); it is considered pure and productive of growth.
One should know that wealth which has come together with one's wife is matrimonial; all such property is to be understood as conducive to the fulfillment of Dharma.
Whatever is given at the time of marriage, intended for the bridegroom on behalf of the maiden,
all that wealth belongs to her and is not to be divided by her kinsmen.
But wealth recorded in a document, as well as that designated for the sake of Dharma and Artha, water-rights, a slave, and any hereditary property; // K_882 //
The garments and ornaments that have been brought should be arranged by the kinsmen so that they are appropriate to the occasion; they must not be unsuitable.
Bṛhaspati says that pasture land for cattle, protection, and clothing already fitted to the body should not be divided, as they are intended for the sake of dharma.
Whatever law has been proclaimed for a country, a caste, a guild, or a village by Bhṛgu, one should determine the distribution of inheritance according to that very law.
[The Division of Concealed Property: If property that was concealed is later discovered, it shall be divided equally with the brothers; for in the absence of the father, the sons [are the heirs].
Bhṛgu has declared that property which was withheld from one another, or which was improperly divided, shall be redistributed with equal shares once it is later recovered.

Whatever wealth is obtained by one who has already divided [the inheritance] shall belong to him alone; likewise, what was seized, lost, or subsequently recovered, as well as what was previously mentioned, shall be shared again.
One should not cause property seized by a relative to be returned by force;
nor should one cause the enjoyment of property belonging to undivided relatives to be surrendered.
Having abandoned a common field and resorted to another country,
a share must undoubtedly be given to a descendant of that lineage who has returned.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh [birth],
if one's births are not fully known, one shall receive the share that has come down in succession.

The land acquired by those born of the lineage who have arrived through succession, and whom the primary and neighboring lords recognize as their master, must be granted by those born of the same clan.
If those who have been divided from the paternal estate live together again, they should divide it once more; he shall receive two shares, because he was the one from whom [the others] prospered.
Those brothers who, having distinct marks and so forth, live for ten years with separate religious duties and separate activities,
should be known as divided from the paternal wealth.
[The definition and types of women’s property: That which is received before the fire, that which is received at the wedding procession, that which is given out of affection by her [relatives],
and that which is obtained from her brothers, mother, and father— this sixfold kind is declared to be a woman’s property.
That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagni* (given near the fire), a form of woman's property (*strīdhana*).
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives as she is being led away from her father's house,
as well as the *adhyāvahanika*, is declared to be her *strīdhana* (woman’s property).
Whatever is given out of affection by either the mother-in-law or the father-in-law,
as well as that which is given upon the salutation of their feet— that is called "gifts of affection" (prītidatta).
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, draft animals, those to be milked, ornaments, or laborers— that is proclaimed as the toll (śulka).
That which is obtained by a woman from her husband’s family after marriage is called *anvādheya*; likewise, that which is obtained from her own paternal kin is also so designated.

Whatever has been obtained after marriage from her father-in-law, from her parents, from her husband, or out of affection from her kinsmen— that, Bhṛgu says, is the woman's *anvādheya* (subsequent property).
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried girl, what is obtained from the husband’s father’s house, or from a brother, or from her parents, is known as *saudāyika* (a woman’s separate property).

[Consideration of Ownership and Other Matters Regarding Women’s Property: The father, mother, husband, brother, or kinsmen must give property to a woman according to their ability, up to a maximum of two thousand [paṇas], with the exception of immovable property.
However, that which is given with a specific condition, or by reason of a [religious] practice, by a father, a brother, or a husband— that is not considered to be a woman’s property.

Whatever wealth has been acquired through crafts, or whatever else obtained through affection from others, the husband's ownership extends over that; the remainder, however, is declared to be the woman’s property.
Upon receiving her dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by their [relatives] as a means of subsistence out of compassion.
It is proclaimed that women always have independence over their *saudāyika* (dowry) property;
they may dispose of it as they wish, even in the case of immovable assets, whether by sale or by gift.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman may dispose of her husband’s inheritance as she pleases; however, while he is still living, she must preserve it, otherwise she shall forfeit it to his family.
But if he has two wives and does not treat her with affection again,
even if she was given away out of love, he must be compelled by force to restore her.
Wherever a woman is deprived of food, clothing, and shelter, she may take for herself her own property; likewise, she shall receive a share from the heirs.
This is the law regarding one who has been written [in a will]: she shall live in the husband's family when [he is] present;
but if she is diseased, she may go to her kinsmen at the time of his death.
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over a woman’s property, whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
For if even one among these should forcibly consume the woman's property,
he shall be compelled to restore it with interest and shall also incur a fine equal to its value.
If one should eat that very same thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay its price, provided that he is wealthy.
Having learned that someone is ill, beset by calamity, or oppressed by creditors, one should give out of affection what has been relinquished, according to one's own will.
While she is alive, her husband, sons, brothers-in-law, fathers, and kinsmen are declared to have no power over a woman's property; those who misappropriate it, however, are liable to punishment.
The sons must repay the woman's property as a debt, just as they would a loan promised by her husband;
she who remains in her husband’s family shall not dwell in her father’s family.
The sisters, together with their kinsmen, shall divide the property of a deceased woman who has a husband;
this is the law regarding a woman's property, and thus the division has been ordained.
In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall go to the sons;
but what was given by kinsmen goes to the kinsmen, and in their absence, it goes to the husband.
Furthermore, whatever immovable property has been given by both parents to a daughter always goes to her brothers if she dies childless and without a husband.
Whatever property a woman has obtained from her father-in-law and others, whether it be her own wealth or an inheritance from her father,
in the absence of her offspring, that is declared to belong to her mother and father.

[On the inheritance of property belonging to one who has no son: A sonless widow, preserving her husband’s bed, remaining under the authority of her elders, and living patiently, shall enjoy the estate until her death; after that, the heirs shall take possession.
But when the husband has gone to heaven, the wife is entitled to food and clothing;
however, if the share of the wealth has not been divided, she receives it until her death.
One devoted to serving the teacher deserves to receive the allotted portion;
however, if he does not perform service, one should employ him in tasks such as gathering rags or begging for alms.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman who protects the family shall receive her husband’s share;
for as long as she lives, she has no ownership over it regarding giving, mortgaging, or selling.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, established in celibacy,
and constantly delighted in self-restraint and charity, shall go to heaven even if childless.
The wife who is faithful shall inherit her husband's wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall go to the daughter, provided she be unmarried.
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters are mentioned;
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [the heirs].
When the estate has been partitioned and settled, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the paternal grandmother, in that order. [But this does not apply to a wife] who is guilty of misconduct, shameless, or a squanderer of wealth.
And a woman who is devoted to adultery does not deserve her husband's property.
Indeed, if a woman performs funeral rites for the deceased without being authorized by her father, husband, or son,
that act of hers shall be fruitless.

Property that has no heir shall go to the king; likewise, the estate of a woman and the funeral expenses for the deceased. However, setting aside the property of a *śrotriya*, he should bestow that upon other *śrotriyas*.
Those who are reunited shall inherit from those with whom they were reunited; those who live separately shall inherit from those who lived separately.
In the absence [of such], they are to be known as takers of the property; those without seed (nirbīja) share with one another.
[Regarding gambling and betting: One should never indulge in gambling, for it increases anger and greed;
it is cruel, produces wicked people, and destroys the wealth of men.
Since strife inevitably arises from gambling, just as venom issues from the mouth of a serpent, therefore a king should desist from it; for that is indeed a vice regarding his domain.
If it should be visible, however, with its gateway and archway standing out,
one should have hand-marks made there for the sake of the noble ones' non-confusion.
The master of the gaming house shall conduct the gambling match; he himself shall pay the king the fee due, and he may take a ten percent profit from the stakes lost.

The victor shall give his own wealth; from the one defeated, [the stake] should be taken after three fortnights, or immediately by the master of the assembly itself—of this there is no doubt regarding gambling.
Whether appearing as one form or two forms, victory is seen for that gambler at dice upon whom protection is established.
Alternatively, a gambler, having given the king his share as prescribed, may engage in gambling openly; in this way, no fault is found.
One should cause that which is due to be paid by force in that place and not otherwise;
for in that case, the master of the hall has won, as the legal procedure depends upon him.

One who is ignorant but has been defeated should be released; one who is knowledgeable but has been defeated in private should not be released. Even when all one's possessions have been won, one should not cause the one who possesses knowledge to surrender his entire wealth.
In disputes over victory or gain in fraudulent gambling,
the master of the gaming hall is the authority, provided that the master of the hall is himself upright.
There is no certainty regarding the king for those who follow the conduct practiced by barbarians, outcasts, rogues, gamblers, and ascetics.

[The Miscellaneous: That which remains unsaid from what was previously stated, and that which has fallen away from its proper context— having been extracted from other treatises and composed incoherently— is the miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka).
That which is established by means of an illustration at the conclusion of a treatise,
or that statement which is repeated according to this rule, shall be known as *prakīrṇaka* (scattered or miscellaneous).
The duties of kings, one's own specific duties, the discussion of doubtful points,
and whatever remains unsaid from what was previously mentioned— all that constitutes the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇaka).
Taking a sixth part as tax and toll, likewise [theft] from a pit,
causing dissension in battle, and violating another's wife.
The desire to kill cows or Brahmins, as well as the destruction of crops—
the king himself should investigate these ten offenses.

The failure to perform expiations, the transgression of prohibitions and injunctions, the destruction of the system of castes and stages of life, and the neglect of the rules for the intermixture of lineages; // K_949 //
A treasure that yields no fruit, wealth for a poor man, and the arrival of riches for one already wealthy—
the king himself, having learned of these through his spies, should prevent them.
Those matters which are not recorded in the scriptures, the ritualistic assertions of disputants, the provocation of the constituent elements, and mutual secret signals— these should be avoided.
And whatever among his subjects proceeds contrary to the scriptures,
the king should pacify these matters by means of such expedients as conciliation and sowing dissension.
One should employ verbal punishment toward friends and others, saying, "Shame on you, wretched woman!
One should do to him exactly what was said; as for what was not said, it should be properly devised.
But whoever should accomplish a transaction by means of a false measure, or by a forged seal, or even by a counterfeit stamp, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Those who are addicted to royal diversions, those who subsist on the king's service,
and whoever speaks what is unpleasant— he should carry out their execution.
Those who manufacture counterfeit coins, those who examine them, those who distribute them,
and those who steal the king’s revenue shall suffer various forms of capital punishment.
A Śūdra who has taken up the life of a renunciant, as well as one devoted to the muttering of prayers and burnt offerings—
if such a sinner is found, he shall be punished by execution or fined double the usual penalty.
Even if the crime is accompanied by evidence, one should inquire into the cause of the offense;
then, having carefully established the fault, one should determine the punishment.
But when all those of virtuous conduct should commit an offense,
even involuntarily through the power of fate, one should not impose punishment in that case.
Kings who administer punishment correctly are worthy of worship even by the gods.
One should impose the lowest fine at the first offense; it is recorded that for a repeated offense, the middle fine is prescribed.
Indeed, whoever is subject to a specific punishment shall receive exactly that which has been ordained for them.
Kings and ministers likewise shall especially attain such [results] through the failure to punish the wicked and through the infliction of punishment upon those who submit.
And whoever are dependent on others, and those who exist in a state of servitude—
they are designated as "the helpless," and their punishment is beating.
Beating, binding, and likewise humiliation—this indeed is the punishment for a slave; a monetary fine is not prescribed.
One who deserves death shall pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
for one deserving the amputation of a limb, half of that; and for exile, twenty-five.
Toward those of noble birth, the Aryas, and distinguished persons, as well as toward those who are lowly, he should act according to their status;
having confiscated all their property, he should swiftly banish them from the city.
Those who are destitute should be placed in confinement; one must never carry out the death penalty for any of those guilty of crimes, according to the specific provisions of the treatises.
A Brahmin deserving of execution or the amputation of limbs should enter a prison free from restraints;
for, being deprived of those [punitive] acts, his conduct therein constitutes his true discipline.
One who gives false testimony should be banished; one who accepts gifts from the wicked should be publicly proclaimed as such;
and one who maims a limb should be deprived of that limb by means of imprisonment according to his own law.

In those cases as well, one should apply this same principle to those who have committed equal offenses; for children, the elderly, the sick, and women, there shall be no punishment other than a beating as a fine.
A righteous lord of the earth should cause the woman's property to be given as a fine;
a woman who is destitute and has committed an offense deserves the punishment of being beaten.

One should deposit wealth acquired through improper means into the treasury as part of the treasury; for the sake of accomplishing a task, one should not cause the ruin of that task—a wise person should not bring about such destruction.
Having given all that wealth arising from fines to the Brahmins,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should depart for the forest.
Thus should the earthly king, ever disciplined, conduct himself according to the principles of dharma;
he should likewise employ all his servants in what is beneficial for the world.

**The Vyavahāramayūkha** **Text (Reconstructed), Translation, Notes and Introduction** By P. V. Kane Reprint from the *Hindu Law Quarterly*, Bombay, 1933 **PLAIN TEXT VERSION** **I. Introduction** The *Vyavahāramayūkha* is one of the most celebrated works of the great Maratha jurist, Śrīmad Bhaṭṭa Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara, who flourished in the early part of the seventeenth century. It forms part of his monumental digest, the *Bhagavantabhāskara*, which is divided into twelve sections (*mayūkhās*), each dealing with a specific branch of Dharmaśāstra. The *Vyavahāramayūkha* specifically treats the law of procedure (*vyavahāra*) and civil and criminal justice. Nīlakaṇṭha was a versatile scholar, deeply versed not only in the legal literature of the Smṛtis but also in the Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and other branches of traditional learning. His style is characterized by its lucidity, logical rigor, and reliance on authoritative sources. He frequently cites the views of earlier commentators such as Vijñāneśvara, Aparārka, and the Mitākṣarā, while also offering his own reasoned interpretations. The work is structured around the eighteen titles of law (*aṣṭādaśa-vivādapadas*) enumerated in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*. These include matters concerning debt, deposits, partnership, slavery, recovery of gifts, non-payment of wages, non-performance of agreements, rescission of sale and purchase, disputes between owners and herdsmen, boundary disputes, assault, defamation, theft, adultery, duties of husband and wife, partition of inheritance, gambling, and miscellaneous offenses. In his treatment of these topics, Nīlakaṇṭha demonstrates a keen awareness of the practical administration of justice. He discusses the qualifications of judges, the methods of evidence, the types of ordeals, and the various modes of punishment. His analysis of the rules of evidence is particularly noteworthy for its systematic approach to the admissibility of witnesses and the evaluation of testimony. The *Vyavahāramayūkha* remains a foundational text for the study of Hindu jurisprudence, especially within the tradition of the Benares School. Its influence is evident in later digests and in the judicial decisions of modern Indian courts, which continue to refer to it as an authority on ancient Hindu law. **II. Textual Basis and Reconstruction** The present edition is based primarily on the manuscript of the *Vyavahāramayūkha* preserved in the collection of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune. This manuscript, though containing occasional lacunae and scribal errors, provides the core text for this reconstruction. Where necessary, readings have been supplemented or corrected by consulting parallel passages in the *Vīramitrodaya*, the *Smṛticandrikā*, and other related works of Nīlakaṇṭha. **III. Translation** [The translation follows the reconstructed Sanskrit text, providing a literal yet idiomatic rendering into English, preserving the technical terminology of the original. **IV. Notes** Each section of the translation is accompanied by detailed notes. These notes identify the sources cited by Nīlakaṇṭha, clarify obscure points of law or procedure, and provide comparative insights into the evolution of Hindu legal thought. Special attention is given to the definitions of technical terms and the historical context of the legal maxims discussed. **V. Conclusion** Through the *Vyavahāramayūkha*, Śrīmad Bhaṭṭa Nīlakaṇṭha offers a comprehensive and authoritative exposition of the Hindu system of justice. His work stands as a testament to the sophistication of traditional Indian legal scholarship and continues to serve as an indispensable resource for scholars and practitioners alike. --- *End of Plain Text Version* **Note:** The actual Sanskrit text, translation, and notes would follow this structural outline in the full publication. www.sub.uni-goettingen.de/ebene_1/fiindolo/gretil/gretdias.pdf Kātyāyanasmṛtisāroddhāraḥ [The Qualities of a King]
A king should be disciplined, accomplished in the sciences, endowed with a treasury and valor,
devoted to the Brahmins, liberal in giving, and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
Free from arrogance, malice, slander, fickleness, and anger;
he is confident yet humble, not overbearing, sociable, and pleasant to behold.

Prosperity attends to the utmost degree one who has his senses under control, who has conquered himself, who wields the rod of punishment against those who deserve it, who acts after careful deliberation, and who is wise.
[On the Duties of Kings: Due to an abundance of valor, learning, and wealth, and especially because of their sovereign power,
the minds of kings constantly fall into delusion for these reasons.
Therefore, the mind should always be awakened by the twice-born regarding the duty of kings;
one must not transgress the words of the Smṛti, which are supremely purifying and meritorious.
By the power of the sound of the Vedas, even the gods who dwell in heaven rejoice there,
being satisfied by the worship of the twice-born.
Therefore, kings should always perform the worship of the twice-born with great effort;
by that means, they shall repeatedly attain the status of Śakra as well as the sovereignty of men again and again.
The superintendent of liquor, fallen from heaven, dwells in the form of a king;
he must constantly perform that by which he may attain the ultimate reality.
Kings who remain established in their own dharma attain the state of Śakra;
whereas those who always behave contrary to proper conduct dwell in the Avīci hell.
That king who, failing to understand correctly, goes under the sway of anger, will dwell in a terrible hell for half a kalpa; of this there is no doubt.
One should appoint as a minister for the deliberation of affairs a Brāhmaṇa who possesses these very qualities, who is devoted to the king, and who upholds his lineage.
Where the ministers, courtiers, and physicians speak only pleasant words,
the king there will swiftly fall away from his kingdom, his dharma, and his happiness.
One should not give way to anger at his words;
for these [words] must always be spoken by them as that which is just and well-established.
Where the king personally oversees legal affairs in accordance with dharma,
there the subjects, practicing virtuous conduct, shall dwell in happiness.
The constant protection of the subjects, the clearing away of thorns,
and the honoring of the twice-born— for this purpose was the king created.
The king is always declared to be the lord of the earth, and not of other property;
for he receives a sixth part of its fruit, and not otherwise.
Because those beings dwell therein, his lordship over them is proclaimed;
his duty consists of receiving a sixth part of their produce, arising from both auspicious and inauspicious causes.
O lord of men, for that king who acts in this way, having abandoned greed,
sons are born to him, and his kingdom and treasury increase.
For that king who, by unjust means, takes taxes, fines, a share of the crops, and tolls from his kingdom, partakes in sin.
Having abandoned what is taught in the treatises on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*), one should follow what is taught in the treatises on righteousness (*dharmaśāstra*).
Even if a king is wicked, his kingdom shall not perish,
because he does not engage in unrighteous acts without the consent of his subjects.
But that king who, without hardship, properly presents [the gift] to one who requests it, saves an infinite number of beings; such is the gift for the sake of Dharma.
That which is acquired by kings after conquering an enemy through lawful means is pure; that should be given as tribute, for it is never acceptable when obtained otherwise.
The king should appoint as his domestic priest a learned Brahmin who is well-disposed toward him,
accomplished in Vedic study, free from greed, and truthful in speech.
In the extensive exposition of logic (nyāya) known as Dharma— which is characterized by conventional usage and so forth, and which is achieved through effort and is subject to interruption—
that debate which has the object of proof as its root is called "legal procedure" (vyavahāra).
In the sense of "diversity" (vi), when there is doubt, the act of removing it is called *hāra*;
because it removes diverse doubts, it is traditionally known as *vyavahāra*.
But a king should not, out of a desire for power or greed for wealth,
personally adjudicate the legal cases of men who have not yet reached a settlement.
For he who commits violence or does not bestow what is to be given, and who,
when entreated, acts with immorality— he shall be dragged away by order of the king.
When the two lines reach eighteen words due to the distinction of the objects to be accomplished (sādhya),
they become eighteen thousandfold through the distinction of the ritual actions (kriyā).
The root of the doctrine of what is to be proven (sādhya) is that which has been presented by the proponent;
"failure to give what is due" and "violence" are said to be the two grounds for defeat (utthāna).
The plaint, the reply, the rejoinder, and the stage of proof— by these it is declared to have four feet.
In the treatises on Dharma and Artha, however, two branches are cited;
victory and decisive settlement are declared to be the two fruits.
But he who, though urged by the king, first reports a matter condemned by the scriptures— being primarily intent on his own wealth— is declared to be a *stobhaka* (a slanderer).
He who, appointed by the king himself to examine defects in official positions,
reports what he has learned to the king, is designated as a "sūcaka" (an informer).

[The consideration of the relative strength and weakness of legal proceedings, customary practice, conduct, and royal edicts: But where, in a dispute, the wrongdoer may claim authorship while the owner of the wealth claims it as his own property, the decision must be made by the law alone. // K_035 //
Whatever Smṛti scripture has been proclaimed by those who establish Dharma for the purpose of deciding legal cases is indeed known as Vyavahāra (judicial procedure).
Whatever is practiced by someone, whether it be righteous or unrighteous,
through the constant practice of a region, that is proclaimed as *caritra* (customary law).
Whatever dharma the king establishes in accordance with the treatises on logic and likewise according to local custom,
that is the just royal decree.
But where a matter is consistent with reason and devoid of divine proof,
there dharma is overridden by legal procedure, and not otherwise.
Regarding those born of inverse unions and those dwelling in outcaste regions, they say that their practice of dharma is necessarily contrary [to the norm]; one should not unsettle them from that.
But when the king makes a decision according to that dharma, then the legal procedure is superseded by that very custom.
If, however, a legal practice is established by kings that is contrary to reason,
such a practice should be set aside there by the king's command.
Whatever subsequent sublation is joined with this method,
where there is sublation by another means, there dharma is destroyed.
When one's own word exists, personal action leads away from heaven, causes the destruction of the world, brings fear to enemy armies, and robs kings of their life-span and progeny.
Therefore, the king should settle legal matters in accordance with the scriptures;
however, in the absence of scriptural statements for all cases, he should decide them according to local custom.
Whatever custom has been established in a particular region and persists for all time,
provided it does not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, that is called a "local practice" (deśadṛṣṭa).
For those who dwell in regions, ports, and cow-pens, or in cities and villages, [the law] is determined by their own conventions;
for others, it is according to the Dharmaśāstras, together with them.
The settlement that has been determined with the consent of the country itself must always be recorded in writing and sealed with the royal seal.
Having examined it, one should determine [the truth], for that which is to be done by those established in the scriptures must be protected with effort according to the treatises;
indeed, whatever has been committed to writing and settled by those following the Vedic tradition [must be upheld].
Therefore, that [cognition] should proceed accordingly and not otherwise;
for that which is observed in a particular place by means of valid cognition is determined to be "thus."
Where an unprecedented act has been performed that is approved by the Śruti and Smṛti, it should not be done otherwise; one should avoid what is devoid of justice.
[The Court of Justice]:
That place where the investigation of the treatises on Dharma is conducted for the purpose of discerning the root and the essence is indeed the Dharmādhikaraṇa (the Court of Justice).

Having risen in the morning and performed his purification with a concentrated mind, the king [should honor] his guru, the astrologer, the physicians, the gods, the Brahmins, and the domestic priests.
Having honored these [deities] as is appropriate with fine flowers, ornaments, and garments,
and having paid homage to the preceptors and others, one should enter the assembly hall with a cheerful countenance.
Having entered the assembly hall with modest attire and composed mind, the king,
seated and facing the east, should remain there and attend to the legal affairs of the litigants,
together with those aged in the three Vedas and with ministers skilled in counsel.
Accompanied by the judge, his ministers, the Brahmins and the domestic chaplain, and the members of the assembly, the king remains in heaven according to dharma as a witness.
Together with his councilors—who were steadfast, disciplined, wise, hereditary, and the best among the twice-born;
who were skilled in the meaning of the treatises on dharma and proficient in the treatises on statecraft.
It should be presided over by a few merchants who possess noble lineage, good conduct, youth, virtuous behavior, and wealth, and who are free from envy, acting as true members of the community.
In that case, the listeners should be like merchants who perceive what is right.
[The time for seeing legal cases: In the assembly halls during the forenoon, the king, the subduer of enemies, shall decide legal cases according to the path prescribed by the scriptures.
Except for the eighth part of the day, the three periods of time that remain are declared in the scriptures to be the supreme times for legal proceedings.
That period which consists of three parts of the day following the first eighth part of the day is seen by the wise in the scriptures as the time for legal proceedings.
[The Judge]: When the king himself does not carry out the decision of a legal case,
then he should appoint there a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the scriptures.
One who is capable, of noble birth, impartial, not causing agitation, steady,
fearful of the next world, most righteous, diligent, and free from anger.
One who is gentle, sweet-natured, affectionate, patient, discerning,
energetic, and free from greed should be appointed by the king to matters of debate.
One who studies only a single treatise cannot attain certainty regarding what ought to be done;
therefore, kings should ensure that they possess extensive knowledge of many scriptures in legal disputes.
Where, however, no Brāhmaṇa is available, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.

Therefore, whatever task has been performed by others in an unjust manner should be recognized as such by those appointed [to oversee it], even if it appears to be right by chance or according to the scriptures.
It is the established rule that he asks the question concerning the matter based on legal procedure;
because he investigates (vivecayati) within that [matter], he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
But if the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding a matter that has not yet been decided,
he shall be punished, and the members of the court even more so.
[The members of the assembly] should be the best of the twice-born, free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all the scriptures.

Where the members of the court have reached a decision by overstepping the science of logic (nyāyaśāstra), there dharma, being struck down by adharma, destroys [the wrongdoer]; of this there is no doubt.
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the court look on, there the members of the court are themselves slain.
But the members of the court must not overlook an action that has proceeded unrighteously;
for by overlooking it, they, along with the king, go headlong into hell.
Even those members of the assembly who follow him as he proceeds by unjust means share in that guilt;
therefore, they must instruct that king.
But having recognized that the king's mind has strayed from the path of justice, one should speak what is pleasing to him; in doing so, the member of the assembly shall not incur guilt.
A member of the assembly must necessarily speak words consistent with dharma and artha;
if the king does not listen, then that member of the assembly would be sinless.
When the king should direct the litigants toward unrighteousness, the member of the court,
having informed the monarch, should then set aside the case.
Whether out of affection, ignorance, greed, or even delusion,
if a member of the assembly speaks otherwise than the truth therein, he is considered non-member and shall be punished.
Having correctly understood the determination of the matter, the member of the court should then speak;
otherwise, he must not speak at all, for the speaker shall be subject to a double fine.
But that which is lost due to the fault of the court members must then be paid by those members;
however, once the matter of the litigants has been definitively settled, one must not overturn it.
[The relative weight of the decision-makers:
Families, guilds, assemblies, and the authorized king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
One should have the affairs of ascetics carried out by those learned in the three Vedas,
and likewise by those skilled in the application of *māyā*, but not by oneself, for fear of provoking anger.
One endowed with perfect knowledge should not offer instruction to those of superior birth and character, nor to gurus, teachers, and ascetics.

But that which is their abiding in the lineage, which comes about in due order through the nature of reality (dharmatā), they call the "family dharma" (kuladharma); one should protect it in that very same way.
[The manner of questioning:
At the appropriate time, he should question the petitioner who stands before him with a bowed head:
"What is your business? What is your affliction? Do not fear; speak, O man!"

"By whom, toward whom, when, and for what reason should one who belongs to the assembly ask? When asked thus, that which he says should be [accepted] by the members of the assembly together with the Brahmins."
Having deliberated upon the matter, if it is found to be just, he should thereafter issue a summons;
otherwise, he should deposit a seal upon it or appoint an official to handle it.

One who is appointed as a representative by the plaintiff and appears before the judicial authority is to be known as a *pratinidhi* (proxy); likewise, one who is himself accepted as the defendant is also considered such.
The right [to sue] belongs to the plaintiff, not to anyone else, because there is no connection;
yet even the other [the defendant] is considered to have been made an opponent by the plaintiff.
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
Slaves, laborers, disciples, servants, and likewise kinsmen who act as advocates shall not be punished; however, anyone other than these is subject to punishment.
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and other such heinous crimes, no opposing witness is admitted.
In the case of killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
eating what is unfit to be eaten, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden;
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, no adversary shall be permitted; the perpetrator himself must plead his case.

The king should summon those who are eager for the Dharma, those seeking prosperity, and even the sick or the dull-witted; however, he should not summon those who are mentally unwell, intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or women.
A young woman born of noble family who has not yet had offspring,
even if she is the best among all castes, is considered to remain under the authority of her paternal kinsmen as long as she is unmarried.
The summoning of those women who are dependent on others for their livelihood, those who are wanton, courtesans, those of ruined families, and those who have fallen from their caste is prescribed.
One who speaks in debate while armed, without an upper garment, with disheveled hair, seated upon a throne,
or with his left hand [holding a weapon], shall incur punishment.
But if one who is capable should, when summoned, disregard the king’s command,
the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law.
In minor cases, the fine shall be fifty [paṇas]; in middling cases, it shall be no less than two hundred;
and for serious matters, the punishment shall always be no less than five hundred.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense, the king should diligently collect either a fine in paṇas or the monetary value equivalent to that penalty.
He who commits violence or fails to pay what is due,
having been summoned despite his misconduct, shall be arrested by the king’s command.
But once the matter has been reported to the king and he has promised to decide it without doubt,
one should then apply a stay of proceedings until the appearance of the defendant at the summons.
One who is fit for restraint but has not been restrained deserves punishment upon departing.
[Those who are not to be obstructed:
But he who, by means of restraining the senses, or by means of speech, breathing, and so forth,
should obstruct one who is not to be obstructed— he is to be punished, but the other is not an offender.
Those who have climbed trees or mountains, those stationed on elephants, horses, chariots, or boats,
and all those situated in difficult terrain— none of these should be obstructed by those seeking to accomplish their purpose.
Those afflicted by disease, those in distress, as well as sacrificers,
those who have not yet crossed over [to the other side], and likewise those who are intoxicated, insane, or mentally dull, are not to be obstructed.
A farmer does not [reap] at the time of sowing, nor does a soldier at the time of marching;
having made a vow, one sets out, and once the appointed time has come, there is no turning back in the interim.

A farmer who is diligently engaged in his crops, from the commencement of work until the harvest, shall not be sued during that time even upon the arrival of water; however, it is the settled rule that one who restrains a person who should not be restrained shall be punished by the king.
Whether accused, imprisoned, or staying by the king's command, no other person should act on his behalf; the wise know him as one who is under accusation.

When the task has been accomplished by the messenger, depending on whether it took one day, two days, or more, and depending on the place, time, and other factors, one should cause him to be given food as a reward.
The knowers of reality understand that eating is prescribed in accordance with place, time, age, strength, and so forth; this applies everywhere to the one who acts.
[They are not to be apprehended as witnesses:
neither a master, nor an enemy, nor one appointed by a master,
nor one who has been imprisoned or fined, nor those in a state of legal uncertainty, under any circumstances.
Neither an heir nor one who is destitute, nor those who dwell in perpetual residence,
nor men appointed to royal service, nor those who have renounced the world (pravrajita).
One who is incapable of paying the debt to the creditor and an equivalent fine to the king,
or one whose father is still living and acts according to his own will,
should not be accepted as a surety for the performance of the obligation when he is unknown [as such].
If there is no surety for a litigant who is fit to plead,
he, being protected, shall at the end of the day give a fee to the messenger.
A twice-born man who lacks a surety should be protected by guards stationed outside;
however, Śūdras and others who lack a surety should be bound with fetters.
If he transgresses or departs, he should be fined eight paṇas;
however, the obstruction of the daily rites of all social classes must be avoided.
According to the principle of not grasping what has already been grasped, the king should not initiate legal proceedings;
rather, he should either hand over the case to that person or entrust it to another.
[The Order of Speech for the Plaintiff and Others:
In that regard, the plaintiff (abhiyoktṛ) should speak first, and the defendant (abhiyukta) immediately thereafter;
at the conclusion of those two, the members of the assembly (sadasya) shall speak, and after that, the presiding judge (prāḍvivāka).
He for whom there is greater suffering or for whom the matter at hand is more significant shall be the plaintiff;
it is not he who first reports the case.
If a person suffers either a loss of wealth or a severe physical affliction, the defendant's plea may be granted;
however, it shall not be granted to one who did not report it previously.
[The nature of the formal proposition:
Having established the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, as well as the date, the hour, the region, the subject matter, the location, the caste, the appearance, and the age; K_124 //

He [should know] the object to be proven, the means of proof, the substance, the number, and likewise the name of himself; as well as the names of the kings in their proper order, their residence, and the name of the person to be proven.
Having announced the name of the defendant, one should sequentially state the names of the ancestors, the injury, the plaintiff and the defendant,
the signs of forgiveness, and other matters, before establishing the case.
The country, as well as the location, the settlement, the caste, the name, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
And likewise, the ancestral lineage of the father and grandfather, and the mention of former kings—
these ten he should cause to be inscribed upon immovable property in disputes concerning them.
If one should state that [the opponent] has been provoked by even one of the passions such as attachment,
then one should write "Oṃ" for all of it upon the board or other materials of the disputant.
One should correct excessive matters and supplement those that are deficient;
one should establish them on paper as long as the case remains unsettled.
The judge shall cause the plaintiff's statement, as it was naturally expressed, to be recorded on a wooden board with chalk;
thereafter, once it has been refined, it shall be written upon a formal document.
A righteous king should punish like a thief anyone who writes down one thing while stating something else in the words of the plaintiff or the defendant.
He obtains a period of relaxation for either three days or seven days,
as long as the thought arises in him when he wishes to speak in the debate.
Since a firm determination is reached only after a long time from the commencement of an action,
one who is diligent does not waste time, for he is one who possesses the opportune moment.
When the intellect of two parties desiring to settle a matter is unable to reach a decision in their dispute,
time should be granted there to both the plaintiff and the defendant.
A plaint that is contrary to the interests of the state, one that has been rejected by the king,
or one that is confused by multiple points does not succeed.
Even a case involving many assertions that has been settled in legal proceedings,
the king may, if he desires to ascertain the truth, take it up again at his pleasure.
A thesis that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number, and deficient in the measure of what is to be proven, is considered unacceptable.
If he does not wish to act according to justice, or if he acts unjustly,
or if he fails to have it recorded in writing in this manner, his case shall not succeed.
One should avoid a fallacious thesis (pakṣābhāsa) that is unestablished, unassailable, devoid of meaning, purposeless,
impossible to prove, or contradictory.

Those who know the thesis understand the *pakṣa* (the subject of proof) to be that which is free from defects of the proposition, is yet to be proven, is endowed with valid reasons, is certain, and is established by worldly consensus.
It consists of very few syllables yet contains abundant meaning; it is free from doubt and free from confusion;
it is devoid of contradictory causes and serves as a refutation of opposing views.
But when such a position has been formulated by the proponent,
the opponent should then provide a response connected to that very position.
For when a matter is being stated by a petitioner and is not obstructed,
or when one remains silent at the time of a gift, that matter is approved.

[The reply should be given either immediately or after a period of time: Having heard the matter set forth in writing, if the defendant requests a delay in the dispute for a specific reason, it should undoubtedly be granted to him.
Depending on the gravity or lightness of the matter, one may obtain [the result] immediately, after one day, five days, or three days;
or in cases such as debts and the like, it may take three fortnights or seven days.
Having ascertained the time, the capacity [of the parties], and the relative strength or weakness of the matters at hand,
the sovereign should grant the defendant a period of time, whether it be short or long.
Whether it be a day, half a month, a full month, a season, or even a year—
the time for the subsequent gift should be determined in accordance with the duration of the ritual performance.
Where respect disappears, whether through destruction or abandonment, one should not wait for the proper time; for that matter is urgent.
In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and likewise in procreation;
in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and similarly in buying and selling.
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, acts of violence, embezzlement of a deposit, fraud, and perjury, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.
Bṛhaspati states that in cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusation regarding cattle, or a grave emergency, one may dispute over land immediately, even outside the prescribed season.
In matters that have been recently committed, the lord should institute a lawsuit immediately;
or, in cases where time has elapsed, he should grant a period of time to the defendant.
If [the death] occurred immediately, the impurity lasts for that very day; if it occurred more than a month ago, it lasts one day;
if six years have passed, it lasts three nights; and if twelve years have passed, it lasts seven days.
At twenty years of age, he shall receive ten days or half a month;
at thirty years, a month; and beyond that, it shall be three fortnights.
One may perform it at a time before a year has passed, according to one's own desire;
however, for one who is dull-witted, insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by disease, [the period] is one year.
Or when the matter has reached a distant region, or when the subject matter is unknown,
or when the foundational documents or witnesses are situated in a foreign land.
In that case, the time for men [to pay] would be until their return to their own country;
even when the time has been granted, it may still be paid later due to the gravity of the matter.
But the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case,
should immediately thereafter present the counter-argument connected to the subject matter of that case.
Regarding the determination of conduct, the giving of materials, sacrifices, duties, and service:
when no one is present to provide such service, one should not take advantage of that situation to act deceitfully.
If at that time a fault caused by a king or by fate should occur,
he shall not be defeated merely because his legal document has been obstructed.
One should establish a fault caused by a king or by fate through witnesses;
however, for one who acts with deceit, that wealth shall be made to pay as a fine.
One who is being prosecuted shall never prosecute the prosecutor,
except in cases of assault, theft, adultery, and crimes involving mortal sin.
Whatever established practice has been handed down through successive tradition in a particular place,
the king, having considered that according to what is right, shall cause a reply to be given.
The reply is of four kinds:
the true reply, the false reply, the counter-attack, and likewise the application of a prior legal decision; thus the reply is fourfold.
But when another, having heard the meaning of what was spoken, refutes it either in terms of its meaning or its words, that reply should be known as false.
If a defendant,
when accused, should deny the charge, one should know that his defense in the legal proceeding is false.
The truthful speech of one who is to be converted is declared to be "practice" (pratipatti).
"This is false; I do not know it; I was not present there at that time;
and I was unborn at that time"—thus, falsehood is fourfold.
If the defendant admits the very claim that has been stated by the plaintiff,
the Teacher (Guru) declared that one should state the grounds for his own superiority.
If one who has been defeated according to the established procedure is made to write again,
he is said to be "previously defeated," and that case is called *prāṅnyāya*.
I shall establish this through witnesses, by family records, or by written documents;
furthermore, this threefold plea of prior judgment has already been won by me.
[These are] the fallacious rejoinders or the faults of the rejoinder:
that which is unestablished, contradictory, too little, or excessive; as well as those characterized by great defects—namely, the doubtful, the impossible, the unclear, and the irrelevant.
An answer that is non-comprehensive, disjointed in its phrasing, obscure in meaning, confused,
requiring interpretation, or lacking substance is not praised by the wise.

An answer that consists of disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is likewise confused, requires interpretation to be understood, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the accomplishment of one's own purpose.
If, however, one does not understand the sign,
the form, or the convention, or if it is stated in a different language, that answer is considered unestablished (aprasiddha).
"I returned it in my youth; indeed, I did not return it"—when one says this, that contradictory reply should be understood as the [defeated] rejoinder here.
To say, "This was previously conquered by me for this purpose," where one says "previously by me" when it is not so, is known as the *ūna* (deficient) rejoinder.
When it should have been said, "It was taken," he instead said, "The task was performed by me;
that wealth which was previously taken was exceedingly great."
When one ought to say "it must be given by me," saying instead "it is not to be given by me"—
the wise should then recognize such an answer as ambiguous in legal proceedings.
In the past, this [doctrine] was established by force;
they consider this unspoken [intention] to have been stated for some other purpose.
When it is said, "I have given this thousand together with myself," that which is returned as half of that is known here as the "non-pervasive" (avyāpaka).
As long as the proponent has not properly established his case, what he says— such as "I previously accepted this"— is called a "deviant statement."
"Will anyone give a lotus that has not been taken?"—
this answer, spoken according to worldly convention, contains a hidden meaning.
"Should that very person always give, or should it be given by me?"—
those who know the truth understand that this answer is considered improper.
The reply that "a crow has no teeth" or "it does have them," and so forth,
is considered a truly inadequate response because it is devoid of essence.
One should not disregard what is presented if it is meager, indistinct, deficient or excessive, inconsistent, incomplete, unsubstantial, doubtful, or subject to opposition.
Anything else that is ambiguous, too little, or too much compared to the subject under discussion—
even if it were to pervade only a portion of the opponent's position— cannot constitute a valid rejoinder.
That which is true regarding one part of the thesis, but is a reason regarding another part,
and is false regarding yet another part, is not a valid rejoinder because of its inconsistency.
In a single dispute, there should not be two means of proof for both disputants;
there can be no establishment of the point for both, nor can there be two means of proof in one case.

If, after having employed the grounds that cause the defeat of an argument, one should state another, more significant reason contained within the opponent's reply, then indeed that [latter reason] is what is established, and not the other.
One should give a truthful answer and cause even one who does not ask to pay,
by means of conciliation, sowing dissension, and other such methods, until that matter has been fully resolved.
Whether out of delusion or through deceit, whatever was not stated by the proponent but is included within the reply, that too should be accepted by both parties.
But he who, though being urged by various means, does not give an answer,
is considered defeated once seven nights have passed and must pay the debt.
Having caused [the opponent] to hear [the proof], he should abandon what was to be done and say something else;
by that, he has resorted to another side, and thus the proponent is defeated.
One should not speak of another's case after having been appointed to one's own;
if one speaks falsely in this manner, one should likewise designate that person as defeated.
But if a litigant, having had a statement written down, should later speak of it as being deficient or excessive, he shall be defeated; he does not deserve to maintain his formal charge.
The members of the court and the witnesses themselves are to be understood by the wise as the "action" (kriyā).
He who, out of delusion, hates that action is called a "hater of the action."
Through failure to attend when summoned, one is immediately cast out.
Even if he is prepared, one should not speak; he deserves immediate imprisonment.
On the second day, one should know that the defeat of that evil-minded person has occurred.
But when one seeks to prolong the debate by means of a pretext,
one should recognize that as "pretextual argument" (sāpadeśa), which is recorded as causing the defeat of the debate.
One who speaks falsely shall pay five paṇas; one who shows malice toward the legal proceeding, ten paṇas;
one who does not appear for the hearing, twelve paṇas;
one who remains silent when questioned, sixteen paṇas; and one who flees after being summoned shall be made to pay twenty paṇas.
The lord of the earth should discipline that man who, having been summoned three times, does not come, who flees when called, or who has exceeded the limit of five nights.
Where one should divide even one of the legal matters that have been announced,
and should also entice the litigant with greed— one should designate him as defeated.
If he causes fear, or division, or intimidation, or obstruction,
he loses his case in the legal proceeding regarding the matter of the disputants.
When the defendant has been summoned in accordance with the fault [of his non-appearance], there shall be no retrial.
Once both parties have committed their statements to writing and the determination of the case has begun,
he who speaks what is improper therein is defeated on that point.
But that plaintiff who, having pointed out witnesses, does not proceed to litigate intentionally,
is defeated after thirty nights have passed.

Because fleeing is not the ultimate [way], and because of relying on another's position, the debate of one who is inferior is accepted; however, this does not apply to one who has been defeated by his own words.
The wise know that one who is defeated by a deficient statement may be rescued;
however, for one who is himself deficient in his own statement, no rescue exists.
Those who, having presented their case, reach a settlement between themselves after the matter has been brought forward,
shall all be fined double, as they have deceived the king.
[Kriyāpāda:

For even the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) attains the status of a conclusion (uttara) by virtue of its cause; therefore, action (kriyā) is then said to be that which establishes the prima facie argument.
When the reply has been properly examined and written down, being thus free from defects,
the taking of evidence by either the defendant or the plaintiff is desired.

That which the proponent intends to establish clearly for himself is the *sādhya* (the probandum); that by which it is established is the *sādhana* (the proof), through which the entire *sādhya* is proven.
[The Means of Proof, and the Consideration of Their Relative Strength]:
They know that the means of proof are threefold: written documents, witnesses, and possession.
Reasoning consists of the indication of a slight trace, while the ordeals here include poison and so forth.
Even when the plaintiff's claim has been written down in its entirety, letter by letter,
he must establish it through evidence in the third stage of the trial.
For it has been stated that the "effect" (kārya) is that which is to be accomplished, while the "means" (sādhana) is called the action (kriyā).
That [action], moreover, should be known as being of two kinds: divine (daivikī) and human (mānuṣī).
Human means consist of documents, witnesses, and so forth; divine means are considered to be [ordeals] such as the water-ordeal and others.
When witnesses are available, a wise man should avoid divine means of proof;
for by employing divine means when witnesses are available, he is defeated thereby.
If one person should state human evidence and another should state divine evidence,
the king should accept the human evidence in that case, but not the divine procedure.
If a human action exists even when it pervades only a single part [of the truth], it should be accepted by men who speak; however, even if it is complete, a divine action [is not to be accepted].
The divine [oblation] is of five kinds, while the human is recorded as being of three kinds.
He who, having abandoned a strong means of proof, resorts to a weak one,
shall not obtain that means of proof again once the victory has been determined by the members of the court.
One should abandon that action which, having set aside the essential point, accomplishes many non-essential things; one should abandon from afar that action which is devoid of essence;
and one should abandon that action which attempts to accomplish two opposing sides.
Human action is not declared to be [the sole means] when divine means exist;
nor, when there is documentary evidence in lawsuits, are there either ordeals or witnesses.
A document loses its validity over time, as does one that is legally defective. In a lawsuit lacking documentary evidence or witnesses, one should assign it to divine means (ordeals).
One should not employ human effort or a document in a matter that must be resolved by divine means.
Regarding the established status of guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, which has been fully proclaimed, its proof is documentary evidence; neither ordeal nor witnesses are required.
Likewise, in matters such as the use of doors, paths, water conduits, and so forth,
possession alone shall be the weightier proof, neither documentary evidence nor witnesses.
Furthermore, when a dispute arises between a master and his servants regarding what has been given or not given,
or concerning a sale, a gift, or a transaction, he may pay the money after having purchased it.
In matters of gambling, betting, and when a dispute has arisen, witnesses are declared to be the means of proof; neither divine ordeal nor written documents are required.
In cases of assault, verbal abuse,
physical violence, or threats involving force, witnesses or even divine ordeal (divya) may be employed.
But for those who commit secret crimes, examination by means of ordeals is appropriate,
as well as [judgment] based on reasoning, physical marks, gestures, facial expressions, speech, eyes, and behavior of men.
And in all cases of the highest severity,
Bhṛgu says that one should investigate the true state of affairs by means of divine ordeals when there are no witnesses present.
Where there is equality among witnesses, one should even then purify [the matter] by means of ordeals.
In cases of dispute where the penalty involves the loss of life, if witnesses are available,
the plaintiff who resorts to an ordeal shall not question the witnesses.
For a debt, documentary evidence, witnesses, or even fragments of reasoning,
or divine proof (ordeals) have been declared as means of proof for the subjects out of a desire for their welfare.
A formal demand at the appropriate time, a modicum of logical reasoning, and likewise a third means, an oath— by these, one should recover a debt in due order.
Even if he is repeatedly exhorted, he should not reject those words;
rather, after three, four, or five times, he should act according to the purpose.
But when there is an objection or contradiction,
one should resort to fragments of reasoning based on place, time, the connection between objects, measure, action, and so forth.
Even when arguments are insufficient, one should resolve the matter by means of oaths alone—
such as those involving fire, water, or meritorious deeds— taking into account the nature of the case, the time, and the relative strength of the parties.
Where there may be a document involving fraud, if it has been presented to the king,
the king, seated upon the seat of justice, shall have it cleared by means of an ordeal.
In cases of verbal abuse and regarding land, one should not employ divine ordeals.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should employ ordeals;
however, one should establish the matter through witnesses, documentary evidence, and possession.
In all disputes whatsoever, the lord of men should always reach a definitive conclusion by means of authoritative proofs, through reasoning, or even by divine means.
A written document, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the threefold means of proof; the wise know inference to be the logical reason, and likewise, reasoning.
In the absence of the former, one should proceed by means of the latter alone, and never otherwise— namely,
by means of the proofs adduced by the disputant, such as possession, documents, and witnesses.
No one should cause the accuser to undergo an ordeal;
those expert in ordeals should administer the ordeal to the defendant.
In the case of a false statement, it shall consist of four parts; likewise in the case of a counter-attack (pratyavaskandana).
It should be understood as having two parts in the case of a plea of prior judgment (prāṅnyāya) and in cases of admission (saṃpratipatti).

Defeat is said to be of two kinds: that declared by another and that declared by oneself. The defeat declared by another is of ten types, while that declared by oneself is recorded as being of one type.
The shifting of the debate to another matter, contradiction between the preceding and the following,
refutation by one's own actions, and the justification of the opponent's statement.
The non-indication of the place, the indication of the wrong place and time, the instigation of witnesses, and the suborning of testimony; K_248 //

A document is said to be of two kinds: that written by one's own hand and that written by another; likewise, it may be without witnesses or with witnesses. The validity of these two depends upon their established usage in the particular region.
A document written by the debtor's own hand, accompanied by witnesses, should be known as a "handwritten document" (svahastalekhya); it is declared by the wise to be valid evidence.
One should record the date of birth, the caste, and the amount of wealth;
for one who acts thus, even if he remembers, his unrecorded claim shall perish.
A document, however, should be executed with witnesses, with the sequence of its letters unbroken,
conforming to the established customs of the region, and complete in all its matters.

A written document that is endowed with correct phonemes, syntax, and action; that is free from ambiguity and possesses distinct syllables; and that maintains its sequence and signs without omission—such a document shall attain validity.
The status of the four classes of Vidyādharas, guilds, corporations, citizens, and so forth,
as well as any document written for the purpose of establishing that status, shall be known as a *sthitipatraka* (a deed of status).
When the curse has been lifted and the expiation has been performed by the people,
a certificate of purification should be obtained from them, accompanied by witnesses.
