When all the most excellent [witnesses] have assembled and a formal accusation has been brought forward,
that written record of the events as they occurred is to be known as a *sandhipatra* (a treaty or settlement document).
When a dispute over a boundary has been resolved, a formal deed concerning the boundary is to be prepared.
A royal document is defined as one bearing the king’s own hand,
marked with his seal, and containing witnesses for all matters.
The statements of the plaintiff and the defendant, the testimony of witnesses,
the decision regarding the case, and how it was determined by himself.
One should record this according to the syllables in writing as previously set forth;
first, one should record the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant.

Thereafter, he should cause the decision of the legal treatises (smṛti-śāstra), representing the opinion of the members of the court, the presiding judge, or the families [of witnesses], to be recorded right there.
Once the disputant has been joined with the proven matter, the king, preceded by marks of respect,
should give him a written document bearing his own signature.
And those members of the assembly who are present there, being experts in the treatises on law (smṛti),
should likewise have their own signatures placed there according to the rules for drawing up a document.
The wise know that a document executed according to this procedure is a *paścātkāra*.
However, where a legal action has been refuted by the plaintiff himself through evidence, a *paścātkāra* may be granted; it is not prescribed in all cases.
To those other than those who are deficient in speech and so forth, [the decision] is granted;
and that which is established through the narration of the facts shall be the document of victory (jayapatra).
[Examination of Documents: Having summoned the parties by the king’s command, he should investigate the case according to justice:
a document is examined by the rules governing documents, and witnesses by the rules governing witnesses.

A written document that is endowed with correct phonemes, syntax, and action; that is free from ambiguity and possesses distinct syllables; and that maintains its sequence and formal marks, shall attain validity.
A document is said to be [valid] when it includes the local customs, the year, and the increase in months,
fortnights, and so forth, and bears the hand-signatures of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
When letters have been displaced from their positions, are out of order, are ambiguous,
or deviate from their characteristic forms, then that document is considered a forged writing.
That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which has been executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is devoid of a valid claim— all such deeds are defective.
A document executed by one who is intoxicated, by one who fears a legal restriction, by one who is insane,
by those who are afflicted, by women, or by children or those who are not independent, is not valid.
If, once it has been proclaimed, no one should revoke it on the second day,
then it shall stand as authoritative, except in the case of that which was performed by one who is intoxicated or insane.
A document may indeed be rendered invalid due to the fault of the witnesses, or that of the scribe,
or due to the fault of fraud on the part of the creditor or the debtor.
A document written by the wicked should be declared invalid, while one written by the pure should be declared valid;
such a document [is invalidated] by witnesses, scribes, and executors who are corrupted by fraud.
For those defects of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which are to be stated must be pointed out by the disputant;
however, those that are hidden [but] manifest [to others] should be pointed out by the members of the assembly at the proper time through the citation of authoritative treatises.
Just as the witnesses, the scribe, and the author of the document fall into falsehood,
so too should faults be attributed [to them] by the wicked, for thus the document becomes corrupted.
"If it was not written by the scribe, nor witnessed by the witnesses," when the defendant has stated this, the document is declared to be forged.
One should not invalidate a means of knowledge through a fault that is not factual;
for in the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
In this way, when a case involving a wicked person is being adjudicated in the king's court,
he should deliberate together with Brahmins and examine the defects of the written petition.
By that [same criterion] by which witnesses, scribes, and executors fall into falsehood, by that the document shall be deemed corrupt; one should declare it valid when the parties are pure.
A document written by the creditor's own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall be considered forged unless the maker can prove, "It was indeed executed by me."
If the debtor denies a signature in his own hand that was given on the document,
he shall be questioned by the witnesses recorded in the document or according to the opinion of the scribe.
In disputes concerning what has been done or not done, the determination of the case is made by witnesses through the written document;
if the document is challenged, the plaintiff must then point out those who are recorded therein.
Confusion may arise for people regarding even the three kinds of written documents;
therefore, one should establish their validity through the testimony of the debtor, the witnesses, and the scribe.
Then, if the scribe along with the witnesses has met his death, he shall be purified by their own handwriting and other such evidence; of this there is no doubt.
When there is doubt regarding a debt, whether the debtor is living or dead,
the determination of that document is made by other writings in his own hand.
Even in the ocean, even in a written record, all those who have died remain;
for that which is written is authoritative even when they have passed away.
Direct perception is never sublated by inference;
therefore, the testimony of witnesses may override a defective written document.
For a decision regarding one's own property indeed invalidates the document itself;
a written document must be countered by another written document, and that which has witnesses must be countered by witnesses.

When a false statement has been made, the document shall be cleared by the testimony of the witnesses and the scribe; he who does not purify it when it is proven false shall be made to pay the highest fine.
If one who is capable does not request repayment from a wealthy person standing nearby,
that document may be rendered invalid due to the suspicion that it represents a pure debt.
A document that is more than thirty years old, and which has neither been seen nor heard by [the parties],
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still be present.
But if, when the profit has been realized, the debtor does not produce the written document,
nor does he request it from the creditor, he shall not obtain success in that matter.
Thereafter, one should carefully examine whatever is recorded as a cause;
if it is indeed consistent with reason, then that written document is authoritative.
Otherwise, a legal matter that has been decided once again from afar—
wherein an untruth was established as truth due to a confusion of knowledge—
must be overturned, even if it was carried out with great effort by kings; for such a decision would lack valid authority.
A royal edict attains purity when it is purified by the seal, purified by the formal act, purified by the enjoyment [of the recipient], and provided with its insignia;
it is rendered pure by the king's own hand.
But that document which is proclaimed to be faultless shall attain validity.
If the debtor, upon seeing the document, does not state the manifest defects therein,
then the document, having remained for twenty years, shall be considered valid.
A document by which property is enjoyed for twenty years in the presence of a capable person is free from defects.
If a pledge has been enjoyed for twenty years with absolute certainty,
its validity is established by that document, provided it is free from defects of the writing.
When a boundary dispute has been settled, a boundary document (sīmāpatra) is issued;
its defects must be declared for as long as twenty years.
Where a debt, together with the details of its deposit, is recorded in writing, they know that— even if witnesses have died— it is valid evidence in cases involving small amounts.
If something has been received by him, or if a gift has been bestowed without being formally specified,
even without a seal, such a document is authoritative as evidence when witnesses have died.
If something has been received, or if a designation has been made,
then the document itself is indeed authoritative, even if the witnesses have died.
A document is established as valid in all cases— even when the witnesses have died— if it was presented at the proper time, and if it was accepted and likewise remembered [by the parties].
A written document is never invalidated even by divine witnesses;
for the rule of documentary evidence is always superior, and thus it is not set aside by anything else.
The act of writing should always be avoided by means of a counter-document associated with that [original] or one superior to it; it can never be avoided by any other means.
Just as a reflection in a mirror appears to be real though it is unreal,
so too do skilled people create images for painting.
A document that is delivered to another after having received property, one that is concealed, or one that has been tampered with, or one kept in the house of another; K_309.
Whether the document has been delivered or the object itself has been handed over, and provided it was previously recorded in writing,
this same rule is to be understood as the means for determining the validity of the document.
He who forges a document concerning the sale or mortgage of immovable property shall be thoroughly interrogated and then deprived of his tongue, hands, and feet.
If a painting is marred by stains, burnt, torn, or even faded, one should have another painting made; likewise, if it has been rubbed away by perspiration.

A written document, witnesses, and possession— these three are accepted as means of proof. Among these proofs, for men, possession is traditionally held to be equal in authority to a written document.
When there is doubt regarding the exit from a street, a gate, a watercourse, and so forth,
it is the settled conclusion that possession alone is the weightiest among the means of proof.
An inference is weightier than a witness; a written document is weightier than witnesses;
and possession by three generations, when uncontradicted, is weightier than these.
Neither the one who seized them nor their son should exert force to enjoy cattle, women, men, and so forth; such is the established law.

Enjoyment is said to be of two kinds: with lineage (sāgamā) and without lineage (anāgamā). That which extends through three generations and is independent is [enjoyment] with lineage; however, if it is limited, it is without lineage.
Possession inherited from a grandfather is considered primary, as is that inherited from a father;
when uninterrupted by these three, it is regarded as stable possession for sixty years.
But when that which was eaten is proven by documentary evidence to have been properly consumed, the one who brought it forth recovers it; it must never be taken away from him.
When a plaintiff has lost the written document or relies solely on possession,
he must declare the duration of time, the amount given, and his title in the assembly.
In the period of memory (smārtakāla), possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by title;
in the period beyond memory (asmārta), however, because there is no means of tracing it back, it is valid when it has been passed down through three generations in succession.
In the beginning, however, there is the title-deed; in the middle, possession accompanied by [the document];
but where possession alone has been continuous for three generations, that is the sole title-deed.
The acquirer, even if he possesses possession, must clear the defects of the document;
his son, however, must clear the defects of possession, but shall not incur the defects of the document.
For whatever property has been taken up by someone, that person alone, being the rightful owner, shall recover it;
even if possession has lasted for a long time, such enjoyment is not recognized as belonging to anyone else.
Out of greed, one should not disturb long-standing wealth that has been unknown.

But whatever property was enjoyed by the father in accordance with the practice of enjoyment and according to dharma, when he has died, no objection can be raised against it; for that was obtained by him through such enjoyment.
But if land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law,
even in the absence of a written document, a fourth person may acquire it there.
Just as milk produces curd endowed with flavor after a period of time,
so too does the cause of a gift result in enjoyment for three generations after a lapse of time.
In the scriptures, possession (*bhukti*) that is continuous and long-standing is powerful;
it should be understood as such even if interrupted, provided it was previously established.
One should not entertain desire for women, nor for the wealth of a god or a king;
and children, Vedic scholars, and wealth [are acquired] respectively from the mother and the father.
A certain man might practice celibacy for thirty-six years without observing the vows,
or a man seeking wealth might dwell in another country for a long time.
After returning from his studies, one who has not yet taken up the vows of a householder may then seek out his own wealth;
possession for fifty years constitutes the seizure of that wealth.
It is traditionally taught that twelve years is the period for those seeking knowledge;
for those seeking the knowledge of crafts, it is proclaimed to last until mastery is attained.
Whatever property of these men was enjoyed by their friends and kinsmen while they were unaware of it,
and likewise that of those who offended the king, does not lapse with the passage of time.

Whatever has been enjoyed by kinsmen of the same lineage, by relatives, and likewise by one's own people—there is no accomplishment through enjoyment in that case; one should direct the enjoyment elsewhere.
[The Principle:
But he who, being requested by a petitioner, does not provide assistance,
shall become a debtor to that other person after three, four, or five attempts.
Giving, causing [the enemy] to be apprehended, sowing dissension, the act of enticement,
and the removal of their resolve— these indeed are the means for causing [the enemy] to waste away.

Whichever among these has been established by the proponent, that shall constitute the fundamental proof; however, if the proponent retracts what he has established, then the burden of proof falls upon him.
The king must not allow a delay in the testimony of witnesses;
for through time, a great evil arises characterized by the turning away from Dharma.
The king himself should examine the witnesses who have been presented;
he should investigate the statement spoken by the witnesses together with the members of the court.
The time for witnesses to be summoned is when there is a need for a thorough understanding of the correct course of action;
however, where the testimony is doubtful, one should settle the dispute immediately and clearly.
Within the assembly, the presiding judge, consoling them, shall appoint all the witnesses in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant according to this rule:
Whatever you two know of each other’s mutual conduct regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for your witness is required here.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either north or east.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are all of known conduct and who understand the matter— one should question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths.
But that which has been personally experienced due to the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant—that testimony of the witnesses must be accepted; otherwise, it is not so, says Bṛhaspati.
Those who are of renowned family and character, free from greed and delusion,
trustworthy, pure, and distinguished— their testimony is undoubtedly valid.
A witness should be examined by the litigant in such a manner that they are of equal status;
one who is superior or inferior should never be made to testify as a witness.
Bhṛgu spoke to the wearers of sectarian marks, to guilds and associations, to groups of merchants, and to others who exist as collectives, as well as to other classes of people.
Among the groups of slaves, wandering performers, wrestlers, and those who live by elephants, horses, and weapons—
each having its own leaders and members—
their disputes within their respective groups are settled by those members acting as witnesses among them.
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes.
Where it is impossible for residents of a foreign land to appear in person,
one should admit documentary evidence sent by those learned in the three Vedas as proof.
In the case of a deposit, however, even a single witness may be declared;
even a single messenger sent by the plaintiff becomes a witness.
Whatever commodity has been refined by whom, that he alone shall demonstrate;
in a dispute concerning it, he alone is declared to be the authority.
The scribe, the presiding judge, and the members of the court, in their respective order,
are declared to be witnesses when they observe the case while the king is looking on.
Furthermore, others who have not been specifically designated are declared to be witnesses for litigants:
the village headman, the presiding judge, and the king.
One who is an insider in legal affairs, one who has been sent by the plaintiff, and members of a family in disputes concerning that family— these also may be witnesses.
But when a dispute regarding the division of inheritance arises and doubt is present, the testimony of the kinsmen is the authority in that case; in their absence, [the testimony of] others.
Among witnesses— whether they are written down or specifically designated by the plaintiff—
if even one of them speaks otherwise than the rest, all are disqualified as witnesses due to that discrepancy.
For one person should not bring a lawsuit against another on behalf of a witness who was appointed by someone else;
in his absence, however, either a commissioned agent or a relative may bring the suit.
Furthermore, those who live by his profession, those who perform services for him,
his kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates are not eligible to be witnesses.
Daughters of maternal aunts, sons of uterine brothers, and sons of maternal uncles—these are declared to be "sapinda" (blood relations); one should not employ them as witnesses.

Relatives by birth, kinsmen, those with whom one has formed a marriage alliance, the husband of one’s sister, the father, a paternal relative, a paternal uncle, a father-in-law, and likewise teachers;
Those royal officers appointed to positions in cities, villages, and districts,
as well as those who are favorites and devoted, shall not be questioned.
In matters such as debts and in cases involving stable transactions, one should examine the witnesses;
in cases of violence and urgent offenses, examination is likewise prescribed in certain instances.
In cases of obstruction of the king’s command, in matters of seizure and acts of violence,
and likewise in theft and verbal assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.
If the accusation concerns what occurred inside a house at night, or outside a village,
one should not examine witnesses in these cases.
Testimony should never be spoken by witnesses unless they are questioned by the plaintiff;
testimony should not be offered among them unless one applies it to oneself.
The written record and the testimony of witnesses are endowed with two paths.

Now, if that very same person, having ascended by his own hand, should remain standing alone and yet fail to recognize [the others], one should establish [his identity] by means of those very hands of his.

A witness who is brought by the plaintiff himself and recorded in the document is called a "written witness" (likhita-sākṣin); one who is not present on the document is called a "reminded witness" (smārta).
But that witness who, having seen the matter for the sake of accomplishing the legal case, is reminded again and again by the plaintiff— is called "one who has been reminded" (smārita) here.
One who has been brought for a specific purpose and one who has arrived by chance—
these two, though not recorded as witnesses, are effective in proving the plaintiff's case.
He who, remaining hidden, has been clearly informed by the plaintiff for the sake of establishing his own case regarding the statement of the defendant,
is called a secret witness.
That witness who gives testimony repeatedly,
either by hearing it himself or by causing others to hear it, is designated as an *uttara-sākṣin* (subsequent witness).
He who, through his trustworthiness, is told what should be whispered or informed of a task,
and who likewise understands the mission, is to be known as a secret agent.
Where the plaintiff has perished, there the witness is one whose testimony is based on hearsay;
and where the defendant has perished, it is likewise ruled in that case.

[The disclosure of defects in witnesses: Whatever defects of the document may exist, as well as those attributed to the witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been stated.
But he who, when the meaning of the statement has been established, should defame witnesses who have not previously been defamed,
and does not state the reason for that [defamation], shall incur the first amercement.
One should not invalidate a means of valid cognition through a fault that is not untrue;
however, in the case of a false accusation, one shall be punished and shall also lose the matter to be proven.
Furthermore, when the defendant or the plaintiff establishes a defect in the witnesses,
this does not constitute a separate legal proceeding, because it is relevant to the matter at hand.
The defects of the witnesses must be declared by the defendant in the assembly;
having written all of them down on a document, he should then state his rebuttal.
But they can never serve as witnesses regarding the actual practice [of the rite];
therefore, they must be conceived otherwise by the defendant through his action.
If the defendant fails to substantiate his claim for wealth, he must be compelled to pay it;
all witnesses who have been produced must be clearly examined according to the rules governing witnesses.
One should discern the internal state of that person through their facial expressions, bodily gestures, and movements;
thus, the opponent is recognized as being defeated by means of inference.
Trembling, perspiration, then agitation, dryness of the lips, touching [the ground], scratching the earth, loss of one's position, looking sideways or upwards,
and a change in the voice— these the wise declare to be the signs of a corrupted [witness].
Witnesses must give their testimony while remaining within the assembly hall, and not elsewhere;
for this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.

In the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, and while the subject matter of the suit is present, one should give testimony directly; never under any circumstances should one give it out of sight.
The meaning [of the rule] should be stated above; in some cases, it applies even without those two.
This law applies to four-footed creatures as well as to bipeds and immovable beings.
Even in the absence of weights, measures, or commodities to be measured, one may dispute;
in all formal agreements, witness-hood applies, and not otherwise than that.
If there is the killing of living beings, one should cause the witness to speak in the presence of Śiva;
in the absence of that, however, one should not cause it to be proclaimed otherwise than by means of a mark.
The testimony of those witnesses, which is stated spontaneously and free from defects, must be accepted;
once it has been spoken, the witnesses should not be questioned again by the king.
Whatever they may say by its very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is meaningless.
But that which is seen by those assembled together must be stated exactly as it was;
however, that which pertains to individual or separate tasks must be stated separately for each.
But when a matter is discovered at a different time, Bhṛgu says that one should have each witness questioned there separately; for that is what constitutes a "separate occasion."
In disputes concerning debts and the like, which are generally of a stable nature, once a decision has been reached,
the matter to be proven is not established if the amount stated is either less or more than the truth.
Even when the portion of the matter to be proven has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established;
this applies to matters involving sexual intercourse, violent acts, and theft, which have been determined as the points to be proven.
But where there may be a deficiency or an excess, one should reject that testimony;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
Where a witness contradicts [the facts regarding] place, time, wealth, number, form, caste, appearance, or age, the wise know that testimony to be unspoken.
If a witness, when questioned regarding the matters specified,
does not speak in accordance with the facts as they occurred, that testimony shall not be considered properly delivered.
Where witnesses state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too should be known as improper; this is the determination regarding witnesses.
[The Faults and Punishments of Witnesses: When witnesses speak entirely without being questioned, or likewise fail to speak when questioned,
they should be restrained, censured, and punished according to the law.
In cases of verbal abuse, fraud, or litigation, they shall be fined three hundred panas;
in disputes concerning debts and the like, they shall be made to pay the money, and likewise the debt itself.
That lowest of men who, though not designated as a witness, nor summoned, nor even presented,
should speak either falsely or even the truth, he too shall be punished.
If a witness does not state the testimony, he shall bear the debt and pay an equal fine;
in other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred [paṇas].
And those who, having spoken one way, speak otherwise, being possessed of verbal quibbling, should be punished.
Having confiscated all the property of one by whom false witnesses were appointed out of greed for the outcome of a case, he should thereafter banish him from the realm.
When the matter has indeed been established by witnesses for the plaintiff,
if the defendant should then prove the case otherwise,
the former witnesses shall be considered false witnesses, especially if they are numerous or of noble birth.
When an action is purified through logical reasoning, then its verbal expression is purified;
and that which is purified from a purified verbal expression is the purified meaning—this is the established principle.
One should recognize that a witness speaks falsely when, within seven days, illness, fire, or the death of a kinsman occurs; or within fourteen or twenty-one days;
or even within forty-six days, depending on the differences in the nature of the object and other factors.
[The divine ordeals and the rules concerning their subject matter:
No one should cause the accuser to undergo the divine ordeals;
the experts in divine ordeals should administer the ordeal to the accused.
For those who are suspected by kings, one should employ the balance and other ordeals;
however, in the performance of self-purification, one should not include the [ordeal of] the head.

For those who are defiled by public scandal and those suspected by bandits, scales and other such ordeals should be employed; however, Bhṛgu says that the head ordeal should certainly not be used in those cases.
One should never employ head-caskets for doubtful cases;
rather, one should cause headless divine ordeals to be administered to the king’s officers.
In matters of suspicion or establishing trust, in the partitioning of inheritance among heirs, and in the performance of collective undertakings, one should always cause a deposit (kośa) to be made.
Where there is a denial of what has been given, one should determine the proof;
in cases of theft or violence, one should cause an ordeal to be administered even when the matter is of small value.
Having ascertained the measure of all the substances, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [image].
Having calculated the number of gold pieces, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
however, upon the loss of eighty, one should indeed offer oneself to the fire.
If sixty [coins] are lost, water should be given as an ordeal; for forty, indeed, a jar [of water];
and for the loss of twenty or ten, the drinking of holy water (kośapāna) is prescribed.
Or, upon the loss of more than five [māṣakas], there should be rice [as a fine] equal to half of that;
but upon the loss of half of that again, one should touch the head of a son or another [relative].
But when even half of that half is lost, worldly activities are prescribed;
reflecting thus, a king does not fall away from dharma and artha.

[The regulations for divine ordeals according to the caste and craft of the plaintiff and defendant: One should employ fire in the case of a Kṣatriya, the water-pot (ghaṭa) in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, and water in the case of a Vaiśya;
or one may employ any divine ordeal for all castes, except poison, which is to be avoided for the twice-born.
He should cause those who tend cattle, merchants, artisans, actors,
servants, and usurers to treat the twice-born like Śūdras.

One should never administer fire to metalworkers, water to those who subsist on water, nor poison to those who know the application of mantras. One should not employ rice-grains as a test for one who observes a vow or one who suffers from diseases of the mouth.
One should avoid fire for those suffering from skin diseases, water for those with asthma and coughing,
and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with disorders of bile and phlegm.
The treasury should not be given by the wise to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the way of nihilism.
For those who kill their mother, father, a twice-born, a teacher, children, women, or a king;
for those burdened with mortal sins (mahāpātaka), and especially for atheists.
But for those who bear the marks [of asceticism], who are arrogant, who know the rituals of mantras and yoga,
who are born from the mixture of castes, and who persist in the practice of evil—
In these very charges and in those that are censurable, a king devoted to dharma should not, with effort, administer an ordeal.
Those virtuous persons appointed by these very [means] deserve the ordeal by divine [test].
Where virtuous persons do not consent, there those to be cleared should be tested by their own men.
The ordeal must not be administered to those guilty of mortal sins, especially to atheists,
nor to those who are habitually engaged in sinful acts.
In these disputes, divine ordeals are strictly prohibited;
one should have them performed by honest men, for Manu says that one who has been falsely accused should not be abandoned.
For those who are untouchable, the lowest of slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions, there is no fixed rule regarding the king;
in cases of doubt concerning them, one should prescribe the ordeals well-known among them.
[The divine regions:
One should employ these [mantras] at the royal gate for those who have committed great sins, who are accused in the abode of Indra, and who have engaged in treason against the king.
For those born of inverse unions, the ordeal should be administered at a crossroads;
for others besides these, the wise know that the ordeal should be administered in the midst of the assembly hall.
But when there is a conflict regarding time or place, one should determine what is appropriate;
in such a case of reversal, one should have the ordeal administered by another person—this is the rule.
Those [mantras] given at an improper place or time, and those performed outside of the dwelling,
undoubtedly cause deviation from the true purpose in this world.
Indeed, when there is a contradiction with the means of proof, one should establish that which is to be proven once again;
for even if the divine ordeals have been administered as prescribed, the king should avoid them [if they are flawed],
and they must certainly be administered again by those who are foolish, greedy, or corrupt.
Therefore, the experts should administer the ordeal according to the prescribed rule;
for when applied contrary to the rule, it is not capable of establishing the truth.
If the sling breaks, or the balance beam, or likewise the cord,
or if there is doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man again.

[The Procedure for the Fire Ordeal: If the accused stumbles or is burned in a place other than the designated spot, the gods do not consider him burnt; one should have him undergo the ordeal once more.
[The Procedure for the Divine Water Test:
For the sake of purity, one should prepare arrows with tips not made of iron;
they may even be made of bamboo stalks, and the thrower should discharge them with great firmness.
When [the vessel] has been cast [into the water], one must perform the immersion; the departure is simultaneous [with the casting].
Upon the departure, however, the return must be performed; another man shall enter the water.
If, upon entering the water, only his head should be seen and neither his ears nor his nose, one should declare that person also to be pure.
If a man who has submerged himself is seen by living beings as he emerges,
he should submerge once more in that very place, which is identified by its local landmarks.
[The Procedure for the Poison and Divine Ordeals:
That which resembles a goat's horn, dark green, and very thick, produced from a horn,
and which has the appearance of ginger when broken— that is known as the poison of horned animals.
One should make that red [substance] black and hard according to its characteristics;
by this method, the divine [nature] is to be known by those expert in the divine.
Yellow and resembling the vatsanābha [poison], this is the certainty through the knowledge of its color;
one should recognize it as vatsanābha when its fracture has the shape of a pearl-oyster shell or a conch.
When combined with honey and milk, it becomes clear in that very instant;
thus has the external characteristic been described by those who accomplish the Dharma.
In the forenoon, one should administer poison to living beings in a cool place;
it should be finely ground, mixed with thirty times its weight of clarified butter, and made smooth.
From six palas of poison, that portion which is the twentieth part should be taken;
having reduced it by one-eighth, it should be given to the person to be cleared, saturated with clarified butter.
[The Procedure for the Divine Ordeal of the Treasure: When the offense is slight, one should cause the gods to bathe in water infused with weapons;
he who drinks it and undergoes no physical change is pure, while one who is impure shall be restrained. Otherwise, he is pure.
[The Procedure for Rice] Regarding the divine consumption of rice for the bathing water of the deities:
one who has spat out pure saliva is pure and may be employed; otherwise, one is impure.
If a person is accused while under arrest, even if he is proven pure by means of the treasury [of evidence],
the king should compel the accuser to pay both a fine and the legal costs;
however, a righteous king should honor a man who has been proven pure by ordeal.
Where blood is seen, where the jaw-hair droops,
and whose body trembles— one should designate such a person as impure.
Then, if there is a discrepancy with fate, after three times seven days,
one should cause the accused to pay that matter with effort, as well as a fine.
If that disease, fire, death of a kinsman, or debt were to befall only one person and not the entire community, he alone shall be made to pay the fine.
Consumption, dysentery, and eruptions, pain in the palate and bones,
eye disease, throat disease,
as well as insanity, headache, and the breaking of the arms— these are the divine diseases that arise for men.
One who is pure should be made to pay fifty; one who is impure shall be subject to punishment.
One should prescribe punishment in order for poison, water, fire, the balance, the sacred vessel (kośa), rice grains,
and the ordeal of the heated gold coin (taptamāṣaka).
One should arrange one thousand, six hundred, five hundred,
and likewise four, three, two, or even one [of the offerings] in descending order for those who are inferior.
[The Procedure for Oaths:
Where a ritual action is prescribed but the specific limb of the performer is not mentioned,
it should be understood that the right hand is the one that carries the action to completion.
If no terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone within fourteen days, he should be known as pure in his oath.

[An Examination of What Is Done by the Insane, the Dependent, and Others: Whatever is given or whatever is done by one who is insane, intoxicated, or likewise under the influence of another state of being— that shall have no legal validity whatsoever.
The master should annul any transaction performed by one who is not independent;
no one other than the master may dispute it, except in cases involving what was done by one who is terrified or insane.
A father who lacks independence, a son, a brother, or even a nephew; one who is younger, or one whose property is undivided; likewise a slave or a laborer.
Transactions involving fields, houses, or slaves— whether gifts, mortgages, or sales— performed by those who are not independent do not attain validity, nor have they been so described.
All of these are authoritative in the buying and selling of merchandise,
provided that they are approved even as they carry out their transactions.
In the same way, the brother, the brother's son, or the son may act for the fields and other assets if they have been authorized by the departing elder to perform his duties.
But he who has been authorized with full power regarding a particular matter is indeed the master in that matter;
his employer cannot undo the business transacted by him otherwise than as done.
A father has authority over his son’s wife in matters of instruction,
but he has no authority over his son regarding sale or gift.
[The function of determination: Purification has been declared by those who know the true principles of the scriptures to be medical treatment;
it is traditionally held to be twofold, consisting of expiation and punishment.
Even when multiple claims are brought forward, the creditor receives only as much wealth as he establishes through witnesses;
only that much proven wealth does he obtain.
Bṛhaspati states that one who, having made a total denial, should later confess even a small portion of it, must be made to pay the entire amount when charged.
Thus, seated upon the seat of justice and remaining impartial, the judge should observe the determination of legal cases together with Brahmins, and not otherwise.
Having personally examined the legal proceedings, either by seeing them himself or hearing them from the presiding judge,
the king should then issue a certificate of victory for the sake of formal recognition.
[The Procedure for Punishment:
The king, however, should cause a Brahmin to pay the debt to the owner by means of peaceful persuasion alone;
but others who are wicked, he should cause to pay by inflicting pressure according to local custom.
Bhṛgu declared that one should cause even an heir or a friend to pay by means of artifice; this applies likewise to merchants, farmers, and artisans.
Having ascertained that he is unable to pay the fine, one should compel him to perform labor under one's own supervision;
if he is incapable of even that, he should be cast into prison, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa.
But he should cause the cultivators—whether they be Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras—who are making an effort [to pay], to pay [the tax].
In the case of offenses committed against the teacher, the father, the mother, and likewise one's kinsmen, no punishment whatsoever is prescribed for them.
But where an improper act has been committed in a situation involving the loss of life, there shall be no punishment at all; this is the law remembered by Bhṛgu.
One must never kill a Brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of sin;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and unharmed.
For members of all four castes who fail to perform penance,
the king shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both their person and their property.
By whatever fault a Śūdra incurs a punishment according to the law, if that same fault is committed by a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be double, double [the penalty].
A Śūdra who has entered the life of a renunciant and is devoted to the recitation of prayers and burnt offerings,
if he commits a sin, should be punished by death or else fined double the usual penalty.
In all offenses, whatever monetary fine is prescribed for a man, women shall pay half of that; however, in the case of killing, the man's limb shall be cut off.
Women who are not independent should not be held accountable; in such cases, it is the man who commits the offense.
They are to be disciplined by their master, but the king shall deal with the man.
If a woman whose husband is away from home is apprehended,
she shall be kept in confinement for as long as it takes for her lord to return.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular offense, that fine shall be collected from the offender with diligence,
or its equivalent value shall be paid to the king.
Wherever a fine is imposed, whether it be one māṣa or two māṣas,
it should be understood that if not specifically stated, one māṣaka is to be prescribed.
Where a fine is stated in *māṣakas*, one should specify that it is in silver;
where it is stated in *kṛṣṇalas*, that indeed shall be the determination of the stated fine.
A māṣa should be known as one-twentieth of a kārṣāpaṇa;
a kākaṇī, however, is one-fourth of a māṣaka and of a paṇa.
In the region of the Five Rivers, this is the conventional terminology:
four *kārṣāpaṇa* coins are known as one *dhānaka*;
twelve of those are a *suvarṇa*; and a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
[Furthermore, the legal principle:

That position which is determined by the members of the court as "unreal" or "real" is declared to be "decided," whereas that which is established through the testimony of witnesses is proclaimed as "adjudicated."
But for one who has not attained satisfaction even when [the truth] has been ascertained by his family and others,
the king, having investigated that deed, should overturn what was wrongly done.
[Consideration of Interest on Loans] One should never grant a loan to women, slaves, or children;
the lender does not recover that [interest], though he may give them whatever wealth he possesses.
However, whatever interest exceeding [the legal rate] has been stipulated by the debtor,
being contracted during a time of distress, must always be paid as agreed;
otherwise, interest that is not so agreed shall never be paid under any circumstances.
But where one should purify the interest so that it increases exclusively,
and [the debtor] pays it at every period, that is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (compound interest).
Satisfaction is proclaimed as the fruit from the house, and the acquisition of enjoyments from the field.
But that which is entirely for the purpose of enjoyment, where interest is merely nominal,
and where such is the application [of the loan], that is called "enjoyment-pledge" (ādhibhoga).
[Ākṛtavṛddhi]:
If one who has taken a loan should depart for another region without returning it,
that debt shall bear interest after the lapse of one year.
If one who has been asked for a loan makes an advance but departs for another region without returning it,
that debt shall accrue interest after the lapse of three months.
But if one who resides even in his own country does not pay when requested at any time,
the king shall compel him to pay that interest which has accrued, even if he is unwilling.
A gift given out of affection does not increase so long as it has not been asked for;
however, if it is not returned when requested, it increases by five percent per month.
Interest on a deposit, the remainder of interest, and likewise profit from buying and selling—
if these are not paid when demanded, they increase by five percent per hundred.
If one who has taken merchandise should depart for another region without paying the price,
that wealth shall accrue interest after three seasons have passed.
Interest shall never accrue on leather, grain, liquor, stakes in gambling, the price of goods, the bride-price for women, and debts incurred as surety.
The amount of interest to be taken shall always be double the principal lent by creditors;
if he does not receive the double, he may again stipulate further interest.
The profit on gems, pearls, corals, gold, silver, and on woven cloth,
woolen blankets, and sheepskins remains doubled.
The increase for all types of oils, as well as for liquors, clarified butter,
molasses, and salt, should be known to be eightfold.
Base metals are considered to be fivefold [the value of the land], and land likewise eightfold;
because of the statement "immediately," it is delivered immediately.
[Discharge of Debt] [The Rule for When Multiple Debts Are Combined]: That debt which has been recorded on a single day, one should discharge as an equal sum.
Grasping, protecting, and obtaining; otherwise, however, they follow in their respective order.
But when there is a combination of various debts, whichever was contracted first must be paid first; after that, the debt to the king and the one to a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) shall be paid.
If one should prove that a commodity was acquired by means of another's property,
that property must be returned by the debtor to him alone, and not otherwise.
If, having taken a substance as collateral, one gives it for the sake of interest so that it may be used,
whether it be movable or immovable, that is called a pledge for use (bhogyādhi).
Having paid a higher price, one may acquire one's own field and so forth.
If one should make a deposit with two persons, what should be the procedure?
Of those two, the prior agreement is to be accepted; the one who violates it shall receive the punishment of a thief.
When a document concerning a mortgage, sale,
or gift is contradicted by a single act, that document is considered fraudulent.
Kātyāyana declared that a document which is unspecified, specified, and written in one place, yet contains a specific detail, is superior.
If one were to first assume something non-existent, whose nature is unindicated and which is like space, that [assumption] would itself remain unindicated;
whatever might exist for him at that time, that he should point out as being indicated.
But if one were to deposit all one's property after first marking it with one's name both before and after,
how could that not be more strongly established as marked?
When a field or even a village is marked by boundary signs,
and those villages and so forth are recorded [in writing], then one shall attain success.
But whatever has been pledged as collateral that is destroyed by fate or by the king,
the debtor shall be made to pay the debt to the creditors along with interest.
If, however, [the debtor] should fall ill or die due to a fault of the creditor,
the debtor shall be released from the debt, provided that the creditor makes him pay for another pledge.
If one should compel a person to perform work against their will and without their consent, he shall be made to pay the fruit of that labor; he does not receive interest.
But he who, while another is performing work as a pledge, should oppress or threaten him with words, physical force, or acts,
shall incur the first amercement.
If one should forcibly enter a pledge that was not surrendered and which one does not desire,
he shall incur the first degree of violence, and the pledgor shall recover his pledge.
If a creditor enjoys a pledge by means of a fraudulent document from a debtor,
the king, having caused him to pay a fine, shall cause that fraudulent document of pledge to be destroyed.

But where there is no depositor, the creditor shall report the pledge to the king; then it is the established rule that it may be sold publicly. Having received the amount together with interest, he should hand over the remainder to the king.
[The Procedure for Sureties]:
In matters of gifts, attendance, and disputes, as well as for the purpose of trust and oaths, one should certainly cause a surety to be taken; in other cases, it should be done accordingly.
If a surety for appearance does not produce the defendant at the proper place and time,
he shall pay the debt therefrom, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
For the purpose of searching for what has been lost, however, a period of up to three fortnights should be granted;
if he can produce it there, the surety shall be released.
If, after the lapse of time, the surety does not produce that person, he shall be made to pay that debt; this same rule is ordained even in the case of his death.
Wherever a pledge has been taken such that the debtor remains under its obligation,
the son shall be made to pay that debt from his own wealth, even in the absence of his father.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
he shall pay the debt from his own property to that person if he fails to produce him.
The first two [types of witnesses], if found to be false, shall be made to pay the wealth that was reported at the time [of the transaction];
the latter two, however, in case of contradiction, shall be made to pay it, as shall their sons in their absence.
If all the sons reside under one roof, they should pay the debt together; however, if the father is away on a journey, the son should pay it.
But when the father has died, Bṛhaspati says that the son shall pay only his own paternal share, not the debts of others.
When those who have entered under a single liability are seen there, they must pay;
if the debtor is away on a journey, his son must pay the whole; but if he is dead, the son must pay the father's share.
But he who, being pressured, gives a guarantee for another while himself being guaranteed,
shall be entitled to receive double the amount of that property after three fortnights have passed.
For whatever purpose, by whomsoever, and whatever was given according to the prescribed rule upon being requested,
the surety shall receive that very thing when he has been proven [guilty] by the witnesses.
In the event of a breach of a solemn agreement (satyaṃkāra), one should cause double the amount to be paid;
for if he does not do so, that [agreement] shall be lost—this is the purpose of the solemn agreement.

One should know that a debt contracted by a father or others for the sake of the family, or taken out by one who is incapable or afflicted by illness, or incurred due to a calamity, is considered a debt contracted in times of distress.
Whatever was done for the marriage of a daughter and whatever was performed for funeral rites—
all this that was done by the family must be given to the master.
According to the law, a debt incurred by a son need not be paid by the father;
however, that which has been promised or which has been approved must be paid.
Bhṛgu says that even for one who is away on a journey, a debt contracted for the sake of the family by a slave,
a wife, a mother, a pupil, or a son, shall be paid.
A debt contracted in this manner—whether jointly with a husband or a son, or by oneself alone—must be paid; otherwise, that which was contracted by a woman [alone] need not be paid.

If a woman is declared by her husband who is desirous of dying, "This debt must be paid by you," she shall be compelled to pay it even if she has not consented, provided that wealth was entrusted to her.
Even if he is afflicted by disease or has gone abroad from his own country,
a debt contracted by the father must be paid by the sons within twenty years.
In the case of those who are diseased, insane, or aged, as well as those who have been away on long journeys,
one should cause such debts to be paid by their sons, even while the fathers are still alive.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons once it has been proven;
this applies even if the father is blind from birth, an outcast, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, or similar diseases.
Since fathers are liberated from their lowest debt only by means of the gifts made by the sons born to them,
for that reason fathers desire sons.
When the father has passed away, the inheritance must never be given by one who has not yet attained the legal capacity for transactions;
rather, it should be given at the proper time according to the prescribed rule. Otherwise, they shall dwell in hell.
If one who has not attained legal capacity is independent even here, he remains liable for debt;
for independence is traditionally attributed to the eldest, based on seniority, virtue, and age.
That which was seen by [the father] or remains after what was given is the paternal debt that must be paid;
however, a debt that is defective, contested by the father, or not at all given by him should never be paid.

But as for the debt seen by the father that has descended in succession from the grandfather, which was free from defect and not discharged by the sons, it must be paid by the grandsons; so says Bhṛgu.
But that which was ancestral property not given by the sons while they were living in a state of illness—
of such a kind, the ancestral share must be given equally by the grandsons.
One should compel the son to pay the debt if he is free from affliction, capable of wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not compel the son to pay.
Whatever must always be given by the fathers, in their absence it should be paid from that wealth;
or else that wealth should be given to the owner of it by the sons or the grandsons.
While the debt to the ancestors remains unpaid, a son shall not take the inheritance;
that wealth must be given to the creditor, for he who takes it after [the father] has died shall be made to pay it back.
In the absence of a son, however, the debt must be paid diligently by the grandson;
it should not be paid by the fourth descendant, for it ceases with him.
A grandson must never pay a debt incurred through suretyship;
however, a father’s debt must always be paid by his son, even if he is still a minor.
The debt must be paid by the inheritor of the estate; in his absence, by the wife;
in her absence, by the sons; and in their absence, by others entitled to inherit the property, in due order.
As long as a son does not obtain existing paternal property,
the debtor shall not be made to pay, even if the son is very wealthy.
Whether it be a written document or a verbal promise,
whatever has been promised to a woman who previously belonged to another, one should know that among men this is done out of lust.
For that which is spoken after having produced violence or having destroyed property out of anger, even if it brings satisfaction, one should know that to be "done out of anger."
Whether healthy or afflicted, one should give what has been promised for the sake of dharma;
if he dies without having given it, his son must be made to pay—of this there is no doubt.
But whatever debt has been contracted by those who are destitute, childless, or such as liquor-sellers and the like,
the one who enjoys their wives must indeed pay that debt.
The supervisor of the wives of a vintner, a hunter, a moneylender, a cowherd,
or a sailor shall be made to pay their debts incurred in the business activities of their husbands.
And a debt incurred by a wife shall never belong to the husband, except for what was contracted during a time of distress;
for men have extensive obligations toward the maintenance of their family.
Except in the case of the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and liquor-sellers;
for their livelihood is dependent on those [professions], and their families rely upon them.
If a woman, being without a husband, should resort to another man for the sake of her son,
that wealth must be taken away by the son alone, excluding the daughters.
One should take up the thread for the sake of the debt, never for the sake of pleasure;
for one should not cause the parents to pay when there is no justifiable reason.
If a woman who has sons, even if she is capable, should abandon her own son after having taken his mother’s property,
Manu says that the father’s debt must be cleared from that property.

And when a woman with young children has recourse to another man for the sake of her husband's welfare, the one she has resorted to shall pay that debt; this is declared to be the rule regarding women with young children.

Property belonging to those who have been away on a long journey, those who are friendless, the dull-witted, the insane, the afflicted, or those wearing the marks of a religious order, must be given to them even while they are still alive by those who hold their wives' property.
When a son is overwhelmed by calamity, or when a child is seen [to be incapable], the one who took the property must be made to pay; in his absence, the one who took the wife must pay.
First, the one who takes the wealth shall give; after him, the one who takes the wife;
in the absence of a daughter, or if the son is utterly destitute, the son himself shall give.

A debt contracted by a wife must be paid by her husband, and a debt contracted by a mother must be paid by her son; likewise, that which was contracted for the sake of the husband must be paid if she has departed to another region after having declared it.
That which is done for the sake of a son should be considered as given;
likewise that which has been described, that which was done without being requested, and that which was performed after hearing it but not being urged.
A debtor who has been detained should be held publicly in an assembly of people until he pays what is due,
in accordance with the established customs of the region.
If a person being carried should feel the urge to void excrement or urine,
he should be followed behind, or one should release him once he has been securely bound.
Having provided a guarantor, he should be released day by day;
at the time of eating and at night, the guarantor remains bound.
He who cannot find a guarantor for his appearance, nor can rely upon one,
should be confined in prison or kept under guard after being informed of the matter.
A noble person who is trustworthy and pure should not be confined in prison;
whether he is unbound or bound by oath, he should be released.
A creditor who has first attempted to recover his debt through labor, legal proceedings, and conciliation may then compel the debtor to pay by means of confinement and restriction.
He may take wealth in this manner, whether by pretext or by conduct; he should cause the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—whether they be of equal or inferior status—to pay it through their labor.
One should cause a king, a master, or a Brahmin to pay by means of conciliation alone;
however, one should settle with an heir or a friend even through deception.
Bhṛgu said to the merchants, the farmers, and the artisans:
"They should be made to pay according to local custom; having oppressed the wicked, one should cause them to pay."
But where a creditor oppresses a debtor who speaks justly,
he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to its value.
For if he should cause an unrighteous act to be performed that was not previously commanded,
he would first incur the penalty for violence, and the debtor would be released from his debt.
He who takes a loan or other such items and does not return them to the owner is born as that person's slave, servant, wife, or animal in his household.
[The Deposit]: That which is deposited by one who has gone abroad, that which is placed as a pledge, that which is sent for delivery, that which is borrowed,
and that which is handed over in exchange for the livelihood of a Vaiśya— that is known as *upanidhi*.
Whatever has been deposited with someone, that person should protect it with effort;
any destruction of it other than what is caused by fate or the king is declared to be his own fault.
If anything is destroyed or stolen through his fault,
he shall be made to pay for that property with interest, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
If the object is destroyed immediately after being requested—even if the destruction was caused by fate or the king—the borrower must be made to pay its value; of this there is no doubt.
He who has consumed, neglected, or destroyed another's property through ignorance must be made to restore that very thing.
If [the deposit] has been consumed, he shall be made to pay it with interest; if it has been neglected, he shall be made to pay its equivalent;
if it has been destroyed through negligence, he shall be made to pay a small portion less.
If a deposit, even when not caused by the king or fate, is lost where it was placed,
that loss is said to belong to the depositor along with the goods, provided they were not taken back by the recipient.
If the giver deposits [the object] with someone after learning of the loss of his own property,
the receiver shall not be made to pay it back even if all means of recovery have failed.
For whatever is lost due to the fault of the purchaser belongs to the purchaser;
when that [item] is lost or stolen, the buyer shall pay its value.
A deposit should be reclaimed at the proper time; however, one should avoid reclaiming it when the time has passed.
One who returns it after the time has elapsed is subject to a fine and must be made to pay double the value.
These rules have been proclaimed for all types of deposits.

If the deposit is being processed by the artisan over a fixed number of days, he should complete it after that period; even if it is damaged by fate, the artisan must restore it and be made to pay for it.
If destruction occurs due to a fault in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), that [liability] shall not be imposed upon the artisan;
however, if it is due to a fault of the artisan, he shall be made to provide for the restoration of whatever was entrusted for that purpose.
Moreover, if even a very small amount of work is lost by a hired servant,
it shall be sufficient cause for that master to lose his wages if he refuses to accept the labor already performed.

If, having been requested for the sake of a specific task or with a fixed time limit, he does not deliver it when that task is half-finished or when the time has not yet arrived, he shall not be compelled to pay.
If a task has been performed when the time for it had arrived, one should not pay even when asked;
or, if that [work] has perished, the recipient shall recover the value.
If, when being entreated, he does not give, he shall be compelled to pay it along with interest.
Moreover, if there is a failure in the work, that loss shall fall upon the employer himself;
however, if the time has not yet arrived, he must be made to pay even for work that is only half-finished.
He who, having taken a loan, does not return it when asked, shall be seized by force and compelled to pay; and he who does not pay at all shall be fined.
When, following up on a transaction, one says "You should give this to another" by my word, that which is thus delivered is called here an *anvādhi* (sub-mortgage).
[On Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner:
He shall annul a sale by one who is not the owner, as well as a gift and a pledge.
The plaintiff shall first provide the wealth from his own kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the purchaser shall provide it through his own relatives.
But the owner who has lost his property should have that wealth restored by its owners;
having established that it was not given, abandoned, or sold, he recovers his own wealth.
He may either make a public purchase or provide the original source;
however, a period for bringing the source must be granted according to the number of *yojanas* [from which it was obtained].
One should perform the purchase publicly with virtuous kinsmen and one's own people;
no other procedure is prescribed there, whether divine or human.
When, having first presented the original source (mūla), the proponent subsequently speaks of the purchase (kraya), he should simply produce that original source; there is no need for the purchase.
But one who cannot produce the root source [of his title] must clear up the purchase itself;
once the purchase has been cleared up by the king, he should not be questioned about anything further.
If he does not produce the original document or purify the purchase by proving its legitimacy,
he shall be made to pay the money to the creditor according to the claim, as well as a fine.
If one who has lost his wealth does not recover it through his own efforts nor through his kinsmen,
he deserves punishment like a thief in order to prevent further attachment to such loss.
Where goods have passed through the market-streets and been recognized by royal officers, yet were purchased from an unknown source, or where the seller has died; ||| K_621 |||
The owner, having paid half the value, may take back his own property;
in that case, according to legal procedure, half of both [the value and the stolen item] shall be considered lost.
Failure to recognize the purchase and likewise failure to provide protection—
these two have been declared by the Buddhas to be causes of the loss of property.
[Joint Undertaking: Whatever physicians or merchants may be joined together,
the fruit obtained therein by those who have not divided it among themselves is equal.

Established by a formal agreement, they shall, without deviation, perform the inspection of goods, the collection of dues, the accounting of expenditures, and the assessment of the weight, quality, and value of the merchandise.
But for those who carry out the transaction with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to whether their shares are equal, deficient, or excessive.
If a single man, who is approved by many, should give wealth or cause a debt to be incurred, it shall be considered as having been done by all of them.
A debt to kinsmen, relatives, and friends must be paid even if it is secured by a pledge;
for others, it must likewise be accompanied by a guarantor, as well as a written document and witnesses.
Gold may be given at one's own will, as may liquids and grain according to the prescribed rule;
it should be given and likewise received in accordance with the local custom of the region.
But that which is given by those who have assembled together must likewise be requested;
whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain.
But whoever recovers property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of it shall be given to him; this is the rule in all such cases.
The instructors, those skilled in the superknowledges, and the preceptors— these artisans shall receive one, two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order.
Whatever wealth may have been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves under the king’s command,
they shall divide it according to the rule after setting aside one-tenth for the king.
But the leader of the thieves shall take four shares from that;
the brave one, three shares; the capable one, two; and each of the others, only one share.
If any among them who have gone forth should incur a seizure [of property],
they shall bear, according to their respective shares, whatever has been given for the sake of his release.
This indeed is the law declared by the virtuous regarding dancers:
one who knows the rhythm (tāla) receives half, while the singers share equally;
those who are the leaders deserve two shares—this is the rule for those performing in concert.
This is the ruling for all merchants, farmers, thieves, artisans, and those who set their own wages without restraint.
Whether it concerns the non-payment of what has been given or the refusal to give what has been promised,
one should not force those who are unwilling to carry out a sale or a gift; however,
one may personally employ one's wife, sons, and all one's property for one's own purposes.
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the property] may be performed;
otherwise it should not be undertaken—this is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Except for one's entire estate and the dwelling, whatever wealth remains after providing for the maintenance of the family is one's own to give; otherwise, it should not be given.
Therefore, while a father has authority over his children and wife regarding their instruction,
he does not have authority over his son regarding his sale or his gift.
He who, having voluntarily promised a gift to a Brahmin,
does not give it, shall be made to pay it as a debt and shall incur the first amercement.
By failing to give what was promised and by misappropriating what has been given,
a mortal is born for a hundred million eons in the animal realm.
Where a gift is prescribed for the purpose of obtaining something not yet known,
that which is obtained through the act of acquisition is proclaimed as "wages" (bhṛti).

One should understand that what is obtained through this method for the sake of protection from fear, for the purpose of guarding, or for the accomplishment of a task, is [the result] of a reciprocal service.
"Even if it were said, 'I shall give my entire possessions to whoever rescues me from this life-threatening danger,' it would not necessarily come to pass."

That which has been given by those who are not self-controlled due to lust or anger, by the distressed, by the impotent, by the insane, by the deluded, or out of error or in jest, may be taken back again.
But as for a bribe that has been promised for the sake of accomplishing a task,
even if that matter has been accomplished, it must not be given under any circumstances.
If, however, she had already been given away previously, he must be made to give her back by force;
furthermore, Gārgya and Mānava state that a fine eleven times the value shall be imposed.
Because of praising thieves, violent criminals, the depraved, and adulterers;
because of seeing one whose livelihood has been ruined; and likewise because of promoting untruth.
Whatever has been obtained by these [mediators] is called a bribe;
in such a case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall bear the guilt.
But if one who has been appointed to official duties should receive a bribe,
he shall be made to pay that entire amount as well as a fine eleven times its value.
But if one who has not been appointed should accept a bribe for the sake of accomplishing a task,
there is no fault in him provided it is for the purpose of returning a favor.

Whether given by one who is healthy or by one who is afflicted, provided it was promised for the sake of dharma—if he dies without having delivered it, his son must be made to pay; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given, or accepted through fraud,
or whatever one perceives to have been done with deceit— that entire transaction one shall annul.
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall receive one-tenth of the profit,
the cattle, and the crops, respectively.
Regarding the non-payment of wages:
"But he who, having undertaken a task, does not bring it to completion, must be made to perform it by force; if he does not do so, he deserves punishment."
If the carrier causes an obstruction, he shall be made to pay double the wage for the journey.
But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or destroyed by fire, or carried away by water.

He who abandons a companion on the road—whether he be exhausted or afflicted by disease—shall first incur the punishment for violence; if he fails to provide care in a village, he shall do so for three days.
But if that merchandise should be lost or stolen on the road,
he shall receive wages proportional to the distance already traveled.
He who, having taken elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, camels, and so forth on lease,
does not return them because his purpose has been accomplished, shall be made to pay the lease along with a fine.

If one takes houses, warehouses, shops, or the like on lease and does not return them to the owner, he shall be made to pay the value of those items along with the rent for as long as they have been withheld.
[The Dispute between Owner and Herdsman]:
Bṛhaspati states that for animals entering fields, groves, pastures, houses, or cattle-pens, there shall be either their seizure or their beating.
In cases where an owner disputes the beating of animals— whether they be of low, high, or middle quality—
the king shall determine the punishment in that instance.
One should erect a great enclosure even before the crops have grown;
for deer, having once tasted their sweetness, are with difficulty kept away from them in this world.
One should cause a quarter-pana to be paid for a cow, two quarters for a buffalo,
and likewise, a quarter is declared as the fine for goats, sheep, and calves.
Neither the violation of an agreement nor the transgression of a formal convention [is permissible];
rather, those who belong to a corporate body should always perform all their affairs according to the law of that body, remaining established in their own respective duties.
The royal edict has issued in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, its practice must first be carried out by the king's command.
That man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king is blameworthy and sinful; he deserves punishment for violating the royal decree.
He who destroys what is logically consistent, he who provides no opportunity for the speaker,
and he who speaks what is illogical, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
The perpetrator of a rash act, the sower of dissension, and the destroyer of the community's property—all these must be executed after being publicly proclaimed to the king; thus said Bhṛgu.
Furthermore, whoever eats from the same vessel or in the same row as another,
if he does not report that person's fault, he shall be punished in the same manner as that person.
Whatever debt may have been incurred or consumed on behalf of the community,
or whatever has been expended for its own sake, that must be repaid by those very same individuals.
Those who have entered into the status of members of guilds, corporations,
or associations shall all receive equal shares of the previous wealth or debts.

In the same way, regarding the performance of the duty of giving gifts, whether they consist of food or other divisible property, one who remains within the community shall receive a share; however, one who has departed does not receive a share.
Whatever has been acquired or preserved by them for the sake of the community, or whatever debt has been contracted,
as well as what was obtained through the favor of the king— all that belongs equally to everyone.
[The definition of the designations beginning with *naigama*: A *naigama* is proclaimed to be a collection of various citizens;
those who have assembled as groups bearing various weapons are proclaimed to be *vrātas*.
A collection of merchants and the like is proclaimed to be a *pūga*;
those who have settled into the life of renunciation are proclaimed to be *pāṣaṇḍas*.
A multitude of Brāhmaṇas is proclaimed to be a *gaṇa*;
those who subsist by means of crafts are proclaimed to be artisans (*śilpin*).
The assembly of Arhats and followers of the Sugata is called a *saṅgha*;
the assembly of Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and others is called a *gulma*.

Bṛhaspati says that *gaṇas*, heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), associations (*pūgas*), guilds (*vrātas*), as well as trade unions (*śreṇis*), and whatever other groups exist that are designated as "classes" (*vargas*), are [to be treated as follows].

[Regarding the remorse concerning buying and selling: having bought or sold, or having given it away. If one who has purchased something does not accept what was obtained, or if one does not give back what was sold and which is undamaged, he shall recover his own property by paying a tenth part of the price.
If the time for performing the purposeful action has not arrived, one should certainly not cause it to be performed;
such is the rule for ten days, but beyond that, there is no longer a formal objection.
In the case of land, the impurity lasts ten days for both the seller and the buyer;
for the sapindas, it lasts twelve days, and after that, it is even less.
If a person, having purchased a commodity such as a milch cow or the like, should abandon it while still harboring a lingering regret,
provided the item is not defective and he returns it at the proper time, he shall pay one-tenth of the price as a fine.
If a buyer, having purchased [an item], departs with regret once it has come into his hand,
the wise man should abandon what was bought by paying one-sixth of its value there.
But that which was purchased without being recognized as defective, yet later discovered to be so, must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned.
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its value and an equal amount as a fine.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss falls upon the seller alone for having sold it without delivering it.
If a buyer does not accept a purchased commodity being offered,
or if a seller sells that same item elsewhere after it has been sold, neither of them shall be held at fault.
