That which is sold by one intoxicated with liquor, or for a low price out of fear, or by one who is not independent or is deluded, must be relinquished; it shall revert to that [original] owner.
One should examine [the milk] for three days, or indeed for five days, until it is fit for export;
however, for pearls, diamonds, and corals, the examination should last for seven days.
For bipeds, however, it is half a month for males, but double that for females;
for all seeds, it is ten days, and for metals and clothes, it is one day.
Therefore, if a defect in the merchandise should arise before that time,
it must be returned to the seller, and the buyer shall recover the purchase price.
However, a garment that has been worn, which is discolored and soiled—
even if it is defective— the seller shall not take it back after it has been purchased.
But that which has been purchased as common property, the lowest of men should not give away alone;
nor should he take it, nor should he accept it, nor indeed should he sell it.
If, after purchasing a commodity for a price, the buyer considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it has not been examined [for defects].
If the buyer delivers [the goods] on the second day, he shall pay one-third of the price as a fine;
if on the third day, double that amount; thereafter, the loss falls solely upon the buyer.
Having divided the value of the commodity into five parts, three parts are called the price;
the fourth part is the profit, and the fifth is called the truth.
Whether through a joint, an exchange, or an unequal transaction involving the three types of enjoyment,
or even by command or purchase, one may rescind [the sale] within ten years.
It is the settled conclusion that even the practice of buying and selling land does not exist if one has not obtained the permission of relatives and others who are nearby and blameless.
In one's own village, it shall last ten nights; in another village, three fortnights;
in other kingdoms, six months; but if there is a difference in dialect, it shall last a year.
But when a taxpayer has fled along with his surety for the tax,
the members of the assembly may sell the taxpayer's land for the sake of the tax.
But by neighboring lords who are assembled together, knowledgeable, and fearful of wrongdoing,
[the boundaries] of fields, groves, houses, and so forth, as well as of bipeds and quadrupeds, [should be determined].
They say that the price is "determined" after dividing it into eight parts;
a price exceeding one part or falling short of it is considered improper.
Even after a hundred years have passed, all of that is revoked;
in the case of buying and selling, whatever price a commodity rightfully deserves is what must be paid.
If, when the sale has been concluded, the price is deficient by a fourth, a fifth, a sixth, a seventh, or even an eighth part; ||| K_708 |||
All that which is of inferior value shall be as if unmade even though it has been made;
when the inferiority is less than what was stated, the purchase is not at all vitiated.
By that portion as well, it would be diminished in value in buying and selling;
other people who know the Dharma say that even such a small amount makes the transaction invalid.
A purchase is successful when the price is half more than the market rate; a profit exceeding ten percent is as stated.
A lease may be made for a third of the value, while a sale by mutual consent (rucikraya) takes effect immediately.
Even if only a small portion of the price is given, the sale shall be considered completed;
in the case of compound interest (cakravṛddhi), the debt must be paid according to that agreement, except in the absence of such a stipulation.

[Non-compliance after having agreed: But he who, having accepted [the pupil], does not cause him to learn the craft and instead makes him perform other tasks, shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from that, the pupil may withdraw.
Even if he has been trained, a pupil may practice his own desires as he pleases;
however, whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs solely to the teacher.
Bhṛgu maintains that by giving away one's own independent self, one enters into servitude like that of a wife;
this state of servitude is to be understood as applying to the three [lower] castes, but never to a Brāhmaṇa.
Servitude is permitted for the castes in the direct order of succession, not in the inverse order;
for the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras lose their independence by [accepting] it.
Even one of equal caste must never compel a Brahmin to servitude;
for by the servitude of a Brahmin, O King, the majesty of the ruler is destroyed.
But Bṛhaspati says that a Brāhmaṇa should never, under any circumstances, be made to perform the duties of a slave or the occupations of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra by one of his own caste.

Even toward one who is endowed with virtue and Vedic study, a superior twice-born man should not intentionally perform any action that falls short of the standard; nor indeed should he perform anything inauspicious toward him.
The cleansing of feces and urine, as well as massaging while naked,
and the tending of cows and other livestock— these tasks are generally performed by the sons of slave-women.
Where the three castes, beginning with the twice-born, have resorted to the life of renunciation,
the king shall cause the Brāhmaṇa to be banished, while the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya shall be made slaves.
But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, one should make into a slave;
for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for the purpose of servitude.
If a man should have intercourse with his own female slave and she subsequently gives birth,
she and her offspring shall not remain a slave, provided that the seed [of the father] is taken into account.
Whatever wealth a slave may possess, it is traditionally held that the master is its owner;
however, as for what has been openly sold, the master does not deserve that wealth.
A female slave who is married by a male slave shall also attain the status of a slave;
for her husband is her master, and since the master is dependent upon his own owner.
If anyone should take a Brahmin woman as a wife, or likewise purchase her, that act is considered undone by the king; all of them shall be punished.
But he who, out of lust, should make a woman of good family a slave by force,
or should transfer her to another, shall be punished, and that [marriage] shall be as if it had not been performed.
He who enjoys the service of a nurse for a child or a non-servant woman as if she were a slave,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a devoted female slave while she is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
And he who, being himself not independent, offers himself [to another] saying, "I am yours," shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall regain him.
A slave who has entered the religious life must not be released by anyone;
however, one who has been maintained against his will during times of distress is freed from slavery by giving a pair of cattle.
[Disputes concerning boundaries: Excess, deficiency, a partial share, existence and non-existence,
possession without enjoyment, and the boundary— these six are the causes for disputes over land.
In that case, the enjoyment [of the property] should be applied while all witnesses remain present;
for a witness is of two kinds: one recorded in writing and the other not, thus following two paths.
In disputes between two parties concerning fields, buildings, tanks, wells, groves, or embankments, as well as in all other matters, the neighbors are the authoritative witnesses.
In cases concerning neighboring lands, one should determine the boundaries of fields and so forth by means of non-adjacent neighbors;
likewise, this applies to village boundaries, as well as those of cities and districts.
A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village, a field the neighbor of a field,
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house, for they embrace it on all sides.
In their absence, the neighbors, the original owners, the elders, the excavators, and so forth [should be consulted];
there should be no hesitation regarding these six types of immovable property.
When the vassals are thus closely joined, and those further beyond them are likewise closely joined,
such formations— where those who are joined are joined with those who are joined— are proclaimed as being in the shape of a lotus.

When neighboring kings have become hostile toward the accomplishment of one's own purpose due to the weight of their interests, one must nevertheless effect a rescue through those who are closely allied with them;
of this there is no doubt.
But those who are attached to those who are themselves attached to faults are declared to be "associated with them";
however, a king who understands the Dharma should not punish those who are not actually corrupt.
For neighbors are not released from liability regarding a decision simply by claiming ignorance;
if they declare ignorance, the king should fine them and then re-examine the boundary.
If a dispute should arise after the matter has been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest amercement.
Having abandoned wicked vassals and having associated with others who are hereditary and so forth, he should have the boundary established; thus do those who know the Dharma understand.
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the sages as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that very place.
Those endowed with human virtues who witness a task being accomplished—
whether they be old or not old— are proclaimed as "the aged" (vṛddha).
Because they rescue [beings] from that [suffering], being characterized by eavesdropping, enjoyment, performing tasks, and narration,
they are therefore known as "The Rescuers" (Uddhṛta).
The neighboring kings are considered to possess one unit of quality when they state their objections first;
those who respond with twice that merit are known as the "superior" (uttara); others beyond them are held to possess three units of merit.
Just as one person, clad in red garments and composed in mind, might lead both parties to a boundary somewhere, placing the earth upon his head.
It was composed by King Bhayavarjita himself when all [other resources] were lacking.
And also for fields, wells, and tanks; for rice-paddies and groves;
and for houses, palaces, dwellings, royal residences, and temples of the gods.
But if those who have been appointed as witnesses, being many in number, do not reach a unanimous decision due to fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
In the case of crossing a boundary, [theft] from a treasury, and likewise touching with the foot,
a period of three fortnights, one fortnight, or seven days is prescribed for offenses against the gods or the king.
One should not obstruct the girdle-closet, the window, or the lattice; by damaging a water-channel or the foundation of a house, one shall be liable to a fine.
After the time of settling [the house], these [rites] should never be performed again;
one should not cast a glance or create a water-channel toward another's house.
One should construct dwellings against the walls of others, leaving a space of two cubits for the ramparts of excrement, urine, and water, as well as for the fire and the drainage pits.
That by which all people always travel is the crossroads;
that which is unobstructed at the proper time is called the royal highway.
One should not plant anything there, nor should one cause any harm to it by any means;
however, one incurs punishment for obstructing the path of the Guru, the Teacher, the King, and others.
If anyone there should out of desire deposit refuse in pits or chasms, or even plant trees [in such places], his fine shall be one māṣaka.
He who destroys tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing-places with impure matter shall first have that impurity cleared away and then be fined the first amercement.
One who defiles established holy fords (tīrtha) set up by great-souled ones—
those which are meritorious and purifying— shall incur the penalty for the first-degree violent offense (sāhasa).
But for trees grown within the boundary of two fields,
one should declare that their fruits and flowers belong in common to the owners of both fields.
But for those born in another's field whose branches are supported elsewhere,
one should know him to be the owner in whose fields they are supported.
But he who performs a restoration of a house, garden, or tank without the consent of the owner does not obtain ownership of it.
If an expenditure has been incurred when the master has arrived and it was not reported to the king,
yet it is subsequently reported and authorized, one receives that expenditure as being for his account.
If, due to incapacity, he does not pay the expenses incurred for the purpose of clearing the fallow land,
the cultivator shall receive the produce minus one-eighth;
he shall be the enjoyer for eight years, after which it belongs to the owner.
If someone should cultivate a field when its owners are incapable, deceased, or lost, he may enjoy the fruit thereof without being hindered.
If a field is being dragged away [by another], the owner of the field may return;
by providing all the customary labor for its cultivation, he shall regain that field.
Then, by a reduction of one-eighth each year, when seven years have passed and the eighth year is completed, he shall obtain the field that has been enjoyed [by another].
[Harsh Speech]: To mimic or to utter sounds such as "hum" or coughing, and whatever else is censured in the world—
that is called harsh speech.
Because of its harshness, vulgarity, and intensity, that [abuse] is also recorded as being threefold:
censure is to be known as the harsh; what is termed a physical defect is the vulgar; and the wise say that intensity consists of insults involving acts leading to loss of caste.
When one disparages another by means of limbs that are designated as non-existent—
whether they are unreal or even real— it is called harsh speech by the wise.
When one, out of anger, uses speech to cause the humiliation of another's conduct,
country, family, and so forth, that is considered by the wise to be *aślīlā* (obscene speech).
That speech which binds one with the noose of great sins, which produces passion and hatred, or which causes the loss of caste, is known as "intense" (tīvra).
Those who, out of anger, proclaim the faults of one who is faultless, or who, though lacking virtues themselves, pretend to recognize virtue,
or who are preoccupied with false notions— they know such a person to be corrupt in speech.
One who proclaims the faults of an innocent person for the sake of causing harm,
and one who speaks with evasive pretexts— they know such a man to be corrupt in speech.
Whatever has been spoken by me out of delusion, negligence, rivalry, or affection,
"I shall not speak thus again"— for such a person, one should prescribe half the punishment.

Where there might otherwise be a fault, there shall be no blame if one makes a declaration for the sake of exoneration, provided that he has been cast out by that [declaration] and can demonstrate it according to the scriptural injunction.

Otherwise, there would be an equal fault; however, in the case of speaking falsely, it is recorded as the highest [offense]. One should overcome a man who is corrupt in speech through great application of effort.
The king should investigate with diligence any testimony that is not true;
for those whose habit is to speak falsehoods, the cutting off of the tongue is the means of purification.
[Regarding assault:
If one cannot perceive the grounds for assault through the evidence of causes and so forth,
one should employ witnesses or divine ordeals in that case.
Furthermore, that man who strikes with a terrifying weapon,
even if he has not been previously harmed, is declared to be subject to punishment.
According to Bhṛgu, for the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest fine is prescribed; for piercing them, the middle fine.
When an offense is committed for the sake of causing suffering to humans or animals,
one should inflict punishment in proportion to the degree of that suffering.
For those who are untouchable, for rogues, slaves, Mlecchas, evildoers,
and those born of inverse unions, corporal punishment is not a fine in terms of its purpose.
That [wind] becomes fourfold when it reaches vomit, urine, feces, and so forth;
it is sixfold within the middle of the body, and is traditionally held to be eightfold in the head.
For raising a hand [to strike], a fine of twelve [paṇas] shall be imposed;
for actually striking those of one's own caste, that same fine is declared to be double.
Just as the punishments for verbal abuse have been declared according to the inverse and direct order [of the castes],
so too shall the punishments be inflicted in due order for physical assault.
But when the body or the sense organs are destroyed,
the wise should impose a fine, as well as provide for his satisfaction and his recovery;
furthermore, he shall pay the expenses for his recovery until the wound is healed.

Those against whom verbal censure or physical punishment has been prescribed for their offenses shall be made to restore what was stolen or broken; however, those who possess no wealth shall be purified through labor.
If a man yokes animals such as donkeys, cows, buffaloes, or camels when they are exhausted, afflicted by thirst, or hungry at an improper time, he shall incur the first amercement.
For the killing of deer and birds, the fine is two or twelve paṇas;
for the killing of snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, and pigs, the fine for men is the same.
One who drives a cow, a young heifer, a sacrificial animal, a castrated bull,
or a full-grown bull with violence shall first incur a fine of one thousand [paṇas], and for the most extreme case, capital punishment.
In the case of killing living beings, one should provide a substitute for them, or pay its equivalent value; so Manu has declared.
It is the established rule that the punishment for injuring any of the forest trees should be proportional to the degree of their utility.
If the teacher should strike the disciple with anger without using a cane,
such that excessive pain is caused, there would be a dispute between the disciple and the father.
[Sāhasa]: An action performed impulsively is declared to be *sāhasa*.
Theft is defined as the taking away of property by force, whether accompanied by violence or not, as well as acts of rashness; it is also described as the concealment of such an act.
But when a matter proceeds without signs [of guilt] and is termed an act of daring (*sāhasa*), it should be cleared by means of oaths; this is the rule in all such cases.
If many enraged men should kill a single person,
he among them who strikes the vital organ is considered the slayer.
One who commits such an act through malice shall incur various forms of execution;
however, one should indeed slay without hesitation an approaching person who intends to cause destruction.
There is no fault for the slayer of evildoers who are intent upon their crimes;
however, when they have desisted from their undertaking, taking them captive is not considered killing.

In the case of an assailant who is superior by virtue of asceticism, Vedic study, or birth, there should be no killing; however, Bhṛgu maintains that killing is permissible for one who is inferior in merit.
One who wields a raised sword, poison, or fire, as well as one who holds a raised bow, one who slays by means of the Atharva-veda, and likewise a slanderer against the king; ||| K_802 |||
One who violates his wife and one who is intent on seeking out one's vulnerabilities—
one should recognize all such persons as *ātatāyin* (assassins).
They say that those who steal one's reputation or conduct, and those who seize one's dharma or wealth, are sinners.
But one who commits an offense against someone who has never previously accused him,
or who seizes his life or property— one should know such a person as an *ātatāyin* (an assailant).
In the killing of those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins,
as well as elephants, horses, and others, the slayer incurs no guilt.
One who causes an abortion is a thief; likewise, even a Brāhmaṇa, having killed an innocent woman, must be put to death with a weapon.
A man who causes injury, breakage, or crushing to goods shall be subject to the first amercement; the owner of the goods is declared to be the one who receives compensation.
If one should carry off, break, or burn an image of the gods,
or likewise destroy its temple, he shall incur the first amercement.
Whoever should breach a wall, cause it to fall, or likewise demolish it,
or block the course of water, shall incur the first amercement.
Whether it be in secret or in public, by night or by day,
the taking of another's property is proclaimed to be theft.
One should carefully examine a stolen object that has fallen from another's hand, been picked up on the ground unintentionally, or dropped by a thief.
One who deals with weights, measures, and counter-measures that are marked with false representations,
whether openly or secretly, shall incur the first amercement.
If something is stolen from a house, however, the king should compel the thieves' catchers, the guards,
and the local wardens to pay for it, provided that the thief is not apprehended.
Property stolen within a village shall be made good by the village headman;
in a pasture, it shall be paid by the owner, and in a forest, by the forest-guardian.
Whatever has been kept by anyone in his own country must be returned by the king;
having investigated it, the monarch himself should take back what was lost and recovered.
If property has been stolen by thieves, he should diligently restore it to its original form;
in the absence of that, there should be payment of its value; otherwise, the king incurs sin.
Even if the thief has been apprehended, if the stolen property is not recovered from him,
he shall either pay that value himself or cause the thief to be made to pay it as desired.
If, however, there should be doubt regarding the guilt of those being compelled to pay,
the one who was robbed shall be made to swear an oath, or he may clear himself through his kinsmen.
Since the owner has recovered only a small portion of the property stolen from him,
he shall receive the remainder once the owner has made a claim for it.
Those who would strike at their own country, as well as those who obstruct the royal highway— the king, having confiscated all their property, shall impale them on a stake.
Property recovered by those intent on searching for thieves shall be made over to the thief;
in that case, the king should cause double that amount to be paid as a fine.
With whichever limb a thief commits an injury against another,
the king shall cut off that very limb, so that he may not do it again.
One who takes two each of cucumber and gourd, five mangoes and five pomegranates, or a handful of dates, jujubes, and the like, does not incur fault.
Mānavas declare that the immediate banishment of those caught in adultery (sahoḍha) is contrary to the views of Gautama, as it is censurable because it results in the destruction of living beings.
Whether the offense was committed in the presence of witnesses or not,
once the perpetrator has been apprehended and his violent act established by the facts, he shall be punished by confiscation of all his property after being publicly proclaimed as a criminal.
But those who are bound with iron chains, though receiving meager food, being endowed with strength, shall perform services for the king until death; so says Kauśika.
When property has been brought from a foreign land by a foreigner, the king,
having taken that property for himself, should dismiss him without imposing a fine.
Those who provide food to thieves, as well as those who supply them with fire and water,
those who purchase their goods, those who receive them,
and those who conceal them— all these are declared by the law to be subject to the same punishment.
If there should be an ignorant officiating priest or an unstable teacher,
the king, having punished both of them with the penalty for theft, should establish them on the right path.
[Adultery with a woman]: If he employs a female messenger, stays at an improper time or place,
or seizes her by the throat, hair, or the ears, nose, hands, and so forth;
Staying in one place, sitting, and eating—this gathering [of requisites] is traditionally taught as being ninefold.
When a man forcibly indulges in sexual intercourse with women, he should proceed to kill him; for that is indeed a transgression of duty.
But a wanton woman who, afflicted by lust, desires [her lover] of her own accord,
shall be released by the king's command after being publicly proclaimed in the presence of the people.
The initiator, the accomplice, as well as the instructor of the path, the refuge, the provider of weapons, and the provider of food for those who commit misdeeds; // K_832 //
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction,
one who is intent on indifference toward what ought to be done, and one who approves of the speaker of faults.
If there should be those who are unable to prevent [an offense], all of them must perform that task;
however, one should assign punishment to them in accordance with their respective capacities.
A woman who desires not to be separated from her husband,
who possesses good fortune and wishes for lifelong widowhood, should serve the sacred fire with humility and devotion to her husband.
By means of service to her husband alone, a woman enjoys all desires;
returning here from heaven, she becomes a treasure-house of happiness.
The virtuous woman who, upon the death of her husband,
remains steadfast in celibacy and conducts herself like Arundhatī, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[The Partition of Inheritance: When the father and the brothers take the entire collection of property in equal shares, that partition is declared to be in accordance with dharma.
The paternal estate is common to both the father and the son;
however, regarding property acquired by the father himself, the son does not possess ownership.
Whatever was inherited from the grandfather, whatever was inherited from the father, and whatever else was acquired by oneself—
all this is divided when there is a partition among the heirs.
When there is suspicion of hidden property, visible items such as a house, a field, or quadrupeds may be divided; in that case, an oath is declared to be the means of proof.
Household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and those engaged in manual labor are divided while being visible; regarding hidden property, Bhṛgu said it goes to the treasury.
Upon the division of property during one's lifetime, a father shall not treat one son as distinct from the others;
nor shall he disinherit one son suddenly, without cause.
And the partition [of property] is ordained for those who have attained legal capacity;
for men, such capacity arises at the sixteenth year.
And the wealth of those who have not yet attained legal majority, as well as that of those who have gone abroad, shall be deposited with kinsmen and friends, free from any expenditure.
All [the heirs] shall protect that share belonging to one who has gone abroad;
when a son dies while still a child, his inheritance must be protected by his maternal relatives (tantubandhu);
but once he has reached the age of puberty (paugaṇḍa), they shall divide it according to their respective shares.
A debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle for the sake of the family must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition.
That debt must be paid to the creditor; one should not cause it to be paid otherwise.
If it has been proven by evidence, then [the debtor] shall pay from that point onward, even if there is a contradiction.

A debt that was contracted for the sake of dharma, or given out of affection, or one that was stipulated, should be divided while it is still visible; however, there is no obligation to pay such a debt from the paternal estate.
A debt of this kind— whether ancestral, cleared by means of ancestral property, or one's own personal debt— must be settled by the kinsmen together during the partition of the estate.
Having paid off debts and provided for those who have shown affection, one should divide the remainder.
Before the son has acquired property, the father shall take two shares or half;
when the father has died, the mother also receives a share equal to that of a son.
In whatever manner the wealth obtained through partition may be employed for the purpose of sacrifice,
in that same manner should the learned increase the weightiness of the shares.
Even in the division of inheritance in the world, no one shall exercise ownership;
rather, only enjoyment may be exercised, but neither giving nor selling is permitted.
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights regarding immovable property;
for no single person is empowered in any case to give, mortgage, or sell it.
If a younger brother dies while the estate is undivided, one should provide for his son’s maintenance from that which was not already received by him from the grandfather.
He shall receive his paternal share from his uncle or from that uncle’s son;
for that share rightfully belongs to all the brothers.
His son may also receive it, but beyond him there should be cessation [of the claim].
When a legitimate son has been born, sons of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a fourth part of the inheritance;
those of a different caste (asavarṇa), however, are entitled only to food and clothing.
For unmarried daughters, however, one-fourth share is prescribed;
for sons, there are three shares. But equality is ordained when the wealth is small.
But if one should produce fruit even with the consent of the field-owner,
both of them are indeed sharers of that fruit here, for fruit does not arise from only one.
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast husband, takes another husband,
the son born of her from that second husband clearly belongs to his biological progenitor.
He whose urine is not frothy and whose feces sink in water,
and who lacks the penis, insanity, and semen— he is called a *klība* (impotent).
A son born of a woman married out of order, one born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra),
and one who has fallen from the religious life— none of these are entitled to inherit property.
But the son of a woman married out of order inherits the estate if he is of the same caste as his father;
so too does the son born of a woman of a different caste who was married in the proper order.
The son of a woman born in the inverse order of castes does not inherit property;
it is held that his kinsmen should provide him with food and clothing for as long as they live.
In the absence even of kinsmen, he shall obtain that paternal property;
however, kinsmen should not be compelled to pay back wealth that was not inherited from a father.
[The following are] indivisible:
that which was taken away by one's own power, that which was lost, and that which was acquired by oneself;
all of this is not to be given by the father to the sons at the time of partition.
Whatever wealth is obtained through that knowledge which was acquired by means of utilizing the food provided by another,
that is called "wealth acquired through knowledge" (vidyāprāpta).
But that which is obtained through learning after it has been offered as a wager should be known as "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam); it is not to be divided in a partition of inheritance.
That which is obtained from a pupil, from officiating at a sacrifice, from answering questions, from resolving doubts through inquiry,
from praising one's own knowledge, from debate, and from recitation—
this they call "wealth of learning," and it is not to be divided during partition.
For this same rule applies even to artisans regarding that which exceeds the price.
Whatever is obtained through learning after having set aside other means, such as by means of gambling and the like,
Bṛhaspati declares that to be "wealth acquired through learning" (vidyādhanam), which is not subject to partition.

That which is obtained through a promise of instruction, that which is received from a disciple, and that which is acquired according to the rule of the officiating priest (ṛtvij)— Bhṛgu declares this to be "wealth acquired through learning" (vidyādhana).

That which is acquired through the power of learning, as well as from officiating at sacrifices or from teaching students—this they call the property of learning; anything other than this is common property.
Bṛhaspati says that wealth acquired through valor by brothers who have been trained in the sciences within the family, or even by a father, is subject to partition.
A physician should never give away any portion of his medical wealth to those who are ignorant;
however, he may give that wealth to those whose knowledge is equal to or superior to his own.
When one performs an action by forcibly entering into a state of uncertainty,
and the master, being pleased with that action, bestows his favor,
whatever wealth is obtained therein through such valor shall belong to him.
That which is acquired through valor, that which is obtained through learning, and that which is traditionally declared to be a woman's property—
all this must not be divided by the heirs during partition.
That which is acquired by means of a banner (dhvajāhṛta) is declared by the legal tradition to be indivisible.
That which is acquired from battle after putting to flight the enemy force,
having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, is called "acquired by means of a banner."
Whatever is obtained at the time of giving along with a maiden of one's own caste, that wealth is known as "situated in a maiden" (kanyāgata); it is pure and productive of growth.
One should know that wealth brought by a wife at the time of marriage belongs to the husband; all such property is to be understood as conducive to the fulfillment of dharma.
Whatever is given to the bridegroom at the time of marriage with reference to the bride,
all that wealth belongs to her and is not to be divided by her kinsmen.
Wealth recorded in documents, property designated for religious purposes, water-rights, a slave, and any hereditary pledge; these are [not lost by adverse possession].
Clothing and ornaments that may not be suitable should be adjusted by kinsmen so that they are appropriate for the occasion.
Bṛhaspati states that pasture land for cattle, protection, and clothing provided for the body shall not be divided, but shall be used [in common] for the sake of dharma.
Whatever law has been declared for a country, a caste, a community, or a village by Bhṛgu,
one should determine the distribution of inheritance according to that very law.

[The re-division of concealed property: If property that was concealed is later discovered, it shall be divided equally with the brothers; indeed, in the absence of the father, the sons [shall divide it].
Whatever property has been taken away from one another or was improperly divided, if it is recovered later, it should be divided into equal shares; so says Bhṛgu.
Whatever wealth is acquired by one [co-heir] alone shall belong to him alone;
likewise, what was seized, lost, or recovered, as well as what was previously mentioned, shall be divided again.
One should not compel the return of property seized by a relative by force;
nor should one compel the payment of a share from the enjoyment of undivided relatives.
Having abandoned the common field and resorted to another country,
a share must undoubtedly be given to one who returns from that lineage.
Whether it be the third, the fifth, or even the seventh birth,
if the births are not fully known, one shall receive the portion that has come down in due order.

Land that has been held by the primary and neighboring lords through tradition as belonging to their master must be given to one who comes from that same lineage, even if he is born of a different clan.
If those who were divided from the paternal estate are living together again, they should divide it once more; he shall receive two shares from whatever source his increase arose.
Having distinct marks and so forth, they should live for ten years with separate religious duties and separate activities;
those brothers are to be known as "divided" once they have been separated from the paternal wealth.
[The definition and types of woman's property: That which is received before the fire, that which is received at the wedding procession, that which is given out of affection by her [relatives],
and that which is obtained from her brothers, mother, or father— this is declared to be the sixfold woman's property.
That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as "adhyagnika" (fire-acquired) woman's property.
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being led away from her father’s house,
as well as the *adhyāvahanika*, is declared to be her *strīdhana* (woman's property).
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given for the purpose of saluting their feet, is called "affectionately given" (prītidatta).
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, and articles for manual labor, that is proclaimed as *śulka* (toll/duty).
Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage is called *anvādheya*; likewise, that which is obtained from her own kinsmen is also so designated.

Whatever is obtained later from her husband, from her parents, or from her father-in-law, whether through formal gift-giving (saṃskāra), out of affection, or as a subsequent gift, that is called anvādheya by Bhṛgu.
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried girl, that which is obtained from the husband, from the father’s house,
or from a brother or from the parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman's property).

[Consideration of Ownership and Other Matters Regarding Women’s Property: Women’s property (strīdhana) should be given to a woman by her father, mother, husband, brothers, or paternal kinsmen according to their ability, up to a maximum of two thousand [paṇas], with the exception of immovable property.
That which is given with a condition, or that which is given through the power of a religious practice (yoga) by the father, brother, or husband, is not intended to be woman’s property.

Whatever wealth has been acquired through crafts or obtained from others out of affection, the husband's ownership extends over that; the remainder, however, is declared to be the woman's separate property (strīdhana).
Upon receiving her dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was given by them as a means of subsistence out of compassion.
Women's independence regarding their dowry is always proclaimed;
they have full authority over its sale and gift, even in the case of immovable property.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman may dispose of her husband’s inheritance as she pleases;
however, while he is alive, she should preserve it, or otherwise spend it for the sake of the family.
But if he has two wives and does not treat her with affection again,
even if she had been given to him out of love, he must be compelled by force to restore her.
Wherever a woman is deprived of food, clothing, and shelter,
she may take for herself her own property as well as a share from the heirs.
This is the law regarding a written document: she shall reside in the husband's family when the time arrives;
however, if she is afflicted by disease, she may go to her own kinsmen at the time of his death.
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over the woman's property,
whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
For if even one among them should consume the woman's property by force,
he shall be compelled to restore it along with interest and shall also incur a fine.
If he should eat that very same thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure,
he should be made to pay its value, provided that he is wealthy.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, in distress, or oppressed by creditors, he may, out of his own will and with affection, give what has been relinquished [as a gift].
While she is alive, her husband, sons, brothers-in-law, fathers, and kinsmen are declared to have no authority over a woman's property; those who misappropriate it are liable to punishment.
The sons must repay the woman's property as a debt, just as they would a loan promised by their father;
she who remains in her husband’s family shall not live in her father’s family.
The sisters, together with their kinsmen and accompanied by their husbands, shall divide the property of a deceased woman;
this is the law regarding a woman's property, and this division has been ordained.
In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall go to the sons;
but property given by kinsmen goes to the kinsmen, and in their absence, it goes to the husband.
Furthermore, whatever immovable property has been given by both parents to a daughter always goes to her brothers,
provided she dies childless and without a husband.
Whatever paternal wealth a woman has obtained from her father's side among Āsuras and other [forms of marriage],
it is ordained that in the absence of her offspring, it belongs to her mother and father.

[On the inheritance of the property of one who dies without a son: A sonless widow, remaining under the protection of her elders and preserving her husband’s bed, may enjoy his estate until her death; after she passes away, the heirs shall take possession.
When the husband has gone to heaven, the wife is entitled to food and clothing;
however, if the property has not been divided, she receives her share until her death.
She who is devoted to serving her teacher deserves to enjoy her allotted share;
if she does not perform service, she should be employed in tasks such as weaving cloth or gathering alms.
Upon the death of her husband, a woman who protects her family's honor shall receive her husband’s share;
however, she has no ownership over it for as long as she lives, nor can she give it away, mortgage it, or sell it.
One who is devoted to vows and fasting, firmly established in celibacy,
and constantly delighting in self-restraint and generosity, shall go to heaven even if she is childless.
The wife who is faithful to her husband shall be the heir to his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried.
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters are designated;
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [as heirs].
When [the estate] has been partitioned and settled, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the father’s mother, in that order.
[But she who is] addicted to misconduct, shameless, or a squanderer of wealth [is excluded].
And a woman who is devoted to adultery does not deserve that wealth.
If a woman performs funeral rites for the deceased without being authorized by her father, husband, or son,
that act of hers shall be fruitless.
Property that has no heir goes to the king; likewise, the estate of a woman and the funeral expenses for servants go to the king.
However, setting aside the property of a learned Brahmin (śrotriya), he should bestow it upon other learned Brahmins.
But those who are united [in marriage] shall inherit from those united, and those who live separately from those living separately;
in the absence [of heirs], they should be known as the takers of the property, being seedless and sharing with one another.
[Regarding gambling and betting: One should never indulge in gambling, for it increases anger and greed;
it is cruel, produces wicked people, and destroys the wealth of men.
Since strife inevitably arises from gambling, just as poison does from the mouth of a serpent,
therefore a king should desist from it, for it is indeed a vice within his domain.
If it should be visible, with a gateway situated at the door,
one should have that "hand-position" (karapada) constructed for the sake of preventing the confusion of the noble ones.
The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and personally pay the dues to the king;
furthermore, he may take a ten percent interest from the loser.
The winner shall give his own wealth, and from the loser, the stake must be recovered within three fortnights, or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house; of this there is no doubt.
Whether appearing as a single form or a double form, victory belongs to that gambler at dice upon whom protection is established.
Alternatively, a gambler, having given the king the share as prescribed, may engage in gambling openly; in this way, no fault is found.
One should compel the payment of what is due in that very place and not otherwise;
for in that case, the loser is indeed the master of the assembly, and the legal proceeding depends upon the authority of the master of the assembly.

One who is unskilled and defeated should be released; one who is skilled and defeated should not be released. Even when all one's possessions have been won and the opponent is skilled, one should not cause him to surrender his entire property.
In disputes over victory, gain, or the methods used by fraudulent gamblers,
the keeper of the gambling hall is the authority, provided that the keeper of the hall is himself pure.
There is no certainty regarding the king for those who follow the conduct established by barbarians, outcasts, rogues, gamblers, and ascetics.

[The Miscellaneous Section: Whatever remains unsaid from what was previously stated, and whatever has fallen away from its proper context— having been extracted and composed for the sake of another treatise— is inconsistent.
That which stands as a restatement at the end of a treatise for the sake of providing an illustration,
and whatever sentence follows by this method, shall be considered *prakīrṇaka* (a miscellaneous or supplementary statement).
The duties of kings, one's own specific duties, the discussion of doubtful points,
and whatever remains unsaid from what was previously mentioned— all that constitutes the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇaka).
The sixth-part tax and the toll must likewise be paid at the pit;
so too for one who causes dissension in battle, a thief, or one who violates another's wife.
The intent to kill cows or Brahmins, as well as the destruction of crops—
the king himself should investigate these ten offenses.

The failure to perform expiations, the transgression of prohibitions and injunctions, the destruction of the system of castes and stages of life, and the neglect of the prevention of the intermixture of castes; // K_949 //
A hidden treasure, wealth that yields no fruit, and the acquisition of riches by a pauper—
the king himself should prevent these when they have been thoroughly discovered through spies.
Those matters should not be disclosed: the affairs of disputants who advocate for action, the provocation of the elements, and mutual secret signals.
Whatever among his subjects proceeds contrary to the injunctions of the scriptures,
the king should pacify those matters by means of the expedients of conciliation, sowing dissension, and so forth.
One should employ verbal punishment toward friends and others, saying, "Shame on you, wretched woman!
One should do for him exactly what was said; even if it was not explicitly stated, one should act with virtuous intent.
But whoever should accomplish a transaction by means of a false measure, or by a forged seal or a counterfeit stamp, shall indeed be made to pay the highest fine.
Those who are addicted to royal amusements, those who subsist on the king’s service,
and whoever speaks what is unpleasant— against them he should carry out the death penalty.
Those who manufacture counterfeit coins, those who examine them,
those who distribute them, and those who steal for the sake of the king shall receive various forms of capital punishment.
A Śūdra who has entered the life of a renunciant and is devoted to the recitation of prayers and burnt offerings—
one such evildoer should be punished by execution, or else fined double the usual penalty.
Even if a crime is accompanied by clear evidence, one should inquire into the cause of that crime;
then, having carefully ascribed the fault, one should determine the punishment.
But when an offense occurs among all those of good conduct,
even if it happens involuntarily through fate, one should not impose punishment in that case.
Kings who administer punishment correctly are worthy of worship even by the gods.

At the commencement of an offense, one should impose the first [lowest] fine; in the case of its repetition, the middle fine is prescribed. Indeed, whoever has been assigned a specific punishment shall receive that which is sufficient for him.
Kings and ministers especially shall attain such [merit] by not failing to punish the wicked and by inflicting punishment upon those who bow [in submission].
Furthermore, those who are dependent and those who exist in a state of servitude are designated as being without a protector; for them, the punishment is beating.
Beating, binding, and likewise humiliating—this indeed is the punishment for a slave; a monetary fine is not ordained.
One who deserves death shall pay a fine of one hundred gold pieces;
for one deserving the amputation of a limb, half of that; and for one deserving exile, twenty-five.
According to the status of those who are noble, distinguished, or low-born,
he should confiscate their entire property and swiftly banish them from the city.
Those who are destitute should be placed in confinement; one must never carry out their execution.
For all those guilty of crimes, the specific application of punishment is determined according to the scriptures.
A Brahmin deserving of execution or the amputation of limbs shall enter a bond of total renunciation;
for, being freed from that [sinful] act, his livelihood consists in that very restraint.
A false witness should be banished after being publicly proclaimed; one who accepts gifts from the wicked should be disgraced;
and one who mutilates a limb should be separated from his own dharma by means of imprisonment.

In the case of those who have committed equal offenses, one should determine the penalty there as well; however, for children, the elderly, the sick, and women, there is no corporal punishment—their fine shall consist only of a beating.
A righteous lord of the earth shall cause the fine to be paid from the woman's property;
however, a woman who is destitute and has committed an offense deserves the punishment of a beating.
One should deposit into the treasury wealth acquired through unjust means; for the sake of accomplishing a task, one should not cause the ruin of the treasury, as a wise man would never do so.
Having given all that wealth arising from fines to the Brahmins,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should depart for the forest to meet his end.
Thus should a king, a ruler of the earth, always act with discipline regarding his duties and for the welfare of the world; he should employ all his servants accordingly.
The End of the Manusmṛti (The Code of Manu)

www.sub.uni-goettingen.de/ebene_1/fiindolo/gretil/gretdias.pdf Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, the great seers honored him according to custom and spoke these words: Manu 1.01a: Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, Manu 1.01c: having honored him according to custom, they spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, you ought to declare to us the duties of all the social classes in their proper order, as well as those born of intermediate castes."
For you alone,
O Lord, are the knower of the true purpose and the nature of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Thus questioned by those high-souled ones,
he of immeasurable vigor duly honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen."
In the beginning, this universe was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, devoid of distinguishing marks,
beyond the reach of reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Then the Lord Svayambhū, the unmanifest,
who dispels darkness and possesses the vital energy of all that has come into being, appeared, manifesting this world beginning with the great elements.

He who is beyond the grasp of the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself came forth. Desiring to bring forth various creatures from his own body, he meditated upon it.
In the beginning, he emitted the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
That egg became golden, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The waters are called "nara"; indeed, the waters are the offspring of Nara. Since they were his first place of resort (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That unmanifest, eternal cause, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent—
emanated from that, the Puruṣa is celebrated in the world as Brahmā.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditation, divided that egg into two parts.
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, he created the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
From himself, he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego (ahaṃkāra), the presiding self-consciousness.
He also drew forth the Great Self (mahān ātmā) and all things composed of the three qualities (triguṇa).
And the five senses, which grasp their respective objects, [should be subdued] gradually.

Having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [gods] of immeasurable power with the portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings. Those subtle parts which were the components of their forms, these six [elements] take as their support.
Therefore, the wise call his form "the body" (śarīra).
Into that enter the great elements together with their functions,
as well as the mind with its subtle components— the imperishable creator of all beings.
But from the subtle constituent elements of form belonging to these seven immensely powerful persons, this perishable world arises from the imperishable.
But each succeeding one among these acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position in the sequence, it is declared to possess that many qualities.
But in the beginning, he assigned the names and the distinct functions of all beings,
as well as their various conditions, from the words of the Veda itself.
And that Lord created the gods whose nature is action among living beings,
as well as the subtle host of Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.
From Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains.
Desiring to create these living beings, he emitted austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger, as well as this entire creation.
And for the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.
The minute particles of the five elements that are recorded as perishable—
along with these, this entire universe comes into being in successive order.
But whatever task the Lord first assigned to each being,
that very same task he performed himself when being created again and again.
Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—
whatever he ordained for each at the beginning of creation, that very quality entered into it of its own accord.
Just as the seasons, at the change of seasons, spontaneously assume their own respective characteristics according to the time,
so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.
For the sake of the increase of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Having divided his own body into two parts, he became a man with one half;
with the other half, he became a woman, and in her, the Lord created Virāj.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that creator of this entire universe, whom the Supreme Person Virāj himself created after performing austerities.
Desiring to create offspring, I performed most difficult austerities; then, in the beginning, I created ten great sages as the lords of creatures:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
And Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada as well.
These seven Manus of great splendor whom [Brahmā] created,
as well as the gods, the hosts of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power— Manu 1.36.
The Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various hosts of Pitṛs;
as well as lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, and red and Indra’s bows (rainbows).
He should also observe meteors, atmospheric thunderclaps, comets, and the various celestial luminaries.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth.
And worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings.
Thus, by my command, all this—
both the stationary and the moving— was created by those high-souled ones according to their respective karma through the power of their ascetic penance.
I shall now declare to you, according to their respective order of birth, what kind of action has been prescribed for each of these beings in this world.
Cattle, wild animals, and beasts of prey with two rows of teeth;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans—these are born from the womb (jarāyuja).
Birds, snakes, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises are born from eggs (aṇḍaja).
And those other things of this same kind that originate from dry land as well as from water.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from sweat;
and whatever else is of this same nature is likewise produced from heat.
All stationary beings are born from sprouts, growing from seeds or slips;
plants that bear abundant flowers and fruit and end with the ripening of their fruit are called herbs (oṣadhi).
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*.
Various kinds of shrubs and thickets, as well as species of grasses, those that grow from seeds or from slips, as well as creepers and climbing plants; these are the fifth [class of living beings].
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
These states, beginning with Brahmā, are declared to end here;
in this terrible cycle of existence of living beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time.
When that God is awake, then this world is active;
when he, whose self is tranquil, sleeps, then everything closes its eyes.
While he sleeps in a state of well-being, however, the embodied beings whose nature is action cease from their respective activities,
and the mind falls into exhaustion.
But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.
But when he remains for a long time resorting to darkness (tamas), though still possessed of his senses, he does not perform his own duty; then he departs from his bodily form.
When, having become as minute as an atom, he enters the seed— both the stationary and the moving—
he then, being united with it, casts off his form.
Thus, through waking and sleeping, that Imperishable One constantly brings all this— both moving and unmoving— to life and causes it to perish.
Having composed this treatise, he himself first caused me to receive it according to the prescribed rule; and I, in turn, [taught] the sages beginning with Marīci.
"Bhṛgu will recite this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of it from me without exception."
Then, having been thus addressed by the great seer Manu, Bhṛgu, with a pleased soul, spoke to all those sages: "Let it be heard."
Of this Svāyambhuva Manu, there were six other great-souled and immensely powerful Manus belonging to his lineage, who each created their own respective progeny.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly effulgent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed great splendor;
each, having produced all this world of moving and non-moving beings within his own interval, brought it to completion.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* constitute one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those are a *kalā*,
thirty *kalās* make a *muhūrta*, and a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of as many [muhūrtas].
The sun divides the day and night for humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of living beings, and the day is for the performance of actions.
In the ancestral realm (Pitṛloka), a month constitutes a day and a night; its division is by the two fortnights.
Of these, the dark fortnight is the day for the performance of rites, while the bright fortnight is the night for sleep.
For the gods, a day and a night equal one year; furthermore, their division is as follows:
the northern course of the sun is their day, and the southern course is their night.
Now learn, in brief and in due order, the measure of each of the ages (yugas) that constitutes a single day and night of Brahmā.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three ages, together with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
This four-age cycle that has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand [years], is called a yuga of the gods.
A thousand cycles of divine ages, by calculation,
should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration.
They know that holy day of Brahmā to end after a thousand such ages.
And those people who know day and night consider that very same duration to be the night as well.
At the end of that day and night, he who was asleep awakens;
and having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
The mind, impelled by the desire to create, undergoes transformation;
from it, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.
From Vāyu, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness;
that radiant entity is said to have the quality of form (rūpa).
From light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
That which was previously described as the divine age (yuga) consisting of twelve thousand [years],
multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a manvantara.
The Manvantaras are innumerable, as are the creations and dissolutions;
the Supreme Lord performs these again and again, as if in play.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete in all four quarters, as was Truth;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred for men through unrighteousness.
In the other ages, however, Dharma has been diminished by one quarter at each step due to the influence of material gain.
And through theft, falsehood, and deceit, righteousness departs foot by foot.
In the Kṛta age, men are free from disease, have all their goals accomplished, and live for four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter at each stage.
The lifespan of mortals declared in the Veda, as well as the fruits of their ritual actions, likewise diminish.
In this world, the fruits and the powers of embodied beings ripen according to the age.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are one way, in the Tretā another, and in the Dvāpara yet others;
in the Kali age they are different again, according to the decline of the ages.
Austerity is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is the means in the Dvāpara, and giving alone in the Kali age.
But for the protection of this entire creation, that one of great splendor ordained distinct duties for those born from his mouth,
arms, thighs, and feet.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving and receiving gifts.
The protection of subjects, the giving of gifts, sacrifice, study,
and non-attachment to sensual objects— this, in brief, is the duty of the Kṣatriya.
The protection of cattle, the giving of gifts, sacrifice, and study— this is the duty of the Vaiśya.
Trade, lending at interest, and agriculture are the duties of a Vaiśya.
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra:
service toward these very same castes, performed without malice.
A man is declared to be increasingly pure from the navel upward;
therefore, his mouth has been called the purest part by the Self-existent One himself.
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation.
For the Self-existent One, having performed austerities, created him from his own mouth in the beginning,
for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the inhabitants of heaven always consume the sacrificial offerings (havya),
and the ancestors likewise consume the ancestral offerings (kavya)?
Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by the intellect;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brahmins, the learned are superior; among the learned, those of firm resolve;
among those of firm resolve, the performers of duty; and among the performers, those who know Brahman.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is destined for union with Brahman.
For a Brāhmaṇa, being born upon this earth,
is born as a sovereign over all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
"Everything whatsoever that exists in this world is the property of the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and his noble lineage, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this."
A Brāhmaṇa eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
for it is through the Brāhmaṇa’s compassion that other people enjoy their food.
For the purpose of discerning the duties of those remaining in their proper order,
the wise Manu, the son of the Self-existent, composed this treatise.
This [work] should be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa,
and it should be correctly expounded to his pupils by him alone, and not by anyone else.
A Brāhmaṇa who studies this treatise and is firm in his vows is never tainted by the defects of action arising from mind, speech, or body.
He purifies his lineage and seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even alone, he is worthy of this entire earth.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this brings fame and long life; this is the supreme means to the highest good.
In this [work], dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions.
And the eternal conduct of all four castes is likewise [to be observed].
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śruti and the Smṛti;
therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly devoted to it.

A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda; however, one who is endowed with right conduct becomes a partaker of the full fruit. Having thus observed the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages—
They have grasped right conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.
And [he shall declare] the origin of the world,
the rules for the sacraments, the practice of religious observances, and the supreme rule for the ritual bath.
The taking of a wife, the characteristics of the various forms of marriage,
the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
The characteristics of the various modes of livelihood, as well as the observances of a Snātaka;
what may and may not be eaten, ritual purity, and the purification of substances.
The duties pertaining to women, the life of asceticism, liberation, and renunciation;
the entire duty of the king, and the adjudication of legal cases.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife,
the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns (criminals).
[He shall describe] the service of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes,
the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation.
Furthermore, he shall explain the threefold journey through saṃsāra arising from action,
the supreme good resulting from actions, and the examination of the merits and defects of those actions.
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families,
and the laws of heretical sects and guilds.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me,
so now you also should learn it from me.
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise, the virtuous, and those always free from hatred and passion,
and which is approved by the heart.
A nature driven solely by desire is not praised, nor indeed is there such a thing as desirelessness in this world;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual acts are both rooted in desire.
Desire indeed has its root in intention; sacrifices originate from intention;
and vows and the duties of self-restraint are all recorded as being born of intention.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
By conducting oneself properly toward these [elders], one goes to the world of the immortals;
and here on earth, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the tradition (smṛti) and the conduct (śīla) of those who know it,
as well as the practice of the virtuous and the satisfaction of one's own self.
Whatever duty has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all that is declared in the Veda, for it contains all knowledge.
But having surveyed all this entirely with the eye of knowledge,
a learned man, relying on the authority of the revealed scripture, should indeed remain steadfast in his own duty.
For a man who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and supreme happiness after death.
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed the Smṛti;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them Dharma has shone forth.
That twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic (hetuśāstra), would hold those two roots in contempt—
he is an atheist and a reviler of the Veda, and he should be excluded by the virtuous.
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—
they say that this fourfold set is the direct definition of Dharma.
For those who are not attached to wealth and sensual pleasure, the knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the Veda is the supreme authority.
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of them have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise.
"When the sun has risen, when it has not yet risen, and likewise at the time of twilight—sacrifice is performed in every way;
such is the Vedic revelation."
He for whom the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral pyre are prescribed by means of sacred mantras—
only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
which was created by the gods, they call Brahmāvarta.
In that region, whatever custom has been handed down through a continuous tradition among the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes— that is called "right conduct" (sadācāra).
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and the Śūrasenakas—
this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣideśa), which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this land,
all men on earth should learn their respective duties.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains,
extending eastward from Vinaśana and westward from Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country).
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
and between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief.
Learn now the origin of all this, as well as the duties of the social classes (varṇas).

For the twice-born, the purifying sacrament of the body, beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception rite), must be performed through meritorious Vedic rites; it is sanctifying both after death and in this world.
By means of oblations for the fetus, and by the rites of birth, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass,
the sin of the seed and the sin of the womb are wiped away from the twice-born.
By the study of the Veda, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the knowledge of the three Vedas, by sacrifices, by sons,
by the great sacrifices, and by other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.
Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed for the male child;
it includes the ceremonial feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
One should cause his naming ceremony to be performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end with a word for "shelter" (śarman); that of a king (Kṣatriya) should be endowed with a word for "protection" (rakṣā);
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with a word for "prosperity" (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be connected with a word for "service" (preṣya).
For women, [the name] should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning,
captivating, auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and containing a word of benediction.
In the fourth month, the infant's first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food, or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.
The *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) for all twice-born classes must, according to the law,
be performed in the first or third year, as enjoined by the *Śruti*.
One should perform the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception.
In the eleventh year from conception for a king, and in the twelfth year from conception for a Vaiśya.
For a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster, the initiation should be performed in the fifth year;
for a Kṣatriya seeking power, in the sixth; and for a Vaiśya desiring worldly prosperity in this life, in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this time, if these three [classes] likewise remain uninitiated at the proper time,
they become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vratyas, and despised by the Aryas.
A Brāhmaṇa shall never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the rule.
The skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat are for the religious student (brahmacārin).
They shall wear, in the respective order, garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.
In the absence of muñja grass, however, [the girdle] should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass;
it should have a single triple-knotted cord, or three, or even five.
The sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen yarn.
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vāṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to reach the hairline in length;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, but that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose.
All those [sacrificial posts] should be straight, free from blemishes, pleasing to the sight,
not causing alarm to men, possessed of their bark, and undamaged by fire.
Having received the desired alms and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and then go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should beg for alms using the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya should place it at the end.
[He should beg from] his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt.
He should beg for alms from the first person who does not treat him with contempt.
Having collected that alms-food as much as is required without guile,
