and having offered it to his teacher, he should eat while facing the east, pure and having sipped water.
Eating while facing east promotes longevity; eating while facing south brings fame;
eating while facing west procures prosperity; and indeed, eating while facing north partakes of truth.
Having sipped water, the twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
and having eaten, he should properly sip water again and touch the cavities of the head with water.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way.
For food that is always eaten with reverence bestows strength and vigor;
however, that same food, when eaten without reverence, destroys both of these.
One should not give the remains of one's food to anyone, nor should one eat while in an intermediate state [of impurity];
one should certainly not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to the attainment of heaven;
it is meritless and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
A Brahmin should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
or he may use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya tīrtha.
They declare that the base of the thumb is the *brāhma* tīrtha;
the root of the fingers is the *kāya*; the tips are the *deva*; and below those two is the *pitrya*.
First, one should sip water three times; then, one should wipe the mouth twice.
One should also touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head.

One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand (tīrtha), in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north.
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that is merely swallowed; and a Śūdra, by water touched at the extremity [of the lips].
When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when it is on the left, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*.
Having cast his girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others accompanied by the appropriate mantras.
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, it is in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya, it is considered to be two years later than that.
This entire sequence of rites for women must be performed without mantras,
for the sake of purifying the body, at the proper time and in the proper order.
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and household duties are their tending of the sacred fires.
This rite of initiation for the twice-born has been declared; it is meritorious and manifests their true birth. Now learn the application of their duties.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.
But when about to study, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north,
he should be taught with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light clothing, and with his senses subdued.
At the beginning and at the end of the study of the Veda, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the hands together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
But when the student is about to begin his recitation, the teacher, always alert, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when [the student] says, "May there be a pause."
A Brahmin should always utter the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end [of his recitation];
for that which is not preceded by *oṃ* flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
Sitting upon the eastern bank [of a river] and purified by means of purifiers,
one who is cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.
Prajāpati milked from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*,
as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone,
Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
But by repeating this triad a thousand times outside [the village],
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One who is devoid of this Ṛgvedic verse, as well as of timely performance of his own duties,
incurs reproach among the virtuous, even if born from the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya.
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) preceded by the syllable Oṃ,
and the three-footed Sāvitrī— these should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of offering oblations and sacrificing flow away;

however, the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as difficult to perform, for it is both Brahman and Prajāpati. The sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice performed according to ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña).
The whispered recitation is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation is recorded as being a thousandfold.
The four types of *pākayajña* sacrifices, together with those prescribed by ritual injunctions (*vidhiyajña*),
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*).
A Brāhmaṇa attains perfection through the recitation of sacred texts alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a true Brāhmaṇa.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining his senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
The eleven faculties which the ancient sages have declared—
I shall explain them correctly, in their proper order and according to the truth.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
Among these, the five beginning with the ear are known in their proper order as the organs of perception (buddhīndriya).
The five organs of action among these are said to be the anus and so forth.
The mind is to be known as the eleventh, which by its own nature partakes of both;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more.

He who attains all these [objects of desire] and he who renounces them entirely— the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment. These [senses] cannot be so effectively restrained by mere abstinence [from objects].
Just as [the senses] are constantly restrained from their objects by means of knowledge.
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and ascetic penances—
none of these ever lead to success for one whose disposition is corrupted.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled [objects of sense],
neither rejoices nor feels dejection, is to be known as one who has conquered his senses.
If even one among all the senses leaks away,
through that [leakage] his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Having brought the collection of the senses under control and likewise restraining the mind,
one should accomplish all goals by means of yoga, without exhausting the body.

Standing, one should recite the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but sitting, one should do so during the evening twilight until the stars are clearly visible. By standing and reciting during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed during the night.
But sitting facing the west, he destroys the impurity produced during the day.
But he who does not stand for the morning [prayer], nor performs the evening one—
he, like a Śūdra, is to be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born.
Restrained and established in the daily rite near water,
he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Sāvitrī.
In the case of the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, in the daily private recitation of the Veda,
and indeed in the mantras for the fire-oblation, there is no restriction regarding days when study is forbidden.
In the daily recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice."
The merit of an oblation offered to Brahman is as great as that of an oblation accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call, even when performed during a period when study is forbidden.
He who, being self-controlled and pure, studies his own Veda for a year according to the prescribed rule—
for him this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, ghee, and honey.

Having been initiated with the sacred thread, a twice-born man shall perform the tending of the sacred fires, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and doing what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return home (samāvartana).

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and a kinsman— these ten are to be taught according to the law.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even though he knows the truth, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in the world.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two perishes or incurs enmity.
Where neither spiritual merit nor material wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve,
there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil.
A teacher of the Veda should, if he so desires, die together with his knowledge;
even in times of dire distress, he must never sow it upon barren soil.
Knowledge, having approached a Brāhmaṇa, said: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to a scorner, so that I may remain most powerful."

"But speak to that Brahmin alone whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a student of sacred knowledge— to such a one, who is a guardian of the treasure and free from negligence, do you impart me. However, he who should obtain the Veda from one who is studying it without having received permission..."
He who is guilty of stealing the Veda falls into hell.
One should first pay homage to that person from whom one receives knowledge— whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he has mastered the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods.
One should not sit upon a bed or a seat that has been used by a superior;
moreover, while remaining on one's bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation.
For when an elder approaches, the vital breaths of a youth indeed rise upward;
by rising to meet him and by saluting him, he recovers them once again.

For one who is habitually respectful in salutation and constantly serves the elders, four things increase: life-span, merit, fame, and strength. When a Brahmin, after performing a salutation, addresses an elder...
He should announce his own name, saying, "I am named so-and-so."
To those who do not know how to address one by name,
a wise man should say "I am [name]," and he should do the same for all women.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the state of being "bhoḥ" is the essential nature of names.
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one";
and at the end of that person's name, the preceding syllable should be pronounced with a protracted *pluta* vowel followed by the sound *a*.
A Brahmin who does not know the proper response to a salutation should not be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Upon meeting, one should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (*kuśala*), a Kṣatriya about his freedom from affliction (*anāmaya*),
a Vaiśya about his prosperity (*kṣema*), and a Śūdra about his health (*ārogya*).
One who is initiated should not be addressed by name, even if he is younger;
one who knows the Dharma should address him by using the words "bho" or "bhavat" at the beginning.
But a woman who is the wife of another and is not related by birth—toward her he should speak thus: "Lady," "Fortunate one," or "Sister."
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself,
saying, "I am so-and-so."
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one's guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
The wife of a brother of the same caste is to be saluted every day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the women who are one's paternal or maternal relatives are to be saluted.
Toward his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, and his elder sister as well, he should maintain the same conduct as toward his mother;
yet the mother is more venerable than they.
Friendship among citizens is said to last ten years; that among artists, five years;
that among those learned in the Vedas, three years; and among those of the same lineage, it lasts even for a very short time.
A ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king—one should recognize these two as father and son; yet, between the two, the Brahmin is the father.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—
these are the grounds for respect, each subsequent one being weightier than the preceding.
Among the three social orders, these five qualities exist in greater measure and with greater excellence in some than in others.
Wherever such persons may be found, even a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade of life is worthy of honor in that place.
Way must be yielded to one in a carriage, to one who is in his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one carrying a burden, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
Among all these gathered together, the bath-graduate (snātaka) and the king are to be honored;
and between the king and the bath-graduate, the bath-graduate alone receives the honor due to a sovereign.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil,
teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya.
But he who teaches even a single portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the prescribed rules,
and supports [the child] with food, is called a guru.
He who, being chosen, performs for another the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others,
is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as mother and father; one should never bear him malice.
An Ācārya outweighs ten Upādhyāyas; a father outweighs a hundred Ācāryas;
but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in venerability.
Between the biological progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world.
One should understand that the birth which a mother and father produce for him through mutual desire is his physical birth,
insofar as he is born from the womb.
But the caste which his teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is true, that is undecaying, and that is immortal.
One should know that person to be a teacher here as well, by virtue of that service rendered through sacred learning, whether it be little or much, which has benefited him.
One who effects a Vedic birth and is an instructor of one's own duty becomes,
according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child.
The young Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his fathers;
having embraced them with his knowledge, he addressed them as "my little sons."
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them: "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant man is indeed a child; he who imparts the sacred mantras becomes his father. For they call the ignorant man a "child," but one who imparts the mantras is called a "father."
Not by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) is great.
The seniority of Brahmins is based on knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas on valor,
that of Vaiśyas on grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone on birth.
One does not become an elder merely because one's head is gray;
the gods know him as an elder who, even if young, is devoted to study.
As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three bear the name [only] in name.
As a eunuch is fruitless with women, as a cow is fruitless with another cow,
and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
The instruction of living beings should be carried out through non-violence alone for the sake of their welfare;
and one who desires dharma should employ speech that is both sweet and gentle.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always properly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit that is reached through the Vedanta.

One should not be a wounder of others' vitals even when afflicted, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds of malice toward others; one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech leads away from the world of light.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if at poison;
he should always long for contempt as if it were nectar.
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in peace and wakes in peace.
One moves with ease in this world; he who treats others with contempt perishes.
By this sequential method, a twice-born man whose self has been consecrated,
dwelling with his guru, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the acquisition of the Veda.
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (the Upanishads), must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific forms of austerity and vows prescribed by rule.
A twice-born man of the highest order, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is declared to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin in this world.
Even that twice-born man who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability, performs the highest austerity even unto the tips of his nails.
The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his descendants.
The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
Among those, that which is his birth from the Veda, marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass—
therein the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, and the teacher his father.
They declare the teacher to be a father because of his imparting the Veda;
for no ritual duty whatsoever is enjoined upon him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
One should not pronounce the Veda, except when offering the *svadhā* libation;
for he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born into the Veda.
For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) is prescribed,
as well as the formal acquisition of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa), in due order according to the rules.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, and girdle are prescribed for him,
whatever staff and whatever garment [are prescribed], those same shall be used by him even during his religious observances (vrata).
A student living with his teacher must observe these following rules,
restraining the entire collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors;
likewise, he should perform the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes, and carrying an umbrella;
as well as lust, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments—these he should avoid.
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, and likewise falsehood;
gazing at and touching women, and injury to others—[one should avoid these].
One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen.
For by intentionally emitting semen, one indeed destroys his own vow.
If a twice-born student (*brahmacārī*) should involuntarily emit semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and kuśa grass—
as much as required— and he should go out for alms every day.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, who are praiseworthy in their own duties.
One should not beg for alms within the family of one's teacher, nor among the families of one's paternal or maternal kin;
however, if other houses are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding category in turn.
Or, if those previously mentioned are not available, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, but avoiding those who are under accusation.
Having fetched fuel-sticks from a distance, he should place them in the open air;
and evening and morning, he should offer oblations with them into the fire without weariness.

If, while not being afflicted by illness, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇi-vrata).
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the subsistence of a vow-holder on alms is equal to fasting.
At a rite for the gods, he should eat like one observing a vow; at a rite for the ancestors, like a seer.
If requested, he may eat at his pleasure; his vow is not thereby violated.
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Rājanya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not ordained in such a manner.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. He should likewise control his body, his speech, his intellect, his senses, and his mind.
Restraining himself and with palms joined in reverence, he should stand gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always have his hand uplifted, maintain virtuous conduct, and be well-restrained; and when told, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire.
He should rise before him and go to rest after him.
One should not engage in conversation or respond to a call while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away.

Standing, one should serve him while he is seated; approaching, one should serve him while he is standing; going out to meet him, one should serve him as he comes toward oneself; and running after him, one should serve him while he is running.
Facing one who has turned his back, approaching one who is at a distance,
bowing down to one who is lying down, and standing by the side of one who is giving orders.
His bed and seat must always be low in the presence of his teacher;
moreover, within the range of the teacher's vision, he must not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one ever imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or even slander of one's teacher occurs,
there the ears must be covered, or one should depart from that place to another.
From reviling others one becomes a donkey; from censuring others one indeed becomes a dog; one who eats another's food becomes a worm; and one who is envious becomes an insect.
Standing at a distance, he should not honor him; nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman;
and while standing in a vehicle or on a seat, he should descend before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher either downwind or upwind;
nor, even if out of his hearing, should one utter anything at all concerning the teacher.
One may sit together with one's teacher on vehicles drawn by cattle, horses, or camels, on a palace, on a grass mat, on mats made of reeds, or on stone slabs, wooden planks, and boats.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher;
and unless permitted by the teacher, one should not pay homage to one’s own elders.
In this very same way, one should always behave toward teachers of knowledge, toward one's own elders,
and also toward those who restrain one from unrighteousness and instruct one in what is beneficial.

One should always behave toward those who are superior exactly as one does toward one’s guru— toward the guru’s sons who are noble, and also toward the guru’s own kinsmen. A child, a contemporary, or even a pupil may act thus during the performance of a sacrificial rite.
A teacher’s son who teaches deserves honor like that given to the teacher himself.
One should not perform the rubbing of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one wash his feet.
The wives of the guru who are of the same caste (sa-varṇā) should be honored like the guru himself;
those who are not of the same caste (a-savarṇā), however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these must not be performed for the wife of one's guru.
But a young wife of one's guru must not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world by a man who has completed twenty years of age and who discerns between virtue and vice.
This is the nature of women: they are a source of corruption for men in this world. Therefore, the wise do not become negligent regarding women.
For in this world,
a woman is indeed capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
However, at his own will, a young man on the ground should perform a formal salutation to the wives of his elders who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey, one should clasp the feet of the teacher's wives and offer daily salutations,
remembering the dharma of the virtuous.
Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water,
so does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge that resides with the teacher.

He may be shaven-headed, or he may wear matted hair, or he may have a single lock of matted hair on his crown; the sun must never set while he is still in a village, nor should it ever rise upon him there.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own will,
or if it should set while he is unaware, he shall fast for the day while muttering prayers.
For he who lies down when the sun is setting, or who rises while the sun is already up,
and fails to perform the penance, shall be joined with great sin.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to the two twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule.
If a woman, or one of lower birth, should perform any virtuous act, he should practice all of that with diligence; and whatever brings him mental delight, that too he should practice.
Dharma and wealth are said to be the highest good; so too are pleasure and wealth, or even dharma alone.
Or perhaps wealth alone is the highest good in this world; such is the established position regarding the three aims of life.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with disrespect even by one who is distressed, especially by a Brahmin.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
The suffering that parents endure at the birth of human beings cannot be compensated for even in a hundred years.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times;
for when these three are satisfied, all austerity is accomplished.
Service to these three is declared to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
For these indeed are the three worlds, these are the three stages of life;
these indeed are the three Vedas, and these are said to be the three sacred fires.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, a householder shall conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By devotion to his mother he attains this world; by devotion to his father, the middle world;
and by service to his teacher, he likewise attains the world of Brahman.
All religious duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual acts are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not serve anyone else;
he should constantly perform service toward them alone, devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to them.
Whatever one may perform for the sake of the next world, provided it does not obstruct those [prior duties],
that should be announced to them through thought, word, and deed.
For in these three, a man's duty is fully accomplished;
this is the supreme dharma directly perceived, while any other is called a secondary dharma.
One who possesses faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a person of lower status;
likewise, one should accept the highest dharma even from another, and a jewel of a woman even from a family of low birth.
Even from poison, one should take the nectar; even from a child, a well-spoken word;
even from an enemy, good conduct; and even from an impure place, gold.
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, well-spoken words,
and various arts— these are to be accepted from everyone.
In times of distress, studying under one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is permitted;
likewise, following after and serving such a teacher must continue for as long as the study lasts.
A student should not dwell for life with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher,
nor with a Brāhmaṇa who has not mastered the Veda, if he desires the highest goal.
But if he should prefer to dwell permanently in the house of his teacher,
he should serve him with diligence until the liberation from the body.
That Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes directly to the eternal abode of Brahman.
One who knows the Dharma should not offer anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when about to perform the final bath, he may, upon being commanded by the teacher, procure wealth for the teacher according to his ability.

A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, a seat, grain, vegetables, or clothing— one should bring these to the teacher to produce his satisfaction. When the teacher has indeed passed away, one should serve the teacher's son if he is endowed with good qualities.

One should behave toward the wife of a guru or toward a sapinda relative as one does toward the guru himself. When these [elders] are not present, one who remains steadfast in standing, sitting, and movement, and who performs service to the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body.
The Brahmin who thus practices the vow of celibacy without fail goes to the highest station and is not born again in this world.
One should observe the vow pertaining to the three Vedas under a teacher for thirty-six years;
or half of that, or a quarter, or until they have been mastered.
Having studied the three Vedas, or two, or even one, in due order,
and having remained inviolate in his vow of studentship, he shall enter the stage of the householder.
When he has been recognized by his own conduct as the one who inherits the Veda from his father,
one should first honor him— who is wearing a garland and seated upon the couch— with a cow.
Having bathed with the permission of his guru and returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
A woman who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of one's mother and who is not of the same *gotra* as one's father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union.
Even if they possess great wealth in cattle, goats, sheep, money, and grain—
In matters concerning marriage, one should avoid these ten types of families.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.
One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a bear, a tree, or a river, nor one whose name is that of a low-caste person or a mountain.
Nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant, nor one with a terrifying name.
He should marry a woman who has no missing limbs, whose name is auspicious, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
A wise man should not marry a girl whose brother does not exist or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) and thus subject to the fault of illegitimacy.
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] are permissible in descending order.
A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as the wife for a Śūdra; she and one of his own [caste] are prescribed for a Vaiśya;
she and those two and one of his own [caste] for a Kṣatriya; and they and one of his own [caste] for a man of the highest birth (a Brāhmaṇa).
For even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of lower castes,
quickly lead their families, along with their descendants, to the status of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having that son as one's offspring.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests have that [guest] as their primary element, neither the ancestors nor the gods eat; he does not go to heaven.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a Śūdra woman, for one who has been defiled by her breath,
and for one begotten by her— no atonement is prescribed.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women, which are beneficial or harmful both after death and in this world for all four castes.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura;
the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
I shall declare to you all that which is the lawful duty for each caste, as well as their respective virtues and faults, and the merits and demerits regarding their offspring.

Six [forms of marriage] in order are for a Brāhmaṇa; for a Kṣatriya, the four lower ones; but one should know that those same [six], excluding the Rākṣasa form, are lawful for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra. The wise know the first four to be recommended for a Brāhmaṇa.
The Rākṣasa form is the one [permitted] for a Kṣatriya; the Āsura form is for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of these five, however, three are declared here to be lawful and two unlawful:
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.
The two previously mentioned forms of marriage, whether performed separately or combined,
namely the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— these two are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Having clothed and honored him according to his learning and character,
the gift of a daughter by personally inviting him is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
But when a sacrifice has been properly commenced and a priest is performing the ritual,
the giving of a daughter after having adorned her is declared to be the *daiva* rite.
Having received one or two pairs of cattle from the groom according to the law,
the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite.
Having addressed them with the words, "May you both perform your duty together," and having honored them,
the giving away of the maiden is recorded as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva form; it arises from passion and has sexual intercourse as its purpose.
Having slain, having cut, and having pierced [the groom], while she is crying out and weeping,
the forcible abduction of a maiden from her home is called the Rākṣasa rite.

He who approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged— this is the most sinful of marriages, the eighth and lowest, known as the Paiśāca. For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is distinguished as the best.
But for the other castes, [the marriage] is by mutual desire.

O Brahmins, listen as I fully proclaim all those qualities which Manu has declared for each of these forms of marriage; hear them all as I recite them. [One who marries according to the first form delivers] ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman, if he performs meritorious deeds, liberates his ancestors from sin.
A son born of a wife wedded according to the Daiva rite rescues seven ancestors and seven descendants;

a son born of a wife wedded according to the Ārṣa rite rescues three ancestors and three descendants; and a son born of a wife wedded according to the Kāya (Prājāpatya) rite rescues six ancestors and six descendants.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, in their proper order,
sons endowed with Vedic luster are born, esteemed by the learned;
they are possessed of beauty, goodness, and virtue, wealthy, and renowned.
Having sufficient enjoyments and being most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
But from the remaining improper marriages are born sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and the sacred law.
Through blameless marriages of women, the offspring becomes blameless; through blameworthy ones, it becomes blameworthy. Therefore, a man should avoid blameworthy marriages.
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known regarding the marriage ceremony with women of different castes.
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman during a marriage with a man of higher caste.

He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may approach her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days (parvan).
The natural fertile period (*ṛtu*) of women is traditionally held to consist of sixteen nights,
together with the four other days that are censured by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four are censured, as are the eleventh and the thirteenth;
the remaining ten nights, however, are praised.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on the even nights.
A male is born when the male seed is in excess, and a female when the female seed is in excess;
when they are equal, a neuter is born, or twins of both sexes; and when the seed is depleted or scanty, the opposite occurs.
Avoiding women on the eight censured nights and on the other [inauspicious] nights,
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī), regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits.
A wise father of a maiden should not accept even the slightest bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property—
whether it be her carriage, her clothing, or anything else— those sinners go to a downward state.

Regarding the *ārṣa* marriage, some say that the pair of cattle is a bride-price (*śulka*), but that is false; for whether it be small or large, it remains a sale nonetheless. When the kinsmen do not take a bride-price from those [girls], that is not a sale.
That honor shown to young maidens is merely an act of compassion; however,
these women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands,
and brothers-in-law who desire abundant prosperity.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all rituals there are fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family perishes quickly;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Those houses which female relatives curse when they have not been honored perish on all sides, as if struck by a magical spell (*kṛtyā*). Therefore,
these women should always be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Men who desire prosperity should always honor one another during rites of hospitality and at festivals.
In that family where the husband is constantly content with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband,
there indeed is certain and perpetual well-being.

For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight her husband; and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed. But when a woman is pleased, the entire family is pleased.
But when she does not shine, everything indeed fails to shine.

(Manu 3.62c) Through improper marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the neglect of Vedic study, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble families fall into a state of ignobility. (Manu 3.63)
[One falls from caste] through crafts, through trade, and by having offspring solely with Śūdra women;
through cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king;
and also through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and through atheism regarding ritual acts.
Families that are deficient in sacred knowledge quickly perish;
however, families that are enriched by sacred knowledge, even if they possess little wealth,
attain the rank of noble lineages and acquire great renown.
[From hereon, the verse numbering is "-10"] A householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rule in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five sacrifices and the daily cooking.

A householder has five slaughter-houses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water-jar; by using these, he is bound. To provide atonement for all of these in their respective order, the great seers have prescribed—
Five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) are prescribed for householders to be performed every day.
Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation (tarpaṇa) is the sacrifice to the ancestors;
the burnt offering (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.

He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while living constantly in the house, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse. He who [provides for] the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—
He who does not offer oblations to these five is not truly living, even though he breathes.
They declare that the five sacrifices are indeed the *ahuta*, the *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *brāhmya-huta*, and the *prāśita*.
Recitation is the *ahuta* sacrifice; the *homa* oblation is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits is the *prahuta*;
the *brāhmya-huta* is the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*.

One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) as well as to rites directed toward the gods (daiva-karman) in this world; for it is by being engaged in rites directed toward the gods that one sustains this entire universe, both moving and stationary.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.

Just as all living beings exist by depending upon the wind, so do all other stages of life (āśramas) exist by depending upon the householder. For the members of the other three stages of life are daily supported by the householder with both knowledge and food.
The householder alone supports [the other stages]; therefore, the householder’s stage is the foremost.

It must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven, and it must be maintained with extreme care by one who desires happiness in this world—though it is difficult for those of weak senses to maintain.
The seers, the ancestors, the gods, all beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act toward them.
One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Veda, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule,
the ancestors with śrāddha rites and food offerings, and all living beings with the bali offering.
Day after day, one should perform the śrāddha for the ancestors with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing them satisfaction.
At the fivefold sacrifice performed for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in this regard, one should not feed any twice-born man specifically for the Vaiśvadeva rite.
A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform an oblation in the domestic fire with the prepared food of the Vaiśvadeva, according to the prescribed rule, for these deities.
First to Agni and to Soma, and then to both of them together;
and to the Viśvedevas and to Dhanvantari.
To Kuhū, to Anumati, and to Prajāpati;
together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and likewise finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.

Having thus properly offered the oblation, he should present the *bali* offering to Indra, Antaka (Yama), Appati (Varuṇa), and Indu (Soma), together with their followers, proceeding clockwise in all directions.
One should cast [food] at the door with the words, "To the Maruts," and also into the water with the words, "To the Waters.
Likewise, one should offer [food] upon the pestle and mortar with the words, "To the Vanaspatis."
One should offer an oblation to Śrī at the head of the bed and to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
furthermore, one should present an offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
He should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
and likewise for the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night.
On the back of the house, one should offer a bali-oblation for the sake of the welfare of all beings;
then, one should carry all the remainder of the bali toward the south for the ancestors.

He should gently scatter on the ground the remains for dogs, for outcasts, for dog-cookers, for those afflicted with foul diseases, for birds, and for worms. The Brāhmaṇa who thus daily honors all beings in this manner—
He, embodied as light, goes by the straight path to the supreme abode.
Having performed this rite of offerings (bali-karman) in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
and he should give alms to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) according to the prescribed rule.
Whatever meritorious fruit a twice-born householder obtains by giving a cow to his guru according to the prescribed rule,
that same meritorious fruit he obtains by giving alms.
Having honored even a morsel of alms or a vessel of water according to the prescribed rule,
one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
The offerings to the gods and the ancestors (*havya-kavya*) of men who lack discernment perish,
when they are offered out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes.
But that which is offered into the fires of the mouths of Brahmins who are enriched by learning and austerity [is imperishable].
And he delivers [the giver] from misfortune and even from great sin.
To a guest who has arrived, he should offer a seat and water,
as well as food according to his ability, having honored him in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Even for one who constantly gathers grains from the chaff and constantly offers oblations into the five fires, [the guest is superior].
A Brāhmaṇa who dwells unhonored takes away all the merit of his host.
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the houses of the virtuous.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent period, he is therefore called a guest.
One should not consider a Brahmin who lives in the same village, nor even a traveling companion,
to be a guest when he has arrived at one's house, whether it be where the wife resides or where the sacred fires are maintained.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food of others go,
after death, to the state of cattle as those who provide such food.
A guest brought by the sun in the evening must not be turned away by a householder; whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not first offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.
One should provide a seat, a dwelling, a bed, attendance, and respectful service:
the best for the best, the lowly for the lowly, and equal for equals.
But if another guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, one should give him food also according to one's ability; one should not, however, perform the Bali offering again.
A Brahmin should not announce his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by proclaiming them for the sake of a meal, he is called a "vomiter-eater" by the wise.
But for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya is not called a guest in his house;
nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, or even a teacher.
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may,
if he so desires, feed him as well once the Brahmins have finished eating.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra who have arrived at the household also partake of the status of guests.
He should feed those two together with his dependents, practicing compassion.
Other guests as well, such as friends and the like, who have come to his house out of affection,
he should feed with his wife, providing food according to his ability.
One should feed these— women whose husbands are living, young maidens, the sick, and pregnant women— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that foolish man who eats before giving to them is a sinner.
While eating, he does not realize that he himself is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, his own dependents, and the servants have finished eating,
the husband and wife may afterwards eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the seers, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from the sacrifice.

One should honor with the *madhuparka* offering the king, the officiating priest, the *snātaka*, and the guru, as well as one's beloved father-in-law and maternal uncle, again after a year has passed.
Both a king and a Śrotriya, when present at a sacrificial rite, are to be honored with the madhuparka; it is the settled rule that they are not so honored when there is no sacrifice.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer the *bali* oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is indeed called the *vaiśvadeva*, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
But having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should, on the waning of the moon,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha monthly.
The wise know the monthly *śrāddha* for the ancestors as the *anvāhārya*;
and that should be performed with effort using excellent meat.
In that regard, I shall describe in their entirety those best of the twice-born who are to be fed, those who are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food.
At a rite for the gods, he should feed two; at a rite for the ancestors, three; or one at each of the two.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should not be intent upon a large company.
He should attend to hospitality, the place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins.
These five [vices] destroy one's prosperity; therefore, one should not seek after abundance.
This rite for the deceased, performed at the waning of the moon, is known by the name "Pitrya" (ancestral).
For one who is constantly engaged in that [rite], even his worldly activity becomes a rite for the deceased.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods (havya) and offerings to the ancestors (kavya) must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
What is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
At a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, one should feed even a single learned man; by doing so, one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
he is the proper channel for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is considered a guest.
For where a thousand times a thousand ignorant men eat,
one who knows the mantras, being pleased, deserves all of them according to dharma.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavyas) and offerings to the gods (havīṃṣi) should be given to one who is preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
As many mouthfuls as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows from the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*),
for so many [years] does that deceased person swallow glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls.
Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity;
some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established among those devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be presented according to the rule to all four [classes] alike.

If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but his son has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*), or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered the Vedas; [in either case, the son shall perform the rites].
Of these two, one should know the elder to be him whose father is a *śrotriya*;
however, the other deserves hospitality for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; his acquisition should be made by means of wealth.
One should feed that twice-born man at a śrāddha whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend.
He whose śrāddhas and sacrificial offerings have friends as their primary recipients gains no fruit after death from those śrāddhas or those offerings.
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms social alliances through a *śrāddha* offering,
falls from the heavenly world, being a friend to the *śrāddha* rather than to the gods.
That which is given by eating together is declared by the twice-born to be the *paiśāca* dakṣiṇā;
it remains in this very world like a blind cow in a single house.
Just as a sower, having sown seed in barren soil,
does not obtain a fruit, so too a giver, having offered an oblation to one who has not studied the Vedas, does not obtain a fruit.
By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the rules to one who is learned, he makes both the giver and the receiver partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death.
At a śrāddha, one may at will honor a friend, but never an enemy, even if he be highly distinguished.
For an oblation eaten by one who hates [the recipient] becomes fruitless after death.
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at someone's *śrāddha*,
the satisfaction of that person's ancestors shall be eternal for seven generations.
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors);
but this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the husband of a daughter, a relative, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors has arrived, he should examine him with great care.
Manu 3.150a: Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and those who follow the ways of nihilists;
Manu 3.150c: Manu has declared that such men are unworthy Brahmins for the offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who wear matted hair but do not study the Veda, nor those who are weak, nor gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for corporate groups.
Physicians, temple-priests, and likewise meat-sellers,
as well as those who live by trade— these should be excluded from offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).

A village servant, a servant of the king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fire, and likewise a usurer; Manu 3.153a [143m]: A village servant, a servant of the king, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; Manu 3.153c [143mc]: One who opposes his teacher, as well as one who has abandoned the sacred fire, and a usurer.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has abandoned the sacred study, an enemy of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a social guild— these are [excluded from the Śrāddha].
An actor, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a Śūdra woman,
the son of a remarried woman, a one-eyed man, and he in whose house a paramour resides.
One who teaches for a fee, one who is taught for a fee, one whose pupil is a Śūdra,
one who is the teacher of a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka.
One who has abandoned his mother, father, or teacher without cause;
and one who has entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial alliances.

An arsonist, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress), a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; [these are those from whom one must not accept food].
One who disputes with his father, a gambler, as well as a drinker of intoxicants,
one afflicted with a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (poisons).

The maker of bows and arrows, he who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, the betrayer of a friend, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; 3.160.
One who suffers from epilepsy, one with a goiter, one afflicted with white leprosy,
as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and a reviler of the Vedas— these are to be excluded.
One who trains elephants, cattle, horses, or camels; one who lives by the stars (an astrologer); one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of war—these are [excluded].
