One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists as a servant to a low-caste person, and one who performs sacrifices for groups of people; 3.164a–c.
One who is devoid of proper conduct, one who is impotent, as well as one who is constantly begging,
one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous— these are unworthy of gifts.
A shepherd, a keeper of buffaloes, the husband of a woman previously married to another,
and likewise a carrier of corpses— these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man of the highest rank among the twice-born should avoid these lowest of the twice-born, who are of censured conduct and unworthy of the company at a meal, in both circumstances.
But a Brāhmaṇa who does not study the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one must not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.

I shall explain in its entirety that result which accrues to the giver after death from giving to those unworthy of the company (*apāṅktya*) at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors— whether it be an oblation (*havis*) or a funeral offering (*pitrya*). Likewise,
that which is eaten by twice-born men who have not fulfilled their vows, or by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), and so forth.
What is eaten by those unworthy of the row and by others, that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
He who enters into marriage and the consecration of the sacred fires while his elder brother remains unmarried is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, meanwhile, is a *parivitti*.
The elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who so marries, she with whom the marriage is contracted,
the giver of the girl, and the officiating priest— these five all go to hell.
He who, out of lust, would carnally desire the wife of a deceased brother—
even though she has been appointed to him according to dharma— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from the wives of others:
the Kuṇḍa is born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is born when the husband is dead.
Those two beings born in the field of another, both after death and in this world,
destroy the sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya) given by the donors.
As many members of a company as an unworthy guest looks upon while they are eating,
for that many the foolish donor receives no fruit from that act.
Having looked [at the gift], a blind man destroys the fruit of ninety [cows]; one who is one-eyed, of sixty; one with white leprosy, of a hundred;
but one afflicted by a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand for the donor.
As many Brāhmaṇas as a priest who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
so much of the fruit of the donor's meritorious gift shall not accrue to him.
Even a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, by accepting a gift from such a person out of greed,
quickly goes to destruction, like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
Feces are [the reward] for one who sells Soma; pus and blood for a physician;
what is given to a temple-attendant (devalaka) is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
But that which is given to a merchant, that bears fruit neither in this world nor in the next;
it is like an offering poured into ashes, so too is a gift to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
But regarding other unworthy persons who are unfit to sit in the company (apāṅktya), as previously specified,
the wise declare that their food is like fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
Learn now in full about those foremost of the twice-born who purify a row (*paṅkti*) that has been defiled by those unworthy of the company (*apāṅktya*). (Manu 3.183)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the explanatory treatises (pravacana),
and who are born into lineages of those learned in the Veda (śrotriya)— they alone are to be known as the purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana).

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the Veda was given as a dowry, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a teacher, a lifelong celibate student, and one who has given a thousand gifts.
And those Brāhmaṇas who have lived for a hundred years should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
On the day before, or on the very day, when the Śrāddha rite is at hand,
one should properly invite at least three Brahmins who are as described [in the rules].
Once invited for a rite for the ancestors, a twice-born man should always remain self-restrained.
And one should not recite the Vedic meters at that place where the śrāddha is being performed.
For the ancestors attend upon those invited twice-born men;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.
But that best of the twice-born who, having been duly invited to a rite for the gods or the ancestors,
somehow neglects it, being a sinner, shall go to the state of a pig.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha, rejoices with a Śūdra woman,
incurs all whatever evil deed has been committed by the giver.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, and ever-continually chaste,
the Pitṛs— the ancient deities— are highly blessed and have laid down their weapons.
Since the origin of all these [sons] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now by what rules they are to be attended to and by whom.
The sons of all those sages, beginning with Marīci, who were the offspring of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha, are recorded in tradition as the groups of Pitṛs.
The Virājas, sons of Virāj, are remembered as the Soma-drinking ancestors (pitaras) of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are those of the Marīcis and the gods.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are recorded as the ancestors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rakṣases,
Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among Brahmins they are named Somapas; among Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs;
among Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among Śūdras, Sukālins.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kavyas, the Barhiṣads,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas and the Saumyas, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins.
These principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed—
of them also, it should be understood here, the lineage of sons and grandsons is endless.
From the sages were born the ancestors; from the ancestors, the gods and human beings;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—in due order.
Even water, when given with faith using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible merit for them.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitr-kārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daiva-kārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the *rakṣas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection.

One should perform that [rite] beginning and ending with the gods; it should not begin and end with the ancestors. For one who performs it beginning and ending with the ancestors, he perishes quickly along with his lineage.
One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow-dung;
one should also diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south.
In open spaces, on clean ground, and indeed upon the banks of waters,
as well as in secluded places, the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered.
When separate seats provided with sacrificial grass have been prepared,
he should cause those Brahmins, who have properly sipped water, to sit down upon them.
Having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the deities.
Having brought water for them, as well as sesame seeds along with purifiers,
a Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the offering in the fire together with them.
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors according to the rule by the offering of the oblation.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place the offering in the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras.

The ancients call these best of the twice-born the gods of the *śrāddha*, who are free from anger, easily propitiated, and intent upon the nourishment of the world. Having performed the circumambulation of the fire in a counter-clockwise direction, one should complete the entire rite.
With his left hand, he should pour water upon the ground.
Therefore, having formed three pindas from that remainder of the sacrificial oblation, he, being composed,
should offer them facing the south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water libation.
Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) there according to the prescribed rule while remaining pure,
he should wipe that hand on those blades of darbha grass for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ).
Having sipped water and turned toward the north, having slowly restrained his breath three times,
he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the piṇḍas;
and with a concentrated mind, he should smell those piṇḍas in the order they were offered.
Having taken very small portions from each of the rice balls in successive order, he should first cause those same seated Brahmins to eat them according to the prescribed rule.
While the father is still living, one should perform the offering for the ancestors alone;
or else, at the *śrāddha*, one may feed one's own father as if he were a guest (*vipravat*).
In the case of one whose father has passed away but whose grandfather is still living, [one should offer to the grandfather].
Having proclaimed the name of his father, he should proclaim the name of his great-grandfather.
"Or his grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
or, being duly permitted, he may perform it himself at his will.
Having poured water mixed with sesame seeds and *pavitra* grass-grass blades into their hands,
he should offer the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them. Then,
having himself taken hold of the increased amount of food with both hands...
Meditating upon his ancestors, he should gently place [the food] near the Brahmins.
When food is brought that is released from both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras suddenly seize it away.
Being pure and composed, he should first place upon the ground itself the various condiments such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
Various kinds of food to be chewed and food to be swallowed, as well as roots and fruits,
meats that are pleasing to the heart, and fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that [food] forward, he should serve it slowly and with great composure,
remaining pure and extolling all its qualities.
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
Tears send the deceased to the state of ghosts; anger, to enemies; falsehood, to dogs;
touching with the foot, to Rākṣasas; and shaking [the head], to evildoers.
Whatever may be pleasing to the Brahmins, that he should give without avarice;
and he should engage in discussions concerning the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should cause [the guests] to hear the Vedic study, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them slowly and steadily;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and drink as well as with words of praise.
One should diligently feed even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow at a Śrāddha ceremony;
one should provide a Kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds. Furthermore, three things are praised here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot; they should eat while remaining silent. And the twice-born should not describe the qualities of the sacrificial offerings when asked by the giver.
The ancestors eat as long as there is steam in the food, as long as those who eat remain silent,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offerings have not been described.
Whatever one eats with one's head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
A Cāṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
as well as a woman in her courses and a eunuch— these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these [impure persons] during an oblation, a gift, or a meal—
whether it be an offering to the gods or one to the ancestors— that becomes ineffective.
A pig destroys [the merit] by its smell; a cock, by the wind of its wings;
a dog, by the casting of its gaze; and one born of the lowest caste, by touch.
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should have such a person removed once again.
A Brahmin who has arrived seeking alms for the sake of a meal should be honored according to one's ability, with the permission of the other Brahmins.
Having collected food fit for all castes and sprinkled it with water,
he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have finished eating.

For those who die before receiving the sacraments, for those who abandon their families, and for women of the household, the food-remnant and that which is scattered upon the *darbha* grass shall be their allotted share.

That which has fallen on the ground from the remnants of the meal belongs to the group of slaves; they declare this to be their share at a rite for the ancestors, provided the giver is neither crooked nor deceitful.
For a twice-born man who has died, until the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
one should feed him at a *śrāddha* without offerings to the gods (*adaiva*) and offer a single rice-ball (*piṇḍa*).
But when the *piṇḍakriyā* has been performed for him according to the law,
the sons must perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* by this very same procedure.
He who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*,
that fool goes headlong to the Kālasūtra hell.
If one who has partaken of a śrāddha meal approaches the bed of a Śūdra woman on that same day,
his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement.
Having asked, "Was it well-savored? he should then cause those who are satiated to rinse their mouths;
and once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be happy on all sides."
Immediately after that, the Brāhmaṇas should say to him, "May there be *svadhā*. For the utterance of *svadhā* is the highest benediction in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, after they have eaten, he should present the remainder of the food;
as the twice-born may direct, so he should act, having been authorized by them.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "It is well-savored" (*svaditam*); at a rite for cows, "it is well-cooked" (*suśṛtam*);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (*saṃpannam*); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (*rucitam*).
Likewise, the afternoon, *darbha* grass, the preparation of the site, and sesame seeds [are required].
The creation [of food], its refinement, and the foremost of the twice-born are the perfections in the performance of śrāddha rites.
Darbha grass, a purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (havirya),
as well as whatever purifying substances were mentioned previously, should be understood as the requisites for the oblation.
The food of sages, milk, soma, meat that has not been seasoned, and salt that is not processed— these are said to be, by their very nature, sacrificial oblations (havis).

Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, silent, and pure, and looking toward the southern direction, he should ask these boons of his ancestors: *Manu 3.258a–c*: "Having dismissed those Brahmins, being restrained, silent, and pure, looking toward the southern direction, he should ask these boons of his ancestors."
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having thus performed the offering of the funeral cakes (nirvapaṇa), he should immediately thereafter cause a cow,
a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire to consume those cakes, or else cast them into water.
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes only after [the cremation];
others cause them to be eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water.
A devoted wife, faithful to her husband, intent upon the worship of the ancestors,
and desiring a son, should then properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and wisdom,
as well as one who is wealthy, possessed of offspring, virtuous, and righteous.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen;
having given hospitality to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives.
That remnant of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed.
"Thereafter, one should perform the domestic offering (gṛhabali); thus the law is established."
I shall describe in its entirety that sacrificial offering which, when given to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for many nights and even for eternity.
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, or fruits are offered according to the prescribed rules,
the ancestors of men are satisfied for one month.
For two months [one lives] by means of fish-meat, for three months by the meat of the hariṇa deer,
then for four months by the meat of sheep, and for five months indeed by the meat of birds.

With the flesh of a goat, they are satisfied for six months; with the flesh of a spotted deer (pārṣata), indeed for seven; with the flesh of a black antelope (aina), for eight; and with the flesh of a Ruru deer, for nine. With the meat of boars and buffaloes, however, they remain satisfied for ten months.
But with the flesh of the hare and the tortoise, one satisfies [the ancestors] for exactly eleven months.
But by means of cow’s milk, milk-rice,
and the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa (a ram), there is satisfaction for twelve years.
Black pot-herbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and red deer, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for sages lead to infinite results.
Whatever mixed with honey one may offer on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā constellation.
"May he be born in our lineage who would give us milk-rice with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth day, and during the shadow of an elephant cast toward the east."
Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
In the dark fortnight, beginning from the tenth day and excluding the fourteenth, these lunar days are recommended for the Śrāddha rite;
other days are not so.
By performing [the śrāddha] on days with odd lunar mansions, one attains all desires;
but by performing it on days with even lunar mansions, one obtains abundant offspring for all the ancestors.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for the performance of a śrāddha.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the offering properly circumambulated from right to left,
and remaining alert, one should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion, holding *darbha* grass in the hand.
One should not perform a Śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.
By this rule, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the Hemanta, Grīṣma, and Varṣā seasons— and the rites pertaining to the five sacrifices daily.
The oblation belonging to the ancestral sacrifice is not prescribed for a common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born man who has consecrated the sacred fires, except on the occasion of the New Moon.
Whatever fruit the best of the twice-born obtains by performing the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), he attains that entire fruit simply by satisfying the ancestors with water after bathing.
They call the ancestors Vasus, the grandfathers Rudras, and the great-grandfathers Ādityas; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
He should always be one who eats *vighasa*, or always one whose food is *amṛta*. *Vighasa* is the remnant of what has been eaten; likewise, *amṛta* is the remnant of a sacrifice.
"All this rule concerning the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now hear the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born."
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, the twice-born man,
having taken a wife, shall dwell in his house during the second quarter of his life.
Adopting a mode of life that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury, a Brahmin should live during times when he is not in distress.
For the purpose of securing only the necessities of life,
he should accumulate wealth by means of his own irreproachable occupations, without causing hardship to his body.
One may live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*, or even by the *satya* and the *anṛta*; but never by the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*).
Gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains is to be known as *ṛta*; that which is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
But begging for alms is *mṛta*, while agriculture is traditionally called *pramṛta*.
Trade, however, consists of both truth and falsehood; one may live by that as well. Service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood"; therefore, one should avoid it.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or grain sufficient for a jar;
or he may have enough for three days, or even be one who does not provide for the morrow.
Among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of worlds.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one [proceeds] with two; but the fourth lives by the "Brahma-sacrifice" (brahmasattra).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭi sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
One should never, for the sake of a livelihood, follow the conduct of the worldly;
rather, one should live by the pure, straightforward, and honest way of life of a Brāhmaṇa.
Relying upon supreme contentment, one who seeks happiness should remain self-restrained;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering.
A twice-born Snātaka living by any one of these means of livelihood should observe these following vows, which lead to heaven, long life,
and fame: he should constantly perform his own duty as prescribed in the Veda without sloth.
For by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
One should not pursue wealth through excessive attachment nor by means of forbidden actions;
nor should one seek it from here and there when wealth already exists, even in times of distress.
One should not become attached out of desire to any of the objects of the senses.
And he should mentally restrain any excessive attachment to these [objects].
One should abandon all pursuits that conflict with the study of the Veda;
for one who teaches in whatever manner possible, that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his duty.
Conforming his dress, speech, and disposition to those of his age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage, he should conduct himself here in this world.
He should constantly study the scriptures that quickly increase intelligence, as well as the Vedic Nigamas, for they are auspicious and beneficial.
For in whatever measure a man masters the scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his specialized knowledge shines forth.

One should never, according to one's ability, neglect the sacrifice to the sages (ṛṣiyajña), the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña), the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūtayajña), the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña), and the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the very senses while remaining free from worldly striving.
Some always offer the breath into speech and speech into breath,
perceiving in speech and breath the imperishable accomplishment of the sacrifice.
Other Brahmins always perform these sacrifices through knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of wisdom that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.
One should always offer the Agnihotra at the beginning and the end of day and night;
likewise, one should perform the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice as well.

At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should worship with the *navasasyeṣṭi* sacrifice; likewise at the end of each season, he should worship with *adhvara* sacrifices; at the beginning of each solstice (*ayana*), he should worship with an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should worship with Soma sacrifices. A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires must not fail to perform the *navasasyeṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice.
One who desires to live a long life should not eat new grain or meat.
For his sacred fires, greedy for new grain and meat offerings, desire to consume his very life-breaths when they are not honored with new grain and animal oblations.
No guest who is capable of being honored should dwell in his house without being properly honored with a seat, food, a bed, water, roots, or fruits.
One should not honor, even with mere words, heretics, those who persist in improper acts, those who follow the "cat-vow," the deceitful, sophists, and those who act like herons.

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, who are learned in the Vedas, and who are householders; one should avoid those who are the opposite.
A householder should give to those who do not cook for themselves according to his ability,
and he should provide a share for all beings without causing hardship to himself.

A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from his patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a resident pupil; it is settled that he must not do so from anyone else.
A learned Snātaka Brahmin who is capable should never suffer from hunger in any way,
nor should he wear worn-out or dirty clothes if he possesses the means.
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in acts beneficial to the self.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot filled with water,
the sacred thread, a Veda-text, and two auspicious golden earrings.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor run while it is raining;
nor should one look at one's own reflection in water—this is the settled rule.
One should circumambulate clockwise earth, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees.
Even if he is overcome by passion, he must not approach his wife when her menses are visible;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman overwhelmed by her menstrual flow,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan are diminished.
For him who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by the menses,
wisdom, splendor, strength, sight, and lifespan indeed increase.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
or while she is sneezing or yawning, nor while she is seated at her ease.
A twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one giving birth.
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked. One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
Neither on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain;
neither in a ruined temple, nor ever on an anthill.
Not in pits inhabited by living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
not having reached the bank of a river, nor on the peak of a mountain.
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows,
one should never discharge feces or urine.
Having covered himself with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or similar materials, he should pass by;
restraining his speech, being purified, with his limbs wrapped and his head veiled.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night and during the two twilights, one should face south, as during the day.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction that is comfortable to him, as well as when there is danger to his life.
One's intelligence perishes by urinating facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man; likewise, facing a cow or facing the wind.
One should not blow on a fire with one’s mouth, nor should one look at a naked woman.
One should not throw impure substances into the fire, nor should one warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it beneath oneself, nor should one step over it;
one should not place it underfoot, nor should one cause any injury to its vital parts.
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor travel, nor even lie down;
one should not scratch the ground, nor remove one's own garland.

One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water, nor anything else smeared with impurity, nor blood, nor poisons. One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person. [One may sleep in an empty house.]
One should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor should one go to a sacrifice unless invited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling its calf, nor should one tell anyone about it;
likewise, a wise man, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone.
One should not dwell in a village ruled by the unrighteous, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one live for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one crowded with unrighteous people; nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating.
Neither too early, nor too late, nor having eaten in the evening, should he eat in the morning.
One should not engage in useless exertion, nor should one drink water with the hollowed palms;
one should not eat food in one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor, being impassioned, raise a clamor.
He should never wash his feet in a vessel made of bell-metal.
One should not eat from a broken vessel, nor from one that is defiled by its appearance.
One should not wear shoes, a garment,
a sacred thread, an ornament, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others.
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those disfigured by their tails.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without lashing them excessively with a goad.
He should avoid the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and likewise a broken seat.
He should not clip his nails or hair with his teeth, nor should he tear at his nails.
He should not crush a clod of earth with his feet, nor should he cut grass with his fingernails. He should not perform any fruitless action, nor anything that results in unhappiness for the future.

A man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails goes quickly to destruction, as does one who is a slanderer or impure. He should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should he wear a garland outside [of his garment].
And riding on the back of cows is in every way utterly censured.
One should not pass through a village or a walled house except by the gate;
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
He should never play with dice, nor should he carry his own sandals;
he should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with his food held in his hand, nor while seated on a chair.
One should not eat anything related to sesame after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep naked here, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
for by eating with wet feet, one attains a long life.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or skull fragments; nor should he step upon cotton seeds or husks.
One should not dwell with outcasts, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with those of the lowest castes, nor with Antyāvasāyins.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remnants of food, nor that which has been prepared as an oblation;
nor should one teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.
For he who explains his duty, and he who prescribes his vow,
sinks into the darkness called *asaṃvṛta* along with him alone.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor, while impure from food, should one touch it, nor bathe without water.
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking the head;
and having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse,
a wheel, or a banner, or who live by the profession of a courtesan.
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a tavern is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten taverns; and a king is equal to ten brothels.
A king is declared by tradition to be equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughter-houses; therefore, the acceptance of gifts from him is terrible.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures goes in succession to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the Naraka Kālasūtra, and Mahānaraka;
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pratimūrtika; Lohaśaṅku, Ṛjīṣa, Panthāna, and the Śālmalī river.
And indeed the Forest of Sword-leaves, and likewise the Iron-Boar.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and who desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king.
One should wake up during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as physical austerities rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, having purified himself and composed his mind,
he should stand reciting the morning twilight prayer for a long time at its proper hour, and likewise the evening prayer. By virtue of their prolonged twilight prayers, the seers attained long life.
Wisdom, fame, renown, and indeed the splendor of sacred knowledge;
Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rules on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin,
being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.
On the day of the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the external dismissal of the Vedas;
or he may do so when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon.
Having thus performed the ritual dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside according to the scriptures,
he should abstain for a "bird-night" (two days and nights), that is, for one full day and night.
From this point forward, however, he should recite the Vedic hymns with self-restraint during the bright fortnights;
and he should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.
One should not study the Veda indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras;
having studied the Veda at the end of the night, one should not sleep again while still fatigued.
A twice-born man who is disciplined and free from distress should always recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule;
indeed, he should always avoid these occasions when study is forbidden while he is engaged in recitation.
And while teaching his pupils according to the prescribed rule, he should [behave as follows].

When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when there is a swirling of dust by day— those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions to be times of non-study during the rainy season.
In the event of lightning, thunder, and rain, or when there is a falling of great meteors,
Manu has declared that there shall be no study for the remainder of the day.

One should know that when these [phenomena] appear while the fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, even outside the rainy season, when clouds appear.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies,
one should know that these occasions constitute times when study is suspended for the duration of the day, even during the proper season.
But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be no study as long as the light remains;
for the remainder of the night, it is as during the day.
There shall always be a perpetual suspension of Vedic study in villages and in towns for those who desire perfection in dharma, as well as whenever there is a foul odor. Likewise,
there is a suspension when a corpse is within a village or in the presence of a *vṛṣala*.
There is no study when there is weeping, nor in the midst of a crowd of people.
In water, at midnight, upon voiding excrement or urine,
while impure from food, or after eating at a *śrāddha*, a learned twice-born man should not entertain even a thought [of reciting the Veda].
Having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a wise twice-born man [should likewise refrain].
For three days, one should not recite the Veda during the birth-impurity of a king or during the birth-impurity of Rāhu (an eclipse).
As long as the fragrance and the residue of a funeral meal for a single ancestor remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed one's knees upon a cloth (or seat), nor after eating meat, nor food belonging to one in a state of birth-impurity.
In mist, in the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon day and the fourteenth day, and on the full moon day and the Aṣṭakā festivals; Manu 4.113.
The new moon day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the eighth day of Brahmā and the full moon day [destroy the Veda]; therefore, one should avoid them.

A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a dust storm, when the quarters of the sky are aflame, when jackals howl, or while dogs, donkeys, or camels are barking, nor while in a row [of people].

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a śrāddha ceremony.
Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha, upon touching that, there shall be no study; for the twice-born is remembered as one whose hand is his mouth.
When a village is harassed by thieves, during a panic caused by fire,
and during all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is a suspension of study for the duration of the event.
At the commencement of the term (upākarma) and at its conclusion (utsarga), a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
likewise, on the Aṣṭakā days and on the nights marking the end of the seasons, the suspension lasts for one day and night.
One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant;
nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing in a barren spot, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
Not during a legal dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when suffering from sour eructations.
Nor when one has not taken leave of a guest; nor while a strong wind is blowing;
nor when blood is flowing from the body; nor when one is wounded by a weapon.
One should never recite the *Ṛg* and *Yajur* Vedas while the sound of the *Sāman* is heard;
nor should one do so after having completed the study of the Veda, or after having studied the *Āraṇyaka*.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deity; the Yajurveda belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Knowing this daily extraction of the essence of the three Vedas,
the learned first practice it in due order and afterwards study the Veda.
Upon the passage between [the teacher and the student] of a domestic animal, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat,
one should know that there is no study for a day and a night.
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study:
an impure place for Vedic recitation and an impure self.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon day, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during his wife’s fertile period.
One should not perform a ritual bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in a body of water that is unknown.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a guru, a king, a *snātaka*, a teacher, a tawny person (*babhru*), or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents, water used for bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm,
spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor an ally who is an enemy,
nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
For there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world.
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, show contempt for a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a Brāhmaṇa deeply learned in the Vedas, even if they appear weak.
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
One should not despise oneself because of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity, and one should not consider it difficult to attain.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak an untruth that is pleasant—this is the eternal dharma.
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (may it be well) or simply say "bhadram" (may it be well); one should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when the sun is at its zenith;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with Śūdras.

One should not insult those who are deficient in limbs, those with redundant limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth. A Brahmin, while impure from eating, must not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or a fire.
One who is impure should not look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky during the day, nor when standing in a state of well-being [at night].
Having touched these, one who is impure must always touch the vital breaths with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own orifices without a specific reason;
he should likewise avoid all the hair of his private parts.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
and he should constantly, without weariness, recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire.
For those who are constantly engaged in auspicious conduct and pure in soul,
and who recite prayers and offer oblations, no misfortune exists.
One should constantly recite the Veda itself at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty.
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity alone,
and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Remembering his former birth, he practices the Veda once again;
and by the constant practice of the Veda, he enjoys infinite bliss.
On the new and full moon days, he should constantly perform the Sāvitra and Śānti oblations;
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days.
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, far from where one has washed one's feet,
and far indeed from where the remains of food have been disposed.
One should perform acts of friendliness, grooming, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium,
and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone.
He should visit the deities and righteous, most excellent twice-born men;
and on the sacred festival days (parvan), he should also visit the Lord for protection and his own gurus.
He should salute the elders and offer them his own seat.
With palms joined in reverence, he should wait upon them; as they depart, he should follow behind them.
One should, with vigilance, practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma and is properly established in one's own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly shares in suffering, being diseased and short-lived.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who follows the conduct of the virtuous,
who is full of faith and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
Whatever action depends on others, that he should carefully avoid.
Whatever is under one's own control, that one should diligently cultivate. All that is dependent on others is suffering; all that is under one's own control is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the definition of happiness and suffering.
Whatever action he performs that brings satisfaction to his inner self, that he should perform with effort; but he should avoid the opposite.
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities;
one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and cruelty.
One should not raise a staff against another in a fit of rage, nor should one strike him down.
Except for his son or pupil, he may beat those two for the purpose of correction.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brāhmaṇa with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [a Brahmin] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in sinful wombs.
Having caused blood to flow from the body of a Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting,
a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death.
As many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth,
for so many years in the hereafter is the shedder of that blood devoured by others.
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor cause blood to flow from his body.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who is constantly devoted to violence— he does not prosper in happiness in this world. Even if he is suffering, he should not, by means of righteousness, set his mind upon unrighteousness.
Quickly perceiving the downfall of unrighteous and sinful men.
Unrighteousness practiced in the world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow;
but as it turns slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.

If [the fruit of an action] is not seen in oneself, it appears in one's sons; if not in the sons, then in one's grandsons. But an unrighteous act (adharma) once committed never fails to bear fruit for the doer. Through unrighteousness one prospers for a time, and thereafter one beholds auspicious things.
From that, he conquers his rivals, and [the enemy] perishes along with its very roots.
He should always apply himself to truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and he should instruct his pupils in accordance with dharma, restraining his speech, his arms, and his belly.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness,
and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future unhappiness or is censured by the world.
He should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes; he should not be crooked, nor fickle with his speech, nor intent on actions that harm others.
By that path which his fathers have traveled, by which his grandfathers have traveled—that path of the virtuous he should follow; going by that way, he does not come to harm.

By officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers; by maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; by children, the elderly, and the sick; and by physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and blood relations.
One should not engage in a dispute with one's mother or father, with female relatives, with a brother, with a son, with a wife, with a daughter, or with the group of servants.
By renouncing disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, the householder conquers all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra, and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.

Female relatives dwell in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice dwell in the world of the Viśvedevas; maternal relations dwell in the world of the Waters; and one's mother and maternal uncle dwell upon the earth.
Children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as the lords of the open air.
An elder brother is equal to a father; one's wife and son are one's own body.
One's own shadow, the group of slaves, a daughter, and one's own poverty are the ultimate [refuges];
therefore, when insulted by these, one should always endure it without distress.
Even if he is capable of receiving gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by the act of receiving, his spiritual luster (*brāhmatejas*) is quickly extinguished.
A wise man, even if perishing from hunger, should not accept a gift without first understanding the lawful rule regarding the objects to be received.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold and food increase one's lifespan; land and a cow likewise nourish the body;
a horse [increases] the eyesight, clothing the skin, ghee the vital energy, and sesame seeds progeny.
But a twice-born man who lacks austerity, does not study the Vedas, and delights in accepting gifts,
sinks along with that very recipient, like one in water using a stone as a raft.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear every kind of gift;
for by even a very small one, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
A knower of the Dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who follows the "cat-vow," nor to one who follows the "heron-vow" and is sinful,
nor to one who is ignorant of the Veda.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rule, when given to these three [types of persons],
results in misfortune for both the giver and the receiver in the next world.
Just as one who attempts to cross water by means of a boat made of stone sinks down,
so do both the giver and the recipient sink to the bottom when they are ignorant.
One who makes a banner of dharma, ever greedy, hypocritical, and a deceiver of the world;
One who is injurious and a deceiver of all should be known as a "cat-vowed" person (baiḍālavratika).
A twice-born man who keeps his eyes cast downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own selfish ends, crafty, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata).
Those Brahmins who follow the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
for by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras.
Such Brahmins, both after death and in this world, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda;
and whatever vow is practiced in secret goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, not being a bearer of the [prescribed] marks, lives by the livelihood of one who bears those marks,
incurs the sin of those who bear the marks and is born into the womb of an animal.
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the sin of the person who constructed the reservoir.
If one makes use of his vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given, he shall incur a fourth part of the sin.
One should always perform one's ablutions in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, and in lakes, as well as in hollows and springs.
A wise man should constantly practice the *yamas*, but not the *niyamas* exclusively;
for by failing to perform the *yamas* while devoting himself solely to the *niyamas*, he falls.
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one performed by a priest for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
"This is offensive to the virtuous, wherein these men offer the oblation;
this is contrary to the gods, therefore one should avoid it."
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease;
nor that which is contaminated by hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched with the foot.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan), touched by a woman in her courses (udakyā),
pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit for consumption].
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food [served] after a public proclamation,
the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned— [these one should avoid].
The food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been consecrated for sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound or fettered; 4.210–211a.
The food of one who has been accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as that which is soured, stale, and the leavings of a Śūdra—these must not be eaten.
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats the leavings of others;
the food of a fierce man, the food of a woman in childbirth, and that at which one has rinsed the mouth but where ten days have not yet passed since a death—these are forbidden.

Meat that has not been honored, meat killed for no sacred purpose, the food of a woman who has no male relatives, the food of an enemy, the food of a city-dweller, the food of an outcast, and food sneezed upon— these one should avoid.
The food of a slanderer and a liar, as well as that of one who sells the rewards of sacrifices (or sacrificial implements), the food of an actor, a tailor,
and indeed the food of an ungrateful person— [these should not be eaten].
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a goldsmith, a basket-maker, and likewise a seller of weapons; [Manu 4.215].
Of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, of the washerman of clothes,
of the dyer, of the cruel man, and of him in whose house a paramour resides;
and of those who tolerate a paramour, and of all those who are ruled by women.
And food from one recently deceased within ten days, as well as that which causes dissatisfaction, [must not be eaten].
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame.
The food of an artisan destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a guild and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Regarding those others who have been declared in due order as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise declare that their skin, bones, and hair constitute their food.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, poison, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance.

A learned twice-born man shall not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha). However, if he has no other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night. [He should likewise avoid the food] of a miserly Vedic scholar and that of a liberal usurer.
Having deliberated upon both, the gods ordained food to be equal.
Prajāpati, approaching them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal!
That which is purified by faith from a liberal giver is [efficacious]; the other is destroyed by a lack of faith."

One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with faith, remaining unwearied; for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired by righteous means, those two become inexhaustible.
One should constantly practice the duty of giving (*dānadharma*) consisting of sacrifices and charitable works,
with a completely satisfied disposition, whenever a worthy recipient is encountered, according to one's ability.
Whatever may be asked for, it should be given without malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who shall deliver one from all [sins].
The giver of water attains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra; the giver of a horse, the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the summit of the sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of security obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of the Veda is distinguished as superior to the giving of water,
food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter.
With whatever disposition one bestows any gift,
with that very same disposition one receives it in return, duly honored.
He who accepts what is unhonored, or he who gives what is indeed honored—both of them go to heaven;
but in the reverse case, they go to hell.
One should not be proud of one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice.
Even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift.
A sacrifice perishes through falsehood, and asceticism perishes through pride.
One's lifespan is diminished by speaking ill of Brahmins, and one's merit is lost by boasting of one's own gifts.
One should gradually accumulate dharma, like termites building an anthill,
without causing pain to any living beings, for the sake of having a companion in the next world.
For neither father nor mother remain as companions in the next world;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—dharma alone stands by one.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the kinsmen depart with averted faces; dharma alone follows him.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
The radiant one, whose body is the ether, swiftly leads to the next world that man who is preeminent in dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity.
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form connections with the most excellent, and should avoid those who are inferior.
By approaching only those who are superior and avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence; by the opposite conduct, he reaches the state of a Śūdra.
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
he who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and generosity.
One may accept from anyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, food offered spontaneously, honey, and the gift of safety (abhayadakṣiṇā).
Prajāpati has declared that alms brought and offered spontaneously, without having been previously solicited, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
His ancestors do not eat [his offerings] for fifteen years.
And Agni does not carry the sacrificial oblation for him who treats her with contempt.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or vegetables.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself must not find satisfaction therein.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always receive it from virtuous persons.
A sharecropper, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—
these among Śūdras are whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Whatever his own nature may be, whatever he intends to do,
and how he would serve him— he should disclose himself accordingly.
He who represents himself to virtuous men as something other than what he truly is, is the greatest sinner in the world; he is a thief who steals his own soul.
All objects of speech are fixed; they have speech as their root and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals this speech is a thief of all things.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule, [he may proceed].
Having entrusted everything to his son, he should live having adopted an attitude of neutrality.
He should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for himself;
for by reflecting alone, he attains the highest good.
This eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder has been declared,
as well as the auspicious ritual procedure for the vows of a Snātaka, which increases one's inner strength.
A Brahmin who, learned in the Vedic scriptures, conducts himself according to this mode of life,
being eternally free from sin, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they were declared, the seers spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: Manu 5.01: Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they were declared, the seers spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire.
O Lord, how does death prevail over those Brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duties and are learned in the Vedic scriptures?
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay the Brahmins."
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of right conduct,
laziness, and the defects of food, death seeks to slay the Brahmins.
[Likewise, one should avoid] garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms.
And those things produced from impure substances are not to be eaten by the twice-born.

One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions; likewise, one should avoid *śelu* fruit and the milk of a cow within the first seven days after calving (*peyūṣa*).
One should also avoid *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, and *apūpa* when prepared for no sacred purpose.
Meat that has not been consecrated, as well as food intended for the gods and sacrificial oblations (havis), [should not be eaten].
The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of camels, of one-hoofed animals,
as well as the milk of sheep, of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away;
and the milk of all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo— Manu 5.8–9a.
The milk of a woman and all sour substances must likewise be avoided.
Among sour substances, curd is fit for consumption, as is everything produced from curd;
and likewise those [liquids] that are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.

One should avoid all carnivorous birds as well as those that dwell in villages; likewise, one should avoid those with uncloven hooves that have not been specifically permitted, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the swan (*haṃsa*), the *cakravāka*, the village cock,
the *sārasa*, the *rajjuvāla*, the *dātyūha*, the parrot, and the *sārikā*; likewise,
birds that peck (*pratudān*), web-footed birds, the *koyaṣṭi*, and those that scratch with their claws (*nakhaviṣkirān*).

The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; [these one should avoid].
He who eats the flesh of any creature is said to be an eater of that very creature's flesh;
since an eater of fish is an eater of all kinds of flesh, one should therefore avoid fish.
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are the first two permitted for use in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Likewise, the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all *saśalka* fish may be eaten.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds whose species are unknown.
Likewise, one should avoid all five-toed animals that have been specified as fit for consumption.
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—
these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel.
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village pig, garlic, a village cock,
onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unintentionally eaten these six [forbidden things], one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance;
or else, for the remaining cases, one should observe a fast for a day and perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa.

An excellent twice-born man should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance during the course of a year for the sake of purification from food eaten unknowingly; however, for food known [to be forbidden], he must perform it specifically.
"Commendable wild animals and birds may be killed by Brāhmaṇas for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sake of maintaining their dependents;
for Agastya did so in ancient times."

For even in ancient sacrifices and in the rites of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) were made from the meat of wild animals and birds. Whatever food, whether chewed or swallowed, is mixed with oil or fat and is not censured, [may be offered].
That which has become stale is still fit to be eaten, as is any remnant of an oblation.
Even if it has been stored for a long time, all food made from barley or wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born even if they have not been treated with oil.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas,
or when one is engaged according to the rules, or indeed when there is a danger to one's life.
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa):
both the stationary and the moving; indeed, everything is the sustenance of the vital breath.
Non-moving creatures are the food of moving ones; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs; those without hands are the food of those with hands; and cowards are the food of the brave.
The eater does not incur sin by eating edible creatures day after day;
for the Creator himself created both the creatures to be eaten and the eaters.
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance;
any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance."
Having purchased it himself, or even having produced it, or having received it as a gift from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having honored the gods and the ancestors.
A twice-born man who knows the law must not eat meat contrary to the rule when he is not in distress;
for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he is helplessly devoured after death by those very creatures he has consumed.
The sin incurred by one who kills deer for the sake of wealth is not as great as the sin that befalls one after death who eats meat in vain.
But that man who, though duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat the meat,
goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births.
A Brahmin, adhering to the eternal rule, must never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, he may eat those consecrated with mantras.
In case of necessity, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the animal, or likewise with an animal made of flour;
but one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal,
so many times does the one who kills an animal in vain undergo death after death in successive births.
"Animals were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."
Herbs, cattle, trees, animals,
and birds that meet their death for the sake of sacrifice attain higher rebirths once again.
[In the case of] the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the sacrifice, and rites for the ancestors and the gods, [they do so].
"Manu has declared that cattle may be killed only in this [context] and not elsewhere."
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, while killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animal to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-controlled twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
One should know that violence toward the moving and unmoving creatures ordained by the Veda in this world is indeed non-violence; for from the Veda, dharma shone forth.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or dead.
He who does not desire to inflict the pains of bondage or death upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherein one fixes one's delight—
that one obtains without effort, provided that one harms nothing at all.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having thoroughly considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and binding of embodied beings,
one should desist from the eating of all meat.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the ritual injunctions like a Piśāca,
does not become unpopular in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are considered killers.
He who seeks to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another,
without first honoring the ancestors and the gods— there is no doer of more demeritorious deeds than he.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
By subsisting on pure fruits and roots, or by eating the food of ascetics,
one does not obtain that fruit which is gained from the total renunciation of meat.
"He shall eat me in the next world, whose meat I eat here"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of meat.
There is no fault in the eating of meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
for this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit.
I shall now proclaim the purification for the deceased, as well as the purification of objects,
for all four castes duly and in their proper order.

When a child dies after the teeth have emerged, or after they have been lost, or when the tonsure ceremony has been performed, all the relatives remain impure; the same is declared to be the case during a birth (sūtaka).
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
it may last until the collection of the bones, or for three days, or even for one day.
The status of being a *sapiṇḍa* ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a *samānodaka* persists as long as there is knowledge of birth and name.

Just as this period of impurity on account of a death is prescribed for the *sapiṇḍas*, so too should it be in the case of a birth for those who desire complete purity. For all others, there is impurity on account of a death; however, for the mother and father, there is *sūtaka* (impurity on account of birth).
The birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall belong to the mother alone; having performed ritual ablution, the father becomes pure.
But a man, having emitted semen, becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
Those who touch a corpse are purified by one day and night, and those who offer water by three sets of three nights; those who offer water are purified after three days.
A student who performs the funeral rites for his deceased teacher becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse. In the case of a miscarriage,
one is purified by a number of nights equal to the months of gestation.
When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who was menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath.

For men whose tonsure ceremony has not yet been performed, purification is declared to take one night; but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights. [Manu 5.67] Relatives should place a deceased child less than two years of age outside the village. [Manu 5.68a]
Having adorned [the body], one should place it on pure ground, except for the collection of the bones.

No consecration with fire (agnisaṃskāra) should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation (udakakriyā) be performed. Having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should observe impurity for exactly three days.
The water-libation should not be performed by his relatives for one who has not reached three years of age.
Or they may perform it for one whose teeth have appeared, or even when the naming ceremony has been completed.
When one day has passed for a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), a single day’s fasting is prescribed;
however, in the case of the birth of those who share the same water-ancestors (*ekodaka*), purification is held to occur after three nights.
But for female relatives who have not been consecrated [with marriage], the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those who share the same ancestry (sapindas) become pure according to the very rule already stated.
They should eat food that is free from pungent substances and salt, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should abstain from eating meat and sleep separately on the ground.
This rule for impurity due to death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
when one is absent, this following procedure is to be known by the relatives and kinsmen.
But he who hears that a person residing in a foreign land has died within ten days [of the period of impurity] shall remain impure for only as long as remains of those ten nights.
If the ten-day period has passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a relative or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed,
a man becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on in water.
When a child, one who has gone to another country, or a person belonging to a different lineage (pṛthakpiṇḍa) has died,
one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water while still wearing one's clothes.
If death or birth should occur again within the ten-day period,
