the Brāhmaṇa remains impure for as long as that subsequent period has not yet expired.
When the teacher has passed away, they say that the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it is established that the impurity lasts for one day and night.
Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has arrived [as a guest], one shall remain impure for three nights;
likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, the impurity lasts for a "winged night" (a day and a night).

When a king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun] lasts; however, if the king is not a *śrotriya*, the impurity lasts for a full day, and likewise when a teacher (*guru*) who is well-versed in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) has died. A Brahmin is purified in ten days, and a king (Kṣatriya) in twelve days.
A Vaiśya is purified in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires;
and while performing those rites, even a kinsman does not become impure.
Having touched a divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse,
or one who has touched such a person, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water and being constantly pure, he should recite, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his energy and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability.
Having touched a human bone that still has marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been assigned a penance shall not perform the water-libation until the completion of that vow;
but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after three nights.
For those born of improper intermixture and for those who persist in wandering asceticism (pravrajyā), [the following applies].
The water-libation rite shall be withheld for those who have abandoned themselves [through suicide].
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their own lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor— [one should abandon them].
Having carried out the funeral rites for his own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother,
or guru who has passed away, one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
however, for the twice-born, they should be carried out through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions;
for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman.
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high office;
and the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting his subjects.
And for those killed in a riot or in battle, by lightning or by the king;
and for one who died for the sake of cows or a Brāhmaṇa, or for whomever the king so desires.
The king bears the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vitta-pati, and Yama.
The king is presided over by the Lord of the World; therefore, no period of impurity is ordained for him.
For the purity and impurity of mortals are the very source and dissolution of their worlds.
For one slain in battle with raised weapons while following the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed; such is the established rule regarding the period of impurity.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, his vehicle or weapon;
a Vaiśya, his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, his staff.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding *sapiṇḍa* relatives has been declared to you;
now learn the purification for the deceased concerning all those who are not *sapiṇḍas*.

Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, as if he were a kinsman, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights; the same applies to the maternal relatives of his mother.
If he eats their food, however, he is purified in ten days;
if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.
Having followed a deceased kinsman or even a non-kinsman at his own request,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
One must not have a dead Brahmin carried by a Śūdra while other [eligible] men are present.
For that oblation, defiled by contact with a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, and anointing;
wind, ritual action, the sun, and time—these are the agents of purification for embodied beings.
Of all forms of purity, purity in respect to wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in respect to wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water.
The learned are purified by forbearance; those who have committed forbidden acts are purified by charity;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by the recitation of prayers; and those most proficient in the Vedas are purified by austerity.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This has been declared to you as the definitive rule for the purification of the body.
Listen now to the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.
For objects made of metal, for gems, and for everything made of stone,
purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
A golden vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone;
the same applies to vessels made of substances born of water, those made of stone, and silver, provided they have not been tarnished.
From the union of water and fire, gold and silver were produced;
therefore, for these two, purification by their own source is more effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
The purification for all liquid substances is declared to be straining;
for solid objects, it is sprinkling, and for wooden articles, it is planing.
In the performance of sacrificial rites, the purification of sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* ladles is by washing.
The purification of sacrificial pots (caru), as well as the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), is by means of hot water;
so too for the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the cart (śakaṭa), and the pestle and mortar (musala-ulūkhala).
The purification for large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed.
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is held to be the same as for grain.
Silk and woolen cloth are purified with alkaline earth (*ūṣa*), and *kutapa* blankets with *ariṣṭaka* fruit.
Silk garments [are purified] with bilva fruits, and linen garments with white mustard seeds.
The purification of linen, conch-shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow’s urine or water.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again.
Earthenware that has been defiled by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus,
or blood cannot be purified even by re-firing.
[But] by sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, sprinkling, and scraping, it is purified.
And ground is purified by the dwelling of cows for five days.
That which has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed over,
and that which is defiled by hair or insects, is purified by the scattering of earth.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by an impure substance do not depart from an object smeared by it,
so long must earth and water be applied for the purification of all such articles.
The gods ordained three things as pure for Brāhmaṇas:
that which has not been seen [to be defiled], that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by word of mouth.
Water found on the ground is pure if it is sufficient to satisfy the thirst of a cow,
provided it is not contaminated by impure substances and possesses its natural smell, color, and taste.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
almsfood received by a religious student is always pure—this is the settled rule.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Manu has declared that the meat of an animal killed by dogs is pure;
so too is the meat of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and other such robbers.
All those apertures of the body that are above the navel are pure in every respect;
those that are below are impure, as are the excretions that issue from the body.
One should declare that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch.
For the purpose of purification after voiding feces or urine, earth and water should be used in sufficient quantity;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of men.
One application of earth on the penis, three in the anus, ten on one hand,
and seven on both hands must be applied by one desiring purity.
This is the purification for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should touch the apertures of the body;
likewise always when about to study the Veda and when eating food.
One desiring bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so only once each.
Śūdras who conduct themselves according to the law must have their heads shaved once a month;
their rules for purification shall be like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of twice-born men.
The primary drops that fall upon the body do not make one impure by leaving a residue;
nor do the hairs of the beard that enter the mouth, nor what remains between the teeth.
The drops that touch the feet of one who is making others sip water for purification are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure by them.
But if one whose hands hold an object is somehow touched by something defiled, [he must act accordingly].
Having merely set that object down and sipped water, he shall attain purity.

One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then perform the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). After eating food, one should simply rinse the mouth; bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and after speaking untruths;
having drunk water, and when about to study, one should sip water (ācamana) even if one is already pure.
This entire rule for purification, as well as the purification of objects, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women.
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an aged woman,
no action whatsoever should be performed by a woman independently, even within her own home.
In childhood, she should remain under the control of her father; in youth, under that of her husband;
and when her husband has died, under that of her sons. A woman must never enjoy independence.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or her sons;
for by being separated from them, she would bring reproach upon both families.
She should always remain cheerful and be skillful in her household duties; she should keep the utensils well-maintained and be not wasteful in her expenditures.
To whomsoever her father may give her, or her brother with the father’s consent,
she shall serve him while he lives and must not disregard him when he has passed away.
For the sake of auspiciousness, the rite of *svastyayana* and sacrifice to Prajāpati are performed at their marriage;
however, the formal gift (*pradāna*) is the cause of [the husband's] ownership.

A husband who performs the consecration with mantras both outside the fertile season and during the fertile season is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next.
Whether he be of bad character, or acting according to his lusts, or even devoid of all virtues,
a husband must always be attended upon like a god by a virtuous wife.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even a fast;
by that through which she serves her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should do nothing whatsoever displeasing to her husband, whether he is alive or dead.
She may, at her will, emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
Until death, she should remain patient, self-restrained, and chaste,
desiring that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband.
Many thousands of young brahmin celibates have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for their lineage.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those lifelong students of sacred knowledge.
But that woman who, out of a desire for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
In this world, there is no offspring produced by another man, nor even upon the wife of another;
nor is a second husband ever prescribed for virtuous women anywhere.
She who, having abandoned her own husband though he be inferior, resorts to one who is superior,
shall indeed be censured in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband."
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs censure in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by evil diseases.
She who does not act treacherously toward her husband through thought, word, or deed— she attains the world of her husband and is called a "virtuous woman" by the righteous.
By this conduct, a woman who is self-restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains preeminent fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.

A twice-born man who knows the law should cause a wife of equal caste, who has conducted herself in this manner and who dies before him, to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements.
Having offered the sacred fires for the funeral rites of a wife who has died before him,
he may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life.
Having thus dwelt in the stage of the householder according to the rules, the twice-born graduate (snātaka),
self-controlled and with his senses conquered, should live in the forest in the prescribed manner.
But when a householder perceives his own skin wrinkled and his hair turned grey, and sees likewise the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest.
Having completely abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, or else go with her.
Having taken up the *agnihotra* and the domestic implements for the sacred fires,
let him depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained.
He should subsist on various kinds of pure food fit for ascetics, or on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rules.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as a beard, body hair, and nails.
From whatever food he himself eats, he should offer the *bali* oblation and give alms according to his ability.
He should honor those who have come from the various stages of life (*āśrama*) with water, roots, fruits, and alms.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), self-controlled, friendly toward all beings, and composed in mind.
He should always be a giver, never a taker, and compassionate toward all living beings.
He should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the prescribed rule,
not omitting the New Moon sacrifice and performing the Full Moon sacrifice with proper application.

He should perform the *ṛkṣeṣṭi*, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices; likewise, he should perform the *turāyaṇa* and the *dakṣāyana* in due order. With pure food fit for sages, gathered by himself from the spring and autumn harvests, he should subsist.
He should offer the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the cooked rice (caru) separately, according to the prescribed rule.
Having offered that most pure wild grain as an oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder himself, as well as salt prepared by his own hand.
One may eat vegetables growing on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots,
and fruits produced by pure trees, and oils derived from fruits;
but one should avoid honey, meat, and mushrooms that grow from the earth.
Earth, grass, the śigruka plant, and the fruits of the śleśmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously accumulated,
as well as his worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plow, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots or fruits grown in a village [or flowers and fruits].
One may either subsist on food cooked by fire, or eat only what is ripened by time.
Or he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may be one who washes away his impurities immediately, or one who stores up for a month;
he may be one who accumulates for six months, or even one who stores up for a year.
One should eat food at night or during the day, having procured it according to one's ability; or one may take food at every fourth mealtime, or even at every eighth mealtime.
Or he may pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he may eat a single meal of boiled barley-gruel.
Or, remaining in accordance with the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots,
and fruits that have ripened in their due time and fallen of their own accord.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for the duration of the day;
he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the times of the three libations.
In summer he should practice the "five-fire" penance; during the rainy season, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.
Performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he should satiate the ancestors and the gods;
and practicing increasingly severe austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself according to the rule,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, observing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, having no sense of ownership even over shelters, and making his dwelling at the roots of trees; ||| 6.26 ||
He should obtain alms sufficient for his sustenance from ascetic Brahmins alone,
and from other twice-born householders who dwell in the forest.
Or, dwelling in the forest, he may eat eight morsels after bringing them from the village,
having received them either in the hollow of his hand, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd.
A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiatory rites,
as well as various Upaniṣadic teachings, for the sake of attaining self-perfection.
These have been practiced by the seers and by brahmins who were householders,
for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body.
Or, having taken his stand in the Aparājita direction,
he should proceed straight forward until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air.
Having cast off the body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
Having gone from one stage of life to the next, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by the practice of begging and making offerings, he who renounces the world prospers after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having offered sacrifices to the best of his ability, he should fix his mind on liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may depart from his home to the life of a wandering mendicant.
He who, having granted freedom from fear to all beings, departs from his home as a wandering mendicant—
for him, the expounder of Brahman, there are worlds consisting of radiant light.
Since not even the slightest fear arises for living beings from the twice-born,
there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever for him when he is liberated from the body.
Having departed from his house, purified by sacred observances, and become a silent sage (muni),
he should wander as a mendicant, indifferent toward all objects of desire when they are presented to him.
He should always wander alone for the sake of perfection, without any companion;
seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons it nor is he abandoned by it.
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, and he may resort to a village only for the sake of food.

Indifferent, free from the use of the staff, a sage whose mind is absorbed in the ultimate reality—[Manu 6.43c]; an alms-bowl, the roots of trees, tattered rags, solitude, and equanimity toward all things—this is the characteristic of one who is liberated. [Manu 6.44]
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this physical body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter untruthful speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated in contemplation, indifferent to worldly objects and free from desire for material gain,
he who seeks happiness should wander about this world with the self alone as his companion.
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology or the interpretation of bodily marks,
nor by giving instructions or engaging in debate.
He should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, or dogs, nor with other mendicants.
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly, self-controlled, without causing pain to any living beings.
His vessels should be made of non-metallic materials and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.
A gourd, a wooden vessel, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for an ascetic.
He should go for alms once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for a mendicant who is attached to alms becomes attached even to sensual objects.
When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has been completed— then a mendicant should always go for alms.

If he does not obtain [alms], he should not be dejected; and if he obtains them, he should not rejoice. He should possess only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of life, being entirely free from attachment to material things.
But he should avoid at all times gains obtained through being honored;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated is bound by gains obtained through being honored.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should restrain the senses when they are being carried away by their objects.
By the restraint of the senses, by the destruction of passion and hatred,
and by non-violence toward all living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
He should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
The separation from loved ones and likewise union with those who are disliked,
being overcome by old age and the affliction of diseases;
The departure from this body, the subsequent conception in a womb,
and the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of births.
He perceives that the connection with suffering for embodied beings arises from unrighteousness (adharma),
while the imperishable union with happiness arises from righteousness (dharma) and wealth (artha).
And by means of yoga, he should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low. Even if he is corrupted, he should practice dharma, remaining devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) he finds himself in.
He should be impartial toward all living beings; outward appearance is not the cause of dharma.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water,
the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name.
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk upon the earth after carefully inspecting it, even when his body is in distress.
Whatever living beings an ascetic kills unintentionally during the day or the night,
for the sake of purifying himself from those, he should bathe and perform six breath-suppressions (prāṇāyāmas).
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed according to the rule by a Brāhmaṇa,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burned away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses consumed by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
One should burn away faults by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and evil by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and the qualities that are not divine by means of meditation (dhyāna).
One should perceive, through the yoga of meditation, the course of this inner self within beings of various kinds— a course that is difficult for those of unrefined souls to discern.
One who is endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of such vision enters the cycle of transmigration.
By non-violence, by detachment from the senses, by Vedic rites,
and by the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.
One should abandon this temporary abode of the elements, which is like a woman in her menses.
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so too one who abandons this body is liberated from the crocodile of distress.
Having cast off his good deeds upon those dear to him and his evil deeds upon those who are not dear,
he attains the eternal Brahman through the yoga of meditation.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition,
then one attains eternal happiness both after death and in this world.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments,
and being liberated from all pairs of opposites, he abides in Brahman alone.
All this that has been declared here is indeed based on meditation;
for no one who is ignorant of the supreme self (adhyātma) ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
One should constantly recite the Veda concerning sacrifice, that concerning the deities,
and that concerning the self, as well as whatever is declared in the Vedāntas.
This is the refuge for the ignorant, and this indeed for those who possess knowledge;
this is for those seeking heaven, and this for those seeking the infinite.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant according to this sequential method,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics whose selves are disciplined;
now learn the yoga of action for those who have renounced the Vedas.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these [duties], when practiced in their proper order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
And among all these, according to the injunctions of the Veda and the Smṛti,
the householder is declared to be the best, for he supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the other stages of life find their support in the householder.
Moreover, by these four twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life,
the tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort.
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity,
control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma,
and having studied them, live according to them, attain the supreme goal.
Having performed the dharma characterized by ten attributes with a concentrated mind,
and having heard the Vedānta according to the rules, a twice-born man, free from debts, may renounce the world.
Having renounced all ritual acts and cast off the defects of karma,
he should live happily under the protection of his sons, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing,
he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
This fourfold duty of a Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you;
it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the duty of kings.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself,
how his origin comes about, and how he attains supreme success.
By a Kṣatriya who has duly received the Brāhmaṇical consecration,
the protection of all this [world] must be performed according to the law.
For when this world was without a king and fled in every direction out of fear,
the Lord created a king for the protection of all this.
Having extracted the eternal particles from Indra, Anila, Yama, Arka, Agni, Varuṇa, Candra, and Viteśa, [the Creator fashioned the Kṣatriya].
Since the king was fashioned from the constituent parts of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in his splendor.
He burns with the brilliance of the sun, scorching both eyes and minds;
and no one on earth is able even to look directly upon him.
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama);
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra. Even as a child, a lord of the earth must not be disregarded on the grounds that he is merely a human being.
For this is a great deity who exists in human form.
Fire consumes only the man who approaches it incautiously;
but the king’s fire, like the fire of destruction, consumes the entire family along with its cattle and its store of wealth.
Having truly considered the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-seated Śrī, in whose prowess dwells victory,
and in whose anger dwells death— for he indeed consists of all splendor.
But he who hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king quickly sets his mind upon that man's destruction.
Therefore, whatever law that king has determined for those he holds dear,
and whatever is ordained for those he dislikes— he should not deviate from that law.
For his sake,
the Lord created in the beginning the Staff, born of his own self, the protector of all beings, consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, exist for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duty.
Having duly considered the place, the time, the capacity, and the learning [of the offender],
he should impose a penalty upon men who act unjustly in accordance with what is appropriate.
He is the king, he is the personification of punishment, he is the leader and the ruler;
he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
Punishment governs all subjects; punishment alone protects them. Punishment keeps watch while others sleep; the wise know punishment to be dharma.
When properly maintained after due deliberation, he gladdens all his subjects;
but when applied without due deliberation, he destroys them on every side.
If the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it,
the stronger would devour the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and a dog might lick the oblation (havis);
likewise, ownership would cease to exist in anything, and the lower would prevail over the higher.
The entire world is kept in check by punishment, for a man who is naturally pure is hard to find;
indeed, through fear of punishment, the whole world is fit for the enjoyment of life.
Gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—
even they are rendered fit for enjoyment only when constrained by punishment.
All social classes would become corrupt and all boundaries would be broken;
indeed, there would be universal upheaval of the world through the misuse of punishment.
Where the dark, red-eyed Punishment stalks about, destroying evil,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, kama, and artha, is the one who should be appointed as the administrator of that [dharma].
A king who administers that [rod of punishment] properly prospers in the three aims of life;
but one whose soul is dominated by passion, who is unjust and base, is destroyed by that very rod.
For the rod is a most mighty power, difficult to be wielded by those of unrefined souls.
One who has strayed from dharma destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world of mobile and immobile beings,
as well as the sages dwelling in the intermediate space and the gods.
He cannot be led by justice by one who is without assistance, foolish, greedy, of unrefined intellect,
and attached to sensual objects.
The rod of punishment can be wielded by one who is pure, true to his word, acting according to the scriptures, possessing good assistants, and being wise.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, yet be severe in punishment toward his enemies;
he should be straightforward toward his friends and affectionate toward Brāhmaṇas, while being endowed with forbearance.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning grains from the stones,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water.
But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered himself,
his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are established in their respective duties in due order.
Whatever must be done by him, together with his servants, while protecting his subjects—
that I shall declare to you exactly and in due order.
Having risen early in the morning, the king should attend upon Brāhmaṇas who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.
One should constantly serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who always serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
Even though his own nature is disciplined, he should constantly acquire discipline from them;
for a king whose nature is disciplined never perishes.
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those living in the forest have attained kingdoms through discipline.
Vena was ruined through his lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa,
Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi.
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera attained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he should learn the triple Veda, the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti),
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) which is the knowledge of the Self, and the practical applications of the economic arts from the people.
Day and night, he should apply himself to the discipline of conquering the senses;
for one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control.
One should strive to avoid with great effort these ten vices arising from desire, as well as those eight born of anger, which lead to miserable ends.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self.
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], and idle wandering— this is the tenfold group born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, detracting from others' merits, and the spoiling of wealth,
as well as verbal and physical cruelty— this is the eightfold group born of anger.
One should strive to conquer greed, which all wise men know to be the root of both these [vices]; for both these groups originate from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— in this sequence,
one should know that this group of four is the most grievous among those arising from desire.

One should always know that this triad— the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the defilement of property— is always painful, even though it belongs to the group of offenses arising from anger.

A self-controlled man should know that among this group of seven vices which follow one everywhere, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more painful.
One who is addicted to vices sinks lower and lower; one who dies free from vices goes to heaven.

He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, successful in their aims, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. For even a task that is easy to perform becomes difficult when undertaken by one person alone.
Especially since he is without assistance, how much more so should he consider the kingdom of great consequence?
He should constantly deliberate with them regarding common matters—
both peace and war— as well as the stationing of troops, the collection of revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired.
Having ascertained their respective individual opinions,
both separately and collectively, he should, in all matters, ordain what is for his own welfare.
But with all of them, the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brāhmaṇa.
Always placing full confidence in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he should then begin his work.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.
He should appoint as many diligent,
capable, and discerning men as are required to carry out his duties.
For their sake, he should appoint those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth to the mines;
and those who are pure for the work of the interior apartments, and those who are timid for the inner residence.
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and physical movements, who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.
One who is loyal, pure, skillful, possessed of a retentive memory, knowledgeable of place and time,
handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised as a messenger for a king.
Punishment is dependent upon the minister; the administration of justice depends on punishment;
the treasury and the kingdom depend on the king; and peace and its opposite depend on the envoy.
For it is the messenger alone who unites those who are divided and indeed breaks apart those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated.
He should discern, through secret gestures and movements,
the king's facial expression, his hints, his conduct, and what he intends to do regarding his affairs, as well as the intentions of his servants.
Having understood in its true essence everything intended by the enemy king,
he should exert such effort as not to cause suffering to himself.
He should dwell in a region that is arid yet rich in crops, inhabited mostly by Āryas, free from turbulence, pleasant, with submissive neighbors, and providing a means of livelihood.
Having taken refuge in a desert-fortress, an earth-fortress, a water-fortress, or even a forest-fortress,
or a human-fortress, or a mountain-fortress, he should dwell in his city.
But with every effort, he should take refuge in a mountain fort;
for among all these, the mountain fort is distinguished by its many advantages.
Among these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, those living in holes, and those dwelling in water;
the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods.
Just as enemies do not harm these [creatures] when they have taken refuge in a fortress,
so too enemies do not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight off a hundred; a hundred can fight off ten thousand. Therefore, a fortification is ordained.
That [fortress] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
it should also be provided with Brāhmaṇas, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
In the center of that [village], he should have his own house constructed— spacious,
well-protected against all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
Having mastered that [Veda], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, pleasing to the heart, and endowed with beauty and virtue.
He should appoint a domestic priest and likewise choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.
The king should sacrifice with various kinds of sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins.
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy agents;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects like a father.
He should appoint various wise supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men engaged in their work for him.
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable Brāhma-treasure of kings.
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this imperishable treasure with the Brāhmaṇas.
It does not overflow, it does not fail, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.
A gift given to a non-Brahmin yields equal merit; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields double;
to one who has studied the Vedas, it yields a hundred-thousandfold; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields infinite merit.
Indeed, this depends upon the excellence of the recipient and upon the degree of one's own faith.
Whether it be small or great, one enjoys the fruit of giving after death.
Whatever substance is given with faith to a worthy recipient, according to the rules regarding place and time—
that is the means for accomplishing dharma. But when summoned by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, the king, while protecting his subjects, [must act].
Remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, he should not retreat from battle.
Not retreating from battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to Brāhmaṇas— these are the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
In battles, when kings, desiring to slay one another,
fight with all their might while not turning their backs, they go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he shall not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are set ablaze with fire.
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."
One must not strike one who is sleeping, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed,
nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should not strike one who has encountered a calamity involving his weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away from the battle.
But he who, being afraid, turns back in battle and is slain by his enemies,
incurs all whatever evil deed his master has committed.
Moreover, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter,
the husband takes all of that from one who is slain while retreating.
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all types of property, and base metals— whatever one wins belongs to him.
And they shall give a special share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually.
This eternal law of warriors has been declared in its unadorned form;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, must not deviate from this dharma.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should know that these fourfold [means] have the human goals as their purpose;
one should always perform their practice correctly and without sloth.
One should seek what has not been obtained by means of force; one should protect what has been obtained with vigilance;
one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his manly prowess,
always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of the rod alone.
He should conduct himself with absolute sincerity and never by deceit;
remaining ever well-guarded, he should constantly be aware of the deception employed by his enemies.
An enemy should not discover one's own vulnerability, but one should discover the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should hide one's limbs and guard one's own weak points.
One should deliberate upon one's goals like a heron, exert oneself like a lion,
snatch like a wolf, and retreat like a hare.
Thus, for one who is conquering, whatever adversaries may stand in his way,
he should bring them all under his control by employing the expedients beginning with conciliation (*sāman*).
If, however, they do not abide by those [commands] through the first three means,
he should bring them under control gradually by force, using punishment alone.
Among the four means of policy, conciliation and the others, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom.
Just as a wood-gatherer clears away the undergrowth while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
That king who, out of delusion and through lack of oversight, oppresses his own kingdom,
shall soon be deprived of both his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
He should constantly observe this rule for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness.
He should establish a military outpost (*gulma*) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for groups of one hundred villages throughout the kingdom.
He should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The village headman himself shall gradually report any evils arising in the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten shall report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should present all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, however, should himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Those items to be given daily by the village residents to the king—
such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth— the village headman shall receive them.

The collector of ten households shall enjoy the produce of one household; the collector of twenty, five households; the superintendent of a hundred villages, a village; and the lord of a thousand, a city.
Their village affairs as well as their private matters should be overseen by a trusted minister of the king, other than [the judge], who attends to them with vigilance.
In every city, he should appoint one official as the overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a high place and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly investigate their conduct in the provinces through spies who move about among them.
For the servants appointed by the king to protect [the people] generally become deceitful and seize the property of others; therefore, he should guard these subjects from them.
Those evil-minded men who seize wealth solely from litigants,
the king shall confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment.

The king should daily determine the livelihood and the station for women engaged in his service and for the class of servants, according to their specific tasks. A paṇa should be given as the wage for a low-ranking servant, and six paṇas for a high-ranking one.
Likewise, clothing is provided every six months, and a *droṇa* of grain is provided every month.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food and its incidental expenses, as well as the security of the goods, the king should cause the merchants to pay taxes.

Having considered how both the king and the performer of actions may be joined with their respective fruits, the king should always fix the taxes within his realm. Just as water-creatures, calves, and bees consume their food little by little,
so should the annual tax be taken from the realm by the king in small amounts.
The king shall take a fiftieth part of livestock and gold;
an eighth, a sixth, or even a twelfth part of grain.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, liquids, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits.
Of leaves, vegetables, grass, hides, and articles made of split bamboo;
of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone.
Even when dying, a king must not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya living within his realm perish from hunger.
In whose kingdom a Śrotriya suffers from hunger,
that king’s realm also shall soon perish from hunger.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son.
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and even his kingdom increase.
The king should cause even the common people in his realm who live by trade to pay some small amount of tax, designated as *kara*, for each year.
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month.
One should not, out of excessive greed, cut off one's own root or that of others;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them.
The lord of the earth, having considered the matter at hand, should be both stern and mild;
indeed, a king who is both stern and mild is held in high esteem.
When exhausted by the inspection of the affairs of men, the king should appoint to that seat his chief minister— one who knows the law, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Having thus ordained all this duty for himself,
he should protect these subjects, being both diligent and vigilant.
If the subjects of a king's realm are carried off by bandits while crying out for help, and he looks on with his servants, he is dead though he breathes; he does not truly live.
The highest duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed rewards is truly united with righteousness.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed purification and composed his mind,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with joy;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a terrace,
or having gone to a secluded spot in a forest devoid of undergrowth, he should deliberate unobserved.
That king whose secret counsel common people do not discover even when they have gathered together enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of a treasury.

At the time of reciting the mantras, one should remove those who are mentally dull, mute, blind, or deaf; those of animal origin; those who have passed the age of youth; as well as women, Mlecchas, the diseased, and the deformed.
Those who are despised, as well as animals, and especially women, disclose a secret; therefore, one should be careful in that regard.
At midday or at midnight, having rested and being free from fatigue,
he should reflect— either alone or together with them— upon virtue, pleasure, and wealth,
and upon the means of acquiring these when they are mutually conflicting.
The giving away of maidens and the protection of boys.
The dispatching of messengers, as well as the remaining business to be done,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
He should know in truth the entire eightfold business and the fivefold group,
as well as loyalty and disloyalty, and the conduct of the circle of states.
He should diligently ascertain the movements of the middle king, the activities of one who desires conquest, the conduct of the neutral king, and likewise that of the enemy.
In brief, these eight constituent elements are the foundation of the circle of states; they are further declared to be twelve when the others are included.
The five others known as ministers, the kingdom, the fort, the treasury, and the army—these have each been described briefly; thus, they total seventy-two.
One should know that the enemy's immediate neighbor is likewise a partisan of the enemy; the neighbor of the enemy is a friend, and beyond those two is the neutral king.
He should win them all over by means of conciliation and other such expedients,
both individually and collectively, through personal effort and statesmanship.
He should always deliberate upon the six measures of foreign policy: peace, war, marching, sitting encamped, dividing his forces, and seeking refuge.
Having carefully considered the matter at hand, he should employ sitting in wait, marching, peace, war, the double policy, or seeking refuge.
A king should know that alliance (saṃdhi) and likewise conflict (vigraha) are each of two kinds;
marching (yāna) and sitting encamped (āsana) are also two, and seeking refuge (saṃśraya) is recorded as being of two kinds.
When the undertaking of the journey is common to both, as well as when it is the opposite,
then that peace, joined with future prospects, is to be known as having two characteristics.

War is declared to be of two kinds: that which is undertaken by oneself for the sake of a specific objective, either out of season or at the proper time, and that which is waged against a friend who has done one harm.
When an urgent matter arises by chance, marching alone is prescribed;
likewise, marching in alliance with a friend is said to be the second kind of expedition.
For one who has been gradually depleted by fate or by his own past actions,
or out of consideration for a friend, two kinds of neutrality (āsana) are prescribed.
The dual policy (*dvaidha*) of both the army and its master, intended for the accomplishment of the purpose at hand,
is proclaimed as being of two kinds by those who know the qualities of the six measures of statecraft (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
Seeking refuge with the virtuous is recorded as being of two kinds: for the purpose of accomplishing one's objectives, or when one is being oppressed by enemies.
When he perceives that his own superiority in the future is certain,
and that there will be only slight suffering in the present, then he should resort to peace.
When he considers all his constituent elements to be exceedingly well-pleased,
and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war.
When he perceives through his inner state that his own army is joyful and well-nourished,
while that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is completely depleted of both vehicles and troops,
then he should remain diligent, gradually conciliating his enemies.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect,
then, having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose.
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of an enemy,
he should then quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king.
He who effects the suppression of his own subjects as well as those of the enemy should be constantly served with all efforts, just like a teacher.
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from seeking refuge,
he should then engage in fair combat without hesitation.
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him.
He should examine the future and the present state of all undertakings,
as well as the merits and defects of all past actions in their true nature.
One who understands the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who knows the remaining tasks from the past, is not overcome by enemies.
He should arrange everything in such a way that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.
Then the lord should set out toward the enemy's kingdom;
at that time, he should advance slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition;
or else, according to his strength, he may do so during the months of Phālguna or Caitra.
But at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth after declaring war, especially when a calamity has arisen for his enemy.
Having made provision for his family and for his journey according to the rules,
and having secured a place of refuge and properly stationed spies;
Having thoroughly secured his threefold path and his sixfold power,
he should march against the enemy's city according to the rules for a campaign.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a friend who serves the enemy while remaining hidden, as well as one who has gone abroad and returned; for such a person is a most dangerous foe.
He should march along that road in the *daṇḍavyūha* (staff-array), or the *śakaṭa* (cart-array),
or the *varāha* (boar-array), the *makara* (crocodile-array), the *sūcī* (needle-array), or the *garuḍa* (eagle-array).
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, toward that side he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always encamp in the lotus formation (*padmavyūha*).
He should station the commander-in-chief and the chief of the army in all directions;
and from whichever direction he anticipates danger, he should designate that as the eastern quarter.
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides,
who are skilled in both staying their ground and fighting, who are fearless, and who are incorruptible.
One should make a few soldiers fight in a compact formation, but one may extend many as desired;
having arrayed them in the *sūcī* (needle) or *vajra* (thunderbolt) formations, one should cause them to fight.

On level ground, he should fight with chariot-horses; likewise, on marshy ground, with boats and elephants; in places covered by trees and shrubs, with bows; and on firm ground, with swords, shields, and other weapons.
One should employ men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena, as well as those who are tall and those who are short, in the vanguard of the army.
Having arrayed his forces, he should cheer them and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of his enemies even as they are fighting.
Having besieged the enemy, he should sit and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly spoil his fodder, food, water, and fuel.
He should break down its tanks, as well as its walls and moats;
he should mount it by assault and likewise terrify it at night.
He should instigate those who can be sown with discord, and he should remain vigilant regarding their actions;
when fate is favorable, he should fight, free from fear and desiring victory.
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension— either collectively or individually— and never by means of war;
for victory is seen to be uncertain for two parties engaged in combat.
And there is defeat in battle; therefore, one should avoid combat.
When even the three previously mentioned means are not possible,
he should fight in such a manner that, being well-prepared, he may conquer his enemies.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brāhmaṇas;
he should grant exemptions for the sake of protection and proclaim amnesties of safety.
But having ascertained briefly the intended purpose of all these [claimants],
he should install there a member of that same lineage and establish a formal agreement.
And he should establish authoritative legal codes for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and he should honor him with jewels along with his principal officers.
Taking what is unpleasant and giving what is pleasant—
these are praised when applied at the proper time regarding desired objects.
All this action depends upon the divine and the human ordinances.
Of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human [realm], action exists.
The following three verses are found only in M. (Jha’s edition does not include them in its textual numbering, though Medhātithi provides a commentary on them).
[Manu 7.207ma] That which proceeds as human action, joined with divine ordinance, [Manu 7.207mc] Accomplishes its purpose despite great hardship.
Even for one who is joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort,
the field yields fruit without human effort.
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water likewise [are ineffective].
In this world, [results] are accomplished through destiny and through human effort with diligence.
Or, being prepared, he should march together after having carefully made a treaty,
perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of an ally, gold, or land.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*) as well as the ally-in-distress (*ākranda*) within the circle of states,
he shall obtain the fruit of his expedition from either a friend or even an enemy.
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by obtaining a firm friend who, though weak, is capable of future endurance.
One who knows the dharma, is grateful, has contented subjects, is devoted,
and is firm in his undertakings— such a light friend is highly praised.
The wise declare that an enemy who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, capable, generous, grateful, and resolute is difficult to overcome.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, compassion,
constant generosity, and the emergence of the quality of impartiality.
A king should, without hesitation, abandon for his own sake even land that is secure, productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle.
One should protect one's wealth for the sake of times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
and one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Having thoroughly observed all calamities that may arise together,
a wise man should employ all means, both combined and separate.
Having fully relied upon these three— the pursuer, the object to be pursued, and all the means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Having thus deliberated upon all this with his ministers,
the king, having exercised himself and bathed at midday, shall enter the inner apartments to eat.

In that regard, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who have become like his own self, who know the proper time, and who cannot be bribed, using mantras that neutralize poison.
He should treat all his belongings with anti-poisonous medicines; he should purify all his goods with anti-poisonous waters;
and, being self-restrained, he should always wear gems that counteract poison.
Women who have been examined by means of fanning, water, and incense,
and who are purified by their dress and ornaments, shall touch him with concentrated minds.
One should exercise such care regarding one's vehicle, bed, seat, and food;
likewise, regarding bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
Having dined, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself, he should at the proper time again attend to his duties.
Adorned with ornaments, he should inspect the armed troops again,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and equipment.

Having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), he should, while bearing his weapon, listen within the inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his secret agents.
Having gone to another chamber and having dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again for the purpose of eating, surrounded by women.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to bed at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
however, if he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
But a king desiring to examine legal cases should enter the court, disciplined and accompanied by Brāhmaṇas as well as ministers who are experts in counsel.
Seated there, or even standing, having raised his right hand,
with his dress and ornaments modest, he should examine the cases of the litigants.
Day by day, by means of reasons observed in local custom and those observed in the scriptures,
[the cases] are decided separately according to the eighteen titles of law.
Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt;
then the deposit, sale without ownership, and partnership; then the non-delivery of what has been given, the non-payment of wages, and the breach of agreement.
Rescission of purchase and sale, and the dispute between the owner and the keeper.
The law concerning boundary disputes; verbal and physical assault;
theft; violence; and the abduction of women.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these eighteen titles constitute the basis of legal procedure here.
In these matters, for men who are most frequently engaged in disputes,
he should make a final decision on the case by relying upon the eternal Dharma.
But when the king does not personally attend to the examination of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to examine those cases.
Surrounded by three members of the court, he should examine his judicial affairs,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together,
along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly to be a *brahma-sabhā*.
When Dharma, pierced by Adharma, enters an assembly,
and the members of that assembly do not extract the arrow from him, they themselves are pierced.
One should either not enter the assembly hall, or one should speak what is just; for by neither speaking nor speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
Where righteousness is slain by unrighteousness, and truth by falsehood, while the members of the court look on, they too are slain there.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when protected, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma destroy us. For the blessed Dharma is a bull; he who does violence to it, indeed, [destroys it].
The gods know him as a *vṛṣala*; therefore, one should not violate the Dharma.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even in death;
for everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes free from sin, as do the members of the court;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured.
Or he may, at his will, be one who merely lives by his caste and calls himself a Brahmin;
however, a Śūdra can never be the expounder of dharma to the king under any circumstances.
But that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma, his kingdom perishes while he looks on, like a cow in the mud.
That kingdom which is predominantly composed of Śūdras, overrun by atheists, and devoid of the twice-born,
quickly perishes in its entirety, afflicted by famine and disease.
Having ascended the seat of justice, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
and having bowed to the guardians of the world, he should begin the examination of legal cases.
Having understood both profit and loss, as well as pure merit and demerit,
he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, facial expressions, gaze, and movements.
By outward appearances, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.
The king should protect the inheritance, such as the property of a minor,
until he has returned from his teacher’s house or until he has passed his childhood.
The same protection should be afforded for barren women, those who have no sons, and those who are without kinsmen.
And toward women who are devoted to their husbands, as well as widows and those who are afflicted by illness.
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still living,
the righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years;
within three years the owner may take it back, but after that period, the king may take it for himself.
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule; after verifying the appearance, number, and other characteristics, the owner deserves to recover that property.
If one fails to report the true place and time of a lost item,
as well as its color, appearance, and size, he deserves a fine equal to the value of that object.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth part of goods lost and then found, or even a tenth or a twelfth part.
Property that has been lost and found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
whatever thieves the king may catch therein, he shall have them executed by an elephant.
If a man should declare a treasure with the truth, "This is mine," the king should take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own property,
or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very deposit.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the lord of all.
But whatever ancient treasure the king may discover buried in the earth,
he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in the treasury.
But regarding ancient treasures and minerals found in the earth, the king is entitled to half the share because of his protection; for he is the lord of the soil.
The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, shall establish the individual's own duty.
Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world.
The king himself should not initiate a lawsuit, nor should his official;
nor should he, in any way, swallow up a case brought forward by another.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood, so should the king follow the trail of justice.
In that manner, the king should discover the track of dharma through inference.
Established in the procedure for legal proceedings, he should consider the truth, the matter at hand, himself, the witnesses, the place,
the nature of the case, and the time.
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men,
that one should ordain for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not inconsistent with the sacred law.
Urged by the creditor for the purpose of recovering the debt,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount of the claim proven to the creditor.
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth,
by those very means he should constrain the debtor and compel him to pay.
One should recover a debt that has been lent through righteous means, through legal procedure, through artifice, through customary practice,
and fifthly, by force.
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own efforts must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own.
But one who denies a debt when it has been proved by evidence,
the king shall compel him to pay the creditor’s money and a small fine according to his ability.
When a debtor, having been told "Pay!
in the presence of an assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff shall point out the place [of the transaction] or specify another means of proof.
