He who, having made a pretext or a false excuse, subsequently flees;
and he who, when questioned, does not acknowledge a matter that has been properly presented.
He who converses privately with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden,
he who does not wish to answer when a question is being put to him, and he who walks away— [these are liable to punishment].
If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he fails to substantiate what he has said,
or if he cannot distinguish between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that point.

If one says, "I have witnesses," but when told "Point them out," he does not point them out; or if he says, "There are those who know [the facts],"—the judge, by these grounds, should declare him to be defeated.
If the plaintiff does not speak, he should be bound and punished according to the law.
If he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the legal matter, he is defeated.
If one should falsely deny a certain amount of wealth, or if one should speak falsely regarding a certain amount,
those two, being ignorant of the Dharma, must be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth, denies his obligation while remaining in his position,
must be proven guilty by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
I shall fully describe what kind of witnesses should be appointed by creditors in legal proceedings,
and how the truth must be spoken by them.

Householders who have sons, who are of established lineage, and who are born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes— when summoned for the sake of the matter— are fit to give testimony, and not just anyone, except in times of emergency.
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be appointed as witnesses in legal matters;
those who know all the laws and are free from greed should be chosen, while one should avoid those who are the opposite.
Those who have a financial interest, those who are relatives, those who are associates, or those who are enemies;
those whose faults are known, those afflicted by disease, or those who are corrupt—these should not be appointed as witnesses.
The king shall not be made a witness, nor an artisan, nor an actor;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one who dwells in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
One who is not dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
nor one who is aged, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane, nor oppressed by hunger or thirst;
neither one afflicted by fatigue, nor overcome by passion, nor angry, nor even a thief [should be questioned].
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
and virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras, while those of the lowest birth for those of the lowest castes.
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants in the interior of a house, in a forest, or even in the event of a threat to life; Manu 8.69.
In the absence of a woman, the business may be conducted by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick, when they testify falsely,
as well as that of those with agitated minds, is unstable.
In all cases of violence, in theft and adultery,
and in both forms of verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.

In a conflict between witnesses, the king should accept the majority; but when the numbers are equal, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and when there is a conflict between those equally virtuous, he should accept the best among the twice-born.
Testimony is established by seeing or even by hearing in the presence [of the parties].
In that case, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from merit or wealth.
A witness who declares in an assembly of noble men anything other than what he has seen or heard goes headfirst to hell after death and is excluded from heaven.
Even where he is not formally enrolled as a witness, if he should see or hear anything,
when questioned, he must declare it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
A single person who is free from greed may be a witness, but even many pure women shall not;
for the intellect of women is unstable, and others who are tainted by faults are likewise disqualified.
Whatever they may state by their very nature is to be accepted as pertaining to legal procedure;
whatever else they might say, even for the sake of dharma, is useless.
When the witnesses have arrived within the court in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant,
the presiding judge shall examine them, consoling them with this following procedure.
"Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter, declare all of that according to the truth; for your role here is that of witnesses."
By speaking the truth in his testimony, a witness attains abundant worlds that are beyond reproach;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking untruth in testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred future births, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
A witness is purified by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all the social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self. Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
Evil-doers think, "No one sees us";
but the gods see them, as does their own inner self.
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, and the wind, as well as night,
the two twilights, and Dharma, are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he, being pure himself, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth during the forenoon, while they are facing either northward or eastward.
One should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak! and the King (Pārthiva), "Speak the truth! One should question the Vaiśya with reference to his cattle, seed-corn, and gold, but the Śūdra with all the sins.

Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the murderer of women and children, and for the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful— those shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely.
"O good man, whatever merit you have performed since birth—
all that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise."
"O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, 'I am alone'— this sage, the witness of merit and sin, dwells eternally within your heart."
The divine Yama, son of Vivasvat, who dwells here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then go neither to the Ganges nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a begging bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst,
and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy.
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell—
he who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely in response.
That man who, having entered the court, speaks of a discrepancy in the facts without having witnessed them himself, eats fish along with their bones, like a blind man.
For the gods know no other man in this world to be more excellent than him whose inner self (kṣetrajña), being wise, does not feel suspicion when he speaks.
Hear now, O gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen a man destroys by speaking falsehood in a given legal testimony.
In a falsehood concerning small livestock one kills five; in a falsehood concerning cattle one kills ten;
in a falsehood concerning horses one kills a hundred; in a falsehood concerning humans one kills a thousand.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking a falsehood regarding land—do not, therefore, speak a falsehood regarding land.
Regarding water, they say it is like land; likewise with the enjoyment of women and sexual intercourse, as well as with aquatic gems and all those made of stone.
Having considered all these evils that arise from speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen, straightforwardly.
One should treat like Śūdras those Brāhmaṇas who are cattle-herders, traders, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers.
A man who, though knowing otherwise, speaks in accordance with dharma regarding legal matters, does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that speech divine.
In cases where the execution of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa would result from speaking the truth, one should speak an untruth; for that is superior to the truth.
And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial offerings (carus) dedicated to the deity of Speech,
performing the highest atonement for that sin of falsehood.

Or he may offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, or with the verse beginning "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the waters. A man who,
being healthy, does not give testimony regarding debts and other matters within three fortnights [is liable for the debt].
He shall incur that entire debt, as well as a tenth part as a fine in every case.
If, within seven days of giving his testimony,
a witness should suffer from disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, or debt, he shall be made to pay the fine.
But in matters concerning which there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot discover the truth in its actual state, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.
Oaths have been taken by the great seers and by the gods for the sake of establishing the truth;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Paijavana.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, he perishes both in this world and after death.
[However, it is permitted] in matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cows, and likewise fuel.
And in the case of an oath taken for the sake of assisting a Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin.
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by means of truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, seed-corn, and gold, and a Śūdra by all the mortal sins.
Or he should cause him to carry fire, or cause him to immerse himself in water;
or he should have his sons and wife touch his head individually.
He whom the kindled fire does not burn, whom the waters do not force to emerge [unsubmerged],
and who does not quickly meet with misfortune— he should be known as pure in his oath.
For in ancient times, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother,
the fire— the witness of the world— did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness.
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been carried out, it shall be as if undone.
"Out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger,
as well as ignorance and childishness, false testimony is spoken.
Whoever should give false testimony on account of any one of these grounds," [Manu 8.118–119].
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for that offense.
If [he does so] out of greed, he shall be fined one thousand; if out of delusion, the first amercement;
if out of fear, two middle amercements; if out of friendship, four times the first amercement.
If committed out of lust, the first [fine] is tenfold; out of anger, it is three times the latter;
out of ignorance, it is two full hundred; but out of childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony,
intended to ensure that justice does not deviate and to restrain unrighteousness.
But a righteous king, having punished the three castes who give false testimony, should banish them;
however, he should only exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the Self-existent, has declared ten places for the infliction of punishment;
among these, a Brāhmaṇa may pass through unhurt in the case of the three [lower] castes.
The genitals, the stomach, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body itself.
Having fully ascertained the motive, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered the capacity [of the offender] and the gravity of the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys reputation and ruins fame;
it also prevents one from attaining heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
First, one should inflict the punishment of speech; immediately after that, the punishment of censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines; and after that, the punishment of corporal punishment.
But when he is unable to restrain these [offenders] even by execution,
then he should employ all these four means against them.
I shall declare in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening—
that they declare to be the first of measurements, the *trasareṇu*.
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* by measure;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium-sized barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, and ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *māṣakas* make one silver *dharaṇa*, which is also called a *purāṇa*.
A copper coin weighing one karṣa is to be known as a kārṣāpaṇa or a paṇa.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one silver *śatamāna*;
furthermore, a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure to consist of four *suvarṇas*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand is indeed the highest.
When a debt is admitted as due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, that fine shall be double—such is the ordinance of Manu.
A moneylender may stipulate the interest prescribed by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Or, remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two per cent;
for by taking two per cent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth.
One may take two, three, four, or five percent per month as interest,
according to the order of the social classes.
But one shall never receive interest on a usufructuary pledge;
nor is there any transfer or sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
Both a pledge (*ādhi*) and a deposit (*upanidhi*) do not suffer from the lapse of time;
if they remain for a long duration, they may be forfeited.
Cattle being used with mutual consent are never lost [to the owner]:
this applies to a milch cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal employed for taming.
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while he is present,
yet remains silent, he is not entitled to recover it.
If the owner is neither mentally incapacitated nor a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another in his presence, that possession is defeated by the legal action;
the enjoyer deserves to forfeit that property.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, and women [are not lost by mere enjoyment].
The property of the king and the property of a Śrotriya are not lost through adverse possession.
He who, being unwise, enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must relinquish half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
in the case of grain, fruit, wool, or beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.
An interest exceeding the legal rate, or one that is excessive, is not valid;
they call that the way of usury, for it deserves a fine of five percent.
One should not take interest exceeding one year's duration, nor that which is not previously established;
namely, compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*), periodical interest (*kālavṛddhi*), stipulated interest (*kāritā*), and corporeal interest (*kāyikā*).
If a debtor who is unable to pay the debt wishes to enter into a new transaction, he may do so.
Having paid the interest that has been earned, he may renew the legal instrument.
Without having shown [the object], he should return the gold right there;
he ought to pay as much interest as may have accrued.
One who has entered into a contract for compound interest (cakravṛddhi), fixed according to place and time,
shall not obtain its fruit if he violates that place and time.
But whatever rate of interest those who are experts in sea-voyages and who perceive the requirements of place, time,
and purpose may establish, that shall apply in respect to the acquisition of wealth therein.
If a man stands as a surety for another's appearance here, failing to produce him,
he shall pay that person's debt from his own property. He should strive to pay what was promised as a surety,
as well as a frivolous gift, a gambling debt, and a debt incurred through drinking.
Nor is a son liable to pay the remainder of a fine or a toll.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the rule previously ordained shall apply;
if the surety for payment has died, the judge should compel even his heirs to pay.
But if the guarantor has died, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt from the surety, provided that the nature of the debt is well known and the debtor himself is unable to pay?
But if the surety has been assigned wealth and possesses sufficient assets, he shall pay that from his own property;
such is the settled rule regarding one who has been assigned wealth.

A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent, or by a child, or by an elderly person, as well as one entered into by someone who is not legally competent, is not valid.
A statement does not become true even if it is well-established,
if it is spoken outside of the fixed legal procedure.
Whatever is mortgaged, sold, or purchased through fraud, whatever gift or acceptance of a gift is obtained through fraud, or wherever one perceives deceit— let him annul all that.
If the borrower should be lost and the expenditure was made for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by the relatives from their own property, even if they have already divided it.
Whatever legal transaction even a dependent (*adhyadhīna*) might carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or abroad, the master shall not annul it.
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—
Manu has declared all transactions effected by force to be as if they were not done."
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a surety, and a family;
yet four prosper: a learned Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.
Even if he is impoverished, a king must not take what is not to be taken;
nor, even if he is prosperous, should he relinquish what is rightfully his, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by refusing what should be taken, the weakness of the king is proclaimed; he perishes both in this world and after death.
From taking what is his own, from preventing the intermixture of castes, and from protecting the weak, the power of the king is generated; he prospers both in this world and after death.
Therefore, like Yama himself, the master should personally set aside both the pleasant and the unpleasant;
with anger conquered and senses subdued, he should conduct himself according to the manner of Yama.
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, conducts legal affairs unjustly,
his enemies will soon bring under their control.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, examines matters according to dharma—
his subjects follow him, just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
He who reports to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will shall be made to pay a fourth part of that amount to the king, and the debt itself to the creditor.
A debtor should repay the creditor even by means of labor;
one of equal or lower caste should do so immediately, but one of higher caste should pay it gradually.
By this procedure, the king should bring to a state of impartiality the legal cases of men disputing with one another, which have been established on the basis of witnesses.

A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is born of noble family, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large circle of supporters, wealthy, and honorable.
In whatever manner a person deposits an object in the hand of another, in that very same manner it must be received back; as was the delivery, so shall be the recovery.
If a person, when being asked for it, does not return a deposit to the depositor,
he shall be summoned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.

In the absence of witnesses, having caused gold to be deposited with the true facts by means of secret agents endowed with appropriate age and appearance, and under various pretexts; [he should have it recovered].
If he should restore it exactly as it was deposited and in the condition it was made,
there exists nothing therein for which he may be accused by others.

If, however, he does not return that gold to them according to the prescribed rule, then, having restrained both, he should be made to pay it; such is the established principle of Dharma. A deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must never be handed over to a next-of-kin.
These two perish in the event of a downfall, but they do not perish if there is no downfall.
But if one should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
He should investigate that matter with kindness and without guile;
or, having examined his conduct, he should settle the case through conciliation alone.
In all these cases of deposits, this same rule shall apply to their recovery;
however, in the case of a sealed deposit, the depositor shall not receive anything if the depositary does not extract it from that [seal].
If [the property] has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire,
he shall not pay for it, provided that he did not take anything from it himself.
One should seek out the embezzler of a deposit and likewise the person who never deposited it by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths.
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands what he did not deposit—
both of these should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of that [deposit].
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value;
likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit, without distinction.
Any man who, by means of fraudulent devices, should seize the property of another,
he, together with his accomplices, shall be put to death publicly by various modes of execution.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses—that same amount must be recognized as it was; one who declares otherwise deserves punishment.
If a gift has been made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
In this same manner, the king should reach a decision regarding property that has been deposited or affectionately entrusted,
without causing hardship to the holder of the deposit.
He who sells another's property, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, one should not admit as a witness; for he is a thief who considers himself no thief.
If he has kin, he shall be fined six hundred panas and his property shall be confiscated;
if he has no kin and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
Where possession is observed but no title is seen anywhere, there title is the decisive factor, not possession; such is the settled rule.
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family,
he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified.

Now, if one has cleared his title by means of a public purchase, yet the original source of the goods cannot be recovered, he shall be released by the king without punishment; the owner of the lost property shall recover his wealth.
An item whose form has been mixed with another is not fit for sale;

nor is that which is valueless, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is far away, nor that which is concealed. (Manu 8.203) If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom, [he may rescind the marriage]. (Manu 8.204a)
"Let him marry both of them with a single fee," so Manu has declared.
A giver does not deserve punishment if he has previously declared the defects of a girl who is insane, afflicted with leprosy, or one who has already experienced sexual intercourse.
If a chosen officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should abandon his own duties during a sacrifice,
a share corresponding to his work must be given to him by the co-performers.
If, after the sacrificial fees have been given, one abandons his own work,
he shall receive his entire share and have it performed by another.
In whatever ritual those specific fees for individual components may have been prescribed,
he alone shall receive them, or all [the officiants] together may share them.
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the fire-consecration;
the Hotṛ may also take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Among all [the sons], the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third share, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth share.
When men here perform their respective duties in association with one another,
the apportionment of shares must be made according to this prescribed rule.

If a person gives wealth to someone who asks for it for the sake of dharma, but later that wealth does not serve its intended purpose, that gift must not be given to him; it shall belong to him [the original owner].
If, however, he should recover that [property] out of pride or greed, he shall be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king; that shall be the expiation for his theft.
This has been declared as the lawful manner of non-payment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
If a hired laborer, though not ill, should out of pride fail to perform his work as it was prescribed,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid to him.
But if one who was incapacitated should, once restored to health, perform the work as originally stipulated from the beginning,
he shall receive that very wage even after a long period of time.
Whether afflicted by illness or in good health, if one does not perform the work as agreed,
his wages must not be paid, even if the work is only slightly incomplete.
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
A man who, having made a covenant in good faith with a village, a district, or an assembly,
should break it out of greed, the king shall banish from the realm.
Having restrained him, the king shall cause that violator of the compact to pay four *suvarṇas*, six *niṣkas*, and one royal *śatamāna*.
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate established agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies.
If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have cause for regret,
he may return or take back that object within ten days.
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the object] to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king.
But if a man gives away a girl who has defects without having disclosed them,
the king himself shall inflict upon him a fine of ninety-six paṇas.
But that man who, out of malice, declares of a maiden,
"She is not a virgin," shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas] if he fails to demonstrate her fault.
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are established as applying only to virgins;
they never apply to non-virgins among women, for such women have their religious rites sublated.
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be recognized by the learned as occurring at the seventh step.
In whatever matter one may have cause for regret after it has been performed,
he should be restored to the path of righteousness by this procedure.
I shall now duly declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding cattle.

If the loss occurs during the day, the blame falls on the keeper; if at night, it falls on the owner, provided the animal was in his house. Otherwise, if the security of the property was not maintained, the keeper shall incur the blame.
A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten;
that shall be the wages for the herdsman if no other wage is provided.
But the keeper alone shall restore what has been lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, died in a dangerous place,
or [perished] through a lack of human effort.
But if cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he informs his own master of it at the proper place and time.
When animals have died, one should give the ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinew, and gallstone to the owners, and show them the identifying marks.
But when goats and sheep are obstructed by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid—
If a wolf should kill a cow by force, that guilt shall fall upon the keeper.
If, among those cows that have been penned up and are grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that case.
There should be a pasture-land of one hundred bows all around a village;
for a city, however, it shall be three times that, or else three throws of a yoke-pin.
If cattle should damage unenclosed grain there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals. In that case,
he should construct a fence such that even a camel cannot look over it.
And he should guard against every vulnerability that might be entered by the snouts of dogs and pigs.

On a road, in an enclosed field, or likewise on the outskirts of a village, the herdsman is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for the cattle; however, he should drive away the cattle that are without a herdsman.
But for cattle in other fields, one deserves a fine of one and a quarter paṇas;
however, in all cases, a sixth part of the crop must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule.
Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved within ten days, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods—
whether they have a keeper or are unattended.
In the event of the owner of the field's negligence, the fine shall be ten times the share [of the crop];
however, the fine for the servants shall be half of that, provided it was due to the owner's lack of knowledge.
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions involving owners of cattle, the cattle themselves, and the herdsmen.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.
And he should establish boundary trees—*nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees;
*śālmalī*, *sāla*, and *tāla* trees, as well as milky sap-bearing trees.
By planting various shrubs and bamboos, as well as *śamī* trees, creepers, and mounds,
and by [planting] reeds and *kubjaka* shrubs, the boundary line does not perish.
Reservoirs, wells, large tanks, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made that are concealed,
having observed the constant confusion among men in this world when the boundaries are unknown.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes,
potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand.
And whatever other such marks the earth might not erode over time,
those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at the junctions of the boundary.
By these signs, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties.
And by continuous prior possession, as well as by the flow of water.
If there should be doubt even when the characteristic marks are visible,
the decision regarding the dispute over the boundary must depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses.
The witnesses concerning the boundary should be examined in the presence of the village communities and their families.
The boundary markers should be questioned by those two litigants themselves. Whatever decision they may unanimously declare regarding the boundary when thus questioned,
he shall fix the boundary accordingly and record all of them by name.
Having grasped the earth with their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and having been sworn by their respective good deeds, they shall lead the case justly.
Leading [the case] in the manner prescribed, those who speak the truth as witnesses are purified;
but leading it in the opposite manner, they shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants of the neighboring villages [or those living on the village boundaries],
being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king.

In the absence of neighboring witnesses who are original inhabitants of the boundary, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forest: Manu 8.259: "In the absence of neighboring witnesses who are original inhabitants of the boundary, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forest."
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers— [these he shall exempt from taxes].
When they have been questioned, whatever mark they declare regarding the boundaries between the two villages,
that the king shall establish according to dharma for both villages.
The determination of boundaries and landmarks for fields, wells, tanks, groves,
and houses is to be understood as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary mark,
all of them shall be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.
When a boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, being a knower of dharma, should assign the land to those who derive benefit from it; such is the settled rule.
This entire law concerning the determination of boundaries has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of verbal assault.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred, but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be forty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
For the twice-born castes, when there is an offense against an equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve;
in cases of unspeakable disputes, that same fine shall be doubled.
A once-born man who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall have his tongue cut out, for he is of low origin.
But for one who maliciously utters their name or caste,
a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
If a king, out of arrogance, provides instruction on the Dharma to Brahmins, he should have boiling oil poured into that person's mouth and ears. [He should likewise pour it into] the ear.
Furthermore, [he should punish one who falsely claims] learning, country, caste, occupation, or even his own body.
Speaking falsely out of arrogance, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Even if one speaks the truth regarding someone who is one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise similarly disabled, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa.
One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher,
as well as one who does not yield the path to his teacher, shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
But a wise king should inflict punishment upon a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement.
In the case of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, the same rule applies exactly with respect to their own respective castes;
the settled conclusion is that the infliction of punishment shall be carried out in this manner, excluding the cutting off [of limbs].
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.
If a low-born man should injure a superior person with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu.
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the severing of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the severing of that foot.
A person of lower birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of higher rank should be branded on the hip and banished,
or else his buttock should be cut off.
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
likewise, he shall have the penis of one who urinates [upon him] cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
If one seizes [another] by the hair, he shall have both hands cut off without hesitation;
likewise for seizing [another] by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
"According as the utility of all forest trees [is determined], so should the fine be imposed for injuring them; such is the settled rule."
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the purpose of causing pain,
the king shall impose a punishment in proportion to the severity of the suffering inflicted.
In cases of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of a wound or blood,
he shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery, or else the full fine.
If anyone should damage the goods of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he shall provide satisfaction to the owner and pay an equivalent amount to the king.
In the case of goods made of leather or leather-work, and those made of wood or clay,
as well as in the case of flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
They say there are ten circumstances under which the driver, the passenger, and the owner of the vehicle are exempt from liability; in all other cases, punishment is ordained.
When the nose-string is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal comes from the side or from the front,
when there is a breakage of the axle of the vehicle, or likewise a breakage of a wheel;
and when there is a snapping of the fastenings, as well as of the thongs and the reins.
And in the case of a cry for help, "Get away!", Manu has declared that there shall be no punishment.
But where a vehicle goes astray due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and shall pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
If the driver be trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas].
But if he, while obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
should cause the death of a living being, the punishment there is not to be deliberated upon.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is immediately the same as that of a thief;
in the case of large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, it is half [of that guilt].
For the injury of small animals, however, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the fine shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, however, the fine shall be five *māṣas*;
for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one *māṣa*.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—
when they have committed an offense, these may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one should strike the body from behind, never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one would incur the guilt of a thief.
This determination of assault has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
The king should exert the greatest effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase.
For that king who is the giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra), which has fearlessness as its sacrificial fee, prospers forever.
A sixth part of the merit from all sources accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of the demerit accrues to him who fails to protect.
Whatever he studies, whatever he sacrifices, whatever he gives, and whatever he worships—
the king becomes the recipient of a sixth part of that through his proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and causing those deserving of death to be executed,
the king performs sacrifices every day with sacrificial fees of hundreds and thousands.
That king who takes tribute, taxes, tolls, the periodic share,
and fines without providing protection, shall immediately go to hell.
They say that a king who does not protect his subjects while taking a sixth part of their produce as tax is the one who takes away the entire impurity of all the world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, who is plundering,
who fails to protect, and who devours his subjects, goes to a low state of existence.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrifices.
A lord who seeks his own welfare must always forgive those litigants who revile him,
as well as children, the elderly, and the sick.
He who, when reviled by those in distress, forgives them, is glorified in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not forgive, goes to hell because of that.
The king should be approached by the thief running with disheveled hair, confessing that theft: "I am a doer of such an act; punish me."

Through punishment or through release, a thief is freed from the guilt of theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the sin of the thief.
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
But he who steals a rope or a water-jar from a well, or who destroys a water-shed,
shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place.
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value as a fine, and that property shall be restored to its owner.
Likewise, for stealing more than a hundred units of things measured by weight—
such as gold, silver, and the like, as well as the finest garments— the punishment is death.
But when the value exceeds fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially of women,
as well as for the theft of the most precious gems, one deserves the death penalty.
Upon considering the time and the circumstances of the offense, the king shall determine the punishment for the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicinal herbs.
In the case of cows belonging to Brāhmaṇas, for piercing them with a knife,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, an immediate punishment of cutting off half a foot shall be inflicted.
Of thread, cotton, fermenting agents, cow dung, molasses, curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass; [Manu 8.326].
In the case of stealing vessels made of bamboo or split cane, as well as salts, and likewise earthenware, clay, or ashes; [the fine shall be equal to the value of the goods].
Of fish, birds, oil, clarified butter,
meat, honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
In the case of other such intoxicating drinks, of cooked rice,
and of all kinds of prepared food, the fine shall be double their value.
In the case of flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*.
In the case of cleaned grains, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits,
the fine shall be one hundred paṇas if there is no prior connection with the owner, and fifty paṇas if such a connection exists.
An act committed by force with the owner present is *sāhasa* (violence);
it becomes *steya* (theft) when committed in the absence of the owner and when one denies having taken it.
But that man who steals these prepared goods,
as well as he who would steal fire from the house, the king shall punish first. With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against men, with that very limb shall the king strike him.
The king should confiscate that very property of the [offender] as a deterrent.
Neither a father, a teacher, a friend, a mother, a wife, a son,
nor a domestic priest is exempt from punishment by the king if he does not abide by his own duty.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
For a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be sixty-four, or even a full hundred;
or twice sixty-four, for he is indeed an expert in the qualities of those offenses.
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cattle, does not constitute theft.
A Brāhmaṇa who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—
even by officiating at his sacrifices or by teaching him— is exactly like a thief.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose means of subsistence are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane and two roots from another's field, does not deserve to pay a fine.
One who joins together those who are ununited, one who releases those who are bound,
and one who seizes a slave, a horse, or a chariot, shall incur the guilt of a thief.
By suppressing thieves according to this rule,
a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
Desiring to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, eternal fame,
a king should not overlook a man who commits an act of violence even for a moment.
A man who commits violence through harsh speech, theft, or even by means of physical punishment,
should be known as the worst among evildoers.
But that king who tolerates one who persists in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred.
Neither for the sake of friendship nor for the sake of a vast influx of wealth should a king release perpetrators of violence who bring fear to all living beings.
Weapons may be taken up by the twice-born when their duty is obstructed,
and during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time.
In self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees,
and in coming to the aid of women or Brahmins, one who kills in accordance with dharma incurs no guilt.
One may indeed kill an assailant who approaches, without hesitation— even if he be a teacher, or a child, or an elder, or a Brahmin deeply learned in the Vedas.
There is no fault whatsoever for a slayer in killing an assailant, whether done openly or in secret; fury recoils upon that fury.
When men are intent on violating the wives of others, the king,
having branded them with punishments that cause public alarm, shall banish them;
for from such acts arises the confusion of castes among the people.
For by that unrighteous act which destroys the root, everything is liable to perish.
A man who engages in secret conversation with another's wife,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out for a valid reason,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.
He who addresses the wife of another at a sacred bathing place, in a deserted spot, or even in a forest,
or likewise at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery.
Service, playful dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments,
and even sitting together on the same bed— all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he allows himself to be touched by her when she does so,
it is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) provided there is mutual consent.
A non-Brāhmaṇa deserves the death penalty for adultery;
the wives of men of all four castes must always be protected most carefully.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice,
and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
but he who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who subsist by their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away.

But he who engages in conversation with such women should be made to pay a small fine; so too for those who converse with female slaves who have a single master, or with female ascetics in secret. He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution.
A man of equal status who defiles a willing woman shall not incur the death penalty.
A maiden who chooses a man of superior caste, he shall not cause her to pay anything at all;
but one who serves a man of inferior caste, he shall cause to live confined within the house.
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
however, if he has intercourse with a woman of equal caste, he should pay the bride-price if her father so desires.
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
his two fingers shall be immediately cut off and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
However, one who defiles a willing maiden of equal status shall not suffer the amputation of his fingers.
But for the sake of preventing a recurrence, he should be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
If a maiden herself should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a whip.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being dragged along by a donkey.
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, transgresses against her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with people.
One should cause the wicked man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they shall pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise, for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī*, the fine is exactly that much.

A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she be protected or unprotected—is punished as follows: for an unprotected woman, he is deprived of his limbs and all his property; for a protected woman, he is deprived of everything. A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year.
A Kṣatriya should be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of those very men, having violated a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
should be punished like Śūdras or burned in a fire of straw.
A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force should be fined one thousand [paṇas];
if he has united with her through her consent, he should be fined five hundred.

Shaving the head is ordained as the capital punishment for a Brāhmaṇa; however, for the other castes, the punishment may be one that ends in death. One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he has committed every possible crime.
He should banish him from the kingdom, taking all his wealth with him, provided he remains unscarred.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a guarded Vaiśya woman,
both of them deserve the same punishment as that prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa woman who is unguarded.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, who approaches those two (Kṣatriya and Vaiśya women) when they are protected, shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
For a Vaiśya approaching an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, the fine is five hundred.
A Kṣatriya, however, should seek either tonsure with urine or a fine as punishment.

If a Brāhmaṇa approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman, he should be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (Antyaja), he should be fined one thousand.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with a rod, shares the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm by the king brings about universal sovereignty among his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world.
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer,
when both are capable of performing the rite and free from fault, the punishment for each of them shall be one hundred [paṇas].
Neither a mother, nor a father, nor a wife, nor a son deserves to be abandoned.
One who abandons these when they have not fallen from their status shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
When twice-born men dispute among themselves regarding their duties in the various stages of life (āśramas),
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold righteousness should not issue a hasty judgment.
Having honored these [offenders] as is appropriate, together with the Brahmins,
the king should first pacify them with conciliation and then cause them to adhere to their own duty.
If a Brahmin does not feed his immediate neighbor and his next-door neighbor when twenty twice-born men are invited to a festive occasion,
provided they are worthy, he deserves a fine of one *māṣaka*.
A learned *śrotriya*, failing to feed another virtuous *śrotriya* at auspicious rites,
shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold.
A blind man, an idiot, a cripple who moves on a board, and one who is seventy years old— these are exempt from taxes.
And those who provide service to Vedic scholars (śrotriyas) shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone.

The king should always honor a learned scholar of the Vedas, one who is afflicted by disease or distress, a child, an elder, one who possesses nothing, and one born of a noble family and of honorable conduct.
On a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood, the washerman shall gently wash clothes;
he shall not exchange garments for garments, nor shall he let them dry together.
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread with one pala added as his fee;
if he acts otherwise than this, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
Those skilled in the places where tolls are collected and expert in all types of merchandise shall fix the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth.
If a person, out of greed, exports those goods belonging to the king that are well-known or prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property.
One who evades a toll station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
and one who speaks falsely regarding the quantity [of goods], shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
Having investigated the source, the destination, the storage period, as well as both the increase and the decrease of all commodities,
he shall regulate their purchase and sale.
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed,
the king should publicly determine the value of these commodities.
All balances, weights, and measures shall be properly marked;
every six months, one should have them re-examined.
A vehicle should be made to pay one *paṇa* at a ferry; a man with his load, half a *paṇa*;
an animal and a woman, a quarter *paṇa*; and an empty-handed man, half of that quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods should be made to pay the ferry toll according to their value.
Empty vessels and whatever else [is lost], as well as men who are without their belongings; [these are not subject to a fine].
On a long journey, the ferry fare shall be according to the place and according to the time;
one should know that this applies to the banks of rivers, but there is no fixed rate for the sea.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering mendicant, a sage,
and Brāhmaṇas wearing the marks of their religious orders, shall not be made to pay the ferry-toll at a crossing.
Whatever on a boat is damaged through the fault of the boatmen must be paid for by those very boatmen,
having assembled together, each from his own share.
This decision regarding legal disputes for those traveling by boat has been declared:
there is no punishment for damage caused by the fault of the boatmen on the water, nor for that which is due to an act of God.
He should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, moneylending, and agriculture;
and the Śūdra to perform the tending of cattle and service to the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa should support with compassion both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.
But a Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed and by virtue of his power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servile labor against their will,
shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, he shall make to perform servitude;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that [servitude] is innate to him, so who can remove it?
One captured under a banner (a slave won in war), one who serves for food, one born in the house, one bought, one given,
one inherited from ancestors, and one enslaved as punishment— these seven are the origins of slavery.
The wife, the son, and the slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he possesses nothing of his own, since his wealth is to be taken by his master.
The king should diligently compel the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own respective duties;
for if these two deviate from their own duties, they would throw this entire world into disorder.
Day by day, he should inspect the completion of his works, the vehicles,
the fixed income and expenditure, the mines, and the treasury itself.
Thus, by settling all these legal disputes, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.
For the man and the woman who abide in the path of dharma,
I shall declare the eternal laws regarding their union and their separation.
Women must be kept in a state of dependence by their own men day and night;
and if they become attached to sensual objects, they must be restrained under one's own control.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth;
in old age, the sons protect her. A woman does not deserve independence.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.
Women must be protected especially from even the slightest opportunities for transgression;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring grief upon two families.
For seeing this as the highest duty among all the social orders,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they themselves are weak.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, a man protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (Manu 9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here again;
for that is the reason she is called "jāyā" (wife), because he is born (*jāyate*) from her once more.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard women with great effort.
No one is able to protect women by force;
however, they can be protected by the application of these following means.
He should employ her in the collection and expenditure of wealth,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
Those women who, confined within the home by trustworthy servants,
protect themselves by their own efforts, are well-protected.
Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about,
sleeping [at improper times], and dwelling in another's house— these six are the vices that corrupt women.
They do not examine their appearance, nor is there any fixed regard for their age; whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection, these women—
even when guarded with great effort— act perversely toward their husbands in this world.
Having thus understood their nature, born of the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the utmost effort toward their protection.
Manu ordained for women the use of beds, seats, ornaments, as well as desire, anger, dishonesty, ignobility, a disposition toward malice, and misconduct (Manu 9.17).
There is no ritual efficacy for women through sacred mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma (Manu 9.18).
"For women are devoid of sensory restraint and lack the sacred mantras; thus stands the rule that they are untruthful. (Manu 9.18c).
Likewise, many Vedic verses have been chanted even in the Nigamas.
Listen now to the expiations for them, intended for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics. (Manu 9.19).
"Whatever my mother, wandering about and unfaithful to her husband, was lustful for—that seed may my father take unto himself"; this is the scriptural illustration for this [rule].
Whatever undesirable thing she may contemplate in her mind for her husband,
this [following] is declared to be the proper means for the concealment of that transgression.
With whatever qualities a woman is united to a husband according to the prescribed rule,
she acquires those same qualities, just as a river does when it joins the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerable status through her union with Vasiṣṭha; and Śāraṅgī reached a state of high honor through Mandapāla.
These and other women of low birth in this world have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.

Thus has been declared the auspicious course of worldly life for husband and wife, which yields happiness in this world and after death; now learn the duties concerning progeny, which result in future bliss.
For the sake of procreation, highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in households, there is no difference whatsoever.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— each of these is visibly dependent upon the woman.
Offspring, the performance of religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure [all depend on her].
Likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent upon the wife.
She who does not act treacherously toward her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called a "virtuous woman" by the righteous.

Through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs censure in this world; she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. Regarding the son who has been extolled by the virtuous and by the great seers of old—
Learn this meritorious exposition, which is beneficial for all people.

They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict in the sacred texts regarding the progenitor. Some say he belongs to the one who produces him, while others know him to belong to the owner of the field.
Woman is declared to be the field, and man is declared to be the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the womb of the woman;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
Of both the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the offspring of all living beings is characterized by the traits of the seed. Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, [such is the nature of the harvest].
Such a seed grows upon that soil, manifested by its own inherent qualities.
For this earth is said to be the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth.
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at different times by farmers are produced here in various forms according to their own nature.
Rice, *śāli* rice, mung beans, sesame seeds, beans, and likewise barley,
as well as garlic and sugarcane, sprout according to their respective seeds.
"It is not possible that one thing is sown and another is produced;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts."
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never procreate upon the wife of another.
In this regard, those who know the past recite these verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a man should not sow seed in the possession of another..."
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sky when one shoots after it as it has been pierced,
so too does seed quickly perish when sown in the possession of another.
Even those who know the ancient lore recognize this entire earth as the wife of Pṛthu.
They say that one who cuts down a tree stump [commits the same sin as] one who destroys a field of rice, and one who kills a deer [commits the same sin as] one who destroys a field of rice.
"A man consists of this much alone:
his wife, himself, and his offspring—so the learned brahmins have declared; likewise, he who is the husband is considered to be the woman."
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati.
The share falls once; once is a maiden given;
once does one say "I give"—these three things happen but once among the virtuous.
Just as it is with cows, horses, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, and sheep...
The progenitor does not share in the offspring, even in the case of other women.
Those who possess seed but have no field, and sow it in the field of another,
never obtain any share of the crop that is produced.
If a bull were to father a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another’s field produce a benefit for the owner of the field; the sower of the seed does not receive the fruit.

But when no agreement regarding the fruit has been made between the owner of the field and the sower, the benefit clearly belongs to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed. However, that which is given for the sake of the seed is due to the acceptance of the undertaking of the work.
In this world, both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen as sharers of the offspring.

If seed carried away by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone’s field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. This same rule applies to cattle, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, and sheep.
And regarding the offspring of birds and female buffaloes, it should be understood that [the rule] applies to their birth.
Thus has been proclaimed to you the relative importance and insignificance of seed and womb;
hereafter I shall declare the law for women in times of distress.
The wife of an elder brother is like the wife of a guru to a younger brother;
conversely, the wife of a younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder brother.

The elder brother who approaches the wife of the younger, or the younger brother who approaches the wife of the elder— even if they are authorized [to do so]— become outcasts, unless there be a state of distress.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized may obtain the desired offspring from her brother-in-law or from a sapinda relative.
One appointed to a widow, however, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent,
may procreate one son at night, but never a second under any circumstances.
Some who are experts in this matter consider a second procreation upon women to be permissible,

seeing that the purpose of the *niyoga* for those two [husband and wife] has not been fully accomplished according to the law. But when the purpose of the *niyoga* regarding a widow has been accomplished according to the rule—
And they should behave toward each other like a teacher and a pupil, and like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.
If those two, being thus enjoined, should act according to their own desire by disregarding the rule,
both of them would become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma.
Nowhere in the mantras used at weddings is "appointment" (niyoga) mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for marriage.
"For this practice of animal behavior, though censured by learned twice-born men, was indeed prescribed even for humans while Vena was ruling the kingdom. (Manu 9.66)
In ancient times, that preeminent royal sage, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social classes, his mind being struck down by lust.
From that time forward, virtuous men censure any man who, out of delusion, attempts to appoint a woman whose husband has died to procreate offspring.
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule.
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she who wears white garments and observes pure vows—
he shall enjoy her in private once at each menstrual season until she gives birth.
A wise man, having given his daughter to anyone, should not give her again;
for by giving her away once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of lying regarding a human being.
Even after accepting a maiden according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon her if she is blameworthy,
diseased, severely defiled, or was presented through deception.
But if one should bestow a maiden who has defects without having disclosed them,
he shall annul that gift of the evil-minded giver of the bride.
A man who has business abroad should depart only after providing for his wife's maintenance;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live observing the prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should subsist by means of blameless crafts.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be waited for eight years;
one for the sake of learning or fame, six years; but one for the sake of pleasure, three years.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who hates him;
but after a year, having taken back her property, he shall no longer live with her.
If she should transgress against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease,
she shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, an outcast, impotent, seedless, or afflicted with a loathsome disease;
nor is there any exclusion from inheritance for her if she is hostile.
A wife who drinks liquor, behaves wickedly, or is rebellious;
or one who is diseased, cruel, or constantly wastes wealth—she may be superseded by another wife.
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year, one whose children have died in the tenth,
one who gives birth only to daughters in the eleventh, but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately.
But a wife who may be diseased, yet is beneficial and endowed with good character, should be superseded only after obtaining her permission; she must never be treated with contempt.
But a superseded wife who goes out from the house in anger should be immediately confined or abandoned in the presence of the family.
If a woman, though forbidden, drinks liquor even at festive occasions,
or goes to a spectacle or a public assembly, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
If twice-born men should marry both women of their own caste and those of other castes,
seniority, honor, and the right to the household shall belong to them according to the order of their castes.
A woman of her own caste alone— and never one of a different caste— should perform the personal service to the husband and his daily religious duties for all [the men in the family].
But he who, out of delusion, causes these to be performed by another woman while a woman of his own caste is available, [is at fault].
Just as a Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla was seen before, so indeed is he.
To a bridegroom who is eminent, handsome, suitable, and of equal status—
even if she has not reached the marriageable age— one should give the daughter to him according to the prescribed rule.
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father’s house at his pleasure until death;
yet he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may find a husband of equal status.
If she approaches her husband of her own accord when he does not take her back,
she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does the man whom she approaches.
A maiden choosing her own husband (svayaṃvarā) shall not take for herself the ornaments belonging to her father;
if she should take those given by her mother or by her brothers, she would be a thief.
But he who takes a girl who has reached puberty shall not pay the nuptial fee to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping the father's ownership.
A man of thirty years should marry a pleasing girl of twelve;
or, if he is in distress regarding his religious duty, one of twenty-four years may marry an eight-year-old with haste.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
he should always support that virtuous woman, acting in a manner pleasing to the gods.
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common [to both] with the wife.
If the giver of the bride-price should die after the price has been paid for a maiden, she should be given to the husband's brother,
provided the maiden consents.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not take a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, he effects a concealed sale of his daughter.
But this which is done— promising one thing and then giving it to another— neither those before nor any virtuous men after them have ever practiced.
We have never heard of such a thing even in former births:
the sale of a daughter disguised under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
Mutual fidelity until death—
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief.

Likewise, a woman and a man who have performed their rites should always strive so that, even when separated from one another, they do not commit infidelity toward each other. This dharma pertaining to sexual pleasure has been declared for you regarding women and men.
In times of distress, the acquisition of offspring [is permitted]; now learn the law of inheritance.
