After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive.
The eldest alone, however, shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the remaining brothers shall depend upon him just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of sons and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off debts and through whom one attains immortality—he alone is the son born of dharma; they know the others to be born of desire.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons;
and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as toward a son.
The eldest son either causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an eldest brother should—like a mother, like a father—is he;
but he who does not behave as an eldest brother should be honored merely as a kinsman.
In this manner, they may live together or separately out of a desire for dharma;
for dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma.
The eldest shall receive an additional portion consisting of one-twentieth of the entire estate and whatever is the most excellent;
half of that shall be the share of the middle son, and a fourth for the youngest.
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those who are others than the eldest and the youngest shall receive the middle portion of the wealth.
Of all kinds of property, the eldest shall take the best;
and he shall also receive whatever is particularly excellent, as well as one choice item from every ten.
There is no preferential share (*uddhāra*) among those who are all equally accomplished in their respective duties;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the elder as a mark of respect.
Thus, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should allot equal portions;
but if no preferential shares have been set aside, this following shall be the distribution of shares for them.
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger than him, one and a half shares;
and each younger than that, one share each—thus is the law established.
The brothers shall severally give portions to their unmarried sisters from their own respective shares;
they shall each give a fourth part from their own share, for those who refuse to give shall become outcasts.
One should never divide goats, sheep, and animals with uncloven hoofs unequally;
however, it is ordained that an unequal share of goats and sheep shall belong to the eldest alone.
If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law.
According to the law, it is not possible for the subordinate to supersede the principal;
the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him according to dharma.

If a doubt should arise as to how the division [of the estate] should be made in a case where the youngest son is born of the eldest wife, and the first-born son is born of the youngest wife: *Manu 9.122*: "If there should be a doubt as to how the partition should be made in such a case..."
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall take bulls according to their seniority, each receiving fewer than the elder in proportion to their mothers.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take fifteen cows and one bull as his share;
the remaining sons shall divide the rest according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no distinction;
seniority is not determined by the mother, but is said to be according to birth.
Even in the *Subrahmaṇyā* liturgical formulas, it is recorded that the invocation is made according to birth-order seniority;
and in the case of twins conceived simultaneously, seniority is declared to be determined by the order of birth.

A sonless man may, according to this rule, make his daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), [stipulating]: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be for me the performer of the ancestral rites."
According to this very rule,
Dakṣa himself, the lord of creatures, formerly made daughters in order to increase his own lineage.
With a delighted soul, he gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them all.
As one’s own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son. While she remains as his very self, how could another take the wealth?
Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the share of the unmarried daughter;
and the son of the daughter (dauhitra) alone shall take the entire estate of one who leaves no sons.
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] sons;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
In this world, there is no difference between a grandson and a daughter's son according to the law;
for both of them are produced from the very body of their mother and father.

But if, after a daughter has been appointed as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate there shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without having borne a son,
her husband shall, without hesitation, take that property.
Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if a man obtains a son from a similar man,
that grandson makes his maternal grandfather the recipient of the *piṇḍa* offering and shall inherit his wealth.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
In this world, no distinction is found between a grandson and a daughter's son;
for even a daughter's son saves him in the hereafter, just like a grandson.
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to that father’s father.
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and the inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives it to the wrong lineage.

The son of a woman not authorized [to bear a child], and the son obtained from her husband’s brother by a woman who already has a son— both of these, being born of an adulterer and born of lust, do not deserve a share of the inheritance.
Even if born of a woman duly appointed,
a man produced contrary to the prescribed rule is not at all entitled to his father's inheritance, for he is begotten by one who has fallen from his caste.
A son born from a woman duly appointed in that matter shall be considered as an *aurasa* (legitimate) son;
for according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*), and so does the offspring.
He who takes charge of the wealth and the widow of his deceased brother shall,
having procreated offspring for that brother, hand over that very wealth to that [offspring].

If a woman, having been authorized, should obtain a son from another man or even from her husband’s younger brother (*devara*), they declare that son to be born of lust, not entitled to the inheritance, and born in vain. This rule is to be understood as applying to the partition of property among children born of a single mother.
And learn now regarding those born of many wives of various castes from a single man.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order of castes,
this rule for partition is prescribed when sons have been born from them.
A plowman, a breeding bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house—these, as well as the share of the eldest, should be given to the Brāhmaṇa; furthermore, one principal share should be given to him.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares of the inheritance; the son of a Kṣatriya wife, two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya wife, one share and a half; and the son born of a Śūdra wife shall take one share.
Or, having divided that entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
the knower of dharma should perform a righteous partition according to this rule.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
This remains so whether there is a legitimate son (son of a wife of equal caste) or even no legitimate son at all.
According to the law, one should not give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra wife.
The son of a Śūdra born to a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya shall not be an heir to the estate;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
All sons born of wives of equal caste to twice-born men,
having given a preferential share to the eldest, should divide the remainder equally.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is prescribed, and no other;
the sons born of her shall have equal shares, even if there should be a hundred sons.
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has declared for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, and six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the adopted son, the son made,
the son secretly born, and the son cast off— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a pregnant bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava),
the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the son of a Śūdra woman (śaudra)— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit property.
Just as one obtains such fruit when crossing water with bad boats,
so does one obtain such fruit when crossing over darkness with bad sons.
If there should be two sons sharing a single inheritance— the legitimate son of the body and the son begotten on the wife—
each shall take that paternal property which belongs to his own biological father, and not the other.
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a means of subsistence.
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa), distributing the estate, should give a sixth share of the father’s wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja),
or even a fifth share.
The legitimate son of the body (aurasa) and the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja) are the two heirs to the father's estate;
the other ten, however, in their respective order, are entitled to a share of the lineage and the inheritance.
But that son whom one himself procreates upon his own consecrated wife,
him one should know as the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, the first in rank.
He who is born on the bed of one who is deceased, impotent, or diseased,
by means of a woman appointed according to her own duty, is known as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja).
If the mother or the father should give a son with water in times of distress—
one who is similar [in status] and given with affection— he is to be known as a *dattima* (given) son.
But he whom one may make similar [to oneself], who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as a *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
But he who is born in the house and it is not known whose he is—he is one born secretly in the house; he shall belong to him on whose wife he was begotten.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his mother and father, or by either of them,
is called an *apaviddha* (cast-off).
But the son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father’s house, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born of the maiden and belongs to the man who marries her.
If a woman who is already pregnant is married— whether her condition be known or unknown—
that child belongs to the husband and is called *sahoḍha* (one born with the bride).
But he whom one purchases from his mother and father for the sake of offspring is his "bought" son (krītaka), whether he be of equal or unequal status.
A son whom a woman, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, bears through her own desire after marrying again,
is called a *paunarbhava*.
If she is still a virgin, even if she has returned from another,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her new husband.
He who, being deprived of his mother and father, or abandoned by them without cause,
offers himself to someone, is known as a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given son).
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is called a Pāraśava, because he is capable of crossing over (pārayan) the corpse (śava). Thus is he remembered.
Whether born of a Śūdra’s slave woman or of his slave woman’s slave woman, the son who is thus born shall, with the permission [of his father], take a share; such is the established law.
The wise declare these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as they have been described, to be substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
Regarding these sons born from the seed of others who have been mentioned incidentally:
they belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else.
Manu 9.182: Among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, Manu has declared them all to be possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
If among all the wives who have but one husband, one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by means of that son.
In the absence of each more excellent [heir], one who is less excellent is entitled to the inheritance.
But if there are many of equal status, they all share the inheritance.
Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the inheritors of the father’s estate.
The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall the brothers.
Water-offerings should be made for three ancestors, and the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) extends to three;
he is the fourth who offers them, and a fifth does not exist.
The property of a deceased person shall belong to whoever is the nearest among his *sapiṇḍas*;
after them, it shall go to a *sakulya*, or else to the teacher or the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs of the estate; thus the Law is not violated.
The property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be confiscated by the king; this is the settled rule. However, in the absence of all other heirs, the king may take the property of the other castes.
For one who has died without offspring, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage (sagotra).
Whatever property may have been acquired there, that he should deliver to him. But if two sons born of two [different] men should dispute over the wealth of a woman,
each of them shall take what belonged to his own father, and not the other.
But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother’s inheritance equally.
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection.
That which is given before the fire, that which is given at the wedding procession, and that which is given as a token of affection;
that which is received from a brother, a mother, or a father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
The property given as a subsequent gift (anvādheya), and that which was given by the husband out of affection—
this shall be the wealth of the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.
Whatever property was acquired in marriages of the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, or Prājāpatya types, it is ordained that,
upon the death of the wife without issue, it belongs to the husband alone.
But whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others,
that is ordained for her mother and father when she dies childless.
But whatever property may have been given to a woman by her father in any manner whatsoever,
the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take that, or it shall belong to her offspring.
Women should not make a withdrawal from the household for their own benefit when it is situated among many members,
nor indeed from their own property without the permission of their husband.
If ornaments have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them;
those who do divide them fall from their caste.
Eunuchs, outcasts, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the mentally dull, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of [vital] faculties, are not entitled to a share.
However, it is right for the wise man to give to all of them according to his ability;
for he who fails to provide food and clothing perpetually becomes an outcast.
If, however, there should be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others by any means whatsoever,
their offspring is entitled to the inheritance once they have produced a lineage.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died,
the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning.
But if all those who are unlearned should acquire wealth through their own exertion, the division of that property shall be equal; it is not ancestral—this is the settled rule.
But whatever is his wealth acquired through learning—that shall belong to him alone;
as also that which is obtained through friendship, at marriage, and from the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka).
But among brothers, he who, though capable of supporting himself by his own labor, does not desire a share of the wealth,
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.
That which has been acquired by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained through one's own exertion— that he need not give if he is unwilling.
But if a father should acquire ancestral property that he had not previously obtained,
he need not share it with his sons against his will, as it was acquired by himself.
If those who were previously divided choose to live together again, their subsequent division shall be equal; in that case, the right of primogeniture does not exist.
If among them the eldest or the youngest is excluded from the distribution of shares,
or if either one should die, his share is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having assembled together in union, shall divide it equally;
as shall those brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall forfeit his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings.

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should the eldest brother make a separate property for himself without giving anything to the younger brothers.
If brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance should live together,
the father must never, under any circumstances, give unequal shares to his sons.
But a son born after partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or he shall share it with those who may have reunited with him.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that they shall divide equally.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security of possession (yogakṣema), and pasture grounds— they declare these to be indivisible.
This division of property among sons and the rule for their rites has been declared to you;
now learn, in due order, the law concerning gambling and betting.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
for these two vices bring about the destruction of kings who rule the earth.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "dyūta" (gambling) in the world;
that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "samāhvaya" (betting).
The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
Gamblers, actors and singers, cruel men, those who adhere to heretical sects,
those engaged in improper occupations, and liquor-sellers— he should quickly banish from the city.
These, existing in the kingdom as the king's hidden thieves,
constantly oppress the virtuous subjects through their performance of forbidden acts.
In a former age, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not practice gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whether he practices it secretly or openly, whatever man indulges in that [prohibited act],
there shall be a variety of punishments for him according to the king's will.
But a man born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, being unable to pay a fine, shall discharge his debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it gradually.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king shall prescribe punishment with whips, split cane, ropes, and the like.
But those who, having been appointed to official duties,
ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth— the king shall render them destitute.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the ministers,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, as well as those who serve his enemies.
Whatever has been adjudicated and whatever has been instructed, wherever it may be, one should know that to be established according to dharma; one must not reverse it again.
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly,
the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
A killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed— [these are the four mortal sins].
All these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
And for these four who do not perform penance,
he shall prescribe a lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the foot of a dog should be made; and for killing a Brahmin, a headless male figure.
Indeed, they shall not eat together, nor sacrifice together, nor study together, nor intermarry.
They shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties.
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their paternal and maternal relatives;
they are to be treated without compassion and without salutation—this is the instruction of Manu.
But when people of all castes perform the prescribed penance as ordained, they shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
In cases of offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement shall be imposed upon him alone;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his property and his belongings.
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
A righteous king must not take the property of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for if he takes it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt.
Having cast that punishment into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should bestow it upon a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and good conduct.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Where the king avoids the acquisition of wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time as long-lived.
And the crops of the people ripen according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and no deformed offspring is born.
But a king should put to death with various terrifying methods of execution a person of low caste who, out of desire, oppresses Brāhmaṇas.

As great as the demerit seen for a king in executing one who should not be executed, so great is the merit for him in releasing one who deserves execution; for he who restrains [the wicked] performs dharma.
Thus has been declared in detail this decision regarding legal procedure in its eighteen titles for two parties engaged in mutual dispute.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet won and protect those already acquired.
Having properly settled his territory and constructed fortifications according to the treatises,
he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to heaven.
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven.
But that kingdom which is free from fear, relying upon the strength of his arms,
increases constantly like a tree being watered.
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should know that there are two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are concealed.
Those who live by various wares and deceive people openly are "open cheats"; but those such as thieves, forest-dwellers, and the like, who deceive in secret, are "hidden cheats."

Those who take bribes, those who practice fraud through deception, cheats, gamblers, those who live by prescribing auspicious rites, fortune-tellers, together with those who subsist by looking at omens,
as well as high officials and physicians who act improperly; [Manu 9.258–259].
And courtesans skilled in the arts and refined manners are expert in their trade.
One should recognize such persons as manifest thorns of society,
as well as others who move in secret, being ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble.
Having identified them through well-conducted secret agents who perform those same tasks,
and through spies stationed in various disguises, he should incite them and bring them under his control.
Having publicly proclaimed their offenses according to the truth in relation to each respective deed, the king shall impose punishment properly, in accordance with the gravity of the offense.
For without punishment, it is impossible to restrain the wicked,
especially those thieves of sinful intent who move about secretly upon the earth.
Courthouses, water-stations, bakeries, houses of prostitution, taverns, and food-sellers;
crossroads, sacred trees, public assemblies, and places of spectacle.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans, empty houses, groves, and pleasure parks; [these are places where one may study].
In such regions, the king should cause patrols consisting of both stationary and mobile troops,
as well as spies, to move about for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
He should discover them through their accomplices who follow them and are familiar with various activities,
and he should eliminate them by means of clever former thieves.
By means of instructions regarding various kinds of food, by the sight of Brāhmaṇas,
and by discussions of heroic deeds, they should bring about their meeting.
Those who do not approach there, as well as those who are secretly dispatched, [should be examined].
The king shall forcibly slay them, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
A righteous king shall not have a thief executed unless he is caught with the stolen goods;
however, if caught with the goods and the implements [of theft], he should be executed without hesitation.
Moreover, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves,
or give them space for their goods— all of those as well he should cause to be executed.
Those appointed to protect the realms, as well as the neighboring chieftains who have been exhorted,
he should quickly punish like thieves if they remain indifferent during attacks.
And even one who lives by the law, if he has fallen away from the established rule of dharma,
the king should burn him with punishment indeed, for he has strayed from his own duty.
In the event of a village raid, the destruction of irrigation works, or the sighting of robbery on the road,
those who do not run to assist to the best of their ability shall be banished along with their belongings.
He shall cause those who steal from the king’s treasury, those who stand in opposition,
and those who instigate enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment.
But those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking through a wall,
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake.
In the first apprehension of a finger-ring thief, the king should cause his fingers to be amputated;
in the second, his hand and foot; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
The king should punish those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter,
as well as those who facilitate the theft, just like the thief himself.
One who destroys a reservoir should be killed, or else executed by drowning in water;
or, if he should repair it, he must be made to pay the highest fine.
One should put to death without hesitation those who break into granaries, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established,
or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
He who, except in times of distress, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity.
But one who has fallen into distress, or an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a verbal reprimand; and that [offense] must be expiated—this is the settled rule.
For all physicians who practice their craft falsely, there shall be punishment:
for animals, the first amercement; but for humans, the middle amercement.
One who destroys a bridge, a banner, a sacrificial post,
or images shall repair all of that damage and pay five hundred [paṇas].
For the spoiling of goods that are not defective, as well as for breaking them,
and likewise for boring gems in the wrong place, the punishment is the first amercement.
But he who treats equals unequally, whether by measure or by price,
shall incur either the first or the middle amercement.
And the king should establish all prisons along the royal highway,
where the suffering and deformed evildoers may be seen.
One should immediately banish the breaker of a wall, the filler of moats,
and likewise the destroyer of gates.
In all cases of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;

likewise for the practice of roots (*mūlakarman*) and various types of sorcery (*kṛtyā*) performed by those who are not authorized. Furthermore, a seller of non-seed as seed, as well as one who has uprooted a superior seed, [shall be punished].
And one who breaks a boundary mark shall suffer mutilation as his punishment.
But the king shall cut a goldsmith— who is the most wicked of all thorns—
into pieces with razors, if he persists in unlawful conduct.
In the case of the theft of agricultural implements, weapons, or medicine, [the same penalty applies].
Having considered the time and the nature of the offense, the king shall determine the punishment.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; indeed, the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Among these seven constituent elements of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order,
each preceding one is more important and its misfortune more grievous.
In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels another because of the specific excellence of their mutual qualities.
In various specific tasks, however, this or that particular limb excels; whichever part accomplishes a given purpose is said to be the most excellent for that purpose.
Through spies, through the application of energy, and by the very execution of his duties,
the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain both his own strength and that of his enemy,
as well as all forms of oppression and likewise all types of vices.
Then, having reflected upon the relative weight and lightness of the matter, he should undertake the task.
One should indeed undertake tasks again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who undertakes actions.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the conducts of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.
Kali is asleep; when he is awake, it is the Dvāpara age;
when he is intent upon actions, it is Tretā; but when he is moving about, it is the Kṛta age.
A king should practice the conduct of those whose essence is splendor: of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and Pṛthivī.
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should the king, performing the vow of Indra, shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays during eight months, so should the king take tax from his kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun.
Just as the wind moves about after having entered all living beings, so too should one enter [the enemy's territory] by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-vow" (māruta-vrata).
Just as Yama restrains both friend and foe when the appointed time arrives, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should the king restrain the wicked; for this is the vow of Varuṇa.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow (cāndravrata).
One who is endowed with majesty and full of splendor should always be intent upon punishing those who commit evil deeds;
being a destroyer of wicked neighbors—that is remembered as the vow of Agni.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so too is the duty of a king who sustains all beings.
Employing these and other means, always remaining vigilant,
the king should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in those of others.
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke Brāhmaṇas;
for they, when enraged, could instantly destroy him along with his army and his vehicles.
By whom was fire made to consume all things, and the great ocean rendered undrinkable?
By whom was the waning moon made to wax? Who would not perish by provoking them?
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked to anger, might create other worlds and other world-protectors,
or turn gods into non-gods?
Who, desiring to live, would harm those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend,
for whom the Veda itself is wealth?
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like the fire, a great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the brilliant fire is not defiled;
when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of unworthy deeds,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme deity.
When the Kṣatriya power becomes excessively overbearing in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇical power alone shall be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya has its origin in the Brāhmaṇa.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brāhmaṇical power, nor does the Brāhmaṇical power increase without the Kṣatriya power;
when the Brāhmaṇical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they prosper both in this world and in the next.
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins the wealth arising from all fines,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle.
Acting thus and ever intent upon the duties of a king, the monarch—
And he should employ all his servants in works that are beneficial to the world.
This eternal rule of action for a king has been declared in its entirety;
one should know this same rule of action to apply to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra respectively.
But a Vaiśya, having performed the purificatory rites and taken a wife,
should be constantly engaged in agriculture and trade, as well as in the protection of cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya should not have the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
and when the Vaiśya is willing, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
One should understand the relative value and worth of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven fabrics,
perfumes, and liquids.
He should know the sowing of seeds and the defects or virtues of the soil;
he should understand the application of measures and all methods of weighing with scales.
He should also know the quality or lack thereof of merchandise, and the advantages and disadvantages of various regions.
The profit and loss on commodities, and the breeding of livestock;
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the proper storage and application of goods, as well as buying and selling.
He should exert the greatest effort to increase his wealth through righteous means,
and he should diligently provide food for all living beings.

For a Śūdra, however, the highest duty leading to supreme beatitude is indeed the service of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious. Being pure, intent on serving those superior to him, gentle in speech, and free from arrogance— *Manu* 9.334–335a.

One who constantly relies upon a Brāhmaṇa or others attains a superior birth. This auspicious rule for the duties of the social classes in times of no distress has been declared; now learn their respective duties in times of distress as well.
The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study;
however, it is certain that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound [the Veda], not the other two.
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others, and he himself should likewise act accordingly.
Due to his superiority, the excellence of his origin, his observance of restrictive rules,
and the distinction of his sacraments, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social orders.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are the twice-born.
The fourth, however, is the once-born Śūdra; there is no fifth.
Among all castes, sons born of wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity,
through unions in the direct order of classes, are to be known as belonging to those same castes.
Sons begotten by the twice-born on women of the next lower caste are said to be equal [in status] to their fathers,
yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women whose caste is immediately below [the father's];
one should know this rule to be the righteous law for those born of women two or one degree below.
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra mother is born a Niṣāda, who is also called a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Śūdra is born a being named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.
Among the three castes for a Brāhmaṇa, among the two castes for a Kṣatriya,
and among the one caste for a Vaiśya— these six are recorded as base-born (apasada) sons.
From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa is born a Sūta by birth;
from a Vaiśya [and the daughters of a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa] are born a Māgadha and a Vaideha, who are the sons of a royal and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.
From a Śūdra, by women of the Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men— these being the offspring of the mixture of castes.
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and the Ugra are declared to be born from a one-interval union in the direct order,
so too are the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka born from a one-interval union in the inverse order.
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women of the next lower caste, as described in due order,
are designated by the name "Anantara" (next-in-order) because of the inferiority of their mothers.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta;
from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra, but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra through women of the higher castes in the reverse order of classes.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone. These three others are also base-born (apasada), being produced in the inverse order.
A son born to a Niṣāda from a Śūdra woman is by birth a Pukkasa;
but one born to a Niṣāda woman from a Śūdra is known as a Kukkuṭaka.
Likewise, one born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
but one produced by a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhā mother is called a Veṇa.
Those offspring whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances—
one should designate them as *vrātyas*, fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*.
From a *vrātya* Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhūrjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.
From a Vrātya of the Kṣatriya caste are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchivi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khaśa, and the Draviḍa.
From a *vrātya* Vaiśya, however, are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Through the adultery of the castes, through marrying those who should not be married,
and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises.
I shall now describe in their entirety those of mixed origin who are born from inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) unions, as well as those who have intermarried with one another.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Āyogava, and the Kṣattṛ (or Kṣatrajāti),
these six beget offspring similar to themselves when they procreate within their own respective wombs.

They procreate offspring belonging to the caste of their mothers in marriages with women of higher castes. Just as for the three castes, a son of one's own self is born from two [wives] of immediate [caste],
so too is the sequence for those outside [the caste system].
And they, moreover, procreate upon the wives of one another many outcastes who are even more defiled than they, and are held in contempt.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste offspring upon a Brāhmaṇī woman,
so does an outcaste beget an even more outcaste offspring within the four castes.
Acting in opposition [to their husbands], women of the outer castes give birth to even more outward [sons]; being degraded, they procreate fifteen further degraded castes.

An Ayogava begets upon a Vaideha woman a Sairandhra, who knows how to attend to personal adornment and grooming, who is not a slave but lives by the life of a slave, and subsists by means of snares. A Vaideha, however, procreates a Maitreyaka, also known as a Mādhūka, upon a Māhiṣya woman.
Manu 10.33c: He who, like one who strikes a bell, does not constantly praise [the gods] at the break of dawn, is censured.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by working as a boatman;
him the inhabitants of Āryāvarta call a Kaivarta.
Upon women who wear the clothes of the deceased, who eat forbidden food, and who are of ignoble birth— namely, upon Āyogava women— these three distinct, outcaste groups are born.
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born as a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehika are born the Andhra and Meda, who have their dwellings outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī woman is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī woman.

But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pukkasa woman, is born the sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-digging and is always censured by the virtuous. From a Caṇḍāla, however, by a Niṣāda woman, is born a son called Antyāvasāyin.
She gives birth to one who frequents the cremation ground, despised even among those outside the caste system.
These castes born of intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
they are to be known by their respective occupations, whether they are concealed or manifest.
The six sons born of women of their own caste and those immediately following in the order of castes possess the duties of the twice-born;
however, all those born of degradation from the Śūdra caste are recorded as having the same duties as Śūdras.
But by the power of their austerity and their seed, they undergo, age after age,
both increase and decrease among human beings here from birth.
But through the gradual neglect of sacred rites and by the failure to see Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya tribes have fallen to the status of Śūdras in this world.
These are the Pauṇḍrakas, the Coḍas, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, and the Śakas.
The Pāradas, Pahlavas, Cīnas, Kirātas, Daradas, and Khaśas; 10.44c.
Those castes in the world who are born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet [of the four original orders],
whether they speak the speech of Mlecchas or the speech of Āryas, are all remembered as Dasyus.
Those who are known as the base-born (apasada) of the twice-born, as well as those born of transgression (apadhvaṃsaja),
should subsist by means of the occupations of the twice-born that are considered censurable.
For Sūtas, the management of horses and chariots; for Ambaṣṭhas, the practice of medicine;
for Vaidehakas, service to women; and for Māgadhas, the way of trade.
The killing of fish is the occupation of Niṣādas, while that of Āyogavas is carpentry;
the killing of wild animals is the occupation of Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.
For the Kṣattṛs, Ugras, and Pukkasas, however, their livelihood shall be dwelling in holes, killing, and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, it shall be working with leather; and for the Veṇas, it shall be playing drums.
These known [outcasts] shall dwell near sacred trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves,
subsisting by their own prescribed occupations.
But for the Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, their dwelling shall be outside the village;
they must be made to use discarded vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Wearing the clothes of the deceased, eating from broken vessels,
ornaments of black iron, and perpetual wandering— these are their duties.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them;
their mutual dealings and marriages are only with their own equals.
Their food should be given by others in a broken vessel;
they must not wander about in villages or towns at night.
They should move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the disposal of a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the settled rule.
They shall constantly execute those deserving of death by the king's command in accordance with the scriptures;
they shall take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of those condemned to death.
One should discern a man of impure origin— who has fallen from his caste, is unknown,
and though appearing noble is actually ignoble— by his own actions.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a disposition toward the neglect of sacred duties—
these reveal in this world a man born of a defiled womb.
He inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or indeed both;
however, one born of a low womb cannot in any way suppress his own innate nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth (yonisaṃkara),
that man inevitably adopts the character of that [lineage], whether to a small or great degree.
But where these corrupters of the social orders are born through moral collapse,
that kingdom, along with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly.
Sacrificing one’s body without regard for reward, whether for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, [is meritorious].
And the protection of women and children is the cause of success for those living outside [the caste system].
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu has declared this to be the summary of the dharma for the four castes.
If one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother procreates with a man of superior status,
he attains the caste of his superior parent up to the seventh generation.
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise attains the status of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly how it occurs for those born from a Kṣatriya and likewise from a Vaiśya.
If it should be asked: "Wherein might there be superiority— between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa to a non-Aryan woman,
and one born from a non-Aryan man to a Brāhmaṇa woman?"— one born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan through his qualities.
Even one born to an Ārya woman from a non-Ārya man is determined to be a non-Ārya.

The law is settled: both of these are ineligible for the sacraments; the former because of the defectiveness of his birth, and the latter because he was born in the inverse order. Just as a good seed sown in good soil comes to fruition, so it is with one born of a good womb from a good seed.
Likewise, one born of an Ārya father and an Ārya mother is entitled to all sacramental rites.

Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the settled rule is as follows: Manu 10.70: Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; yet others praise both the seed and the field. In this regard, the established principle is as follows: [The field is the source of the crop, but the seed is the source of the species. (Manu 10.71) [A field that is well-plowed and sown with good seed yields an abundant harvest. (Manu 10.72) [But a field that is not plowed, even if sown with good seed, does not yield a harvest; nor does a seed sown in an unplowed field. (Manu 10.73) [Therefore, both the seed and the field should be carefully examined by those who desire offspring of excellent quality. (Manu 10.74) [A Śūdra woman is the wife of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman of a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya woman of a Kṣatriya, and a Brāhmaṇa woman of a Brāhmaṇa. (Manu 10.75) [But a Brāhmaṇa may take three wives from the [other] castes in the direct order of classes, or two, or one. (Manu 10.76) [In the same way, a Kṣatriya may take two wives, and a Vaiśya one, from the castes below his own. (Manu 10.77) [But for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, the wife of a lower caste is not recommended, even if she has been married according to the prescribed rites. (Manu 10.78) [From women of equal caste, sons are born who resemble their fathers; from women of lower castes, base-born sons are produced who follow the condition of their mothers. (Manu 10.79) [Sons born of women in the reverse order of classes are called vrātyas; they are excluded from inheritance and are declared to be the lowest of men. (Manu 10.80) [A son born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is a Pāraśava; he is the seventh among the sons and is called a "son of the field" (kṣetraja) because he was conceived in the field of another. (Manu 10.81) [A son born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is an Ambaṣṭha; one born from a Kṣatriya woman is a Sūta; these two are known as "in-between" (antarapātinau). (Manu 10.82) [A son born to a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman is a Niṣāda; one born from a Vaiśya woman is a Mahiṣya; these two are also called "in-between. (Manu 10.83) [A son born to a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is an Ugra; he is the last of the six sons born in the natural order of classes. (Manu 10.84) [Now, sons born to a Brāhmaṇa from women of the three lower castes in the reverse order are respectively called a Ratha-kāra, a Pāraśava, and a Cāṇḍāla. (Manu 10.85) [A son born to a Kṣatriya from a Śūdra woman is an Āyogava; and one born to a Vaiśya from a Śūdra woman is a Vaiṇa. (Manu 10.86) [These six are called "in-between" (antarapātinaḥ); they are born from women of lower castes than their fathers and are considered base-born (vṛṣalāḥ). (Manu 10.87) [From a Śūdra are born in the reverse order a Kṣatta, a Māgadha, and a Vaidehaka; and from a Vaiśya, an Āyogava. (Manu 10.88) [From a Kṣatriya, a Sūta; and from a Brāhmaṇa, a Cāṇḍāla, who is the lowest of men; these are the six base-born sons born in the reverse order of classes. (Manu 10.89) [The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is a Cāṇḍāla; the son of a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is a Vaiṇa; and the son of a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is a Kṣatta. (Manu 10.90) [The son of a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is an Āyogava; the son of a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is a Kṣatta; and the son of a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla, the most despicable of men. (Manu 10.91) [The son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is a Sūta; the son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Māgadha; the son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is a Rathakāra. (Manu 10.92) [These three are also called "in-between"; they are born from women of higher castes than their fathers and are considered base-born. (Manu 10.93) [The son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Sūta; the son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is a Māgadha; the son of a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla. (Manu 10.94) [The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is an Ambaṣṭha; the son of a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is a Niṣāda; these two are also called "in-between. (Manu 10.95) [The son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is a Sūta; the son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Māgadha; the son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is a Rathakāra. (Manu 10.96) [These three are also called "in-between"; they are born from women of higher castes than their fathers and are considered base-born. (Manu 10.97) [The son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Sūta; the son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is a Māgadha; the son of a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇḍāla. (Manu 10.98) [The son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is an Ambaṣṭha; the son of a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is a Niṣāda; these two are also called "in-between. (Manu 10.99) [The son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is a Sūta; the son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Māgadha; the son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is a Rathakāra. (Manu 10.100) [These three are also called "in-between"; they are born from women of higher castes than their fathers and are considered base-born. (Manu 10.101) [The son of a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Sūta; the son of a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is a Māgadha; the son of a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is a Cāṇ
Seed sown in a non-field perishes in the very middle;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
Since, by the power of the seed, even those born as animals have become seers (*ṛṣi*).
Because they are honored and praised, the seed is therefore highly esteemed.
Having considered the non-Aryan who performs the deeds of an Aryan, and the Aryan who performs the deeds of a non-Aryan, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Brāhmaṇas who abide in the source of the Veda and remain steadfast in their own duties should properly subsist by means of the six occupations in their proper order.
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices,
giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.

"In the same way, these [duties] should cease with respect to the Vaiśya; such is the settled rule. For Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them (the Śūdras). Bearing arms and missiles is the duty of the Kṣatriya, while trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture belong to the Vaiśya."
But for the sake of livelihood, the duty consists of giving, study, and sacrifice.
The study of the Vedas is the specific duty of the Brāhmaṇa, protection is that of the Kṣatriya,
and the occupation of agriculture and trade is that of the Vaiśya— these are the distinguished duties among their respective occupations.
But if a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own aforementioned occupation,
he may live by the duty of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best alternative for him.
But if it should happen that he cannot subsist by either of these two,
he may live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing.
But even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which involves much violence and is dependent on others.
They consider agriculture to be an excellent livelihood, yet that occupation is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wooden plough destroys both the earth and those creatures that dwell within it.
But for one who, due to a deficiency in livelihood, abandons skill in the dharma,
this may be sold as merchandise for the increase of wealth, provided that the reserved portion has been set aside.
One should exclude all liquids, as well as cooked food together with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, domestic animals, and human beings.
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as fabrics made of hemp, flax, and wool— even if they are undyed— likewise fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass.
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and all one-hoofed animals likewise;
and having produced [these goods] at will through cultivation, the farmer himself may sell them.
A Śūdra may sell sesame seeds that have not been kept for long, provided it is for the sake of dharma.
But if he uses sesame seeds for anything other than eating, anointing, or giving as a gift,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors.
He falls immediately from his caste by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk.
But by selling other commodities here out of desire,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, and sesame seeds for grain in equal quantities.
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all these means;
however, he must never at any time consider a higher mode of livelihood as his own.
If one who is inferior by birth should, out of greed, live by the occupations of those superior to him,
the king shall strip him of his wealth and banish him immediately.
One's own duty, even if performed imperfectly, is better than the duty of another well-performed;
for by living according to the duty of another, one immediately falls from one's caste.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may also live by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts, he should desist from it once he is capable [of supporting himself otherwise].
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born,
having fallen into distress regarding his sons and wife, may live by the crafts of artisans.
Those occupations of artisans and various crafts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— [these are the duties of a Śūdra].
A Brāhmaṇa who remains established on his own path, yet finds himself distressed by a lack of livelihood while unable to subsist through the occupation of a Vaiśya,
should practice this following rule.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a purifier should become defiled—this is not logically tenable according to the Dharma.
No fault attaches to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts— even from those that are censured— for they are like fire and water.
One who, having fallen into a situation where life is at stake, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
Vāmadeva, though skilled in discerning between dharma and adharma, did not eat dog’s flesh even when distressed and desiring to consume it,
for the sake of preserving his life.
But Bharadvāja, the great ascetic, afflicted by hunger in the lonely forest along with his sons,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra,
who was discerning of dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise from teaching,
for a Brahmin, the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those who have been consecrated;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra or one of the lowest birth.
The sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by silent recitations (japa) and burnt offerings (homa);
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renunciation and austerity.
If a Brahmin cannot subsist [by his own means], he may gather grains from anywhere;
gleaning ears of grain (śila) is better than receiving gifts, and picking up individual grains (uñcha) is praised even more than that.
When Snātaka Brahmins are in distress, desiring base metals or wealth, they may request it from the lord of the earth; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned by them.
From a cultivated field, unprepared land is less blameworthy; likewise for cattle, goats, and sheep, gold, grain, and food—the earlier mentioned being less blameworthy than the later.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, investment, the performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Knowledge, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing,
trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever lend money at interest;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may indeed give a small amount to a person of evil character as one wishes.
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress,
a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.
Victory is his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle. Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapons, he should collect a lawful tribute from them:
one-eighth of their grain, and one-twentieth of their money, with a minimum of one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Śūdras who assist with work, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [are those who may serve].
But if a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya,
or if a Śūdra desires to live by serving a wealthy Vaiśya, he may do so.
He should propitiate Brahmins for the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed is his fulfillment of duty.
Service to Brahmins alone is declared to be the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs, that becomes fruitless for him.
They shall provide for his maintenance from their own family resources as is appropriate,
having regard to [the giver's] wealth, [the recipient's] skill, and the number of dependents he must support.
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments,
the shriveled husks of grain, and old household utensils.
There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor is he entitled to sacramental rites;
he has no obligation regarding dharma, yet there is no prohibition against dharma.

But those who desire to know the Dharma, who understand the Dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur sin by omitting the sacred mantras; rather, they receive praise. For to the extent that one free from malice adheres to the conduct of the good, [so much does he gain merit].
In that same measure, being blameless, he attains both this world and the next.
Even if he is capable, a Śūdra should not accumulate wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by properly performing them, they attain the supreme goal.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rules for penance.
One seeking offspring, one intending to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions,
one seeking wealth for the sake of his teacher, for the sake of his father or mother, one seeking wealth for Vedic study, and one who is afflicted by illness— [these may be exempted from taxes].
One should indeed not consider those Brāhmaṇas who beg for the sake of dharma as mere Snātakas;
gifts should be given to these [others] who are destitute, according to the excellence of their learning.
For to these foremost of the twice-born, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given;
for others, it is said that cooked food is to be given outside the sacrificial altar (bahirvedi).
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon those Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas, according to their merit, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of performing sacrifices.
If a man who has already taken a wife obtains another wife by begging for her, his reward is merely sexual pleasure; the offspring, however, belongs to the giver of the wealth.
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins according to one's ability—
upon those who are learned in the Vedas and live in seclusion— and thereby enjoys heaven after death.
He whose food supply for three years is sufficient to maintain his dependents...
Or even if he possesses more wealth than that, he is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, if a twice-born man drinks Soma when he possesses very little wealth,
even though he has previously drunk Soma, he does not obtain its fruit.
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery—
that counterfeit dharma has a taste like honey at first, but its relish is like poison.
Whatever funeral rite one performs by causing distress to one's dependents results in unhappiness both for the living and for the deceased.
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the absence of even a single constituent part—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, provided that a righteous king is in power— then [the following applies].
If there be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of completing a sacrifice.
He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for the Śūdra has no entitlement to sacrificial rites whatsoever.

He who possesses a hundred cows but has not established the sacred fires, and he who possesses a thousand cows but has not performed sacrifices— from the households of these two as well, one may take [food] without hesitation.
And from one who is constantly intent on taking and who does not give back what was taken, he should seize [the property];
thus his fame spreads and his dharma increases.
Likewise, having fasted for six meals, one may take food at the seventh mealtime from a person of low conduct who follows the practice of not providing for the morrow.
Whether it is obtained from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or from wherever else it may be found,
it must be reported to him if he asks.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, if he lacks a means of livelihood, he is entitled to take the property of a Dasyu or one who neglects his religious duties.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and causes both of them to cross over.
The wise know that the wealth of those who are devoted to sacrifice is the property of the gods;
however, the wealth of those who do not perform sacrifices is said to belong to the asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger.

Having ascertained his dependents, the lord of the earth should determine a righteous means of livelihood for him, after taking into account his own family's needs and having examined his learning and character.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from that protected person, the king obtains one-sixth of the merit.
A Brahmin should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for by begging for it while performing a sacrifice, he is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
If a Brahmin, having begged wealth for the purpose of a sacrifice, does not give it all away,
he shall become a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of a Brāhmaṇa—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures.

At the end of each year, he should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the purpose of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.
If a twice-born man performs his duty according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress,
it has been determined that he does not obtain the fruit thereof in the hereafter.
By the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great Ṛṣis,
fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the prescribed rule was established.
He who, though capable of following the primary rule,
conducts himself according to the secondary rule, for that person of evil intellect there exists no reward pertaining to the hereafter.
A Brāhmaṇa who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king;
rather, by his own power alone, he should discipline those offending men.
One's own power is more effective than the power of a king;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own power alone.
"Without hesitation, one should employ the Atharva-Angirasa hymns;
for the speech of a Brahmin is indeed a weapon, and with that, the twice-born man shall slay his enemies."
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own distress by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by their wealth; but the best of the twice-born by silent recitation and burnt offerings.
The Brāhmaṇa is called the ordainer, the punisher, the teacher, and the friend;
one should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted,
nor likewise one who is unconsecrated, shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*.

For these fall into hell while performing the oblation, as does he for whom it is performed. Therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.
If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, does not give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya),
he remains one who has not established the fires (anāhitāgni).
One who is faithful and has conquered his senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, he should by no means perform sacrifices here with small sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys the senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires becomes equal to one who has slain a hero;
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra fire,
are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
By treading with his foot upon the heads of those who constantly serve the fires of Śūdras out of ignorance, the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and is addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable for penance. The wise know that when a sin has been committed unintentionally, there must be a penance.
Some say that this applies even when committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scripture (Śruti).
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of penances.
If a twice-born man, having incurred the necessity of penance due to fate or by reason of his past deeds,
does not perform that penance, he must not associate with the virtuous.
In this world, some wicked men suffer a transformation of their physical form due to their current misdeeds, while others do so because of actions performed in the past.
A thief of gold incurs deformed nails; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a slayer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the Guru’s bed, a skin disease.
An informer receives a foul-smelling nose; a slanderer, a foul-smelling mouth;
a thief of grain, a deficiency of limbs; and one who adulterates goods, an excess of limbs.
The stealer of food becomes afflicted with disease; the stealer of speech becomes mute;
the stealer of clothing suffers from leucoderma; and the stealer of horses becomes lame.
Thus, by reason of specific actions, they are born despised by the virtuous—
stupid, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.
Therefore, an expiation must always be performed for the sake of purification;
for those who have not removed their sin are born endowed with despicable physical marks.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—
they call these the great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them.
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, malicious talebearing directed toward the king,
and persistent malice toward a teacher— these are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Abandoning the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food,
and eating what is censured— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land,
diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.
Emission of semen into women who are one's own uterine sisters, into virgins,
or into women of the lowest castes (antyajā), as well as into the wives of a friend or a son, they know to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed.
Killing a cow; officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed or sacrificing for such a person; adultery; selling oneself;
abandoning one’s teacher, mother, father, or son; and neglecting the study of the Veda or the sacred fires—[these are minor sins].

The state of being a *parivitti* when the younger brother has not yet married, as well as the act of *parivedana* (giving away the elder brother in marriage first); the giving away of a daughter by those two [the elder brother and the younger], and officiating at a sacrifice for those very two.
The defiling of a maiden, usury, the violation of a vow,
and the sale of a tank, a grove, a wife, or a child.
Becoming a *vrātya*, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages,
receiving instruction for wages, selling goods that should not be sold,
exercising authority over all types of labor, and operating large-scale mechanical works.
Injuring medicinal plants, living off women, malevolent incantations, and root-magic.
Cutting down green trees for the sake of fuel, undertaking activities solely for one's own benefit, and likewise eating forbidden food; 11.64a–c.
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts, studying improper scriptures, and engaging in the performance of arts for pleasure; 11.65. [64]a-c.

The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the drinking of intoxicants and consorting with forbidden women; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or intoxicating drinks,
crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are declared to be acts that cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats and sheep,
and likewise of fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as causing loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from censurable persons, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths are to be known as acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa).
The killing of worms, insects, and birds; eating food mixed with liquor;
stealing fruits, firewood, and flowers; and lack of fortitude—these are acts that cause impurity.
Now, learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins, each separately, are expiated.
A killer of a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having built a hut,
subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
Or, by his own will, he may become a target for those who bear arms among the learned;
or he may cast himself headlong three times into a blazing fire.
Or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
