Or, for the removal of the sin of killing a Brahmin, he may travel a hundred *yojanas* while reciting one of the Vedas, eating sparingly and with his senses restrained.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas;
for wealth is sufficient for a livelihood, or even a house together with its furnishings.
Or, eating sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī river upstream;
or, with his diet restricted, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village or even in a cow-pen,
or in a hermitage or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, one should immediately sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or a Brāhmaṇa is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.

Or by resisting him three times, or by recovering all his property, or if the Brahmin’s life is saved for that reason, he is released from the sin. Thus, one who is always firm in his vows, a celibate student (brahmacārī), and composed in mind—
When the twelfth year is completed, he removes the guilt of killing a Brahmin.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods on earth (the Brahmins) at an assembly of kings,
he is released from it after bathing in the *avabhṛtha* rite of a horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya its summit. Therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified.
By his very birth from Brahmā, he is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā alone is the cause in this matter.

Regarding them, even three who know the Veda should declare the means of complete expiation for the sin; that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying. Therefore, having adopted one of these rules, a Brahmin, being composed, [should proceed].
By means of self-control, he removes the sin committed through the killing of a Brahmin.
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also for having killed a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has performed a sacrifice, or a woman who is an Ātreyī.
Having given false testimony, likewise having obstructed a teacher,
having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend—
this purification has been declared for having unintentionally killed a twice-born man.
For the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks *surā*, he should drink *surā* that is red-hot like fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he may drink cow’s urine the color of fire, or water;
or milk, ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung, until death.
Or, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, he shall eat either grain-particles or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing garments of hair, with matted locks, and carrying a flag.
Liquor is indeed the impurity of foods, and it is called the impurity of sin;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that distilled from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that from honey (mādhvī).
Just as one is [forbidden], so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
The food of Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas, as well as intoxicants, meat, and spirituous liquors—
these must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation for the gods.
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might even recite Vedic texts; or, deluded by intoxication, he might perform some other improper act.
He whose Veda, residing within his body, is once overwhelmed by liquor— his Brahminhood departs and he attains the state of a Śūdra.
This expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared in its various forms;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should confess his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me."
Having seized a club, the king himself shall strike him once.
A thief is purified by execution, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who desires to remove by austerity the impurity born of stealing gold shall,
clothed in bark, perform in the forest the penance prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he may expiate the sin of approaching the wife of a guru by means of these same vows.
Having committed the sin of violating the Guru’s bed, he should lie upon a heated iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing metal image (sūrmi), and by death he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his cupped hands, he should walk straight toward the south-west until he falls down dead.
He should proceed toward the south-western direction in a straight line until he falls down.
Carrying a staff with a skull at its end, clothed in rags, or with his beard grown, he should dwell in a lonely forest and,
with a concentrated mind, perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley-gruel (yavāgū), in order to remove the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
By these penances, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows.
One who has killed a cow and is thus afflicted by a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley-gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
He should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his bath using cow urine.
During the day he should follow the cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust raised by them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain at night in the *vīrāsana* posture.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should walk after them.
Likewise, sitting while they are sitting, self-restrained and free from envy, he should eat.

One should rescue by all possible means a woman who is ill, or one who is threatened by dangers such as thieves or tigers, or one who has fallen, or one stuck in the mud— even at the cost of one's own life.
One should do so whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind is blowing violently.
One should not seek one's own protection without first having done what is possible for the sake of the cow.
Whether in one's own house or in the house of others, whether in a field or in a threshing floor,
one should not speak of a cow that is eating, nor of a calf that is drinking.
The cow-killer who follows a cow according to this rule removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
Having successfully completed his vow, he should give ten cows and one bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) shall perform this same vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the student who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), or else they may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. However,
the student who has broken his vow of chastity shall, at a crossroads, [sacrifice] a one-eyed donkey...
One should worship Nirṛti at night according to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
Having offered the oblations into the fire according to the rule with the verse beginning "Then," he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Vahni.
The knowers of dharma, the exponents of the Veda, declare that for a twice-born man observing a vow, the intentional emission of semen constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The four— the Maruts, Indra (Puruhūta), Bṛhaspati (Guru), and Agni (Pāvaka)—
approach the Vedic splendor of the student who has broken his vow.
When this sin has been incurred, having clothed himself in the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.

Subsisting on alms obtained from those [persons], eating only once a day, and performing ritual ablutions at the three times of the day, he becomes purified after one year. Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, [he shall perform this penance].
If he does so unintentionally, he shall perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra or the Prājāpatya penance.
For acts that cause the mixture of castes or render one unworthy of receiving gifts, the purification is the Aindava (moon-fast) for one month;
for acts that cause defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
A fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the killing of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part is for a Vaiśya who abides in his proper conduct, while a sixteenth part is to be known for a Śūdra.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having properly observed his vow, shall give a thousand cows and one bull.
Or, with restrained senses, wearing matted hair, he may perform for three years the penance prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin,
dwelling far away from the village and making his home at the foot of a tree.

The best of the twice-born, having killed a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, shall perform this very same penance for one year and give one hundred and one cows. A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months.
Or else, he should give ten white cows and one bull to a Brahmin.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog,
as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Or he may drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana;
or he may perform ablutions in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the Waters (Āpohiṣṭhīya).
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
having killed a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of clarified butter; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a crane, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or a peacock,
as well as a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for an elephant, five dark-blue bulls;
and for having killed a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
having killed non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
For having killed women of the four castes who have not been lawfully wedded, one should give, for the sake of purification, a worn-out bow, a goat, and a sheep respectively.
If a twice-born man is unable to expiate the killing of snakes and other such creatures by means of giving gifts,
he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate creatures,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the slaying of a Śūdra.
But for killing animals with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred *ṛc* verses are to be recited as a prayer;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all creatures born from food, born from fluids,
and those arising from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete means of purification.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
By these vows, the sin arising from violence may indeed be removed;
now hear concerning the entire [expiation] for eating what is forbidden, whether done intentionally or unintentionally.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite alone; but if it was done intentionally, the penance is beyond prescription—it is a matter of ending one's life. This is the settled rule.
Having drunk water that has been in a vessel for spirituous liquor, or likewise water that has stayed in a container for intoxicants,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, having accepted it according to rule,
or having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Even after drinking fermented liquids or astringent decoctions, though they are pure,
a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [liquid] has not passed downward.
Having consumed the urine or excrement of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth,
and anything situated in a slaughterhouse that was unknown, one should perform this very same penance.
Upon eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as humans, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher’s house eats food offered at a monthly Śrāddha,
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.
But a student who, in any way whatsoever, should eat honey or meat,
having performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance, shall complete the remainder of his vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog,
or a mongoose, or food defiled by hair or insects, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.

One who desires his own purity must not eat food that is unfit to be eaten. However, if it has been consumed unintentionally, it must be expelled from the body or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites.
This various rule for penances regarding the eating of forbidden food has been declared;
now hear the rule for those penances which remove the guilt of theft.

Having intentionally committed thefts of grain, cooked food, or wealth from the house of a member of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
But for the abduction of human beings, women, fields, and houses,
as well as for [the theft of] water from wells and tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification.
Having committed theft of articles of little value from another's house,
one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance after returning those goods for the sake of self-purification.
For the theft of edible and consumable foods, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats,
and for the theft of flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, and molasses;
for clothing, skins, and meat; one shall undergo a fast of three nights.
For gems, pearls, corals, copper, and silver; [one shall likewise undergo a fast of three nights].
And for iron, bronze, and stone vessels, one should subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For cotton, silk, wool, animals with cloven hooves,
and those with solid hooves, as well as for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk alone for three days.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall expel the sin of approaching a woman who should not be approached by means of these same vows.

Having discharged semen into women who are his own uterine sisters, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, one shall perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
Having approached the daughter of his father’s sister, the daughter of his mother’s sister,
or the daughter of his mother’s brother— having approached these, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. A wise man, however, should not take any of these three as his wife.
One should not approach those women as kinswomen; for by approaching them, one falls low.

If a man discharges semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper source of offspring, or even into water, he shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a male or a female,
a twice-born man shall perform a bath along with his clothes in a cow-cart, in water, or during the daytime.

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brāhmaṇa falls [from his caste] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes their equal.
A husband shall confine a wife who has become seriously corrupted in a single room;
he shall cause her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.
If she should again become corrupt, having been enticed by one of equal status,
then the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting [sacred texts] for three years.
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who have associated with outcasts.
By associating with an outcast for one year, one becomes an outcast;
[this occurs] through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or [forming] a matrimonial alliance, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
Whichever among these outcasts a man associates with,
he must perform that very same penance for the sake of purification from that association.

The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has become an outcast (patita) outside the village on an inauspicious day during the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.
A female slave shall overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
the kinsmen, together with her, shall observe impurity for one day and night.
Therefore, they should desist from conversing with him, from sitting together with him,
from giving him an inheritance, and even from ordinary social intercourse.
Seniority shall cease, as shall the wealth obtainable by the eldest;
however, a younger brother who is superior in virtue shall receive the share of the eldest.
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe and together with him alone cast a new pitcher full of water into a sacred body of water.
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the rites for his kinsmen as before.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have become outcasts;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they must live near the house.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins and have not been purified;

yet, once they have performed the rites of purification, one should never despise them. This includes even those who have killed children or those who are ungrateful, provided they have been purified according to the law.
One should not dwell with those who kill one who has sought refuge, nor with those who kill a woman.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
But for those twice-born men who, engaged in improper acts, desire to perform penance,
and who have been abandoned by the Veda— one should prescribe this very same [penance] for them as well.
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire by means of a censurable occupation,
they are purified from it by renouncing that wealth, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity.
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting gifts from unworthy persons.
When he has returned again from the cow-pen, emaciated by fasting and bowing down, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equality? (Manu 11.195).
But having spoken the truth before Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for cows;
when the ford has been opened by the cows, they should perform his funeral rites there.
By performing sacrifices for Vratyas, performing funeral rites for others,
practicing malevolent magic (abhicāra), or officiating at an Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Having abandoned one who has come for refuge, or having caused the Veda to be lost,
a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One who has been bitten by dogs, jackals, or donkeys, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or boars, becomes pure through breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
as well as the daily performance of all *Śākala* oblations, are the means of purification for those unworthy of sitting in the same row (*apāṅktya*).
Having intentionally mounted a vehicle drawn by camels or a vehicle drawn by donkeys, [one must likewise perform these penances].
But having bathed, a Brahmin who is naked becomes pure by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Whether he is without water or even in the midst of water, if one is afflicted and has discharged bodily excrement, he becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on, touching a cow, and then performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Upon the omission of the obligatory rites prescribed in the Veda,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, fasting is the expiation.

Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" or having addressed one who is superior with "thou," he shall bathe and spend the remainder of the day without eating, and after prostrating before him, he shall seek his favor.
Even if he has struck her with a blade of grass, or bound her by the neck with a garment,
or defeated her in an argument, he should propitiate her by bowing down.
Having merely threatened a Brahmin for a hundred years, and having actually struck him for a thousand years,
one falls into hell through the intent to kill a Brahmin.

As many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth, for that many thousands of years shall the shedder of it dwell in hell. Having merely threatened [to strike], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; if he actually strikes him down, he must perform the *atikṛcchra*.
Having caused the shedding of blood from a Brahmin, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances.
But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been prescribed,
one should determine an appropriate penance after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
I shall describe to you those means by which a human being removes his sins— means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors.
For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should eat food that has not been asked for;
for the final three days he should not eat at all—this is the Prājāpatya penance performed by a twice-born man.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a fast for one night— this is known as the *Sāṃtapanakṛcchra*.
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat only a single mouthful for three periods of three days each, as previously described,
and should fast for the final three days.
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed.
For one who has controlled the self and is vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called *parāka*,
which removes all sins.
One should decrease the rice-ball by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three times of the day, this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, being self-restrained and beginning with the bright fortnight, should observe this entire rule in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama (barley-middled) form.
Restraining his self and eating sacrificial food, one performing the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* penance should eat eight mouthfuls at midday when the sun has reached its zenith.
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning;
four when the sun has set—this is known as the Śiśucāndrāyaṇa.
By eating with a concentrated mind any kind of sacrificial food (haviṣya) for three hundred and eighty mouthfuls in one month, he attains the same world as the Moon.
The Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus observed this vow,
as did the Maruts together with the great seers, for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
One should personally perform the oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
Three times during the day and three times during the night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
furthermore, he should never speak to women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
If he is unable [to fast], he should pass his time by standing and sitting; or he may sleep on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of vows, and worship his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
He should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to his ability;
in all such vows, he should thus be diligent for the sake of expiation. By these vows, the twice-born whose sins have been made public shall be purified;
however, those whose sins have not been made public, he should purify with mantras and burnt offerings.
By confession, by repentance, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act,
confesses it, to that same extent he is released from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
To the extent that his mind reproaches his evil deed,
to that same extent is his body released from that unrighteousness.
For having committed a sin and felt remorse, one is indeed released from that sin;
however, he is purified by the resolve of abstention, thinking, "I shall not do this again."
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the emergence of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform auspicious deeds through his thoughts, speech, and physical form.
Whether performed through ignorance or through knowledge, having committed a censurable act,
one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time.
In whatever action he has performed that causes unease in his mind,
he should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction.
All this happiness, whether pertaining to the gods or to humans, has austerity as its root;
it has been declared by the wise who perceive the Vedas that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.
The austerity of a Brāhmaṇa is knowledge; the austerity of a Kṣatriya is protection;
the austerity of a Vaiśya is trade and agriculture; and the austerity of a Śūdra is service.
Sages who have restrained their selves and subsist on fruits, roots,
and air perceive the three worlds, with all things mobile and immobile, through austerity alone.
Medicinal herbs, antidotes, knowledge, and the various states of divine beings—all these are accomplished through austerity alone; for austerity is the means to achieve them.

Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish— all that can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed hard to surpass. Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts, [are purified by it].
By means of well-performed austerity alone, they are liberated from that sin.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even immobile beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.
Whatever sin people commit through mind, speech, or body,
those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone.
For a Brāhmaṇa who has been purified by austerity alone,
the inhabitants of heaven accept his sacrifices and increase his desires.
The Lord Prajāpati created this treatise through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity.
The gods declare this to be the great power of austerity (*tapas*),
seeing that the merit arising from this austerity is supreme among all things.
The daily study of the Veda according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), and forbearance— *Manu* 11.245a.
They quickly destroy even those sins born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka).
Just as fire, having reached fuel, consumes it in an instant with its brilliance,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil by the fire of knowledge.
Thus has the expiation for these sins been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret offenses.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the syllable Om,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin within a month.
By muttering the *kautsa* hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the verse of Vasiṣṭha beginning with "prati," the *māhitra*,
and the *śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
Having recited the *Āsyavāmīya* and the *Śivasankalpa* even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant after stealing gold.
Having recited the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and having muttered the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from that sin.
Desiring the removal of both gross and subtle offenses, [one should perform this].
He should recite for a year the verse beginning with "ava" (RV 8.61.13), or else the verse beginning with "yat kiṃ ca idam" (RV 10.190.1).
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
But one who has committed many offenses becomes pure by performing the Soma-Rudra rite for a month,
while practicing the ritual bath in a flowing river and reciting the three verses beginning with "aryamṇām."
One who has committed these seven offenses should mutter the hymn beginning with "Indraḥ" for half a year;
but having performed a censurable act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.
A twice-born man, having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras belonging to the Śākala-homa, destroys even the most grievous sin;
or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ."
One who has been joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by reciting the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms, he becomes purified.
Or, having purified himself with three *parāka* penances, he who, being self-restrained, recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest is released from all sins.
But by fasting for three days while remaining self-controlled and bathing in water three times a day,
and by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, one is released from all sins.
Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
Even if he has destroyed these three worlds and eats food from anywhere at all,
a Brahmin who retains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
Having recited the *Ṛg-saṃhitā* three times with a concentrated mind, or that of the *Yajus* verses,
or that of the *Sāmans* together with their secret doctrines (*rahasya*), one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does all evil conduct sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda.
The *ṛg*-verses, the *yajus*-formulas, and various other *sāman*-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
That which is the primordial three-syllabled Brahman, in which the triple Veda is established— that other secret threefold Veda, he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
O sinless one, you have declared this entire dharma of the four castes;
now tell us truly about the ultimate accomplishment of the fruits of actions.
The righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire application of ritual action."
Action arising from mind, speech, and body bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious;
the destinies of living beings born of action are superior, inferior, or middling.
Of that embodied being here, who is of three kinds, has three bases,
and is endowed with ten characteristics, one should know the mind to be the instigator.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable in one's mind,
and adherence to false doctrines— this threefold action is mental.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form,
and idle chatter— these constitute the fourfold nature of verbal misconduct.
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the prescribed rules,
and adultery with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [sin].
This person experiences the mental [karma] as mental, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
the action performed by speech through speech, and that which is physical through the body alone.
Through defects of action arising from the body, a man goes to the state of stationary objects;
through those of speech, to the state of birds and wild animals; and through those of the mind, to the status of the lowest castes.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a "triple-staffed" ascetic (tridaṇḍin).

Having cast aside this triple staff among all living beings and having thoroughly restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection. That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field).
But he who performs actions is called the "soul of beings" (bhūtātman) by the wise.
There is another internal self, distinct from the body, known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
it is by means of this that one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.
Both of these—the Great One (mahat) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which resides within all beings, high and low.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from those very five constituent elements for the purpose of undergoing torment.
Having experienced those torments of Yama with this very body, they dissolve,
part by part, back into those same elemental constituents.
Having experienced those defects arising from attachment to sense objects, which result in future unhappiness, he—
freed from taint— returns to those very two who possess great splendor.
Vigilant, they both behold his merit and his sin together;
through them, he obtains happiness or unhappiness, both in this world and after death, when joined with them.
If he practices dharma for the most part and adharma only to a small degree, then,
enveloped by those very elements, he enjoys happiness in heaven.
But if he mostly practices unrighteousness and only slightly practices righteousness,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from its impurities,
returns again to those very five elements, part by part.

Having observed these destinies of this living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— he should always fix his mind upon righteousness.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self (*ātman*),
by which the Great One (*mahat*) pervades and remains within all these states (*bhāva*) without exception.
Whenever one of these qualities is preponderant in the body in its entirety,
it then makes that embodied being consist mostly of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is said to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive form, which rests within all beings.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself that is joined with joy,
tranquil as it were and possessing a pure luster— that one should understand to be *sattva*.

But that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know that to be *rajas*, which is constantly carrying away embodied beings. But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, and characterized by sense objects—
One should understand that to be darkness which is inconceivable and unknowable.
I shall now declare in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— whether superior, middling, or inferior.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses,
performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of *sattva*.
Delight in undertaking [actions], lack of fortitude, engaging in improper deeds,
and constant indulgence in sensual objects— these are the characteristics of the quality of *rajas*.
Greed, excessive sleep, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
a habit of begging, and negligence are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Moreover, regarding these three qualities as they reside in the [three] worlds,
this should be known as the summary definition of their qualities in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having performed it, while performing it, or even when intending to perform it—
that should be known by the wise as entirely characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
and does not grieve over failure, should be known as *rājasa*.
That which one desires to know with one's whole being, that which one does not feel shame in practicing,
and that by which one's own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic mark of the quality of *sattva*.
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*), and their excellence increases in the order mentioned.
I shall now briefly describe, in their proper order, the transmigrations that each of these beings undergoes according to their respective qualities.
Those characterized by *sattva* attain divinity; those characterized by *rajas*, the state of humanity;
and those characterized by *tamas* always attain the state of animals—such is the threefold destiny.
This secondary course of existence is to be understood as threefold and of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the distinction of one's actions and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
as well as cattle and wild animals— these constitute the lowest state of darkness (tāmasī gati).
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas,
as well as lions, tigers, and boars, constitute the middling Tāmasa destiny.
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men,
as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas— this is the highest destination among those characterized by darkness (tāmasī).
Jhallas, Mallas, and Naṭas, as well as men who live by the sword,
those addicted to gambling and drinking, and those of the lowest sort— this is the Rājasa state.
Kings, Kṣatriyas, the domestic priests of kings,
and those who specialize in debate and warfare— this is the middling Rājasī state.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, constitute the highest destination among those born of the rājasa quality.
Ascetics, renunciants, Brahmins, and the hosts of celestial chariot-dwellers,
as well as the lunar mansions and the Daityas— this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries,
the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, sattvic goal.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—
these the wise call the highest Sāttvika state.
All this has been fully set forth regarding the threefold action;
thus the entire transmigratory existence of all beings is threefold and of three kinds.
Through attachment to the senses and by failing to practice dharma,
the ignorant and lowest of men go to sinful transmigrations.
Learn now all those various wombs into which this living soul enters in this world, one after another, according to its respective actions.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, upon the exhaustion of that [karma],
those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations (saṃsāra).
A killer of a Brāhmaṇa enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; and of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, venomous creatures, birds, and predatory beasts.
A Brahmin who is a thief [incurs the same fate] thousands of times for killing spiders, snakes, lizards, other crawling creatures that move in water, predatory beasts, and Piśācas.
The violator of the Guru’s bed becomes, by hundreds, [the body] of grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as of carnivorous animals, fanged beasts, and those who commit cruel deeds.

After death, those who eat the flesh of others become carnivorous beasts; those who consume impure things become worms; and thieves who consort with women of the lowest castes become creatures that devour one another.
Having had sexual intercourse with outcasts or with another man’s wife,
and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa.
Having stolen gems, pearls, and corals, or various other precious stones, out of greed, a man is born among the workers in gold.

By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing juice, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [becomes] flesh, a cormorant fat, a bird that feeds on oil oil,
a cricket salt, and a crane curd.
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge; having stolen linen, a frog;
having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; for stealing a cow, an iguana; and for stealing molasses, a rat.
The muskrat [eats] auspicious fragrances, while the peacock [eats] leaf-vegetables;
the porcupine [eats] various kinds of prepared food, while the hedgehog [eats] unprepared food.
Having stolen fire, one becomes a crane; having stolen household utensils, one becomes a *gṛhakārī* (a small bird);
and having stolen dyed garments, one is born as a *jīvajīvaka* (a pheasant).
A wolf [destroys] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruit and roots;
a bear, a woman; a chataka bird, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock.
Having forcibly seized any property whatsoever belonging to another,
a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal, as does one who has consumed an oblation that was not consecrated by fire.
Women also, having stolen [these things] according to this same rule, shall incur guilt;
they become wives of these very creatures.
For when the social classes (*varṇas*) fall away from their respective duties during times of non-distress,
they undergo miserable transmigrations and fall into servitude among their enemies.
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own duty becomes a *preta* (ghost) who eats vomit and has a mouth like a flaming torch.
A Kṣatriya who eats impure things and corpses becomes a Kaṭapūtana; a Vaiśya, having fallen from his own duty, becomes a Maitrākṣajyotika Preta that feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra, having fallen from his own dharma, becomes a Cailāśaka.
To the extent that those whose nature is directed toward sense-objects indulge in sense-objects,
to that same extent skillfulness in them arises for them.
Due to the repeated performance of those sinful acts, those of small intellect obtain sufferings in various wombs here in this world.
The tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra and others,
and the binding and cutting in the Forest of Sword-Leaves and similar places.
Various kinds of torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand and gravel, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he undergoes births in various wombs that are mostly full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears.
Repeated dwelling within the womb and dreadful births;
various forms of bondage and servitude to others;
separation from kinsmen and loved ones, and living together with wicked people.
The acquisition of wealth and its loss, as well as the gaining of friends and enemies.
And likewise, old age which is without remedy, the torment of various diseases,
those manifold sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
With whatever disposition one performs each particular action,
with a body of that same nature one experiences the corresponding fruit.
This entire arising of the fruits of actions has been declared to you;
now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
And among all these auspicious actions here,
some particular action has been declared to be more conducive to the highest good for a person. Yet, among all these as well, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme.
For that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained through it.
Of all these six types of actions, both in this world and after death,
the Vedic rite should always be known as the most conducive to the highest good.
But in the application of Vedic rites, all these [observances] without exception are included in their respective ritual injunctions,
one after another.

Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the path of active engagement and the path of withdrawal.

Action performed with a desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called "pravṛtta" (active). But action performed without desire, preceded by knowledge, is taught as "nivṛtta" (withdrawn).
By practicing the path of active action (*pravṛtta-karma*), one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing the path of renunciation (*nivṛtta-karma*), one indeed transcends the five elements.
Seeing himself in all beings and all beings in himself as equal, the one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty.
Even having abandoned the duties as they have been described, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Veda.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
having attained this, the twice-born man has truly accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.
The Veda is the eternal eye of the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.
Those Smṛtis which are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all of these are fruitless after death, for they are declared to result in darkness.
Whatever other things there may be that arise from this [dharma] and then pass away,
they are fruitless and false because they are of recent origin.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately—
the past, the present, and the future— all these are established from the Veda.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
From the Veda alone they are produced; their birth is according to their qualities and actions.
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of this living being.
One who knows the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a judge, and even lordship over the entire world.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does one who knows the Veda burn away the defects of his own actions born of past deeds.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedic scriptures, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
is fit for becoming Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

Those who merely memorize the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely memorize; those who possess true knowledge are superior to those who merely retain the texts; and those who act upon that knowledge are superior to those who merely possess it.
Austerity and sacred knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity he destroys sin, and by sacred knowledge he attains immortality.
Perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditional teachings—
these three must be well understood by one who desires purity in dharma.
He who examines the instruction on dharma given by the Ṛṣis through reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows dharma, and no other.
This action leading to supreme bliss has been declared in its entirety as prescribed;
now the secret doctrine of this treatise of Manu is being taught.
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those duties not mentioned in the traditional scriptures:
That which learned Brahmins declare shall be the Dharma, free from doubt.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired through righteous means—
they are to be known as the cultured *śiṣṭas*, those Brahmins who are the direct authorities for the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
An assembly of at least ten, or even three, who are established in good conduct, shall determine the law; that law they must not set aside.
One learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the three [members] of the preceding stages of life— this assembly shall consist of at least ten members.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this assembly of at least three members is to be recognized as authoritative for the resolution of doubts concerning dharma.

Even if he is alone, whatever dharma a most excellent twice-born man who knows the Veda determines, that should be recognized as the supreme dharma; it is not superseded by tens of thousands of ignorant men.
Even if they have gathered by the thousands, those who lack vows, who lack sacred mantras, and who subsist merely on their caste— among them, no true assembly exists.
That which fools, who are shrouded in darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, proclaim as Dharma— that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after those who speak it.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has declared to me this entire supreme secret of Dharma.
Composed in meditation, one should perceive both the existent and the non-existent within oneself;
for by perceiving everything within oneself, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The Self alone is all the deities; everything is established in the Self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with karma for these embodied beings.
One should dissolve space into the cavities, wind into movement and touch,
the supreme fire into digestion and sight, water into moisture, and earth into solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the step,
Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle,
radiant like gold, and perceivable by the intellect through meditation.
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati;
some call him Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state.
A twice-born man reciting this treatise of Manu, as proclaimed by Bhṛgu—
By being constantly possessed of right conduct, he shall attain whatever destination he desires.
[The Mānava Dharmaśāstra is completed. End of the Manu-Smṛti (plain text).

"The great seers, having approached Manu as he sat with a one-pointed mind..."
Having honored him according to the rule, they spoke these words.
O Blessed One, you ought to declare to us the duties of all the social classes in their proper order, as well as those born from intermediate unions.
For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true purpose and the reality of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Being thus duly questioned by those high-souled great seers, he of immeasurable luster honored them all and replied, "Listen."
In the beginning, this was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks,
beyond reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Then the Lord Svayambhū, the unmanifest, making this manifest—
the primary elements and the rest— appeared, his power having come forth, dispelling the darkness.
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal,
consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself appeared of his own accord.
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from his own body, he first created the waters alone;
into them he cast his seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The waters are called "nara," for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his first place of motion (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of both being and non-being—
from that was that Puruṣa emitted, who is celebrated in the world as Brahman.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditation, divided that egg into two parts.
From those two fragments, he fashioned the heaven and the earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
And from himself he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the presiding lord who is the conceiving subject.
And [he created] the Great Self (mahān ātmā), all things characterized by the three qualities (triguṇa),
and the five sense organs that gradually grasp the objects of the senses.
But having arranged the subtle constituent parts of those six [great elements], each possessing immeasurable power, within their own respective portions, he fashioned all living beings.
The six subtle components of form take refuge in these [elements];
therefore, the wise call that which possesses such form "the body."
Then the great elements, together with their functions, and the mind with its subtle components, enter that imperishable creator of all beings.
From the subtle constituent particles of the forms of these seven immensely powerful beings, this perishable world arises from that which is imperishable.
But among these, each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position in the sequence, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.
But at the beginning, he fashioned the individual names, the specific actions, and the distinct social orders of all beings from the words of the Veda itself.
And that Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings,
the subtle host of Sādhyas, and the eternal sacrifice itself.
From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman—
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman— for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and both the level and the uneven terrain.
Desiring to bring forth these creatures, he emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger.
And for the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated dharma and adharma;
he also joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.
The subtle, perishable particles that are said to constitute the five elements—
along with these, this entire universe comes into being in successive order.
Whatever specific duty the Lord first assigned to each being,
that very same duty it performed spontaneously, being created again and again.
In the creation, whatever he assigned to each— whether violence or non-violence, gentleness or cruelty, righteousness or unrighteousness, truth or falsehood— that entered into it of its own accord.
Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, naturally assume their own respective characteristics, so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became male with one half and female with the other; in her, the Lord created Virāj.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person, whom he himself created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this.
Desiring to create living beings, however, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers as the lords of creatures.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
These seven Manus of immense splendor created the gods,
the classes of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power.
And [he created] the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various classes of Pitṛs.
Lightnings, thunderclouds, and red clouds; rainbows of Indra; meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and various celestial lights of diverse kinds.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth.
And worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings.
Thus, by my command, all this— both the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of austerity, each according to their respective karma.
But whatever kind of occupation has been prescribed here for each of these beings,
that I shall declare to you accordingly, as well as the sequence of their births.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans—these are born from the womb.
Birds born from eggs, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises—
whatever other such kinds there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from moisture;
and whatever else is of this kind arises from heat.

All stationary beings that sprout from the soil are called *udbhijja*; those that grow from seeds or slips are plants (*oṣadhi*), which bear many flowers and fruits and perish after the ripening of their fruit.
Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses,
those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as creepers and climbing plants.
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
But these destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, have been declared to end here in this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is eternal and constantly moving.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time.
When that God is awake, the world thus moves;
when he sleeps with his soul at peace, then everything closes its eyes.
While that self remains soundly asleep, the embodied beings whose nature is action cease from their respective activities,
and the mind falls into exhaustion.
But when they all dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.
But when it remains for a long time supported by darkness (tamas) along with the senses,
yet does not perform its own function, then it departs from the body.
When, having become as minute as an atom, he enters, conjoined with it, the seed— whether stationary or moving— then he assumes a physical form.
Thus, by means of waking and dreaming, that imperishable one incessantly brings all this world of moving and non-moving beings to life and causes it to perish.
Having composed this treatise, he himself first caused me to learn it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, taught it to Marīci and the other sages.
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of this from me in its fullness.
Then, having been thus addressed by the great seer Manu, Bhrigu, with a joyful heart, spoke to all those sages: "Listen! (Mn 1.60).
After this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, six other high-souled and most powerful Manus of his lineage have created their own respective subjects.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval, produced and protected this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those make one *kalā*,
thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*, and a day and night consists of as many [muhūrtas].
The sun divides the day and night for both humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of living beings, and day is for the performance of actions.
A month is a day and a night for the ancestors; its division is by the two fortnights.
The dark fortnight is their day for active exertion, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep.
For the gods, a year constitutes day and night; their division is as follows:
the northern course of the sun is their day, and the southern course is their night.
Now learn, in brief and in their proper order, the measure of each of the ages that constitute a single day and night of Brahmā.
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three ages, together with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
This cycle of four ages, which has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand [years], is called an age of the gods.
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation,
should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration.
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration.
At the end of that day and night, having been asleep, he awakens;
and once awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth the creation;
from that, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.
From the wind, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness;
it is radiant and is said to have the quality of form (rūpa).
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
That divine age (yuga) which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years],
multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a Manvantara.
The Supreme Lord, as if in play, repeatedly brings about innumerable Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma exists in its entirety with all four feet, and truth alone prevails;
no acquisition whatsoever occurs for men through unrighteousness.
In the other [ages], Dharma exists by means of tradition (āgama), but it is diminished quarter by quarter;
through theft, falsehood, and deceit, Dharma likewise departs quarter by quarter.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, have all their goals accomplished, and live for four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
The lifespan ordained for mortals by the Vedas, as well as the fruits of their ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to each successive age.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, in the Tretā another, and in the Dvāpara yet others;
in the Kali age they are different again, according to the decline of the ages.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity is the one thing held in highest regard.
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
The protection of subjects, the giving of gifts, the performance of sacrifice, the study of the Vedas,
and non-attachment to sense objects— this, in brief, is the duty of a Kṣatriya.
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifices,
studying, trade, money-lending, and agriculture are the duties of the Vaiśya.
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra:
to serve these very castes with a mind free from malice.
The human being is declared to be more pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been called the most pure by the Self-Existent One.
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation.

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying oblations to the gods and ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the inhabitants of heaven always consume the sacrificial offerings to the gods (havya),
and the ancestors consume the offerings to the manes (kavya)?
Among beings, the living creatures are the best; among living creatures, those who live by their intelligence are the best;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, the Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brahmins, the learned are superior; among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected;
among those with perfected intellects, the performers of ritual acts; and among the performers, those who know Brahman.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is destined for union with Brahman.
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born on earth,
he is born as a lord over all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
All this that exists in the world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble birth, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this.
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brahmin’s compassion that other people eat at all.
For the sake of discerning that karma, the wise Svāyambhuva Manu composed this treatise for the remaining [topics] in their proper sequence.
This must be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa and correctly expounded to his pupils; it must not be taught by anyone else.
A Brahmin who studies this treatise and is firm in his vows is never tainted by the defects of action arising from mind, speech, or body.
He purifies his lineage and seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even a single such person merits this entire earth.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this brings fame and long life; this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.
In this [work], dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions,
and the eternal conduct of all four castes.
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śruti and in the Smṛti;
therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda;
but one who is endowed with right conduct shall partake of the full reward.
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through conduct, the sages adopted conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.
And [he shall explain] the origin of the world, the rules for the formative forces (saṃskāra),
the practice and observance of vows, and the supreme rule for ritual bathing.
The taking of a wife, the characteristics of marriages,
the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, as well as the vows of the Snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, purification, and the cleansing of objects.
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
the entire duty of kings, and the determination of legal cases.
The rules for examining witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife,
the laws of partition, gambling, and the removal of social thorns.
The conduct appropriate for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation; Mn 1.116.
The course of transmigration, which arises from the threefold karma,
as well as the supreme good resulting from action and the examination of the merits and defects of actions.
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and guilds.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so now do you also learn it from me.
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart.
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet here there is no such thing as being entirely without desire;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices arise from volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all these are traditionally held to be born of volition.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
By conducting oneself correctly toward these, one goes to the world of the immortals;
and here on earth, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it,
the practice of the virtuous, and also the satisfaction of one's own self.
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge.
But having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge,
the wise man should indeed abide in his own duty according to the authority of the revealed scripture.
For a man who practices the dharma declared in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Smṛti is indeed the Dharmaśāstra;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them the Dharma shone forth.
That twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would show contempt for their source— the Veda— should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda.
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—
they say that this fourfold is the direct definition of Dharma.
For those who are unattached to wealth and sensual pleasures, knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the Veda is the supreme authority.
But where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of them have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise.
Whether the sun has risen, has not yet risen, or is at the juncture of dawn, the sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.
He for whom the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral pyre have been prescribed by means of mantras—
only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
that land created by the gods they call Brahmāvarta.
Whatever custom has been handed down by tradition in that region for the social classes and the intermediate castes, that is called "right conduct" (sadācāra).
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
From one born in this land, a man of the first caste,
all men on earth should learn their respective duties.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
and between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature should be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This source of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the origin of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes (varṇas).

For the twice-born, the purifying sacraments of the body, beginning with the rite of impregnation, must be performed through meritorious Vedic rites; these bring sanctification both in this world and after death.
By means of the fire-oblations pertaining to the womb, and by the rites of birth, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle,
the taint derived from the seed and that derived from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born.
By the study of the Vedas, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the knowledge of the three Vedas, by sacrifices, by sons,
and by the great sacrifices as well as other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.
For a male child, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it includes the ritual consumption of gold, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by sacred mantras.
One should cause his naming ceremony to be performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word denoting happiness (*śarman*); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word signifying protection (*rakṣā*);
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with a word for prosperity (*puṣṭi*); and that of a Śūdra should be connected with a word for service (*preṣya*).
For women, [the speech] should be easy to pronounce, gentle, clear in meaning, charming, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction.
In the fourth month, the child's first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food, or whatever auspicious rite is desired by the family.
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to the Dharma in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Śruti.
One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh year from conception; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception.
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a Kṣatriya seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya desiring worldly prosperity in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year,
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this, if all three of these remain uninitiated for the prescribed period,
they become Vrātyas who have fallen from the Sāvitrī and are censured by the Āryas.
A Brāhmaṇa should never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules.
