Students of the Veda should wear, in the proper order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat; and likewise garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya, however, should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya, a cord of hempen threads.
In the absence of muñja grass, however, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass,
with three, one, three, or five knots.
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads.
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to reach the hair at the top of the head according to its proper measure;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose.
All those [reeds] should be straight, without blemishes, pleasant to behold,
not causing alarm to men, with their bark intact, and undamaged by fire.
Having accepted his desired staff and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go about for alms using the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle, and a Vaiśya, at the end.
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt, or from one who will not treat him with contempt.
Having collected that alms-food as much as is needed without guile,
and having offered it to his teacher, he should eat, facing the east, pure and having sipped water.
Eating while facing the east promotes longevity; facing the south brings fame;
facing the west brings prosperity; and indeed, facing the north, one eats according to the eternal truth (Ṛta).
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
after eating, he should sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these.
One should not give the leavings of one's food to anyone, nor should one eat between the prescribed meal times;
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven;
it is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
A Brahmin should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
he may also use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya.
They declare that the *brāhma* tīrtha is at the base of the thumb;
the *kāya* [tīrtha] is at the base of the fingers, the *daiva* at their tips, and the *pitrya* below those two.
First, one should sip water three times; then, one should wipe the mouth twice.
One should likewise touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head.
One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand, in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north.
A Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity.
When the right arm is raised, a twice-born man is called *upavītī*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*.
Having thrown his girdle, deer-skin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a member of the royal caste (rājanyabandhu), it is in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, it is considered to be two years later than that.
This entire series of rites for women must be performed without omission at the proper time and in the proper order, for the purpose of purifying the body.
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and the tending of the sacred fires is their domestic duty.
This has been declared as the sacred rite of initiation for the twice-born, which manifests their true birth; now learn the application of their duties.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.
But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north,
he should be instructed while wearing light clothing, with his senses subdued, and having formed the *brahmāñjali* gesture.
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda, the feet of the teacher must always be clasped;
one should study with hands joined together, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
But when the pupil is about to begin his recitation, the teacher, always alert, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude with, "May there be a pause."
A Brahmin should always utter the syllable Om at the beginning and at the end [of his recitation].
What is not preceded by Om slips away, and what is not followed by it falls apart.
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One born of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes who is deprived of this Ṛc, as well as of his own timely ritual duties, incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as difficult to attain, for it is both Brahman and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña),
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, he who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
I shall now correctly enumerate, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven organs which the wise of old have declared.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
Of these, the five sense organs are the ear and so forth in their respective order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth.
The eleventh, the mind (manas), should be known as being of a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
Between one who might attain all these [desires] and one who might renounce them entirely,
the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
These [senses], when excessively attached to their objects, cannot be so effectively restrained by abstinence as they can by constant application of knowledge.
Neither the Vedas, nor renunciation, nor sacrifices, nor observances, nor austerities ever lead to success for one whose disposition is corrupted.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
But if even one among all the senses leaks away,
through that his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind,
he should accomplish all his goals through yoga without wasting his body.
One should stand during the morning twilight, reciting the Sāvitrī until the sun appears; but one should sit during the evening twilight, reciting it properly until the stars become visible.
Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night;
sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by the day.
But he who neither remains at the morning [service] nor performs the evening [service] is to be excluded from all duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
Restrained and established in the daily rule, he should go to the forest and, with a concentrated mind, recite the Sāvitrī near water.
There is no restriction regarding days unsuitable for study (anadhyāya) in the case of the Vedāṅgas, in the daily private recitation of the Veda,
and indeed in the mantras used for burnt offerings.
In the daily recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice";
it is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call even during times when study is otherwise suspended.
For him who, being self-controlled and pure, studies his own Veda for a year according to the prescribed rule,
this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.

A twice-born man who has undergone initiation shall, until his formal return home (samāvartana), maintain the sacred fire, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher.

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman— these ten are to be taught according to the law.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in the world.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two dies, or incurs enmity.
Where neither dharma nor artha are found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve,
there knowledge should not be sown, just as a good seed is not sown in saline soil.
A teacher of the Veda should rather die along with his knowledge;
even in times of terrible distress, he must never sow it in barren soil.
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said to him: "I am your treasure; protect me.
Do not give me to one who is censorious, so that I may remain most powerful. (Manu 2.114)
But speak to that brahmin whom you know to be pure, who is disciplined in his student life, who guards the treasure [of knowledge], and who is free from negligence.
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission is guilty of the theft of Brahman and falls into hell.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, he from whom one receives it should first be saluted.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he has mastered the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods.
One should not sit upon a bed or seat already occupied by a superior;
likewise, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation.
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed depart when an elder approaches;
he recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase: life-span, merit, fame, and strength.
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name. (Mn 2.122)
To those who do not know how to respond to his name,
a wise man should say "I am he," and the same applies to all women.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is identical to the essential form of names.
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one";
and at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with a protracted (pluta) first syllable.
That Brahmin who does not know the proper response to a salutation should not be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask after his welfare; a Kṣatriya, after his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, after his well-being; and a Śūdra, after his health.
One who knows the law should address an initiated person by name only if he is younger; otherwise, he should address him using the honorifics *bhoḥ* or *bhavat*.
But toward the wife of another who is not related by birth,
he should address her as "Lady," "Fortunate One," or "Sister."
Having risen, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "I am so-and-so."
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
The wife of one's brother, if she is of the same caste, should be saluted day after day;
however, the women who are kinswomen or relatives by marriage should be saluted only upon returning from a journey abroad.
One should behave toward one's father's sister, one's mother's sister, and one's elder sister as toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they.
Friendship with fellow citizens is established by ten years; that with artists, by five years;
that with Vedic scholars, by three years; and among those of the same lineage, it is formed even by a very short period.
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet, between the two, the Brahmin is the father.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding.
Among the three [higher] castes, he who possesses many qualities and is superior among the five [classes] is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth decade of his life.
Way must be yielded to one holding a wheel, to one who has reached his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
Among those who have come together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the royal *snātaka* and the [ordinary] *snātaka*, the *snātaka* receives the honor due to a king.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya.
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the child] with food, is called a guru.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as mother and father; one should never bear him malice.
Ten preceptors are equal to one teacher; a father exceeds a hundred teachers in venerability;
but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in venerability.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for the Brahmin, both after death and in this world.
One should understand that his birth, which occurs when he is produced by his mother and father through mutual desire, is merely his physical conception in the womb.
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is true, and it is free from old age and death.
One should know that person as a teacher in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever assists one with their knowledge, whether it be little or much.
One who effects a Vedic birth and is a teacher of his own duty becomes,
according to the law, the father of an elder Brahmin, even if he is a child.
The wise child of Aṅgiras taught his elders;
having encompassed them with his knowledge, he addressed them as "little sons."
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant man is indeed a child, while the giver of sacred knowledge is a father;
for they call the ignorant man a "child" and the giver of sacred knowledge a "father. (Manu Smṛti 2.153)
The sages have established that dharma is not by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great.
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kshatriyas by valor,
that of Vaishyas by grain and wealth, and that of Shudras alone by birth.
One does not become an elder merely because one's head is gray;
the gods know him to be an elder who, though young, is learned in the Vedas.
Just as an elephant made of wood, as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with a bull,
and just as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
One who desires righteousness should instruct living beings toward their welfare through non-violence alone,
and should employ speech that is sweet and gentle.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit described in the Vedānta.
Even when afflicted, one should not be a wounder of others' vital parts, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm others;
one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if at poison;
he should always long for dishonor as if for nectar.
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in peace and wakes in peace;
he moves through this world in comfort, while the scorner perishes.
By this gradual method, the twice-born man, having purified his self, should while dwelling with his teacher slowly accumulate the austerity that leads to the attainment of Brahman.
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (Upanishads), must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule.
An excellent twice-born man, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is declared to be the highest austerity for a Brahmin in this world.
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingertips who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.
That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his progeny.
The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass;
the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
Among these, that which is his birth from Brahman, marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass,
in that case Sāvitrī is said to be his mother and the teacher his father.
They declare the teacher to be a father because of his imparting the Veda;
for no ritual duty whatsoever is enjoined upon him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
One should not utter the Veda except when offering the *svadhā* oblation;
for as long as he is not born into the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra.
For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony, the instruction in the observances and the formal reception of the Veda are prescribed to be performed in due order according to the rule.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, girdle, staff, and garment have been prescribed for him, those same items he must wear even during his religious observances.
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules,
fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
Having bathed daily and become pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella, as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments; Mn 2.178.
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, as well as falsehood;
gazing at and touching women, and the injury of others.
One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one destroys one's own vow.
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth,
and kusha grass as much as required, and he should go out for alms every day.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praised for their own duties.
One should not beg for alms from the family of one's teacher, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives;
however, if houses of others are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding category in preference for the next.
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, but he must avoid those who have been accused of crimes.
Having fetched fuel-sticks from a distance, he should place them in the open air;
and with these, he should untiringly offer oblations into the fire every evening and morning.
If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of chastity.
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the livelihood of a vow-observer sustained by alms is equal to fasting.
In a rite dedicated to the gods, one should eat like one observing a vow; likewise in a rite for the ancestors, one may eat at will when invited, like a seer (ṛṣi); his vow is not thereby violated.
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not ordained in this manner.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply effort to his studies and to the welfare of his preceptor.
Having restrained his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind,
he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always have his right hand raised, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him.
One should not engage in conversation with a reply while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor while facing away.

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is standing; going forward to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running, one should attend to one who is running after.
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is at a distance,
bowing down to one who is lying down, and standing by the side of one who is giving instructions.
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat must always be low;
within the teacher's line of sight, he should not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone even in his absence,
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or even slander of the teacher occurs,
one should cover one's ears there or depart from that place to another.
From reviling others one becomes a donkey; indeed, a slanderer becomes a dog; one who consumes another's property becomes a worm, and a miser becomes an insect.
One should not salute him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher either upwind or downwind of him,
nor should one say anything at all within hearing distance of the teacher that he would not wish to hear.
He may sit together with his teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on a palace terrace, on mats, on stone slabs, on wooden planks, or in a boat.
When the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
nor, unless permitted by his teacher, should one pay homage to one's own teachers.
In the same way, this conduct is always required toward teachers of knowledge, toward one's own kinsmen,
and toward those who forbid unrighteousness as well as those who impart what is beneficial.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as toward one's own teacher—
toward the sons of the teacher, toward those who are noble, and toward the teacher’s own kinsmen.
Whether he be of equal age, a child, or a pupil, the son of a teacher deserves honor like the teacher himself when he is teaching during a sacrificial rite.
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one wash his feet.
The wives of one's gurus who are of the same caste should be honored like the gurus themselves;
those who are of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair must not be performed for the wife of one's teacher.
But a young wife of the guru should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who is twenty years of age and capable of discerning virtues and faults.
This is the inherent nature of women: to corrupt men in this world.
Therefore, the wise do not place their trust in women for the sake of their interests.
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place even with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
However, on this earth, a young man should, according to the prescribed rule, perform a salutation to the wives of his elders who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives every day and offer salutations, remembering the duty of the virtuous.
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade,
so does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge residing in a teacher.
Whether he be shaven-headed or wear matted hair, or have his hair in a single lock on the crown,
the sun must never set or rise while he is still inside a village.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while muttering prayers.
For he who, while lying down, is overtaken by the setting sun or awakened by the rising sun,
becomes joined with great sin if he does not perform an expiation.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule.
If a woman or a person of lower status should practice anything that is beneficial, one should diligently perform all of that; and whatever brings him joy, he should also practice.
Some say that spiritual merit and wealth constitute the highest good; others say it is pleasure and wealth, or even merit alone.
Or again, some say that wealth alone is the highest good in this world; yet the established doctrine is that the threefold aggregate [of dharma, artha, and kāma] is the highest good.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and an elder brother must not be treated with disrespect even by one who is distressed, especially by a Brahmin.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
The suffering that parents endure for the birth of their children cannot be repaid even in a hundred years.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times;
when these three are satisfied, all austerity is fully accomplished.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
For these indeed are the three worlds, these are the three stages of life;
these indeed are the three Vedas, and these are said to be the three sacred fires.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, a householder shall conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world;
and by service to one's teacher, one likewise attains the world of Brahmā.
All duties are honored by him who honors these three;
but for him who does not honor them, all ritual acts are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not attend to anyone else;
he should constantly perform service for them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Whatever one may perform for the sake of the next world, provided it does not conflict with their interests,
that one should announce to them through thought, word, and deed.
For a man’s duty is fully accomplished through these three;
this is the supreme dharma directly perceived, while any other is called a secondary dharma (upadharma).
One who possesses faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a person of lower status;
likewise, one should accept the highest dharma even from another, and a jewel of a woman even from a lowly family.
Nectar should be taken even from poison; a well-spoken word even from a child;
good conduct even from an enemy; and gold even from an impure place.
Women, jewels, knowledge, dharma, purity, well-spoken words,
and various arts are to be acquired from everywhere.
In times of distress, studying under one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
however, he must follow and serve that teacher for as long as the study lasts.
A pupil who desires the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied the Veda.
But if he should prefer a lifelong residence in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation of the body.
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahman.
One who knows the Dharma should not provide any service to the teacher beforehand;
however, when about to perform the final bath, being commanded by the teacher, he should procure wealth for the teacher's sake according to his ability.
A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, a seat, grain,
vegetables, and garments— one should bring these to the teacher to produce his satisfaction.
But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who possesses good qualities,
or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, exactly as toward the teacher himself.
In the absence of these, one who maintains the postures of standing, sitting, and walking,
and practices the service of the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body.
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this manner, remaining unbroken in his vow of celibacy,
goes to the highest station and is not born again in this world.
The vow pertaining to the three Vedas requires a student's conduct toward the teacher for thirty-six years;
or it may be half of that, or a quarter, or even until the [Veda] has been mastered.
Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in the proper order,
and having remained inviolate in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own duty, who inherits the father's Vedic legacy, and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland.
Having bathed with the permission of his teacher and returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man shall marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
A woman who is not a sapinda of one's mother and who is not of the same gotra as one's father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union.
Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain,
one should avoid these ten families in forming a marriage alliance.

Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, those with excessively hairy bodies or hemorrhoids, and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.

One should not marry a woman named after a bear, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one whose name is terrifying.

He should marry a woman who has no deficient limbs, whose name is auspicious, who walks with the gait of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
But a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter).
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] are permitted in descending order.

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra; she and a woman of his own caste are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and a woman of his own caste for a Kṣatriya; and those three and a woman of his own caste for a Brāhmaṇa.
For it is taught that under no circumstances whatsoever— not even in times of distress— can a Śūdra woman be prescribed as a wife for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests have that [greed] as their primary motive, neither the ancestors nor the gods eat; he does not go to heaven.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a Vṛṣalī, who has been defiled by her breath,
and who has begotten offspring upon her, no atonement is prescribed.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four castes, which lead to welfare or harm both in this world and after death.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya,
the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
I shall declare to you all that which is the lawful duty for each caste, as well as the virtues and vices belonging to each, and the merits and defects pertaining to procreation.
One should know that for a Brahmin there are six marriages in the direct order, and for a Kṣatriya, four lower ones;
for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, however, one should know those same [four] to be lawful, excluding the Rākṣasa form.
The wise know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra.
Of these five, three are considered lawful and two unlawful in this world;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Having clothed her and honored her, and having invited one who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, the giving away of the daughter by oneself is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) rite.
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law,
the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite.
Having addressed them with the words, "May you both perform your religious duties together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is sexual in nature and arises from passion.
Having slain, cut, and broken [through obstacles], while she cries out and weeps, the forcible abduction of a maiden from her home is called the Rākṣasa rite.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is the eighth and most base of marriages, the sinful Paiśāca form.
For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is prescribed as the most distinguished;
for the other castes, however, it is by mutual desire.
O Brahmins, listen as I proclaim all the specific qualities of each of these forms of marriage that were described by Manu.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has performed meritorious deeds delivers ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin.
A son born of a woman married according to the Daiva rite delivers seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants;
a son born of a woman married according to the Ārṣa rite delivers three of each; and a son born of a woman married according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite delivers six of each.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born in due order.
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and being most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
But from the remaining improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and the Law are born.
Offspring becomes irreproachable through blameless marriages with women; it becomes blameworthy for men through blameworthy ones. Therefore, one should avoid those that are blameworthy.
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known regarding the marriage ceremony with women of different castes.
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste.
He should approach his wife during her season and always remain devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days.
The natural menstrual period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights,
together with the four other days that are censured by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights are commended.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on the even nights.
A male is born when the male seed is in excess; a female when that of the female is in excess.
When they are equal, a neuter is born, or sometimes both a male and a female; when they are deficient or scanty, the opposite occurs.
Avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and the other [four],
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits.
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, subsist upon the property of women—
whether it be vehicles, clothing, or other goods— are sinners who go to a downward state.
Regarding the rite of the seers (ārṣa), some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price; but that is surely false.
Whether it be small or large, it remains nothing other than a sale.
When the kinsmen do not take a fee for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely an honoring of the maidens and an act of pure compassion.
These women should be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual acts there become fruitless.
That family where female relatives grieve perishes quickly;
but that family where they do not grieve indeed prospers forever.
Those households which female relatives, being unhonored, curse,
perish on all sides as if struck by a malevolent spell.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always honor these women with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at regular ceremonies and during festivals.
In whatever family the husband is always content with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband, there indeed prosperity is certain.
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight her husband; and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed.
When a woman is radiant, the entire family shines; but when she does not shine, the whole family indeed fails to shine.
Families fall into a state of unworthiness through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins.
By means of crafts, trade, and the exclusive offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king.
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras perish quickly through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, as well as through atheism regarding the efficacy of ritual acts.
But families that are enriched by the power of mantras, even if they possess little wealth,
are reckoned among the noble lineages and acquire great renown.
In the nuptial fire, the householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound [by sin].
For the purpose of expiating all of these in their proper order, the great seers have prescribed five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability,
even while living constantly in the house, is not defiled by the faults of the slaughterhouse.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
They declare that the five sacrifices are the *ahuta*, the *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *brāhmya-huta*, and the *prāśita*.
Recitation is the *ahuta* offering; the fire-oblation is the *huta*; the offering to the elements is the *prahuta*;
the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya-huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and to rites directed toward the gods;
for it is by being engaged in rites directed toward the gods that one sustains this entire world, both moving and stationary.
An oblation duly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Just as all living beings exist by depending upon the air,
so do all the stages of life (āśramas) exist by depending upon the householder.
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone through both knowledge and food,
therefore the householder's stage is the most excellent.
This must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven and absolute happiness in this world— even that which is difficult for those of weak faculties to uphold.
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act for them.
One should honor the ṛṣis with the private recitation of the Veda, the gods with burnt oblations according to the rule,
the ancestors with funeral offerings (śrāddha), men with gifts of food, and the spirits with the bali offering.
One should perform the *śrāddha* rite day after day with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
In the performance of the five sacrifices for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in the rite of the Vaiśvadeva, one should not feed any Brahmin at all.
A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform an oblation in the domestic fire with the Vaiśvadeva food that has been prepared, according to the prescribed rule, for these deities.
First to Agni and to Soma, then to both of them together,
to the Viśvedevas, and to Dhanvantari.
To Kuhū and Anumati, and to Prajāpati,
together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having thus offered the oblation correctly, he should present the sacrificial food (bali) to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, along with their followers, while circumambulating in all directions.
One should throw [food] at the door with the words "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water with "To the Waters";
one should offer it upon the pestle and mortar with "To the Vanaspatis."
He should offer an oblation to Śrī at the head of the bed, and to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
he should present an offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
And he should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
One should offer a Bali oblation on the back of the house for the sake of all beings;
as for the remainder of the Bali, one should carry it all to the south for the ancestors.
One should gently place on the ground the food intended for slaughterers, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, birds, and insects.
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by the straight path to the supreme abode, his very form consisting of light.
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
he should also give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge.
Whatever merit a householder twice-born man obtains by giving a cow to his teacher according to the prescribed rule,
that same merit he obtains by giving almsfood.
One should respectfully offer even alms or a vessel of water, according to the prescribed rule,
to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when given out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes. (Manu Smṛti 3.97)
An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, who are enriched by knowledge and austerity,
delivers one from misfortune and even from great sin.
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water,
as well as food according to one's ability, honoring him with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Even from one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning or offers oblations into the five fires,
a Brāhmaṇa who dwells unhonored takes away all his merit.
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these things are never lacking in the house of the virtuous.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is traditionally called a guest (*atithi*);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore termed a guest.

One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who has come from another village, as well as one who has arrived by chance, when he has presented himself at the house where the wife resides or even where the sacred fires are maintained.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go,
after death, to the state of cattle as those who have given away their food and other provisions.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not give to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.
One should provide a superior seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance for those who are superior; inferior for those who are inferior; and equal for those who are equal.
But if another guest should arrive after the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed,
one should give him food according to one's ability, but one need not perform the Bali offering again.
A Brahmin should not announce his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by praising them for the sake of a meal, he is called a "vomit-eater" by the wise.
A Kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a Brāhmaṇa;
nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, or even a teacher.
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house as a guest, he may,
if he so desires, feed him after the Brahmins have finished eating.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at the household as one who possesses the status of a guest,
he should feed them along with his dependents, practicing compassion toward them.
He should also, together with his wife, feed other friends and relatives who have come to his house out of affection, providing them with food according to his ability and their rank.
One should feed these— married women, young maidens, the sick, and pregnant women— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins and his own servants have finished eating,
the husband and wife should then eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.

One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, a sacrificial priest, a snātaka, a guru, a beloved father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, provided it has been a year since they were last honored.

Both a king and a learned brahmin, when present at a sacrificial rite, are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the established rule that this does not apply when there is no sacrifice.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali-oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both evening and morning.
But having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors on the new moon day, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires shall perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
The wise know that the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors is called the Anvāhārya;
and that should be performed with effort using commendable meat.
In this regard, I shall explain in full detail which of the best of the twice-born are to be fed, which are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food.
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large company.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.
This rite for the deceased, known as the ancestral offering (pitrya), is prescribed at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that [observance], it is always considered merely a worldly rite for the dead.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
One should examine from afar a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas;
he is considered a worthy recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is declared to be a guest.
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda are fed,
a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to the law.
The offerings for the ancestors (kavyas) and the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
As many mouthfuls as one who is ignorant of the mantras consumes at offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya),
so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls does that deceased person consume.
Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established among those devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be given according to the rule to all four [classes of Brahmins].
If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas but his son has mastered the Vedas, or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered them; Mn 3.136.
Of these two, one should know the elder to be him whose father is a Vedic scholar;
the other, however, deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
One should feed at a śrāddha that brahmin whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend.
He whose ancestral offerings and sacrificial oblations are dominated by friends gains no fruit from those *śrāddhas* or sacrifices after death.
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships with those performing śrāddhas through such śrāddhas, falls from the heavenly world and its realms.
That which is given by the twice-born for the sake of a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be the Piśāca dakṣiṇā;
it remains right here in this world like a blind cow in a single house.
Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit,
so too a donor who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit.
By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the rule to one who is learned, he makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death.
At a śrāddha, one may certainly honor a friend even if he is not distinguished, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by one who hates the giver becomes fruitless after death.
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his recensional branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at his *śrāddha*,
the satisfaction of his ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations.
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
however, this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed one's maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, sister's son, father-in-law, teacher, daughter's son, wife's brother, kinsman, officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors has arrived, he should examine him with great care.
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or those who live as atheists to be unworthy of offerings made to the gods and the ancestors.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who officiate as priests for a man with matted hair who does not study the Vedas, nor for one who is weak, nor for a gambler, nor for groups of such persons.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; Mn 3.153.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who neglects the sacred fires, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, and one who belongs to a religious guild— these are unfit to be invited.

One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a Śūdra woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour; // Mn 3.155 //
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, a teacher of a Śūdra, one of foul speech, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka; Mn 3.156.
Having abandoned, without cause, one's mother, father, or teacher;
and having entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections.
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats food from a base vessel, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; Mn 3.158.
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (poisons).

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, one who betrays a friend, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; Mn 3.160.

One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with white leprosy, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be avoided.
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare. // Mn 3.162 [152M] //
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise one who plants trees; Mn 3.163 [153M]
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists as a servant to Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for guilds; Mn 3.164.
One who is devoid of proper conduct, one who is impotent, a constant beggar,
one who lives by agriculture, and one who has elephantiasis are indeed censured by the virtuous.
A butcher of sheep, a butcher of buffalo, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and one who carries out the dead for a fee— these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid both of these lowest of the twice-born, whose conduct is censurable and who are unworthy of sitting in the row for a meal.
But a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer an oblation to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.
I shall now describe in its entirety that fruit which arises for a donor after death from giving to one who is unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors.

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder, and by others excluded from the company at a meal— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
He who, while his elder brother remains, enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* sacrifice, is to be known as a *parivetta*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him,
she with whom he marries, the giver of the girl, and the officiating priest as the fifth— all these go to hell.
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—
even if she has been appointed [to bear a son] according to dharma— should be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is born when the husband is dead.
Those two beings, born in the field of another, destroy both in this world and after death the offerings of sacrificial oblations and ancestral gifts given by their donors.
As many members of a company as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating,
for so many does the foolish donor fail to obtain the fruit of that gift.

A blind man, upon seeing [the gift], destroys the fruit of ninety; one who is one-eyed, that of sixty; one with white leprosy, that of a hundred; but one afflicted with a foul disease, that of a thousand donors.
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift.
Even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, by accepting a gift from him out of greed,
quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood;
what is given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
That which is given to a merchant, however, yields no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an offering poured into ashes, as is the case with a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
But regarding the others who are unworthy of the company— those unrighteous persons previously specified—
the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born, the sanctifiers of the company, by whom a row defiled by those unworthy of the company is purified. (Manu 3.183)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions,
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the Veda was given as a religious gift, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; Mn 3.185.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a reciter, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand gifts,
and one who lives for a hundred years— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
When the Śrāddha rite is about to take place, either on the preceding day or on the following day,
one should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described.
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns while that śrāddha is taking place.
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.
But that best of the twice-born who, having been invited according to the rule for offerings to the gods or the ancestors,
somehow transgresses, becomes a sinner and shall go to the state of a pig.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a Śūdra woman,
takes upon himself whatever evil deed the giver has committed.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, the highly fortunate ancestors are the deities of the past.
Since the origin of all these [castes] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now those rules by which they are to be occupied with their respective duties.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others, who were the sons of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha— are recorded as the classes of Pitṛs.
The sons of Virāj, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods, the offspring of Marīci.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are traditionally held to be the ancestors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among the Brahmins they are called Somapas; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmants were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kavyas, the Barhiṣads,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas and the Saumyas, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins.
Regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are likewise infinite.
From the sages were born the ancestors; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—in due order.
Even water given with faith in silver vessels, or in those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible merit for them.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection.
One should seek that which has the gods at its beginning and end; it should not have the ancestors at its beginning and end.
For one who seeks that which has the ancestors at its beginning and end perishes quickly, along with his lineage.
One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung and,
with great care, ensure that it slopes toward the south.
For the ancestors are always satisfied by what is given in open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and in secluded places.
When separate seats provided with sacred grass have been prepared,
he should cause those Brahmins, having duly sipped water, to sit down upon them.
Having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with those representing the gods.
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds and purifiers (pavitra),
the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire together with the Brāhmaṇas.
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama according to the rule by means of the offering of oblations, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place the offering directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras.

The ancients describe these best of the twice-born as those who are free from anger, easily propitiated, intent on the nourishment of the world, and to whom the gods look for offerings at the ancestral rites.
Having circumambulated the fire keeping it to his left and having performed the entire rite in reverse order,
he should pour water on the ground with his left hand.
Having formed three balls from that remainder of the sacrificial food, he, being composed,
should offer them with the same rite as for the water-libation, facing the south.
Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) then, being self-restrained and according to the prescribed rule,
he should wipe that hand on those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "smear-partakers" (lepabhāginaḥ).
Having sipped water and turned toward the north, having slowly restrained his breath three times,
he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls;
and with a concentrated mind, he should smell those rice balls in the order they were placed.
Having taken small portions from each of the food balls in succession,
he should first cause those same seated Brahmins to eat according to the rule.
While his father is still living, however, he should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone;
or else, like a Brahmin [at a Śrāddha], he should cause his own father to eat at the Śrāddha.
If one's father has passed away but the grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father's name and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
or, being duly authorized, he may perform it himself at his pleasure.
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the sacred grass (pavitra) into their hands,
he should offer them the first portion of that funeral cake (piṇḍa), saying, "May there be svadhā for them."
Having himself taken the increased portion of food with both hands,
he should place it slowly near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors.
The food that is brought forth and placed between both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras suddenly seize and plunder it.
With self-restraint and concentration, he should first place upon the ground the various side dishes such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
Various kinds of food and edibles, roots and fruits,
as well as savory meats and fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure,
being purified and extolling all its qualities.
One should never shed tears, one should not become angry, and one should not speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
Tears cause the hungry ghosts to depart; anger, the enemies; falsehood, the dogs;
the touch of one's foot, the Rākṣasas; and shaking [the head], the evildoers.
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without avarice;
he should also engage in discussions concerning the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause the recitation of one's own Vedic study, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
sacred narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and other delicacies, praising their qualities.
One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
At a Śrāddha ceremony, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a blanket made of goat’s hair (kutapa), and sesame seeds.
Furthermore, they praise three qualities in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born, when asked by the giver, speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
The ancestors eat as long as there is steam from the food, as long as those who have restrained their speech continue to eat,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offerings are not mentioned.
Whatever one eats with one's head covered, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
a woman in her menses, and a eunuch— these must not look upon twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these at the giving of a house or at a meal—
whether at an offering to the gods or one to the ancestors— that becomes ineffective.
The pig destroys [the merit of the meal] by its smell, the cock by the wind of its wings;
the dog by the casting of its glance, and the low-caste man by touch.
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove such a person as well.
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has approached for the sake of food, he should,
with the permission of the Brahmins, honor him according to his ability.
Having gathered various kinds of food and sprinkled them with water,
he should cast them upon the ground before those who have finished eating.
The leavings on the *darbha* grass and whatever food is scattered there shall be the portion for those who have died an unnatural death and for women who have abandoned their families.
That which remains on the ground as leavings for those who are straightforward and honest is declared to be the share of the group of servants at a rite for the ancestors.

Until the performance of the rite of offering funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa) for a deceased member of the twice-born caste, one should perform a śrāddha ceremony without an offering to the gods, feeding the Brahmins and offering a single rice-ball.
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the law, his sons must perform the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) by this very same procedure.
That fool who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*,
goes head-first to the Kālasūtra hell.
If one who has partaken of a śrāddha feast approaches a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) on that same day,
his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement.
Having asked, "Was it well-tasted?", he should then cause those who are satisfied to sip water;
and once they have sipped water, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you rest at your pleasure."
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhāstu" (Let there be Svadhā);
for the utterance of "Svadhā" is the highest blessing in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
he should do exactly as they say, having been authorized by the twice-born.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "it is well-savored" (svaditam); at a rite for cattle, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (rucitam).
The afternoon, as well as *darbha* grass, the preparation of the site,
sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent twice-born men— these are the perfections in rites for the ancestors (*śrāddha*).
Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial foods (haviṣya),
as well as whatever purifying substances were mentioned previously, should be understood as the requisites for the sacrificial offering (havya).
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned, and salt produced naturally— these are called sacrificial oblations by their very nature.

Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, restrained in speech, and pure, he should look toward the southern direction and request these boons from the ancestors: "May my ancestors be satisfied; may they grant me contentment. May they grant me prosperity; may they grant me offspring. May they grant me cattle; may they grant me the splendor of sacred knowledge. May they grant me fame; may they grant me heaven. (Mn 3.259) "Whatever I have done today out of ignorance, whether through negligence or even intentionally, may the ancestors forgive all that of mine. (Mn 3.260) "Whatever sin has been committed by me through thought, word, or deed, may the ancestors entirely release me from that. (Mn 3.261) "May the ancestors who dwell in the world of the ancestors, those who have gone to the world of the gods, and those who have gone to the world of men—may they be pleased with me. (Mn 3.262) "May they bestow upon me sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons who shall live for a hundred autumns; may they grant me wealth and every kind of happiness.
