(Mn 3.263) "May there be no loss of progeny nor loss of wealth; may there be no loss of [Vedic] study nor loss of self. May you grant me these boons, O ancestors; may I always be victorious over my enemies. (Mn 3.264) Having thus addressed the ancestors, he should circumambulate them three times from left to right and then depart as he came. "May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."

Having thus performed the offering of the water libations, he should immediately thereafter cause those funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be eaten by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else he should cast them into the water.
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes only afterwards;
others cause them to be eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water.
Then, the devoted and lawful wife, intent on the worship of the ancestors and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of offspring, virtuous, and likewise righteous.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide a meal primarily for his kinsmen;
having given what is honored to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives.
That remnant of food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established.
I shall now describe in its entirety that sacrificial offering which, when given to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for a long time and even for eternity.
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rule,
the ancestors of men remain satisfied for a month.
For two months he may subsist on the flesh of fish, for three months on that of the deer,
for four on that of sheep, and for five indeed on that of birds.
For six months with the meat of a goat, and for seven indeed with that of the spotted deer;
for eight months with the meat of the ena deer, and for nine indeed with that of the ruru deer.
They are satisfied for ten months with the flesh of boar and buffalo;
however, with the flesh of rabbit and tortoise, they are satisfied for exactly eleven months.
But with cow's milk and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as with the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa, there is satisfaction for twelve years.
Black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red goat, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for ascetics are prescribed for the sake of infinite [merit].
Whatever one may give mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
May there be born in our family one who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, and before the shadow of an elephant has turned eastward.
Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly, and endowed with faith—
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
In the dark fortnight, the lunar days beginning with the tenth—excluding the fourteenth—are recommended for the Śrāddha rite;
other days are not so highly regarded.
By performing [the śrāddha] on even lunar days and under even asterisms, one attains all desires;
but by performing it on odd days and under odd asterisms, one obtains abundant progeny for all the ancestors.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too is the afternoon superior to the forenoon for a śrāddha rite.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the offering properly made counter-clockwise, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the rite for the ancestors according to the rule until its conclusion.
One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only just risen.
By this rule, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the rites pertaining to the five sacrifices daily.
The oblation belonging to the ancestral sacrifice is not prescribed for the common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires without the Darśa sacrifice.
When that best of the twice-born, having bathed, gratifies the ancestors with water,
he thereby obtains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is the eternal Vedic revelation.
He should always be an eater of vighasa, and always an eater of amṛta;
vighasa is the remnant of what has been eaten, and likewise, the remnant of a sacrifice is amṛta.
All this rule regarding the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now let the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born be heard.
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, O twice-born ones,
he should dwell in his house as a married man during the second quarter of his life.
A Brahmin should live in times of no distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury. (Manu Smṛti 4.2)
For the sake of accomplishing the mere requirements of life,
he should accumulate wealth by means of his own irreproachable occupations, without causing hardship to his body.
One may live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*, or even by the *satya* and the *anṛta*; but one should never live by the "dog's mode of life."
Gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains is to be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta* (the nectar);
begged alms are *mṛta* (the dead); and agriculture is recorded as *pramṛta* (the very dead).
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed subsist by it;
service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or grain sufficient for a single jar;
or he may have enough for three days, or he may not even have enough for tomorrow.
And among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one should be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmasattra).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭi sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
He should not, under any circumstances, follow worldly conduct for the sake of his livelihood; rather, he should live the pure life of a Brahmin, free from crookedness and guile.
Seeking happiness, one who desires ease should remain self-controlled by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering.
A twice-born Snātaka, however, living by any one of these modes of livelihood, should observe these vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: [Mn 4.13]
One should constantly perform, without sloth, one's own duty as declared in the Veda;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
One should not seek wealth through excessive attachment, nor by forbidden actions;
one should not seek it from here and there when wealth already exists, nor even in times of distress.
One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should also restrain the mind from excessive attachment to them.
One should abandon all worldly interests that obstruct one's own Vedic study;
however, one may teach them in whatever manner possible, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's duty.
One should move about in this world conducting oneself in conformity with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage, through similarity in dress, speech, and intellect.
One should constantly study the treatises that quickly increase the intellect, as well as those which are auspicious and beneficial, and likewise the Vedic scriptures.
For in whatever measure a person masters a treatise,
in that same measure he understands it, and his specialized knowledge shines forth.
One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to the ancestors, according to one's ability.
Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly desire.
Some offer the breath into speech and speech into breath at all times,
perceiving the imperishable completion of the sacrifice within both speech and breath.
Other brahmins always perform these sacrifices with knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.
One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night,
as well as the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice at the full moon.
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should worship with the sacrifice of new grain; likewise at the end of the seasons with sacrifices;
at the beginning of the solstice with an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year with Soma sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, desiring to live a long life, must not eat new grain or meat without having first performed the sacrifice of the first-fruits and the animal sacrifice.
For his sacred fires, greedy for new grain and meat, desire to consume his very life-breaths if they are not honored with offerings of new grain and animal sacrifices.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits.

One should not honor with even a word or a gesture those who follow heretical paths, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, the deceitful, those who rely on mere reasoning, and those who behave like herons.

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those householders who are learned in the Vedas, purified by their study and vows, and well-versed in sacred scripture; one should avoid those who are the opposite.
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves,
and he should make a distribution among all living beings without causing hardship to his own dependents.

A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; it is the settled rule that he must not seek it from anyone else.
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger if he is capable [of providing for himself],
nor shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes as long as he possesses the means.
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, dressed in white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly devoted to the study of the Veda and to what is beneficial for the self.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot filled with water,
the sacred thread, a Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor run while it is raining, nor look at one's own reflection in water; such is the rule.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees.
Even if he is intoxicated, he should not approach a woman during her menstrual period;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish.
For one who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by the menses,
wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even lifespan increase.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease.
A twice-born man who desires luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with unguents and uncovered, nor one giving birth. (Manu Smṛti 4.44)
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked;
one should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
Never on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain,
nor in a ruined temple, nor on an anthill.
He should not study in pits inhabited by living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing;
nor having reached the bank of a river, nor on the peak of a mountain.
Seeing the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows,
one should never discharge feces or urine.
Having covered [the ground] with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or the like, he should pass over it,
restraining his speech, being pure, with his limbs wrapped and his head veiled.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night, one should face south; and during the two twilights, as during the day.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as also when there is danger to his life.
The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man,
or facing a cow or the wind, perishes.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it on the ground, nor should one step over it;
one should not place it at one's feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings.
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel, nor should one lie down;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor should one remove one's own garland.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water,
nor anything else defiled by impurities, nor blood, nor poisons.
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one awaken a superior person;
one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice uninvited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling her calf, nor should one inform anyone of it;
likewise, upon seeing a rainbow in the sky, a wise man should not point it out to anyone.
He should not dwell in a village where unrighteousness prevails, nor in one that is excessively plagued by disease;
he should not set out on a journey alone, nor should he reside for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people;
nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating;
one should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor in the evening if one has already eaten in the morning.
One should not engage in useless exertion, nor drink water from one's cupped hands;
one should not eat food while holding it in one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor utter cries when impassioned.
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal;
nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature.
One should not wear sandals, clothing, a sacred thread, an ornament, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (Manu Smṛti 4.66)
One should not travel with oxen that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are mutilated.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without lashing them excessively with the goad.
The heat of the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.
He should not crush a lump of clay, nor should he tear grass with his fingernails;
he should not perform fruitless labor, nor anything that results in unhappiness for the future.
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites his nails, is a slanderer,
or is impure, quickly goes to destruction.
One should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should one wear a garland outside [the house].
Riding on the backs of cows is in every way condemned.
One should not enter an enclosed village or house except through the gate;
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's sandals oneself.
One should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
And one should not eat anything mixed with sesame after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one attains a long life.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at excrement or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds, nor cotton seeds, nor husks.
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with the lowest castes, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor food prepared for a sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.
For he who teaches his dharma and he who prescribes his vow sink together with him into the darkness called "the unrestrained."
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using it.
One should avoid seizing others by the hair and striking them on the head;
moreover, after bathing the head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya lineage, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse, a cart, or a tavern flag, nor from those who live by prostitution.
A cart is equal to ten slaughter-houses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten brothels.
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is terrible.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in due course, go to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the Kālasūtra hell, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pratimūrtika.
The iron spike, the parched grain scrap, the path, the Śālmalī river,
the forest of sword-leaves, and likewise the iron-tipped darts.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and who desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king.
One should wake up during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as the bodily hardships rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, having purified himself and being composed,
he should stand for a long time reciting prayers during the morning twilight, and likewise at its proper time during the evening twilight.
By virtue of their long observance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), the seers (*ṛṣis*) attained long life,
as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rules on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedic hymns for four and a half months.
Under the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the external ceremony of the suspension of Vedic study (utsarjana);
or he may do so when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, in the forenoon.
Having thus performed the formal dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside according to the scriptures,
he should cease [studying) for a night with its two flanking days— that is, for one full day and night.
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and one should study all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas during the dark fortnights.
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night, one should not sleep again while still fatigued.
A twice-born man who is disciplined and not in times of distress should daily recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule, as well as the Brāhmaṇas composed in meters.
One who is studying should always avoid these occasions when study is forbidden,
as should one who is teaching disciples according to the prescribed rule.
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when it raises clouds of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.
In the event of lightning, thunder, and rain, as well as when there is a falling of great meteors,
Manu has declared that there shall be no study for the remainder of the day.
One should know that when these [omens] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, so too when clouds are seen out of season.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as during the day.
For those who desire perfection in dharma, there shall always be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as wherever a foul odor is present.
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a low-caste person (vṛṣala),
nor while one is weeping, nor in a gathering of people.
In water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine,
while impure from food, or after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha), one should not even mentally contemplate [forbidden things].

Having accepted an invitation for an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the period of impurity following the death of a king or an eclipse of Rāhu.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of a funeral meal (ekānudiṣṭa) remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should one not recite the Veda.
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor while sitting with a cloth tied around the knees; nor after eating meat, nor food provided by one in a state of birth-impurity.
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon and the fourteenth days, and on the full moon and the Aṣṭakā days; Mn 4.113.
The new moon day destroys the teacher, and the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the full moon and the eighth day of the lunar fortnight destroy the Veda; therefore, one should avoid those days.
A twice-born man should not recite while there is a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking or braying in a row.

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a funeral rite (śrāddha).

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever constitutes an offering for a śrāddha, upon touching that there shall be no study; for the twice-born is traditionally declared to have his hand as his mouth.
When a village is harassed by thieves, during a panic caused by fire,
and during all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study for the duration of that day.
At the Upakarman and the Utsarga ceremonies, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
likewise on the Aṣṭakās, at the ends of the seasons, and during the nights [of the new moon], it lasts for one day and night.

One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is acidity of stomach.
Nor should one study without having first taken leave of a guest, nor while a strong wind is blowing,
nor when blood flows from the body, nor when it is wounded by a weapon.
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of Sāman chanting is heard;
nor after having completed the study of the Veda, nor after having studied the Āraṇyaka.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Knowing this, the learned daily first practice the essence of the three Vedas in their proper order, and afterwards they study the Veda itself.
If any of these— cattle, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat—
should pass between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night.
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study:
an impure place for Vedic recitation and an impure self.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born *snātaka* must always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in a body of water that is unknown.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king, a *snātaka*, an *ācārya*, a tawny person (*babhru*), or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
At midday and at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should not intentionally step upon a body-scrub, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this life.
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak.
For these three, when insulted, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
One should not despise oneself on account of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal law.
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being) or simply say "bhadram" (well-being);
one should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those deficient in learning, those advanced in age, those lacking beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.
A Brahmin who has not washed after eating should not touch a cow, a Brahmin, or fire with his hand;
nor, while impure, should he look at the luminaries by day, even if he is otherwise healthy.
Having touched these while being impure, one should always touch the vital organs with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily apertures without a reason;
he should avoid touching all the hairs on his private parts as well.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should constantly recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.
For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, who are ever self-restrained,
and who recite prayers and offer oblations, no misfortune exists.
One should constantly study the Veda at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty.
Through constant study of the Veda, through purity, and indeed through austerity—
And by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Remembering his former birth, he practices Brahman once again;
and through the constant practice of Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss.
He should constantly perform the Sāvitra oblations and the propitiatory fire-sacrifices on the Parvan days;
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days.
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, far from the water used for washing the feet,
and likewise far from where leftover food is disposed of.
In the forenoon alone, one should perform the preparation of unguents, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities.
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the sovereign for the sake of protection, and his teachers.
He should salute his elders, offer them his own seat,
wait upon them with palms joined in reverence, and follow behind them as they depart.
One should, unwearied, always practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly prescribed in one's own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes in suffering, being diseased and short-lived.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
Whatever action depends on another, that one should avoid with effort;
but whatever depends on oneself, that one should practice with diligence.
"Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering."
Whatever action brings satisfaction to one's inner self while performing it, that one should perform with diligence; but one should avoid the opposite.
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities;
one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness.
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down;
except for a son or a pupil, whom one may strike for the sake of discipline.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in evil wombs.
A man who, through lack of wisdom, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting,
incurs very great suffering after death.
For as many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth,
for that many years shall the shedder of that blood be devoured by others in the next world.
Therefore, a learned man should never threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who is constantly devoted to violence— such a person does not prosper in happiness in this world.
Even if he suffers for it, he should not, on account of his own righteousness, turn his mind toward unrighteousness;
for he quickly perceives the downfall of the wicked who act contrary to dharma.
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
but turning back slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.

If [the fruit of unrighteousness] does not fall upon oneself, it falls upon one's sons; if not upon the sons, then upon the grandsons; but an unrighteous act committed never fails to bear fruit for the doer.
By unrighteous means one prospers for a time, and thereafter sees auspicious results;
then one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes along with their very roots.
He should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and he should instruct his pupils in accordance with the Dharma, restraining himself in speech, arms, and belly.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future unhappiness or is censured by the world.
He should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, nor crooked; he should likewise not be fickle with his speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others.
By that path by which his fathers have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; traveling by that way, he does not come to harm.
With officiating priests, family chaplains, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants.
By abandoning disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the sovereign in the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra, and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.

Sisters-in-law are the kinsmen of the world of the Apsarases; relatives by marriage are those of the world of the Viśvedevas; and maternal uncles and mothers are the kinsmen of the world of the waters and the earth.
Children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords of space;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body.
One's shadow, one's group of servants, and one's daughter are exceedingly pitiable;
therefore, when insulted by these, one should always endure it without feverish resentment.
Even if he is capable of accepting gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, his Brahmanic luster is quickly extinguished.
Without knowing the righteous rule for the acceptance of gifts,
a wise man should not accept a gift, even if he is perishing from hunger.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold and food increase one's lifespan; land and a cow nourish the body;
a horse [increases] the eyesight, clothing the skin, ghee the vital energy, and sesame seeds progeny.
But a twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study, and who delights in accepting gifts,
sinks along with that very recipient, like one in water using a raft made of stone.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear accepting gifts from whomever they may come; for even by means of a very small gift, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat,
nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Veda.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, given to these three types of persons,
results in misfortune for the giver and for the recipient in the next world.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks,
so too do the ignorant giver and recipient sink to the bottom.
One who carries the banner of righteousness while being always greedy, hypocritical, and a deceiver of the world;
one who follows the "vow of a cat," being violent and a detractor of all—such a person is to be known as a mere pretender to virtue.
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own self-interest, dishonest, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow."
Those Brahmins who practice the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma,
concealing that sin with the vow while practicing deception upon women and Śūdras.
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda;
and a vow performed through deceit goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, not being a bearer of the marks, subsists by the dress of one who bears the marks,
takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.
One should never bathe at water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the sin of the person who constructed the reservoir.
One who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given incurs a fourth part of the sin.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in mountain clefts and springs.
A wise man should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not the observances (niyamas) exclusively;
for by failing to perform the restraints while devoting himself solely to the observances, he falls.

A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one offered by a priest who officiates for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these people offer the oblation;
it is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it.

One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease; nor food into which hair or insects have fallen, nor that which has been intentionally touched with the foot.
Food looked upon by a killer of a fetus, touched by a woman in her courses,
pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit for consumption].
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food [announced by] public proclamation;
the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned.
And the food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound in fetters.
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as sour gruel, stale food, and the leavings of a Śūdra.
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, and one who eats leavings;
the food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that which has been tasted by someone and is less than ten days old.

Meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, the food of a woman who has no hero (husband or son), the food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of an outcast, and food upon which someone has sneezed.
The food of the slanderer and the liar, as well as that of one who sells the fruits of sacrifices, the food of an actor and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person; Mn 4.214 [215M]
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player,
a goldsmith, a basket-maker, and likewise a seller of weapons.
From those who keep dogs, from vintners, from a washerman, from a dyer,
from a cruel man, and from one in whose house a paramour resides.
Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely dominated by women,
food from one recently deceased (within ten days), and that which is simply disagreeable— these are forbidden.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Regarding those others who have been successively proclaimed as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.
If one has eaten the food of any of these [outcastes] unintentionally, there shall be a fast for three days;
but if one eats it intentionally, or consumes semen, feces, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance.
A learned twice-born man should not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform śrāddha rites;
however, in the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him enough raw grain for one night.
Having deliberated upon both— the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer— the gods ordained their food to be equal.
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
the gift of a liberal man purified by faith is [efficacious], while the other is destroyed by lack of faith."
With faith, one should constantly perform sacrifices and works of public utility without sloth;
for when performed with faith using wealth acquired by lawful means, those two become inexhaustible.
One should constantly practice the duty of giving, consisting of both sacrifices and charitable works,
with a contented disposition whenever a worthy recipient is encountered, according to one's ability.
Whatever may be asked for should be given without malice;
for a worthy recipient (pātra) will arise who delivers one from all [suffering].
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses, the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a draft-ox, abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow, the celestial realm of the Sun.
The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of freedom from fear obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Of all gifts— water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter— the gift of the Veda (brahmadāna) is preeminent.
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift,
with that very same disposition one receives it back in return, duly honored.
He who accepts a gift that has been honored, or he who gives a gift that has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell.
One should not take pride in one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice;
even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride;
life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes through boasting of it.
One should gradually accumulate merit, as termites build an anthill,
for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings.
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remain for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—dharma alone stands by one.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; dharma alone follows him.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate dharma for the sake of companionship;
for with dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads to the next world that man who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity.
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form alliances with the most eminent; he should avoid those who are inferior.
By approaching only the most excellent and avoiding the inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra.
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
one who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and charity.
One may accept from anyone fuel for the fire, water, roots, fruits,
food that is offered, honey, and the gift of safety.
Prajāpati considered alms that have been brought forward and offered spontaneously, without being previously solicited, as acceptable even from one of evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years from him who treats her with contempt, nor does the fire carry his oblations.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, gems, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or vegetables.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself must not find satisfaction therein.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept [gifts] from virtuous persons.
A partner in business, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave,
and a barber— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Whatever his own nature may be, whatever he intends to do,
and how he would treat him, in that manner should he present himself.
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is when among virtuous people is the greatest evildoer in the world; he is a thief who robs his own self.
All objects of speech are fixed; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals that speech is a thief of everything.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live adopting an attitude of neutrality.
Alone, he should constantly reflect in solitude upon what is beneficial for himself;
for by reflecting alone, he attains the highest good.
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder,
as well as the auspicious ritual of the Snātaka vows, which increases one's inner strength.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from sin and is glorified in the world of Brahma.

Having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: 1. Having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire:
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duties and are learned in the Vedas and the Shastras?
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay the Brahmins."
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct,
laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms,
as well as those things produced from impure matter, are not to be eaten by the twice-born.
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those originating from incisions, and the śelu fruit, along with cow's colostrum (peyūṣa).
One should not eat kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, or cakes in vain, nor meat that has not been consecrated, nor food intended for the gods, nor sacrificial oblations.
The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals,
that of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away— [these are forbidden].
And among all wild animals, except for the buffalo,
as well as the milk of females and all fermented acids, these indeed are to be avoided.
Among sour substances, curd is fit for consumption, as is everything produced from curd,
and those [liquors] which are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds as well as those that dwell in villages,
single-hoofed animals that have not been specifically permitted, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the domestic cock,
the sārasa, the rajjuvāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; Mn 5.14.
He who eats the flesh of any creature is called an eater of that very creature's flesh;
one who eats fish is an eater of all kinds of flesh; therefore, one should avoid fish.
The pāṭhīna and rohita fish are the first to be prescribed for offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
likewise, all rājīvas, siṃhatuṇḍas, and scaled fish are permitted.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown,
nor all five-toed creatures, even if they are specified among those permitted for consumption.
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and likewise the hare—
they say these are among the five-toed animals that may be eaten, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel.
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, village cocks,
onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall from his caste.
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining forbidden foods, one should fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single Kṛcchra penance for the sake of purification from food eaten unknowingly; however, for food known [to be forbidden], he must perform it specifically.
Excellent wild animals and birds may be slain by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sake of maintaining their dependents; for Agastya did so in ancient times.
For even in ancient sacrifices and in the rites of Brahmins and Kshatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) consisted of the flesh of wild animals and birds. (Manu Smṛti 5.23)
Whatever food, whether solid or soft, that is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured,
may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as may any remnant of sacrificial oblation (havis).
Even if it has been kept for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born even if they have not been treated with oil.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is enjoined according to the rule, or indeed when life is in danger. (Manu Smṛti 5.27)
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa);
both the stationary and the moving—all is the sustenance of the vital breath.
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs;
the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave.
The eater is not defiled by eating those living beings that are fit to be eaten, even day after day;
for both the eaters and the beings to be eaten were created by the Creator himself.
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance; any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance. (Manu Smṛti 5.31)
Having purchased it, or having produced it himself, or even having received it as a gift from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having first honored the gods and the ancestors.
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when there is no distress;
for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he is helplessly devoured after death by those very creatures.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great after death as that of one who eats meat in vain.
But that man who, though duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat meat,
goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births.
A Brahmin shall never eat animals that have not been consecrated by mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated by mantras.
In times of distress, one may offer an animal made of ghee, or likewise an animal made of flour;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death after death in future births.
"Beasts were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing. (Manu Smṛti 5.39)
Herbs, animals, trees, quadrupeds, and likewise birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher rebirths once again.
"Manu has declared that animals may be slain only on these occasions— the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), at a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods— and nowhere else."
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animal to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
One should know that violence which is ordained by the Veda and restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings is indeed non-violence; for from the Veda dharma shone forth.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or dead.
He who does not desire to inflict bondage, death, or affliction upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, enjoys ultimate happiness.
Whatever he meditates upon, whatever he does, and wherever he fixes his delight—
that he obtains without effort, provided he harms nothing whatsoever.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should avoid meat.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the manner of a Piśāca,
does not fail to attain popularity in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are slayers.
There is no doer of greater unmeritorious deeds than he who, without having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another.
He who should perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots or by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'flesh-ness' (māṃsatva) of flesh."
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
for these are the natural inclinations of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit.
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased, as well as the purification of objects,
for all four castes, duly and in their proper order.

When a child dies after the eruption of teeth, or after the cutting of the hair-tuft (cūḍā), all the relatives remain impure; the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka). Impurity on account of death (śāva) for ten days is prescribed for those who are sapinda relations.
Until the collection of the bones has taken place, [the impurity lasts] for three days or for one day alone.
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka persists as long as there is knowledge of the common ancestry or the name.
Just as this impurity on account of a corpse is prescribed for the sapinda relatives,
so too shall it be in the case of a birth for those who desire complete purity.
For all others, there is impurity due to death; however, for the parents, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Birth-impurity shall belong to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ablutions.
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by sipping water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three triple-nights;
those who offer water for the deceased are purified after three days.
A disciple who performs the funeral rites for his deceased preceptor becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse.
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified after as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
once her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath.
For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is declared to take one night;
but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights.
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside [the village],
having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones.
For him, no consecration with fire should be performed, nor should the water-rite be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should observe impurity for only three days.
The ritual offering of water should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, they may perform it once the child has teethed or when the naming ceremony has been completed.
If a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin) has died, it is prescribed that purification occurs after one day;
however, for those who offer water libations together (ekodaka), purification is held to take place after three nights following the birth [of a child].
In the case of women who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the paternal kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, the uterine relatives become pure according to the very rule already stated.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves in water for three days,
they should abstain from eating meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground.
This rule for impurity caused by death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure is to be understood as applying to relatives and kinsmen when one is absent.
But he who hears that one staying in a foreign land has died within ten days shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights.
When ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a relative who has not yet passed ten days, or of the birth of a son,
a man becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on in water.
If a child, a person residing in another country, or one who has become an outcast (pṛthakpiṇḍa) dies,
one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes.
If death or birth should occur again within ten days,
a Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period of ten days has not yet elapsed.
When a teacher has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it is settled that the impurity lasts for one day and night.

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya, one shall remain impure for three nights; for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one shall remain impure for a period of two days and the intervening night.
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun or stars] lasts;
but if the king is not learned in the Vedas, the impurity lasts for a full day, and likewise when a teacher who has mastered the Veda has died.
A Brahmin becomes pure in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra becomes pure in a month.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the ritual acts performed with the sacred fires;
furthermore, even a kinsman performing that rite does not thereby become impure.
Having touched a public singer, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth,
a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability.
Having touched a human bone that still has fat adhering to it, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of fat, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been formally initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libations, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
The water libation shall be withheld from those born of illicit unions, from those who persist in false ascetic orders,
and from those who commit suicide.
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor. // Mn 5.90 [89M] //
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or preceptor who has died, one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.
One should carry out a dead Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
but for the twice-born, one should do so through the western, northern, or eastern gates, as appropriate.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions; for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman.
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high office;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting his subjects.
And for those killed in a riot, by lightning, or by a king;
and for one who has died for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whom the king so desires.
The king bears the body of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Appati, and Yama.
A king who is empowered by Lokeśa is not subject to impurity;
for purity and impurity belong to mortals, arising from and dissolving into the worlds.
For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons while fulfilling the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed; such is the rule regarding the purification of impurity.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle or weapon;
a Vaiśya, by his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, by a staff.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you;
now learn the purification for the dead concerning all those who are not sapindas.
Having carried out a deceased twice-born person who is not a sapinda, or the maternal relatives of his mother, as if they were kinsmen, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights.
If one eats their food, however, one is purified in ten days;
but if one does not eat their food and does not dwell in that house, one is purified in a single day.
If one follows out of desire a deceased kinsman or even a stranger,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay],
wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Among all forms of purity, purity in respect to wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in respect to wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water.
The wise are purified by forbearance; those who have committed forbidden acts, by charity;
those whose sins are concealed, by the muttering of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas, by austerity.
That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This determination regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.
The purification of luminous gems, as well as of all things made of stone,
has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
A gold vessel that is unstained is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they are not ornamented.
Gold and silver were produced from the union of water and fire;
therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
For all liquid substances, purification is declared to be straining;
for solid objects, sprinkling; and for wooden articles, scraping.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* and *graha* cups is by washing.
The purification of the *caru* vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar, is by means of hot water.
The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is performed by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed.
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is held to be the same as for grains.
Silk and woolen garments [are purified] with alkaline salts; blankets of Kutapa wool with Aṛiṣṭaka fruits; fine linen cloths with Bilva fruits; and linen garments with white mustard seeds.
One who knows the rules of purification should perform the cleansing of conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory with cow’s urine or water, just as one does for linen cloth.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again.
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, saliva, pus,
or blood can never be purified even by re-firing.
The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by smearing with cow-dung, by sprinkling with water, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at,
or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from an object smeared with it,
so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances.
The gods have ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word.

Water on the ground that is pure, which can satisfy the thirst of a cow, is fit for use provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (Manu Smṛti 5.128)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the established rule.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Manu has declared that the meat of an animal killed by dogs is pure,
as is the meat of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcastes (caṇḍālas) and other such robbers.
The apertures of the body that are above the navel are entirely pure;
those below it are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body.
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch.
For the purpose of purifying the discharge of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken in sufficient quantities;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of men.
One application of earth should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand,
and seven on both hands by one desiring purification.
This is the rule of purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always before studying the Veda and while eating food.
One who desires bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so once each.
For Śūdras who live according to the law, a monthly shaving of the head must be performed;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born.
The primary [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants, nor do drops that fall upon the body;
nor are the beard hairs considered part of the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth.
Drops that touch the feet of one who is giving water for rinsing to others are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
If one who holds something in his hand is somehow touched by leavings,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that object down.
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and having spoken untruths;
and after drinking water when about to study, one should sip water (ācamana) even if already pure.
The entire rule for purification and likewise the cleansing of objects has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women.
Neither by a girl, nor by a young woman, nor even by an aged woman should any action whatsoever be performed independently, even within the home.
In childhood, she should remain under the authority of her father; in youth, under that of her husband; and when her husband has died, under that of her sons. A woman must never enjoy independence.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, husband, or sons;
for by being separated from them, she brings reproach upon both families.
She should always be cheerful, skillful in her household duties, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in expenditure.
To him whom her father or her brother— by the father's consent— may give her,
she should serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not disregard him.
For their sake, auspicious rites, blessings for well-being, and sacrifices are performed by Prajāpati at the wedding;
however, the formal giving away of the bride is the cause of his ownership over her.

A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with sacred formulas is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next, whether she be outside her season or during her fertile period.
Whether he be devoid of virtue, addicted to sensual pleasures, or destitute of good qualities,
a husband must always be treated by a virtuous wife like a god.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is glorified in heaven.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should not do anything displeasing to her husband, whether he be living or dead.
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but once her husband has died, she must not even utter the name of another man.
Until death, let her remain patient, self-controlled, and devoted to the religious life,
longing for that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband.
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without producing offspring for the continuation of their lineage.
When her husband has died, a virtuous wife who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who practice lifelong celibacy.
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
No offspring born here belongs to anyone other than the biological father, nor does it belong to another’s possession;
for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere prescribed.
She who, abandoning her own husband though he be inferior, devotes herself to one who is superior,
becomes indeed contemptible in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband."
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
She who does not act treacherously toward her husband through thought, word, or deed attains the world of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains preeminent fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.

A twice-born man who knows the law should cause his wife— who is of the same caste, of virtuous conduct, and who dies before him— to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements.
Having given the sacred fires to a wife who has died before him during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the marriage ceremony and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life.

Having thus lived in the householder stage according to the rules, the twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies should dwell in the forest, self-restrained and with his senses fully conquered, in accordance with the law.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair,
and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should resort to the forest.
Having abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
he should entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
Having taken up the Agnihotra sacrifice and the implements for the domestic fire,
he should depart from the village for the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as a beard, body hair, and nails.
From whatever food he may have, he should offer the ritual oblation (bali) and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
he should always be a giver and never a taker, showing compassion toward all living beings.
And he should perform the Vaitānika Agnihotra sacrifice according to the rules,
not omitting the new-moon and full-moon festivals through the practice of yoga.
He should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dakṣāyaṇa in their proper sequence.
He should separately prepare sacrificial cakes and boiled rice offerings according to the rules, using pure food fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons.
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities, he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots,
and fruits produced from pure trees, along with oils derived from fruits.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the ground,
