bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleśmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored,
as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a ploughshare, even if it has been discarded by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots and fruits grown within a village.
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may be one who washes away his impurities immediately, or one who stores up for a month;
he may be one who stores up for six months, or even one who stores up for a year.
He should eat food at night or during the day, having gathered it according to his ability; or he may eat only every fourth mealtime, or even only every eighth mealtime.
Or he may pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he may eat a single meal of boiled barley gruel.
Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots,
and fruits that have ripened in their season and fallen of their own accord, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the three ritual libations.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.
Performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should become a sage without fires and without a fixed dwelling, subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, he should be a celibate student, sleeping on the ground,
having no sense of ownership over shelters, and making his dwelling at the foot of a tree.
He should obtain alms for his sustenance only from brahmins who are ascetics,
or from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from a village,
receiving them either in the hollow of his hand, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd.
Living in the forest, a Brahmin should practice these and other initiations,
as well as various Upanishadic scriptures for the sake of self-perfection.
These [rites] are practiced by sages, brahmins, and indeed by householders for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body.
Or, having taken his stand upon the Aparājitā [direction], he should proceed straight ahead toward that quarter until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air.
Having cast off his body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
a Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life dwelling in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by alms and offerings, one who renounces increases after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of his ability, he should direct his mind toward liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa should go forth from his home as a wandering ascetic.
For him who, having granted freedom from fear to all beings, departs from his home to the life of renunciation,
there are worlds consisting of splendor, O teacher of Brahman.
Since not even the slightest fear arises from living beings for the twice-born,
there is no fear whatsoever for him once he is liberated from the body.
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by sacred observances,
should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him.
One should always wander alone for the sake of accomplishment, without a companion;
seeing that success belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons his path nor is he abandoned by it.
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food;
indifferent, free from agitation, a sage whose being is concentrated in meditation.
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, tattered rags, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should step forth with the foot purified by vision; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to worldly objects, and free from sensual desire,
he who seeks happiness should wander about in this world with himself alone as his companion.
A mendicant should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by giving instructions or counsel.
He should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants.
Having his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, not causing pain to any living beings.
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for an ascetic.
He should go for alms only once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached to sensual objects as well.
When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms.
He should not be dejected in the event of failure to obtain [alms], nor should he rejoice upon obtaining them;
he should take only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material things.
But he should utterly despise gains obtained through being honored;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through being honored.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
he should restrain the senses when they are being carried away by their objects.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
He should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
Separation from those who are dear, as well as union with those who are unpleasant,
being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases.
He perceives the departure of this inner self from the body, its rebirth in a womb,
and its wanderings through thousands of millions of wombs.
He should know that for embodied beings, the connection with suffering arises from unrighteousness (adharma),
while the inexhaustible union with happiness arises from righteousness (dharma) and wealth (artha).
And by means of yoga, he should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.
Even if he is corrupted, one should practice dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) one may be;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of dharma.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (Manu Smṛti 6.67)
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk after scanning the ground, even when his body is exhausted.
Whatever living beings an ascetic injures unintentionally by day or by night,
for the sake of purifying himself from that, he should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) after bathing.
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa and joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
Through the yoga of meditation, one may perceive the course of this inner self among beings of high and low station— a course that is difficult for those of unrefined soul to understand.
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of such vision enters into the cycle of transmigration.
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the rigorous practice of austerities, they attain that state in this world.
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of living beings, which is beset by old age and sorrow, a seat of disease and affliction, full of passion, and impermanent.
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so too, by abandoning this body, one is released from the crocodile of hardship.
Having relinquished both his good deeds toward those dear to him and his evil deeds toward those who are not dear,
through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition,
then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments and being liberated from all pairs of opposites, he abides in Brahman alone.
All this that has been described here is indeed based on meditation;
for no one who is not self-realized ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and whatever is declared in the Vedāntas.
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this very same is for those who possess knowledge;
this is for those seeking heaven, and this is for those seeking the infinite.
The twice-born man who wanders as a mendicant according to this sequential method,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action (karmayoga) for them.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
Moreover, among all these [orders], according to the injunctions of the Vedas and the Smṛtis,
the householder is declared to be the best, for he supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the other stages of life find their support in the householder.
Moreover, this tenfold duty must always be practiced with diligence by the twice-born belonging to all four stages of life.
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-control, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
wisdom, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma and,
having studied them, live according to them, attain the supreme goal.
Having practiced the tenfold dharma with a concentrated mind and having heard the Vedānta according to the prescribed rule, the twice-born man, freed from his debts, should renounce the world.
Having renounced all ritual actions and having cast off the defects of action, he should, being self-restrained,
study the Veda and dwell happily under the sovereignty of his son.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing,
he destroys his sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
This fourfold duty of a Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you;
it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the duty of kings.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how he may attain supreme success.
Having received the Vedic consecration according to the prescribed rule, a Kṣatriya must duly provide protection for all this [world].
For in this world without a king, everyone would flee in fear from all sides; therefore, the Lord created a king for the protection of this entire world.
Having extracted the eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, Ārka, Agni, Varuṇa, Candra, and Vitteśa, [he created Brahmā].
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore overcomes all beings by his splendor.
Like the sun, he dazzles both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look directly at him.
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama);
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and the great Indra.
A king must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking "he is merely a human being";
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form.
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king’s fire, like the fire of destruction, consumes the entire family along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
Having truly considered the task at hand, his own power, and the place and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-born Śrī, in whose prowess victory, and in whose anger death; for he is composed of all splendor.
But whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon that person's swift destruction.
Therefore, that king should determine what is right for those he holds dear,
and he should not deviate from that duty even regarding those he dislikes.
For its sake, the Lord formerly created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, remain devoted to their own duties and do not deviate from them.
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of those people],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is remembered as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be Dharma itself.
When properly guided after due deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when implemented without deliberation, he destroys them on every side.
If the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and a dog might lick the oblation (havis);
there would be no sense of ownership in anything at all, and the low would rise above the high.
The entire world is subdued by punishment, for a pure man is indeed rare;
through fear of punishment, the whole world is fit for the enjoyment of life.
Even the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, birds,
and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when they are oppressed by the rod alone.
All social classes would become corrupted, all boundaries would be broken,
and there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment.
Where the dark-hued, red-eyed Punishment stalks about, destroying evil,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who properly leads it.
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
however, one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by that very punishment.
For punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those who have not disciplined their souls;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.
He cannot be led by the right path by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect,
and attached to sensual objects.
Punishment can be effectively administered by one who is pure, true to his word, follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward his enemies,
straightforward toward his friends, and full of forbearance toward affectionate Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered his own self,
his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are each established in their respective duties in due order.
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his servants,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon Brāhmaṇas who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.
One should always serve aged Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
Even though he is already self-disciplined, he should constantly learn the principles of discipline from them;
for a king who is self-disciplined never perishes.
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those living in the forest have obtained kingdoms through discipline.
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (Mn 7.41)
Pṛthu obtained the kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained wealth and sovereignty, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he shall learn the triple knowledge (trayī), the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti),
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the science of the self (ātmavidyā), and the practical applications of the economic arts (vārtā) from the people.
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered the senses is able to keep the subjects under control.
One should strive with diligence to avoid these ten calamities arising from desire and those eight born of anger, which end in misery.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived even of his own self.
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], and idle wandering— this is the tenfold group born of passion.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault with others' merits,
and the harshness of speech and punishment— this is the group of eight born of anger.
One should strive to conquer greed, which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these classes arise from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— one should know this tetrad to be the most grievous among the group of vices born of desire.
One should know that this triad— inflicting physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the deprivation of property— is always difficult to endure, even when it arises from the group born of anger.
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the one following it.
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
the man of calamities sinks lower and lower, while the man free from calamities goes to heaven when he dies.
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone to accomplish, especially so without assistance; how much more so the sovereignty of a kingdom, which brings great prosperity?
With them, he should constantly deliberate upon common matters:
peace and war, stability, acquisition, protection, and the consolidation of what has been gained.
Having ascertained their respective individual intentions, he should act for his own welfare regarding the affairs of both the individuals and the collective.
But the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his ministers.
Constantly placing his trust in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he may then undertake his work.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.
He should appoint as many men who are unwearied, skillful, and discerning as may be required for the performance of his duties.
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in industrial works;
and those who are pure and timid within the inner apartments.
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and movements, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.
A messenger who is devoted, pure, skillful, mindful, knowledgeable of place and time, handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised by kings.
Punishment depends upon the minister; the administration of discipline depends upon punishment; the treasury and the kingdom depend upon the king; and peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy.
For it is the messenger indeed who unites those who are divided and also divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated.

He should discern, through secret hints and gestures, the outward appearance, the internal disposition, and the intended actions of this king regarding his undertakings, as well as those of his servants.
Having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king,
he should apply such effort as will not cause him suffering.
He should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of livelihood.
Having taken refuge in a desert fortress, an earth fortress, a water fortress, a forest fortress, a human fortress, or a mountain fortress, he should dwell in a city.
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for, by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Of these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, burrow-dwellers, and aquatic creatures;
the latter three are inhabited respectively by monkeys, humans, and gods.
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress,
so too do foes not injure a king who has taken refuge in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is ordained.
That city should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
it should also be provided with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
In the center of that [land], he should have his own house built— spacious,
well-protected against all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue.
He should appoint a domestic priest and likewise choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.
The king should perform various sacrifices accompanied by liberal sacrificial fees,
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins.
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy men;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects like a father.
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of men as they carry them out.
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher's house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable Brahman-treasure of kings.
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brāhmaṇas.
It overflows not, it fails not, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward; to one who has studied the Vedas, it yields a hundred-thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields an infinite reward.
For it is specifically through the excellence of the recipient and through faith that one enjoys the fruit of a gift, whether small or great, after death.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient according to the rules of place and time, that is the means for accomplishing dharma.
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, a king protecting his subjects must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya.
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to the Brāhmaṇas— these are the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another and fight with all their might, never turning their backs, go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with barbed ones, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are ablaze with fire.
One should not strike one who has climbed onto dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."
One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed,
nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the duty of the virtuous, one should not strike one who is suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely mangled, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away in flight.
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies,
incurs all whatever evil deeds his master has committed.
Furthermore, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter,
the master takes all of that from one who is killed while retreating.
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all types of goods, and base metals— whatever anyone conquers belongs to him.
And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually.
This eternal law of warriors has been declared as unadorned;
a Kṣatriya, while slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should know that this fourfold purpose serves the goals of human life;
one should perform its constant practice correctly and without sloth.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired by means of force; protect what has been acquired with vigilance;
increase what has been protected through growth; and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment uplifted, always display his prowess,
always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds his rod of punishment uplifted;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod.
He should conduct himself with complete sincerity and never by deceit;
remaining ever well-guarded, he should also recognize the deception employed by his enemy.
An enemy should not discover his own weak point, but he should discover the weak point of the enemy;
he should hide his own limbs like a tortoise and guard his own vulnerability.
He should deliberate on his objectives like a crane, display valor like a lion, snatch his prey like a wolf, and flee like a hare.
While he is thus victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation.
If, however, they do not abide by these [means], he should gradually bring them under control by force alone, using the first three expedients.
Among the four expedients beginning with conciliation, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom.
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
That king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, oppresses his own kingdom,
shall soon be deprived both of his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
He should always observe this rule for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness.
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom.
He should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The village headman himself shall gradually report any faults arising in the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten shall report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty, however, shall report all that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, in turn, shall himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Whatever is to be given daily by the village dwellers to the king— such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth— the village headman shall receive those.
The collector of ten should enjoy five families, and the collector of twenty, five hundred;
the superintendent of a hundred villages should enjoy a village, and the lord of a thousand, a city.
Indeed, another minister of the king, who is affectionate and vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their individual duties.
And in every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs,
occupying a high position and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through his spies.
For the king's protectors are generally servants who seize the property of others and are deceitful; he should guard these subjects from them.
Those of evil intent who would seize wealth solely from litigants,
the king shall confiscate their entire property and carry out their banishment.
The king should daily provide maintenance and a place of residence for women and servants engaged in his service, according to their respective tasks.
A paṇa is the wage for the lowest servant, and six for the highest;
likewise, clothing is given every six months, and a droṇa of grain every month.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of property and person, the king should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants.
Having considered how the king and the performer of actions may both be joined with their respective fruits, the king should always apportion taxes within his realm accordingly.
Just as water-birds, young calves, and bees consume their food very little by little,
so should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is very small.
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
And of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and wickerwork;
of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone.
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his kingdom perish from hunger.
In whose kingdom a learned Śrotriya suffers from hunger,
his entire realm likewise perishes from hunger before long.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, he should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
and he should protect him in every way, like a father protects his own biological son.
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
The king shall cause even the common people in his realm who live by trade to pay some small amount known as a tax for the sake of the year.
The lord of the earth shall cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month.
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one harms both oneself and them.
The lord of the earth should be both severe and mild, having regard for what needs to be done;
indeed, a king who is both severe and mild becomes esteemed.
When exhausted by overseeing the affairs of men, the king should appoint to that seat his chief minister— one who knows the law, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Having thus performed all these duties incumbent upon himself,
he should protect these subjects, remaining both disciplined and vigilant.
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried away by robbers while they cry out for help,
even though he looks on with his servants, is dead and does not truly live.
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed rewards is joined with righteousness through that very act.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications with a concentrated mind,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with a joyful greeting;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended to a mountain ridge, or having gone to a secluded spot,
or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate on counsel unobserved.
That king who, even if destitute of treasure, enjoys the entire earth while ordinary people, having come together, do not know his secret counsel.
At the time of reciting the mantras, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; animals; those past their youth; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed.
Those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, disclose a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue,
he should reflect upon virtue, pleasure, and wealth, either together with those [pursuits] or alone.
He should also effect the reconciliation of those who are at variance with one another,
the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of his sons.
The dispatching of envoys, as well as the remaining tasks to be performed,
the conduct within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
He should truly understand all eightfold action and the five classes [of spies],
as well as loyalty and disloyalty, and the conduct of the circle of states.
He should diligently investigate the conduct of the middle king, the activities of one who desires to conquer, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy.
These constituent elements are, in brief, the foundation of the circle [of kings];
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
The five others are known as the minister, the kingdom, the fort, the treasury, and the army;
each of these has been described briefly, making seventy-two in total.
Immediately after [the conqueror], one should know the enemy and likewise the one who serves the enemy; next to the enemy is the friend, and beyond those two is the neutral party.
He should win over all of them by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation—
both individually and collectively— and through personal prowess and statesmanship.
He should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.
Having carefully considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment, marching, alliance, and war, as well as double-dealing and seeking refuge.
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds;
likewise, marching and sitting encamped are two-fold, and seeking shelter is recorded as being of two kinds.
When the undertaking of the journey is common to both, or likewise when it is the reverse,
that peace treaty should be known as having two characteristics and being connected to future consequences.
War is declared to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of one's own purpose, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged against an enemy who has wronged a friend.
When an urgent matter has arisen by chance,
marching alone or in alliance with a friend is said to be the two-fold way of marching.
When one's own power has gradually diminished, whether due to fate or by one's own prior actions,
or out of consideration for a friend— this is declared to be the two-fold "sitting" (āsana) policy.
The maintenance of both the army and the sovereign for the sake of accomplishing the objective is declared to be of two kinds as "duplicity" by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy.
Seeking refuge with the virtuous for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose when oppressed by enemies is considered to be of two kinds.
When he perceives that his own superiority in the future is certain,
while the suffering in the present is slight, then he should resort to peace.
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased,
and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he may wage war.
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit,
and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is completely depleted of both mounts and troops,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.
When the king considers his enemy to be in every way more powerful,
he should then divide his army into two parts and accomplish his own purpose.
But when he becomes most vulnerable to the forces of the enemy,
then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king.
One should constantly serve with all efforts that king who effects the suppression of both his subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would a teacher.
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from seeking refuge,
he should engage in fair combat itself, free from hesitation.
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him.
He should examine all future undertakings as well as those of the present, and he should truly discern the merits and defects of all past actions.
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who understands the consequences of past actions, is not overcome by his enemies.
He should arrange everything in such a way that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.
Then the lord should mount his vehicle toward the enemy's kingdom;
at that time, he should proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
or else in the months of Phālguna or Caitra, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition according to his strength.
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for his enemy.

Having performed the ritual arrangements at the root [of the tree] and the preparations for the journey according to the rules, and having secured a place of residence and properly stationed his spies; Mn 7.184 [185M]
Having cleared the threefold path and his own sixfold forces according to the rules for a campaign,
he should march toward the enemy's city.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a secret friend who serves the enemy, as well as one who has gone away and returned;
for such a person is a most dangerous foe.
He should march along that road in the staff-array, or the wagon-array,
or the boar-array, the crocodile-array, the needle-array, or the eagle-array.
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, in that direction he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus formation (*padmavyūha*).
The commander-in-chief and the general shall station their forces in all directions;
and whichever direction he suspects danger from, that he shall designate as the front.
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—
men who are skilled in both their positions and in battle, who are fearless and steadfast.
One should make a small number of troops fight in close formation, while one may at will spread out a large number;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.
One should fight on level ground with chariots and horses, on marshy ground with boats and elephants,
in places covered with trees and shrubs with bows, and on open ground with swords, shields, and other weapons.
He should station men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena,
as well as those who are tall and those who are short, at the vanguard of the army.
Having arrayed his army, he should encourage it and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of the enemies as they fight.
Having besieged his enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly spoil his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel.
He should break down tanks as well as walls and moats;
he should also launch a sudden assault upon him at night and likewise cause him terror.
He should instigate those who can be instigated and remain aware of their actions;
when fate is favorable, he who desires victory should fight, free from fear.
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension— either collectively or individually— and never by means of war.
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two combatants,
as is defeat in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
If even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible,
he should fight in such a way that, being well-equipped, he conquers his enemies.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions for their livelihood and proclaim amnesties of safety.
But having understood the intended purpose of all these [claimants] in brief,
he should install one of their lineage there and establish a formal covenant.
And he should establish authoritative legal codes for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and he should honor him with precious gifts along with his principal officers.
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving causes pleasure;
at the proper time, the practice of acquiring desired objects is highly praised.
All this action is dependent upon the two ordinances, the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists the possibility of action.
Human effort, when joined with destiny,
proceeds toward the attainment of its goal, though it may involve great hardship.
Even when joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort,
the field yields fruit only through human effort.
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water,
are brought about here by destiny through the exertion of human effort.
Or, being prepared, he may even march together with him after carefully concluding a treaty,
provided he perceives a threefold result consisting of a friend, gold, or territory.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and the ally within the circle of states,
whether from a friend or even from an enemy, one should obtain the fruit of the expedition.
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend who, though currently weak, is capable of future endurance.
A light friend who knows the Dharma, is grateful, has a contented nature, is loyal, and is steadfast in his undertakings is highly praised.
The wise declare it a hardship to have for an enemy one who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and resolute.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, compassion, great-souled munificence, and the constant arising of the qualities of an indifferent person; these are the marks of a king.
A king should, without hesitation, abandon for his own sake even land that is secure, productive of crops, and constantly conducive to the increase of cattle.
One should save wealth for times of misfortune, and protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together,
the wise man should employ every means, both those that are combined and those that are separate.
Relying upon these three— the seeker, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
after exercising and bathing at midday, shall enter the inner apartments to eat.
There, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be seduced, and who have neutralized poison with mantras.
He should employ all substances that counteract poison along with anti-venomous medicines;
and, remaining self-controlled, he should always wear gems that destroy poison.
And women who have been thoroughly examined, whose dress and ornaments are pure, and who are well-composed, should touch him with fans, water, and incense.
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food,
as well as bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties.
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the military personnel again,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, while bearing his weapon, listen within the inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again for the purpose of eating, surrounded by women.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to bed at the proper time and rise free from fatigue.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
however, when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
But when the king desires to inspect legal cases, he should enter the court modestly, accompanied by Brahmins as well as ministers who are experts in counsel.
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal affairs of the litigants.
Every day, they shall be recorded separately according to the eighteen titles of law, using reasons based on local custom as well as those found in the scriptures.
Of these, the first is non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
The non-payment of wages, the breach of a compact, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and his herdsman; Mn 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes; verbal and physical assault;
theft; violence; and the abduction of women.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these are the eighteen titles of law established here for judicial procedure.
In these matters, the king should determine the legal case by relying upon the eternal dharma for those men who are most frequently engaged in disputes.
But when the king himself does not personally conduct the investigation of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate those cases.
Surrounded by three members of the assembly, he should examine his duties,
having entered the foremost court while either seated or standing.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together,
along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly as a court of Brahman.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, approaches an assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (Manu Smṛti 8.12)
One should either not enter the assembly hall or speak what is just;
for by not speaking or by speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
For where dharma is destroyed by adharma, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the assembly look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, one must not violate Dharma, lest Dharma, being violated, destroy us.
For the Blessed Dharma is indeed a bull (vṛṣa); those who act against it, the gods know as a vṛṣala (outcaste). Therefore, one should not violate the Dharma.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even in death;
for everything else surely perishes along with the body.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are released; for where one deserving of censure is censured, the guilt goes to the perpetrator.
One who merely lives by his birth may, if he so desires, be called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇabruva) as the expounder of dharma to the king; but a Śūdra shall never be so under any circumstances.
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while onlookers look on.
That kingdom which is predominantly composed of Śūdras, overrun by atheists, and devoid of the twice-born,
quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease.
Having occupied the seat of justice, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.
Having understood both the beneficial and the harmful, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, eyes, and movements.
By outward forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his minority.
The same protection should be afforded to women who have no sons,
to those whose families have perished, to women devoted to their husbands, to widows, and to those who are afflicted by illness.
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still alive,
a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that period, the king may take it.
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule;
having verified the form, number, and other characteristics, the owner deserves that property.
One who fails to report the place and time of the lost item accurately,
as well as its color, form, and size, deserves a fine equal to the value of that object.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king may take a sixth part of lost property that has been recovered, or even a tenth or a twelfth.
Property that has been lost and then found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch there he shall cause to be executed by an elephant.
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own property,
or a smaller fraction of the value of that very deposit.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the master of all.
If a king should discover an ancient treasure buried in the earth,
he shall give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury.
The king is entitled to half the share of ancient treasures and minerals found in the earth, for he is indeed the lord of the soil.
The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
Having duly examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, one who knows the law should establish the specific duty for each individual.
Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world.
Neither the king himself nor his official should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another.
Just as a hunter tracks the path of a deer by drops of blood,
so should a king track the path of dharma by means of inference.
Abiding by the rules of legal procedure, he should examine the truth and the matter at hand, as well as himself, the witnesses, the place, the appearance, and the time.

Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, that one should establish as the law for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not inconsistent with the sacred tradition.
When urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering the debt,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount established as due to the creditor.
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own property,
by those very means he should compel the debtor to pay, having first won him over.
One should recover a debt through legal procedure, by artifice, by customary practice,
and by force as the fifth means.
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own.
But if a debtor denies the debt, yet it is proven by evidence,
the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor's due and a small fine according to his ability.
When a debtor, being addressed with "Pay!
in the assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff must point out the person who can testify or produce another means of proof.
He who points out what should not be pointed out, he who denies after having pointed it out, and he who does not comprehend the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows; // Mn_8.53 //
Furthermore, he who, having stated his case and what is to be stated, subsequently retracts it, or who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly established; Mn 8.54.
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when questioned, or he who runs away; Mn 8.55.
If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said,
or if he cannot distinguish between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that account.
If a person, having said "I have witnesses," is told "Produce them" and fails to produce them,
the judge shall declare him to be defeated on these grounds.
If the plaintiff does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he shall be bound and punished according to the law as a defeated party.
If a person conceals an object to whatever extent, or if he speaks falsely regarding its value to whatever extent,
both of them, being ignorant of the law, shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth while remaining in his place, denies the charge,
must be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas.
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be employed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them.

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, are worthy of being called upon for testimony when they are summoned for the sake of the matter; but no others whatsoever, except in times of emergency.
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be made witnesses in legal matters;
they must be knowers of all duties and free from greed, while those who are the opposite should be avoided.
One should not employ as witnesses those who have a financial interest in the matter, nor friends, nor allies, nor enemies;
nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt.
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a learned Vedic scholar, nor one who dwells in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
One who is not dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
nor one who is aged, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane, nor oppressed by hunger or thirst;
neither one afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by lust, nor angry, nor even a thief [should be questioned].
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men who are similar [in status] for twice-born men;
and virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras, while those of the lowest birth for those of the lowest castes.
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants in a private house, in a forest, or even in a matter involving the loss of life; Mn_8.69.
In the absence of a woman, the duty may be performed by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, the sick, and those who speak falsely in witness-depositions is unstable, as is the speech of those whose minds are agitated.
In all cases of violence, theft,
and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.

In the case of a conflict between witnesses, O King, the ruler should accept the majority; but when the numbers are equal, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and when there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.
Testimony is established by seeing or hearing in person;
a witness who speaks the truth therein does not fall away from merit or wealth.
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men regarding anything other than what was seen or heard goes headfirst to hell after death and is excluded from heaven.
Even where one has not been formally appointed, if one should see or hear anything,
even when questioned there, one should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but not women, even if they are many and pure;
for the intellect of women is unstable, and others as well who are beset by defects [are inadmissible].
Whatever they may say by their very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is meaningless.
When the witnesses have arrived within the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant,
the judge shall examine them, consoling them with this following procedure.
Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for your role here is that of witnesses.
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
he also gains unsurpassed fame in this world—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking falsely when giving testimony, one is bound tightly by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred births, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
A witness is purified by truth; righteousness increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
"Evil-doers think, 'No one sees us';
yet the gods see them, as does their own inner self."
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, Yama, wind, night,
the two twilights, and Dharma are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either the north or the east.
One should question a Brāhmaṇa with "Speak"; a Kṣatriya with "Speak the truth";
a Vaiśya with [the threat of] his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra with all [possible] sins.
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the murderer of women and children,
and for the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful— those shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely.
O gentle one, whatever merit you have acquired since birth—
all that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
O virtuous one, as for you who think of yourself, "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and demerit is ever present within your heart.
If you have no dispute with that god Yama Vaivasvata who resides within your heart,
then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty,
and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar.
He who, when questioned during a legal determination, speaks falsely in response to a question, shall go headlong into the darkness of hell as a sinner. (Manu 8.94)
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts or what he has not personally witnessed, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man.
For the gods know no other person in this world to be more excellent than that learned man whose inner self (kṣetrajña) does not harbor suspicion when he speaks.
Listen now, gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony, in due order, for each respective case.
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Therefore, do not speak falsehood regarding land.
They say that [the law of] the earth applies to women in matters of enjoyment and sexual intercourse,
as well as to aquatic gems and all those made of stone.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen.
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers as one would Śūdras.
When a man speaks thus regarding matters of law, even though he knows otherwise, he does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods.
Where the death penalty would be prescribed for a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, or a Brāhmaṇa upon the telling of the truth, there one must speak an untruth; for that is superior to the truth.
And they should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to Vāgīśvarī,
thereby effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood.
Or he may offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the Waters.
If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth of the total amount.
If, within seven days of the testimony being given,
sickness, fire, or the death of a relative should befall the witness, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine.
But in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot discover the truth in its actual state, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.
Oaths have been taken by great seers and gods for the sake of accomplishing their purposes;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Paijavana.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death.
In matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cattle, fuel,
and in coming to the aid of a Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin in taking an oath.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons;
a Vaiśya, by cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all mortal sins.
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should make him touch the heads of his son and wife individually.
He whom the kindled fire does not burn, whom the waters do not cause to float up,
and who does not quickly meet with misfortune, should be known as pure in his oath.
For in ancient times, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother,
even a single hair of his was not consumed by fire, for he was a witness to the world through truth.
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; what has been done shall be as if undone.
Testimony is declared to be false when given out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger, as well as ignorance and childishness.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any one of these cases.
For taking [property] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first amercement;
for out of fear, two middle amercements; and for out of friendship, four times the first amercement.
From lust, the first [penalty] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold;
from ignorance, it is two full hundred; but from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony to be for the purpose of ensuring that justice does not fail and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
A righteous king, having punished them with fines, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the Self-existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
in these three castes, however, a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered the strength of the offender and the gravity of the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame;
it also prevents access to heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
One should first employ the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal chastisement.
But when he is unable to restrain them even by execution,
then he may employ all these four methods against them.
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are established on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
The minute particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is called the *trasareṇu*, the first of all measurements.
Eight *trasareṇus* (motes of dust) are to be known as one *likṣā* (nit) in measurement;
three of those [make] a *rājasarṣapa* (black mustard seed), and three of those [make] a *gaurasarṣapa* (white mustard seed).
Six mustard seeds make one middle-sized barleycorn; three barleycorns make one kṛṣṇala;
five kṛṣṇalas make one māṣa; and sixteen of those make one suvarṇa.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, and ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together should be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa* or a *paṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* are to be known as one silver *śatamāna*;
a *niṣka* is to be understood by its measure as consisting of four *sauvarṇikas*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest.
When a debt is admitted as due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent;
if he denies it, the fine is double that—such is the ordinance of Manu.
A moneylender may stipulate an interest that increases his wealth as ordained by Vasiṣṭha;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two per cent;
for by taking two per cent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth.
One may take two, three, four, five,
or ten percent as monthly interest, according to the order of the social classes.
But one shall not receive interest on a secured loan if it remains idle;
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
Both an open deposit and a sealed deposit do not suffer from the lapse of time;
however, if they remain for a very long duration, they may be forfeited.
Things enjoyed through mutual affection are never lost;
this applies to a cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal being trained for work.
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he is not entitled to recover it.
If the owner is not an idiot and is not a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another, that [enjoyment] is nullified by legal process;
the enjoyer deserves to forfeit that property.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property,
and the property of a Vedic scholar are not lost through adverse possession.
The unwise man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of the owner must relinquish half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
for grain, fruit, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.
An interest exceeding the legal rate is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for it is only right to charge five percent per month.

One should not take interest exceeding that for a year, nor that which is not sanctioned; likewise, one should not take compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, or bodily interest.
He who is unable to pay the debt and wishes to enter into a new transaction shall,
after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond.
Without showing the gold back there, he may exchange it;
he ought to pay as much interest as has accrued.
One who has entered upon the increase of his capital and is established in the proper place and time will not obtain that fruit if he disregards the requirements of place and time.
Those who are skilled in sea voyages and who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose establish whatever profit; that is what constitutes the gain in such a case.
If a man stands as a surety for another's appearance here,
failing to produce him, he shall pay the debt from his own property.
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous loan, what is owed for gambling or spirituous liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
however, if the surety for payment has died, the judge should compel even his heirs to pay.
But if the debtor does not pay, and the surety—who was known for his reliable character—has died, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt? (Manu 8.161)
But if the surety has been designated with wealth and possesses sufficient assets, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who has been designated.
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, or dependent, or by a child, or by an elderly person,
or one that is otherwise invalid, is not upheld.
Even if a statement is well-established, it does not constitute truth if it is spoken outside the context of established legal conventions regarding worldly affairs. (Manu Smṛti 8.164)
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, or given away through fraud, or whatever has been received as a gift through fraud,
or wherever one perceives deceit— let him annul all that.
If the borrower should perish after having incurred an expenditure for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by his kinsmen, even if they are divided in property, from their own resources.
Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it.
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—
Manu has declared all such matters effected by force to be as if not done at all."
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.
A king, even when impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death.
Through the collection of taxes, the blending of castes, and the protection of the weak, the strength of the king is produced; he prospers both in this world and after death.

Therefore, like Yama himself, the king, having personally abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant, should conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, having conquered his anger and subdued his senses.
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, conducts affairs unjustly,
his enemies soon bring under their control.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to righteousness—
the subjects follow him, just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
He who reports to the king a creditor who is recovering his debt by his own will shall be made to pay a fourth part of that amount to the king, and the debt itself to the debtor.
A debtor should repay the creditor in equal installments;
one of equal or lower caste may pay at once, but one of superior caste should pay it gradually.
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of equality the legal cases of men disputing with one another, as established by the evidence of witnesses.
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in the Dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable.
