Whatever object a man deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the recovery.
When one who has been asked for a deposit does not return it to the depositor,
he shall be questioned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with trustworthy persons endowed with age and physical beauty under various pretexts, he should proceed.
If he should restore it exactly as it was deposited and in the condition it was made,
there exists therein nothing for which he may be prosecuted by others.
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the prescribed rule, he shall be seized by both [parties] and compelled to pay; such is the established principle of the law.
A deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must never be handed over to a next-of-kin;
they are lost in the event of his misfortune, but they do not perish if he does not meet with misfortune.
But if one should personally deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the relatives of the depositor.
He should seek to recover that property with honesty and with affection;
or, having investigated the man's conduct, he should settle the matter through conciliation alone.
In all these cases of deposits, this rule shall apply regarding their recovery;
however, if the depositary does not withdraw anything from it, he shall incur no liability in the case of a sealed deposit.
If [the property] has been stolen by thieves, washed away by water, or consumed by fire,
he need not pay it back, provided that he has not taken anything for himself from that [property].
One should seek out the thief of a deposit and even the person who did not deposit it by all possible means and by Vedic oaths.
He who does not return a deposit and he who demands it back without having made a deposit—
both of them should be punished like thieves, or be made to pay a fine equal to the value of that [item].
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates an open deposit, without distinction.
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should carry off the property of another,
shall be put to death publicly with various modes of execution along with his accomplices.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; he who declares otherwise deserves punishment.
If a gift has been made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
In such cases, the king shall make a decision regarding both deposited wealth and that which has been handed over out of friendship, without causing hardship to the holder of the deposit.
One who sells another's property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, one should not admit him as a witness; he is a thief who considers himself no thief.
He shall be liable to forfeit his property along with his family and pay a fine of six hundred;
if he has no family and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
But a gift or a sale made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
Where enjoyment is observed but no source of acquisition is seen anywhere, there the source of acquisition is the cause [of ownership], not the mere enjoyment; such is the settled rule.
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family members,
he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified.

Now, if the root source [of the property] cannot be recovered, but it has been cleared by means of a public sale, the seller is not to be punished by the king and is released; the original owner (nāṣṭika) recovers his wealth.
An object whose form has been mixed with another is not fit for sale;
nor is that which is worthless, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is concealed at a distance.
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the groom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for a single bride-price.

A giver who has previously declared the defects [of the bride] does not deserve punishment, provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already engaged in sexual intercourse. Mn 8.205.
If an officiating priest, having been chosen for a sacrifice, should fail to perform his own duty,
a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the co-performers.
If, after the sacrificial fees have been distributed, he causes his own work to be neglected,
he shall receive his entire share even if he has it performed by another.
In whatever ritual act specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, that very person shall receive them; or else, all [the officiants] may share them together.
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the fire-consecration;
the Hotṛ may also take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Among all of them, the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those with a third share receive a third part, and those with a fourth share receive a fourth part.
When men here join together to perform their respective duties,
the apportionment of their shares must be determined by this application of the rule.
If wealth has been given by someone to another who asks for it for the sake of dharma,
and if that wealth does not subsequently serve that purpose, then it should not have been given to him.
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed,
he shall be made to pay one suvarṇa by the king as atonement for that theft.
Thus has been declared the lawful method for the non-repayment of what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
If a hired laborer, being neither ill nor distressed, should out of pride fail to perform the work as prescribed,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid.
But one who, having been ill, performs the work once he has recovered, exactly as it was described from the beginning,
shall indeed receive that wage even after a long period of time.

As it has been said: "Whether he be distressed or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be paid, even for work that is only slightly incomplete. (Manu Smṛti 8.217)
This law concerning the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law regarding those who violate an agreement.
A man who, having made a formal agreement with a village, a district, or a corporation,
should break that agreement out of greed, the king shall banish from the realm.
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the compact to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one royal śatamāna.
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate the agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies.
If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have regret,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.
But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king.
But for him who gives away a girl who has defects without having disclosed them,
the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas.
But if a man, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating any fault in her, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (Manu 8.225)
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are established for maidens alone;
they are never for women who are not maidens, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites.
The mantras recited at the time of taking the hand are the definitive mark of wifehood;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step.
In whatever matter a person may feel remorse after it has been done,
he should be established on the path of righteousness by this procedure.
I shall now duly declare, according to the principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock.
During the day, the responsibility for reporting any loss falls on the herdsman; at night, it falls on the owner if the animals are in his house.
Otherwise, if the security of the herd is otherwise maintained, the herdsman shall incur the responsibility for reporting any loss.
A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; this shall be the wages for a herdsman if he receives no other pay.
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place,
or if it has failed through lack of human effort, the keeper alone shall make restitution.
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time.
When animals have died, one should give their ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinews, and bile to the owners, and show them the identifying marks.
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman.
If, among those cows that have been penned up and are grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
The common pasture ground around a village shall be one hundred bows on all sides, or three throws of a yoke-pin;
for a city, however, it shall be three times that amount.
If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there,
the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals.
One should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it,
and one must block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass.

If cattle enter a field that is enclosed on a path, or one situated near a village, the owner of the cattle, if they have a herdsman, deserves a fine of one hundred; if they are without a herdsman, he should drive them away.
In other fields, however, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
in all cases, a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule.

Manu has declared that a cow that has recently calved within ten days, bulls, and animals dedicated to the gods— whether they have a keeper or are unattended— are not subject to punishment for damage.
In the event of a failure on the part of the owner of the field, the fine shall be ten times his share;
however, if it occurs through the negligence of the servants, the fine for the owner of the field shall be half of that.
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions committed by owners, cattle, and herdsmen.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.
And he should plant boundary trees— banyan, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees,
as well as *śālmalī*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and milky-exuding trees.
By means of shrubs, various kinds of bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and plots of ground,
as well as reeds and clusters of kubjaka shrubs, the boundary shall not perish.
Ponds, wells, large tanks, and springs;
And at the junctions of boundaries, he should establish works of public utility and temples for the deities.
And he should cause other boundary marks to be made concealed,
having observed that among men in this world there is constant confusion regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand; Mn 8.250.
And whatever objects of this kind the earth might swallow due to the lapse of time,
he should cause them to be placed hidden at junctions and on the boundaries.
By these marks, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant arrival of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties.
If there were doubt even when the marks are visible,
the decision regarding a boundary dispute would depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses.
In the presence of the village families and the two litigants themselves, witnesses should be questioned regarding the boundary marks at the border.
But having questioned them, he should establish the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, and he should record all of them by name.
Bowing their heads to the earth, wearing garlands and red garments,
and swearing oaths by their own good deeds, they shall lead the case to a just conclusion.
Those witnesses who lead the case according to what was stated are purified;
but those who lead it otherwise shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
In the absence of witnesses, however, four neighboring villagers shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
But in the absence of neighboring witnesses within the boundary of the original inhabitants,
he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers.
Whatever those witnesses may declare when questioned regarding the boundary marks at the junctions,
the king shall establish that between the two villages in accordance with the law.
The determination of boundaries for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
the king shall punish each of them individually with the middle amercement.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.
When a boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, who knows the law, shall assign land to some [parties] on account of their utility; such is the settled rule.
Thus has the law regarding the determination of boundaries been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya deserves half of that or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
in the case of a Vaiśya, the fine should be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
When twice-born men of equal caste commit an offense against one another, the fine shall be twelve [paṇas];
in the case of unspeakable disputes, that same fine shall be doubled.
But one of low birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is born from a base origin.
But for one who utters their names or castes with malice,
a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
If he gives instruction in the Dharma to Brahmins out of pride,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
One who, out of pride, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, occupation, or even their body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas.
Whether one speaks of someone as being one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly impaired— even if the statement is true— one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa.
One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher,
as well as one who does not yield the path to his teacher, shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
A wise king must impose punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (Manu Smṛti 8.276)

In the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the same rule applies toward their own respective classes; it is the settled conclusion that the administration of punishment shall be carried out exactly as before, with the exception of physical mutilation.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared in accordance with the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.
If a person of the lowest caste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu.
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the cutting off of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of that foot.
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of a superior caste shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be gashed.
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
likewise, he shall have the penis of one who urinates [upon him] cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
One who seizes him by the hair should have his two hands cut off without hesitation;
likewise for seizing him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred; likewise, one who causes blood to flow. But he who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while the breaker of bone shall be banished.
The rule is that for the destruction of any kind of trees, a fine must be imposed in proportion to the utility of each.
When an assault is committed against humans or animals,
the king shall inflict a punishment in proportion to the extent of the suffering caused.
And in the case of crushing a limb, or likewise in the case of a wound or blood,
he shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for recovery, or even the full fine.
If one should damage the goods of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king.
For leather and leatherwork, for articles made of wood or clay,
and for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
They say there are ten exemptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in any other case, punishment is ordained.

When the nose-rope is cut, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction, and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheel of the vehicle; Mn 8.291.
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of mechanical devices, nor likewise for the snapping of yokes or reins, nor when one cries out "Get away! to avoid an accident.
If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and shall pay a fine of two hundred panas.
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred.
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
he should cause the death of living beings, the punishment there is not to be deliberated upon.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is incurred immediately, just as in the case of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, it is half [of that].
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the penalty shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
but for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother,
when they have committed an offense, may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one must strike on the back of the body, and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief.
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
A king should exert the greatest effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase.
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is ever-prosperous, having the gift of fearlessness as its sacrificial fee.
A sixth part of all merit accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of the demerit accrues to him who fails to protect.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes entitled to a sixth part of that through his providing proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to the law and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices every day with sacrificial fees of hundreds and thousands.
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls,
shares of produce, and fines, shall go immediately to hell.
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects while taking a sixth part of their produce as tax is the remover of all the impurities of the entire world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect his subjects, and who devours them instead, is destined for a downward path.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrificial rites.
A lord who seeks his own welfare must always forgive those litigants who revile him,
as well as children, the elderly, and the sick.
He who, when insulted by those in distress, forgives, is glorified in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not forgive, goes to hell because of that.
The thief must go to the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I have committed such an act; punish me."
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood,
or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod, he should carry it on his shoulder.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.

The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
But men who have committed sins, having been punished by kings,
go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
But he who draws a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who breaks a water-trough,
shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place.
For one who steals more than ten jar-measures of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he should be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property must be restored to its owner.
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments, death is the penalty when the amount exceeds one hundred.
But for an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
One deserves the death penalty for stealing men of noble birth, women especially, and the most precious of gems.
In cases of the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicine,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the circumstances of the act.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for piercing them with a knife,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, the punishment of half a foot (amputation) shall be carried out immediately.
Of thread, cotton, fermenting agents, cow dung, molasses, curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass; Mn 8.326.
Likewise, for the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, of salts, of earthenware, and of earth or ashes; Mn 8.327.
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter,
of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
For other such intoxicating drinks, for boiled rice,
and for all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value.
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five kṛṣṇalas.
When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been winnowed,
the fine shall be one hundred paṇas for stealing them if they belong to an unrelated person, and fifty paṇas if they belong to a related person.
An act committed by force with the owner's presence is *sāhasa* (violence);
that which is done without his presence, or where one takes and then denies it, is *steya* (theft).
But the king shall punish first that man who steals these prepared materials, as well as he who would steal the fire from the house.
With whichever limb a thief acts among men,
that very limb the king shall remove as a deterrent.
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest— there is no one who, failing to abide by his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, the king should be fined one thousand; such is the established rule.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
For a Brahmin, it shall be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he is one who knows both the faults and the merits of those [offenses].
Manu has declared that wood from trees, roots and fruits, firewood for the sake of the sacred fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, are not subject to the charge of theft.
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—
even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching— is exactly like a thief.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted does not deserve to be fined for taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field.
One who binds those who are not bound, releases those who are bound,
and seizes the slaves, horses, and chariots of others, shall incur the guilt of a thief.
By suppressing thieves according to this rule,
a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
Desiring to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, eternal glory,
a king should not overlook a man of violent deeds even for a moment.
A man who commits an act of violence is to be known as the worst of evildoers, surpassing even one who is foul-mouthed, a thief, or one who injures with a staff.
But that king who tolerates one who persists in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred.
Neither for the sake of friendship nor from the acquisition of vast wealth should a king release perpetrators of violence who bring fear to all living beings.
The twice-born may take up arms when their duty is obstructed,
or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time.
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or for the protection of a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin, provided he acts according to dharma.
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin,
one should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation.
No guilt whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin, whether done openly or in secret; it is fury that meets that fury.
The king, having punished with terrifying penalties those men who have set out to violate another's wife, shall banish them.
For from that arises the intermixture of castes among people,
by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total destruction.
A man who engages in conversation with another's wife in secret,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out for a valid reason,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, or even in a forest,
or at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery.
Courtship, dalliance, touching her ornaments and clothes,
and even sitting together on the same bed— all this is recorded as adultery.
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he is touched by her and consents to it,
it is all considered *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction) when there is mutual consent.
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected with the utmost care.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice,
and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
however, he who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away.
But he who engages in conversation with such women,
or with female slaves who eat only a single meal a day, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine.
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in status, shall not suffer death.
One should not cause a maiden who is associating with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one who is serving an inferior man should be kept confined in the house.
A man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
however, if her father desires it, he may have intercourse with her upon paying a bride-price.
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
shall have two fingers immediately cut off and deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who defiles an unwilling one— namely, the cutting off of a finger—
but he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred for the purpose of preventing a recurrence.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being carried away on a donkey.
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, would transgress against her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with people.
One should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they shall pile wood upon him, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise, it shall be the same for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī*.

A Śūdra who dwells with a member of the twice-born caste, whether that person is protected or unprotected, shall lose his limb if the victim was unprotected, and his entire property if the victim was protected. (Manu Smṛti 8.374)
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king shall fine the Vaiśya five hundred and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of them, having committed adultery with a guarded Brahmin woman,
shall be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw.
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas];
he who has sexual intercourse with one who consents shall be fined five hundred.
Shaving the head is ordained as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa that ends with his life;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends with their lives.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is engaged in every possible sin;
one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and his body uninjured.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive of his execution in his mind.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a guarded Vaiśya woman,
both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman.
A Brahmin, however, approaching those two women while they are guarded, shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
If a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, the fine is five hundred;
however, the Kṣatriya should desire either tonsure with urine as the penalty or the fine itself.

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with a rod, shares in the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm brings imperial sovereignty among his kinsmen and indeed confers glory upon him in the world.
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—
provided that each is capable of performing the rite and free from fault— the punishment for both shall be one hundred [paṇas] each.
Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned.
He who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their caste, shall be fined six hundred by the king.
When twice-born men in hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties,
a king who desires his own welfare should not pronounce a legal decision himself.
Having honored these men according to their merit along with the Brahmins,
and having first pacified them with gentle words, the king should cause them to adhere to their own duty.
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor when twenty Brahmins are invited for an auspicious occasion, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.
If a learned Brahmin does not feed another learned and virtuous Brahmin during rites for prosperity,
he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold.
One who is blind, one who is mentally infirm, one who moves about on a board, and one who is seventy years old or older,
as well as one who serves those learned in the Vedas, shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone.
The king should always honor a learned Vedic scholar, those afflicted by disease or distress, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous.
On a smooth board made of śālmalī wood, a washerman shall wash clothes gently;
he shall not rub garments against one another, nor shall he let them dry together.
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread increased by one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
Those skilled in customs houses and expert in all types of merchandise shall determine the value according to each commodity; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.
If one, out of greed, exports those articles which are the king's famous wares or those which are prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property.
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the toll.
Having investigated the importation, exportation, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he shall regulate their purchase and sale.
Every five nights, or else at the end of every fortnight,
the king should perform the formal offering of water (argha) in their presence.
All scales and measures must be clearly marked;
they shall be re-examined every six months.
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
cattle and women, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half of a quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without luggage, shall pay whatever is appropriate.
On a long journey, one should know that a crossing may be found according to the place and the time on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such certainty on the ocean.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a renunciant,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay the ferry toll at a crossing.
Whatever on board a ship may be damaged through the negligence of the boatmen,
that must be made good by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together, each from his own share.
This has been declared as the decision regarding legal disputes for those traveling by boat:
in the event of an injury on water caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment; however, in the case of an act of God, there is no liability.
One should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and the Śūdra [should perform] service for the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa should support out of compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of greed and by virtue of his superior power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will,
he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, one should compel to perform service;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (Mn 8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave by being given as food, one born in the house, one purchased, one received as a gift, one inherited from ancestors, and one enslaved for a fine— these seven are the sources of slavery.
Wife, son, and slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra;
for he has nothing of his own, as his wealth is to be taken by his master.
The king should cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own duties with diligence; for if these two deviate from their respective duties, they would throw this entire world into turmoil.
Day by day he should inspect his undertakings and his vehicles, as well as his fixed income and expenditure, his mines, and his treasury.
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.
I shall now declare the eternal duties for a man and a woman who abide in the path of dharma, both in their union and in their separation.
Women must be kept under subjection day and night by their own men; and if they become attached to sensual pleasures, they must be restrained within their own control.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.
Women must be protected especially from even the slightest of opportunities for misconduct;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring sorrow upon two families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma.
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here;
for that is the reason she is called "jāyā" (wife), because he is born again from her.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard a woman with great effort.
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded by means of these applications of expedients.
He should employ her in the collection and expenditure of wealth,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
Those women who, though confined at home by trustworthy male guards,
protect themselves by their own efforts, are truly well-protected.

Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at improper times], and dwelling in another's house—these six are the causes of a woman's corruption. (Manu Smṛti 9.13)
They do not examine their appearance, nor do they take into account their age;
whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection,
these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
Having thus understood their nature as produced by the Creator at the beginning of creation,
a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection.
Manu assigned to women beds, seats, ornaments, lust, anger, dishonesty, ignobility, a malevolent disposition, and bad conduct.
"Women have no ritual action with mantras"—such is the established rule in the Dharma.
For women are without [Vedic] authority and without mantras; it is settled that they are untruthful. (Manu Smṛti 9.18)
And likewise, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas;
listen now to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics.
"Whatever my mother, wandering about unfaithful, lusted after, may my father take that seed of mine"—this is the illustration for this [rule]. (Manu 9.20)
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind for her husband,
this is declared to be the proper means of averting that transgression.
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, such qualities she acquires, just as a river does when it merges with the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained honor by being united with Vasiṣṭha; and Śāraṅgī reached a state of venerability through Mandapāla.
These and other women of low birth in this world have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in their worldly life, which yields happiness both in this world and after death; now learn the duties concerning progeny.
For the sake of procreation, highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
there is no difference whatsoever between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) within households.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those already born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— women are the visible foundation for all this.
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for both one's ancestors and oneself depends upon her.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous.
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been proclaimed by the virtuous and by the great seers of old concerning a son.
They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict of scriptural authorities regarding the progenitor.
Some say he belongs to the one who produces him, while others know him to belong to the owner of the field.
Woman is considered to be the field, and man is considered to be the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed.
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time,
that very kind of seed grows therein, manifested with its own inherent qualities.
For this earth is said to be the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth.
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers arise here in various forms according to their own nature.
Rice, paddy, mung beans, sesame, kidney beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcane, sprout according to their respective seeds. (Manu Smṛti 9.39)
That one thing is sown and another is produced is not tenable;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth.
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a man should not sow seed in what belongs to another... (Manu Smṛti 9.42).
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sight of one who continues to pierce the air where it was struck,
so indeed does a seed sown in the possession of another quickly perish.
Those who know the past recognize this earth as the wife of Pṛthu;
they say that the field belongs to Sthāṇuccheda and the deer to Śālyavān.
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have declared; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (Manu Smṛti 9.45)
A wife is not released from her husband by means of sale or divorce;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati.
A share of inheritance is allotted but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once;
and "I give" is said but once—these three things happen only once among the virtuous.
Just as one who begets offspring on cows, mares, female camels, slave-girls, buffaloes, goats, or sheep does not share in the ownership of that offspring, so it is likewise with the wives of others.
Those who possess seeds but do not own a field, yet sow them in another's field,
never obtain any fruit of the crop that is produced.
If a bull were to beget a hundred calves upon the cows of others, those calves belong only to the owners of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit.
But when no reward is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs clearly to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed.
But when this [seed] is given for the purpose of sowing because of an agreement regarding the labor,
both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in the crop.
If seed carried by the current of a flood sprouts in someone’s field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit.
This law regarding the offspring of cattle, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood.
Thus has been declared to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter I shall proclaim the duty of women in times of distress.
The wife of an elder brother is the teacher’s wife for the younger;
but the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law for the elder. (Manu Smṛti 9.57)

An elder brother who approaches the wife of a younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of an elder brother— even if they have been authorized to do so— become outcasts, unless there be a state of distress.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring.
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent, shall procreate a single son at night; he must by no means procreate a second.
Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [duty],
seeing that the purpose of the appointment (niyoga) for those two is not fulfilled according to dharma.
When the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been accomplished according to the rule,
the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.
If those two, being appointed, should act according to their own will, disregarding the prescribed rule,
they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal dharma.
Nowhere in the mantras used for marriage is "authorization" (niyoga) mentioned;
nor, furthermore, is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies.
For this practice, which is a mere custom of beasts, was censured by learned brahmins even when Vena was ruling the kingdom of men.
In former times, that most excellent of royal sages, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social orders because his mind was struck by lust.
From that time forward, virtuous men censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring.
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall marry her according to this rule.
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she who is clothed in white garments and observes pure vows—
they should unite with one another once each during her fertile seasons until conception occurs.
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of falsehood regarding a human being.
Even after having accepted her according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon a bride who is blameworthy,
diseased, severely corrupted, or one who was presented through deception.
But if one should bestow a girl who has defects without having disclosed them,
he shall render that gift void for that evil-minded giver of the bride.
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for the maintenance of his wife;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live observing the prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should maintain herself by means of blameless crafts.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be waited for eight years;
if for the sake of knowledge or fame, six years; but if for the sake of pleasure, three years.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who shows him hostility;
but after a year has passed, he may take back her property and cease to live with her.
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, barren, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the inheritance for her.
A wife who drinks liquor, is of bad conduct, or is hostile;
or one who is diseased, injurious, or constantly wasteful of wealth, may indeed be superseded by another wife.
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately.
But a wife who is sickly, yet endowed with kindness and virtuous conduct, may be superseded by another only after she has been informed; she must never be treated with contempt.
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, goes out from the house in anger,
must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family.
If a woman, though forbidden, should nevertheless drink liquor even on festive occasions, or should go to a public spectacle or assembly, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
If twice-born men should marry women of their own caste as well as of other castes,
seniority, honor, and the principal dwelling shall belong to them according to the order of their castes.

The wife alone shall perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [the deceased husbands]; never, under any circumstances, may one who is not of the same caste do so.
But he who, out of delusion, causes that [rite] to be performed by another woman of the same caste who is already established [in marriage],
is indeed a Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla, just as previously described.
To one who is eminent, handsome, excellent, and worthy,
he should give his daughter according to the prescribed rule, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age.
A maiden may remain in her father's house even after reaching puberty until her death,
but he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may seek a husband of equal status.
If she should obtain a husband on her own initiative when not being given away in marriage,
she incurs no sin, nor does he whom she obtains.
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself the ornaments given by her father, her mother, or her brother; if she should take them, she would be a thief.
One who takes a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his rightful authority.
A man thirty years of age should marry a charming girl twelve years old,
or one twenty-four years old an eight-year-old, if he is in haste to fulfill his religious duty.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
he should always support her, being virtuous, while performing what is pleasing to the gods.
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both husband and wife.
If the giver of the bride-price should die after the price has been paid for a maiden,
she should be given to his brother-in-law, provided that the maiden consents.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not accept a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, he effects a concealed sale of his daughter.
But this is what neither others nor other virtuous men have ever done:
that after promising something to one person, it is given again to another.
For we have never heard of such a thing, even among our ancestors in former births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
Let there be mutual fidelity until death;
this, in brief, should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife.
Likewise, a man and a woman who have performed their rites should always strive so that,
even when separated from one another, they do not violate their mutual fidelity.
This law concerning men and women, together with the rules for sexual pleasure, has been declared to you;
as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress—now learn the law of inheritance.
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive.
The eldest alone, however, shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the remaining brothers shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of a son and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, that son deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off debts and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as born of desire.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father.
The eldest son causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder is like a mother and like a father;
but he who does not behave as an elder is to be honored merely like a kinsman.
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma.
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods;
half of that shall belong to the middle son, and a fourth to the youngest.
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall receive the middle portion of the wealth.
The eldest brother shall take the best of all kinds of property, as well as whatever is particularly excellent; moreover, he may receive one choice item from each ten.
There is no share-out for those who have performed their own duties among ten;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the elder as a means of increasing his honor.
Thus, when an extra portion has been set aside, one should assign equal shares;
but when no such portion has been set aside, this following shall be the distribution of shares for them.
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the one born after him, one and a half shares;
and each younger brother shall take one share—thus is the law established.
But the brothers shall each separately give to their unmarried sisters a fourth part from their own respective shares; those who are unwilling to give would become outcasts.
He should never divide goats, sheep, and one-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that an unequal division of goats and sheep may be made for the eldest alone.
If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law.
Subordination to the principal is not logically consistent with dharma;
the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him according to dharma.
If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in a case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife: // Mn_9.122 //
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall then receive bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull as his special share and sixteen [other shares] from the remainder;
thereafter, the rest shall divide according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority based on the mother; seniority is said to be determined by birth [order].
Even in the Subrahmaṇyā liturgical formulas, it is recorded that the invocation is made according to birth-order;
and among twins conceived simultaneously, seniority is declared to be determined by birth.
A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter his appointed daughter (*putrikā*), with the agreement:
"Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs the ancestral offerings for me."
In former times, Dakṣa himself, the lord of creatures, created these daughters according to this rule for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
With a joyful heart, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them all.
As one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take away the wealth?
Whatever may be the separate property of the mother, that indeed is the share of the unmarried daughter;
and the son of the daughter (dauhitra) alone shall take the entire estate of a man who dies without sons.
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
In this world, there is no difference between a son’s son and a daughter’s son according to the law;
for both of them are born from the very body of their parents.
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without having borne a son,
her husband shall, without hesitation, take that wealth.

Whether she was formally appointed or not, whichever son a woman bears from a man of equal status, through that son the maternal grandfather becomes the possessor of a grandson; he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-existent One himself.
In this world, no distinction is found between a son's son and a daughter's son;
for the daughter's son also delivers him to the next world, just like a son's son.
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to her father’s father.
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives it to the wrong lineage.

Both the son born of an unauthorized woman and the son obtained from the brother-in-law of a woman who already has a son are unworthy of a share, as they are born of an adulterer and born of lust respectively.
Even if a man has procreated on an appointed woman,
a son born contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to the paternal inheritance, for he was begotten by one who has fallen from his status.

A son born to a woman appointed for that purpose is considered equal to a legitimate son of the body (aurasa); according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring.
He who takes charge of the wealth and the wife of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him.
If a woman, being appointed by another, obtains a son from her brother-in-law or another [kinsman],
they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and begotten in vain.
This rule for the division [of inheritance] among those born of a single womb should be understood;
now learn that which applies to those born of many wives of different castes.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the prescribed order of castes,
this rule for partition is ordained when sons are born to them.
A ploughman, a bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house—
these should be given to the Brahmin as his preferential share (oddhārika), along with one principal portion from the remainder.
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa should take three shares, the son of a Kṣatriya two shares,
the son born of a Vaiśya one and a half shares, and the son of a Śūdra should take one share.
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous partition according to this rule.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
Even if he has a virtuous son or even no son at all,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra wife.
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya does not inherit property;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste to twice-born men shall,
after giving a preferential share (uddhāra) to the eldest, divide the remainder equally.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other;
those born of her shall have equal shares, even if there be a hundred sons.
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has mentioned for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, and six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the bought son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a bad boat obtains such a result,
so does one who attempts to cross the darkness [of rebirth] with bad sons obtain such a result.
If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are joint heirs,
each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other.
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of avoiding cruelty toward the others, he should provide them with a means of subsistence.
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share.
The son begotten on one's own wife and the son born of the wife of another are both entitled to share in the paternal inheritance;
however, ten other types of sons, in their respective order, are entitled to share in the family name and a portion of the estate.
But that son whom one should procreate oneself in one's own wedded wife, prepared for conception, one should know as the legitimate (aurasa) son, belonging to the first age.
The son born on the bed of a man who has died, or who is impotent, or diseased, through a woman duly appointed according to the sacred law, is known as the *kṣetraja* (son of the wife).
If, in times of distress, the mother or the father should give a son who is similar [to themselves] with water and with affection, he is to be known as a "given" (dattrima) son.
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the "adopted" (kṛtrima) son.
But he who is born in the house and whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he shall belong to him by whose wife he was begotten.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha* (cast-off).
But the son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father's house, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born from the maiden and belongs to the man who marries her.
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the husband;
such a son is called "sahoḍha" (one taken with the bride).
If one should purchase from his mother or father a son for the sake of offspring,
that son is his "bought" (krītaka) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [in status].
A woman who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces offspring through her own will after marrying again, is called *paunarbhava*.
If she is still a virgin, or even if she has returned after having left,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with a husband who is her second husband.
One who, being deprived of his parents or abandoned by them without cause,
offers himself to someone, is known as a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) son.
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may procreate through lust upon a Śūdra woman is called a Pāraśava, because he is like a corpse (śava) even while still alive.
If a son is born to a Śūdra by a female slave or the female slave of a slave, he may, with permission, take a share; such is the established law.
The wise declare these eleven sons, beginning with the son of the wife (kṣetraja) as previously described, to be substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as being born from the seed of others belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else.
Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son.
If among all the wives who have but one husband, one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
In the absence of a more worthy person, one who is less worthy is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, they all share the inheritance.
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons, are the heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall the brothers.
Water must be offered to three; the funeral cake (piṇḍa) proceeds for three;
the fourth is the giver to them; a fifth is not possible.
The property of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda;
after him, it shall go to a sakulya, or else to the teacher, or even to the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; thus the law is not violated.
The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; this is the settled rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take their property when no heirs exist.
For one who has died childless, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage;
whatever property there may be, that one should bestow upon him.
But if two [sons] born of two [different men] should dispute over the wealth of their mother,
each shall take what belonged to his own father, and not the other.
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally.
To those who may be their daughters, something from the maternal grandmother's wealth should also be given with affection, according to what is appropriate for each.

What is given before the nuptial fire, what is received from the father's house, and what is given as a token of affection; that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
That which was given as a post-nuptial gift (anvādheya), and that which was given by a husband who is well-pleased,
shall be the property of the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.

Whatever property exists in marriages according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites, it is ordained that upon the death of the wife without offspring, it belongs to the husband alone.
Whatever property may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that upon her death childless, it shall belong to her mother and father.
Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her daughter, or to her offspring.
Women should not make a disposal from the household property held in common with many others,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their caste.
Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.
However, it is right for a wise man to give to all of them food and clothing according to his ability; for he who does not give becomes an outcast.
If, however, eunuchs and others should somehow have a desire for wives,
their offspring, having produced progeny, shall be entitled to the inheritance.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after his father has died,
the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning.
But if all the unlearned [sons] should acquire wealth through their own efforts,
the rule is that there shall be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property.
But whatever is his wealth acquired through learning shall belong to him alone;
the same applies to what is received from a friend, what is given at marriage, and what is offered with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth,
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.
That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained by one's own effort, he is not obliged to give away unless he so desires.
But if a father should acquire ancestral property that was previously unobtained,
he need not share it with his sons against his own will, as it was acquired by himself.
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that instance.
If the eldest or the youngest is deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them dies, his portion is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having come together and being united, shall divide that property equally,
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall forfeit his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings.

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should the eldest brother make a separate acquisition for himself without giving a portion to the younger ones.
If there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who have not divided their inheritance,
the father must under no circumstances allot unequal shares to their sons.
But one born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all of that they shall divide equally.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security of possession, and pasture land are declared to be indivisible.

This division of property and the rule for the performance of rites for sons—beginning with the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the others—has been declared to you; now learn the law concerning gambling.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the destruction of kings who rule the earth.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called gambling (dyūta) in the world;
but that which is performed with animate beings should be known as betting (samāhvaya).
The king shall execute all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the emblems of the twice-born.
Gamblers, actors, cruel men, those who adhere to heretical sects,
those engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers— he shall quickly banish from the city.
Existing in the kingdom as secret thieves of the king,
these people constantly afflict the virtuous subjects through their improper conduct.
In a former age, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whether secretly or openly, whatever man should practice such [forbidden acts],
there shall be a discretionary punishment for him according to the king's will.
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra caste who is unable to pay a fine shall discharge the debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it back gradually, little by little.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king shall administer punishment with a whip, a split bamboo cane, a rope, or similar means.
But those who, having been appointed to duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth, the king shall render them destitute.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies.
Whatever has been decided and adjudicated anywhere, one should know that to be established according to dharma; it shall not be overturned again.
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly,
the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
And for these four who do not perform expiation,
he shall prescribe a lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.

For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag; for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
For they shall be excluded from communal meals, excluded from sacrifices, excluded from Vedic recitation, and excluded from marriage;
wretched and cast out from all religious duties, they shall wander the earth.
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives;
they shall be without compassion and without salutation—such is the command of Manu.
