But those of all castes who perform the prescribed expiation as ordained shall not have a mark branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement must be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his property and his belongings.
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they committed them intentionally, they deserve banishment.
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt.
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he may present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
but the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Where the king avoids receiving wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time with long lives.
And the crops of the people ripen according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and nothing deformed is born.
But a king should slay with various terrifying means of execution that person of low caste who, out of lust, oppresses Brāhmaṇas.
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; but merit accrues to him who restrains [the wicked].
Thus has been declared in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties engaged in mutual dispute across the eighteen titles of law.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with the Dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet won and protect those already acquired.
But one who has properly settled in a location and constructed a fortress according to the treatises should always exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to heaven.
But that king who collects taxes without punishing thieves,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven.
But that kingdom which is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered.
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who act openly and those who act in secret.
Those who live by various kinds of merchandise are "open deceivers," while those such as thieves and forest-dwellers are "concealed deceivers."

Those who take bribes, those who practice fraud, cheats, gamblers, those who live by predicting auspicious events, fortune-tellers, and those who examine the bodily marks [of men and women]— all these are to be avoided.
Likewise, high officials who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of crafts, and clever courtesans [should be avoided].
One should recognize such manifest thorns of the world,
as well as others who move in disguise— ignoble men wearing the marks of the noble.
Having identified them through secret agents who follow good conduct and perform their duties,
and through spies in various disguises, he should uproot them and bring them under his control.

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king shall duly administer punishment based on the nature of the offense and the status of the person.
For indeed, without punishment,
it is impossible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who harbor evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles—these are [places to be avoided].
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans, empty houses, groves, and pleasure-gardens; Mn 9.265.
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military units, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
He should discover them through their accomplices who follow them and are familiar with their various activities,
and he should eliminate them by means of clever former thieves.
They should bring about their meeting by means of instructions regarding food and drink, by visits to Brāhmaṇas, and under the pretext of discussing deeds of heroism.
Those who do not approach him there, as well as those who have been instigated from the root,
the king shall forcibly slay, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen property;
however, he may execute one caught with the stolen goods and the tools [of the crime] without hesitation.
Moreover, those in the villages who provide food to thieves,
as well as those who give them shelter for their goods— all of them he shall cause to be executed.

In the territories, he should swiftly punish those appointed to protect the realm and the vassal chiefs who have been exhorted [to act], if they remain neutral during attacks, just as one punishes thieves.
Moreover, even one who lives by the Dharma but has fallen away from the covenant of the Dharma should be scorched with punishment alone, for he has strayed from his own duty.

Those who do not run to the aid of others to the best of their ability when a village is being plundered, when a well is being destroyed, or when a robbery is seen on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings.
He shall cause those who steal the king’s treasury, those who stand in opposition to him,
and those who instigate his enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment.
But those thieves who, having broken through a wall, commit robbery at night— the king,
having cut off their hands, should impale them on a sharp stake.
In the first offense, one who breaks a seal should have his fingers amputated;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
The king should punish those who provide fire, food, weapons,
or shelter to thieves, as well as those who facilitate their theft, just like the thief himself.
One who destroys a tank should be killed, or else executed by drowning in water;
or, if he repairs it, he should be made to pay the highest fine.
One should execute without hesitation those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established,
or cuts off the flow of water, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
He who, except in times of distress, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity.
Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child deserve only a verbal reprimand, and that [offense] must be purified; such is the settled rule.
For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement for offenses against non-human beings, but the middle amercement for those against human beings.
One who breaks down the archways, flagstaffs,
or images shall repair all of that damage and pay five hundred panas as a fine.
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods,
as well as for their breaking or the false boring of gems, the punishment is the first amercement.
For a man who deals unfairly with those who are equal, whether by measure or by price,
shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement.
And the king should establish all prisons along the road,
where those who have committed evil deeds may be seen suffering and disfigured.
One should immediately banish the breaker of a rampart, the filler of moats, and the destroyer of gates.
In all cases of malevolent incantations, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for root-magic, and for various kinds of sorcery, until the perpetrator is apprehended.
One who sells seeds, one who steals seeds from the field,
and likewise one who violates a boundary, shall suffer the punishment of mutilation.
But the king shall cause a goldsmith who is most wicked among all thorns and who practices injustice to be cut into pieces with razors.
In cases of the theft of Sītā (grain), goods, weapons, or medicine,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Among these seven constituents of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one is more serious and its misfortune more grave.
In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels another because of the specific excellence of their mutual qualities.
In various specific tasks, however, one particular limb excels;
whichever part accomplishes a given purpose is said to be the most excellent for that task.
Through his movements, through the application of energy, and through the very performance of his duties,
the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain both his own strength and the strength of his enemies.
Having reflected upon the gravity or lightness of all oppressions as well as calamities, he should then undertake his task.
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.
When asleep, he is the Kali age; when awake, he is the Dvāpara age;
when intent upon his duties, he is the Tretā age; but when moving about, he is the Kṛta age.
A king should conduct himself with the splendor and conduct of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and the Earth. (Manu Smṛti 9.303)
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should he who observes the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should the king take taxes from his kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun.
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves about within them, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-like" vow (māruta-vrata).
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should he restrain the wicked; for this is indeed the Vāruṇa vow.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow (*cāndravrata*).
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, ever intent on evil deeds against wicked vassals, and a destroyer of them— that is known as the Agneya vow.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so too does the king who upholds the duty of a ruler support all beings.
Employing these and other means, always vigilant,
the king should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in those of others.
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke the Brāhmaṇas;
for they, when enraged, could destroy him instantly, along with his army and his vehicles.
By whom was fire made to consume all things, the great ocean rendered undrinkable, and the moon made to wane and wax—who would not perish by provoking them? (Mn 9.314)
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked to anger, might create other worlds and other guardians of the world, and turn gods into non-gods? (Manu 9.315)
Who, desiring to live, would harm those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, and for whom Brahman itself is their wealth? (Manu 9.316)
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like the fire, which is a great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
rather, when oblations are offered into it at sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable occupations,
Brahmins are in every way worthy of honor, for they are the supreme deity.
When the Kṣatriya power has become excessively overbearing in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇical power alone shall be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
Neither does the Kṣatriya power prosper without the Brāhmaṇical power, nor does the Brāhmaṇical power flourish without the Kṣatriya power;
when the Brāhmaṇical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next.
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle.
Acting thus and ever intent upon the duties of kingship as well as the welfare of the world, the monarch should employ all his servants.
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order.
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the sacraments and taken a wife,
should be constantly engaged in agriculture and commerce, as well as in the protection of cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya should not entertain the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
One should know the relative value of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven fabrics,
perfumes, and liquids.
He should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the soil;
he should also understand the application of measures and all the applications of weights.
He should consider the worth and worthlessness of merchandise, the merits and defects of various regions,
the profit and loss on commodities, and the proper rearing of livestock.
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their purchase and sale.
He should exert the greatest effort to increase his wealth through righteous means,
and he should diligently provide food for all living beings.
For a Śūdra, however, the service of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious, is indeed the highest dharma leading to supreme beatitude.
Pure, devoted to the highest service, gentle in speech, free from egoism,
and always taking refuge in Brahmins and the like, one attains a superior birth.
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them even in times of distress.
The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound [the Veda], and not the other two.
The Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others, and he himself should likewise act accordingly.
On account of his distinction, the excellence of his origin, his observance of the rules,
and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth, however, is once-born, the Śūdra; there is no fifth.
Among wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity,
those born in the direct order [of castes] are to be known as belonging to that very same caste.
Sons begotten by the twice-born on women born immediately after them in the social order are said to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this to be the righteous rule for those born of women two or three degrees lower.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Śūdra is born a Niṣāda, who is also called a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Śūdra is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.

These six are declared to be base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin woman by men of the three [lower] castes, those born from a Kṣatriya woman by men of two [lower] castes, and those born from a Vaiśya woman by a man of one [lower] caste.
From a Kṣatriya on the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a Sūta is born by birth;
from a Vaiśya [on the daughters of a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa], a Māgadha and a Vaideha are born as the sons of a king and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.
From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men— through the intermixture of castes.
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and the Ugra are declared to arise from a one-removal (ekāntara) union in the natural order,
so too do the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka arise from a one-removal union in the inverse order of birth.
Those sons of twice-born men who are born of women of the next lower caste, as described in due order,
are designated by the name "anantara" (next-in-order) because of the inferiority of their mothers.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra; and from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra in the reverse order of castes.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone is born.
These others are also the three base-born (apasada) sons who are produced in the inverse order.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pukkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka.
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhī woman is called a Veṇa.
Those whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances and excluded from the Sāvitrī, one should designate as Vrātyas.
From a Vratya Brahmin, however, are born the evil-natured Bhurjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.
From a Kṣatriya Vratya are born the Jhalla, the Malla, the Nicchivi,
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khaśa, and the Draviḍa.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Through the violation of caste rules, through the marrying of those who should not be married,
and through the abandonment of one's own prescribed duties, the intermixture of castes arises.
I shall now describe in their entirety those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural unions, as well as those who are mutually intermingled.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Āyogava, and the Kṣattṛ caste.
These six beget similar castes upon women of their own kind;
they also procreate offspring upon women of the mother's caste and upon women of higher castes.
Just as for the three castes, a son is born from two [wives] of his own [caste] through immediate succession, so too is the order among the outsiders (bāhya).
And they also procreate upon the wives of others many outsiders, even more corrupted than themselves, who are despised by one another.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste child upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, so does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste upon a woman of the four castes.
Acting in opposition to their own kind, those who are outsiders beget yet more outsiders; being low, they give birth to even lower castes—indeed, fifteen such castes in all.
From a Dasyu and an Ayogava woman is born a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply cosmetics and personal adornments, who is not a slave yet lives like one, and subsists by means of snares.
The Vaideha begets a Maitreyaka from a Mādhūka woman;
he is one who incessantly praises men and strikes a bell at the break of dawn.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those who dwell in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.
These three distinct, outcaste groups are born from Āyogava women who wear the clothes of the dead and consume despised food.
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born, who is a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehika are born the Āndhra and Meda, whose dwellings are outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pukkasa woman, is born the sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-digging and is always despised by virtuous people.
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman gives birth to a son called an Antyāvasāyin,
who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system.
These castes resulting from intermixture, as shown according to their fathers and mothers,
are to be known by their respective occupations, whether they are concealed or manifest.
Six sons born of women of their own caste or of those immediately below it possess the status of the twice-born;
however, all those born of women further removed are declared to be of the same nature as Śūdras, being born of a violation of the law.
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age.
But by the gradual neglect of sacred rites and by the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya tribes have fallen to the state of Śūdras in this world.
The Pauṇḍrakas, Auḍras, Draviḍas, Kāmbojas, Yavanas, Śakas,
Pāradas, Pahlavas, Cīnas, Kirātas, Daradas, and Khaśas.
Those castes in the world who are outside those born from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet—
whether they speak the speech of barbarians or the speech of the Aryas— are all remembered as Dasyus.
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of a violation of the natural order,
shall subsist by means of the despised occupations of the twice-born themselves.
For Sūtas, the management of horses and chariots; for Ambaṣṭhas, the practice of medicine;
for Vaidehakas, service to women; and for Māgadhas, the way of trade.
The killing of fish is the occupation of the Niṣādas, while that of the Āyogava is carpentry;
and the slaughter of wild animals is the work of the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.
For the Kṣattragus, Pukkasas, and Bilaukovas, their livelihoods are killing and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, working with leather; and for the Veṇas, playing drums.
These known [Vrātyas], subsisting by their own occupations, may dwell at sacred shrines, near trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves.
The dwellings of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, however, must be outside the village;
they are to be made outcaste from the community of the twice-born, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead; their food shall be from broken dishes;
their ornament shall be black iron; and they must constantly lead a life of wandering mendicancy.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them;
their mutual dealings and marriages should be with their own equals.
Their food, dependent on others, should be given to them in a separate vessel;
they must not wander about in villages or cities at night.
They may go about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the funeral of a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the settled rule.
They shall constantly execute those condemned to death by the king's command in accordance with the scriptures;
they shall also take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of the executed.
One should discern by their own actions a man who has fallen from his caste, who is unrecognizable, and born of a defiled womb— an ignoble man appearing in the form of a noble one.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty,
and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world a man born from a defiled womb.
He inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or indeed both;
however, one born of a low womb cannot in any way suppress his own innate nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there is a confusion of birth (yonisaṃkara),
that man will surely adopt the conduct of those [of mixed origin], whether to a small or great extent.
But that kingdom where these corrupters of the social orders are born from promiscuity, along with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly.

The self-sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or a cow, or for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those of the outer castes, provided it is performed without seeking reward.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of the duty for the four castes.
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with a superior man,
he attains the higher caste of his progenitor by the seventh generation.
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise descends to the status of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father to a non-Aryan mother, and one born from a non-Aryan father to a Brāhmaṇī mother?"—Mn_10.66.
A son born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan by his qualities;
however, one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is certainly a non-Aryan—this is the settled rule.
The law is established that both of these are ineligible for the sacraments:
the former because of the deficiency of their birth, and the latter because of being born in the inverse order.
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition,
so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement.
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established rule is as follows: // Mn_10.70 //
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
Since sages born of animal wombs became honored and praised by virtue of the power of their seed, therefore the seed is highly esteemed.
Having considered one who is ignoble but performs noble deeds, and one who is noble but performs ignoble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Those Brāhmaṇas who abide in the womb of Brahman and remain steadfast in their own duties should properly subsist by means of the six occupations in their proper order.
Teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.
It is the established rule that these [prohibitions] should likewise cease with respect to a Vaiśya;
for Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them.
The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya.
But the duty [of all] for the sake of subsistence consists of giving, study, and sacrifice.
The study of the Vedas is the distinguished duty among one's own duties for a Brāhmaṇa, protection for a Kṣatriya,
and the occupation of trade and agriculture for a Vaiśya.
But if a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own aforementioned duty,
he may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the one immediately next to him.
But if he should find it impossible to live by either of these two, how should he act? He may indeed live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing.
Even if he must live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and depends upon others.
People consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and the creatures dwelling within it.
But for one who, due to a deficiency of livelihood, abandons his skill in the Dharma,
this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth, provided that the choice pieces have been extracted.
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, domestic animals, and human beings.
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as hemp, linen, and woolen fabrics—
even if they are undyed— as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all types of perfumes;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass.
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals.
Having himself produced them through agriculture,
a farmer may sell sesamum seeds of inferior quality for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long.
If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or as an ointment,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors.
One falls immediately from one's caste by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brahmin becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk.
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal.
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into distress may live by all these means,
yet he must never at any time take pride in a livelihood superior to his own.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed,
the king, having deprived him of his wealth, shall banish him immediately.
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another;
for by living according to the duty of another, one immediately falls from one's caste.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may also live by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided that he does not perform forbidden acts and, when capable, desists from such improper conduct.
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born and has fallen into distress regarding his wife and children may live by the crafts of artisans.
Those occupations of artisans and various crafts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are [the duties of the Vaiśya].
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path,
should practice this duty when he is distressed by the lack of a livelihood and is suffering.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
it is not logically consistent with dharma to say that his purifier becomes defiled thereby.
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or accepting gifts— even from censurable sources— for they are like fire and water.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not defiled by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
Desiring to eat dog-meat when distressed, Vāmadeva— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— did not defile himself, for the sake of preserving his life.
But Bharadvāja, a man of great asceticism, being afflicted by hunger in a lonely forest along with his sons,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Between accepting gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching,
the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured for a Brahmin after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are performed constantly by those who have been consecrated;
however, the acceptance of gifts is performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth.
Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
but that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renunciation and by austerity.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from anywhere;
gleaning ears of corn is better than receiving gifts, and picking up individual grains is praised even more than that.
A lord of the earth should be entreated by Snātaka Brahmins who are sinking, desiring base metals, or seeking wealth; if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.

From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, from a non-cultivated field, one may take prepared grain, cattle, goats, sheep, gold, grain, or food; among these, each preceding item is less objectionable than the one following it.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Learning, craftsmanship, labor for hire, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, they may at will give even a small amount to a sinner.
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he may collect the lawful tribute.
The toll on grain for the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide services, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [are subject to this].
But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, may serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek to maintain himself.
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both worlds, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose.
Service to the Brahmins alone is declared to be the distinguished duty of the Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him.
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family resources as is appropriate,
having regard for their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they maintain.
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments,
the shriveled grain of the harvest, and old household utensils.
For a Śūdra there is no sin whatsoever, nor does he deserve any sacramental rite;
he has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against dharma for him.
But those who desire righteousness, who know the dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous,
do not incur sin by doing so— provided they omit the sacred mantras— and they even receive praise.
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides by virtuous conduct,
in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the next.
For even a Śūdra who is capable should not accumulate wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by properly performing them, they attain the supreme goal.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rule for expiation.

One who belongs to a lineage of sacrificers, one who is about to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one who seeks wealth for the sake of his teacher, for the sake of his father or mother, one seeking wealth for Vedic study, and one who is afflicted by illness. (Manu 11.1)
One should indeed know those Snātakas who are Brāhmaṇas seeking alms for the sake of dharma;
gifts should be given to these destitute ones according to the excellence of their learning.
For food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial enclosure (bahirvedi).
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas as is appropriate, and likewise provide sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice.
He who, having already taken a wife, obtains another by begging her, gains only the fruit of pleasure; the progeny, however, belongs to the giver of the wealth.
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and live in seclusion according to one's ability; thus, after death, one enjoys heaven.
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, that twice-born man who drinks Soma when the substance is very small,
even if he has previously drunk Soma, does not obtain its fruit.
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery—this is a mere semblance of dharma; it is like drinking honey with a taste of poison at the end.
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death.
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the absence of even a single constituent part—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, while a righteous king is in power— then [the following applies].
If there be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of completing a sacrifice.
He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for a Śūdra has no proprietary right over anything in sacrifices.
If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—
one may take [food] from the households of even these two without hesitation.
One may take from a non-giver who is habitually acquisitive;
in this way, his fame spreads and his merit increases.
Likewise, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one may take food from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found,
one must inform that person who asks, provided he does indeed ask.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he may take the property of a Dasyu or one who neglects his religious duties if he cannot otherwise subsist.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and carries both across.
The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods;
however, the wealth of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of the asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him,
for it is through the folly of a Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa suffers from hunger.
Having ascertained his dependents and his own family members, and having recognized their learning and character, the lord of the earth should provide them with a righteous means of subsistence.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from one thus protected, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit of righteousness.
A Brahmin should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the purpose of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who has begged thus is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the purpose of a sacrifice, does not give it all away,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of a Brahmin—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures.

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the sake of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.
If a twice-born man performs a religious duty by means of a substitute rite when no such occasion for it exists, he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter; so it has been determined.
By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great seers,
when they were afraid of death in times of distress, a substitute for the sacred law was established.
He who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary rule, gains no fruit pertaining to the hereafter; such is the case for that man of perverted intellect.
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king regarding those human disciples who have done him harm; he should deal with them by his own power alone.
Between one's own effort and the effort of a king, one's own effort is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own effort alone.
One should employ the hymns of the Atharva-Angirases without hesitation;
for the weapon of a Brahmin is indeed speech, and with that a twice-born man may slay his enemies.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by their wealth; but the best of the twice-born by means of silent recitation and burnt offerings.
One who is a provider, a ruler, a speaker, and friendly is called a Brāhmaṇa;
one should not speak what is unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, shall be the officiating priest for the Agnihotra.
For these fall into hell while offering oblations, as does he for whom they offer;
therefore, the officiating priest (hotṛ) should be skilled in the sacrificial ritual and one who has mastered the Vedas.

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, fails to give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he remains one who has not established the fires. (Manu 11.38)
One who is faithful and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should by no means perform sacrifices in this world with meager sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with small sacrificial fees destroys one's senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
If a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should abandon those fires out of his own will, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice,
are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
Trampling with his foot the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the *vṛṣala*, the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and is addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to penance.
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some say it is also required for one committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scripture.
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.
Having incurred the necessity of penance, whether by fate or by his own past actions,
a twice-born man shall not associate with the virtuous as long as that penance remains unperformed.
In this world, some wicked-souled men undergo a transformation of their physical form due to their current misconduct, while others do so because of what they have done in the past.
A thief of gold incurs deformed nails; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the bed of his teacher, a skin disease.
A slanderer shall have a putrid nose; an informer, a foul-smelling mouth;
a stealer of grain, a deficiency of limbs; and one who adulterates goods, an excess of limbs.
The stealer of food suffers from chronic disease; the stealer of speech, from dumbness;
the stealer of clothing, from leucoderma; and the stealer of a horse, from lameness.
Thus, by the particularity of their actions, they are born censured by the virtuous—
stupid, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.
Therefore, one must always perform penance for the sake of purification;
for those whose sins are not expiated are born with despicable physical marks.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—
they call these the great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them.
False testimony regarding one's own excellence, malicious slander directed at the king,
and persistent falsehood toward a teacher are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Abandoning Brahmanas, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend,
eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.

They consider the emission of semen into women who are one's own female relatives, into virgins, into women of the lowest castes, and into the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the bed of a guru.

Killing a cow, officiating at a sacrifice for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, selling oneself, abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, sacred study, the sacred fires, or one's son; Mn 11.59 [58M]

The elder brother remaining unmarried while the younger is married is *parivitti*, and the younger brother marrying before the elder is *parivettṛ*; the giving away of the girl to either of them, and officiating at their sacrifice, are likewise [forbidden].
Violating a maiden, usury, the breaking of a vow, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child; Mn 11.61 [60M].
The state of being a *vrātya*, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages, receiving instruction from a servant, and the sale of goods that ought not to be sold; Mn 11.62 [61M]

Exercising authority over all forms of work, operating large mechanical contrivances, dealing in harmful medicinal herbs, living off women, performing malevolent incantations, and performing root-rites (mūlakarma).
Felling green trees for the sake of fuel, undertaking activities solely for one's own benefit, and likewise eating censured food; Mn 11.64 [63M]
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts, studying wicked treatises, and the practice of the arts of the stage; Mn 11.65.
The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; associating with women who drink liquor;
killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).
Causing pain to a Brahmin, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats,
sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from those who are censured, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths should be known as acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa).
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
Now learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins, each individually, are expiated.
A killer of a Brāhmaṇa, having constructed a hut, shall dwell in the forest for twelve years for the sake of self-purification,
subsisting on alms and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
Or he may become a target for weapon-wielders at his own will;
or, with his head hanging down, he may throw himself three times into a blazing fire.
Or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or, for the expiation of the murder of a Brahmin, he may travel one hundred yojanas to Japan or another [holy place], eating sparingly and with his senses restrained.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas—
be it wealth sufficient for a livelihood or a house together with its furnishings.
Or, subsisting on sacrificial food, he should follow the Sarasvatī upstream;
or, with his diet restricted, he should recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village,
or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should immediately sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or of a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Or he who has resisted [the king] three times, or having seized all the property of a Brahmin, or when his life was at stake on that account, is released from [the sin].
Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly chaste, and concentrated,
removes the guilt of killing a Brahmin at the completion of the twelfth year.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods on earth (the Brahmins) at an assembly of kings,
he is liberated from it after bathing at the concluding rite (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya its summit;
therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified.
By his very birth, he is the deity even of the gods;
he is indeed the authority for the world, for Brahmā alone is the cause in this matter.
Those three who know the Vedas shall declare for them a complete expiation for the offense;
that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying.
Therefore, by adhering to any one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin removes the sin committed through the killing of a Brahmin through his self-control.

Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows the Veda, or a woman who has bathed after her courses.
Having given false testimony, having obstructed a preceptor, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; Mn 11.88.
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for killing a Brāhmaṇa intentionally, no atonement is prescribed.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he shall drink liquor that is the color of fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he may drink cow’s urine that is fire-colored, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung, until death.
Or, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, he shall eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks, and carrying a banner.
Surā is indeed the dregs of food, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā.
Sura is to be known as threefold: that distilled from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that from honey (mādhvī).
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
that must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation for the gods.
A Brāhmaṇa deluded by intoxication might fall into impurity, or recite the Veda, or perform some other improper act. (Manu 11.96)
He whose Brahmanical nature, residing within his body, is once drenched by liquor—
his status as a Brāhmaṇa departs, and he sinks to the state of a Śūdra.
This manifold expiation for drinking liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for stealing gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king and proclaimed his own deed, should say: "May Your Majesty punish me."
Taking up a pestle, the king himself shall strike the thief once;
by this execution the thief is purified, but a Brāhmaṇa thief is purified by austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove the impurity born of stealing gold by means of austerity,
shall wear rags and perform in the forest the penance prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall expel the sin of approaching the wife of his teacher by means of these same vows.
Having addressed the sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie upon a heated iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing iron image of a woman; by death, he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his own penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms,
he should walk straight toward the region of Nirṛti until he collapses.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard, in a solitary forest,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley gruel, in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows.
One who has killed a cow through a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at every fourth mealtime, and perform his bath using cow's urine.
By day he should follow those cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust raised by them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While [the others] stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should follow;
likewise, while they sit, he should sit, self-restrained and free from envy.
One should rescue by every possible means a woman who is afflicted by illness, or accursed, or threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen, or one stuck in the mud.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
One should not speak of a cow eating in one's own house, or in the field or threshing-floor of oneself or others, nor of a calf drinking.
But he who, following this rule, attends upon a cow as a killer of a cow,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.
Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka),
with the exception of one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), shall perform this same penance for the sake of purification, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa.
But one who has spilled his semen shall, at night, sacrifice a one-eyed donkey at a crossroads according to the procedure for a *pākayajña* to Nirṛti.
Having duly performed the oblations in the fire,
he should finally offer oblations of clarified butter with the verse [beginning with] "sam" to Vāta, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni.
Those who know the Dharma and expound the Veda declare that for a twice-born man observing a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The fourfold Brahmanic splendor of one who has violated his vow approaches Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka.
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go about for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day,
and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year.
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness to receive alms, the purification is the lunar penance (*aindava*) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
one-eighth for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, and it should be known as one-sixteenth for a Śūdra.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having observed his vow well, shall give a thousand cows with one bull.
Or, with his hair matted and remaining self-restrained, he shall perform for three years the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa,
dwelling far away from a village and making his home at the foot of a tree.
The best of the twice-born shall perform this very penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, and he shall also give one hundred and one cows.
A slayer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or he shall give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
or even a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one shall perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Or he should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana,
or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the waters (Ab-daivata).
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
For killing a boar, one must give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a curlew, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, a peacock,
a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should touch a cow and give it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for killing an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for killing a goat or a sheep, an ox; and for killing a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
having killed non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; and having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
Having killed women of the four castes who have not been consecrated, one should give, for the sake of purification, a bow of Jina, a bull, a goat, and a sheep, respectively.
If a twice-born man is unable to purify the slaughter of snakes and other such creatures through the gift of wealth,
he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate beings,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one shall perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
But for killing a boneless creature, one should give something to a Brahmin;
however, for injuring creatures that have bones, one is purified by a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for cutting shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete means of purification.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the penances] regarding the eating of forbidden food.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone; but for drinking it intentionally, the penance is beyond prescription—it results in the end of life—such is the settled rule.
Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for spirituous liquor or likewise in a container for wine,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rules,
or having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes purified by thrice suppressing his breath in water and consuming clarified butter.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the religious observances—
all these are discontinued for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Even after drinking fermented acids and astringent decoctions, though they are purifying, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [substance] has not passed downward.
Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth,
or meat from a slaughterhouse that was unknown [to be such], one should observe this very same penance.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, cocks, humans, crows, and donkeys,
the Taptakṛcchra penance is the means of purification.
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher's house should eat food given on the monthly ancestral offering (māsika),
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.
But a religious student who should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever must perform the ordinary Kṛcchra penance and then complete the remainder of his vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or those of a dog or a mongoose,
or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit to be eaten;
however, if it was consumed through ignorance, it should be vomited up or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites.
Thus has been declared the various rule for the vows regarding the eating of forbidden food;
now hear the rule for those vows which remove the guilt of theft.
Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
But for the abduction of human women, as well as for the seizure of fields,
houses, wells, tanks, or water, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification.
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house,
one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance and restore the property for the sake of self-purification.
For stealing food that is chewed or eaten, as well as vehicles, beds, seats, and flowers,
roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
cloth, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast for three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver,
iron, brass, or stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed and single-hoofed animals,
birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk for three days.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
but he shall expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these same vows.

Having discharged semen into women of his own lineage, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, one must perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed.
Having approached the daughter of his father’s sister, the daughter of his own sister, or the daughter of his mother’s brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives;
they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by marrying them he falls low.
Having discharged semen in non-human females, in a woman during her courses, in those not born from a womb, or in water, one shall perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance.
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman,
a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock-cart, in water, or during the daytime.

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or having eaten from them, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes their equal.
A husband should confine a wife who has become corrupted in a single room;
he should compel her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.
If, however, she should become defiled again after being approached by a man of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting sacred texts for three years.
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who have associated with outcasts.

One falls by associating for a year with one who has fallen, through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance; but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
Whichever among these a man associates with through a fallen act,
he must perform that very person's vow for the sake of purification from that association.
The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen from his caste outside the village on an inauspicious day,
in the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.
A female slave should overturn a water-pot full of water with her foot as if for a dead person;
the kinsmen, together with her, shall observe impurity for a day and a night.
From him, however, they must desist from conversation, sitting together,
the giving of inheritance, and even ordinary social intercourse.
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as shall the wealth obtainable by the eldest;
however, a younger brother who is superior in merit shall receive the share of the eldest.
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe in a sacred body of water and together with him cast a new pitcher full of water into it.
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the rites for his kinsmen as before.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they should dwell near the house.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins and have not been purified; yet, once they have undergone purification, one should never despise them.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they have been purified according to the law.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and being abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform expiation.
When Brahmins acquire wealth through a reprehensible action,
they become pure by relinquishing that wealth, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity.
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
But when he has returned from the cow-pasture, emaciated by fasting and bowing before them, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (Mn 11.195)
But having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
when the sacred bathing place has been opened by the cows, they should perform his formal reception there.
Having performed sacrifices for Vrātyas, having performed funeral rites for others,
or having practiced malevolent magic (abhicāra) and the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Having abandoned one who has sought refuge or having caused the Veda to be lost,
a twice-born man expiates that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Eating only at the sixth mealtime for a month, or the constant recitation of the Saṃhitā,
as well as all the regular burnt offerings, are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals.
Having mounted a camel-carriage or, out of desire, a donkey-carriage,
a Brahmin who has bathed while naked becomes pure through breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
If one is afflicted while away from water or even within water, having performed the bodily purification,
he becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow.
If one neglects the obligatory rites prescribed in the Vedas,
or violates the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" and an elder with "thou," one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and seek their favor by offering a respectful salutation.
Even after striking him with a blade of grass, or binding him by the neck with a garment,
or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by bowing down.
But by threatening a Brahmin, one enters hell for a hundred years; and by striking him with intent to kill, one enters it for a thousand years.
For as many particles of dust as the blood collects upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the shedder of it dwell in hell.
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.
But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
I shall describe to you those means, practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors, by which a human being removes his sins.
A twice-born man performing the Prājāpatya penance should eat food obtained unasked for three days in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should not eat at all.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a fast for one night— this is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance.
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat only a single morsel for three periods of three days each as before, and should fast for the final three days. (Manu 11.213)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind.
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is the penance known as Parāka; it removes all sins.
One should decrease the morsels of food by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase them during the bright fortnight;
performing ritual ablutions at the three periods of the day, this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, beginning with the bright fortnight and remaining self-restrained, should observe this entire procedure in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama variety.
Restraining his soul and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa should eat eight mouthfuls at midday when the sun has reached the meridian.
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, three hundred and sixty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in this manner over the course of a month, one attains the same world as the Moon.
The Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus,
together with the Maruts and the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
One should personally perform the fire-oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
Three times during the day and three times at night, he shall enter the water with his clothes on;
and he shall never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable to do so, he may lie on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of his vows, worshipping his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and other purificatory texts according to his ability;
for in all vows, one who is intent on expiation should act in this manner.
The twice-born whose sins have been made public shall be purified by these vows;
however, those whose crimes have not been disclosed, one should purify with sacred mantras and burnt offerings.
By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act,
confesses it, to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
To the extent that his mind reproaches his evil deed,
to that same extent his body is released from that unrighteousness.
For having committed a sin and felt remorse, one is released from that sin;
however, by the resolve "I shall not do this again," one is purified through abstention.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform auspicious deeds through his thoughts, words, and physical gestures.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable act,
one who seeks liberation from it should not commit it a second time.
If, after performing a particular action, there should be a lack of lightness in his mind,
he should perform penance for that act until it brings him satisfaction.
All happiness, whether divine or human, has austerity as its root;
it is declared by the wise who perceive the Vedas that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.
The austerity of a Brāhmaṇa is knowledge; the austerity of a Kṣatriya is protection;
the austerity of a Vaiśya is agriculture and trade; and the austerity of a Śūdra is service.
Sages who have restrained their selves, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air,
perceive the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, through austerity alone.
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of divine power—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is their means of attainment.
Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—
all this can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable.
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts,
are freed from that guilt by means of well-performed austerity alone.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven through the power of austerity.
Whatever sin people commit through their thoughts, words, or physical actions,
those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone.
The gods accept the sacrifices of a Brahmin purified by austerity alone, and they fulfill his desires.
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity.
Thus the gods proclaim this great majesty of austerity,
perceiving the supreme merit of all this austerity.
The daily study of the Vedas to the best of one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices,
and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes.
Just as fire, having reached its fuel, consumes it in an instant with its heat,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil by the fire of knowledge.
Thus has the expiation for these sins been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret offenses.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a fetus within a month.
By muttering the Kautsa hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the Vasiṣṭha verse beginning with "prati," the Māhitra hymn,
and the Śuddhavatī verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant.
By practicing the Haviṣpāntīya hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and by reciting the Puruṣasūkta, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from sin.
