Desiring the removal of gross and subtle sins,
one should mutter for a year either the verse beginning with "ava" or that beginning with "yat kiṃ cedam."
Having accepted what should not be accepted or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
But one who has committed many sins is purified by performing the Soma-Raudra rite for a month,
while practicing ritual bathing in a flowing river and reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with "aryamṇām."
One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "Indraḥ pramādāt" for half a year;
but having performed a blameworthy act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.
Having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras used for the Śakala-homa, a twice-born man destroys even very grave sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ."
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year and subsisting on alms-food, he becomes purified.
Or, having purified himself by three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest; he is liberated from all sins.
One who, being self-controlled, fasts for three days and approaches water three times a day,
is released from all sins by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
Even having slain these three worlds and eating [their inhabitants] from here and there,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
Having recited the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times, or the Yajurveda, or the Sāmaveda along with its secret portions, with a concentrated mind, one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does all evil conduct sink away when it reaches the threefold Veda.
The Rig-veda verses, the Yajus-formulas, and various other Saman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
That which is the primordial Brahman consisting of three syllables, in which the triple Veda is established—that other secret triple Veda is it; he who knows that is a knower of the Veda.
O sinless one, you have declared this entire dharma for the four social orders;
now tell us truly and in its highest form about the production of the fruits of actions.
The righteous Bhṛgu, son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire system of action."
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, yields auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
the destinies of men—superior, inferior, and middling—are born of action.
One should know that for this embodied being— who possesses these three types [of action], who has three bases, and who is endowed with ten characteristics— it is the mind that is the instigator.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— this threefold action is mental.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form,
and idle chatter— these constitute the fourfold nature of speech.
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the rules, and adultery with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [evil].
This person experiences the mental [karma], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind itself;
the action performed by speech through speech, and that which is bodily through the body alone.
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or beasts; and through those of the mind, to the status of a person of the lowest caste.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a "triple-staffed" ascetic (tridaṇḍin).
Having laid down this triple staff toward all beings and having restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.
That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise.
There is another inner self, distinct [from the body], known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
by means of it, one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout births.
Both of these—the Great Principle (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they remain pervading that which abides within high and low beings.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from those very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment.
Having experienced those tortures with the body here in the world of Yama,
they dissolve respectively back into those very same elemental constituents.
Having experienced the evils born of attachment to sense objects, which result in future suffering, he,
freed from impurity, approaches those same two of great splendor.
Together with him, those two unweariedly perceive both his merit and his sin,
by which he, when joined with them, attains happiness or misery both in this world and after death.
If he practices dharma for the most part and adharma only to a small degree,
he enjoys happiness in heaven, enveloped by those very same elements.
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and righteousness only slightly,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from defilement,
returns once again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.
Having observed with his own mind these destinies of the living being resulting from both righteousness and unrighteousness, he should always fix his mind upon righteousness.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self;
pervaded by these, the Great One (*mahat*) stands encompassing all these states without exception.
Whichever of these qualities predominates entirely within the body at any given time,
it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is traditionally held to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as associated with joy,
tranquil and appearing pure— that one should understand to be *sattva*.
But that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know that to be *rajas*, which is constantly carrying away embodied beings against their will.
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects,
inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
Furthermore, I shall describe in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— the highest, the middling, and the lowest.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses,
performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Delight in undertaking enterprises, lack of fortitude, engagement in ignoble deeds,
and constant indulgence in sensual objects are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
a habit of begging, and negligence are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
And for these three qualities abiding in the three [states],
this should be known as the concise definition of their characteristics in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels shame for after having done it, while doing it, or even when about to do it—
all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world and does not grieve over failure should be known as rajasic.
That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel ashamed to practice,
and that by which one's own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
the characteristic of *sattva* is righteousness (*dharma*). Among these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.
I shall now describe, in brief and in their proper order, the qualities by which each of these transmigrates through the various states of existence.
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is this threefold destiny.
This secondary course of transmigration should be understood as being threefold and of three kinds—
namely, low, middling, and superior— according to the distinction between one's actions and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts constitute the lowest state of darkness (tāmasī gatiḥ).
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling state of darkness.
The Cāraṇas, the Suparṇas, deceitful men,
Rākṣasas, and Piśācas constitute the highest state among those belonging to Tamas.
Jhallas, Mallas, and actors, as well as men who live by the sword, those addicted to gambling and drinking, and those of low character— this is the Rājasa state.
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings,
as well as those whose primary concern is the science of war, constitute the intermediate Rājasa state.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, find their highest state among those characterized by passion (rājasī).
Ascetics, self-restrained practitioners, Brahmins, the hosts of celestial beings in their chariots,
the lunar mansions, and the Daityas— this is the first, characterized by goodness (sāttvikī), destination.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, the sāttvika goal.
The wise declare that Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest— this is the supreme state characterized by sattva.
Thus has been fully described the entire transmigratory existence consisting of all beings, which is threefold and of three kinds, arising from the three types of action.
Through attachment to the senses and by not practicing the Dharma,
the ignorant and lowest of men go to evil states of existence.
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living soul enters in this world, and by what particular karma it does so, in due succession.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations upon the exhaustion of that [karmic residue].
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; or that of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or even that of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.
A Brahmin who steals [gold] becomes a spider, a snake, a lizard, or aquatic animals, as well as predatory beasts and Piśācas, for thousands of births.
The violator of the Guru's bed becomes [the seed] of grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as of carnivorous animals, fanged beasts,
and those who perform cruel deeds, by the hundreds.

Those who eat the wives of others become carnivorous beasts after death; those who steal become worms that feed on impurities; and those who consort with women of the lowest castes become predators that devour one another.
By entering into association with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
A man who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, corals,
and various other precious stones, is born among the goldsmiths.

By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl; by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing meat, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [eats] meat, a cormorant [eats] fat, a bird that feeds on oil [eats] oil,
a cricket [eats] salt, and a crane [eats] curd.
Having stolen silk, a partridge [becomes a partridge]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, an iguana; and having stolen molasses, a rat.
The chuchundarī [eats] auspicious fragrances; the peacock, leafy vegetables;
the porcupine, various kinds of prepared food; and the śalyaka, unprepared food.
Having stolen fire, one becomes a *baka* crane; having stolen household utensils, one becomes a *gṛhakārī* (house-builder bird);
and having stolen dyed garments, one is born as a *jīvajīvaka* (pheasant).
A wolf [destroys] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruits and roots;
a bear, a woman; a cuckoo, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock.
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property, or having consumed an oblation that has not been offered in sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
Women also, by stealing in this same manner, incur guilt;
they become wives of those very same creatures.
For when the social classes fall away from their respective duties in times of no distress,
they undergo sinful transmigrations and enter into a state of servitude toward their enemies.
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha, who eats what has been vomited;
and a Kṣatriya becomes a *kaṭapūtana*, who eats impure matter and corpses.
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta that feeds on pus, known as Maitrākṣajyotika;
and a Śūdra who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a Cailāśaka.
To whatever extent those whose nature is directed toward sense objects indulge in them,
to that same extent skillfulness in those very things arises within them.
Due to the repeated practice of those sinful deeds, those of small intellect encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world.
There is tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra and others,
as well as [suffering] in the Forest of Sword-leaves and so forth, involving binding and cutting.
And various torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of sand mixed with grit, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he undergoes births in various non-womb-born states that are mostly full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat and manifold fears.
Again and again, there is dwelling in the abodes of the womb and dreadful birth,
as well as wooden fetters and even servitude to others.
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people,
the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies.
And [he considers] old age which is beyond remedy, the affliction caused by diseases,
various kinds of sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action,
with a body of that same nature one experiences its respective fruit.
This entire arising of the fruits of actions for you has been fully declared;
now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
And among all these auspicious actions here,
a certain action has been declared to be more conducive to the highest good for a person.
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme;
for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained through it.
Of all these six types of actions, both in this world and after death,
it should be known that the Vedic rite is always the most conducive to the highest good.
But in the Vedic yoga of action, all these [stages] without exception are included, respectively, within each specific rule of ritual action.

Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the path of active engagement and the path of withdrawal.
Action performed with a desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called "active" (pravṛtta); but action free from desire, preceded by knowledge, is taught as "withdrawn" (nivṛtta).
By practicing active (pravṛtta) action, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renunciation (nivṛtta), one indeed transcends the five elements.
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self,
one who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty.
Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
having attained this, the twice-born man has truly accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all those are fruitless after death, for they are declared to be grounded in darkness.
Whatever other things there may be that arise and pass away from this [cycle],
they are fruitless and false because they belong to the past.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four distinct stages of life—
the past, the present, and the future— all these are established through the Veda.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are produced from the Veda alone; their manifestation arises from the qualities and actions [of the elements].
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a living being.
One who knows the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a judge, and even the lordship over all the world.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does one who knows the Veda burn away the defects of his own actions born of karma.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely possess the texts; those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who act with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge.
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
through austerity he destroys evil, and through knowledge he partakes of immortality.
One who desires the purification of dharma should thoroughly understand this triad: perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions.
He who investigates the instruction on Dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows Dharma, and no other.
This action leading to supreme bliss has been declared in its entirety;
now the secret doctrine of this treatise of Manu is being taught.
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those duties not specifically prescribed,
whatever learned Brahmins may declare as Dharma, that shall be the Dharma, free from doubt.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered in accordance with the Dharma,
are to be known as cultured Brahmins, who are the very source of the revealed scriptures and direct perception.
Whatever dharma an assembly of at least ten members may determine,
or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct— that dharma one must not overturn.
One who possesses the threefold knowledge, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the first three classes of ascetics— these constitute an assembly of at least ten members.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this assembly of at least three is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding dharma.

Whatever dharma even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Vedas may determine, that should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not [the dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.
Even if they gather by the thousands, those who lack vows, lack sacred mantras, and subsist on their birth alone do not possess the status of an assembly.
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the foolish who do not know the Dharma, declare to be dharma—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after those who spoke it.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of dharma.
Composed in meditation, one should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the Self;
for by perceiving everything within the Self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
One should place the ether within the cavities, the wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, the waters within moisture, and the earth within solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the steps,
Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call this Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some call it Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self by means of the self within all beings,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state.
A twice-born man who recites this Institutes of Manu, proclaimed by Bhṛgu,
becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal.
The End of the Manusmṛti (The Code of Manu)

www.sub.uni-goettingen.de/ebene_1/fiindolo/gretil/gretdias.pdf Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, the great seers, having honored him according to the rule, spoke these words: Manu 1.01a: Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, Manu 1.01c: having honored him according to the rule, they spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, you ought to tell us the duties of all the social classes in their proper order,
as well as those born from intermediate unions."
For you alone,
O Lord, are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Thus questioned by those high-souled ones,
he of immeasurable vigor duly honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen."
In the beginning, this universe was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, devoid of distinguishing marks,
beyond the reach of reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely immersed in sleep.
Then the blessed Self-existent One, unmanifest and dispelling darkness, appeared— his vital energy having been aroused— to manifest this world consisting of the great elements and the rest.

He who is beyond the grasp of the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself came forth. Desiring to bring forth various creatures from his own body, he meditated upon it.
In the beginning, he emitted the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
That egg became golden, possessing a brilliance equal to the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The waters are called "nara"; indeed, the waters are the offspring of Nara. Since they were his first place of motion (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
That unmanifest, eternal cause, which consists of both being and non-being—
emanated from that, the Puruṣa is celebrated in the world as Brahmā.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditation, divided that egg into two parts.
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the intermediate space, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
From himself, he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, he drew forth the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the presiding lord who identifies with objects.
He also drew forth the Great Self (mahān ātmā) and all things composed of the three qualities (guṇas).
And one should gradually withdraw the five senses, which seize upon their respective objects.
But having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [great elements], each of immeasurable power,
with the portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings. Those subtle constituent parts of the forms [of the elements] are what these six [beings] take as their support.
Therefore, the wise call his form "the body" (śarīra).
The great elements, together with their functions, enter that [unmanifest], as does the mind with its subtle components; thus it is the imperishable creator of all beings.
But from these seven persons of great power,
this perishable world arises from the imperishable through the subtle constituent elements of form.
But each succeeding one among these acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position in this sequence, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.
But at the beginning, he assigned the individual names and actions of all beings,
as well as their distinct social orders, solely from the words of the Veda.
And that Lord created the gods, whose nature is action, as well as living beings;
he also created the subtle host of Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.
From Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of the successful accomplishment of sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains.
Desiring to create these offspring, he emitted austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger, as well as this entire creation.
For the sake of distinguishing between actions, he separated right from wrong;
and he joined these creatures with pairs such as pleasure and pain.
The subtle particles, which are said to be perishable and consist of the five [subtle elements],—
with these together, all this [universe] comes into being in due order.
But whatever task the Lord first assigned to each being,
that very same task he performed himself when being created again and again.
Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—
whatever he ordained for each at the time of creation, that very thing entered into them of its own accord.
Just as the seasons, at the change of seasons, spontaneously assume their own respective characteristics according to the signs of the time,
so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.
For the sake of the increase of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Having divided his own body into two parts, he became a male with one half;
with the other half he became a female, and into her the Lord created Virāj.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that creator of this entire universe, whom the Supreme Person Virāj himself created after performing austerities.
Desiring to create offspring, I performed most difficult austerities; then, in the beginning, I created ten great seers as the lords of creatures:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
And Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada as well.
These seven Manus of great splendor whom [Brahmā] created,
as well as the gods, the hosts of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power— Manu 1.36.
The Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various hosts of Pitṛs;
as well as the lightning-flashes, thunderbolts, clouds, and the red and Indra-bows.
And meteors, thunderclaps, comets, and various celestial bodies of diverse kinds.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth.
Worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bugs;
all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings.
Thus, by my command, all this—
both the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones according to their respective actions through the power of their austerity.
But whatever kind of action is proclaimed here for these beings,
that I shall declare to you accordingly, as well as the sequence of their birth.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans are born from the womb.
Birds, snakes, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises are born from eggs.
And those things of this kind which originate on land as well as in water.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from sweat;
as are whatever other such things exist that arise from heat.
All stationary beings are born from sprouts; they grow from seeds or slips.
Herbs are those that perish after the ripening of their fruit and bear abundant flowers and fruit.
Those which bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those which bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*.
But various kinds of shrubs and bushes, as well as species of grasses, those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines; 1.48.
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
These states, beginning with Brahmā, are declared to have this as their limit;
in this terrible cycle of existence of beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time.
When that God is awake, then this world is active;
when He, whose soul is tranquil, sleeps, then everything closes its eyes.
While he sleeps in a state of well-being, however, the embodied beings whose nature is action cease from their respective activities,
and the mind falls into exhaustion.
But when they all dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and in peace.
But when he remains for a long time having resorted to darkness (tamas), though still possessed of his senses, he does not perform his own duty; then he departs from his physical form.
When, having become minute in size, he enters the seed— both the stationary and the moving—
he then, being united with it, casts off his form.
Thus, by means of waking and sleeping,
that Imperishable One incessantly brings to life and causes the destruction of all this world, both moving and unmoving.
Having composed this scripture, he himself first caused me to receive it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, [taught] Marīci and the other sages.
"Bhṛgu here will recite this treatise to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of it from me without exception."
Then, having been thus addressed by the great seer Manu, Bhrigu, with a joyful heart, spoke to all those sages: "Listen!"
Of this Svāyambhuva Manu, there were six other high-souled and immensely powerful Manus belonging to his lineage, who each created their own respective progeny.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval (antara), produced and sustained all this world of moving and non-moving beings.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those make one *kalā*,
thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*, and a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of as many [thirty] *muhūrtas*.
The sun divides the human and divine day and night:
the night is for the sleep of living beings, and the day is for the performance of actions.
In the realm of the ancestors (Pitṛs), a month constitutes a day and a night; its division is by the two fortnights.
Of these, the dark fortnight is the day for the performance of rites, and the bright fortnight is the night for sleep.
For the gods, a day and a night consist of a year; furthermore, their division is as follows:
the northern course of the sun (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night.
Now learn, in brief and in due order, the measure of the night and day of Brahmā,
as well as that of each of the Yugas individually.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its morning twilight is of equal duration, and its evening twilight is likewise.
In the other three ages, along with their twilights and their twilight-parts,
they proceed by decreasing one thousand and one hundred [years] respectively.
This cycle of four ages (yuga), which has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand years, is called a yuga of the gods.
A thousand cycles of divine ages, by calculation,
should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration.
They know that holy day of Brahmā to end after a thousand such ages.
And those people who know day and night consider that very same duration to be the night as well.
At the end of that day and night, he who was asleep awakens;
and having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes a transformation of its creative power;
from it, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.
From Vāyu, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness;
that radiant entity is said to have the quality of form (rūpa).
From light, as it undergoes transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
That divine age (*yuga*) which was previously declared to consist of twelve thousand [years] is here said to be multiplied by seventy-one; this is called a *manvantara*.
The Manvantaras are innumerable, as are the creations and the dissolutions;
the Supreme Lord performs these again and again, as if in play.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete in all four quarters, as was Truth;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred for men through unrighteousness.
In the other ages, however, Dharma has been diminished by one quarter with each successive age due to the influence of worldly acquisition.
And through theft, falsehood, and deceit, righteousness departs one quarter at a time.
In the Kṛta age, men are free from disease, have all their aims accomplished, and possess a lifespan of four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
The lifespan of mortals declared in the Veda, as well as the fruits of their ritual acts, diminish accordingly.
In this world, the fruits and the powers of embodied beings ripen according to the age.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different,
and those in the Kali age are yet another, in accordance with the decline of the ages.
Austerity is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is for the Dvāpara, and charity alone in the Kali age.
But for the protection of this entire creation,
that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving and receiving gifts.
The protection of subjects, the giving of gifts, sacrifice, study,
and non-attachment to sensual objects— this, in brief, is the duty of a Kṣatriya.
The protection of cattle, the giving of gifts, sacrifice, and study— this is likewise his duty.
Trade, usury, and agriculture are the duties of a Vaiśya.
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra:
to serve these very same castes without malice.
Manu 1.92a: A man is declared to be more pure above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been called the most pure part by the Self-existent One.
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he maintains the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation.
For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, created him from his own mouth in the beginning,
for the purpose of conveying the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the inhabitants of heaven always consume the *havya* offerings,
and the ancestors likewise consume the *kavya* offerings?
Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by their intellect;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brāhmaṇas, the learned are superior; among the learned, those of firm resolve;
among those of firm resolve, the performers of action; and among the performers, those who know Brahman.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is destined for union with Brahman.
For a Brāhmaṇa, upon being born, is indeed born preeminent on earth;
he is the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
"Everything whatsoever that exists in this world is the property of the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and his noble lineage, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this. (Manu 1.100)
A Brāhmaṇa eats his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
for it is through the Brāhmaṇa’s compassion that other people eat.
For the purpose of discerning the duties of that [king], as well as those of the remaining [classes] in their proper order,
the wise Manu, the son of the Self-existent, composed this treatise.
This [law-code] should be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa,
and it should be correctly expounded to his pupils by him alone, and not by anyone else.
A Brāhmaṇa who studies this treatise and whose vows are praised is never tainted by the defects of actions arising from mind, speech, or body.
He purifies his lineage of seven ancestors and seven descendants, and even this entire earth; indeed, such a person alone deserves it.
This is the most excellent means for attaining well-being; this increases the intellect;
this brings fame and long life; this is the supreme means for the highest good.
In this [work], dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions.
And the eternal conduct of all four castes is likewise [to be maintained].
Conduct is the highest dharma, whether declared in the Śruti or prescribed in the Smṛti;
therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it.

A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas; however, one who is endowed with right conduct becomes a partaker of the full fruit. Having thus observed the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages [declared him] to be a partaker of the full fruit.
They have grasped good conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.

The origin of the world, the rules for the sacraments, the practice of religious observances, and the supreme rule for the ceremonial bath; Manu 1.111a: And the origin of the world, and the very procedure for the sacraments; Manu 1.111c: The performance of vows and observances, and the highest rule for the ritual bath.
The taking of a wife, the characteristics of the various forms of marriage,
the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
The characteristics of the various modes of livelihood, as well as the observances of a Snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, ritual purity, and the purification of objects.
The duties of women, the practice of asceticism, liberation, and renunciation;
the entire duty of the king, and the decision of legal cases.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife,
the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns (criminals).
And [he shall describe] the service of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes,
the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation.
He shall also explain the threefold journey through transmigratory existence arising from action,
as well as the supreme good resulting from actions and the examination of their merits and defects.
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families,
and the laws of heretical sects and guilds.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me,
so now you also should learn it from my presence.
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous who are always free from hatred and passion,
and which is approved by the heart.
To be driven solely by desire is not praised, yet there is no such thing as being entirely free from desire in this world;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic rituals are themselves objects of desire.
Desire indeed has its root in intention; sacrifices originate from intention;
vows and the duties of restraint are all recorded as being born of intention.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
By conducting oneself properly toward these [elders], one goes to the world of the immortals;
and here on earth, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the tradition (smṛti) and the conduct (śīla) of those who know it,
as well as the practice of the virtuous and the self-satisfaction of one's own conscience.
Whatever dharma of anyone has been proclaimed by Manu,
all that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge.
But having examined all this entirely with the eye of knowledge,
a learned man should indeed abide in his own duty according to the authority of the Śruti.
For a man who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and supreme happiness after death.
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed the Smṛti;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them Dharma has shone forth.

That twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic (hetuśāstra), would show contempt for these two roots [the Vedas], is an atheist and a reviler of the Veda; he should be excluded by the virtuous.
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—
they say that this fourfold set is the direct definition of Dharma.
For those who are not attached to wealth and desire, the knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those who wish to understand Dharma, the Śruti is the supreme authority.
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are remembered as Dharma;
for both of those have been correctly declared as Dharma by the wise.
"When the sun has risen, when it has not yet risen, and likewise at the time of twilight—sacrifice is performed in every way;
such is the Vedic revelation."
He for whom the rites beginning with conception and ending with the funeral pyre are prescribed by means of mantras—
only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta.
In that region, whatever custom has come down through a succession of tradition among the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes— that is called "good conduct" (sadācāra).
Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pañcālas, and the Śūrasenakas—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
From the presence of a twice-born man born in this land,
all men on earth should learn their respective duties.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains,
to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country).
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
and between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief.
Learn now the origin of this entire world and the duties of the social classes.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body—beginning with the rite of impregnation (*niṣeka*)—must be performed through meritorious Vedic rites; it is sanctifying both after death and in this world.
By means of oblations for the fetus, and by the rites of birth, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass,
the sin of the seed and the sin of the womb are wiped away from the twice-born.
By the study of one's own Veda, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the knowledge of the three Vedas, by sacrifices, by sons,
by the great sacrifices, and by other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.
Before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is ordained for a male child;
it includes the ceremonial feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
On the tenth or the twelfth day after birth, one should cause his naming ceremony to be performed on an auspicious lunar day,
at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word meaning "shelter" (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word meaning "protection" (rakṣā);
that of a Vaiśya should be joined with a word meaning "prosperity" (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be joined with a word meaning "service" (preṣya).
For women, [the name] should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning,
captivating, auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and containing a word of benediction.
In the fourth month, the infant's first outing from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.

The rite of tonsure (cūḍākarma) for all twice-born classes must be performed according to dharma in either the first or the third year, as prescribed by the Śruti. One should perform the initiation (upanayana) of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception.
In the eleventh year from conception for a king, and in the twelfth year from conception for a Vaiśya.
For a Brahmin desiring spiritual luster, the initiation should be performed in the fifth year;
for a Kṣatriya seeking power, in the sixth; and for a Vaiśya desiring worldly prosperity in this life, in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this time, if these three also remain uninitiated according to the prescribed time,
they become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vrātyas, and are censured by the Āryas.
A Brahmin shall never, even in times of distress, form connections through Vedic study or marriage with those who have not been purified according to the rule.
The skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat are for the religious student (brahmacārin).
They shall wear, in the respective order, garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya, however, should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya, a cord made of hempen threads.
In the absence of muñja grass, however, [the girdle] should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja;
it should have a single threefold knot, or three, or even five.
The sacred thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and tripled;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen yarn.
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vāṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to reach the hairline in length;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, but that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose.
All those [reeds] should be straight, without blemishes, pleasant in appearance,
not causing alarm to men, with their bark intact, and undamaged by fire.
Having received the desired alms and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go for alms using the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, at the end.
[He should beg from] his mother, or his sister, or his mother's own sister.
He should beg for alms first from that woman who would not treat him with contempt.
Having collected that alms-food, as much as is required and without guile, he should announce it to his guru; then, having sipped water, being pure and facing the east, he should eat.
Eating while facing east promotes longevity; eating while facing south brings fame;
eating while facing west brings prosperity; and indeed, eating while facing north brings truth.
Having sipped water, the twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
and having eaten, he should properly sip water again and touch the cavities of the head with water.
One should always honor food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way.
For food that is always eaten with reverence bestows strength and vigor;
but that which is eaten without reverence destroys both of these.
One should not give the remains of one's food to anyone, nor should one eat between [meals];
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to the attainment of heaven;
it is meritless and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
A Brahmin should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha;
or he may use the Kāya or Traidaśika tīrthas, but never the Pitrya.
They declare that the base of the thumb is the *brāhma* tīrtha;
the *kāya* at the roots of the fingers, the *daiva* at their tips, and the *pitrya* below those two.
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should also touch the cavities of the head with water, as well as the body and the head itself.

One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand (tīrtha), in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north.
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water that reaches the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity.
When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when it is on the left, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*.
Having cast away his girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, it is in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya, it is considered to be two years later than that.
This entire sequence of rites for women must be performed without mantras,
for the sake of purifying the body, at the proper time and in the proper order.
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the guru, and the tending of the sacred fires is their domestic duty.
This rite of initiation for the twice-born has been declared; it is meritorious and manifests their true birth. Now learn the application of their duties.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the worship at the twilights.
But when about to study, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north,
he should be taught with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light clothing, and with his senses subdued.
At the beginning and at the conclusion of the study of the Veda, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the hands together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left [foot] is to be touched with the left [hand], and the right [foot] with the right [hand].
But whenever the teacher is about to begin his instruction, he should always, without weariness, say to the pupil, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when [the pupil] says, "Let there be a pause."
A Brāhmaṇa should always utter the syllable Om at the beginning and at the end [of his recitation];
for that which is not preceded by Om flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
Sitting on the eastern bank [of a river] and purified by means of purifiers,
one who is cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) is then worthy of the syllable Om.
Prajāpati milked from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*,
as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
From the three Vedas alone,
Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out each quarter-verse of this Sāvitrī beginning with "Tat."
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and these [Vyahritis] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One who is devoid of this Ṛgvedic verse, as well as his own timely ritual action,
being born from the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya, incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) preceded by the syllable Oṃ,
and the three-footed Sāvitrī— these should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of ether.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice perish;

however, the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as difficult to perform, for it is both Brahman and Prajāpati. The sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice performed according to ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña).
The whispered recitation is a hundredfold [more effective], and the mental recitation is recorded as being a thousandfold.
The four types of *pākayajña* sacrifices, together with those prescribed by ritual injunctions (*vidhiyajña*),
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*).
A Brāhmaṇa attains perfection through the chanting of prayers alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining his senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
The sages of old have spoken of eleven organs;
I shall describe them correctly, in their proper order and according to the truth.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
Among these, the five beginning with the ear are known in their respective order as the organs of perception (buddhīndriya).
The five organs of action among these are said to be the anus and the others.
The mind is to be known as the eleventh, which by its own nature partakes of both [the external and internal];
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more.
He who should attain all these [objects of desire], and he who should renounce them entirely—
for the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
These [senses] cannot be so effectively restrained by mere non-indulgence as they can be by other means.
Just as [the senses] are constantly restrained from their objects through knowledge.
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and austerities—
none of these ever lead to success for one whose disposition is corrupted.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled [objects of sense],
neither rejoices nor desponds, is to be known as one who has conquered his senses.
But if even one among all the senses leaks away,
through that his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restraining the mind,
he should accomplish all his goals without wasting his body through disciplined yoga.

Standing, one should recite the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but during the evening twilight, one should remain seated until the stars are clearly visible. By standing and reciting during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed during the night.
But sitting facing west, one destroys the impurity produced during the day.
But he who does not stand for the morning [prayer], nor performs the evening one—
he, like a Śūdra, is to be excluded from all the rites of the twice-born.
Restrained and established in the daily rite, he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Sāvitrī near water.
In the case of the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, in the daily private recitation,
and indeed in the mantras for the fire-oblation, there is no restriction regarding days unfit for study.
In the daily recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the "Brahma-sacrifice."
The merit of an oblation offered by a Brahmin is as if it were offered with the Vaṣaṭ-call, even though no formal suspension of study has been declared.
He who, being self-restrained and pure, studies his own Veda for a year according to the prescribed rule—
for him this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man shall perform the tending of the sacred fires, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and doing what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return home (samāvartana).

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman— these ten are to be taught according to the law.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks in an improper manner;
for even though he knows the truth, a wise man should behave like one who is dull-witted in this world.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two dies or incurs enmity.
Where neither spiritual merit nor material wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve,
there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil.
A teacher of the Veda should, if he so desires, die with his knowledge alone;
for even in times of dire distress, he must never sow it in barren soil.
Knowledge, having approached a Brāhmaṇa, said: "I am your treasure; guard me.
Do not give me to a scorner, so that I may be most powerful."

But to that Brahmin whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and observant of the vow of celibacy— to such a guardian of the treasure who is free from negligence, speak to me. However, he who should acquire the Veda from one who is studying it without having received permission...
He who is guilty of stealing the Veda falls into hell.
From whomever one receives knowledge— whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual— one should first offer salutation to that person.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī mantra,
than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all kinds of goods.
One should not sit upon a bed or seat that has been used by a superior;
moreover, while remaining on one's bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and offer salutation.
For when an elder approaches, the vital breaths of a youth depart upward;
by rising to meet him and by saluting him, he recovers them once again.

For one who is habitually respectful in salutation and constantly serves the elderly, four things increase: life-span, merit, fame, and strength. When a Brahmin, after performing a salutation, greets an elder...
He should announce his own name, saying, "I am named so-and-so."
To those who do not know how to address one by name,
a wise man should say "I am [Name]," and he should do the same for all women.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the state of being "bhoḥ" is the essential nature of names.

When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one. Furthermore, at the end of that person's name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced as a protracted (*pluta*) sound, with the preceding syllable being lengthened.
A Brahmin who does not know the proper response to a salutation should not be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask after his welfare (*kuśala*); a Kṣatriya, after his health (*anāmaya*);
a Vaiśya, after his well-being (*kṣema*); and a Śūdra, after his freedom from disease (*ārogya*).
One who is initiated should not be addressed by name, even if he is younger;
one who knows the law should address him by prefixing "bho" or "bhavat."
But as for a woman who is another's wife and not related by birth,
he should address her simply as "lady," or as "fortunate one," or as "sister."
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself,
saying, "I am so-and-so."
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
The wife of a brother of the same caste should be saluted every day;
however, upon returning from a journey, the women who are one's paternal or maternal relatives should be saluted.
Toward his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, and his own elder sister, he should maintain a conduct as toward his mother;
yet the mother is more venerable than they.
Friendship among citizens is said to last ten years; among artists, five years;
and among those learned in the Vedas, three years—even for those of the same lineage, it lasts but a very short time.
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son;
yet between the two, the Brahmin is the father.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—
these are the grounds for respect, each subsequent one being weightier than the preceding.
Among the three social classes, these five qualities should be present in abundance and be excellent.
Wherever such persons may be found, even a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade is worthy of honor in that place.
Way must be yielded to one in a carriage, to one in his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one carrying a burden, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
Among all these gathered together, the bath-graduate (snātaka) and the king are to be honored;
and between the king and the bath-graduate, the bath-graduate alone receives the honor due to a sovereign.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil,
teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpa and the Rahasya, him they call an Ācārya.
But he who teaches even a single portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
That brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the prescribed rules,
and supports [the child] with food, is called a guru.
He who, having been chosen, performs for another the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the great sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others,
is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as one's mother and father; one should never bear him malice.
An *ācārya* outweighs ten sub-teachers (*upādhyāya*), a father outweighs a hundred *ācāryas*,
but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in terms of venerability.
Between the one who procreates and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world.
One should understand that the "origination" (saṃbhūti) of this person— which consists in his being born from the womb— is that which his mother and father produce together through mutual desire.
But that caste which his teacher, who has mastered the Vedas,
produces for him according to rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is real, undecaying, and immortal.
One should know that person as a teacher here in this world by virtue of that service rendered through sacred learning, whoever benefits one with it, whether little or much.
One who effects a Vedic birth and is the instructor of one's own duty becomes,
according to the law, the father of an elder Brahmin, even if he is a child.
The young Kavi, the son of Aṅgiras, taught his fathers;
having embraced them with his knowledge, he addressed them as "little sons."
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant man is indeed a child; he becomes a father when he imparts the sacred mantras. For they call the ignorant man a "child," but one who imparts the mantras is called a "father."
Not by years, nor by grey hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who has studied the Vedas is great.
The seniority of Brahmins is based on knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas on valor,
that of Vaiśyas on grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone on birth.
One does not become an elder merely because his head is gray;
the gods know him alone to be an elder who, even if young, is devoted to study.
As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three bear only the name.
As a eunuch is fruitless with women, as a cow is fruitless with a bull,
and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
The instruction of living beings should be performed for their welfare through non-violence alone;
and one who desires dharma should employ speech that is both sweet and gentle.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always properly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit that is reached through the Vedānta.

Even when afflicted, one should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor should one have a mind intent on acts of malice toward others; one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech leads away from the world of the righteous.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if it were poison;
he should always long for contempt as if it were nectar.
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in comfort and wakes in comfort.
One moves about happily in this world; he who treats others with contempt perishes.
By this sequential application, the twice-born man, having purified his self,
should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the acquisition of the Veda while dwelling with his teacher.
By means of various specific forms of austerity and vows prescribed by rule,
the entire Veda, together with its secret portions (the Upanishads), must be mastered by the twice-born.
A twice-born man of the highest order, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda alone;
for the study of the Veda is declared to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin in this world.
That twice-born man indeed performs the highest austerity unto the very tips of his nails,
who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.
The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly becomes a Śūdra even while still alive, along with his progeny.
The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass;
the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
Among those, that which is his birth from the Veda, marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass—
therein the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, and the teacher his father.
They declare the teacher to be a father because of his imparting the Veda;
for no ritual duty whatsoever is enjoined upon him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
One should not pronounce the Veda except when offering the *svadhā* libation;
for he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born [into the Veda].
For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony, the instruction in the observances is prescribed;
likewise, the acquisition of the Veda is to be performed in due order according to the rule.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, and girdle have been prescribed for him,
whatever staff and whatever garment [he has], those same shall also be his during his religious observances.
A student living with his teacher must observe these following rules,
restraining the entire collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors;
likewise, the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and the injury of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella,
as well as lust, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments— these he should avoid.
Gambling, idle gossip, slander, as well as falsehood;
gazing at and touching women, and injury to others—[he should avoid these].
He should always sleep alone and should never spill his semen.
For by intentionally emitting semen, one indeed destroys his own vow.
If a twice-born student (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow dung, earth, and kuśa grass—
as much as required— and he should go out for alms every day.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, who are praised for their own duties.
One should not beg for alms within the family of one's teacher, nor among the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives;
however, if other houses are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding category in turn.
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech with self-control, but avoiding those who are accused of crimes.
Having fetched fuel-sticks from a distance, he should place them in the open air;
and both evening and morning, he should unwearyingly offer oblations with them into the fire.

If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇivrata).
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the subsistence of a vow-holder on alms is equal to fasting.
At a rite for the gods, one should eat like a deity, and at a rite for the ancestors, like a seer;
however, if invited, he may eat according to his desire, and his vow is not thereby violated.
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Rājanya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in this manner.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. He should likewise control his body, speech, intellect, senses, and mind.
Having restrained himself, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always keep his hand uplifted, maintain virtuous conduct, and remain well-restrained; and when told, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher.
He should always have inferior food, clothing, and dress in the presence of his teacher.
He should rise before him and go to rest after him.
One should not engage in conversation or respond to a call while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away.

Standing, one should serve him while he is seated; approaching, one should serve him while he is standing; going out to meet him, one should serve him while he is coming toward one; and running after him, one should serve him while he is running.
Facing one who has turned his back, approaching one who is at a distance,
bowing down to one who is lying down, and likewise standing near one who is giving orders.
His bed and seat must always be low in the presence of his teacher;
moreover, within the range of the teacher's vision, he must not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or even slander of one's teacher occurs,
there one must either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
Through reviling others one becomes a donkey; through censuring others one becomes a dog; one who consumes another's food becomes a worm; and one who is envious becomes an insect.
Standing at a distance, he should not honor him; nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman.
And while standing in a vehicle or on a seat, he should descend before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher either downwind or upwind;
nor, even if out of earshot of the teacher, should one utter anything at all.
He may sit together with his teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on a palace, on a grass mat, on mats of woven straw, or on a stone slab, a wooden plank, or a boat.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher;
and unless permitted by the teacher, one should not pay homage to one's own elders.
In the same way, this constant conduct is required toward teachers of knowledge, toward one's own elders,
and toward those who restrain one from unrighteousness as well as those who impart what is beneficial.

One should always behave toward those who are superior as one does toward one's own teacher— toward the sons of the teacher who are noble, and likewise toward the teacher’s own kinsmen. Even a child, or one of equal age, or a pupil, [must act thus] during the performance of sacrificial rites.
A teacher’s son who teaches deserves honor like that shown to the teacher himself.
One should not perform the rubbing of the limbs, bathing,
or eating of the leftovers for the teacher's son, nor should one perform the washing of his feet.
The wives of the preceptor who belong to the same caste as he should be honored like the preceptor himself;
those who are of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair— these must not be performed for the wife of one's guru.
But a young wife of one's guru must not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world by a man who has completed twenty years of age and who understands virtues and faults.
This is the nature of women: they are the corrupters of men in this world. Therefore, wise men do not become negligent regarding women for the sake of their interests.
For in this world,
a woman is capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
But at will, a young man on the ground should perform a prostration according to the rule before the wives of his gurus who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives every day and offer salutations,
keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous.
Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water,
even so does one who is intent on service obtain knowledge that resides with the teacher.
