He may be shaven-headed, or he may wear matted hair, or he may have a single lock of matted hair on his crown;
the sun must never set or rise while he is still in the village.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own will,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while muttering prayers.
For he who, while lying down, is overtaken by the setting sun or by the rising sun,
and fails to perform the penance, shall be joined with a great sin.
Having sipped water, being pure and concentrated, he should constantly attend upon both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the prescribed rule.
If a woman, or one of lower status, should perform anything that is beneficial, he should practice all of that with diligence; and he should do whatever his mind finds pleasure in.
Dharma and wealth are said to be the highest good, as are pleasure and wealth, or dharma alone;
yet in this world, wealth alone is the highest good—such is the established view regarding the three aims of life.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and the elder brother must not be treated with contempt even by one who is distressed, especially by a Brāhmaṇa.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahmā; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
The suffering that parents endure at the birth of human beings cannot be compensated for even in a hundred years.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times;
for when these three are satisfied, all asceticism is accomplished.
Service to these three is declared to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
For these indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three stages of life (āśramas);
these indeed are the three Vedas; and these are said to be the three sacred fires.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, a householder shall conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By devotion to his mother he wins this world; by devotion to his father, the middle world;
and by service to his teacher, he likewise attains the world of Brahmā.
All the religious duties of that man are honored who honors these three;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual acts are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not serve anyone else;
he should always perform service toward them alone, devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to them.
Whatever one may perform for the sake of the next world, provided it does not interfere with those [duties],
that one should announce to them through thought, word, and deed.
For in these three, a man's duty is fully accomplished;
this is the supreme dharma directly perceived, while any other is called a secondary dharma.
A person of faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a lowly source;
likewise, one should accept the highest dharma even from another, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
Even from poison, one should take the nectar; even from a child, a well-spoken word;
even from an enemy, good conduct; and even from an impure place, gold.
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, dharma, purity, eloquent speech,
and various arts— these are to be acquired from everywhere.
In times of distress, studying under one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is permitted;
however, one must follow and serve that teacher for as long as the study continues.
A student should not dwell for life with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher,
nor with a Brāhmaṇa who has not mastered the Vedas, if he desires the highest goal.
But if he should choose to dwell permanently in the family of his guru,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation of the body.
That Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahman.

One who knows the Dharma should not offer anything to the teacher beforehand; however, when about to perform the final bath, he should, upon being commanded by the teacher, provide for the teacher's needs according to his ability.

A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, a seat, grain, vegetables, or clothing— one should bring these to the teacher to produce his satisfaction. But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should serve the teacher’s son, provided he is endowed with good qualities.
One should behave toward the wife of a guru or toward a sapinda relative as one would toward the guru himself.
When these [elders] are not present, remaining steady in standing, sitting,
and moving about, one should perfect one's own body by practicing service to the sacred fire.
The Brahmin who thus practices the vow of celibacy without fail goes to the highest station and is not born again in this world.
One should observe the vow pertaining to the three Vedas under a teacher for thirty-six years,
or for half that time, or for a quarter, or until they have been mastered.
Having studied the three Vedas, or two, or even one, in due order,
and having remained unbroken in his vow of celibacy, he shall enter the stage of the householder.
When he has been recognized by his own conduct as the heir to his father’s Vedic knowledge,
one should first honor him— who is wearing a garland and seated upon the couch— with a cow.
Having bathed with the permission of his teacher and returned home according to the prescribed rule,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
A woman who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of one's mother and who is not of the same *gotra* as one's father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union.
Even if they possess great wealth in cattle, goats, sheep, money, and grain—
In matters concerning marriage, one should avoid these ten types of families.

Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, and those afflicted with excessive body hair, hemorrhoids, consumption, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy;

Manu 3.7: Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, and those afflicted with excessive body hair, hemorrhoids, consumption, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy; [should be avoided].
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.
One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a bear, a tree, or a river, nor one whose name is that of a low-caste person or a mountain.
Nor one whose name is that of a bird, a snake, or a servant, nor one with a terrifying name.

He should marry a woman who has no missing limbs, whose name is auspicious, whose gait is like that of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair on the head, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
But a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother, or whose father is unknown, for fear of the illegality of her being an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended first for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] are inferior in the given order.
A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as the wife for a Śūdra; she and one of his own [caste] are prescribed for a Vaiśya;
she and one of his own for a Kṣatriya; and they, along with one of his own, for a Brāhmaṇa.
For even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of a lower caste,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having that [son] as one's offspring.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed deprived of his Brāhmaṇahood.
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests have that [study] as their primary element, the ancestors and gods do not eat; nor does he go to heaven.
For one who has drunk the foam from a Śūdra woman's mouth, for one who has been defiled by her breath,
and for one begotten by her— no atonement is prescribed.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women, which bring benefit or harm both after death and in this world to all four social classes.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura;
the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
I shall declare to you all that which is the lawful duty for each caste, as well as their respective virtues and vices, and the merits and defects pertaining to their offspring.
Six [forms of marriage] in order are for the Brāhmaṇa; for the Kṣatriya, the four lower ones;
but for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, one should know those same [four] to be lawful, excluding the Rākṣasa form.
The wise know the first four to be recommended for the Brāhmaṇa.
The Rākṣasa [form] is the one for a Kṣatriya; the Āsura [is permitted] for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of these five, however, three are declared here to be lawful and two unlawful:
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.
The two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— whether performed separately or combined, are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Having clothed and honored a man of learning and good character,
and having invited him himself, the giving away of a daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
When a sacrifice has been properly commenced and a priest is performing his duty,
the giving of a daughter after having adorned her is declared to be the *daiva* rite.
Having received one or two pairs of cattle from the groom according to the law,
the formal giving away of the daughter is called the Ārṣa rite.
Having addressed them with the words, "May you both perform your duty together," and having honored them,
the bestowing of the maiden is recorded as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma.
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it arises from passion and has sexual intercourse as its purpose.
Having slain, mangled, and pierced [the kinsmen], and having carried off a weeping and crying maiden from her home by force,
this is declared to be the Rākṣasa rite.

He who approaches a woman while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged in secret— this is the most sinful of marriages, the eighth and lowest, known as the Paiśāca. For the foremost of the twice-born, the giving away of a daughter with water alone is distinguished as the best.
But for the other castes, [the marriage is contracted] through mutual desire.

O Brahmins, listen as I fully proclaim all the qualities of these forms of marriage that have been described by Manu for each; [listen] as I proclaim them all correctly. By this, one purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman, if he performs meritorious deeds, liberates his ancestors from sin.
A son born of a woman married according to the Daiva rite purifies seven ancestors and seven descendants;

a son born of a woman married according to the Ārṣa rite purifies three ancestors and three descendants; and a son born of a woman married according to the Kāya (Prājāpatya) rite purifies six ancestors and six descendants.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, in their proper order,
sons endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasvin*) are born, esteemed by the learned;
they are possessed of beauty, goodness, and virtue, wealthy, and renowned.
Having sufficient enjoyments and being most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
But from the remaining censured marriages are born sons who are cruel, speakers of untruth, and haters of the Veda and the sacred law.
Through blameless marriages with women, the offspring becomes blameless; through blameworthy ones, it becomes blameworthy. Therefore, a man should avoid blameworthy marriages.
The sacrament of taking the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa) is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known regarding the marriage ceremony for women of different castes.
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by the daughter of a Vaiśya,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste.

He should approach his wife during her fertile period and always remain devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may approach her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days.
The natural fertile period of women is traditionally held to be sixteen nights,
together with the four other days condemned by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four are censured, as is the eleventh;
the remaining ten nights, however, are commended.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night.

A male is born when the male seed is in excess; a female is born when the female seed is in excess. When the two are equal, the offspring is either a eunuch or twins; if the seed is diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs.
Avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and on the other [inauspicious] nights,
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī), regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits.
A wise father of a maiden should not accept even the slightest bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman’s property—
whether it be her carriage, her clothing, or anything else— those sinners go to a downward state.

Regarding the *ārṣa* form of marriage, some say that the pair of cattle is a bride-price (*śulka*), but that is false; whether it be small or even great, it is still nothing other than a sale. When the kinsmen do not receive a bride-price for the girls, that is not a sale.
That honor shown to young maidens is merely an act of compassion; however,
these women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands,
and brothers-in-law who desire abundant prosperity.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, there all ritual acts become fruitless.
Where female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever.
Those houses which female relatives, when not properly honored, curse,
perish on all sides as if struck by a magical spell (*kṛtyā*).
Therefore, these women should always be honored with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Men who desire prosperity should always honor [guests] during auspicious rites and festivals.
When a husband is content with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband,
in whatever family this is constant, there indeed is certain and lasting well-being.

For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight her husband; and from a lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed. But when a woman is pleased, the entire family is pleased.
But when she does not shine, nothing at all shines.

(Manu 3.62c) Through improper marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble lineages fall into a state of ignobility. (Manu 3.63)
By means of crafts, by trade, and by having offspring solely from Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king;
and by officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, as well as by atheism regarding religious duties.
Families that are deficient in sacred knowledge quickly perish;
however, families that are enriched by sacred knowledge, even if possessing little wealth,
attain the status of being counted among the great lineages and acquire immense renown.
[From hereon, the verse numbering is "-10"] A householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules in the nuptial fire,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.

A householder has five slaughter-houses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water-jar; by using these, he is bound [by sin]. For the sake of expiating all of these in their respective order, the great seers [prescribed the following]:
Five great sacrifices are ordained for householders to be performed every day.
Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña);
the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods (daivayajña); the bali-offering is the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūtayajña); and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).

He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while living constantly in the house, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse. He who [provides for] the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—
He who does not offer the five [great sacrifices] does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The *ahuta*, the *huta*, the *prahuta*,
the *brāhmya-huta*, and the *prāśita*— these are declared to be the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*).
The silent recitation of mantras is the *ahuta* sacrifice; the burnt offering (*homa*) is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits (*bhūta*) is the *prahuta*;
the oblation to beings (*bali*) is the *brāhmya-huta*; the honoring of the foremost of the twice-born is the *prāśita*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *pitṛ-tarpaṇa*.

One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) and likewise to rites for the gods (daiva-karman) in this world; for it is by being engaged in rites for the gods that one sustains this entire universe, both moving and unmoving.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.

Just as all living beings exist by depending upon the wind, so do all other stages of life (āśramas) exist by depending upon the householder. For the members of the other three stages of life are supported daily by the householder with both knowledge and food.

The householder alone supports [the other stages]; therefore, the householder’s stage is the foremost. It must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven, and it must be maintained by one who desires ultimate happiness in this world—though it cannot be maintained by those of weak senses.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, all living beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act toward them.
One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule,
the ancestors with śrāddha rites and food offerings, and all living beings with the bali offering.
One should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day by day with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
At the rite of the five sacrifices performed for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in this regard, one should not feed any twice-born man specifically for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
A Brāhmaṇa should daily perform a fire-oblation in his domestic fire with the prepared food of the Vaiśvadeva, according to the prescribed rule, for these deities.
First to Agni and to Soma, and then to both of them together;
then to the Viśvedevas and to Dhanvantari.
And [he offers] to Kuhū, to Anumati, and to Prajāpati;
likewise to Dyāvāpṛthivī together, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.

Having thus properly offered the oblation, he should present the bali-offering to Indra, Antaka (Yama), Appati (Varuṇa), and Indu (Soma), along with their attendants, while proceeding clockwise in all directions.
One should cast [the food] at the door with "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water with "To the Waters";
one should offer it to the Vanaspatis upon the pestle and the mortar.
One should offer a bali-oblation to Śrī at the head of the bed, and to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
furthermore, one should present a bali-oblation to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
He should cast the bali offering into the air for all the gods,
and likewise for the beings that roam by day and those that roam by night.
On the back part of the house, he should offer a bali-oblation for the sake of all beings;
then, he should carry all the remainder of the bali toward the south for the ancestors.

He should gently scatter on the ground the remains of food for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, birds, and insects. The Brāhmaṇa who thus daily honors all beings in this manner—
He, having the form of light, goes by the straight path to the supreme abode.
Having performed this rite of offerings (bali-karman) in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
and he should give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student (brahmacārin).
Whatever meritorious fruit a twice-born householder obtains by giving a cow to his teacher according to the prescribed rule,
that same meritorious fruit he obtains by giving alms.
Having honored even a portion of alms or a vessel of water according to the prescribed rule,
one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
The offerings to the gods and the ancestors (*havya-kavya*) of men who lack discernment perish,
when they are given out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes.
But when offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins who are enriched by learning and austerity, those offerings reach the deities.
And he delivers [the giver] from misfortune and even from great sin.
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water,
as well as food according to one's ability, honoring him in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Even for one who constantly gathers grains from the chaff and constantly offers oblations into the five fires, [the guest remains superior].
A Brāhmaṇa dwelling unhonored takes away all the merit of his host.
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the house of the virtuous.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally called a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest.
One should not consider a Brahmin who lives in the same village, nor one who is merely a casual acquaintance,
as a guest when he arrives at the house, even if the wife or the sacred fires are present there.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food prepared by others go,
after death, to the state of cattle as those who provide such food.
A guest brought by the sun in the evening must not be turned away by a householder; whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
honoring a guest brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.
One should provide a seat, a dwelling, a bed, attendance,
and respectful service to the highest among the high, to the lowest among the low, and to those who are equal, that which is equal.
But if another guest should arrive after the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, one should give him food according to one's ability; however, one should not perform the Bali offering again.
A Brahmin should not announce his own family and lineage for the sake of a meal;
for by proclaiming them for the sake of food, he is called a "vomit-eater" by the wise.
But for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya is not called a guest in his house;
nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, or even a teacher.
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may,
if he so desires, feed him as well once the Brahmins have finished eating.
Even a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, when they have arrived at one's household, are entitled to the treatment due to a guest.
He should feed those two together with his dependents, practicing compassion.
To others as well, such as friends and the like, who have come to his house out of affection,
he should, according to his ability, provide food along with his wife.
One should feed these— women whose husbands are living, young maidens, the sick, and pregnant women— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that foolish man who eats before giving to them is a sinner.
While eating, he does not realize that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, as well as his own dependents, have finished eating,
the husband and wife may afterwards eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities,
the householder should thereafter eat the remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.

One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) the king, the officiating priest, the bath-graduate (snātaka), and one's guru, as well as one's dear father-in-law and maternal uncle, again after the lapse of a full year.

Both a king and a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), when present at a sacrificial rite, are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the settled rule that they are not so honored when there is no sacrifice.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer the *bali* oblation without the recitation of mantras;
for this is indeed called the *vaiśvadeva*, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, on the waning of the moon,
perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
The wise know the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors as the Anvāhārya;
and that should be performed with effort using excellent meat.
In that regard, I shall explain in their entirety who those best of the twice-born are who should be fed, and who are to be avoided; how many there are, and with what kinds of food.
At a rite for the gods, he should feed two; at a rite for the ancestors, three; or one in each case.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should not be intent upon a large number of guests.
He should attend to hospitality, the place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins.
These five [vices] destroy one's prosperity; therefore, one should not seek after abundance.
This rite for the deceased, performed at the waning of the moon, is celebrated as "Pitrya" (the ancestral rite).
For one who is constantly engaged in that [ancestral rite], the worldly rite for the deceased is effectively accomplished.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
At a rite for the gods or the ancestors, one should feed even a single learned man; by doing so, one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
he is the proper recipient for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is considered a guest.
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda eat,
a single man who knows the mantras, being pleased, rightfully supersedes them all according to dharma.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and offerings to the gods (havis) should be given to one who is preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
As many mouthfuls as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows during offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya),
so many glowing iron balls, spears, and spikes shall the deceased swallow.
Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, while others are devoted to austerity;
some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavyas) should be diligently established with those who are devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havyas) may be given according to the rule to all four [classes] alike.
If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but his son has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*), or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered the Vedas— *Manu* 3.136.
Of these two, one should know the elder to be him whose father is a *śrotriya*;
however, the other deserves hospitality for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.
One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; his acquisition should be made with [other] wealth.
One should feed that twice-born man at a *śrāddha* whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend.
He whose śrāddhas and sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) have friends as their primary recipients obtains no fruit after death from those śrāddhas or from those oblations.
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms social alliances through a *śrāddha* offering, falls from the heavenly world; he is a friend to the *śrāddha* [only in name].
That which is given by eating together is declared by the twice-born to be the Paiśāca form of gift;
it remains right here in this world, like a blind cow in a single house.
Just as a sower, having sown seed in barren soil,
does not obtain a harvest, so too a donor, having given an oblation to one ignorant of the Vedas, does not obtain the fruit.
By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the rules to one who is learned, he makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death.
At a śrāddha, one may at will honor a friend, but never an enemy, even if he be learned.
For an oblation consumed by one who harbors hatred becomes fruitless after death.
One should diligently feed at the Śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his recitation.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at someone's *śrāddha*,
the ancestors of that person shall enjoy eternal satisfaction for seven generations.
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors);
however, this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the lord of the village, a kinsman, the officiating priest, and the person for whom one sacrifices.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors is at hand, he should examine him with great care.
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or who follow the ways of atheists to be unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who wear matted hair but do not study the Veda, nor those who are weak, nor gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for groups of people.
Physicians, temple-priests, and likewise meat-sellers,
as well as those who live by trade— these should be excluded from offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fire, and likewise a usurer; [these are excluded from the Śrāddha].

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has abandoned the sacred study, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a guild— all these are unworthy of receiving gifts.
An actor, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a Śūdra woman,
the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house a paramour resides— these are unfit to be invited.
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a paid teacher,
one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one whose teacher is a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka— these are excluded.
One who has abandoned his mother, father, or teacher without cause;
and one who has entered into alliances with outcasts through Vedic study or matrimonial ties.
An arsonist, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress), a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; 3.158.
One who disputes with his father, a gambler, a drinker of intoxicants,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids [are unworthy of inheritance].

The maker of bows and arrows, he who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, the betrayer of a friend, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; [these are excluded from the Śrāddha].

One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with white leprosy, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be excluded [from the company].
One who trains elephants, cattle, horses, or camels; one who lives by the stars (an astrologer); one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare.
He who diverts the currents of rivers, he who delights in obstructing them, one who constructs houses, a messenger, and likewise one who plants trees; [these are those who must be avoided].
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, a violent man, one who subsists as a servant to a low-caste person, and one who performs sacrifices for guilds (gaṇas).
One who is devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, a constant beggar,
one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous— these are unworthy of receiving gifts.
A sheep-butcher, a buffalo-breeder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and likewise a carrier of corpses— these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man, the best among the twice-born, should avoid both of these lowest of the twice-born, who are of censurable conduct and unworthy of the company at a meal.
But a Brāhmaṇa who does not study is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.
I shall describe in its entirety the fruit that accrues to the giver after death from giving to those unworthy of the *paṅkti*— whether at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors—
when it is consumed by twice-born men who have not fulfilled their vows, or by those such as a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*).
Whatever is eaten by those unworthy of the row and by others, that indeed the *rakṣas* consume.
He who enters into marriage and the consecration of the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.

The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, the younger brother who so marries, she with whom the younger brother cohabits, as well as the giver [of the bride] and the officiating priest— the fifth— these all go to hell.
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of a deceased brother—
even though she has been appointed to him according to dharma— should be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from the wives of others:
the Kuṇḍa is born while the husband is alive; the Golaka is born when the husband is dead.
Those two beings, having been born in the field of another,
cause the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* given by the donors to perish, both in this world and after death.
As many members of a company as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating, for that many the foolish giver receives no fruit from that act.
One who is blind from birth destroys the merit of ninety cows, one who is one-eyed that of sixty, one with white leprosy that of a hundred,
and one afflicted by a foul disease that of a thousand given by the donor.
As many Brāhmaṇas as a priest who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [Brāhmaṇas] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the gift consisting of a religious work (paurtika).
Even a Brahmin who knows the Veda, having accepted a gift from him out of greed,
goes quickly to destruction like an unbaked earthen vessel in water.
Feces are [the reward] for one who sells Soma; pus and blood for a physician;
what is given to a temple-attendant (devalaka) is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
But that which is given to a trader brings no reward either in this world or the next;
it is like an oblation poured into ashes, so too is a gift given to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
But regarding other unworthy persons who are unfit to sit in the row (apāṅktya), as previously specified,
the wise declare that their food is like fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.

Learn now in full about those foremost of the twice-born who purify a row (paṅkti) defiled by those unworthy of the company (apāṅktya). 3.183cd–184ab [173cd–174ab] Manusmṛti 3.183ab [173ab]: "A row defiled by those unworthy of the company is purified by those best of the twice-born. Manusmṛti 3.183cd [173cd]: "Learn them in their entirety, those foremost of the twice-born who purify the row. Manusmṛti 3.184ab [174ab]: "One should know that the following are the purifiers of the row: those who have studied the Vedas, those who know the Vedas, those who are devoted to austerities, those who are self-restrained, those who are free from greed, and those who are born of noble lineage. Manusmṛti 3.184cd [174cd]: "Those who have mastered the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda; those who know the Atharvaveda; those who are devoted to the study of the Purāṇas and the Itihāsas; and those who are devoted to the six auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas). Manusmṛti 3.185ab [175ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Upaniṣads; those who are devoted to the study of the Mīmāṃsā; those who are devoted to the study of the Nyāya; and those who are devoted to the study of the Dharmaśāstra. Manusmṛti 3.185cd [175cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Śikṣā; those who are devoted to the study of the Kalpa; those who are devoted to the study of the Jyotiṣa; and those who are devoted to the study of the Nirukta. Manusmṛti 3.186ab [176ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Vyākaraṇa; those who are devoted to the study of the Chandas; those who are devoted to the study of the Śrauta-sūtras; and those who are devoted to the study of the Gṛhya-sūtras. Manusmṛti 3.186cd [176cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Dharma-sūtras; those who are devoted to the study of the Artha-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Kāma-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Yoga-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.187ab [177ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Sāṃkhya; those who are devoted to the study of the Vaiśeṣika; those who are devoted to the study of the Pātañjala; and those who are devoted to the study of the Bhāgavata. Manusmṛti 3.187cd [177cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Jainas; those who are devoted to the study of the Buddhists; those who are devoted to the study of the Lokāyatikas; and those who are devoted to the study of the Cārvākas. Manusmṛti 3.188ab [178ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Āyurveda; those who are devoted to the study of the Dhanurveda; those who are devoted to the study of the Gāndharva-veda; and those who are devoted to the study of the Artha-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.188cd [178cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Kāvya-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Nāṭya-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Alaṃkāra-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Śilpa-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.189ab [179ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Jyotiṣa-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Vāstu-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Ratna-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Dhātu-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.189cd [179cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Maṇi-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Auṣadha-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Yantra-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Tantra-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.190ab [180ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Mantra-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Tarka-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhana-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Siddhi-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.190cd [180cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Abhyāsa-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Anuṣṭhāna-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Prayoga-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Phala-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.191ab [181ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Hetu-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Upāya-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Kriyā-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Karma-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.191cd [181cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Guṇa-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Doṣa-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Lakṣaṇa-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Parīkṣā-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.192ab [182ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhya-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhaka-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhanika-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhita-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.192cd [182cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhya-siddhi-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhaka-siddhi-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhanika-siddhi-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhita-siddhi-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.193ab [183ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhya-nirṇaya-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhaka-nirṇaya-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhanika-nirṇaya-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhita-nirṇaya-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.193cd [183cd]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhya-vicāra-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhaka-vicāra-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhanika-vicāra-śāstra; and those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhita-vicāra-śāstra. Manusmṛti 3.194ab [184ab]: "Those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhya-prakaraṇa-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sādhaka-prakaraṇa-śāstra; those who are devoted to the study of the Sād
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions of the sacred texts,
and who are born into lineages of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), should be known as the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one who is the offspring of a lineage where the Veda was given as a gift, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; likewise, one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a teacher, a celibate student, and one who has given away a thousand cows.
And those Brahmins who have lived for a hundred years are to be known as purifiers of the assembly.
On the day before or on the very day that the Śrāddha rite is to take place,
he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who have been described as qualified. Once invited to a rite for the ancestors, a twice-born man should always remain self-restrained.
And one should not study the Vedic meters at that place where the śrāddha is being performed.
For the ancestors attend upon those invited twice-born men;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.
But the best of the twice-born who, having been duly invited to a rite for the gods or the ancestors,
somehow neglects it, that sinner shall go to the state of a pig.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha, rejoices with a Śūdra woman,
takes upon himself whatever evil deed the giver may have committed.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, and ever-continually practicing celibacy,
the ancestors— the ancient deities— are highly fortunate and have laid down their weapons.
Since the origin of all these [castes] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now the rules by which those who are to be served by others should be served.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others— who were the offspring of Manu, the son of Hiranyagarbha, are recorded in tradition as the groups of Pitṛs.
The Virājas, sons of Virāj, are remembered as the Soma-drinking ancestors (Pitṛs) of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are those of the Marīcis and the gods.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are recorded as the ancestors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rakṣases,
Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among Brahmins they are named Somapas; among Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs;
among Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among Śūdras, Sukālins.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
One should designate the Agnidagdhas, the Anagnidagdhas, the Kavyas, the Barhiṣads,
as well as the Agniṣvāttas and the Saumyas, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins.
These principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed—
of them too, it should be understood here, the lineage of sons and grandsons is endless.
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, the gods and human beings;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—arose in due order.
Even water given with faith in vessels made of silver, or those adorned with silver, serves as an inexhaustible provision for them.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
for it is traditionally taught that the rite for the gods is the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection.

One should perform that [rite] beginning and ending with the gods; it should not begin and end with the ancestors. For one who performs it beginning and ending with the ancestors, he perishes quickly along with his lineage.
One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung;
one should also ensure that it slopes toward the south with great care.
In open spaces, on clean riverbanks,
and indeed in secluded places, the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered.
When separate seats provided with sacred grass have been prepared,
he should cause those Brahmins, who have properly sipped water, to sit down.
Having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the deities.
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds accompanied by purifiers (pavitra),
a Brāhmaṇa, being authorized, should perform the rite in the fire together with other Brāhmaṇas.
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors according to the rule by the offering of the oblation.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is said by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras to be the very fire itself.

The ancients describe these best of the twice-born as gods of the *śrāddha*, free from anger, easily propitiated, and intent upon the nourishment of the world. Having performed the circumambulation of the fire in the counter-clockwise direction (*apasavya*), one should complete the entire ritual procedure.
With the left hand, he should pour water upon the ground.
Therefore, having formed three pindas from the remainder of that sacrificial oblation, he, being composed in mind,
should offer them facing south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water-libation.
Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) there according to the prescribed rule while remaining pure,
he should wipe that hand on those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāgins).
Having sipped water, turned toward the north, and slowly restrained his breath three times,
he should pay homage with mantras to the six seasons and to the ancestors.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the *piṇḍas* again;
and with a concentrated mind, he should smell those *piṇḍas* in the order in which they were placed.
Having taken very small portions from each of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) in successive order,
he should first cause those same Brahmins, who are seated, to eat according to the rule.
While the father is still living, one should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone;
or else, at the *śrāddha*, one may feed one's own father as if he were a *vipra*.
In the case of one whose father has passed away but whose grandfather is still living, [the same rule applies].
Having announced the name of his father, he should announce the name of his great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
or, with his permission, he may perform it himself at will.
Having poured water with sesame seeds and *pavitra* grass-grass blades into their hands,
he should offer them the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for these. Then,
having himself taken up with both hands the increased quantity of food, [he should proceed].
Meditating on his ancestors, he should gently place [the food] near the Brahmins.
When food is brought that is released from both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras suddenly seize it away.
Being self-controlled and composed, he should first place upon the ground the various qualities such as soups, vegetables, milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.
Various kinds of food to be chewed and food to be swallowed, as well as roots and fruits,
meats that are pleasing to the heart, and fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that [food], he should, being composed and purified, serve it slowly while praising all its qualities.
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
Tears send the deceased to the state of ghosts; anger, to enemies; falsehood, to dogs;
contact with the feet, to Rākṣasas; and shaking [the head], to evildoers.
Whatever may please the Brahmins, that he should give without avarice;
and he should engage in theological discourses (*brahmodya*), for this is what is desired by the ancestors.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should cause [the Brahmins] to hear the Vedic study, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and the supplementary texts (khilas).
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually, little by little;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and drink as well as with various qualities.
One should diligently feed even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.

Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds. Furthermore, three qualities are praised in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born, when asked by the giver, speak of the qualities of the sacrificial oblation.
As long as the food remains warm, as long as they eat in silence,
and as long as the qualities of the oblation have not been described, for so long do the ancestors eat.
Whatever one eats with one's head covered, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
as well as a woman in her menses and a eunuch— these must not look upon twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these [defilers] during an oblation, a gift, or a meal—
whether it be an offering to the gods or one to the ancestors— that becomes ineffective.
The pig destroys [the merit] by smell; the cock, by the wind from its wings;
the dog, by the casting of its gaze; and one born of the lowest caste, by touch.
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove him as well.
A Brahmana or even a mendicant who has approached for the sake of food,
he shall honor according to his ability, with the permission of the Brahmanas.
Having gathered food fit for all castes and sprinkled it with water,
he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have finished eating.

For those who have died without the sacramental rites, for those who have abandoned their families, and for women of the household, the food-remnant on the *darbha* grass and that which is scattered thereon shall be their allotted share.
The remnants of the meal that have fallen upon the ground are declared to be the share of the group of slaves at a rite for the ancestors, provided they are neither crooked nor deceitful.
Until the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for a deceased member of the twice-born caste,
one should perform a *śrāddha* without offerings to the gods (*adaiva*), feeding [the guests] and offering a single *piṇḍa*.
But when the *piṇḍakriyā* has been performed for him according to the law,
the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍanirvapana*) must be performed by his sons according to this very same procedure.
He who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leavings to a *vṛṣala*,
that fool goes headlong to the Kālasūtra hell.
If a partaker of a Śrāddha feast approaches the bed of a Śūdra woman on that very day,
his ancestors lie for that entire month in her excrement.
Having asked, "Was it well-savored? he should then cause those who are satisfied to sip water. And when they have sipped water, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be happy on all sides."
Immediately after that, the Brāhmaṇas should say to him, "May there be *svadhā*. For the utterance of *svadhā* is the supreme benediction in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, after they have eaten, he should present the remainder of the food;
as the twice-born may direct, so he should do, being authorized by them.
At a rite for the ancestors (pitrya), one should say "It is well-eaten" (svaditam); at a rite in a cow-pen, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity (abhyudaya), "it is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods (daiva), "it is pleasing" (rucitam).
Likewise, the afternoon, darbha grass, the preparation of the site, and sesame seeds [are required].
The creation [of food], its purification, and the foremost of the twice-born are the perfections in the performance of śrāddha rites.
Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣya);
as well as whatever purifying substances were mentioned previously—these should be known as the requisites for the oblation.
The food of sages, milk, soma, meat that has not been seasoned, and salt that is not processed— these are by their very nature called sacrificial oblations (havis).

Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-controlled, silent, and pure, and facing the southern direction, he should request these boons from his ancestors: *Manu 3.258*: "Having dismissed those Brahmins, being restrained, silent, and pure, looking toward the southern quarter, he should ask these boons of the ancestors. *Manu 3.258c*: "[...he should ask these boons of the ancestors]."
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having thus performed the offering of the funeral cakes (nirvapaṇa), he should immediately thereafter cause a cow,
a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire to consume those cakes, or else cast them into the water.
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) only after [the cremation];
others cause them to be eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water.
A devoted wife, faithful to her husband, intent upon the worship of the ancestors,
and desiring a son, should then properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and wisdom,
as well as one who is wealthy, possessed of progeny, virtuous, and righteous.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen;
having given hospitality to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives.
That remnant of the meal should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed.
Thereafter, one should perform the domestic offering (gṛhabali); thus the law is established.
I shall explain in its entirety that sacrificial offering which, when given to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for many nights and even for eternity.
By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, or fruits,
the ancestors of men are satisfied for a month when given according to the prescribed rule.
For two months one may subsist on the flesh of fish, for three months on that of the hariṇa deer,
for four months on the flesh of sheep, and for five months indeed on the flesh of birds.

With the flesh of a goat, they are satisfied for six months; with that of the spotted deer (pārṣata), for seven; with the flesh of the black antelope (aina), for eight; and with that of the ruru deer, for nine. With the meat of boar and buffalo, however, they remain satiated for ten months.
But with the flesh of the hare and the tortoise, one [is purified] for exactly eleven months.
But by means of cow's milk, milk-rice,
and the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa (a ram or a rhinoceros), there is satisfaction for twelve years.
Black pot-herbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red goat, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for sages lead to infinite rewards.
Whatever mixed with honey one may offer on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
"May he be born in our lineage who would give us milk-rice with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, while the shadow of an elephant still falls toward the east."
Whatever one gives according to the rule, properly and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
In the dark fortnight, beginning from the tenth day and excluding the fourteenth, these lunar days are recommended for the Śrāddha;
other days are not so.
By performing [the śrāddha] on days with odd lunar mansions, one attains all desires;
but by performing it on days with even lunar mansions, one obtains abundant progeny for the ancestors.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too is the afternoon superior to the forenoon for the performance of a śrāddha.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the palm of the hand turned toward the left, and remaining alert,
one should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion, holding *darbha* grass in the hand.
One should not perform a Śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen.
By this rule, one should offer the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the Hemanta, Grīṣma, and Varṣā seasons— and perform the five great sacrifices daily.
The oblation belonging to the ancestral sacrifice (paitṛyajña) is not prescribed for the common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires, apart from the New Moon sacrifice (darśa).
Whatever fruit the best of the twice-born obtains by performing the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), he obtains that entire fruit simply by bathing and satiating the ancestors with water.
They call the ancestors Vasus, the grandfathers Rudras, and the great-grandfathers Ādityas; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
He should always be an eater of *vighasa*, or always an eater of *amṛta*. *Vighasa* is the remains of what has been eaten; likewise, *amṛta* is the remains of a sacrifice.
"All this rule regarding the five great sacrifices has been declared to you;
now hear the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born."
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher,
the twice-born should dwell in his house as a married man during the second quarter of his life.
Adopting a mode of life that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury, a Brahmin should live in times of non-distress.
For the sake of securing merely the means of subsistence through his own irreproachable occupations,
he should accumulate wealth without causing hardship to his body.
One may live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*, or even by the *satya* and the *anṛta*; but one must never subsist by the "dog's mode of life" (*śvavṛtti*).
Gleaning ears of grain (*uñcha*) and picking up single grains (*śila*) should be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
But begging for alms is called *mṛta*, and agriculture is traditionally known as *pramṛta*.
Trade consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may indeed subsist by that;
however, service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or indeed grain sufficient for a single jar;
or he may have enough for three days, or even be one who does not provide for the morrow.
Among these four twice-born householders,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior in terms of dharma and as more victorious over the worlds.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the "sacrifice of Brahman" (brahmasattra).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭi sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
He should not, under any circumstances, follow the conduct of the world for the sake of his livelihood;
rather, he should live the pure life of a Brāhmaṇa, free from crookedness and guile.
Seeking happiness, one who desires ease should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering.
A twice-born Snātaka, living by any one of these modes of livelihood,
should observe these following vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame:
he should perform his own duty as prescribed in the Veda constantly and without sloth.
For by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.

One should not pursue wealth through excessive attachment nor by means of forbidden actions; nor should one do so when wealth is already available, even in times of distress, nor from hither and thither. One should not, out of desire, become excessively attached to any of the objects of the senses.
And he should mentally restrain excessive attachment to these.
One should abandon all worldly pursuits that conflict with Vedic study;
however, one may teach them in whatever manner is appropriate, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his duty.
Conforming to the likeness of his age, occupation, wealth, learning,
and lineage, as well as his dress, speech, and intellect, he should conduct himself here in this world.
He should constantly study the scriptures that quickly increase wisdom, as well as the beneficial and auspicious Vedic Nigamas.
For in whatever measure a man masters the scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his specialized knowledge shines forth.

One should never, according to one's ability, neglect the sacrifice to the seers (ṛṣiyajña), the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña), the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūtayajña), the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña), and the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves while remaining free from worldly exertion.
Some always offer the breath into speech and speech into breath,
perceiving the imperishable completion of the sacrifice within both speech and breath.
Other Brahmins always perform these sacrifices through knowledge alone,
perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.
One should always offer the Agnihotra at the beginning and end of day and night;
likewise, one should perform the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice as well.

At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the *navasasyeṣṭi* sacrifice; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the *adhvara* sacrifices; at the beginning of the solstice (*ayana*), he should perform the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*); and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices. A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires must not fail to perform the *navasasyeṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice.
One who desires to live a long life should not eat new grain or meat.
For his sacred fires, greedy for new grain and meat offerings, desire to consume his very life-breaths when they are not honored with new offerings and animal sacrifices.
No guest who is capable of doing so should dwell in his house without being honored with a seat, food, a bed, water, roots, or fruits.
One should not honor, even with mere words, heretics, those who persist in forbidden acts, those who act like cats, the deceitful, sophists, and those who live like herons.

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and who are householders; one should avoid those who are the opposite.
A householder should give, according to his ability, to those who do not cook for themselves;
and he should provide a distribution to all living beings without causing hardship to his own household.
A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from his patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a resident pupil; but not from anyone else—this is the settled rule.
A learned Snātaka Brahmin who is capable should never suffer from hunger in any way,
nor should he wear worn-out or dirty clothes if he possesses the means.
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self.
He should carry a staff of bamboo, a water-pot with water,
the sacred thread, a Vedic text, and two auspicious earrings made of gold.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor should one run while it is raining;
nor should one look at one's own reflection in water—this is the settled rule.
One should circumambulate clockwise earth, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees.
Even if he is impelled by passion, he must not approach his wife when her menses are visible;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman overwhelmed by her menstrual flow,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan are diminished.
For him who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by the menses,
wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and lifespan indeed increase.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
or while she is sneezing or yawning, nor while she is seated at her ease.
A twice-born man who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one giving birth.
One should not eat food wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked. One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
Neither on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain;
neither in a ruined temple, nor on an anthill, under any circumstances.
Not in pits containing living beings, nor while walking, nor while standing;
not having approached the bank of a river, nor on the peak of a mountain.
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows,
one should never discharge feces or urine.
Having covered [the mouth] with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or similar materials,
restraining his speech, purified, with his limbs wrapped and his head veiled, he should speak.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night and during the two twilights, one should face south, as during the day.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction that is comfortable to him, as well as when there is danger to his life.
One's intelligence perishes by urinating facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man; likewise, facing a cow or facing the wind.
One should not blow on a fire with one’s mouth, nor should one look at a naked woman.
One should not throw impure substances into the fire, nor should one warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it underneath anything, nor should one step over it;
one should not place it at the level of one's feet, nor should one cause any injury to living beings by means of it.
He should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should he travel, nor even lie down;
nor indeed should he scratch the ground, nor should he remove his own garland.

One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water; nor should one cast into it anything else smeared with impurity, blood, or poisons. One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person from sleep. [One may sleep in an empty house.]
One should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor should one go to a sacrifice unless invited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brāhmaṇas,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling, nor should one tell anyone about it;
likewise, a wise man, having seen a rainbow in the sky, should not point it out to anyone.
One should not dwell in a village ruled by unrighteousness, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one live for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one crowded with unrighteous people;
nor in one overrun by groups of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating.
Neither too early, nor too late, nor having eaten in the evening and morning.
One should not engage in useless exertion, nor should one drink water with the hollowed palms;
one should not eat food placed on the lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor, being impassioned, raise a clamor.
He should never wash his feet in a vessel made of bell-metal.
One should not eat from a broken vessel, nor from one that is defiled by its condition.
One should not wear shoes, a garment,
a sacrificial cord, an ornament, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others.
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those disfigured by maimed tails.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without striking them excessively with the goad.
He should avoid the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and likewise a broken seat.
One should not clip one's nails or hair with the teeth, nor should one tear at the nails.
One should not crush a clod of earth with the feet, nor should one cut grass with the fingernails. One should not perform fruitless labor, nor anything that results in unhappiness for the future.
A man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails,
as well as one who is a slanderer or impure, quickly goes to destruction. He should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should he wear a garland outside [of his garment].
And riding on the back of cows is in every way utterly condemned.
One should not pass through a gateless opening into an enclosed village or house;
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
He should never play with dice, nor should he carry his own sandals;
he should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with his food held in his hand, nor while seated on a seat.
One should not eat anything mixed with sesame seeds after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep naked here, nor walk anywhere while still impure from food.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to sleep with wet feet;
by eating with wet feet, one obtains a long life.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds; nor should he step upon cotton seeds or husks.
One should not live together with outcasts (patita), nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with the lowest castes, nor with those who dwell on the outskirts of society.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for a sacrificial offering;
nor should one teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a religious vow for him.
For he who explains his duty, and he who prescribes a vow for him,
sinks into the darkness called *asaṃvṛta* along with that very person.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor, while impure from food remnants, should one touch it, nor bathe without using water for that purpose.
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking the head;
moreover, having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse,
a wheel, or a banner, nor from those who live by the profession of a courtesan.
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a tavern is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten taverns; and a king is equal to ten brothels.
A king is declared to be equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughter-houses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is a terrible thing.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures goes,
in succession, to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the Naraka Kālasūtra, and Mahānaraka;
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika,
Lohaśaṅku, Ṛjīṣa, Panthāna, Śālmalī, and the River.
And also the Forest of Sword-leaves and the Forest of Iron Spikes.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse upon the Veda and who desire their own welfare after death do not accept gifts from a king.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā, he should wake up and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as bodily hardships rooted in those two and the true meaning of the Veda.
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, having purified himself and composed his mind,
he should stand reciting the morning twilight prayer for a long time at its proper hour, and likewise the evening prayer. By virtue of their prolonged twilight prayers, the seers attained long life.
Wisdom, fame, renown, and indeed the splendor of sacred knowledge.
Having performed the ritual commencement (upākarma) according to the rule on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin,
being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.
On the day of Puṣya, a twice-born man should perform the external dismissal of the Vedic hymns;
or he may do so when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, in the forenoon.
Having thus performed the ritual dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside [the village] according to the scriptures,
he should observe a fast for a "bird-night" (two days and two nights), or for that very same day and night.
From this time forward, however, he should, being self-restrained, recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights;
and he should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.
One should not study when the recitation is indistinct, nor in the presence of Śūdras;
nor, having finished his Vedic study at the end of the night, should one go back to sleep while still exhausted.

A twice-born man who is disciplined and not in times of distress should daily recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule; for he is indeed joined with the sacred word (*brahman*) and that which is composed in meters. While studying, he should always avoid these occasions when study is forbidden.
And while teaching his pupils according to the prescribed rule, he should likewise act.

When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when it stirs up clouds of dust during the day— those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions to be times of non-study during the rainy season.
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when great meteors fall,
there shall be an interruption of study for the remainder of the day.

One should know that when these [phenomena] appear while the fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, even outside the rainy season, when clouds are seen.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the celestial bodies,
