one should know that these occasions constitute times when study is forbidden, even during the proper season.

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be no study as long as the light remains; in other cases, it is as at night [during such phenomena] as it is by day.
There shall always be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and in cities for those who desire proficiency in the Dharma, as well as whenever there is a foul odor. Likewise,
there is a suspension of study within a village where a corpse lies and in the presence of a *vṛṣala*.
There is no study when there is weeping, nor in the midst of a crowd of people.
In water, at midnight, upon voiding excrement or urine,
while impure from food, or after eating at a *śrāddha*— even in his mind—
a learned twice-born man should not contemplate the invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite once he has accepted it. (Manu 4.109–110a)
For three days, one should not recite the Veda during the period of impurity following the birth of a king or during the eclipse of Rāhu.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of food offered at a funeral rite for a single ancestor remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor while sitting in the *avasakthikā* posture; nor after eating meat, nor food from a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the fourteenth and new moon days, and on the full moon and *aṣṭakā* days; Manu 4.113.
The new moon day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
and the eighth day of Brahmā and the full moon day [destroy the Veda]. Therefore, one should avoid those days.

A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a dust storm, when the quarters of the sky are aflame, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, and camels are barking or braying, nor while in a row.

One should not study near a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, or after accepting food offered at a funeral rite (śrāddha).

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony—upon touching that, there shall be a suspension of Vedic study; for the twice-born is traditionally declared to have his hand as his mouth.
In a village harassed by thieves, during a panic caused by fire,
and during all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study for the duration of the event.
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
likewise on the Aṣṭakās, for a day and a night, and on the nights at the end of the seasons.
One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant;
nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing in a barren spot, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
Not during a legal dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while suffering from indigestion, nor after vomiting, nor when there is sour eructation.
Nor when he has not taken leave of his guest; nor while a strong wind is blowing;
nor when blood flows from his body, or when he is wounded by a weapon.
One should never recite the *Ṛg* or *Yajur* Vedas while the sound of the *Sāman* is heard;
nor should one do so after having completed the study of the entire Veda, or after having studied the *Āraṇyaka*.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deity; the Yajurveda belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as pertaining to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Knowing this daily extraction of the essence of the three Vedas,
the learned first practice it in due order and afterwards study the Veda itself.
When cattle, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose,
or a rat pass between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night.
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study:
an impure place for Vedic recitation and himself when he is impure.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon day, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born *snātaka* should always remain celibate, even during the fertile period.
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in a body of water that is unknown.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, of one's teacher, of a king, of a *snātaka*, of an *ācārya*, nor of a brown-hued person or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents used for rubbing the body, water used for ritual bathing, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor the ally of an enemy,
nor an unrighteous person, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
For there exists nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world.
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a Brāhmaṇa deeply learned in the Vedas, even if they appear weak.
For these three, when treated with contempt, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
One should not despise oneself because of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity, and one should not consider it difficult to attain.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak an untruth that is pleasant—this is the eternal dharma.
One should say "May it be well, may it be well," or simply say "May it be well. One should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone.
One should not go out too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when the sun is at its zenith;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with *vṛṣalas*.

One should not insult those who are deficient in limbs, those with redundant limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth. A Brahmin, while impure from eating, must not touch a cow, a Brahmin, or a fire with his hand.

One who is impure should not look at the hosts of luminaries in the sky during the day, nor when he is in a state of well-being. Having touched these, while remaining constantly impure, one should touch the vital breaths with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own orifices without a specific reason;
he should likewise avoid touching all the hair on his private parts.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should daily mutter prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.
For those who are ever devoted to auspicious conduct, whose souls are constantly restrained,
and who recite prayers and offer oblations, no downfall exists.
One should constantly study the Veda itself at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty.
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity,
and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Remembering his former birth, he practices the Veda once again;
and by the constant practice of the Veda, he enjoys infinite bliss.
He should always perform the *sāvitra* oblations and the *śānti* homas on the *parvan* days;
and he should constantly worship the ancestors on the *aṣṭakā* days and the subsequent *anvaṣṭakā* days.
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, far from where one has washed one's feet,
and likewise far from where one has discarded the remains of food.
One should perform acts of friendliness, grooming, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium,
and the worship of the deities during the forenoon itself.
He should visit the deities and righteous, most excellent twice-born men;
and on the sacred festival days (parvan), he should likewise visit the Lord for protection and his own gurus.
He should salute the elders and offer them his own seat.
With palms joined in reverence, he should wait upon them; as they depart, he should follow behind them.
One should unweariedly practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma, properly established in one’s own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly experiences suffering, is afflicted by disease, and is short-lived.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who follows the conduct of the virtuous,
who is full of faith and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
Whatever action depends on others, that he should carefully avoid.
Whatever is under one's own control, that one should diligently cultivate. All that is dependent on others is suffering; all that is under one's own control is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.
Whatever action he performs that brings satisfaction to his inner self, that he should perform with effort; but he should avoid the opposite.
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities;
one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness.
One should not raise a staff against another in a fit of rage, nor should one strike him down.
Except for his son or his pupil, he may strike those two for the purpose of correction.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brāhmaṇa with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [a cow] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in the wombs of sinful creatures.
Having caused blood to flow from the body of a Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting,
a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death.
As many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth,
for so many years in the next world is the shedder of that blood devoured by others.
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who is constantly devoted to violence— he does not prosper in happiness in this world. Even if he suffers for the sake of dharma, he should never set his mind upon adharma.
Seeing the swift downfall of unrighteous evildoers, (he should act accordingly).
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow;
but turning back slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.

If [the fruit of an action] does not manifest in oneself, it appears in one's sons; if not in the sons, then in one's grandsons. But an unrighteous act (*adharma*) that has been committed never becomes fruitless for the doer. Through unrighteousness one prospers for a time, and thereafter one beholds auspicious things.
From that, he conquers his rivals, and they perish along with their very roots.
He should always apply himself to truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and, restrained in speech, arms, and belly, he should instruct his pupils in accordance with the Dharma.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness,
and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in unhappiness or is censured by the world.
He should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, nor crooked;
he should likewise not be fickle with his speech, nor intent on actions that harm others.
By that path which his fathers have traveled, by which his grandfathers have traveled—that path of the virtuous he should follow; going by that way, he does not come to harm.

By officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers; by maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; by children, the elderly, and the sick; and by physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and blood relations.
One should not engage in a dispute with one's mother or father, female relatives, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of slaves.
By renouncing disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.

Female relatives dwell in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice dwell in the world of the Viśvedevas; maternal relatives dwell in the world of the Waters; and one's mother and maternal uncle dwell upon the earth.
Children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as the lords of space;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body.
One's shadow, one's own group of slaves, a daughter, and a dependent are one's supreme refuge;
therefore, when insulted by these, one should always endure it without resentment.
Even though he may be capable of receiving gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by the acceptance of gifts, his spiritual luster (*brāhmatejas*) is quickly extinguished.
A wise man, even if he is perishing from hunger, should not accept a gift without first understanding the lawful rule regarding the objects to be received.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold and food increase one's lifespan; land and a cow likewise nourish the body;
a horse [increases] the eyesight, clothing the skin, ghee the vital energy, and sesame seeds progeny.
But a twice-born man who lacks austerity, does not study the Vedas, and delights in receiving gifts,
sinks down along with that very person, like one in water with a stone for a raft.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear every kind of gift;
for by even a very small one, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
A knower of the Dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who follows the "cat-vow," nor to one who follows the "heron-vow" and is sinful,
nor to one who is ignorant of the Veda.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the prescribed rule, when given to these three types of persons,
results in misfortune for both the giver and the receiver in the next world.
Just as one who crosses water by means of a boat made of stone sinks down,
so do the ignorant giver and receiver sink to the bottom.
One who makes a banner of righteousness, who is always greedy, a hypocrite, and a deceiver of the world;
One who is injurious and a deceiver of all should be known as a "cat-vowed" person (baiḍālavratika).
A twice-born man who keeps his eyes cast downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own selfish ends,
fraudulent, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata).
Those Brahmins who follow the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
for by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception toward women and Śūdras.
Such Brahmins, both after death and in this world, are censured by the exponents of the Veda; and whatever vow is practiced under false pretenses goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, not being a bearer of the marks, lives by the livelihood of one who bears the marks,
takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born into the womb of an animal.
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the person who constructed the reservoir.
If one makes use of his vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given, he shall incur a fourth part of the sin.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, and in lakes, as well as in hollows and springs.
A wise man should constantly practice the *yamas*, but not the *niyamas* exclusively;
for by failing to perform the *yamas* while devoting himself solely to the *niyamas*, he falls.
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one performed by a priest for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
"This is offensive to the virtuous, wherein these men offer the oblation;
this is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it."
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease;
nor that which is contaminated by hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by a foot.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan), touched by a woman in her courses (udakyā),
pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit for consumption].
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food proclaimed [for sale],
food belonging to a group, food belonging to a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned— [these one should avoid].
The food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, and a usurer;
and that of one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, and one who is bound in fetters—these are forbidden.
The food of one who is accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as food that is sour, stale, or the leavings of a Śūdra—[these must not be eaten].
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats the remnants of another's meal;

the food of a fierce man, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that which has been tasted by someone before being served; the food of one whose ten-day period of impurity has not yet passed.

Meat that has not been honored, meat killed for no sacred purpose, the food of a woman who has no male relatives, the food of an enemy, the food of a city-dweller, the food of an outcast, and food sneezed upon— these one should avoid.
The food of a slanderer and a liar, as well as that of one who sells the results of sacrifices;
the food of an actor, a tailor, and indeed the food of an ungrateful person.
[The food] of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a goldsmith, a basket-maker, and likewise a seller of weapons; 4.215.
Of those who keep dogs, of liquor-sellers, of the washerman of clothes,
of the dyer, of the cruel man, and of him in whose house a paramour resides;
and of those who tolerate a paramour, and of all those who are ruled by women.
And food from one recently deceased within ten days, as well as that which fails to provide satisfaction, [should not be eaten].
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame.
The food of an artisan destroys one's offspring, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Regarding those others who have been described in succession as persons whose food is not to be eaten,
the wise declare that their skin, bones, and hair constitute their food.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one must fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, poison, or urine, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance.

A learned twice-born man shall not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha). If he has no other means of subsistence, he may take from him raw grain sufficient for one night. [He should avoid the food] of a miserly Vedic scholar as well as that of a liberal usurer.
Having deliberated upon both, the gods ordained food to be equal.
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal!
That which is purified by faith belongs to the generous giver; the other is destroyed by a lack of faith."

One should always perform sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*) with faith and without indolence; for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired by righteous means, these two become inexhaustible.
One should constantly practice the duty of giving, consisting of sacrifices and works of public utility,
with a cheerful disposition whenever a worthy recipient is found, according to one's ability.
Whatever may be asked for should be given without malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who will deliver one from all [sins].
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra; the giver of a horse attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the highest station of the sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of security obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of the Veda is preeminent;
so too are the gifts of water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter.
With whatever disposition one bestows any gift,
with that very same disposition one receives it in return, duly honored.
He who accepts what is unhonored, or he who gives what is indeed honored—both of them go to heaven;
but in the reverse case, they go to hell.
One should not be proud of one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice;
even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift.
A sacrifice perishes through falsehood, and asceticism perishes through pride.
One's lifespan is diminished by speaking ill of Brahmins, and one's merit is lost through the public proclamation of one's own gifts.
One should gradually accumulate merit, as termites build up an anthill,
without causing pain to any living beings, for the sake of having a companion in the next world.
For neither father nor mother remain there in the next world for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains—dharma alone stands by one.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the kinsmen depart with averted faces; dharma alone follows him.
Therefore, one should constantly accumulate dharma little by little for the sake of a companion;
for with dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
The radiant one, whose body is ether, swiftly leads to the next world that man who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity.
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form connections with the most eminent; he should avoid those who are inferior.
By approaching only those who are superior and avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains excellence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra.
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
one who is non-violent and observes such vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and charity.
One may accept from anyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, food offered spontaneously, honey, and the gift of safety.
Prajāpati considered that alms brought and offered spontaneously, without having been previously solicited, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat [the offerings] of that person for fifteen years.
And Agni does not carry the sacrificial oblation for him who treats her with contempt.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or vegetables.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself must not find satisfaction in that alone.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
seeking a means of livelihood for himself, he should always accept it from a virtuous person.
A sharecropper, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave,
and a barber— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Whatever his disposition may be, whatever he intends to do,
and how he would treat him, in that manner he should present himself.
He who represents himself to virtuous men as something other than what he truly is, is the greatest sinner in the world; he is a thief who steals his own soul.
All objects of speech are fixed, rooted in speech, and issued from speech;
he who steals that speech is a man who commits every kind of theft.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule, [he may enter the forest].
Having entrusted everything to his son, he should live adopting an attitude of neutrality.
Alone, he should constantly reflect upon what is beneficial for himself in solitude;
for by reflecting alone, he attains the highest good.
This eternal mode of life for a Brahmin householder has been declared,
as well as the auspicious ritual of the vows for a Snātaka, which increases one's inner strength.
A Brahmin who, learned in the Vedic scriptures, conducts himself according to this mode of life,
being eternally free from sin, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they were declared, the seers spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: *Manu 5.01a-c* (as cited above) [The seers said: "O venerable one, you have explained the duties of the *snātaka*. Now we wish to hear about the duties of householders."
O Lord, how does death prevail over those Brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own specific duties and are learned in the Vedic scriptures?
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen, O Brahmins, to the fault by which death seeks to destroy you."
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of right conduct,
laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to destroy the Brahmins.
[Likewise, one should avoid] garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms.
And those things produced from impure substances are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born.

One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions; likewise, one should avoid *śelu* fruit and the colostrum (*peyūṣa*) of a cow. One should also avoid *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, and cakes when prepared for no sacred purpose.
Meat that has not been consecrated, as well as food intended for the gods and sacrificial oblations, [should not be eaten].
The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of camels, of one-hoofed animals, of sheep,
the milk of a *sandhinī* (a cow in heat), and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away;
and the milk of all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo— these are forbidden.
The milk of a woman and all sour substances must likewise be avoided.
Among sour substances, curd is fit for consumption, as is everything produced from curd;
and likewise those [liquids] which are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds as well as those that dwell in villages;
one should also avoid those with uncloven hooves that have not been specifically permitted, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the swan (*haṃsa*), the *cakravāka*, the village cock, the *sārasa*, the *rajjuvāla*, the *dātyūha*, the parrot, and the *sārikā*; also the birds that peck (*pratuda*),
those with webbed feet, the *koyaṣṭi*, and the clawed scratchers (*viṣkira*).
And fish-eaters who sink [into the water], meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; [these one should avoid].
He who eats the flesh of any creature is said to be an eater of that very creature's flesh;
since an eater of fish is an eater of all kinds of flesh, one should therefore avoid fish.
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are fit to be eaten when employed in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Likewise, the *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and all *saśalka* fish may be eaten.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown.
Likewise, one should avoid all five-toed animals that have been specified as fit for consumption.
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—
these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with one row of teeth, excluding the camel.
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village pig, garlic, a village cock,
onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unintentionally eaten these six [forbidden things], one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance;
or else, for the remaining cases, one should observe the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa or fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for a year for the sake of purification from food eaten unknowingly; however, for food known [to be forbidden], the penance must be specifically more severe.
Commendable wild animals and birds may be killed by Brāhmaṇas for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sake of maintaining dependents; for Agastya did so in ancient times.

For even in ancient sacrifices, including those performed by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) consisted of the meat of wild animals and birds. Whatever food, whether chewed or swallowed, is mixed with oil or fat and is not censured, [is fit for sacrifice].
That which has become stale is still fit to be eaten, as is what remains from an oblation.
Even if it has been stored for a long time, all food made from barley or wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be eaten by the twice-born even if they have not been smeared with oil.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
One may eat meat that has been consecrated with sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas,
or when one is appointed according to the rule, or indeed when there is danger to one's life.
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa):
both the stationary and the moving; indeed, everything is the sustenance of the vital breath.
Non-moving creatures are the food of moving ones; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs; those without hands are the food of those with hands; and cowards are the food of the brave.
The eater does not incur sin by eating edible creatures day after day;
for the Creator himself created both the creatures to be eaten and the eaters.
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance;
any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance."
Having purchased it, or having produced it himself, or even having received it from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having honored the gods and the ancestors.
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when he is not in distress;
for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he becomes a ghost and is helplessly devoured by those very creatures.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth who kills deer for profit is not as great as the sin that awaits one who eats meat in vain after death.
But that man who, having been duly appointed, does not eat meat,
goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births.
A Brahmin, adhering to the eternal rule, must never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, he may eat those consecrated with mantras, remaining established in the perpetual ordinance.
In case of necessity, one may perform an animal sacrifice with clarified butter, or likewise with an animal made of flour;
but one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death after death in successive births.
"Animals were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice; sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."
Herbs, cattle, trees, animals,
and birds that meet their death for the sake of sacrifice attain higher rebirths once again.
[At the honey-mixture offering, at a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods.]
"In this very case alone may animals be killed, and not elsewhere," so said Manu.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, while killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animal to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-controlled twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
One should know that the injury to moving and unmoving beings which is prescribed by the Veda and regulated in this world is indeed non-injury; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor after death.
He who does not desire to inflict the sufferings of bondage or death upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherein one fixes one's pleasure—
that one obtains without effort, provided that one harms nothing at all.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having thoroughly considered the origin of meat and the killing and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from the eating of all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the ritual injunctions like a Piśāca,
does not become unpopular in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the one who buys or sells, the one who prepares the meat,
the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are considered killers.
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another,
without first honoring the ancestors and the gods— there is no doer of more demeritorious deeds than he.
He who might perform the horse-sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots, nor by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total renunciation of meat.
"He shall eat me in the next world, whose meat I eat here"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "meat" (māṃsa).
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
for this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit.
I shall now declare the purification for the dead, as well as the purification of objects,
for all four castes, duly and in their proper order.

When a child dies after the teeth have emerged, or after they have been lost, or when the tonsure ceremony has been performed, all the relatives remain impure; the same is declared to be the case during a birth.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapindas;
it may last until the collection of the bones, or for three days, or even for one day.
The status of sapinda-relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka (a kinsman by water) persists as long as there is knowledge of the birth and the name.
Just as this impurity on account of a death is prescribed for the *sapiṇḍas*,

so too should it be in the case of a birth for those who desire complete purity. For all others there is impurity on account of a death, but for the mother and father there is *sūtaka* (impurity on account of a birth).
The birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall belong to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (upaspṛśya).
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
By one day and night, and by three periods of three nights, those who touch a corpse are purified;
those who offer water are purified after three days.
But a pupil who performs the funeral rites for his deceased teacher becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse. In the case of a miscarriage,
one is purified by nights equal in number to the months [of pregnancy].
When her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who was menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath.

For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is declared to take one night; but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights. A deceased child less than two years old, the kinsmen should place outside the village.
Having adorned [the body], one should place it on pure ground, except for the collection of the bones.
No funeral rites with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water libation be offered;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should remain in mourning for exactly three days.
The water libation need not be performed by his relatives for one who has not reached the age of three years.
Or they may perform it for one whose teeth have emerged, or even when the naming ceremony has been completed.
When one day has passed for a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), a single day's fasting is prescribed;
however, for those who share the same funeral water (*ekodaka*) upon birth, purification is held to occur after three nights.
But for female relatives who have not been consecrated with marriage rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sapinda) become pure according to the very rule already stated.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should abstain from eating meat and sleep separately on the ground.
This rule for impurity due to death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure is to be understood by relatives and kinsmen for when one is absent.
But he who hears that one who had departed and was staying in a foreign land has died within the ten-day period shall remain impure for only as long as remains of those ten nights.
If ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a relative or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed,
a man becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on in water.
If a child, one who has gone to another country, or a person belonging to a different *piṇḍa* lineage dies,
one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water while still wearing one's clothes.
If death or birth should occur again within ten days,
the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure for as long as that period has not yet expired.
When the teacher has passed away, they say that the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it is settled that the impurity lasts for one day and night.
Upon the death of a *śrotriya* who has arrived as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights;
likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, one remains impure for a night with its two surrounding days (*pakṣiṇī rātri*).

When a king dies, one who resides in his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun or moon] persists; however, if the king is not a *śrotriya*, the impurity lasts for a full day, and likewise when a teacher who has mastered the Vedas (*anūcāna*) dies. A Brahmin is purified in ten days, and a king (Kṣatriya) in twelve days.
A Vaiśya is purified in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the rites performed in the sacred fires;
and while performing those rites, even a kinsman does not become impure.
Having touched a Divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse,
or one who has touched such a person, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water and become pure, he should always recite, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his energy and *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability.
Having touched a human bone that still has marrow, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of marrow, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been initiated for a vow shall not perform the water-libation until the completion of that vow;
but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after three nights.
For those born of illicit intermixture and for those who persist in the life of wandering mendicants (pravrajyā), [the same penance applies].
The water-libation rite shall be withheld from those who have abandoned themselves.

And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their own lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor— [the king shall confiscate the entire property].
Having carried out the funeral rites for his own teacher, a sub-teacher, his father, his mother, or a guru who has died,
one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.
One should carry out a deceased Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
however, for the twice-born, they should be carried out through the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions;
for they always occupy the station of Indra and have become one with Brahman.
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high office;
and the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting his subjects.
And for those killed in a riot or in battle, by lightning, or by the king;
and for one who died for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whomever the king so desires.
The king bears the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vitta-pati, and Yama.
The king is presided over by the Lord of the World; no impurity (āśauca) is ordained for him. For the purity and impurity of mortals are the origin and dissolution of their worlds.
For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons while following the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is completed immediately, and likewise the period of impurity; such is the settled rule.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, his vehicle or weapon;
a Vaiśya, his goad or reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, his staff.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you;
now learn the purification for the dead concerning all those who are not sapindas.
Having carried out a deceased twice-born man who is not a *sapiṇḍa* as if he were a kinsman, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights; the same applies to the maternal relatives of his mother.
If he eats their food, however, he is purified in ten days;
if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.
Having followed a deceased kinsman or even a non-kinsman at his own wish,
he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
One should not have a dead Brahmin carried by a Śūdra while other [eligible] men are present.
For that oblation would not lead to heaven, being defiled by contact with a Śūdra.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, and ointment;
wind, ritual action, the sun, and time—these are the agents that bring about the purification of embodied beings.
Of all forms of purity, purity of wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water.
The wise are purified by forbearance; those who have committed forbidden acts are purified by charity;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by the silent recitation of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas are purified by austerity.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This decision regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you.
Listen now to the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.
For objects made of metal, for gems, and for everything made of stone,
purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
A golden vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone;
the same applies to vessels made of substances born in water, those made of stone, and silver that has not been alloyed.
Through the combination of water and fire, gold and silver were produced;
therefore, for these two, purification by their own source is more effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
For all liquids, purification is declared to be straining;
for solid objects, sprinkling; and for wooden items, scraping.
In the performance of sacrificial rites, the purification of sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of *camasa* cups and *graha* ladles is by washing.
The purification of sacrificial pots (caru), as well as the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva), is by means of hot water;
likewise for the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the cart (śakaṭa), and the pestle and mortar (musala-ulkhala).
The purification for large quantities of grain and clothing is by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification is prescribed by washing them with water.
The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and that of woven bamboo articles is likewise;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is prescribed to be the same as for grain.
Silk and woolen cloth are purified with alkaline salts, and blankets (*kutapa*) with *ariṣṭaka* fruit.
Silk fabrics [are purified] with *śrīphala* fruits, and linen cloths with white mustard seeds.
The purification of linen, conch-shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow’s urine or water.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again.
Earthenware that has been defiled by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus,
or blood cannot be purified even by re-firing.
[But] by sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, sprinkling, and scraping, it becomes pure.
And ground is purified by the five-fold process involving cattle.
(5.124c) What has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or spat upon, and what is defiled by hair or insects, is purified by the scattering of earth. (5.125)
As long as the odor and the stain caused by an impure substance do not depart from that which has been smeared by it,
so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of objects.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by word.
Water found on the ground is pure if it is sufficient to satisfy the thirst of a cow,
provided it has not been contaminated by impure substances and possesses its natural odor, color, and taste.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
almsfood received by a religious student is always pure—this is the settled rule.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Manu has declared that the meat of an animal killed by dogs is pure,
as is the meat of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and other such robbers.
All those apertures of the body that are above the navel are pure in every respect;
those below it are impure, as are the excretions that issue from the body.
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch.
For the purpose of purification after voiding feces or urine, earth and water should be used in sufficient quantity;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
One application of clay should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten to one hand,
and seven applications of clay should be given to both hands by one desiring purification.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise, one who is about to study the Veda and one who is eating food should always do so.
One who desires bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice;
however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so once each.
Śūdras who conduct themselves according to the law must have their hair shaved every month;
their rules for purification shall be like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of food left by twice-born men.
The primary drops that do not fall upon the body do not make one impure by leavings;
nor do beard hairs that have entered the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth.

The drops that touch the feet of one who is making others sip water for purification should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure by them. However, if one whose hands hold an object is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants (ucchiṣṭa), [he must purify himself].
Having set that object down, one who has sipped water (ācānta) shall attain purity.

One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then perform the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). After eating food, one should simply sip water; for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse, bathing is prescribed.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, and after speaking untruths;
and after drinking water, as well as when about to study, one should sip water even if one is already pure.
This entire rule for purification, as well as the purification of objects, has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women.
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an aged woman,
no action whatsoever should be performed independently by a woman, even within her own home.
In childhood, she should remain under the control of her father; in youth, under that of her husband;
when her husband has died, under that of her sons. A woman must never enjoy independence.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or her sons;
for by being separated from them, she would bring reproach upon both families.
She should always remain cheerful and be skillful in her household duties; she should keep the utensils well-maintained and be not wasteful in her expenditures.
To whomsoever her father may give her, or her brother with the father’s consent,
she shall serve him while he lives and must not disregard him when he has passed away.
For their auspiciousness, for their well-being, and as a sacrifice to Prajāpati, these rites are performed at the wedding;
however, the formal giving away of the bride is the cause of the husband’s ownership.

The husband who performs the consecration with mantras both outside the fertile season and during the fertile season is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next.
Whether he be of bad character, or acting according to his lusts, or even devoid of all virtues,
a husband must always be attended upon by a virtuous wife like a god.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, and no fasting;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should do nothing whatsoever displeasing to him who took her hand, whether he be living or dead.
She may, at her will, emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died.
Until death, she should remain patient, self-controlled, and chaste,
desiring that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband.
Many thousands of young Brahmins who have observed the vow of celibacy have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for their lineage.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those lifelong students of the Veda.
But that woman who, out of a desire for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
In this world, there is no offspring produced by another man, nor even one born of another's wife;
furthermore, it is taught that for virtuous women, there is never a second husband.
She who, having abandoned her own husband though he be inferior, resorts to one who is superior,
shall indeed be censured in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband."
But through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs censure in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by diseases resulting from her sin.
She who does not practice sorcery against her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the world of her husband and is called a "virtuous woman" by the righteous.
By this conduct, a woman who is self-restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains preeminent fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.

A twice-born man who knows the Dharma should cause his wife of equal caste— who has conducted herself in this manner and dies before him— to be cremated with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial implements.
Having offered the sacred fires to a wife who has died before him during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five great sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life.
Having thus dwelt in the householder stage according to the rules, the twice-born Snātaka,
with his senses subdued, should live in the forest, self-controlled and in accordance with the law.
But when a householder perceives his own skin wrinkled and his hair turned grey,
and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest.
Having completely abandoned village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, or else [go] together with her.
Having taken up the *agnihotra* and the domestic fire-utensils,
and having departed from the village for the forest, he should dwell there with his senses restrained.
He should subsist on various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, a beard, body hair, and nails.
From whatever food he himself may eat, he should offer the *bali* oblation and alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come from the various stages of life (*āśrama*) with water, roots, fruits, and alms.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), self-controlled, friendly toward all beings, and composed in mind.
He should always be a giver, never a taker, and compassionate toward all living beings.
He should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the prescribed rule,
not omitting the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices at their proper times.

He should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsyas; likewise, he should perform the Turāyaṇa and the Dakṣāyaṇa in due order. With pure food fit for sages, gathered by himself from the spring and autumn harvests, he should subsist.
One should offer the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the cooked rice oblations (caru), each separately and according to the prescribed rule.
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities,
he should consume the remainder himself, as well as salt prepared by his own hand.
One may eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots,
and fruits produced from pure trees, and oils derived from fruits; however,
one should avoid honey, meat, and mushrooms growing from the ground.
Earth, grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleśmātaka tree;
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the food of sages previously stored,
as well as worn-out clothes and vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plow, even if it has been abandoned by anyone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots and fruits grown in a village [or flowers and fruits].
One may either subsist on food cooked by fire, or indeed eat only what is ripened by time.
Or he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may be one who washes away his food immediately, or one who stores for a month;
he may be one who accumulates for six months, or even one who accumulates for a year.
Having gathered food according to his ability, he should eat it either at night or during the day;
or he may eat at every fourth mealtime, or even at every eighth mealtime.
Or he should pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he should eat boiled barley-gruel only once.
Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots,
and fruits that have ripened in their season and fallen of their own accord, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of Vaikhānasa.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for the duration of the day;
he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching the waters at the times of the three libations.
In summer he should practice the five-fire penance; in the rainy season, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, gradually increasing his austerity.
Performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
and practicing most intense austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself according to the prescribed rule,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a silent sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, observing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, having no sense of ownership even in shelters, and making his dwelling at the roots of trees; ||| 6.26 ||
He should obtain alms sufficient for his sustenance from ascetic Brahmins alone,
as well as from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Or, living in the forest, he may eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from a village,
having received them either in a leaf-cup, in his hand, or in a potsherd.
A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiatory rites,
as well as various Upanishadic teachings, for the sake of attaining self-perfection.
These have been practiced by the seers and by brahmins who were householders,
for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body.
Or, having taken his stand in the Aparājita direction,
he should proceed straight ahead until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air.
Having cast off the body by means of one or another of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
Having gone from one stage of life to the next, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by the practice of begging and making offerings, he who renounces the world prospers after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of his ability, he should direct his mind toward liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes downward.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may go forth from his home into the life of a wandering ascetic.
He who, having granted freedom from fear to all beings, departs from his home as a wandering mendicant—
for him, the expounder of Brahman, the worlds consist of radiant light.
Since not even the slightest fear arises for living beings from the twice-born,
there is no fear whatsoever for him when he is liberated from the body.
Having departed from his house, purified by sacred observances, and become a silent sage (muni),
he should wander as a mendicant, indifferent toward all objects of desire when they are presented to him.
He should always wander alone for the sake of perfection, without any companion;
seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons it nor is he abandoned by it.
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food.

Indifferent, free from the use of weapons, a sage whose mind is absorbed in the ultimate reality—[Manu 6.44a: an alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude, and equanimity toward all things: these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure.
One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter untruthful speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated in meditation, indifferent to worldly objects and free from carnal desires,
he who seeks true happiness should wander about this world with the self alone as his companion.
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks,
nor by instructions or threats.
He should not approach a house that is crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, or dogs, nor with other beggars.
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, not causing pain to any living beings.
His vessels should be made of non-metallic materials and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.
A gourd, a wooden vessel, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Svāyambhuva Manu has declared, are the vessels for an ascetic.
He should go for alms once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for a mendicant who is attached to alms becomes attached even to sensual objects.

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has taken place— at these times a mendicant should always go for alms.

If he does not obtain [alms], he should not be despondent; and if he obtains them, he should not rejoice. He should possess only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material things.
But he should avoid gains obtained through honor in every way;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated is bound by gains obtained through honor.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should restrain the senses when they are being carried away by their objects.
By the restraint of the senses, by the destruction of passion and hatred,
and by non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
He should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
The separation from beloved ones and likewise union with those who are disliked, being overcome by old age and the affliction of diseases; [these he should reflect upon].
The departure from this body, the subsequent conception in a womb,
and the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of births— [all these he perceives].
And [he perceives] the connection with suffering for embodied beings as arising from unrighteousness,
and the imperishable union with happiness as arising from righteousness and wealth.
And by means of yoga, he should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low. Even if he is defiled, he should practice dharma, regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he is devoted to.
He should be equal toward all beings; outward appearance is not the cause of dharma.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water,
the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name.
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk upon the earth after carefully scanning the ground, even when his body is at risk of exhaustion.
Whatever living beings an ascetic kills unintentionally by day or by night,
for the sake of purifying himself from those [karmas], he should bathe and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas),
performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa and joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and sin by means of concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
One should perceive, through the yoga of meditation, the course of this inner self among various beings— a course that is difficult for those of unrefined soul to discern.
One who is endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of such vision enters the cycle of transmigration.
Through non-violence, by restraining the senses, through Vedic rites,
and by the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.
A body with bones for its pillars, bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement;
possessed by old age and sorrow, it is a dwelling place of disease and afflicted by pain.
One should abandon this impermanent abode of the elements, which is as fleeting as a woman in her menses.
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so too one who abandons this body is liberated from the crocodile of suffering.
Having relinquished his good deeds among those dear to him and his evil deeds among those not dear,
through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman.
When one becomes free from longing toward all objects through one's inner disposition,
then one attains eternal happiness both after death and in this world.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments,
and being liberated from all pairs of opposites, he remains established in Brahman alone.
All this that has been declared here is indeed mental;
for no one who is ignorant of the supreme self (adhyātma) ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
He should constantly recite the Veda concerning sacrifice, that concerning the deities,
and that concerning the self, as well as whatever is declared in the Vedāntas.
This is the refuge for the ignorant, and this very same thing for those who possess knowledge;
this is for those seeking heaven, and this for those seeking infinity.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant according to this sequential method,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics whose minds are self-restrained;
now learn the application of ritual action for those who have renounced the Vedas.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these [stages of life], when practiced in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
And among all these, according to the ordinances of the Veda and the Smṛti,
the householder is declared to be the best, for he supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the other stages of life find their support in the householder.
Moreover, by these four twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas),
the tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort.
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, abstention from theft, purity, control of the senses,
wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this tenfold set is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma,
and having studied them, live according to them, attain the supreme goal.
A twice-born man, having performed the dharma characterized by ten marks with a concentrated mind,
and having heard the Vedānta according to the rule, may renounce his worldly ties once he is free from debt.
Having renounced all ritual actions and cast off the defects of karma,
he should live happily under the protection of his sons, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing,
he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
This fourfold duty of a Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you;
it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the duty of kings.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself,
how his origin comes about, and how his supreme success is achieved.
Having received the Vedic initiation according to the prescribed rule,
a Kṣatriya must provide protection for all this [world] in accordance with justice.
For in this world, when it is without a king, everything flees in every direction out of fear;
therefore, the Lord created the king for the protection of all this.
Having extracted the eternal particles from Indra, Anila, Yama, Arka, Agni, Varuṇa, Candra, and Viteśa, [the Creator fashioned the Kṣatriya].
Since the king was fashioned from the constituent parts of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in his splendor.
He burns with the brilliance of the sun, scorching both eyes and minds;
and no one on earth is able even to look directly upon him.
By his power, he becomes Agni and Vāyu; he is Arka, Soma, and Dharmarāja;
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra. Even as a child, a king must not be disregarded on the grounds that he is merely a human being.
For this is a great deity who abides in human form.
Fire consumes only the man who approaches it incautiously;
but the king’s fire consumes the entire family, along with its cattle and its store of wealth.
Having duly considered the task, his own power, and the place and time,
he assumes various forms again and again for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-seated Śrī, in whose valor dwells victory,
and in whose anger dwells death— for he indeed consists of all splendor.
But he who, out of delusion, hates him [the king] will undoubtedly perish;
for the king quickly sets his mind upon his destruction.
Therefore, that king should determine what is dharma regarding those who are dear to him;
and he should not deviate from that dharma even regarding those who are not dear to him.
For his sake, the Lord created in the beginning the Staff, born of his own self, consisting of the splendor of Brahman, the protector of the dharma of all living beings.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, remain devoted to their own duties and do not deviate from them; thus they become fit for enjoyment.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the capacity, and the learning [of the offender],
he should duly inflict punishment upon men who act unjustly.
He is the king, he is the personification of punishment, he is the leader and the ruler;
he is recorded as the surety for the dharma of the four stages of life.
Punishment governs all subjects; punishment alone protects them. Punishment keeps watch while others sleep; the wise know punishment to be Dharma itself.
When properly maintained after due deliberation, that [king] delights all his subjects;
but when administered without due deliberation, it destroys them on every side.
If the king, unwearied, were not to inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and likewise a dog might lick the oblation (havis);
there would be no ownership over anything, and the lower would prevail over the higher.
The entire world is kept in check by punishment, for a man who is naturally pure is hard to find;
indeed, through fear of punishment, the whole world is fit for the enjoyment of life.
Gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—
even these are rendered capable of enjoyment only when constrained by punishment.
All social classes would become corrupt and all boundaries would be broken;
indeed, there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment.
Where the dark, red-eyed Punishment stalks about, destroying evil,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who should be appointed as the administrator of that [dharma].

A king who administers that rod of punishment properly prospers in the three aims of life; but one whose soul is dominated by passion, who is unjust and base, is destroyed by that very rod. For the power of the rod is exceedingly great and difficult to be wielded by those who have not disciplined their souls.
One who has deviated from dharma destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen.
Consequently, he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world of moving and non-moving beings,
as well as the sages dwelling in the intermediate space and the gods.
He cannot be led to act with justice by one who is without assistance, foolish, greedy, of undisciplined intellect,
and attached to sensual pleasures.
The rod of punishment can be wielded by one who is pure, true to his word, acting according to the scriptures, possessing good assistants, and endowed with wisdom.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, yet be severe in punishment toward his enemies;
he should be straightforward with his friends and affectionate toward Brahmins, while being endowed with patience.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he subsists by gleaning ears of grain from the threshing floor,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered himself,
his fame diminishes in the world like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are established in their respective duties according to their order.
Whatever must be done by him, together with his servants, while protecting his subjects—
that I shall declare to you exactly and in due order.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon Brāhmaṇas who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.
One should constantly serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who always serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
Even though his own self is disciplined, he should constantly acquire discipline from them;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes.
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those living in the forest have attained kingdoms through discipline.
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa,
