Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi.
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained wealth and sovereignty, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he shall learn the triple Veda, the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti),
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) which is the knowledge of the Self, and the methods of commerce from the people.
Day and night, he should apply himself to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control.
One should strive to avoid with great effort these ten vices arising from desire, as well as those eight born of anger, which lead to miserable ends.
For a king addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; however, one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of his very self.
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication,
the triple symphony [of song, dance, and instrument], idle wandering, and [vain] curiosity— this is the tenfold group born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, detracting from others' merits, and the spoiling of wealth,
as well as verbal and physical cruelty— this is the eightfold group born of anger.
That which all wise men know to be the root of both these [two groups], one should strive to conquer that greed; for both these classes arise from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— these four, in their respective order,
one should know to be the most grievous among the group of vices born of desire.
One should always know that this triad— the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the defilement of property— is always grievous, even within the category of offenses born of anger.
A self-possessed man should know that among this group of seven vices which follow one another everywhere, each preceding one is more serious than the next.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more grievous.
One who is addicted to vices sinks lower and lower; one who dies free from vices goes to heaven.

He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, proven in their aims, and of noble birth; they must be thoroughly tested. For even a task that is easy to perform becomes difficult when undertaken by a single person alone.
Especially by one who is without assistance, how much less can he rule a kingdom of great consequence? Therefore,
he should constantly deliberate with them regarding common matters— both peace and war— as well as the stationing of troops,
the collection of revenue, protection, and the pacification of conquered territories.
Having ascertained their respective individual opinions,
both separately and collectively, he should, in all matters, ordain what is for his own welfare.
But with all of them, the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, learned Brāhmaṇa.
Constantly placing full confidence in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he should then begin his work.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.
He should appoint as many diligent,
capable, and discerning men as are required to carry out his duties.
For their sake, he should appoint those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth to the mines;
and those who are pure for the work of the treasury, and those who are timid within the inner apartments.
And he should appoint as an envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and movements, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.
One who is devoted, pure, skillful, possessed of a retentive memory, knowledgeable of place and time,
handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised as a messenger for a king.
The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of justice depends on punishment; the treasury and the kingdom depend on the king; and peace and its opposite depend on the envoy.
For it is the messenger alone who unites those who are divided and indeed breaks apart those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated.
He should discern, through secret gestures and movements,
the king's facial expression, his hints, his conduct, and what he intends to do regarding his undertakings among his servants.
Having understood in its true essence everything intended by the enemy king,
he should apply such effort as will not cause him suffering.
He should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, inhabited mostly by Āryas, free from turmoil, pleasant, with submissive neighbors, and providing a means of self-sustenance.
Having taken refuge in a desert-fortress, an earth-fortress, a water-fortress, or even a forest-fortress,
or a human-fortress, or a mountain-fortress, he should dwell in a city.
But with every effort, he should take refuge in a mountain fort;
for among all these, the mountain fort is distinguished by its many advantages.
Among these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, those dwelling in holes, and aquatic creatures;
the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods.
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress,
so too enemies do not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight off a hundred; a hundred can fight off ten thousand. Therefore, a fort is ordained.
That [fortress] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
it should also be provided with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
In the center of that [village], he should cause to be built for himself a house that is spacious,
well-protected, suitable for all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, pleasing to the heart, and endowed with beauty and virtue.
He should appoint a domestic priest and likewise choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.
The king should perform various sacrifices accompanied by ample sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins.
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trustworthy agents,
and he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world, behaving toward his subjects like a father.
He should appoint various wise supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men who are performing their duties for him.
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher's house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable Brahman-treasure of kings.
Neither thieves nor enemies carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brāhmaṇas.
It does not overflow, it does not waver, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.
A gift given to a non-Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward;
to one who has studied extensively, a hundred-thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, an infinite reward.
Indeed, this depends upon the excellence of the recipient and upon one's own faith.
Whether small or great, one enjoys the fruit of giving after death.
Whatever substance is given with faith to a worthy recipient, according to the regulations regarding place and time—
that is the means of accomplishing dharma. But when summoned by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, the king, while protecting his subjects, [should act as follows].
Remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, he should not retreat from battle.
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects,
and service to the Brāhmaṇas— these are the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
In battles, when kings, desiring to slay one another,
fight with their utmost strength and do not turn their backs, they go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he shall not strike them with deceptive weapons,
nor with those that are barbed, nor with those smeared with poison, nor with those whose tips are set ablaze with fire.
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor one who is impotent, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."
One should not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed,
nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is merely looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one must not strike one who is beset by a calamity involving his weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned away from the battle.
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies,
incurs all whatever evil deed his master has committed.
And whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter—
all that his husband takes away from him when he is slain while retreating.
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all types of goods, and base metals— whatever one conquers belongs to him.
And they shall give a special share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which was not won individually.
This eternal law of warriors has been declared in its unadorned form;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, must not deviate from this dharma.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should know that these fourfold [means] have human purpose as their goal;
one should always perform their practice correctly and without sloth.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired by means of force; one should protect what has been acquired with vigilance;
one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment uplifted, always display his manly prowess,
always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod alone.
One should conduct oneself with absolute sincerity and never by means of deceit;
being always well-guarded, one should constantly perceive the deceit employed by enemies.
An enemy shall not discover his own vulnerability, but he should discover the vulnerability of the enemy;
like a tortoise, he should withdraw his limbs and guard his own weak points.
One should deliberate upon one's goals like a heron, display prowess like a lion,
snatch [the prey] like a wolf, and retreat like a hare.
Thus, for one who is victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by employing the means beginning with conciliation (*sāman*).
If, however, they do not abide by those [injunctions] through the first three means,
he should bring them under control by force, using the rod of punishment alone, but gradually.
Among the four means of policy, conciliation and the others, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom.
Just as a wood-gatherer pulls up the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
That king who, out of delusion and through lack of foresight, exhausts his own kingdom,
shall soon be deprived both of his realm and his life, along with his kinsmen.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings waste away through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings waste away through the emaciation of the kingdom.
He should constantly implement this ordinance for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness.
He should establish a military guard (gulma) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for groups of one hundred villages throughout the kingdom.
He should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The village headman shall himself gradually report any faults arising within the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten shall report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty, however, should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, moreover, should himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Those items, such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth, which are to be given daily by the village-dwellers to the king, the village headman (grāmika) shall receive them.
The collector of ten should enjoy the produce of one family, while the collector of twenty should enjoy five families;
the superintendent of a hundred villages should enjoy a village, and the lord of a thousand should enjoy a city.
Their village affairs as well as their private matters should be supervised by a trusted minister of the king, other than [the judge], who should look after them with vigilance.
In every town, he should appoint one official to oversee all matters,
stationed in a high place and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.
He himself should always inspect them all one by one;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the provinces through spies who move among them.
For the servants appointed by the king to protect [the subjects] generally become deceitful and seize the property of others; therefore, he should guard these subjects from them.
Those evil-minded men who seize wealth from litigants shall have all their property confiscated by the king and be banished.

The king should daily determine the livelihood and the station for women and servants engaged in his service, according to their respective tasks. A paṇa should be given as the wage for the lowest laborer, and six for the highest.
Likewise, clothing is to be provided every six months, and a droṇa of grain every month.
Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food and its expenses, and the security of the goods, the king should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants.

Having considered how both the king and the performer of actions may be joined with their respective fruits, the king should always apportion taxes within his realm. Just as water-creatures, calves, and bees consume their food little by little,
so should the annual tax be taken from the kingdom by the king in small amounts.
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits.
Of leaves, vegetables, grass, hides, and articles made of split cane;
of earthenware vessels and of all things made of stone.
Even when dying, a king must not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya living within his realm perish from hunger.
But in whose kingdom a Śrotriya perishes from hunger,
his kingdom also will perish from hunger before long.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous means of livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son.
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
The king should cause even the common people living by trade within his realm to pay some small amount known as a tax for each year.
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and even Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work one day each month.
One should not, out of excessive greed, cut off one's own root or that of others;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them.
The lord of the earth, having examined the matter at hand, should be both stern and mild;
indeed, a king who is both stern and mild becomes esteemed.
When weary from overseeing the affairs of men, the king should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the law, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Having thus ordained all this duty pertaining to himself,
he should protect these subjects with diligence and vigilance.
If the subjects of a king's realm are carried off by bandits while crying out for help, and he looks on with his servants, he is dead though he breathes; he does not truly live.
The highest duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the fruits as they are prescribed is joined with merit through that righteous act.
Having risen during the last watch of the night, having performed purification and being composed in mind,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with joy;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a terrace,
or having gone to a secluded spot in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate unobserved.
That king whose counsel ordinary people do not discover even when they gather together enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of a treasury.

At the time of reciting the mantras, one should remove those who are mentally dull, mute, blind, or deaf; those of animal origin; those who have passed the age of youth; as well as women, Mlecchas, the diseased, and the deformed.
Those who are despised, as well as animals, and especially women, disclose a secret; therefore, one should be careful in that regard.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue,
he should reflect— either together with them or alone— upon virtue, pleasure, and wealth,
and upon the acquisition of these when they are mutually conflicting.
The giving away of daughters and the protection of sons.
And he should know in truth the entire eightfold business, the fivefold group [of spies],
the loyalty and disloyalty [of his subjects], and the conduct of the circle of states.
He should diligently ascertain the movements of the middle king, the activities of one who desires conquest, the conduct of the neutral king, and likewise that of the enemy.
In brief, these eight constituent elements are the foundation of the circle of states; yet, when others are included, they are recorded as being twelve in total.
The five others known as ministers, the kingdom, the fort, the treasury, and the army—each of these has been described briefly; thus, they total seventy-two.
One should know that the enemy's immediate neighbor is likewise a friend of the enemy; the neighbor next to the enemy’s neighbor is one’s own friend, and beyond those two is the neutral king.
He should employ all these measures— conciliation and the rest—
both individually and collectively, along with personal effort and statesmanship.
He should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.
Having carefully considered the matter at hand, he should employ sitting in wait, marching, peace, war, the double policy, or seeking refuge.
A king should know that alliance is of two kinds, as is conflict;
likewise, marching and sitting encamped are both twofold, and seeking refuge is recorded as being of two kinds.
When the undertaking of the journey is common to both, and likewise when it is the opposite,
that peace should be known as having two characteristics and being connected to future prospects.

War is declared to be of two kinds: that undertaken by oneself for the sake of a specific objective, whether at the improper time or at the right time; and that waged against a friend who has done one harm.
When an urgent matter arises by chance, marching alone is prescribed;
likewise, marching with an ally is also said to be a twofold form of expedition.
For one who has gradually declined due to fate or by reason of past actions,
or out of regard for a friend, two kinds of neutrality (āsana) are recorded.

The strategic stationing of both the army and its master for the sake of accomplishing the objective is declared to be of two kinds as "dual policy" (dvaidhībhāva) by those who know the qualities of the six measures of statecraft.
Seeking refuge with the virtuous is recorded as being of two kinds: for the purpose of accomplishing one's objectives, and when one is being oppressed by enemies.
When he perceives that his own superiority in the future is certain,
and that there is only slight hardship in the present, then he should resort to peace.
When he considers all his constituent elements to be exceedingly well-pleased,
and likewise himself to be highly exalted, then he should wage war.
When he perceives through his own disposition that his own army is joyful and well-nourished,
and that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is depleted of both vehicles and troops,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect,
he should then divide his army into two parts and accomplish his own purpose.
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of his enemies,
then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king.
One should constantly serve with every effort that king who exercises restraint over his own subjects and over the enemy's forces, just as one would serve a teacher.
If even there he should perceive a fault arising from seeking refuge,
he should then engage in fair combat without hesitation.
A king who understands policy should employ every possible means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him.
He should deliberate upon the future and the present state of all undertakings,
as well as the merits and defects of all past actions in their true nature.
One who understands the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who knows the remaining tasks from the past, is not overcome by enemies.
He should arrange everything in such a way that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not plot against him; this is the summary of political strategy.
Then the lord should set out on his expedition toward the enemy kingdom;
at that time, he should advance slowly toward the enemy city according to this rule.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition;
or else, according to his strength, he may do so during the months of Phālguna or Caitra.
But even at other times, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth after declaring war, especially when a calamity has arisen for his enemy.
Having made provision for his family and for his journey according to the rules,
and having secured a place of refuge and properly stationed spies;
Having thoroughly secured his threefold path and his sixfold power,
he should march against the enemy's city according to the rules for a campaign of war.
One should be especially vigilant toward a friend who serves the enemy in secret, and likewise toward one who has gone abroad and returned; for such a person is a most dangerous foe.
He should march along that path in the *daṇḍavyūha* (staff-array), or the *śakaṭa* (cart-array),
or the *varāha* (boar-array), the *makara* (crocodile-array), the *sūcī* (needle-array), or the *garuḍa* (eagle-array).
From whatever direction he anticipates danger, toward that side he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus array (*padmavyūha*).
He should station the commander-in-chief and the chief of the army in all directions;
and in whichever direction he suspects danger, he should designate that as the "east."
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides,
who are skilled in both their positions and in battle, fearless and incorruptible.
One should cause a small number of troops to fight in close formation, but one may extend a large number at will;
having arrayed them in the *sūcī* (needle) or *vajra* (thunderbolt) formations, one should make them fight.

On level ground, he should fight with chariot-horses; likewise, on marshy ground, with boats and elephants. In places covered by trees and shrubs, he should fight with bows; and on firm ground, with swords, shields, and other weapons.
One should employ men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena,
as well as those who are tall and short, in the vanguard of the army.
Having arrayed his forces, he should encourage them and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of his enemies even as they are fighting.
Having besieged his enemy, he should sit and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly spoil his supply of fodder, food, water, and fuel.
He should break down its tanks, as well as its walls and moats;
he should launch a surprise attack upon it at night and likewise terrify it.
He should instigate those who are susceptible to sowing dissension, and he should remain vigilant regarding their actions.
When the auspicious omens have appeared, he should fight, free from fear and desiring victory.
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension— either collectively or individually— and never by means of war;
for victory is seen to be uncertain for two parties engaged in combat.
And there is defeat in battle; therefore, one should avoid combat.
When even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible,
he should fight with full preparation so that he may conquer his enemies.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties.
But having ascertained briefly the intended purpose of all these [disputants],
he should install a member of their own lineage there and establish a formal agreement.
And he should establish authoritative legal codes for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and he should honor him with jewels along with his principal officers.
Taking what is unpleasant and giving what is pleasant—
these are praised when applied at the proper time regarding desired objects.
All this action depends upon both divine and human ordinances.
Of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, but human action exists within the human realm.
The following three verses are found only in M. (Jha’s edition does not include them in its textual numbering, though Medhātithi provides a commentary on them):
[Manu 7.207a] That which proceeds as human action, joined with divine ordinance, [Manu 7.207c] Accomplishes its purpose only through great hardship; [not in K] [Jha: *ayuktam*] [not in K]
Even for one who is joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort,
the field does not yield fruit without human exertion.
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water likewise [depend on human action].
In this world, things are accomplished through destiny and through diligent human effort.
Alternatively, being prepared, he should march together after having carefully made a treaty,
perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and the ally in the circle of states,
he shall obtain the fruit of his expedition from either a friend or even an enemy.
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend who, though currently weak, is capable of future growth.
One who knows the dharma, who is grateful, whose nature is contented,
who is devoted, and who is steadfast in his undertakings— such a light friend is highly praised.
The wise declare that an enemy who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, capable, generous, grateful, and resolute is difficult to overcome.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, compassion,
constant generosity, and the manifestation of the qualities of one who remains impartial.
A king should, without hesitation, abandon for his own sake even land that is secure, productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle.
One should protect one's wealth for the sake of times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Having thoroughly examined all calamities that have arisen together,
a wise man should employ all means, both those combined and those separate.
Having fully relied upon these three— the pursuer, the object to be pursued, and all the means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Having thus deliberated upon all this with his ministers,
the king, having exercised himself and bathed at midday, shall enter the inner apartments to eat.

In that regard, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who have become like his own self, who know the proper time, and who cannot be bribed, using mantras that destroy poison.
He should treat all his belongings with anti-poisonous medicines; [or: he should purify all his belongings with anti-poisonous waters].
Furthermore, being self-controlled, he should always wear gems that counteract poison.
Women who have been examined by means of fanning, water, and incense,
and who are purified by their dress and ornaments, should touch him with a concentrated mind.
One should exert such effort regarding one's vehicle, bed, seat, and food,
as well as in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties.
Adorned [with ornaments], he should inspect the armed troops again,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), he should, while bearing a weapon, listen within his inner apartments to the reports of those who reveal secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to bed at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
however, when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
But a king who desires to examine legal cases should enter the court, modestly accompanied by Brāhmaṇas as well as ministers skilled in counsel.
Seated there, or even standing, having raised his right hand,
and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he shall examine the legal cases of the litigants.
Day by day, by means of reasons observed in local custom and those observed in the scriptures,
[the king] should decide cases separately according to the eighteen titles of law.
Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt;
then the deposit, sale without ownership, and partnership; then the non-delivery of what has been given, the non-payment of wages, and the breach of agreement.
The dispute between an owner and a keeper concerns rescission of purchase and sale.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these eighteen titles constitute the basis of legal procedure here.
In these matters, for men who engage in frequent disputes,
he should determine the outcome of the case by relying upon the eternal Dharma.
But when the king does not personally attend to the investigation of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate those cases.
Surrounded by three members of the court, he should examine his judicial duties,
having entered the foremost assembly hall and being either seated or standing.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together,
along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly as a *brahma-sabhā*.
But where Dharma, pierced by Adharma, approaches the assembly,
and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart from it, they themselves are pierced.
One should either not enter the court, or speak what is just; for by failing to speak or by speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members of the court look on, they too are slain there.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when protected, protects.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma destroy us. For the Blessed Lord Dharma is a bull; he who does violence to him indeed commits a great offense.
The gods know him as a *vṛṣala*; therefore, one should not destroy the Dharma.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even in death;
for everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes free from sin, as do the members of the assembly;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured.
Or, one who merely lives by his caste may at will be called a "Brāhmaṇa-in-name";
however, a Śūdra can under no circumstances be the expounder of dharma to the king.
But that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma, his kingdom perishes while he looks on, like a cow in the mud.
That kingdom which is predominantly composed of Śūdras, overrun by atheists, and devoid of the twice-born,
quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease.
Having ascended the seat of justice, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should bow to the guardians of the world and begin the examination of legal cases.
Having understood both gain and loss, as well as pure righteousness and unrighteousness,
he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, facial expressions, gaze, and movements.
By outward appearance, by gestures, by gait, by movement, and by speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.
The king should protect the inheritance, such as the property of a minor,
until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his childhood.
The same protection should be afforded for female cattle without calves, and likewise for women who have no family.
And toward women who are devoted to their husbands, as well as those who are widows or afflicted by illness.
But if their kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still living,
the righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that period, the king shall take it.
He who says "this is mine" shall be questioned according to the rule; having verified the appearance, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property.
One who does not truly report the place, the time,
the color, the appearance, and the size of a lost item deserves a fine equal to its value.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth part of goods lost and then found, or even a tenth or a twelfth.
Property that has been lost and found shall remain under the supervision of officials appointed for the purpose;
whatever thieves the king may catch there, he should have them executed by an elephant.
If a man should declare with truth regarding a treasure-trove,
"This is mine," the king should take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own property,
or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very deposit.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the lord of all.
But whatever ancient treasure the king may discover buried in the earth,
he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury.
But regarding ancient treasures and minerals found in the earth, the king is entitled to half the share because of his protection; for he is the sovereign lord of the land.
The king must restore to all social classes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that property for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, shall establish the specific duty for each individual.
Even when they are far away, men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world.

The king himself should not initiate a legal case, nor should his official; nor should he ever suppress a matter brought before him by another. Just as a hunter tracks the path of a deer by drops of blood, so should the king follow the trail of justice.
In that manner, the king should discover the track of dharma through inference.
Established in the procedure for legal proceedings, he should consider the truth, the matter at hand, himself, the witnesses, the place,
the nature of the case, and the time.
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men,
that one should establish for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not inconsistent with the sacred law.
Urged by the creditor for the purpose of recovering the debt from the debtor,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the proven amount to the creditor.
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own property,
by those same means he should constrain the debtor and compel him to pay.
One should recover a loaned object by means of moral persuasion, legal procedure, artifice, customary practice,
and fifthly, by force.
A creditor who recovers his own property from a debtor by his own means shall not be prosecuted by the king for recovering his own wealth.
But one who denies a debt when it has been proven by evidence shall be made to pay the amount to the creditor and a small fine according to his ability.
When a debtor, having been told "Pay!
in the presence of an assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff must point out the place [of the transaction] or specify another means of proof.

He who, having made a pretext or having provided a false excuse, subsequently flees;
and he who, when questioned, does not acknowledge a matter that has been properly presented.
He who converses privately with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when questioned, and he who walks away; 8.55.
If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he fails to substantiate what he has said,
or if he cannot distinguish between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that point.

If one says, "I have witnesses," but when told "Produce them," he does not produce them; or if he says, "There are those who know [the facts]"—the judge should declare him to be defeated on these grounds.
If the plaintiff does not speak, he should be bound and punished according to the law.
If he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the legal matter, he is defeated.
If one should deny a matter for whatever amount, or if one should speak falsely regarding whatever amount,
the king should indeed cause those two— who are ignorant of dharma— to pay a fine double that amount.
But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth, denies his involvement after having established his position,
must be proved [guilty] by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
I shall now fully declare what kind of witnesses should be appointed by creditors in legal proceedings,
and how the truth must be spoken by them.

Householders who have sons, who are of noble birth, and who are born from the *kṣatriya*, *vaiśya*, or *śūdra* castes— when summoned for the sake of the matter— are fit to give testimony, but not just anyone, except in times of emergency.
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be appointed as witnesses in legal matters;
they must be knowers of all dharmas and free from greed, while those who possess the opposite qualities should be avoided.
Neither those with financial interests, nor relatives, nor associates, nor enemies;
neither those whose faults have been observed, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt—such persons should not be appointed [as witnesses].
The king shall not be made a witness, nor an artisan or an actor;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is subject to verbal abuse, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an aged man, nor a child, nor one who is alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired senses.
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane, nor oppressed by hunger or thirst;
neither one afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by passion, nor angry, nor even a thief [should be questioned].
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
and virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras, while those of low birth shall testify for those of low birth.
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants in the interior of a house, in a forest, or even in the event of a threat to life; Manu 8.69.
In the absence of a woman, the business may be carried out by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick, when they testify falsely,
as well as that of those with agitated minds, is unstable.
In all cases of violence, in theft and adultery,
and in cases of verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses.

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, the king should accept the majority; but if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.
Testimony is established by seeing or hearing in the presence [of the court].
In that case, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from merit or wealth.
A witness who declares in an assembly of noble men anything other than what he has seen or heard goes head-first to hell after death and is deprived of heaven.
Even where he is not formally bound [to the court], if he should see or hear anything,
when questioned there, he should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
A single person who is free from greed may be a witness, but even many women, though pure, are not witnesses;
for the intellect of women is unstable, and others who are tainted by defects are likewise excluded.
Whatever they may state by their own nature is to be accepted as the judicial decision;
whatever else they might state contrary to that for the sake of dharma is useless.
When the witnesses have arrived within the court in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant,
the presiding judge shall examine them, consoling them with this following procedure.
"Whatever you know to have been transacted privately between these two regarding this matter, declare all that in truth; for your role here is that of witnesses."
By speaking the truth in testimony, a witness attains abundant and irreproachable worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this speech is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking untruthly in testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred births, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
A witness is purified by truth; dharma increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all the social classes.
For one's own self is indeed the witness of oneself, and likewise, the self is the refuge of oneself. Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness among men.
"Evil-doers think, 'No one sees us';
but the gods see them, as does the inner person within their own selves."
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, and the wind;
night, the two twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of all embodied beings.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
he, being pure himself, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they are facing either northward or eastward.

One should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak! and the King, "Speak the truth! One should question the Vaiśya by means of [threats regarding] cattle, seed-grain, and gold, but the Śūdra by all [the aforementioned] sins.

Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the murderer of women and children, and for the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful— those same worlds shall be his who speaks falsely.
"O good man, whatever merit you have performed since birth—
all that shall go to a dog if you speak otherwise."
"O auspicious one, you who think of yourself, 'I am alone'— this sage, the witness of merit and sin, is eternally situated within your heart."
The god Yama, son of Vivasvat, who dwells here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then go neither to the Ganges nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a begging bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst,
and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy.
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell—
he who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely in response.
That man who, having entered the court, speaks of a deficiency in the facts or of something not witnessed by himself, eats fish along with their bones, like a blind man.
For the gods know no other man in this world to be superior to him, whose inner self (*kṣetrajña*) does not feel suspicion when he speaks as a learned man.
Hear now, O gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen a man destroys by speaking falsehood in a particular kind of testimony.
He kills five by lying about small cattle; he kills ten by lying about cows;
he kills a hundred by lying about horses; he kills a thousand by lying about men.
By speaking falsehood for the sake of gold, one destroys both those born and those unborn;
by a falsehood regarding land, one destroys everything. Therefore, do not speak a falsehood concerning land.
Regarding water, they say it is like land; likewise for the enjoyment of women and sexual intercourse, as well as for aquatic gems and all those made of stone.
Having considered all these evils that arise from speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as you have heard and as you have seen, straightforwardly.
One should treat like Śūdras those Brahmins who are cattle-herders, traders, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers.
A man who, though knowing otherwise, speaks in accordance with dharma regarding legal matters, does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that speech divine.
Where the death penalty would otherwise be incurred for speaking the truth regarding Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Brāhmaṇas, there a falsehood must be spoken; for that is superior to the truth.
And they should sacrifice to Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (caru) dedicated to Speech as the deity,
performing the supreme expiation for that sin of untruth.
Or he may offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the waters.
A man who does not speak the truth regarding testimony in matters such as debts becomes diseased within three fortnights.
He shall incur that entire debt, as well as a tenth part as a fine, in every case.
If, within seven days of giving his testimony,
a witness should suffer from disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine.
But in matters where there are no witnesses, between two parties disputing with one another,
if he cannot ascertain the truth in its reality, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.
Oaths were taken by the great seers and by the gods for the sake of establishing the truth;
and Vasiṣṭha also swore an oath before King Paijavana.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, he perishes both in this world and after death.
[This applies except] in matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cows, and likewise fuel.
And in an oath taken for the sake of assisting a Brāhmaṇa, there is no sin.
One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, seed-corn, and gold, and a Śūdra by all the mortal sins.
Or he should cause him to carry fire, or make him immerse himself in water;
or he should have his sons and wife touch his head individually.
He whom the kindled fire does not burn, whom the waters do not force to emerge [unwillingly],
and who does not quickly meet with misfortune— he should be known as pure in his oath.
For in ancient times, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother,
the fire— the witness of the world— did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness.
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; even if it has been decided, it shall be as if undecided.
"From greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, and likewise from anger,
as well as from ignorance and childishness, false testimony is spoken.
He who gives false testimony on account of any one of these grounds [is guilty]."
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for such an offense.
Out of greed, he should be fined one thousand; out of delusion, the first amercement;
out of fear, two middle amercements; and out of friendship, four times the first.
Ten times the first [fine] is for intentional acts; three times the highest is for acts out of anger;
two full hundreds are for ignorance; and exactly one hundred is for childishness.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony, proclaimed for the purpose of ensuring that justice does not fail and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
A righteous king, having punished them with fines, shall banish those of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony;
however, he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
in these ten, the Brāhmaṇa may depart unhurt among the three other castes.
The genitals, the stomach, the tongue, the hands, and fifthly the feet;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body itself.
Having thoroughly ascertained the motive, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered the capacity and the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys reputation and ruins fame;
it also prevents one from attaining heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
First, one should administer the punishment of speech; immediately after that, the punishment of censure;
thirdly, the punishment of fines; and beyond that, the punishment of corporal chastisement.
But when he is unable to restrain these [offenders] even by execution,
then he should employ all four of these measures against them.
I shall declare in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
That minute particle of dust which is seen when the sun's rays pass through a lattice is called the *trasareṇu*,
the first of all measures of weight.
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* by measure;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium-sized barley grain; three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*, and ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *māṣakas* make one silver *dharaṇa*, which is also called a *purāṇa*.
A copper coin weighing one karṣa is to be known as a kārṣāpaṇa or a paṇa.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one silver *śatamāna*;
a *niṣka* should be understood by measure as consisting of four *suvarṇas*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest.
When a debt is admitted as due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, that fine shall be double—such is the ordinance of Manu.
A moneylender may stipulate an interest rate ordained by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Or, remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two per cent;
for by taking two per cent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth.
One may take two, three, four, or five percent per month as interest,
according to the order of the social classes.
But one shall never receive interest on a usufructuary pledge;
nor is there any transfer or sale of a pledge due to the lapse of time.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
Both a pledge (*ādhi*) and a deposit (*upanidhi*) do not suffer loss due to the lapse of time;
however, if they remain for a very long period, both may be forfeited.
Cattle being used with mutual consent are never lost;
this includes a milch cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal employed for training.
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while he is present,
yet remains silent, he is not entitled to recover it.
If the owner is neither mentally incapacitated nor a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another in his presence, that possession is subverted by the legal process;
the enjoyer deserves to forfeit that property. [The enjoyer deserves that wealth.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, and women [are not lost by adverse possession].
The property of the king and the property of one learned in the Vedas are not lost through adverse possession.
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must relinquish half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
in the case of grain, fruit, wool, or beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.
An interest rate exceeding the legal maximum, or one that is excessive, is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for it deserves a fine of five per hundred.
One should not take interest exceeding one year's duration, nor interest that has not been previously stipulated.
Interest may be of four kinds: compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*), periodical interest (*kālavṛddhi*), contractual interest (*kāritā*), and corporeal interest (*kāyikā*).
If a debtor is unable to repay the debt, he who wishes to do so may enter into a new transaction.
Having paid the interest that has been earned, he may renew the bond.
Without having shown [the object], he should recover the gold right there;
he ought to pay as much interest as may have accrued.
One who has entered into a contract for compound interest (cakravṛddhi), having fixed the terms regarding place and time,
shall not obtain its fruit if he violates those limits of place and time.
But whatever interest those who are skilled in sea-voyages and who perceive the requirements of place, time,
and profit may establish, that shall apply in such cases regarding the recovery of the loan.

If a man stands as a surety for another's appearance in this world, failing to produce him, he shall pay that person's debt from his own property. He should strive to pay what was guaranteed by surety,
as well as gifts made in vain, debts incurred at dice, and those contracted through drinking.
Nor is a son liable to pay the remainder of a fine or a toll.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the rule previously ordained shall apply;
however, if the surety for payment has died, the judge should cause even the heirs to pay.
But when the surety for payment has died, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt from the surety for appearance,
whose character was previously well known?
But if the surety has been assigned wealth and possesses sufficient assets, he shall pay that from his own property;
such is the settled rule regarding one who has been assigned wealth.
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by pain, dependent, a child, or an elderly person,
as well as one performed by an unrelated party, is not valid.
A statement does not become true even if it is well-established,
provided it is spoken outside of the fixed legal procedure.
Whatever is mortgaged or sold through fraud, whatever gift or acceptance is obtained through fraud,
or wherever one perceives deceit— that entire transaction he shall annul.
If the borrower should have perished while the expenditure was made for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by his kinsmen from their own property, even if they are divided.
Whatever legal transaction even a dependent (*adhyadhīna*) might carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or abroad, the superior (the master) shall not annul it.
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—
Manu has declared all transactions effected by force to be as if they were not done."
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a surety, and a family;
yet four prosper: a learned Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.
A king, even if he is impoverished, must not take what is not to be taken;
nor should he, even if he is prosperous, relinquish what is rightfully his, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by refusing what should be taken, the weakness of the king is proclaimed; he perishes both in this world and after death.
From the seizure of property, from the intermixture of castes, and from the failure to protect women, the strength of a king is destroyed;
yet by the opposite of these, his strength is born, and he prospers both in this world and after death.
Therefore, like Yama himself, the master should personally set aside both the pleasant and the unpleasant;
with his anger conquered and his senses subdued, he should conduct himself according to the manner of Yama.
But that king who, out of delusion, conducts legal affairs unjustly—
his enemies soon bring that evil-minded man under their control.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, examines matters according to dharma,
his subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean.
If a debtor, being pressed for payment at his own will, reports the creditor to the king,
he shall be made by the king to pay one-fourth of that amount as a fine, and the debt itself to the creditor.
A debtor of equal caste to the creditor shall discharge the debt even through manual labor;
one of lower caste shall do so immediately, but one of higher caste shall pay it gradually.
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of justice the legal cases of men disputing with one another, which have been established on the basis of witnesses.

A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is born of a noble family, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in the law, truthful, possessed of a large circle of kinsmen, wealthy, and honorable.
In whatever manner a person deposits an object in the hand of another, in that very same manner it must be received back; as the delivery was, so shall be the recovery.
If one, when being asked for it, does not return a deposit to the depositor,
he shall be summoned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.

In the absence of witnesses, having caused gold to be deposited with the true nature of the matter by means of secret agents endowed with appropriate age and appearance, and under various pretexts; 8.182cd.
If he should restore it exactly as it was deposited and in its original condition,
there is nothing therein for which he can be accused by others.

If, however, he does not return that gold to them according to the prescribed rule, both [the depositary and the receiver] shall be restrained and made to pay it; such is the established principle of the law. A deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must never be handed over to the next-of-kin.
These two perish upon his downfall, but they do not perish if there is no downfall.
But if one should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
He should seek that matter with sincerity and with affection;
or, having investigated his conduct, he should settle it through conciliation alone.
In all these cases of deposits, this rule shall apply regarding their recovery:
one who has deposited [property] in a sealed casket shall not receive anything if he does not produce it from that [container].
If [the property] has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire,
he need not pay for it, provided that he did not take anything from it himself.
One should seek out the misappropriator of a deposit, as well as the person who never deposited it,
by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths.
He who does not restore a deposit, and he who demands what he did not deposit—
both of these should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of that [deposit].
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value;
likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates an open deposit, without distinction.
Any man who, by means of fraudulent devices, should seize the property of another,
shall be put to death publicly along with his accomplices by various modes of execution.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses—that same amount it must be recognized as; one who declares otherwise deserves punishment.
A gift that was made privately by someone, or accepted privately, must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
In this same manner, the king shall reach a decision regarding property that has been deposited or handed over out of friendship,
without causing loss to the holder of the deposit.
One who sells another's property without being the owner or without the consent of the owner— one who is a thief yet considers himself no thief— should not be made a witness.
If he has kin, he shall be fined six hundred panas and his property shall be confiscated;
if he has no kin and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
Where possession is observed but no title is seen anywhere, there title is the decisive factor, not possession; such is the settled rule.
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family, he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase;
for it is purified by such a transaction.

Now, if the seller has cleared his title by proving a public purchase, yet the root of the title cannot be produced, he shall be released by the king without punishment; the original owner shall recover his property.
One thing mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;

nor that which is valueless, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is far away, nor that which is concealed. (Manu 8.203) If, having shown one girl, another is given to the bridegroom, [he may rescind the marriage]. (Manu 8.204a)
"Let him marry both of them with a single dowry," so Manu has declared.
A giver does not deserve punishment if he has previously declared the defects of a girl who is insane, afflicted with leprosy, or one who has already experienced sexual intercourse.
If a chosen officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should abandon his own duties during a sacrifice,
a share corresponding to the portion of work he has performed must be given to him by the other co-performers.
If, after the sacrificial fees have been given, he abandons his own work,
he shall receive his entire share and have it performed by another.
In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed,
the performer alone may take them, or all the priests may share them together.
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot at the establishment of the sacred fires, and the Brahman shall take a horse;
or the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Of all [the priests], the chief ones receive half; others receive half of that;
those who receive a third part get one-third; and those who receive a fourth part get one-fourth.
When men here perform their respective duties in concert,
the distribution of shares must be carried out according to this prescribed rule.

If a person has given wealth to someone who asks for it for the sake of dharma, but later that wealth does not turn out to be used for such a purpose, it shall not be given to him; it must be taken back.
If, however, he should recover that [property] out of pride or greed,
he must be made to pay one *suvarṇa* by the king as atonement for that theft.
This has been declared as the lawful manner of non-payment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
If a hired laborer, though not ill, should out of pride fail to perform his work as prescribed,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid to him.
But one who is ill, having recovered his health, shall perform the work as originally stipulated from the beginning;
he shall receive that very wage even after a long period of time.
Whether afflicted by illness or in good health, if one does not perform the work as agreed,
his wages must not be paid, even if the work is only slightly incomplete.
This entire law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
A man who, having made a covenant in good faith with a village, a district, or an assembly,
should break it out of greed, the king shall banish from the realm.
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of agreements to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one royal śatamāna.
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate established agreements within villages, castes, or assemblies.
If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have cause for regret,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the object] to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But if a man gives away a girl who has defects without having disclosed them,
the king himself shall impose upon him a fine of ninety-six paṇas.
But that man who, out of malice, says of a maiden "she is not a virgin," shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas] if he fails to demonstrate her fault.
The mantras used at the taking of the hand are established as applying only to virgins;
they never apply to non-virgins among women, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites.
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be recognized by the learned as occurring at the seventh step.
In whatever matter one may have cause for regret after it has been performed,
he should be restored to the path of righteousness by this procedure.
I shall now duly declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from transgressions between owners and herdsmen regarding cattle.

If the loss occurs during the day, the blame falls on the keeper; if at night, it falls on the owner, provided the animal was in his house. Otherwise, if the security of the property was not maintained, the keeper shall incur the blame.
A cowherd who is supported by milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be his wages if he is otherwise not paid. This is the fee for a herdsman.
But the keeper alone must restore what is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, or died on uneven ground,
provided it was not due to human negligence.
But if cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he informs his own master of it at the proper place and time.
When animals have died, one should give the ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinew, and gallstone to the owners, and show them the identifying marks.
But when goats and sheep are obstructed by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid—
If a wolf should kill a cow by force, the guilt for that shall fall upon the keeper.
If, among those cows that have been penned up and are grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that case.
There shall be a pasture-land of one hundred bows all around a village;
for a city, however, it shall be three times that, or else three throws of a yoke-pin.
If cattle should damage unenclosed grain there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals. In that case,
he should have a fence constructed such that even a camel cannot look over it.
And he should guard against every vulnerability that might be entered by the snouts of dogs or pigs.

On a path, in an enclosed field, or likewise on the outskirts of a village, the keeper of the cattle is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unattended.
But for cattle in other fields, one deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
however, in all cases, a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule.
Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved within ten days, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods—
whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper.
In the event of the owner of the field's negligence, the fine shall be ten times the share [of the crop];
however, if the field-owner is ignorant, the fine for his servants shall be half of that.
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions involving owners of cattle, the cattle themselves, and herdsmen.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary during the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.
And he should establish boundary trees—*nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees;
*śālmalī*, *sāla*, and *tāla* trees, as well as milky-sap trees.
By means of various thickets, bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and mounds,
as well as reeds and *kubjaka* shrubs, the boundary is not lost.
Reservoirs, wells, tanks, and springs,
as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries.
And he should cause other boundary marks to be made that are concealed,
having observed the constant confusion among men in the world when boundaries are unknown.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand; [these are to be used for filling up the pits].
And whatever other such marks the earth might not erode over time,
those he should cause to be made inconspicuous at junctions and boundaries.
By these signs the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties.
And by continuous prior possession, as well as by the flow of water.
If there should be doubt even when the characteristic marks are visible,
the decision regarding the dispute over the boundary shall depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses.
[Witnesses] concerning the boundary should be examined in the presence of the village assemblies and their families.
The boundary markers should be questioned by both of those litigants. Whatever determination they all declare when questioned regarding the boundary,
he shall fix the boundary accordingly and record the names of all of them.
Having grasped the earth with their heads, wearing garlands and red garments,
and having been made to swear by their respective good deeds, they shall lead the case justly.
Leading [the case] in the manner prescribed, those truthful witnesses are purified;
but leading it otherwise, they shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
In the absence of witnesses, however, four inhabitants of the neighboring villages [or those dwelling on the village boundaries],
being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
But in the absence of neighboring elders who can serve as witnesses to the boundary, he should also interrogate these following persons who frequent the forests: [Manu 8.259].
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers— [these he should exempt from taxes].
Whatever mark they may declare when questioned regarding the boundaries between the two villages,
the king shall establish that in accordance with dharma for both villages.
The determination of boundaries and landmarks for fields, wells, tanks, groves,
and houses is to be understood as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
the king shall punish each of them individually with the middle amercement.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.
When a boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, being a knower of dharma, shall assign the land to those who have benefited it; such is the settled rule.
This entire law regarding the determination of boundaries has been declared;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of verbal assault.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be forty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment shall be twelve.
For the transgression of twice-born men against a woman of equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve;
in cases of unspeakable disputes, that same fine shall be doubled.
But a man of one birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall have his tongue cut out, for he is of low origin.
But for one who, out of malice, utters their name and caste,
a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
If a king, out of arrogance, provides instruction on the Dharma to Brahmins,
he should have boiling oil poured into his mouth and his ears. [He should likewise pour it into] his ears,
his native region, his caste, his occupation, and his very body.
Speaking falsely out of arrogance, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Even if one speaks the truth regarding someone who is one-eyed, or lame, or otherwise similarly disabled, he shall be made to pay a fine of at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher.
A wise king must impose punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement.
In the case of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, the same rule applies exactly regarding their own respective castes;
the settled legal principle is that the infliction of punishment shall be carried out with the exception of mutilation.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.
If a person of the lowest caste should injure a member of the highest caste with any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu.
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the severing of his hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the severing of his foot.
A person of lower birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of higher rank should be branded on the hip and banished,
or his buttock should be cut off.
If a man spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both his lips to be cut off;
if he urinates [upon him], his penis; and if he passes wind [against him], his anus.
If one seizes another by the hair, he shall have both hands cut off without hesitation;
likewise for seizing by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
One who pierces the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
"For all trees, according to the degree of their utility, so should the fine be imposed for injuring them; such is the established rule."
When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the purpose of causing pain,
the king shall impose a punishment in proportion to the severity of the suffering inflicted.
In cases of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of wounds or blood,
the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery, or else the full fine.
If anyone should damage the goods of another, whether intentionally or even unintentionally,
he shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king.
In the case of goods made of leather or leather products, or those made of wood or clay,
as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
They declare that there are ten exemptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in all other cases, a punishment is ordained.
When the nose-string is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or comes from the front;
