likewise, when there is a breakage of the axle of the vehicle or a breakage of a wheel;
and also when there is a snapping of the fastenings, the thongs, or the reins.
And in the case of a cry for help, "Get away!", Manu has declared that there shall be no punishment.
But where a vehicle goes astray due to the negligence of the driver,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred paṇas.
If the driver be trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas].
But if he, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
should cause the death of a living being, the punishment there is not to be deliberated upon.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is immediately the same as that of a thief;
in the case of large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, it is half [of that].
For the injury of small animals, however, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the fine shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, however, the fine shall be five *māṣas*;
but for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one *māṣa*.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother—
when they have committed an offense, these may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one must strike only on the back part of the body, never on the head;
for striking otherwise, one incurs the guilt of a thief.
This decision regarding assault has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
The king should exert the greatest effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and kingdom increase.
For that king who is the giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra), which has fearlessness as its fee, prospers forever.
A sixth part of the merit from all sources accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of the demerit accrues to him who fails to protect.
Whatever he studies, whatever he sacrifices, whatever he gives, and whatever he worships—
the king becomes the recipient of a sixth part of that through his proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death,
the king performs sacrifices every day with fees of a hundred thousand.
That king who takes tribute, taxes, tolls, the customary share,
and fines without providing protection, shall immediately go to hell.
They call that king who fails to protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part as tax, the one who carries away the entire impurity of all the world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, who is plundering, who fails to protect, and who consumes [the wealth of his subjects], goes to a low state.
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are purified by sacrifices.
A lord who seeks his own welfare must always forgive those litigants who revile him,
as well as children, the elderly, and the sick.
He who, when reviled by those in distress, endures it, is glorified in heaven because of that;
but he who, out of pride in his power, does not endure it, goes to hell because of that.
A thief must approach the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me."
Carrying on his shoulder a pestle, or even a club made of *khadira* wood,
or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron staff;
By punishing or by releasing him, the thief is freed from the guilt of theft;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the sin of the thief.
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
But he who steals a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who destroys a watering-trough,
shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place.
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value as a fine, and that property shall be returned to its owner.
Likewise, for stealing more than a hundred units of things measured by weight— such as gold, silver, and the like— and for the theft of the finest garments, the punishment is death.
But when the value exceeds fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially of women,
as well as for the theft of the most precious gems, one deserves the death penalty.
For the theft of large animals, weapons, and medicinal herbs,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the circumstances of the act.
For stealing cows belonging to Brahmins, for piercing them with a knife,
and likewise for the theft of other animals, one must immediately have half a foot amputated.
Of thread, cotton, fermenting agents, cow dung, and molasses;
of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass.
In the case of stealing articles made of bamboo or split cane, as well as various kinds of salt,
and likewise for stealing earthenware, earth, or ashes, [the fine shall be equal to the value of the goods].
Of fish, birds, oil, clarified butter,
meat, honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
In the case of other such intoxicating drinks,
as well as boiled rice and all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value.
For taking flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*.
In the case of cleaned grains, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits,
the fine shall be one hundred paṇas if there is no prior connection [with the owner], and fifty paṇas if such a connection exists.
An act committed by force with the owner present is *sāhasa* (violence); that which is committed without the owner being present, or where one takes and denies it, is *steya* (theft).

But the king shall punish first that man who steals these prepared articles, as well as he who would steal fire from a house. With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against men, with that very same limb shall the king strike him.
The king shall confiscate that very same [property] of him as a deterrent.
Neither a father, a teacher, a friend, a mother, a wife, a son,
nor a domestic priest is exempt from punishment by the king if he does not abide by his own duty.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*, the king should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
For a Brāhmaṇa, it shall be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he is indeed an expert in the merits and defects of those offenses.
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cattle, does not constitute theft.
A Brāhmaṇa who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given—
even by officiating at sacrifices or by teaching— is exactly like a thief.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose means of subsistence have failed, taking two stalks of sugarcane and two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished.
One who binds those who are not bound, one who releases those who are bound,
and one who seizes a slave, a horse, or a chariot, shall incur the guilt of a thief.
By suppressing thieves according to this rule,
a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
Desiring to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, eternal fame,
a king should not overlook a man who commits an act of violence even for a moment.
A man who commits violence through harsh speech, theft, or even by means of physical punishment,
should be known as the worst among evildoers.
But that king who tolerates one who persists in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred.
Neither for the sake of friendship nor due to the acquisition of vast wealth should a king release perpetrators of violence who bring fear to all living beings.
Weapons may be taken up by the twice-born when their duty is obstructed,
and during the upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time.
In self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees,
or in coming to the aid of a woman or a Brahmin, one who kills in accordance with dharma incurs no guilt.
One may indeed kill, without hesitation, an assailant (ātatāyin) who approaches, even if he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brāhmaṇa deeply learned in the Vedas.
In the killing of an assailant, no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer;
whether done openly or in secret, it is fury that meets that fury.
When men are intent upon violating the wives of others, the king,
having branded them with punishments that cause public alarm, shall banish them;
for from such acts arises the confusion of castes among the people.
By that unrighteousness which destroys the root, everything is liable to perish.
A man who, having been previously accused of offenses, engages in secret conversation with another's wife,
shall incur the first amercement.
But he who, having previously been unaccused, speaks out for a valid reason,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a deserted spot, or even in a forest,
or likewise at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery (saṃgrahaṇa).
Service, playful dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments,
and even sitting together on the same bed— all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, consents to it,
it is all recorded in tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse), provided there was mutual consent.
A non-Brāhmaṇa deserves the death penalty for adultery;
the wives of all four castes must always be protected most carefully.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for a sacrifice,
and artisans may converse with women without being hindered.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
but he who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers (cāraṇas), nor to those who subsist on their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away.

But he who engages in conversation with such women should be made to pay a small fine; as should one who converses in secret with female slaves who have only one master, or with female ascetics. He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate corporal punishment.
A man of equal status who violates a woman who consents to it shall not suffer the penalty of death.
If a maiden chooses a man of higher caste, he shall not be made to pay anything at all;
but if she serves one of lower caste, he should keep her confined in the house.
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves corporal punishment;
however, if he has intercourse with a woman of equal caste, he should pay a bride-price if her father so desires.
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
However, one who defiles a willing maiden of equal status shall not suffer the amputation of his fingers.
But for the sake of preventing a recurrence, he should be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
If a maiden herself should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being led away on a donkey.
But that woman who, arrogant because of her kinsmen or her own virtues, violates her husband,
the king shall cause her to be devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with people.
One should cause the wicked man to be burned on a red-hot iron bed;
they shall pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise, for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī* woman, it shall be exactly that much.

A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she be protected or unprotected—is punished as follows: for an unprotected woman, he is deprived of his limb and all his property; for a protected woman, he is deprived of everything. A Vaiśya shall be fined all his property after being imprisoned for one year.
A Kṣatriya should be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
he should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of those very men, having violated a guarded Brāhmaṇa woman,
should be punished like Śūdras or burned in a fire of straw.
A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand;
he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred.

Shaving the head is ordained as the capital punishment for a Brāhmaṇa; however, for the other castes, the punishment may indeed be the loss of life. One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he has committed every possible crime.
He should banish him from the kingdom, taking all his wealth with him, provided he remains unscarred.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brāhmaṇa;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a guarded Vaiśya woman,
both of them deserve the same punishment as that prescribed for one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, approaching guarded women of those two castes, should be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
For a Vaiśya approaching an unguarded Kṣatriya woman, the fine is five hundred.
But a Kṣatriya should desire the shaving of his head with urine, or else pay a fine.

If a Brāhmaṇa approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman, he should be fined five hundred; but for approaching a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he should be fined one thousand.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with a staff, shares in the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm by the king secures universal sovereignty among his kinsmen and brings him glory in the world.
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—
provided that he is capable of the task and free from fault— the punishment for both of them shall be one hundred [paṇas] each.
Neither a mother, nor a father, nor a wife, nor a son deserves to be abandoned.
One who abandons these when they have not fallen from their status shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
When twice-born men dispute among themselves regarding their duties in the various stages of life (āśramas),
a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold righteousness should not issue a hasty judgment.
Having honored these [offenders] as is appropriate together with the Brahmins, the king,
having first pacified them with gentle words, should cause them to return to their own duty.
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and the neighbor next door when twenty twice-born men are invited to a festive occasion,
he deserves a fine of one *māṣaka*.
A learned Śrotriya who does not feed another virtuous Śrotriya at auspicious rites shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one *māṣaka* of gold.
A blind man, an idiot, one who moves about on a board, and one who is seventy years old [are exempt from this obligation].
And those who provide service to Vedic scholars shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone.
The king should always honor a Vedic scholar, those afflicted by disease or distress, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous.
On a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood, the washerman shall gently wash the clothes;
he shall not exchange garments for other garments, nor shall he allow them to be worn [by others].
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread with an additional one pala;
if he acts otherwise than this, he should be made to pay a fine of twelve paṇas.
In the customs houses, those who are skilled and expert in all types of merchandise shall determine the value of each commodity;
from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.
If someone, out of greed, exports goods that are the king’s own property, or those that are prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire wealth.
One who evades the toll-station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
and one who gives a false account in the reckoning, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
Having considered the source, the destination, the storage period, as well as both the increase and the decrease,
he should regulate the purchase and sale of all marketable goods.
Every five nights, or else at the end of every fortnight,
the king should publicly determine the value of these commodities.
All weights and measures must be clearly marked;
every six months, one should have them re-examined.
A vehicle should be made to pay one *paṇa* at a ferry; a person, half a *paṇa*;
an animal and a woman, a quarter *paṇa*; and an empty-handed man, half of that quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods should be made to pay the ferry fare according to their value.
Empty vessels and whatever else, as well as men who are without belongings; [these are exempt from search].
On long journeys, the toll shall be according to the place and according to the time;
one should know that this applies to riverbanks, but there is no fixed rule for the ocean.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering mendicant, a sage,
and Brāhmaṇas wearing the marks of their religious orders, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing.
Whatever may be damaged on a boat through the fault of the boatmen,
that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together, each from his own share.
This decision regarding legal disputes for those traveling by boat has been declared:
there is no punishment for damage caused by the fault of the boatmen on the water, nor for that which is caused by fate.
One should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, moneylending, and agriculture;
and the Śūdra to perform the tending of cattle and service toward the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa should support with compassion a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.
But a Brāhmaṇa who, out of greed and by virtue of his power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servile labor against their will,
shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But a Śūdra, whether bought or even unbought, one should make to perform service;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (Manu 8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given as a gift, one inherited from an ancestor, and one enslaved by way of punishment— these seven are the origins of slavery.
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property.
Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take goods from a Śūdra;
for he possesses nothing of his own, as his wealth is to be taken by his master.
The king should cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own duties with diligence; for if these two deviate from their respective duties, they would throw this entire world into disorder.
Day after day, he should inspect the completion of his works, the vehicles,
and the fixed income and expenditure, as well as the mines and the treasury.
Thus, by settling all these legal disputes, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.
For the man and the woman who abide in the path of dharma,
I shall declare the eternal laws concerning their union and their separation.
Women must be kept in a state of dependence by their own men day and night; and if they become attached to sensual pleasures, they must be restrained within their own control.
The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth;
the sons protect her in old age. A woman does not deserve independence.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is to be censured; a husband who does not approach his wife is to be censured;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is to be censured.
Women must be protected especially from even the slightest of attachments;
for if they are not guarded, they will bring sorrow upon two families.
For seeing this as the supreme duty for all social classes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak themselves.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, a man protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (Manu 9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here again;
for that is the reason she is called "jāyā" (wife), because he is born (*jāyate*) from her once more.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard women with great effort.
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded by the application of these following means.
He should employ her in the accumulation of wealth and in its expenditure,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
Women who are confined at home and guarded by trustworthy men,
yet protect themselves by their own efforts— they are well-protected.
Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about,
sleeping [at improper times], and dwelling in another's house— these six are the vices that corrupt women.
They do not examine their appearance, nor is there any fixed regard for their age; whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection, these women—
even when guarded with great effort— act perversely toward their husbands in this world.
Having thus understood their nature, born of the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection.
Manu ordained for women the use of beds, seats, ornaments, passion, anger, dishonesty, ignobility, a malevolent disposition, and misconduct (Manu 9.17).
It is established in the Dharma that women have no ritual efficacy through sacred mantras (Manu 9.18).
"For women are devoid of sensory restraint and lack the authority of sacred mantras; such is the established rule that they are untruthful. (Manu 9.18c).
Likewise, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas.
Listen now to the expiations for them, intended for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics. (Manu 9.19).
"Whatever my mother, wandering about unfaithful to her husband, lusted after—may my father take that seed away from me"; this is the scriptural basis for this [rule].
Whatever undesirable thing she meditates upon in her mind for her husband,
this is declared to be the proper means of averting that transgression.
With whatever qualities a woman is united to her husband according to the prescribed rule,
she becomes possessed of those same qualities, just as a river is by the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained honor by being united with Vasiṣṭha; and Śāraṅgī reached a state of venerability through Mandapāla.
These and other women in this world who were born of low origin have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.
Thus has been declared the ever-auspicious conduct for men and women in this world; now learn the duties regarding progeny, which yield happiness both in this life and after death.
For the sake of procreation, highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
there is no difference whatsoever between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) within households.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— each of these is visibly dependent upon the woman.
Offspring, the performance of religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure [all depend on her].
Likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent upon the wife.
She who does not act treacherously toward her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called a "virtuous woman" by the righteous.

But by infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world; she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. [M.śṛgālayoniṃ] Regarding a son, the virtuous and the great seers of old have declared: [Manu 9.31a]
Learn this meritorious discourse, which is beneficial for all people.

They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict in the sacred texts regarding the progenitor. Some say he belongs to the one who produces him, while others know him to belong to the owner of the field.
Woman is declared to be the field, and man is declared to be the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the womb of the woman;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
Of both the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the offspring of all living beings is characterized by the traits of the seed. Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, [such is the fruit that arises].
Such [a child] is born from him, that seed being manifested by its own inherent qualities.
For this earth is said to be the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth.
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at different times by farmers are produced here in various forms according to their own nature.
Rice, *śāli* rice, mung beans, sesame seeds, masha beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcane— these all sprout according to their respective seeds.
"It is not possible that one thing is sown and another is produced;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts."
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man,
who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical experience and desires a long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another.
In this regard, those who know the past recite these verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a man should not sow seed in another's field..."
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sky when one shoots after it as it pierces its mark,
so too does seed quickly perish when sown in the possession of another. Those who know the ancient lore recognize this entire earth as the wife of Pṛthu.
They say that a field full of rice is the equivalent of cutting down a tree-stump, and a deer is the equivalent of a field.
"A man consists of just this much: his wife, himself, and his offspring—so the learned Brahmins have declared. Likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as being the very self of the woman."
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the law as it was ordained of old by Prajāpati.
The inheritance is divided once; a daughter is given away in marriage once;
and once has a man said, "I give"—these three things happen but once among the virtuous.
Just as it is with cows, horses, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, and sheep...
The progenitor does not share in the offspring, even in the case of other women.
Those who possess seed but have no field, and sow it in the field of another,
never obtain the fruit of the crop that is produced.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field produce a benefit for the owner of the field; the sower of the seed does not obtain the fruit.

But when no agreement regarding the fruit has been made between the owner of the field and the sower, the benefit clearly belongs to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed. However, this [fruit] which is given for the sake of the seed arises from the acceptance of the labor.
In this world, both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen to be sharers of the offspring.

If seed carried away by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone's field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. This same rule applies to cattle, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, and sheep.
And regarding the offspring of birds and female buffaloes, it should be understood that [the ownership] depends upon the birth.
Thus has been proclaimed to you the relative importance and insignificance of seed and womb;
hereafter, I shall declare the law for women in times of distress.
The wife of an elder brother is the teacher's wife for the younger brother;
but the wife of the younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law for the elder.

The elder brother who approaches the wife of the younger, or the younger brother who approaches the wife of the elder— even if they are authorized [to do so]— become outcasts, unless there be a state of distress.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized may obtain the desired offspring from her brother-in-law or from a sapinda relative.
One appointed to a widow, however, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent,
may procreate one son at night, but by no means a second.
Some who are experts in this matter consider a second procreation with women to be permissible,
seeing that the purpose of the *niyoga* for those two [husband and wife] has not yet been fully accomplished according to the law.
However, once the purpose of the *niyoga* with a widow has been accomplished according to the prescribed rule...
And they should behave toward each other like a teacher and a pupil, and like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.
If those two, being thus enjoined, should act according to their own desire by disregarding the rule,
they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal dharma.
Nowhere in the marriage mantras is the practice of *niyoga* mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for marriage.
"For this practice of animal behavior has been condemned by learned twice-born men;
yet it was proclaimed even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom."
In former times, that most excellent of royal sages, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social classes, his mind being struck down by lust.
From that time forward, virtuous men censure any man who, out of delusion, attempts to appoint a widow whose husband has died to procreate offspring.
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule.
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she being dressed in white garments and pure in her observances—
he should unite with her in private once at each menstrual period until conception occurs.
A wise man, having given his daughter to anyone, should not give her again;
for by giving her once and then giving her away again, he incurs the sin of falsehood regarding a human being.
Even after accepting a maiden according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon her if she is blameworthy,
diseased, severely defiled, or was offered through deception.
But if one should bestow a maiden who has defects without having disclosed them,
he shall nullify that gift of the evil-minded giver of the bride.
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's maintenance;
for a woman, even one of firm character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live observing the prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she may live by means of blameless crafts.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be waited for eight years;
one who has gone for the sake of learning or fame, six years; but one who has gone for the sake of pleasure, three years.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who hates him;
but after a year has passed, he may take back her property and no longer live with her.
If she should transgress against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease,
she shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, outcast, impotent, seedless, or afflicted with a foul disease;
nor is there any forfeiture of her inheritance. And the same applies to one who is hostile.
A wife who drinks liquor, behaves wickedly, is hostile,
is afflicted by disease, is violent, or is constantly wasteful of wealth may be superseded by taking another wife.
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year, one whose children have died in the tenth,
one who gives birth only to daughters in the eleventh, but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately.
But a wife who may be diseased, yet is devoted and endowed with good character, may be superseded only after obtaining her permission; she must never be treated with contempt.
But a superseded wife who goes out from the house in anger should be immediately confined or abandoned in the presence of the family.
If a woman, though prohibited, drinks liquor even at festive occasions,
or if she goes to a spectacle or a public assembly, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
If twice-born men should marry women both of their own caste and of other castes,
seniority, honor, and the principal residence shall belong to them according to the order of their castes.
A woman of her own caste alone, and never one of a different caste, should perform the personal service to the husband and his daily religious duties for all [the brothers].
But he who, out of delusion, causes those duties to be performed by another woman while a woman of his own caste is available, [is at fault].
Just as a Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla was seen before, so indeed is he.
To a distinguished, handsome, and suitable suitor who is of equal status,
one should give that maiden according to the prescribed rule, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age.
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father’s house at his pleasure until death;
but he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may choose a husband of equal status.
If she approaches her husband of her own accord when he does not take her back,
she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does the man whom she approaches.
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself the ornaments belonging to her father;
whether they were inherited from her mother or given by her brother, she would be a thief if she should take them away.
But he who takes a girl who has reached puberty shall not pay the nuptial fee to her father;
for by obstructing the periods, he would overstep the father’s right of ownership.
A man thirty years of age should marry a pleasing girl of twelve;
or one twenty-four years old may marry an eight-year-old, if he is in haste to fulfill his religious duty.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
he should always support her if she is virtuous, performing what is pleasing to the gods.
Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage;
therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both, performed together with the wife.
If the giver of the bride-price should die after the price has been paid for a maiden, she should be given to the husband's brother,
provided the maiden consents.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, should not take a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, one effectively commits a concealed sale of the daughter.
But this which is done— promising to one and then giving to another— neither those of old nor any other virtuous men have ever practiced.
We have never heard of such a thing even in former births:
the sale of a daughter disguised under the name of a "bride-price" (śulka).
Mutual fidelity until death—
this is to be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief.

Likewise, a man and a woman who have performed their rites should always strive so that they do not violate each other when separated. This dharma concerning sexual union has been declared for you regarding husband and wife.
In times of distress, the acquisition of offspring [is permitted]; now learn the law of inheritance.
After the death of both the father and the mother, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the parents are alive.
The eldest alone, however, shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the remaining brothers shall depend upon him just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a father of sons and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off a debt and through whom one attains immortality—he alone is the son born of dharma; they know the others to be born of desire.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons;
and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as toward a son.
The eldest son causes the family to prosper, or conversely, he destroys it;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an eldest brother should—like a mother, like a father—is he;
but he who does not behave as an eldest brother should is to be honored merely as a kinsman.
Thus they may live together, or separately if they desire to fulfill their duty; for dharma increases through separation; therefore, separation is consistent with dharma.
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as an additional share, and whatever is the best among all the goods;
half of that shall be the share of the middlemost, and a fourth for the youngest.
The eldest and the youngest shall take [their shares] as prescribed;
those who are others than the eldest and the youngest shall receive the middlemost portion of the wealth.
Of all kinds of property, the eldest shall take the best;
and whatever is particularly excellent, he shall also receive as his choice from among ten.
There is no preferential share (*uddhāra*) among those who are all equally proficient in their respective duties;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the eldest as a mark of respect.
Thus, when the preferential shares have been extracted, one should allot equal portions;
but if no preferential shares have been extracted, this following distribution of shares shall apply.
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the younger than him, one and a half shares;
and the youngest sons, one share each—thus is the law established.
Brothers shall give portions to their unmarried sisters from their own respective shares;
each sister shall receive a fourth part of her brother's share. Those who are unwilling to give shall become outcasts.
One should never divide goats, sheep, and single-hoofed animals unequally;
however, an unequal share of goats and sheep is ordained for the eldest alone.
If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law.
According to the law, the subordinate cannot rightfully take the place of the principal;
the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him according to dharma.

If a doubt should arise as to how the division [of the estate] should be made in a case where the youngest son is born of the eldest wife, and the first-born son is born of the youngest wife— Manu 9.122: "The younger son born of the eldest wife, and the elder son born of the youngest wife—if a doubt should arise as to how the partition should be made in that case..."
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall take bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take the best bull and fifteen other shares;
the remaining sons shall divide the rest according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority based on their mothers; rather, seniority is said to be according to birth [from the father].
Even in the *Subrahmaṇyā* liturgical formulas, it is recorded that the invocation is made according to birth-order seniority;
and in the case of twins conceived simultaneously, seniority is declared to be determined by the order of birth.
A sonless man may, by this rule, make his daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), [stipulating]: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs my ancestral rites."
According to this very rule, Dakṣa himself, the Lord of Creatures, formerly made daughters in the form of appointed daughters (*putrikā*) for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
With a pleased heart, he gave ten daughters to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them with due respect.
As one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son. While she stands as his very self, how could another take the wealth?
Whatever may be the separate property of the mother, that is the share of the unmarried daughter alone;
and the daughter's son shall inherit the entire estate of one who leaves no son.
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
In this world, according to the law, there is no difference between a grandson and a daughter's son;
for both of them are born from the bodies of one's own mother and father.

But if, after a daughter has been appointed as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate there shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
But if the appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without having borne a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.

Whether she has been formally appointed or not, if a man obtains a son from a similar man, that grandson makes his maternal grandfather the recipient of the funeral cake; he shall inherit the property.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
In this world, no distinction is found between a grandson and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son saves him in the hereafter, just like a grandson.
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to that [father's] father.
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall never inherit the family name or the estate of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and the estate, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives [the son away].

Both the son born of a woman not authorized [to bear a child] and the son obtained from her brother-in-law by a woman who already has a son— these two, being born of an adulterer and born of lust, do not deserve a share of the inheritance.
Even if born of a woman duly appointed [for levirate],
a son produced contrary to the prescribed rule is not at all entitled to the paternal inheritance, for he is begotten by one who has fallen from his status.
A son born from a woman duly appointed in that matter shall be like a legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*);
for according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring.
He who takes charge of the wealth and the widow of his deceased brother shall,
having procreated offspring for that brother, hand over that very wealth to that [offspring].

If a woman, having been authorized, should obtain a son from another man or even from her brother-in-law, they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and begotten in vain. This rule is to be understood as applying to the division of property among children born of a single womb.
Now learn concerning those born of many wives of various castes from one [man].
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order of castes,
this rule for partition is prescribed when sons have been born from them.
The plowman, the breeding bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house—
these should be given to the Brāhmaṇa as his preferential share, along with one principal portion from the inheritance.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares of the inheritance; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya woman, one share and a half; and the son born of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
Or, having divided that entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous partition according to this rule.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
This is so whether there be a legitimate son (son of a wife of equal caste) or even no legitimate son at all.
According to the law, one should not give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra wife.
The son of a Śūdra born to a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya does not inherit the estate;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
All sons born of wives of equal caste to twice-born men,
having given a preferential share to the eldest, should divide the remainder equally.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is prescribed, and no other;
those born of her shall have equal shares, even if there be a hundred sons.
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has declared for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, and six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the son made,
the son secretly born, and the son cast off— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried woman, the son received with a pregnant bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman,
the self-given son, and the Śūdra son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
Just as one obtains such fruit when crossing water with bad boats,
so does one obtain such fruit when crossing over darkness with bad sons.
If there should be two sons, an aurasa and a kṣetraja, who are heirs to the same estate,
each shall take that paternal property which belongs to his own biological father, and not the other.
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the rest, he should provide them with a livelihood.
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa), upon distributing the estate, should give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja),
or even a fifth share.
The legitimate son of the body (aurasa) and the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja) are the two heirs to the father's estate;
the other ten, however, in their respective order, are entitled to a share of the lineage and the inheritance.
But that son whom one himself begets upon his own wedded wife who has been consecrated,
one should know him to be the legitimate (aurasa) son, the first in rank.
He who is born on the bed of one who is deceased, impotent, or diseased,
by means of a woman duly appointed according to her own dharma, is known as the son of the soil (kṣetraja).
If the mother or the father should give away a son with water in times of distress—
one who is similar [in status] and given with affection— he is to be known as a *dattima* (given) son.
But he whom one may make similar [to oneself], who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the "artificial" (kṛtrima) son.
But he who is born in the house and it is not known whose he is—he is one secretly born in the house; he shall belong to him on whose wife he was begotten.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his mother and father, or by either of them,
is called an *apaviddha* (abandoned son).
But the son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father’s house,
one should call him by the name Kānīna, born of a maiden, belonging to the one who marries her.
If a woman who is already pregnant is married— whether her condition be known or unknown—
that embryo belongs to the husband and is called *sahoḍha* (born with the bride).
But he whom one purchases from his mother and father for the sake of offspring—
whether he be similar or dissimilar to him— that son is his "bought" (krītaka) son.
He who, having become a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), whether she has been abandoned by her husband or is a widow, procreates by her own will, is called a *paunarbhava*.
If she is still a virgin, even if she has returned from another,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with a husband who takes a second wife.
He who, being deprived of his mother and father, or abandoned by them without cause,
offers himself to someone, is known as a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) son.
But the son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman—
he is called a Pāraśava, because he is merely capable of carrying a corpse.
If a son is born to a Śūdra by a female slave or the female slave of a slave, he shall, with the permission [of his father], take a share; such is the established law.
The wise declare these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as described above, to be substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
These sons born from the seed of others who have been mentioned here incidentally belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else.
Manu 9.182: Among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, Manu has declared them all to be possessed of sons through that son.
If among all women who have had only one husband, one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
In the absence of each more excellent [heir], one who is less excellent is entitled to the inheritance. But if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate.
Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the takers of the father's inheritance.
The father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall the brothers.
Water-offerings must be made for three ancestors, and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) extends to three;
he who offers it is the fourth, and a fifth does not exist.
The wealth of a deceased person shall belong to his nearest *sapiṇḍa*;
after him, it shall go to a *sakulya*, or else to the teacher or the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs of the inheritance; thus the Dharma is not abandoned.
The property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be confiscated by the king; this is the settled rule. However, in the absence of all [heirs], the king may take the property of the other castes.
For one who has died without offspring, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage (sagotra).
Whatever property may have been acquired there, that he should bestow upon him. But if two sons born of two [different] men should dispute over the wealth of a woman,
each of them shall take what belonged to his own father, and not the other.
But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally.
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something from the maternal grandmother's wealth should be given according to their merit and with affection.
That which is given before the fire, that which is given at the wedding procession, and that which is given as a token of affection;
that which is received from her brothers, her mother, or her father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
The property given as a subsequent gift (anvādheya), as well as that which was given by the husband out of affection—
this shall be the wealth of the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.
Whatever property was acquired in marriages of the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, or Prājāpatya types, it is ordained that,
upon the death of the wife without issue, it belongs to the husband alone.
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others,
that is ordained to belong to her mother and father when she dies childless.
But whatever property may have been given to a woman by her father in any manner whatsoever,
that a Brāhmaṇī daughter shall take, or it shall belong to her offspring.
Women should not make a removal of property from the midst of a large family,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband.
If ornaments have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them;
those who do divide them fall from their caste.
Eunuchs, outcasts, those born blind or deaf,
as well as the insane, the mentally dull, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs, do not receive a share of the inheritance.
However, it is just for the wise man to give to all of them, according to his ability, food and clothing for life; for by not giving these, he becomes an outcast.
If, however, there should be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others by any means whatsoever,
their offspring is entitled to the inheritance once they have produced progeny.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died,
the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning.
But if all those who are unlearned should acquire wealth through their own exertion, the division of that property shall be equal; it is not ancestral—this is the settled rule.
But whatever is his wealth acquired through learning shall belong to him alone;
the same applies to what is received from a friend, what is obtained at a wedding, and what is received as the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
But among brothers, he who, though capable of supporting himself by his own labor, does not desire a share of the wealth,
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.
That which has been acquired by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained through one's own effort— that he need not give if he is unwilling.
But if a father should acquire ancestral property that was previously unobtained,
he need not share it with his sons against his will, as it was acquired by himself.
If those who were previously divided should live together again and divide once more, the division in that case shall be equal; there, the right of primogeniture does not exist.
If among them the eldest or the youngest is excluded from the distribution of shares,
or if either one of them dies, his share is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having come together and being united, shall divide it equally;
as shall those brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall lose his status as the eldest, be deprived of his share, and be restrained by the kings.

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should an elder brother make a separate acquisition for himself without giving a portion to the younger brothers.
If there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance,
the father must under no circumstances allot unequal shares among their sons.
But one born after partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or he shall share it with those who may have reunited with him.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be divided equally.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security of possession (yogakṣema), and pasture grounds— they declare these to be indivisible.
This division of property among sons and the rule for their rites has been declared to you;
now learn, in due order, the law concerning gambling for those born of the wife and the others.
The king shall prohibit gambling and betting from the realm;
for these two vices are the destroyers of kings who rule the earth.
This gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always be diligent in suppressing them.
That which is carried out by means of inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world;
that which is carried out by means of animate beings is to be known as "betting with living creatures" (samāhvaya).
The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
Gamblers, actors and singers, cruel men, those who adhere to heretical sects,
those engaged in improper occupations, and liquor-sellers— he shall quickly banish from the city.
These, existing in the kingdom as the king's secret thieves,
constantly oppress the virtuous subjects through their illicit occupations.
In a former age, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not practice gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whether it be done secretly or openly, whatever man should practice that [forbidden act],
there shall be a variety of punishments for him according to the king's pleasure.
But a man born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, being unable to pay a fine, shall attain freedom from debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, should pay it gradually.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king shall prescribe punishment by means of whips, split cane, ropes, and the like.
But those who, having been appointed to official duties,
ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth— the king shall strip them of their property.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the ministers,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies.
Whatever has been adjudicated and whatever has been instructed, wherever it may have occurred, one should know that to be established by dharma; one must not reverse it.
Whatever legal matter the ministers or the judge might decide incorrectly,
the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
A killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed— [these are the four mortal sins].
All these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
And for these four who do not perform penance,
the king shall prescribe a righteous punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.
For violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the man should be branded with the mark of a headless corpse.
Indeed, they shall not be allowed to eat together, nor to sacrifice together, nor to study together, nor to intermarry.
They shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties.
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their paternal kinsmen and relatives;
they are to be without compassion and without salutation—this is the instruction of Manu.
But when people of all castes perform the prescribed penance as ordained, they shall not have a mark branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
In cases of offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement shall be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom along with his property and his belongings.
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
A righteous king must not seize the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by seizing it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt.
Having cast that fine into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should bestow it upon a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and good conduct.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Where the king avoids the acquisition of wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time with long lives.
And the crops of the people ripen according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and no deformed offspring is born.
But a king shall put to death with various and terrifying methods of execution a person of low caste who, out of malice, oppresses Brāhmaṇas.

As great as the demerit incurred by a king for executing one who should not be executed, so great is the demerit seen for releasing one who deserves execution; but merit accrues to him who restrains [the guilty].
Thus has been declared in detail this decision regarding legal proceedings in the eighteen titles of law for two parties engaged in mutual dispute.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired.
But having properly settled his territory and constructed fortifications according to the treatises,
he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.
By protecting those who follow the conduct of the noble and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to heaven.
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven.
But that kingdom which is free from fear, relying upon the strength of his arms,
increases constantly for him like a tree being watered.
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should know that there are two kinds of thieves who seize the property of others: those who are open and those who are concealed.
Those who live by various wares and deceive people openly are "open deceivers"; those such as thieves, forest-dwellers, and the like, who deceive in secret, are "concealed deceivers."
Those who take bribes, those who practice fraud, deceivers, gamblers, those who subsist by prescribing auspicious rites, fortune-tellers, together with those who stage spectacles for profit,
and high officials and physicians who act improperly; 9.259.
And courtesans who are skilled in the arts and refined manners are clever in their trade.
One should recognize such persons as open thorns of society,
as well as others who move in secret, being ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble.

Having identified them through well-conducted secret agents who perform their specific tasks, and by means of spies stationed in various disguises, he should incite them and bring them under his control.
Having fully proclaimed their faults in accordance with their respective deeds, the king should duly administer punishment according to the gravity of the offense and the strength of the offender.
For indeed, without punishment, it is impossible to restrain the wicked,
especially those thieves of sinful intent who move about secretly upon the earth.
A court of justice, a water-shed, a bakery, a dwelling, a tavern, and a food-vendor;
crossroads, sacred trees, assemblies, and places of spectacle.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans, empty houses, groves, and pleasure parks; 9.265cd.
In such regions, the king should cause patrols consisting of both stationary and mobile units,
as well as secret agents, to move about for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
He should discover them through their accomplices who follow them and are familiar with various activities,
and he should eliminate them by means of clever former thieves.
By means of instructions regarding various kinds of food, by the sight of Brāhmaṇas,
and by instructions regarding acts of heroism, they should bring about their meeting.
Those who do not approach there, as well as those who are secretly dispatched from the capital.
The king should forcibly slay them, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
A righteous king shall not have a thief executed unless he is caught with the stolen goods;
however, if he is caught with the goods and the implements [of theft], he should be executed without hesitation.
Furthermore, whoever among those in the villages provide food to thieves,
or even give them space for their goods— all of them the king shall cause to be executed.
Those appointed to protect the realms, as well as the neighboring kings who have been exhorted,
if they remain indifferent during attacks, he should punish them swiftly like thieves.
And even one who lives by the law but has fallen away from the covenant of righteousness—
him too the king should burn with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty.
In the event of a village raid, the destruction of irrigation works, or the sighting of a robbery on the road,
those who do not run to assist to the best of their ability shall be banished along with their belongings.
He shall cause those who steal from the king’s treasury, those who persist in hostile acts,
and those who instigate enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment.
But those thieves who commit burglary at night by breaking through a wall,
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake.
In the first seizure, the king shall cause the fingers of a cutpurse to be amputated;
in the second, both hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
The king should punish like a thief those who provide fire, food, weapons, or shelter,
as well as those who facilitate the theft.
One who destroys a water reservoir should be killed, or else executed by drowning in water;
or, if he should repair it, he must be made to pay the highest fine.
One should indeed put to death, without hesitation, those who break into granaries, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots.
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established,
or obstructs the flow of its waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
He who, when not in distress, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two *kārṣāpaṇas* and must immediately clean away that impurity.
But one who has fallen into distress, or an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a reprimand; and that [debt] must be cleared—such is the settled rule.
For all physicians who practice their craft improperly, there shall be a fine:
the first amercement for animals, but the middle amercement for human beings.
One who destroys a bridge, a banner, a sacrificial post,
or an image shall repair all of that damage and pay five hundred [paṇas].
For the spoiling of unblemished goods, as well as for their breaking,
and for the boring of gems in the wrong place, the punishment is the first amercement.
If one should deal unequally with equals, whether by measure or by price,
that man shall incur either the first or the middle fine.
And the king should establish all prisons along the royal highway,
where the suffering and disfigured evildoers may be seen.
One should immediately banish the breaker of a wall, the filler of moats,
and likewise the destroyer of gates.
In all cases of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for root-magic (*mūlakarman*) performed by those who are not related, and for various kinds of sorcery (*kṛtyā*).
Furthermore, a seller of non-seed and one who has extracted the best seed [from a field] shall be punished in the same manner.
And one who breaks a boundary mark shall suffer the punishment of mutilation.
But the king should have a goldsmith, who is the most wicked of all thorns and who proceeds unjustly,
cut into pieces with razors.
In the case of the theft of agricultural implements, weapons, or medicine, [the same punishment applies].
Having considered the time and the nature of the offense, the king shall determine the punishment.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements;
thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Among these seven constituent elements of the kingdom, one should know that, in their respective order,
each preceding one is more important and its calamity more serious.
In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels another due to the specific excellence of their mutual qualities.
In various specific tasks, however, this or that particular limb is distinguished;
whatever organ accomplishes a given purpose is said to be the most excellent for that purpose.
Through spies, through the application of energy, and by the actual performance of his duties,
the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain his own strength and the strength of his enemy,
as well as all forms of oppression and likewise all vices.
Then, having reflected upon the relative gravity or lightness of the matter, he should undertake the task.
One should indeed undertake tasks again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who undertakes actions.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.
Kali is asleep; when he is awake, it is the Dvāpara age;
when he is intent upon actions, it is Tretā; but when he is moving about [actively], it is the Kṛta age.
A king should practice the conduct of those whose essence is splendor: Indra, Arka (the Sun), Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra (the Moon), Agni, and Pṛthivī (the Earth).
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should the king, observing the vow of Indra, shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays during eight months, so should the king draw taxes from his kingdom; for that is the constant vow of the sun.
Just as the wind moves about, having entered all living beings, so too should one penetrate [the enemy's domain] by means of spies; for this is the vow of the Wind-god.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should the king restrain the wicked; for this is the vow of Varuṇa.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow (cāndravratika).

One who is endowed with majesty and possesses brilliance should always be intent upon punishing those who commit evil deeds; and one who is destructive toward wicked neighbors—that is remembered as the vow of Agni.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so is the duty of a king who sustains all beings.
Employing these and other means, always remaining vigilant,
the king should suppress thieves within his own kingdom and even in those of others.
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke Brāhmaṇas;
for they, when enraged, could instantly destroy him along with his army and his vehicles.
By whom was fire made to consume all things, the great ocean rendered undrinkable,
and the moon made subject to waning and waxing— who would not perish by provoking them?
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked, might create other worlds and other world-protectors,
or turn gods into non-gods?
Whoever desires to live should never harm those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, and for whom the Veda itself is their wealth.
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like the fire, which is a great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the brilliant fire is not defiled;
when oblations are offered to it in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of unworthy actions,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are indeed the supreme deity.
When the Kṣatriya power becomes excessively overbearing in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brahman alone shall be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya has its origin in the Brahman.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own sources.
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brāhmaṇical power, nor does the Brāhmaṇical power increase without the Kṣatriya power;
when the Brāhmaṇical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next.
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle.
Acting thus and always disciplined in the duties of a king, the monarch—
And he should employ all his servants in works that are beneficial for the world.
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should know this same rule of action to apply to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra respectively.
But a Vaiśya, having performed the purificatory rites and taken a wife,
should be constantly engaged in agriculture and the protection of cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya should not entertain the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
and when the Vaiśya is willing, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
One should understand the relative value and worthlessness of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven fabrics,
perfumes, and liquids.
He should know the sowing of seeds and the defects or virtues of the soil; he should understand the application of measures and all methods of weighing with scales;
and he should know the quality or lack thereof of merchandise, as well as the advantages and disadvantages of various regions.
The profit and loss on merchandise, and the increase of livestock;
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the proper storage and application of goods, and indeed the rules for buying and selling.
He should exert the greatest effort toward the increase of wealth through righteous means,
and he should diligently give food to all living beings.

For a Śūdra, however, the highest duty leading to supreme beatitude is indeed service to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious. Being pure, intent on serving those superior to him, gentle in speech, and free from arrogance— this is his path.
One who constantly relies upon a Brāhmaṇa or others attains a superior birth. This auspicious rule of action for the social classes has been declared for times of no distress;
now learn that which pertains to them in due order even in times of distress.
The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study [the Veda];
however, it is settled that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound it, not the other two.
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others, and he himself should likewise act accordingly.
Due to his preeminence, the excellence of his origin, his observance of restrictive rules,
and the distinction of his sacraments, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth, however, is once-born, the Śūdra, and there is no fifth.
Among all castes, sons born in the direct order (ānulomya) from wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity are to be known as belonging to that same caste.
Sons procreated by twice-born men on women of the next lower caste are said to be equal [in status] to their fathers,
yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women from the next lower caste;
one should know this rule to be the righteous law for those born of women two or three castes below.
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya maiden is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra maiden is born a Niṣāda, who is also called a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra maiden is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.
Among the three castes for a Brāhmaṇa, among the two castes for a Kṣatriya,
