and among the one caste for a Vaiśya— these six are declared to be base-born (apasada).
From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa is born a Sūta by birth;
from a Vaiśya are born a Māgadha and a Vaideha, who are the sons of a royal and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.
From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men— these being the offspring of the intermixture of castes.
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and the Ugra are remembered as being born from a one-generation interval in the direct order (ānulomya),
so too are the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka born from a one-generation interval in the inverse order (prātilomya).
Those sons of twice-born men who are born of women of the next lower caste, as described in due order,
are designated by the name "Anantara" (next-in-order) on account of the inferiority of their mothers.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta;
from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra, but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—are born from a Śūdra through women of the higher castes; these three are outcasts (apasada) born in the reverse order of castes.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone is born. These three others are also base-born (apasada), though they are born in the reverse order.
A son born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by caste a Pukkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is indeed known as a Kukkuṭaka.
Likewise, one born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is proclaimed a Śvapāka;
but one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhī woman is called a Veṇa.
Those whom twice-born men beget upon wives of their own caste, but who are devoid of the vows,
one should designate as *vrātyas*, fallen from the *Sāvitrī*.
From a Vratya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhūrjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.
From a Vrātya of the Kṣatriya caste are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchivi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khaśa, and the Draviḍa.
From a Vratya Vaiśya, however, are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Through the adultery of the castes, through marrying women who should not be married,
and through the abandonment of their own duties, the intermixture of castes arises.
I shall now describe in their entirety those of mixed origin who are born from inverse (pratiloma) and natural (anuloma) unions, as well as those who are mutually intermingled.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Āyogava, and the Kṣattṛ (or Kṣatrajāti),
these six beget offspring similar to themselves when they procreate within their own respective wombs.
They are born with the caste of their mother even when procreated in superior wombs. Just as for the three castes, the son of one’s own self is born from two [wives],
so too is the sequence for those born outside [the caste], according to the order of immediate proximity to their own womb.
And they, moreover, procreate upon the wives of one another many outsiders who are even more defiled than themselves and are held in contempt.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman,
so does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste among the four castes.
Acting in opposition [to their duties], those excluded castes produce even more excluded offspring;
being degraded, they give birth to fifteen further degraded castes.

A Dasyu begets upon an Āyogava woman a Sairandhra, who knows how to attend to personal adornment and grooming, who is not a slave but lives by the life of a slave, and subsists by means of snares. A Vaideha, however, procreates a Maitreyaka, also known as a Mādhūka.
Manu 10.33c: He who, like a bell-ringer, does not ceaselessly praise [the gods] at the break of dawn, is censured.
The Niṣāda begets a Mārgava, a slave who lives by working with boats;
those who dwell in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.
Among women who wear the clothes of the dead and eat forbidden food— namely,
among Āyogava women— these three base-born castes are separately produced.
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born as a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehika are born an Andhra and a Meda, both of whom have their dwellings outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī woman is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī woman.

From a Caṇḍāla and a Pukkasa woman is born the sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-extraction and is always censured by virtuous people. From a Caṇḍāla and a Niṣāda woman is born a son called Antyāvasāyin.
She gives birth to one who frequents cremation grounds, despised even by those outside the caste system.
These castes born of intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their respective occupations.
The six sons born of women of their own caste and those immediately following in the order of castes possess the duties of the twice-born;
however, all those born of degradation (apadhvaṃsaja) are declared to share the same duties as Śūdras.
But by the power of their austerity and their seed, they undergo, age after age,
both advancement and decline among human beings here from birth.
But through the gradual neglect of their duties and by the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya tribes have reached the state of Śūdras in this world.
These are the Pauṇḍrakas, the Cūḍas, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, and the Śakas.
The Pāradas, Pahlavas, Cīnas, Kirātas, Daradas, and Khaśas; 10.44c.
Those castes in the world who are born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet [of the primordial man],
whether they speak the language of Mlecchas or the language of Āryas— all of them are recorded as Dasyus.
Those who are known as the base-born (apasadāḥ) of the twice-born, as well as those born of transgression (apadhvaṃsajāḥ),
should subsist by means of those very occupations of the twice-born that are considered censurable.
For Sūtas, the management of horses and chariots; for Ambaṣṭhas, the practice of medicine;
for Vaidehakas, service to women; and for Māgadhas, the way of trade.
The killing of fish is the occupation of Niṣādas, while that of Āyogavas is carpentry;
the killing of wild animals is the occupation of Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.
For the Kṣattṛ, Ugra, and Pukkasa, however, their livelihoods shall be dwelling in holes, killing, and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, working with hides; and for the Veṇas, playing drums.
These known [outcasts], subsisting by their own prescribed duties, shall dwell near sacred trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves.
But for the Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, their dwelling shall be outside the village;
they must be made to use discarded vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Wearing the clothes of the deceased, eating from broken vessels,
having ornaments of black iron, and perpetual wandering are their duties.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them;
their mutual dealings and marriages are only with their own equals.
Their food, dependent on others, should be given to them in a broken vessel;
they must not wander about in villages or towns at night.
They shall move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts;
and they shall carry out a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the settled rule.
They shall always execute those deserving of death by the king's command in accordance with the scriptures;
they shall take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of those condemned to death.
One should discern a man of impure origin who has fallen from his caste, who is unknown,
and who, though appearing noble in form, is actually ignoble by his own actions.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a disposition toward neglecting one's duties—
these reveal in this world a man born of a defiled womb.
He inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or even both;
for one born of a low womb cannot, under any circumstances, suppress his own innate nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth,
that man inevitably adopts the character of that [lineage], whether to a small or great degree.
But where these corrupters of the castes are born through moral decay,
that kingdom, along with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly.
The abandonment of one's body, unconditionally, for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow—
And assisting women and children is the cause of success for those of the outer castes.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of dharma for the four castes.
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with a man of superior caste,
he attains the caste of his superior parent up to the seventh generation.
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise descends to the status of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly how it occurs for those born from a Kṣatriya and likewise from a Vaiśya.
If it should be asked where superiority lies— between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa to a non-Aryan woman,
and one born from a non-Aryan man to a Brāhmaṇa woman— the son born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father would be an Aryan by virtue of his qualities.
Even one born from a non-Aryan father and an Aryan mother is determined to be a non-Aryan; this is the settled rule.
The law is settled that both of these are ineligible for the sacraments:

the former because of the defect of his birth, and the latter because he was born in the inverse order. Just as a good seed sown in good soil comes to fruition, so it is with one born of a high-caste father and a low-caste mother.
Likewise, one born of an Ārya father from an Ārya mother is worthy of all sacramental rites.

Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the settled rule is as follows: Manu 10.70: Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the settled rule is as follows.
Seed sown in a non-field perishes in the very middle;
likewise, a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
Since, by the power of the seed, even those born as animals have become seers (ṛṣis).
Because they are honored and praised, therefore the seed is held in high esteem.
Having considered the non-Aryan who performs Aryan deeds and the Aryan who performs non-Aryan deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Brahmins who abide in the source of the Veda and remain steadfast in their own duty should properly subsist by performing the six duties in their proper order.
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices,
giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.

"In the same way, these [duties] should cease with respect to the Vaiśya; such is the settled rule. For Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them (the Śūdras). Bearing arms and missiles is the duty of the Kṣatriya, while trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture belong to the Vaiśya."
But for the sake of livelihood, the dharma consists of giving, study, and sacrifice.

The study of the Vedas is the specific duty of the Brāhmaṇa, protection is that of the Kṣatriya, and the occupation of trade is that of the Vaiśya; these are the distinguished duties among their respective occupations.
But if a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own occupation as prescribed,
he may live by the duty of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best alternative for him.
If it should happen that he cannot subsist by either of these two,
he may live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing.
But even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which involves much violence and is dependent on others.
They consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is despised by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood [of the plow] destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.
But for one who, due to a lack of livelihood, abandons the perfection of dharma,
this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth, provided that the reserved portion has been set aside.
One should exclude all liquids, as well as cooked food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, domestic animals, and human beings.
All dyed woven cloth, as well as hempen, linen,
and woolen fabrics— even if they are undyed— and likewise fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass.
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and all one-hoofed animals likewise;
having produced these at will through cultivation, the farmer himself may sell them.
A Śūdra may sell sesame seeds that have not been kept for long, provided it is for the sake of dharma.
But if he uses sesame seeds for anything other than eating, anointing, or giving as a gift,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors.
One falls immediately from his caste by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra in three days by selling milk.
But by intentionally selling other commodities here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these [latter] in equal quantities.
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into distress may live by all these means;
however, he must never at any time consider a higher mode of livelihood for himself.
If one who is inferior by birth should, out of greed, live by the occupations of those superior to him,
the king shall strip him of his wealth and banish him immediately.
One's own duty, even if performed imperfectly, is better than the duty of another well-performed;
for by living according to the duty of another, one immediately falls from one's caste.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
however, he should avoid forbidden acts and, when capable, he should desist from such conduct.
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born,
having fallen into distress regarding his sons and wife, may live by the crafts of artisans.
Those occupations of artisans and various crafts by which the twice-born are served when they are practiced; 10.100.
A Brāhmaṇa who remains established on his own path, yet finds himself distressed by a lack of livelihood while unable to subsist through the occupation of a Vaiśya,
should practice this following rule.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that "the purifier becomes defiled" is not logically tenable according to the Dharma.
No fault attaches to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts— even from censurable ones— for they are like fire and water.
One who, having fallen into a situation where life is at stake, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, being famished, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
Vāmadeva, though he was an expert in discerning between dharma and adharma, did not eat dog's flesh even when distressed and desiring to consume it,
for the sake of preserving his life.
But Bharadvāja, the great ascetic, being afflicted by hunger in a desolate forest together with his sons,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra,
who was discerning of dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise from teaching,
for a Brahmin, the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those who have been consecrated;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra or one of the lowest birth.
The sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by silent recitations (japa) and burnt offerings (homa);
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renouncing them and by austerity.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist [by other means] may gather grains from anywhere;
among these, gathering ears of grain (śila) is better than receiving gifts, and gleaning (uñcha) is praised even more than that.
If they are suffering, desiring base metals, or seeking wealth, the lord of the earth should be petitioned by Snātaka Brahmins; however, if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.
From cultivated land, uncultivated land is less blameworthy; likewise for cattle, goats, and sheep;
and among gold, grain, and food, each preceding one is less blameworthy than the following.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, investment, the performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing,
trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury— these are the ten means of livelihood.
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever lend money at interest;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may indeed give a small amount to a person of evil character as one wishes.
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress,
the Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.
Victory is his own duty; he should not turn his back in battle. Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he should collect the lawful tribute from them.
One-eighth of the grain is the tax for the Vaiśyas, and one-twentieth of their profits on merchandise, provided it is at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Śūdras who provide services for work, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [shall be maintained].
But if a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya,
or if a Śūdra wishes to live, he may do so by serving a wealthy Vaiśya.
He should propitiate Brahmins for the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed is his fulfillment of duty.
Service to Brahmins alone is declared to be the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs, that becomes fruitless for him.
They shall provide for his maintenance from their own family resources as is appropriate,
having regard to [the family's] capacity, his skill, and the number of dependents he maintains.
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments,
the shriveled husks of grains, and old household utensils.
There is no sin whatsoever in a Śūdra, nor is he entitled to sacramental rites;
he has no obligation regarding dharma, yet there is no prohibition against dharma for him.
But those who desire righteousness, who know the law, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous—
provided they avoid the sacred mantras— they do not incur sin and they attain praise.
For to the extent that one free from malice adheres to the conduct of the good, [so much does he gain merit].
In that same measure, being blameless, he attains both this world and the next.
Even if he is capable, a Śūdra should not accumulate wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by properly performing them, they attain the highest goal.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rules for expiation (prāyaścitta).
One seeking offspring, one intending to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions,
one seeking wealth for the sake of his teacher, for the sake of his father or mother, one seeking wealth for Vedic study, and one who is afflicted by illness— [these may be supported].
One should indeed not consider those Brāhmaṇas who beg for the sake of dharma as mere Snātakas;
gifts should be given to these [others], who are destitute, according to the excellence of their learning.
For to these foremost of the twice-born, food together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given;
for others, it is said that cooked food is to be given outside the sacrificial altar (bahirvedi).
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas, according to their merit, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice.
If a man who has already taken a wife obtains another wife by begging for her, the fruit of that act is mere sexual pleasure; the offspring, however, belongs to the giver of the wealth.
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins according to one's ability—
upon those who are learned in the Vedas and live in seclusion— and thereby enjoys heaven after death.
He whose food supply for three years is sufficient to maintain his dependents...
Or even if he possesses more wealth, he is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, if a twice-born man drinks Soma when the wealth [required for the sacrifice] is very small,
he does not obtain the fruit of that rite, even though he has previously drunk Soma.
One who is capable of giving to strangers, yet fails to give to his own kin who live in misery—
that counterfeit dharma has a taste like honey at first, but is poison in its effect.
Whatever funeral rite one performs by causing distress to one's dependents results in unhappiness both for the living and for the deceased.
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by the absence of even one component—
especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa, provided that a righteous king is in power— then [he must perform a penance].
If there be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of completing a sacrifice.
He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for the Śūdra has no entitlement whatsoever to sacrifices.

He who possesses a hundred cows but has not established the sacred fires, and he who possesses a thousand cows but has not performed sacrifices— from the households of even these two, one may take [food] without hesitation.
And from a creditor who is constantly intent on collecting but refuses to pay, one may take [the debt] by force;
in this way, his fame spreads and his merit increases.
Likewise, having fasted for six meals, one may take food at the seventh mealtime from a person of inferior conduct, provided that one does not store food for the morrow.
Whether it is from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever else it may be found,
if he asks, that [stolen property] must be reported to him who inquires.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, if he is unable to subsist, he may take the property of a Dasyu or of one who neglects his religious duties.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and carries both of them across.
The wise know that the wealth of those who are devoted to sacrifice is the property of the gods;
however, the wealth of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of the asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth must not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger.

Having ascertained the number of his dependents, the lord of the earth should determine a righteous means of subsistence for them from his own household, after having examined their learning and character.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from that protected man, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit of dharma.
A Brahmin should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for by begging for it, a sacrificer is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
If a Brahmin, having begged wealth for the purpose of a sacrifice, does not give it all away,
he shall become a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of a Brāhmaṇa—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world upon the leavings of vultures.

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice for the purpose of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.
If a twice-born man performs a duty according to the rule for times of distress when he is not in distress,
it has been determined that he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter.
By the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great Ṛṣis,
fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the prescribed rule was established.
He who, though capable of following the primary rule,
conducts himself according to the secondary rule, for that person of evil intellect there exists no fruit pertaining to the next world.
A Brāhmaṇa who knows the law should not report anything to the king;
he should discipline those offending men by his own power alone.
One's own power is more effective than the power of a king;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own power alone.
One should employ the Atharva-Angirasa hymns without hesitation;
for the weapon of a Brahmin is indeed speech, and with that, the twice-born man shall slay his enemies.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own adversity by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by wealth; but the best of the twice-born by silent recitation and burnt offerings.
The Brāhmaṇa is called the ordainer, the punisher, the teacher, and the friend;
one should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool,
nor likewise one who is afflicted or unconsecrated, shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*.
For these fall into hell, as does he for whom they perform the sacrifice while offering oblations;
therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, fails to give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he remains one who has not established the fires. *Manu 11.38* [37ma]–[37mc]
One who is faithful and has conquered his senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, he should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with small sacrificial fees destroys the senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires becomes liable to perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra fire—
these are the officiating priests of Śūdras, and they are censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
By treading with his foot upon the heads of those who constantly serve Śūdras and fires while remaining ignorant [of the sacred law], the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and is addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to penance. The wise know that when a sin has been committed unintentionally, penance is required.
Some say that this applies even when committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scripture (śruti).
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of penances.
Having incurred the necessity of penance, whether by fate or by his own past actions,
a twice-born man must not associate with the virtuous until that penance has been performed.
In this world, some wicked-souled men undergo a transformation of their appearance due to evil conduct in this life, while others do so because of deeds performed in previous lives.
A thief of gold [incurs] deformed nails; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
A slanderer shall have a foul-smelling nose; a backbiter, a foul-smelling mouth;
a thief of grain, a deficiency of limbs; and one who adulterates goods, an excess of limbs.
The stealer of food becomes afflicted with disease; the stealer of speech becomes mute;
the stealer of clothing suffers from leucoderma; and the stealer of horses becomes lame.
Thus, by reason of specific actions, they are born despised by the virtuous—
dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.
Therefore, an expiation must always be performed for the sake of purification;
for those whose sins have not been atoned for are born endowed with censurable physical marks.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher's wife—
these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them.
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, slander directed at the king,
and persistent malice toward one's teacher are equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Abandoning the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food,
and eating what is censured— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as [the theft] of men, horses, and silver, and of land,
diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.
They consider the emission of semen into women of one's own womb, into virgins, into women of the lowest castes,
and into the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the bed of a guru.

Killing a cow, officiating at a sacrifice for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, selling oneself, abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, sacred study, the sacred fires, or one's son; [these are minor sins].

The state of being a *parivitti* when a younger brother has not yet married, as well as the act of *parivedana* (giving away a daughter in marriage to such a man), the giving of a maiden to those two, and officiating at a sacrifice for them; [these are grounds for loss of caste].
Defiling a maiden, usury, the violation of a vow,
and the sale of a tank, a grove, one's wife, or a child.
Becoming a *vrātya*, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for wages,
receiving instruction for wages, selling goods that ought not to be sold,
exercising authority over all forms of labor, and operating large-scale mechanical works.
Injuring medicinal plants, living off women, malevolent incantations, and magical rites using roots.
Felling green trees for the sake of fuel, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating forbidden food; [these are acts that cause one to fall].
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts,
studying heterodox scriptures, and engaging in the performance of arts for pleasure.

The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the drinking of intoxicants and consorting with forbidden women; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute minor offenses (upapātaka).
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or intoxicants,
crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are declared to be acts that cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats and sheep,
and likewise of fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as an act that causes loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from censurable persons, trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths are to be known as acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa).
The killing of worms, insects, and birds; eating food mixed with liquor;
stealing fruits, firewood, and flowers; and lack of fortitude—these are defiling acts.
Now, learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins, each individually, are expiated.
A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having built a hut,
subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
Or, by his own will, he may become a target for those who bear weapons, provided they are learned;
or he may throw himself headlong three times into a blazing fire.
Or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or else with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or, for the removal of the sin of killing a Brahmin, he may travel one hundred *yojanas* while reciting one of the Vedas, eating moderately and with his senses restrained.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas;
for wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings, [is what should be given].
Or, eating sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī river against its current;
or, with his diet restricted, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village or even in a cow-pen,
or in a hermitage or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow, one should immediately sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or of a Brāhmaṇa is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.

Or by resisting him three times, or by recovering all his property, or if the Brahmin’s life is saved on that account, he is released from the debt. Thus, one who is always firm in his vow, a celibate student (brahmacārī), and composed in mind—
When the twelfth year is completed, he removes the guilt of killing a Brahmin.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods on earth (the Brahmins) in an assembly of kings,
he is liberated from it after bathing at the *avabhṛtha* rite of a horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Kṣatriya its summit;
therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified.
By his very birth from Brahmā, he is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā alone is the cause in this matter.

Regarding them, even three who know the Veda should declare the means for the complete expiation of their sin; that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying. Therefore, having adopted one of these rules, a Brahmin, being composed, [should proceed].
By means of self-control, he removes the sin committed through the killing of a Brahmin.
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this same vow; as also for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who has performed a sacrifice, or a woman of the Ātreya clan.
Having given false testimony, likewise having obstructed a teacher,
having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend—
this purification has been declared for having unintentionally killed a twice-born man.
For the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no expiation is ordained.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks *surā*, he should drink *surā* that is glowing like fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he may drink cow’s urine the color of fire, or water;
or milk, ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung until death.
Or he may eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing garments of hair, with matted locks, and carrying a flag, in order to remove the sin of drinking liquor.
Wine is indeed the impurity of foods, and it is called the impurity of sin;
therefore, the Brāhmaṇa, the Rājanya, and the Vaiśya shall not drink wine.
Sura is to be known as threefold: that distilled from molasses, that made from flour, and that from honey.
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
The food of Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas, as well as intoxicants, meat, and spirituous liquors—
these must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation for the gods.
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might even recite Vedic texts; or, deluded by intoxication, he might perform some other forbidden act.
He whose Veda, residing within his body, is once defiled by liquor— his Brahminhood departs and he falls into the state of a Śūdra.
This expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared in its various forms;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, shall proclaim his own deed and say: "May your majesty punish me."
Having seized a club, the king himself shall strike him once.
A thief is purified by execution, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove by austerity the impurity born of stealing gold,
shall wear clothes of bark and perform in the forest the penance prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin.
By these vows, a twice-born man may expiate the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall remove the sin of approaching the teacher’s wife by means of these following vows.
Having committed the sin of violating the Guru’s bed, he should lie upon a heated iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing metal image (sūrmī), for by death he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, he should proceed.
He should proceed toward the direction of Nirṛti, walking straight until he falls down.
Carrying a staff topped with a skull, clothed in rags, or with his beard grown, he should dwell in a lonely forest and,
with a concentrated mind, perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley-gruel (yavāgū), in order to remove the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
By these penances, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their taint;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows.
One who has killed a cow and is thus afflicted by a minor offense (upapātaka) shall drink barley-gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
He should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime;
for two months, with his senses restrained, he should perform his bath using cow urine.
During the day he should follow the cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust raised by them.
Having performed service and paid homage, he should remain in the *vīrāsana* posture at night.
He should stand when they stand and follow them when they walk.
Likewise, sitting while they are seated, self-controlled and free from envy, he should offer the water.

One should rescue by every possible means a woman who is ill, or one accused [of adultery], or one threatened by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one fallen [into a pit], or one stuck in the mud— even at the cost of all one’s life. Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, [one should protect her].
One should not seek one's own protection without first having done what is possible for the sake of the cow.
Whether in one's own house or in the house of others, whether in a field or in a threshing floor,
one should not speak of a cow that is eating, nor of a calf that is drinking.
But he who, as a killer of a cow, follows a cow according to this rule,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
Having successfully completed the vow, he should give ten cows and one bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) shall perform this very same vow for the sake of purification, with the exception of the student who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), or else they may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. But the student who has broken his vow of chastity shall, at a crossroads, [sacrifice] a one-eyed donkey.
One should worship Nirṛti at night according to the procedure for the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
Having offered the oblations into the fire according to the rules with the verse beginning "Then indeed" (*samaḥ*),
he should finally offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Agni.
The knowers of dharma, the exponents of the Veda, declare that for a twice-born man observing a vow, the intentional emission of semen constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The four— Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka—
approach the Vedic splendor of the student who has broken his vow.
When this sin has been incurred, having clothed himself in the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.

Subsisting on alms obtained from them for a single meal a day, and performing ritual ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified after one year. Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, [he must perform this penance].
If he does so unintentionally, he shall perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra or the Prājāpatya penance.
For acts that cause the mixture of castes or render one unworthy of receiving gifts, the purification is the Aindava (moon-fast) for one month;
for acts that cause defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
A fourth part of the penalty for killing a Brāhmaṇa is prescribed for the killing of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, and a sixteenth part should be known for a Śūdra.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having properly observed his vow, shall give a thousand cows and one bull.
Or, with his hair matted and self-restrained, he may perform for three years the vow prescribed for the slayer of a Brahmin,
dwelling far away from the village and making his abode at the foot of a tree.

The best of the twice-born, having killed a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, shall perform this very same penance for one year and give one hundred and one cows. A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months.
Or he may give ten white cows and one bull to a Brahmin.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog,
as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Or he may drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana* on the road;
or he may perform ablutions in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the Waters (*ab-daivata*).
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
having killed a eunuch, he should give a load of straw and one māṣaka of lead.
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a crane, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or a peacock,
as well as a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for an elephant, five dark-blue bulls;
and for having killed a goat, a sheep, an ox, or a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
having killed non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; and having killed a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
For having killed women of the four castes who were not virtuous, one should give, for the sake of purification, a worn-out bow, a goat, and a sheep respectively.
If a twice-born man is unable to atone for the killing of snakes and other such creatures by means of giving gifts,
he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate creatures,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
But for killing animals with bones, one should give something small to a Brahmin;
indeed, for injuring boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
But for cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred *ṛc* verses are to be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering vines.
For all beings born from food,
born from moisture, and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the means of purification.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
By these observances, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the rules] regarding the eating of forbidden food.

Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite alone; but if it was done intentionally, the penance is indeterminate, for the settled rule is that it ends only with life.
Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a vessel for other intoxicants,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rule,
and having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
But a Brāhmaṇa who drinks Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes pure by performing three suppressions of the breath in water and consuming clarified butter.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
Having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, as well as the leavings of women or Śūdras,
and having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Even after drinking fermented liquids or astringent decoctions, though they be pure,
a twice-born man remains impure as long as that liquid has not passed downward.
Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth,
or any unknown meat found in a slaughterhouse, one should perform this very same penance.
Upon eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks,
as well as humans, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher's house eats food belonging to a monthly śrāddha,
he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day.
But a religious student (brahmacārī) who should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever,
having performed the ordinary Kṛcchra penance, shall complete the remainder of his vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog,
or a mongoose, or food into which hair or insects have fallen, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.

One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit to be eaten. However, if it has been consumed unknowingly, it must be expelled from the body or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites.
This various rule for penances regarding the eating of forbidden food has been declared;
now hear the rule for those penances that remove the guilt of theft.

Having intentionally committed thefts of grain, cooked food, or wealth from the house of a member of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
But for the abduction of human beings, women, fields, and houses,
as well as for [the theft of] water from wells and tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the purification.
Having committed theft of articles of little value from another's house,
one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance after returning those goods for the sake of self-purification.
For the theft of edible and consumable foods, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats, and for flowers,
roots, and fruits, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, and molasses;
for clothing, skins, and meat; there shall be a fast of three nights.
For jewels, pearls, corals, copper, and silver; [the same applies].
And for iron, bronze, and stone [vessels], one should subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For cotton, silk, wool, animals with cloven hooves,
and those with solid hooves, as well as for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk alone for three days.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he shall expel the sin of approaching a woman who should not be approached by means of these same vows.

Having discharged semen into women who are his own uterine sisters, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, one must perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
Having approached a daughter of his father’s sister, a daughter of his mother’s sister,
or a daughter of his mother’s brother— having approached these, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. A wise man, however, should not take any of these three as a wife.
One should not approach those [women] as kin; for by approaching them, one falls low.
If a man discharges semen into non-human females, into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper source [of offspring],
or even into water, he shall perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance.
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a male or a female,
a twice-born man shall perform a bath along with his clothes in a cow-cart, in water, or during the day.

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or other lowest castes, or having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes their equal.
A husband shall confine a wife who has become seriously corrupted in a single room;
he shall compel her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.
If she, however, should become corrupt again when enticed by a man of equal status,
then the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years.
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who associate with the outcastes.
By associating with an outcast for a year, one becomes an outcast;
[this occurs] through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or [forming] a matrimonial alliance, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
Whichever among these outcasts a man associates with,
he must perform that very same penance for the sake of purification from that association.
The sapinda relatives and kinsmen should perform the water-libation for one who has become an outcast (patita) outside the village on an inauspicious day,
in the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.
A female slave shall overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
they, together with their kinsmen, shall observe impurity for a day and a night.
Therefore, they should desist from conversing with him, sitting together on the same seat,
giving him an inheritance, and even engaging in ordinary worldly dealings.
Seniority shall cease, as well as the wealth that is acquired by virtue of being the eldest;
however, a younger brother who is superior in merit shall receive the share of the eldest.
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe and together with him alone cast a new pitcher full of water into a sacred body of water.
Having cast that jar into the waters and entered his own home,
he should perform all the rites for his kinsmen as before.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they must live near the house.
One should not engage in any transaction with those who have committed sins and have not been purified; yet, once they have performed the rites of purification, one should never despise them.
This includes even those who have killed children or are ungrateful, provided they have been purified according to the law.
One should not dwell with those who kill one who has sought refuge, nor with those who kill a woman.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
But for those twice-born men who, engaged in improper acts and abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform penance—
for them also one should prescribe this very same [penance].
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation,
they become purified by relinquishing it, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity.
Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
When he has returned from the cow-pen, emaciated by fasting and bowing down, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (Manu 11.195).
But having spoken the truth before Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for cows;
when the ford has been made accessible by the cows, they should perform his funeral rites.
Having performed the sacrifice for Vratyas, the funeral rites for others,
malevolent magic, or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes that taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Having abandoned one who has come for refuge, or having allowed the Veda to be lost,
a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One bitten by dogs, jackals, or donkeys, or by domestic carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or boars, becomes pure through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Eating only at every sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the *Saṃhitā*,
as well as the daily performance of all the *Śākala* oblations, are the means of purification for those unworthy of sitting in the company at a meal (*apāṅktya*).
Having intentionally mounted a vehicle drawn by camels or a vehicle drawn by donkeys, [one must perform the same penance].
But having bathed, a Brahmin who is naked becomes pure by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Whether without water or even in the midst of water, if one is distressed and has discharged bodily excrement, he becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on, touching a cow, and then performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Upon the omission of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.

Having uttered the sound "huṃ" to a Brāhmaṇa, or having addressed one who is superior with the word "thou," he shall bathe and spend the remainder of the day without eating, and then seek forgiveness by offering salutations.
Having struck her even with a blade of grass, or having bound her by the neck with a garment,
or having defeated her in a dispute, he should propitiate her by prostrating himself.
Having merely threatened a Brāhmaṇa, one enters hell for a hundred years; having struck him, for a thousand years; and by the mere intent to kill a Brāhmaṇa, one likewise falls into hell.

As many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth, for so many thousands of years shall the shedder of that blood dwell in hell. Having merely threatened [to strike], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; if he actually strikes, he should perform the *atikṛcchra*.
Having caused the blood of a Brāhmaṇa to flow, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances.
But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been specified,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
I shall describe to you those means by which a human being removes his sins— means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors.
For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should eat food obtained unasked;
for the final three days he should not eat at all—this is the Prājāpatya penance performed by a twice-born man.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a one-night fast, is declared to be the *Sāṃtapanakṛccha*.
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat only a single mouthful for three periods of three days each, as previously described,
and should fast during the final three days.
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind.
For one who has controlled the self and is vigilant, fasting for twelve days is the penance known as Parāka;
it removes all sins.
One should decrease the rice-ball by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three times of the day, this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, being self-restrained and beginning with the bright fortnight, should observe this entire rule in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama (barley-middled) form.
Restraining his self and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached midday.
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning;
when the sun has set, he should eat four more. This is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, three hundred and sixty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever over the course of a month, one attains the same world as the Moon.
The Rudras, as well as the Ādityas,
the Vasus, and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
Every day, he himself should perform the fire-oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
he should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
Three times during the day and three times during the night, he should enter the water while still wearing his clothes;
furthermore, he must never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
If he is unable [to fast], he should pass his time by standing and sitting; or he may sleep on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of his vows, and he should worship his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
He should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to his ability;
likewise, in all vows, he should be diligent for the sake of expiation. By these observances, the twice-born whose sins have been made public are to be purified;
however, those whose sins are not public, he should purify with mantras and burnt offerings.
By confession, by repentance, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the evildoer is released from sin.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act,
confesses it, to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
To the extent that his mind reproaches his evil deed,
to that same extent his body is released from that unrighteousness.
For having committed a sin, one is indeed released from that sin by feeling remorse;
however, he is purified even more by the resolve, "I shall not do this again," through such abstention.
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the emergence of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform auspicious deeds through his mind, speech, and body.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable act,
one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time.
In whatever action he has performed that causes unease in his mind,
he should perform penance for it until it brings him satisfaction.
All this happiness, whether pertaining to gods or humans, has austerity as its root;
it has been declared by the wise who perceive the Vedas that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.
For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge; for a Kṣatriya, austerity is protection;
for a Vaiśya, austerity is agriculture and trade; and for a Śūdra, austerity is service.
Sages who have restrained their selves and subsist on fruits, roots,
and air perceive the three worlds, with all that is moving and unmoving, through austerity alone.
Medicinal herbs, antidotes, knowledge, and the various states of divine power—all these are accomplished through austerity alone; for austerity is their means of realization.

Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish— all that can be achieved through austerity (*tapas*), for austerity is indeed hard to surpass. Even those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*) and others who have performed forbidden acts, [are purified by it].
By means of well-performed austerity alone, they are liberated from that sin.
Insects, snakes, moths, domestic animals, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.
Whatever sin people commit through thought, word,
or deed, those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone.
For a Brāhmaṇa who has been purified by austerity alone,
the inhabitants of heaven accept his sacrifices and increase his desires.
The Lord Prajāpati created this treatise through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity.
The gods proclaim this to be the great majesty of austerity (tapas),
perceiving the supreme merit arising from all this austerity.
The daily study of the Veda according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices, and forbearance— *Manu 11.245a*.
They quickly destroy even those sins born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka).
Just as fire, having reached fuel, consumes it in an instant with its brilliance,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil by the fire of knowledge.
Thus has the expiation for these sins been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret offenses.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the syllable Om,
performed day after day, purify even the killer of an embryo within a month.
By reciting the *kautsa* hymn beginning with "apa," the verse of Vasiṣṭha beginning with "prati," the *māhitra*,
and the *śuddhavatī* verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
Having stolen gold, one becomes stainless in an instant by reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasankalpa hymns just once.
By reciting the *Haviṣpāntīya* and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and by muttering the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the preceptor’s bed is released from that sin.
Desiring the removal of both gross and subtle offenses, [one should perform these rites].
For one year, he should mutter the verse beginning with "ava" (RV 8.75.14), or else the verse beginning with "yat kiṃ cedam" (RV 10.16.6).
Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
But one who has committed many offenses becomes purified by performing the *somāraudra* rite for a month,
while practicing bathing in a flowing river and reciting the three verses beginning with "aryamṇām."
One who has committed these seven offenses should mutter the hymn beginning with "Indra" for half a year;
however, having performed a censurable act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.
Having offered clarified butter for a year with the *śākala* oblation mantras, a twice-born man destroys even a very heavy sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namaḥ."
One who has been joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by reciting the Pāvamānī verses for a year and subsisting on alms-food, he becomes purified.
Or, having purified himself by three *parāka* penances, he who, being self-restrained, recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest is released from all sins.
But by fasting for three days, remaining self-controlled, and bathing in water three times a day,
he is released from all sins after reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
Even if he has destroyed these three worlds and eats food from anywhere at all,
a Brahmin who retains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
Having recited the *Ṛksaṃhitā* three times, or the *Yajus* with a concentrated mind,
or the *Sāmans* together with their secret doctrines (*rahasya*), one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does every evil deed sink away when one is immersed in the threefold Veda.
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and various other Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
That which is the primordial three-syllabled Brahman, in which the triple Veda is established— that other secret threefold Veda, he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
O sinless one, you have fully declared this entire dharma of the four castes;
now tell us truly the supreme accomplishment of the fruits of actions.
The righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this application of ritual action."
Action arising from mind, speech, and body bears fruit that is auspicious or inauspicious;
the destinies of living beings, whether superior, inferior, or middling, are born of action.
Of that embodied being here, who is of three kinds, has three bases,
and is endowed with ten characteristics, one should know the mind to be the instigator.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable in one's mind,
and adherence to false doctrines— this threefold action is mental.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form,
and incoherent prattle— this constitutes the fourfold sin of speech.
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the prescribed rules,
and adultery with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [sin].
This person experiences the mental [karma], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind alone;
the karma performed by speech through speech, and that which is physical through the body alone.
Through defects of action arising from the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, he becomes a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, he attains birth among the lowest castes.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a "tridaṇḍin" (one who possesses the triple staff).

Having cast aside this triple staff among all living beings and having thoroughly restrained desire and anger, a human being then attains perfection. They call him the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) who is the director of this self.
But he who performs actions is called the "soul of beings" (bhūtātman) by the wise.
There is another internal self, distinct [from the body], known as the *jīva*, which is innate to all embodied beings;
it is by means of this that one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.
Both of these—the Great One (mahat) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they abide pervading that which exists within high and low beings.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.
For men who have committed evil deeds, after death, another body certainly arises from those very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment.
Having experienced those torments of Yama with this very body, they dissolve,
part by part, back into those same elemental constituents.
Having experienced the misfortunes arising from attachment to sense objects, which result in future unhappiness, he,
freed from all taints, returns to those very two who possess great splendor.
Vigilant, they both behold the merit and the sin of that man together;
through these two, being united with them, he attains happiness or unhappiness both in this world and after death.
If he practices dharma for the most part and adharma only to a small degree, then,
enveloped by those very elements, he enjoys happiness in heaven.
But if he mostly practices unrighteousness and only rarely practices righteousness,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmya realm, that living being, freed from impurity,
returns once more to those very five elements, part by part.

Having observed these destinies of this living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— he should always fix his mind upon righteousness.
One should know that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are the three qualities (*guṇa*) of the Self (*ātman*),
by which the Great One (*mahat*), pervading all these states of being, remains present without exception.
Whenever one of these qualities is preeminent throughout the body,
it then makes that embodied being consist predominantly of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is traditionally held to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive form, which rests within all beings.
In that regard, whatever one perceives within oneself as conjoined with pleasure,
tranquil and possessing a pure luster— that one should understand to be *sattva*.

But that which is joined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know that to be *rajas*, which is constantly carrying away embodied beings against their will. And that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, and characterized by sense objects—
One should understand that to be darkness (tamas), which is inconceivable and unknowable.
I shall now declare in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— the highest, the middling, and the lowest.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of dharma,
and contemplation of the self— these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva.
Delight in undertaking [new projects], lack of fortitude, engagement in improper actions,
and constant indulgence in the objects of the senses— these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Greed, excessive sleep, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct,
a habit of begging, and negligence— these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Of these three qualities, which abide in the three [states],
this should be known as the summary definition of their characteristics in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when intending to do it—
that should be known by the wise as entirely characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
and does not grieve over failure, should be known as *rājasa*.
That which one desires to know with one's whole being, that which one does not feel shame in practicing,
and that by which one’s own self is satisfied— this is the characteristic of the quality of *sattva*.
Lust is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
righteousness is the characteristic of *sattva*. Their superiority follows this respective order.
I shall now briefly describe, in their proper order, the transmigrations that each of these beings undergoes according to their respective qualities.
Those characterized by *sattva* attain the state of gods; those characterized by *rajas*, the state of humans;
and those characterized by *tamas* always attain the state of animals—such is this threefold destiny.
This secondary course of existence is to be understood as threefold and each of those threefold again—
namely, low, middling, and superior— according to the distinction of one's actions and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts— these constitute the lowest state of darkness.
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling Tāmasa state.
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men,
as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas— this is the highest destination among those born of tamas.
Jhallas, mallas, and naṭas, as well as men who live by the sword,
those addicted to gambling and drinking, and those of the lowest sort— this is the rājasa destiny.
Kings, Kṣatriyas, the domestic priests of kings,
and those whose primary activities are debate and warfare— this is the intermediate Rājasī state.
Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases— this is the highest destination among those born of the rājasa quality.
Ascetics, renunciants, Brahmins, and the classes of Vaimānika deities,
as well as the lunar mansions and the Daityas— this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries,
the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second, sattvic goal.
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—
these the wise call the highest Sāttvika state.
Thus has been fully described the entire threefold nature of action;
the whole transmigratory existence, consisting of all living beings, is likewise threefold and of three kinds.
Through attachment to the senses and by failing to practice dharma,
the ignorant and lowest of men go to sinful transmigrations.
Learn now all those various wombs into which this living soul enters in this world, one after another, according to its specific actions.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, upon the exhaustion of that [karma],
those who have committed mortal sins enter these transmigrations.
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, a camel, a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, a bird, a Caṇḍāla, or a Pukkasa.
A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, venomous snakes, birds, and predatory beasts.
A Brahmin who is a thief [incurs the same fate] thousands of times for killing spiders, snakes, lizards, other crawling creatures that move in water, and predatory Piśācas.
The violator of the Guru’s bed becomes, by hundreds of births, a grass, a shrub, a creeper, a carnivorous animal, a fanged beast, or even one who performs cruel deeds.

After death, those who eat the food of the impure become carnivorous beasts; thieves become creatures that devour one another; and those who have sexual intercourse with women of the lowest castes become worms.
Having had sexual intercourse with outcasts, having approached another man's wife,
and having stolen the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa.
Having stolen jewels, pearls, and corals, or various other gems, out of greed, a man is born among the workers in gold.
By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl;
by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing savory juices, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [becomes] meat, a cormorant fat, a "tail-eater" bird oil,
a cricket salt, and a crane curd.
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge; having stolen linen, a frog;
having stolen woven cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, an iguana; and having stolen molasses, a rat.
The muskrat [destroys] auspicious fragrances; the peacock, leafy vegetables;
the porcupine, various kinds of prepared food; and the pangolin, unprepared food.
Having stolen fire, one becomes a crane; having stolen household utensils, one becomes a *gṛhakārī* (house-builder);
and having stolen dyed garments, one is born as a *jīvajīvaka* bird.
A wolf [destroys] a deer, a tiger a horse, and a monkey fruit and roots;
a bear [destroys] a woman, a chataka bird water, a camel vehicles, and a goat livestock.
Whatever another's property it may be, having forcibly seized it,
a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal, as does one who has consumed an oblation that was not consecrated by fire.
Women also, by stealing according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives to these very same creatures.
For when the social classes (*varṇas*) fall away from their respective duties during times of non-distress,
they pass through miserable transmigrations and fall into servitude under their enemies.
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own duty becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha, who eats vomit.
A Kṣatriya who eats impure things and corpses becomes a Kaṭapūtana;
a Vaiśya becomes a Maitrākṣajyotika preta that feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a Cailāśaka.
To the extent that those whose nature is directed toward sense-objects indulge in sense-objects,
to that same extent skillfulness in them arises for them.
Due to the habitual practice of those sinful deeds, those of small intellect encounter various sufferings here in these respective wombs.
They experience tossing about in the terrible hells such as Tāmisra,
as well as the forests of sword-leaves and other forms of bondage and mutilation.
Various kinds of torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand and grit, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he undergoes births in various wombs that are mostly full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears.
Repeated dwelling in the womb and dreadful births;
various forms of imprisonment and servitude to others;
