separation from kinsmen and loved ones, and living together with wicked people.
The acquisition of wealth and its loss, as well as the gaining of friends and enemies.
And likewise, old age which is without remedy, the torment of various diseases,
those manifold sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
With whatever disposition one performs each particular action,
with a body of that same nature one experiences its respective fruit.
This entire arising of the fruits of actions has been declared to you;
now learn this action which brings about the supreme good for a Brahmin.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
Among all these auspicious actions prescribed here for a person, some are said to be more conducive to spiritual welfare than others. Yet,
among all of these, the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna) is traditionally held to be supreme.
For that is the foremost of all branches of knowledge, for through it immortality is attained.
Of all these six types of actions, both after death and in this world,
the Vedic rite is always to be known as the most conducive to spiritual welfare.
But in the application of Vedic rites, all these [duties] without exception are included,
respectively, within each specific rule of action.

Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the path of active engagement and the path of withdrawal.

Action performed with a desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is designated as *pravṛtta* (active); however, action free from desire, preceded by knowledge, is taught as *nivṛtta* (withdrawn).
By practicing active worldly action (*pravṛtta-karma*), one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renunciation (*nivṛtta-karma*), one indeed transcends the five elements.
Seeing himself in all beings and all beings in himself, he who performs the sacrifice of the self (*ātmayājī*), beholding them all as equal, attains sovereign rule (*svārājya*).
Even having abandoned the duties as they have been prescribed, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, in tranquility, and in the study of the Veda.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
having attained this, the twice-born becomes one who has accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is impossible to master and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture.
Those legal codes that are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all of these are fruitless after death, for they are declared to result in darkness.
Whatever other things there may be that arise from this and then pass away,
they are fruitless and false because they are merely of recent origin.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four distinct stages of life—
whatever has been, is, and will be— all this is established from the Veda.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
They are produced from the Veda alone; their birth is according to their qualities and actions.
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of this living being.
The command of an army, sovereignty, the office of a judge,
and even lordship over the entire world— these a knower of the Vedic scriptures deserves.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does one who knows the Veda burn away the defects born of his own actions.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whichever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

Those who merely memorize the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely memorize; those who possess true knowledge are superior to those who merely retain the texts; and those who act upon that knowledge are the best of all.
Austerity and sacred knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity he destroys sin, and by knowledge he attains immortality.
Perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions—
these three must be well understood by one who desires purity in dharma.
He who examines the instruction on dharma given by the Ṛṣis through reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows dharma, and no other.
This action leading to the supreme good has been declared in its entirety as prescribed. Now, the secret doctrine of this treatise of Manu is being taught.
If it should be asked, "How should one act regarding those duties not mentioned in the revealed scriptures? [the answer follows].
Whatever learned Brāhmaṇas declare, that shall be the Dharma, free from doubt.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired through righteous means—
they are to be known as cultured *brāhmaṇas*, who are the direct authorities for the revealed scripture.
An assembly of at least ten, or even three, who are established in virtuous conduct, shall determine the law; that law they must not set aside.
One learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the three [members] belonging to the first stages of life— this assembly shall consist of at least ten members.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this assembly of at least three persons is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts regarding dharma.

Even if he is alone, whatever dharma a most excellent twice-born man who knows the Veda determines, that should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not [the dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of the ignorant.
Even if they have gathered by the thousands, those who lack vows, who lack sacred mantras, and who subsist merely on their caste— among them, the status of an assembly is not found.
That which ignorant fools, being shrouded in darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, proclaim as such—
having become a hundredfold, that sin follows after those who speak it.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has declared to me all this, the supreme secret of dharma.
Composed in meditation, one should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within oneself;
for by perceiving everything within oneself, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The Self alone is all the deities; everything is established in the Self.
For it is the self that produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
One should dissolve space into the cavities, wind into movement and touch,
the supreme fire into digestion and sight, water into moisture, and earth into solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the stride, Hara in the strength,
Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle,
possessing the luster of gold, and accessible through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati;
some call him Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with his five forms,
he perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
"He who thus perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self, having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state. Thus,
the twice-born man who recites this teaching of Manu, proclaimed by Bhṛgu,"
By being constantly possessed of right conduct, he shall attain his desired goal.
[The Mānava Dharmaśāstra is completed. End of the Manu-Smṛti (plain text).

Having honored him according to the rule, they spoke these words.
O Blessed One, you ought to speak to us of the duties of all the social classes, as well as those born of intermediate castes, in their proper order and according to the truth.
For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Being thus duly questioned by those high-souled ones of immeasurable luster,
he honored all those great seers and replied, "Listen."
In the beginning, this universe was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, devoid of distinguishing marks, beyond the reach of logic, unknowable, as if entirely asleep.
Then the Lord Svayambhū, the unmanifest,
dispelling darkness and possessing great vital power, appeared, making manifest this world beginning with the great elements.
He who is perceivable by those beyond the senses, subtle, unmanifest, eternal,
consisting of all beings, and inconceivable— he himself appeared of his own accord.
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from his own body, he first created the waters alone;
into them he cast his seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The waters are called "nara," for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his primordial abode, he is therefore known as Nārāyaṇa.
That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of both being and non-being—
from that was that Puruṣa emitted, who is celebrated in the world as Brahmā.
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditation, divided that egg into two parts.
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the sky, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
And from himself he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the lord who is the conceiving subject.
And he [perceived] the Great Self, all the three qualities,
and the five sense organs which gradually grasp the objects of the senses.
But having combined the subtle constituent parts of those six [great elements], each possessing immeasurable power,
with portions of his own self, he fashioned all beings.
The six subtle components of form resort to these;
therefore, the wise call that form of his the "body" (śarīra).
Then the great elements, together with their functions, enter that imperishable creator of all beings, along with the mind and its subtle components.
From the subtle constituent particles of form of these seven highly energetic persons, this perishable world arises from the imperishable.
But among these, each subsequent one acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.
But at the beginning, he fashioned the individual names, the specific functions, and the distinct social orders of all beings from the words of the Veda itself.
And that Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings,
the subtle host of Sādhyas, and the eternal sacrifice.
From fire, wind, and the sun, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of accomplishing sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets;
the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and both the level and the uneven terrain.
Desiring to bring these creatures into existence, he created this creation— namely austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger.
And for the sake of distinguishing actions, he separated merit and demerit;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain.
Those minute, perishable particles which are said to constitute the five elements—
along with these, this entire universe comes into being in successive order.
Whatever action the Lord first assigned to each being,
that very same action it performed spontaneously, as it was created again and again.
In the creation, whatever— whether violent or non-violent, mild or cruel, dharma or adharma, truth or falsehood— the Lord assigned to each being, that entered into it of its own accord.
Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, spontaneously assume their respective seasonal characteristics, so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Dividing his own body into two parts, he became male with one half and female with the other; with her, the Lord created Virāj.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj, the Supreme Person, whom he himself created after performing austerities; I am the creator of all this.
Desiring to create living beings, however, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers, the lords of creatures.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.
These seven Manus of immense splendor created the gods,
the hosts of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power.
And [he created] the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras;
the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas; and the various classes of Pitṛs.
Lightnings, thunderclouds, and red clouds; rainbows of Indra; meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and various celestial lights of diverse kinds.
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and fanged predators.
And worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings.
Thus, by my command, all this— both the stationary and the moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of austerity, each according to their respective karma.
But whatever kind of karma has been proclaimed here for these beings,
that I shall describe to you accordingly, as well as the sequence of their births.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous animals with two rows of teeth;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans—these are born from the womb.
Birds born from eggs, serpents, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises—
whatever other such kinds there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic.
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from sweat;
and whatever else is of this kind arises from heat.

All stationary beings that sprout from the soil are called *udbhijja*; those that grow from seeds or slips are plants (*oṣadhi*), which bear many flowers and fruits and perish at the ripening of their fruit.
Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as *vanaspatis*;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as *vṛkṣas*.
Likewise, there are various kinds of clusters and shrubs, as well as species of grasses,
those that grow from seeds and from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines.
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by their past actions,
these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain.
But these destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is eternal and in constant flux.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew into himself, subduing time with time.
When that God is awake, the world thus moves;
when he sleeps with his soul at peace, then everything closes its eyes.
While that self remains in a state of restful sleep, the embodied beings whose nature is action cease their activities,
and the mind falls into a state of exhaustion.
But when they dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self,
then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and at peace.
But having resorted to this darkness, he remains for a long time endowed with the senses;
yet he does not perform his own functions, and then he departs from the body.
When, having become minute as an atom, it enters, conjoined with it, the seed— whether stationary or moving— then it assumes a physical form.
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that imperishable one perpetually brings to life and causes the destruction of all this world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having composed this treatise himself, he first caused me alone to receive it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, taught it to Marīci and the other sages.
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of this from me without exception.
Then, having been addressed in that manner by the great seer Manu, Bhrigu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those sages: "Listen! (Mn 1.60).
Six other high-souled Manus of great power, belonging to the lineage of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, have each created their own respective progeny.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own period (antara), produced and protected this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
Eighteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, thirty of those make one *kalā*,
thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*, and a day and night (*ahorātra*) consists of as many *muhūrtas*.
The sun divides the day and night for both human beings and gods:
night is for the sleep of living beings, and day is for the performance of actions.
Among the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night; its division is by the two fortnights.
The dark fortnight is their day for active exertion, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep.
For the gods, a year constitutes day and night; their division is as follows:
the northern course of the sun is their day, and the southern course is their night.
Now learn, in brief and in their proper order, the measure of each of the ages that constitute a single day and night of Brahmā.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three ages, along with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
This cycle of four ages (caturyuga), which has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand [years], is called a yuga of the gods.
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation,
should be known as one day of Brahmā, and his night is of the same duration.
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration.
At the end of that day and night, he who has been asleep awakens;
and having awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth the creation;
from that, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality.
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.
From wind, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness;
it is radiant and is said to have the quality of form.
And from light, undergoing transformation, water is said to arise with the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises with the quality of smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
That divine age (yuga) which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand years is here called a Manvantara when multiplied by seventy-one.
The Supreme Lord, as if in play, repeatedly brings about innumerable Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution.
In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete in all four quarters, as was Truth;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred for men through unrighteousness.
In the other [ages], however, dharma is reduced by one quarter through the lack of sacred tradition;
and dharma departs quarter by quarter through theft, falsehood, and deceit.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, achieve all their goals, and have a lifespan of four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
The lifespan ordained for mortals in the Vedas, as well as the fruits of ritual actions and the powers of embodied beings, bear fruit in the world according to each successive age.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, in the Tretā another, and in the Dvāpara yet others;
in the Kali age they are different again, according to the decline of each successive age.
Austerity is said to be supreme in the Kṛta age, knowledge in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is the means in the Dvāpara, and charity alone in the Kali age.
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great splendor assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
The protection of subjects, giving, sacrifice, study,
and non-attachment to sense objects constitute, in brief, the duty of a Kṣatriya.
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifices,
studying, trade, money-lending, and agriculture are the duties of a Vaiśya.
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra:
to serve these very castes without malice.
The upper part of a person above the navel is declared to be more pure;
therefore, his mouth has been called the most sacred by the Self-Existent One.
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda,
the Brāhmaṇa is by law the lord of this entire creation.

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying oblations to the gods and ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
What being is greater than he, from whose mouth the dwellers of heaven always eat the sacrificial offerings (havya) and the ancestors eat the offerings to the manes (kavya)?
Among beings, living creatures are the best; among living creatures, those who live by their intelligence are the best;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brāhmaṇas, those who are learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are perfected;
among those with perfected intellects, those who perform their duties; and among the performers of duty, those who know Brahman.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is destined for union with Brahman.
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born on earth,
he is born as a lord over all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
Everything that exists in this world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble descent, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this.
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brahmin's compassion that other people enjoy their sustenance.
For the sake of discerning the duties of that [king], the wise Svāyambhuva Manu composed this treatise for the remaining [classes] in their proper order.
This must be studied with diligence by a learned Brāhmaṇa and correctly expounded to his pupils; it must not be taught by anyone else.
A Brāhmaṇa who studies this treatise and is firm in his vows is never tainted by defects of action arising from mind, speech, or body.
He purifies his lineage, seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even a single such person is worthy of this entire earth.
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this brings fame and long life; this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss.
In this [work], dharma has been declared in its entirety, as well as the merits and defects of actions,
and the eternal conduct of all four castes.
Conduct is the highest dharma, both that which is declared in the Śruti and that which is prescribed in the Smṛti;
therefore, a twice-born man who possesses self-control should always be constantly devoted to it.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct becomes a partaker of the full fruit.
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through conduct, the sages adopted conduct as the supreme root of all austerity.
And [he shall describe] the origin of the world, the rules for the formative factors (saṃskāra),
the practice of religious observances (vratacaryā) and their application, and the supreme rule for ritual bathing (snāna).
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages,
the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha).
The characteristics of the modes of livelihood, the vows of a Snātaka,
what may and may not be eaten, purity, and the purification of objects.
The application of the duties of women, the practice of asceticism, liberation, and renunciation itself;
as well as the entire duty of kings and the judicial determination of legal cases.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife,
the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of social thorns.
And [he shall describe] the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes, the duties of the social orders in times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation.
The journey through saṃsāra, which arises from threefold action,
as well as the highest good resulting from actions and the examination of their merits and defects.
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and groups.
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so now do you also learn it from me.
Learn that dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous, who are always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart.
A nature of self-centered desire is not praised, nor indeed is a state of desirelessness found here;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices originate from volition;
and vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire.
By conducting oneself rightly toward these, one goes to the world of the immortals;
and here, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended.
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it,
the practice of the virtuous, and also the satisfaction of one's own self.
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all that is stated in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge.
But having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge,
the wise man should indeed abide in his own duty according to the authority of the revealed scriptures.
For a man who practices the dharma declared in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Smṛti is indeed the Dharmaśāstra;
these two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them Dharma has shone forth.
Any twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would show contempt for their source,
should be excluded by the virtuous as an atheist and a reviler of the Veda.
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—
they say that this fourfold is the direct definition of Dharma.
For those who are unattached to wealth and sensual pleasures, knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the Śruti is the supreme authority.
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be Dharma;
for both of them have been rightly declared as Dharma by the wise.
Whether the sun has risen, has not yet risen, or it is the time of twilight, the sacrifice is performed in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.
He for whom the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral pyre have been prescribed by means of mantras—
only he is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī,
which was created by the gods, they call Brahmāvarta.
Whatever custom has been handed down by tradition in that region for the social classes and the intermediate castes is called "good conduct" (sadācāra).
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahmarṣis, which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta.
From one born in this land, a man of the highest caste,
all men on earth should learn their respective duties.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa (the Middle Country).
The wise know Āryāvarta to be the region between those two mountains, extending from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature should be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the source of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes (varṇas).

For the twice-born, the purifying sacraments of the body, beginning with the rite of impregnation, must be performed through meritorious Vedic rites; they lead to purification both in this world and after death.
By means of domestic fire-sacrifices, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle,
the taint derived from seed and the taint derived from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born.
Through private Vedic study, vows, burnt offerings, the knowledge of the three Vedas, sacrifices, sons,
the great sacrifices, and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman.
For a male child, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it consists of the ceremonial feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
One should cause his naming ceremony to be performed on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with good qualities.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word denoting "happiness" (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word signifying "protection";
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with a word meaning "prosperity" (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be connected with a word meaning "service" (preṣya).
For women, [the speech] should be easy to pronounce, gentle, clear in meaning, charming, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction.
In the fourth month, the child's first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food, or whatever auspicious rite is desired by the family.
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to the Dharma in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Veda.
One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh year from conception; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception.
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a Kṣatriya seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya desiring worldly prosperity in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not pass beyond the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa,
nor beyond the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, nor beyond the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya.
Beyond this time, all three of these, if they have not been consecrated at the proper time, become Vrātyas fallen from the Sāvitrī, despised by the Āryas.
A Brahmin should never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules.
Students of the Veda should wear,
in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat, as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of Murvā fibers; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.
If muñja grass is unavailable, however, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass,
with three, one, three, or five knots.
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya should be made of woolen threads.
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made to reach the hair at the crown of the head in length;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose.
All those [reeds] should be straight, without blemishes, and pleasant to the sight;
they should not cause alarm to men, possessed of their sheaths, and undamaged by fire.
Having taken up his desired staff and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go about for alms using the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should place it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, with it at the end.
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt, or from one who will not treat him with contempt.
Having collected that alms-food as much as is needed without guile,
and having offered it to his teacher, he should eat while facing east, pure and having sipped water.
Eating while facing the east promotes longevity; facing the south brings fame;
facing the west brings prosperity; and indeed, facing the north, one eats according to the eternal law (Ṛta).
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
having eaten, he should sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious toward it, and welcome it in every way.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these.
One should not give the leavings of food to anyone, nor should one eat between the prescribed meal times;
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from a meal.
Excessive eating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven;
it is non-meritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
A Brahmin should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
he may use either the Kāya or the Traidaśika tīrtha, but never the Pitrya tīrtha.
They declare that the *brāhma* tīrtha is at the base of the thumb;
the *kāya* tīrtha is at the roots of the fingers, the *daiva* at their tips, and the *pitrya* below those two.
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should also touch the cavities of the head with water, as well as the self and the head itself.
One who knows the Dharma and desires purity should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand, in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north.
A Brahmin is purified by water that reaches the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity.
When the right arm is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*.
Having thrown his girdle, antelope skin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is ordained for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya, it is in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, it is considered to be two years later than that.
This entire series of rites for women must be performed without omission at the proper time and in the proper order, for the sake of purifying the body.
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and the tending of the sacred fires is their domestic duty.
This has been declared as the rite of initiation for the twice-born; it is meritorious and manifests their true birth. Now learn the application of their duties.
Having initiated his pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity,
as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions.
But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north,
he should be instructed while wearing light clothing, with his senses controlled, and forming the *brahmāñjali* gesture.
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda, the feet of the teacher must always be clasped;
one should study with hands joined together, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*.
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
But when the student is about to begin his lesson, the teacher, always alert, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should stop when the student says, "May there be a pause."
A Brahmin should always utter the syllable Om at the beginning and at the end [of his recitation];
for that which is not preceded by Om flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
Seated upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he then becomes worthy of the syllable Om.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [first] quarter of this Sāvitrī verse beginning with "Tat."
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One who is devoid of this Ṛc, and fails in his own duties at the proper time,
being born of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes, incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without sloth reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and having the sky as his form.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of offering oblations and sacrifices flow away;
the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as difficult to attain, for it is both Brahman and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña);
the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is said to be a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña),
all do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses.
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven organs which the wise of old have taught.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth.
Of these, the five organs of perception, beginning with the ear, are enumerated in their proper order;
the five organs of action, beginning with the anus, are likewise declared.
The eleventh, the mind (manas), should be known as being of a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five become conquered.
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
Between one who might attain all these [desires] and one who renounces them entirely,
the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
These senses, when excessively attached to their objects, cannot be so effectively restrained by abstinence as they can by constant application of knowledge.
Neither the Vedas, nor renunciation, nor sacrifices, nor observances, nor austerities ever lead to success for one whose disposition is corrupted.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, is to be known as one who has conquered his senses.
But if among all the senses even one sense leaks away,
through that his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restraining the mind,
he should accomplish all his goals through yoga without wasting his body.
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears,
but during the evening twilight one should remain seated until the stars are clearly visible.
Standing while reciting prayers during the morning twilight, one removes the sin committed at night;
sitting during the evening twilight, however, one destroys the impurity created by the day.
But he who neither remains at the morning [service] nor performs the evening [service] should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra.
Restrained and established in the daily rite, he should go to the forest and, with a concentrated mind, recite the Sāvitrī near water.
Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding non-study days concerning the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, the daily private recitation,
and the mantras for the burnt oblations.
In the daily obligatory recitation, there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as a "sacrifice of Brahman" (brahmasattra);
it is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the exclamation vaṣaṭ even during times when study is otherwise suspended.
For him who, being self-controlled and pure, studies his own Veda for a year according to the prescribed rule,
this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey.

Having undergone the initiation ceremony, a twice-born man shall maintain the sacred fire, practice begging for alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher until his formal return home (samāvartana).

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman— these ten, according to the law, are to be taught.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave among people like one who is dull-witted.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two dies or incurs enmity.
Where neither virtue nor wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve,
there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in salty soil.
A teacher of the Veda should rather die along with his knowledge;
even in the face of terrible calamity, he must never sow it on barren soil.
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; guard me.
Do not give me to one who is censorious, so that I may remain most powerful."
But speak of me to that brahmin whom you know to be pure, who is disciplined in his student life, who guards the treasure, and who is free from negligence.
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission becomes guilty of stealing the Veda and falls into hell.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge,
one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī,
is better than one who is unrestrained, even if he has mastered the three Vedas, eats all kinds of food, and sells all things.
One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by a superior;
moreover, while staying on a bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and salute him.
For the vital breaths of a youth indeed depart when an elder approaches;
one recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves his elders, four things increase: life span, merit, fame, and strength.
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name. (Manu Smṛti 2.122)
To those who do not know how to address him by name,
a wise man should say "I am he," and the same applies to all women.
In greeting, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the seers have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is identical to the essential form of names.
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one";
and at the end of his name, the vowel *a* should be pronounced with the preceding syllable as a protracted *pluta*.
A Brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be greeted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should inquire after his welfare; a Kṣatriya, after his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, after his prosperity; and a Śūdra, after his health.
One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name, even if he is younger, preceded by the words "bho" or "bhavat."
But toward a woman who is the wife of another and not related by birth,
he should address her as "madam," "fortunate lady," or "sister."
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "I am so-and-so."
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one’s guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru.
The wife of one's brother of the same caste may be saluted day after day;
however, the wives of paternal kinsmen and maternal relatives are to be saluted only upon returning from a journey abroad.
One should behave toward one's father's sister, one's mother, and one's elder sister as toward a mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they.
Friendship with fellow citizens is established by ten years; that with artists, by five years;
that with Vedic scholars, by three years; and among those of the same lineage, it is formed even by a very short period.
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; of these two, the Brahmin is indeed the father.
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding.
Among the three [higher] castes, he who possesses the greatest number of qualities and virtues is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached the tenth decade of his life.
The way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one who has reached his tenth decade of life, to the sick, to one carrying a burden, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom.
Among those who have come together, the *snātaka* and the king are to be honored;
and between the royal *snātaka* and the ordinary *snātaka*, the *snātaka* receives the honor due to a king.
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya.
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas,
for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the child] with food, is called a guru.

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world.
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda should be known as both mother and father; one should never bear him malice.
Ten preceptors are equal to one teacher; a father exceeds a hundred teachers;
but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in respect.
Of the two—the progenitor and the giver of the Veda—the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world.
One should know that the birth which occurs when his mother and father produce him together through desire is merely his physical conception within the womb.
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is true, and it is free from old age and death.
One should know that person as a teacher in this world who benefits one with sacred learning, whether it be little or much, by means of that very benefit of learning.
One who brings about a Vedic birth and is a teacher of his own duty becomes,
according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child.
The wise child, the descendant of Aṅgiras, taught his elders;
having encompassed them with his knowledge, he said to them, "O my sons."
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods about that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you."
The ignorant man is indeed a child, while the giver of sacred knowledge is a father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child" and the giver of sacred knowledge a "father."
The sages have established this law: that one is not great by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen; he who has studied the Vedas is great among us.
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kshatriyas by valor,
that of Vaishyas by grain and wealth, and that of Shudras alone by birth.
One does not become an elder merely because his head is gray;
rather, even if he is young, the gods recognize him as an elder who is devoted to study.
Just as an elephant made of wood, as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name.
As a eunuch is fruitless among women, as a cow is fruitless with another cow,
and as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
The instruction of living beings toward their welfare must be carried out through non-violence alone;
and one who desires dharma should employ speech that is both sweet and gentle.
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit that is taught in the Vedānta.
Even when afflicted, one should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor should one have a mind intent on deeds that harm another;
one should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if at poison,
and he should always long for dishonor as if for nectar.
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in peace and wakes in peace;
he moves about this world in comfort, while the scorner perishes.
By this gradual process, the twice-born man, having purified his self, should dwell with his teacher and slowly accumulate the austerity that leads to the realization of Brahman.
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule.
A superior twice-born man, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is declared to be the highest austerity for a Brahmin in this world.
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even to his very fingertips who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability.
The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his progeny.
The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass;
the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti.
Among those, that which is his birth from Brahman, marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass—
therein the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother and the teacher his father.
They declare the teacher to be a father because of his imparting the Veda;
for no ritual duty whatsoever is enjoined upon him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
One should not recite the Veda except when performing the offering of the *svadhā* libations;
for as long as he is not born into the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra.

For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) and the acquisition of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa) are prescribed to be performed in due order according to the rules.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, girdle, staff, and garment have been prescribed for him [in initiation], those same items he must also employ during his religious observances.
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules,
fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own ascetic merit.
Having bathed daily and become pure, he should perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire.
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women,
all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings.
Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes or carrying an umbrella,
as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.
Gambling, public scandal, slander, as well as falsehood;
gazing at and touching women, and injury to another.
One should always sleep alone and never let semen be spilled;
for by emitting semen out of desire, one destroys one's own vow.
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām."
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass—
as much as required— and he should go out for alms every day.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praiseworthy in their own duties.
He should not beg from the family of his teacher, nor from the families of his paternal or maternal relatives;
however, if other houses are unavailable, he should avoid each preceding house in favor of the next.
Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village,
restraining his speech with self-control, but avoiding those who have been accused of crimes.
Having fetched fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air;
and with those, he should unwearyingly offer oblations into the fire every evening and morning.
If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of chastity.
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the subsistence of a vow-observer on alms is equal to fasting.
In a rite dedicated to the gods, one should eat like a person observing a vow; likewise in a rite for the ancestors, one may eat at will when invited, like a seer (ṛṣi); thus his vow is not violated.
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, this duty is not prescribed in this manner.
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged,
he should apply effort to his studies and to the welfare of his preceptor.
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher.
He should always have his right hand raised, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit down facing the teacher.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him.
One should not engage in conversation with a reply while lying down,
nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor while facing away.

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is standing; going forward to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running, one should attend to one who is running.
Facing one who has turned away, approaching the presence of one who is far off,
bowing down to one who is lying down, and standing by the side of one who is giving instructions.
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat must always be low;
within the range of the teacher's sight, he must not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Wherever censure or even reproach of the teacher occurs,
one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
From speaking ill of others one becomes a donkey; indeed, a slanderer becomes a dog; one who consumes another's property becomes a worm; and an envious person becomes an insect.
One should not salute him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him.
One should not sit with one's teacher either downwind or upwind;
nor should one say anything at all within earshot of the teacher that he cannot hear.
He may sit together with his teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on a palace terrace, on mats, on rocks, on wooden planks, or in a boat.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
and without being permitted by one's teacher, one should not pay homage to one's own teachers.

In the same way, one's conduct toward teachers of sacred knowledge, toward one's own parents, and toward those who forbid unrighteousness or instruct one in what is beneficial, must always be constant.
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one would toward the teacher himself—
toward the teacher’s sons, toward venerable persons, and toward the teacher’s own kinsmen.
Whether he is of equal age, a youth, or a pupil, the son of a teacher deserves the same honor as the teacher himself when teaching during a sacrificial rite.
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one wash his feet.
The wives of one's gurus who belong to the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the gurus themselves;
however, those of a different caste should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation.
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs,
and the dressing of the hair should not be performed for the wife of one's teacher.
But a young wife of the guru should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who is twenty years of age and capable of discerning virtues and faults.
This is the very nature of women: they are the corruption of men in this world;
therefore, the wise do not place their trust in young women for the sake of their interests.
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant and even the learned man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
However, on this earth, a young man should, according to the prescribed rule, perform a salutation to the wives of his elders who are themselves young, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher's wives every day and offer salutations,
keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous.
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade,
so does one who is desirous of learning obtain knowledge residing in a teacher.
Whether he be shaven-headed or wear matted hair, or have a single lock of matted hair on his crown,
the sun must never set or rise while he remains in a village.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while muttering prayers.
For he who, while lying down, is overtaken by the setting sun or awakened by the rising sun,
and fails to perform the penance, becomes joined with great sin.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend upon both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule.
If a woman or a younger person should perform any virtuous act, one should practice all of that with diligence; and one should also do whatever brings him mental delight.
Some say that the good consists in virtue and wealth; others, in pleasure and wealth, or in virtue alone;
or again, in wealth alone as the highest good in this world—such is the established position regarding the three aims of life.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and the elder brother must not be treated with disrespect, especially by a Brahmin, even if he has been harmed by them.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself.
The suffering that parents endure for the birth of human beings cannot be repaid, even in a hundred years.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times;
when these three are satisfied, all austerity is fully accomplished.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them.
For these indeed are the three worlds, these are the three stages of life;
these indeed are the three Vedas, and these are said to be the three sacred fires.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, a householder may conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world;
and by service to one's teacher, one likewise attains the world of Brahmā.
All duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless.
As long as those three live, he should not attend to anyone else;
he should constantly perform service for them alone, devoted to their pleasure and welfare.
Whatever one may do for the sake of the next world, provided it does not conflict with their interests,
that very thing one should announce to them through thought, word, and deed.
For a man's duty is fully accomplished through these three;
this is the supreme dharma manifestly, while any other is called a secondary dharma.
One who possesses faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a person of lower status;
likewise, one should accept the highest dharma even from another, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family.
Nectar should be taken even from poison; a well-spoken word even from a child;
good conduct even from an enemy; and gold even from an impure place.
Women, jewels, knowledge, righteousness, purity, well-spoken words,
and various arts are to be acquired from everywhere.
In times of distress, study under one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
he must follow his teacher and serve him for as long as the period of study lasts.
A student who desires the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a non-Brahmin teacher, nor even with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas.
But if he should prefer to dwell permanently in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation of the body.
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes directly to the eternal abode of Brahman.
One who knows the Dharma should not provide anything to the teacher beforehand;
however, when he is about to perform the ceremonial bath and has been instructed by the teacher, he should acquire property for the teacher's sake according to his ability.
A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella, sandals, a seat, grain,
vegetables, and garments— one should bring these to the teacher to produce his satisfaction.
But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with good qualities,
or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, exactly as toward the teacher himself.
When these are not available, one who maintains a regular regimen of standing, sitting, and moving about,
and performs service to the sacred fire, shall perfect his own body.
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this manner, remaining unbroken in his vow of celibacy,
goes to the highest station and is not born again in this world.
The vow pertaining to the three Vedas involves a period of service under a teacher for thirty-six years;
or half of that, or a quarter, or even until they have been mastered.
Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in due order,
and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is well-known for his own duty, who inherits the father's Vedic legacy, and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland.
Having bathed and returned home from his teacher's house according to the prescribed rule with the permission of his guru,
the twice-born man shall marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.
A woman who is not a sapinda of one's mother and not of the same gotra as one's father is recommended for the twice-born in the marriage rite for sexual union.
Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain,
one should avoid these ten families in forming alliances with women.
Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, those with hairy bodies or hemorrhoids,
and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one with reddish-brown eyes.

One should not marry a woman named after a bear, a tree, or a river; nor one named after a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one whose name is terrifying.

He should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has an auspicious name, who walks with the gait of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft.
A wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter).
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following [wives] are permitted in descending order.

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as the wife for a Śūdra; she and a woman of his own caste (Viś) are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and a woman of his own caste for a Kṣatriya; and those three and a woman of his own caste for a Brāhmaṇa.
For it is taught that, even in times of distress, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, regardless of the circumstances.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her.
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from his Brāhmaṇahood.
But he for whom the rites for the gods, the ancestors, and guests are primarily concerned—
if the ancestors and gods do not eat [the offerings] from him, he does not go to heaven.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a Vṛṣalī, for one who has been defiled by her breath,
and for one who has begotten a child upon her, no expiation is prescribed.
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women among all four castes, which lead to welfare or harm both in this world and after death.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya,
the Āsura, the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest.
I shall declare to you all that which is lawful for each caste, as well as the virtues and vices pertaining to each, and the merits and demerits of their offspring.

One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [marriages] in the prescribed order, for a Kṣatriya four [of those] beginning with the lower ones, and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, those same [four], which are lawful and not Rākṣasa.
Sages know that four of the first [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone is for a Kṣatriya, and the Āsura for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Of these five, three are considered lawful and two unlawful in this world;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed.
Whether performed separately or combined, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—
the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa— are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya.
Having clothed and honored her himself, and having invited a man of learning and good character, the giving away of the daughter is proclaimed as the Brāhma rite.
When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest is performing his duty,
the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) rite.
Having received one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law,
the giving away of the daughter according to the prescribed rule is called the Ārṣa rite.
Having addressed them with the words, "May you both perform your religious duties together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is recorded as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability,
the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura rite.
The mutual union of the maiden and the bridegroom through their own desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it is based on sexual union and arises from passion.
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home while she cries out and weeps, after having slain, wounded, or broken down [the resistance], is called the Rākṣasa rite.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is the eighth and most base of marriages, the sinful Paiśāca form.
For the foremost of the twice-born, the gift of a daughter is distinguished by water alone;
for the other castes, however, it is by mutual desire.
O Brahmins, listen as I proclaim all the specific merits of these forms of marriage that have been described by Manu for each of them.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has performed meritorious deeds delivers ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin.
A son born of a woman married according to the Daiva rite delivers seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants;
a son born of a woman married according to the Ārṣa rite delivers three of each; and a son born of a woman married according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite delivers six of each.
In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born in due order.
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned,
possessing sufficient enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
But from the remaining improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and the Law are born.
Offspring becomes irreproachable through blameless marriages with women; it becomes reproachable for men through reprehensible ones. Therefore, one should avoid those that are censurable.
The sacrament of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste;
this following rule is to be known regarding the act of marriage with women of different castes.
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden,
and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste.

He should approach his wife during her fertile period and always remain devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may go to her out of a desire for sexual pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days.
The natural menstrual period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights,
together with the four other days that are censured by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights are commended.
Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights;
therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on the even nights.
If the male seed is in excess, a male is born; if the female seed is in excess, a female is born.
If they are equal, a neuter is born, or sometimes both a male and a female; if they are diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs.
Avoiding women on the eight censurable nights and the other [four],
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he inhabits.
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring.
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off a woman's property—
whether it be her carriage or her clothing— are sinners who go to a downward state.
Some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price according to the Ṛṣi tradition, but that is entirely false;
whether it be small or large, it remains nothing other than a sale.
When the kinsmen do not take a bride-price for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure benevolence.
These women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant prosperity for them.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, there all rites become fruitless.
Where the female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes;
but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers for all time.
Those households which female relatives, when not properly honored, curse,
perish on all sides as if struck by a malevolent spell.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always honor these women with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at daily rites and during festivals.
In whatever family the husband is always content with his wife, and likewise the wife with her husband, there indeed prosperity is certain.
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight her husband; and from the lack of delight on the part of the man, procreation does not proceed.
When a woman is radiant, the entire family shines; but when she is not radiant, the whole family indeed does not shine.
Families fall into a state of worthlessness through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins.
By means of crafts, trade, and solely through the offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king.
Families that are deficient in sacred mantras perish quickly through officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, as well as through atheism regarding the efficacy of ritual acts.
But families that are enriched by the power of mantras, even if they possess little wealth,
are reckoned among the noble lineages and acquire great renown.
In the nuptial fire, the householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rule,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound by sin.
For the sake of expiating all of these in due order, the great seers have ordained five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability is never tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse, even while living constantly in the household.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
