The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the likewise well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these they declare to be the five sacrifices.

Recitation is the *ahuta* offering; the fire-oblation is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits is the *prahuta*; the oblation to the elemental beings is the *bhautika bali*; the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda and to rites directed toward the gods;
for it is by being engaged in rites directed toward the gods that one sustains this entire world, both moving and unmoving.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Just as all living beings exist by depending upon the air,
so do all the other stages of life exist by depending upon the householder.
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by the householder alone with both knowledge and food,
therefore the householder's stage is the most eminent.
This [dharma] must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven,
and by one who desires ultimate happiness in this world— even though it is difficult for those of weak senses to maintain.
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, one who understands his duty must act for them.
One should honor the ṛṣis with the private recitation of the Veda, the gods with burnt oblations according to the rule,
the ancestors with funeral offerings (śrāddha), men with gifts of food, and all beings with the bali offering.
He should perform the *śrāddha* rite day by day with food and drink,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
In the rites of the five sacrifices performed for the ancestors, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, in the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should not feed any Brahmin at all.
A Brahmin should daily perform an oblation in the domestic fire with the prepared Vaiśvadeva food, according to the prescribed rule, for these deities.
First to Agni and to Soma, then to both of them together,
to the Viśvedevas, and to Dhanvantari.
And to Kuhū, to Anumati, and to Prajāpati;
together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.

Having thus offered the oblation correctly, he should present the sacrificial portion (bali) in a clockwise direction toward all the quarters to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, along with their followers.
One should cast [food] at the door with the words "To the Maruts," and likewise into the water with the words "To the Waters";
one should offer [food] upon the pestle and mortar with the words "To the Vanaspatis."
He should offer an oblation to Śrī at the head of the bed and to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
furthermore, he should present an offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
And he should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
One should offer a bali-oblation on the back part of the house for the sake of the welfare of all beings;
however, one should carry the entire remainder of the bali-offering to the south for the ancestors.
And for those who have been executed, for outcasts, for dog-cookers, for those afflicted with loathsome diseases,
for birds, and for insects, he should gently scatter [the food] upon the ground.
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by the straight path to the supreme abode, his very form consisting of light.
Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, he should first feed his guest;
he should also give alms according to the rule to the mendicant and the student of sacred knowledge.
Whatever merit a householder twice-born man obtains by giving a cow to his teacher according to the prescribed rule,
that same merit he obtains by giving alms.
One should respectfully offer even alms or a vessel of water, according to the prescribed rule,
to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when given by donors out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes.
An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, who are enriched by knowledge and austerity,
delivers one from misfortune and even from great sin.
To a guest who has arrived, he should offer a seat and water,
as well as food according to his ability, honoring him with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Even for one who constantly subsists by gleaning grains or offers oblations into the five fires,
a Brāhmaṇa residing unhonored takes away all his merit.
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these things are never lacking in the house of the virtuous.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is traditionally called a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest.

One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who has come from another village, or likewise one who has arrived as a visitor, when he has presented himself at the house where the wife or even the sacred fires are located.
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others go, after death, to the state of cattle for having given away food and other such things.
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by a householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
for the honoring of guests brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.
One should provide a superior seat, lodging, bed, escorting, and attendance for those who are superior; inferior for those who are inferior; and equal for those who are equal.
But if another guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been completed, one should give him food according to one's ability; however, one need not perform the Bali offering again.
A Brahmin should not proclaim his own family or lineage for the sake of food;
for he who announces these for the sake of a meal is called by the wise a "vomit-eater."
However, it is said that for a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya is not a guest in his house;
nor are a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, nor even a friend, a kinsman, or a teacher.
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may,
at will, feed him as well once the Brahmins have finished eating.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at the household as one who possesses the status of a guest,
he should feed them along with his dependents, practicing compassion toward them.
Furthermore, he should, together with his wife, feed with affection his friends and others who have come to his house, providing food according to his ability.
One should feed these— married women, young maidens, the sick, and pregnant women— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins and his own servants have finished eating,
the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.

One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, an officiating priest, a snātaka, a teacher, and one's dear father-in-law, maternal uncle, and father-in-law, once again after a year has passed.

Both a king and a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) who have arrived for the performance of a sacrifice are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the settled rule that this does not apply when there is no sacrifice.
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer an oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon,
perform the monthly Śrāddha known as Piṇḍānvāhāryaka.
The wise know that the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors is the Anvāhārya;
and that should be performed with effort using commendable meat.
In this regard, I shall explain in their entirety who among the best of the twice-born are to be fed, who are to be avoided, how many there are, and with what kinds of food.
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large company.
Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.
This rite for the deceased, known as the ancestral offering (pitrya), is prescribed at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that [rite], it is always considered a worldly duty for the dead.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
One should examine from afar a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas;
he is considered a worthy recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is declared to be a true guest.
For where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda are fed,
a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to the law.
Offerings for the ancestors (kavya) and oblations (haviṣ) should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not purified by blood alone.
As many mouthfuls as one ignorant of the mantras consumes at offerings to the gods or the ancestors,
so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls shall that deceased person consume.
Some twice-born men are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity; some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are devoted to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established with those who are devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) may be given according to the rule to all four classes alike.

If one's father is unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*) but his son has mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*), or if the son is unlearned in the Vedas but the father has mastered the Vedas; [in either case, they may officiate as priests for one another].
One should know the elder of these two to be the one whose father is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya);
the other, however, deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
One should feed at a śrāddha that brahmin whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend.
He whose śrāddha rites and oblations are dominated by friends gains no fruit after death from those śrāddhas or oblations.
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships through a funeral feast, falls from heaven and from the world, he whose friendship is based on the śrāddha.
The *paiśāca* form of marriage is declared by the twice-born to be a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) accompanied by feasting;
yet it remains in this world like a blind cow in a house with only one door.
Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain a fruit,
so too a donor who has given an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain a fruit.
By giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the rules to a learned man, one makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit, both in this world and after death.
At a Śrāddha ceremony, one may by all means honor a friend, even if he is not a distinguished man, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by one who hates the giver becomes fruitless after death.
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda,
or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his recensional branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his studies.
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at his *śrāddha*,
the satisfaction of his ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations.
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
however, this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed one's maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, sister’s son, father-in-law, preceptor, daughter’s son, brother-in-law, kinsman, officiating priest, and the person for whom one performs sacrifices.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors has arrived, he should examine him with great care.
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or who follow the lifestyle of nihilists to be unworthy of offerings made to the gods or the ancestors.
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who officiate as priests for a man with matted hair who does not study the Vedas, nor for one who is weak, nor for a gambler, nor for groups [of such persons].
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; Mn 3.153.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, an outcaste, a hater of the Veda, an elder brother whose younger brother has married first, and one who belongs to a communal group (gaṇa)— these are those from whom food must not be accepted.

One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a Śūdra woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour; // Mn_3.155 //
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a teacher for a fee, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, a teacher of a Śūdra, one who is foul-mouthed, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka; Mn 3.156.
One who has abandoned mother, father, or teacher without cause;
and one who has entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections.
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats food from a base vessel, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; Mn 3.158.
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (such as poison).

One who manufactures bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, one who betrays a friend, one who subsists by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; Mn 3.160 [150M]
One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas— these should be avoided.
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare. // Mn_3.162 //
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them, a house-settler, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees; Mn 3.163 [153M]
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for guilds (gaṇas).
One devoid of proper conduct, one who is impotent, a constant beggar,
one who lives by agriculture, and one with elephantiasis are indeed censured by the virtuous.
A butcher of sheep, a butcher of buffaloes, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and one who carries out the dead for a fee— these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man who is the best among the twice-born should avoid both here and hereafter those lowest of the twice-born who have censurable conduct and are unworthy of the company at a meal.
But a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer an oblation to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.
I shall now describe in its entirety that fruit which arises for a donor after death from giving to one unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors.

Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not kept their vows, as well as by those such as a younger brother whose elder brother is married before him, and by other persons excluded from the company at a meal— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.

He who, while his elder brother remains, enters into the union of marriage and the sacred fire-sacrifice, is to be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder); the elder brother, however, is a *parivitti*.

The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, the younger brother who so marries, she with whom the younger brother marries, as well as the giver and the officiating priest— the fifth— these all go to hell.
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—
even if she has been appointed according to the sacred law— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa is born when the husband is alive, and the Golaka when the husband is dead.
Those two beings, born in the field of another, cause the destruction of the offerings made to the gods and ancestors by the donors, both in this world and after death.
As many members of a company as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating,
so many of them does that foolish donor fail to obtain the fruit of his gift.
A blind man, upon seeing [the gift], destroys the fruit of ninety; a one-eyed man, of sixty; a leper, of a hundred;
but one afflicted with a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand for the giver.
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift.
Even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, by accepting a gift from him out of greed,
quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood;
what is given to a temple-attendant (devalaka) is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
That which is given to a trader brings no benefit either in this world or the next;
it is like an offering poured into ashes, even so when given to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
But regarding other unworthy persons who are unfit to sit in the company at meals, as previously specified,
the wise declare that their food is equivalent to fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born, the purifiers of the row, by whom a row defiled by those unworthy of the company is purified. (Manu Smṛti 3.183)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the sacred law],
and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the Veda was given as a dowry, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman.

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a reciter, a student of sacred knowledge, one who bestows a thousand gifts, and one who lives for a hundred years— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
When the Śrāddha rite is about to take place, either on the preceding day or on the following day,
he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described.
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns, and that [rite] shall be his śrāddha.
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit.
But that best of the twice-born who, having been invited according to the rule for offerings to the gods or the ancestors,
somehow transgresses, becomes a sinner and shall go to the state of a pig.
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a Śūdra woman,
incurs all whatever evil deed the giver has committed.
Free from anger, devoted to purity, ever practicing celibacy,
having laid down their weapons, the highly fortunate Pitṛs are the deities of the ancients.
Since the origin of all these [castes] has been explained in its entirety,
learn now those rules by which they are to be designated according to their respective occupations.
The sons of all those sages— Marīci and the others, who were the sons of Manu, the son of the Golden Womb— are recorded as the classes of Pitṛs.
The sons of Virāj, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, renowned throughout the world, are those of the Marīcis and the gods.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are remembered as the ancestors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among the Brahmins they are named Somapas; among the Kshatriyas, Havirbhujas; among the Vaishyas, Ajyapas; and among the Shudras, Sukalinas.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
One should designate as belonging exclusively to Brahmins those who are consumed by fire, those not consumed by fire, the Kāvyas, the Barhiṣads, the Agniṣvāttas, and the Saumyas.
Furthermore, regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed,
it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite.
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, gods and humans;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—arose in due succession.
Even water given with faith in vessels made of silver, or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible merit for them.
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
One should first appoint a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection.
One should seek that which has the gods at its beginning and end; it should not have the ancestors at its beginning and end.
For one who seeks that which has the ancestors at its beginning and end perishes quickly, along with his lineage.
One should smear a pure and secluded place with cow dung and,
with diligence, ensure that it slopes toward the south.
For the ancestors are always satisfied by what is given in open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and in secluded places.
When separate seats provided with sacred grass have been prepared,
he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them.
Having seated those blameless Brahmins on their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds and purifiers (pavitra),
the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire together with them.
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma,
and Yama according to the rule by means of the offering of oblations, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place the offering directly into the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras.

The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as those who are free from anger, easily propitiated, intent on nourishing the world, and who have the ancestors and the gods as their deities for the śrāddha rite.
Having performed the circumambulation of the fire in the counter-clockwise direction and having completed the entire rite,
he should pour water upon the ground with his hand in the counter-clockwise direction.
Having formed three balls from that remainder of the sacrificial food, he, being composed,
should offer them facing the south according to the very same rite prescribed for the water libation.
Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) then, being self-restrained and according to the prescribed rule,
he should wipe that hand on those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ).
Having sipped water and turned toward the north, having slowly restrained his breath three times,
he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras.
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the rice balls;
then, with a concentrated mind, he should smell those rice balls in the order they were placed.
Having taken small portions from each of the food balls in succession,
he should first cause those same seated Brahmins to eat according to the rule.
But while his father is still living, he should offer the oblation to the ancestors alone;
or else, like a Brahmin [inviting guests], he should cause his own father to partake in the Śrāddha.
If one's father has passed away but one's grandfather is still living,
he should pronounce his father’s name and then proclaim the name of his great-grandfather.
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
or, being duly authorized, he may perform it himself at his pleasure.
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the sacred grass (pavitra) into their hands,
he should offer the tip of that funeral ball (piṇḍa), saying, "May there be svadhā for them."
Holding the increased portion of food with both hands,
he himself should slowly place it near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors.
The food that is brought forth and placed between both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras suddenly seize and plunder it.
And with a restrained mind and composed spirit, he should first place upon the ground itself the various side dishes such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey.
Various kinds of food and edibles, roots and fruits,
as well as savory meats and fragrant drinks.
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure,
being pure and extolling all its qualities.
One should never shed tears, one should not become angry, and one should not speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it.
Tears cause the departed spirits (pretas) to depart; anger, the enemies; falsehood, the dogs;
contact with the foot, the demons (rakṣas); and shaking [the head], the evildoers.
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without avarice;
and he should engage in discourses on the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause the Vedic recitation to be heard, as well as the treatises on Dharma,
narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts.
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and other delicacies, as well as by praising their virtues.
One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
At a funeral feast (*śrāddha*), three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds.
Furthermore, three qualities are praised in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born, when asked by the giver, speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
As long as there is steam from the food, as long as they eat with speech restrained,
so long do the ancestors eat— provided that the qualities of the oblation have not been mentioned.
Whatever one eats with a turbaned head, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
A Cāṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
a woman in her menses, and a eunuch— these must not look at twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these at the giving of a house, at a meal,
or at an offering to the gods or the ancestors, that goes astray from its intended purpose.
The pig destroys [the merit of the gift] by its smell, the cock by the wind of its wings,
the dog by the casting of its gaze, and the low-caste man by his touch.
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove him as well.
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has approached for the sake of food, he should,
with the permission of the Brahmins, honor them according to his ability.
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should cast it upon the ground before those who have finished eating, scattering it there.

The remnants of food and whatever scattering of food (vikiro) is upon the *darbha* grass shall be the allotted portion for those who have died an unnatural death and for women who have left their families.
That which has fallen on the ground as the remains of the meal belongs to the group of servants who are upright and free from deceit;
this they declare to be their share at the ancestral rite (pitrya).
But for a twice-born man who has died, until the performance of the *piṇḍa*-offering rite,
one should perform the *śrāddha* without an invitation to the gods and offer only a single *piṇḍa*.
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the law, his sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by this very same procedure.
That fool who, having eaten at a śrāddha, gives the leavings to a Śūdra,
goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell.
If one who has partaken in a śrāddha ceremony approaches the bed of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) on that same day,
his ancestors lie in her excrement for that entire month.
Having asked "Was it well-tasted? he should then cause those who are satisfied to sip water;
and once they have sipped water, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you rest at your pleasure."
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhāstu! (Let there be *svadhā*);
for the utterance of *svadhā* is the supreme blessing in all rites for the ancestors.
Then, once they have finished eating, he should offer them the remains of the food;
he should do exactly as they say, having been authorized by the twice-born.
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "it is well-savored" (svaditam); at a rite for cattle, "it is well-cooked" (suśṛtam);
at a rite for prosperity, "it is excellent" (saṃpannam); and at a rite for the gods, "it is pleasing" (rucitam).
The afternoon, as well as darbha grass, the preparation of the site,
sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent twice-born men— these are the perfections for śrāddha rites.
Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial foods—
as well as whatever purifying substance was mentioned previously— should be understood as the perfections of the oblation.
The food of hermits, milk, soma, meat that is not seasoned,
and salt that is not processed— these are called by their very nature sacrificial oblations (havis).

Having dismissed those Brahmins, being self-restrained, silent, and pure, and gazing toward the southern direction, he should pray to the ancestors for these boons: "May the ancestors be satisfied; may the ancestors be gratified; may the ancestors be appeased; may the ancestors grant me what is beneficial. (Mn 3.259) "Whatever I have done here with excessive haste, or whatever has been left incomplete, may the ancestors accept all that from me out of compassion. (Mn 3.260) "May the ancestors be satisfied; may the ancestors be gratified; may the ancestors be appeased; may the ancestors grant me what is beneficial. (Mn 3.261) Having thus addressed the ancestors, he should circumambulate them three times from left to right and then dismiss them with the word "Svadhā. (Mn 3.262) Then, having sipped water and being purified, he should offer water-libations to the six classes of ancestors, beginning with the father, in the order in which they were previously mentioned. (Mn 3.263) He should then perform the ancestral rites for his maternal grandfather and other relatives who are not included among those previously named, as well as for friends and associates. (Mn 3.264) Having offered water to all of them according to their seniority, he should honor them with food, drink, and clothing, as well as with fragrant garlands and unguents. (Mn 3.265) The giver of the funeral cake, the one who recites the Veda, and the one who performs the ancestral rite—these three are said to be the sharers of the ancestral offering. (Mn 3.266) The giver of the funeral cake obtains the merit of the gift; the reciter of the Veda, the fruit of the Veda; and the performer of the rite, the fruit of the sacrifice. (Mn 3.267) One should give a cow to the giver of the funeral cake, a horse to the reciter of the Veda, and a garment to the performer of the rite, according to the rule. (Mn 3.268) Alternatively, he may give a single cow to each of them, or even a single cow to all of them collectively, after having first honored them with food and drink. (Mn 3.269) Having thus completed the ancestral rite, he should feed the Brahmins who are proficient in the Vedas, being pure and self-restrained, and should cause them to pronounce the benediction "Svadhā. (Mn 3.270) When they have pronounced "Svadhā," he should say, "Let it be so"; thereafter, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be satisfied by this. (Mn 3.271) Having fed them, he should give them a portion of food, and also a small gift according to his ability, saying, "May you be satisfied by this. (Mn 3.272) After dismissing the Brahmins, being self-restrained, silent, and pure, and gazing toward the southern direction, he should pray to the ancestors for these boons. (Mn 3.258)
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having thus performed the offering of water, he should immediately thereafter cause those rice-balls to be eaten by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else cast them into water.
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes only after [the recitation];
others have them eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water.
Then, the devoted and lawful wife, intent on the worship of the ancestors and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of offspring, virtuous, and likewise righteous.
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen;
having given hospitality to his kinsmen, he should also feed his relatives.
That remnant of food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
then one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established.
I shall now explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for a long time and even for eternity.
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rule,
the ancestors of men remain satisfied for a month.
For two months he may subsist on fish-meat, for three months on the meat of the hariṇa deer,
for four months on the meat of sheep, and for five months indeed on the meat of birds.
For six months with the meat of a goat, for seven indeed with that of the spotted deer (pārṣata),
for eight with the meat of the black antelope (aina), and for nine with that of the ruru deer.
They are satisfied for ten months with the flesh of boars and buffaloes,
and for exactly eleven months with the flesh of hares and tortoises.
But with cow's milk and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as with the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa, one's satisfaction lasts for twelve years.
Black pot-herbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and the red goat, honey,
and all kinds of food fit for ascetics are prescribed for the sake of infinite results.
Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
May there be born in our family one who would give us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day, before the shadow of an elephant has turned eastward.
Whatever one gives according to the rule, properly and endowed with faith,
that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter.
In the dark fortnight, the lunar days beginning with the tenth, excluding the fourteenth, are recommended for the Śrāddha; other days are not so.
By performing [the śrāddha] on even lunar days and under even asterisms, one enjoys all desires;
but by performing it on odd days and under odd asterisms, one obtains abundant progeny for all the ancestors.
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight,
so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for the performance of a śrāddha.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the rite performed correctly from left to right, unwearied,
and holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion.
One should not perform a Śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas;
nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has just risen.
By this rule, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the Pāñcayajñika rites daily.
The oblation pertaining to the sacrifice for the ancestors is not prescribed to be performed in a common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha for a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires without the Darśa sacrifice.
When the best of the twice-born, having bathed, gratifies the ancestors with water,
he thereby obtains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is the eternal Vedic revelation.
He should always be an eater of vighasa, and he should always be an eater of amṛta;
vighasa is the remnant of what has been eaten, while amṛta is likewise the remnant of a sacrifice.
All this rule regarding the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now hear the rule for the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born.
Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, O twice-born ones,
he should dwell in his house as a married man during the second quarter of his life.
A Brahmin should live in times of no distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no injury to living beings, or at least very little injury. (Manu Smṛti 4.2)
For the sole purpose of maintaining his livelihood,
he should accumulate wealth by means of his own irreproachable occupations, without causing hardship to his body.
One may live by means of *ṛta* and *amṛta*, or by *mṛta* and *pramṛta*, or even by *satya* and *anṛta*; but one should never live by the "dog's mode of life."
Gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains is to be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Begging for alms is called *mṛta*, while agriculture is traditionally known as *pramṛta*.
Trade, however, consists of both truth and falsehood; one may live by that as well.
Service is called the "dog's livelihood"; therefore, one should avoid it.
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or grain sufficient for a single jar;
or he may have enough for three days, or he may not even have enough for tomorrow.
Among these four twice-born householders as well,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds.
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmasattra).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the maintenance of the sacred fires,
he should always perform only those sacrifices prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
He should not, under any circumstances, follow worldly customs for the sake of his livelihood; rather, he should live the pure life of a Brahmin, free from crookedness and guile.
Seeking happiness, one who desires ease should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering.
A twice-born Snātaka, living by any one of these modes of livelihood, should observe these vows which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: [Mn 4.13]
One should perform one's own duty as declared by the Veda constantly and without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
One should not seek wealth through excessive attachment, nor by forbidden actions;
one should not seek it from here and there when wealth already exists, nor even in times of distress.
One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should also turn the mind away from excessive attachment to them.
One should abandon all worldly pursuits that obstruct one's Vedic study;
teaching in whatever manner possible is indeed the fulfillment of his duty.
One should move about in this world practicing conformity in dress, speech, and intellect with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage.
He should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, which are auspicious and beneficial, as well as the Vedic Nigamas.
For in whatever measure a man masters a scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his discernment finds delight therein.
One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to the ancestors, according to one's ability.
Some people who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly desire.
Some always offer the breath into speech and speech into breath,
perceiving in speech and breath the imperishable accomplishment of sacrifice.
Other brahmins always perform these sacrifices with knowledge alone,
seeing that the efficacy of their ritual action is rooted in knowledge through the eye of wisdom.
One should always perform the Agnihotra sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night,
and indeed with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month, as well as with the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice.

At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should worship with the sacrifice for new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should worship with sacrifices; at the beginning of each solstice, with animal sacrifices; and at the end of the year, with Soma sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and desires to live a long life shall not eat new grain or meat without having first performed the sacrifice for the new harvest and the animal sacrifice.
For his fires, greedy for new grain and meat, if not honored with the offering of the animal sacrifice, desire to consume his very life-breaths.
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability, whether with seats, food, beds, water, or roots and fruits.

One should not honor with even a word or a limb those who follow heretical sects, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, the deceitful, the rationalists, and those who behave like herons.

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those householders who are learned in the Vedas, purified by their knowledge, sacred learning, and vows; one should avoid those who are the opposite.
A householder should give according to his ability to those who do not cook for themselves,
and he should provide a share for all beings without causing hardship to his own dependents.

A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from a patron for whom he performs sacrifices, or from a pupil; it is the settled rule that he must not seek it from anyone else.
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger if he has the means;
nor, while possessing wealth, shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes.
Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure,
he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot filled with water,
a sacred thread, a Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when it is reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.
One should not leap over a calf's tethering rope, nor run while it is raining, nor look at one's own reflection in water; such is the rule.
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees.
Even if he is intoxicated, he should not approach a woman during her menstrual period;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman who is overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish.
For him who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by menstrual flow,
wisdom, luster, strength, sight, and even lifespan increase.
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
or while she is sneezing or yawning, nor while she is sitting at her ease.
A twice-born man desiring luster should not look at a woman who is anointing her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth.
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked;
one should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
Neither on ploughed land, nor in water, nor on a sacrificial altar, nor on a mountain;
neither in a dilapidated temple, nor ever on an anthill.
He should not study in pits inhabited by living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing;
nor having reached the bank of a river, nor on the summit of a mountain.
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows,
one should never discharge feces or urine.
Having covered [the excrement] with wood, clods of earth, leaves, grass, or the like, he should pass by,
restraining his speech, being pure, with his body wrapped and his head veiled.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day,
facing south at night, and during the two twilights as one does during the day.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction that is comfortable for him, as well as when there is fear of danger to life.
The wisdom of one who urinates facing fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man,
or facing a cow or the wind, perishes.
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it.
One should not place it beneath oneself, nor should one step over it;
one should not place it at the level of one's feet, nor should one act so as to cause injury to living beings.
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel, nor lie down;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor remove one's own garland.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or saliva into water,
nor anything else defiled by impurities, nor blood, nor poisons.
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person from sleep;
one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice uninvited.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling its calf, nor should one inform anyone of it;
likewise, upon seeing a rainbow in the sky, a wise man should not point it out to anyone.
He should not dwell in a village where unrighteousness prevails, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
he should not set out on a journey alone, nor should he reside for long on a mountain.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with unrighteous people;
nor in one overrun by hosts of heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice overeating;
one should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor in the evening if one has already eaten in the morning.
One should not engage in useless exertion, nor drink water from one's cupped hands;
one should not eat food while holding it in one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity.
He should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
he should not clap his hands, nor shout, nor utter cries when impassioned.
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal;
nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature.
One should not wear sandals, a garment, a sacred thread, an ornament, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (Manu Smṛti 4.66)
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are mutilated.
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without lashing them excessively with the goad.
The heat of the morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat are to be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth.
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless labor, nor any action that results in future unhappiness.
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites his nails, is a slanderer,
or is impure, quickly goes to destruction.
One should not engage in censurable conversation, nor should one wear a garland outside [the house].
Riding on the backs of cows is in every way condemned.
One should not enter an enclosed village or house except through the gate;
and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar.
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
One should not eat anything mixed with sesame after the sun has set;
nor should one sleep naked here, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one shall attain a long life.
He should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
he should not look at feces or urine, nor should he cross a river by means of his arms.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds, nor cotton seeds, nor husks.
One should not live together with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Caṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with the lowest castes, nor with those who dwell at the outskirts.
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for a sacrifice;
one should not instruct him in the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow to him.
For he who teaches him the Dharma and he who prescribes a vow sink together with him into the darkness called *asaṃvṛta*.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without using water.
One should avoid seizing others by the hair and striking them on the head;
moreover, having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess a slaughterhouse, a wheel, or a tavern banner, nor from those who live by prostitution.
A cart is equal to ten slaughter-houses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a brothel is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten brothels.
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is a terrible thing.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in due course, go to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava,
the Kālasūtra hell, and Mahānaraka as well.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana,
Saṃhāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pratimūrtika.
The iron spike, the parched husks, the path, the river Śālmalī,
the forest of sword-leaves, and the iron bristles.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire their own welfare after death do not accept gifts from a king.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha,
as well as the bodily hardships rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Having risen and performed the necessary duties, having purified himself and composed his mind,
he should stand for a long time reciting prayers during the morning twilight, and likewise at its proper time during the evening twilight.
By virtue of their long observance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), the seers (*ṛṣis*) attained long life,
as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Having performed the Upākarma ceremony according to the rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being self-controlled, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.
Under the Puṣya asterism, a twice-born man should perform the external ceremony of the suspension of Vedic study;
or he may do so when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon.
Having thus performed the formal dismissal of the Vedic hymns outside according to the scriptures,
he should cease recitation for a "bird-night" (a night with its two flanking days), that is, for one full day and night.
Henceforth, being self-restrained, he should recite the Vedic hymns during the bright fortnights,
and he should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night, one should not sleep again while still fatigued.
A twice-born man who is disciplined should daily recite the Veda composed in meters and the sacred texts (Brahman) composed in meters, except in times of distress.
One who is studying should always avoid these occasions when study is forbidden,
as should one who is teaching disciples according to the prescribed rule.
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when it stirs up clouds of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when great meteors fall,
there shall be a suspension of study for the remainder of the day.
One should know that when these [omens] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should recognize it as a time unfit for study; likewise, when clouds appear out of season.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, the suspension of study shall last as long as the light remains; for the remainder of the night, it is as during the day.
For those who desire proficiency in dharma, there shall always be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, as well as wherever there is a foul odor.
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a low-caste person (vṛṣala),
nor while there is weeping, nor in a crowd of people.
While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine,
while impure from food, or after eating at a śrāddha feast, one should not even mentally contemplate [forbidden things].

Having accepted an invitation to an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the period of impurity following the death of a king or an eclipse of Rāhu.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of food offered at a funeral remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should he not recite the Veda.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food from a house where a birth or death has occurred.
In mist, at the sound of an arrow, during both twilights, on the new moon day, the fourteenth day, the full moon day, and the Aṣṭakā festivals; Mn 4.113.
The new moon day destroys the teacher, and the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the eighth day and the full moon day destroy the Veda; therefore, one should avoid those days.
A twice-born man should not recite [the Veda] during a rain of dust, when there is a conflagration of the quarters, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, or camels are barking in a row.

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a funeral rite (śrāddha).

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a śrāddha ceremony, upon touching that, there is a suspension of study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth.
One should know that there is no study for the remainder of the day when a village is harassed by thieves, when there is a panic caused by fire, and during all extraordinary portents.
On the occasion of the Upākarma and the Utsarga, a suspension of study for three nights is prescribed;
on the Aṣṭakās, however, it lasts for a day and a night, as does the suspension on the nights marking the end of the seasons.
One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant;
nor in a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when food has turned sour.
Nor should one study without having first obtained permission from a guest, while a strong wind is blowing,
or when blood flows from the body due to a wound inflicted by a weapon.
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of the Sāmaveda is being heard;
nor after having completed the study of the Veda, nor after having studied the Āraṇyaka.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda is human;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as pertaining to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure.
Knowing this, the learned daily first practice the extraction of the essence of the three Vedas in sequence, and afterwards they study the Veda itself.
If any of the following— cattle, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat—
should pass between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is a suspension of study for a day and a night.
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study:
an impure place for Vedic recitation and an impure self.
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth,
a twice-born Snātaka must always remain celibate, even during the period favorable for conception.
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king, a *snātaka*, an *ācārya*, a tawny person (*babhru*), or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should not intentionally step upon a body-scrub, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
For there exists nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world. (Mn 4.134)
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they appear weak.
For these three, when insulted, may utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
One should not despise oneself because of former failures;
until death one should seek prosperity and should not consider it unattainable.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood—this is the eternal dharma.
One should say "bhadram, bhadram" (well-being, well-being), or simply say "bhadram";
one should not engage in groundless enmity or dispute with anyone.
One should not travel too early in the morning, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not travel with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts (vṛṣala).
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those devoid of learning, those advanced in age, those lacking beauty or wealth, or those of low birth.
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brahmin, or fire with his hand;
nor should one who is impure look at the hosts of luminous bodies in the sky during the day, even if he is otherwise healthy.
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily apertures without a specific reason;
he should avoid touching all the hairs on his body, especially those of the private parts.
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should daily recite prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness.
For those who are devoted to auspicious conduct, who are always self-restrained,
and who constantly engage in recitation and burnt offerings, no misfortune exists.
One should constantly study the Veda at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty (*dharma*), while any other is called a secondary duty (*upadharma*).
Through constant study of the Veda, through purity, and indeed through austerity—
And by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Remembering his former birth, he practices the Brahman once again;
and through the constant practice of the Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss.
One should constantly perform the Sāvitra and Śānti oblations on the Parvan days;
and one should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days.
One should discharge urine far from one's dwelling, far from the water used for washing the feet,
and likewise far from the place where leftover food is disposed of.
One should perform the application of unguents, bathing, cleaning the teeth, and applying collyrium,
as well as the worship of the deities, only during the forenoon.
On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his teachers.
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart.
One should, unwearied, always practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma and is properly established in one's own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes of suffering, being diseased and short-lived.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
Whatever action depends upon another, that one should avoid with effort;
but whatever depends upon oneself, that one should practice with diligence.
"Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering."
Whatever action brings satisfaction to his inner self while he performs it, that he should perform with diligence; but he should avoid the opposite.
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities;
one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness.
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike them down;
however, one may strike both a son and a pupil for the sake of their correction.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [a Brahmin] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in evil wombs.
A man who, through lack of wisdom, causes blood to flow from the body of a Brāhmaṇa who is not fighting,
incurs very great suffering after death.
For as many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth,
for so many years shall the shedder of that blood be devoured by others in the next world.
Therefore, a learned man should never threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood,
and who is constantly devoted to violence— this man does not prosper in happiness in this world.
Even if he suffers for it, he should not, out of righteousness, turn his mind toward unrighteousness;
for he quickly perceives the downfall of those who are unrighteous and sinful.
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
however, turning back slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.

If [the fruit of unrighteousness] does not fall upon oneself, it falls upon one's sons; if not upon the sons, then upon the grandsons; but an unrighteous act committed never fails to bear fruit for the doer.
By unrighteous means one prospers for a time, and thereafter sees auspicious results;
then one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes along with their very roots.
He should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and he should instruct his pupils in accordance with the Dharma, restraining his speech, his arms, and his stomach.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness; and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future unhappiness or is censured by the world.
He should not be fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, nor crooked; he should likewise not be fickle with his speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others.
By that path by which his fathers have gone, and by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm.
With officiating priests, family chaplains, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with children, the elderly, and the sick; and with physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
One should not engage in dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants.
By renouncing disputes concerning these, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati;
but the guest is the lord of Indra’s world and of the world of the gods, as are the officiating priests.

Sisters-in-law are the kinsmen of the world of the Apsarases; maternal uncles and mothers are the kinsmen of the world of the Viśvedevas; and relatives by marriage are the kinsmen of the world of the Waters on earth.
But those who are children, the elderly, the emaciated, and the sick should be known as lords of space;
an elder brother is equal to a father, and one's wife and son are one's own body.
One's shadow, one's own group of servants, and a daughter are the ultimate objects of compassion;
therefore, one should always endure being insulted by them without any feverish resentment.
Even if he is capable of accepting gifts, he should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, his Brahmanic luster is quickly extinguished.
Without knowing the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of gifts for various substances,
a wise man should not accept a gift, even if he is perishing from hunger.
But an ignorant man who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter is reduced to ashes like wood.
Gold, life-span, and food; land, a cow, and also fuel for the body;
a horse, sight, skin, clothing, clarified butter, splendor, and sesame seeds produce offspring.
But a twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study, and who delights in receiving gifts,
sinks along with that very recipient, like one in water using a boat made of stone.
Therefore, an ignorant man should fear every kind of acceptance;
for even by a very small amount, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat,
nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Veda.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three types of persons,
results in misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world.
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks,
so too do the ignorant giver and receiver sink to the bottom.
One who carries the banner of righteousness while being ever covetous, hypocritical, and a deceiver of the world;
such a person should be known as one who follows the "cat-vow," for he is violent and a betrayer of all.
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own self-interest, dishonest, falsely humble, and who practices the "heron-vow," is so called.
Those Brahmins who practice the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma,
concealing that sin with the vow while practicing deception upon women and Śūdras.
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda;
and a vow practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, being without the marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks,
takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the person who constructed the reservoir.
One who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given incurs a fourth part of the sin.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and in mountain clefts and springs.
A wise man should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not exclusively the observances (niyamas);
for by failing to perform the restraints while devoting himself solely to the observances, he falls.

A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one conducted by a priest who officiates for an entire village, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch.
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these people offer oblations;
it is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it.
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by a foot.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses,
pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog [is unfit for consumption].
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food announced for all to hear; the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned.
The food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer, one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, and one bound in fetters is forbidden.
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as sour gruel, stale food, and the leavings of a Śūdra.
The food of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, and of one who eats leavings;
the food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and that from which no one has sipped water for purification within ten days.
One should not eat meat that has not been honored, meat obtained for no purpose, the food of a woman who has no male relatives,
the food of an enemy, the food of a city, the food of an outcast, or food that has been sneezed upon.
The food of the slanderer and the liar, as well as that of one who sells the results of sacrifices, the food of an actor and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person; Mn 4.214 [215M]
Of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player,
a goldsmith, a bamboo-worker, and likewise a seller of weapons.
From those who keep dogs, from vintners, from a washerman, from a dyer,
from a cruel man, and from one in whose house a paramour resides.

And those who tolerate a paramour, as well as all those who are completely enslaved by women, and food from a deceased person within ten days of death, and that which is simply unsatisfying; [these one should avoid].
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
Regarding those others who have been declared in sequence as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise say that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
A learned twice-born man should not eat cooked food from a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha);
however, in the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night.
Having deliberated upon both the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer, the gods ordained that their food is equal.
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
the gift of a generous man purified by faith is [efficacious], while the other is destroyed by lack of faith."
One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with faith and without sloth;
for those performed with faith, using wealth acquired through righteous means, become inexhaustible.
One should constantly practice the duty of giving— both that which pertains to sacrifices and that which pertains to public works—
with a spirit of complete contentment, whenever one encounters a worthy recipient, according to one's ability.
Whatever may be asked for should be given without malice;
for there will arise a worthy recipient who delivers one from all [suffering].
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desirable offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision.
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow reaches the realm of the Sun.
The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
Of all gifts— water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter— the gift of the Veda is preeminent.
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift,
with that very same disposition one receives it back, duly honored.
He who accepts what has been honored, or he who gives what has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell.
One should not be proud of one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice;
even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, and having given a gift, one should not boast of it.
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride;
life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes through boasting of it.
One should gradually accumulate merit, like termites building an anthill,
