for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings.
For neither father nor mother stand by one in the next world for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman stands there—dharma alone remains.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone that of its evil deeds.
Having abandoned the dead body on the ground like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; Dharma alone follows him.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
Dharma swiftly leads that man who is devoted to righteousness, whose sins have been destroyed by austerity, to the radiant world beyond, where he possesses an ethereal body.
One who desires to lead his family to eminence should always form connections with the most excellent people; he should avoid those who are inferior.
By approaching only the most excellent and avoiding the inferior, a Brahmin attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra.
Firm in action, gentle, self-controlled, and not associating with those of cruel conduct,
he who is non-violent and observes his vows shall conquer heaven through self-restraint and liberality.
One may accept from anyone fuel-wood, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered spontaneously, honey, and the gift of safety.
Prajāpati has declared that alms which have been brought forward and offered spontaneously, without being previously solicited, may be accepted even from one of evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat the offerings of that man for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, who treats her with contempt.
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or vegetables.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself must not be satisfied by that alone.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
he who seeks his own livelihood should always receive it from virtuous persons.
A partner in a business venture, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave,
and a barber— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Whatever his own nature may be, whatever he intends to do,
and how he would treat him, in that same manner he should present himself.
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is when among virtuous people is the greatest evildoer in the world; he is a thief who robs his own self.
All objects of speech are fixed; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals that speech is a thief of everything.
Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he may dwell having adopted an attitude of neutrality.
Alone, one should constantly reflect in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself;
for by reflecting alone, one attains the highest good.
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for the Brahmin householder,
as well as the auspicious ritual of the Snātaka vows, which increases one's inner strength.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from taint and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

Having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: The sages, having heard these duties of the Snātaka as they have been declared, spoke this to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire.
O Lord, how does death prevail over those Brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the Shastras? (Manu Smriti 5.2)
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen to the fault by which Death seeks to slay the Brahmins."
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of proper conduct,
laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms,
as well as anything originating from impure substances, are not to be eaten by the twice-born.
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions, and the śelu fruit, and the colostrum of a cow.
In vain are *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, milk-rice, and cakes; likewise, meat that has not been consecrated, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations.
The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals,
that of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died— [these are forbidden].
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo, the milk of females is to be avoided; likewise, all things that have turned sour must be shunned.
Among sour substances, curd is edible, as is everything produced from curd,
and those [liquors] which are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those that dwell in villages,
unmarked single-hoofed animals, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the domestic cock,
the sārasa, the rajjuvāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic creatures, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish; Mn 5.14.
Whoever eats the flesh of another is called an eater of that being's flesh;
since an eater of fish is an eater of all kinds of flesh, one should therefore avoid fish.
The pāṭhīna and rohita fish are the first to be prescribed for offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
likewise, all rājīvas, siṃhatuṇḍas, and scaled fish are permitted.
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown,
nor all five-toed creatures, even if they are specified among those permitted for consumption.
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and likewise the hare—
they say these are the edible five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel.
Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock,
an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste].
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining forbidden foods, one should fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, the penance for food known [to be forbidden] is specifically greater.
Excellent wild animals and birds may be killed by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sake of maintaining their dependents; for Agastya did so in ancient times.
For even in ancient sacrifices and in the rites of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) consisted of the meat of wild animals and birds. (Manu Smṛti 5.23)
Whatever food, whether hard or soft, is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured, may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as may whatever remains from an oblation.
Even if it has been kept for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, are pure when not mixed with oil, according to the twice-born.
Thus has been declared in its entirety what may and may not be eaten by the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.

One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged according to the rule [in a sacrifice], or indeed when life is in danger. (Manu Smṛti 5.27)
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa):
both the immobile and the mobile; everything is the sustenance of the vital breath.
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs;
the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave.
The eater does not incur guilt by eating edible creatures day after day, for both the eaters and the creatures to be eaten were created by the Creator himself. (Manu Smṛti 5.30)
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine rule; but any practice other than this is called the demonic rule. (Manu Smṛti 5.31)
Having purchased it oneself, or having produced it, or even having received it as a gift from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors.
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when there is no distress;
for having eaten meat contrary to the rule, he is helplessly devoured by those very creatures after death.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain.
But that man who, being duly appointed, does not eat meat according to the rule,
goes after death to the state of a beast for twenty-one births.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras.
In times of distress, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the victim, or likewise with a victim made of flour;
but one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death after death in future births.
"Beasts were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."
Herbs, animals, trees, and likewise crawling creatures and birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher rebirths once again.
"Manu has declared that animals may be killed only in the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods; not elsewhere."
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animal to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
One should know that the violence ordained by the Veda, which is restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings, is indeed non-violence; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or dead.
He who does not desire to inflict bonds, death, or afflictions upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever he meditates upon, whatever he performs, and wherever he fixes his delight—
that he attains without effort, provided that he harms nothing whatsoever.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the manner of a Piśāca,
does not fail to attain popularity in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are considered slayers.
There is no doer of more demerit than he who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another, without having first worshipped the ancestors and the gods.
He who should perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots or by eating the food of hermits, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'flesh-ness' (māṃsatva) of flesh."
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
for these are the natural inclinations of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit.
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased as well as the purification of objects,
for all four castes, duly and in their proper order.

When a child dies after the eruption of teeth, or after the performance of the tonsure ceremony, all relatives remain impure; the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka). Impurity on account of death (śāva) is prescribed for ten days among the sapinda relatives.
Until the collection of the bones has taken place, [the impurity lasts] for three days or for one day alone.
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka (a kinsman by water) continues as long as the birth and the name are not unknown.
Just as this impurity on account of death is prescribed for the sapinda relatives,
so too should it be in the case of birth for those who desire complete purity.
For all others there is impurity due to death (śāva), but for the mother and father there is birth-impurity (sūtaka).
The birth-impurity belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing an ablution.
But having emitted semen, a man becomes pure simply by sipping water;
however, due to the connection arising from the seed, he should observe impurity for three days.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three periods of three nights;
those who offer water for the deceased are purified after three days.
A disciple who performs the funeral rites for his deceased teacher becomes pure after ten nights, together with those who carry the corpse.
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
when her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who has become soiled by it is purified by bathing.
For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, purification is declared to take one night;
but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights.
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside the village,
having adorned it, upon pure ground, but without performing the collection of bones.
For him, neither the rite of cremation with fire nor the water libation should be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should observe impurity for only three days.
The water-rite for one who has not reached three years of age should not be performed by his relatives;
or they may perform it once a tooth has appeared, or when the naming ceremony has been completed.
If a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin) has died, purification is prescribed after one day;
however, for those who share the same funeral water (ekodaka), purity is held to be attained after three nights from the time of birth [of the deceased].
In the case of women who have not been consecrated [by marriage], the kinsmen on the husband's side become pure after three days;
however, the uterine relatives become pure according to the very rule already stated.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, they should immerse themselves in water for three days,
they should not consume meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground.
This rule regarding impurity on account of death has indeed been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure should be understood as applicable to relatives and kinsmen when one is absent.
But he who hears that one staying in a foreign land has died within ten days shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights.
When ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed,
a man becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.
If a child, a person residing in another country, or one who has established a separate household dies,
one becomes pure immediately after immersing oneself in water along with one's clothes.
If death and birth should occur again within ten days,
a Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period of ten days has not yet elapsed.
When a teacher has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise for his son and his wife, it is settled that the impurity lasts for a day and a night.

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has been received as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights; likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, the impurity lasts for a night with its two surrounding days (pakṣiṇī).
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm remains impure for as long as the light [of the sun or moon] lasts;

but if the king is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), the impurity lasts for a full day, as does the same period when a teacher (*guru*) who is well-versed in the scriptures (*anūcāna*) has died.
A Brahmin becomes pure in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra becomes pure in a month.
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the ritual acts performed in the sacred fires;
and while performing those rites, even a kinsman does not become impure.
Having touched a public singer, a menstruating woman, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth,
a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always recite, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability.
Having touched a human bone that still has fat adhering to it, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if the bone is free of fat, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
The water-libation rite shall be withheld for those born of illicit unions, for those who persist in heretical ascetic orders,
and for those who commit suicide.
And for women who have resorted to heresy, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor. // Mn 5.90 [89M] //
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or preceptor who has passed away, one who is under a vow is not released from that vow.
One should carry out a dead Śūdra through the southern city gate;
but those of the twice-born castes should be carried out through the western, northern, or eastern gates, as appropriate.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions; for they always abide in the station of Indra, having become one with Brahman.
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high position;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], intended for the protection of his subjects.
And for those killed in a riot, by lightning, or by a king;
for the sake of a cow or a Brahmin; and for whomever the king may desire [to be so].
The king bears the form of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Appati, and Yama.
A king who is empowered by Lokeśa is not subject to ritual impurity;
for purity and impurity among mortals arise from and dissolve back into the worlds.
For one slain in battle with uplifted weapons while fulfilling the duty of a Kṣatriya, the sacrifice is immediately completed; such is the rule regarding the period of impurity.
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya by his mount or weapon;
a Vaiśya by his goad or reins; and a Śūdra, having performed his duties, by a staff.
O best of the twice-born, this purification regarding sapindas has been declared to you;
now learn the rules for the purification after death in the case of all those who are not sapindas.
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the kinsmen on his mother’s side.
If one eats the food of those [who have died], one is purified in ten days;
if one does not eat their food, one is purified in a single day, provided one does not dwell in that house.
If one follows a deceased person— whether a kinsman or a stranger— out of affection,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing with unguents,
wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Among all forms of purity, purity in respect to wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in respect to wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water.
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts, by charity;
those whose sins are concealed, by the recitation of prayers; and those most learned in the Vedas, by austerity.
That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman whose mind is defiled is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This determination regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.
The purification of luminous gems, as well as of all things made of stone,
has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth.
A gold vessel that is free from stains is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they have not been chemically treated.
Gold and silver were produced from the union of water and fire;
therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, or water.
For all liquids, purification is traditionally held to be straining;
for solid objects, sprinkling; and for wooden items, scraping.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* and *graha* cups is by washing.
The purification of the *caru* vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar, is performed with hot water.
For large quantities of grain and clothing, purification is prescribed by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is ordained.
The purification of skins is like that of cloth, and the same applies to articles made of split cane;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is held to be the same as that of grain.
Silk and woolen cloths are purified with alkaline salts; blankets of Kutapa wool with Aṛiṣṭaka fruits; fine linen cloths with Bilva fruits; and linen garments with white mustard seeds.
A wise person should effect the purification of conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory with either cow’s urine or water, just as one does for linen cloth.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again.
An earthen vessel that has been touched by intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, spittle, pus,
or blood can never be purified even by baking it again.
The ground is purified by these five means: sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, sprinkling water, scraping, and the dwelling of cows.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed at,
or defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
In all purifications of objects, earth and water must be applied as long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart.
The gods ordained three things as pure for Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word.
Water on the ground is pure when it is sufficient to satisfy the thirst of a cow,
provided it has not been contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural odor, color, and taste.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the settled rule.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while it yields milk; and a dog is pure when catching deer.
Manu has declared that the meat of an animal killed by dogs is pure,
as is the meat of one killed by other carnivorous animals or by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and other bandits.
The apertures above the navel are all pure;
those below it are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body.
One should specify that flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch.
For the purpose of purifying the voiding of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken in appropriate quantities;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and sweat— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand,
and seven on both hands by one who desires purification.
This is the rule of purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always before studying the Veda and while eating food.
One who desires bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, a woman or a Śūdra should do so only once each.
For Śūdras who live according to the law, a monthly shaving of the head must be performed;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and they may eat the remnants of the food of the twice-born.
The principal [limbs] do not become defiled by food-particles that fall upon them;
nor do drops that fall on the body [render one impure]; nor do beard-hairs that have entered the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth.
Drops that touch the feet of one who is giving water for rinsing to others are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
If one who holds something in his hand is somehow touched by leavings,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that object down.
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply sip water, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruths,
and having drunk water— even if already pure— one who is about to study should sip water.
The entire rule for purification and likewise the cleansing of objects has been declared to you for all social classes; now learn the duties of women.
Neither by a girl, nor by a young woman, nor even by an aged woman should any action whatsoever be performed independently, even within the home.
In childhood, she should remain under the authority of her father; in youth, under that of her husband; and when her husband has died, under that of her sons. A woman must never enjoy independence.
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or her sons;
for by being separated from them, she would bring reproach upon both families.
She should always remain cheerful, be skillful in household duties, keep the utensils well-maintained, and be not wasteful in expenditure.
To him whom her father or her brother— having obtained the father's consent—
may give her, she should serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him.
For their sake, at the wedding, rites for prosperity, auspicious ceremonies, and sacrifices to Prajāpati are performed;
however, the formal giving away of the bride is the cause of the husband's ownership.

A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with mantras is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife, both in this world and in the next, whether she is outside her season or during her fertile period.
Whether he be devoid of virtue, addicted to sensual pleasures, or destitute of good qualities,
a husband must always be attended upon by a virtuous wife like a god.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is exalted in heaven.
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should never do anything displeasing to him, whether he be living or dead.
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits;
but once her husband has died, she must not even utter the name of another man.
Until death, let her remain patient, self-controlled, and chaste,
longing for that supreme dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband.
Many thousands of brahmins who practiced celibacy from their youth have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for the continuation of their lineage. (Manu Smṛti 5.159)
When her husband has died, a virtuous wife who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who practice lifelong celibacy.
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband,
incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world.
No offspring born here belongs to another, nor does it belong to anyone else's possession;
for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere ordained.
She who, abandoning her own husband though he be inferior, resorts to one who is superior,
shall be censured in the world and is called "one who has had a previous husband."
But by being unfaithful to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
She who does not prove unfaithful to her husband through thought, word, or deed attains the world of her husband and is called a virtuous woman by the righteous.
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech,
and body attains preeminent fame in this world and the world of her husband in the hereafter.
A twice-born man who knows the law should have his wife— who has behaved in this manner, is of equal caste, and dies before him— cremated with the Agnihotra fire and the sacrificial implements.
Having offered the sacred fires to a wife who has died before him during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the marriage ceremony and likewise the re-establishment of the fires.
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life.

Having thus remained in the stage of the householder according to the rules, the twice-born who has completed his Vedic studies shall dwell in the forest, self-restrained and with his senses fully conquered, in the prescribed manner.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair,
and sees the offspring of his offspring, then he should resort to the forest.
Having abandoned village food and all his belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or together with her.
Having taken up the Agnihotra and the domestic implements for the sacred fires,
he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained.
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always bear matted hair, as well as a beard, body hair, and nails.
From whatever food he may have, he should offer a portion as a bali-oblation and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms.
He should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
he should always be a giver, never a receiver, and compassionate toward all living beings.
And he should offer the Vaitānika Agnihotra according to the rules,
not omitting the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices through the practice of yoga.
He should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsyas,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dakṣāyaṇa in their proper sequence.
He should separately prepare sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and oblations (caru) according to the rules, using pure forest foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons.
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities, he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots,
and fruits produced from pure trees, and oils derived from fruits.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the ground,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleśmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored,
as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a ploughshare, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor, even when distressed, should one eat roots and fruits grown within a village.
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what has ripened naturally in its own time;
he may be one who grinds with a stone, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may be one who washes his bowl immediately after a meal, or one who stores food for a month;
he may store it for six months, or even for a year.
He should eat food brought according to his ability either at night or during the day; or he may eat only at every fourth mealtime, or even at every eighth mealtime.
Or he may pass the bright and dark fortnights according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he may eat boiled barley-gruel once.
Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots,
and fruits that have ripened in their season and fallen of their own accord, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the times of the three libations.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity.
Performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing even more intense austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for objects of pleasure, observing celibacy, sleeping on the ground, having no sense of ownership over shelters, and making his dwelling at the foot of a tree; Mn 6.26.
He should collect alms sufficient for his journey from ascetics who are Brahmins,
and from other twice-born householders living in the forest.
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from the village,
receiving them either in the hollow of his hands, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd.
A Brahmin living in the forest should practice these and other initiations,
as well as various Upaniṣadic scriptures, for the sake of self-perfection.
These [sacrifices] are practiced by sages and brahmins who are householders for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity, and for the purification of the body.
Or, taking his stand upon the Aparājitā [direction],
he should proceed straight ahead until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air.
By abandoning the body through any one of these practices of the great seers,
a Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life wandering in the forests,
he should renounce all attachments and go forth as a wandering mendicant during the fourth part of his life.
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations and conquered his senses,
one who has grown weary of seeking alms and making offerings prospers after death by embracing the life of a wandering mendicant.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward.
Having studied the Vedas according to the rules, having procreated sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of his ability, he should direct his mind toward liberation.
A twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, without having procreated sons,
and without having performed sacrifices, desires liberation, goes to perdition.
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having consigned the sacred fires into his own self, a Brāhmaṇa may depart from his home to lead the life of a wandering mendicant.
For him who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, departs from his home to the mendicant life,
worlds consisting of splendor await that teacher of Brahman.
Since not even the slightest fear arises for the twice-born from living beings,
there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever for him who is liberated from the body.
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by sacred observances,
should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him.
One should always wander alone for the sake of perfection, without a companion;
seeing that perfection belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons it nor is he abandoned by it.
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling; he may resort to a village for the sake of food.
Indifferent, free from agitation, a sage whose mind is absorbed in the Supreme Being.
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, tattered garments, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages.
One should step forward with one's gaze purified; one should drink water filtered through a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure.
He should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone;
nor, depending upon this body, should he harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates.
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to worldly objects, and free from sensual desire,
he who seeks happiness should wander about in this world with himself alone as his companion.
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor through the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by means of instructions or discourses.
He should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants.
Having his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, not causing pain to any living beings.
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice.
A gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—
these, Svāyambhuva Manu has declared, are the vessels for an ascetic.
He should go for alms only once a day and should not be attached to an abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached even to sensual objects.
When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal,
and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms.

He should not be dejected when he gains nothing, nor should he rejoice when he gains something; he should take only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material possessions.
But he should utterly despise gains obtained through honor;
for even an ascetic who is already liberated becomes bound by gains obtained through honor.
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
he should restrain the senses when they are being carried away by their objects.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one is fit for immortality.
One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
Separation from those who are dear, union with those who are unpleasant,
being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases.
The departure from this body, the rebirth in a womb again,
and the paths of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs.
And [he understands] the connection with suffering for embodied beings arising from unrighteousness,
as well as the inexhaustible union with happiness arising from righteousness and purpose.
And by means of yoga, one should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self,
as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low.
Even if he is corrupted, one should practice dharma, devoted to whichever stage of life (āśrama) he may be in;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of dharma.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (Manu Smṛti 6.67)
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day,
he should always walk upon the earth after carefully scanning it, even when his body is exhausted.
Whatever living beings an ascetic unintentionally injures by day or by night,
for the sake of purifying himself from those acts, he should bathe and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), performed according to rule by a Brāhmaṇa and joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the highest austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted,
so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).
Through the yoga of meditation, one should perceive the course of this inner self among beings of high and low status— a course that is difficult for those of unrefined soul to understand.
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of such vision enters the cycle of transmigration.
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rites,
and the rigorous practice of austerities, they attain that state in this world.
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement.
One should abandon this abode of living beings, which is beset by old age and sorrow, a locus of disease and affliction, full of passion, and impermanent.
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so he who abandons this body is liberated from the crocodile of distress.
Having cast off his good deeds upon those dear to him and his evil deeds upon those not dear to him,
he attains the eternal Brahman through the yoga of meditation.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition,
then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death.
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments and being liberated from all dualities, he abides in Brahman alone.
All this that has been described here is indeed based on meditation;
for no one who is not self-knowing enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and whatever is declared in the Vedāntas.
This is the refuge for the ignorant, and this indeed for those who possess knowledge;
this is for those seeking heaven, and this for those seeking the infinite.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant according to this sequential method,
having shaken off all evil in this world, attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas;
now learn the yoga of action for those who have renounced the Vedas.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder.
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal.
And among all these, according to the injunctions of the Vedas and the Smṛtis,
the householder is declared to be the best, for he supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
even so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their support in the householder.
Moreover, this tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort by the twice-born belonging to all four stages of life.
Fortitude, forgiveness, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma and,
having studied them, live according to them, attain the supreme goal.

Having practiced the Dharma characterized by the ten marks with a concentrated mind and having heard the Vedānta according to the injunctions, the twice-born man, freed from his debts, should renounce the world.
Having renounced all ritual acts and dispelled the defects of action,
he should live happily under the authority of his son, self-restrained and devoted to the study of the Veda.
Having thus renounced all actions, intent upon his own duty and free from longing,
he destroys his sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal.
This fourfold duty of a Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you;
it is meritorious and yields imperishable fruit after death. Now learn the duty of kings.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how he may attain supreme success.
A Kṣatriya who has received the Vedic consecration according to the prescribed rule must protect all this [world] in accordance with justice.
For in this world without a king, everything would have fled in every direction out of fear;
therefore, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this.
Having extracted the eternal constituent parts of Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; of Agni and Varuṇa; and of Candra and Vitteśa, [he created Brahmā].
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods,
he therefore surpasses all beings in splendor.
Like the sun, he dazzles both the eyes and the minds;
no one on earth is able even to look directly at him.
By his power, he becomes fire and wind; he is the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma (Yama);
he is Kubera, Varuṇa, and Mahendra.
A king must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking "he is merely a human being," for he is a great deity dwelling in human form.
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the king’s fire, that fire of justice, consumes the entire family along with its livestock and accumulated wealth.
Having truly considered the task at hand, his own power, and the place and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-born Śrī, in whose prowess victory, and in whose anger death; for he is composed of all splendor.
But whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon that person's swift destruction.
Therefore, that king should apply the law toward those who are dear to him;
and he should not deviate from that law even when it concerns those who are not dear.
For its sake, the Lord formerly created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
Out of fear of him, all beings— both stationary and moving— submit to their enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties.
Having duly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of those involved],
he should appropriately apply these measures toward men who act unjustly.
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
Punishment governs all subjects; punishment alone protects them.
Punishment keeps watch while others sleep; the wise know punishment to be dharma.
When properly supported after due deliberation, he pleases all his subjects;
but when implemented without deliberation, he destroys them on every side.
If the king were not to tirelessly inflict punishment upon those deserving of it,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and likewise a dog might lick the oblation (havis);
there would be no ownership over anything, and the lower would prevail over the higher.
The whole world is kept in check by punishment, for a pure man is hard to find;
indeed, through fear of punishment, the entire world is fit for the enjoyment of life.
Even the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, birds,
and serpents are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when they are oppressed by the rod alone.
All social classes would become corrupted, all boundaries would be broken,
and there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks about, destroying evil,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts with circumspection, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who properly leads them.
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
however, one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by that very punishment.
For punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those who have not disciplined their souls;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.
He cannot be led by the right path by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect,
and attached to sensual objects.
Punishment can be effectively administered by one who is pure, true to his word, follows the scriptures, possesses good assistants, and is wise.
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward his enemies,
straightforward toward his friends, and full of forbearance toward affectionate Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he subsists by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered his own self,
his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water.
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are each established in their respective duties in due order.
Therefore, whatever must be done by him together with his servants while protecting the subjects,
all that I shall declare to you duly and in proper sequence.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon Brāhmaṇas who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and he should abide by their instruction.
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas.
From them he should constantly learn discipline, even though he is already disciplined himself;
for a king who is disciplined never perishes.
Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those dwelling in the forest have attained kingdoms through discipline.
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (Mn 7.41)
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he shall learn the triple knowledge (trayī), the eternal science of government (daṇḍanīti),
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the knowledge of the self (ātmavidyā), and the methods for undertaking the various means of livelihood (vārtā) from the people.
One should practice the discipline of conquering the senses day and night;
for only one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control.
One should strive with diligence to avoid these ten calamities arising from desire, as well as those eight born of anger, which all end in misery.
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived of them by his very self.
Hunting, gambling, sleeping during the day, slander, women, intoxication, the triple symphony [of song, dance, and music], idle wandering, and [vain] talk— this is the tenfold group born of desire.
Slander, violence, malice, envy, finding fault with others' merits,
and the harshness of speech and punishment constitute the eightfold group born of anger.
One should strive to conquer greed, which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these two groups arise from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting— one should know that this quartet is the most grievous among the set of vices arising from desire.
One should know that this triad— inflicting physical punishment, verbal abuse, and the misappropriation of property— is always grievous, even within the category of offenses born of anger.
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more grievous;
the man of vice sinks lower and lower, while the man free from vice goes to heaven when he dies.
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the scriptures, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone to accomplish, especially without assistance; how much more so the sovereignty of a kingdom, which brings great prosperity?
He should constantly deliberate with them on matters common to all, such as peace and war,
stability, revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired.
Having ascertained their respective individual intentions,
he should act for his own welfare in all matters concerning them collectively.
But the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brāhmaṇa among all his ministers.
Constantly placing his trust in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having deliberated with him, he may then undertake his work.
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.
He should appoint as many men— vigilant, skillful, and discerning— as may be required to accomplish his duties.
For their sake, he should employ those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth at the mines and in the workshops;
and those who are pure and timid within the inner apartments.
And he should appoint as his envoy one who is learned in all the scriptures,
who understands gestures, facial expressions, and movements, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth.
A messenger who is devoted, pure, capable, possessed of a good memory, knowledgeable of place and time, handsome, fearless, and eloquent is praised by kings.

The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of discipline depends on punishment; the treasury and the kingdom depend on the king; and peace and its opposite depend on the envoy.
For it is the messenger alone who unites those who are divided and indeed breaks apart those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are divided.
He should discern, through secret signs, gestures, and actions,
the king's facial expression, his intentions, his conduct, and what he desires to do regarding his undertakings and toward his servants.
Having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king,
he should apply such effort so that he does not bring suffering upon himself.
He should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, inhabited mostly by Āryas, free from turbulence, pleasant, with submissive vassals, and where a livelihood is easily obtained.
Having taken refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort, he should dwell in a city.
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for by its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Of these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, burrow-dwellers, and aquatic creatures;
the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods.
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress,
so too do foes not injure a king who has taken refuge in a fortress.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is ordained.
That [fortress] should be well-equipped with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles; it should also be provided with Brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water.
In its center, he should have a house built for himself that is spacious,
well-protected, pleasant in all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
Having entered upon that [stage], he should marry a wife of his own caste who possesses auspicious marks,
born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue.
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests;
they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires.
The king should perform various sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the Brahmins.
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from his kingdom by trusted agents;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward men like a father.
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry out their work.
He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this is declared to be the imperishable Brahman-treasure of kings.
Neither thieves nor enemies can carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, a king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brāhmaṇas.
It overflows not, it fails not, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices.

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward; to one who has studied the Vedas, it yields a hundred-thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields an infinite reward.
Indeed, according to the excellence of the recipient and the very nature of one's faith,
one enjoys the fruit of a gift— whether small or great— after death.
That which is given to a worthy recipient with faith, according to the rules regarding place and time, is the means for accomplishing dharma.
When challenged by those who are equal, superior, or inferior, a king protecting his subjects must not retreat from battle, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya.
Not retreating in battles, the protection of the subjects,
and service to the Brahmins constitute the supreme means for the welfare of kings.
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another and fight with all their might, never turning their backs, go to heaven.
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with barbed weapons,
nor with those that are hollowed, nor with those smeared with poison, nor with those whose points are blazing with fire.
One should not strike one who has climbed onto dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with joined palms;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours."

One must not strike one who is asleep, nor one who has laid aside his armor, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who is engaged with another.

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, one should not strike one who is afflicted by the loss of weapons, nor one who is distressed, nor one who is severely wounded, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has turned back.
But he who, being afraid, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies,
incurs all whatever evil deeds his master has committed.
Moreover, whatever merit he may have acquired for the sake of the hereafter,
the master takes all of that from one who has turned back and been killed.
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, cattle, women,
all types of property, and base metals— whatever anyone wins belongs to him.
And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which has been won by them collectively, not individually.
This is declared to be the eternal warrior-dharma, unadorned by artifice;
a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired,
increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
One should know that this fourfold [duty] is for the purpose of human goals;
one should perform its constant practice correctly and without sloth.
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired by force; one should protect what has been acquired with vigilance;
one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients.
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his manly prowess, always keep his secrets concealed, and always watch for the vulnerabilities of his enemy.
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds his rod of punishment uplifted;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod.
He should conduct himself with absolute sincerity and never by deceit;
being ever well-restrained, he should also recognize the deception employed by his enemy.
An enemy should not discover one's own weakness, but one should discover the weakness of the enemy;
like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own vulnerability.
One should deliberate on matters like a crane, display prowess like a lion,
snatch away like a wolf, and flee like a hare.
While he is thus victorious, he should bring all those who stand as his adversaries under his control by employing means such as conciliation and the rest.
If, however, they do not abide by these [means], he should gradually bring them under control by force alone, using the first three expedients.
Among the four means of policy, conciliation and so forth, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom.
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain,
so should the king protect his kingdom and slay those who stand as obstacles.
That king who, out of delusion, exhausts his own kingdom through neglect shall,
before long, fall from both his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen.
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
He should constantly employ this ordinance for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness.
He should establish a military outpost (gulma) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages],
and likewise he should organize the collection of taxes for hundreds of villages throughout the kingdom.
He should appoint a lord of a village, and likewise a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and also a lord of a thousand.
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults that have arisen in the village to the leader of ten villages;
the leader of ten should report them to the leader of twenty.
The lord of twenty, however, shall report all that to the lord of a hundred;
and the lord of a hundred villages shall himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Whatever is to be given daily by the village inhabitants to the king,
such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth, the village headman (grāmika) shall receive those.
The collector of ten should enjoy the produce of one family, and the collector of twenty, five families;
the superintendent of a hundred villages should enjoy a village, and the lord of a thousand, a city.
Indeed, another minister of the king, who is affectionate and vigilant, shall oversee their village affairs as well as their individual matters.
And in every city, he should appoint one overseer of all affairs,
occupying a high position and possessing a formidable appearance, like a planet among the stars.
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through spies.
For the king's appointed guardians are generally deceitful servants who seize the property of others; he should protect these subjects from them.
Those of evil intent who seize wealth solely from litigants,
the king shall confiscate all their property and carry out their banishment.
The king should daily provide maintenance and a place of residence for women engaged in work and for servants, according to their respective tasks.
A paṇa is the wage for the lowest servant, and six paṇas for the highest;
likewise, clothing is given every six months, and a droṇa of grain every month.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of their goods, the king should cause the merchants to pay taxes.
Having considered how the king and the performer of actions may both be joined with their respective fruits, the king should always apportion taxes in his kingdom accordingly.
Just as water-creatures, young calves, and bees consume their food little by little,
so should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is small and small.
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
and an eighth, a sixth, or even a twelfth part of grain.
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
And of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and wickerwork;
of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone.
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling in his kingdom perish from hunger.
In whose kingdom a learned Śrotriya perishes from hunger,
his entire realm likewise perishes from hunger before long.
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son.
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king,
by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase.
The king shall cause even the common people in his realm who live by trade to pay some small amount known as a tax at the end of the year.
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month.
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one harms both oneself and them.
The lord of the earth should be both stern and mild, having regard for the task at hand;
indeed, O King, one who is both stern and mild is held in high esteem.
When exhausted by overseeing the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the law, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth.
Having thus performed all these duties incumbent upon himself,
he should protect these subjects, remaining both disciplined and vigilant.
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—
even though he looks on with his servants— he is dead and does not truly live.
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed rewards is truly united with righteousness.
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications and composed himself,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with words of blessing;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended to a mountain ridge, or having gone to a secluded place,
or in a forest free from undergrowth, he should deliberate in secret, unobserved.
That king whose secret counsel ordinary people do not discover, even when they have gathered together,
enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of treasure.
At the time of reciting the mantra, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, animals, the very aged, women, barbarians, the diseased, and the deformed.
Those who are despised, as well as animals and especially women, disclose a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue,
he should reflect upon virtue, pleasure, and wealth, either together with those [who share his aims] or alone.
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory,
the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons.
He should likewise attend to the dispatching of envoys, the remaining matters of business,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of his secret agents.
He should also truly understand the eightfold business in its entirety, the five classes [of spies],
as well as loyalty and disloyalty, and the conduct of the circle of states.
He should diligently ascertain the conduct of the middle king, the activities of one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy.
These constituent elements are, in brief, the foundation of the circle of states;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
The five others known as ministers, the kingdom, the fort, the treasury, and the army—these have each been described briefly; thus, they total seventy-two.
Immediately after [the enemy], one should know the one who serves the enemy;
immediately after the enemy, the friend; and beyond those two, the neutral party.
He should win over all of them by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation,
whether used individually or collectively, as well as through personal prowess and statesmanship.
He should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking protection.
Having carefully considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting encampment, marching, peace, and war, as well as double-dealing and seeking protection.
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds;
likewise, marching forth and sitting encamped are two-fold, as is the practice of seeking refuge.
When the undertaking of the journey is common, as well as when it is the opposite,
then that alliance, joined with future prospects, should be known as having two characteristics.

War is declared to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of accomplishing a purpose, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged because of an injury inflicted upon a friend.
When an urgent matter arises by chance, marching alone or together with an ally— these two types of marching are prescribed.
When one's own resources have gradually diminished, whether due to fate or by one's own prior actions,
or out of regard for a friend— these are recorded as the two types of neutrality (āsana).
The maintenance of both the army and the master for the sake of accomplishing the objective is declared to be of two kinds as "duplicity" by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy.
Seeking refuge with the virtuous for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose when oppressed by enemies is considered to be of two kinds.
When he perceives that his own superiority in the future is certain,
while the suffering in the present is slight, then he should resort to peace.
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly well-pleased,
and likewise considers himself to be in a state of great preeminence, then he should wage war.
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit,
and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe.
But when he is utterly depleted of both mounts and troops,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating his enemies.
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then,
having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose.
But when he becomes most vulnerable to attack by the forces of his enemies,
then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king.
One should constantly serve with all efforts that king who subdues both his subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would a preceptor.
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from seeking refuge,
he should engage in fair battle itself without hesitation.
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his allies,
neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him.
He should examine the future course of all undertakings as well as their immediate results, and he should consider the merits and defects of all past actions according to their true nature.
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present,
and who understands the remaining tasks from the past, is not overcome by enemies.
He should arrange everything in such a way that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not gain the upper hand over him; this is the summary of political strategy.
Then the lord should mount his vehicle toward the enemy's kingdom;
at that time, he should proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this rule.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition,
or toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra, according to his strength.
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory,
he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for his enemy.
Having performed the ritual at the root [of the tree] and the journey-related rites according to rule, and having secured a dwelling place and properly stationed spies; Mn 7.184 [185M]
Having cleared the threefold path and his own sixfold power,
he should march against the enemy's city according to the rules for a campaign of war.
One should be especially vigilant regarding a friend who serves the enemy and one who remains hidden;
likewise, one who has gone abroad and returned is a most dangerous foe.
He should proceed along that road in a staff-like array, or in a cart-like array,
or in the form of a boar, a crocodile, a needle, or a Garuda.
From whatever direction he anticipates danger, in that direction he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus array.
The commander-in-chief and the army supervisor should station themselves in all directions;
and from whichever direction he suspects danger, that he should designate as the "east."
And he should station trusted troops as outposts on all sides—
men who are skilled in both their positions and in battle, who are fearless and steadfast.
One should make a small number of troops fight in a compact formation, but one may extend a large number at will;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy lands;
with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground.
He should station men from Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena,
