as well as those who are tall and those who are short, at the front lines of the army.
Having arrayed his army, he should encourage it and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of the enemies as they fight.
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain encamped and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly spoil his supply of fodder, food, water, and fuel.
He should break down tanks as well as walls and moats;
he should launch a surprise attack upon him at night and likewise cause him terror.
He should instigate those who can be sowed with dissension and remain ever vigilant regarding their actions;
when fate is favorable, he who desires victory should fight, free from fear.
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension— either collectively or individually— but never by means of war.
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two combatants,
as is defeat in battle, one should therefore avoid war.
If even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible,
he should fight in such a manner that, being well-prepared, he may conquer his enemies.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties.
But having understood the intended purpose of all these [claimants] in brief,
he should install there a member of that [deceased's] lineage and establish a formal agreement.
And he should establish authoritative legal codes for them according to the duties as they have been declared;
and he should honor him with precious gifts together with the leading men.
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving causes pleasure;
at the proper time, the practice of acquiring desired objects is highly commended.
All this action depends upon the two ordinances, the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists the possibility of action.
Human activity, when undertaken according to the divine ordinance,
achieves its purpose despite great hardship.
Even when joined with destiny, if it is devoid of human effort,
the field yields fruit only through human effort.
The moon, the sun, and other planets, as well as wind, fire, and water,
are brought about here through destiny and through human effort with diligence.
Or, being prepared, he may even march together with him after having diligently made a treaty, perceiving one of the three kinds of fruit: an ally, gold, or land.
Having carefully considered the rear-attacker and likewise the ally within the circle of states,
one should obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy.
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of gold and land as he does by gaining a firm friend who, though currently weak, is capable of future success.
One who knows the Dharma, is grateful, and is naturally contented;
who is devoted, firm in his undertakings, and light—such a person is praised as a light friend.
The wise declare it a hardship to have for an enemy one who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, capable, generous, grateful, and steadfast.
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, compassion, great-souled munificence, and the constant arising of the qualities of an indifferent person; // Mn_7.211[215M] //
A king should unhesitatingly abandon even a land that is secure, productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for his own sake.
One should save wealth for times of distress; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth.
Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together,
the wise man should employ every possible means, both those that are combined and those that are separate.
Relying upon these three— the seeker, the goal to be sought, and all the means in their entirety— one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king,
after exercising himself and bathing at midday, shall enter the inner apartments to eat.
There, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be led astray, and who have used mantras that remove poison.
He should apply all substances that counteract poison as antidotes;
and, remaining self-controlled, he should always wear gems that destroy poison.
And women who have been thoroughly examined, whose dress and ornaments are pure, and who are well-composed, should touch him with fans, water, and incense.
One should exert effort in this manner regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food;
likewise in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment.
Having eaten, he should indeed enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments;
but having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again reflect upon his duties.
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the armed men again,
as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should, while bearing his weapon, listen within the inner apartments to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people,
he should enter the inner apartments again for the purpose of eating, surrounded by women.
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments,
he should go to bed at the proper time and rise free from fatigue.
A healthy lord of the earth should observe this rule;
but when he is unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
But when the king desires to inspect legal cases, he should enter the court modestly, accompanied by Brahmins as well as ministers who are experts in counsel.
Seated there, or even standing, with his right hand raised and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he shall examine the legal affairs of the litigants.
Every day, they shall be recorded separately according to the eighteen titles of law, based on reasons observed in local custom and those found in the scriptures.
Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given.
The non-payment of wages, the breach of a compact, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and his herdsman; Mn 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes; verbal and physical assault;
theft; violence; and the abduction of women.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—
these are the eighteen titles of law established here in this world.
In these matters, he should decide the legal cases of men who are mostly engaged in disputes by relying upon the eternal Dharma.
But when the king himself does not personally attend to the investigation of legal cases,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to investigate those cases.
Surrounded by three members of the assembly, he should examine his judicial duties,
having entered the foremost court while either seated or standing.
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together,
along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly to be a court of Brahmā.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, appears before an assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (Manu Smṛti 8.12)
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is just;
for by neither speaking nor speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the court look on, there the judges themselves are slain.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, one must not violate Dharma, lest violated Dharma destroy us.
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed the Bull (vṛṣa); the gods know him who treats that Dharma with contempt as a Vṛṣala; therefore, one should not violate the Dharma.
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even in death;
for everything else surely perishes along with the body.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are also released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (Manu Smṛti 8.19)

One who lives merely by his birth may, if he so desires, be called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇabruva) and serve as the king's instructor in dharma; but a Śūdra shall never under any circumstances be so.
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while he looks on.
That kingdom which consists mostly of Śūdras, is overrun by atheists, and is devoid of the twice-born,
perishes quickly, afflicted by famine and disease.
Having occupied the seat of justice, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed,
he should begin the examination of legal cases after bowing to the guardians of the world.
Having understood both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
through their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, eyes, and movements.
By outward forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his minority.
The same protection should be afforded to women who have no sons,
to those whose families are extinct, to women devoted to their husbands, and to widows who are afflicted by illness.
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still living,
a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the penalty prescribed for thieves.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that time the king may take it for himself.
He who says, "This is mine," shall be questioned according to the rule;
after verifying the form, number, and other characteristics, the owner is entitled to that property.
One who fails to report the place, time, color, appearance, and size of a lost item exactly as they are, deserves a fine equal to the value of that object.
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king may take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of property lost and then recovered.
Property that has been lost and then found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch therein, he shall have them executed by an elephant.
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth,
or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very deposit.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the lord of all.
If a king should discover an ancient treasure buried in the earth,
he shall give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury.
The king is entitled to a half-share of ancient treasures and minerals found in the earth, for he is indeed the lord of the soil.
The king must restore to all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds,
and the laws of families, should establish the specific duty (svadharma) for each.
Men who perform their own duties, even when living at a distance,
become dear to the world when they remain steadfast in their respective occupations.
Neither the king himself nor his official should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood,
so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference.
Abiding by the rules of legal procedure, he should examine the truth, the matter at hand, himself, the witnesses, the place, the appearance, and the time.
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men,
that he should establish for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not contradictory [to the sacred law].
When urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering the debt,
the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount proved to the creditor.
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own property,
by those very means he should constrain the debtor and compel him to pay.
One should recover a debt that has been lent by means of legal process, by artifice, by customary conduct,
and by force as the fifth.
A creditor who recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own.
But if the debtor denies the debt, yet it is proved by evidence,
the judge shall compel him to pay the creditor's claim and a small fine according to his ability.
When the debtor denies the debt in the assembly after being told "Pay it," the plaintiff must point out the place [of the transaction] or specify another means of proof.
He who points out what should not be pointed out, he who denies after having pointed it out, and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows; Mn 8.53.
Furthermore, he who, having stated a matter and what is to be stated, subsequently evades it;
and he who, when questioned, does not acknowledge a matter that has been correctly proposed.
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when questioned, or he who runs away; Mn 8.55.
If, when told "speak," he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said,
or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that account.
If a person, having said "I have witnesses," when told "Produce them," fails to produce them,
the judge shall declare him defeated on these grounds.
If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall be bound and punished according to the law;
if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated.
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or whatever amount one may state falsely,
both of those ignorant of the law shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount.
But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth while remaining steadfast, denies the charge,
must be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins.
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be appointed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them.

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, are worthy of being called as witnesses when summoned for a legal matter, but no others except in times of emergency.
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be appointed as witnesses in legal matters;
they must be knowers of all dharmas and free from greed, while those who are the opposite should be avoided.
One should not appoint as witnesses those who have a financial interest in the matter, nor friends, nor allies, nor enemies;
nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt.
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), nor one who dwells in a religious order (*liṅgastha*), nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments.
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is mute, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an elderly man, nor a child, nor one who is alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties.
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane, nor oppressed by hunger and thirst;
neither one afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by lust, nor angry, nor even a thief [should be questioned].
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men;
virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes.
But whoever, being a witness to the facts, should give testimony for litigants within a house, in a forest, or even when there is a threat to life; Mn_8.69.
In the absence of a woman, the work may be performed by a child, an elderly person,
a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant.
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, the sick, and those who testify falsely, as well as that of those with agitated minds, is unstable.
In all cases of violence, theft,
and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely.

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, O King, the ruler should accept the majority; but if the numbers are equal, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those of equal virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.
Testimony is established through seeing in person and likewise through hearing;
by speaking the truth therein, a witness does not fall away from merit or wealth.
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men concerning anything other than what was seen or heard goes headlong to hell after death and is excluded from heaven.
Even where one has not been formally appointed, if one should see or hear anything at all,
even when questioned there, one should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard.
A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but not women, even if they are many and pure;
for the intellect of women is unstable, and others as well who are tainted by defects [should be excluded].
Whatever they may say by their very nature should be accepted as conventional practice;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is useless.
When the witnesses have arrived in the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, the judge shall examine them with this procedure, addressing them with conciliatory words.
Whatever you know of each other’s mutual conduct regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for you two possess the status of witnesses here.
A witness who speaks the truth in his testimony attains abundant worlds;
he also gains unsurpassed fame in this world—for this speech is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking falsely in testimony, one is bound tightly by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred future births, rendered powerless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
A witness is purified by truth; righteousness increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self;
do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
Evil-doers think, "No one sees us," but the gods see them, as does their own inner self.
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, Yama, wind, night,
the two twilights, and Dharma are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings.
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth during the forenoon, while they face either the north or the east.
One should question a Brāhmaṇa with "Speak! a Kṣatriya with "Speak the truth!";
a Vaiśya with [threats regarding] his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra with all [the aforementioned] sins.
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the killer of women and children,
and for the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful— those shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely.
O gentle one, whatever merit you have performed since birth—
all that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, "I am alone"— this sage, the witness of merit and sin, is eternally situated within your heart.
If you have no dispute with that god Yama Vaivasvata who resides within your heart,
then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty,
he who gives false testimony shall go blind to the house of his enemy.
He who, when questioned during a legal determination of dharma, speaks falsely, shall go headlong into the blind darkness of hell as a sinner. (Manu 8.94)
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts or what he has not personally witnessed, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man.
For the gods know no other man in this world to be more excellent than that learned man whose inner self (kṣetrajña) does not harbor suspicion when he speaks.
Hear now, gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely when giving testimony in a lawsuit.
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men.
He who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
he destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a falsehood concerning land.
They say that [the property of] women in their enjoyment and sexual intercourse, as well as in water, in aquatic gems, and in all things made of stone, is like [the property of] land.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and as it was seen, straightforwardly.
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, traders, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers as one would Śūdras.
When a man speaks thus regarding matters of law, even though he knows otherwise, he does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods.
In a case where the death penalty would otherwise be prescribed for a Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Brāhmaṇa, a falsehood should be spoken; for that is superior to the truth.
And they should worship Sarasvatī with oblations of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to Vāc and the Viśvedevas,
effecting the highest expiation for that sin of untruth.
Or he may offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses whose deity is the waters.
If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth of the total amount.
If, within seven days of the testimony being given,
sickness, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall the witness, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine.
But in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot ascertain the truth in reality, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath.
Great seers and gods have taken oaths for the sake of a particular purpose;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Paijavana.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death.
In matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cattle, fuel,
and in providing assistance to Brahmins, there is no sin in taking an oath.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the [great] sins.
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should make him touch the heads of his son and wife separately.
He whom kindled fire does not burn, whom water does not cause to float,
and who does not quickly meet with misfortune, should be known as pure in his oath.
For in ancient times, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother,
the fire— the watcher of the world— did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness.
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be overturned; what has been done shall be as if undone.
Testimony is declared to be false when given out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, desire, anger, as well as from ignorance and childishness.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any of these cases.
For taking through greed, he should be fined one thousand; for taking through delusion, the first amercement;
for taking through fear, two middle amercements; and for taking through friendship, four times the first amercement.
From lust, the first [penalty] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold;
from ignorance, it is two full hundred; but from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony to be for the purpose of ensuring that justice does not fail and for the restraint of unrighteousness.
A righteous king, having punished them with fines, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the Self-existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
in these cases involving the three [lower] castes, a Brāhmaṇa may depart unhurt.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body itself.
Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature,
and having considered the strength of the offender and the gravity of the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it.
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame;
it also prevents access to heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it.
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it,
incurs great infamy and goes to hell.
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal chastisement.
But when he is unable to restrain them even by execution,
then he may employ all these four measures against them.
I shall now declare in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold which are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions.
That minute particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is declared to be the first of measurements, known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight *trasareṇu*s should be known as one *likṣā* in measurement;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*.
Six mustard seeds make one medium-sized barleycorn; three barleycorns make one kṛṣṇala;
five kṛṣṇalas make one māṣa; and sixteen of those make one suvarṇa.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together are to be known as one silver *māṣaka*.
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute one *purāṇa*;
furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, or a *paṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure to consist of four *suvarṇas*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred should be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest.
When a debt is admitted as due, the debtor deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, the fine is double that—such is the ordinance of Manu.
A moneylender may stipulate an interest that increases his wealth as ordained by Vasiṣṭha;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month.
Or, remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two per cent;
for by taking two per cent, he does not become a sinner through wealth.
One may take two, three, four, five,
or ten percent as the monthly interest, according to the order of the social classes.
But one shall not receive interest on a secured loan if it remains with the debtor due to negligence;
nor, because of the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge.
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge.
Both an open deposit and a sealed deposit do not suffer from the lapse of time;
however, if they remain for a very long period, both may be forfeited.
When used with mutual consent, these do not perish at any time:
a milch cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal employed as a beast of burden.
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while he is present and remains silent, he is not entitled to recover it.
If the owner is not an idiot and is not a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another, that [ownership] is subverted by the legal proceeding; the enjoyer deserves that property.
A mortgage, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not perish through adverse possession.
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must relinquish half of the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.
Interest on a loan, when collected at one time, shall not exceed double the principal;
for grain, fruit, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount.
An interest exceeding the legal rate, or one that is excessive, is not valid;
they call that the path of usury, for [the law] allows only five per hundred.
One should not take interest exceeding that for a year, nor that which is not sanctioned;
[the types of interest are] compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and corporal interest.
He who is unable to pay the debt and wishes to enter into a new transaction shall,
after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond.
Without showing the gold, he may exchange it right there;
he ought to pay as much interest as has accrued.
One who has ascended to the increase of his circle of territory, being established according to place and time,
shall not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the proper place and time.
Those who are skilled in sea-voyages and who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose establish whatever rate of interest; that shall be the rate for the recovery of the loan in that case.
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance,
he shall pay that debt from his own property to the creditor if he fails to produce him.
A son is not liable to pay for a suretyship, a frivolous debt, what is owed for gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
if a surety for payment dies, the judge should compel even the heirs to pay.
But if the debtor does not pay, and the surety—who was known for his wealth—is deceased, by what means may the creditor subsequently seek to recover the debt? (Manu 8.161)
But if the surety has been assigned wealth and possesses sufficient funds, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one for whom wealth has been assigned.
A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, or dependent, or by a child, or by an elderly person, or one that is otherwise invalid, is not established.

Even if a statement is well-established, it does not constitute truth if it is spoken contrary to the established facts regarding external objects, except in the case of conventional usage. (Manu Smṛti 8.164)
Whatever is mortgaged, sold, given, or received through fraud,
or where one perceives any deceit, all that he shall annul.
If the borrower should have perished while the expenditure was made for the sake of the family,
that debt must be paid by his kinsmen from their own property, even if they are divided.
Whatever transaction even a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family,
whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it.
"Manu has declared that all matters effected by force— whether given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force— are as if they were not done at all."
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a surety, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.
A king, even when impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be.
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death.
From the enjoyment [of taxes], from the blending of castes, and from the protection of women, the strength of the king arises; he prospers both in this world and after death.
Therefore, like Yama himself, the master should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
and conduct himself with the impartial manner of Yama, having conquered anger and subdued his senses.
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, performs his duties unrighteously,
will soon be brought under control by his enemies.
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives matters according to righteousness—
toward him the subjects turn, as rivers flow toward the ocean.
He who reports to the king a creditor who is recovering his debt by his own will shall be made to pay a fourth part of that amount to the king, and the debt itself to the debtor.
A debtor should repay the creditor in a manner consistent with his own occupation;
one of equal or lower caste may pay at once, but one of superior caste should pay it gradually.
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of resolution the legal matters of men disputing with one another, as established by the evidence of witnesses.
A wise man should entrust a deposit to one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable.
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as the delivery was, so shall be the recovery.
If one who is asked for a deposit does not return it to the depositor,
he shall be questioned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with trustworthy persons endowed with age and physical appearance, and under various pretexts; Mn 8.182.
If he should restore it exactly as it was deposited and in the same condition as it was made,
there exists nothing therein for which he may be prosecuted by others.
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he shall be seized by both parties and compelled to pay; such is the settled law.
A deposit (*nikṣepa*) and a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must never be handed over to a next-of-kin;
for these two are lost in the event of his misfortune, but they are not lost if no misfortune occurs.
But if one should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased,
he must not be prosecuted by the king nor by the kinsmen of the depositor.
He should seek that object with honesty and with affection;
or, having investigated the man's conduct, he should settle the matter through conciliation alone.
In all these cases of deposits, this same rule shall apply regarding their recovery;
however, in the case of an ocean-deposit, one shall receive nothing if the depositary does not produce it from that [ocean].
If he has not taken anything for himself from it, he need not give what has been stolen by thieves, swept away by water, or burnt by fire.
One should seek out the thief of a deposit, as well as the person who did not actually entrust it,
by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths.
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having made a deposit—
both of these should be punished like thieves, or compelled to pay a fine equal to its value.
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit (upanidhi), without distinction.
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should seize the property of another,
shall be put to death publicly with various modes of execution along with his accomplices.
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; one who declares otherwise deserves punishment.
That which has been given as a gift privately, or accepted privately, must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back.
In such cases, the king shall make a decision regarding both deposited wealth and that which was entrusted out of friendship, without causing hardship to the holder of the deposit.
One who sells another's property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, should not be admitted as a witness; for he is a thief, even if he considers himself no thief.
He shall be liable to forfeit [the property] along with his family and pay a fine of six hundred [paṇas];
if he has no connection [to the owner] and no excuse, he shall incur the guilt of a thief.
But a gift or a sale made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings.
Where enjoyment is seen but no source of income is seen anywhere, there the source of income is the cause [of the enjoyment], not the enjoyment itself; such is the established rule.
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family members,
he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified.

Now, if the root source of the property cannot be recovered, but it has been cleared by means of a public sale, the seller is not to be punished by the king and is released; the original owner recovers his wealth.
One thing mixed with another does not deserve to be sold;
nor that which is worthless, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is concealed at a distance.
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom,
Manu has declared that he may marry both for a single bride-price.

A giver who has previously declared the defects of a maiden—provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not had sexual intercourse—is not subject to punishment. (Manu Smṛti 8.205)
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty,
a share proportionate to his work must be given to him by the co-performers.
If, after the sacrificial fees have been distributed, a priest neglects his own duty,
he shall receive his entire share and have the work performed by another.
In whatever rite specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, that very person shall receive them; or alternatively, all [the priests] may share them together.
The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the kindling of the fires;
the Hotṛ may also take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma].
Among all [the priests], the chief ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that;
those entitled to a third receive a third part, and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part.
When men here join together to perform their respective duties,
the apportionment of their shares must be determined according to this rule.
If one has given wealth to someone who asks for it for the sake of a religious duty (dharma),
but that wealth subsequently turns out not to be used for such a purpose, then that gift should not have been given to him.
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed, he shall be made to pay a fine of one suvarṇa by the king; that shall be the expiation for his theft.
Thus has been declared the lawful manner of non-repayment for what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
If one who has been hired, though not ill, fails through arrogance to perform the work as it was prescribed,
he shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas* and his wages shall not be paid.
But one who, having been ill, performs the work once he has recovered, shall receive his wages exactly as stipulated from the beginning,
even after a long period of time.
As it has been said: "Whether he be distressed or healthy, if a person does not perform that work, his wages must not be paid, even if the work is only slightly incomplete. (Mn 8.217)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate agreements.
A man who, having made a formal agreement with a village, a district, or a guild by means of truth,
should break that agreement out of greed— he the king shall banish from the realm.
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the compact to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one royal śatamāna.
A righteous lord of the earth should apply this rule of punishment to those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies.
If, after having purchased or sold anything, one should have remorse regarding it,
he may return that object or take it back within ten days.
But after ten days, one should neither give nor cause to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be fined six hundred by the king.
But for him who gives away a girl who has defects without disclosing them,
the king himself shall impose a fine of ninety-six paṇas.
But that man who, out of malice, declares a maiden to be non-virgin without demonstrating any fault in her, shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (Manu Smṛti 8.225)
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are established for maidens alone;
they are never for non-maidens among men, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites.
The mantras used at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of a wife;
their completion, however, should be understood by the wise to occur at the seventh step.
In whatever matter one may feel remorse after it has been done,
one should establish that person on the path of righteousness according to this procedure.
I shall now duly declare, according to the principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock.
If the safety and security [of the cattle] are maintained otherwise, the keeper shall be held accountable; by day, the liability rests with the keeper, and by night, with the owner or his household.
A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be the wages for a herdsman if he receives no other pay.
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place,
or if it has failed through lack of human effort, the keeper alone shall make it good.
If the cattle have been stolen by thieves after being proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his master at the proper place and time.
When animals have died, one should give their ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinews, and gallstones to the owners, and show them the identifying marks.
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman.
If, among those cows being kept and grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should spring upon and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
The common pasture ground (parīhāra) around a village shall be one hundred bows on all sides, or three throws of a yoke-pin;
for a city, it shall be three times that amount.
If animals should damage grain that is not enclosed there,
the king shall not inflict punishment upon the keepers of the animals.
One should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it,
and one must block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass.

On a path, in a field that is enclosed, or at the edge of a village, the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas] for the cattle; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unattended.
But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter;
however, in all cases, a sixth part must be given to the owner of the field—this is the settled rule.

Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods— whether they have a keeper or are without a keeper— provided it has not passed ten days since their birth.
In the event of a transgression by the owner of the field, the fine shall be ten times his share;
however, if it occurs through the negligence of the servants, the fine for the owner of the field shall be half of that.
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions committed by owners of cattle, the animals themselves, and their keepers.
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages,
one should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible.
And he should plant boundary trees— banyan, sacred fig, and kiṃśuka trees,
as well as silk-cotton trees, sal, palmyra, and milky-sap trees.
By means of thickets, various bamboos, śamī trees, creepers, and level ground,
as well as reeds and clusters of kubjaka shrubs, the boundary is not lost.
Ponds, wells, large tanks, and springs.
He should establish administrative offices and temples at the junctions of the boundaries.
And he should cause other boundary marks to be made concealed,
having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries.
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand; Mn 8.250.
And whatever objects of this kind the earth might consume over time,
those he should cause to be placed inconspicuously at junctions and on boundaries.
By these signs, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king should determine the boundary between two disputing parties.
If there were doubt even when the boundary marks are visible,
the decision in a dispute over a boundary would depend solely on the testimony of witnesses.
In the presence of the village families and the two litigants themselves, witnesses should be questioned regarding the boundary marks at the border.
But having questioned them, he should establish the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, and he should record all of them by name.
Bowing their heads to the earth, wearing garlands and red garments,
they shall lead him with justice, having sworn oaths by their own meritorious deeds.
Those who lead [the case] according to what has been stated are purified as witnesses of truth;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
In the absence of witnesses, however, four villagers residing in the neighboring villages,
being purified, shall determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
But in the absence of neighboring witnesses within the boundary of the original inhabitants,
he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests.
Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers,
snake-catchers, gleaners, and other forest-dwellers.
Whatever those witnesses may declare as the boundary markers at the junctions of the borders,
the king shall establish that accordingly between the two villages in accordance with the law.
The determination of boundaries for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors.
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary,
the king shall punish each of them individually with the middle amercement.
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.
When a boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, who knows the law, shall assign land to some [claimants] based on their relative benefit; such is the settled rule.
Thus has the law regarding the determination of boundaries been declared in its entirety;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya deserves either fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
In the case of an equal caste among the twice-born, the fine for a transgression is twelve [paṇas];
in the case of unspeakable disputes, that same fine shall be doubled.
But one of low birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin.
But for one who pronounces their name or caste with malice,
a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
If he gives instruction on the Dharma to Brahmins out of pride,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
One who, out of arrogance, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, occupation, or even their body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas.
Whether one speaks of someone as being one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly impaired— even if the statement is true— one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa.
One who slanders his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher.
A wise king should impose punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (Manu Smṛti 8.276)
In the case of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes,
the administration of punishment shall be carried out according to the truth, excluding only the cutting off of limbs.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault.
If a person of the lowest caste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu.
Raising his hand or his staff, he deserves the cutting off of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of that foot.
One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of a superior caste shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be gashed.
If one spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both his lips to be cut off;
if he urinates [upon him], his penis; and if he passes wind [against him], his anus.
If someone seizes him by the hair, he shall cut off both hands without hesitation;
likewise if they seize him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished.
The punishment for injuring any of the forest trees should be inflicted in proportion to their utility; this is the established rule.
When an assault is committed against humans or animals,
the king shall inflict a punishment that corresponds exactly to the magnitude of the suffering caused.
And in the case of crushing a limb, or likewise in the case of a wound or blood,
he shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery or even the full fine.
He who destroys the property of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
shall give satisfaction to that person and pay an equal amount to the king.
For leather articles, leather goods, and objects made of wood or clay,
as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
They say there are ten exceptions for the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle; in any other case, punishment is ordained.

When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction, and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheel of the vehicle; Mn 8.291.
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a yoke, a thong, or a rein, nor for shouting "Get away! [to avoid an accident].
If a vehicle turns off its course due to the driver's negligence,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas.
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the punishment;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred.
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot,
he should cause the death of living beings, the punishment there is not to be deliberated upon.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is as swift as that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, and horses, it is half [of that].
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
but for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.
A wife, a son, a slave, a servant, and a uterine brother,
when they have committed an offense, may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one must strike on the back of the body, and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief.
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for determining the punishment of a thief.
A king should exert the greatest effort in the suppression of thieves;
for by suppressing thieves, his fame and his kingdom increase.
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of honor;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is ever-increasing, with the gift of fearlessness as its fee.
A sixth part of the merit from all righteous deeds accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of the demerit from unrighteousness accrues to him who fails to protect.
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—
the king becomes entitled to a sixth part of that through his proper protection.
Protecting all beings according to the law and causing those deserving of death to be executed, the king performs sacrifices every day with sacrificial fees of hundreds and thousands.
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls,
shares of produce, and fines, shall immediately go to hell.
They say that a king who does not protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part of the produce as tax,
is the remover of the entire impurity of all the world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, one who fails to protect his subjects, and one who devours them, is destined for a downward course.
One should diligently suppress the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment.
For by the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are purified by sacrifices.
A lord who seeks his own welfare must always forgive those litigants who revile him,
as well as children, the elderly, and the sick.
He who endures insults when he is tormented by others is exalted in heaven because of that;
but he who does not endure them out of pride goes to hell because of that.
A thief must go to the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I have done this deed; punish me."
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron rod; Mn 8.315.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from the guilt of theft;
however, by failing to punish him, the king incurs the sin of the thief.

The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
But he who draws a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who breaks a water-station,
shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place.
For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times the value and restore that property to its owner.
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments, death is the punishment when the amount exceeds one hundred.
But for an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for any remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially women,
as well as for the theft of the most precious gems, one deserves the death penalty.
In the case of the theft of large animals, weapons, or medicine,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, for piercing them with a knife,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, the punishment of half a foot must be carried out immediately.
Of thread, cotton, and fermenting agents; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass.
For the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, as well as salts, and likewise for the theft of earthenware, clay, or ashes; Mn 8.327.
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter,
of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
For other such intoxicating drinks, for boiled rice,
and for all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value.
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, trees,
and other things that have not been threshed, the fine shall be five kṛṣṇalas.
When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been cleaned,
the fine shall be one hundred panas for a first offense, and fifty panas if it is a repeated offense.
An act committed by force with the owner's presence is *sāhasa* (robbery);
but it becomes *steya* (theft) when committed in the owner's absence, as well as when one takes something and denies having done so.
But the king shall punish first that man who steals these prepared articles, as well as he who would steal the fire from the house.
With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against men,
that very limb the king shall remove as a deterrent.
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—
none who does not abide by his own duty is beyond the king's punishment.
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, there the king should be fined one thousand; such is the settled rule.
For a Śūdra, however, the guilt in the case of theft becomes eightfold;
for a Vaiśya it is sixteenfold, and for a Kṣatriya, thirty-twofold.
For a Brahmin, it shall be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he is one who knows both the faults and the merits of those [offenses].
Manu has declared that wood from trees, roots and fruits, firewood for the sake of the sacred fire, and grass for the fodder of cattle, are not subject to the charge of theft.
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given,
even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching, is exactly like a thief.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be punished.
One who binds those who are not bound, releases those who are bound,
and seizes the slaves, horses, and chariots of others, shall incur the guilt of a thief.
By suppressing thieves according to this rule,
a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, undecaying fame should not overlook a man of violent deeds even for a moment.
The perpetrator of violence— whether through harsh speech, theft, or indeed by physical assault—
is to be known as the worst among evildoers.
But that king who tolerates one who persists in violence quickly goes to destruction and incurs hatred.
Neither for the sake of a friend nor due to the acquisition of vast wealth should a king release those who act with violence,
for they bring fear to all living beings.
The twice-born may take up arms when their duty is obstructed,
and during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time.
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin, provided he acts according to dharma.
One may indeed kill, without hesitation, an assailant who approaches, whether he be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin.
In the killing of an assassin, there is no fault whatsoever for the slayer, whether it be done openly or in secret; the wrath merely encounters that [assassin's] wrath.
The king, having punished with terrifying punishments those men who have set out to violate another's wife, shall banish them.
For from that arises the intermixture of castes among people,
by which unrighteousness, destroying the very root, leads to total destruction.
A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife,
having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement.
But he who, having never before been accused, speaks out for a valid reason,
shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part.
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a wilderness, in a forest,
or even at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery.
Courting, dalliance, touching her ornaments and garments,
and even sitting on the same bed— all this is recorded as adultery.
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, consents to it,
it is all considered *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) when there is mutual consent.
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected most carefully.
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women without being restrained.
One who has been forbidden should not engage in conversation with the wives of others;
however, if he converses despite being forbidden, he deserves a fine of one suvarṇa.
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away.
But he who engages in conversation with such women,
or with female slaves who eat only a single meal a day, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine.
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in status, shall not suffer death.
One should not cause a maiden who is associating with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one who is serving an inferior man should be kept confined in the house.
A man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
however, if her father so desires, he may have intercourse with a woman of equal caste upon paying a bride-price.
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
shall have two fingers instantly cut off and deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
One who violates a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who violates an unwilling one— namely, the cutting off of his fingers—
but he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas to prevent a recurrence of such conduct.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod.
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head,
or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being led away on a donkey.
But a woman who, arrogant on account of her kinsmen or her virtues, violates her husband,
the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public assembly.
One should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they shall pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire.
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise for cohabiting with a *vrātyā* woman or a *caṇḍālī*.

A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the twice-born castes—whether she be guarded or unguarded—is deprived of his limb if she was unguarded, and of his entire property if she was guarded. If she was guarded, he is deprived of everything.
A Vaiśya shall be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya shall be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman,
the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred and the Kṣatriya one thousand.
But both of them, having committed adultery with a protected Brāhmaṇa woman,
shall be punished like Śūdras or burnt in a fire of straw.
A Brahmin who approaches a protected Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand;
he who has sexual union with one who consents shall be fined five hundred.
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa that ends with his life;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends with their lives.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is guilty of every possible crime;
one should banish him from the kingdom with all his property intact and his body unhurt.
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive of his execution in his mind.
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a guarded Vaiśya woman,
both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman.
A Brahmin, however, approaching guarded women of the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya castes, should be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Śūdra woman, the punishment for both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya shall indeed be one thousand.
If a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, the fine shall be five hundred;
however, the Kṣatriya should prefer either having his head shaved with urine as a mark of punishment or paying the fine.

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
no perpetrator of violence, and no one who strikes with a staff, shares the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm brings universal sovereignty for a king among his kinsmen and bestows glory upon him in the world.
If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—
provided that each is capable of the task and free from fault— the punishment for both shall be one hundred [paṇas] each.
Neither a mother, nor a father, nor a wife, nor a son deserves to be abandoned.
One who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their caste, shall be fined six hundred by the king.
When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties,
a king who desires his own welfare should not pronounce a legal decision himself.
Having honored these men according to their merit along with the Brahmins,
and having first pacified them with gentle words, the king should establish them in their own duty.
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor at a festive meal for twenty Brahmins, provided they are worthy, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.
If a learned Śrotriya does not feed another virtuous Śrotriya at auspicious rites,
he shall be made to pay double the value of that food and one māṣaka of gold.
One who is blind, one who is mentally deficient, one who moves about on a board, and one who is seventy years old or older,
as well as one who renders service to those learned in the Vedas, shall not be made to pay tax by anyone.
The king should always honor a learned Vedic scholar, those afflicted by disease or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous.
On a smooth board made of Śālmalī wood, a washerman shall wash clothes gently;
he shall not rub one garment against another, nor shall he let them dry together.
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread increased by one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he should be made to pay a fine of twelve [paṇas].
Those skilled at customs houses and expert in evaluating all types of merchandise shall fix the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax.
If one, out of greed, exports those articles that are either famous or prohibited for the king, the king shall confiscate his entire property.
One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
Having investigated the arrival, departure, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he shall regulate their purchase and sale.
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed,
the king should publicly perform the formal offering of the guest-water (argha) for these [offenders].
All weights and measures must be clearly marked;
they should be re-examined every six months.
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
an animal and a woman, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half of a quarter.
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
empty vessels and men without luggage shall pay whatever little they possess.
On a long journey, one should know that a ford may exist at a particular place and time on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such fixed sign for the ocean.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as an ascetic,
a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those wearing the marks of a religious order, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing.
Whatever on a boat may be damaged through the negligence of the boatmen must be made good by those very boatmen, having assembled together from their own respective shares.

This has been declared as the decision regarding legal disputes for those traveling by boat: in the case of water damage caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment; however, in the case of an act of God (such as a storm), there is no liability.
He should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and he should cause the Śūdra to perform service for the twice-born.
A Brāhmaṇa should support out of compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties.
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of greed and by virtue of his power, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will,
he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
But a Śūdra, whether purchased or even unpurchased, one should compel to perform service;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (Manu 8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave by food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given, one inherited from ancestors, and one enslaved as punishment— these seven are the origins of slavery.
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
A Brāhmaṇa may confidently take property from a Śūdra, for he has nothing that is his own; indeed, his wealth is to be taken by his master.
He should cause the Vaiśya and the Śūdra to perform their own duties with diligence; for if these two deviate from their respective duties, they would throw this entire world into disorder.
Day by day he should inspect his works and his vehicles, as well as his fixed income and expenditure, his mines, and his treasury.
Thus, by settling all these legal disputes, the king,
having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal.
I shall declare the eternal duties of a man and a woman who abide in the path of dharma, both in their union and in their separation.
Women must be kept under subjection day and night by their own men; and if they become attached to sensual pleasures, they must be restrained within their own control.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is censurable; a husband who does not approach his wife is censurable;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is censurable.
Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest of opportunities for misconduct;
for if they are not protected, they will bring sorrow upon two families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes,
husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they are weak.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma.
The husband, having entered his wife and become an embryo, is born here again;
for that indeed is the "jāyātva" (the state of being a wife) of the wife, because he is born from her again.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of offspring, one should guard women with great effort.
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded through the application of these following means.
He should employ her in the collection and expenditure of wealth,
as well as in cleanliness, religious duties, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils.
Those women who, though confined at home by trustworthy male guardians,
protect themselves by their own efforts, are truly well-protected.

Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at inappropriate times], and dwelling in another's house—these are the six things that corrupt women. (Manu Smṛti 9.13)
They do not examine their appearance, nor do they consider their age;
whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Due to their proclivity for men, their fickle-mindedness, and their natural lack of affection,
these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world.
Having thus understood their nature as born from the creation of Prajāpati,
a man should apply the greatest effort toward their protection.
Manu ordained for women the use of beds and seats, ornaments, as well as desire, anger, dishonesty, ignobility, a malicious disposition, and misconduct.
"There is no ritual action for women with sacred mantras; such is the established rule in the Dharma.
For women are devoid of spiritual faculties and are without mantras; it is settled that they are untruthful."
And likewise, many Vedic verses have been sung even in the Nigamas;
listen now to their expiations for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics.
"May my father take that seed which my mother, wandering about unfaithful, lusted after"— this is the scriptural illustration for this.
Whatever undesirable thing she meditates upon in her mind for the sake of her husband,
this is declared to be the proper expiation for that transgression.
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, such qualities she acquires, just as a river does when it merges with the ocean.
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerability through union with Vasiṣṭha;
and Śāraṅgī, through Mandapāla, reached a state worthy of honor.
These and other women in this world, though born of low origin,
have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives.
Thus has been declared the auspicious conduct for men and women in their worldly life, which yields happiness both in this world and after death; now learn the duties concerning progeny.
For the sake of procreation, highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
there is no difference whatsoever between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) within households.
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born,
and the daily conduct of worldly life— woman is visibly the foundation for all this.
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme pleasure depend upon the wife;
likewise, heaven for one's ancestors and for oneself is dependent upon her.
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body,
attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous.
But through infidelity with her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been proclaimed by the virtuous and by the great seers of old concerning a son.
They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict in the sacred texts regarding the progenitor.
Some say he belongs to the one who produces him, while others know him to belong to the owner of the field.
The woman is considered to be the field, and the man is considered to be the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings.
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised.
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed.
