Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time,
that very kind of seed grows there, manifested with its own inherent qualities.
For this earth is said to be the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any qualities of the womb during its growth.
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers arise here in various forms according to their own nature.
Rice, śāli rice, mung beans, sesame, beans, and likewise barley, as well as garlic and sugarcane, sprout according to their respective seeds. (Manu Smṛti 9.39)
That one thing is sown and another is produced is not logically tenable;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth.
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom,
and who desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a man should not sow seed in what belongs to another... (Mn 9.42).
Just as an arrow, once shot, vanishes from the sight of one who continues to pierce the air where it was struck,
so indeed does a seed sown in another's possession quickly perish.
Those who know the past recognize this earth as the wife of Pṛthu;
they say that the field belongs to Sthāṇuccheda and the deer to Śālyavān.
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have declared; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as being the woman. (Manu 9.45)
A wife is not released from her husband by means of sale or abandonment;
thus we know the law established of old by Prajāpati.
A share of inheritance is allotted but once; a daughter is given in marriage but once;
and one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once among the virtuous.

Just as one who begets offspring on cows, mares, female camels, slave-girls, buffaloes, she-goats, or ewes does not share in the ownership of that offspring, so it is likewise with the wives of others.
Those who possess seed but do not own a field, yet sow it in another's field,
never obtain any fruit of the crop that is produced there.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain.
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit.
But when no reward is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs clearly to the owner of the field; for the womb is more important than the seed.
But when this [seed] is given for the sake of the seed because of an agreement regarding the act,
both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers in it.
If seed carried by the current of a flood sprouts in someone's field, that seed belongs to the owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit.
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood.
Thus has been proclaimed to you the essential and the worthless nature of seed and womb;
hereafter I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress.
The wife of an elder brother is the teacher’s wife for the younger;
but the wife of the younger is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder. (Manu Smṛti 9.57)

An elder brother who approaches the wife of his younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of his elder brother— even if they are authorized by law— become outcasts, unless there be a time of distress.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized may obtain the desired offspring from her husband’s brother or from a sapinda relative.
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with clarified butter and remaining silent, shall procreate only one son at night, and never a second under any circumstances.
Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [duty],
seeing that the purpose of the appointment (niyoga) for those two is not fulfilled according to dharma.
But when the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been accomplished according to the rule,
the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law.

If those two, having been appointed, should act according to their own will by disregarding the prescribed rule, they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher.
A widow must not be appointed to another man by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal dharma.
Nowhere in the mantras used for marriage is the appointment [of a widow to her brother-in-law] mentioned;
nor is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules governing marriage.
For this practice, condemned as a law fit for beasts, was indeed proclaimed by learned Brahmins even among men while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
In former times, that foremost of royal sages, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social orders because his mind was struck down by lust.
From that time forward, virtuous men censure anyone who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring.
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this rule.
Having approached her according to the prescribed rule— she being clad in white garments and pure in her vows—
the two shall enjoy each other's company once at each menstrual period until the birth of a child.
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of falsehood regarding a human being.
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rule, one may abandon a bride who is blameworthy,
diseased, severely defiled, or who was offered through deception.
But if one should bestow a girl who possesses defects without having disclosed them,
he shall annul that gift of the evil-minded giver of the bride.
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's maintenance;
for a woman, even one of steadfast character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live observing the prescribed rules;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should subsist by means of blameless crafts.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be waited for eight years;
if for the sake of learning or fame, six years; but if for the sake of pleasure, three years.
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who shows him hostility;
after a year, however, he may take away her property and no longer live with her.
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings.
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen from caste, impotent, sterile, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the gift [of her hand]. (Manu 9.79)
A wife who drinks liquor, behaves improperly,
is hostile, is diseased, is injurious, or is constantly wasteful of wealth may indeed be superseded by another wife.
A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth;
one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately.
But she who is sickly, yet beneficial and endowed with good character, may be superseded only after obtaining her permission; she must never be treated with contempt.
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should depart from the house in anger,
must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family.
If a woman, though forbidden, should drink intoxicants even on festive occasions, or go to a public spectacle or assembly, she shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*.
If twice-born men marry women both of their own caste and of other castes,
seniority, honor, and the principal dwelling shall belong to them according to the order of their castes.
A wife alone shall perform the service of her husband’s body and his daily religious duties for all [the deceased husbands]; never one who is not of the same caste.
But he who, out of delusion, causes that [rite] to be performed by another woman belonging to his own caste while she is present,
is regarded as a Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla, exactly as previously described.
To one who is eminent, handsome, excellent, and worthy,
he should give his daughter according to the prescribed rule, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age.
A maiden may remain in her father's house even after reaching puberty until her death;
however, he must never give her in marriage to one who is destitute of good qualities.
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
but after this period, she may choose a suitable husband for herself.
If she obtains a husband on her own initiative when she is not being given away,
she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does he whom she obtains.
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself any jewelry belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brothers; if she should take it, she would be a thief.
One who takes away a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would overstep his rightful authority.
A man thirty years of age should marry a charming girl twelve years old;
or one twenty-four years old may marry an eight-year-old, if he is quick to falter in his religious duty.
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will;
doing what is pleasing to the gods, he should always support that virtuous woman.
Women were created for the sake of procreation, and men for the sake of continuing the lineage;
therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both husband and wife.
If the giver of the bride-price dies after the price has been paid for the maiden,
she should be given to the husband's brother, provided the maiden consents.
Even a Śūdra, when giving away his daughter, must not accept a bride-price;
for by accepting a bride-price, one performs a disguised sale of the daughter.
But this is what neither others nor other virtuous men have ever done:
that having promised something to one person, it is given again to another. (Manu Smṛti 9.99)
Indeed, we have never heard of such a thing even among our ancestors in former births:
the sale of a daughter under the guise of a price known as a "bride-price."
Let there be mutual fidelity until death;
this, in brief, should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife.
Likewise, once they have performed the marriage rites, the woman and the man should always strive so that,
even when separated from one another, they do not commit adultery.
This law concerning men and women, connected with pleasure, has been declared to you, as well as the acquisition of offspring in times of distress; now learn the law of inheritance.
After the father and mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the parents are alive.
The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father.
By the mere birth of a first-born son, a man becomes a father of a son and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he deserves everything.
He upon whom one pays off debts and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as born of desire.
The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father.
The eldest son causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is never censured by the virtuous.
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder should be honored like a mother and like a father; but he who does not behave as an elder should be respected merely as a kinsman.
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma.
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods;
half of that shall belong to the middlemost, and a fourth to the youngest.
Both the eldest and the youngest shall take their shares as prescribed;
those who are others than the eldest and the youngest shall have the middle portion of the property.
The first-born shall take the best of all kinds of wealth, as well as whatever is most excellent; and he shall also receive one choice item from every ten.
There is no share of the profits from their own occupations for those who have been supported;
however, something whatsoever should be given to the superior as a means of increasing his honor.
Thus, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should assign equal portions;
but if no preferential share has been set aside for them, this following shall be the allotment of shares.
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger brother, one and a half shares;
and the youngest brothers, one share each—thus is the law established.
But the brothers shall each separately give to their unmarried sisters a fourth part from their own respective shares; those who are unwilling to give it shall become outcasts.
He should never divide goats, sheep, or one-hoofed animals unequally;
however, it is ordained that goats and sheep may be divided unequally for the sake of the eldest alone.
If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law.
Subordination to the principal is not logically consistent with dharma;
the father is the principal in procreation, therefore one should honor him according to dharma.
If a doubt should arise as to how the division of property should be made in a case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife: // Mn_9.122 //
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
the others shall then take bulls inferior to that, according to their respective mothers.
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull as his sixteenth share;
thereafter, the remaining sons shall divide the rest according to their mothers—this is the settled rule.
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority according to their mothers; rather, seniority is said to be according to birth [from the father].
Even in the Subrahmaṇyā liturgical formulas, it is recorded that the invocation is made according to birth-order;
and among twins conceived together, seniority is declared to be determined by birth.
A sonless man may, according to this rule, make a daughter an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), with the agreement:
"Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the performer of my funeral rites."
In former times, Dakṣa himself, the lord of creatures, created these daughters according to this rule for the sake of increasing his own lineage.
With a joyful heart, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them all.
As one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take away the wealth?
Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the portion of the unmarried daughter;
and the daughter’s son alone shall take the entire estate of a man who dies without a son.
For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
In this world, according to the law, there is no difference between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for both of them were produced from the body of his own parents.
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
But if an appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without having borne a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation.

Whether she has been formally appointed or not, the maternal grandfather shall obtain as his son a grandson born to her from a husband of equal status; through that grandson, he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-existent One himself.
In this world, no distinction is established between a son's son and a daughter's son;
for even a daughter's son saves him in the hereafter, just like a son's son.
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to that father’s father.
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage.
An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father;
for the funeral cake follows the family name and inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives it to the wrong lineage.
Both the son of an unauthorized woman and the son obtained from the husband's brother by a woman who already has sons do not deserve a share; they are born of adultery and lust.
Even if a man has procreated on an appointed woman,
the son born contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to the paternal inheritance, for he was begotten by one who has fallen from his status.
A son born of a woman appointed for that purpose is considered equal to a legitimate son (aurasa); according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring.
He who takes charge of the wealth and the widow of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to that child.
If a woman, having been authorized by another, obtains a son from her brother-in-law or another [relative],
they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and begotten in vain.
This rule for the division of property among sons born of a single wife should be understood;
now learn the rule for those born of many wives of various castes from one man.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order of castes,
this rule for partition is ordained when sons have been born to them.
A ploughman, a bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house shall be given to the Brāhmaṇa as his preferential share, along with one principal portion from the inheritance.
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya wife two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya wife one and a half shares; and the son of a Śūdra wife shall take one share.
Or, having divided that entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the law should make a righteous partition according to this rule.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share.
Even if there be a virtuous son or even a wicked son,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya does not inherit property;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste for the twice-born may all divide the inheritance equally after giving a preferential share to the eldest.
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is prescribed, and no other;
those born of her shall share equal portions, even if there should be a hundred sons.
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has mentioned for men,
six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the bought son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
Just as one who attempts to cross the water with a bad boat obtains such a result,
so does one who attempts to cross the darkness by means of bad sons obtain such a result.
If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are joint heirs,
each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other.
The son born of the wife alone is the sole master of his father's wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood.
But when the legitimate son (aurasa) divides the paternal inheritance, he should give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share.
The two sons, the aurasa (legitimate) and the kṣetraja (soil-born), are sharers in the father's inheritance;
ten others, however, in their respective order, are sharers in the family name and a portion of the inheritance.
One should recognize as an *aurasa* (legitimate) son, belonging to the first category, that child whom he himself procreates upon his own consecrated wife.
A son begotten upon the wife of one who has died, is impotent, or is afflicted by disease, by a man duly authorized according to the sacred law, is known as a *kṣetraja* (son of the soil).
If, in times of distress, the mother or the father should give a son who is similar [in status] and with affection, accompanied by a libation of water, he is to be known as a *dattima* (given) son.
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults,
and who is endowed with the qualities of a son, is to be known as a *kṛtrima* (adopted) son.
But he who is born in a house and is not known to belong to anyone is one born secretly in the house; he shall belong to him whose wife gave birth to him.
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha*.
A maiden, however, who bears a son in secret within her father’s house,
one should call that child by the name *kānīna* (maiden-born), as he is produced from a maiden by one other than her husband.
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown,
the child belongs to the husband and is called "sahoḍha" (one taken with the bride).
But he whom one may purchase from his mother and father for the sake of offspring is his "bought son" (krītaka), whether he be similar or dissimilar [to the parents].
A woman who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, produces a son by her own will after marrying again, is called *paunarbhava*.
If she is still a virgin, or even if she has returned after having gone [to another],
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her husband from a second marriage.
He who, being deprived of his parents or abandoned by them without cause,
offers himself to someone, is known as one "given by himself" (svayaṃdatta).
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may, out of lust, procreate upon a Śūdra woman is called a Pāraśava,
because he is like a corpse (śava) while yet being carried across (pārayan).
Whether born of a Śūdra’s slave-woman or of his female slave, the son who is born shall, with the father’s permission, take a share; thus the law is settled.
The wise declare these eleven sons, beginning with the son of the field (kṣetraja) as previously described, to be substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites.
These sons born from the seeds of others who have been mentioned incidentally belong to the man from whose seed they were born, and not to any other.
Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father, even one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son.
If among all the wives of one husband even one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
In the absence of a superior [heir], an inferior one is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate.
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are the heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, as shall the brothers.
Water-offerings should be made for three; the offering of funeral cakes proceeds for three; the fourth is the giver to them; a fifth does not exist.
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda;
after him, it shall go to a sakulya, or else to the teacher or the pupil.
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs; thus the law is not violated.

The property of a Brāhmaṇa is eternally incapable of being seized by the king; such is the settled rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take their property when all [other heirs] are absent.
For one who has died childless, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage;
whatever property may have been acquired there, that one should bestow upon him.
But if two [sons] born of two [different men] should dispute over the wealth of their mother,
each shall take what belongs to his own father, and not the other.
But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally.
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection.

What is given before the nuptial fire, what is received from the father's or mother's family, and what is given as a token of affection; that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
That which was given as a post-nuptial gift (anvādheya), and that which was given by the husband out of affection—
this shall be the property of the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living.
Whatever property exists in marriages according to the Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Gandharva, or Prajapatya rites, it is held that upon the death of a childless wife, it belongs to the husband alone.
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, it is ordained that upon her death without offspring, it shall belong to her mother and father.
Whatever property may belong to a woman, however given by her father,
that shall be taken by his Brāhmaṇa wife, or it shall belong to their offspring.
Women should not make a disposal from the family property held in common by many,
nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their husband.
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their caste.
Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those blind from birth, the deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.
However, it is right for a wise man to give to all of them food and clothing according to his ability; for he who does not give becomes an outcast.
If, however, eunuchs and others should somehow have a desire for wives,
their offspring, having produced progeny, shall be entitled to the inheritance.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after the father has died,
the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning.
But if all those who were ignorant of the law should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the division there shall be equal; such is the settled rule regarding what is not ancestral property.
But whatever is his wealth acquired through learning shall belong to him alone;
the same applies to what was received from a friend, what was given at a wedding, and what was offered with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth,
shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence.
That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate,
being obtained by one's own effort, he is not obliged to give away against his will.
But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was not previously obtained,
he need not share that with his sons if he so desires, as it was acquired by himself.
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture in that instance.
If the eldest or the youngest [son] is deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them dies, his share is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having come together and being united, shall divide that property equally;
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers,
he shall forfeit his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings.

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should the eldest brother make a separate provision for himself without giving anything to the younger ones.
If there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who have not divided their inheritance,
the father must under no circumstances allot unequal shares to their sons.
But one born after the partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide it together with them.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.
When all debts and assets have been distributed according to the rule,
whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be divided equally.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women,
security of possession, and pasture lands are declared to be indivisible.
This division of property for you and the rule of procedure for sons—beginning with the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the others—has been declared; now learn the law concerning gambling.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the destruction of kings who rule the earth.
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them.
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called gambling (dyūta) in the world;
but that which is performed with animate beings should be known as betting (samāhvaya).
The king shall execute all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
Gamblers, actors, cruel men, those who adhere to heretical sects,
those engaged in forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers— he shall quickly banish from the city.
Existing in the kingdom as secret thieves of the king,
these men constantly afflict the virtuous subjects through their unlawful actions.
In a former age, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not practice gambling, even for the sake of amusement.
Whosoever man should practice such [an act], whether secretly or openly,
there shall be a discretionary punishment for him according to the king's will.
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra caste who is unable to pay a fine shall attain freedom from debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, should pay it gradually, little by little.
For women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, and the sick,
the king shall administer punishment by means of whips, split bamboo, ropes, and the like.
But those who, having been appointed to duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth, the king shall render them destitute.
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, as well as those who serve his enemies.
Whatever has been adjudicated and instructed by whomsoever it may be, one should know that to be done according to dharma; one should not reverse it again.
Whatever legal matter ministers or a judge might decide incorrectly,
the king himself shall settle that case and fine them one thousand [paṇas].
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—
all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin).
And for these four who do not perform penance,
the king shall ordain a lawful punishment consisting of both corporal and monetary fines.

For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern banner; for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man.
For they shall be excluded from communal meals, excluded from sacrifices, excluded from Vedic recitations, and excluded from marriage;
wretched and cast out from all religious duties, they shall wander the earth.
But these men, having been marked with the signs of their crime, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives;
they are to be treated without compassion and without salutation—such is the instruction of Manu.
But those of all castes who perform the prescribed expiation as ordained shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine.
For offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement must be imposed;
or he may be banished from the kingdom, together with his wealth and his belongings.
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment.
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for if he takes it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt.
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he may present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world.
Where the king avoids deriving wealth from evildoers,
there men are born in due time with long lives.
And the crops of the people ripen individually according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and nothing deformed is born.
But a king should slay with various terrifying means of execution that person of low caste who, out of lust, oppresses Brāhmaṇas.
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; but merit accrues to him who restrains the wicked.
Thus has been declared in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties engaged in mutual dispute across the eighteen titles of law.
Thus, performing his duties in accordance with the Dharma correctly, the lord of the earth should seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired.
But having properly settled his territory and constructed fortifications according to the treatises,
he should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to heaven.
But that king who takes tribute from thieves without punishing them,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is excluded from heaven.
But that kingdom which is fearless and supported by the strength of arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered.
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who act openly and those who act in secret.
Those who live by various kinds of merchandise are open cheats;
but those such as thieves and forest-robbers are concealed cheats.
Those who take bribes, those who practice fraud, cheats, gamblers, those who live by predicting auspicious events, fortune-tellers, and those who examine omens; Mn 9.258.
Likewise, high officials who act improperly, physicians, those skilled in the practice of crafts, and clever courtesans; // Mn_9.259 //
One should recognize such open thorns of the world as these,
as well as others who move in disguise— ignoble men wearing the marks of the noble.
Having discovered them through secret agents who perform their duties with good conduct and by means of spies in various disguises, he should uproot them and bring them under his control.

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king should duly administer punishment based on the gravity of the offense and the strength of the offender.
For indeed, without punishment,
it is impossible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who harbor evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, and shops selling intoxicants and food; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and places of spectacle.
Dilapidated gardens, forests, the workshops of artisans, empty houses, groves, and pleasure-grounds; Mn 9.265.
In such regions, the king should cause patrols consisting of both stationary and mobile military units, as well as spies, to circulate for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
He should discover them through their companions who follow them and are familiar with their various activities,
and he should eliminate them by means of clever former thieves.
They should bring about their meeting by means of instructions regarding food and drink, by inviting Brahmins, and under the pretext of discussing deeds of heroism.
Those who do not submit there, and those who are instigators from the root,
the king shall forcibly slay, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives.
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen goods;
however, he may execute one caught with the booty along with the implements of theft, without further deliberation.
Furthermore, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves or give them space for their goods— all of those as well he should cause to be executed.
In the territories, he should swiftly punish those appointed to guard them and the vassal chiefs who have been exhorted [to act], if they remain neutral during attacks, just as one punishes thieves.
And even one who lives by the Dharma, if he has fallen away from the covenant of the Dharma,
the king should burn him with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty.

Those who do not run to the aid of others to the best of their ability when a village is being plundered, when a well is being destroyed, or when a robbery is seen on the road, shall be banished along with their belongings.
He shall cause those who steal the king's treasury, those who stand in opposition to him,
and those who instigate his enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment.
But those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking through a wall—
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them on a sharp stake.
In the first offense, one should have the fingers of a pickpocket cut off;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty.
The king should punish those who provide fire, food, weapons,
or shelter to thieves, as well as those who harbor stolen goods, just as he would a thief himself.
One who destroys a tank should be executed by drowning in water or by some other pure form of capital punishment;
or else, if he repairs it, he should be made to pay the highest fine.
One should indeed put to death, without hesitation, those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots.
But he who diverts the water of a pre-existing tank,
or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
He who, except in times of distress, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity.
Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child deserve only a reprimand, and that [offense] must be purified; such is the settled rule.
For all physicians who practice falsely, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement for offenses against non-humans, but the middle amercement for those against humans.
One who breaks down bridges, flagstaffs, or pillars, or destroys images,
shall repair all of that and pay five hundred panas as a fine.
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods,
as well as for their breaking or the false piercing of gems, the punishment is the first amercement.
But a man who deals unfairly with those who are equal, whether by measure or by price,
shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement.
And the king should place all prisons along the road,
where those who have committed evil deeds may be seen suffering and disfigured.
One should immediately banish anyone who breaks down a rampart, fills up the moats, or destroys the gates.
In all cases of malevolent magic, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for root-magic performed by one who is not authorized, and for various kinds of sorcery.
One who sells seeds, one who steals seeds from the field,
and likewise one who breaks a boundary, shall suffer the punishment of mutilation.
But a king shall have a goldsmith who is the most wicked of all thorns,
if he practices injustice, cut into pieces with razors.
In cases of the theft of Sītā grass, grain, weapons, or medicine,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the purpose of the act.
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these are the seven constituent elements; thus the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Among these seven constituents of the kingdom, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one is more serious and its misfortune greater than the next.
In this world, of the seven-limbed kingdom which is supported like a triple staff,
nothing excels anything else due to the specific excellence of their mutual qualities.
In various specific tasks, however, one particular limb excels; whichever part accomplishes a given task is said to be the most excellent for that purpose.
Through his movements, through the application of energy, and through the very execution of his duties,
the lord of the earth should constantly ascertain both his own strength and that of his enemy.
Having reflected upon the gravity or lightness of all afflictions as well as calamities, he should then undertake his task.
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted;
for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages are all the conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.
When asleep, he is the Kali age; when awake, he is the Dvāpara age;
when intent upon actions, he is the Tretā age; but when moving about freely, he is the Kṛta age.
A king should emulate the majestic conduct of Indra, Arka, Vāyu, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and the Earth. (Mn 9.303)
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season,
so should he who observes the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the fulfillment of desires.
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should the king take taxes from his realm; for that is the constant vow of the sun.
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves through them, so too should one enter [the enemy's territory] by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-like" vow.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when the time has come, so must subjects be restrained by the king; for that indeed is the vow of Yama.
Just as one who is bound by Varuṇa with his nooses is clearly seen, so should he restrain the wicked; for this is indeed the vow of Varuṇa.
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do his subjects rejoice in that king who observes the lunar vow.
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is known as the Agneya vow.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally,
so too does he who upholds the duty of a king support all beings.
Employing these and other means, the king, ever vigilant, should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in those of others.
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one should not provoke the Brāhmaṇas;
for they, when enraged, could instantly destroy him along with his army and his vehicles.
By whom the fire was made to consume all things, the great ocean was rendered undrinkable,
and the moon was made to wane and wax— who would not perish by provoking them?
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked to anger, might create other worlds and other world-protectors, or turn gods into non-gods? (Manu 9.315)
Who, desiring to live, would harm those upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend, and for whom Brahman itself is their wealth? (Mn 9.316)
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like the fire, a great deity.
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more.
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable occupations,
Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme deity.
When the Kṣatriya power has become excessively overbearing in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇa alone shall be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa.
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone;
the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own respective sources.
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brāhmaṇical power, nor does the Brāhmaṇical power increase without the Kṣatriya power;
when the Brāhmaṇical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next.
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines,
and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle.
Acting thus and always intent upon the duties of a king, the monarch should employ all his servants in matters that are beneficial to the world.
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order.
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the sacraments and taken a wife,
should be constantly engaged in agriculture and trade, as well as in the protection of cattle.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King.
A Vaiśya must not entertain the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya is willing, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
One should know the relative value of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven textiles,
perfumes, and liquids.
He should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the soil;
he should also understand the application of measures and all the applications of weights.
He should also consider the worth and worthlessness of merchandise, the merits and defects of various regions,
the profit and loss on commodities, and the proper rearing of livestock.
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their purchase and sale.
He should exert the greatest effort to increase his wealth in accordance with the Dharma,
and he should diligently provide food for all living beings.
For a Śūdra, however, the service of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious, is indeed the highest dharma leading to supreme beatitude.
Pure, devoted to the highest service, gentle in speech, free from egoism,
and always taking refuge in Brahmins and the like, one attains a superior birth.
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them even in times of distress.
The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study;
however, it is a settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may teach, and not the other two.
The Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others, and he himself should likewise abide by them.
Due to his distinctiveness, the excellence of his origin, his adherence to restrictive rules,
and the distinction of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth, however, is once-born, namely the Śūdra, and there is no fifth.
Among wives of equal caste from all social orders who have not lost their virginity,
those born in the natural order (ānulomya) are to be known as belonging to that very same caste.
Sons begotten by twice-born men on women born in the next lower caste are said to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers.
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this same righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra daughter is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya and the daughter of a Śūdra is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel.

These six are declared to be base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin woman by men of the three [lower] castes, those born from a Kshatriya woman by men of the two [lower] castes, and those born from a Vaishya woman by a man of the one [lowest] caste.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden is born a Sūta by birth; from a Vaiśya father are born a Māgadha and a Vaideha, who are the sons of a royal and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.
From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men— through the intermixture of castes.
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are recorded as resulting from the natural order (ānulomya) with an interval of one caste,
so too do the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka arise from birth in the inverse order (prātilomya).
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife of equal caste], as described in sequence,
are designated by the name "anantara" (immediate) due to the defect of their mothers.
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra; and from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa.
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—are born from a Śūdra in the reverse order; these three are outcastes (apasada).
From a Vaiśya are born the Māgadha and the Vaideha; from a Kṣatriya, however, is born the Sūta alone.
These others are also three base-born (apasada) castes produced in the reverse order.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pukkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka.
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one begotten by a Vaidehaka on an Ambaṣṭhī woman is called a Veṇa.
Those sons whom twice-born men beget on wives of their own caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances, one should designate as *vrātyas*, having fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*.
From a Vratya Brahmin, however, are born the evil-natured Bhurjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.
From a Rājanya Vrātya are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Nicchivi;
as well as the Naṭa, the Karaṇa, the Khasa, and the Draviḍa.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
Through adultery, through the marrying of women who should not be married,
and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises.
But those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural orders,
and those who are mutually intermingled— I shall describe them in their entirety.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, the Caṇḍāla— the lowest of men—
as well as the Māgadha, the Āyogava, and the Kṣattṛ caste.
These six produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs;
they also procreate within wombs of higher castes that are of the same mother-caste.
Just as for the three castes, a son is born from two [wives] of his own caste in immediate succession, so too is the order among those outside [the caste system].
And they also procreate upon the wives of others many outsiders, who are even more corrupted than themselves and are held in contempt.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste child upon a Brāhmaṇa woman, so does an outcaste beget an even more outcaste child upon women of the four castes.
Acting in opposition to their own kind, those who are outsiders beget yet more outsiders; being inferior, they give birth to fifteen even more degraded castes.
A Dasyu begets upon an Āyogava woman a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply ornaments and perfumes, who is not a slave but lives like one, and subsists by means of nets.
The Vaideha, however, procreates a Maitreyaka from a Mādhūka woman;
he is one who incessantly praises men and strikes a bell at the break of dawn.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.
These three distinct, outcaste groups are born among Āyogava women who wear the clothes of the dead and consume despised food.
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born, who is a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehika are born the Āndhra and the Meda, both of whom have their dwellings outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. He is likewise born from a Niṣāda and a Vaidehī.
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pukkasa woman, a sinful Sopāka is born, whose livelihood consists of the root of calamity and who is always censured by virtuous people.
But from a Caṇḍāla, a Niṣāda woman gives birth to a son called an Antyāvasāyin,
who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system.
These castes resulting from intermixture, as demonstrated by their fathers and mothers—
whether they are concealed or manifest— are to be known by their respective occupations.
The six sons born of women of their own caste or of those immediately below it possess the duties of the twice-born;
however, all those born of women further removed are recorded as being of the same nature as Śūdras.
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here in birth after birth, age after age.
But through the gradual neglect of sacred rites and the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya lineages have reached the state of Śūdras in this world.
The Pauṇḍrakas, the Auḍras, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas,
the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, the Daradas, and the Khaśas.
Those castes in the world who are outside the lineages born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—
whether they speak the tongues of barbarians or the speech of the Aryans— are all traditionally known as Dasyus.
Those who are known as the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions,
should subsist by means of those despised occupations of the twice-born themselves.
The management of horses and chariots is for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas;
service to women for the Vaidehakas; and the way of trade for the Māgadhas.
The killing of fish is the occupation of Niṣādas, while that of Āyogavas is carpentry;
the killing of wild animals is the occupation of Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus.
For the Kṣattr, Ugra, and Pukkasa, however, there shall be dwelling in holes and the killing and binding [of animals];
for the Dhigvaṇas, the working in leather; and for the Veṇas, the playing of drums.
These known [Vrātyas] shall dwell at sacred shrines, by trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves, subsisting by their own occupations.
The dwelling of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, however, shall be outside the village;
they must be made outcaste from the community, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead; their food shall be from broken vessels;
their ornament shall be black iron; and they must constantly lead a life of wandering mendicancy.
A man practicing the dharma should not seek association with them;
their dealings shall be among themselves, and their marriages shall be with their own equals.
Their food should be given by others from a broken vessel;
they must not wander about in villages or towns at night.
They may go about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the funeral of a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the settled rule.
They shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures and by the king's command;
they shall take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of the executed.
One should discern a man who is devoid of caste, unknown, and born of a defiled womb,
as being ignoble despite having the appearance of an Ārya, by means of his own actions.
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty,
and an inactive nature reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb.
He inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or indeed both;
for one born of a low womb cannot in any way suppress his own innate nature.
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth-origins (yonisaṃkara),
that person inevitably adopts the conduct of those origins, whether to a small or great extent.
But that kingdom where these corrupters of the social orders are born through intermixture with the inhabitants of the realm quickly perishes.
The unconditioned sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or a cow,
or for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those of the outer castes.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—
Manu declared this to be the summary of the duty for the four castes.
If one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother procreates with someone of a superior caste,
the inferior offspring attains the status of the superior caste up to the seventh generation.
A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise falls to the status of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father upon a non-Aryan mother, and one born from a non-Aryan father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother? (Mn 10.66)
A son born to a non-Aryan woman from an Aryan father may become an Aryan through his qualities;
however, one born to an Aryan woman from a non-Aryan father is certainly a non-Aryan—this is the settled rule.
Both of these are established by law as being ineligible for sacramental rites:
the former because of the deficiency of his birth, and the latter because he is born in the inverse order.
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition,
so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement.
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established rule is as follows.
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
and even a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground.
Since sages born of animal wombs became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is held in high esteem.
Having considered one who is ignoble but performs noble deeds, and one who is noble but performs ignoble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal."
Those Brahmins who abide in the womb of Brahman and remain steadfast in their own duty should properly subsist by means of the six occupations in their proper order.
Teaching, studying, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts— these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts.
The established rule is that these [practices] should likewise cease with respect to a Vaiśya;
for Prajāpati Manu did not prescribe those duties for them.
The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya;
but the duty (dharma) consists of giving gifts, study, and sacrifice.
The study of the Vedas is the distinguished duty of the Brāhmaṇa, protection that of the Kṣatriya,
and the occupation of trade and agriculture that of the Vaiśya, among their respective duties.
But if a Brāhmaṇa cannot subsist by his own aforementioned occupation,
he may live by the duty of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best alternative for him.
But if he should find it impossible to live by either of these two, how should he proceed? He may live by adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, namely agriculture and cattle-rearing.
But even if he lives by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and depends upon others.
People consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the wooden tool tipped with iron destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it.
But for one who, due to a deficiency in livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma,
this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth, provided that the choice portions have been extracted.
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, animals, and human beings.
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as hemp, linen, and woolen fabrics—
even if they are undyed— as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes;
milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass.
All wild animals, fanged creatures, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals.
Having personally engaged in agriculture and produced a profit, a farmer may sell sesamum seeds that have not been long stored, provided they are of inferior quality, for the sake of dharma.
If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than giving them as food or as an unguent,
he becomes a worm in dog dung and sinks there together with his ancestors.
One falls [from caste] immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
by selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days.
But by intentionally selling other types of merchandise here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for other flavors;
prepared food may be exchanged for prepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal.
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all these means;
however, he must never at any time covet a superior mode of livelihood.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed,
the king, having deprived him of his wealth, shall banish him immediately.
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another;
for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste.
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided that he does not practice forbidden acts and, when capable, desists from such conduct.
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born and has fallen into distress regarding his children and wife may live by the work of artisans.
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served, are the duties of artisans.
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path,
should practice this rule when he is distressed by the lack of means of subsistence and is suffering.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a means of purification should become defiled—this is not logically tenable according to the Dharma.
Neither from teaching, nor from officiating at sacrifices, nor from accepting gifts— even those that are censured—
does any fault accrue to Brahmins, for they are like fire and water.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, being hungry, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely performing a remedy for hunger.
Desiring to eat dog-meat when distressed, Vāmadeva— who was discerning of dharma and adharma— did not defile himself for the sake of preserving his life.
But the great ascetic Bharadvāja, afflicted by hunger along with his sons in a lonely forest,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
And Viśvāmitra, though he was an expert in discerning dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla while afflicted by hunger.
Between receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching,
the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured for a Brahmin after death.
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those who have been consecrated;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth.
Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
but that caused by accepting gifts is removed only by renunciation and by austerity.
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from anywhere;
picking up ears of grain (śila) is better than receiving gifts, and gleaning (uñcha) is praised even more than that.
Snātaka Brahmins who are suffering from want, or who desire base metals or wealth, may beg the lord of the earth; if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned.

From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, from a non-cultivated field, one may take cows, goats, sheep, gold, grain, or food—each preceding item being less objectionable than the following.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous.
Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture,
contentment, begging, and usury are the ten means of livelihood.
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give a small amount to a more sinful person.
Even when taking a fourth part as his share during times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin.
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he should not turn his back in battle.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he may collect the lawful tribute from them.
The toll on grain for the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide services, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [shall pay the same].
But a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, may serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek his subsistence.
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both worlds, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose.
Service to the Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him.
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family resources as is appropriate,
having regard for their capacity, their diligence, and the number of dependents they maintain.
Leftover food should be given to him, as well as worn-out clothes,
the shriveled kernels of grain, and old household utensils.
There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve any sacramental rite;
he has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against him from dharma.
But those who desire righteousness, who know the dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur sin when acting except by means of sacred formulas; rather, they receive praise.
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct,
in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the next.
For even a Śūdra who is capable should not accumulate wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves.
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by properly performing them, they attain the supreme goal.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rule for expiation.

One who belongs to a lineage of teachers, one who intends to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking wealth for the sake of a guru, for the sake of his father or mother, one desiring to study the Veda, and one who is afflicted by illness; Mn 11.1.
One should indeed know those Snātakas who are Brāhmaṇas seeking alms for the sake of dharma;
gifts should be given to these destitute ones according to the excellence of their learning.
For food accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial altar (bahirvedi).
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brahmins learned in the Vedas according to their merit, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice.
He who, having already taken a wife, obtains another by begging for her, gains only the fruit of pleasure; the offspring, however, belongs to the giver of the wealth.
One should bestow wealth upon Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and live in seclusion according to one's ability; thus, after death, one enjoys heaven.
He who possesses enough food for three years to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, that twice-born man who drinks Soma when the substance is very small— even if he has drunk Soma before— does not obtain its fruit.
When one who is capable gives to strangers while his own people live in misery, that is a semblance of dharma; it is like the taste of honey followed by the taste of poison.
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one's dependents results in unhappiness both while living and after death.
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by even a single component—
especially that of a Brāhmaṇa— while a righteous king is in power, [he shall perform a penance].
If there be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.
He may take three or two items at will from the house of a Śūdra,
for a Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices.
If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but does not perform sacrifices—
one may take [wealth] from the households of even these two without hesitation.
One may take from a person who does not give back what was borrowed, provided that person is habitually acquisitive;
in this way, his fame spreads and his merit increases.
Likewise, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one may take food from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Whether it be from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found—
if he asks, that [stolen property] must be declared to him who asks.
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he may take the property of a Dasyu or one who neglects his religious duties if he cannot otherwise subsist.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a boat and carries both of them across.
The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods;
however, the wealth of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of the asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger.
Having ascertained his circle of servants and his family members, and having learned of their learning and character, the lord of the earth shall provide them with a righteous means of livelihood.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from that protected person, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit.
A Brahmin should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who begs in this manner is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the purpose of a sacrifice, does not give it all away,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of a Brāhmaṇa—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures.

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the purpose of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.
If a twice-born man performs a religious rite according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress,
it has been determined that he does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter.
And by all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great seers,
fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the prescribed rule was established.
He who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary rule, gains no fruit pertaining to the future life; such is the case for that man of evil intellect.
A Brahmin who knows the law should not report anything to the king;
he should deal with those offending men, his own disciples, by his own power alone.
Between one's own effort and the effort of a king, one's own effort is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own effort alone.
Without hesitation, he may employ the hymns of the Atharva-Angirases;
for the weapon of a Brahmin is indeed speech, and with that, the twice-born man shall slay his enemies.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra by their wealth; but the best of the twice-born by silent recitation and burnt offerings.
One who is a provider, a punisher, and a speaker, yet remains friendly, is called a Brāhmaṇa;
one should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh words.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, shall be the officiating priest for the Agnihotra.
For these fall into hell while offering oblations, as does he to whom that [sacrifice] belongs;
therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, fails to give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he remains one who has not established the fires. (Manu 11.38)
One who is faithful and has conquered his senses may perform other meritorious acts,
but he should by no means perform sacrifices in this world with meager sacrificial fees.
A sacrifice with small sacrificial fees destroys one's senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice.
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should abandon those fires out of his own will, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
Those who, having obtained wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice,
are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the low-born (vṛṣala), the giver shall cross over all difficulties.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and remains addicted to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to penance.
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some say it is also required for one committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the revealed scripture.
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.
Having incurred the state of requiring expiation, whether by fate or by his own prior actions,
a twice-born man must not associate with the virtuous as long as the expiation has not been performed.
In this world, certain evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their physical form due to their own misconduct, as well as by deeds committed in previous lives.
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of spirituous liquor, black teeth;
a slayer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, a skin disease.
A slanderer shall have a putrid nose; a backbiter, a putrid mouth;
