a stealer of grain, a deficiency of limbs; and one who adulterates goods, an excess of limbs.
The stealer of food suffers from chronic disease; the stealer of speech becomes mute;
the stealer of clothing suffers from leucoderma; and the stealer of a horse becomes lame.
Thus, by reason of specific actions, they are born despised by the virtuous—
dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.
Therefore, one must always perform penance for the sake of purification;
for those who have not expiated their sins are born with censurable physical marks.
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—
they call these the great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them.
False testimony regarding one's own excellence, malicious slander directed at the king,
and the persistent fabrication of falsehoods against a teacher are equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Abandoning one's Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend,
eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten— these six are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, silver, land, diamonds, and gems, is declared to be equal to the theft of gold.

They consider the emission of semen into women who are one's own female relatives, into virgins, into women of the lowest castes, and into the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the bed of a guru.

Killing a cow; officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice or sacrificing for one for whom one should not sacrifice; adultery; selling oneself; abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, or son; and neglecting the private recitation of the Vedas or the sacred fires.

The elder brother remaining unmarried while the younger is married; the younger brother marrying before the elder; giving away a daughter in marriage to either of them; and officiating as a priest at a sacrifice for either of them.
Defiling a maiden, usury, the violation of a vow, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child; Mn 11.61.
The state of being a Vrātya, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for a fee,
receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that ought not to be sold.

Exercising authority over all forms [of work], operating large machines, dealing in harmful medicinal herbs, living off women, performing malevolent incantations, and performing root-rites (mūlakarma).
Felling trees that are not dry for the sake of fuel, undertaking actions for one's own sake, and likewise eating censured food; Mn 11.64 [63M].
Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts,
studying improper scriptures, and the practice of the arts of the stage.
The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the habit of drinking liquor or consorting with women [of low caste];
the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, crookedness, and sexual intercourse with a male are declared to cause loss of caste.
The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats,
sheep, fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from those who are censured, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths should be known as acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa).
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food accompanied by liquor; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity.
Now learn correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins are respectively expiated.
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years, having built a hut,
subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification, and carrying the skull of a corpse as his banner.
Or he may become the target of weapon-wielders, according to his own wish;
or he may throw himself headlong three times into a blazing fire.
Or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or he may travel one hundred yojanas toward Japan (the east) or toward any other [direction],
eating sparingly and with his senses restrained, in order to remove the sin of killing a Brahmin.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas—
be it wealth sufficient for a livelihood or a house together with its furnishings.
Or, eating only sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī river against its current;
or, restrained in his diet, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village,
or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage, or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should immediately renounce one's life;
the protector of a cow or of a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Or he is released by resisting [the king] three times, or by winning back all his property,
or when his life is saved on account of that [property] for the sake of a Brahmin.
Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly chaste, and composed in mind,
removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin at the completion of the twelfth year.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods on earth (the Brahmins) at an assembly of kings,
he is liberated from it after bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya its summit;
therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one becomes purified.
By his very birth, he is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā alone is the cause in this matter.
Those three who know the Vedas shall prescribe for them a complete expiation for the offense;
that shall serve as their purification, for the speech of the learned is indeed purifying.
Therefore, by adhering to any one of these rules with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin removes the sin committed through killing a Brahmin by means of self-control.
Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows [the Veda], or a woman who has bathed after her courses.
Having given false testimony, having obstructed a teacher, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; Mn 11.88.
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
no atonement is prescribed for the intentional killing of a Brahmin.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, drinks liquor, he shall drink liquor that is fire-colored;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he may drink cow’s urine the color of fire, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung, until death.
Or, for the purpose of removing the sin of drinking liquor, he shall eat grains or oil-cake once at night for a year,
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks, and carrying a banner.
Surā is indeed the dregs of foods, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that distilled from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that from honey (mādhvī).
Just as one is so are all; none of these should be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
Wine, meat, and spirituous liquors are the food of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas;
these must not be consumed by a Brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation (havis) for the gods.
Intoxicated by pride, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or utter Vedic texts,
or perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication.
He whose Brahmanical nature, residing within his body, is once drenched with liquor—
his status as a Brahmin departs and he becomes a Śūdra.
This manifold expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should confess his own deed and say: "May your majesty punish me."
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, but a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove the impurity born of stealing gold through austerity,
shall wear rags and perform in the forest the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
but he shall expel the sin of approaching the teacher’s wife by means of these very same vows.
Having addressed the sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie down upon a heated iron bed;
or he should embrace a blazing iron image of a woman; by death, he is purified.
Or, having himself cut off his own penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms,
he should walk straight toward the region of Nirṛti until he collapses.
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard and dwelling in a solitary forest,
he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind.
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or barley gruel, in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) may do so by means of these various kinds of vows.
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
Restraining his senses, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at every fourth mealtime; for two months, he should perform his ablutions with cow urine.
By day he should follow those cows, and while standing, he should inhale the dust raised by them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
He should stand when they stand, follow them when they walk,
and likewise sit when they sit, being self-restrained and free from envy.
One should rescue by all possible means a woman who is ill or accused, one who is threatened by dangers such as thieves or tigers, one who has fallen, or one who is stuck in the mud.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
One should not mention a cow that is eating in one's own house, or in the field or threshing-floor of oneself or others, nor should one mention a calf that is drinking.
But he who, following this rule, attends upon a cow,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.
Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka),
with the exception of one who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), shall perform this very same penance for the sake of purification, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa.
But one who has spilled his semen shall, at night, sacrifice a one-eyed donkey at a crossroads according to the procedure for a *pākayajña* to Nirṛti.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rule, and finally having come together with the verse [beginning with "sam"],
he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Agni.
Those who know the Dharma and speak of Brahman declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow.
The fourfold Brahmanic energy of one who has violated his vow approaches Māruta, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka.
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go about begging alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them, eating only once a day,
and performing the ritual ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year.
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one shall perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness to receive alms, purification is achieved by the lunar penance (*aindava*) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel for three days.
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, and a sixteenth part should be known for a Śūdra.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born,
having observed his vow well, shall give a thousand cows and one bull as a gift.
Or, with his hair matted and self-restrained, he may perform for three years the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa,
dwelling far away from a village and making his home at the foot of a tree.
An excellent twice-born man,
having killed a Vaiśya who is established in his duty, shall perform this very same penance for one year and give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or else he shall give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay,
a frog, a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one shall perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Or he should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana,
or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the waters (Ab-daivata).
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
having killed a eunuch, a load of straw and one māṣa of lead.
For killing a boar, one must give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for a curlew, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, a peacock,
a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for an elephant, five dark-colored bulls; for a goat or a sheep, an ox; and for a donkey, a one-year-old calf.
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, one should give a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
Having killed women of the four castes who have not been consecrated, one should give, for the sake of purification, the skins of a Jina, a bow, a bull, and a goat respectively.
If a twice-born man is unable to purify the killing of snakes and other such creatures through gifts,
he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin.
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate creatures,
or for a full cartload of boneless ones, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
But for killing vertebrate animals, one should give something to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛgvedic verses should be recited;
likewise for cutting shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the means of purification.
For the unauthorized plucking of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—is entirely removed; now hear [the rules] regarding the eating of forbidden food.
Having drunk *vāruṇī* through ignorance, one is purified by the purificatory rite alone; but for intentional drinking, the penance is indescribable and ends only with life—this is the settled rule.
Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for *surā* liquor or likewise in a vessel for intoxicating drinks,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rule,
or having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor,
becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of regeneration again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the religious observances—
all these are dispensed with for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Even after drinking fermented acids or astringent decoctions, though they are purifying,
a twice-born man remains impure as long as that [substance] has not passed downward.
Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms growing from the earth,
or meat from a slaughterhouse that was not known [to be so], one should observe this very same vow.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, cocks, humans, crows, and donkeys,
the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
But that twice-born man who, not having yet returned home from his teacher, should eat food given on the first day of the month,
shall fast for three days and dwell for one day in water.
But a religious student who should eat honey or meat in any way whatsoever must perform the ordinary Kṛcchra penance and then complete the remainder of his vow.
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a mouse, or those of a dog or a mongoose,
or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.
One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit to be eaten;
however, if it has been consumed through ignorance, it should be vomited up or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites.
Thus has been declared the various rule for the vows regarding the eating of forbidden food;
now hear the rule for those vows that remove the taint of theft.
Having committed thefts of grain, food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one of his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by performing the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
But for the abduction of human women, as well as for the seizure of fields,
houses, wells, tanks, and water, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification.
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house,
one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that [stolen property].

For stealing food that is chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, seats, and flowers, roots, and fruits, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For consuming grass, wood, trees, dried food,
molasses, clothing, leather, or meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver,
iron, brass, or stone, one must subsist on grain husks for twelve days.
For stealing cotton, silk, wool, cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed animals,
birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk for three days.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
but he shall expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these very vows.

Having discharged semen into women of his own kin, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, he shall perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
Having approached the daughter of his father’s sister, the daughter of his own sister, or the daughter of his mother’s brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives;
they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by marrying them he falls low.
Having discharged semen into non-human females, a woman in her courses, those who are not women, or into water, one should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance.
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman,
a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a vehicle drawn by oxen, in water, or during the daytime.

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, or having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; but through knowledge, he becomes equal [to them].
A husband shall confine a wife who has become corrupt in a single room;
he shall cause her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others.
If, however, she should become defiled after being solicited by one of equal status,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are declared to be her means of purification.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting prayers for three years.
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who have associated with outcasts.
By associating with an outcast for a year—through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance—one becomes an outcast; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
Whichever among these a man associates with by falling into the same state,
he must perform that very person's vow for the sake of purification from that association.
The sapinda relatives and kinsmen must perform the water-libation for one who has fallen [from his caste] outside the village on an inauspicious day,
in the evening, in the presence of his agnates, officiating priests, and teachers.
A female slave should overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a deceased person;
the relatives, together with her, shall observe impurity for a day and a night.
From him, however, they must desist from conversation, sitting together,
the giving of an inheritance, and even ordinary social intercourse.
The status of being the eldest shall cease, as well as the wealth obtainable by the eldest;
however, a younger brother who is superior in merit shall receive the portion of the eldest.
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe and together with him throw a new pitcher full of water into a sacred reservoir of water.
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the duties pertaining to his kinsmen as before.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be provided with clothing, food, and drink, and should live near the house.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins and have not been purified; yet, once they have undergone purification, one should never despise them.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman— even if they have been purified according to the law.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born men who, being engaged in forbidden acts and abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform expiation.
When Brahmins acquire wealth through a reprehensible action,
they become purified by relinquishing it, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity.
Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk in a cow-pen for a month, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
But when he has returned from the cow-pasture, emaciated by fasting and bowing before them, they should ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (Mn 11.195)
Having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
when the sacred bathing place has been established by the cows, they should perform his formal reception there.
Having performed sacrifices for Vratyas, having performed funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic or the Ahina sacrifice, one removes the taint by three Krichchhra penances.
Having abandoned one who has sought refuge or having caused the Veda to be lost,
a twice-born man expiates that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by village-dwelling carnivorous animals,
as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Eating only at the sixth mealtime for a month, or the recitation of the Saṃhitā,
as well as all the regular burnt offerings, are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals.
Having intentionally mounted a vehicle drawn by camels or a vehicle drawn by donkeys,
a Brahmin who has bathed while naked becomes pure through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
If one is afflicted while without water or even in the midst of water, and has used the bodily excretions,
he becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow.
If one neglects the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda,
or violates the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" and an elder with "thou," one should bathe, remain without food for the rest of the day, and seek their favor by offering salutations.
Even after striking him with a blade of grass, or binding him by the neck with a cloth,
or having defeated him in a dispute, one should propitiate him by bowing down.
But by threatening a Brahmin, one enters hell for a hundred years, and by striking him with intent to kill, for a thousand years.
For as many particles of dust as the blood collects upon the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the shedder of it dwell in hell.
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been stated,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
I shall describe to you those means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors, by which a human being removes his sins.

A twice-born man performing the Prājāpatya penance should eat food obtained by begging for three days in the morning, for three days in the evening, for three days he should not ask for anything, and for the final three days he should not eat at all.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
followed by a fast for one night, is known as the *Sāṃtapana* penance.
A twice-born man performing the Atikṛcchra penance should eat only a single morsel for three days each, as before, and fast for the final three days. (Manu Smṛti 11.213)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed.
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called *parāka*, which removes all sins.
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three sessions of the day, this is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, beginning with the bright fortnight and remaining self-restrained, should carry out this entire procedure in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama variety.
Restraining his self and subsisting on sacrificial food, one performing the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* penance should eat eight morsels when the sun has reached midday.
A Brahmin, with a concentrated mind, should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating three times eighty mouthfuls of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in a month, with a concentrated mind, in whatever manner possible, one attains the same world as the Moon.
The Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus,
along with the Maruts and the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
He himself should perform the fire-oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
he should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness.
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
furthermore, he should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable, he may lie down on the ground.
He should remain celibate and observant of his vows, and worship his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and purificatory texts according to his ability;
likewise, in all vows, he should be diligent for the sake of expiation.
The twice-born whose sins have been made public shall be purified by these vows;
however, those whose sins have not been made public, one should purify with mantras and burnt offerings.
By confession, by repentance, by austerity, and by Vedic study,
as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil.
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act,
confesses it, to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
To the extent that his mind reproaches the evil deed he has committed,
to that same extent his body is released from that unrighteousness.
For having committed a sin and felt remorse, one is liberated from that sin;
however, one is purified through the resolve of abstention, thinking, "I shall not do this again."
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death,
he should constantly perform auspicious deeds through thought, word, and deed.
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a censurable act,
one who seeks liberation from it should not perform it a second time.
If, after performing a particular act, there should be a lack of lightness in his mind,
he should perform penance for that act until it brings him satisfaction.
All happiness, whether divine or human, has austerity as its root;
it is declared by the wise who perceive the Veda that austerity is its middle and austerity its end.
The austerity of a Brāhmaṇa is knowledge; the austerity of a Kṣatriya is protection;
the austerity of a Vaiśya is agriculture and trade; and the austerity of a Śūdra is service.
Sages who have restrained their selves and subsist on fruits, roots,
and air perceive the three worlds, with all that is moving and unmoving, through austerity alone.
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of divine power—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is the means to achieve them.
Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—
all this can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable.
Even those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and others who have performed forbidden acts are liberated from that taint solely through well-performed austerity.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds,
and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.
Whatever sin people commit through thought, word,
or deed, those whose wealth is austerity burn it all away quickly by means of austerity alone.
For a Brahmin purified by austerity alone,
the denizens of heaven accept his offerings and increase his desires.
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity.
Thus, the gods proclaim this to be the great power of austerity,
seeing that the merit of austerity is supreme over all this.
The daily study of the Vedas to the best of one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices,
and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes.
Just as fire, having reached its fuel, consumes it in an instant with its heat,
so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil with the fire of knowledge.
Thus has the expiation for these sins been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, learn the expiation for secret offenses.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of an embryo within a month.
By muttering the Kautsa hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the Vasiṣṭha verse beginning with "pratīcīṃ," the Māhitra hymn,
and the Śuddhavatī verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa hymns even once,
one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant.
Having repeated the Haviṣpāntīya hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and having recited the Puruṣasūkta, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated from that sin.
Desiring to remove gross and subtle sins, one should mutter for a year either the verse beginning with "ava" or that beginning with "yat kiṃ cedam. (Manu 11.252)
Having accepted what should not be accepted or having eaten food that is censured,
a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn.
But one who has committed many sins is purified by performing the Soma-Raudra rite for a month,
while bathing in a flowing river and reciting the three verses beginning with "aryamṇām."
One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "Indraḥ pramādāt" for half a year;
but having performed a blameworthy act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.
Having offered clarified butter for a year with the mantras used for the Śakala-homa, a twice-born man destroys even very grave sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "Namaḥ."
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms-food, he becomes purified.
Or, having purified himself by three *parāka* penances, one who is self-restrained and recites the Vedic *saṃhitā* three times in the forest is released from all sins.
One who, being self-controlled, fasts for three days and partakes of water three times a day,
is released from all sins by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, removes all sins,
so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins.
Even if he has slain these three worlds and eats from anywhere at all,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
Having recited the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times, or the Yajurveda, or the Sāmaveda along with its secret portions (rahasya), with a concentrated mind, one is liberated from all sins.
Just as a clod of earth thrown into a great lake perishes,
so does every evil deed sink away when one has mastered the threefold Veda.
The Ṛg-verses, the other Yajus-formulas, and the various Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
That primordial Brahman which consists of three syllables, in which the triple Veda is established— that other secret threefold Veda, he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
O sinless one, you have declared this entire dharma of the four castes;
now tell us truly the supreme outcome of the fruits of actions.
The righteous Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action."
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, yields auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
the destinies of men—superior, inferior, and middling—are born of action.
One should know that for this embodied being— whether characterized by the threefold [path], the three bases, or the ten characteristics— it is the mind that is the instigator.
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— these are the three kinds of mental action.
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form,
and idle chatter— these constitute the fourfold nature of speech.
Taking what has not been given, violence contrary to the rules,
and adultery with another's wife are recorded as the threefold bodily [evil].
This person experiences the mental [result], whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the mind alone;
the action performed by speech through speech, and that which is bodily through the body alone.
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, to the status of a low-born caste.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of body— he in whose intellect these are firmly established is called a *tridaṇḍin*.
Having cast aside this triple staff among all living beings and having restrained desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.
That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise.
The inner self, known as the *jīva*, is distinct and innate to all embodied beings;
it is by means of this that one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births.
Both of these— the Great Principle (mahat) and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)— being joined with the elements,
remain pervading that which resides within high and low beings.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set in motion all beings, both high and low.
After death, for men who have committed evil deeds, another body certainly arises from those very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment.
Having experienced those torments with this very body in the world of Yama,
they dissolve respectively back into those same elemental constituents.
Having experienced those evils born of attachment to sense objects, which result in future suffering, he,
with his taints removed, approaches those same two of great splendor.
Together with him, those two unweariedly perceive his merit and his sin,
through which he, being joined with them, attains happiness or unhappiness both in this world and after death.
If one practices dharma for the most part and adharma only to a small degree,
he enjoys happiness in heaven, enveloped by those very same elements.
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and righteousness only slightly,
abandoned by those elements, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from impurity,
returns again to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.
Having observed with his own mind these destinies of the living soul resulting from both righteousness and unrighteousness, he should always fix his mind upon righteousness.
One should know that sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities of the Self,
by which the Great One (mahat) remains pervading all these states without exception.
Whichever of these qualities predominates entirely within the body at any given time,
it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality.
Goodness is knowledge, darkness is ignorance, and passion is said to be attachment and aversion;
this is their pervasive form, which rests within all beings.
In that state, whatever one perceives within oneself as conjoined with joy,
tranquil and appearing pure— that one should understand to be *sattva*.
But that which is conjoined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, one should know as *rajas*, which is constantly carrying away embodied beings against their will.
But that which is joined with delusion, unmanifest, consisting of sense objects,
inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be *tamas*.
Furthermore, I shall describe in its entirety the arising of the fruits of these three qualities— the highest, the middling, and the lowest.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses,
performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self— these are the characteristics of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Delight in undertaking tasks, lack of fortitude, engagement in improper actions,
and constant indulgence in sensual objects are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa).
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism,
violation of moral conduct, a habit of begging, and negligence are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Furthermore, this should be known as the summary definition of the qualities of these three, as they abide in the three [states], in their respective order.
Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even intending to do it—
all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas).
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve when it fails to be achieved, should be known as rajasic.
That which one desires to know entirely, that which one does not feel ashamed to practice,
and that by which one’s own self is satisfied— this is the defining characteristic of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is said to be that of *rajas*;
righteousness is the characteristic of *sattva*. Among these, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding.
I shall now briefly describe, in their proper order, the qualities by which each of these transmigrates through the various states of existence.
Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans;
and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is this threefold destiny.
This secondary course of existence is to be understood as threefold and of three kinds—
namely, inferior, middling, and superior— according to the distinction between one's actions and knowledge.
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes along with tortoises,
domestic animals, and wild beasts constitute the lowest state of darkness.
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas;
lions, tigers, and boars—these constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati).
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, deceitful men,
Rākṣasas, and Piśācas constitute the highest state among those belonging to Tamas.
Jhallas, Mallas, and Naṭas, as well as men who live by the sword, those addicted to gambling and drinking, and those of base conduct— this is the Rājasa destiny.
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings,
as well as those whose primary occupation is the science of war, constitute the intermediate Rājasa state.
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are attendants of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases, find their highest state among the Rajasic beings.
Ascetics, self-restrained practitioners, Brahmins, the hosts of celestial chariot-dwellers,
the lunar mansions, and the Daityas— this is the first, the Sāttvika state.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas— this is the second path, characterized by goodness (sāttvikī gatiḥ).
The wise declare that Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest— this is the highest state characterized by sattva.
Thus has been fully described the entire transmigratory existence consisting of all beings, which is of three kinds and threefold, arising from the three types of action.
Through attachment to the senses and by not practicing the Dharma,
the ignorant and lowest of men go to sinful states of existence.
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living soul enters in this world, and by what particular karma, in due order. Mn 12.53.
Having endured terrible hells for many series of years, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) enter these transmigrations upon the exhaustion of that [karmic residue].
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; or that of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or even that of a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
A Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures.
A Brahmin who is a thief becomes thousands of spiders, snakes, and lizards; of aquatic animals; and of predatory beasts and Piśācas.
The violator of the Guru's bed becomes a grass, shrub, or creeper, or even a carnivorous, fanged beast,
or one who performs cruel deeds, for hundreds of lifetimes.

Those who eat the wives of others become carnivorous beasts of prey after death; those who steal become worms that feed on impurities; and those who have sexual intercourse with women of the lowest castes become creatures that devour one another.
By entering into union with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.
A man who, out of greed, steals gems, pearls, corals,
and various other precious stones, is born among the goldsmiths.
By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl;
by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing savory food, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [eats] meat, a cormorant [eats] fat, the oil-drinking bird [eats] oil,
a cricket [eats] salt, and a crane [eats] curd.
Having stolen silk, a partridge [becomes a partridge]; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; having stolen a cow, an iguana; and having stolen molasses, a rat.
The chuchundarī [eats] auspicious fragrances; the peacock, leafy vegetables;
the porcupine, various kinds of prepared food; and the śalyaka, unprepared food.
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder wasp; and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [destroys] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruits and roots;
a bear, a woman; a cuckoo, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock.
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property whatsoever, or having consumed an offering that has not been consecrated by sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
Women also, by stealing in this same manner, incur guilt;
they become wives of these very same creatures.
For when the social classes fall away from their respective duties in times of non-distress,
they undergo sinful transmigrations and fall into servitude under their enemies.
A Brahmin who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha who eats what has been vomited;
and a Kṣatriya becomes a *kaṭapūtana* who eats impure matter and corpses.
A Vaiśya who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a preta named Maitrākṣajyotika that feeds on pus;
and a Śūdra who has fallen from his own dharma becomes a Cailāśaka.
To whatever extent those whose nature is directed toward sense objects indulge in them,
to that same extent skillfulness in those very objects arises within them.
Due to the repeated practice of those sinful deeds, those of small intellect undergo sufferings here in various wombs.
There is the tossing about in the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
as well as the forests of sword-leaves and other punishments involving binding and cutting.
And various torments, being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of burning sand mixed with grit, and the dreadful Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he undergoes births in wombs that are generally full of suffering,
as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and various kinds of fears.
Again and again, there is dwelling in the abodes of the womb and dreadful birth,
as well as wooden fetters and even the state of being sent into the service of others.
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people;
the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies.
And likewise, old age which is beyond remedy, the affliction caused by diseases,
various kinds of sufferings, and death itself, which is difficult to overcome.
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action,
with a body of that same nature one experiences its corresponding fruit.
Thus has been fully declared to you the arising of the fruits of all actions;
now learn this action which brings about the highest good for a Brahmin.
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses,
non-violence, and service to the teacher are the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
And among all these auspicious actions here,
some particular action is said to be more conducive to the highest good for a person.
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is declared to be supreme;
for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained through it.
Of all these six types of actions, both in this world and after death,
it should be known that the Vedic rite is always the most conducive to one's welfare.
But in the Vedic path of action, all these [duties] without exception are included, respectively, within each specific ritual injunction.
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, being either active (pravṛtta) or withdrawn (nivṛtta).
Action performed with desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called *pravṛtta* (active); whereas action free from desire, preceded by knowledge, is taught as *nivṛtta* (withdrawn).
By practicing active (pravṛtta) action, one attains equality with the gods;
but by practicing renunciation (nivṛtta), one indeed transcends the five elements.
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self,
he who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty.
Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, in tranquility, and in the study of the Vedas.
For this indeed is the fulfillment of the purpose of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa;
having attained this, the twice-born man has truly accomplished his duty, and not otherwise.
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings;
it is established that the scripture of the Veda is impossible to master and immeasurable.
Whatever Smṛtis are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—
all those are fruitless after death, for they are said to be grounded in darkness.
Whatever other things there may be that arise and pass away from this [Veda],
they are fruitless and false because they are limited by time.
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately—
the past, the present, and the future— all these are established through the Veda.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are produced from the Veda alone; their manifestation arises from the qualities and actions [of the elements].
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all living beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of the goals of this creature.
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a magistrate, and even the lordship over all the world.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does one who knows the Veda burn away the defects of his own karma.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be,
becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world.

Those who possess the texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely possess the texts; those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain them; and those who practice with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge.
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for attaining the highest good for a Brahmin;
by austerity he destroys evil, and by knowledge he partakes of immortality.
One who desires purity in dharma should ensure that these three— direct perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions— are thoroughly understood.
He who examines the instruction on Dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedas and the Shastras knows Dharma, and no other.
This action leading to supreme bliss has been explained in its entirety;
now the secret doctrine of this treatise of Manu is being taught.
If it be asked how one should act regarding those duties not specifically prescribed,
that which learned Brahmins declare shall be the law, free from doubt.
Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered in accordance with the Dharma,
are to be known as the cultured Brahmins (śiṣṭas), who are the authorities for the direct perception of the Śruti.
Whatever legal matter an assembly of at least ten members may determine,
or even one of at least three who are established in virtuous conduct, that law shall not be overturned.
One who is learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the first three orders of life— these constitute an assembly of at least ten members.
One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—
this assembly of at least three persons is to be recognized for the determination of doubts regarding dharma.
Whatever dharma even a single best of the twice-born who knows the Vedas may determine, that should be known as the supreme dharma; it is not so by ten thousand ignorant men who have arisen.
Even if they gather by the thousands, those who lack vows, lack sacred mantras, and subsist on their birth alone do not possess the status of an assembly.
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the foolish who do not know the Dharma, proclaim as dharma—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after those who spoke it.
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
by not falling away from this, a Brahmin attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed Lord, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
has told me all this, the supreme secret of dharma.
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness.
The Self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the Self.
For the Self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings.
One should place the ether within the cavities, the wind within movement and touch,
the supreme fire within digestion and sight, the waters within moisture, and the earth within solid forms.
One should meditate on the Moon in the mind, the Quarters in the ears, Viṣṇu in the steps,
Hara in strength, Agni in speech, Mitra in excretion, and Prajāpati in procreation.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep.
Some call this Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman.
Pervading all beings with its five forms,
this [Self] perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self,
having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state.
A twice-born man who recites this treatise of Manu, proclaimed by Bhṛgu,
becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal.

Mātṛkā 1 [Legal Procedure]:
When men were solely devoted to Dharma and were speakers of truth;
At that time, there was no legal dispute, nor hatred, nor even envy.
When dharma had perished among men, legal disputes came into being;
and the king was appointed as the upholder of the rod of punishment and the arbiter of those disputes.
In this matter, two methods are proclaimed: written documents and witnesses.
For the purpose of clarifying a disputed point between two litigants, that [method] is to be understood as having two characteristics:
with a counter-claim and without a counter-claim.
NM 1.4c: "With a stake" (*sottara*) means where there is a wager (*paṇa*) preceded by a written contract (*vilekhā*).
NM 1.5a-c: In a dispute involving a wager, whichever of the two parties loses therein, he shall be made to pay the wager he himself made, as well as the fine for defeat.
The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the plaint;
if that is abandoned, the plaintiff loses, while he who crosses over it becomes the defendant.
Families, guilds, assemblies, the appointed official, and the king [are the authorities].
The foundation of legal proceedings is established in each successive stage from the teacher onwards.
It is proclaimed to have four feet, four bases, and four means; it is beneficial in four ways, pervasive in four respects, and productive of four results.

It has eight limbs, eighteen titles, and likewise a hundred branches; it has three origins, two types of legal proceedings, two doors, and likewise two goals. It consists of Dharma, Vyavahāra, Caritra, and Rājaśāsana.
This four-footed legal procedure consists of the subsequent [claim] which subverts the prior.
Among these, *dharma* is established in truth; *vyavahāra* (legal procedure) rests upon witnesses;
*caritra* (customary practice) is found in written records; and *śāsana* (the king’s command) resides in royal edicts.
Because it is to be accomplished through the means of conciliation and the others, it is called "having four instruments" (*catuḥsādhana*);
and because it protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), it is "beneficial to the four" (*caturhita*). Furthermore, [it concerns] the doers, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king.
Because it pervades [the treatise] quarter by quarter, it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
Furthermore, because it accomplishes these four— dharma, artha, fame, and public esteem—
it is proclaimed as "four-effecting" (catuṣkārī).
The king, his attendants, the members of the court, the legal treatises, the calculator, and the scribe;
gold, fire, and water—this is declared to be the eightfold constituent of the court.
Indeed, the non-payment of debt, deposits, and partnership concerns [are the first matters of dispute].
Taking back what has been given, failing to perform services after having agreed to them,
non-payment of wages, as well as sale by one who is not the owner, failure to deliver after selling, and likewise regret after buying; 17.
The non-performance of agreements, disputes concerning land,
the relationship between husband and wife, partition of inheritance,
and then violence; verbal abuse, as well as physical assault, have been thus described.
Gambling and miscellaneous matters—thus the law is remembered as having eighteen titles.
Another division of these very titles is recorded as one hundred and eight;
it is said to have a hundred branches due to the diversity of human actions.

Because it proceeds from these three—desire, anger, and greed—that which gives rise to disputes is proclaimed to have three origins; therefore, this triad is called the "threefold source. Furthermore, a lawsuit should be understood as being of two kinds: based on suspicion and based on the actual facts.
But doubt arises among the unwise from association with [the ignorant], as seen in the case of those who have boarded a ship and so forth.
Because it is connected to both sides, it is described as having two doors:
the prima facie argument (*pūrvavāda*) is one side, and the rejoinder (*uttara*) is its counter-position.
Because it follows both reality and deception, that [jāti] is said to have two courses.
Reality is that which is connected with the true meaning; deception is that which is stated through negligence.
In that regard, the king who employs dharma as his instrument should tolerate the remaining deception.
One should resort only to what is factual, since prosperity has its root in dharma.
For a king who is self-disciplined and adjudicates legal disputes according to dharma,
seven virtues arise like the seven flames of fire.
Dharma, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, the winning over of others, great respect from the subjects, and an eternal station in heaven— therefore,
having ascended the throne of justice, the king should be free from envy.
He should be impartial toward all living beings, observing the law of Yama;
placing the treatise on Dharma before him and abiding by the mind of the judge, he should examine the legal cases with a concentrated mind in their proper order.
The scripture (*āgama*) should be established first, followed by the subject matter of the legal proceeding (*vyavahārapada*);
then the desire to know (*vivitsā*) and the final decision (*nirṇaya*). Thus, the judicial process (*darśana*) is fourfold.
One should proceed according to the path without contradicting the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Arthaśāstra*.
Examining the course of legal proceedings with skill, he should lead them to their conclusion.
Just as a hunter, having struck a deer,
follows its tracks by means of a trace of blood in the undergrowth, so should he follow the path of justice.
Where there may be a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra,
one should set aside what is stated in the Arthaśāstra and practice what is stated in the Dharmaśāstra.
However, in the event of a contradiction with the Dharmaśāstra, even that which is supported by logic is not in accordance with Dharma.
For judicial procedure is powerful; by it, even the Dharma is set aside.
(34) For the venerable Dharma is subtle, beyond the senses, and difficult to discern.
Therefore, one should lead the course of legal proceedings through the path of direct perception. (35)
Even one who is not a thief incurs the status of a thief, and a thief attains the status of a non-thief;
through legal proceedings, Māṇḍavya—who was not a thief—was treated as a thief.
[Likewise, one may be accused] regarding women, at night, outside the village, inside a house, or by enemies.
Even if a legal proceeding has been concluded regarding these matters, it may be reopened for further action.
Because of the complexity of disputes and because human memory is unreliable, one may,
out of a desire to ascertain the truth, allow time to pass in cases such as debts and the like.

In cases of theft of cattle, land, gold, or women; in cases of violence, verbal or physical abuse, and crimes of immediate peril; and in cases of assault and defamation, one should institute a lawsuit immediately.
However, he who proceeds with a disputed matter without first reporting it to the king [is liable for the penalty].
He should be restrained by force, yet his purpose shall not be achieved.
The plaintiff should detain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated and who departs from that speech,
until the appearance for the summons at the trial.
Confinement may be of four kinds: by place, by time, by exile, and likewise by labor. One must not violate such confinement while it remains unfulfilled.
[This applies] in cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering a difficult terrain or a calamity.
One who has not yet secured a prohibition does not commit an offense by departing while that prohibition is still unestablished.
(43) He who violates a prohibition during the period when it is being established—by acting otherwise—he is to be disciplined; the one who imposed the prohibition shall incur a fine. (44)
One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one beset by calamity, one similarly assailed by another, and one engaged in the king’s business;
likewise, cowherds while tending cattle and farmers while the crops are ripening. (45–46a)

Artisans, as well as those engaged in weaponry during a conflict, are exempt from being summoned at that time. Furthermore, one who has not yet attained legal majority, an envoy, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and one in a precarious situation shall not be obstructed [in their business], nor shall the king summon them. (NM 1.46c–47)

One who has not been formally charged should not bring a charge against another; nor, having failed to prove his own case, should he seek to strike back at one who has already accused him. Furthermore, he ought not to strike one who has been struck by another.
Whatever matter one brings as a charge, he must not cause that matter to fall into disorder.
One should not shift to another position; by doing so, one loses the previous claim.
(49) One should not bring a false accusation; the fault belongs to the one who makes a false accusation. Whatever penalty has been prescribed for that [offense] shall apply to the accuser. (50)
Making excuses while wasting time, remaining silent in the assembly, speaking words and then contradicting them—these are the signs of one who is losing his case.
Furthermore, he who flees when summoned, or who does not appear for the dispute when it has begun; 51–52.

That person should be punished by the king and indeed excluded from the legal proceeding. In cases where a lawsuit has been adjudicated, even written documents or witnesses become useless if they were not previously presented.
Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grains have already ripened,
so too is evidence useless for those whose legal proceedings have been concluded.
Even that which is untrue, if stated at the appropriate time, is examined.
But that which, through negligence, is not stated, even if it be true, is lost.
If one should think that a case has been concluded or a judgment passed contrary to the law,
the judge, having imposed a double fine, shall reopen that matter.
But when a legal proceeding has been wrongly judged, the members of the court shall incur that same punishment;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of righteousness without the threat of punishment.
(57) He who speaks otherwise than the truth, whether out of passion, ignorance, or greed, [shall be punished].
He who is a member of the assembly but acts unbecomingly of the assembly should be recognized as such; the king should severely punish him.
However, by the king especially, while protecting his own dharma, the quality of being virtuous or non-virtuous must be examined due to the diversity of human minds.
There are men who, out of greed, would give false testimony; there are also other wicked people who forge documents. Therefore, the king must especially examine both of these matters with great care.
A document is [validated] by the conduct of writing, and witnesses by the conduct of witness-hood.
(61) Untruths appear like truths, and truths appear as untruths;
various states of being are seen in this way. Therefore, investigation is appropriate. (62)
The sky appears like a surface, and a firefly like a flame;
yet there is no surface in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
Therefore, even when an object is perceived through direct perception, it is proper to subject it to critical examination.
By making known the matters after having examined them, he does not fall away from *dharma*.
Seeing legal cases in this way at all times, the king, composed in mind,
spreads his radiant glory here and attains the world of the Sun.

Mātṛkā 2 (Mātṛkā 2 is found only in manuscript P). [The second chapter of the Mātṛkā included in Jolly’s edition and translation does not belong to the original Nāradasmṛti (see the Introduction to the text). Its translation is provided in the Appendix.]

Having gained firm confidence through deliberation, the plaintiff— impelled by his own interest and having reached a certainty regarding the matter to be accomplished— should cause the *pūrvapakṣa* (the initial statement of the case) to be written down.
But the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case,
should immediately set forth his counter-argument related to the subject matter of that initial plea.
He may obtain a period of one day for writing, or three days, or even seven days.
In the third quarter, however, the plaintiff is joined; the winner is certainly entitled to immediate [recovery].
(NM 2.3) The reply may be of four kinds: denial (*mithyā*), admission (*saṃpratipatti*), a counter-plea (*pratyavaskanda*), or a plea based on a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāyavidhisādhya*). (NM 2.4)
"This is false; I do not recognize it, for I was not present there at that time, and I was not even born at that moment"—thus, falsehood is fourfold.
Furthermore, "false" (*mithyā*) and "contrary" (*viparīta*) are synonyms.

The reply, which is connected to the meaning of the plaintiff's case, is of four kinds. (NM 2.6c) As long as the defendant has not yet submitted his reply to the *bhāṣā* (the plaint), the plaintiff shall cause it to be written down, including all matters he intends to state. (NM 2.7)
A document that has a different meaning, one that is devoid of meaning, one that lacks authoritative evidence or scriptural support,
and one that is deficient or redundant— these are cited as defects of the statement (bhāṣādoṣa).
Whatever is to be obtained, by whom, from what source, and how— that person shall obtain that very thing from that source.
"But it is not that one is other than another, nor that one is from another; thus, this meaning of 'other' is threefold.
(NM 2.9) "I too have been meditated upon here by your friend with his mind as if I were an enemy;
therefore, it was for this reason—and no other—that I informed you here with great forbearance. (NM 2.10)
That which is deficient in substance and measure, devoid of the object and the recipient of the fruit, and lacking in authority—
one should reject such a document as being defective in its evidence.
One should avoid the defect of lacking a legal title in the first section.

[One should avoid] a case where one person is at odds with many, or where there is opposition between a city and a kingdom. (NM 2.12) If, regarding the drops, measures, words, or syllables, there is a discrepancy—whether deficient or excessive—due to a single irregularity, it becomes useless; one should carefully avoid such a [composition]. (NM 2.13)
But that which is corrupted, poorly situated, or spoiled by water, oil, and the like— even if it is clear in its phrasing— one should avoid it because its meaning is not distinct.
Even if a statement is established, it does not constitute valid testimony if it is not true.
If one falls away from the external duties prescribed by conventional practice,
that which was entrusted to me by him while he resided on Mount Gandhamādana has been forfeited.
This external form of conventional dharma is not established;
(NM 2.16) because of the insertion of different syllables and the resulting shift in meaning, the delivery of the action becomes confused, and the action itself becomes disordered. (NM 2.17)
NM2.18a: Whatever [charge] one [party], being provoked by passion and the like, might state during the proceedings;
NM2.18c: all that should first be written by the judges upon a board or similar surface for the plaintiff.
NM2.19a: This is well-considered by those established in dharma for the sake of unconfused understanding.
Therefore, something other than that—such as a fruit, a leaf, or the like—should be excluded by the proponent.
(NM 2.19) The remaining items, permitted by both disputants and placed upon the board, they should record in writing along with witnesses, as well as the admissions of the two disputants. (NM 2.20)

That which remains from what was written by the two disputants, and which is subsequently remembered by a disputant, is called *pratyākalita*; it is recorded in his own section. Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant, [he acts as the representative].
Between two parties who dispute for the sake of one another, victory and defeat belong to them alone.
He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent,
yet speaks on behalf of another, shall be punished even if he is merely speaking falsely in a legal proceeding.

He who, having abandoned his initial position, resorts again to another, should be known as a debater defeated due to shifting his argument; such indeed is that man. In all disputes, one is not defeated by quibbling over words (*vākchala*).

In cases concerning cattle, women, land, or the non-payment of debt, even one who deserves punishment does not lose his property. If a defendant, when being sued, should deny the charge, the plaintiff must point out the evidence; unless he has been refuted by a counter-claim.
For what was written in the first *pāda* must be presented in its entirety, letter by letter;
however, in the third *pāda*, the plaintiff shall substantiate it through evidence (*kriyā*).
Evidence, moreover, is declared to be of two kinds: human (*mānuṣī*) and likewise divine (*daivikī*).
Human proof is said to consist of written documents and witnesses, while ordeal by the balance and other such means is considered divine.
When a legal proceeding has been conducted during the day in villages or cities,
and provided that witnesses are available, the divine method of proof is not to be employed.

In the forest, in a deserted place, at night, or within a house, in cases of violence, and likewise in the denial of a deposit, divine means of proof are applicable. And when the prima facie case is contradicted by the recognition of the grounds for the claim.
The defendant must indeed be diligent, and the case should be understood as being like the plaintiff's initial claim.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by witnesses, and one who confesses the charge himself— these are the four types of those who have failed their case.

One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the legal procedure, one who does not appear, one who fails to provide a reply, and one who flees after being summoned— these five are recorded in tradition as those who have lost their case.
Gems such as rubies and the like, gold such as dinars and the like;
Pearls, coral, conch shells, and the like, when stolen, shall go to their owner.
But if one steps upon perfume, garlands, ornaments, clothing, or sandals that have not been given— these being called "the King's"— he deserves the death penalty.

The price of merchandise, wages, a deposit, a fine, and whatever is paid as a court fee, as well as gifts made in vain, stakes in gambling, and the wagers of dice— these do not accrue interest if they are not intended to do so.
Those of Śūdra origin who bring false accusations against the twice-born, [shall be punished].

Having cut out their tongues, the king shall have them impaled upon stakes. Whether it be an oral command, a written document, a tablet, a royal edict, a mortgage deed, a sale contract, or a purchase agreement—
whosoever makes the first presentation to the king, his case shall be recognized as the plaintiff's claim by those who know the legal procedure.
When the witnesses are challenged, the first step is the purification of the previous witnesses;
once those witnesses have been cleared, one should thereafter purify the testimony itself.

In the case of witnesses, assessors, and those who have failed in their duties, there is a requirement for a renewed examination; however, for those who have been found deficient through their own conduct, there is no rule for a second trial.
Even one who has confessed of his own accord, though he may have been found deficient through his own conduct, [is not subject to further penalty].

Even one who has failed in his legal action deserves a final determination by the members of the court. (NM 2.41c) But having set aside the arguments, the members of the court must reach a definitive decision on the case. (NM 2.42a) If a decision is reached without setting aside [the arguments], there will be conflict both in this world and after death. (NM 2.42c)
If he is defeated by the jurors themselves, he should subsequently be punished by the king according to his own legal code.
Furthermore, a formal document of victory (jayapatraka) should be granted to the victor as is appropriate.
And this has been declared by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) to be the primary gateway to legal procedure.
For when the opening is pure, there shall be purity of the legal proceeding; not otherwise.
[Mātṛkā 3: The Court]
But one who has been appointed must speak words that are impartial. A member of the court (*sabhyah*) who speaks what is appropriate shall incur neither hatred nor guilt;
however, a member of the court who speaks otherwise shall incur both of those.
The king, however, should appoint righteous assessors who have been well-tested,
capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings like excellent oxen—
those who are skilled in the meaning of the treatises on Dharma, of noble birth, and speakers of truth.
The members of the king’s court should be impartial toward both enemy and friend.
Dharma is said to be established upon them, and the king is the root of Dharma;
therefore, the king should purify legal proceedings in consultation with the virtuous.
In pure legal proceedings, the members of the court attain purity;
their purity indeed arises from *dharma*, therefore they should speak only what is *dharma*.
For where *dharma* is overcome by *adharma*, and where truth is overcome by falsehood, [the court is defiled].
While they look on, justice is slain; the members of the court are themselves slain there.
For when Justice, pierced by Injustice, enters an assembly, if he is not extracted from his wound, the members of that court are pierced as well.

One should either not enter the court, or speak what is just; for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely therein becomes guilty of sin. But those members of the court who, having entered the assembly, sit in silence and deep thought, [are likewise at fault].
All those who do not speak according to what they have perceived are speakers of untruth. One quarter of the demerit goes to the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
