The king becomes guilty by this [act], yet the members of the court are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured.
He who is indifferent eats fish along with the bones, as it were, like a blind man.
13c–14. He who, having entered the court, speaks behind one's back due to a deficiency in the facts—
therefore, a member of the court, having reached the assembly, being free from passion and hatred,
should speak such words that he does not fall into hell.
Just as a learned physician extracts a splinter by means of an instrument,
so should the judge extract the splinter through legal procedure.
Where all the members of the court consider, "This is right," [that is a just decision].
That debate would be free from thorns; otherwise, it would be full of thorns.
(16) That is no court where there are no elders; they are not elders who do not speak according to dharma.
That is not dharma where there is no truth; that is not truth which is pierced by deceit. (17)
Legal Subjects 1. Non-payment of Debt (ṛṇādāna)
That which is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner,
as well as the rules regarding the giving and receiving [of wealth]— this is traditionally known as *ṛṇādāna* (the law of debt).
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares.
Whether they are divided or undivided, those who take up that burden [of the estate] must pay it. Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle or a brother,
or whatever was contracted by the mother for the sake of the family, the heirs shall pay all of that in its entirety.
A debt that has been cleared by sons in due order, having been received without obstruction, must be paid by grandsons for their grandfather's debt; it ceases with the fourth generation.
Since fathers desire sons for the sake of their own interests, [they act] accordingly.

"He will liberate me from my creditors, both those to whom I owe and those who owe me. Therefore, once a son is born, the father should strive with effort to liberate himself from debt through his son, so that he does not fall into hell.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fires dies while still indebted,
both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifice shall become the property of his creditors.
A father need not pay a debt incurred by his son, but a son must pay one incurred by his father.
Except for that contracted on account of lust, anger, liquor, gambling, or acting as a surety;
and except for that which was contracted at the father's own command or for the maintenance of the family;
the father shall pay such debt of his son even in times of distress. (8–9)

Whatever has been set aside for the sake of the family by pupils, resident students, slaves, wives, or those performing domestic service, that must be borne by the head of the household. A son shall not [claim his inheritance] before twenty years have passed while his father is away abroad.

He should pay the debt to the paternal uncle or to the eldest brother. Even if he is the only one remaining, he may be made to pay a debt contracted by those authorized while they were alive; but when they have died, his son is not liable to pay that debt to others.
A woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor likewise one contracted by her son,
except for what was promised by her own consent, or what was contracted jointly with her husband. A childless widow, authorized by her dying husband, shall pay [the debt].
Or rather, he who takes the inheritance shall [pay the debt], for from where the inheritance comes, from there the debt follows.
And a debt contracted by a wife shall not in any way become the husband's obligation, except for what was contracted during times of distress;
for the expansion of the household depends upon the men.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and liquor-sellers,
whose livelihood depends on them and whose families rely upon them;
but a woman who, having sons, abandons her son and resorts to another man, [is liable to punishment].
The son alone shall take the entire inheritance of that woman who is destitute of wealth.
But if a woman who possesses property and has offspring should resort to another man,
he shall pay her husband’s debt, or she may be abandoned by him in that same manner.

For when a man dies without wealth and without sons, he who takes his wife incurs the debt; that very person is declared by tradition to be the heir to his property. Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the burden of the debt.

If there is neither a son nor a husband, the woman who possesses the property shall take it; if there is neither a wife nor a son, the one who possesses the property shall take it. Among women who live as they please (*svairiṇī*), she who is the most excellent, and among remarried women (*punarbhū*), she who is the most excellent—he who marries such a woman must pay the debt contracted by her former husband.
They say that transactions entered into by a woman are invalid when not in times of distress,
especially those involving the giving, mortgaging, or selling of a house or field.
Even these are valid if the husband gives his consent.

In the absence of the husband, the son, or both husband and son, the king may take [the property]. Whatever has been given by a gratified husband to his wife, even when he has died, she may enjoy it as she wishes or give it away, with the exception of immovable property.
Likewise, a deed performed by a slave is declared to be as if not done, except by the master’s command;
for a slave has no authority over himself.
And a deed performed by a son against the will of the father is likewise [invalid].
They say that even such a gift is as good as not given; a slave and a son are equal in this regard.
Even if he is independent, one who has not attained legal capacity is not liable for debt.
Independence, however, is recorded as belonging to the eldest, based on seniority determined by virtue and age.

In this world, there are three who are independent: the king, the teacher, and likewise the householder in his own home for each of all the social classes. All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth alone is independent.
A student is traditionally held to be dependent, whereas independence resides in the teacher.
Women, sons, and slaves, along with their possessions, are dependent;
however, the householder is independent therein, specifically regarding that which has come to him by inheritance.
A child staying in the womb is to be considered equal [to an adult] until the eighth year;
a minor (bāla) is to be known as such until the sixteenth year, and is also termed a pogaṇḍa.
Beyond that age, he is knowledgeable in legal transactions and independent, except in matters concerning his parents.
While both parents are alive, he shall remain dependent even if he is advanced in age.
Of those two, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the eldest brother.
All these [sons] are always independent with respect to their own property,
but regarding instruction, distribution, and sale, they are considered dependent on others.
Whatever act an infant performs, and likewise one who is not independent, [is invalid].
Those who know the treatises declare in the scriptures that such an act is "unperformed.
For even if one is independent, whatever deed they perform while having fallen into a state of non-naturalness,
that too they call "unperformed," because by reason thereof they are no longer independent.
Those who are possessed by lust and anger, afflicted by pain, fear, or calamity, and overwhelmed by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen from their natural state (*aprakṛti*).
Likewise, the eldest in the family, as well as he who is most excellent and remains established in his natural state, [should be respected].
An act performed by such a person shall be considered as not done; what is done by one who lacks independence is not considered done.
All actions have wealth as their root; therefore, effort is deemed necessary for its acquisition.
Its management follows this sequence: protection, increase, and enjoyment.
Furthermore, that [wealth] should be known as threefold: white, variegated, and black;
its seven distinct varieties should be understood individually.
[The first is] that which is acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, a daughter, a pupil, a patron for sacrifice, or inheritance.
Wealth is of seven kinds, and "white" (śukla) wealth is one of them; its increase is likewise of that same kind.
Wealth acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, tolls, the practice of crafts, and what is obtained from one who has received a favor, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).

That which is acquired through bribery, gambling, acting as a messenger, causing distress, forgery, violence, or by means of fraud, is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa). With that [wealth], one may engage in buying, selling, giving, or receiving.
And various activities as well as enjoyments proceed [from it].
Whatever a man performs with whatever kind of substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both here and after death.
Furthermore, that [wealth] is traditionally held to be of twelve kinds based on its relation to the various castes;
it is of three kinds as common property, and the remainder is traditionally held to be of nine kinds. These are:
what has come down by succession, a gift of affection, and what is acquired together with a wife.
N1.47c. For all social classes without distinction, wealth is of three kinds.
N1.48a. The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics:
N1.48c. That which is obtained through receiving gifts, from a patron for whom one performs sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil.
They declare that the specific wealth of a Kṣatriya is also threefold:
what is acquired in battle, tribute, and fines from legal proceedings. (49) The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics. (50a)

For a Śūdra, however, [the means of livelihood] are agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, provided they are performed under the patronage of those [higher castes]. This is the righteous way for all social classes to acquire wealth;
it would be unrighteous if practiced otherwise, unless there is a grave emergency.
In times of distress, the conduct of a Vaiśya is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as the next best alternative; it is never declared to be inferior to that.
Under no circumstances, however, should a Brāhmaṇa perform the work of a Śūdra.
A Śūdra is not entitled to perform the rites of a Brāhmaṇa, for those two [the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya] incur a fall by doing so.
Between those two, no superior or inferior action exists;
for, setting aside the middle actions, all other duties are common to both.
Having crossed over a time of distress by means of wealth acquired through the occupation of a Kṣatriya,
a Brāhmaṇa should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation once he has performed purification for himself. But if a Brāhmaṇa takes delight out of passion in that very occupation, [he must perform penance].
A *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* who has fallen from the path is proclaimed to be unworthy of sitting in the row for meals (*apāṅkteya*).
Among the occupations of a Vaiśya, the following items are not to be sold by a Brāhmaṇa: milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, beeswax, lac, alkali, liquids, and fermented spirits.
Meat, cooked rice, sesame, linen, soma, flowers, fruits, vegetables, humans, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, and climbing plants;
indigo, silk, skins, bones, blankets made of goat hair, one-hoofed animals, and earth.
Curdled milk, hair, oil-cakes, vegetables, and similar medicinal herbs [are forbidden for sale]. However, a Brahmin may sell dry wood and grass,
with the exception of fragrant substances, lac, bamboo, cotton, roots, and chaff.
Split bamboo that has fallen of its own accord, fruits from the jujube and *iṅguda* trees,
a rope, and cotton thread— provided these have not been altered; likewise,
in cases of incapacity for the sake of medicine, or for the purpose of a sacrifice.

If sesame seeds must necessarily be sold, they should be exchanged for an equal amount of grain. A Brāhmaṇa who sells items that are not to be sold has fallen from the path; having been restored to the right path, he shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.

The means of proof must be diligently protected by those who abide by the means of proof; for the means of proof fail when they are not properly established. Written documents, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the threefold means of proof.
In the acquisition of wealth, that by which the owner enjoys his property [is decisive].
A written document is always superior; however, witnesses are valid only while they live.
Possession prevails through the lapse of time—this is the settled rule in the scriptures.

Among these three types of direct evidence (*dṛṣṭa*), each preceding one should be known as more authoritative than the following; possession (*bhukti*) is the most authoritative of them all. For even when a written document exists and witnesses are still living, [possession prevails].
Especially regarding immovable property, that which is not enjoyed does not remain secure.
(68) When a person, out of folly, neglects his own assets while they are being enjoyed by others even in his presence, possession brings those very assets under its control during his lifetime. (69)
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years in his presence while remaining silent, he does not deserve to recover it;
for he stands there silently, showing indifference.
N1.71c. When the previously mentioned time has elapsed, the legal proceeding is not established. N1.72a.
If [the owner] is not mentally incapacitated nor a minor, and his property is enjoyed [by another];
N1.72c. that which has been enjoyed is settled by the legal proceeding; the possessor deserves that wealth.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, an open deposit, a sealed deposit, women, the property of a king, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not become lost through adverse possession.
However, if the owner uses [the property] openly, it is lost after twenty years.
Even property such as deposits and the like is lost through adverse possession, with the exception of the property of a wife and that of a king.
However, the property of a wife and the property of kings are never lost,
even if they have been enjoyed for hundreds of years without a legal title to them.
Where possession is seen but no title is seen anywhere,
there title is the cause, not possession.
That which is enjoyed without title— possession does not override that.

But when the enjoyer has died, the property passes to the state of being enjoyed by his descendants. When one who has taken possession is challenged, he should produce evidence for the objects; possession itself shall be proof of purity, provided it has been obtained through succession from the father.
That which is deposited with another, that which is taken away, that which is left behind, that which is seized by force, that which is borrowed,
and that which is enjoyed in the owner's absence— these six [types of property] are lost without legal title (āgama).
Likewise, when a litigant has died while a lawsuit was pending, [the case continues against his heirs].

That property must be cleared up by the son; possession does not override it. (80) Even that which has been enjoyed for three generations by predecessors without a title, having come down through the succession of three persons, cannot be set aside. (81)
Even if they are virtuous, witnesses are not authoritative after the wealth-owner has died,
except for that which was previously made known by him when death was imminent.
For when the defendant is dead, the testimony of witnesses is not considered valid evidence.
In that case, a legal proceeding accompanied by witnesses shall be the means of proof for reaching a definitive decision.

Furthermore, even if a matter consistent with dharma has been communicated by a dying person, one may serve as a witness therein; this applies also in the six cases beginning with "deposited with another" (anvāhita).
In all matters concerning debts and the like, each subsequent [means of proof] is stronger than the preceding one;
however, among gifts, acquisitions, and purchases, each preceding one is more authoritative than the succeeding.
For the giving and receiving of gifts is intended as the cause for obtaining a specific status or position.
That is declared to be *kusīda* (lending on interest), and by that is the livelihood of moneylenders established.
In the treatises, its interest is recorded as being fourfold: corporeal (*kāyikā*), periodical (*kālikā*), stipulated (*kāritā*), and compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*).
That which is not inconsistent with one's physical capacity and is paid as a fee for services is called bodily interest (*kāyikā*).
That interest which flows month by month is known as periodical interest (*kālikā*).
That interest which is agreed upon by the debtor himself is called stipulated interest (*kāritā*).
Interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*. This rule for the accumulation of interest is recorded as being universally applicable to all debts;
however, there is another rule according to local custom where a debt remains outstanding.
In one place it is double, in another triple, and likewise in another it is fourfold;
in yet another region, it stands at eightfold.
The interest on gold, grain, and cloth is respectively double, triple, and fourfold.
The interest on ghee is eightfold; likewise, the offspring of female cattle and other animals [constitutes the interest].
[So too is it for] thread, cotton, fermenting agents, tin, lead, all types of weapons, leather, copper, and iron.
And for all other [substances] as well, including bricks,
Prajāpati Manu has declared that their increase is inexhaustible;
this is likewise true for all oils, intoxicants, honey, and clarified butter.
The interest on molasses and salt should be known to be eightfold.
Interest on items given out of affection shall never accrue unless it was agreed upon;
however, even if not agreed upon, it increases after half a year has passed.
This rule for interest has been declared according to dharma for one who has grown wealthy. However, that interest which is prescribed for grains is called usury (vārdhuṣya).
A Vaiśya may, at his will, overcome his distress through the practice of usury.
Even in the midst of dire calamities, a Brāhmaṇa must not engage in usury.
If a Brāhmaṇa who has a right to inheritance has no one to whom the debt should be given, he should pay it to a kinsman of his own lineage;
in the absence of such a person, he should pay it to his relatives.

But when there are no kinsmen of his own, nor relatives or blood relations, then he should give it to those of his own caste; if none of these exist, he should cast it into the water. Having received a debtor who has come to him, the creditor shall pay him the principal along with the interest.
But if, when being entreated, he does not give, he shall suffer the loss of his remaining property.
When the debt is cleared, he should provide a written discharge; in the absence of such a document, he should provide a verbal acknowledgment.
In this manner, there shall be mutual clearance between the creditor and the debtor.
In this matter, there are two causes for confidence:
the surety and the pledge; likewise, the written document and witnesses are the two means of proof that bring clarity.
[They serve] for appearance, for delivery, and likewise for assurance.
The wise have observed that a surety is of three kinds, corresponding to exactly three types of matters.
When debtors fail to repay their debts, or when the terms of the agreement are disputed,
the guarantor shall pay that debt, as shall one who fails to produce the debtor.
If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to the agreement;
for when no specific distinction has been made among them, the creditor may act as he pleases.
Whatever amount a surety may pay when pressured by the creditor, the debtor shall reimburse that amount to the surety doubled.
That which is pledged is known as *ādhi*; it should be understood as having two types.
A pledge is of two kinds: that for which the time of repayment has been fixed, and that which remains until the debt is paid;
likewise, it is further declared to be of two types: one to be kept (gopya) and one to be used (bhogya).
In the case of the former, there is a return of the object; in the opposite case, there is a loss of interest.
Similarly, if through negligence the pledge of the owner undergoes deterioration,

or if it is destroyed— except in cases caused by fate or the king— the principal shall be lost. Even when being properly guarded, if the pledge should become worthless over time, [the same rule applies].
Another pledge should be provided, or the debt must be paid to the creditor.
Now, if a debtor should become deprived of his capacity due to a change in circumstances,

he shall be made to pay the debt as it becomes possible, at the appropriate times, according to his income. Or, if he is capable but, out of wickedness, does not give the wealth to the creditor, [he shall be punished].
The king, having taken a twentieth part as his share, should cause [the debtor] to be made to pay.
If, over time, the debtor's debt amount should be lost here [in this world], the restoration of the record of the lineage, name, and residence is declared to be by means of a document.
A document, moreover, should be known to be of two kinds: that written in one's own hand and that written by another.
Whether a matter lacks witnesses or possesses witnesses, its proof depends on the established customs of the region.

A document that is not contrary to local customs, which clearly indicates the subject matter and the parties involved, and whose sequence and characters are uncorrupted, is recognized as valid evidence.
That which is done under intoxication, or by force against women or children,
or that which is done out of fear or through fraud, is not authoritative. Furthermore, where the witnesses, the creditor, the debtor, and the scribe have all died, [the document is invalid].
Even that [document] is written in vain, unless it concerns a pledge (ādhi) which has a stable basis.
The pledge (ādhi) has been declared to be of two kinds: movable and immovable.
In this case, the validity of both depends upon possession; it is not otherwise.
That which has been shown at the proper time, that which has been made known, and that which has been proclaimed [is valid].
A written document is established as valid everywhere, even when the witnesses have died. However,
a document that has not been heard of, one whose meaning has not been seen, or one that is merely for the sake of litigation,
does not attain validity even while the witnesses are still living.

If a document has been deposited in another country, burnt, poorly written, or stolen, the procedure for one who possesses it is the production of a contemporaneous copy; for one who does not possess it, it is the presentation of witnesses. In any case where there is doubt regarding a document—whether it was actually executed or not—the same applies.

One should authenticate it by means of the marks of its being executed by his own hand, possession, and logical reasoning. A document that bears another's name or was produced for some other purpose must be examined when there is a dispute, by means of the reasons regarding its connection and provenance.
Any document that bears another's name or has been produced for some other purpose must,
in case of dispute, be examined by means of connections, traditional accounts, and reasons.
A written document should be contested by means of another written document, and one with witnesses by means of witnesses;

a written document is superior to witnesses, but witnesses are superior to a written document. And in cases where a document is torn, broken, stolen, erased, lost, or poorly written, [it may be contested by other means].
Another document must be executed; this is recorded as the rule for documents.
But when matters are in doubt between two parties disputing,
the ascertainment of the truth is seen to arise from witnesses, because of their having seen, heard, or experienced [the facts].
A witness is to be understood as one who has seen with his own ears and eyes;
for what another says is heard by the ear, and what is done by the body is seen by the eye.
Witnesses are declared by the wise to be of eleven kinds;
among them, five are said to be appointed (*kṛta*) and six are unappointed (*akṛta*). They are:
the written, the reminded, the incidental, and the cognizant.
The secret witness and the corroborating witness: thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
The unestablished [judgment] is also proclaimed by the wise to be of six kinds:
the village, the presiding judge, and the king of those engaged in legal proceedings.
One who is an insider in the affairs [of a family], one who has been sent by the plaintiff, and those from the family in disputes between families— these too may be witnesses.
Worthy witnesses should be of noble birth, upright, pure by birth, conduct, and wealth; they should be at least three in number, irreproachable, honest, and possessed of sound intellect.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and those who are blameless— these may belong to their respective classes, or alternatively, they may all belong to all classes.
In guilds, the members of the guild; in their own groups, those belonging to the group;
among outsiders, the outsiders; and among women, women themselves shall be witnesses.
But if someone among groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred, he shall not be a witness for those very same groups; for all of them would then be his haters.
For even those who are not witnesses are seen by the wise in the treatises to be of five kinds:
[those declared so] by statement, by defect, by division, by self-accusation, and by death in the interval.

Where witnesses are divided in a legal dispute— some being learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) and so forth on account of their testimony, and others being thieves and so forth on account of the perception of their faults— there shall be a conflict of opinions.
One who, not having been designated by his own statement, comes of his own accord and speaks,
is considered a "dead witness" (mṛtāntara), except in the case of one who was made aware of the claim while the plaintiff was dying.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world are not witnesses; this is because of their own statements, and no further reason is cited here.
Thieves, violent assailants, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise murderers—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; in them, truth is not found.
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
those whose testimony differs shall be disqualified as non-witnesses because of that discrepancy.
But he who, not being designated as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks, is called a "sūcī" (informant) in the scriptures; he does not deserve to be a witness.
If the matter that ought to be made known does not exist, or if there is no claimant, where could one exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness.
If the matter that ought to be made known does not exist, or if there is no claimant, where could he exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness.
When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both,
the witnesses shall belong to the one whose case constitutes the *pūrvapakṣa* (the initial claim).
In whatever matter the weakness of the plaintiff's case arises by force of circumstances,
the witnesses of the defendant must be questioned in that dispute.
One should not approach a witness in private at the instigation of another;
nor should one cause him to be divided by means of another. By acting in this manner, one shall surely suffer defeat.
If a witness designated for testimony should die or depart to another land, those who heard it shall be the authority; for the subsequent action depends upon the evidence.
Even after a very long time, that which has been written shall attain validity;
one who knows [how to write] should write it oneself, but one who does not know should have it written by another.
The validity of a witness who has been reminded here is stated to be established from the eighth year;
likewise, the validity of one who appears by chance is established up to the fifth year.
Success for a secret witness is attained up to the third year;
they say that success for a subsequent witness is attained up to one full year.
Alternatively, no fixed time limit has been observed regarding the witness;
for those learned in the scriptures say that the status of a witness depends upon memory.
That man whose memory and hearing are never impaired,
even over a very long period of time, is fit to serve as a witness to a legal matter.
But other six types of disputes are declared to be those where witnesses are not required;
the wise say that for these, the very characteristics [of the case] constitute witness-status.
One who sets fire [to a house] with a torch in hand is to be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer;
and one seized by the hair of the head is a simultaneous adulterer.
One who approaches with a spade in hand should be known as a destroyer of embankments;
likewise, one with an axe in hand is proclaimed to be a cutter of forests.
A man who commits assault is to be recognized by his prominent physical marks;
for these matters of assault are not dependent on witnesses, but rather require careful investigation.
Someone, having marked himself, might harm another out of malice;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of the evidence, the purpose, the circumstances, and the capacity for action.

Those who have a financial interest in the matter, those who are not trustworthy, companions, enemies, those whose faults are known, those afflicted by disease, and those who are corrupted should not be questioned as witnesses.

Slaves, deceitful persons, those lacking faith, the elderly, women, children, and wheelmen (cart-drivers); those intoxicated, insane, negligent, afflicted, gamblers, and village priests; N1.160a/ dāsanaikṛtikāśraddhavṛddhastrībālacākrikāḥ / N1.160c/ mattonmattapramattārtakitavagrāmayājakāḥ //
Long-distance travelers, sea-going merchants, renunciants, and the sick;
hunters, Vedic scholars, those devoid of proper conduct, eunuchs, and actors.

Nihilists, those who have become outcasts (vrātyas), those who abandon their wives and the sacred fire, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from a common vessel, companions of enemies, those who live by trade, and kinsmen; [these are not to be invited].
Actors whose faults have been previously observed, poisoners, snake-charmers, and snake-catchers;
those who administer poison, arsonists, usurers, the sons of Śūdra women, and those born of illicit unions;
the exhausted, the reckless, the weary, the penniless, and outcasts.
Those who have broken their vows, those who have not returned from their studies, the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and root-diggers; N1.164c.

Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to the king, those who predict rain or the position of the stars, those who proclaim impending calamities, those who sell themselves, and those whose limbs are deficient or who live on lewdness; N1.165.

One with deformed nails, one with a dark-complexioned face, one afflicted with vitiligo, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a fierce man, and those who oppose guilds or corporations; N1.166.
A murderer, a painter, a performer, one who has fallen from his caste,
a forger, a cheat, one who has renounced [his vows], a thief, and a king’s servant;
[as well as those who deal in] human beings, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, and climbing plants.
The seller, the Brāhmaṇa, the twice-born usurer, and whoever else [is such].
One who has fallen from his own duty, a member of a guild, a panegyrist, a servant of the low-born,
one disputing with his father, and a creator of dissension— these are non-witnesses.
Even those who have been designated as non-witnesses— such as slaves, rogues, and the like—
may become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it.
In all cases of violence, theft,
and adultery, as well as in both forms of verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a forger,
nor a relative, nor an enemy shall give false testimony.
A child may speak falsely through ignorance, a woman through wicked habit, a forger through malice,
a kinsman out of affection, and an enemy in order to settle a grudge.
Alternatively, one who is agreed upon by two disputing parties—
even if he is otherwise ineligible as a witness— should be questioned as a witness in the assembly.
But he who, because he is broken by his own faults, appears as if unwell,
moves from one place to another and seeks refuge with each one individually.
He coughs restlessly and without cause, sighs repeatedly,
scratches the ground with his feet, and tosses his arms or his garment.
The color of his face changes, and likewise his forehead perspires;
his lips become parched, and he glances upward and sideways.
He who speaks much at random, as if in haste, even when unasked, should be known as a false witness; the king shall punish that sinner.
And he who, having caused others to hear [the testimony], subsequently denies that witness-status, must be punished even more severely; for he is worse than a false witness.
Having summoned the witnesses— who are well-known for their conduct and who understand the matter— the judge should question them individually after binding them with solemn oaths.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by means of truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the heinous sins.
Having greatly terrified the witnesses by means of ancient declarations of dharma, by proclaiming the greatness of truth, and by censuring falsehood, [the judge should proceed].
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a begging bowl, tormented by hunger and thirst, and wretched,
he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar.
He who would give false testimony might find himself besieged in a city, hungry at its outer gate, and beholding his enemies once again.

The night on which a woman is taken as a wife, the night on which one is defeated at dice, and the night on which one’s limbs are tormented by a heavy burden— the speaker of falsehood shall dwell through those nights.
A witness who, when called upon to testify, behaves with the laxity of an ox's ear,
fastens upon himself a thousand nooses of Varuṇa.
When one hundred years of that [time] are completed, he is released from one noose;
in this manner, he is liberated from that bondage after a million years.
Listen, O gentle one, to the number of kinsmen he destroys by speaking falsely in testimony, according to that specific number, in due order.
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men.
By speaking falsehood for the sake of gold, one kills both those born and those unborn;
by falsehood regarding land, one kills everything. Therefore, do not speak falsehood regarding land.
They say that truth alone is the singular, peerless purifier of the self; it is the staircase to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Better than a hundred wells is even a single pond; better than a hundred ponds is a sacrifice; better than a hundred sacrifices is a son; and truth is better than a hundred sons.
The earth supports all by means of truth; by truth the sun rises;
by truth the wind blows; and by truth the waters flow.
Truth alone is the supreme gift; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the highest dharma for the worlds—thus have we heard.
Truth, O gods, is briefly defined as that which belongs to humans, while falsehood is what is traditionally known [as human].
One whose mind is established in truth attains divinity even in this very world.
Speak the truth, abandoning falsehood; by the truth you shall go to heaven.
Having spoken a most terrible falsehood, one will fall into hell.
And in the hells, those fierce and powerful servants of Yama will constantly cut out their tongues and sever them with swords.
And, unprovoked by anger, they shall pierce with spears the wailing man who has no refuge;
having lifted him up with his head downward, they shall throw him into lakes of fire.
And having experienced those painful sensations of hell for a long time,
you shall go here, O unfortunate one, into the wombs of vultures, crows, and other such creatures.
Having understood these faults in falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities in truth, speak the truth and uplift yourself; do not cause yourself to fall.
Neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor even great riches are able to rescue one who is sinking into the fierce darkness.
But the ancestors hang on you when you have become their witness:
"Will he deliver us, or will he cause himself to fall?"
Truth is the self of man; everything is established upon truth. In every way, you shall unite yourself with the self through that which is beneficial.
The interval between the night you were born and the night you will die would be in vain for you, if you were to act otherwise than truthfully.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood;
therefore, especially regarding the duty of a witness, one should speak only the truth.
That lowest of men who employs his own speech for the sake of another—
what would that sinner, who fears not hell, not do for his own sake?
Meanings are indeed fixed in speech; they have their root in speech and have issued forth from speech.
For that man who would steal this speech is a thief of everything.
But in the event of a conflict among witnesses, the majority is the authority;
when they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; and when they are equal in purity, those with the better memory should be chosen.
But where, in a legal dispute, an equality of memory is observed among the witnesses,
the testimony is set aside again because of the subtle nature of the requirements for witness-hood.
If a witness, having been summoned to give testimony regarding the categories of facts specified,
does not speak in accordance with the syllables [of the evidence], that testimony shall not be considered properly delivered.
Where there is a discrepancy regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or caste,
that testimony is said to be false.
Where witnesses state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that too shall be considered as unspoken; this is declared to be the rule for witnesses.
Where, due to negligence, there is neither a document nor witnesses for the creditor,
and the plaintiff denies the matter, the threefold procedure prescribed therein shall apply.
An injunction according to the circumstances, a fragment of reasoning,
and likewise a third means, an oath— by these one should establish the case in due order.
If one who is repeatedly exhorted should reject that advice,
after three, four, or five times, he should bring about his own ruin by disregarding the matter.
But when there is an obstruction to the injunction, one should pursue it by means of fragments of reasoning (yukti) through [considerations of] place,
time, the connection of objects, quantity, action, and so forth.
Even when arguments are insufficient, one should distress the accused with oaths,
taking into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the strength of the case, using fire, water, good deeds, and so forth.
He whom a blazing fire does not burn and whom water holds back [without wetting him] overcomes the curse; in the opposite case, he would be a sinner.
This same rule is prescribed for women in cases of charges regarding their conduct, as well as in cases of theft and violence,
and in all instances of denial of facts.
For even oaths are recorded among the gods and among the sages;
Vasiṣṭha, being suspicious of a Yātudhāna, uttered an oath.
Likewise, when the Seven Sages assembled at Puṣkara for the sake of Indra,
they uttered an oath with undistracted minds for the sake of mutual purification.
If one who has committed an improper act of violence seeks to restore himself to rectitude,
or if he confesses it himself in the assembly, half of the prescribed fine is ordained for him.
But if, out of wickedness, he conceals his sin, he shall be defeated;
in such a case, the members of the court are not satisfied, and a severe punishment is imposed.
2. Deposit (nikṣepa):
Where one deposits one's own property out of trust and without hesitation, that is called "deposit" by the wise; it is a title of legal dispute.
When an object that is separated from other substances and is indeterminate in nature is deposited in another's house, that is known as *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit).
Furthermore, that [debt] is said to be of two kinds: one with witnesses and likewise the other;
in the case of the latter, the proof shall be its repayment or, in the opposite case, [other evidence].
But he who, when requested by the depositor, does not restore the deposit, shall be fined by the king and compelled to pay it; and if it has been lost, he shall be made to pay its equivalent.
And he who should recover the property without the permission of the depositor shall be punished for that act and shall restore it along with its interest.

If that which was lost together with the object is lost to the borrower, it is lost to the lender; the same applies if it is destroyed by fate or the king, provided it was not caused by his own misconduct.
This same rule is seen to apply to articles borrowed or held in trust,
as well as to craftsmen, deposits, bailments, and counter-deposits.
And that man who adopts a minor (pogaṇḍa) along with his property—for him also this same rule shall apply;
these six procedures are equal.
3. Partnership (Saṃbhūyasamutthāna). Where merchants and others perform an undertaking collectively, that is known as partnership, a head of legal dispute.

When those who, for the sake of the fruit, perform their work in combination through a common means, the contribution [of each] serves as the basis; by that [contribution], they shall arise [to share the profit] according to their respective shares.
Whether equal, excessive, or deficient— whatever the proportion of a person may be,
their loss, expenditure, and increase will likewise be of that same kind.
Established in their own duty without deviation, they shall carry out the inspection of merchandise, bundles, expenditures, receipts, loads, and quality.
He who has lost [the property] through negligence, as well as he who has done what was forbidden,
and he who acts without being instructed by all the partners acting in concert, shall be made to pay [the loss].
When a calamity arising from a deity, a thief, or a king has occurred,
he who protects that [property] by his own power is declared to be entitled to a tenth share.
If one [of several brothers] should meet with misfortune, his heir shall receive that [property];
or, if there is no heir, all [the brothers] together, provided they are capable, shall take it.

Likewise, in the event of the misfortune of the officiating priests (ṛtvij), another person may complete that ritual; he shall receive from them the portion of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as it was originally assigned.
If a priest abandons a patron who is blameless and has done him no wrong,
or if a patron abandons a blameless priest, both of them shall be punished.
The officiating priest (ṛtvij) is seen to be of three kinds: one previously engaged, one chosen by oneself, and one who performs the priestly office out of affection and of his own accord.
This rule applies to those who have come by succession and to officiating priests chosen by oneself;
however, regarding a priest engaged by chance, there is no sin in relinquishing him.
A merchant arriving at a customs station shall pay the duty as it is prescribed;
he must not evade it, for this is ordained as a tribute to kings.
One who evades the customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who declares a false quantity, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
If a certain merchant, while traveling from his country, should die as a guest,
the king shall protect his goods until his heirs appear.
If there is no heir, one should entrust that property to relatives or kinsmen;
in their absence, one should keep it well-guarded for ten years.
After ten years, property that has no owner and no heir shall be taken by the king for himself; in this way, the law is not violated.

4.d. Non-delivery of what has been given (Dattāpradānika). N4.01a: When one, having given property improperly, desires to take it back, that is recorded in law as the title of dispute known as non-delivery of what has been given.
That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given—
this fourfold path of giving should be understood in legal proceedings.
For in that regard, eight things are traditionally held to be non-givable, and the givable is said to be of one kind;
one should know that what is given is of seven kinds, and what is not given consists of sixteen types.
A deposit, a borrowed item, a pledge, and that which is held in common;
a trust, as well as one's sons and wife, and one's entire property, when there is a male heir.
For even when a living being is beset by grievous calamities, the teachers declare that certain things must not be given away: namely, that which has already been promised to another.
Whatever wealth remains in excess after supporting one's family must be given away;
if one gives something else instead of that [excess], one incurs fault.

Those who know the law of giving recognize as a gift what is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, in return for a favor, or for the sake of a woman’s dowry or as a mark of favor.
But what is taken without it being given may be so through the force of fear, anger, grief, or illness;
likewise, through bribery, jesting, exchange, or fraud.

That which is performed by one who is a child, confused, not independent, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent [in this matter]."
When one who is not a worthy recipient is declared to be a worthy recipient, or when an act is joined with unrighteousness,
whatever is given through such ignorance is recorded in tradition as "not given."

He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who bestows what should not be given, are both to be punished: the one who takes what is not given, and likewise the giver of that which should not be given.

5. Non-performance of Service after Having Undertaken It (Abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā): But he who, having undertaken service, does not perform it—this legal subject matter is called "non-performance of service after having undertaken it."
In the treatise, the wise have observed five types of attendants;
four types are laborers, and among them, the slaves are fifteen-fold.

Pupils, resident students, and hired laborers—the fourth being the one who performs extra work—these are declared to be "laborers" (karmakaras); slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth.

The wise have declared that their lack of independence is their common characteristic; however, the distinction between them, as well as their specific functions, is said to be determined by their genus and their actions.
Action also should be known as twofold: indeed, both unwholesome and wholesome.
Unwholesome action is said to be the work of slaves; wholesome action is recorded as that of those who perform [righteous] deeds.
Cleaning the house door, impure places, the road, and the refuse heap; touching private parts, the limbs, or what remains after eating; and the handling or discarding of feces and urine.
Service performed for one's own master with one's limbs according to his will is to be known as inauspicious action; other than this, that which follows is auspicious.
Until he has mastered the knowledge, the pupil, being self-restrained, should serve his teacher;
he should likewise adopt the same conduct toward the teacher’s wives and the teacher’s son.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should wander for alms, sleep on the ground, remain unadorned,
go to bed last of all, and rise before everyone else in the house of his teacher.
He should not go anywhere without being commanded, nor should he remain with his teacher unless so instructed; when commanded, however, he should perform his duty without hesitation if he is capable.
One should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not mentally distressed;
sitting below the teacher on a grass mat or a wooden plank, one should remain composed.
If a pupil does not comply after being instructed by his teacher,
the teacher may punish him without causing physical injury, using either a rope or a split bamboo cane.
One should not strike him severely, nor on the head or the chest;
having first instructed and gained his confidence, he may then be punished by the king, otherwise like a teacher.
Having returned from his studies and having presented the teacher's fee to the guru, he should return to his own home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
Desiring to practice his own craft, with the permission of his relatives,
he shall dwell in the presence of a teacher for a period of time that has been well-determined.
The teacher should instruct him, providing food from his own household;
he should not make him perform other work, and he should treat him like a son.
He who abandons a teacher who is instructing him and is not at fault should be compelled to stay by force; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even if he has been trained, the pupil shall receive his fee once the prescribed time has elapsed;
furthermore, whatever work he performs there belongs to the teacher alone, and its fruit is his.
Having mastered the craft within the agreed time and having circumambulated his teacher from left to right, the apprentice, having honored him according to his ability, should take his leave.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages, based on the work performed, should correspond to their ability and devotion.
In this regard, the highest wage-earner is the soldier, the middle is the farmer, and the lowest should be the porter; thus is the hired laborer of three kinds.
He who is authorized over matters of wealth and likewise stands at the head of the household is to be known as an *adhikarmakara*; he is also remembered as a *kauṭumbika*.
These four are declared to be the performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen types of slaves are partakers of lowly labor.
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir, one maintained during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been impregnated by the master; N5.24.
Rescued from great debt, won as a prize in battle,
approached saying "I am yours," and made one who has completed his period of exile— these are the types of slaves.
A slave by gift of food (bhaktadāsa), likewise one supported by a female slave (vaḍavābhṛta),
and one who has sold himself— these are recorded in the treatise as the fifteen kinds of slaves.
Among them, the first four categories are not released from slavery except by the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary.
And whoever among these should rescue his master from a life-threatening danger shall be released from slavery and shall receive a share equal to that of a son.
One who was maintained during a time of famine is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by such an act.
Even if one has pledged the property after receiving payment, if the owner should redeem it,
then he who restores it is next in rank to the purchaser.
Having paid back the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from servitude;
likewise, even one who has entered into a contract for a fixed term is released upon the expiration of that time.
One who has approached [an enemy] saying "I am yours," or one who has entered battle and been defeated in a wager,
is released by the giving of a counter-head through an equal act.
A man who has fallen from the life of a renunciant shall indeed become the slave of the king;
for him there is no release, nor is there any purification whatsoever.
By neglecting his food, a slave for food is immediately released;
and by the punishment of a mare, a slave acquired through a mare is released.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most wretched of them all and is never released from slavery.
Those who have been stolen by thieves and sold, or those who have been forcibly made slaves, must be liberated by the king; servitude is not permitted with respect to them.
Slavery by means of the inverse order of castes is not ordained;
however, for one who abandons his own duty, slavery is considered permissible—except in the case of a wife—as it is otherwise thought of.
And he who, being dependent, offers himself [to another], saying "I am yours," shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall regain him.
N5.39 Only three are declared to be without property: the wife, the slave, and likewise the son;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
If one, with a joyful mind, should desire to make his own slave a non-slave,
he should take a water-pot from that person's shoulder and break it along with its water.
One should sprinkle him on the head with unbroken grains together with flowers;
then, having said three times, "He is no slave," one should release him facing the east.
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
he becomes one whose food may be eaten, one who may accept gifts, and one who is held in high esteem.
6. Non-payment of Wages (Vetanasyānapākarma):
The procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for those who have been hired has already been stated. The non-payment of such wages is recorded as that title of dispute.
The master of the work shall pay wages to the hired laborer according to the sequence agreed upon—
whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the conclusion of the work— as has been determined.
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall receive a tenth part of the profit,
cattle, seed-corn, and crops respectively.
Whatever implements for work have been brought for their task, he should employ them with a sense of trustworthiness;
he should not act with deceit.
If one who has promised to perform work fails to do so, he should be compelled by force to do it after wages have been paid;
if, having received wages, he does not perform the work, he shall pay double the amount of the wages.
If he should abandon his work before the time is complete, he deserves the loss of his wages;
however, if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for what was actually done.

Having agreed upon a wage consisting of a sixth part of the load, one who abandons a beast of burden on the road incurs the loss of that wage; however, if he causes it to work without paying, he must pay the wage along with interest.
Having hired a porter for goods or a vehicle for transport, if one abandons them on the way, he should be made to pay a quarter of the wages; if he abandons them halfway, he must pay half.
Likewise, even a carrier who does not bring [the goods] shall suffer a loss of wages;
however, one who creates an obstacle to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
If the goods should meet with misfortune due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost therein, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the fee; from two hundred, a milch cow.
This is the annual wage for the cowherd, along with the milk produced on the eighth day.
N6.12a: He should cause the cows to be brought back, O cowherd, every day at the end of the night; N6.12c:
having grazed and drunk, those cows the cowherd should bring back in the evening.
If a disaster should befall the cattle, the cowherd shall exert himself therein to the best of his ability;
if he is unable to do so, he must come quickly and report it to his master.
If a cowherd fails to exert himself, cries out [when the herd is lost], or fails to inform the owner,
he deserves to carry that [fine] and must also pay a penalty to the king.
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, or dies in a dangerous place,
or if it has failed through human negligence, the herdsman alone shall forfeit it.
Likewise, when goats and sheep have been obstructed by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
if a wolf should forcibly kill one, the guilt for that shall fall upon the herdsman.
And while those cows are still unweaned and roaming together in the forest,
if a wolf should spring upon and kill one of them, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
But if cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his own master at the proper place and time.
By this, the dispute concerning all guardians has been fully explained;
and in the case of [the animals] having died, the guardian shall be cleared of blame upon the production of marks and other evidence.
Having received the nuptial fee (*śulka*), a courtesan who does not wish [to comply] shall pay that same amount twice;
likewise, a man who does not give the fee after having enjoyed the woman [shall pay the same].
He who approaches a woman in a place other than the womb, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine (vinaya).
If one has built a house within the courtyard and dwells there after having paid the fee,
he should take away that house— its grass, wood, bricks, and so forth— and depart.
One should bring forward the vessels for the hymns when they are full and at the proper time;
otherwise, what is broken or lost shall be the responsibility of the receiver, except in the case of an accident.
7. Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner (Asvāmivikraya):
When property belonging to another—whether it has been deposited, lost, found, or stolen—is sold in the absence of the owner, that should be recognized as sale by one who is not the owner.
Having recovered property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall take possession of it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made openly, whereas there is theft if the purchase was made in secret.
If one purchases a slave from someone who is not the owner with that person's consent, or from a person of ill repute in private,
or buys him for a low price at an improper time, he shall be liable for those defects.
A buyer should not conceal the source of his purchase; his purity [of title] is established by that provenance.
In the opposite case, he incurs the same fault and deserves the punishment for theft.
The seller shall pay the value to the owner and the price paid by the buyer;
likewise, he shall pay a fine to the king—this is the rule regarding sale without ownership.
Having found a treasure deposited by another, one should present it to the king;
for all treasure belongs to the king, with the exception of that which belongs to a Brāhmaṇa.
Even a Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure-trove, shall quickly report it to the king;
he may enjoy what is given by the king, but by failing to report it, he would be a thief.
Having recovered even his own lost property in that manner, he should report it to the king;
he may take possession of it as being pure, otherwise he would be impure.

8. Regret over a Purchase (Krītānuśaya): When, after having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer—that is called the legal head of dispute known as "selling without delivery" (vikrīyāsaṃpradāna).
In this world, there are two kinds of property: that which is mobile and that which is immobile;
all of that is called "merchandise" (paṇya) in matters concerning purchase and sale.
N8.3a. However, the wise have recorded its method of giving and taking as being sixfold:
N8.3c. [Namely] by counting, by weighing, by measuring, and by action, by form, and by beauty.
If, after selling a commodity for its price, one does not deliver it to the buyer,
he shall be made to pay the loss of value for immovable property, and the fruit of the labor for movable property.
If the market price should fall, he shall bring back the merchandise together with its profit;
this rule applies to those who remain stationary, while for those who travel to various regions, the profit is determined by the local market of each direction.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss falls upon the seller alone who, having sold it, does not deliver it.
But he who, having shown an article as faultless, delivers it as faulty,
shall be made to pay double its value and an equal fine for the offense.
Likewise, he who, having sold [an item] into the hand of one person, delivers it to another,
shall be made to pay double that amount and shall be punished to the same extent.
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered for sale,
or if a seller sells it elsewhere after having already sold it, neither of them shall be held at fault.
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if it is not delivered, except by mutual agreement, there is no transgression on the part of the seller.
N8.11 For the sake of profit, merchants engage in the buying and selling of all commodities;
and that profit, having depended upon the market price, may either become great or not.
Therefore, at the proper place and time, a merchant should strive for profit;
he should not proceed by crooked means, for such is the superior path of commerce.
9. Non-delivery after sale (Vikrīyāsaṃpradāna).

N9.1a: When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for its price, does not regard it as satisfactory, this legal subject is called "repentance after purchase" (krītvānuśaya). N9.1c: This is declared to be the title of dispute known as "repentance after purchase."
If, after having purchased a commodity for a price, the buyer considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unspoiled.
If the purchaser delivers [the goods] on the second day, he shall incur a fine of one-thirtieth of the price;
on the third day, that fine is double; after that, the loss falls upon the purchaser alone.
The buyer should personally examine the merchandise beforehand for its qualities and defects;
once it has been examined and purchased with approval, it shall not be returned to the seller.
One should examine a milch cow after three days, but a draft animal after five;
however, the examination of pearls, diamonds, and corals should last for seven days.
For bipeds, the impurity shall last for half a month; for men it is twice that, and for women, double again.
For all seeds, it lasts ten days; for metals and clothes, one day.
Furthermore, a garment that has been worn, which is discolored and soiled—
even if it was sold while still defective— shall not belong to the seller again.
For a garment that has been washed once, one-eighth of its value is lost;
for the second time, one-half; for the third time, one-third; and for the fourth time, exactly one-half [of the remaining value].

But after half has been exhausted, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter [of the lifespan] until it reaches the stage where ten years remain; for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its further decay.
N9.10a. Furthermore, for all metals, the cause [of their transformation] in the process of working with fire is as follows:
N9.10c. It is observed that when they are being refined, their impurities are destroyed through contact with fire.
There is no loss in the case of gold; for silver, the loss is two palas per hundred;
it should be known that for tin and lead, the loss is eight palas per hundred.
One should know that five palas [of impurity] are found in copper, as well as in whatever products are made from it;
because there are many varieties of its ores, there is no fixed rule regarding the loss of iron.
N9.13a. Regarding the processing of woven cloth, the decrease and increase [in weight] have been illustrated.
N9.13c. For threads made of cotton and wool, the increase is ten palas for every hundred.
For those of medium quality with thick threads, the internal loss is declared to be one hundred and five;
however, for very fine threads, it is three palas.
The loss of a garment pierced by a needle is one-thirtieth for those made of wool, but for those made of work-woven cloth, there is neither increase nor loss.
For garments made of silk or bark-cloth, however, there is neither increase nor loss at all.
A merchant who is discerning regarding merchandise should not harbor regret after having purchased;
rather, he should understand the fluctuations in profit and loss as well as the supply of goods.
10. Non-fulfillment of the agreement (samayasyānapākarma).
The established practice of heretics, guilds, and so forth is called an "agreement" (samaya). The non-fulfillment of that agreement is recorded as a ground for litigation.
The king should likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, trade associations, corporations, bands, assemblies, and so forth, both within the fort and in the countryside.
Whatever their duty may be, whatever their action, whatever the rule for their attendance,
and whatever their means of livelihood— let him approve of all that accordingly.
Whatever is contrary to the king's wishes, whatever is naturally despised by his subjects, and whatever is detrimental to his interests— he should turn that away from them.
The king shall not tolerate their mutual forming of factions, the carrying of weapons, or their mutual injury.
Those who divide the separate groups must be especially disciplined;
for if they are neglected, they will bring about terrible danger, like a disease.
Whatever means of action should be defective and not prescribed by the sacred tradition,
that the king who desires his own welfare must cause to be stopped, even if it has already been set in motion.

11. Disputes concerning Land (Kṣetrajavivāda): The determination of watercourses, field boundaries, and the status of cultivated or uncultivated land—wherever such matters pertaining to land arise, that is a dispute concerning land.
In disputes concerning the boundaries of fields, the decision is based on the testimony of the neighbors,
as well as those who are the heads of cities, villages, or guilds, and those men who are the most venerable.
And those who live by agriculture outside the village boundaries, as well as cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest; N11.3.
They should mark out the boundary, characterized by signs such as husks,
charcoal, potsherds, jars, sanctuaries, and trees.
And by means of well-known anthills, level and uneven ground, and the like;
as well as by ancient fields, gardens, paths, and embankments.
In cases where lands have been carried away by rivers, abandoned, or lost their boundary markers,
[the decision] shall be made by inferring the location from that area, as well as by means of measurements and the observation of possession.
If, however, the neighbors should speak falsely in determining that matter,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
But others, such as the heads of guilds and the like, should be made to pay fines individually;
if they persist in falsehood, they should be punished with the first amercement.
A single man, even if he is trustworthy, shall not determine a boundary by himself;
because of the gravity of this legal matter, this procedure is established upon many witnesses.
If there is only one person to mark the boundary, he should do so while fasting and composed in mind,
wearing red garlands and garments, and placing the earth upon his head.
And when there are no knowers of the boundary and no boundary markers,
then the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two parties as he deems fit.
By this very same rule, the procedure for disputes concerning houses, gardens, water-reservoirs, temples, and so forth, as well as those between different villages, has been declared.
One should not obstruct crossroads, temples, carriage-roads, or pathways with refuse-heaps, ground-level pits, chasms, drains, and the like.
A watercourse built in the middle of another's field is not prohibited, provided it yields great benefit and causes little harm; for when there is a loss [to one], an increase [in yield] is desired.

A dam, moreover, should be known to be of two kinds: that which is to be excavated and likewise that which is to be built up. It is called "excavated" because it directs the flow of water, and "built up" because it stops that flow.
Without water, the crop would perish; yet by excessive water, it likewise perishes. That very same fault which exists in the absence of water is recorded as existing in the case of excessive water.
But whoever should construct a new embankment for one that was previously established but has fallen into ruin, without having consulted the owner, shall not partake in its fruit.
But when the owner has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is a human being,
one should then undertake that work of constructing a dam after having petitioned the king.
Otherwise, one would incur affliction by observing the hunter;
for the arrows of him who pierces again what has already been pierced are lost.
If the owners of a field are incapable, deceased, or lost, and no one prevents it,
should someone else cultivate that field, he shall enjoy its fruit.
If the owner of a field returns while it is being ploughed,
he shall recover his own field by paying for all the cultivation of the fallow land.
Then, by a reduction of one-eighth each year, when seven years have passed,
upon the arrival of the eighth year, he shall recover possession of the field that was enjoyed [by the other].
After one year, it becomes half-waste; after three years, it becomes waste;
but a field neglected for five years shall be equal to a wilderness.
A field that has been held for three generations, or a house that has come down by succession—
with the exception of what is granted by royal favor— one should not allow another to take away the enjoyment of such property.
But where cattle or other animals, having broken through the enclosure, cause damage to the crops,
the keeper shall be punished there, provided he does not prevent it to the best of his ability.
But in the case of the destruction of standing crops together with their roots, the owner of the field shall receive an equivalent amount;
the herdsman shall be released from liability by the killing [of the offending animal], and he shall inflict the fine upon the owner.
A cow that has recently calved, as well as bulls, goats, sheep, and elephants, must be kept away from the crops with great effort for ten days; their owner shall not be subject to punishment.
One should cause a cow to pay a fine of one māṣa, and likewise a buffalo two māṣas;
for a goat or a sheep with its young, the fine shall be half a māṣa.
Elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are considered protectors of the people;
likewise, a cow that is pregnant, one that has recently calved, and one that is in heat are exempt from punishment.
But for those who sit twice [in the same manner], it is declared to be fourfold;
likewise, for those who act as overt spies, the punishment of a thief is ordained by tradition.
If cows that have strayed due to the fault of the herdsman take refuge in a field, the owner of the cattle is not to be punished; rather, the herdsman deserves the punishment.
Or seized by a royal predator, or even struck by a thunderbolt; or bitten by a serpent, or even fallen from the summit of a mountain.
If [the animal] is killed by a lion or a tiger, or struck down by diseases,
there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners.
If a man seeks to recover grain that has been eaten by cows,
the neighbor must pay the value of the crop that was sown there;
however, fodder for the cows must be given to the owner of the cattle, while the grain itself belongs to the cultivator.
If a field located on the outskirts of a village, at the edge of a pasture, or by a high road is uncovered,
there is no fault on the part of the guardian if it is destroyed.
Along the road, a fence should be constructed such that a camel cannot look over it,
nor can a beast, a horse, or a boar leap over or break through it.
A house and a field should be understood as the basis for the residence of householders;
therefore, the king should not confiscate them, for they are the very root of householders.
When the realm prospers, the king’s righteousness and treasury increase;
when it declines, they too diminish. Therefore, he should rely upon the causes of prosperity.
12. Strīpuṃsayoga (The Union of Woman and Man).
N12.1a-c: That legal title of dispute known as Strīpuṃsayoga is said to be that wherein the rules for the marriage and other rites of women and men are proclaimed.
But for a man and a woman, the formal choosing (varaṇa) is prescribed first;
after the choosing comes the grasping of the hand, and then the sacramental rite (saṃskāra) characterized by two features.
N12.3a: For those two, the choice [of a wife] is said to be indefinite because of the perception of defects; N12.3c:
the status of being a wife is rendered definite by the taking of the hand and the sacred mantras.
Among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, a wife of one's own caste is superior;
and for a woman, a husband of her own caste is likewise superior.
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are exactly three other wives in the direct order [of castes];
likewise, for a Śūdra woman, there are three other husbands in the inverse order [of castes].
Two wives for a Kṣatriya and one for a Vaiśya are proclaimed;
two husbands are to be known for a Vaiśya woman, and one other for a Kṣatriya woman.
Up to the seventh or the fifth degree from the paternal and maternal relatives,
those who share the same *gotra* as well as those who have the same *pravara* are ineligible for marriage.
A man must be examined for his virility by the very characteristics of his own limbs;
if he is proven to be a male without exception, he is entitled to receive a maiden.
His collarbones, knees, and bones are well-knit; his shoulders and neck are well-proportioned;
his temples are full, his thighs are slender, his skin is thin, and his gait and voice are unhindered.
If his semen floats upon the water and his urine is pleasant-smelling and frothy, he shall be a male;
by the opposite characteristics, however, he is a eunuch.
In the treatise, that [doubt] is seen by the wise to be of fourteen kinds;
the method for treating those that are curable and those that are incurable has been stated in due order.
One who is impotent from birth, one who is castrated, and likewise one who becomes impotent for a period;
as well as one rendered so by a teacher’s curse, by disease, or by the wrath of the gods.
The jealous man (īrṣyāpaṇḍa), the one who must be served (sevya), the one with wind-semen (vātaretas), the one whose vulva is in the mouth (mukhebhaga), the one who is rejected (ākṣipta),
the one whose seed is fruitless (moghabīja), the modest man (śālīna), and likewise the one whose husband is another (anyapati).
Among these, the first two are incurable; the one called *pakṣaka* (hemiplegia) should be treated for a month.
For this triad, the duration of treatment is traditionally recorded as one year in successive order.
The other four [defects] that have been mentioned— jealousy, impotence, and so forth—
must be abandoned by a woman whose womb has been damaged, just as they are by one who has fallen from her caste.
If her husband has been incapacitated or his seed is fruitless, or if he is incapable of performing his duties,
another man is permitted for the woman after she has waited for one year.
Even for a man of refined character, the banner falls through union with a bold woman;
one should therefore approach him when his vigor has subsided, using other women, young girls, and the like.
If a man who is devoted to another woman becomes unfaithful toward his own wife, she may take another husband; this is the ordinance of Prajāpati.
Women were created for the sake of offspring; a woman is the field, and the progeny belongs to the owner of the seed.
The field should be given to one who possesses the seed; one who lacks the seed does not deserve the field.
The father himself, or the brother with the father’s consent, may give away the maiden;
likewise may the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, kinsmen, and relatives.
But in the absence of a mother, if she [the woman] remains in her natural state among all [the suitors],
then when she is no longer in her natural state, those of her own caste shall give her away as a maiden.
But when there is no one at all [suitable], the maiden should approach the king;
with his permission, having found a suitor, she may choose him herself.
He should practice his religious duty together with a wife of the same caste who is suitable in terms of family, appearance, age, and learning; and from her, he should procreate sons.
If a man, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country,
the maiden may choose another suitor after three menstrual seasons have passed.
If a maiden should neglect her dancing, she should inform her kinsmen;
if they do not give her to a husband, they shall be equal to killers of embryos.
As many seasons as have passed for her while she is without a husband,
so many instances of foeticide shall belong to him who does not take her back.
Therefore, before the menses have begun, the father should give away his daughter once;
otherwise, a great sin would touch him—such is the rule of the virtuous.
