A share of inheritance falls [to one] only once; a daughter is given in marriage only once;
and one says "I give" only once—these three things happen but once.
The rule prescribed for these five marriages, beginning with the Brāhma,
is that the giving [of the bride] in the three beginning with the Āsura depends upon [the groom’s] qualities.
If a bridegroom who has received the bride-price should come back when he is superior [to the first],
then a falsehood may be spoken regarding that which is joined with dharma, artha, and kāma.
One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished groom;
however, if a defect exists, there shall be no penalty for the two of them if they mutually abandon each other.
If a man, having given a maiden to a suitor in accordance with the law, does not give her to him while the suitor remains faultless,
he shall be punished by the king like a thief for that offense.
But for him who gives away a girl in marriage without disclosing her defects,
the king shall inflict the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence.
But that man who, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating any fault in her, shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
But if a suitor, having accepted an unblemished maiden, should abandon her, he should be punished—
even if he is unwilling— and he must marry that very same girl again.

Being tall, having a loathsome appearance, being afflicted by disease, being deformed, having had sexual intercourse, being forward, and having her heart set on another— these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden.
One who is insane, outcast, impotent, unfortunate, or has abandoned his kin,
as well as those two defects previously mentioned regarding a maiden— this collection of defects applies to the groom.
Eight forms of marriage have been proclaimed for the sacramental rites of the social classes;
of these, the Brāhma and likewise the Prājāpatya are the first.
The Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura;
the Rākṣasa follows immediately after that, while the Paiśāca is recorded as the eighth.
Having honored the bride and invited her, one should give her away adorned in the Brāhma form;
the Prājāpatya rite is ordained by saying, "May you both perform your religious duties together."
Having given a pair of a garment and a cow, the marriage is called Ārṣa;
but that which takes place within the sacrificial enclosure for the officiating priest performing the ritual is Daiva.
They declare that when he approaches a willing woman, it is the fifth, named the Gāndharva marriage;
whereas the Āsura marriage is to be known as resulting from the transaction of a bride-price.
The Rākṣasa form of marriage is said to result from abduction by force;
the eighth and lowest is the Paiśāca, resulting from approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated.
Of these, the four beginning with the Brāhma [marriage] are declared to be lawful;
the Gāndharva is common to all, but the three following it are unlawful.
But other women who have had previous husbands are said to be sevenfold in sequence;
among them, the *punarbhū* (remarried woman) is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* (self-willed woman) is of four kinds.

A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the grasping of the hand [in marriage], is called the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); she is eligible for the sacramental rite once again.
She who, having abandoned her husband from her youth, resorts to another man and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
When there are no brothers-in-law, a woman who is given by her kinsmen to a man of the same caste who is not a sapinda is proclaimed as the third [form of marriage].
A woman, whether she has borne children or not,
who out of lust resorts to another man while her husband is still alive, is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
If, upon the death of her husband, she should reject even the brothers-in-law who have approached her and,
out of desire, approach another man, she is proclaimed as the second [type of remarried woman].
She who has come from another country, who has been purchased with wealth, and who is afflicted by hunger and thirst,
having approached you saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the third [type].
A woman who, disregarding local customs, is given away by her elders to another man while she has already conceived a passion for him, is indeed declared to be a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman).
This rule has been proclaimed for women who have remarried and for wanton women;
among these, each preceding one is inferior, while each succeeding one is superior.

Regarding those women who were acquired through a bride-price, the offspring belongs to the one who procreated it; however, in the case of a woman who was obtained without a bride-price, that fruit belongs solely to the owner of the field.
If seed is sown in a field without the knowledge of the owner of the field, the owner of the seed has no share therein; that [crop] belongs to the owner of the field alone.
If seed carried by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone’s field, that field-owner shall enjoy the fruit;
the owner of the seed shall not share in the fruit.
If a great bull, while roaming among the cows in someone's pen, should sire calves, those cows belong to him whose bull they are; the bull's seed has been spent in vain.
When seed sown with the owner's consent is produced in another's field,
that offspring is considered to belong to both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.
There can be no crop without a field, nor does it exist without a seed;
therefore, according to the law, offspring is held to belong to both the father and the mother.

When a woman who has a protector is seen by experts in the matter engaged in sexual union with another man in someone else's house, that is considered adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*); however, it is not so if she has come to his own house of her own accord.
There is no offense of violence for one who approaches the wife of a man who is corrupt, has abandoned his wife, is impotent, or is submissive, provided he does so of his own accord.

Standing together with another man’s wife at an improper time or in an improper place, or conversing with her, or engaging in dalliance— these three are the stages of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
At the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords, in groves, and in forests,
if a woman and a man meet together, it shall be considered adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) and they are to be apprehended.
By dispatching female messengers, by sending letters,
and by other such transgressions, all such acts are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or likewise, if he is touched and consents to it, that shall be considered sexual intercourse (*saṃgrahaṇa*) with mutual consent.
Whether by means of foods, or edibles, clothes, and likewise garlands,
or by being sent perfumes— all such acts are recorded in tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction).
Whether out of pride, delusion, or self-praise, if he should say of his own accord,
"This woman was previously enjoyed by me," all such cases are recorded in the law as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery).
If one should seize another by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the hem of the garment, or should say "Stay! Stay!", all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual assault).
When men violate their own caste, the highest fine has been prescribed;
in the reverse case, however, it is the middle fine, but for violating one of a lower caste, it is the death penalty.
If the maiden is unwilling, there shall be the cutting off of two fingers;
but if she is of the highest caste, there shall indeed be execution as well as the confiscation of all property.
But if the maiden is willing, there is no transgression when she is of the same caste;
rather, he alone shall marry her after having adorned and honored her.

A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle or a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law; N12.72.
A daughter, the wife of a teacher, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
Having approached any one of these women, one is called a violator of the Guru’s bed;
the punishment therein is the excision of the penis, and no other is prescribed.
One who commits an offense against an animal of the sacrificial species shall be punished with a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
for offenses against cows, the middle amercement applies, and the same penalty holds for those of the lowest castes.
The punishment urged by the king instructs those who approach women who should not be approached;
in this matter, however, purification is achieved through the performance of penance.

A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— all these women may be approached in the direct order of castes (ānulomya), but not in the inverse order (pratiloma).
But with these very same female slaves, there would be a fault as great as with the wives of others;
for even if they are permissible [as sexual partners], one should not approach them if they are under the protection of another.
If the husband of a woman who has not yet borne children should die, she,
being authorized by her elders, may approach her brother-in-law out of a desire for offspring.
And he should enter upon that [state] in the same manner as from the birth of a son;
when a son is born, he should desist, for otherwise there would be a transgression.
Having anointed his limbs with clarified butter or unrefined oil,
avoiding the contact of mouth with mouth and the touching of limb with limb;

He should not approach a woman who already has a son, one who is barren, one who has ceased to menstruate, one who is unwilling, one who is pregnant, one who is blameworthy, or one who has not been authorized by her kinsmen.
But if a woman not authorized should bear a son to her brother-in-law,
those who speak according to the Dharma say that he is born of an adulterer and is not entitled to the inheritance.
Likewise, if a younger brother approaches his elder brother’s wife without authorization,
or if an elder brother approaches his younger brother’s wife, both of them are guilty of violating the bed of a guru.

But when the family lineage is left with no remaining members, one who is commissioned by his elders may approach the wife of his younger brother for the sake of continuing the line, and not out of lust.
But when the teacher is not present, the king should be informed of the destruction of the family;
then, having instructed her, he should depart with the woman at his word.

Having bathed according to the very procedure previously described during the *puṃsavana* rite, he, being pure, should approach her once; or rather, until the *garbhādhāna* is performed, she is indeed his daughter-in-law once the embryo has been conceived.
Therefore, a man or even a woman who, out of lust, behaves otherwise than this, should be severely punished by the king; for by failing to restrain them, he would become a sinner.
But when a quarrel arises between a husband and wife due to jealousy, envy, or passion, they should settle it among themselves, not before their kinsmen nor before the king.

If a man and a woman who are mutually hostile abandon each other, a snake [as a witness] may be employed; however, this is not the case for a woman who has committed adultery in secret, except when she is concealed.
In the event of infidelity, the woman shall have her head shaved, sleep on the ground, eat poor food, wear wretched clothes, and perform the labor of clearing away refuse.
A woman who has squandered her husband's wealth or her entire property, one who causes an abortion,
or one who seeks the death of her husband, he shall banish from the home.
A wise man should expel from the home that wife who is constantly immoral, speaks unpleasantly, and eats before her husband.
One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a barren woman, one who gives birth only to daughters, one who is censurable, or one who is always hostile; by acting in this way, he incurs fault.
If a man abandons a wife who is compliant, not foul-mouthed, skillful, virtuous, and has borne children, he shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine.

A woman who was married without her fault being known, who has left [her husband] but has not taken refuge with another, should be compelled by her relatives to return; if she has no relatives, she should seek refuge for herself.
When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.

A Brāhmaṇa wife should wait for her absent husband for eight years if she has not borne children, but if she has given birth, she should wait for four years; after that period, she may resort to another man.

A Kṣatriya woman who has not borne children may remain for six years; one who has borne children, for three years. A Vaiśya woman who has borne children shall stay for four years, while the other (the Śūdra woman) shall live with him for two years.
No specific time limit is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is there a transgression of dharma [if she remains longer];
however, in particular, for one who has not borne children, her stay [in her husband's house] is limited to one year.
This rule is ordained for women whose husbands have gone abroad and do not return;
however, if he is heard to be alive, this procedure shall be twofold.
In the production of offspring, this is the creation of living beings by Prajāpati;
therefore, when women go to another [man] for this purpose, no such fault is found.
The birth of castes in the natural order is known as the established rule;
that which occurs in the inverse order is to be understood as the confusion of castes (varṇasaṃkara).

The son born immediately after [the mother] is declared to be a *putra*; likewise, the son born with one degree of separation, and the son born with two degrees of separation, according to the direct order (*anuloma*), and likewise according to the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
The Ugra, the Pāraśava, and the Niṣāda are proclaimed as the three sons born from Śūdra women in the direct order (anuloma) from the three highest castes.
From a Brāhmaṇa woman as well, the Cāṇḍāla, the Sūta, and the Vaidehaka are born;
these three others are to be known as born in the reverse order from the [preceding] three.
The Ambaṣṭha, the Māgadha, and the Kṣattṛ are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman;
among these, one is born in the direct order (ānulomya) and two are to be known as born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
The sons of a Vaiśya woman, however, are the Dauṣṣanta, the Yavana, and the Āyogava;
among these, one is born in the reverse order (prātilomya) and two are to be known as born in the natural order (anuloma).

Those born in the reverse order of castes, such as the Sūta and others, who are produced through the inverse sequence of birth, are the "mixed castes" (saṃkara), beginning with the Śvapāka; their group consists of twenty-one members.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a wife of equal caste is a Savarṇa; from a Kṣatriya wife, he is an Anantara.
Likewise, the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are the sons of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya respectively.
But the son of a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is the Dauṣṣanta, separated by one interval;
likewise, from a Kṣatriya with a Śūdra woman, one born is named a Niṣāda.
A Śūdra woman bears from a Brāhmaṇa a Pāraśava son, who is superior [to her father];
for these are proclaimed to be the sons born according to the natural order (ānulomya) of the castes.
The Sūta, the Māgadha, and likewise the Āyogava are the sons born from the inverse order of the castes; these too are immediate [in rank].
The Sūta is declared to be the son born immediately after [the legitimate son], produced by a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa woman;
likewise, the Māgadha and the Āyogava are the two sons of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra respectively.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears to a Vaiśya a son called a Vaidehaka, who is one degree lower;
likewise, a Kṣatriya woman bears to a Śūdra a son called a Kṣattṛ, who is also one degree lower.
When there is a confusion of castes through inverse order, one who is two steps removed becomes most wicked; a Cāṇḍāla is born when a Brāhmaṇī woman is deluded by a Śūdra.
The king must investigate so that no intermixture of castes occurs;
therefore, the king must especially protect the Triple Veda from such confusion.
13. Partition of Inheritance (Dāyabhāga) N13.1a: Where the division of paternal property is determined by the sons, N13.1c:
that subject of dispute is declared by the learned to be "Partition of Inheritance" (dāyabhāga).
When the father has died, the sons shall divide the father's wealth;
in the absence of sons, the daughters [shall divide it]; in their absence, the daughter's offspring.

When the mother's menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage, or when the father has passed away or has lost all desire for life; N13.3. N13.3a/ mātur nivṛtte rajasi prattāsu bhaginīṣu ca / N13.3c/ niraṣṭe vāpy amaraṇe pitary uparataspṛhe //
Or rather, the father himself, having reached old age, should divide his sons,
giving the eldest a superior share according to his own inclination.
The eldest brother should support all [the others] who desire it, just as a father does;
or a capable younger brother may do so, for in a family, religious rites depend upon one's ability.
Excluding the property acquired through valor, the wife’s property, and whatever may be the wealth acquired through learning— these three are indivisible, as is any gift received from one's father.
And for one to whom his mother has given her own property out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; the mother is as beloved as the father.
That which is received before the sacred fire, that which is received at the wedding ceremony, as well as the gift from the husband,
and [that received] from brothers, mother, and father— this is recorded as the sixfold property of a woman.
N13.9a: That property of a woman belongs to her offspring; in the case of those who have no offspring, it goes to the husband.
N13.9c: They say that in the four [forms of marriage] beginning with the Brāhma, it goes to the father, but in the others, it goes to the husband.
He who maintains the household for a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself is unlearned.
A learned man shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is unlearned,
unless that wealth was acquired by him while depending upon the paternal estate.
When dividing his own property, a father may take two shares for himself;
when her husband has died, the mother shall be entitled to an equal share with the sons.
A larger share should be given to the eldest, for it is traditionally taught that the best [gift] belongs to the eldest;
the remaining [sons] shall share equal portions, as shall an unmarried sister.
Likewise, among sons born according to the law from women of lower castes,
there is a gradual reduction in their shares when they are born from wives who have been duly wedded.
But for those who have been divided by the father himself with unequal shares of wealth—whether inferior, superior, or equal—the same rule shall apply to them; for the father is the master of all.
The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a woman kept in secret (gūḍhaja)— of these,
the man who marries them (the husband) is to be known as their father, and they are recorded as entitled to inherit a share.
He who has an unknown father and is born of an unmarried mother (kānīna) shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his property.
But those who are born of a woman not authorized [to bear children], whether by one man or by many, none of them are sharers of the inheritance;
they are the sons of the biological fathers alone.
They shall give the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the biological father if the mother was obtained through a marriage-price (śulka);
but if she was approached without a price, those cakes belong to the husband alone.
One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these sons of the body (aurasa) shall not receive a share; how much less so those born of the wife (kṣetraja)?

Those seized by long-lasting or severe illness, as well as the mentally dull, the insane, the blind, and the lame, should be maintained within the family; however, their sons shall be entitled to a share of the inheritance.
Those who are *dvairāmuṣyāyaṇas* (belonging to two lineages) should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and water separately to both [fathers];
likewise, they should take half a share from the inheritance for the benefit of both the biological father (*bījika*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrika*).
But the share belonging to those who are reunited (saṃsṛṣṭin) is ordained for them alone;
otherwise, among those without offspring, the others shall take the shares.
If among brothers one should die without offspring, or if he should enter the religious life,
the remaining brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman's property.
They shall provide for his maintenance, as well as for that of the women, until the end of their lives;
provided they preserve the bed of their husband, but otherwise, they may be deprived of it.

N13.26a. It is held that the father’s share for the maintenance of one who has a daughter belongs to her father; N13.26c. he should maintain her until her marriage, but thereafter the husband shall maintain her.
When her husband has died, the husband's kin are the masters of a childless woman;
they are the authority over her employment and protection, and they are the ones responsible for her maintenance.
When the husband’s family has become extinct, devoid of men, and without support,
and when his sapindas are no longer present, the father’s side becomes the authority over the woman.
But at the conclusion of both these alternatives, the king is declared to be the husband of a woman;
he shall provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from the path.
Even women born into noble families perish through independence;
therefore, Prajāpati ordained their lack of independence.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in widowhood; a woman does not deserve independence.
Whatever remains after the father's debts have been paid from the paternal inheritance must be divided by the brothers, so that the father shall not remain a debtor.
And for those whose purificatory rites were not performed in due order by their father,
those rites must be performed by their brothers from the paternal wealth itself.
If paternal property is not available,
the consecratory rites that must necessarily be performed for brothers by those already consecrated should be carried out by taking [funds] from one's own share.
But he who is engaged in the affairs of the family and performs those duties should be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and means of transport.
In cases of doubt regarding the law of partition among heirs,
a decision shall be reached through kinsmen and written records of the shares, as well as by the commencement of separate activities.
Among brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties shall likewise be separate for each.

The giving away, receiving, and possession of cattle, food, houses, and fields, as well as the cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditures of those who have been divided, are to be understood as separate.
Witnessing, standing surety, giving, and receiving—
these brothers who have divided their property may perform among themselves, but not those who have not divided.
Those among whose own kinsmen these transactions occur in the world—
one should recognize them as divided, even in the absence of a written document.
If many sons born of one [father] have separate religious duties,
separate occupations, and are endowed with separate qualities of action, they are not considered eligible for joint undertakings.
If they should give their own shares, or even sell them, they may do all that as they wish; for they are masters of their own property.

The legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), as well as the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with the bride (sahoḍha), and likewise the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna).

The son of a remarried woman, the abandoned son, the received son, the purchased son, the son made [by agreement], and likewise the son who has come of his own accord— these twelve are declared to be sons.
Among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen who are not heirs;
each preceding one is declared superior, and each subsequent one inferior.
For these [sons] would inherit that wealth after their father has died in due order;
in the absence of each elder brother, the younger one shall obtain it.
In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [inherits], because she is seen to provide an equivalent lineage;
for both the son and the daughter are declared to be the perpetuators of the father's lineage.
But in the absence of daughters, the kinsmen (sakulyas) and relatives shall take it; after them, those of the same caste (sajātyas). In the absence of all these, it goes to the king.
Except for a Brāhmaṇa, however, the king devoted to righteousness shall provide a livelihood for women; this is the traditional rule regarding inheritance.
14. Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is called *sāhasa* (violence); here, *saha* is said to mean strength.
Furthermore, that [discipline] is to be known as threefold—namely, the initial, the intermediate, and likewise the superior; its specific characteristics have been stated separately in the treatises.

The destruction, seizure, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and so forth, as well as the implements of cultivation in a field, is declared by the sages to be the first degree of *sāhasa* (violence).
For clothing, cattle, food, drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Malice, the use of poison or weapons, the violation of another's wife, and whatever else is said to be life-threatening constitutes the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa).
For that first [offense], the punishment depends on the circumstances of the act and shall be at least one hundred [paṇas];
for the middle [offense], it should be known by those learned in the treatises as being at least five hundred [paṇas].

Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of that specific limb— these are declared to be the punishments for the highest degree of violence (uttama-sāhasa).
This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction;
except for the death penalty, a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve corporal punishment.
Shaving the head is his punishment, followed by banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall have the mark of his crime branded on his forehead and be paraded on a donkey.
Those two may be considered fit for social intercourse once they have been punished for the first two offenses;
however, even if punished, one who has committed the highest violence (uttamasāhasa) should be known as unfit for social intercourse.

Theft shall be considered a specific variety of that very [act]; the distinction therein is now stated: they say that theft committed by force is *atisāhasa* (extreme violence), whereas that committed by fraud is simply *steya*.
That [theft] also is declared by the wise to be of three kinds, depending on the nature of the object:
namely, from the removal of objects that are small, middling, or superior.
Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, bones, wood, leather, grass, and the like,
as well as pulses such as *śamī* and *mudga*, are declared to be "minor goods" (*kṣudradravya*).
Clothing, excluding silk; likewise cattle, excluding cows;
iron, excluding gold; and also rice and barley—these constitute the middle value.
Gold, gems, silk, women, bulls, elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, Brahmins, and kings, should be known as the highest category of goods.
The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] after having deceived them by various means, or from those who are asleep, negligent, or intoxicated.

Theft is established by the seizure of stolen goods (hoḍha), even in the absence of such goods, through the act of consumption; suspicion arises from association with wicked persons and likewise from irregular income and expenditure.
Those who provide food and shelter to thieves as they move about, and those who,
though capable, look on with indifference, are also partakers of that guilt.
Moreover, those who hear people crying out while their property is being carried away,
yet do not run to the rescue, are also partakers in that offense.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed by the wise for the three types of violent crimes (sāhasa),
that same punishment applies also to theft (steya) of the three kinds of property, in their respective order.
When cattle or other goods have been lost or stolen,
people skilled in the matter should conduct a search by following the tracks until the source is reached.
In a village, a cattle-pen, or a pasture, wherever a footprint should be encountered, it must be carried by that person; unless he carries it elsewhere.
If a foot is confused or broken due to unevenness in the *janāntika* style,
one should instead cast it toward the nearest village or cattle-pen.
When two people are on the same path, the person is generally considered impure by that [fact],
whether he has been seen previously in misdeeds or has associated with evil-minded men.
In the villages, the Caṇḍālas, executioners, and others should conduct the search;
likewise, those who roam outside at night and wander abroad should do so outside.
If thieves cannot be apprehended, the king shall provide restitution from his own treasury; for by neglecting this, he becomes a sinner and falls away from both merit and wealth.
15–16. Verbal and Corporal Abuse (vāgdaṇḍapāruṣye):

Speech that is injurious to [the reputation of] regions, castes, families, and so forth, which is accompanied by insults and slanders, and which has a disagreeable meaning—that is called verbal abuse (vākpāruṣya).
N15-16.2a. Because of being harsh, abusive, or excessive, that [abuse] is also recorded as being of three kinds.
N15-16.2c. According to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment here also increases in that same order.

That which is accompanied by an insult is to be known as "harsh" (*niṣṭhura*); that which is joined with a physical defect is "indecent" (*aślīla*). The wise say that [abuse] involving censure by means of grounds for expulsion is "severe" (*tīvra*).
N15-16.4a-c. Assaulting another’s body with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth, or injuring it with ashes and the like, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (physical violence).
N15-16.5a. For that [offense] as well, three degrees are observed, namely mild, middling, and superior, respectively. N15-16.5c.
These are determined by the sight of a threatening gesture, a discharge without contact, or the appearance of a wound.

For the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior goods, they say there are exactly three types of *sāhasa* (violent crimes); therein lies the purification of the thorns [of the state].
The fivefold procedure has been stated for both of these cases;
therein, purification and the liability to punishment are applied accordingly.
When verbal abuse has occurred due to a fit of passion between two agitated parties,
he who shows forbearance is considered the one who bears the penalty, while he who transgresses further incurs it as well.
When two people are simultaneously engaged in the offenses of harsh speech and being covered by faults,
if no distinction between them is perceived, the disciplinary measure for both shall be equal.
He who first insults another shall certainly be the one to bear the blame;
he who does so afterwards is likewise an offender, but the punishment for the former is more severe.

If one person subsequently instigates two others who have already committed an offense against each other equally, he incurs the same punishment as either of them, whether he was the first or the other.

N15-16.12a–c. [One incurs the same sin] by having intercourse with dog-cookers, eunuchs, Cāṇḍālas, those with physical deformities, those who live by killing, elephant-keepers, Vratyas, the wives of others, and the wives of one's preceptors or teachers.
N15-16.13: When there is a transgression of the boundary, immediate execution alone is the prescribed punishment;
and the wise say that there is no fault in such severity of punishment.
For if these [officials] should transgress against any virtuous person among the subjects, that person alone shall administer the punishment; the king does not incur the guilt for that punishment.
For these are indeed stains among men, and their wealth is of the nature of stain;
the king should have them executed, but he should not punish them with a fine.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brahmin should be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine should be forty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
For twice-born men of equal caste, the fine for transgression is twelve [paṇas] alone;
in cases where speech is not permitted, that same fine shall be doubled.
Even if one speaks truthfully of another who is one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly impaired, he shall be made to pay at least one *kārṣāpaṇa* by the king.

One should not, out of malice, defame one who has performed purification according to the scriptures; nor should one defame one punished by the king, for he who punishes him incurs the same penalty for that transgression.
In this world, two are proclaimed to be beyond reproach and exempt from punishment:
the Brāhmaṇa and the king; for these two sustain this universe.

If one says of an outcast, "He is an outcast," or likewise of a thief, "He is a thief," one incurs an equal degree of guilt through such speech; if the statement is false, one incurs double the guilt.
For one who, out of malice, utters the name or caste of these [twice-born] people,
an iron spike eighteen finger-breadths long shall be driven into the ground for that Śūdra.
If he should out of pride give instruction in the Dharma to the twice-born,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
Whatever limb of a Brāhmaṇa with which a person of a lower caste might offend him, that very limb of his shall be cut off; in this way, he may attain purification.

A man of lower birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of higher rank shall be branded on the hip with the mark of a dog's foot and banished; alternatively, the king may cause the region of his buttocks to be cut off.
If someone spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both his lips to be cut off;
if he urinates [on him], his penis; and if he passes wind [against him], his anus.
If one seizes [the victim] by the hair, the king shall cut off both hands without hesitation;
likewise if he seizes him by the feet, the nose, the neck, or the testicles.
But having reviled a king who is established on his own path,
purification may be attained either by the cutting off of the tongue or by the confiscation of all one's property.
But that evil-minded man who would strike at the king, even though the latter has committed an offense,
shall be cooked on a stake in fire for longer than a hundred killings of Brahmins.
Neither the father is liable for punishment on account of the offense of his son, nor the dog-owner for the offense of his dog,
nor the owner of a monkey for its offense— provided that he did not send them out [to commit it].

17. Gambling and Betting (Dyūtasamāhvaya). Gambling (devana) conducted with crooked means such as dice, fists, or small sticks, as well as betting (paṇakrīḍā) with living creatures—this is the legal category of gambling and betting.
The keeper of the gambling house shall conduct the game and shall pay what is owed for it;
his fee for conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of the total.
When the dice fall twice in favor of the stake for a gambler,
they say that victory belongs to the other player and that the gambler has lost.
Gamblers should remain among gamblers when a dispute arises;
they alone shall be the observers of that matter, and they alone shall be the witnesses.
An impure gambler shall not resort to another gambling hall;
he shall not strike back at the master of the gaming house, nor shall he cause him to pay that debt according to his own will.
The king should expel from the gambling hall those wicked men who play with fraudulent dice;
having placed a rosary of seeds around their necks, for that is declared to be their punishment.

18. Miscellaneous Matters (Prakīrṇaka) Furthermore, in the miscellaneous category, it should be known that legal disputes are those pertaining to the king: namely, the defiance of the king's commands and likewise the failure to perform his duties.
The burning of cities, as well as the sowing of dissension among the subjects;
and the subversion of the laws of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies.
Disputes between father and son, transgression regarding penance,
the failure to accept gifts, and even anger on the part of those belonging to the [four] stages of life (āśrama).
The fault of the intermixture of castes, as well as the restriction of their respective duties,
and whatever was not seen in the previous [sections], all that shall be found in the Prakīrṇaka (Miscellany).
But the king, being attentive, should protect all the stages of life by means of the four expedients prescribed in the treatises, as well as those inherent to his own nature.
Whichever caste should decline, or whichever should follow a course of excess—
seeing each of them fallen from their own path, one should establish them back upon that path.
And regarding other acts not prescribed by the scriptures which are joined with sin,
the king, having duly considered them, shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.

The king should not promote that which is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti and detrimental to the people, nor should he allow it to continue once it has been promoted; rather, he should cause it to cease.
Whatever has been done by another king that is devoid of justice, and whatever has been done through ignorance—
that too, being established unjustly, he should bring back into the path of justice.
Any man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king shall be punished as a sinner and,
for violating the royal decree, shall be put to death.
He shall take the weapons of those who live by arms, the draft animals and so forth of those who live by draft animals,
the ornaments of courtesans, and the musical instruments of those skilled in them.
Whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live their lives— even when all their property is to be confiscated— the king ought not to seize those tools.
He is without beginning and without end, the lord of the earth among bipeds;
for if he had not strayed from the path, he would have been radiant and pure.
If the king were not to administer punishment to all the social classes who have strayed from the path, these subjects would perish.
A Brāhmaṇa may abandon his status as a Brāhmaṇa, and a Kṣatriya may relinquish his Kṣatriya duties;
a Vaiśya may abandon his own specific work, but a Śūdra may abandon all [his duties].
If there were no kings on earth to wield the rod of punishment,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
The constant favoring of the virtuous and likewise the restraint of the wicked—
this is recorded as the duty (*dharma*) of kings, and their purpose (*artha*) is achieved through the affliction of enemies.
Just as fire, though constantly burning these creatures,
is not defiled, so too the king, while inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it, is not defiled.
The authority of kings is their majesty, and that is established in their speech; whatever they may declare, whether it be false or true, that is the law for those engaged in legal proceedings.
This one called the King moves upon the earth as the thousand-eyed Indra in person;
the subjects must never remain anywhere in defiance of his command.
Because he holds the office of protection, because of his sovereignty, and because he is seen to favor living beings, whatever the king ordains—that is authoritative; such is the established rule.
Just as a husband is always worthy of honor by women even if he is devoid of virtues,
so too is a lord of men worthy of honor by his subjects even if he is lacking in merit.
Subjects are purchased by the king through his asceticism; therefore, the monarch is their master.
Consequently, one must abide by his word, and their livelihood is dependent upon him.
Kings of immeasurable power possess five forms:
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Dhanada.
When, due to a specific cause or even without one, a protector of the earth falls under the sway of anger and consumes his subjects, he is then called "Fire."
When a king, desiring victory and with weapons raised, advances against his enemies by relying upon fiery energy, he is then declared to be Indra.
When the king, free from the heat of anger and appearing joyful,
goes to see his subjects, he is then said to be Soma.
When the glorious king, seated upon the throne of justice, wields the rod of punishment with impartiality toward all beings, he is then Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
But when the lord of the earth favors supplicants, teachers, the wise, servants, and others with gifts, then he is remembered as the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
Therefore, one should not despise him, nor revile him, nor treat him with contempt;
one should abide by his command, for death would result from its transgression.
His duty consists of protecting the subjects, attending upon the elderly and the wise, presiding over legal proceedings, and guarding himself.
A king, with a concentrated mind, should constantly attend upon Brahmins;
for the Kṣatriya power joined with Brahmins is the root of the protection of the world.
A Brāhmaṇa is exempt from being bypassed; he has the right to a seat at the head of the Kṣatriyas, the first audience in the morning, and the salutation from all others.
The first-fruits from new crops and the clearing of the path for one who is traveling are [due]; furthermore, entry into another's house for the purpose of begging alms is not forbidden.
Non-stealing consists in not taking sacrificial fuel, flowers, or water that belong to another;
furthermore, it includes not making demands on others and conversing with the wives of others only when permitted.
In the case of rivers, the crossing by those without means of transport should be done first; likewise, there shall be no payment of toll at ferries, provided that crossing is not his means of trade.
A Brāhmaṇa traveling on the road, exhausted, taking for himself two stalks of sugarcane and five radishes while staying overnight, does not commit an offense.
One should not accept [a gift] from those who are accused, nor from outcasts, nor from enemies, nor from atheists;
nor from one who uses deception, nor without a cause, nor by causing distress to the donor.
Because of the vast abundance of wealth and because of the greatness of those from whom it is received,
accepting gifts from kings is superior to that of others, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas.
Both the Brahmin and the king are observers of firm vows; there is no difference between them whatsoever, because both are intent on protecting the subjects and the dharma.
They say that the wealth of even a harsh king— who knows the Dharma, is grateful, and rules for the sake of protecting the impure— is indeed pure.
Just as the confluence of pure and impure waters attains equality within the ocean, so too does the influx of wealth to a king.
Just as gold placed in a blazing fire attains purity,
even so do all the sacred scriptures attain their purity when established among kings.
Whatever person gives his own property to Brāhmaṇas, that must be permitted by the king as well; this is the eternal law.
From whatever other type of land is traditionally designated as yielding a sixth part [of the produce],
that tribute is ordained for him as his wages for protecting the subjects.
That which has been made over to one who is not a Brahmin can be taken back;
however, that which has been given to a Brahmin cannot be taken away again.
Giving, study, and sacrifice—these are his threefold duties; officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts constitute his means of livelihood, the third being the acceptance of gifts.
A twice-born man should remain established in his own duty and subsist on a livelihood he has earned;
he should not accept gifts from the unworthy among the social classes when they lack restraint.
How is it that the king is not a deity— he by whose word an impure man becomes pure, and who instantly makes the pure impure?
Those twice-born ones who know that the king indeed possesses divine status through his immeasurable splendor,
are not defiled when they accept gifts from him.
In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brahmin, a cow, the sacrificial fire, gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise, a king as the eighth.
One should constantly behold these [images], bow to them, and worship them;
one should also circumambulate them, for in this way one's lifespan is not diminished.
Appendix 19. Theft (steya).
N19.1a: Thieves who seize the property of others are to be known as being of two kinds.
The self-possessed king should know them to be both manifest and unmanifest.
In that regard, there are those who deceive by means of illumination, those who rely on false weights and measures, those who take bribes, violent men, gamblers, and courtesans.
Those who produce counterfeits and those who live by pointing out auspicious signs—
these and others like them should be known as deceivers of the light of the world.
They should be known as unmanifest thieves who dwell both outside and within;
they rob men by attacking them while they are asleep or intoxicated.
Those who destroy districts, villages, or houses, those who waylay travelers on the road, and pickpockets— these and others like them should be known as secret thieves.
Having identified them through well-trained spies who perform those specific tasks,
they should be pursued and captured by men stationed in secret.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles.
Empty houses, forests, and temples of the deities—
these must be patrolled by spies intent on the apprehension of thieves.
In the same way, others who are well-disposed, trustworthy, and eloquent may act as spies;
for former thieves might incite those [new] thieves.
By means of providing food and drink, by attending social gatherings and festivals,
and likewise under the pretext of theft, they should bring about their meeting.
Those who do not approach there, even though they have been sent and dispatched,
must be pursued and captured along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Those thieves whom he may apprehend there, having beaten and humiliated them,
and having proclaimed it everywhere, they are to be executed by various methods of capital punishment.
But thieves who have not been caught in the act and do not reappear shall be executed by the king;
however, those caught in the act along with their tools, the king should promptly cause to be punished as thieves.
Those who destroy their own country, as well as those who obstruct the roads— having confiscated all their property, the king should further inflict punishment upon them.
One should interrogate those caught as thieves on suspicion without violence;
through various forms of intimidation and stratagems, they shall speak of the matter exactly as it was done.
Regarding the place, time, direction, caste, name, or residence;
as well as the purpose and the laborers involved—these are the matters that must be questioned when determining the suppression of the offense.
Because of differences in complexion, voice, and appearance; because of reporting with uncertainty;
because of being seen at an improper place or time; and because of not purifying even one's own clothing.
On account of the disappearance of property that was not there before, on account of prior acts of theft, and because of association with those who do not exist [as honest people],
one should be understood through even slight indications, and not by the seizure of stolen goods alone.
If there should be suspicion against a man who follows the way of bandits, or even against a thief,
and he should be touched by even a slight trace [of guilt], then an oath must be administered.
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who supply fire and water,
those who give lodging, those who act as guides, and likewise those who provide assistance;
Purchasers of goods, as well as those who receive them,
are declared by the law to be subject to the same punishment as those who conceal them.
Those appointed as provincial governors and the neighboring chieftains who have been summoned to the provinces,
yet remain indifferent during times of attack— they are exactly like thieves.
If property is stolen within the jurisdiction of a person, he must diligently search for the thieves;
otherwise, he shall be made to pay the value of the theft, unless the tracks of the thieves have disappeared.
But when that footprint has vanished, been lost, or fallen elsewhere,
he should cause the neighbors, the road-keepers, and the guardians of the quarters to pay [the fine].
If a house is indeed robbed, the king shall make the thieves-catchers,
the guards, and the provincial officials pay for it, provided that the thief is not apprehended.
Or, if there is doubt regarding those being compelled to pay in respect to that theft,
the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to swear an oath for the purpose of clearing himself of the charge of theft.
If a person who is not a thief is made to pay for stolen goods on the grounds of clearing him of the charge of theft,
they shall, once the actual thief is apprehended, be made to pay double the amount they were required to pay.
One should diligently restore property stolen by thieves in its original form;
in the absence of that, however, its value shall be paid, and a fine equal to that amount shall be imposed.
Of wood, sticks, grass, and the like, as well as of earthenware, of bamboo and articles made of bamboo, and of cane, sinew, bone, and leather;
In the case of stealing vegetables, greens, and roots, as well as fruits and flowers, products of cow's milk, sugarcane derivatives, and likewise salt and oil;
For cooked grains, prepared foods, intoxicants, and meat—
indeed for all items of low value— the fine shall be five times their price.
In the case of goods measured by weight, by capacity, or by number, as well as those measured by count, the fine for stealing items of superior value from among these shall be ten times their value.
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
however, for stealing less than that, Manu declared that one should be made to pay a fine eleven times the value.
For gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments and the most excellent jewels, the punishment is death if the value exceeds one hundred [paṇas].
For one who abducts a man, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for one who abducts a woman, the forfeiture of all property; but for one who abducts a maiden, the penalty is death.
For one who steals large livestock, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for stealing medium-sized livestock, the middle amercement; and for stealing small livestock, the first amercement.
The first [type of] assembly shall have twenty-four as the minimum, while the maximum shall be ninety-six;
the middle [type] shall have five hundred as the maximum, with two hundred as the minimum.
A fine of one thousand is to be known as the highest, while that which is five hundred less is the lowest;
thus has the threefold punishment for acts of violence been proclaimed by the Self-Existent One.
In the first case of breaking a knot [of a boundary], there shall be the cutting off of the finger and the thumb;
in the second case, the remainder of that [limb] shall be cut off, and the fine shall be the first *sāhasa*.
In the case of cows belonging to Brahmins, there shall be the cutting off of a large piece of flesh;
but for one who abducts a female slave, there shall always be the amputation of half a foot.
"By whichever specific limb a thief acts [to commit theft], that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu."
Whether the offense is more serious or less serious than that of a thief,
one should inflict a punishment upon the thief that is not the same as for the first [offense].
Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared ten places for punishment, which apply to the three social orders; the Brāhmaṇa is always to be protected from them.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the two hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the two ears, wealth, and likewise the body.

Having fully ascertained the offense according to its true nature, as well as the place and time, and having considered the strength of the crime and its consequences, he should impose these punishments.
A perpetrator of violence must not be released by the king on account of friendship or from the acquisition of vast wealth;
he should be abandoned [by the king], for Manu has declared that such a person has already sacrificed his own life.

As much demerit accrues to a king from executing one who should not be executed, so much does he incur from releasing one who deserves execution; yet, for him who restrains the wicked, there is merit.
One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is established in every possible sin;
one may, however, banish him at will—thus the law is settled.
The king shall either take away all his property or leave a fourth part remaining;
remembering the duty toward his dependents, he should follow the law of Prajāpati—this is the established rule.
But for a Brāhmaṇa’s offense, four marks are prescribed:
[for] violating the Guru’s bed, drinking liquor, theft, and the injury of a Brāhmaṇa.
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, a tavern-sign is prescribed;
but for theft, having made the mark of a dog’s foot, one should brand it with peacock bile.
A man who has killed an embryo must be branded on the forehead with the mark of a headless corpse;
furthermore, he must be excluded from social intercourse—this is the instruction of Manu.
A thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I have done this; punish me."
By this act, he becomes a thief because of the execution of his own deed;
that guilt shall touch the king who releases him while he is still defiled by sin.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
Through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor for those whose sins are concealed.
The guilt for theft incurred by a Śūdra is eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is twice eightfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
"Sixty-four [years] for a Brāhmaṇa," thus Svāyambhuva has declared;
and even therein, it should be especially greater among those who are learned.
Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporeal and monetary;
corporeal punishments are said to be tenfold, while monetary punishments are manifold.
The monetary fine begins with a *kākaṇī* and likewise ends with the forfeiture of all property;
the corporal punishment begins with confinement and likewise ends with the loss of life.
The punishment beginning with one *kākaṇī* is traditionally held to end at one *māṣa*;
that which was declared to begin with one *māṣa* ends at one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
But [the fine] beginning with one kārṣāpaṇa and ending at four kārṣāpaṇas is one;
another begins with two and ends at eight; and yet another begins with three and ends at twelve.
All those [fines] beginning with the *kārṣāpaṇa* that have been mentioned shall each be quadrupled;
others, however, should be understood in this same way, up to the first level of the *sāhasa* fine.
In the southern direction, the silver kārṣāpaṇa circulates;
in the eastern direction, however, that same coin is fixed at sixteen paṇas.
A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, however, is one-fourth of both a *māṣa* and a *paṇa*.
In the region of the Five Rivers, however, there is a conventional designation;
by that [designation], the measure of the *kārṣāpaṇa* is indeed fixed here.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* should be known as four *aṇḍikās*, and four of those make a *dhānaka*. Twelve of those [make] a *suvarṇa*; a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
The king should constantly and vigilantly follow the way of livelihood, the three Vedas, and the science of government;
he should strike down those caught with skillful means and suppress the wicked in both the city and the countryside.
When no witness is found for men litigating in a dispute,
then one should examine them by means of divine ordeals and various kinds of oaths.
Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, silver,
the feet of deities and ancestors, and meritorious deeds— these are what have been given.
However, in cases of a great offense, the lord of the earth should cause divine ordeals to be administered.
And when the matter is minor, the best of men should cause the man to swear by oaths;
for these oaths are declared to be easy to perform in cases of slight doubt.
In cases of violence and in accusations of grave crimes, the procedure involving divine ordeals is proclaimed.
N20.5 When the matter is doubtful, especially in cases that are concealed,
the Lord Manu has declared that the fivefold ordeal is to be known [as the means of proof].
N20.6 The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation (kośa).

These divine ordeals have been declared for the purification of those who are accused when the matter is doubtful; furthermore, for the sake of establishing the truth regarding those under accusation, the high-souled Nārada has again proclaimed the means of discerning truth from falsehood.
The wise judge should have the defendant perform this ordeal with the consent of the plaintiff, and not otherwise.
The two feet of the balance are declared to be four cubits in height.
The measured dimension of those two [scales] is observed to be six cubits in length. There should be a distance of one cubit, or even one and a half cubits, between the two feet.
Having suspended two loops from the sturdy crocodile-head supports of the balance-beam (dhaṭa), [the scales are prepared].
Having first weighed the man, one should mark the balance;
then, having lowered him from the balance so that he is equal to the reference point,
the man should be made to mount it again after being bound by the oaths.

When this has been done, if she remains perfectly still while placed in the balance, and if, when weighed, she increases [in weight], the man shall be pure; of this there is no doubt. If he is equal or decreases [in weight], the man shall not be pure.
N20.13 You are designated as the *dhaṭa* by means of words that describe the nature of phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*).
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
you alone, O *dhaṭa*, know those things which human beings do not perceive. 13
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is compared to fire;
you ought to save him from that very state of uncertainty in accordance with dharma. (14) [Fire]
N20.15a. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the ordeal by heated metal (loha).
N20.15c. The distance from one circle to the next circle is thirty-two finger-breadths (aṅgula).
N20.16a. Thus, with eight circles, there are two hundred finger-breadths.
This has been declared as twenty-four by those who perceive the true meaning of the principles of number.
For one who is pure and has likewise dwelt within the imagined mandalas,
[he should place] seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, wrapped with thread, upon his two hands.
One should take a ball of heated iron weighing fifty palas with both hands and walk slowly seven steps;
one must not step beyond the circle, nor should one place a foot within it.
And one should not cause [the fire] to fall before it has reached the ground that has been prepared.
Having crossed over the mandalas according to this rule with a concentrated mind,
that man who remains unburned on all sides shall be purified.

If one who has not been burnt is found to have failed [the ordeal] out of fear, he shall again be made to undergo the iron; this is the ancient rule. By this procedure, the trial by fire is ordained. (21)
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
there is nothing done well or ill by people that remains unknown to you. The secret sins and good deeds of men [are known to you].
20.23c You know exactly as it is those things which human beings do not know.
20.24a This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
20.24c therefore, you ought to protect him, who has fallen into doubt, according to the Dharma.
[Water] N20.25a: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the water.
N20.25c: One should discharge three arrows with a bow that is not excessively harsh. 25
But a middle-sized arrow should be taken by a man who is younger;
then, if that arrow is recovered, the man shall be purified.
Otherwise, he would not be purified, even if he shows a single part [of the body].
Or he may go elsewhere than his place, to where he was previously stationed.
Women, however, must not be forced by force, nor even a weak man;
for through fear, a woman might die, and [force] might bring death even to one who is emaciated.
One might meet all these [consequences] suddenly; therefore, one should not cause them to be submerged.
(28) Having firmly grasped the thighs of the person in the midst of the water, being well-restrained, [the judge acts].
Water and fire are the most effective means for distinguishing between truth and falsehood. (29–30a)
Since fire originated from this [water], water is therefore superior.
Those who know the true nature of Dharma perform the purification of the defiled by means of it;
therefore, O Blessed One, Lord of Waters, you ought to protect me through the power of truth.
Next, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for poison:
having first weighed the poison, this should be administered during the winter season.
One who knows the Dharma should not have [the ordeal] administered in the forenoon, nor at midday, nor during the twilight;
nor should he cause it to be given in autumn, summer, spring, or the rainy season. Furthermore, [the vessel] should not be broken, cracked, smoked, or adulterated.
One should carefully avoid *kālakūṭa* and *alaṃbu* poisons.
That which is produced in the Śārṅga and Haimavata regions, endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste, is recommended;
it should be administered by the king to one who has committed a great offense, out of a desire for the truth.

N20.36. One should not administer poison to children, the sick, or the elderly, nor indeed to those whose offense is very slight; rather, in a case requiring testing, one should give seven barley-corns of poison soaked in clarified butter. N20.37.
Of the sixteenth part of a *pala* of poison, that which is the twentieth part [is the amount to be used].
One should give that [amount] reduced by one-eighth, soaked in ghee,
to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule; having been approved by them upon their touch,
he, while fasting, should eat it in the presence of the gods and Brahmins.
If the poison, having lost its force and its distress, is digested easily, then the king,
recognizing it as pure, shall release him with due honor.
"O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in devotion to truth and righteousness."
Purify this man from sin; by means of truth, become immortal for him.
(40) [The Ordeal of the Sacred Libation] Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for the ordeal of the sacred libation. (41)
In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and is still wearing wet clothes— one who is conscientious and free from vices— the drinking of the *kośa* (sacred water) is prescribed.
The accused should be made to drink that which he habitually consumes, and [the water] consecrated to the deity presiding over it.
If, within seven days or again within fourteen days,
any personal [symptom] whatsoever is observed, that itself is its manifestation.
If, after fourteen days, a great abnormality occurs for someone, [that too is its manifestation].
He should not be subjected to the ordeal by experts because he has already violated the appointed time.

(44) One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (*kośapāna*) in the case of those who have committed a great offense, those devoid of dharma, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, atheists, those who have fallen from their caste (*vrātya*), and slaves. (45)
In the manner described, the king who knows the law should administer the five ordeals to those accused; he shall rejoice both in this world and after death.
He should not administer poison to a Brāhmaṇa, nor should a Kṣatriya take up the ordeal of heated metal.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra shall not be made to undergo the ordeal by water;
one shall not administer the ordeal by poison during the rainy season, nor shall one cause [the accused] to be immersed in water during the winter.
One shall not cause [the accused] to swallow molten metal in the summer, nor shall one administer the ordeal by sacred libation at night.
The Nāradīya Dharmaśāstra is completed.
