Mātṛkā 1 [Legal Procedure]:
When men were solely devoted to the Dharma and were speakers of truth.
At that time, there was no worldly transaction, nor hatred, nor even envy.
When the Dharma has perished among men, legal procedure (vyavahāra) comes into operation;
and the king is made the observer of legal procedures and the wielder of the rod of punishment.
In this matter, two methods are proclaimed for the clarification of a disputed point between two litigants: a written document and witnesses. (Narada Smriti 1.3)
It should be understood as being of two types: with a counter-stake (sottara) and without a counter-stake (anuttara).
That which is "with a counter-stake" is that in which there is a wager preceded by a challenge.
In a dispute involving a wager, whichever of the two parties loses shall be made to pay the wager he himself made, as well as the fine for defeat.
The plaint is declared to be the essence of legal proceedings;
if that is abandoned, the plaintiff loses his case, while he who crosses over it becomes the defendant.
Families, guilds, corporations, and the king as the presiding authority are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.
It is proclaimed as having four feet, four bases, and four means;
it possesses four benefits, pervades four [realms], and accomplishes four [purposes].
It has eight limbs, eighteen steps, and likewise a hundred branches;
it has three origins, two applications, two gates, and likewise two destinations.
Law, legal procedure, custom, and royal edict—
this four-legged legal process consists of these, each subsequent one superseding the preceding.

In that regard, legal procedure (dharma) is based on truth; judicial practice (vyavahāra), however, rests upon witnesses; customary law (caritra) is established by written records; and royal edict (śāsana) is based on the king's command.
Because he accomplishes [his goals] through the means beginning with conciliation, he is called the "one who employs the four means";
and because he protects the four stages of life, he is the "one who benefits the four."
Because it pervades the doer, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king itself, part by part, it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
Because he accomplishes these four— dharma, wealth, fame, and likewise the affection of the world— he is proclaimed as the "Accomplisher of the Four."
The king, the judicial officers, the members of the court, the legal treatise, the astrologer, the scribe, gold, fire, and water— this is declared to be the eightfold constituent of the court.
Recovery of debts, deposits, partnerships, resumption of what has been given, and the failure to perform promised service; Narada 1.16.
Non-payment of wages, as well as sale without ownership, non-delivery after selling, and likewise rescission after buying; Nārada Smṛti 1.17.
The non-performance of agreements, disputes, and the son born of the field; the union between a man and a woman, the partition of inheritance, and then violence.
Likewise, verbal abuse, physical assault, gambling, and miscellaneous matters are declared; thus, [the law] is remembered as having eighteen titles.
Another division of these very [castes] is recorded as one hundred and eight;
due to the diversity of human actions, it is said to have a hundred branches.
Since it proceeds from these three—desire, anger, and greed—it is proclaimed as having three origins; therefore, this triad is the cause of dispute.
A lawsuit, however, should be understood as being of two kinds: based on suspicion and based on facts.
Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while facts are established by the discovery of stolen goods and the like. (Nārada 1.22)
Because it is connected with two sides, it is declared to have two doors:
of these two, the first position is the *pūrvavāda* (the plaintiff's case), and the counter-position is the *uttara* (the defendant's reply).
Because it follows both the real and the deceptive, that [speech] is said to be of two kinds.
The "real" is that which is connected with the true meaning; the "deceptive" is that which is stated through negligence.
In that regard, a king who seeks to accomplish righteousness should tolerate the remaining forms of deception;
he should pursue only what is factual, for prosperity has its root in righteousness.
For a self-disciplined king who adjudicates legal cases according to the Dharma,
seven virtues arise, just as the seven flames of a fire.
Dharma, wealth, fame, the ripening of the world, the winning over of others, great honor from the subjects, and an eternal station in heaven.
Therefore, having attained the seat of dharma, the king, free from envy,
should be impartial toward all beings, upholding the vow of Vaivasvata.
Placing the Dharmaśāstra before him and abiding by the opinion of the judge,
he should examine the legal cases in due order with a concentrated mind.

The scripture (āgama) must come first, then the subject matter of the legal dispute (vyavahārapada), followed by the desire to know (vivitsā) and the decision (nirṇaya); thus, the judicial process (darśana) is fourfold.
Without contradicting the Dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstras, he should skillfully examine and conduct the course of legal proceedings according to the path of justice.
Just as a hunter might track a wounded deer by a trace of blood in the undergrowth, so too should one track the path of the Dharma.
Where there may be a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra,
one should set aside what is stated in the Arthaśāstra and practice what is stated in the Dharmaśāstra.
But when there is a conflict with the Dharmaśāstras, even a legal proceeding that is logically sound is weaker than Dharma; by it, Dharma is set aside.
For the Blessed Dharma is subtle, beyond the senses, and difficult to investigate;
therefore, one should lead the course of worldly conduct by means of direct perception.
Even one who is not a thief incurs the state of being a thief, and a thief attains the state of being a non-thief;
through legal proceedings, Māṇḍavya—who was no thief—was reduced to the status of a thief.
A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, within a private house, or with enemies— even if completed— must be performed again.
Because disputes are profound, and because even one's memory may fail, one may,
out of a desire to know the truth, take as much time as desired regarding debts and other such matters.

In cases involving the theft of cattle, land, gold, or women; in instances of verbal or physical assault; in urgent matters; in acts of violence; and in cases of false accusation, one should seek a legal decision immediately.
But he who proceeds with regard to a doubtful matter without having informed the king should be forcibly punished,
and his case shall not succeed.
The plaintiff shall restrain one who does not abide by the matter to be stated or who departs from it,
until the appearance for the summons.
Confinement may be of four kinds: restricted to a specific place, limited by time, restricted from travel, or restricted from work; one who is not released from such confinement must not violate it.
In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or encountering calamities in difficult regions,
one who oversteps that prohibition before reaching his destination shall not be held at fault.
When the time for seizure has arrived, he who seizes another and then violates that seizure should be punished;
likewise, one who acts otherwise [than the law dictates] becomes liable to a fine.

One who desires to settle a debt, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to perform a sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one assailed by another, and likewise one engaged in royal service; // Nar_M1.45 //
Cowherds [should wait] while the cattle are grazing; farmers while the crops are ripening;
artisans at their respective times; and those who bear arms during a conflict.
A messenger, one who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and one in a precarious situation must not be obstructed; nor shall the king summon them.
One who has been accused should not accuse another in turn before that matter has been resolved;
nor should one who has been accused by another, or pierced, seek to pierce in return.
One should not bring the matter at issue into disorder;
one should not shift to another position, for by doing so, one loses what was previously established.
One should not bring a false accusation; there is fault for the one who brings a false accusation.
Whatever punishment is prescribed in that case shall fall upon the accuser.
Making excuses while wasting time, speaking in the assembly yet remaining silent,
and speaking after having already said what was required— these are the characteristics of one who is losing ground.
He who flees when summoned, or who does not engage in the dispute when it has been brought before him,
shall be disciplined by the king and indeed deprived of his case.
In legal proceedings that have been finalized, even documentary evidence or witnesses become ineffective if they were not previously presented. (Narada Smṛti 1.53)
Just as the qualities of the rainy season are fruitless when the grain is already ripe,
so too is evidence useless for those whose legal case has been decided.
Even that which is untrue, if spoken at the appropriate time, is examined;
but that which is not spoken due to negligence, even if it be true, is lost.
If one should consider that a case has been decided and adjudicated contrary to the law,
the king, having imposed a double fine, should reopen that matter.
But when a legal proceeding is wrongly decided, the members of the court shall incur that same punishment;
for indeed, no one ever remains on the path of righteousness without the threat of punishment.
Whether out of passion, ignorance, or greed, whoever speaks otherwise [than the truth] should be known as an unseemly member of the assembly; the king should severely punish him.
However, by a king who especially desires to protect his own duty,
the goodness or wickedness [of others] must be examined due to the diversity of human minds.
There are men who, out of greed, would give false testimony;
and there are others, evil-minded people, who forge fraudulent documents.
Therefore, both of these must be examined especially by the king:
the written document according to the rules for writing, and the witnesses according to the rules for witnesses.
Unreal things appear like the real, and real things appear as unreal;
various phenomena are seen in this way, therefore investigation is appropriate.
The sky appears as if level, and the firefly like a flame;
yet there is no levelness in the sky, nor is there fire in the firefly.
Therefore, even an object perceived through direct perception ought to be examined;
one who makes known objects after having examined them does not fall away from dharma.
Seeing thus, the king who always remains composed while attending to legal affairs spreads his radiant glory here on earth and attains the realm of the Sun.

Mātṛkā 2 (Mātṛkā 2 is found only in manuscript P. [The second chapter of the Mātṛkā included in Jolly’s edition and translation does not belong to the original *Nāradasmṛti* (see the Introduction to the text).]
[The translation is provided in the Appendix.
[In the vernacular:
One who has gained firm confidence, being desirous and impelled by his own purpose, [should act].
Having reached a definitive conclusion regarding the matter at hand, he should cause the plaintiff's case to be recorded in writing.
But the defendant, having heard the meaning of the plaintiff's case,
shall immediately thereafter present his counter-argument connected to the subject matter of that claim.
He may obtain a written document the next day, or after three days, or even after seven days;
however, if he is a plaintiff, it is certain that he will be victorious immediately upon the third quarter of the day.
The reply may be of four kinds: false admission, a counter-attack, or that which is to be established by the procedure of a prior judgment. (Narada Smṛti 2.4)
"This is false; I do not know it, for I was not present there at that time, and I had not even been born then"—thus, falsehood is of four kinds.
The rejoinder may be of four kinds: false, contradictory, based on the addition of words, or related to the meaning of the opponent's position. // Nar_M2.6 //
The plaintiff shall cause the defendant to submit his answer only as far as the matter intended to be asserted has been set down in writing by the plaintiff. (Narada Mīmāṃsā 2.7)

A document that has a different purpose, one devoid of meaning, one lacking authoritative sources or traditional transmission, and one with omissions or additions, is declared to have defects of expression. (Narada Smṛti 2.8)
Whatever is to be obtained by someone, from whatever source, that person shall obtain that from that source;
for one thing cannot come from another, nor can another thing come from a different source—thus, this [principle] is threefold for the sake of establishing the distinction between things.
I too have been meditated upon here by your friend with a mind like that of an enemy;
it was for this reason, and no other, that I informed you of this through great patience.
That which lacks the value of the commodity, that which is devoid of the basis for the fruit,
and that which is lacking in legal formalities— one should discard such a document as being defective in its writing.
In the first chapter, one should avoid a fault that is devoid of scriptural authority,
as well as a case involving one person against many, or one that involves opposition to a city or a kingdom.

If there be a deficiency or excess in the drops (bindu), measures (mātrā), words (pada), or syllables (varṇa) due to a single irregularity, it becomes useless; one should therefore avoid such [a recitation] with effort.
One should clearly avoid even that which is corrupted, poorly articulated, or obscured by liquids, oils, and the like; such speech, though seemingly clear, lacks distinct meaning. (Nar_M2.14)
Even if a statement is well-established, it does not constitute truth if it deviates from the Dharma, whether that Dharma be the established legal convention or the ultimate truth.
That [gift] was offered by me to him while he was staying on Mount Gandhamādana;
this is external to the dharma of worldly conduct and is not established.
By the insertion of other syllables and by shifting to another meaning,
the gift of the ritual action becomes confused, and the ritual action itself becomes confused.
Whatever one has stated in the course of the procedure when provoked by passion or other such emotions,
all of that should first be written down by the proponent on a wooden board or similar surface.
For the sake of unconfused understanding, that which has been well-examined by those established in the Dharma should be accepted;
therefore, the proponent must exclude anything else, such as the [mere] fruit and so forth.
With the permission of the two disputants, they shall record in writing upon a wooden board the remaining points,
along with the witnesses and the admissions of both disputants.
Whatever remains from what was written by the two disputants, which is then recalled by the disputant, is called the *pratyākalita*; it is recorded by him at his own place.
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
whoever litigates on behalf of another, victory and defeat belong to those two [parties].
He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent,
yet speaks for the sake of another, shall be punished if he gives false testimony even in a legal proceeding.
He who abandons his former position and takes up another again should be known as a man of inferior argument, due to his shifting of the debate.

In all disputes, one does not lose the case through verbal quibble; however, in matters concerning cattle, women, land, and the non-payment of debts, even if one is punished, one does not lose the substance of the claim.
If the defendant denies the charge, the plaintiff must point out the evidence;
provided that he has not been caught in a contradiction.
For whatever has been written in the first quarter-verse (pāda) in its entirety, according to the syllables,
the plaintiff shall establish it by means of action in the third quarter-verse.
Action is also said to be of two kinds: human and likewise divine.
Human action is known through documents and witnesses; the ordeal by balance and so forth is remembered as divine.
When a legal procedure has been conducted during the day in villages or cities,
and witnesses are available, a divine ordeal is not to be employed as a means of proof.
In a forest, in a deserted place, at night, inside a house,
in cases of violence, and likewise in the denial of a deposit, the ordeal by divine proof is applicable.

When the prima facie case has been refuted by the demonstration of the [correct] cause, the defendant must indeed act with diligence; it should be understood as being like the prima facie case itself.
One who flees when summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses, and one who confesses of his own accord— these are the four kinds of defeated litigants.

One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance of legal acts, one who does not appear, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these are recorded as the five kinds of defeated parties.

Gems such as rubies and the like, gold such as dinars and other coins, and items such as pearls, coral, and conch shells—when these are stolen, they go to the owner if they are of high quality. // Nar_M2.34 //
"Perfumes, garlands, or even ornaments and garments that have not been given, as well as sandals—O King, it is said that one who steps upon such things deserves death. (Nar_M2.35)
The price of merchandise, wages, a deposit, a fine, and whatever is paid as a legal fee,
as well as gifts made in vain, stakes at dice, and gambling bets, do not increase [with interest] unless they are intended to do so.
Those of Śūdra birth who bring false accusations against Brāhmaṇas,
the king shall have their tongues cut out and impaled upon a stake.

Whether it be an edict, a letter, a copper-plate grant, a royal decree, a mortgage deed, a sale, or a purchase—those who know the law should recognize that the party who first makes a formal complaint to the king possesses the prima facie case (*pūrvapakṣa*). // Nar_M2.38 //
In a case involving the refutation of witnesses, the purification of the previous witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been cleared, one should thereafter purify the testimony.

If witnesses, assessors, or members of the court are found to be corrupt, there shall be a retrial; however, for those who have reached a conclusion through their own conduct, there is no rule for a second proceeding.
Even if he has admitted his own guilt, or even if he has been caught in his own misdeed,
or even if he has failed in his duty, he deserves the final judgment of the assembly.
The members of the court must set aside the arguments and determine the outcome of the case;
for if a decision is made without setting them aside, there will be conflict both in this world and after death.
If he is defeated by the assessors themselves, he shall subsequently be punished by the king according to his own legal code;
and a formal document of victory (jaya-patraka) should be granted to the victor in the proper manner.
This gateway to legal procedure was previously declared by the Self-Existent One;
for when the gateway is pure, the legal proceeding shall be pure, and not otherwise.
But the one appointed to the assembly (mātṛkā) must speak words that are free from partiality.
A member of the assembly who speaks what is appropriate shall incur neither hatred nor guilt;
but a member of the assembly who speaks otherwise shall incur both of those.
The king, however, should appoint righteous councilors who have been well-tested and who are capable of bearing the burden of legal proceedings, like excellent oxen.
The members of the king’s court should be well-versed in the meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, of noble birth, speakers of truth, and impartial toward both enemy and friend.
Dharma is known to be established upon that [truth], and the king is the root of Dharma;
therefore, the king, together with the virtuous, should purify legal proceedings.
In pure legal proceedings, the members of the court attain purity;
their purity indeed arises from dharma, therefore one should speak only of dharma.
Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood,
while the members of the assembly look on, there they too are slain.
For when Dharma, pierced by Adharma, approaches the assembly,
if it is not extracted as the arrow, then the members of that assembly are themselves pierced.
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is right;
for by neither speaking nor speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
But those members of the assembly who, having entered the court, sit in silence and deep thought,
and do not speak according to what they have perceived— all of them are speakers of falsehood.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness,
one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes [sinless], and the members of the assembly are released from guilt;
the sin goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (Narada Smṛti 3.12)
He who, having entered an assembly, speaks behind one's back due to a deficiency of wealth, eats like a blind man who disregards the fish along with their bones.
Therefore, a member of the assembly, having entered the court, should speak such words as are free from passion and hatred, so that he himself does not fall into hell.
Just as a learned physician extracts a splinter by means of an instrument,
so should the judge extract the splinter through legal procedure.
Where all the members of the assembly consider, "This is well done," that dispute shall be free from thorns; otherwise, it shall be thorny.
That is no assembly where there are no elders; they are not elders who do not speak the Dharma.
That is not the Dharma where there is no truth; that is not truth which is pierced by deceit.
The titles of legal procedure (vyavahārapada):
1. Non-payment of debt (ṛṇādāna).
Debt consists of that which is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and in what manner, and what [is to be paid].
And from the duty of giving and receiving, the law of lending and borrowing (ṛṇādāna) is traditionally known.
When the father has passed away, the sons shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, provided that they bear that burden.
Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle, or by a brother,
or by a mother for the sake of the family, the heirs shall pay all of that in its entirety.
The debt that was cleared by sons, which they inherited in succession without obstruction, their grandsons must repay; that obligation ceases with the fourth generation.
"Ancestors desire sons for their own sake, thinking from every perspective:
'This one will liberate me from my creditors. (Nar_1.05)
Therefore, once a son is born, he should strive diligently to liberate his father from debt so that he does not fall into hell.
If an ascetic who maintains the sacred fire dies while still burdened by debt,
both his asceticism and his fire-sacrifice become the wealth of those who possess riches.
A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his son, but a son may pay one contracted by his father, except for debts incurred through lust, anger, liquor, gambling, or acting as a surety.
If a debt was contracted by the father himself, or for the sake of maintaining the family,
or incurred during a time of distress, the father shall pay that debt to the son.
Whatever has been set aside for the sake of the family by disciples, resident students, servants, wives, and those who perform services must be carried by the head of the household.
If the father has gone abroad, the son shall not pay the debt before twenty years have passed,
nor to a paternal uncle, nor even to an elder brother.

Even a single son shall be made to pay the debt contracted by his authorized representatives while the others were alive; however, when they have died, his son is not liable to pay that debt of others.
A woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor likewise one contracted by her son,
except for what she has promised herself, or what was contracted jointly with her husband.
A sonless widow who has been authorized by her husband, or whoever shall take his inheritance, must pay the debt;
for from whom the inheritance comes, from him the debt follows.
And a debt incurred by a wife shall never become the husband's responsibility, except for what was contracted during times of distress; for the expansion of a household depends upon the men.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and vintners;
their livelihood depends upon them, and their families rely on them for support.
But a woman who, having sons, abandons her own son and resorts to another man, shall have all her property seized; however, for a woman who is destitute of wealth, the son alone shall take it.
But if a woman who is already provided for, together with her children, should resort to another man,
he shall pay her husband's debt or release her from it in that same manner.
For when a man dies without wealth or a son, he who takes his wife incurs the debt;
he alone is considered to be the heir to that man's property.
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;

between one who has no son and one who possesses the wife's property, the one who takes the wife shall bear it; and between one who possesses wealth and one who has a son, the one who takes the wealth shall bear it.
She who is a self-willed woman (*svairiṇī*) is the best among those who have remarried (*punarbhū*);
he who marries either of these two must pay the debt incurred by her husband.
They say that transactions carried out by a woman are invalid when not in times of distress, especially those concerning the gift, mortgage, or sale of a house or field. (Narada Smṛti 1.22)
These authorities are also valid if the husband permits them;
or, in the absence of the husband, the son; or, in the absence of both husband and son, the king.
Whatever has been given by a gratified husband to his wife, she may enjoy or give away as she pleases even after he has died, with the exception of immovable property.
Likewise, a deed performed by a slave is declared to be as if unperformed, except by the master's command;
for a slave has no authority over himself.
Even that deed which a son performs against the will of his father is said to be as if unperformed; for a slave and a son are considered equal in this regard.
For even one who is independent is not liable for debt if he has not attained legal capacity;
indeed, independence is traditionally held to belong to the eldest, where seniority is determined by both merit and age.
In this world, three are independent: the king, the teacher, and likewise the householder in his own home for each and every member of the castes. (Nar_1.28)
All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent.
A disciple is traditionally held to be dependent, whereas the teacher possesses independence.
Wives, sons, and slaves, along with all that is acquired, are not independent;
however, the householder therein is independent regarding whatever has come to him by inheritance.
One should know that a child is similar to one still in the womb until the eighth year;
one is known as a *bāla* (child) until the sixteenth year, and is also termed a *pogaṇḍa*.
One who knows legal procedure is independent with respect to others, except for his parents;
while they live, he shall remain dependent, even if he is advanced in age.
Of these two as well, the father is superior, because the importance of the seed is observed;
in the absence of the progenitor, the mother [is superior], and in her absence, the elder brother.
All these [members of the family] are always independent with respect to those who are dependent;
they are considered masters in matters of instruction, dismissal, and sale. (Nar_1.34)
Whatever action a child performs, or likewise one who is not independent,
those who know the scriptures declare that in the treatises it is considered "unperformed."
For even that effect which one who is independent might produce when not subject to external conditions, they say is as good as unproduced; for he is not truly independent by virtue of his cause.
Those who are overcome by desire and anger, afflicted by distress, fear, and calamity,
and enveloped by passion and hatred, should be known as having fallen into a state contrary to their true nature.

Whatever is performed by the eldest in the family, or by one who is most excellent and established in his natural state, that deed shall be considered as done; what is done by one who is not independent is not considered as done.
All activities have wealth as their root; therefore, effort is considered necessary for its acquisition.
Its method, in due order, consists of protection, increase, and enjoyment.
Furthermore, that [conduct] should be known as threefold: white, variegated, and black; its distinct divisions should be understood separately as sevenfold.

Wealth acquired through learning, heroism, austerity, daughters, disciples, sacrificial clients, and inheritance—this sevenfold wealth is "pure" (śukla), and its increase is likewise of that same nature. (Nar_1.41)
That which is obtained through idleness, agriculture, trade, customs duties, the practice of crafts, or from one who has rendered assistance, is declared to be "stained" (śabala). // Nar_1.42 //
That which is acquired through gambling, acting as a messenger, distressing others, hypocrisy, violence, or under some pretext is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa). // Nar_1.43 //
By means of that [ignorance], buying and selling, giving and receiving,
as well as various activities and even the enjoyment of pleasures, all proceed.
Whatever a person performs with a particular kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both here and after death.
Furthermore, that [suffering] is remembered as being of twelve kinds based on the distinction of castes;
it is threefold when considered collectively, and the remainder is remembered as being ninefold.
Inherited property, a gift of affection, and what is acquired together with one's wife—
these are the three kinds of wealth for all castes without distinction.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics:
that which is obtained through receiving gifts, from a patron for officiating at sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil.
They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific kinds of wealth: what is acquired in battle, taxes, and fines from legal proceedings.
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should also be known as having three characteristics:
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade; whereas that of a Śūdra consists of service to these [higher castes].
This is the righteous way for all social classes to acquire wealth;
by the opposite method it would be unrighteous, unless there is a grave emergency.
In times of distress, the conduct of a Vaiśya is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa as the next best alternative; it is never declared to be inferior to that.
A Brāhmaṇa should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform the work of a Brāhmaṇa; for those two acts lead to their downfall.
For them, no action—whether superior or inferior—is found;
for, having abandoned actions that are middling, those two are indeed common to all.
Having crossed over the calamity by means of wealth acquired through the occupation of a Kṣatriya,
the Brāhmaṇa should abandon that Kṣatriya occupation once he has performed purification for himself.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, out of passion, delights in that very way of life—
he is fallen from the path, known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, and declared unfit to sit in the row for a meal.
In the occupation of a Vaiśya, the following are not to be sold by a Brāhmaṇa: milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, beeswax, lac, alkali, juice, and fermented liquor.
Meat, rice, sesame, linen, Soma, flowers, fruits, leaves, humans, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, and climbing plants. // Nar_1.58 //
Indigo, silk, skins, bones, blankets made of goat hair, and one-hoofed animals; likewise earth, buttermilk, hair, oil-cakes, vegetables, and other medicinal herbs.
However, for a Brāhmaṇa, dry wood and grass may be sold,
with the exception of fragrant substances, iron, flax, cotton, roots, and chaff.
He may use wood that has fallen of its own accord and split bamboo, as well as fruits from the jujube and *iṅguda* trees;
and he may use a rope made of cotton thread, provided it remains unaltered.
In cases of incapacity for the sake of medicine, and likewise for the purpose of a sacrifice,
sesame seeds may indeed be sold, provided they are exchanged for an equivalent amount of grain.
A Brāhmaṇa who sells items that ought not to be sold has fallen from the path;
having been restored to the path once more, he should be punished severely by the king.
The means of valid cognition must be diligently protected by those who abide by the means of valid cognition;
for the means of valid cognition fail when they are not properly established.
A written document, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the threefold means of proof by which an owner enjoys his property. (Narada 1.65)

A written document is always powerful, while witnesses are indeed effective only as long as they live; through the passage of time, possession becomes authoritative—this is the settled conclusion in the scriptures.
Among these three types of perceived means of knowledge, each preceding one should be known as more authoritative than the next; among them, direct experience is the most weighty.
Even when a written document exists and witnesses are still living,
that which has not been enjoyed— especially in the case of immovable property— is not secure.
If one, out of folly, neglects one's own wealth while it is being enjoyed by others,
that very enjoyment brings it under their control even while he is alive before his eyes.
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent and present, he does not deserve to recover it.
If he remains silent and indifferent while this time previously mentioned elapses, his legal claim does not succeed.
If he is not an idiot and not a minor, and the property is enjoyed by him in his presence, that enjoyment is established by legal usage; the possessor deserves that wealth.
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, an open deposit, a sealed deposit, women, royal property,
and the property of a Vedic scholar do not become lost through adverse possession.
And through direct enjoyment, twenty years of the owner [pass]; even property such as deposits and the like is lost, with the exception of the wealth of a wife or a king.
And the property of women and kings is never lost,
even if it is enjoyed for hundreds of years without a legal title to its acquisition.
Where enjoyment is not observed, scripture is not observed anywhere;
in that case, scripture is the authority, and enjoyment is not the authority.
That which is enjoyed without having been acquired does not transcend the nature of enjoyment;
however, when the enjoyer has passed away, that wealth becomes the property to be enjoyed by his descendants.
One who is accused as a taker of property should produce documentary evidence;
for those acquired from one's father in due succession, possession itself shall be the proof of clear title.
That which is deposited, that which is taken away, that which is left behind, that which is seized by force, that which is borrowed,
and that which is enjoyed in one's absence— these six are [lost] without a legal title.
When a deceased litigant has thus engaged in a lawsuit, his property must be investigated by his son; possession does not override that [legal claim].
Even without scriptural authority, that which was enjoyed by the three preceding ancestors cannot be set aside,
as it has been inherited through a succession of three generations.
Even honest people would not be valid witnesses after the death of the wealthy man,
unless they had been informed by him himself when he was near death.
For when the defendant is deceased, the testimony of witnesses is not a valid means of proof;
in that case, the instrument accompanied by witnesses would be the authority for reaching a certain conclusion.

Even if it is merely made known by a sick person, whatever matter connected with dharma has been stated, one may be a witness to that even after [the person] has died; this applies also in the case of the six types of transactions, such as deposits and the like.
Among all [debts], such as those for ritual acts and so forth, each subsequent one is more powerful;
among those incurred through acceptance of gifts, each preceding one is weightier.
For the acceptance of gifts is intended for the purpose of obtaining a place [of residence]; that is declared to be usury, and by means of it comes the livelihood of usurers. // Nar_1.86 //
In the treatises, his interest is said to be fourfold: bodily, timely, commissioned, and likewise compound interest known as the "wheel-increase."
That which does not conflict with one's physical well-being and is paid as a fee for services is known as bodily interest;
that increase which flows month by month is traditionally called periodical interest.
Interest that is caused to be paid by the debtor himself is called *kāritā*;
interest upon interest is declared to be *cakravṛddhi*.
This rule regarding the accumulation of interest on debts is declared to be universal;
however, there is another rule according to local custom where a debt remains outstanding.
In one region it remains double, in another triple, and likewise in yet another quadruple;
thus, in various regions, it exists as eightfold.
The interest on gold, grain, and clothing is two, three, and fourfold respectively;
the interest on ghee is eightfold, and for women and cattle, it is offspring.
Of cotton thread, silk-cotton, and fermenting agents; of gourds and lead; of all weapons; and of leather, copper, and iron.
And for all other bricks as well,
Prajāpati Manu has declared that their increase is inexhaustible.
The increase for all types of oils, liquors, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as for molasses and salt, should be known to be eightfold.
Interest on gifts given out of affection shall never accrue if they have not been requested;
however, even if unrequested, it increases after half a year has passed.
This rule for interest has been declared according to dharma for one who has grown wealthy; however, that interest which is applied to grains is designated as usury (vārdhuṣya).
A Vaiśya may indeed overcome distress through the practice of usury at his will;
however, even in the midst of the most dire calamities, a Brāhmaṇa must never engage in usury.
If there is no descendant of a Brāhmaṇa to whom the gift should be given, one should offer it to a kinsman of his;
in his absence, to his relatives.
But when there are no kinsmen, nor relatives or blood-kinsmen, then one should give to those of one's own caste; if none of these exist, one should cast [the offering] into the water.
The creditor shall deliver the principal with interest to the debtor who has come to collect it;
but if he refuses when requested, he shall incur the loss of the remainder.
When the debt has been cleared, one should provide a written document; in its absence, a verbal acknowledgment (pratiśrava).
In this manner, there shall be mutual clearance between the creditor and the debtor.
In this matter, there are two causes for confidence: a guarantor and a pledge;
and two means of proof that bring clarity: a written document and witnesses. (Narada 1.103)
For attendance, for giving, and likewise for providing security—
wise men recognize three kinds of sureties with respect to these three purposes alone.
If debtors fail to repay, or if there is a dispute regarding the transaction, the guarantor shall pay that debt; likewise, he shall pay it if they fail to appear.
If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to the agreement;
for when no specific distinction has been made among them, the creditor may act as he pleases.
Whatever amount the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
the debtor shall reimburse that amount to the surety twofold.
That which is pledged is known as *ādhi*; it should be understood as having two characteristics:
that for which a time limit has been set, and that which remains until the debt is paid. (Narada Smṛti 1.108)
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: that which is to be guarded and likewise that which is to be enjoyed.
Likewise, there is its restitution, and in the opposite case, there is loss of profit.
Similarly, if through negligence the pledge of a wealthy person undergoes deterioration or is destroyed—
unless caused by fate or the king— the principal shall be lost.
If a pledge, even when being kept, should become worthless with the passage of time,
another pledge must be provided, or the debt must be paid to the creditor.
Now, if he becomes devoid of resources due to the reversal of time and remains a debtor,
he shall be made to pay the debt as it can be afforded, at each appropriate time according to his income.
If a debtor, though capable, does not repay the wealth to the creditor due to wickedness,
he shall be compelled by the king to pay it, after the king has taken a twentieth part as a fee.
If the amount of a debt owed by a debtor should be extinguished here over time,
the recovery of the [debtor's] caste, name, and residence is said to depend upon the written document.
A written document should be known to be of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another;
it may be without witnesses or with witnesses, and its validity depends on its standing in the local custom.

A document that is not contrary to local customs, which possesses the characteristics of a clear subject matter, and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is recognized as valid evidence. (Narada 1.116)
That which is done by one intoxicated, or by a woman, a child, or through force;
likewise, that which is done out of fear or through fraud—such acts constitute invalid legal evidence.
Where the witnesses, the creditor, the debtor, and the scribe have all died,
that document is also invalid, except in the case of a pledge which serves as a stable basis.
The pledge (ādhi) is said to be of two kinds: movable and immovable;
in this case, the realization [of ownership] for both occurs if there is enjoyment [by the creditor], and not otherwise.
A document that has been shown at the appropriate time, and whatever has been read aloud or caused to be heard,
is established as valid everywhere, even when the witnesses have died.
A document that has not been heard of, one whose meaning is not seen, and one intended merely for worldly transaction does not attain validity,
even if witnesses are still living.

When a document has been deposited in another country, burnt, poorly written, or stolen, there shall be a determination of its validity based on the time; if it does not exist, proof must be established by witnesses who have seen it.
If there should be any doubt regarding a document concerning facts, whether real or unreal,
one should resolve it by means of the signature of the party's own hand, identifying marks, possession, and logical reasoning.
Any document that bears another's name or has been produced for some other purpose must,
in case of dispute, be examined by means of connections, provenance, and motives.
Any document that bears another's name or was produced for some other purpose must,
in case of dispute, be examined by means of connections, provenance, and motives.
A written document should be contested by means of another written document, and witnesses by means of witnesses;
however, a written document is superior to witnesses, and witnesses are inferior to a written document. // Nar_1.125 //
In cases where a document is torn, broken, stolen, wiped out, lost, or poorly written, another document should be executed; this is the traditional rule for documents as recorded in the Smṛti.
But when matters are in doubt and two parties are disputing, the clarification [of the truth] is seen to come from witnesses, because they have seen, heard, or experienced [the events]. (Nar_1.127)
A witness is to be understood as one who has seen with both ears and eyes:
that which another says is for the ear, and that which is bodily action is for the eye. (Nar_1.128)
That witness is seen by the wise to be of eleven kinds;
among them, five are said to be appointed (kṛta) and six are said to be unappointed (akṛta).
The written witness, the reminded witness, the witness by chance,
the secret witness, and the corroborating witness— thus is the witness declared to be of five kinds.
Furthermore, the wise have proclaimed that it is sixfold,
consisting of the village, the presiding judge, and the king for those engaged in legal proceedings.
Those who are insiders in a matter, those sent by a litigant, and those from the family involved in disputes between families— these also may serve as witnesses.
Those who are of noble birth, upright, pure by birth, by conduct, and by wealth;
at least three in number, blameless, pure, and possessed of sound intellect—such persons shall be witnesses. (Narada Smṛti 1.133)
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, or even those who are blameless— let them all belong to their respective castes, or alternatively, let them all belong to every caste.
Guildsmen shall be witnesses for guildsmen, members of a group for those in their own group, outsiders for those residing outside, and women for women. // Nar_1.135 //
But if someone within groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred,
he must not be a witness for those very same groups, for they would all be his haters.
For even in the treatises, the wise have observed five kinds of non-witnesses:
one who speaks [falsely], one who is tainted by vice, one who is divided [by enmity], one who has testified for himself, and one whose testimony was given after death.

Where witnesses are divided— some being learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) based on their testimony, and others being thieves or the like based on the perception of their faults— there shall be a conflict of opinions.
One who, not being designated by the party himself, comes of his own accord and speaks,
is considered a "dead-witness" (mṛtāntara), except in the case of one who was made to hear the claim while the claimant was on the verge of death.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world are not witnesses; no reason for this has been stated here.
Thieves, violent criminals, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise executioners—these are not witnesses because of their wickedness; in them, truth is not found.
When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
if their testimony diverges, they shall be considered non-witnesses due to that disagreement.
But he who, not being designated as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks, is called a "sūcī" (informant) in the scriptures; he does not deserve the status of a witness.
If the matter that ought to be heard does not exist, or if there is no petitioner, where could one exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness. (Narada 1.144)
If the matter that ought to be heard were absent, or if there were no seeker of justice, where could one exercise witnesshood? Thus, one who dies in the interval is not a witness.
When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both,
the witnesses shall belong to the one whose case constitutes the prima facie claim (pūrvapakṣa).
In whatever matter the weakness of the plaintiff's case arises by virtue of his own will,
there the witnesses of the defendant must be questioned in that dispute.
One should not approach a witness in private at the instigation of another;
nor should one cause him to be divided by means of another. By acting in this manner, one will surely suffer defeat.
If the witness designated should die or depart to another region, those who heard him shall be the authority; for the subsequent action is the authority.
Even after a very long period of time, that which has been written shall attain its fulfillment;
one who knows should write it oneself, but one who does not know should have it written by another.
Success is declared for a witness who is reminded here within eight years;
likewise, success is achieved for one who appears voluntarily within five years.
The validity of a secret witness is established until the third year;
they say that the validity of a subsequent witness lasts for one full year.
Alternatively, no fixed time limit has been observed regarding a witness;
for those learned in the scriptures say that witnesshood depends upon memory.
That man whose memory and hearing have not been impaired,
even over a very long period of time, is fit to serve as a witness for testimony.
But other six types of disputes are declared to be those where there is no reliance on witnesses;
the wise say that for these, the very characteristics [of the case] constitute witness-status.
One with a firebrand in hand should be known as an arsonist; one with a weapon in hand is a murderer;
and one seized by the hair is a simultaneous adulterer.
One who approaches with a spade in hand should be known as a destroyer of embankments;
likewise, one with an axe in hand is proclaimed to be a cutter of forests. // Nar_1.156 //
A man who commits physical assault is to be recognized by prominent signs;
for these matters of assault are not dependent on witnesses, but rather require careful investigation.
Someone, having made a mark upon themselves, might out of hatred cause harm to another;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of the logical grounds, the purpose, the context, and the capacity of the situation.
Those who have a financial interest, those who are not trustworthy, those who are associates, or those who are enemies;
those whose faults are known, those afflicted by disease, and those who are corrupted—these should not be questioned.
Slaves, those who act with deceit, the faithless, the elderly, women, children, and followers of the Cākrīka sect;
those intoxicated, insane, negligent, afflicted, gamblers, and village priests; // Nar_1.160 //
Long-distance travelers, sea-faring merchants, renunciants, and the sick;
hunters, Vedic scholars, those devoid of proper conduct, eunuchs, and professional musicians.

Those who deny the afterlife, those who have abandoned their wives and the sacred fire, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who eat from the same vessel, those who associate with enemies, and those who are kinsmen by birth. // Nar_1.162 //

Actors who have previously been seen to commit faults, those who live by poison, snake-charmers, poisoners, arsonists, usurers, the sons of Śūdra women, and those who approach others' wives for illicit intercourse; // Nar_1.163 //
Those exhausted by reckless acts, the weary, the destitute, and the outcastes;
those of broken conduct, those who have not returned from their studies, the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and root-diggers.

Those possessed by spirits, those hostile to kings, those who predict rain or the positions of the stars, those who proclaim their own misfortunes, those who sell themselves, those with missing limbs, and those who live by the service of prostitutes; // Nar_1.165 //

One with deformed nails, one with a dark-complexioned face, one afflicted with leprosy, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a fierce man, and those who oppose guilds or assemblies; // Nar_1.166 //
A murderer, a painter, a wandering performer, an outcaste, a forger, a cheat, one who has turned back from his vows, a thief, and a royal officer; ||| Nar_1.167 |||
One who sells human beings, poison, weapons, water, salt, cakes, or climbing plants; a Brāhmaṇa who is a usurer; and likewise any twice-born man who is a moneylender.
One who has fallen away from his own duty, a member of a guild, a panegyrist, a servant of the lowly,
one who disputes with his father, and a sower of discord— these are non-witnesses.
Even those who have been designated as non-witnesses, such as slaves, rogues, and others,
may become witnesses when the gravity of the matter requires it.
In all cases of violence, theft,
adultery, and both forms of harsh speech, one should not examine the witnesses.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a deceitful person, nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give false testimony. (Nar_1.172)
A fool may speak falsely out of ignorance; a woman, from habitual wickedness; a forger, from deceit; a kinsman, from affection; and an enemy, from the desire for revenge. (Nar_1.173)
Alternatively, if a person is agreed upon by two disputing parties,
even if he is the only witness, he should be questioned as a witness in the assembly.
But he who, because he is pierced by his own defects, appears as if unwell,
should move from one place to another and resorts to each [remedy] one by one.
He coughs uncontrollably and suddenly, sighing repeatedly;
he scratches the ground with his feet and tosses his arms and garments.
The color of his face changes and likewise his forehead perspires;
his lips become parched, and he looks upward and sideways. (Nar_1.177)
He who speaks much at length without being asked, as if in a hurry and without foundation, should be known as a false witness; the king shall punish that sinner.
And he who, having caused [the matter] to be heard by others, then denies his testimony, must be punished even more severely; for he is worse than a false witness.
Having summoned the witnesses, he should question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths—
those who are all of known conduct and who have knowledge of the matter.
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by the truth, a Kṣatriya by his vehicle and weapons,
a Vaiśya by his cattle, grain, and gold, and a Śūdra by all sins.
Having greatly terrified the witnesses with ancient declarations of dharma, with praises of the greatness of truth, and with condemnations of falsehood; ||| Nar_1.182 |||
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, wretched—
he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar.
One who gives false testimony shall be imprisoned in the city, hungry at the outer gate, and shall behold his enemies once again.
The night that a woman is taken as a wife, the night one is defeated at dice, and the night one’s limbs are tormented by a heavy burden— the speaker of evil words shall dwell through all of them.
A witness who, when questioned regarding the matter at hand, gives testimony with the laxity of a cow's ear,
fastens upon himself a thousand nooses of Varuṇa.
When a hundred years have passed for him, one noose is released;
in this manner, he is liberated from that bondage after a million years.
O gentle one, hear now in due order the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely when giving testimony in each case.
One kills five by lying regarding cattle, ten by lying regarding cows;
one kills a hundred by lying regarding horses, and a thousand by lying regarding men.
One who speaks a falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those already born and those yet unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking a falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a falsehood concerning land.
They say that truth alone is the singular, peerless purifier of the self; it is the ladder to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
A single well is better than a hundred pits; a sacrifice is better than a hundred wells;
a son is better than a hundred sacrifices; and truth is better than a hundred sons.
By truth the earth supports all; by truth the sun rises;
by truth the wind blows; and by truth the waters flow.
Truth alone is the supreme gift; truth alone is the supreme austerity;
truth alone is the highest dharma for the worlds—thus have we heard.
In brief, O gods, truth is the mark of humans, while falsehood is traditionally held to be their nature;
yet for one whose mind is established in truth, divinity is attained even in this very world.
Speak the truth, abandoning falsehood; by truth you shall go to heaven.
Having spoken a most terrible lie, one will fall into hell.
And in the hells, those powerful and cruel servants of Yama will constantly cut out your tongue and sever it with swords.
Enraged, they will pierce with spears the one who cries out for help and has no refuge;
and having lifted him up with his head downward, they will hurl him into lakes of fire.
And having experienced those long-lasting sufferings of hell,
you shall go here to the wombs of unworthy beings, such as vultures, crows, and the like.
Having understood these faults in falsehood and having understood the excellent qualities in truth, speak the truth and uplift yourself; do not cause yourself to fall.
Neither kinsmen, nor friends, nor even great riches are able to rescue one who is sinking into the fierce darkness.
The ancestors, however, look down upon you now that you have become their witness:
"Will he deliver us, or will he cause himself to fall? (Nar_1.203)
Truth is the self of a human being; everything is established upon truth.
In every way, you shall unite yourself with your own self through that which is most beneficial.
The interval between the night you were born and the night you will die would be spent in vain, if you were to act otherwise than truthfully.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood;
especially regarding the duty of a witness, one should therefore speak only the truth.
That lowest of men who employs his own speech for the sake of another—
what would that sinner not do for his own sake, being fearless of hell?
Meanings are indeed fixed in speech; they have their root in speech and have issued forth from speech.
For that man who would steal this speech is a thief of all things.
But when witnesses disagree, the majority is the authority;
if they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; if they are equal in purity, those with better memories should be followed.
But where, in a legal dispute, an equality of memory is observed among the witnesses,
the testimony is set aside again because of the subtle nature of the requirements for witness-status.
When the categories of facts have been set forth and the witness has arrived to testify,
if he does not speak in accordance with the syllables [of the deposition], that shall not be considered as having been declared.
Where there is disagreement regarding place, time, age, substance, quantity, appearance, or caste,
that testimony is said to be invalid.
If witnesses should state a matter that is either deficient or excessive, that which remains unstated must also be understood [as part of the testimony]; this is recorded as the rule for witnesses.

Where, due to negligence, there is neither a written document nor witnesses for a wealthy man, and the plaintiff denies the matter, the threefold procedure prescribed therein shall apply. // Nar_1.214 //
An accusation at the proper time, a fragment of reasoning,
and likewise a third, an oath— by these very means one should establish [the truth] in due order.
If one who is being repeatedly exhorted should reject those words,
then after three, four, or five times, one should bring about that goal for him.
But when there is an obstruction to the injunction, one should investigate it by means of fragments of reasoning,
such as place, time, the relationship between objects, measure, action, and so forth.
Even when arguments are ineffective, one should distress him with oaths—
such as those involving fire, water, or meritorious deeds— taking into account the nature of the matter, the time, and the strength of the case.
He whom a blazing fire does not burn and whom the waters hold back shall overcome the curse; in the opposite case, he shall be a sinner.
This same rule is seen to apply to women in cases of offenses against virtue, as well as in theft and acts of violence, and in all instances of denial of one's property.
For even oaths are recorded among the gods and the sages;
Vasiṣṭha uttered a curse when he was suspicious of a Yātudhāna.
Then the seven ṛṣis, having assembled for the sake of Puṣkara,
solemnly took an oath with undistracted minds for the sake of mutual purification.
If one who has committed an improper act of violence seeks reconciliation,
or speaks for himself in the assembly, it is ordained that his punishment shall be half [of the standard].
But if, out of wickedness, he conceals his sin, he shall be defeated;
the members of the court are not satisfied with this, and a severe punishment is inflicted.
2. When one deposits one's own property with another out of trust and without hesitation,
that is declared by the wise to be the legal title known as "Deposits" (nikṣepa).
When an object, separated by other substances and being neutral (avyākṛta),
is deposited in another's house, that is known as an open deposit (aupanidhika).
Furthermore, that [debt] is said to be of two kinds: one with witnesses and likewise the other;
in the case of the latter, there should be proof through restitution or by means of an ordeal.
But he who, when requested by the depositor, does not return the deposit, shall be fined by the king and compelled to pay it; and if it has been lost, he shall be made to pay its equivalent.
And whoever should recover the property without the permission of the depositor,
he too shall be punished and must restore that property along with its interest.
That which is lost together with the object by the receiver is lost to the giver,
provided it was not caused by fate or the king, nor was it brought about through fraud.
This same rule is seen to apply in cases of borrowed goods, items held for safekeeping, and so forth;
as well as in the case of artisans, deposits, trusts, and counter-deposits.
And this same duty applies to that man who adopts a minor son along with his property;
these six rules are equal.
3. Partnership in Undertaking Business: When merchants and others perform an enterprise collectively, that is known as "partnership in undertaking business," a head of legal dispute. (Nar_3.01)
For those who, through skillful means, perform actions in combination for the sake of the fruit, the *prakṣepa* serves as their support; by it, they may arise from their respective portions.
Whatever portion of a thing is equal, superior, or inferior,
its depletion, expenditure, and increase will likewise be of that same nature.

Established in their own duty, they shall without deviation attend to the inspection of merchandise, the collection of revenue, the expenditure of funds, the recovery of debts, and the assessment of the weight and quality of goods.

He who has destroyed [the property] through negligence, as well as he who has done what was forbidden, and he who acts without being instructed by all the partners acting in concert, shall be made to pay for it. // Nar_3.05 //
When a calamity arising from gods, thieves, or the king has occurred,
he who protects [the person] by his own power is declared to be entitled to a tenth share.
If one person should meet with misfortune, his heir shall receive that property;
or, in the absence of an heir, all those who are capable [of inheriting] shall receive it.
Likewise, in the event of a misfortune befalling the officiating priests, another person may complete that rite;
he shall receive the portion of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) assigned from it.
If a priest should abandon a sacrificer who is blameless and has done no wrong, or if a sacrificer should abandon a blameless priest, both of them are to be punished. (Narada Smṛti 3.09)

The officiating priest (ṛtvij) is seen to be of three kinds: one who has served in previous generations, one appointed by oneself, and one who performs the priestly office out of free will and with affection. (Nar_3.10)
This rule applies when the officiating priests have been chosen according to tradition or by oneself;
however, if the priests are engaged by chance, there is no fault in abandoning them.
When a merchant arrives at a customs station, he should pay the toll as it is prescribed;
he must not evade it, for this has been ordained as a tribute to the kings.
One who evades the customs house, one who buys or sells at an improper time,
or one who declares a false quantity, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty.
If some merchant, while traveling from his country, should die as a stranger,
the king shall protect his merchandise until his heirs appear.
If there is no heir, one should entrust it to kinsmen or relatives;
in their absence, one should keep it well-guarded for ten years.
After ten years, property that has no owner and no heir shall be taken by the king for himself; in this way, the law is not violated.
4. Non-delivery of what has been given: When one, having given property improperly, desires to take it back, that is recorded in law as the legal dispute known as *dattāpradānika*.
That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given—
this fourfold path of giving should be understood in legal proceedings.
For in that regard, eight things are traditionally held to be non-givable, and the givable is said to be of one kind;
one should know that what is given is of seven kinds, and what is not given consists of sixteen types.

That which has been deposited as collateral, that which has been borrowed, a pledge, that which is held in common, a trust, one's wife and children, and one's entire property when there is offspring; // Nar_4.04 //
For even when a person is beset by dire calamities,
the teachers declare that certain things must not be given away— namely, that which has already been promised to another.
Whatever wealth remains after supporting one's family should be given away; if one gives something other than that, even if it is offered as a gift, one incurs fault.

Those who know the rules of giving understand that what is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return for a favor, or for the sake of a bride-price or as a mark of grace, constitutes a gift.
But what is taken without it being given may be so through the force of fear, anger, grief, or illness;
likewise, through bribery, jesting, exchange, or by means of deception. // Nar_4.08 //

That which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my agent" and "This is my deed. // Nar_4.09 //
If one says "this is a worthy recipient" when he is unworthy, or if a gift is given for a purpose joined with unrighteousness,
that which is given out of ignorance is also declared to be as if not given.
He who takes what is not given out of greed, and he who bestows what should not be given—both the taker of the ungiven and the giver of the ungivable deserve punishment. (Nar_4.11)
5. Breach of Service:
But when one who has undertaken service does not perform it, this legal ground for dispute is called "breach of service after undertaking. (Nar_5.01)
In the treatise, the wise have observed five kinds of attendants;
four kinds are laborers, and fifteen kinds are slaves.

Disciples, resident pupils, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer for extra tasks—these are declared to be laborers (karmakarāḥ); slaves (dāsāḥ), however, are those born in the house and so forth.

The wise declare that their lack of independence is their common characteristic; however, the distinctions among them, as well as their specific modes of livelihood, are said to be determined by their caste and their actions.
Action, too, should be known to be of two kinds: indeed, the unwholesome and the wholesome.
The unwholesome is said to be the work of a slave; the wholesome is remembered as the work of those who perform virtuous deeds.
The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; the touching of private parts, the handling of food remnants, and the evacuation and disposal of feces and urine. // Nar_5.06 //
Furthermore, the worship of the Lord with one's own limbs according to one's desire is to be known as inauspicious action; that which is other than this is auspicious.
Until he has mastered the knowledge, the disciple should serve his teacher with self-restraint;
he should behave toward the teacher’s wives and likewise toward the teacher’s son in the same manner.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should wander for alms, sleep on the ground, remain unadorned,
go to bed last of all, and rise before everyone else while in the teacher’s house.
One should not set out or even remain anywhere near one's teacher without being instructed;
once instructed, if one is capable, one should perform the task without hesitation.
He should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not troubled in mind;
he should sit attentively on a grass mat or a wooden plank below the teacher.
If a disciple, though instructed by his teacher, does not comply,
the teacher may punish him without causing physical injury, using either a rope or a split bamboo cane.
One should not strike him excessively, nor on the head or the chest;
rather, having instructed and gained his confidence, he should be disciplined by the king like a teacher.
Having completed his studies and having presented the teacher’s fee to the guru, he should return to his own home; this is declared to be the conduct of a student.
Desiring to master his own craft with the permission of his relatives,
he should dwell in the presence of a teacher for a well-determined period of time.
The teacher should provide him with food from his own home and instruct him;
he should not make him perform any other work, and should treat him like a son.
He who abandons a teacher who is instructing him and is free from malice should be compelled to dwell with him by force; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment.
Even if he has been trained, the pupil shall receive his fee once the time [of training] is completed;
furthermore, whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone.
Once he has mastered the craft, the apprentice, having circumambulated his teacher at the proper time and honored him according to his ability, should take his leave.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Their wages, based on their work, should correspond to their capacity and devotion. (Nar_5.20)
In this regard, the highest type of hired laborer is the warrior, the middling is the cultivator, and the lowest is the porter; thus, the hired servant is of three kinds.
He who is authorized over the affairs of the family is to be known as the *adhikarmakara*; he is also remembered as the *kauṭumbika*.
These four are declared to be performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen types of servants are partakers of inferior karma.
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir, one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one begotten by the master; // Nar_5.24 //
Rescued from great bondage, won as a prize in battle,
and having approached you saying "I am yours," he was made to renounce his life as a wandering ascetic.
One who becomes a slave through devotion, one supported by a female slave,
and one who sells himself— these are declared in the scripture to be the fifteen kinds of slaves.
In that regard, the first four classes are not released from servitude except through the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary. (Nar_5.27)
And whoever should liberate their master from a life-threatening danger shall be released from slavery and receive a share equal to that of a son.
One who has maintained a slave during a time of famine is released from servitude by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by such an act.
Even if he has been pledged after money was paid, if the owner should redeem him,
then he may cause him to return to that person immediately after the sale.
Having paid back the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery;
likewise, even one who was made a slave is released by the lapse of the agreed-upon time.
Having approached you saying "I am yours," and having been won as a stake when the battle was joined,
he is released by the giving of a counter-head through an equal act.
But a man who has fallen from the religious life shall become the slave of the king alone; for him there is no liberation from that state, nor is there any purification by any means whatsoever.
By neglecting his devotee, the master is immediately released from his status as a slave to that devotee;
and by the restraint of the mare, the one who maintains the mare is released.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most wretched of them all and is never released from servitude.
Those who have been abducted by thieves, sold, or forcibly enslaved must be liberated by the king; servitude is not permitted for them.
Slavery by means of the inverse order of castes is not ordained;
except for those who have abandoned their own duty, slavery is considered to be like marriage.
And he who, being dependent, offers himself saying "I am yours," shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall regain him.
Only three are declared to be without property: the wife, the slave, and likewise the son;
whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong.
If one, with a joyful mind, should wish to make his own slave a non-slave,
he should take a water-pot from that person's shoulder and break it along with its water.
One should scatter unbroken grains together with flowers upon his head;
then, having said "He is no slave" three times, one should release him while facing eastward.
From that time forward, he should be addressed as one protected by the favor of his master;
he becomes one whose food may be eaten, one who may be accepted [as a guest], and one who is held in high esteem.
6. Non-payment of Wages: The prescribed procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for those who have been hired has been stated;
the non-payment of such wages is recorded as that title of dispute. (Narada 6.1)
The master of the work shall pay wages to the laborer according to the sequence agreed upon—whether at the beginning, the middle, or the end of the task—as has been determined. (Narada Smṛti 6.2)
But when the wages are not fixed, the merchant, the cowherd, and the farmer shall receive a tenth part of the profit, the cattle, the seed, and the crop, respectively.
Whatever tools for work have been brought for their labor, he should employ them with a sense of trustworthiness; he should not act with deceit.
If one has promised to perform work but does not do it, or if one has been forced to work after receiving wages,
he who takes the wages but fails to work shall pay double the wages as a fine.
If one abandons the work before the time is complete, he deserves the loss of his wages;
however, if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for what was actually done.

Having agreed upon a wage consisting of a sixth part of the produce, if he abandons the laborer on the road while the work is still being done by the draft animals, he must pay the full wage along with interest; likewise, if he causes the work to be done without paying the wage at all, he must pay the wage together with interest.
If one hires carriers for goods by means of vehicles or draft animals, they should be made to pay a fourth part of the wage; however, if one abandons them on the way, the payment shall be half.
In this same way, even a porter who fails to bring [the goods] shall suffer a loss of wages;
however, one who creates an obstacle to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
If the goods should meet with misfortune due to the fault of the carrier,
he shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
From a hundred cows, a young heifer shall be the cowherd's fee; from two hundred, the milk of one milch-cow every day, and on the eighth day, the entire yield of milk.
"O cowherd, you must bring back the cows every day at the end of the night;
having grazed and drunk, the cowherd should bring them back in the evening."
If a calamity should befall the cattle, the cowherd should strive to remedy it to the best of his ability;
if he is unable to do so, he should quickly return and report the matter to his master.
If he does not exert himself to recover it, nor raises a cry for help, nor informs his owner,
the cowherd must pay the value of that [lost] animal and also a fine to the king.
One should cause even a cow that is lost, ruined, infested with worms, struck by a dog, dead in a dangerous place,
or deficient in human effort to be disposed of.
Likewise, when goats and sheep are obstructed by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid,
if a wolf should kill one by force, that guilt shall fall upon the herdsman.

If the herd has been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay,
provided he reports it to his master at the proper place and time.
By this, the dispute regarding all guardians has been fully explained;
and in the case of those who have died, purification shall occur through the sight of their marks and other signs.
Having received the fee, a courtesan who does not wish to comply shall pay double that amount;
likewise, a man who does not grant the woman after having paid the fee shall suffer the same penalty.
He who approaches a woman in an improper place, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine (vinaya).
But he who, having built a house on another's threshing floor and offered praise, should dwell there, must take away that house—its grass, wood, bricks, and so forth—and depart. (Nar_6.22)
One should bring forward the vessels for carrying the *stoma* when they are full and their time has come;
otherwise, what is broken or lost shall be the responsibility of the receiver, except in the case of an accident.
7. Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner:
