When property belonging to another—whether deposited, lost, found, or stolen—is sold in the absence of the owner, that should be known as "sale by one who is not the owner."
Having recovered property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall regain it;
the buyer is cleared of guilt if the purchase was made openly, whereas the act is theft if the purchase was made in secret.
One who purchases [a slave] in secret from a person who is not his master, from one who is not his own offspring,
for an insufficient price, or at an improper time, shall be a partaker in that fault.
A purchaser shall not conceal the source of his acquisition; his purity is established by that provenance.
In the opposite case, he incurs the same fault and deserves the punishment for theft.
The seller shall pay the value of the object to the owner, the price paid by the buyer, and likewise a fine to the king; such is the rule regarding sale without ownership.
If one finds a treasure deposited by another, he should present it to the king;
for all treasure belongs to the king, with the exception of that which belongs to a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin, having found a treasure-trove, should also promptly inform the king;
he may enjoy what is given by him, for by failing to inform, he would be a thief. (Nar_7.7)
If one recovers even one's own lost property in that same manner, one should report it to the king;
having been cleared therein, one may take possession of it, otherwise one would be guilty. (Narada 7.8)

8. Regret over a Purchase: When, after having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer—that failure to deliver after sale is called the legal head of dispute known as *vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*. (Narada 8.1)
In this world, there are two kinds of substances: the mobile and the immobile;
all of these are called "merchandise" in the context of the laws of buying and selling.
The wise have recorded his method of giving and receiving as being of six kinds:
by counting, by weighing, by measuring, and by way of labor, form, and splendor.
If one who has sold a commodity does not deliver it to the buyer for its price,
he shall be made to pay the loss of value for immovable property, and the fruit of the labor for movable property.
If the profit is lost, one should recover the merchandise along with the interest;
this is the rule for local traders, while those who travel to foreign regions receive the profits of their respective quarters.
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss belongs solely to the seller who, having sold it, does not deliver it.
But he who, having shown an item as faultless, delivers one that is defective,
shall be made to pay double its value and an equal amount as a fine.
Likewise, he who sells [an item] into one person's hand and then delivers it to another shall be made to pay double that amount and shall be punished to the same extent.
If a buyer does not accept a commodity being offered for sale,
or if a seller sells it elsewhere after having already agreed to sell it, neither of them shall be held at fault.
This rule has been proclaimed regarding merchandise for which the price has been paid;
if the price has not been paid, there is no transgression on the part of the seller, except in the case of a prior agreement.
For the sake of profit, merchants engage in the buying and selling of all commodities; yet that profit, even upon reaching the market price, may or may not become great. (Nar_8.11)
Therefore, in that place and at that time, a merchant should investigate the market price;
he should not proceed with deceit, for such is the superior path of commerce.
9.1. Non-delivery after sale:
When a buyer, having purchased a commodity for its price, does not regard it with favor, this is called the legal head of dispute known as "repentance after purchase."
If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase,
it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it is still unblemished.
If the buyer returns it on the second day, he shall pay a thirtieth part of the price as a fine;
on the third day, that fine is double; after that, the loss falls solely upon the buyer.
A buyer should personally examine a commodity beforehand for its merits and defects;
once it has been examined and purchased with approval, it cannot be returned to the seller.
One should examine what is to be milked after three days, but what is to be carried [as a load] after five;
for pearls, diamonds, and corals, the examination period shall be seven days.
For bipeds, the impurity lasts half a month for males and twice that for females;
for all seeds, it lasts ten days; and for metals and clothes, one day.
Furthermore, a garment that has been worn, which is discolored, soiled, and even defective, once sold, shall not belong to the seller again. // Nar_9.7 //
The value of a garment that has been washed once is reduced by one-eighth;
if washed twice, by one-half; if thrice, by one-third; and if washed four times, by one-half.
But beyond the point when half has been exhausted, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage until it reaches the state of being worn out;
for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its further decay.
For all metals as well, the cause of their depletion during the process of refinement is seen to be their contact with fire. // Nar_9.10 //
There is no loss in the case of gold; in silver, there is a loss of two palas per hundred;
it should be known that for tin and lead, the loss shall be eight palas per hundred.
One should know that five palas [of ash] result from copper, as well as from whatever alloys are made thereof;
because there are many such metals, there is no fixed rule regarding the reduction of iron.
Regarding the processing of woven cloth, the decrease and increase have been illustrated:
for threads made of cotton or wool, the increase is ten palas for every hundred.
For those of medium thickness like thick thread, five hundred [turns] are prescribed;
for very fine threads, three palas is declared to be the limit of depletion.
For that which is pierced by a needle, there is a loss of one-thirtieth of what was produced by the work;
however, for silks and bark garments, there is neither increase nor decrease.
A merchant skilled in commodities should not harbor regret after having purchased;
rather, he should understand the profit and loss of goods as well as their supply.
10. Non-abandonment of established custom (*samayasyānapākarma*):
The established practice (*samaya*) of heretics, guilds, and so forth is called "custom. The non-abandonment of that custom is recorded as this title of dispute. (Nar_10.1)
The king should likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, corporations, associations, bands, and assemblies, both within the fort and in the countryside.
Whatever the duty, whatever the action, whatever the manner of attending to them,
and whatever the means of their livelihood— let him approve of all that accordingly.
Whatever is contrary to the king's wishes, whatever is naturally despised by the subjects, and whatever is detrimental to their interests— one should turn them away from those things.
The king should not tolerate their forming secret alliances, their bearing of weapons, or their mutual injury. (Nar_10.5)
Those who would divide the separate groups must be especially disciplined;
for if they are neglected, they will bring about terrible danger, like a disease.
Whatever instrument of action is defective and not prescribed by the sacred tradition,
even if it has been set in motion, a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be withdrawn.

11. Disputes concerning fields—determinations regarding embankments, fallow land, boundaries, cultivated and uncultivated plots—wherever such matters pertaining to fields arise, that is a dispute concerning fields. // Nar_11.1 //
In disputes concerning the boundaries of fields, the decision is based on the testimony of the neighbors,
as well as the leaders of cities, villages, and guilds, and those men who are the most venerable.
And those who live outside the village boundaries by means of agriculture, as well as cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest— Nar_11.3.
They should mark out the boundary,
characterized by husks, charcoal, potsherds, water-jars, shrines, and trees.
And by means of well-known anthills, level ground, depressions, and elevations, as well as by ancient fields, groves, paths, and embankments; // Nar_11.5 //
On lands where the marks have been lost because they were swept away by the waters of rivers,
[the ownership] is determined by inference from those regions, as well as by measurements and the observation of possession.
If, however, the neighbors should speak falsely in determining that matter,
they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
But others, such as the head of a guild and so forth, should each be made to pay a fine;
if they persist in falsehood, they should be punished with the first amercement.
A single man, even if he be trustworthy, shall not determine a boundary by himself;
because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established upon many.
If one person alone should mark out the boundary, he must do so while fasting and composed in mind,
wearing red garlands and garments, and placing the earth upon his head.
And when there are no knowers of the boundary nor any marks of it,
then the king himself shall determine the boundary between the two [villages] as he sees fit.

By this very same method, the procedure for resolving disputes regarding houses, gardens, water reservoirs, temples, and so forth, as well as those between different villages, has been declared. // Nar_11.12 //
One should not obstruct crossroads, shrines of the gods, or carriage ways with refuse heaps, pits, ditches, drains, and the like. (Nar_11.13)

A boundary embankment in the middle of another's field is not forbidden, provided it yields great benefit with little harm; for when there is a loss [to one], an increase [to another] is desired. // Nar_11.14 //
A dam should be known to be of two kinds: that which is to be dug out and likewise that which is to be built up.
It is "to be dug out" by causing water to flow through it, and "to be built up" by stopping that flow.
Without water, the crop would perish; yet by excessive water it likewise perishes.
That very same fault which exists in the absence of water is recorded as existing in the case of excessive water.
But whoever should initiate a dam that was previously begun and then abandoned, without having consulted his master, shall not partake in its fruit.
But when the master has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is no longer present,
one should consult the king and then carry out that work on the embankment.
Otherwise, one would incur affliction by observing the hunter;
for the arrows of him who shoots after what has already been pierced are wasted. (Nar_11.19)
If someone should cultivate a field when the owners are incapable, deceased, or lost, he may enjoy the fruit of it without being hindered. // Nar_11.20 //
If a field-owner returns while his field is being ploughed,
he shall recover his own field by paying for all the cultivation of the fallow land.
Then, through a reduction of one-eighth each year for up to seven years,
when the eighth year is reached, he shall recover the field that was enjoyed [by another].
If neglected for half a year, it becomes fallow; if for three years, it is truly fallow;
but a field abandoned for five years becomes like a wilderness.
Whether it be a field that has passed through three generations or a house inherited in succession,
except by royal favor, one should not transfer the enjoyment of such property to another.
But where the destruction of crops by cattle and other animals occurs after they have broken through the enclosure,
the keeper shall be punished there, provided he does not prevent it to the best of his ability.
But when standing crops are destroyed along with their roots, the owner of the field shall receive an equal amount as compensation;
the keeper shall be released from liability by the killing [of the animal], but he shall inflict a fine upon the owner.
A cow that has recently calved, as well as bulls, goats, sheep, and elephants, must be restrained with great effort for ten days; their owner shall not be subject to punishment.
One should cause a fine of one māṣa to be paid for a cow, two māṣas for a buffalo,
and for a goat or sheep with its young, the fine shall be half a māṣa.
Elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are considered protectors of the people;
likewise, a cow that is pregnant, one that has recently calved, and one that is in heat are exempt from punishment.
For those who sit twice [in the same manner], the punishment is declared to be double; for those who dwell there [longer], it is fourfold.
Likewise, the punishment for a thief is prescribed for those who act as direct spies.
If cows that have strayed due to the fault of the herdsman take refuge in a field, there is no punishment for the owner of the field; rather, the herdsman deserves that punishment.
Whether seized by a king's grasp, or struck by a thunderbolt of diamond, or bitten by a serpent, or even fallen from the summit of a mountain; // Nar_11.32 //
Even if [the animal] is killed by lions or tigers, or struck down by diseases, there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners. (Nar_11.33)

If a man seeks to recover grain that has been eaten by cows, the neighbor must pay the fine for the damage; the grain sown there should be given to the owner of the cattle, while the fodder should be given to the farmer. // Nar_11.34 //
And if a field located at the edge of a village, at the boundary of a pasture, or on a great highway is uncovered,
there is no fault on the part of the guardian if it is destroyed.
A fence should be constructed around the field on the path such that a camel cannot look over it,
nor can a beast, a horse, or a boar leap over or break through it.
A house and a field should be known as the basis for the dwelling of householders;
therefore, the king should not confiscate them, for they are indeed the root of householders.
When the population increases, the king’s righteousness and treasury increase;
when it declines, they too decline. Therefore, one should rely upon the causes of growth.
12. *Strīpuṃsayoga*:
That title of a legal dispute (*vivādapada*) called *strīpuṃsayoga* is said to be that wherein the rules for marriage and so forth concerning women and men are proclaimed. (Narada 12.1)
From the union of a woman and a man, the formal choosing (varaṇa) is prescribed first;
after the choosing comes the grasping of the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa), and then the rite of two-fold character (saṃskāra).
For those two, marriage is said to be indefinite because of the possibility of perceiving faults;
it becomes definite as the characteristic of a wife through the taking of the hand and the recitation of the mantras.
Among the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, a wife of one's own caste is superior; and for a woman, a husband of her own caste is likewise superior.
For a Brāhmaṇa, there are three other wives in the direct order [of castes],
while for a Śūdra woman, there are likewise three other husbands in the inverse order.
Two wives for a Kṣatriya and one for a Vaiśya are proclaimed;
two husbands for a Vaiśya are to be known, and one other for a Kṣatriya wife.
Up to the seventh or the fifth degree from the paternal and maternal relatives,
those of the same *gotra* as well as those with the same *pravara* are ineligible for marriage.
A man must be examined for his virility by the very marks of his own limbs;
if he is a man without deficiency, he is worthy to obtain a maiden.
His collarbones, knees, and bones were well-knit; his shoulders and neck were firmly set;
his temples were broad, his thighs and skin were slender, and his gait and voice were unhindered.
His semen floats upon the water, and his urine is pleasant-smelling and frothy;
by these characteristics he would be a man, but by the opposite characteristics, he is a eunuch.
In the treatise, that [disease] is seen by the wise to be of fourteen kinds;
the method for treating those that are curable and those that are incurable has been stated in due order.
One who is impotent by nature, one who is castrated, and likewise one who becomes impotent due to a factional dispute;
as well as one rendered so by a teacher’s curse, by disease, or by the wrath of the gods. (Nar_12.12)

The jealous man, the eunuch, he whose semen is wind, the one whose vulva is in the mouth, the one who is rejected, the one with sterile seed, the modest man, and likewise the husband of another. Nar_12.13.
Among these, the first two are incurable; one should observe the treatment known as *pakṣa* for one month.
For this triad, the duration is traditionally recorded as one year in successive order.
The other four [defects] that have been proclaimed— envy, ignorance, and so forth—
must be abandoned even by a woman whose womb has been violated, just as one would a fallen man.
If her husband is one who has cast away his seed in vain or is incapable of performing his duties,
another man is permitted for the woman after she has waited for one year.
Even for a modest man, the penis becomes flaccid through union with a bold woman;
therefore, one should employ other women, young girls, and the like to stimulate his diminished vigor. (Nar_12.17)
If a man should become unfaithful to another woman, he shall find another husband for her; this is the ordinance of Prajāpati.
Women were created for the sake of offspring; a woman is the field for the seed-bearer to produce progeny.
The field should be given to one who possesses the seed; one without seed does not deserve the field.
The father himself should give away the daughter, or the brother with the father's consent;
likewise the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the paternal kinsmen, and other relatives.
But in the absence of a mother, if she is present in her natural state,
then when she is not in that natural state, those of the same caste shall give their daughter [in marriage].
But when there is no one at all [suitable], the maiden, having obtained the king's permission and relying upon a suitor, may choose for herself.
He should practice dharma together with a wife of the same class who is suitable in terms of family, appearance, age, and learning; and from her, he should procreate sons.
If a man, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country,
and after three menstrual seasons have passed, she may choose another groom.
A maiden may postpone her marriage and inform her kinsmen;
if they do not give her to a husband, they shall be equal to killers of embryos.
As many seasons as have passed for her without a husband,
so many instances of foeticide shall belong to him who does not give her away.
Therefore, before menstruation has begun, the father should give his daughter away once;
otherwise, a great sin would touch him—for this is the rule of the virtuous.
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once.

In these five marriages, beginning with the Brāhma, the rule is prescribed as being based on merit; however, in the three beginning with the Āsura, the giving [of the bride] depends upon [material] considerations.
If a bridegroom who is superior should arrive after the bride-price has already been received for a maiden,
a falsehood may be uttered there that is consistent with dharma, artha, and kāma.
One should not defile an unblemished maiden, nor should one defile an unblemished bridegroom;
for if a fault exists, there is no sin for the two of them if they mutually abandon one another.
If one who has given a maiden according to the law does not deliver her to the groom,
and the groom is not at fault, he shall be punished by the king like a thief.
But for him who gives away a maiden who has defects without having disclosed them,
the king shall inflict the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence.
But that man who, out of malice, declares a maiden to be "not a virgin" without demonstrating her fault, shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (Narada 12.34)
But if a groom, having accepted an unblemished maiden, should abandon her, he must be disciplined—
even against his will— and he shall marry that very same girl again.

Being afflicted by long-standing or loathsome diseases, being physically deformed, having engaged in sexual intercourse, being forward, and having her heart set on another— these are proclaimed as the defects of a maiden.
One who is insane, fallen from caste, impotent, unfortunate, or abandoned by kinsmen, as well as those two previously mentioned defects of a maiden— this is the collection of defects in a bridegroom.
Eight forms of marriage have been proclaimed for the sake of the sacramental rites of the social classes;
of these, the Brāhma is the first, and likewise the Prājāpatya.
The Ārṣa, the Daiva, the Gāndharva, and likewise the Āsura;
the Rākṣasa follows immediately after that, while the Paiśāca is recorded as the eighth.
Having invited the girl and honored her, one should give her adorned with ornaments in the Brāhma rite;
having said, "May you perform your religious duties together," it is ordained as the Prājāpatya rite.
Having given a pair of a cow and a bull, the marriage is called Ārṣa;
that which takes place within the sacrificial altar for the officiating priest performing the rite is Daiva.
When one desires a woman who also desires him, they call that the fifth marriage, named Gāndharva;
while the Āsura marriage is to be known as that which arises from the transaction of a bride-price.
Marriage by abduction is called the Rākṣasa form;
likewise, the eighth and lowest is the Paiśāca, resulting from approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated.
Of these, the four beginning with the Brāhma are declared to be lawful;
the Gāndharva is common to all, while the three beyond that are unlawful.
Other women who have had previous husbands are said to be of seven types in their respective order;
among them, the *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) is of three kinds, while the *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman) is of four kinds.

A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage, is called the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); she is eligible for the sacramental rite once again.
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, resorts to another man and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second type.
When no suitable bridegrooms are available, a woman who is given by her kinsmen to a man of the same caste who is not a sapinda is proclaimed the third [form of marriage].
If a woman, whether she has borne children or not,
out of desire resorts to another man while her husband is still alive, she is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
She who, upon the death of her husband, rejects even the brothers-in-law who have approached her and,
out of desire, goes to another man, is proclaimed as the second [type of widow remarriage].
She who has come from another land, purchased with wealth, and afflicted by hunger and thirst,
approaching you saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the third type.
A woman who, disregarding local customs, is given by her elders to one man but then commits an act of violence against another,
is indeed remembered as a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman).
This rule has been proclaimed for women who marry again and for wanton women;
among these, each preceding one is inferior, while each succeeding one is superior.

Regarding the procreation of offspring, that which is obtained from a woman who was acquired for a price belongs to the biological father; however, in the case of one who has approached him without a price, the fruit belongs solely to the owner of the field.
If seed is sown in a field without the knowledge of the owner of the field, there is no share for the owner of the seed; that [crop] belongs to the owner of the field alone. // Nar_12.55 //
If seed carried by the force of a flood sprouts in someone's field, that person who possesses the field shall enjoy the fruit;
the owner of the seed shall not share in the fruit.
If a great bull, while roaming among the cows in the pen, were to sire calves,
those cows would belong to him— the bull— and the bull's virility would have been in vain for the others.
When seed, approved by the owner of the field, is sown in someone else's field,
that offspring is considered to belong to both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field.
There would be no crop without a field, nor would there be a crop without a seed;
therefore, according to the law, offspring are considered to belong to both the father and the mother.

Experts recognize adultery as occurring when a woman who has a protector is seen in another's house in the company of a man; it is not so recognized if she has come to his own house of her own accord.
There is no offense of violence for one who approaches the wife of a man who is corrupt, has abandoned his wife, is impotent, or is forgiving, provided he does so of his own will.

Standing together with another's wife at an improper time or in an improper place, as well as conversing or sporting with her in secret—these three constitute the stages of adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*). (Narada 12.62)
When a woman and a man meet at the confluence of rivers, at sacred fords, in groves, or in forests, their act of sexual union shall be considered adultery.
By means of dispatching female messengers, by sending letters, and through other such transgressions, all such acts are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
If one touches a woman in an improper place, or likewise, if being touched he consents to it, and this occurs with mutual consent, that shall be considered *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
Whether by means of foods, or edibles, garments, and likewise garlands,
or by being sent perfumes— all this is recorded as "gathering" (saṃgrahaṇa).
Whether out of pride, delusion, or self-praise, if one should say of her own accord,
"She was previously enjoyed by me," all such cases are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
If one should seize another by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the hem of the garment, or say "Stay! Stay!", all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual solicitation).
When men violate their own caste, the highest fine is prescribed;
in the reverse case, however, it is the middle fine, but for violating the inverse order, it is the death penalty.
If the maiden is unwilling, there shall be the excision of two fingers;
in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there shall indeed be execution as well as the confiscation of all her property.
But when a maiden is willing and he is of the same caste, there is no transgression; however, having adorned her and honored her, he alone shall marry her.

A mother, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, a maternal uncle’s wife, a paternal aunt, the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend, a female disciple, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law; // Nar_12.72 //
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge, a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and she who is of the highest caste. // Nar_12.73 //
Having approached any one of these women, one is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
the cutting off of the penis is the punishment prescribed there, and no other.
One who violates a female animal should be disciplined with one hundred lashes;
for cows, the middle amercement applies, and the same penalty holds for those of the lowest castes.
For one who approaches a woman who should not be approached, the king, being urged on, inflicts punishment;
yet in this matter, according to the rules for expiation, the purification consists of the performance of penance.

A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brahmin woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— all these women may be approached in the direct order of the castes (ānulomya), but never in the inverse order (pratiloma).
But with these very female slaves, there would be a fault as great as with the wives of others;
for even if they are permissible, one should not approach them if they are under the protection of another.
If the husband of a woman who has not yet borne offspring should die, she,
being authorized by her elders, may approach her brother-in-law out of a desire for a son.
He should proceed toward her in that very manner until the birth of a son;
once a son is born, he should desist, for otherwise there would be a transgression.
Having anointed his limbs with clarified butter or unrefined oil, avoiding contact of mouth with mouth and limb with limb; (Nar_12.81)

One should not approach a woman who already has a son, one who is barren, one who is menstruating, one who is unwilling, one who is pregnant, one who is censurable, or one who has not been authorized by her kinsmen.
But if a woman who has not been authorized should bear a son to her husband's younger brother,
those who speak according to dharma say that he is born of an adulterer and is not entitled to the inheritance.
Likewise, if a younger brother approaches the wife of an elder brother without being so authorized,
or if an elder brother approaches the wife of a younger brother, both of them are guilty of violating the bed of a guru.

If the family lineage is left with only him remaining, he may, at the command of his elders and for the sake of the continuity of the line— and not out of lust— approach the wife of his younger brother.
But if no guru is present, the king should be informed of the destruction of the family;
then, having received his permission, he should depart with his wife after giving her instructions.
Having bathed according to the very procedure previously described during the *puṃsavana* rite, the pure husband [should approach her];
or rather, until the *garbhādhāna*, she is as a daughter-in-law once the embryo has been conceived.
Therefore, a man or even a woman who acts otherwise out of lust must be severely punished by the king; for by failing to restrain them, he becomes a sinner.
But when a quarrel arises between a husband and wife, caused by envy or malice and rooted in passion, they should not dispute it before their kinsmen nor before the king.
If a man and a woman who are mutually hostile abandon each other, the serpent-nature arises; except in the case of a woman whose transgression remains concealed.
In the event of infidelity, the woman shall undergo shaving of the head, sleeping on the ground,
eating wretched food, wearing poor clothing, and the labor of clearing away refuse.
A woman who has squandered her husband's wealth, one who has caused the miscarriage of a fetus,
or one who desires the death of her husband, shall be banished from the home.
A wise man should expel from his home that wife who is constantly inclined toward what is harmful, speaks unpleasantly, and eats before her husband.
One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a woman who is barren, who gives birth only to daughters, who is blameworthy, or who is always hostile; by acting thus, one incurs fault.
One who abandons a wife who is compliant, free from verbal abuse, capable, virtuous, and a mother of children, shall be restrained by the king with a heavy punishment.

If a woman has been married by her kinsmen without the fault being known, and she departs without having taken refuge with another, she should be reinstated by them; if she is without kin, she should seek refuge on her own.
"When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women."
A Brāhmaṇa woman whose husband has gone abroad shall wait for eight years if she is childless, but only four years if she has borne children; after that time, she may resort to another man.
A Kṣatriya woman who has not borne children may remain [in her husband's house] for six years;
a Vaiśya woman who has borne children, for four years; but a woman of the other [Śūdra] caste shall dwell there for two years.
No specific time for cohabitation is prescribed for a Śūdra woman, nor is there any transgression of dharma;
however, if she has not borne a child, her stay [in the house] is limited to one year.
This law is prescribed for women whose husbands have gone abroad and from whom no news is received;
however, if he is heard to be alive, this rule shall be doubled.
This creation of living beings by Prajāpati occurs for the sake of the continuation of progeny;
therefore, no such fault exists for women in approaching another man in this manner.
The birth of castes in the natural order is known as *vidhi*;
that which occurs in the reverse order should be understood as *varṇasaṃkara* (the mixing of castes).

The son born of a woman one degree lower is known as the *anantara*; likewise, the son born of a woman two degrees lower is the *ekāntara*, and the son born of a woman three degrees lower is the *dvyantara*—this being according to the natural order (*anuloma*), and the same applies to the inverse order (*pratiloma*).
The Ugra, the Pāraśava, and the Niṣāda are proclaimed as the three sons born of Śūdra women from the three highest castes in the direct order of birth.
From a Brāhmaṇa woman as well, the Cāṇḍāla, the Sūta, and the Vaidehaka are born;
these three others are to be known as born in the reverse order (pratiloma).
The Ambaṣṭha, the Māgadha, and the Kṣattṛ are the sons of Kṣatriya women;
among them, one is born in the natural order (ānulomyena), while two are to be known as born in the inverse order (pratilomataḥ).
The sons of a Vaiśya woman, however, are the Dauṣṣanta, the Yavana, and the Āyogava;
among these, one is born from the reverse order (prātilomya) and two are to be known as born from the natural order (anuloma).
The Sūtas and others who are born in the reverse order of castes (pratiloma) are those born from the inverse crossing of castes;
they are the mixed castes (saṃkara), such as the Śvapākas and so forth, and their group consists of twenty-one.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa from a woman of the same caste is a Savarṇa; from a Kṣatriya woman, he is an Anantara.
Likewise, Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are the sons of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya respectively.
But the son of a Vaiśya woman from a Brāhmaṇa is the Dauṣṣanta, separated by one interval;
likewise, from a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra woman, one named Niṣāda is born.
A Śūdra woman bears a Pāraśava son from a Brāhmaṇa;
these are indeed proclaimed to be the sons born according to the natural order (ānulomya) of the castes.
The Sūta, the Māgadha, and likewise the Āyogava— these are the sons born from the castes in the reverse order (prātilomya), and they are likewise immediate [in their status].
The Sūta is declared to be the son born immediately after [the Brāhmaṇa], produced from a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman;
likewise, the Māgadha and the Āyogava are the two sons of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra respectively.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears to a Vaiśya a son called a Vaidehaka, who is one degree lower;
likewise, a Kṣatriya woman bears to a Śūdra a son called a Kṣattṛ, who is also one degree lower.
When there is an inversion of the order and a confusion of castes, a most wicked Caṇḍāla is born from a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother who has lost her virtue. // Nar_12.116 //
The king must exercise such scrutiny that no intermixture of castes occurs;
therefore, the king must especially protect the three Vedas from such confusion.
13.1. Where the division of paternal property is determined by the sons,
that subject of dispute is called "partition of inheritance" (dāyabhāga) by the learned.
When the father has died, the sons shall divide the father's wealth;
in the absence of daughters, the daughters [inherit], and in their absence, the offspring of those daughters.
When the mother’s menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage, or when the father has passed away, having lost all desire for life; ||| Nar_13.3 |||
Or rather, the father himself, having reached old age, should divide his sons,
giving the eldest a superior share according as he deems fit.
The eldest brother should support all his brothers who so desire, just as a father does;
or a capable younger brother may do so, for in a family, religious rites depend upon one's ability.
Excluding the wealth acquired through valor or marriage, as well as that which constitutes the wealth of learning—
these three are indivisible, as is any gift received from a father.
And for one to whom his mother has given her own wealth out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; for the mother is as beloved as the father.

What is given before the sacred fire, what is received at the wedding, as well as the inheritance from the husband, and that which is received from brothers, the mother, and the father— this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
The property of a woman belongs to her children; if she leaves no offspring, it goes to her husband.
However, in the case of marriages such as the Brāhma and the other first four, they say it goes to her father; but in the others, it goes to the husband.
He who maintains the family of a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself has not studied.
A physician shall not, against his will, give a portion from his own wealth to one who is unqualified, unless that person has acquired it by relying upon the paternal estate. (Narada 13.11)
When dividing his own property, a father should allot two shares to himself;
after her husband has died, the mother shall be entitled to an equal share with the sons.
A larger share should be given to the eldest, for a special boon is ordained for the eldest;
the remaining brothers shall share equal portions, as shall an unmarried sister.
Likewise, among sons born of wives of lower castes according to the law,
there is a gradual reduction of shares for those born of women married [in the prescribed order].
But for those who have been divided by their father with unequal shares of wealth— whether inferior, superior, or equal—
that very same rule shall apply, for the father is indeed the master of all.

The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son taken with the bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a concealed maiden (gūḍhaja)— for these, the one who marries them is to be known as the father, and they are declared to be entitled to a share of the inheritance.
And he who is fatherless, being the son of an unmarried woman whose mother has not been wedded,
shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his property.
Those who are born of an unauthorized woman by one man, or likewise by many, are all non-partakers of the inheritance; they are the sons of the seed-owners alone.
If the mother was taken for a bride-price, they shall offer the funeral cake to the progenitor;
but if she was approached without a bride-price, the offering of the cake belongs to the husband alone.

One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these, though born of the body (aurasa), shall not receive a share; how much less so those born of the wife (kṣetraja)? || Nar_13.20 ||

Those in the family who are seized by long-lasting or severe illness, or who are dull-witted, insane, blind, or lame, must be supported; however, their sons shall be entitled to a share of the inheritance.
Those who have two fathers (dvirāmuṣyāyaṇas) should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and water separately to both;
likewise, they should take half a share from the inheritance for both the progenitor (bījika) and the owner of the field (kṣetrika).
The share of those who have lived together in union is held to belong to them alone;
otherwise, among those who have no offspring, the heirs shall go to the others.
If a brother should die without offspring, or if he should renounce the world,
the remaining brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman's separate wealth.
They should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives, provided they preserve the bed of their husband; however, if they do not, they may forfeit their inheritance from the others.
It may be that for one who has a daughter, the paternal share is intended for her maintenance;
he should support her until her marriage, but thereafter the husband shall maintain her.
When her husband has died and she is childless, the husband's kin are the authority over the woman;
they are the masters regarding her employment, her protection, and her maintenance.
When the husband's family is extinct, devoid of men, and without support,
and when his sapinda relatives are no longer present, the father’s side becomes the woman's authority.
At the conclusion of both [the husband's] life and his absence, the king is declared to be the woman's protector;
he shall provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from the path.
Even women born into noble families fall away through lack of independence;
therefore, Prajāpati ordained that they should not possess independence.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the sons protect her in widowhood; a woman does not deserve independence.
Whatever remains after the paternal inheritance has been given and the father’s debt has been paid,
that is to be divided by the brothers, so that the father does not remain a debtor.
And for those whose purificatory rites have not been performed in due order by their father,
these must be performed by their brothers from the paternal wealth itself.

If paternal wealth is not available, the sacramental rites that must necessarily be performed should be carried out by brothers who have already had their own rites performed, using a portion drawn from their own shares.
He who is engaged in the affairs of the family and performs those duties should be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and vehicles.
In cases of doubt regarding the law of partition, for the determination of inheritance among heirs,
[the matter is settled] by kinsmen and by written records of the shares, through the commencement of separate activities.
For brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single dharma prevails;
once division has occurred, their dharma shall also become distinct for each.

The giving and receiving of gifts, the ownership of cattle, food, houses, and fields, as well as cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditure, are to be understood as distinct for those who have been partitioned.
Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, stand surety, give gifts, and receive them from one another; those who have not divided may not do so.
One should understand those among one's own kinsmen for whom these customary rites are performed in the world to be divided, even in the absence of a written document.
If many who are born of one source possess separate natures, separate activities,
and are endowed with separate qualities of action, they are not considered capable of accomplishing tasks together.
If they should give their own shares, or even sell them, they may do all that as they wish; for they are masters of their own property. (Nar_13.42)

The legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), and the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), as well as the son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), and likewise the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna).
The son born again, the abandoned, the received, the purchased, the made,
and likewise the one who has come of his own accord— these are declared to be the twelve kinds of sons.
Among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen who are not heirs;
each preceding one is considered superior, and each subsequent one is inferior.
For these [sons] would inherit that wealth after the father has died in due order;
in the absence of each elder brother, the younger one shall obtain it.
In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [is the heir] because her lineage is seen to be equal [to his];
for both the son and the daughter are declared to be the perpetuators of the father's lineage.
In the absence of daughters, however, the kinsmen on the father's side (sakulya) shall take it; after them, those of the same caste (sajāti). In the absence of all these, it goes to the king.
Except for a Brahmin, however, a king devoted to righteousness shall provide a livelihood for women; this is recorded as the rule for inheritance.
Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is called *sāhasa* (recklessness); here, *saha* is said to mean strength.
Furthermore, that [discipline] is to be known as threefold—namely, the first, the middle, and the highest; its specific characteristics have been explained separately in the treatises. (Nar_14.2)
The destruction, seizure, or crushing of fruits, roots, water, and other such agricultural implements is declared to be the first degree of violence (sāhasa).
Regarding clothing, livestock, food and drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Malice, the use of poison or weapons, the violation of another's wife, and whatever else is said to cause the loss of life— these are declared to be the highest form of violence (uttamasāhasa).
For that first [offense], the punishment depends on the nature of the act and shall be at least one hundred;
for the middle [offense], it should be known by those learned in the scriptures as being at least five hundred.
Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of limbs— these are declared to be the punishments for the highest degree of violence.
This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction, except for the execution of a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death.
Shaving the head is his punishment, as is banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall bear the mark of his crime on his forehead and travel upon a donkey.
Those two may be considered fit for social intercourse once they have been punished for the first two offenses;
however, even one who has been punished for the highest violence (uttamasāhasa) should be known as one with whom no social communion is permitted.
Theft is a specific variety of that very [violence], and its distinction is stated here: they say that theft committed by force is extreme violence, whereas that done by deceit is theft.
That [gift] is also declared by the wise to be of three kinds, depending on the material substance:
namely, from the removal of inferior, middling, or superior materials.

Whatever consists of earthenware, seats, beds, bones, wood, leather, grass, and so forth, as well as pulses such as *śamī* and *mudga*, is declared to be minor property (*kṣudradravya*). (Narada 14.13)
Clothing, with the exception of silk; likewise cattle, with the exception of cows;
iron, with the exception of gold; and also rice and barley—these constitute the middle [gift]. (Nar_14.14)
Gold, jewels, silk garments, women, men, cattle, elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, Brahmins, and kings, should be known as the highest category of wealth.
The wise declare that theft consists of the removal of these [goods] by deceiving them through various means, such as when they are asleep, careless, or intoxicated. (Nar_14.16)

Theft is established by the seizure of stolen goods; in the absence of such goods, it is established by the enjoyment [of the property]. Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, as well as from the lack of income and expenditure.
Those who provide shelter to thieves as they move about,
and those who, though capable, neglect them, also partake in the guilt of that crime.
And those who, having heard the cries of people while their wealth is being carried off, do not run to its rescue, they too share in that guilt.
Whatever punishment has been prescribed by the wise for the three types of violent acts, that same punishment applies to theft as well, according to the sequence of the three kinds of property.
When cattle and other such property have been lost or stolen,
those who know how should conduct a search by following their tracks until the source is reached.
In a village, a cow-pen, or a pasture, wherever his foot may fall, he must carry it;
otherwise, he shall not lead it elsewhere.
If his foot should stumble or break due to uneven ground in a crowded place,
he should cast it down there at whichever village or herd-station is nearest.
In that same place where two [opposites] coexist, people are generally impure;
they are either seen through their past misdeeds or have associated with those of evil character.
The Caṇḍālas, executioners, and others should conduct their search within the villages,
while those who roam outside and wander at night should conduct it outside.
If stones cannot be obtained, the king should provide them from his own wealth;
for by neglecting this, he becomes a sinner and falls away from both merit and prosperity.

1516. Harshness of speech (*vāgdaṇḍapāruṣya*) consists of words that are contrary in meaning and joined with insults or slanders regarding one's country, caste, family, and so forth; this is called verbal harshness. // Nar_1516.1 //
Because it is harsh, abusive, and excessive, that [speech] is also recorded as being threefold;
and according to the sequence of their gravity, the punishment here is also progressively heavier.

The wise say that speech accompanied by reproach and harshness is "indecorous" (aślīla), while that joined with the mention of physical defects and severe censures leading to expulsion is called "fierce" (tīvra).
Assault with violence against the bodies of others by means of hands, feet, weapons, and so forth,
as well as injury caused by ashes and similar substances, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (physical violence).
His [the king's] vision was also seen to be of three kinds— mild, middling, and supreme— respectively,
as indicated by his threatening gestures, his falling away from attachment, and the appearance of wounds.
Because of the transgression involving inferior, middling, and superior objects,
they say there are exactly three types of fines for the removal of thorns (criminals) in that regard.
The procedure for both of these has been stated to be fivefold; therein, purification and the liability to punishment are applied according to the circumstances.
When harshness arises from agitation between two agitated parties,
he who forgives is considered the one who bears the burden, while he who transgresses is the one who suffers the penalty.
If no distinction were seen between two people who are simultaneously engaged in conduct veiled by the fault of harshness, then discipline would be the same for both.
He who first utters an accusation will certainly be the one to bear the fault;
he who does so later is also an offender, yet in the former case, the censure is more severe.
Furthermore, he who instigates two people who have already fallen out with each other incurs the same punishment as either of them—
the first one or the other.
[One should not have intercourse] with dog-cookers, eunuchs, Caṇḍālas, the deformed, those who live by killing,
elephant-drivers, the wives of Vratyas, nor with the wives of one's preceptor or teacher.
When there is a transgression of the established rule, immediate execution alone is the punishment;
and the wise say that there is no fault in such severity of punishment.

For if these [ministers] should transgress against a virtuous person among men, that person alone should administer discipline; the king does not share in the responsibility for that lack of discipline.
For these are indeed stains among men, and their wealth is of the nature of stain;
the king should have them executed, but he should not punish them with a fine of money.
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas];
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
A Brahmin shall be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.
For twice-born men of equal caste, the fine is twelve [paṇas] for an offense;
in cases where speech is not to be uttered, that same fine shall be doubled.
If one speaks even truthfully of another who is one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly afflicted, he shall be made to pay at least one *kārṣāpaṇa* by the king.
One should not, out of malice, defame one who has performed purification according to the scriptures;
nor should one defame one punished by the king, for the latter incurs the penalty for such transgression.
In this world, two are proclaimed to be beyond reproach and exempt from punishment:
the Brāhmaṇa and the king; for these two sustain this universe.
If one says "fallen" regarding a fallen person, or again "thief" regarding a thief, one incurs an equal fault by that statement; if it is false, one incurs double the fault.
For a Śūdra who maliciously utters the name or caste of these [twice-born],
an iron spike eighteen finger-breadths long shall be driven into his head.
If he should arrogantly provide instruction on the Dharma to the twice-born,
the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
Whatever limb of a Brahmin by which he might commit an offense against a person of lower caste, that very limb of his must be cut off; in this way, he shall attain purification.

One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of superior caste shall be branded on the hip with the mark of a dog's foot and banished; alternatively, the fleshy part of his buttocks shall be cut off.
If one spits out of arrogance, the king shall cause both his lips to be cut off;
if he urinates upon him, his penis; and if he passes wind against him, his anus.
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off both hands without hesitation;
likewise for seizing him by the feet, the nose, the neck, or the testicles.
But if one reviles a king who is established on his own path,
purification occurs either by cutting out the tongue or by the forfeiture of all one's property.
But that evil-minded person who would strike a king, even if the latter has committed an offense,
shall be cooked on a spit in fire for longer than the duration of a hundred killings of Brahmins.
A father does not incur punishment for the offense of his son, nor does a dog-owner for that of his dog,
nor does the owner of a monkey for that of his monkey— provided they were not dispatched by those very individuals themselves.
17. Gambling and betting:
playing for stakes with dice, fists, sticks, or small rods, conducted through deceitful means; and games involving animals as stakes—these constitute the category of gambling and betting. (Nar_17.1)
The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and pay what is owed for it;
his fee for conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of the hundred.
When the dice fall twice in favor of the side on which a gambler has placed his stake,
they say that victory belongs to the other player and that the gambler has met with defeat.
Gamblers should remain among gamblers regarding their disputes;
they alone shall be its observers, and they alone shall be the witnesses.
An impure gambler shall not resort to another gambling circle;
he shall not strike back at the master of the gaming house, nor shall he cause him to pay that stake as he pleases.
One should expel from the gambling hall those wicked men who play with fraudulent dice;
for it is ordained that their punishment consists of having a rosary of beads tied around their necks.
18. Miscellaneous Matters:
Furthermore, among miscellaneous matters, it should be known that legal disputes depend upon the king;
such as the obstruction of the king’s commands and likewise the performance of his duties. (Narada 18.1)
The burning of cities, the sowing of dissension among the subjects, as well as the subversion of the laws of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies; Nar_18.2 //
Disputes between father and son, the transgression of penances,
the failure to accept gifts, and even anger on the part of those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas).
The fault of the intermixture of castes, as well as the restriction of their respective duties,
and whatever was not seen among the previous [treatises]— all that shall be found in the Prakīrṇaka.
But the king, being attentive, should protect all the stages of life by means of the four expedients prescribed in the treatises as well as those inherent [to his office].
Whichever caste should decline, or whichever should attain excess—
seeing each of them fallen from their own path, one should establish them back upon that path.
And regarding other acts not prescribed by the scriptures that are joined with sin,
the king, having carefully considered his own capacity, should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
The king should not promote that which is contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti and detrimental to the people, nor should he allow it to continue once it has been set in motion.
Whatever has been done by another king that is devoid of justice, or whatever was done through ignorance— even that which was improperly ordained— he should restore to the path of justice.
That man who does not observe the laws set forth by the king is a sinner who should be punished; he who violates the royal decree deserves death. (Nar_18.10)
He gave weapons to those who live by arms, draft animals and the like to those who subsist on transport,
ornaments to courtesans, and musical instruments to those skilled in playing them.
Whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live their lives—
the king ought not to seize these even when all other property is being confiscated.
He is without beginning and without end, the lord of the earth among bipeds;
for if he had not strayed from the right path, he would have been radiant and pure.
If the king did not administer punishment to all the social classes who have strayed from the path, these subjects would perish.
A Brahmin may abandon his status as a Brahmin, and a Kshatriya may relinquish his Kshatriya duties;
a Vaishya may abandon his own specific work, but a Shudra should distinguish himself in all respects.
If there were no kings on earth to wield the rod of punishment,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
The constant favoring of the virtuous and likewise the restraint of the wicked—
this is remembered as the duty of kings, and their purpose is achieved by the oppression of enemies.
Just as fire, though constantly burning these creatures,
is not defiled, so too the king, while inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it, remains undefiled.
The authority of kings is their majesty, and that is established in their speech; whatever they may say, whether it be false or true, that is the law for those engaged in legal proceedings.
This one called a king moves upon the earth as the thousand-eyed Indra in person;
the subjects should never remain in a state that transgresses his command.
Because he holds the office of protection, because of his sovereignty, and because he is seen to favor living beings, whatever the king ordains is authoritative; such is the established rule.
Just as a husband is always worthy of honor by women even if he is devoid of virtues,
so too is a lord of men worthy of honor by his subjects even if he is lacking in merit.
The subjects were purchased by the king through his asceticism; therefore, the king is their master.
Consequently, one must abide by his word, and their livelihood is dependent upon him.
Kings of immeasurable power bear five forms:
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Dhanada.
When a king, driven by some cause or even without cause, falls under the sway of anger and consumes his subjects, he is then called "Fire."
When a king, desiring victory and with weapons raised, advances against his enemies by relying upon his fiery energy (tejas), he is then declared to be Indra.
When the king, free from the heat of anger and appearing joyful,
goes to visit his subjects, he is then called Soma.
When the illustrious king, seated upon the throne of justice,
wields the rod of punishment with equanimity toward all beings, he is then Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
But when the lord of the earth favors supplicants, teachers, the wise, servants, and others with gifts, then he is considered a giver of wealth (Dhanada).
Therefore, one should not despise him, nor revile him, nor treat him with contempt;
one should abide by his command, for death would result from its transgression.
His duty consists of protecting the subjects, serving the elderly and the wise, presiding over legal proceedings, and guarding himself.
A king, with a concentrated mind, should constantly attend upon the Brahmins;
for the Kshatriya power joined with the Brahmins is the root of the protection of the world.
A Brāhmaṇa is exempt from the obligation of yielding his seat to a Kṣatriya;
he is the first to be seen in the morning and is to be saluted by all. (Nar_18.33)
The first portion of the new grain belongs to them, as does the right-of-way for those traveling;
furthermore, entry into another's house for the purpose of begging alms is not forbidden to them.
One should practice non-stealing regarding the gathering of sacrificial fuel, flowers, and water because they belong to others;
one should not make demands upon others, nor should one converse with the wives of others.

On rivers, there shall be free passage for those who are unconscious, as well as for those crossing first; likewise, there shall be no payment of tolls on ferries, unless that person is engaged in trade.
A Brahmin who is traveling on the road, exhausted, and taking for himself two stalks of sugarcane and five radishes while staying nowhere else, does not commit an offense. (Nar_18.37)
Not from those who are accused, nor from outcasts, nor from enemies, nor from atheists; not from one who uses deception, nor without cause, nor by afflicting the donor.
Because of the great variety of objects and because they are given by high-souled beings,
accepting gifts from kings is superior [to receiving them] from others, with the exception of Brahmins.
Both the brahmin and the king are observers of firm vows;
there is no difference between them, for both are devoted to the protection of the subjects and the dharma.
They say that even for a sharp-witted king who knows the Dharma, who is grateful, and who rules by punishing the impure for the sake of protection, wealth is indeed pure.
Just as the confluence of pure and impure waters attains equality within the ocean, so too does the influx of wealth for a king.
Just as gold attains purity when placed in a blazing fire,
even so do all sacred scriptures attain their true purity through kings.
Whoever bestows his own property upon Brahmins, that should be permitted by the king as well; this is the eternal dharma.
That tribute, prescribed from other appropriate lands designated as one-sixth [of the produce],
is his wages for the protection of the subjects.
That which has been made over to one who is not a Brahmin can be taken back;
but that which has been given to a Brahmin cannot be seized again.
Giving, study, and sacrifice—these are his threefold duties;
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts are his means of livelihood, the third being the acceptance of gifts.
A twice-born man should remain steadfast in his own duty and subsist on a livelihood he has earned;
he should not accept gifts from the unworthy among the social classes when they lack self-restraint.
How is it that the king is not a deity—he by whose word an impure man becomes pure, and a pure man instantly becomes impure? (Nar_18.49)
O Vidura, those twice-born ones who accept the gifts of that king of immeasurable splendor, which are indeed of a divine nature, are not defiled.
In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brahmin, a cow, fire, gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise, a king as the eighth.
One should constantly behold these, pay homage to them, and worship them;
one should also circumambulate them, for in this way one's lifespan is not diminished. (Nar_18.52)
Appendix 19: Theft.
Thieves who seize the property of others are to be known as being of two kinds.
A self-possessed king should know them to be both manifest and unmanifest.
There were deceivers who relied on false measures and scales,
extortionists, violent men, gamblers, and courtesans.
Those who produce counterfeits and those whose livelihood consists of pointing out auspicious signs—
these and others like them should be known as deceivers of the light of the world.
They should be known as unmanifest, residing both outside and within;
they rob men by overpowering them while they are asleep or heedless.
Those who destroy districts, villages, and houses, those who waylay travelers, and pickpockets— these and others like them should be known as secret thieves.
Having learned of them, those men who are highly skilled at performing such tasks should follow and seize them by means of secret agents stationed there.
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, taverns, and shops selling meat; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and theaters.
Empty houses, forests, and shrines for deities—
these must be patrolled by those intent on capturing thieves.
In the same way, others who are appointed, trustworthy, and eloquent speakers—
spies indeed— should incite those thieves, just as former thieves would do.
They should bring about their meetings by means of providing food and drink, by attending social gatherings and festivals, and likewise under the pretext of theft.
Those who do not approach there, even though they have been sent and dispatched,
must be pursued and captured along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Whichever thieves he might capture there, having beaten and humiliated them,
and having proclaimed it everywhere, they were to be executed by various forms of capital punishment.

But thieves who do not admit their guilt and have no means of identification should be executed by the king; however, those caught in the act with the stolen goods and the tools of their crime, he should have the thieves punished immediately.
Those who would strike at their own country, as well as those who obstruct the highways— having confiscated all their property, one should further subject them to public censure.
One should interrogate those caught as thieves on suspicion by means of various terrifying ordeals; thus they will speak exactly as it was done.
Regarding the place, time, direction, caste, name, or residence,
as well as the purpose and the laborers involved, they should be questioned for the sake of a definitive determination.
Because of differences in complexion, voice, and appearance; because of reporting with uncertainty;
because of being seen at an improper place or time; and because even his clothing was not purified.

One should be apprehended even by slight signs— such as the expenditure of what is not one's own, prior acts of theft, or association with the wicked— and not solely by the possession of stolen goods.
If there should be suspicion against a man who follows the way of a bandit, or even against a thief,
and if he should be touched by even a slight [taint], then an ordeal must be administered.
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who give them fire and water, those who provide lodging, guides, and likewise those who provide provisions; // Nar_19.20 //
Those who purchase goods, those who receive them as gifts,
and those who conceal them— all these are declared by the law to be subject to equal punishment.
In the kingdoms, those appointed as provincial governors and the feudal lords who have been incited likewise remain indifferent during attacks; they are exactly like thieves.
If a person’s property is stolen within his own domain, he must diligently search for the thieves;
otherwise, he shall be made to pay the value of the theft, unless the tracks of the robbers have already departed.
When that footprint has vanished, been lost, or fallen elsewhere,
one should cause the neighboring kings, the guardians of the roads, and the guardians of the quarters to pay restitution.
If a house has indeed been plundered, the king shall cause the thieves to be apprehended from the guards and the provincial officials, provided that the thief cannot be found.
Or, if there is doubt regarding those being compelled to pay in that theft,
the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to swear an oath for the sake of clearing himself of the charge of theft.
If a non-thief is made to pay for theft on account of a judicial purification of the charge of thievery,
they shall receive double that amount once the actual thief is apprehended.

One should diligently restore to its owner property stolen by thieves, returning it in its original form; in the absence of the object itself, its value shall be paid, and a fine equal to that amount shall be imposed.
Of pieces of wood, stalks, grass, and the like, as well as those made of clay;
of bamboo and vessels made of bamboo, and of cane, sinew, bone, and leather.
In the case of stealing vegetables, greens, and roots, as well as fruits and flowers, products of cow's milk, sugarcane derivatives, and likewise salt and oil; ||| Nar_19.30 |||
For cooked foods, prepared foods, intoxicants, and meat—
indeed for all items of low value— the fine shall be five times their price.
For all goods measured by weight, by measure, or by number, the fine shall be ten times their value if they are of superior quality. // Nar_19.32 //
Manu declared that for one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death; however, for stealing less than that, he should be made to pay a fine eleven times the value.
For stealing gold, silver, and the like, as well as excellent garments and the finest jewels, the punishment is death for more than one hundred [such items].
For one who abducts a man, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for one who abducts a woman, the forfeiture of all property; but for one who abducts a maiden, the penalty is death.
For one who steals large cattle, the punishment is the highest fine;
for stealing a medium-sized animal, the middle fine; and for seizing a small animal, the first fine.
The former [minimum] is twenty-four, while the latter [maximum] would be ninety-six;
the middle [maximum] is five hundred, while its minimum is two hundred.
A thousand is to be known as the highest, while five hundred is the lowest;
thus has the threefold punishment for violent crimes been proclaimed by the Self-Existent One.
In the first case of breaking a knot, there shall be the cutting off of the fingers and the thumb;
in the second case, the remaining part of that [limb] shall be cut off, and the first amercement shall be the fine.
For cutting the udder of cows belonging to Brahmins, there shall be the amputation of a large portion;
for one who abducts a female slave, however, there shall always be the amputation of half a foot.
"By whatever specific limb a thief acts out his offense, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu. (Nar_19.41)
Whether the offense is more serious or not more serious,
one should inflict a heavier punishment upon a thief than that prescribed for the first offender.
The self-existent Manu has declared ten grounds for punishment which apply to the three [lower] castes; the Brāhmaṇa, however, is always to be protected.
The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Having fully understood the offense and the true nature of the place and time, and having considered the strength of the crime and its consequences, he should prescribe these punishments.
A king must not release a perpetrator of violence for the sake of a friend or because of the acquisition of vast wealth;
such a person has abandoned his own life, as Manu declared.

As much demerit accrues to a king from the execution of one who should not be killed, so much does he incur from releasing one who deserves death; yet, for him who restrains the wicked, there is merit.
One must never kill a brahmin, even if he is established in every kind of sin;
one may, at will, banish him—thus the dharma is settled.
The king may take away all his property, or he may leave a fourth part remaining;
remembering the duty toward his dependents, he should follow the established rule of the Prājāpatya.
But for the offense of a Brahmin, four marks are prescribed:
[the branding] for violating the Guru's bed, for drinking liquor, for theft, and for the injury of a Brahmin. (Nar_19.50)
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ should be made; for drinking liquor, a flag is prescribed;
but for theft, having fashioned the footprint of a dog, one should brand it with the bile of a peacock.
A man who has killed an embryo must be branded on the forehead with the mark of a headless corpse;
furthermore, he must be rendered unfit for social intercourse—such is the ordinance of Manu.
The thief must go before the king with disheveled hair, running and confessing that theft, saying: "I have done this; punish me. (Nar_19.53)
By this act, one becomes a thief through the execution of his own deed;
that sin touches the king who releases him while he is still guilty.
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
Whether through punishment or through release, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
but for those whose sins are concealed, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra is eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is twice eightfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
"Sixty-four [years] for a Brāhmaṇa"—thus Svāyambhuva has declared;
and even therein, it should be especially greater among the learned.
Punishment is traditionally held to be of two kinds: corporal and monetary;
corporal punishments are said to be tenfold, while monetary punishments are manifold.
The monetary fine begins with a *kākaṇī* and likewise ends with the confiscation of all one's property;
the corporal punishment begins with confinement and likewise ends with the loss of life.
The punishment beginning with a *kākaṇī* is traditionally held to culminate in a *māṣa*;
that which is declared to begin with a *māṣa* culminates in a *kārṣāpaṇa*.
But for offenses beginning with a *kārṣāpaṇa* and ending with four *kārṣāpaṇas*, another [fine] begins with two and ends with eight; and another begins with three and ends with twelve.
All those [fines] mentioned, beginning with the kārṣāpaṇa, shall each be quadrupled; others, however, should be understood in the same way, provided they are below the first amercement (pūrvasāhasa).
In the southern direction, the silver kārṣāpaṇa circulates;
in the eastern direction, it is fixed at sixteen paṇas.
A *māṣa* should be known as one-twentieth of a *kārṣāpaṇa*;
a *kākaṇī*, however, is one-fourth of both a *māṣa* and a *paṇa*.
In the region of the Five Rivers, however, there is a conventional designation;
by that [designation], the measure of a *kārṣāpaṇa* has indeed been fixed here.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* is to be known as equal to four *aṇḍikās*, and four of those make one *dhānaka*. Twelve of those [make] a *suvarṇa*; a *dīnāra* is recorded as being equal to a *citraka*.
The king should constantly follow the threefold Vārttā, the Trayī, and the science of government (Daṇḍanīti) with unflagging vigilance;
he should strike down those caught in his city and kingdom by skillful means, and restrain the wicked.
When no human witness is available in a dispute between litigants,
then one should examine the case by means of ordeals and various kinds of oaths.
Truth, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, and silver;
the ancestors and the gods, as well as the meritorious deeds performed—these have been bestowed.
In cases of great offense, the lord of the earth should cause divine ordeals to be administered;
but for minor matters, O best of men, he should cause the man to swear by oaths.
For these oaths have been declared as easy to perform when the doubt is slight;
however, in cases of violent crimes and formal accusations, the divine ordeal is proclaimed as the rule.
"In matters that are doubtful, and especially in those that are concealed, the fivefold ordeal is to be known as the means of proof; so said the Blessed Manu. (Narada Smṛti 20.5)
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation—
these are declared to be the ordeals for the purification of those who are accused.
For the sake of purifying those who are accused in doubtful cases, the high-souled Nārada further proclaimed these means of discerning truth from falsehood;
a wise man should cause this to be performed with the consent of the litigant, and not otherwise.
The two pillars of the balance are proclaimed to be four cubits in height;
their measurement in width is seen to be six cubits.
The distance between the two feet should be one cubit and a half;
having suspended two balance-beams upon the sturdy joints of the scale-beam.
Having first weighed the man, one should mark the balance;
then, having lowered him from the balance so that he is equalized with the empty space [of the scale], [one should proceed].
Having secured him with these pledges, the man should mount him once again;
when this has been done, if she remains perfectly still while being placed upon his side, [he should know her to be faithful].
If, when weighed, he increases [in weight], he is pure; of this there is no doubt.
If he remains equal or decreases, the man would not be pure.
By the words of this legal discourse, you are called the "Balance" (dhaṭa).
You know the sins and the good deeds of all living beings;
you alone, O Balance, know those things which human beings do not perceive.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed in that same manner;
you ought to save him from this state of uncertainty in accordance with dharma.
Henceforth, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the metal ordeal:
the circles shall measure thirty-two finger-breadths, with an equal interval between each circle.
Thus, by means of eight circles, two hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths have been declared by those who perceive the true meaning of the principles of enumeration.
Having thus dwelt within the imagined mandalas, even though he was pure,
he wrapped seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree with thread around his two hands.
One should take a ball of heated iron weighing fifty palas with both hands and walk slowly for seven steps.
