He should not step beyond the mandala, nor should he set foot within it;
and he should not let his foot fall before reaching the ground that has been prepared.
Having crossed over by means of this procedure with a concentrated mind, that man who remains unburned on all sides shall become purified.

If one who has not been burnt casts down [the metal] out of fear, or if he is found to be trembling, he shall have to carry that iron again; this is the ancient rule. By this procedure, the ordeal by fire is ordained.
O Agni, you move within all living beings like a witness;
there is no good deed or evil deed in the world that remains unknown to you.
You know exactly as they are the hidden sins and good deeds of men— those which human beings themselves do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from his state of uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Henceforth I shall proclaim the supreme ritual for water:
one should discharge three arrows with a bow that is not excessively harsh.
But a man of lesser age should accept the middle arrow;
then, once it has been brought back, that man shall be purified.
Otherwise, he would not be pure; he might reveal even a single sign, or depart from his place to another location where he had previously been stationed. (Nar_20.27)

Women should not be made to act by force, nor should a weak man; because of their timidity, death may come to a woman, and force might cause even a frail man to commit all [these sins]. Therefore, one should not cause them to sink into such acts suddenly.
In the midst of the water, he firmly grasped the man's thighs with great restraint.
Water and fire are the most effective means for distinguishing between truth and falsehood;
and since fire originated from this [water], water is therefore superior.
The purification of those who have been defiled is performed by those who know the true nature of reality;
therefore, O Blessed One, Lord of Waters, you ought to save me through the power of truth.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for poison:
having first weighed the poison, this should be administered at the onset of winter.
One who knows the Dharma should not cause [the gift] to be given in the forenoon, nor at midday, nor at twilight;
nor during the autumn, summer, spring, or the rainy season.
One should carefully avoid *kālakūṭa* and *alaṃbu* poisons, as well as those that are broken, split, fumigated, or mixed. (Nar_20.34)
The Śārṅga and Haimavata types are praised as being endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste;
they should be given by the king to one afflicted by great defects, out of a desire to know the truth.

One should not administer seven barley-grains soaked in ghee as poison to children, the sick, or the elderly, nor to those who have committed only minor offenses; however, it may be given to one who is to be interrogated.
From six palas of poison, one should take that portion which is the twentieth part;
having reduced that by one-eighth, one should administer it soaked in clarified butter to the person to be cleared of suspicion.
Having touched the Brahmins according to the prescribed rite and having received their approval,
he, while fasting, should eat in the presence of the gods and the Brahmins.
If the poison is digested easily, free from its violent onset and exhaustion,
the king, knowing it to be pure, should honor him and release him.
O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in devotion to truth and righteousness;
purify this man from sin, and by means of his truth, become nectar for him.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme method for the treasury.
In the forenoon, for one who has fasted, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes,
who possesses a beard and is free from vices, the drinking of the ordeal liquid (kośapāna) is prescribed.
One should cause the accused to drink that which belongs to the deity to whom he is devoted;
whatever personal [symptom] is observed within seven days or again within fourteen days, that indeed is the manifestation of his guilt.
If, after two weeks have passed, a person suffers a major transformation of the humors,
he should not be prosecuted by the wise, because the prescribed time limit has expired.

One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the sacred vessel (kośapāna) in the case of those who have committed a great offense, those devoid of dharma, the ungrateful, the impotent, the contemptible, atheists, those who have not undergone the initiatory rites (vrātya), and slaves.
In the manner described, the king who knows the Dharma should administer the five ordeals to those accused; thus he rejoices both in this world and after death.
One should not give poison to a Brāhmaṇa; a Kṣatriya should not take away gold;
a Vaiśya should not immerse himself in water; and one should not make a Śūdra drink from the royal treasury-vessel.
One should not administer poison during the rainy season; one should not cause [the enemy] to drown in water during the winter;
one should not extract iron [as tribute] in the summer; and one should not make [the enemy] drink from the treasury at night.
The Nāradīya Dharmaśāstra is completed.
End of the Parāśara-smṛti.

Then, therefore, on the peak of the Snowy Mountain, in the abode of the Devadāru forest,
the sages of old questioned Vyāsa as he sat with one-pointed concentration.
"O son of Satyavatī, please describe correctly the dharma beneficial for human beings, as well as the rules of purification and conduct, during the present Kali age."
Having heard those words of the sage, the king, who resembled the sun and possessed great splendor, being well-versed in the Śruti and Smṛti, replied together with his disciples.
"I am not an omniscient knower of all truths; how then could I speak on Dharma? My father alone should be questioned," so Vyāsa, the son, replied.
Then all those sages, desiring to know the true meaning of the principles of Dharma,
placed the sage Vyāsa at their head and went to the hermitage of Badarikā.
It was strewn with various flowers, adorned with fruit-bearing trees,
endowed with rivers and springs, and graced by sacred bathing places.
Abounding with the cries of deer and birds, it was filled with shrines of the deities,
and adorned with the dances and songs of yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
In that assembly of sages, the one of great splendor beheld Parāśara, the son of Śakti, seated at ease and surrounded by a multitude of preeminent munis.
Having joined his palms in reverence, Vyāsa, together with the ṛṣis,
honored him with circumambulations, salutations, and hymns of praise.
Then, with a heart full of contentment, the great sage Parāśara, that bull among munis, sat down and said: "Welcome; speak."
Having said, "It is well, it is right," Vyāsa immediately asked:
"O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, if you know [the answer], out of affection for me or because of my devotion..."
"O father, please discourse on the Dharma for me, for I am worthy of your favor.
I have already heard the laws of Manu, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa."
The Gārgeyas and the Gautamīyas, as well as those recorded by Uśanas; likewise those of Atri, Viṣṇu, Saṃvarta, Dakṣa, and Aṅgiras.
From Śātātapa and Hārīta, as well as from Yājñavalkya; likewise, the laws composed by Āpastamba, Śaṅkha, and Likhita.
I have indeed heard these works composed by Kātyāyana as well as those of the sage Prācetasa; having been spoken by you, their meaning has not been forgotten by me.
In this Manvantara, throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā,
all dharmas are born in the Kṛta age and all are lost in the Kali age.
Tell me something regarding the common conduct of the four castes— that which is shared by all four castes and must be performed by those learned in dharma.
"Speak in detail, O knower of the true nature of Dharma, concerning its subtle and gross aspects.
At the conclusion of Vyāsa's speech, Parāśara, the foremost of sages, [replied].
He has declared the determination of Dharma, both subtle and gross, in detail.
Listen, my son, I shall speak; let the sages likewise listen.
In every kalpa, through their destruction and manifestation, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśvara are always the determiners of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.
No one is the author of the Veda; rather, the four-faced Brahmā remembers the Veda.
In the same way, Manu remembers the dharmas at the beginning of each successive kalpa.
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind; in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages they are different;
and in the Kali age they are yet another, according to the nature of each respective age.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so.
In the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; in the Kali age, charity alone.
In the Kṛta age, however, the laws of Manu are prescribed; in the Tretā, those of Gautama;
in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, those of Parāśara are recorded.
In the Kṛta age one should abandon the country; in the Tretā age, one should leave the village;
in the Dvāpara age, the single family; but in the Kali age, only the perpetrator.
In the Kṛta age, one falls by mere conversation; in the Tretā, by touch;
in the Dvāpara, by taking food; but in the Kali age, one falls through action alone.
In the Kṛta age, a curse takes effect immediately; in the Tretā, after ten days;
in the Dvāpara, after one month; but in the Kali age, after a year.
In the Kṛta age, a gift is given after approaching [the recipient]; in the Tretā, it is given after being invited;
in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali age, it is given through service.
The highest gift is that given after approaching [the recipient]; the middling is that given by summoning [them];
the lowest is that given to one who begs; but a gift given through servitude is fruitless.
In the Kali age, dharma is indeed conquered by adharma, and truth by falsehood;
kings are defeated by thieves, and men by women.
In this Kali Yuga, the Agnihotra sacrifices fall into ruin, reverence for teachers perishes, and maidens constantly give birth [to children].

In the Kṛta age, however, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā, they are dependent on the flesh; in the Dvāpara, they are in the blood; but in the Kali age, they are situated in food and other such things.

One must not engage in censure of the dharmas that exist in each respective age, nor of the twice-born who exist in those various times; for those twice-born ones are indeed the very forms of the ages themselves.
In every age, however, the remaining capacity [for penance] has been explained by the Sage;
furthermore, the expiation prescribed by Parāśara is also ordained.
"Having recollected all of that this very day, I speak it to you;
O bulls among sages, listen to the conduct of the four castes."
The meritorious thought of Parāśara, which is purifying and destructive of sin,
was conceived for the sake of the Brahmins and for the establishment of Dharma.
The conduct of all four castes is the protector of Dharma;
for those whose bodies have fallen away from conduct, Dharma becomes turned away.
A Brahmin who constantly delights in the six duties, honors the deities and guests, and eats only the remnants of the oblation, does not come to ruin.
Bathing at the twilights, silent recitation, burnt offerings, worship of the deities and guests,
hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice— these are the six duties to be performed day after day.
Whether he be beloved or hateful, a fool or even a scholar,
whoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is a guest who brings about the attainment of heaven.

One should recognize as a guest (atithi) one who has arrived from a long journey, who is weary, and who arrives at the time of the Vaiśvadeva offering; one who arrives before that time is not a guest.
One should never accept as a guest someone who belongs to the same village;
since he has arrived without fixed regularity, he is therefore called an *atithi* (guest).
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other such courtesies,
by offering water for the hands (*arghya*), a seat, and by washing his feet.
With faith, by the gift of food, by pleasant inquiries and replies,
and by following one who is departing, the householder should generate affection.
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
the ancestors of that person do not eat for fifteen years.
For one whose guest departs with frustrated hopes, the burnt offering is as useless as a thousand loads of wood and a hundred jars of clarified butter.
One should sow seed in a good field and bestow wealth upon a worthy recipient;
for what is sown or given in a good field and to a worthy recipient does not perish.
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, school, Vedic recitation, or learning;
for he is composed of all the gods, one should conceive of him as a god within one's own heart.
Just as a Brahmin who observes excellent vows is unprecedented, and likewise a guest who arrives unexpectedly,
so too those two who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas become unprecedented [in their merit] day by day.
When the Vaiśvadeva rite has begun and a mendicant arrives at the house,
one should set aside food for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva and then dismiss the mendicant.
Both the ascetic and the student are the rightful owners of cooked food.
Having eaten without first giving food to these two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A wandering mendicant should give three portions of alms to other mendicants and to celibate students;
thereafter, if he has the means, he may give as much as desired, provided it is not forbidden.
One should give water in the hand of the ascetic, and then give alms-food, and again give water;
that alms-food is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is comparable to the ocean.
He whose parasol, horse, and elephant are indeed possessed of supernatural power (ṛddhi) may occupy the station of Indra; therefore, one should not challenge him.
A monk is capable of removing the evil committed during the *vaiśvadeva* offering;
however, the *vaiśvadeva* offering does not remove the faults committed by the monk.
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva offering are all to be known as fruitless; they fall into an impure hell.
Those who are deprived of the Vaiśvadeva offering and excluded from hospitality all go to hell and enter the womb of a crow.
Whether he be a sinner, a Caṇḍāla, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a killer of his father— if such a person arrives when the Vaiśvadeva ceremony has begun, he is a guest who leads one to heaven.
He who eats with his head wrapped, he who eats facing south,
or he who places his hand on his left foot— verily, the Rākṣasas consume that food.
But that village where twice-born men wander for alms while remaining without vows and unlearned in the Vedas—
the king should punish that village, for it provides sustenance to thieves.
For a Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and wielding the rod of punishment,
should conquer the enemy armies and protect the earth according to Dharma.
One should pluck flower after flower, but should not cause the destruction of the roots; like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-maker.
Acquiring wealth, trade, gems, and the protection of cattle,
as well as agriculture and commerce, are declared to be the occupations of the Vaiśya. For the Śūdra, service to the twice-born is said to be the highest duty.
If one performs anything otherwise than this, that shall be fruitless for him.
Salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—these do not cause defilement for those of the Śūdra caste; one may sell them among all [classes].
By selling the meat of carnivorous animals, by eating that which is forbidden to eat,
and by having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his caste at that very moment.
By drinking the milk of a tawny cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Veda, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla. Hereafter [is described] the conduct and duties of the householder in the Kali age.
One should, according to one's ability, promote the common dharma that pertains to the four castes and the stages of life.
I shall first proclaim that according to the words of Parāśara:
a Brahmin engaged in the six duties may also perform the work of agriculture.
One should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted.
A Brahmin should not drive an ox that is deficient in limb, diseased, or impotent.
One should cause a bull that has firm limbs, is well-fed, pleasant-voiced, and free from castration to pull [the cart] for half the day; thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath.
One should practice the recitation of mantras (*japa*), the worship of the deity, the fire sacrifice (*homa*), and the private study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*).
A twice-born man should feed one, two, three, or four *snātaka* Brahmins.
Likewise, he should do so with grains produced by his own plowing and earned by his own efforts.
He should perform the five sacrifices and cause the initiation for a sacrificial rite to be carried out.
One who sells sesame seeds or liquids is equal to one who sells grain;
such is the livelihood for a Brahmin, as is the selling of grass, wood, and the like.
If a Brahmin should practice agriculture, he incurs a great fault;
the sin that a fisherman incurs in a single year, he incurs by that [act].
With an iron-tipped wooden stick, Lāṅgalin [kills] in a single day;
so too does the snarer, the fisherman, the hunter, and the fowler.
The one who does not give and the cultivator—both of these share equally [in the merit].
Having cut down trees, having broken the earth, and having killed insects and worms.
A farmer is liberated from all sins by means of the threshing-floor sacrifice (khala-yajña),
provided that he does not fail to give to the twice-born when he has arrived at the root of his harvest heap.
He is a thief, he is most wicked; one should designate him as a slayer of a Brahmin.
Having given a sixth part to the king and a twenty-first part to the gods, [he may be purified].
By giving a thirtieth part of his wealth to Brahmins, he is liberated from all sins.
A Kṣatriya, too, having engaged in agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins.
A Vaiśya and likewise a Śūdra should practice agriculture, trade, and the arts.
Śūdras who abandon service to the twice-born perform improper actions.
They indeed become short-lived and go to hell without a doubt.
This is the eternal law for all four castes as well.
Therefore, I shall now declare the purification regarding birth and likewise death:
Brahmins become pure after three days in the case of a death or a birth.
A Kṣatriya is purified in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days,
and a Śūdra becomes pure in a month, according to the word of Parāśara.
In the case of attending upon Brahmins, O dear one, purification of the limbs occurs;
however, in the case of the birth of Brahmins or contact with a deity, it is ordained [that the entire body be purified].
In the case of birth, a Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days,
a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in one month.
A Brahmin who is endowed with both the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day; one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days, while one devoid of both is purified in ten days.

One who has fallen away from [proper] birth and conduct, and who is devoid of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*), is merely a Brahmin in name; he shall remain in a state of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days.
Those who share a single funeral cake (inheritance) but have separate wives and dwellings,
for them there shall be the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) upon a birth and likewise upon a death.
That birth-impurity (sūtaka) remains within the lineage until the fourth generation;
however, at the fourth or the fifth person born of one's own family, the right to inheritance (dāya) comes to an end.
In the fourth [case], there shall be ten nights; in the fifth, for a male, six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days.
In the case of death by leaping from a cliff or by fire, as well as death in a foreign land,
and when a child dies or one who has renounced the world (saṃnyasta) dies, immediate purification is prescribed.

If it is heard that someone belonging to one's own lineage has died in another country, one becomes pure by bathing immediately; there is no need for three nights or a single day and night of impurity.
If a Brahmin who has gone to another country meets his death due to exhaustion or the passage of time, and the lunar day [of his passing] is not known;
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
one should perform the offering of water, the offering of funeral cakes, and the śrāddha ceremony.
For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb,
there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water libations.
Par3.15ab: If the fetus of a woman should perish or be miscarried;
Par3.15cd: for as many months as the fetus had remained, for that many days there is *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth).
Up to the fourth month, there shall be a miscarriage; in the fifth and sixth months, it is a birth. Beyond that, it is a delivery, and for ten days there shall be *sūtaka* (birth-impurity).
When one who has teethed, one who has been born after [the first child], or one for whom the tonsure ceremony has been performed dies,
they shall remain impure for three nights during the cremation with fire.

Until the eruption of teeth, impurity is said to be immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is one night; until the instruction for the vows (vratādeśa), it is three nights; and beyond that, it is ten nights.
For those in whose house a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) resides, and in which the consumer of oblations (the sacrificial fire) is offered,
there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka), provided they do not engage in social contact [with outsiders].
A Brahmin becomes defiled by contact [with impure persons] at birth as well as at death;
however, for one who has withdrawn from such contact, there is neither impurity due to a death nor impurity due to a birth.
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female and male slaves,
barbers, kings, and those well-versed in the Vedas are proclaimed to be immediately pure.

A twice-born man who is observant of his vows, purified by a sacrificial session (*satra*), and one who has maintained the sacred fires— there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) for these, nor for a king, or for one whom the monarch desires [to be pure].
When a Brahmin who has been invited for a funeral rite or a gift is in distress and is ready to depart,
the sages have observed that he becomes pure according to the time [of his departure].
If a householder does not cause a mixture of impurities during childbirth,
the mother is purified after ten days, provided she has immersed herself in water, while the father is pure immediately.
Par3.24ab: For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca); however, for the mother and father, there is birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Par3.24cd: Birth-impurity shall belong to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual sipping (upaspṛśya).
If a twice-born man has sexual intercourse with a wife who has recently given birth,
he incurs the impurity of *sūtaka*, even if that Brahmin is learned in the six Vedāṅgas.
"From association arises fault; indeed, there is no other fault for a twice-born man.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid association with every effort."
But during marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if a death or birth impurity occurs in the interval,
there is no fault in giving away wealth that was previously intended for the purpose.
If death or birth occurs again within ten days,
the Brāhmaṇa shall remain impure for as long as that [second period] remains within its own ten-day term.
For those who perish for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, as well as for those killed while rescuing a captive or cattle,
and for those who perish in battles, the period of impurity lasts for one night.
"O Sūrya, these two persons in the world pierce the solar orb: the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and the warrior slain while facing the enemy in battle."
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not utter words of cowardice.
Upon seeing a Brahmin who has renounced the world (saṃnyasta), the sun moves from its place [to honor him], thinking:
"Having pierced through my orb, he shall proceed to the supreme abode."
But he who, when the armies are broken and fleeing in every direction,
goes forth as their protector, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
Whose body has been mangled by arrows, mallets,
and clubs, even the daughters of the gods carry off that hero and take delight with him.
Thousands of celestial maidens run in haste toward the hero slain in battle, crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine!"
Par3.36ab: Just as the Brahmins, seeking heaven, go there by means of multitudes of sacrifices and through austerity;
Par3.36cd: even so do heroes go there in an instant, relinquishing their lives in a noble battle.
By victory, one gains fortune; even by death, one obtains celestial nymphs.
Since this body perishes in an instant, what anxiety can there be regarding death in battle?

When blood flowing from the region of the forehead enters the mouth during battle, that is indeed equal to the drinking of soma; it is seen by tradition as being performed according to rule in the sacrifice of war.
Those twice-born who carry the corpse of a deceased Brāhmaṇa who has no protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due succession.
For those who perform auspicious deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, purification is ordained immediately upon immersion in water.
Having carried and cremated a deceased person who was neither a relative nor a kinsman, even if that person were the best of the twice-born, one becomes pure by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having followed a deceased person— whether a kinsman or even a non-kinsman— at his own request,
one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a deceased Kṣatriya out of ignorance,
he becomes impure for one day and is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a Vaiśya follows a corpse out of ignorance while a Brāhmaṇa is present,
he shall observe impurity for two nights and perform six breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse while being carried away,
he shall remain impure for three nights.
When three nights have thus passed, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he becomes purified by consuming clarified butter.
When a Śūdra has been cremated and has reached the edge of the water,
the twice-born must then follow him; this is the eternal law.
Whether out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or even fear,
if a woman or a man should commit suicide, this [following] course of action is prescribed.
Filled with pus and blood, he sinks into blinding darkness;
for sixty thousand years, he enters hell.
One should not cause impurity, nor the offering of water, nor the fire, nor the shedding of tears;
likewise, this applies to those who carry the corpse, those who provide the fire, and those who cut the bonds.
"Purification is attained through the *taptakṛcchra* penance"— thus spoke Prajāpati—
regarding that which was killed by cows, as well as that which was hanged or slain by a Brāhmaṇa.
Those brahmins who touch [the corpse], those who carry it, those who provide the fire, others who follow behind, and those who cut the bonds; Par4.5cd. // 4.5 //
Having been purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance, they should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee to a learned Brāhmaṇa.
For three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot milk;
for three days one should drink hot clarified butter; and for three days one should subsist on air alone.
One should drink six palas of water, three palas of milk, and one pala of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
If a Brahmin should unintentionally associate with those who have fallen [from their caste] and so forth,
he shall observe this for five days, or ten days, or even twelve days.
For half a month, a full month, or even two months; for half a year, a year, or even one year; or beyond that—[if he studies] for the same duration, he becomes equal to him.
In the first fortnight, one should observe a three-night fast; in the second, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance;
and in the third fortnight, one should perform a *sāṃtapana kṛcchra*.
In the fourth [case], there shall be a ten-night penance; in the fifth, a parāka is prescribed.
In the sixth, one should perform a cāndrāyaṇa; but in the seventh, two aindavas.

For the sake of purification, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six months during the eighth period; the number of suvarṇas to be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is determined by the number of fortnights.
But that woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband,
goes to hell when she dies, and becomes a widow again and again.
He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of foeticide; there is no doubt in this matter.
She who treats her husband with contempt— whether he be poor, diseased, or foolish—
is born as a female dog after death, and again and again as a sow.
If a woman, while her husband is still living, observes a fast or undertakes a vow, she takes away the lifespan of her husband; that woman shall go to hell.
If a woman performs a vow without having first asked her husband's permission, all of that goes to the Rākṣasas; thus Manu has declared.
But she who behaves wickedly toward her kinsmen or those of her own caste,
or she who causes an abortion— one should never speak with her.
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin, that same sin is doubled in the destruction of an embryo. There can be no expiation for such an act; rather, her abandonment is ordained.
Neither by his house nor again by the Agnihotra sacrifice does he become [pure];
he becomes a Cāṇḍāla in action who is averse to Dharma.
If seed carried by a flood or the wind sprouts in someone's field, that owner of the field receives the crop;
the owner of the seed does not deserve a share.
In the same way, two types of sons born of another's wife are recorded in tradition as the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka:
the Kuṇḍa is he whose father is still living, and the Golaka is he whose husband has died.
The legitimate son (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the adopted son (datta), and the made son (kṛtrima)— if the mother or the father gives him away, he becomes an adopted son (dattaka).
The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, the younger brother who so marries,
the woman with whom he marries, as well as the giver and the officiating priest— these five all go to hell.
For the elder brother who marries before his younger brother, two *kṛcchra* penances; for the maiden, a single *kṛcchra*;
for the giver, a *kṛcchra* and an *atikṛcchra*; and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
There is no fault in marrying a girl from among those who are humpbacked, dwarfish, eunuchs, stammerers, or mentally dull,
nor from those who are blind from birth, deaf, or mute.
The son of a paternal uncle, the son of a co-wife, and likewise the son of another's wife—
there is no fault in superseding these in the matter of marriage or the establishment of the sacred fires.
When an elder brother is present, one should not perform the *ādheya* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires).
However, with his permission, one may do so; such is the word of Śaṅkha.
When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has become an outcast—
under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women.
When her husband has died, the woman who remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy attains heaven upon her death, just like those lifelong students of the Veda.
As many hairs as there are on a human being— three and a half crores—
for that long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
so too does a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoice together with him.
But that best of the twice-born who has been bitten by wolves, dogs, jackals, or the like—
Having bathed, he should mutter the Gāyatrī, the purifier, the mother of the Vedas.
Bathing with water from a cow's horn at the confluence of great rivers,
or even by beholding the ocean, one bitten by a dog shall become pure.
If a twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies, sciences, and vows is bitten by a dog,
he becomes pure by bathing with water containing gold and consuming clarified butter.
But one who has been bitten by a dog while observing a vow should fast for three nights;
having drunk ghee mixed with water infused with *kuśa* grass, he should complete the remainder of his vow.
Whether he be without vows or even with vows, a twice-born man who has been bitten by a dog becomes purified by prostrating himself and being gazed upon by Brahmins with their eyes.
For food that has been smelled by a dog, licked, or scratched with its claws,
it is prescribed that one should wash it with water and heat it over fire.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf,
she becomes pure immediately upon seeing a planet or a lunar mansion that has risen.
When the moon is never visible during the dark fortnight,
one should look toward whichever direction the moon happens to have moved.
If the best of the twice-born is bitten by a dog in a village where no Brāhmaṇas reside,
he becomes pure immediately after circumambulating a bull and bathing.
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is struck by a Caṇḍāla, a dog-cooker, cattle, or other Brahmins; or if he dies from poison or commits suicide; [he shall not go to heaven].
A Brahmin shall burn that Brahmin in the world-fire (lokāgni) without the recitation of mantras;
and having touched him, carried him, or burned him, one is likewise affected in every way among the sapinda relatives.
Afterwards, at the instruction of the Brahmins, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having collected the burnt bones once more, the twice-born man should wash them with milk.
One who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) may, when departing on a journey impelled by time, cremate [the body] again with his own fire independently, each separately.
When his body has met its destruction, the sacred fire remains in his house;
O best of sages, hear now the ritual for the consecration of the deceased’s *agnihotra* fire.
Having spread out a black antelope skin and fashioned a human figure with *kuśa* grass,
one should [place] six hundred and one stalks of *palāśa* wood.
One should place forty [beads] on the head, one hundred on the neck;
one should place one hundred on the two arms, and exactly ten on the fingers.
One should apply one hundred [strokes] on the buttocks, and likewise two hundred on the abdomen;
one should apply eight on the testicles and place five on the penis.
One should assign twenty-one [parts] to the two thighs, two hundred to the knees and shanks, and six to the toes of the feet; thereafter, one should place the sacrificial vessel.
Having placed the *śamyā* on the penis and the two *araṇīs* on the testicles,
he should place the *juhū* in his right hand and the *upabhṛt* in his left.
One should place a mortar on the ear and set a pestle upon the back;
having placed a grinding stone on the chest, one should put rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds in the mouth.
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* water on the ears and the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthalī*) on the two eyes;
one should then place pieces of gold in the ears, the eyes, the mouth, and the nose.
He should deposit all the implements for the *agnihotra* sacrifice there without exception, offering a single oblation once with the words: "This [is] for the heavenly world, svāhā! (Par5.22).
The son, or a brother, or even another kinsman, should perform the cremation rite; it should be carried out by the wise in the same manner as the funeral ceremony.
One should perform such a rite as this; it is traditionally taught that [the deceased] attains the world of Brahmā.
Those twice-born who cremate him, however, go to the supreme goal.
Driven by their own deluded intellects, they perform actions in a contrary manner;
indeed, they become short-lived and fall into an impure hell.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the atonement for the killing of living beings.
It was previously spoken by Parāśara and also expanded upon in the work of Manu.
By eating the krauñca, sārasa, haṃsa, cakravāka, kukkuṭa, jālapāda,
and śarabha birds, one is purified in one day and night.
The crane, the lapwing, the parrot, and the dove,
as well as the snake and the crocodile-eater, are purified by eating only at night.
One who kills wolves, crows, pigeons, śāris,
or partridges is purified by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) both at the morning and evening twilights while remaining within the water.
One who kills vultures, hawks, rabbits, dogs, or owls,
and eats uncooked food, shall remain standing for a day, subsisting on air during the three periods of the day.
The *valgūṇī*, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the cuckoo, the *khañjarīṭaka*,
the *lāvika*, and those with red wings are purified by eating only at night.
Having killed a kāraṇḍava, a cakora, a piṅgalā, a kurara,
or one beginning with the bhāradvāja crane, one becomes purified by worshipping Śiva.
Upon hearing the cries of the bheruṇḍa, the blue jay, the hawk, the pigeon, and the kapiñjala,
as well as from all other birds, one must fast for a day and night.
Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a *ḍuṇḍubha* [non-venomous snake],
one should feed the Brahmins rice mixed with sesame and peas (*kṛsara*), and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having killed a young deer, a monitor lizard, a tortoise, or a porcupine,
as well as one who has eaten eggplant, is purified after a day and a night.
One who kills a wolf, a jackal, a bear, a hyena, a dog,
or a hunter should give a *prastha* measure of sesame seeds to a twice-born man and subsist on air for three days.
For the killing of an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, or a camel,
the penance is one day and night, along with immersion in water at the three junctions of the day.
By killing a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger,
one is purified in three nights by means of satiating the Brahmins with offerings.
A killer of deer, female antelopes, boars, sheep,
or goats shall fast for one day and night and eat only food that has not been ploughed by the furrow.
In this manner, having stayed for a day and night among all these four-footed forest-dwellers, he should remain standing and recite prayers to Jātavedas.
He who causes the death of an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman,
shall perform two Prājāpatya penances and give eleven bulls as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
If one should strike a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya who is free from fault,
he too shall perform two Kṛcchra penances and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee.
Having killed a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who is devoted to his duties, or a most excellent twice-born man who stands in improper occupations,
one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give thirty cows as a sacrificial fee.
If someone has killed a Caṇḍāla in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa,
he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee.
Whether it be by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or indeed by anyone else,
when the death penalty for a Caṇḍāla has been incurred, one is purified by half of the Kṛcchra penance.
If a thief, a dog-cooker, or a Caṇḍāla are struck by a Brāhmaṇa,
he becomes pure after staying overnight and bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If thieves, dog-cookers, or Caṇḍālas are struck by a Brahmin,
he becomes pure after staying there for a day and night and bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one has slept together with Caṇḍālas, one should fast for three nights;
having traveled along a path used by a Caṇḍāla, one becomes pure by the recollection of the Gāyatrī.
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun;
upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
If a person of the highest caste drinks water from wells or ponds dug by Caṇḍālas out of ignorance, he becomes pure after one day and night, provided he eats only one meal.
Having drunk water from a well that has been touched by the vessels of a Caṇḍāla,
one attains purification after three nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
If a twice-born man drinks water contained in a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he who spits it out at that very moment should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If one does not discharge water [from the penis] while the food in his body is still undigested, the Prājāpatya penance should not be given; instead, he should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
A Brahmin shall perform the Sāṃtapana penance; a Kṣatriya, the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya shall perform half of that; and a Śūdra shall perform one quarter of it.
If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk contained in a vessel belonging to an outcaste (antyaja), [he must undergo penance].
For the twice-born, expiation is by means of the Brahmakūrca fast;
for a Śūdra, it is by fasting as well as by giving gifts according to his capacity.
O best of the twice-born, if one should ever eat the food of a caṇḍāla out of ignorance,
he becomes pure after ten nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel.
One should eat each mouthful of cow-urine and barley-gruel separately;
one who observes this restraint for ten days should be declared to have fulfilled that vow.
But where a Caṇḍāla stays in a house out of ignorance,
the twice-born perform a favor for one who has approached them once that [fact] is known.
Those who have mastered the Vedas and know the Dharma, singing the teachings that have issued from the mouth of the Sage,
shall rescue him as he falls from the mixture of sin.
One should eat curd, clarified butter, milk, cow's urine, and barley-gruel; and one should perform immersion in water at all three junctions of the day.
For three days he should eat with curd, for three days he should eat with clarified butter,
and for three days he should eat with milk— one [substance] for each of the three days.
One should not eat food that is defiled by its nature, nor that which is leftover, nor that which is infested with worms;
however, one may consume three palas of curd, one pala of milk, and one pala of clarified butter.
The purification of both copper and bronze is achieved by means of ash;
that of garments by washing with water; and that of earthenware by discarding it.
Having placed safflower, molasses, cotton, salt, oil,
and clarified butter at the door, one should place the grains inside the house and set fire to them.
Thus purified, he should thereafter perform the satiation of the Brahmins;
he should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Furthermore, one is purified by plastering, digging, offering oblations, and reciting prayers;
and for Brahmins, no defect of the ground exists when it serves as a foundation.
If one has contact with Caṇḍālas for a month or even for half a month,
one becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel (yāvaka).
A washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter, or a basket-maker—
she who stays unrecognized in the house of one belonging to the four castes.
Having recognized [the offense], one should perform expiation; for that which was previously mentioned, one should indeed perform half.
One should not set fire to the house, but should carry out all the rest.
If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone's house,
he must be expelled from that dwelling, and the earthenware vessels must be discarded.
One should never discard a vessel that is full of liquid;
likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
If a worm should arise from the opening of a wound in a Brāhmaṇa where pus and blood have formed, what is the expiation for him?
Having bathed and drunk cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter for three days, one who has been defiled by worms shall become pure.
A Kṣatriya, having given five māṣas of gold,
should likewise prescribe a cow as the sacrificial fee for a Vaiśya and a fast;
for Śūdras there shall be no fasting, as a Śūdra is purified by giving.
"That which the gods of the earth call a 'flawless' statement."
Having bowed with one's head, it should be accepted, for that indeed yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whatever flaw there may be in recitation, whatever flaw in austerity, and whatever flaw in the performance of a sacrificial rite—[all these are remedied by this].
Everything provided by Brahmins becomes flawless,
even in times of disease, calamity, exhaustion, famine, or likewise during a violent upheaval.
Fasting, vows, and burnt offerings are indeed accomplished through the agency of the twice-born;
or rather, when the Brāhmaṇas are satisfied, they bestow grace for everything.
One obtains all desires in this world through those things prepared by the twice-born.
Likewise, it is declared that favor should be shown toward the weak, as well as toward children and the elderly.
Otherwise, there would be a fault; therefore, it is not considered a favor.
Whether out of affection, greed, fear, or even ignorance, [it is so].
But those who show favor to such people, that sin goes to them;
for they speak of religious observances only when the dissolution of the body has arrived.
One should never perform [a rite] while in good health by obstructing a great task;
for fools who speak without restraint cause such obstruction even when one is healthy.
Those who create obstacles for him fall into an impure hell—
he who, having himself undertaken a vow, treats a Brahmin with contempt.
His fast would be in vain; he does not partake in the merit [of it]. That very rule alone is to be accepted if even a single twice-born man should speak [in its favor].
One should speak to the twice-born; otherwise, one becomes a killer of an embryo.
For Brahmins are a moving tirtha, for the virtuous are indeed the very embodiment of sacred fords.
By the water of their very words, even defiled people are purified;
whatever the Brāhmaṇas speak, the gods consider that to be true.
A Brahmin embodies all the gods; his word is never otherwise.
Fasting, religious vows, ritual bathing, pilgrimage to sacred sites, recitation of mantras, and austerity [all derive their power from him].
The fruit of that [gift] belongs entirely to him for whom it has been prepared by a Brahmin.
When food and other such items are infested with insects or defiled by flies and hair, [one should act as follows].
If one touches water during that interval, one should touch that food with ashes. Furthermore, a Brahmin who, while eating, touches his foot with his hand [should likewise do so].
He eats his own leavings from the vessel with his hand after it has been set aside;
he should not eat while standing on footrests, nor while seated upon a couch.
One should avoid eating food while being watched by a dog or a Caṇḍāla;
likewise, one should observe the rules regarding forbidden food and the purification of food.
Just as it was spoken by Parāśara, so do I speak to you:
food boiled from a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* measure that has been defiled by crows or dogs [is rendered unfit].
"By what means is this purified?"—thus one should inquire of the Brāhmaṇas.
However, food in the measure of a *droṇa* that has been licked by a crow or a dog should not be discarded.
By Brahmins who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and who uphold the Dharmaśāstras,
thirty-two prasthas are recorded as one droṇa, and two prasthas are known as one āḍhaka.
Therefore, those who know the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* understand that food in the amount of a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* [is not defiled] if it has been licked by a crow or a dog,
or smelled by a cow or a donkey.

A Brahmin should discard even a very small amount of food; purification occurs when there is one *droṇa* or one *āḍhaka* remaining. Having removed from the food that portion which has been defiled by saliva, [the rest may be consumed].
Having sprinkled the gold with water, one should heat it with fire alone;
[the ordeal is considered valid when] touched by both the fire and the golden water.
By the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins, that food becomes pure at that very moment;
but how can there be purification for the oil or even the cow's milk in that case?
In that case, one should discard a small portion [of the milk] and purify it by straining the fat;
the purification of cow's milk is prescribed by means of the flame of fire. (This concludes the section on the purification of substances.)
Now, therefore, follows the purification of substances according to the words of Parāśara: the purification of wooden vessels is held to be by planing.
Bell-metal is purified by ashes; copper is purified by acid;
a woman who does not go to her husband is purified by her menses.
One is purified by the current of a river if no loss [of water] is visible;
this applies when step-wells, wells, and tanks have been somehow defiled.
Having indeed drawn out a hundred jars [of water], one becomes pure through the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
A girl of eight years is a *Gaurī*, while one of nine years is a *Rohiṇī*.
A girl becomes marriageable at ten years of age; beyond that, she is subject to menstruation.
But when the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not bestow his daughter [in marriage]—
Month after month, her menstrual blood is drunk by the ancestors themselves—
namely, the mother, the father, and likewise the eldest brother.
Three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses:
he who would marry such a girl, and the Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by passion, marries her.
For that Brahmin who serves a *vṛṣalī* for even a single night becomes unfit to be spoken to and excluded from the sacrificial row (*apāṅkteya*). (Parāśara Dharma Śāstra 7.8)
Subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [the sacred texts], he is purified in three years. When the sun has set, [if he touches] a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or a woman...
Par7.10ab: And for one who touches a woman who has recently given birth, how is purification prescribed?
Par7.10cd: By looking at fire, gold, and the path of the moon.
If two Brāhmaṇa women who are menstruating touch one another, they become pure by bathing with the permission of a Brāhmaṇa.
She should remain without food for that long; she becomes pure after three nights alone.
If a Brahmin woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another, the former shall perform an Ardhakṛcchra penance, and the latter a single quarter-penance.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their menses, should touch one another;

If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another, she who is of the Brāhmaṇa caste shall perform the penance prescribed for the first [grade of] offense, while the other shall perform a penance reduced by one quarter.
A Śūdra woman previously [married] becomes pure through a Kṛcchra penance; she becomes pure through a gift. A menstruating woman who has bathed becomes pure on the fourth day.
One should perform rites for the gods, the ancestors, and so forth upon the cessation of the menstrual flow;
however, that flow which occurs daily in women due to illness is not subject to this rule.

Because she is not impure due to that [menstrual flow], it is considered to be *vaikālika* (permissible at any time). However, she should not be regarded as one of virtuous conduct (*sādhv-ācārā*) as long as the menstrual flow continues.
When the menstrual flow has ceased, a woman is approachable for sexual intercourse and indeed for household duties;
however, on the first day she is a Caṇḍālī, and on the second day she is a slayer of a Brahmin.
On the third day she is said to be a washerwoman; on the fourth day she becomes pure. When a bath is required due to illness, one who is not ill must bathe ten times.
Having bathed again and again, he should touch that [corpse]; then that afflicted person shall become pure.
A twice-born man who has been touched by one who is impure from eating, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra, [should likewise act].
Having fasted for one night, one is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Upon being touched by a Śūdra who is not rendered impure by food remnants, bathing is prescribed.
One who has been touched by that leavings (ucchiṣṭa) should perform a Prājāpatya penance.
Bell-metal (kāṃsya) is purified by ashes, provided it has not been smeared with liquor.

An object touched by even a trace of *surā* is purified by scrubbing with fire; likewise, vessels of white copper (*kāṃsya*) that have been sniffed by a cow or defiled by dogs and crows are purified in the same manner.
Those items which have been defiled by the remnants of a Śūdra are purified by ten alkaline substances;
likewise, after rinsing the mouth and washing the feet, one may use a vessel made of bell-metal (kāṃsya).
Having buried iron objects in the ground for six months and then having dug them up again, one should bring them forth;
likewise, the purification of iron and lead [instruments] is by means of fire.
One should cleanse with water these items: ivory, bone, beeswax, silver, golden vessels, and bowls made of gems or stone.
Furthermore, for stone, purification is declared to be by scrubbing;
for earthenware, purification is by burning; and for grains, it is also by winnowing.
The purification of bamboo, bark, rags, linen, cotton cloth, woolen blankets,
and silk cloths is prescribed by means of sprinkling them with water.
For items made of muñja grass, household utensils, winnowing baskets, hemp, fruits,
skins, grass, wood, and ropes, sprinkling with water is prescribed as the purification method.
Cushions such as those made of cotton wool, as well as red garments and the like,
attain purity by being dried in the sun and then sprinkled with water.
Manu has declared that cats, flies, insects, moths, worms,
and frogs do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa* (rendered impure by food remnants), even though they touch what is pure and what is impure.
Manu has declared that water which has reached the earth after being touched, as well as mutual droplets [from the mouth],
the remnants of food, and oily substances, do not make one impure by leaving a residue.

They know it to be lawful that one is not considered impure by remnants (ucchiṣṭa) when consuming betel, sugarcane, or fruit; likewise after applying oil or ointments, or when partaking of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) or the Soma juice.
Roads, mud, water, boats, paths, and grass,
as well as structures built of baked bricks, are purified by wind and the sun.
A continuous stream that is not turbid, dust raised by the wind,
women, the elderly, and children— these are never considered defiled.
In the event of the ruin of one's country, during exile, or even amidst diseases and calamities, one must certainly protect one's own body and so forth; thereafter, one should practice the Dharma.

By whatever means possible— whether mild or harsh— one who is capable should rescue oneself from distress and practice dharma. But once the time of calamity has passed, one should attend to the rules of purification and proper conduct.

Afterwards, having attained purification, one who is restored to health should practice the Dharma. (Parva 7.38cd) If death should occur through the ropes or harnesses used for tethering cows due to unintentional negligence, what is the expiation for a sin committed unintentionally? (Parva 8.1ab–cd)
One should confess one's own sin to those who are learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who understand the Dharmaśāstras, and who are Brahmins devoted to their own duties.
Par8.3ab. Regarding the Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī, the twilight devotions, and the fire-rituals:
Par8.3cd. Those Brahmins who perform agriculture out of ignorance are merely bearers of the name.
Even if they have gathered by the thousands, those who lack vows, lack mantras, and subsist merely on their caste-status possess no status as an assembly (*pariṣad*).
Whatever those who are deluded by darkness, fools, and ignorant of the Dharma may say,
that sin becomes tenfold and falls upon those who speak it.
He who prescribes an expiation without having understood the treatises on Dharma becomes purified through that very act of expiation, while the guilt passes to the assembly.
What four or even three persons who have mastered the Vedas may declare, that should be known as Dharma; not so by thousands of others.
Evil recoils from those who proclaim the Dharma while seeking the path of valid cognition, for they speak of qualities that truly exist.
Just as water remaining upon a stone is purified by wind and sun,
so too may one destroy that person's evil deed through the instruction of the assembly.
It does not go to the doer, nor does it go to the assembly;
through contact with wind, sun, and so forth, evil perishes like water.
Whether they be four or even three Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, maintain the sacred fires, and are competent— such an assembly is designated as a *pariṣad*.
Those others who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas—
whether they be five or three— who are knowers of the Dharma, are proclaimed to be an assembly (pariṣad).
Even a single person who is a sage, a knower of the self, a twice-born, a performer of sacrifices, and one who has completed his studies under the Vedic vows may constitute an assembly.
I have previously described five [types of assemblies]; in their absence, there are three.
That assembly which is content with its own livelihood is proclaimed as such.
But from this point forward, those Brahmins who merely bear the name—
there is no status as an assembly among them, even if they number in the thousands.
Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
Just as a village site is empty, just as a well is without water,
and just as an oblation is offered into what is not fire, so too is a Brahmin who lacks the sacred mantras.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, and just as a saline field is fruitless,
and just as a gift given to an ignorant person is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless.
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by means of many constituent parts,
so too is Brahminhood [attained] through purificatory rites preceded by mantras.
Those twice-born men who merely bear the name of the twice-born and prescribe penances [for those who do not deserve them],
being performers of evil deeds, have all gone together to hell.
Those twice-born who recite the Veda and those who are devoted to the five sacrifices—
they rescue the three worlds, even if they are attached to the five senses.
A well-kindled fire blazing in cremation grounds is a consumer of all things;
likewise, a Brahmin learned in the Vedas is a deity, even if he consumes all things.
Just as all impure things are cast into water,
even so, O twice-born one, should one cast all sin into the fire.
A Brahmin devoid of the Gāyatrī becomes more impure even than a Śūdra; those twice-born ones who know the reality of Brahman through the Gāyatrī are honored by people.
Even a twice-born man of bad character is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses.
Who would abandon a cow that is ill-behaved and instead milk a she-ass, however well-behaved?
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas,
are said to possess the supreme Dharma in whatever they declare, even if spoken in jest.
One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), a reciter of the Dharma,
and the three principal orders (*āśrama*)— this assembly (*parṣad*) consists of at least ten members.
Having remained with the king's permission, one should prescribe the penance (*prāyaścitta*);
one must not perform it oneself, but rather a small expiation (*niṣkṛti*) should be performed.
Whatever a king desires to do by transgressing against those Brahmins,
that sin becomes tenfold and follows after the king.
One should always offer an expiation (prāyaścitta) before the sanctuary of a deity;
having then performed the self-purification (ātma-kṛcchra), one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas (Sāvitrī).
Having shaved his head together with the top-knot, he should bathe at the three junctions of the day;
he should dwell among cows at night and follow after them during the day.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor,
nor of a calf drinking.
One should drink water when they are drinking, and go to bed when they are going to bed;
one should rescue with all one's strength a woman who has fallen or is mired in the mud.
He who would sacrifice his life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow is released from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa;
he is a protector of both the cow and the Brāhmaṇa.
One should prescribe the Prājāpatya penance in proportion to the amount of cattle wealth;
that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra is then divided into four types.
For one day he shall eat a single meal, for one day he shall eat only at night;
for one day he shall eat food that is unasked for, and for one day he shall subsist on air alone.
For two days he should eat only one meal a day, and for two days he should eat a single meal;
for two days he should be one who does not beg, and for two days he should subsist on air alone.
For three days he should eat only one meal a day; for three days he should eat only at night;
for three days he should be a non-seeker of alms (fasting); and for three days he should subsist on air alone.
For four days he should eat a single meal [a day], for four days he should eat only at night;
for four days he should be one who does not beg for food, and for four days he should subsist on air alone.
When that penance has been performed, he should provide a feast for Brahmins;
the twice-born man should give sacrificial fees to the Brahmins and recite purificatory prayers.
Having fed Brāhmaṇas, the cow-killer is purified; of this there is no doubt.
For the purpose of protecting cows, one does not incur sin through confining or tethering them.
One should not consider that killing [of a cow] to have been committed, whether intentionally or unintentionally.
If, after the initial blow with a staff, one should cause [the cow] to fall by another means,
then the penance prescribed for killing a cow should be performed twice.
Confinement, binding, yoking, and slaughter—these are the four kinds [of injury].
One should perform one quarter-penance for confinement, and two quarters for binding.
If the offense should be less than a quarter [of a *puruṣa*] in those cases, one should perform the entire penance for the killing.
This applies whether it occurs in a cow-pen, in a house, in a difficult place, or on uneven ground.
In rivers, in oceans, or in other [bodies of water], but not at the mouths of rivers;
when cows die in a burnt region, it is called *stambhana* (obstruction).
If a cow should die while bound in a house or even in a forest by means of a yoke-tie, a tethering rope, a halter, or ornaments such as neck-ornaments;
One should know that very same thing to be bondage, whether it is caused by desire or by lack of desire;
such as when one is oppressed by men with a plow, a cart, a line [of oxen], or on their back.
The master of the cattle meets his death; such is the nature of the yoke-tie.
Whether intoxicated, negligent, insane, conscious, or even unconscious—[the same fate awaits].
Whether acting out of desire or without desire, if one strikes with sticks or stones in anger,
or causes another to be struck or even killed, that indeed constitutes the cause for the penalty of execution.
If he has fainted or fallen, or has been struck by a staff,
yet when he rises and walks five, seven, or ten paces,
or if he takes a mouthful of food or even drinks water; [then he is purified].
If he was previously afflicted by disease, no expiation is required.
If one kills an embryo while it is still a mere mass of flesh (*piṇḍastha*), the penance is one quarter; if it has reached the stage of a distinct fetus (*garbhasammite*), it is two quarters.
For killing an insentient embryo, the vow is declared to be three-quarters of the full penance.
For a minor offense (pāda), there shall be the shaving of the hair on the limbs; for a double offense (dvipāda), the beard as well;
for a triple offense (tripāda), everything except the topknot; but for a complete downfall (nipātana), including the topknot.
For one-quarter [of the penance], a pair of garments; for two-quarters, a bronze vessel;
for three-quarters, one should give a bull; and for the fourth, it is traditionally taught that two cows should be given.
But if he is seen with all his limbs fully formed and endowed with consciousness,
complete in every major and minor limb, he shall perform the cow-vow (go-vrata) for double the duration.
If a cow is struck by a stone or a staff,
one should perform one quarter-penance for breaking its horn, and two quarters for injuring its eye.
If a cow is struck by means of a stone or a staff,
he shall perform one quarter-penance for breaking a horn, and two quarters for injuring an eye.
For striking the tail, one should perform a Pāda-kṛcchra penance; for breaking a bone, two Pādas;
for cutting off an ear, three Pādas; and for causing death, one should perform the full penance.
In the case of breaking a horn, breaking a bone, and likewise breaking the hip—
if he survives for six months, no penance is prescribed.
When a wound has been treated, an oil massage with the hand should be performed;
furthermore, fodder should be provided until the animal has regained its full strength.
As long as all its limbs are complete, so long should the man nourish it;
having first paid homage to the form of the cow as representing the Brahmin, he should release it.
If one should have a deficient body with incomplete limbs,
then one should prescribe an expiation for that person on account of their being a cow-killer.
If one who is arrogant forcibly kills a cow with wood, clods of earth, stones, or even a weapon,
one should prescribe the following purification for him.
One should perform the Sāṃtapana penance for killing a wooden post, the Prājāpatya for a clod of earth,
the Tapta-kṛcchra for a stone, and the Atikṛcchra for a weapon.
In the Pañcasāntapana penance there are five cows; likewise, in the Prājāpatya, three;
in the Tapta-kṛcchra, there are eight; and in the Atikṛcchra, thirteen.
In the case of killing living beings, one should give a substitute for that [life];
or one should pay its equivalent value—so Manu has declared.
Except for branding and marking, as well as for the purpose of transport and release,
and for the sake of securing them at night, one does not incur guilt by confining or tethering [animals].
In cases of excessive burning, excessive carrying [of loads], as well as piercing the nose,
and traveling across rivers or mountains, one should prescribe an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
In the case of excessive burning, one should perform a quarter-penance; for riding [on a vehicle], one should perform two quarters.
For piercing the nose, one should perform three-quarters, but for killing [the animal], one should perform the entire penance.
But if an ox, restrained by the yoke-halter, dies from being burnt,
it has been stated by Parāśara himself that one quarter [of the penance] applies according to the rule.
Confinement, binding, carrying loads, striking, driving through difficult terrain, and the use of a yoke— these six are the causes of death.
If a cow or other domestic animal dies with its limbs tightly bound by a tethering rope,
the owner of that dwelling shall be sinful and deserves half of the prescribed penance. [Furthermore,
one should not use] coconut fibers, hemp fibers, muñja grass, or cords made of bark for such purposes.
Cows should not be tied up with these [materials]; even when they have been tied, one should remain standing there holding an axe.
One should bind the sacrificial animal, facing south, with kuśa and kāśa grass. There is no expiation required for those [animals] burnt by fire while caught in a snare.
If there should be wood in that [place], how could there be an expiation? By reciting the purifying goddess, one is liberated from that sin.
By causing [water] to be diverted from wells and tanks, by felling trees,
or by selling fodder for cattle and horses, one thereby incurs the same sin as the killing of a cow.
But when anyone who has been won over becomes one whose ranks are broken—
whether his ears and heart are pierced, or he is submerged in the narrowness of a well— [then he must be abandoned].
If a person dies there due to emerging from a well, or because of a fracture in the neck or feet [caused by the well],
one should perform three-quarters of the penance.
This applies also to the digging of a well, the construction of a bank, the building of a river-dam, and at water-stations (*prapā*).
For those who have perished in water, no expiation is prescribed.
In the case of digging a well, a pond, or a long trench,
as well as in other such religious excavations, no expiation is prescribed.
For a man who desires to dig a pit at the door of a house, in dwellings,
or for his own business or for digging a house, one should prescribe an expiation.
For those who die at night while confined by fetters, those killed by snakes or tigers,
and those perished by fire or lightning, no expiation is prescribed.
In the case of the destruction of a village by a flood of arrows, the collapse of a house due to its falling,
or those killed by excessive rain, no penance is prescribed.
For those killed in battle, those who have perished in their homes by fire,
and those who died in forest fires or village conflagrations— for these, no penance is prescribed.
When a cow is restrained for the purpose of medical treatment or to release a dead fetus,
if she should perish despite the effort being made, no expiation is prescribed.
One should prescribe an expiation for many people who have perished while being bound or confined,
as well as for a physician who has administered treatment incorrectly.
In the event of the death of oxen or bulls, all those people who were looking on and did not prevent it shall incur the sin of a fallen act.
When a single person has been killed by many acting together, and it is not known from the impact who struck him,
the slayer must be identified through divine means by those appointed by the king and then removed.
If a single woman is killed by several people by chance,
they shall each perform one quarter of the penance for killing separately.
If blood is seen, [the victim] has been killed; if seized by disease, he becomes emaciated.
Saliva appears when bitten; such is the method of investigation.
Or even if urged for the sake of food, he does not go on his journey;
thus has it been stated by Manu alone, who knows all the scriptures.
The expiation prescribed by him for a cow-killer is that he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
however, for the sake of preserving his hair, he should observe double the vow.
When a vow is prescribed as being twofold, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall likewise be twofold;
this applies whether it be a king, a prince, or a Brahmin deeply learned in the Vedas.
Without performing the shaving of his head, one should prescribe an expiation for him:
having pulled out all the hair, he should have two finger-breadths cut off.
In this manner, the shaving of the head for women and young girls is prescribed;
however, there is no shaving of the hair for a woman, nor must she sleep or eat at a distance [from her husband].
He shall not stay overnight in a cow-pen, nor shall he follow the cows during the day;
especially so in rivers, at their confluences, and in forests.
For women, there is no skin garment as clothing; rather, they should observe the vow itself.
It is said that bathing at the three junctions of the day and likewise the worship of the gods [are their duties].
In the midst of their kinsmen, their penance consists of the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such observances;
they should remain constantly in their homes, pure and practicing self-restraint.
He who, having committed the slaughter of a cow in this world, desires to conceal it,
goes without doubt to the terrible hell known as Kālasūtra.
Released from that hell, that man is born in the world of mortals as a eunuch,
a sufferer, and one afflicted with leprosy for seven births.
Therefore, one should not proclaim the sins of others; one should constantly practice one's own duty.
One should avoid excessive anger toward women, children, servants, cows, and Brahmins. (Parāśara 9.61) I shall declare the beneficial expiation for all the four social orders. (Parāśara 10.1)
And for approaching those who should not be approached, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification.

One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight; on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa.
One should indeed take a morsel of food the size of a hen's egg;
otherwise, through the fault of improper disposition, there is neither dharma nor purification.
After that, once the penance has been performed, one should provide a meal for a Brahmin;
one should give two cows, a pair of garments, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
If a twice-born man approaches a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī,
he shall fast for three nights according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
Having performed the *pavana* rite along with the topknot (*śikhā*), one should perform two *prājāpatya* penances;
Pārāśara has declared that the purification is achieved by giving two cows as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya has sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman,
he should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give away a pair of cattle consisting of a bull and a cow.
If a Śūdra has sexual intercourse with a dog-cooker woman (Śvapākī) or a Caṇḍālī woman,
he shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of four cows as a gift.
If one should approach his mother, his sister, or likewise his own daughter—
if, deluded, he has approached these three, he shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
One should perform three cāndrāyaṇa penances; one is purified by the cutting off of the penis.
And likewise, for sexual intercourse with one's mother's sister, there shall be the excision of one's own penis.
But he who should go [to her] out of ignorance shall perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
he should give a pair of ten cows—this is the purification, as Pārāśara has declared.
Having violated the wife of a father, a sister born of the same mother,
the wife of a teacher, a daughter-in-law, and likewise the wife of a brother;
If one has sexual intercourse with a maternal aunt or a woman of the same lineage (sagotra), one should perform three Prājāpatya penances;
one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and one is purified—of this there is no doubt.
Having approached female animals, female slaves, and the like, as well as female buffalo, female camels, female monkeys,
female donkeys, and female pigs, one shall perform the Prājāpatya vow.
One who has approached a cow is purified by a three-night fast upon giving a single cow to a Brāhmaṇa;
however, one who has approached a female buffalo, a female camel, or a female donkey is purified in a single day and night.
In times of plague, in battle, during famine, or when people are perishing;
or when captured as prisoners or afflicted by fear—one should always look upon one’s own wife.
If a woman forms an association with Caṇḍālas,
she should then make ten excellent Brahmins witness and confess her own transgression.
In a well dug up to the neck, filled with a mire of cow-dung and water,
one should remain there without food and emerge after a day and night. Having shaved the head together with the top-knot, one should eat a meal of barley-gruel.
Having fasted for three nights, one should dwell in water for one night.
Having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper,
along with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should drink the water.
Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
as long as she performs that vow, she shall dwell outside [the house].
Then, when the penance has been performed, one should feed Brahmins;
Pārāśara declared that one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee for purification.
For women of the four castes, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa vows are prescribed.
As is the earth, so is a woman; therefore, one should not defile her.
If a woman has been enjoyed by force—having been captured as a prisoner, killed, or bound out of fear—she is purified by performing the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance; so said Pārāśara.
But a woman who has been enjoyed once by those of evil deeds against her will is purified by the Prājāpatya penance and by the flow of menses.
Half of the body of that man falls [from grace] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is ordained.
Reciting the Gāyatrī while performing the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance,
one should consume cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with Kuśa grass, each accompanied by the Gāyatrī mantra.
A fast for one night is declared to be the *sāṃtapana* penance.
[If she] should conceive a child by a paramour when her husband is dead, missing, or has gone abroad, [this is the rule].
In another kingdom, one should abandon that woman who has fallen and committed evil; but when a Brāhmaṇa woman goes forth united with another man, [she must be abandoned].
She is declared lost and there is no hope of her return.
