But she who, out of lust or delusion, departs having abandoned her kinsmen, children, and husband—
But she is lost in the next world, especially among human beings— namely,
a woman who has fallen into intoxication and delusion, and who, out of anger, strikes with a staff or other implements.
And having gone to the state beyond duality, there shall be no returning again;
when the tenth day has arrived, no expiation is required.
For ten days one should not abandon a woman; likewise, one should abandon her if she has lost her sense of sacred learning (*śruti*).
The husband shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance, and his kinsmen half a *kṛcchra*.
Having eaten from or drunk from their [vessels], one is purified after a day and night. But when a Brāhmaṇī woman, being free from any other man, should have intercourse with another man...
Having gone [to a woman], she passes through the hundred [generations] of men; however, her agnates (gotriṇas) shall exclude her.
If a man should go to a woman’s house, that house becomes impure.
Whatever is the house of the husband’s mother, that indeed is the house of the paramour.
Having scraped that house, one should afterwards sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should discard earthen vessels and purify clothes and wooden ones;
all ritual materials made of cow-hair and those produced from fruits should be cleansed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Copper vessels [are purified] with the five products of the cow, and bronze vessels with ashes ten times over; the Brahmin should perform the expiation as prescribed by the Brahmins.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee, or one should perform two Prājāpatya penances.
For others, the purification consists of fasting for one day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are purified by fasts, meritorious vows, ritual bathing, the twilight devotions, worship, and so forth; as well as by the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, compassion, and gifts.
Space, wind, fire, earth, and water are pure;
likewise, *darbha* grasses do not become defiled in sacrifices, just like the sacrificial cups (*camasa*).
[However, they are defiled by] impure semen, cow-flesh, or even the food of a *caṇḍāla*.
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food], he should perform the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the same way, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should also perform half a Cāndrāyaṇa;
and when a Śūdra eats in this manner, he should perform a Prājāpatya.
A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while a twice-born man should drink the brahmakūrca;
or they should give one, two, three, or four cows respectively, according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇa.
The food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), and the food of one whose food is unfit to be eaten;
likewise, food that is suspected [of being forbidden], prohibited food, and the leavings of another.
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food] out of ignorance or due to distress,
he should perform the purifying Brahmakūrca penance once he becomes aware of it.
When food has been defiled by children, mongooses, or cats, it is purified by sprinkling it with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water; there is no doubt in this matter.
When Brahmins are seated in a single row for a communal meal,
if even one person sets aside his vessel, the remaining food must not be served.
If a Brahmin should eat the leavings from that row out of delusion,
he must perform the Kṛcchra penance as well as the Sāṃtapana penance.
Milk, white garlic, eggplant, and *gṛñjana*;
leeks, tree exudations, and mushrooms that grow on sacred ground.
If a twice-born man consumes camel’s milk or ewe’s milk through ignorance,
he is purified by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having eaten a frog as well as the flesh of a mouse, a Brahmin,
knowing [the nature of the offense], is purified by subsisting on barley-gruel for a day and a night.
A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are diligent in their duties and pure in their vows—
food from their houses may always be eaten by the twice-born at rites for the gods and the ancestors.
Having gone to the bank of a river, a Brahmin may eat ghee, oil, milk, or food cooked with fat, even if it is the food of a Śūdra.
A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is constantly addicted to liquor and meat and who engages in base occupations, as if he were a dog-cooker.
A twice-born man should never abandon those Śūdras who are devoted to serving the twice-born, who abstain from liquor and meat, and who are constantly intent upon their own duties.
If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka),
how should one prescribe the expiation for them in each respective caste?
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs through eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī;
for a Vaiśya, it is through five thousand, and for a Kṣatriya, through three thousand.
When one eats at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, one should cause two thousand [cows] to be given;
or else, one is purified by the single Vāmadevya Sāman alone.
Manu has declared that dry food, cow's milk, and oily substances obtained from the house of a Śūdra are fit to be eaten,
provided they have been cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
If a Brahmin has eaten in the house of a Śūdra during times of distress,
he shall be purified by mental remorse or by reciting the Drupadā verse one hundred times.
A slave, a barber, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who shares half the harvest—
these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
A son born from a Śūdra maiden who has been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Dāsa through that consecration; however, if he is not consecrated, he is a Nāpita.
The son who is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra maiden is to be known as a Gopāla; he may be fed by Brahmins, without a doubt.
A son born from a Vaiśya maiden who has been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa is known as an Ārdhika; he is to be fed by the Brāhmaṇas, without a doubt.
If one unintentionally consumes water, curd, ghee, or milk that has been placed in a vessel used for forbidden foods,
what should the expiation be?
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who approaches [for instruction],
the expiation for one of the twice-born castes is the Brahmakūrca fast.
For Śūdras there should be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts. Even for a dog-cooker, the *brahmakūrca* rite performed for a day and night shall bring purification.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with kuśa grass—
this is designated as the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya), which is purifying and cleanses away sin.
Cow’s urine from a black cow, cow dung from a white one,
milk from a copper-colored cow, and curd from a red cow are to be taken.
Clarified butter should be taken from a tawny cow, or indeed all [products] from a tawny cow;
one should provide one *pala* of urine and half the size of a thumb of cow dung.
One should give seven palas of milk; it is said that three palas of curd are to be given;
one pala of ghee should be given, and one pala of kuśa-water.
Having taken cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārām," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhi krāvṇaḥ."
With the mantra "Thou art brilliance, thou art pure," he should place clarified butter; with "Thee for the God," the water with *kuśa* grass;
and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), purified by the *ṛc*, he should set down in the vicinity of the fire.
Having stirred [the water] with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should consecrate it with the mantra "mānastoke.
Furthermore, there should be seven blades of *darbha* grass that are not cut at the tips and are as bright as a parrot.
Having extracted these [substances], one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the rule,
with the mantras "Irāvatī," "Idam Viṣṇuḥ," and "Mā nas toke," which are auspicious.
With these [verses] the twice-born should offer oblations, and he should drink the remains of the offering;
having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, and likewise having churned it with the *praṇava*.
Having extracted [the sin] with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink [the water] with the *praṇava* as well;
for whatever sin residing in the bones remains within the bodies of embodied beings, [it is removed by this].
The Brahmakūrca burns everything away, like a blazing fire consumes fuel;
it is a purifier in the three worlds, presided over by the deities.
Varuṇa resides in cow urine, and the bearer of oblations (Agni) in cow dung;
Vāyu is declared to be in curd, Soma in milk, and the Sun in clarified butter.
If one drinks water that has fallen from the mouth into a vessel, one should know that it is unfit for consumption; having drunk it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a twice-born man sees a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
or if he drinks water that has become impure by contact with bones, skin, or other such things fallen therein, [he must perform penance].
A human corpse, a crow, a village pig, a donkey, and a camel;
likewise a gavaya, a supratīka, a peacock, and a rhinoceros.
If one falls into a well containing the skin of a tiger, a bear, or a lion,
or if one has drunk the water of a defiled pond;
By this entire sequence, the expiation for a man shall be determined in its proper order:
a Brahmin is purified in three nights, while a Kṣatriya is purified in two days.
A Vaiśya, however, is purified in one day, while a Śūdra is purified by eating only at night.
Of one who has desisted from cooking for others, yet delights in cooking for others.
Having eaten food from one who is unworthy (an *apaca*), a twice-born man should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
and as for the gift given by such an unworthy person, how can there be any fruit for the giver?
Both the giver and the receiver—these two go to hell. Having taken the sacred fire and established it, he shall not fail to perform the five great sacrifices.
He who has desisted from cooking for others is proclaimed by the sages as one who,
having himself performed the five sacrifices, subsists on the food of others.
That brahmin who, though devoted to the householder's duty, constantly rises early in the morning and takes delight in cooking for others, yet remains devoid of giving— [he is a thief].
The seers who knew the true essence of dharma have proclaimed that there is no cooked food [for them];
for in every age, there are those twice-born ones who follow their respective dharmas.
One must not utter censure against them, for those twice-born ones are the very form of the age (yuga).
Having uttered the sound "hum" to a Brahmin, or the word "you" to one who is superior;
Having bathed, he should remain standing for the remainder of the day and, having offered salutations, seek his favor;
even if he has struck him with a blade of grass or bound him by the neck with a garment.

Even after winning a dispute, one should appease the opponent by bowing down; however, for threatening someone, the penance is one day and night, and for causing them to fall to the ground, it is three nights.

In the case of blood, one should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance; in the case of internal bleeding, the *kṛcchra*. One who performs the *atikṛcchra* should eat only as much food as fills the palm for nine days.
One who fasts for three nights performs what is called the *atikṛcchra* penance;
this is prescribed when a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred.

The Gāyatrī, when practiced ten thousand times, is the supreme means of purification. If one sees a bad dream, or after vomiting, or following a shaving, or after sexual intercourse, or from exposure to the smoke of a funeral pyre, bathing alone is prescribed.
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or that which has been touched by *surā* liquor,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of regeneration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
The deerskin, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the religious observances—
all these are set aside for the twice-born upon the performance of the rite of re-initiation.
One who eats feces or urine shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for purification;
furthermore, having bathed and drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one shall become pure.

Regarding those who have committed suicide by water, fire, or falling [from a precipice], or through renunciation of the world (pravrajyā) or fasting unto death (anāśaka), and regarding those of the castes who have fallen away from their status— how is their purification ordained?
By performing two *prājāpatya* penances, by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
and by the gift of eleven bulls, those three castes are purified.
I shall now declare the penance for a Brahmin who, having gone to a forest crossroads, has his hair shorn including the topknot; he should perform two Prājāpatya penances.
Svāyambhuva has declared that one should give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee for purification;
by that, one is released from that sin and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
The wise have proclaimed five meritorious types of bathing:
that of fire, that of water, that of Brahman, that of wind, and that of heaven.

The *āgneya* bath is performed with ashes; the *vāruṇa* bath is by immersion in water; the *brāhma* bath is performed with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭha"; and the *vāyavya* bath is said to be [bathing] in the dust raised by cows.
But that which is performed with heat and rain is called divine bathing;
having bathed there, a person becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā.
When a twice-born man goes to bathe, all the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors,
travel along with him in the form of wind, afflicted by thirst and seeking water.
When the wringing out of the garment is performed, they return disappointed.
Therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having performed the libation for the ancestors.
He who, having placed [sesame] in his pores, satisfies the ancestors with sesame seeds—
by him the ancestors are satisfied with blood and with filth.
He who shakes his hair after bathing, or who discharges impurity,
or even one who sips water while standing in the water— that twice-born man is excluded from the rites of the ancestors and the gods.
Having covered one's head or neck, or with the lower garment tucked up or the topknot loosened,
or without the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one remains impure even after sipping water (ācamana).
One standing on land should not sip water while remaining in the water, nor one standing outside should sip water while remaining in the water.
Having touched both [the water and the ground], one who has sipped water becomes pure in both places.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
Upon sneezing, spitting, or having food remaining between the teeth, as well as upon speaking an untruth or conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear.
Manu has declared that the sacred sites beginning with Prabhāsa, as well as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā,
reside within the right ear of a Brahmin.
Likewise, fire, water, the Vedas, Soma, the Sun, and the Wind [reside there].
But all [the sacred fires] of a Brahmin remain in the right ear.
Bathing during the day is praised when purified by the rays of the sun;
bathing at night is not recommended, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [during an eclipse].
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and burnt offerings should be performed during an eclipse of Rāhu;
however, at other times, the night is impure, and therefore one should avoid it.
The Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—these deities all dissolve into Soma; therefore, a gift should indeed be given during that planetary conjunction.
At a sacrifice of the wicked, at a wedding, at the sun’s passage into a new sign, and likewise during an eclipse, there is indeed the giving of gifts at night;
it is not ordained for any other occasion.
Giving is praised at the birth of a son, during a sacrifice, and likewise for rites performed to avert calamity; it is also praised upon the sighting of Rāhu, but not otherwise at night.
The middle two watches of the night should be known as the "great night" (mahāniśā). During the first and last watches, one should perform bathing as during the day.
A sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), a funeral pyre (*citī*), a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a *caṇḍāla*, and a seller of Soma [are places where one should not void urine].
But having touched these, a Brāhmaṇa should enter the water with his clothes on.
Before the collection of the bones, one should weep and then perform a ritual bath;
however, for a Brahmin, if this occurs within ten days [of death], there need only be sipping of water (ācamana).
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, all water is equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā;
the same has been declared regarding the bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites during a lunar eclipse.
A bath purified by *kuśa* grass, or when a twice-born man sips water with a *kuśa* blade,
or water drawn up with a *kuśa* blade— each of these becomes equal to the drinking of Soma.
Those who have neglected the fire-ritual, those who have abandoned the worship of the twilights (saṃdhyā),
and those who do not study the Veda— all these are declared to be *vṛṣalas*.
Therefore, a Brahmin who is especially afraid of a Śūdra should study at least a portion [of the Veda],
even if he is unable to master it all.
Even for one who studies constantly, chants, or offers oblations, if he is nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra,
no higher destiny exists for him.
Eating the food of a Śūdra, associating with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra,
and receiving knowledge from a Śūdra— even one who is blazing with merit— will cause him to fall.
That twice-born man who constantly causes food to be cooked by a Śūdra woman, and whose housewife is a Śūdra woman, is excluded from the ancestors and the gods; he goes to the Raurava hell.
A twice-born man whose body is nourished by the food of a Śūdra, having consumed that which grows from the dead and the impure, does not understand this: into what various wombs shall he go?
A vulture [is reborn] for twelve births, a pig for ten births, and one shall be in the womb of a dog for seven births; thus Manu has declared.
But that Brahmin who, seeking a fee, should offer the oblation for a Śūdra,
would become a Śūdra, while the Śūdra would become a Brahmin.
Having undertaken the vow of silence, a twice-born man should not speak while seated;
for if he should speak while eating, one must avoid that food.
If a Brahmin drinks water from that vessel while half of its contents remains uneaten,
he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and brings harm upon himself.
But he who, while the Brahmins are eating, releases his vessel first—he is a fool, he is most sinful; indeed, he is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
If the twice-born perform the rite of *svasti* while the vessels remain [unemptied],
the gods do not attain satisfaction, and likewise the ancestors depart disappointed.
One should not eat without having bathed, nor without having muttered prayers, nor without having offered oblations to the fire;
one should not eat from the back of a leaf, nor likewise at night without a lamp.
But the householder, endowed with compassion, should reflect only upon dharma;
being of sound intellect and abiding by justice, he should do so for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those whom he must support.
One must indeed protect oneself by means of wealth acquired through righteous means;
however, he who lives by unrighteous means is excluded from all ritual acts.

A fire-priest, a tawny cow, one who performs a long sacrificial session, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify by the mere sight of them; therefore, one should look upon them constantly.
One should keep these things in the house: the fire-drill, a black cat, sandalwood, a fine gem, ghee, sesame seeds, a black antelope skin, and a goat.
Where a hundred cows with one bull remain unrestrained,
that field is declared to be a "cow-hide" (go-carma), calculated as ten times [the standard measure].
A mortal [is purified] from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, which arise from the actions of mind, speech, and body;
by the gift of this ox-hide, he is released from all taints.
That gift which is given to a householder who is poor, and especially to one learned in the Vedas,
that gift brings about auspicious results.
One who seizes land is not purified by means of step-wells, wells, tanks, and the like, nor by hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, nor even by the gift of ten million cows.
Within eighteen days, a woman in her menses must indeed bathe;
beyond that, she must observe a three-night period of impurity—so the sage Uśanas has declared.

One yuga, two yugas, three yugas, and four yugas [are the periods of impurity] for a caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and one who has fallen from his caste, respectively.
Then, by the mere presence [of the corpse], one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Having bathed, if one has touched [the corpse] through ignorance, one should gaze at the sun.
A Brahmin who is weak in knowledge, while gold is available in his hand, drinks water from his mouth;
he will certainly be born in the womb of a dog.
But if a man, being angry, should declare his wife to be unapproachable,
yet later desires her again, he must have it proclaimed in the midst of the Brahmins.
One who is exhausted, angry, blinded by darkness, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear—
if such a person fails to perform a meritorious gift, the expiation is three days.
One should perform ablutions three times a day at the confluence of great rivers;
and upon the completion of the vow, one should give a cow and feed ten Brahmins.
Having eaten the food of a Brahmin who is of evil conduct and who practices forbidden acts,
a twice-born man should fast for one day.
By eating the food of a Brahmin who follows the sixfold conduct and likewise knows the end of the Vedas,
a man is released from sin within the interval of a day and night.
One who has food remaining above the mouth, food remaining below the mouth, or who has eaten during the menstrual period,
as well as one who has touched a corpse during a period of impurity, should perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
O Goddess, [one should perform] a *kṛcchra* penance, ten thousand repetitions [of a mantra], two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
and a bath at a sacred ford (*puṇyatīrtha*) with the head not wet, twelve times in number.

For a householder who intentionally causes the emission of semen upon the ground, a single *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed for every two *yojanas* traveled on a pilgrimage to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).

One who is endowed with the fourfold knowledge should recite the mantra of the Goddess one thousand times along with three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the rule, even for the slayer of a Brahmin.
One should prescribe going on a bridge over the ocean as the penance;
he should beg for alms from the four castes along the path of the bridge-construction.
Avoiding those engaged in forbidden occupations, and devoid of the parasol and sandals, he should say:
"I am indeed a doer of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins."
"I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms, a slayer of a Brahmin;
let him dwell among herds of cows, in villages, or in cities."
In penance groves, at sacred fords, or by rivers and springs—
having gone to these places and to the ocean, he shall proclaim his sin and [attain] merit.
Ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length,
it was constructed by Nala at the command of Rāmacandra.
Having seen the bridge of the ocean, one removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having seen the bridge, with a purified soul, one should plunge into the sea.
Or rather, the king who is the lord of the earth should perform the horse sacrifice;
once he has returned home, he may approach for the purpose of dwelling there.
Together with his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for the Brahmins;
he should also give one hundred cows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the four classes of officiants.
Through the grace of the Brahmins, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated.
Having killed a woman who is engaged in a ritual sacrifice, one should observe the vow for the killing of a Brahmin.
A twice-born man who drinks liquor should go to a river that flows into the ocean;
once he has performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, he should then provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas.
And one should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee to Brahmins.
Having drunk liquor even once, one should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire.
Having himself stolen gold from a Brāhmaṇa, he then torments both himself in this world and in the next.
Taking up a club, he should go into the presence of the king for execution;
then, having been released by the king, he attains purification.
But that which is done intentionally deserves death, and not otherwise;
[this applies] from sharing a seat, a bed, a vehicle, conversation, or eating together.
For sins indeed pass away like a drop of oil upon water;
[the penances for them are] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal fast (yāvaka), and the Tulāpuruṣa.
And following after cows destroys all sins. This is the treatise of Parāśara, consisting of five hundred verses;
it is a compendium of the Dharmaśāstra containing nine hundred and two [verses].
Just as the ritual acts of Vedic study [are to be observed], so too is this Dharmaśāstra;
it should be studied with diligent effort by one who is intent on attaining heaven.
[No sūtra on *vyavahāra* (legal procedure); only the commentary of Parāśaramādhava]

[Volume I, Part 1: The Section on Conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa), concerning the conduct of the four social classes (cāturvarṇya).
Then, in ancient times, on the peak of the snowy mountain in a dwelling within a forest of Devadāru trees, the sages questioned Vyāsa as he sat with one-pointed concentration. (I.1.1)
O son of Satyavatī, please describe the Dharma beneficial for human beings in the current Kali age, as well as the rules of purification and conduct exactly as they are.
Having heard those words of the sage, he—resplendent like fire and the sun, possessed of great luster, and learned in the Śruti and Smṛti—replied along with his disciples. (I.1, p. 65) // Par_1.3 //
"I am not an omniscient knower of all truths; how then could I speak of the Dharma?
Our father alone should be questioned," thus Vyāsa spoke to his son.
Then all those sages, desiring to know the true meaning of dharma, placed the sage Vyāsa at their head and went to Badarikāśrama. (I,1, p. 68) // Par_1.5 //
It was strewn with various flowering creepers, adorned with fruit-bearing trees, provided with rivers and springs, and graced by sacred bathing places. (I.1, p. 70) // Par_1.6 //
It was rich with the cries of beasts and birds, filled with temples of the gods,
and adorned by the dances and songs of yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
In the midst of that assembly of sages, the highly effulgent [Vyāsa] approached Parāśara, the son of Śakti, who was seated comfortably, surrounded by a multitude of eminent sages. (I.1.8)
With palms joined in reverence, Vyāsa, together with the sages,
honored him with circumambulations, salutations, and hymns of praise.
Then, with a heart full of contentment, the great sage Parāśara, that bull among munis, sat down and said, "Welcome; speak. (I.1, p. 75) // Par_1.10 //
Having said, "It is well; you have spoken correctly," Vyāsa immediately asked:
"O you who are kind to your devotees, if you know [the answer], then out of affection for me, [tell me] my devotion. (I.1.11, p. 77)
"Tell me the Dharma, O Father, for I am worthy of your favor.
I have heard the Dharmas of Manu, as well as those of Vasiṣṭha and Kāśyapa. (I.1.78)
The Gārgya and Gautama [Smṛtis], as well as those remembered by Uśanas, Atri, Viṣṇu, Saṃvarta, Dakṣa, and likewise Aṅgiras; Parāśara 1.13.
And likewise from Śātātapa, Hārīta, and Yājñavalkya;
[I have extracted] the laws composed by Āpastamba, as well as those of Śaṅkha and Likhita.
Those composed by Kātyāyana and likewise those of the sage Prācetasa have been heard by me; indeed, these meanings of the Vedas spoken by you have not been forgotten. (I,1, p. 79) // Par_1.15 //
In this Manvantara, throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā, all dharmas were born in the Kṛta age, and all dharmas are lost in the Kali age. (I,1, p. 80) // Par_1.16 //
Tell me something of the common conduct of the four castes—that which is to be performed by all four castes, as known by those learned in dharma. (I,1, p. 87) // Par_1.17 //
"Speak at length, O knower of the true nature of Dharma, concerning both the subtle and the gross.
At the conclusion of Vyāsa’s words, Parāśara, the foremost of sages, [replied]. (I.1.18)
He has declared the determination of Dharma, both subtle and gross, in detail.
"Listen, my son, I shall speak; let the sages likewise listen. (I.1, p. 93) // Par_1.19 //
In every kalpa, through their emergence and dissolution, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśvara are always the determiners of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous.
No one is the author of the Veda; rather, having remembered the Veda, the four-faced Brahmā likewise remembers the Dharmas, as does Manu in each interval between kalpas. (I.1, p. 112) // Par_1.21 //
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are one thing, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages another, and those in the Kali age yet another, according to the nature of each age. (I,1, p. 117) // Par_1.22 //
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone. (I,1, p. 119) // Par_1.23 //

In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu are prescribed; in the Tretā, those of Gautama; in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, those of Parāśara are remembered. (I,1, p. 122) // Par_1.24 //
One should abandon the country in the Kṛta age, leave the village in the Tretā age,
the single family in the Dvāpara age, but in the Kali age, one should abandon the perpetrator alone.
In the Kṛta age, [one falls] merely by conversation; in the Tretā, by touch; in the Dvāpara, by taking food; but in the Kali age, one falls through action alone. (I,1, p. 123) // Par_1.26 //
In the Kṛta age, the curse takes effect immediately; in the Tretā, after ten days;
in the Dvāpara, after one month; but in the Kali age, after a year.
In the Kṛta age, a gift is given after approaching [the recipient]; in the Tretā, it is given after being invited;
in the Dvāpara, it is given to one who asks; and in the Kali, it is given through service.

The highest gift is that given by approaching [the recipient]; the middling is that given by calling out; the lowest is that given to one who has already begged; but a gift given through service is fruitless. (I,1,p.124) // Par_1.29 //
For in the Kali age, righteousness is conquered by unrighteousness and truth by falsehood; kings are defeated by thieves, and men by women.
The Agnihotra sacrifices fall into neglect, reverence for the guru perishes, and maidens give birth [to children]—this is always the case in this Kali Yuga. (I,1, p. 125) // Par_1.31 //

In the Kṛta age, however, the vital breaths reside in the bones; in the Tretā, they depend on the flesh; in the Dvāpara, on the blood; but in the Kali age, they are situated in food and such. (I,1, p. 126) // Par_1.32 //

One should not criticize the religious duties that exist in each age, nor the twice-born who exist in each respective place; for those twice-born ones conform to the nature of their particular age. (I.1, p. 128) // Par_1.33 //
In every age, however, the remaining capacity [for penance] has been described by the Sage;
furthermore, the expiation declared by Parāśara is hereby prescribed. (I,1, p. 131) // Par_1.34 //
"Having recollected all of that this very day, I speak to you; O bulls among sages, listen to the conduct of the four social classes. (I.1, p. 140) // Par_1.35 //
The meritorious doctrine of Parāśara is pure and the destroyer of sins;
it was contemplated for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas and for the establishment of Dharma. (I.1, p. 141) // Par_1.36 //
The conduct of all four castes is the protector of Dharma;
for those whose bodies have fallen away from right conduct, Dharma turns its back. (I,1, p. 143) // Par_1.37 //

A Brahmin who is constantly devoted to the six duties, who worships the deities and guests, and who eats only the remnants of the sacrificial oblation, does not come to ruin. (I,1, p. 145) // Par_1.38 //

Bathing at the two twilights, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, worship of the deities and guests, hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice—these are the six duties to be performed day after day. (I.1, p. 218) // Par_1.39 //
Whether he be beloved or hateful, a fool or even a scholar, a guest who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is indeed a bringer of heaven. (I,1, p. 395) // Par_1.40 //

One should recognize as a guest a person who has come from a long journey, who is weary, and who arrives during the Vaiśvadeva offering; one who has arrived previously is not a guest. (I,1, p. 396) // Par_1.41 //
One should never treat a resident of one's own village as a guest; because he comes without fixed regularity, he is therefore called a guest (atithi). (I, 1, p. 398) // Par_1.42 //
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and the like, by offering the respectful water (arghya), a seat, and by washing his feet. (I.1, p. 399) // Par_1.43 //
A householder should generate affection by giving food with faith, by pleasant inquiries and replies, and by following one who is departing. (I,1, p. 400) // Par_1.44 //
If a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated, the ancestors of that person do not eat for fifteen years. (I,1, p. 401)
If a guest departs with his hopes frustrated, the fire-sacrifice of one who has offered a thousand loads of wood and a hundred jars of ghee is rendered useless. (I,1, p. 402) // Par_1.46 //
One should sow seed in a good field and bestow wealth upon a worthy recipient; for what is sown and given in a good field and to a worthy recipient does not perish. (I,1, p. 403) // Par_1.47 //
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or learning;
rather, one should conceive of the deity within the heart, for he embodies all the gods. (I.1, p. 404) // Par_1.48 //

For the Brahmin who is unprecedentedly observant of his vows and the guest who is unprecedentedly excellent—both of them, ever devoted to the study of the Vedas, become truly extraordinary day by day. (I.1, p. 406) // Par_1.49 //
When the Vaiśvadeva rite has commenced and a mendicant has arrived at the house, one should set aside food for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva and then dismiss the mendicant. (I,1, p. 408) // Par_1.50 //
Both the ascetic and the student are the masters of cooked food;
having eaten without first giving food to those two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

A wandering mendicant should give three portions of alms to the ascetic and the student; thereafter, if he has the means, he may give as much as desired without restriction. (I,1, p. 409) // Par_1.52 //
One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, then offer alms, and again give water;
that alms is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is like the ocean.
One whose parasol and horse belong to a prosperous elephant-riders’ guild should occupy the station of Indra; therefore, one should not question him. (I,1, p. 410) // Par_1.54 //
A mendicant is capable of removing the sin committed during the Vaiśvadeva rite;
however, the Vaiśvadeva rite does not remove the faults committed by a mendicant. (I,1, p. 411) // Par_1.55 //
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite—all of them should be known as fruitless and fall into an impure hell. (I,1, p. 412) // Par_1.56 //
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and excluded from hospitality all go to hell and enter the womb of a crow.
Whether he be a sinner, a Caṇḍāla, a slayer of a Brahmin, or a killer of his father— if such a person arrives when the Vaiśvadeva rite has begun, he is a guest who leads one to heaven.
He who eats with his head wrapped, he who eats facing south, or he who places his hand upon his left foot—verily, the Rākṣasas eat that food. (I,1, p. 413) // Par_1.59 //
For the king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being devoid of vows and unlearned; for such a village provides sustenance for thieves. (I.1, p. 445) // Par_1.60 //
For the Kṣatriya, protecting his subjects with weapon in hand and wielding the rod of punishment,
should conquer the enemy armies and rule the earth according to dharma.
One should pluck flower after flower without cutting the root,
like a gardener in a grove, and not like a charcoal-maker.
The acquisition of wealth, as well as dealing in gems, the protection of cattle, agriculture, and trade—these are declared to be the occupations of a Vaiśya. (I.1, p. 476) // Par_1.63 //
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is declared to be the supreme duty;
if he does anything otherwise, that shall be fruitless for him. (I.1, p. 480) // Par_1.64 //
Salt, honey, oil, curd, buttermilk, ghee, and milk—these do not become defiled for those of the Śūdra caste; one may sell all of them. (I,1, p. 484) // Par_1.65 //

By selling the meat of an animal that may not be eaten, by eating what is forbidden to eat, or by having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, a Śūdra falls from his status at that very moment. (I,1, p. 486) // Par_1.66 //
By drinking the milk of a tawny cow, by having sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman,
and by deliberating upon the syllables of the Vedas, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Cāṇḍāla.
[Volume I, Part 2:

Hereafter, [I shall describe] the ritual conduct of the householder in the Kali age—the common dharma pertaining to the four castes and stages of life according to one's capacity. (I,2,p.1) // Par_2.1 //
I shall first declare that according to the words of Parāśara:
a Brahmin, engaged in the six duties, may also perform the work of agriculture. (I.2.2)
One should not yoke an ox that is hungry, thirsty, or exhausted;
a Brahmin should not drive a bull that is deficient in limb, diseased, or impotent. (I,2, p. 6) // Par_2.3 //

One should cause [the bull] to carry for half a day— provided it has firm limbs, is free from disease, is well-fed, bellows pleasantly, and is not castrated— and thereafter, one should perform a ritual bath.

A twice-born man should practice the recitation of prayers, the worship of the gods, burnt offerings, and the study of his own Veda; he should feed one, two, three, or four Snātaka Brahmins. (I,2, p. 8) // Par_2.5 //
In a field ploughed by himself, and with grains earned by his own efforts, he should perform the five sacrifices and cause the initiation for a sacrifice to be conducted. (I,2,p.9) // Par_2.6 //
Sesame seeds and liquids must not be sold; however, grains and things equal to them may be sold.
For a Brahmin, such is his livelihood, as is the selling of grass, wood, and the like.
If a Brahmin should practice agriculture, he incurs a great fault; the sin that a fisherman incurs in a year, he incurs in a single year. (I,2, p. 13) // Par_2.8 //
With an iron-tipped wooden stake, the plowman, the fisherman with his net, the hunter, and likewise the fowler [kill] that [creature] in a single day. (Pariccheda 2.9)
The non-giver and the cultivator alike share equally in the consequences;
for they have cut down trees, broken the earth, and killed worms and insects.
A farmer is liberated from all sins by means of the threshing-floor sacrifice;
he who, having arrived at the root of his harvest, does not give to the twice-born. (I,2, p. 14) // Par_2.11 //
One should designate that thief and that most wicked man as a slayer of a Brahmin, after giving a sixth part to the king and a twenty-first part to the gods. (I,2, p. 15) // Par_2.12 //
By giving a thirtieth part to the Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins;
even a Kṣatriya, having practiced agriculture, should worship the gods and the Brahmins.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra should likewise engage in agriculture, trade, and the arts;
however, those Śūdras who abandon service to the twice-born perform forbidden acts. (I,2, p. 16) // Par_2.14 //
They indeed become short-lived and undoubtedly go to hell;
this is the eternal dharma for all four castes.
Therefore, I shall now declare the purification regarding birth and likewise death: Brāhmaṇas become pure after three days in the event of a death or a birth (impurity). (I,2,p. 204) // Par_3.1 //
A Kṣatriya is purified in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days,
and a Śūdra is purified in a month, according to the words of Parāśara.
By attending upon Brahmins, purification of the limbs occurs;
however, upon the birth of Brahmins, touching their bodies is prescribed. (I,2, p. 212) // Par_3.3 //
A Brahmin is purified by ten days, a Kṣatriya by twelve days, a Vaiśya by fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified by one month upon the birth [of a son]. (I,2, p. 213) // Par_3.4 //
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days; but one who is devoid of both is purified in ten days. (I,2, p. 215) // Par_3.5 //

One who has fallen away from his birth-rites and duties, who neglects the twilight prayers, and who is a Brahmin in name only, shall remain impure for ten days due to birth-impurity. (I,2, p. 217) // Par_3.6 //

But heirs who share a single funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), yet have separate wives and dwellings—for them, that period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) shall apply both at a birth and in the event of a death. (I,2, p. 219) // Par_3.7 //
That impurity (sūtaka) within the lineage ceases with the fourth generation through inheritance; or rather, it ends with the fifth person born of one's own family line. (I, 2, p. 221) // Par_3.8 //
In the fourth [generation], there should be ten nights; in the fifth for a male, six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, after three days. (I,2, p. 222) // Par_3.9 //

In the case of the death of Bhṛgu or Agni, as well as when one has died in a foreign land, or when a child has died, or in the case of one who has renounced the world (saṃnyasta), immediate purification is prescribed. (I,2, p. 223) // Par_3.10 //

If it is heard that someone who is a member of one's own lineage has died in another country, one should remain impure for three nights; otherwise, for a day and a night; or, having bathed immediately, one becomes pure. (I,2, p. 232) // Par_3.11 //
If a Brahmin who has gone to another country meets his death due to exhaustion or the passage of time, and the lunar day [of his passing] is not known, (I,2, p. 236) // Par_3.12 //
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight,
one should perform the offering of water, the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the ancestral rite (śrāddha).

For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb, there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water libations. (I.2, p. 237) // Par_3.14 //
If the fetus of a woman miscarries or is aborted, the period of impurity (sūtaka) lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had remained in the womb. (Parāśara-smṛti 3.15)
Until the fourth month there may be a miscarriage; in the fifth and sixth months, it is a "falling" [of the fetus].
Beyond that, it shall be a birth, and for ten days there shall be impurity due to childbirth (*sūtaka*). (I,2, p. 240) // Par_3.16 //
Upon the death of one whose teeth have emerged, one who has cut his first teeth, or one for whom the tonsure ceremony has been performed,
there shall be impurity for three nights during the cremation rites.
Immediate purification is prescribed until the eruption of teeth;
until the tonsure ceremony, it is considered to last for one night; until the initiation into the vows, three nights; and beyond that, ten nights. (I,2, p. 243) // Par_3.17 //

For those householders in whose home the student of sacred knowledge dwells and the sacrificial fire is offered, there shall be no birth-impurity, nor do they incur contact with such impurity. (I,2, p. 253) // Par_3.18 //
A Brahmin becomes impure through contact at birth as well as at death;
however, for one who has desisted from such contact, there is neither impurity from a corpse nor impurity from birth. (I,2, p. 254) // Par_3.19 //
Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, male and female slaves,
barbers, kings, and those learned in the Vedas are proclaimed to be pure immediately.

A twice-born man who observes his vows, is purified by the Sattra sacrifice, and maintains the sacred fires, incurs no impurity from the birth of a king, provided the monarch so desires. (I,2, p. 255) // Par_3.21 //
When a Brahmin who has been invited for a funeral rite or a gift is distressed,
the sages have observed that he becomes pure at that very moment through the passage of time.
But during childbirth, if no confusion of castes has occurred, the householder shall not perform [the full rites];
the mother becomes pure after ten days, while the father is purified by bathing. (I,2, p. 259) // Par_3.23 //
For all [relatives], there is impurity due to death; however, for the mother and father, there is impurity due to birth.
The impurity due to birth belongs to the mother alone; the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution.
If a twice-born man has sexual intercourse when his wife has given birth, he incurs the impurity of birth (sūtaka), even if the Brahmin is learned in the six Vedāṅgas. (I,2, p. 260) // Par_3.25 //
"Defilement arises from contact; indeed, there is no other defilement, O twice-born one.
Therefore, a wise man should avoid contact with every effort. (I,2, p. 261) // Par_3.26 //

However, during marriages, festivals, or sacrifices, if a death or birth-impurity occurs in the interim, there is no fault in giving away wealth that was previously intended for the purpose. (I.2, p. 262) // Par_3.27 //
If death or birth occurs again within the ten-day period, the Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that [second] period has not yet elapsed. (I,2, p. 263) // Par_3.28 //
For those who perish for the sake of a Brahmin, or likewise in the capture of prisoners of war, or for those who perish in battles, there is impurity for one night. (I, 2, p. 268) // Par_3.29 //
These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant disciplined in yoga, and the warrior slain while facing the enemy in battle.
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain, he attains imperishable worlds, provided that he does not speak like a coward. (I,2, p. 269) // Par_3.31 //
Upon seeing a Brahmin who has renounced the world, the sun moves from its place, thinking: "Having pierced my orb, this man shall proceed to the supreme station. (I,2, p. 270) // Par_3.32 //
But he who, when the armies are broken and fleeing in all directions, goes forth as their protector, shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice. (I,2, p. 271) // Par_3.33 //
But for that hero whose body is wounded by arrows, mallets, and clubs,
celestial maidens carry him away and delight him.
Thousands of celestial nymphs run forward in haste toward the hero slain in battle, each crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine! (I.2, p. 272).
Just as the Brahmins seeking heaven go there by means of hosts of sacrifices and asceticism,
so indeed do heroes go there in an instant by relinquishing their lives in a noble battle.
"By victory one gains fortune; even by dying, one obtains celestial maidens.
Since this body perishes in an instant, what anxiety can there be regarding death in battle? (I,2, p. 273) // Par_3.37 //
When blood flowing from the forehead enters the mouth in battle, it is indeed equal to the drinking of Soma; this is seen to be performed according to rule in the sacrifice of combat.
Those twice-born who carry the deceased Brahmin who is without a protector obtain, step by step in due order, the fruit of a sacrifice. (I,2, p. 274) // Par_3.39 //
For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any sin;
for them, immediate purification is ordained by immersion in water.

Having carried and cremated a member of the highest twice-born caste who is of a different lineage, unrelated by kinship, and deceased like a hungry ghost, one becomes pure through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (I, 2, p. 275) // Par_3.41 //

If one follows out of desire a deceased person—whether a kinsman or even a stranger—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. (I.2, p. 280) // Par_3.42 //
If a Brāhmaṇa follows a deceased Kṣatriya out of ignorance, he becomes impure for one day and is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (I, 2, p. 281) // Par_3.43 //
If a Brāhmaṇa follows the corpse of a Vaiśya out of ignorance, he shall observe impurity for two nights and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). (I.2, p. 282) // Par_3.44 //
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse while being carried away,
he shall remain impure for three nights.
When those three nights have passed, he goes to a river that flows into the ocean,
performs one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and by consuming clarified butter, he becomes purified.
When the Śūdras have been turned back and have reached the edge of the water, the twice-born should then follow them; this is the eternal law. (I, 2, p. 283) // Par_3.47 //
[Volume II, Part 1: The Section on Expiation (Prāyaścittakāṇḍa).
Whether out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or even fear—
Whether it be a woman or a man, one should hang oneself; this is the course prescribed. (II,1, p. 18) // Par_4.1 //
Filled with pus and blood, he sinks into blinding darkness;
for sixty thousand years, he falls into hell. (II,1, p. 19) // Par_4.2 //

One should not cause impurity, nor the offering of water, nor the lighting of fire, nor the shedding of tears; likewise, those who carry the body, those who provide the fire, and those who cut the bonds [should not perform these]. (II,1, p. 23) // Par_4.3 //

"Purification occurs through the Taptakṛcchra penance"—thus said Prajāpati regarding that which was killed by cows, as well as that which was hanged or slain by a Brāhmaṇa. (II,1, p. 25) // Par_4.4 //
But those Brahmins who touch [the corpse], those who carry it, those who provide the fire, others who follow as attendants, and those who cut the bonds; // Par_4.5 //
Having been purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, they should feed Brahmins and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin.
For three days one should drink warm water; for three days one should drink warm milk;
for three days one should drink warm clarified butter; and for three days one should subsist on air alone. (II,1, p. 26) // Par_4.7 //
One should drink six palas of water, three palas of milk, and one pala of clarified butter; this is prescribed as the Tapta-kṛcchra penance.

If a Brahmin should, unintentionally, associate with those who have fallen [from their caste] and others, he should observe a penance for five days, ten days, or even twelve days. (II,1, p. 27) // Par_4.9 //
Whether for half a month, one month, or even two months;
or for half a year, one year, or even beyond that, he remains equal to them.

In the first fortnight, one should fast for three nights; in the second, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance; and in the third fortnight, one should perform a *sāṃtapana-kṛcchra*. (II,1, p. 29) // Par_4.11 //
In the fourth [case], it should be a ten-night fast; in the fifth, a parāka is prescribed;
in the sixth, one should perform a cāndrāyaṇa; and in the seventh, two cāndrāyaṇas.

For the sake of purification, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six months during the eighth [period]; gold coins, equal in number to the fortnights, should also be given as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 30) // Par_4.13 //
But that woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband, goes to hell after death and becomes a widow again and again. (II,1, p. 33) // Par_4.14 //
He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of killing an embryo; of this there is no doubt.
She who despises her husband— whether he be poor, diseased, or foolish—
is born as a female dog after death, and again and again as a sow.
That woman who, while her husband is alive, observes a fast or undertakes a vow, takes away the lifespan of her husband; such a woman shall go to hell.
"And whatever vow a woman performs without having asked her husband, all of that goes to the Rākṣasas; thus Manu has declared. (II.1, p. 34) // Par_4.18 //
She who commits misconduct toward her kinsmen and relatives,
or she who causes an abortion— one should never speak with her at any time.
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin, that same sin is doubled in causing an abortion;
there can be no atonement for her, for her abandonment is ordained.
Neither by the domestic fire nor again by the Agnihotra sacrifice is any purpose accomplished for him who is averse to dharma; he indeed becomes a Cāṇḍāla in his actions.
If seed carried by the current of a flood sprouts in someone’s field, that owner of the field receives the crop; the owner of the seed does not deserve a share. (II,1, p. 42) // Par_4.22 //
In the same way, two types of sons born of another's wife are recorded as the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka:
the Kuṇḍa is one whose father is still living, while the Golaka is one whose husband is dead.

The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the given son, and the made son—whom the mother or the father may give away, that son becomes a "given" (dattaka) son. (II,1, p. 48) // Par_4.24 //
The elder brother who is superseded, the younger brother who supersedes him, and she by whom he is superseded—
all these go to hell, with the giver [of the bride] and the officiating priest as the fifth.
For the elder brother who marries before his younger brother, there are two *kṛcchra* penances; for the girl, a single *kṛcchra*;
for the giver, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*.
There is no fault in lamenting over those who are hunchbacked, dwarfs, eunuchs, those with stammering speech, the mentally dull, those born blind, the deaf, or the mute. (II,1, p. 51) // Par_4.27 //

There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] when the one being superseded is the son of a paternal uncle, the son of a co-wife, or the son of another man's wife, provided he is united with a wife and the sacred fires. (II,1, p. 52) // Par_4.28 //
As long as the elder brother remains, one should not perform the fire-consecration (ādhāna);
however, having obtained his permission, one may do so, according to the word of Śaṅkha.
"When her husband is lost, dead, has renounced the world, is impotent, or has fallen from his caste—under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. (II,1, p. 53) // Par_4.30 //
A woman who, upon the death of her husband, remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy,
attains heaven when she dies, just like those lifelong celibates.
As many hairs as there are on a human being—three and a half crores—for that long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven. (II,1, p. 54) // Par_4.32 //
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole, so too a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoices together with him. (II,1, p. 57) // Par_4.33 //

O best of the twice-born, that foremost of the twice-born who has been bitten by a wolf, a dog, a jackal, or similar animals, should bathe and recite the Gāyatrī, the purifier and mother of the Vedas. (II,1, p. 61) // Par_5.1 //
One bitten by a dog becomes pure by bathing with water from a cow's horns at the confluence of great rivers, or even by beholding the ocean.

If a twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies, knowledge, and vows is bitten by a dog, he becomes pure by bathing with water containing gold and consuming clarified butter. (II,1, p. 62) // Par_5.3 //
But he who, while observing a vow, has been bitten by a dog, should fast for three nights;
having drunk ghee and water infused with *kuśa* grass, he should complete the remainder of his vow.

Whether he be one who has failed to observe his vows or one who observes them, a twice-born man bitten by a dog becomes purified by prostrating himself and being gazed upon by Brahmins with their eyes.
For food that has been smelled by a dog, licked, or scratched with its claws,
it is prescribed that it be washed with water and singed over a fire.
But a Brāhmaṇī woman bitten by a dog, a jackal,
or a wolf becomes pure immediately upon seeing the risen planets and stars.
When the moon is not visible at all during the dark fortnight,
one should gaze toward whichever direction the moon has gone.
If the best of the twice-born is bitten by a dog in a village inhabited by those who are not Brahmins,
he becomes pure immediately by circumambulating a bull and bathing.
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is killed by a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapāka, cattle, or other Brahmins, or if he dies by poison or commits suicide; (II,1, p. 69) // Par_5.10 //
A Brahmin should burn that Brahmin in the world-fire (lokāgni) without the use of mantras;
this applies in every way to one who has touched, carried, or cremated [the corpse] among the sapinda relatives.
Thereafter, at the instruction of the Brahmins, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
the twice-born man should then take the burnt bones again and wash them with milk. (II,1, p. 70) // Par_5.12 //

Furthermore, one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) may, when departing on a journey impelled by time, cremate [the body] separately with his own independent fire. (II,1, p. 71) // Par_5.13 //
"O bulls among sages, listen now to the consecration of the *agnihotra* for the deceased, whose body has perished and whose fire remains in his house."
Having spread out a black antelope skin with *kuśa* grass arranged in the shape of a human being,
[he should place] seven hundred stalks of *palāśa* wood, including their bases.
One should place forty [beads] on the head, one hundred on the neck;
one should place one hundred on the two arms, and ten indeed on the fingers. (II,1, p. 72) // Par_5.16 //
One should apply one hundred [strokes] on the buttocks, two hundred on the abdomen,
eight on the testicles, and place five on the penis.
One should offer twenty-one [oblations] with the two thighs, two hundred with the knees and shanks, and six with the toes of the feet; thereafter, one should place the sacrificial vessel.
Having placed the *śamyā* upon the penis and the *araṇī* upon the testicles,
he should place the *juhū* in his right hand and the *upabhṛt* in his left.
One should place a mortar upon his ear, set a pestle upon his back,
cast a grinding stone upon his chest, and put rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds into his mouth.
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* water on the ears and the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthalī*) on the eyes;
one should then place pieces of gold in the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose.
One should deposit all the implements of the *agnihotra* there and offer a single oblation once, saying: "To this world of heaven, svāhā! (II,1, p. 73).
Whether it be the son, a brother, or even another relative,
the wise should perform the cremation rite exactly as prescribed.
One should perform such a rite as this; it is traditionally taught that one attains the world of Brahmā.
Those twice-born who cremate him indeed go to the supreme goal. (II,1, p. 74) // Par_5.24 //
Driven by their own deluded intellects, they perform actions in a contrary manner;
indeed, they become short-lived and fall into an impure hell.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the expiation for the killing of living beings, as previously declared by Parāśara and expanded upon in the *Manusmṛti*. (II,1, p. 77) // Par_6.1 //
By eating a curlew, a crane, a swan, a ruddy goose, a cock, a web-footed bird, or a śarabha, one is purified in a day and night. (II,1, p. 78) // Par_6.2 //
Whether it be a crane, a lapwing, a parrot, or even a pigeon, as well as one who kills snakes or crocodiles, is purified by eating only at night. (II,1, p. 79) // Par_6.3 //
One who kills wolves, crows, pigeons, peacocks, partridges, or hawks is purified by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) while submerged in water during both twilights. (II,1, p. 80) // Par_6.4 //
One who kills vultures, hawks, dogs, or owls, and eats uncooked food, shall remain standing during the day and subsist on air alone for three periods of time. (II,1, p. 81) // Par_6.5 //
One is purified from eating at night by [refraining from] the *valgu*, *guṇī*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, the *kokila*, the *khañjarīṭaka*, and birds with red wings such as the *lāvika*. (II,1, p. 82) // Par_6.6 //
Having killed a kāraṇḍava duck, a cakora partridge, a piṅgala bird, a kurara osprey, a bhāradvāja crane, or others, one becomes purified by worshipping Śiva. (II,1, p. 83) // Par_6.7 //
And for the bheruṇḍa, the blue jay, the hawk, the pigeon, and the francolin partridge—
for all such birds, there shall be a fast of one day and night.

Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a water-snake, one should feed the Brahmins *kṛsara* (rice and peas with sesame), and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 85) // Par_6.9 //
Likewise, having killed a porpoise, an iguana, a tortoise, or a porcupine, one is purified by fasting for a day and a night, provided one subsists on eggplant. (II,1, p. 87) // Par_6.10 //
One who kills a wolf, a jackal, a bear, a hyena, a dog, or a predator should give a *prastha* of sesame seeds to a twice-born man and subsist on air for three days. (II,1, p. 89) // Par_6.11 //
For the killing of an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, or a camel,
the penance is a fast for a day and night and bathing at the three junctions of the day.
By killing a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger, one is purified in three nights by means of libations to the Brahmins. (II,1, p. 91) // Par_6.13 //
A killer of deer, female deer, boars, sheep, or goats, having fasted for a day and a night, shall eat food grown without the use of a plow. (II,1, p. 92) // Par_6.14 //
In this manner, having stayed for a day and night, he should remain among all four-footed forest-dwellers; indeed, he should recite the Jātavedas hymns. (II,1, p. 93) // Par_6.15 //
He who causes the death of an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman,
shall perform two Prājāpatya penances and give a bull as the eleventh among ten cows as a sacrificial fee.
Whoever should strike a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya who is innocent must perform two Kṛcchra penances and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 95) // Par_6.17 //

Having killed a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who is devoted to ritual acts, or a most excellent twice-born man who stands in improper action, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give thirty cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 105) // Par_6.18 //
If someone has killed a Caṇḍāla in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 106) // Par_6.19 //
Whether it be a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or anyone else,
when the death penalty for killing a Caṇḍāla has been incurred, one is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance.

If a thief, a dog-cooker, or a Caṇḍāla is struck by a Brāhmaṇa, he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (II,1, p. 107) // Par_6.21 //
If a Brahmin converses with a dog-cooker or even a Caṇḍāla, he should perform conversation with the divine waters and mutter the Sāvitrī once. (II,1, p. 108) // Par_6.22 //
If one has slept together with Caṇḍālas, one should fast for three nights;
having traveled along a path used exclusively by Caṇḍālas, one becomes pure by recollecting the Gāyatrī.
Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should immediately look at the sun;
upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. (II,1, p. 109) // Par_6.24 //
If an elder brother drinks water from wells or ponds dug by Caṇḍālas out of ignorance, he becomes pure after one day and night of eating only a single meal. (II,1, p. 111) // Par_6.25 //
Having drunk water from a well that has been touched by a Caṇḍāla’s vessel, one attains purification after three nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel. (II,1, p. 112) // Par_6.26 //
If a twice-born man drinks water that has been contained in a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla,
he should perform a Prājāpatya penance if he discharges it at that very moment.
If one does not discharge water [from the penis] and yet his body undergoes digestion [of semen], the Prājāpatya penance should not be given; he should instead perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
A Brahmin shall perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; a Kṣatriya, the *prājāpatya*;
a Vaiśya shall perform half of that, and a Śūdra shall perform a quarter of it. (II,1, p. 113) // Par_6.29 //

If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk contained in a vessel belonging to the lowest castes, [he must perform penance]. (II,1, p. 114) // Par_6.30 //
For the twice-born, expiation is achieved through the Brahmakūrca fast;
for a Śūdra, it is through fasting as well as by giving gifts according to his capacity.

If a most excellent twice-born man should somehow eat the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance, he becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow's urine and barley gruel. (II,1, p. 115) // Par_6.32 //
One should eat each mouthful of cow-urine and barley-gruel; for one who remains under this restraint for ten days, that is designated as the vow. (II,1, p. 116) // Par_6.33 //
But where a Caṇḍāla remains in a house unrecognized, O twice-born ones, once he is known, the twice-born show favor to one who has become purified. (II,1, p. 118) // Par_6.34 //
Those who have mastered the Vedas and know the Dharma, singing the teachings issued from the mouth of the Sage,
shall rescue him as he falls from the mixture of sin.
He should eat barley-gruel with curds, ghee, milk, and cow urine; and he should perform ablutions at all three junctions of the day. (II,1, p. 119) // Par_6.36 //
For three days one should eat with curd, for three days one should eat with clarified butter,
and for three days one should eat with milk— each for a period of three days.
One should not eat food that is defiled by intention, nor that which is left over, nor that which is infested with worms;
[one may consume] three palas of curd and milk, and one pala of ghee. (II,1, p. 120) // Par_6.38 //
The purification of both copper and bell-metal is achieved by means of ash;
that of garments by washing with water; and that of earthenware by discarding it.
Having placed safflower, jaggery, cotton, salt, oil,
and clarified butter at the door, one should place grains and fire within the house.
Having thus become purified, he should thereafter perform the satiation of the Brahmins;
he should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins. (II,1, p. 121) // Par_6.41 //
Furthermore, it is purified by smearing, digging, fire-offerings, and recitations;
and for Brahmins who provide the foundation, no defect of the ground exists.
If one has contact with Caṇḍālas for a month or even half a month, one becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow's urine and barley gruel. (II,1, p. 122) // Par_6.43 //
A washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter, and a basket-maker may dwell unrecognized in the house of one belonging to the four castes. (II,1, p. 123) // Par_6.44 //
Having ascertained [the nature of the offense], one should perform atonement; specifically, one should do only half of what was previously prescribed.
One should not set fire to the house, but should carry out all the rest. (II,1, p. 124) // Par_6.45 //
If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone's house,
he must be expelled from that dwelling, and one should discard the earthenware vessels.
One should never discard a vessel that is full of liquid;
likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
If a worm should arise in the opening of a wound of a Brāhmaṇa where pus and blood have formed, what would be the expiation for that? (II,1, p. 126) // Par_6.48 //
By bathing and drinking cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk,
and clarified butter for three days, one who has been defiled by worms becomes pure.
A Kṣatriya, having given five māṣas of gold,
should likewise prescribe a cow as the sacrificial fee for a Vaiśya, along with a fast.
For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts. "It is flawless," so say the gods of the earth. (II,1, p. 127) // Par_6.51 //

Having bowed with one's head, that [gift] should indeed be accepted, for it yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; it fills whatever gap there may be in recitation, whatever gap in austerity, and whatever gap in the performance of sacrificial rites. (II,1, p. 128) // Par_6.52 //
Everything provided by the Brahmins becomes flawless,
even in times of disease, calamity, exhaustion, famine, or likewise during a violent upheaval.
Fasting, vows, and burnt offerings are indeed accomplished by means of the twice-born;
or rather, when the Brahmins are satisfied, they bestow grace for everything. (II,1, p. 129) // Par_6.54 //
One obtains all desires here through those things provided by the twice-born; likewise, favor toward the weak, as well as toward children and the elderly, is prescribed. (II,1, p. 130) // Par_6.55 //
Otherwise, a fault would arise; therefore, it is not considered a favor.
Whether out of affection, or greed, or fear, or even from ignorance— (II,1, p. 131) // Par_6.56 //
But those who show favor [to such a person], that sin goes to them;
for those who, when the end of the body has arrived, speak [only] of religious observances, (II,1, p. 132) // Par_6.57 //
One who is healthy should never neglect his duties due to the obstruction of great tasks;
those fools who do so for one who is healthy speak what is contrary to the rule. (II,1, p. 133) // Par_6.58 //
Those who create obstacles for him fall into a foul hell—
he who, having himself undertaken a vow, treats a Brahmin with contempt.
His fast would be in vain, and he would not be joined with merit;
that very rule alone is to be accepted if even a single twice-born man should say so. (II,1, p. 134) // Par_6.60 //
One should obey the word of the twice-born; otherwise, one becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
For Brāhmaṇas are a moving sacred ford (tīrtha), and the virtuous are indeed the very embodiment of sacred fords.
By the water of their words alone, defiled people are purified; whatever the Brahmins speak, the gods consider that to be authoritative. (II,1, p. 135) // Par_6.62 //
A Brahmin embodies all the gods; his word is never otherwise.
Fasting, vows, ritual bathing, pilgrimage, recitation, and austerity [all depend upon him]. (II,1, p. 136) // Par_6.63 //
The fruit belongs entirely to him for whom [the rite] has been properly performed by the Brahmins.
When food is infested with insects or defiled by flies and hair, [it must be purified].
If one should touch water during that interval, one should touch that food with ashes;
and the Brahmin who, while eating, touches his foot with his hand [should likewise do so].
He eats his own leftovers from the hand when the vessel has been set aside;
he should not eat while standing on sandals, nor even while seated upon a couch. (II,1, p. 138) // Par_6.66 //
One should avoid eating food seen by a dog or a caṇḍāla; likewise, one should observe the rules regarding prohibited food and the purification of food.
"Just as it was stated by Parāśara, so do I speak to you:
food cooked from a droṇa or an āḍhaka measure that has been defiled by crows or dogs. (II,1, p. 139) // Par_6.68 //
One should inform the Brahmins as to how this [food] may be purified;
however, one should not discard a *droṇa* measure of food that has been licked by a crow or a dog. (II,1, p. 140) // Par_6.69 //
By Brahmins learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) and observers of the Dharmaśāstras,
thirty-two prasthas are known as a droṇa, and two prasthas are remembered as an āḍhaka.

Therefore, those who know the Śruti and Smṛti understand that food from a droṇa or an āḍhaka measure is pure, even if it has been licked by crows or dogs, or smelled by a cow or a donkey. (II,1, p. 141) // Par_6.71 //

A Brahmin should discard even a small amount of food; purification occurs when the quantity is one *droṇa* or one *āḍhaka*. One should remove from the food that portion which has been touched by saliva. (II,1, p. 142) // Par_6.72 //
Having sprinkled it with golden water, one should heat it with fire;
thus it is touched by both fire and golden water.
By the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins, food becomes pure at that very moment;
but how can there be purification for oil or even cow’s milk in such a case? (II,1, p. 144) // Par_6.74 //
In that case, one should discard a small portion by means of purifying the oil;
the purification of cow's milk is prescribed by means of the flame of fire.

**Purification of Substances:** Now, therefore, follows the purification of substances according to the words of Parāśara: "The purification of wooden vessels is held to be by planing. (II.1, p. 147) Parāśara-smṛti 7.1.
Bell-metal is purified by ashes; copper is purified by acid; a woman is purified by her menses, provided she does not have intercourse during her period. (II,1, p. 150) // Par_7.2 //
A river is purified by its current provided that no pollution is visible; but how is it when step-wells, wells, or tanks have been defiled in any way? (II,1, p. 153) // Par_7.3 //
Having indeed drawn out a hundred jars [of water], one is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
A girl of eight years is *Gaurī*, while one of nine years is *Rohiṇī*.
A girl becomes a maiden at ten years of age, and beyond that, she is menstruating;
however, when the twelfth year has arrived, he who does not give away his daughter [is at fault]. (II,1, p. 157) // Par_7.5 //
Month after month, her own fathers—the mother, the father, and likewise the eldest brother—drink her menstrual blood themselves. (II,1, p. 158) // Par_7.6 //
Three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses:
he who would marry such a girl, and the Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by passion, weds her.

For that Brahmin who, being twice-born, indulges in the company of a *vṛṣalī* for even a single night is unfit to be spoken with and excluded from the ritual row (*apāṅkteya*). (II,1, p. 159) // Par_7.8 //
Eating only almsfood and reciting prayers constantly, he is purified in three years;
even when the sun has set, [he is purified by avoiding] a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or a woman.
And for one who touches a woman who has recently given birth, how is purification ordained?
By looking at fire, gold, and the path of the moon.

And having bathed with the permission of Brāhmaṇas, she becomes pure; likewise, if two Brāhmaṇa women who are menstruating touch one another, [they become pure by bathing]. (II,1, p. 160) // Par_7.11 //
She should remain without food for that long; she becomes pure after three nights if a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman, both in their courses, touch one another, the former shall perform half a *kṛcchra* penance and the latter one quarter.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another, the former shall perform three-quarters of the penance, and the latter one-quarter.
A Śūdra woman is purified by a penance with difficulty; she is purified by a gift.
A menstruating woman who has bathed becomes pure on the fourth day. (II,1, p. 164) // Par_7.15 //
One should perform rites for the gods, ancestors, and so forth upon the cessation of the menstrual flow;
however, that flow which occurs daily in women due to illness [is not subject to this restriction]. (II,1, p. 165) // Par_7.16 //
Therefore, she is not impure because of that; thus, it is considered that [the period] lasts for one day and night.
As long as the flow of blood continues, she shall not be of virtuous conduct. (II,1, p. 168) // Par_7.17 //
Indeed, when her menses have ceased, a woman may be approached for domestic duties;
however, on the first day she is like a Caṇḍālī, and on the second day she is like a slayer of a Brahmin.
On the third day she is called a washerwoman, and on the fourth day she becomes pure;
however, when an impurity arises due to illness, one who is not ill must bathe ten times.

A twice-born man who has been touched by someone who is impure due to having eaten leftovers, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra, shall become pure by bathing again and again until he touches this [water]. (II,1, p. 170) // Par_7.20 //
Having fasted for one night, he is purified by means of the five products of the cow;
upon being touched by a Śūdra who is not rendered impure by food remnants, bathing is prescribed. (II,1, p. 171) // Par_7.21 //
If one is touched by the leavings of another, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance;
bell-metal that has not been smeared by liquor is purified by ashes. (II,1, p. 172) // Par_7.22 //

Vessels made of bell-metal that have been touched by even a trace of liquor are purified by scrubbing with fire and stones; likewise those smelled by a cow or defiled by dogs and crows. (II,1, p. 172) // Par_7.23 //

Those items that have been defiled by the remnants of a Śūdra's meal, as well as those used for rinsing the mouth or washing the feet in a bronze vessel, are purified by ten applications of alkaline substances.
Having buried [the iron] in the ground for six months, one should extract it and bring it back;
this is the purification of iron items and lead in fire. (II,1, p. 173) // Par_7.25 //
One should wash with water ivory, bone, beeswax, silver, golden vessels, and bowls made of gems or stone. (II,1, p. 174) // Par_7.26 //
Furthermore, rubbing on a stone is declared to be the purification for [stone vessels];
for earthenware, purification is by burning; and for grains, it is also by winnowing. (II,1, p. 176) // Par_7.27 //
The purification of bamboo, bark, rags, linen, cotton garments, and woolen or net-like cloths is held to be achieved by sprinkling water. (II,1, p. 179) // Par_7.28 //
