For items made of muñja grass, equipment, winnowing baskets, hemp, fruits, hides, straw, wood, and ropes, sprinkling with water is prescribed. (II,1, p. 181) // Par_7.29 //
Cushions made of wool and the like, as well as red garments and similar items, attain purity by being dried in the sun and then sprinkled with water. (II,1, p. 184) // Par_7.30 //

Manu has declared that cats, flies, insects, moths, worms, and frogs do not cause one to become *ucchiṣṭa* (rendered impure by food remnants), even though they touch both pure and impure things. (II.1, p. 185) // Par_7.31 //

Manu has declared that water which has reached the ground, as well as mutual droplets [from the mouth], food remnants, and oily substances, do not constitute *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants of a meal). (II.1, p. 186) // Par_7.32 //

According to the law, they know that there is no such thing as "leavings" (ucchiṣṭa) in the case of betel, sugarcane, fruit, anointing with oil after a meal, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the Soma juice.
Roads, mud, water, boats, paths, and grass,
as well as structures built of baked bricks, are purified by wind and the sun.
An unbroken stream [of water], dust raised by the wind, women, the elderly, and children—these are never considered defiled. (II,1, p. 188) // Par_7.35 //

In the event of the ruin of one's country, during exile, or even amidst diseases and calamities, one should certainly protect one’s own body and so forth; thereafter, one should practice the Dharma. (II,1, p. 196) // Par_7.36 //
By whatever means possible, whether gentle or harsh, one should rescue oneself from distress; once capable, one should practice the Dharma. (II,1, p. 197) // Par_7.37 //
But once the time of calamity has passed, one should attend to the rules of purity and conduct;
having subsequently established purification, being restored to health, one should practice the Dharma.
If death should occur among cattle through their tethering ropes unintentionally, what expiation shall there be for a sin committed unintentionally? (II,1, p. 199) // Par_8.1 //

One should confess one's own sin to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who understand the treatises on Dharma, and who are devoted to their own duties. (II,1, p. 205) // Par_8.2 //

Those Brahmins who, out of ignorance, perform agriculture while neglecting the Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī, the twilight devotions, and the fire-rituals, are merely bearers of the name. (II,1, p. 207) // Par_8.3 //
Even if thousands of those who lack vows, lack mantras, and subsist on mere birth should assemble together, they do not possess the status of an assembly (*pariṣad*). (II,1, p. 209) // Par_8.4 //
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, proclaim—that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it. (II,1, p. 210) // Par_8.5 //
He who prescribes an expiation without having studied the treatises on Dharma becomes purified by that very act of expiation, while the guilt falls upon the assembly.
Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas may declare, that should be known as Dharma, and not that which is proclaimed by thousands of others. (II,1, p. 212) // Par_8.7 //
Evil recoils from those who proclaim the Dharma while seeking the path of valid cognition, for they speak of qualities that truly exist.
Just as water situated within a stone is purified by wind and sun, so too shall his evil deed be destroyed through the command of the assembly. (II,1, p. 213) // Par_8.9 //
It goes neither to the doer nor to the assembly;
through contact with wind, the sun, and so forth, evil perishes like water. (II,1, p. 214) // Par_8.10 //
Whether they be four or even three Brahmins who possess knowledge of the Vedas, maintain the sacred fires, and are capable, that assembly is so designated. (II,1, p. 215) // Par_8.11 //
Those others who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet are masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences—
whether five or three— who are knowers of the Dharma, are proclaimed to be an assembly (pariṣad).
Even a single person who is a sage, a knower of the self, a twice-born man who performs sacrifices, and one who has been initiated into the Vedic vows, may constitute an assembly.
Five [types of assemblies] were previously mentioned by me; in their absence, there are three:
that assembly which is proclaimed as being satisfied with its own livelihood is one such.
But beyond this, those Brahmins who are merely bearers of the name do not possess the status of an assembly, even if they number in the thousands. (II,1, p. 218) // Par_8.15 //
Just as an elephant made of wood, or a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.

Just as a village site is empty, just as a well is without water, and just as an oblation offered where there is no fire, so too is a Brahmin who lacks the sacred mantras. (II,1, p. 219) // Par_8.17 //

Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a saline field is fruitless [for cultivation], and just as a gift given to an ignorant person is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. (II,1, p. 220) // Par_8.18 //
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by means of many parts, so too is brahminhood [realized] through consecrations preceded by mantras. (II,1, p. 221) // Par_8.19 //
Those twice-born ones who merely bear the name and prescribe penances—
those twice-born ones of sinful deeds went together to hell.

Those twice-born who recite the Veda and those who are devoted to the five sacrifices—they rescue the three worlds, even if they are attached to the pleasures of the five senses. (II,1, p. 222) // Par_8.21 //
Just as a consecrated fire blazing in cremation grounds is a consumer of all things, so too is a Brahmin learned in the Vedas a deity, even if he consumes all things. (II,1, p. 224) // Par_8.22 //
Just as all impurities are cast into water, so too should one cast all sin into the fire of the twice-born. (II,1, p. 227) // Par_8.23 //
A Brahmin devoid of the Gāyatrī becomes more impure even than a Śūdra;
those twice-born ones who know the true essence of the Gāyatrī-Brahman are honored by people.
Even a twice-born man of immoral conduct is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses.
Who would abandon a wicked cow to milk a well-behaved she-ass? (II,1, p. 228) // Par_8.25 //

The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas, whatever they may declare—even in jest—that is remembered as the supreme Dharma. (II,1, p. 229) // Par_8.26 //

One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), a reciter of the Dharma, and the three principal stages of life—this assembly consists of at least ten members. (II,1, p. 230) // Par_8.27 //
Abiding by the king's consent, one should prescribe the penance;
it must not be performed by oneself alone, but a small expiation should be carried out [under his authority]. (II,1, p. 232) // Par_8.28 //
Whatever sin a king commits by overstepping those Brahmins in what he desires to do, that sin becomes tenfold and follows after the king. (II,1, p. 233) // Par_8.29 //
One should always offer an expiation in front of a deity’s shrine;
then, having performed the *ātmakṛcchra* penance, one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas (*vedamātṛ*).
Having shaved his head together with the top-knot, he should bathe at the three junctions of the day;
he should dwell among cows at night and follow after them during the day. (II,1, p. 237) // Par_8.31 //

Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (II,1, p. 238) // Par_8.32 //
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not speak of a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor of a calf drinking.
One should drink water when they are drinking, and lie down when they are lying down;
one should rescue with all one's strength a woman who has fallen or is mired in the mud. (II,1, p. 239) // Par_8.34 //
He who would sacrifice his life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin; he is a protector of both the cow and the Brahmin.
One should prescribe a Prājāpatya penance in accordance with the killing of a cow;
one should then divide that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra into four types. (II,1, p. 240) // Par_8.36 //
For one day he ate a single meal, for one day he ate only at night;
for one day he ate what was unasked for, and for one day he subsisted on air alone.
For two days he should eat but one meal a day, for two days he should take a single meal;
for two days he should be one who does not beg, and for two days he should subsist on air alone.
For three days he should eat a single meal a day, for three days he should eat only at night,
for three days he should not beg for food, and for three days he should subsist on air alone.

For four days he should eat a single meal [a day], for four days he should eat only at night; for four days he should not beg for food, and for four days he should subsist on air alone. (II,1, p. 241) // Par_8.40 //
Then, when the penance has been performed, he should provide a feast for Brahmins;
he should give sacrificial fees to the Brahmins and the twice-born man should recite purificatory prayers.
But having fed the Brahmins, the cow-killer is purified; of this there is no doubt.
For the sake of protecting cattle, one does not incur sin through their confinement or tethering;
however, one should not consider the killing of them as such, distinguishing between whether it was done intentionally or unintentionally. (II,1, p. 255) // Par_9.1 //
If one should cause [a cow] to fall by means other than a staff after it has been struck, then the penance prescribed for killing a cow must be performed twice. (II,1, p. 256) // Par_9.2 //
Imprisonment, confinement, the yoking of cattle, and execution constitute the fourfold [set of punishments].
For imprisonment, one should perform one quarter of the penance; for confinement, two quarters. (II,1, p. 257) // Par_9.3 //
If [a cow] falls while being tied with a rope, the penance shall be one-quarter less;
however, if it falls in a cow-pen, in a house, in a difficult terrain, or on uneven ground, he must perform the entire penance. (II,1, p. 258) // Par_9.4 //

Furthermore, when cows die in rivers, in the oceans, or in other places—provided they are not at the mouth of a river—and in a scorched region, this is called *stambhana* (obstruction) due to the blocking [of the flow]. (II,1, p. 259) // Par_9.5 //
If a cow, whether in the house or in the forest, should die while bound with a tethering rope, a halter, or ornaments such as necklaces and trinkets; ||| Par_9.6 |||

One should know that very thing to be bondage, whether it be caused by desire or lack of desire; such as when one is oppressed by men with a plow, a cart, a line [of oxen], or on their back. (II,1, p. 260) // Par_9.7 //
The master of cattle incurs death; the yoke-strap is his slaughter.
Whether intoxicated, heedless, insane, conscious, or unconscious—(II,1, p. 261) // Par_9.8 //
One who has been provoked to anger by desire or by lack of desire may strike with sticks or even with stones;
whether they are struck or die, that indeed is the cause of their downfall.
"Thick as a thumb and measuring a cubit in length, moist and with its leaves intact—this is called a staff. (II,1, p. 262) // Par_9.10 //
Whether he has fainted and fallen, or has been struck by a staff,
when he rises and walks five, seven, or ten paces, [he is purified].
If he should take a morsel of food or even drink water, provided he was previously afflicted by disease, no expiation is required. (II,1, p. 263) // Par_9.12 //

Having killed an insentient embryo while it is still in the form of a mass, one-fourth of the penance is prescribed; if it is in the stage of a distinct shape, two-fourths; and if it has reached the stage of a fully formed fetus, three-fourths of the vow is ordained.
For an offense involving one-quarter [of a limb], there is the shaving of the body hair; for two-quarters, also the beard;
for three-quarters, everything except the top-knot; but for a fatal blow, including the top-knot. (II,1, p. 264) // Par_9.14 //
For one-fourth [of the penance], a pair of garments; for one-half, a bronze vessel;
for three-quarters, one should give a bull; and for the fourth part, two cows are prescribed.

But if he is seen with all his limbs fully formed and endowed with consciousness, complete in every major and minor limb, he shall perform the cow-vow (govrata) twice over. (II,1, p. 265) // Par_9.16 //
If one strikes cows with a stone or a staff, he shall perform one quarter-penance (*pāda*) for breaking a horn, and two quarters for injuring an eye. (II,1, p. 266) // Par_9.17 //

For striking the tail, one should perform a quarter-penance; for breaking a bone, two quarters; for striking the ear, three quarters; and for causing its fall, one should perform the entire penance. (II,1, p. 267) // Par_9.18 //
In the case of a broken horn, a broken bone, or likewise a broken hip, if he lives for six months, no penance is prescribed. (II,1, p. 268) // Par_9.19 //
When the wound has been treated, an oil massage with the hand should be performed,
and fodder should be provided until he has regained his full strength.
As long as all its limbs are complete, so long should a man nourish it; having bowed before a Brāhmaṇa in the form of a cow, he should release it. (II,1, p. 269) // Par_9.21 //
If his body were incomplete in its limbs and thus deficient in form,
then one should prescribe an expiation for that cow-slayer on his behalf.
One who, being arrogant, violently kills a cow with wood, clods of earth, stones, or even a weapon—for him, one should prescribe purification. (II,1, p. 270) // Par_9.23 //
If he strikes with a wooden stick, he should perform the Sāṃtapana penance; if with a clod of earth, the Prājāpatya;
if with a stone, the Taptakṛcchra; and if with a weapon, the Atikṛcchra.
In the *saṃtapanakṛcchra* there are five cows; likewise, three in the *prājāpatya*;
in the *taptakṛcchra* there are eight, and thirteen in the *atikṛcchra*.
In the case of killing living beings, one should give an equivalent [animal] as restitution, or its corresponding value; thus Manu has declared.

Except for branding and marking, as well as for the purpose of transport and release, and for the sake of protection in the evening, there is no fault in confining or tethering [the animal]. (II,1, p. 271) // Par_9.27 //

In cases of excessive burning, excessive carrying, as well as piercing the nose, or transporting [the animal] across rivers and mountains, one should prescribe an expiation. (II,1, p. 272) // Par_9.28 //

In the case of excessive burning, one should perform a quarter-penance; for carrying [the load], one should perform two quarters; for piercing the nose, one should perform three-quarters; but for killing, one should perform the entire penance.
But from being burned, a draft ox yoked to the harness perishes;
for it has been stated by Parāśara himself according to the rule: "One foot [of the penance], as prescribed" (II,1, p. 273). // Par_9.30 //
Confinement, bondage, the imposition of a burden, striking, driving through difficult terrain, and the use of a yoke— these are the six causes of death.
If a cow or beast dies while its limbs are well-secured by a tethering rope within the house, the owner shall be considered guilty; he deserves half the penance. (II,1, p. 274) // Par_9.32 //

Cows should not be tied with coir ropes, nor with hempen cords, nor even with those made of muñja grass, nor with fetters of bark; even when they have been tied, one should remain standing there holding an axe.
Parivāra 9.33.
One should bind the sacrificial animal facing south with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass.
There is no expiation for [the animal] burnt by fire that has become entangled in the ropes. (II,1, p. 276) // Par_9.34 //
If there should be wood in that place, what would be the expiation?
By reciting the purifying Goddess, one is released from that sin.

By driving [cattle] into wells or ponds, by causing them to fall into the felling of trees, or by selling them as fodder for oxen, one thereby incurs the sin of killing a cow. (II,1, p. 277) // Par_9.36 //
But when someone who has been won over should become separated from his rank—
his hearing and heart divided, or plunged into the peril of a pit— then [one must act].
If he dies there from climbing out of a well, or if his neck or feet are broken,
one should perform three-fourths of the penance.
There is no expiation for those who perish in the excavation of a well, in the embankment of a tank, in the damming of a river, or at water-stations (prapās), provided they died while in the water.
In the case of digging a well, a pond, or a large trench, as well as in other such meritorious excavations, no expiation is required. (II,1, p. 279) // Par_9.40 //
For a man who desires to dig a pit at the door of a house or within his dwellings— for such pits dug for one's own purposes or for the house— one should prescribe an expiation.
For those imprisoned at night, those killed by snakes or tigers, and those perished by fire or lightning, no expiation is prescribed. (II,1, p. 280) // Par_9.42 //
In the case of those killed by a shower of arrows during a village raid, by the collapse of a house, or by excessive rain, no penance is prescribed. (II,1, p. 281) // Par_9.43 //
For those killed in battle, or those who have perished in fires within their homes, or in forest fires and village destructions, no expiation is prescribed. (II,1, p. 282) // Par_9.44 //
If a cow is restrained for the purpose of medical treatment or to deliver a dead fetus,
and she dies despite efforts being made, no expiation is required.
One should prescribe an expiation for the death of many people, or for their imprisonment or confinement, as well as for a physician's improper treatment. (II,1, p. 284) // Par_9.46 //
And in the event of a calamity involving bulls, as many people as are present as spectators shall incur sin, provided they do not attempt to prevent it. (II,1, p. 285) // Par_9.47 //

When one man is killed by many acting together, and it is not known whose blow caused his death, the slayer must be discovered through divine means and turned back by those appointed by the king. (II,1, p. 286) // Par_9.48 //
If some single person is killed by many through fate,
they shall each perform a quarter of that killing individually.
If blood is seen, it indicates hatred; if one is afflicted by disease, it indicates emaciation;
if saliva is present in those bitten, such is the manner of investigation.
"Even when urged for the sake of food, he does not go on a journey;
thus it was stated by Manu alone, who knew all the scriptures. (II.1, p. 288) // Par_9.51 //
However, the expiation prescribed by him is that the killer of a cow shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
for the sake of preserving his hair, he shall perform double the vow. (II,1, p. 290) // Par_9.52 //
When a vow is prescribed as being twofold, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be twofold;
whether it be a king, a prince, or a Brāhmaṇa deeply learned in the Vedas.
Without performing the shaving, one should prescribe an expiation for him:
having pulled out all the hair, one should cut off two finger-breadths. (II,1, p. 291) // Par_9.54 //
Thus, for women and young girls, shaving the head is prescribed;
however, for a woman, there is no shaving of the hair, nor staying at a distance, nor sleeping on the ground. (II,1, p. 292) // Par_9.55 //
He should not stay in the cow-pen at night, nor should he follow the cows by day,
especially at river confluences and in the forests.
Women should not wear deerskin as clothing; rather, they should observe their vows alone.
It is said that they should bathe at the three junctions of the day and likewise perform the worship of the gods. (II,1, p. 293) // Par_9.57 //
In the midst of their kinsmen, they should observe vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa;
remaining constantly at home, they should remain pure and practice self-restraint.
In this world, he who, having committed the slaughter of a cow, desires to conceal it, goes without doubt to the terrible hell known as Kālasūtra. (II,1, p. 294) // Par_9.59 //
Released from that hell,
that man is born in the world of mortals for seven births as one who is impotent, miserable, and afflicted with leprosy.
Therefore, one should disclose one's sin and constantly practice one's own duty;
one should avoid excessive anger toward women, children, servants, cows, and Brahmins.

I shall declare the beneficial expiation for all the four castes; for purification after approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (II,1, p. 297) // Par_10.1 //
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (II,1, p. 298) // Par_10.2 //
One should indeed determine the size of a morsel to be equal to a hen’s egg;
otherwise, due to the fault of improper disposition, there is neither dharma nor purification. (II,1, p. 304) // Par_10.3 //

Once the penance has been performed, one should then provide a meal for Brahmins; one should give two cows and a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins. (II,1, p. 305) // Par_10.4 //
If a twice-born man approaches a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī,
he shall fast for three nights according to the instruction of the Brahmins.

Having allowed his hair-lock to be blown away by the wind, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances; he should give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee—thus Pārāśara has declared purification. (II,1, p. 306) // Par_10.6 //
If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should have sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman,
he should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give away two pairs of cattle.
If a Śūdra has sexual intercourse with a Śvapākī or a Caṇḍālī,
he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance and give four pairs of cattle as a gift.
If one should approach his mother, or likewise his sister or his own daughter, having approached these out of delusion, he shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (II,1, p. 311) // Par_10.9 //

One should perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; one is purified by the cutting off of the penis. Likewise, for sexual intercourse with a mother’s sister, there is the excision of one's own member. (II,1, p. 316) // Par_10.10 //
But he who should approach [her] out of ignorance shall perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances and give ten pairs of cattle; Pārāśara has declared this to be purification. (II,1, p. 317) // Par_10.11 //
Having approached the wife of his father, the sister of his mother’s kinsman, the wife of his teacher, his daughter-in-law, and likewise the wife of his brother; (II,1, p. 319) // Par_10.12 //

If one approaches the wife of a maternal uncle or a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā), one should perform three Prājāpatya penances; one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and one is purified—of this there is no doubt.
Having approached female animals for sexual intercourse—such as a buffalo, a camel, a monkey, a she-ass, or a sow—one should perform the Prājāpatya vow. (II,1, p. 339) // Par_10.14 //

One who has had intercourse with a cow is purified by three nights if he gives a single cow to a Brāhmaṇa; however, one who has had intercourse with a female buffalo, a camel, a she-ass, or a female sheep is purified by a day and a night. (II,1, p. 342) // Par_10.15 //
In a riot or in battle, during a famine or a massacre of people,
or when captured as a prisoner or afflicted by fear, one should always look upon one's own wife.
If a woman maintains contact with Caṇḍālas, she should then make ten excellent Brahmins witnesses and confess her own transgression. (II,1, p. 343) // Par_10.17 //
Standing in a pit reaching up to her neck, filled with cow-dung, water, and mud,
she should remain there without food and emerge after a full day and night.
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should eat barley-rice;
having fasted for three nights, he should dwell in water for one night.
Having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper,
along with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should drink the water.
Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
as long as she observes that vow, she shall dwell outside [the community]. (II,1, p. 344) // Par_10.21 //
Once the penance has been performed, one should provide a feast for Brāhmaṇas; Pārāśara declared that purity is attained by giving two cows as a sacrificial fee. (II,1, p. 345) // Par_10.22 //
For women of the four castes, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa vows [are prescribed].
As is the earth, so is a woman; therefore, one should not defile her. (II,1, p. 346) // Par_10.23 //

If a woman has been enjoyed by a robber who has killed and bound her by force out of fear, she is purified by performing the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance; so said Pārāśara. (II,1, p. 347) // Par_10.24 //
If a woman has been enjoyed but once by those of evil deeds against her will,
she shall be purified by the Prājāpatya penance and by the flow of menses.
Half of the body of that man whose wife drinks liquor falls away;
for one whose half-body has fallen away, no atonement is prescribed. (II,1, p. 349) // Par_10.26 //

While muttering the Gāyatrī, one should perform the Sāṃtapanakṛccha penance, consisting of cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with Kuśa grass. (II,1, p. 351) // Par_10.27 //
A fast for one night is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance.
[If she] should conceive a child by a paramour when her husband is dead, missing, or has departed [abroad], (II,1, p. 352).

Others should abandon that woman in another kingdom, for she is fallen and a doer of evil; but when a Brāhmaṇa woman goes forth united with another man, [she must be abandoned]. (II,1, p. 354) // Par_10.29 //
She who, out of delusion and lust, departs having abandoned her kinsmen, children, and husband, is declared lost; there is no returning for her again. (II,1, p. 356) // Par_10.30 //
But she is lost in the next world, especially among human beings— this woman who has fallen into intoxication and delusion, and who was struck with sticks and other weapons out of anger.
If she has departed as one who is not to return, there is no expiation once the tenth day has arrived. (II,1, p. 358) // Par_10.32 //
For ten days one should not abandon a woman, yet one should abandon her if she has lost her hearing;
the husband shall perform the Kṛcchra penance, and his kinsmen half of that Kṛcchra.
Having eaten and drunk with them, one is purified after a day and night; but when a Brāhmaṇī woman, being free from desire, goes to another man... (II,1, p. 359) // Par_10.34 //
Having gone [to another], she passes through a hundred men; her kinsmen should abandon her.
If she should go to the house of a man, that house would become impure. (II,1, p. 360) // Par_10.35 //
Whatever belongs to the husband’s mother’s house is indeed the house of the paramour;
having smeared that house with [cow dung], one should afterwards sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should discard earthen vessels and purify those made of cloth or wood;
one should purify all ritual materials, including those derived from fruits, by means of cow-hair.
Copper vessels [should be purified] with the five products of the cow, and bell-metal vessels with ashes ten times over;
a Brahmin should perform the expiation as prescribed by the Brahmins.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee and perform two Prājāpatya penances;
for others, purification consists of fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are purified by fasts, meritorious vows, ritual bathing, twilight devotions, worship, and so forth, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, compassion, and charity. (II,1, p. 361) // Par_10.40 //
Space, wind, fire, water on the earth, and *darbha* grass do not become defiled, just as the sacrificial cups (*camasa*) do not in sacrifices. (Parāśara-smṛti 10.41)
If a Brahmin has consumed impure semen, beef, or even the food of a Caṇḍāla, he shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (II,1, p. 364) // Par_11.1 //
In the same way, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya should perform half a Cāndrāyaṇa;
likewise, when a Śūdra eats [forbidden food], he should perform a Prājāpatya penance. (II,1, p. 374) // Par_11.2 //
A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while a twice-born man should drink the Brahmakūrca;
or else, he should give one, two, three, or four cows, respectively, according to the order starting with the Brāhmaṇa.

The food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a state of birth-impurity, and indeed the food of one whose food is unfit to be eaten; food that is suspected [of being forbidden], prohibited food, and likewise the leavings of another—(II,1, p. 375) // Par_11.4 //
If a Brahmin has eaten [forbidden food] out of ignorance or due to distress, he should,
upon realizing it, perform the purifying Brahmakūrca penance.
When food has been defiled by children, mongooses, or cats, it is purified by sprinkling it with sesame, darbha grass, and water; of this there is no doubt. (II,1, p. 390) // Par_11.6 //
When Brahmins are seated in a single row eating together, if even one should set aside his vessel, the remaining food must not be eaten. (II,1, p. 398) // Par_11.7 //
If a Brahmin should eat from that row where food is being consumed as leavings out of delusion,
he must perform the Kṛcchra Sāṃtapana penance.
Milk, white garlic, eggplant, *gṛñjana*, onion, tree resin, and mushrooms (II,1, p. 399).
If a twice-born man consumes camel’s milk or sheep’s milk through ignorance,
he is purified by a three-night fast and the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having eaten a frog as well as the flesh of a mouse, a Brahmin, knowing this, is purified by subsisting on barley-gruel for a day and a night. (II,1, p. 405) // Par_11.11 //

A Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya who are diligent in their duties and pure in their observances—food from their houses may always be eaten by the twice-born at offerings to the gods and the ancestors. (II,1, p. 410) // Par_11.12 //
If a Brahmin goes to the bank of a river and eats ghee, oil, milk, or food cooked with fat, he partakes of the meal of a Śūdra. (II,1, p. 411) // Par_11.13 //
A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is constantly addicted to liquor and meat and who engages in base occupations, as he would a dog-cooker. (II,1, p. 416) // Par_11.14 //
A twice-born man should not abandon those Śūdras who are devoted to serving the twice-born, who abstain from liquor and meat, and who are constantly engaged in their own duties.
If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity, how should one prescribe the expiation for them in each respective caste? (II,1, p. 417) // Par_11.16 //
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs through eight thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī;
for a Vaiśya, through five thousand; and for a Kṣatriya, through three thousand.
When one eats at the house of a Brahmin, one should cause two thousand [cows] to be given;
or else, one is purified by the Vāmadevya Sāman alone.

"Manu has declared that dry food, cow's milk, and oily substances, even if they have come from the house of a Śūdra, are fit to be eaten provided they have been cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa. (II.188, p. 427) // Par_11.19 //
If a Brahmin eats in the house of a Śūdra during times of distress,
he may be purified by mental remorse or by reciting the Drupadā verse one hundred times.

A slave, a carpenter, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who shares half his earnings—these among the Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (II,1, p. 429) // Par_11.21 //
One born from a Śūdra maiden but consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Dāsa through that consecration; however, if he is not consecrated, he is a Nāpita.
The son who is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra maiden should be known as a Gopāla; he is to be fed by Brahmins, without a doubt.
One born of a Vaiśya maiden but consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa is to be known as an Ārdhika; he may be eaten by Brāhmaṇas, without a doubt.
If one unintentionally consumes water, curd, ghee, or milk that has been kept in a vessel used for forbidden foods, what should the expiation be? (II,1, p. 432) // Par_11.25 //
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra who approaches [for sexual intercourse],
the expiation for one of the twice-born castes is the Brahmakūrca fast.
For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts.
The *brahmakūrca* rite, observed for a day and night, would purify even a dog-eater.

Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—this is designated as the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), which is purifying and cleanses one of sin. (II,1, p. 433) // Par_11.28 //
Cow’s urine from a black cow, cow dung from a white one,
milk from a copper-colored cow, and curd taken from a red cow.
Ghee should be taken from a tawny cow, or everything may be from a Kapila cow;
one should add one *pala* of urine and half the size of a thumb of cow dung. (II,1, p. 434) // Par_11.30 //
One should provide seven palas of milk, three palas of curd are prescribed,
one pala of ghee should be given, and one pala of kuśa-water.
Taking cow's urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇaḥ. (II,1, p. 435) // Par_11.32 //

With the mantra "Thou art splendor, thou art semen," one should place clarified butter; with "Thee for the sake of the god," water from *kuśa* grass; and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), purified by a *ṛc*, one should set down in the vicinity of the fire.
Having stirred [the water] with the mantra "āpohiṣṭhā," one should recite over it the mantra "mānastoke.
Then, taking seven blades of *darbha* grass that are not cut at the tips and are as bright as a parrot, (II,1, p. 436) // Par_11.34 //

Having extracted these [ingredients], one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the rule, reciting the verses beginning with "irāvatī," "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," "mā nas toke," and "śaṃvatī. (II,1, p. 437) // Par_11.35 //
The twice-born should offer oblations with these very [mantras] and drink the remainder of what has been offered;
having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, he should churn it out with the *praṇava*. (II,1, p. 438) // Par_11.36 //
Having drawn it up with the *praṇava* alone, one should drink it with the *praṇava*;
for whatever sin resides within the bodies of embodied beings, even that which has entered the bones, [is removed].
The Brahmakūrca burns everything away like a blazing fire consumes fuel;
it is a purifier in the three worlds, presided over by the deities. (II,1, p. 439) // Par_11.38 //
Varuṇa is indeed in cow urine, Havyavāhana (Agni) in cow dung;
Vāyu is declared to be in curd, Soma in milk, and Ravi (the Sun) in clarified butter.

If one drinks water that has fallen from the mouth into a vessel, one should know that it is unfit for consumption; having drunk it, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (II,1, p. 440) // Par_11.40 //
And having seen a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well,
or having seen bones, skin, and such things fallen there, or having drunk impure water, a twice-born man [must perform penance].
The corpse of a human, a crow, a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a gavaya, a supratīka, a peacock, and likewise a rhinoceros; // Par_11.42 //
If one sinks into a well containing the skin of a tiger, a bear, or a lion, or if one has drunk the water of a defiled pond, [one must perform purification]. (II,1, p. 441) // Par_11.43 //
By this entire sequence, the expiation for a man shall be performed in its proper order:
a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after three nights, while a Kṣatriya becomes pure after two days.

A Vaiśya is purified in one day, while a Śūdra is purified by eating only at night, provided he abstains from the food of others and does not delight in the food of others. (II,1, p. 446) // Par_11.45 //
Having eaten the food of an *apaca*, a twice-born man should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance;
as for the gift given by an *apaca*, how can there be any fruit for the donor?
Both the giver and the receiver go to hell; having taken the fire and established it, one must not fail to perform the five sacrifices. (II,1, p. 447) // Par_11.47 //
He who has desisted from cooking for others is thus proclaimed by the sages;
having himself performed the five sacrifices, he subsists on the food of others.
That Brahmin who, though observing the duties of a householder, constantly rises at dawn and is devoted to food cooked by others, yet gives nothing away, [is as one who eats alone].

The sages who know the true nature of dharma have proclaimed that the *apaca* [is the lowest]; for in each successive age, there are specific duties and specific twice-born classes associated with them. (II,1, p. 451) // Par_11.50 //
One must not revile them, for those twice-born ones are indeed the embodiments of the age itself;
having uttered the sound "hum" to a Brahmin, or the address "thou" to one who is superior, [one incurs great sin].
Having bathed and remained standing for the remainder of the day, he should greet [the teacher] and propitiate him,
even if he has struck him with a blade of grass or bound him by the neck with a cloth.

Even after winning a legal dispute, one should prostrate and appease the opponent; however, for threatening [another], the penance lasts a day and night, and for striking [the ground] with the hand, it lasts three nights. (II,1, p. 455) // Par_11.53 //
The *atikṛcchra* penance is performed when blood is present; the *kṛcchra* is for internal bleeding.
One who eats a handful of food for nine days shall perform the *atikṛcchra*. (II,1, p. 459) // Par_11.54 //
One should fast for three nights; that is called the *atikṛcchra*. This applies when a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred. (II,1, p. 460) // Par_11.55 //
The Gāyatrī, when practiced ten thousand times, is the supreme purification.

If one sees a bad dream, or after vomiting, undergoing a haircut, engaging in sexual intercourse, or being exposed to the smoke from a funeral pyre, bathing alone is prescribed. (II,2,p.1) // Par_12.1 //
Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or anything touched by *surā* liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite once again. (II,2, p. 5) // Par_12.2 //
The deerskin, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are set aside for the twice-born upon the performance of the purificatory rite.
One who has consumed feces or urine should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for purification;
having bathed and drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one shall become pure. (II,2, p. 6) // Par_12.4 //

And for those who have committed suicide by drowning or fire, or through renunciation or fasting unto death, how is purification ordained for those of the outcaste classes? (II,2, p. 7) // Par_12.5 //
By performing two *prājāpatya* penances, by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
and by the gift of eleven bulls, those three castes are purified.
I shall declare the penance for a Brāhmaṇa: having gone to a forest at a crossroads and shaved his head, including the topknot, he should perform two Prājāpatya penances.
Svāyambhuva declared that one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee for purification;
by that, one is released from that sin and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
The wise have proclaimed five meritorious baths: those of fire, water, Brahman, wind, and the celestial. (II,2, p. 13) // Par_12.9 //

The fire-related bath is performed with ashes; the water-related bath is by immersion; the Vedic bath is performed with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the wind-related bath is traditionally said to be [bathing] in the dust raised by cows.
That which occurs during a shower of rain is called the divine bath;
having bathed there, a person becomes as one who has bathed in the Gaṅgā.
All the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, follow behind the twice-born man as he goes to bathe;
transformed into the nature of wind, they move along, afflicted by thirst and seeking water. (II,2, p. 17) // Par_12.12 //
They return disappointed once the wringing out of the garment has been performed;
therefore, one should not wring out the garment without having first offered the libation to the ancestors.
He who, having applied sesame seeds to the pores of his skin, offers libations to the ancestors, satisfies the ancestors with his own blood and filth. (II,2,p.18) // Par_12.14 //
He who shakes his hair after bathing, he who casts off impurity,
or he who sips water even while standing in the water— such a person is excluded from the rites of the ancestors and the gods.
Having covered his head or his neck, or even with his lower garment or topknot hanging loose, one becomes impure even after sipping water if he is without the sacred thread (II.2, p. 19).

One standing on land should not perform ritual sipping while in the water, nor one standing outside should do so while in the water; having touched both [the water and the ground], and having performed the sipping, one becomes pure in both respects.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road, and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water should sip water again. (II,2, p. 20) // Par_12.18 //
Upon sneezing, spitting, or being defiled by food particles from the teeth, as well as when speaking untruths or conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear.
Manu has declared that the sacred fords beginning with Prabhāsa and the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā reside within the right ear of a Brahmin. (II, 20)
Fire, water, the Vedas, as well as the moon, the sun, and the wind—
all these indeed abide in the right ear of the Brahmin.
Bathing during the day, purified by the rays of the sun, is praised;
bathing at night is not recommended, except upon the sighting of Rāhu [during an eclipse]. (II,2, p. 21) // Par_12.22(21) //
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and burnt offerings should be performed during the appearance of Rāhu;
otherwise, the night is impure, and therefore one should avoid it.
The Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—indeed, all the deities—are absorbed into Soma; therefore, a gift should be given upon its reception. (II,2, p. 22) // Par_12.24(23) //

At a sacrifice for the common folk, at a wedding, at the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign, and likewise during an eclipse, giving is indeed prescribed for the night; it is not ordained for any other occasion.
Giving at the birth of a son, during a sacrifice, in times of emergency, or upon the sight of Rāhu (an eclipse), is praised; it is not recommended at other times during the night.
The "great night" (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle watches;
during the first and last watches, one should perform ablutions just as during the day.
A sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, and a seller of Soma—a Brāhmaṇa who has touched these must enter the water with his clothes on. (II,2, p. 24) // Par_12.28(27) //
Before the collection of the bones, one should weep and then perform a ritual bath;
for within the ten-day period of a Brahmin’s death, bathing is required, whereas after that period, merely sipping water (ācamana) suffices.
When the sun is seized by Rāhu, all water is equal to the Gaṅgā; the same is said regarding the eclipse of the moon for rites such as bathing and giving gifts. (II,2, p. 25) // Par_12.30(29) //
A bath purified by *kuśa* grass, a twice-born man who sips water with *kuśa*, or water drawn up with *kuśa*—each of these is equal to the drinking of Soma. (II,2, p. 26) // Par_12.31(30) //
Those who have fallen away from the fire-ritual, those who have abandoned the twilight devotions,
and those who do not study the Veda— all these are declared to be *vṛṣalas*.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who is afraid of a Śūdra, especially if he is unable to study the whole, should at least study a single portion. (II,2, p. 27) // Par_12.33(32) //
Even for one who studies constantly, recites prayers, or offers oblations, if he is nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, no upward path exists for him.

The food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together on the same seat as a Śūdra, and even the acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra—these would cause one to fall, even if one is blazing like fire. (II,2, p. 28) // Par_12.35(34) //

That twice-born man who constantly has food cooked by a Śūdra woman, and whose housewife is a Śūdra woman, is excluded from the rites for the ancestors and the gods, and he goes to the Raurava hell. (II,2, p. 29) // Par_12.36(35) //
With my body nourished by the impurity of death and birth, and subsisting on the food of a Śūdra, O twice-born one,
I do not know what various wombs I shall enter.
"A vulture for twelve births, a pig for ten births, and one shall be in the womb of a dog for seven births—thus Manu has declared. (II,2, p. 30) // Par_12.38(37) //
But that Brahmin who, for the sake of a fee, should offer the oblation for a Śūdra,
would become a Śūdra, and the Śūdra would become a Brahmin.
Having undertaken the vow of silence, a twice-born man should not speak while seated;
for if he should speak while eating, one must avoid that food. (II,2, p. 31) // Par_12.40(39) //
If a Brahmin drinks water from that same vessel while only half his meal remains,
he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and brings harm upon himself.
But he who sets down his vessel first while the Brahmins are still eating—that fool is most wicked; indeed, he is called a slayer of a Brahmin. (II,2, p. 32) // Par_12.42(41) //
If those twice-born ones utter a blessing while the vessels still stand [empty],
the gods do not attain satisfaction, and likewise the ancestors depart disappointed.
One should never eat without having bathed, nor without having muttered prayers, nor without having invoked the fire;
one should not eat from the back of a leaf, nor likewise at night without a lamp.

But a householder, endowed with compassion, should reflect only upon dharma; being of sound intellect and walking in the path of justice, he should do so for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those whom he is bound to support. (II,2, p. 33) Par_12.45(44)
One must indeed protect oneself by means of wealth acquired through righteous means;
however, he who lives by unrighteous means is excluded from all sacred rites.

One who has built the sacred fire-altar, a tawny cow, one who performs long sacrificial sessions, a king, a mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify by the mere sight of them; therefore, one should look upon them constantly. (II,2, p. 34) // Par_12.47(46) //
One should keep these things in the house: the fire-drill, a black cat, sandalwood, a fine jewel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, a black antelope skin, and a goat. (II,2, p. 35) // Par_12.48(47) //
That field where a hundred cows and one bull stand unrestrained is proclaimed to be ten times that amount as a *gocarma*.

A mortal is liberated from all sins, including the killing of a Brahmin, which arise from the actions of mind, speech, and body, by means of this gift of a *gocarma* cowhide. (II,2, p. 36) // Par_12.50(49) //
Whatever gift is given to a householder who is poor, and especially to one learned in the Vedas, that gift brings about auspicious results. (II,2, p. 37) // Par_12.51(50) //
One who seizes land is not purified by means of constructing ponds, wells, and tanks, nor by hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, nor even by the gift of ten million cows.

The sage Uśanas declared that for a woman with menstrual flow, bathing alone is required within eighteen days; beyond that, there shall be a three-night period of impurity. (II,2, p. 38) // Par_12.53(52) //

One *yuga*, two *yugas*, three *yugas*, and four *yugas* [are the periods of impurity] for a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and one who has fallen from his caste, respectively.
Then, by mere proximity, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
having bathed, one should look at the sun if one has touched [the corpse] through ignorance. (II,2, p. 39) // Par_12.55(54) //
If a Brahmin, though possessing hands, drinks water from his mouth due to weakness in knowledge,
he will certainly be born in the womb of a dog.
If a man, in anger, declares his wife to be unapproachable,
yet later desires her again, he must proclaim this before an assembly of Brahmins.
One who is exhausted, angry, blinded by darkness, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear,
having failed to perform a meritorious gift, must observe a three-day penance.
One should perform ablutions at the confluence of great rivers during the three periods of the day;
and upon completing the vow, one should give a cow and feed ten Brahmins.
Having eaten the food of a Brahmin who is of evil conduct and who practices forbidden acts, a twice-born man should observe a fast for one day. (II,2, p. 45) // Par_12.60(59) //
By eating the food of a Brahmin who is of virtuous conduct and likewise a knower of the Vedanta, a man is released from sin within the interval of a day and night.

One who consumes food from the upper part of a meal, from the lower part of a meal, or from the middle of a meal, as well as during the menstrual period, or likewise upon the death of someone in a state of impurity, should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (II,2, p. 46) // Par_12.62(61) //
O Goddess, one should perform ten thousand *kṛcchra* penances and two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
as well as bathe twelve times at a sacred ford (*puṇyatīrtha*) with the head unwetted.
A pilgrimage of two yojanas is prescribed as the equivalent of one *kṛcchra* penance for a householder who intentionally causes the emission of semen upon the ground. (II,2, p. 48) Par_12.64(63)

One who is endowed with the fourfold knowledge should recite the mantra of the Goddess a thousand times, together with three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), according to the rule even for the slayer of a Brahmin. (II,2, p. 50) [Par_12.65(64)]
One should prescribe the journey to the bridge over the ocean as the expiation;
on the path of the bridge-construction, one should practice begging for alms from the four castes.
Avoiding those engaged in forbidden occupations, and devoid of an umbrella and shoes, he says:
"I am indeed a doer of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins. (II,2, p. 51) // Par_12.67(66) //
I stand at the doors of houses seeking alms, a slayer of Brahmins;
I may dwell in cow-pens, or indeed in villages or cities.
Having gone to these—penance groves, sacred fords, or rivers and waterfalls—proclaiming his sin, he should then go to the ocean. (II,2, p. 52) // Par_12.69(68) //
Ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long,
it was constructed by Nala at the command of Rāmacandra.
Having seen the bridge over the ocean, one casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having seen the bridge, one whose soul is purified may plunge into the sea.
Or the king, the lord of the earth, should perform the horse sacrifice;
then, having returned home, he approaches it for the purpose of dwelling.
Together with his sons and servants, he should provide a feast for the Brahmins;
he should also give one hundred cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those who are proficient in the four Vedas.
Through the grace of the Brahmins, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated;
having killed a woman engaged in a sacrifice, one should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin. (II,2, p. 76) // Par_12.74(73) //
And a twice-born man who drinks liquor shall go to a river that flows to the ocean;
then, having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, he should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas. (II,2, p. 77) // Par_12.75(74) //
And one should give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee to Brahmins.
Having drunk liquor even once, one should drink liquor that is red-hot like fire. (II,2, p. 80) // Par_12.76(75) //
Having himself stolen gold from a Brāhmaṇa, he then purifies himself both in this world and in the next. (II,2, p. 84) // Par_12.77(76) //
Taking a pestle, he should go into the presence of the king for execution;
then he attains purification, and he is indeed released by the king.
But if an act is committed intentionally and not otherwise, one deserves death;
[this applies] from sharing a seat, a bed, a vehicle, conversation, or eating together. (II,2, p. 90) // Par_12.79(78) //
For sins spread abroad like a drop of oil upon water;
[the remedies for them are] the Cāndrāyaṇa, the barley-meal fast, and the Tulāpuruṣa. (II,2, p. 91) // Par_12.80(79) //
Following after cows also destroys all sins.
This compendium of the Dharmaśāstra, composed by Parāśara, consists of five hundred and ninety-two verses. (II,2, p. 287; BI: 534)
Just as the rites of Vedic study [are to be observed], so too must this treatise on Dharma be studied with diligent effort by one who is intent on going to heaven. (II,2, p. 288) Par_12.[82](81)

Vi_1 When the night of Brahmā had passed and the Lotus-born One had awakened:
Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged by the waters.
Just as in former kalpas, he who delights in sporting in the waters took on the auspicious form of a boar and lifted up the earth.
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts his fangs, the rituals his teeth, and the fire-altars his mouth;
Agni is his tongue, the *darbha* grass his hair, Brahman his head, and he is possessed of great ascetic power.

Divine, with day and night as his eyes, adorned with the Vedāṅgas and the Śruti, having clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his beak, and the great sound of Sāman chants for his voice; || Vi_1.4 ||
He consists of the truth of the Dharma, is glorious, and is honored by his successive strides;
he has the great snout of expiation, knees like those of a sacrificial animal, and a magnificent form.
The Udgātṛ-priest is its intestines; it has the oblation as its characteristic mark; the seeds and medicinal herbs are its great fruit;
the altar is its inner self; the mantras are its buttocks; and the Soma is its blood. || Vi_1.6 ||
The altar was his shoulder, the oblation his fragrance; he possessed the momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the *prāgvaṃśa* hall was his body, radiant and endowed with various initiations.
The Great One consists of the great mantra, with the sacrificial fee as his heart and Yoga as his body;
he is beautiful with the Upākarma rite as his lips and adorned by the Pravargya ceremony as his whorls of hair.
He whose path of movement consists of various meters, who is seated upon the secret Upanishads,
and who is accompanied by his consort Chāyā, has indeed arisen like the peak of a jewel.
The Lord, having entered the single ocean, beheld the earth— bounded by the sea and including its mountains, groves, and forests—
submerged in the waters of that single ocean.
Having lifted it up with the tip of his tusk out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
the Primordial God, the Great Yogi, fashioned the earth anew.
Thus, in ancient times, having assumed the form of the Sacrificial Boar and desiring the welfare of all beings, the divine Earth was raised up from the depths of the netherworld.
Having extracted them and established them in their own respective places where they were motionless,
Madhusūdana divided the waters according to their proper locations.
And those born of the ocean were in the oceans, those of the rivers were in the rivers,
those of the ponds were in the ponds, and those born of lakes were in the lakes.
He created the seven netherworlds as well as the seven worlds,
and the various locations of the continents and the oceans.
The guardians of the quarters, the world-protectors, the rivers, the mountains and trees,
the seven seers who know the Dharma, the Vedas with their auxiliary branches, and the gods and asuras.
Piśācas, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans;
beasts, birds, wild animals, and the fourfold assembly of living beings;
as well as clouds, rainbows, lightning, and various kinds of sacrifices.
Thus the Blessed One Varāha, having created this world with its moving and unmoving beings,
departed for that destination of the worlds which is unknown.
When Janārdana, the god of gods, had departed for an unknown destination, the Earth reflected: "What support will there be for me?"
"I shall go and ask Kaśyapa; he will undoubtedly tell me [the answer], for that great sage is constantly occupied with my concerns."
Having thus made her resolve, the goddess, assuming the form of a woman, went to see Kaśyapa; and Kaśyapa beheld her.

Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her face resembled the autumnal moon, her hair was adorned with swarms of bees, and she was radiant and auspicious, with lips as red as the bandhujīva flower.
She had beautiful eyebrows, very fine teeth, a lovely nose, and arched brows;
she possessed a neck like a conch shell, joined thighs, and full, broad hips and thighs.
Her two breasts shone forth—equal, full, and close together;
resembling the frontal lobes of Indra’s elephant and possessing a luster like that of gold.
His arms are as tender as lotus stalks, his hands resemble young sprouts;
his thighs are like pillars of gold, and his knees are well-concealed and closely set.
Her shanks were hairless and perfectly symmetrical, her feet exceedingly beautiful,
and her hips broad, while her waist was like that of a lion cub.
Her copper-colored nails were endowed with radiance, and her form was enchanting to all;
she constantly made the quarters of space appear filled with blue lotuses by her glances.
The goddess, making the quarters free from darkness with her radiance,
was dressed in very fine white garments and adorned with the finest jewels.
Making the earth appear as if covered with lotuses by her footsteps,
she was endowed with beauty and youth, yet stood before him with humility.
Seeing her approach and having honored her, Kaśyapa said to that woman of beautiful hips: "O lady of noble form, what is in your heart has been understood by me."
"O large-eyed lady, hold this fast; go, O Goddess, to Janārdana.
He will tell you everything regarding how your steadfastness shall come to pass."
"O fair-faced one, O lady of beautiful limbs, through the power of meditation and by his grace, I have learned that he dwells in the Ocean of Milk for your sake."
Having been addressed in this manner, the Earth then paid homage to Kaśyapa and departed for the Ocean of Milk, the sea of Keśava, to behold him.
She beheld that ocean of nectar, enchanting with the rays of the moon,
and agitated by hundreds of waves produced by the turbulence of the wind.
Resembling the Himalayas, it was like another circle of the earth,
seemingly summoning the ground with its moving hands of waves.
By those very rays, as if incessantly bestowing whiteness upon the moon,
his every stain was removed by Hari dwelling within him.
Therefore, he possessed a very bright and powerful body,
white, moving through the air, inaccessible [to others], and dwelling in the lower world.
Rich with sapphire-like tawny [minerals], it was like the sky turned upside down;
it was as if covered by a multitude of forests produced from rows of fruit.
Indeed, seeing that [palace] situated in the middle there, with its exceedingly vast interior like the slough of the serpent Śeṣa, he beheld the abode of Keśava.
Upon that [bed], he beheld Madhusūdana reclining on his side, his dimensions indescribable and endowed with inconceivable supernatural power.
The lotus of his face was difficult to discern due to the rays from the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa;
it resembled a hundred moons and possessed a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.
Akṣobhya, clad in yellow garments and adorned with all kinds of jewels, is resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and two earrings. || Vi_1.42 ||
His pair of feet were being massaged by the auspicious palms of Lakṣmī,
and he was being attended on all sides by personified weapons.
Having seen that lotus-eyed Madhusūdana, he prostrated himself and, falling upon his knees on the ground, then addressed him with this request:
O Lord Viṣṇu, I who had gone to the depths of the netherworld have been uplifted by you and established in my own place out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
"In this situation, O Lord of Gods, what stability will there be for me now?
When she had spoken thus, the God addressed these words to the Goddess: Vi_1.46.
O Earth, virtuous people devoted to the conduct of their castes and stages of life, and solely intent upon the scriptures, will sustain you; upon them your burden has been placed.
Thus addressed, Vasumatī spoke to the God of gods:
"O Eternal One, tell me of the duties of the social classes and the stages of life."
I wish to hear from you, for you are my supreme refuge.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O destroyer of the strength of the enemies of the gods!
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace;
O Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, you of great strength and prowess!
O beyond-the-senses one, O most difficult to cross over, O God who wields the Śārṅga bow, O Boar, O Terrible One, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person! Vi_1.51 ||
O golden-haired one, O all-seeing one, O embodiment of sacrifice, O stainless one;
O Lord of the field and the knower of the field, O God, O you who recline upon the ocean of waters!
O you who are the mantra, the inconceivable bearer of mantras, whose body is the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
and who are the cause of the creation and destruction of this entire world.
O Knower of Dharma and Adharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons;
O Viṣvaksena, O Nectar, O Space, O Slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
O Great One, you are to be known as the nourisher of all; you grant fearlessness to everyone.
O Sinless One, most excellent one, you are the cloud that brings forth the creation of the world.
O nourisher of the waters, abode of the elements, support of consciousness, and actionless one;
O teacher of the seven-headed sacrifice, Supreme Puruṣa of antiquity! Vi_1.56 ||
O Lord of the eternal syllable, most subtle Master, compassionate toward devotees, and purifier!
You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of those who discourse on Brahman.
O Supreme Person, you are the goal for those who have known what is to be known;
O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Master, the Lord of Speech.
To Subrahmaṇya, the unassailable, the son of Vasu, the bestower of wealth;
to him endowed with the power of great yoga, the one born from the speckled cloud (Pṛśnigarbha), who maintains the radiant flame.
To the high-souled Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed, the infallible one;
to the god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, the all-pervading Lord, the Great Sovereign of all beings.
"O Blessed One, tell me of the single manifestation, the four-armed one, the cause of the causes of the world, and the eternal dharmas of the four social orders."
"Endowed with the conduct of the stages of life (āśrama), together with their secret doctrines and their compendiums"—
having been addressed thus by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth.
Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes,
together with the conduct of the stages of life, along with their secret doctrines and their essential summaries.
But for those virtuous ones who shall uphold you, be the ultimate refuge;
sit down, O lady of beautiful thighs, upon this excellent golden seat.
Seated comfortably, understand the duties as I proclaim them;
at that time, the Earth, seated comfortably, heard the Vaiṣṇava duties.
Vi_2 Om. The four social classes (varṇas) are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. Vi_2.1.
Among them, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the entire collection of rituals, beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with the funeral rites at the cemetery, is performed according to the mantra.
And their dharmas are as follows.
Teaching the Veda to a Brāhmaṇa. // Vi_2.5 //
For a Kṣatriya, there is constant devotion to weapons.
For the Vaiśya, cattle-rearing.
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born.
For the twice-born, [the duties are] sacrificing and studying.
Now, their functions are as follows: Vi_2.10.
For a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and receiving gifts [are lawful means of livelihood].
The duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the earth.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and the breeding of livestock are the duties of a Vaiśya.
For a Śūdra, all crafts are [permitted].
In times of distress, one may resort to the next lower mode of livelihood.
Forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion.
Uprightness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise freedom from malice— this is called the common dharma.
Now, the duties of kings. 3.1.
The protection of the subjects.
The establishment of the castes and stages of life each in their own respective duty.
And the king should take refuge in a region that is arid yet suitable for cattle and endowed with crops.
And it shall consist mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
In that regard, one should take refuge in one of the following types of fortresses: a desert, a marsh, water, trees, or a mountain.
And remaining there, he should appoint the local chiefs over their respective villages.
And ten superintendents.
[He should appoint] supervisors over a hundred.
And [he should appoint] provincial governors.
The village headman shall provide a remedy for the faults of the village.
If he is unable [to do so], he should report it to the superintendent of ten villages.
He too, being unable [to do so], [reports it] to the superintendent of a hundred.
If he too is unable, [he should report it] to the district governor.
Even the ruler of a region should eliminate faults with his whole being.
He should appoint trustworthy persons to oversee mines, tolls, ferries, elephants, and forests.
Those who are most righteous in their religious duties.
Skilled in matters concerning wealth and purpose.
[He sees] heroes in their deeds of battle.
The fierce ones among the fierce.
[One should not give] eunuchs among women. // Vi_3.21 //
For the sake of tribute from the subjects, he shall take a sixth part of the grain every year.
And from all grain. // Vi_3.23 //
Two hundred [paṇas] for animals, gold, and garments.
From meat, honey, ghee, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, fruits, juices, wood, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and wickerwork, the king shall take a sixth part.
One should not collect taxes from Brahmins.
For they are the ones who bring about the king's righteousness.

And he should put to death those who defile it.

One should perform the worship of the virtuous.

The dust particle situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice window is known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [translucent particles] make one nit (*likṣā*).
Three of those make one rājasarṣapa.
Three of those make one white mustard seed (gaurasarṣapa).
Six of those [yūkās] make one barley grain (yava).
Three of those [rattis] constitute one *kṛṣṇala*.
Five of those [rathikas] make one māṣa.

Half an *akṣa*, together with four *māṣakas*, is one *suvarṇa*.

"This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed upon you;

if, when weighed, he increases in weight, then he is pure according to the law.

for in this way, knowledge free from doubt arises, resulting in a definitive conclusion.
Now, regarding the fire: 11.1. Then the fire. 11.1.

The gods are the deities who are beyond perception; the brahmins are the deities who are directly perceptible.

Twelve thousand divine years constitute a cycle of four yugas.
