And a thousand cycles of four yugas is a kalpa.
And that [period] is one day of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
And his night is of the same duration.
By calculating months and years according to such a day and night, the lifespan of the entire Brahmā is one hundred years.
And a human day is delimited by the lifespan of a Brahmā.
At its conclusion is a great eon (mahākalpa).
For him, the night lasts exactly that long.
There is no counting at all for the human days and nights that have passed.
And not of those yet to be.
Because time is without beginning or end.
Thus, in this supportless time that flows on incessantly,
I do not perceive any such entity whose stability could be permanent.
The grains of sand in the Ganges, or the torrents of rain when Indra pours it down, might be counted in this world; but the grandfathers who have passed away cannot be counted.
In every kalpa, fourteen lords of the gods perish,
as do the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of the Daityas have perished here through time; what then can be said of mortal men?
And many royal sages, endowed with all virtues,
as well as gods and celestial seers, have met their end in the course of time.
Even those who are capable of causing the creation and destruction in this world are led away by Time; for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Overcome by time, every living being is led to the next world under the power of the noose of karma; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no help to be found in this world.
Since grieving people do not benefit the deceased here in this world, one should certainly not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
For one who departs with both good and evil deeds as his two companions,
what need has he for kinsmen, whether they grieve or not?
While the period of impurity for his kinsmen lasts, the deceased finds no rest;
therefore, he goes to those very ones who offer the funeral cakes and water.
"One who has died remains a *preta* until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed;
offer food along with a water-pot to him who has gone to the world of the *pretas*. (ViDh 20.33)
And having gone to the world of the ancestors, one eats food at the śrāddha that is equal to the svadhā offering;
therefore, offer the śrāddha for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
Whether in the state of a deity, in a place of torment, likewise in the animal realm,
or in the human state, one receives the śrāddha offered by one's own kinsmen.
When the śrāddha has been performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer of the rite is certain.
Therefore, having abandoned useless grief, the śrāddha should always be performed.
This much alone should always be done for a deceased relative by his kinsmen; a man should not help either the deceased or himself by grieving.
Seeing the world without refuge and kinsmen dying,
O men, always choose the Dharma alone as your companion.
Even when dead, a kinsman is unable to follow a deceased person;
for, with the exception of a wife, the path to Yama is blocked for everyone else.
Dharma alone follows him wherever he may go;
indeed, in this essence-less world of men, practice Dharma without delay.
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished.
Death seizes and departs with one who is attached to fields, shops, and houses, and whose mind is directed elsewhere, just as a she-wolf carries off a lamb.
Time has no one dear to it, nor is there anyone it hates;
when the karma that sustains life is exhausted, it forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings, nor repeated recitations can save a human being who is overtaken by death or even by old age.
For even with hundreds of precautions, one is unable to ward off an impending misfortune; what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so too does previously performed karma unfailingly find its doer.
Beings have an unmanifest beginning and a manifest middle, and likewise an unmanifest end;
what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
Just as a person here takes up a garment after discarding one previously worn,
so too does the embodied being take up a new body bound by karma.
Weapons do not cut this; fire does not burn it;
waters do not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it up.
This is indestructible, this is unburnable, this is indeed unmoistenable and un-dryable;
it is eternal, ever-moving, fixed, immovable, and ancient.
This Self is said to be unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable;
therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.

Vi_21.1 Then, when the period of impurity has passed, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as he is able, facing northward, and honored with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and so forth.
In the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, one should modify the mantras so that they refer to a single person.
In the vicinity of the leavings, he should offer a single pinda with the mention of that person's name and lineage.

When the Brahmins have finished eating and have been honored with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), he should offer the inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) while pronouncing the name and lineage of the deceased, and then construct three trenches: four finger-breadths wide, that deep, and one span long, dug at intervals of that same distance from one another.
Having established three fires near the trench and strewn grass around them, he should offer three oblations into each one.
To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! Homage!
To Agni Kavyavāhana, the bearer of offerings to the ancestors, svadhā! Homage!
To Yama, the descendant of Aṅgiras, svadhā! Homage!
And at the three places, one should perform the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) as previously described.
Having filled three pits with rice, curd, ghee, honey, and meat, he should mutter the mantra "This for thee" (etat te).
In this manner, one should perform [the rites] every month on the anniversary of the death.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins, preceded by the gods, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
In this case, one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and the offering of water for the feet (pādya).
With the mantra "May the earth unite with you, and [the waters] common to all," he should join the water from the guest's foot-washing vessel to the three vessels for the ancestors' foot-washing.
One should offer four rice-balls in the vicinity of the remnants of the meal.
And having followed the Brahmins who have sipped water for purification and to whom sacrificial fees have been given, he should dismiss them.
Then, one should place the *piṇḍa* for the deceased (*preta*) among the three *piṇḍas*, just like the water from the vessel for the feet (*pādya*).
The same applies even when in close proximity to three furrows.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, like the monthly offerings, should be performed either after completing the *śrāddha* for twelve days or on the thirteenth day.
For Śūdras, however, [the rite] takes place on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras.
If an intercalary month should occur within the year, then one should increase the period for the monthly rite by one day.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for women should be performed in this same manner;
likewise, one should perform the *śrāddha* every year as long as one lives.
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of a year.
Vi_22.1 For a Brāhmaṇa, there is a period of impurity lasting ten days for the birth or death of those who are sapinda.
For a member of the royal caste (rājanya), it lasts twelve days.
For a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days.
For a Śūdra, it is one month.
And the sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person.
During a period of ritual impurity, the performance of fire-oblations, giving, receiving gifts, and the private recitation of the Veda are suspended.
During a period of impurity, one should not eat the food of anyone.
If one eats food even once from a Brāhmaṇa or others while they are in a state of impurity, his own period of impurity lasts as long as theirs.
Upon the removal of the impurity, one should perform the penance.

If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a person of his own caste, he should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
But a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted during the period of impurity caused by the death of a Kṣatriya, becomes pure after performing this very rite.
And a Kṣatriya [is impure] during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya.
In the case of impurity due to the death of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
During the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and during the period of impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya shall go to a flowing river and mutter the Gāyatrī five hundred times.
And a Vaiśya, during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a Śūdra shall perform a bath during the period of impurity of the twice-born.
A Śūdra, having bathed during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For wives and slaves, the period of impurity is equal to that of their master, according to their respective order of birth.
When the master has died, it belongs to oneself.
When those of lower caste marry sapiṇḍas of higher caste, purification occurs at the end of that [latter's] period of impurity.
For a Brāhmaṇa, among sapinda relatives who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods of impurity are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively.
For a Kṣatriya [impurity resulting from the death] of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra lasts for six nights or three nights respectively.
For a Vaiśya among Śūdras, purification occurs in six nights.
In the case of a miscarriage, the penance consists of days and nights equal in number to the months [of gestation].
In the case of a child born dead or one who dies shortly after birth, there is immediate purification for the family.
If a child who has not yet grown teeth dies, the impurity lasts for that very day.
For him there is no consecration by fire, nor the rite of water-libation.
But for one whose teeth have appeared but who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony performed, purification occurs after one day and night.
But if the tonsure ceremony has been performed yet no other sacraments have been completed, purification occurs after three nights.
Thereafter, at the time as previously stated.
Marriage is the sacramental rite for women. Vi_22.32.
There is no period of impurity on the paternal side for women who have been refined [by marriage].
If her birth or death should occur while she is in her father's house, then the impurity lasts for one night and three nights respectively.
If another birth-impurity should occur during the midst of a birth-impurity, then purification occurs upon the cessation of the preceding impurity. (ViDh 22.35)
At the end of the night, it is completed in two days.
At dawn, after three days.
Likewise, if a relative dies during a period of impurity caused by death, the same rule applies.
One who hears of a birth or a death while residing in another country shall become pure by means of the remainder of the period of impurity.
But when the period of impurity has passed at the end of a year, [one becomes pure] in one night.
After that, by means of bathing. // Vi_22.41 //
When both the teacher and the maternal grandfather have passed away, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
When sons born of other than one's own loins have been born and have died, and when wives who previously belonged to another have given birth and have died; || Vi_22.43 ||
If the teacher’s wife, a son, a preceptor, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a fellow student, or a pupil has passed away, [one remains impure] for one night.
And also toward the king of one's own country. // Vi_22.45 //
And when a person who is not a sapinda dies in one's own house. // ViDh 22.46 //
There is no period of impurity for those killed by Bhṛgu, fire, fasting, water, battle, lightning, or the king.
Nor [should one eat] at the royal meal-offering for kings. // Vi_22.48 //
Nor [is it a transgression] for those observing a vow while they are in the state of that vow.
Nor [should one eat] at the sacrifice of those performing a sacrificial session.
Nor [is there any fault] in the work of artisans regarding their own craft. // Vi_22.51 //
It does not apply to those who carry out the king's commands, by virtue of his will.
Nor [should one eat] at the installation of a deity or at a wedding, if the provisions were previously prepared.
Not when there is confusion regarding the location. // Vi_22.54 //
And even in times of extreme distress.
Those who commit suicide and those who are outcasts do not partake in the impurity rites or the water libations.
On the day of death, the female slave of one who has fallen [from caste] should overturn a water-pot with her foot.
He who cuts the noose of one who has died by hanging is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
And he who performs the funeral rites for those who have sacrificed their own lives. // Vi_22.59 //
And one who causes the shedding of tears [is also guilty]. // Vi_22.60 //
For every deceased person, having shed tears together with their relatives, [one should perform purification] by means of bathing.
If the collection of bones has not yet been performed, [one becomes pure] by bathing with one's clothes on.

A twice-born man, having followed the funeral procession of a Śūdra corpse, should go to a river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
For the funeral rites of a deceased twice-born man, one hundred and eight [offerings] are required.
A Śūdra, having followed a deceased person, should perform a ritual bath.
Upon inhaling the smoke from a funeral pyre, all social classes should perform a ritual bath.
After sexual intercourse, a bad dream, when blood has reached the throat, and after vomiting or purging. // Vi_22.67 //
And also when the work of shaving has been performed.
And having touched one who has touched a corpse, as well as a menstruating woman, a Caṇḍāla, or a sacrificial post; Vi_22.69.
Except for edible [meat], one should avoid the corpse of a five-toed animal and its bone-marrow.
In all these ritual baths, one should not wear a garment that has not been washed.
A woman in her menses becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
Having touched a woman of lower caste who is menstruating, or having been touched by a menstruating woman, one should not eat until she has become pure.
Having touched a woman of the same caste or of a higher caste, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or being desirous of eating or studying; having drunk, bathed, spat, or put on a garment; having stepped onto a road, or having voided urine or feces; and having touched the bone of a five-toed animal that is not greasy—one should sip water for purification.
And also when conversing with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas. (Vi 22.76)
If one is defiled by bodily impurities below the navel or on the arms, or by wine and intoxicants, that limb shall be purified by washing it with earth and water.
If it has been defiled elsewhere, one should wash that limb with earth and water and then bathe.
But if it has been defiled by the mouth [of an impure person], one should fast and bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And one whose lips have been bitten by the teeth.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, nails, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. || Vi_22.81 ||
Sura is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses, that made from honey, and that made from flour;
just as each one is, so are all of them, and they must not be drunk by the twice-born.

The honey-wine (mādhūka), the sugarcane wine (aikṣava), the ṭāṅka, the kaula, the dates and breadfruit wines, the grape-wine (mṛdvīkārasa), the madhvīka, the maireya, and that produced from coconut; || Vi_22.83 ||
These ten kinds of intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them.
A disciple, however, performing the funeral rites for his deceased preceptor,
becomes pure there after ten nights together with those who partake of the offerings for the deceased.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, the one observing a vow is not deprived of his vow.
One who has been formally initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
however, once it is completed, having offered the water libations, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water,
smearing [with cow-dung], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Of all forms of purity, purity regarding food is declared to be supreme;
for he who is pure in food is truly pure, not he who is merely purified by earth and water.
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts by giving;
those whose sins are concealed by silent recitation; and those most learned in the Vedas by austerity.
That which requires purification is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
This determination regarding bodily purification has been declared to you;
now hear the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.
That which is defiled by bodily excretions, by fermented liquors, or by intoxicants is considered utterly defiled.
Every metal vessel that has been excessively defiled shall be purified by being cast into fire.
One made of jewels, one made of stone, and a lotus are purified by burying them in the earth for seven nights.
[It may be] made of horn, ivory, or bone by means of carving.
One should discard [the vessel] made of wood or that made of clay.
If a garment that has been excessively damaged becomes free of stains when washed, one should cut it away.
Objects made of gold, silver, lotus, or gems are purified by water, provided they are free from stains.
And [the purification] of cups and vessels made of stone.
The *caru*, *sruc*, and *sruva* ladles [should be cleaned] with hot water.
In the performance of a sacrifice, by wiping the sacrificial vessels with the hand.
By sprinkling [water] upon the wooden sword, the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar.
And of beds, vehicles, and seats.
And [the same applies] for many. Vi_23.13.
And [the same applies] to grains, skins, ropes, woven cloth, split bamboo, thread, and cotton garments.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, fruits, and flowers.
And [the same applies] to grass, wood, and dry leaves.
By washing these.
And [the same applies] to those who are few in number.
Silk and woolen cloth may be purified with alkaline substances.
With *ariṣṭaka* fruits for the *kutapa* goats.
[One should give] wood-apples for silken garments.
[The purification] of linen garments is with white mustard seeds.
And [the same applies] to those made of horn, bone, or ivory.
[The purification] of those made of deer-hair [is performed] with lotus seeds.
For those made of copper, brass, tin, and lead, [the purification is] with acidic water.
With ashes, [one should purify] bell-metal and iron.
[It is] by carving for wooden objects. // Vi_23.27 //
[The purification] of fruits is by means of cow-hair brushes.
For those that are clustered together, purification is by sprinkling.
By means of purifying, [the purification] of liquids [is achieved]. // Vi_23.30 //
By giving water and fire for the abundant products of sugarcane, such as molasses and the like, which have been stored in one's house.
And [the same applies] to all types of salt.
Furthermore, earthenware vessels [are purified] by firing again.
By re-consecrating images of deities that have been cleansed like material objects. // Vi_23.34 //
Of the food that has not yet been prepared, one should discard only that portion which is defiled and then proceed with the threshing and washing of the remainder.
Food that has been prepared in an amount exceeding one *droṇa* is not defiled even if it is touched by a dog.
Having removed only that which has been defiled from it, one should pour gold-infused water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra into it, and show it to a goat and to the fire.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon,
sneezed at, or defiled by hair or insects is purified by scattering earth over it.
In all purifications of objects, earth and water should be applied as long as the odor and the stain caused by the impure substance do not depart.
Goats and horses are pure by their mouths; cows and humans are not defiled by impurities;
and roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.
The mud and water in a street, even when touched by outcasts, dogs, or crows, are purified by the wind alone; and likewise, structures built of baked bricks are purified in the same way.
Furthermore, for all living beings whose bodies have been excessively defiled, one should constantly and without negligence perform purification with earth and water.
Water found on the ground is meritorious where it quenches the thirst of a cow, provided it is not contaminated by impurities; the same applies to water situated upon a stone.
From a well containing a dead five-toed animal or otherwise severely defiled,
one should draw out all the water and purify the remainder with a cloth.
One should perform the kindling of fire in a well constructed with baked bricks;
thereafter, one should deposit the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in a newly arisen body of water.
Furthermore, O Earth, in the case of small and stagnant reservoirs, purification is said to be like that of a well; however, there is no impurity in those that are large.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by speech.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale; likewise, almsfood offered through a Brāhmaṇa and all mines are pure.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while yielding milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
The meat of an animal killed by dogs is declared to be pure,
as is that of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and other such bandits.
One should declare those apertures which are above the navel to be pure;
those which are below are impure, as are the impurities that have fallen from the body.
Flies, droplets, shadows, a cow, an elephant, a horse,
rays of light, dust, earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure.
The principal [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants; nor do droplets that fall upon the body [cause impurity];
nor do the beard hairs that have entered the mouth, nor what is caught between the teeth.
The drops that touch the feet of one who is rinsing the mouth for others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down.
A house [is purified] by sweeping and smearing; a book by sprinkling;
and [the ground] by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and scraping. || Vi_23.56 ||
The earth is purified by burning or else by the dwelling of cows;
cows are purifying and auspicious, and upon cows the worlds are established.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all evil.
Cow-urine, cow-dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and yellow pigment—these are the products of the cow.
This sixfold water from the horns of cows is supremely auspicious; it is the most excellent of cow-products, meritorious, and the destroyer of all sins.
Scratching the bodies of cows indeed destroys all impurities;
by giving morsels of food to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
For the Gaṅgā dwells here in the footprint of cows; likewise, their nourishment increases in their dust;
fortune resides in their dried dung, and dharma in bowing to them; therefore, one should always offer salutation to them. || Vi_23.61 ||
Now, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives according to the order of the castes. 24.1.
A Kṣatriya has three [wives]. // Vi_24.2 //
There are two for the Vaiśya.
One [stick] for a Śūdra.
Among those women, the hand should be taken in marriage when one marries a woman of the same caste.
In the case of marrying a girl of a different caste, a Kṣatriya girl [should be given] an arrow.
A goad [is the emblem] of a Vaiśya maiden.
[He was born] from within the hem of the garment of a Śūdra maiden.
One should not take as a wife a woman who is of the same lineage (sagotrā) or who shares the same ancestral seers (samānārṣapravarā).
But from the mother's side up to the fifth generation, and from the father's side up to the seventh generation.
[The same applies to] the nākulī [plant]. Vi_24.11.
Nor one who is diseased. Vi_24.12.
Nor one with an extra limb. // Vi_24.13 //
Nor one who is deficient in a limb. // Vi_24.14 //
Nor one who is excessively tawny. // Vi_24.15 //
Nor one who is talkative. // Vi_24.16 //
Now, there are eight forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, the Gāndharva, the Āsura, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca. // Vi_24.18 //
The Brāhma marriage consists of inviting a virtuous man and giving him one's daughter.
The Daiva [marriage] is that which is given to an officiating priest at a sacrifice.
The term "cow-pair" (gomithuna) is used here according to the usage of the sages.
Through the granting of what is requested, one becomes equal to Prajāpati.
The Gāndharva marriage is the union of two people who have mutual desire, but who are without the presence of their mother and father.
An Asura is born through purchase. // Vi_24.24 //
The Rākṣasa [is characterized] by seizing through battle.
The Paiśāca rite consists of approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated. Vi_24.26.
Among these, the first four are lawful.
The Gāndharva marriage is also [permitted] for Kṣatriyas.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman purifies twenty-one men.
The son of Daivī was Caturdaśa.
And there are seven sons of the Ṛṣis. 24.31.
The Prājāpatya penance lasts for four days.
By giving away a daughter in the Brāhma form of marriage, one causes her to go to the world of Brahmā.
By fate, one attains heaven. // Vi_24.34 //
The Vaiṣṇava [rite] is performed according to the Ṛṣi tradition.
By the Prājāpatya penance, one attains the world of the gods.
By the Gāndharva rite, one goes to the world of the Gandharvas.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, the maternal grandfather, and the mother are the givers of a maiden.
In the absence of the preceding one, each subsequent [state] is established in its own nature.
A maiden should choose her own husband only after having waited for three menstrual periods;
once those three periods have passed, she always has the power over herself.
A maiden who sees her menses while still in her father’s house and remains unconsecrated by marriage is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; one who carries her off does not incur sin.
Now, the duties of women. 25.1.
The practice of observing vows identical to those of her husband.
The honoring of one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, teachers, deities, and guests.
Having well-prepared utensils. // Vi_25.4 //
The state of having open hands.
Keeping one's belongings well-secured. // Vi_25.6 //
A lack of delight in fundamental activities.
Dedication to the practice of auspicious conduct.
When the husband has gone abroad, she should refrain from the practice of personal adornment.
Not entering the houses of others. // Vi_25.10 //
One should not remain stationed at doorways or windows.
Lack of autonomy in all actions.
Even in childhood, youth, and old age, there is dependence upon the father, the husband, and the son, respectively.
When her husband has died, she should observe celibacy or ascend the funeral pyre after him.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by serving her husband, however, she is exalted in heaven.
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living,
she takes away his life-span and goes to hell.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates.
When there are many wives of equal caste, he should perform religious duties together with the eldest wife.
And in the case of mixed castes, [the son] belongs even to the youngest wife who is of the same varna as the father.
But in the absence of a woman of the same caste, one may take a woman of the next lower caste.
But a twice-born man must never [beget a son] with a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra wife for a twice-born man can never serve the purpose of dharma;
she is declared to be for the sake of pleasure alone for him who is blinded by passion.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth,
quickly lead their families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
But for one whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are primarily concerned with that [wealth],
neither the ancestors nor the gods will eat, and he does not go to heaven.
When the embryo becomes clearly perceptible, the rite of impregnation (niṣeka-karman) is performed. Vi_27.1.
The *puṃsavana* rite is performed before the quickening of the fetus.
The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is performed in the sixth or eighth month. (6) Vi_27.3 //
And when the boy is born, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed.
The naming ceremony shall take place once the period of impurity has passed.
Auspiciousness belongs to the brahmin.
It belongs to a powerful Kṣatriya. // Vi_27.7 //
That which is endowed with wealth belongs to the Vaiśya.
That which is loathsome for a Śūdra.
In the fourth month, the showing of the sun.
In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.
In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed.
These same rites for women are performed without mantras.
Their marriage is accompanied by mantras.
The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year from conception.
In the eleventh month from conception, [the birth] of the king.
For Vaiśyas, [initiation] is in the twelfth year from conception.
For them, the girdles are made of muñja grass, bowstring, or balbaja grass, and consist of muñja grass.
The sacred threads and garments may be made of cotton, hemp, or wool.
The skins are those of the black antelope, the tiger, and the spotted deer.
The staffs are made of Palāśa, Khadira, or Udumbara wood.
The hairline, the forehead, and the nose are equal in measure. // Vi_27.22 //
Or rather, all [of them] indeed.
They are not crooked and possess their skin intact. // Vi_27.24 //
One should wander for alms at the beginning of the day, in the middle of the day, and at the end of the day.
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year,
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
Beyond this point, all three of these, if they remain uninitiated at the proper time,
become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vratyas, and are censured by the Aryas.
Whatever hide is prescribed for him, whatever cord and girdle, whatever staff and whatever garment— each of these remains his even during his religious observances.
Having cast away the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread,
and the water-pot when they are worn out into the water, he should take others while reciting the appropriate mantras.
Now follows the residence of students in the house of the teacher (gurukula). Vi_28.1.
The worship of the two twilights.
One should recite the morning prayer while standing, and the evening prayer while seated.
The performance of the consecration and fire rituals occurs at two times.
Submerging oneself in water like a staff.
Studying when summoned [to do so]. Vi_28.6.
Acting for the pleasure and welfare of the guru.
Wearing a girdle, a staff, a deerskin, and a sacred thread.
Except for the teacher's household, he should wander for alms among those possessed of virtuous qualities.
The consumption of almsfood is permitted only when authorized by the guru.

One should avoid salt and fermented liquids offered at ancestral rites, stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, the remnants of others' meals, injury to living beings, and vulgar speech.
Sleeping on the ground. Vi_28.12.
One should rise before the teacher and go to sleep after him.

Sinful evildoers who have committed transgressions, immediately after giving up their lives,
reach the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering.
Just as they are dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama, and are led away with great difficulty and groaning.
They are being devoured by dogs, jackals, and flesh-eating creatures such as crows, herons, and cranes, as well as by fire-mouthed beings, serpents, and scorpions.
Being burned by fire, pierced by thorns,
split apart by saws, and tormented by thirst;
Tormented by hunger and likewise by packs of fierce tigers,
they fainted at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
Desiring the food and drink of others, they are beaten by the henchmen with faces resembling those of terrifying crows, herons, cranes, and other such birds.
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places they are beaten with pestles;
and likewise in some places they are crushed upon iron anvils and upon stone slabs.
In some places they eat what has been vomited; in some, pus and blood;
in some, excrement; and in others, flesh that is foul-smelling like pus—most dreadful indeed.
They remain in dreadful darkness, and in some places they are being devoured by worms with most terrible fire-like mouths.
In some places they are afflicted by cold, and in others they dwell amidst impurities;
furthermore, in some places those most dreadful pretas devour one another.
In some places they are struck by spirits, and likewise in some places they are suspended;
in some places they are pelted with showers of arrows, and likewise in some places they are flayed.
With their feet placed upon their throats and entwined by the coils of serpents,
they were likewise tormented by mechanical devices and dragged along by their knees.
With their backs, heads, and necks broken, and with most dreadful needle-like throats,
they possess bodies as large as multi-storied palaces, capable of enduring the torments of hell.
Thus, having experienced the consequences of their sins and being deeply afflicted by suffering, those who have committed transgressions enter into animal births and endure various miseries.
Vi_44.1 Now, for those of evil nature who have experienced suffering in the hells, there are rebirths among the animal wombs.

One who commits a heinous crime becomes afflicted with leprosy.

A drinker of spirituous liquor has black teeth.

And the Atisāntapana [penance] consists of practicing this for three days.
The consumption of oil-cake, water from boiled rice, sour gruel, and barley meal, alternating with days of fasting, constitutes the Tulāpuruṣa penance.
The *parṇakṛcchra* consists of drinking water boiled with the leaves of each of the following—kuśa, palāśa, udumbara, padma, śaṅkhapuṣpī, vaṭa, brāhmī, and suvarcalā—individually.
Having undergone a shave, he should perform all these penances (kṛcchras),
bathing daily at the three sessions of the day, sleeping on the ground, and keeping his senses subdued.
One should avoid excessive conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts;
one should constantly recite purificatory texts and offer oblations according to one's ability.
Now, furthermore, the Cāndrāyaṇa [penance]. Vi_47.1.
One should eat mouthfuls that do not cause transformation [of the body].

One should increase those [meals] during the waxing of the moon's phases and decrease them during its waning; one should not eat at all on the new moon day. This is the Cāndrāyaṇa penance known as "Barley-shaped" (yavamadhyama).
Or it may have the middle of an ant.
That [lunar day] which occurs in the middle of the new moon is called "ant-waisted" (pipīlikāmadhya).
He whose full moon day falls on the fifteenth of the waxing fortnight is one who is "barley-shaped" (yavamadhyas).
If one should eat eight morsels every day for a month, that is the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*.
Eating four morsels each evening and four each morning constitutes the Śiśucāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one should eat three hundred and sixty morsels in a month in any manner whatsoever, that is the common Cāndrāyaṇa.
O Earth, in ancient times, having performed this vow, the stainless Seven Sages,
as well as Brahmā and Rudra, attained the supreme abode.
Vi_48.1 Now, if one should consider oneself heavy due to actions performed by oneself, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel for one's own sake.
One should not offer oblations into the fire after that.
And there is no offering of oblations here.
One should consecrate with mantras that which is uncooked, that which is being cooked, and that which is already cooked.
While it is being cooked, one should perform a protective rite.
Brahmā among the gods, the pathfinder for the poets, the seer among the sages, the buffalo among wild beasts,
the hawk among vultures, the axe among the forests— Soma goes forth singing across the filter.
Thus he binds the darbha grass. Vi_48.6.
And having poured that boiled [milk-rice] into a vessel, he should eat it.

"Those gods who are born of the mind, who delight in the mind, who are highly skillful, whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they favor us; to them be homage, to them be *svāhā*!"—with these words, one should offer the oblation into oneself.
Then, having sipped water, he should touch his navel.

"O waters, you who have been bathed and drunk, remain within our bellies as barley; may they be free from disease, free from consumption, and sinless for us—divine, immortal, and increasers of cosmic order. // Vi_48.10 //
One who desires intelligence should observe this for three nights.
One who commits a sin [is purified] in six nights.
Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself from any one of the great sins.
Within twelve nights, one burns away even the sins committed by one's ancestors.
Having drunk [it] for a month, all sins [are purified].
And for twenty-one nights, [the penance consists of] barley grains that have been released from their husks.
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey.
You are the expeller of all evils, a purifier upheld by the seers.
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is indeed the nectar of immortality;
may all [these] purify my sin, whatever evil deed I have committed.
O barley grains, destroy the misfortune and the ill omen known as Kālakarṇī that has been committed by speech, performed through action, or conceived with a wicked mind.
O barley grains of mine, purify that which has been licked by a sow or a pig, that which is defiled by leavings, and the failure to serve one's mother and father.
The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or a period of impurity,
the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral— purify these with my barley.
The deceit of children, unrighteousness, and whatever is done at the king's gate;
the theft of gold, the neglect of vows, and the officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice; the reviling of Brahmins—purify these for me with barley.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva on the twelfth day.
By means of flowers, incense, ointments, lamps, and food offerings, as well as by the propitiation of fire and Brahmins.
Having observed this vow for one year, one becomes purified from sins.
Having practiced this for as long as one lives, one attains Śvetadvīpa.
By observing the twelfth lunar days of both fortnights in this manner for one year, one attains the heavenly world.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, [one goes] to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the same way, this also applies to the fifteenth days.
By attending upon Keśava, who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day, and who has become Yoga itself, one shall attain the Great.
In that year, when the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky,
that full-moon day is declared to be the "Great Full Moon" (Mahatī Paurṇamāsī).
In that [time], acts such as giving and fasting are proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
likewise so is the twelfth day of the bright fortnight which is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism.
Having constructed a leaf-hut in the forest, he should dwell there.
One should bathe at the three sessions of the day.
Without proclaiming his own deeds, he should practice begging for alms from village to village.
And he should sleep on a bed of grass.
This is the great vow.
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform [the penance] for twelve years.
A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who is present at a sacrifice.
Nor one who is pregnant or menstruating. // Vi_50.8 //
Or a woman of the Atri lineage.
Or a friend. // Vi_50.10 //
In the case of killing a king, one should perform the Great Vow (mahāvrata) itself twice over.
In the case of killing a Kṣatriya, it is three-quarters [of that].
In the case of killing a Vaiśya, the penance is half [of that].
Half of that [penance] is for killing a Śūdra.
In all [these cases], he should have a human skull as his banner.
Having shaved his head, he should follow cows for one month.
While they are seated, he should sit.
And when they are stationary, he should remain stationary.
And one should rescue those who have fainted. // Vi_50.19 //
And one should protect them from fears.
Without having provided protection for them from cold and other such hardships, one should not provide it for oneself.
One should bathe with cow urine.
And one should subsist on cow's milk products.
One should perform this cow-vow in the event of killing a cow.
Having killed an elephant, one should give five blue bulls as a gift.
A horse or a garment. Vi_50.26.
For killing a donkey, one should give a one-year-old ox.
And also for the killing of a ram or a goat. // Vi_50.28 //
For the killing of a camel, one *kṛṣṇala* of gold.
Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights.

Having killed any one of a mouse, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a water-snake, or a python, one who has fasted should feed a Brahmin with *kṛsara* (rice and peas) and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee.
One should fast for three nights upon killing a hyena, an owl, a crow, or a fish.
Having killed any one of these—a swan, a crane, a balākā, a water-fowl, a monkey, a hawk, a vulture, or a cakravāka—one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a snake, one should give a black iron hoe as a gift.
Having killed a eunuch, one [receives] a load of straw.
Having killed a boar, one obtains a jar of clarified butter.
A partridge [is equal to] one drona of sesame seeds.
A parrot that is two years old, like a calf.
A three-year-old curlew. Vi_50.39.
Upon killing a carnivorous beast, one should give a milch cow.
For killing a non-carnivorous wild animal, [one should give] a heifer.
If one kills a deer unintentionally, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon killing a bird, one should eat only at night.
Or he should give a silver māṣa.
Having killed an aquatic creature, one should observe a fast.
But for the killing of a thousand boneless beings,
or for a full cartload of boneless beings, one should perform the vow prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra.
But for the killing of bone-bearing creatures, one should give something to a Brahmin;
indeed, for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting down fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification.
For the unauthorized cutting of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while observing a milk-vow.
One who has drunk liquor is excluded from all ritual acts; he shall subsist on grain-particles for one year.
Upon consuming any one of the impure substances or intoxicants, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And [the same applies] to eating garlic, onions, leeks, things with a similar odor, village pigs, village cocks, monkeys, and the flesh of cows.
In all these cases, at the conclusion of the penance, one should perform the sacramental rite for the twice-born once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—these are to be avoided during the rite of re-consecration.
If one eats the meat of five-toed animals, excluding the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one should fast for seven nights.
Having eaten the food of a member of a religious community, a courtesan, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights.
The food of a carpenter and of a leather-worker.
And [the water] of usurers, misers, those initiated for sacrifice, those bound in fetters, those accused of crimes, and eunuchs [is not to be used].
And [the same applies] for those who eat the leftovers of unchaste women, hypocrites, physicians, hunters, cruel people, and fierce people.
And [the food] of a woman whose husband is not a hero, of a goldsmith, of one whose husband is an enemy, and of one who has fallen from the religious life.
And [the sin] of those who speak slander and falsehoods, those who violate the dharma, and those who sell their own bodies for pleasure.
And [the same applies] to actors, weavers, ungrateful persons, and washermen.
And [the same applies] to those who perform manual labor, those who sit in attendance, actors on the stage, lute players, and sellers of weapons.
And [one should not eat the food] of dog-cookers, liquor-sellers, oil-pressers, weavers, and washermen.
And [one should not eat] from those who live in the same house as a menstruating woman or with a paramour.
Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow.
If it is intentionally touched with the foot or sneezed upon. Vi_51.18.
And for those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted.
Meat that has not been honored and meat obtained in vain.
If one eats the flesh of any fish except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohitaka*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* species, one should fast for three nights.
And also for eating the flesh of any aquatic creature.
Having drunk water that has been kept in a vessel for liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights.
And those who have stayed in a vessel containing liquor [become pure] after five nights.

One who drinks soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk *surā*, shall immerse himself in water, recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times, and perform the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*).
For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having consumed unknown meat from a slaughterhouse, as well as dried meat. 51.27.
For eating the flesh of carnivorous beasts or birds, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
One should fast for three nights upon eating the flesh of the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, haṃsa, rajjudāla, sārasa, dātyūha, śuka, sārikā, baka, balākā, kokila, or khañjarīṭa birds.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of single-hoofed animals and those with two rows of teeth.
And for eating the flesh of any bird, with the exception of the partridge, the grey partridge, the common quail, the francolin, and the peacock, there is a fast of one day and night.
If one eats insects for one day, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of dogs. // Vi_51.33 //
For eating mushrooms and fungi, one must perform the Sāntapana penance.
Having avoided preparations of barley, wheat, and milk, as well as oily substances, fermented liquids, and *khāṇḍava*, one should consume whatever has become stale and then observe a fast.
And those tree exudations that arise from incisions or from impure sources, as well as those that are red.
Lotus roots, rice cooked with sesame, *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, milk-rice, cakes, fried pastries, food intended for the gods, and sacrificial oblations; // Vi_51.37 //
And all kinds of milk, with the exception of that of cows, goats, and buffaloes.
Those [days] as well, if they are within ten days [of birth]. Vi_51.39.
And the milk of a cow that flows [excessively], one that is pregnant, or one whose calf has died. // Vi_51.40 //
And those who eat impure substances. // Vi_51.41 //
And those that are sour, excluding curd. // Vi_51.42 //
A student in the stage of celibacy (brahmacaryāśramin) who eats at a funeral feast (śrāddha) shall fast for three nights.
And he should dwell in water for one day.
For eating honey or meat, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
If one eats the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.
If one eats the leavings of another on the following day, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For eating the excrement or urine of five-toed animals, [the penance lasts] seven nights.
If one eats at a funeral rite for a raw corpse (āmaśrāddha), one should subsist on milk for three nights.
A Brahmin who eats the leavings of a Śūdra must undergo this for seven nights.
For eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, one must fast for five nights.
For eating the remnants of a Kṣatriya, one must observe a fast for three nights.
But for eating the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa's meal, the penance lasts for one day.
A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra must fast for five nights.
One who eats the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal shall observe a fast for three nights.
A Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra [is also excluded].
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights.
Having eaten prepared food, one must perform the Parāka penance.
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated by mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated by mantras.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal, for that many times does the killer of animals undergo slaughter here;
he obtains no atonement either in this world or after death.
"Beings were created for the sake of sacrifice by the Self-Existent One himself;
for sacrifice leads to the prosperity of all, therefore killing in sacrifice is not killing. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 51.61)
The sin incurred by a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain.
Herbs, animals, trees, as well as crawling creatures and birds,
having met their end for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states once again.
In the honey-mixture offering, in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—
only in these instances may animals be slain, and never under any other circumstances.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, by killing animals for the sake of sacrifice,
leads both himself and those animals to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Vedas, even in times of distress.
One should know that the violence ordained by the Veda, which is restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings, is indeed non-violence; for from the Veda, dharma has shone forth.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor even when dead.
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage or death,
seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherever one fixes one's delight—
that very thing one attains without effort, provided that one harms nothing at all.
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and bondage of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, avoiding the manner of a Piśāca,
becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are killers.
There is no doer of unmeritorious deeds greater than he who, without having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another.
The merit of one who performs the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years is equal to the merit of one who does not eat meat.
One does not obtain that fruit by means of divine foods consisting of fruits and roots, nor by the consumption of the various foods of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'meat-ness' of meat."
One who has committed the theft of gold, confessing his deed to the king, shall hand over a wooden mallet.
Through either killing or renunciation, one becomes purified.
Or one should observe the great vow for twelve years.
And one who misappropriates a deposit. // Vi_52.4 //
And one who steals grain or wealth shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
For the theft of a human being, a woman, a well, a field, or a pond, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is required.
The *sāṃtapana* penance is for objects of little value.
For those who consume food, drink, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, and fruits, there is the drinking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should fast for three nights after consuming grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses, clothing, leather, or meat.
For [stealing] gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one should eat grains for twelve days.
For stealing cotton, silk, wool, and so forth, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon stealing animals with cloven hooves or solid-hoofed animals, one should fast for two nights.
For stealing birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or articles made of split bamboo, one should fast for a day.
Having returned the stolen property to the creditor by some means,
one should then perform an expiation for the removal of that taint.
Whatever a person who is unrestrained might take from others,
by that very thing he shall be deprived when he is born again in whatever state he is reborn.
Since both life and the desire for the Dharma are established upon wealth,
one should therefore avoid harming wealth through every possible effort.
He who is intent on harming living beings and likewise he who is intent on harming wealth—
of these two, the one intent on harming wealth encounters the greater suffering.

Now, regarding sexual intercourse with one who has approached [forbidden women], he shall dwell in the forest for one year, clothed in bark garments, and perform the Prājāpatya penance according to the rules of the Great Vow.
And in approaching another's wife. // Vi_53.2 //
And for sexual intercourse with a cow, one must observe the cow-vow.
In the case of a man [having intercourse] with a non-vaginal opening, in space, in water, during the day, or while riding in a vehicle, he should perform a bath wearing his clothes.
By having sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman, one attains equality with her.
And if it was done out of ignorance, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
And for approaching a female animal or a prostitute, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a woman who has once been unfaithful to her husband should perform that same vow which applies to a man regarding another's wife.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting prayers for three years.
Whichever evil-minded person associates with another, he shall perform the same penance as that person.
Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-toed animal or from one that is utterly defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
A member of the royal caste [should wait] for two days.
For one day, I was indeed a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra [should eat] at night.
And at the conclusion of the vow, everyone should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A Śūdra who drinks the five products of the cow and a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor—
both of them go to the hell known as Mahāraurava.
If he approaches his wife during her season except on the forbidden days, he shall fast for three nights.
A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brahmin.
If one voids urine or excrement in a place lacking water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform a burnt offering (homa) with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One who has been released after sunrise should bathe with his clothes on and repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
If one is bitten by a dog, a jackal, a village pig, a donkey, a monkey, a crow, or an unchaste woman, one should go to a river and perform sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
One who has extinguished the sacred fires of the Vedas shall bathe three times a day, sleep on the ground, and subsist for one year on almsfood received only once a day.
For falsely exaggerating one's own qualities, for making false accusations against a teacher, and for reviling him, one should subsist on milk alone for one month.
An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of Brahmins—these shall subsist on alms for one year.

The elder brother who is superseded, the younger brother who supersedes him, the woman by whom he is superseded, the giver [of her in marriage], and the officiating priest—all these should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells living beings, land, merit, or Soma must perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.

One who sells fresh medicinal herbs, fragrances, flowers, fruits, roots, skins, cane, bamboo splints, husks, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, milk products, oil-cakes, or sesame oil must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
One who sells phlegm, lac, beeswax, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, tin, lead, black iron, copper, or swords shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells dyed red cloth, gems, perfumes, molasses, honey, or wool shall fast for three nights.
One who sells meat, salt, lac, or milk shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And one should further bring him back to it.
Having traveled by camel or donkey, or having bathed naked, slept, or eaten, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, having performed funeral rites for others, and having performed malevolent magic or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
This same [penance] should be prescribed even for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and been cast out from the Brahminical state, desire to perform an expiation.
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation,
they are purified by its renunciation, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and austerity.
In the event of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
as well as the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra.
One should not engage in any business with those who have been purified from sin;
however, one who knows the Dharma should not despise them once they have undergone purification.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who had sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they are pure according to the Dharma.
A child who is less than sixteen years old, or one who is eighty years of age,
as well as women and the sick, deserve half of the prescribed penance.
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been stated,
one should prescribe an atonement after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
Now, there follow the secret penances. 55.1.

Having reached a flowing river, one who bathes daily, performs sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with their proper characteristics, and eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) once a day, becomes purified from the murder of a Brahmin within a month.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
By means of the vow and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, one who has drunk liquor becomes purified.
By reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one who has committed the theft of gold [is purified].
One who has violated the teacher’s bed is purified by fasting for three nights and performing the recitation and fire-oblation of the Puruṣasūkta.
Just as the horse sacrifice, the king of rituals, removes all sins,
so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins.
A twice-born man should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
indeed, all the sins of a twice-born man are consumed by breath controls.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that [first] quarter of this Sāvitrī verse beginning with "Tat. || Vi_55.11 ||
A Brahmin who knows the Vedas, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas.
Having practiced this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One who is devoid of these three, yet performs his own duties at the proper time,
incurs reproach among the virtuous if he belongs to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya caste.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
as well as the three-footed *gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and having the sky as his form.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī mantra; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
however, the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as the Imperishable, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña);
the whispered (upāṃśu) recitation is said to be a hundredfold more effective, and the mental (mānasa) recitation a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with those performed according to ritual injunctions (vidhiyajña),
all together do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a true Brahmin.
Now, therefore, follow the purifiers of all the Vedas. 56.1.
By means of whose recitations and burnt offerings the twice-born are purified from their sins.

Now, those who should be avoided: Vi_57.1.
The Vrātyas. // Vi_57.2 //
They have fallen.
Those who are impure for three generations on both the mother's and the father's side [are ineligible].
All of them are indeed unfit to be eaten from and unfit to receive gifts from.
And one should avoid the habit of accepting gifts from those whose gifts are not to be accepted.
Through the acceptance of gifts, the Vedic splendor of Brahmins perishes.
He who accepts a gift without knowing the rules for accepting material objects sinks down together with the donor.
And he who, though capable of accepting gifts, refrains from accepting them, attains the world of the givers.
One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection, meat, honey, bedding, seats, houses, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered.
Prajāpati considered that alms offered spontaneously upon being invited, presented before one without prior solicitation, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years of him who treats her with contempt, nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblation.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the ancestors and the gods,
he may accept gifts from all sources, but he himself should not find satisfaction therein.
Even when capable of receiving these [gifts] for the sake of such duties,
one should not accept them from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or likewise from an enemy.
But when the teachers have passed away, or when living at home without them,
one seeking one's own livelihood should always receive it from a virtuous person.
A partner in a business, a family friend, a slave, a cowherd, and a barber—
these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Now, for one living in the householder stage of life (gṛhāśramin), there are three kinds of wealth (artha).
White, variegated, and black.
Whatever funeral rites he performs with pure wealth, by that he attains divinity.
That which is variegated is human existence.
That which was done by Kṛṣṇa resulted in his birth as an animal.
That which is acquired by one's own labor is "white" for everyone.
That which is acquired through immediate succession is variegated.
And that which is acquired through an activity separated by one [moment] is black.
Inheritance received in due order, a gift of affection obtained together with one's wife,
and wealth acquired without distinction— all such property is declared to be "white" (śukla).
That which is obtained through bribery or taxes, or by selling what should not be sold,
or received from one who has rendered a service, is declared to be "stained" (śabala).
That which is acquired through gambling, theft, fraud, forgery, violence, or by means of a pretext is declared to be "black" wealth. || Vi_58.11 ||
Whatever a person performs with whatever kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both in this world and after death.
A householder should perform the *pākayajñas* in the nuptial fire.
And one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice both in the evening and in the morning.
One should offer oblations to the deities. Vi_59.3.
One should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa offerings at the times of the conjunction and the opposition of the moon and the sun.
The expiation is by means of an animal sacrifice.
And in the autumn and summer, one should perform the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
Or when rice and barley have been cooked. // Vi_59.7 //
We have more than enough for three years.
Every year, [he should sacrifice] with the Soma sacrifice.
In the absence of wealth, [one should perform] the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice.
One should bestow in its entirety all the wealth obtained by begging for the sake of a sacrifice.
One should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering every evening and morning.
And one should give alms to the monk.
By giving alms to one who has been honored, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
In the absence of a monk, one should give even a single mouthful of food to the cows.
Or one should cast it into the fire.
Even when food is already being eaten, one should not refuse a mendicant.
The mortar and pestle, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and household utensils—these are the five slaughter-houses of the householder.
And for the sake of expiating that, one should perform sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the spirits, the ancestors, and men.
The private recitation of the Veda is the sacrifice to Brahman.
The human being is divine.
The libation for the ancestors is the ancestral rite.
Bali is a ghost.
The sacrifice to men consists of honoring guests.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts; therefore, the one in the householder stage of life is the best.
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
By constantly practicing the three aims of life, giving food, worshipping the gods, honoring Brahmins,
engaging in the study of the Vedas, and performing libations for the ancestors, a householder attains the station of Śakra.

women and Śūdras are purified by water once touched at the extremities.
Now, for the sake of security and well-being, one should approach the Lord.

And one should exert the utmost effort in honoring guests.
One should diligently honor a guest who arrives in the evening.

By worshipping that, one attains heaven.
From whose house a guest returns with his hopes frustrated, he takes away that person's merit and bestows upon him their demerit.
For a Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest;
because he stays for an uncertain time, he is therefore called an *atithi*.
One should consider a Brahmin guest who comes from another village, as well as a traveling companion,
as a guest when he arrives at one's house, whether it be one's own home or where the sacred fires are maintained.
But if a Kṣatriya has come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may,
at will, feed him as well after the Brahmins have finished eating.
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at his household as one entitled to the status of a guest,
he should feed them along with his dependents, practicing compassion toward them.
Furthermore, he should, together with his wife, feed with affection other friends and relatives who have come to his house, providing them with ordinary food according to his ability.
One should feed these— female relatives living in the house, a maiden, a sick person, and likewise a pregnant woman— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise person who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
And when the Brahmins and his own servants have finished eating,
the husband and wife should then eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the ancestors, human beings, servants, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains.
He who cooks for his own sake alone eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.
A householder does not attain such worlds through the private recitation of scripture, the agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, or ascetic penance, as he does from honoring a guest.
In the evening and in the morning, one should offer a seat and water to a guest,
as well as food according to one's ability, having honored them in accordance with the prescribed rule.
By giving a shelter, as well as bedding and an oil massage for the feet along with a lamp,
one obtains through each individual gift a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.

One who desires righteousness and has conquered the senses should practice that conduct which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, which is consistent with dharma, and which is practiced by the virtuous.
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, the desired state;

Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.

This world and the next belong to the self-controlled.

Through self-restraint, one obtains everything that one desires in the mind.
He traveled in a chariot yoked with five horses, which moved at the speed of thought and followed the noble path;
provided that the horses do not carry off that chariot, the enemies shall not defeat the Tathāgata.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
Now, one who desires to perform a *śrāddha* should invite the Brahmins on the day before.

On the second day, during the forenoon of the bright fortnight or the afternoon of the dark fortnight, he should cause the Brahmins—having bathed well and performed the ritual sipping of water—to sit upon seats covered with *kuśa* grass, arranged according to their seniority in age.

On the new moon days, by means of the supreme pentad.

Having performed the invocation with the mantra, "May all those ancestors come to me first; O ancestors, this is for you," and having offered water for washing the feet (*pādya*) mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds using the mantras "Those who stand as immortal speech" and "That which my mother [gave]," and having prepared and offered the respectful oblation (*arghya*), applied unguents, and honored the Brahmins according to his ability with *kuśa* grass, sesame, garments, flowers, ornaments, incense, and lamps, he should take food soaked in ghee and look at it while reciting, "O Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus," saying, "I shall perform the offering into the fire."
Having said that, and being told by the Brahmins, "Do so," one should offer three oblations.

Having performed the consecration of the oblation with the mantras, "O my ancestors, this is for you, O ancestors, here is the sacrifice," he should first offer food—specifically in vessels as they are available, preferably those made of silver—to the two facing east, saying, "Homage to all the gods."

And one should adorn it with all kinds of perfumes and jewels.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should cause a prastha of powdered salt with a golden center to be given to a Brahmin at the rising of the moon.
By this karma, one is born endowed with beauty and good fortune.

If the full moon day of Pauṣa should coincide with the Puṣya asterism, on that day one whose body has been rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds, who has been consecrated with a jar filled with cow's ghee, and who has bathed with all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, and all seeds, should bathe the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva with ghee; having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, and having offered oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava, Śākra, and Bārhaspatya mantras, he should cause the Brahmins to pronounce blessings with ghee mixed with gold.
