On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, when it is conjoined with the Āṣāḍhā nakṣatra, by giving food and drink one obtains that very same merit in an inexhaustible manner.
By giving a water-cow along with cooked rice, covered with a pair of garments, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa when it is joined with the asterism Śravaṇā, one attains heaven.
On the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, when it is conjoined with the Proṣṭhapadā constellation, one becomes liberated from all sins by the gift of a cow.

In the month of Āśvayuja, when the moon has entered the constellation Aśvinī, by giving a vessel filled with ghee and accompanied by gold to a Brahmin, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire.

If the full moon day of Kārttika should coincide with the Kṛttikā constellation, one who, at the rising of the moon, gives a white bull or one of another color—endowed with all kinds of grain, jewels, and perfumes—in the midst of lamps to a Brāhmaṇa, shall not experience fear in the wilderness.

Having fasted on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one who has worshipped Śrī Vāsudeva with unbroken grains (akṣata), and having offered oblations and given gifts of those same grains, becomes purified from all sins.
And whatever one gives on that day attains imperishability.

When the full moon of Pauṣa has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who has fasted, bathed with sesame seeds, offered a libation of sesame, worshipped Vāsudeva with sesame, and likewise offered oblations, given gifts, and eaten, becomes purified from sins.

When the full moon day of Māgha has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, having observed a fast and reached the Śravaṇa asterism, one should offer two lamps with two large wicks before the venerable Vāsudeva.

In that very month, by feeding Brahmins daily with products of the cow, one becomes a sharer in the kingdom.

Every month, when the moon is conjoined with the asterism Revatī, one who feeds Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee as an offering to please Revatī, and thereby gratifies Revatī, becomes a possessor of beauty.
In the month of Māgha, having offered oblations of sesame seeds into the fire every day and having fed Brahmins with boiled grain mixed with ghee, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire.
Having bathed in river water on every fourteenth lunar day and having worshipped Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from all sins.
If one desires vast enjoyments that follow the movements of the moon, the sun, and the planets, one should always bathe in the morning for two months: Māgha and Phālguna.
Then, when water begins to flow from that well dug by the excavator, half of his evil deed is destroyed.

Twofold for one who is a Brāhmaṇa in name only.

Sisters, daughters, and sons-in-law. // Vi_93.6 //

One who subsists on fruits.

Vi_96.1 Now, having ripened his passions through the three stages of life and having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, he should give away all his possessions as the sacrificial fee and become one belonging to the stage of wandering mendicancy.

One should not beg from a mendicant.

In a vessel made of clay, a wooden bowl, or a gourd vessel.
And their purification shall be by means of water.
One should be wary of gains obtained through honor.
One should make one's dwelling in an empty house.
Or one who makes the foot of a tree his dwelling.
He should not dwell for a second night in a village.
He should take only as much clothing as is sufficient to cover his private parts.
One should set down one's foot purified by sight.
One should take water that has been filtered through a cloth.
One should speak that which is purified by truth.
One should act only with what is purified by the mind.
One should desire neither death nor life.
One should endure harsh words.
One should not despise anyone at all.
One should be free from desire.
He is beyond salutation. // Vi_96.22 //
Whether one person hacks at his one arm with an axe or another anoints his other arm with sandalwood paste,
he should think neither ill of the former nor well of the latter.
One should be constant in breath control, concentration, and meditation.
One should perceive the impermanence of saṃsāra.
The impurity of the body.

O lotus-navelled Hṛṣīkeśa of great strength and prowess!
O Viṣṇu, O one beyond the senses, O god whose further shore is very difficult to reach, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
O Varāha, O Bhīma, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person!
O golden-haired one, O universal-eyed one, O embodiment of sacrifice, O stainless one;
O Lord of the field, the knower of the field, and the Lord of gods, O you who recline upon the ocean of waters!
O Viṣṇu, you who are the mantra, the bearer of mantras, the inconceivable one whose body is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and the cause of the creation and destruction of this entire world.
O Knower of Dharma and Adharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons;
O Viṣvaksena, O Immortal One, O Sky, O Slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
O Viṣṇu, the nourisher of the great, the unknowable, the all-encompassing, the bestower of fearlessness to all;
O most excellent, sinless one, the cloud-like creator of the world.
O nourisher of the waters, O abode, O support of consciousness, O inactive one;
O teacher of the seven-headed sacrifice, O Supreme Ancient Person!
O Viṣṇu, eternal, imperishable, most subtle Lord, compassionate toward Your devotees, purifier! You are the refuge of all the gods; You are the refuge of those who discourse on Brahman.
"O Supreme Person, you are the goal for those who have known all that is to be known;
O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Master, the Lord of Speech."
Viṣṇu 1.59: [I praise him who is] the one most skilled in sacred knowledge (*subrahmaṇya*), the unassailable, the army of wealth (*vasuṣeṇa*), the bestower of wealth;
he who is endowed with the power of great yoga (*mahāyogabala*), the offspring of *pṛśni* (*pṛśnigarbha*), and the bearer of radiance (*dhṛtārcis*).
Vāsudeva, the Great Soul, the lotus-eyed, the Infallible;
the God who is the teacher of gods and asuras, the All-pervading Lord, the Supreme Sovereign of all beings.
"O Blessed One, tell me of Viṣṇu, who is the single manifestation with four arms, the cause of the cause of the world, and [tell me] the eternal duties of the four castes."
"Those [dharmas] connected with the conduct of the stages of life (āśramas), together with their secret doctrines and their compendiums"—
having been thus addressed by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth.
"Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes,
together with the conduct of the stages of life (āśramas), along with their secret doctrines and their essential summaries."
O fair-thighed one, sit down upon this excellent golden seat, which shall be the ultimate refuge for those virtuous ones who uphold you.
"Sit comfortably and learn from me as I proclaim the duties," [said] Viṣṇu 1.65a;
"Then Dharā, sitting comfortably, heard the Vaiṣṇava duties," [it is said in] Viṣṇu 1.65c.
Viṣṇu 2.01: Om! The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—these are the four castes.
Among them, the first three are the twice-born.
Viṣṇu 2.03: For them, there is a collection of rites beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral pyre, performed according to the sacred mantras.
And their duties are as follows. (Viṣṇu 2.04)
Viṣṇu 2.05: Teaching the Veda is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 2.06: For a Kṣatriya, there is constant devotion to weapons.
For a Vaiśya, [the duty is] the tending of cattle. (Viṣṇu 2.07)
For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is [the duty]. (Viṣṇu 2.08)
For the twice-born, [the duties are] sacrificing and studying (Viṣṇu 2.09).
Now, Viṣṇu 2.10: furthermore, these are their modes of conduct.
For a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and accepting gifts [are lawful means of livelihood]. (Viṣṇu 2.11)
For a Kṣatriya, the duty is the protection of the earth.
Viṣṇu 2.13: Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and the cultivation of the soil are the duties of the Vaiśya.
For a Śūdra, all crafts [are lawful]. (Viṣṇu 2.14)
Viṣṇu 2.15: In times of distress, the next lower mode of livelihood is permitted.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, generosity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion— Viṣṇu 2.16.
Uprightness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise absence of malice— this is declared to be the common dharma.
Viṣṇu 3.01 Now, the duties of the king.
Viṣṇu 3.02: The protection of the subjects.
Viṣṇu 3.03: The establishment of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas) each in their own respective duty (dharma).
And the king should take refuge in a region that is arid, suitable for cattle, and endowed with crops. (Viṣṇu 3.04)
And [the world] will consist mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras. (Viṣṇu 3.05)
Therein, he should take refuge in one of the various types of fortresses: those situated in a desert, among men (an inhabited stronghold), on the ground, by water, among trees, or on a mountain.
And remaining there, he should appoint the respective village headmen.
Viṣṇu 3.08: [He shall appoint] ten superintendents.
Viṣṇu 3.09: [He shall appoint] supervisors over groups of one hundred.
And [he should appoint] provincial governors, Viṣṇu 3.10.
The village headman shall provide a remedy for the faults of the village. (Viṣṇu 3.11)
If he is unable [to do so], he should report it to the superintendent of ten villages.
He too, being unable [to do so], shall report it to the superintendent of a hundred.
If he too is unable, he shall report it to the district magistrate (deśādhyakṣa).
The provincial governor, too, should eliminate wrongdoing with all his soul.
Viṣṇu 3.16: He should appoint trustworthy persons to oversee mines, tolls, ferries, elephants, and forests.
Viṣṇu 3.17: [He should appoint] those most devoted to dharma for matters concerning dharma.
Viṣṇu 3.18: Those who are skillful in matters of wealth and purpose.
Viṣṇu 3.19: [He should appoint] heroes for the duties of battle.
Viṣṇu 3.20: [He should place] fierce [deities] among the fierce.
Viṣṇu 3.21: [One should not eat food] from eunuchs or from women.
Viṣṇu 3.22: For the sake of tribute from the subjects, he shall take a sixth part of the grain every year.
And from all kinds of grain, [one should give] according to Viṣṇu 3.23.
Viṣṇu 3.24: Two hundred [paṇas] for animals, gold, and clothes.
Viṣṇu 3.25: From meat, honey, ghee, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, fruits, juices, wood, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and wickerwork, the king shall take a sixth part.
Viṣṇu 3.26: One shall not collect taxes from Brāhmaṇas.
For they, indeed, are the performers of the king's duty.
And the king receives a sixth part of the merits and demerits from his subjects. (Viṣṇu 3.28)
And from the merchandise of his own country, he shall take a tenth part as the toll.
And from merchandise brought from foreign lands, [the king shall take] a twentieth part. (Viṣṇu 3.30)
One who departs from a toll station shall incur the forfeiture of all his property.
Viṣṇu 3.32: Artisans and those who live by manual labor shall perform one month's work for the king each year.
Viṣṇu 3.33: The sovereign, the minister, the fort, the treasury, the army, the territory, and the ally are the constituent elements [of sovereignty].
And he should slay those who revile him. (Viṣṇu 3.34)
Viṣṇu 3.35: He should have spies as his eyes both within his own kingdom and in the kingdoms of others.
One should perform the worship of the virtuous. (Viṣṇu 3.36)
And he should slay the wicked ones. (Viṣṇu 3.37)
Viṣṇu 3.38: One should employ conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force against enemies, friends, neutrals, and those in between, as appropriate and at the proper time.
One should resort to peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, and duplicity at the appropriate times.
Viṣṇu 3.40: Or one should set out on the journey in the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa.
Or during the misfortune of another, according to Viṣṇu 3.41.
Upon arriving in a foreign land, one should not abolish the customs of that country. (Viṣṇu 3.42)
And when attacked by an enemy, he should protect his own kingdom with his whole soul. (Viṣṇu 3.43)
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.44: For kings, there is no duty equal to the sacrifice of one's body in battle.
Those who are killed while protecting cows, brāhmaṇas, kings, friends, wealth, wives, or their own lives, partake in the heavenly realm.
And [this is] for the sake of protecting the intermixture of castes (varṇa-saṃkara), Viṣṇu 3.46.
Viṣṇu 3.47: Upon the conquest of an enemy's city, the king should install there a member of that [enemy's] family.
Viṣṇu 3.48: One should not exterminate the royal family.
Viṣṇu 3.49: Except from a royal family that is not of noble birth.
One should avoid addiction to hunting, gambling, women, and drinking.
And [the same applies] to verbal cruelty and physical violence, Viṣṇu 3.51.
One should not cause the loss of wealth. (Viṣṇu 3.52)
One should not cut off the primary gateways. (Viṣṇu 3.53)
Viṣṇu 3.54: One should not shower [gifts] upon an unworthy recipient.
Viṣṇu 3.55: He may take everything from mines.
Having found a treasure, one should give half of it to Brahmins.
Viṣṇu 3.57: One should cause the second half to enter the vessel.
A Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure-trove, may take it all for himself.
A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king, a fourth part to the Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself.
A Vaiśya, however, should give a fourth part to the king, half to the Brāhmaṇas, and take a fourth part for himself.
And a Śūdra, having divided what he has acquired into twelve parts, shall give five shares to the king, five shares to the Brāhmaṇas, and take two shares for himself.
Viṣṇu 3.62: One should confiscate everything belonging to a person who is known to have consumed food that has not been offered [to the gods].
Viṣṇu 3.63: From what has been hidden by themselves, they should give a twelfth part to the king, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu 3.64: One who claims that what was deposited by another was deposited by oneself shall incur a fine equal to the value of the deposit.
The king should protect the wealth of children, the destitute, and women. (Viṣṇu 3.65)
And Viṣṇu 3.66 states: "Having recovered wealth stolen by a thief, one should give it all back to those of all social classes."
And even if he cannot obtain it from his own treasury, he should still give it. (Viṣṇu 3.67)
One should pacify the afflictions caused by fate through means such as rites for peace (*śānti*) and auspiciousness (*svastyayana*).
And [he should provide for] the destruction of enemy armies through constant readiness with weapons. (Viṣṇu 3.69)
Viṣṇu 3.70: One should choose as a domestic priest (purohita) one who is well-versed in the Vedas, the Itihāsas, and the Dharmaśāstras, of noble birth, free from physical defects, and ascetic.
Viṣṇu 3.71: [He should appoint] those who are pure, free from greed, attentive, endowed with capability, and capable of assisting in all matters.
Viṣṇu 3.72: He himself should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu 3.73: Or, when examining legal proceedings, he should appoint a Brāhmaṇa.

Viṣṇu 3.74: The king should appoint as members of his council those who are endowed with noble birth, virtuous conduct, and observance of vows; who are impartial toward both enemy and friend; and who cannot be subverted by desire, anger, fear, greed, or other motives related to their duties.
And the king shall be dependent upon the astrologer in all his affairs. (Viṣṇu 3.75)
One should constantly worship the gods and the Brahmins. (Viṣṇu 3.76)
One should serve the elderly. (Viṣṇu 3.77)
And one who performs sacrifices is [also purified], Viṣṇu 3.78.
And in his realm, no Brāhmaṇa shall perish, oppressed by hunger.
And no one else either, even if devoted to virtuous deeds.
Viṣṇu 3.81: And he should bestow land upon Brāhmaṇas.

Viṣṇu 3.82: To those to whom he bestows it, he should give a document—written on cloth or a copper plate, inscribed with the names of his own ancestors, the dimensions of the land, and a description of the boundaries of the gift, and marked with his own seal—for the information of future kings.
And one should not seize land given by another. (Viṣṇu 3.83)
Viṣṇu 3.84: He should bestow all gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas.
But one should protect oneself from all sides. (Viṣṇu 3.85)
And he shall be of beautiful appearance.
And he should be one who maintains the mantras for antidotes that destroy poison.
Viṣṇu 3.88: One should not consume anything that has not been examined.
One should address others with a smile, preceded by a smile.
Even toward those deserving of death, one should not knit one's brows in anger. (Viṣṇu 3.90)
And he should cause punishment to be inflicted upon those deserving of it, in accordance with their offense. (Viṣṇu 3.91)
Viṣṇu 3.92: He should administer punishment properly.
Viṣṇu 3.93: He would not forgive a second offense from anyone.
Viṣṇu 3.94: There is no one who, failing to observe his own duty, is exempt from punishment by kings.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks fearlessly,
there the subjects flourish, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
In his own kingdom, he should administer justice through punishment; he should be severe in punishing enemies;
straightforward toward friends; and endowed with forbearance toward affectionate Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
The king who finds happiness in the happiness of his subjects and who is grieved by their suffering,
being endowed with fame in this world, is glorified in heaven after death.
The particle of dust situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [atoms] are a nit (likṣā). Viṣṇu 4.02.
Three of those [mustakas] are one royal mustard seed (rāja-sarṣapa).
Those three [mustard seeds] constitute one white mustard seed (gaura-sarṣapa).
Six of those [viṣṇus] make one barleycorn (yava).
Those three [māṣas] constitute one *kṛṣṇala*.
Five of those [rathikas] make one māṣa.
Twelve of those [muhūrtas] make half an akṣa. (Viṣṇu 4.08)
A *suvarṇa* consists of exactly two *akṣas* and four *māṣakas*.
Viṣṇu 4.10: Four suvarṇas constitute one niṣka.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together constitute one silver *māṣaka*.
Viṣṇu 4.12: Sixteen of those [māṣas] constitute one dharaṇa.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* consists of one *karṣa* of copper.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred are to be known as the middle, and one thousand is the highest.
Viṣṇu 5.01: Now, all those who have committed great crimes (mahāpātakin), with the exception of Brāhmaṇas, are liable to capital punishment.
Viṣṇu 5.02: No corporal punishment shall be inflicted upon a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 5.03: He shall banish from his own country a Brāhmaṇa who has been branded with a mark.
And in the case of killing a Brahmin, one should fashion a headless human figure on his forehead.
Viṣṇu 5.05: For drinking liquor, the mark of a tavern-sign.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.06: For theft, the punishment is the mark of a dog's foot.
Viṣṇu 5.07: [The penance for] approaching the bed of a guru is the Bhaga.
Viṣṇu 5.08: Even in other cases involving capital punishment, one should banish the offender along with his entire property, provided he remains unhurt.
And the king shall put to death those who forge royal edicts. (Viṣṇu 5.09)
And those who forge documents, [the king shall punish] according to Viṣṇu 5.10.
Viṣṇu 5.11: Those who administer poison, those who set fire [to property], violent robbers, and those who kill women, children, or men.
And those who would steal more than ten jars of grain; Viṣṇu 5.12.
Viṣṇu 5.13: [The fine for] things measured by weight shall be more than one hundred [paṇas].
And those of low birth who might desire sovereignty; (Viṣṇu 5.14)
And those who cause the breach of a dam (Viṣṇu 5.15).
And those who forcibly provide shelter, food, or provisions to thieves, [Viṣṇu 5.16].
Viṣṇu 5.17: Except in cases of inability on the part of the king.
Viṣṇu 5.18: [One may take] a woman whose husband is incapable [of providing for her] and who disregards him.
Viṣṇu 5.19: If a person of lower caste commits an offense against one of higher caste with a particular limb, that very limb of his shall be mutilated.
One who sits upon the same seat [as the king] or one who has made a mark on the king's waist shall be banished.
Having spat, one should act so as to be free from both lips.
And one who cannot control flatulence becomes deprived of the anus.
And one who reviles others is "fork-tongued" (vijihva). Viṣṇu 5.23.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.24: The king shall cause hot oil to be poured into the mouths of those who, out of arrogance, provide instruction on the Dharma.
And for the malicious utterance of another's name or caste, a ten-finger-long wooden stake shall be driven into his body.
One who speaks falsely regarding what has been heard, or regarding country, caste, or occupation, shall be fined two hundred kārśāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.26)
According to Viṣṇu 5.27, even one who speaks the truth regarding those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise disabled, shall be fined two kārṣāpaṇas.
One who insults his teachers shall pay two hundred *kārśāpaṇas*.
Viṣṇu 5.29: But when an accusation of a crime causing loss of caste is made against another, the highest amercement shall be imposed.
For one who has committed a secondary sin (upapātaka), the middle [amercement] applies. (Viṣṇu 5.30)
Viṣṇu 5.31: [The punishment for] reviling those advanced in the three Vedas and for [reviling] groups of people based on caste.
And for [theft from] a village or a district, the first amercement shall be imposed.
For a defamatory statement involving a physical deformity, the fine shall be one hundred kārṣāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.33)
But when it is joined with the mother, it is the highest [type]. (Viṣṇu 5.34)
In the case of insulting someone of equal caste, one shall be fined twelve paṇas.
For reviling one of a lower caste, the fine is six [paṇas]. (Viṣṇu 5.36)
Viṣṇu 5.37: For insulting a member of the highest caste at the appropriate time, the punishment shall be equal to that [offense].
Or three kārṣāpaṇas, according to Viṣṇu 5.38.
In the case of speaking words that are acidic or harsh, the same [penance] applies.
According to Viṣṇu 5.40: "One who commits adultery with a woman of his own caste shall be punished with the highest amercement."
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.41: For approaching a woman of inferior caste, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
And also for sexual intercourse with a cow, [one shall perform penance] according to Viṣṇu 5.42.
Viṣṇu 5.43: He who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the lowest caste shall be put to death.
Viṣṇu 5.44: For sexual intercourse with an animal, one shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who gives away a daughter without disclosing her defects [is also liable]. (Viṣṇu 5.45)
And he should support her. (Viṣṇu 5.46)
One who falsely accuses an innocent woman of being guilty incurs the highest fine.
One who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, a cow, or a bull should be made one-handed and one-footed.
And one who sells meat is [born as] a *viḍvarāha*. Viṣṇu 5.49: And one who sells meat is [born as] a *viḍvarāha*.
One who kills domestic livestock shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
He shall pay its value to the owner of the animal. (Viṣṇu 5.51)
One who kills a wild animal shall pay fifty kārṣāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.52)
One who kills birds and one who kills fish shall pay ten kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who kills insects shall pay a kārṣāpaṇa fine.
But one who cuts down a tree that bears fruit at the proper time commits the highest degree of violence.
One who cuts down a tree that is frequented by flowers incurs the middle amercement.
One who cuts down creepers, shrubs, or climbing plants shall pay a fine of one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
One who cuts grass [commits] one [offense]. (Viṣṇu 5.58)
And all [the sons] shall take that [property] from their respective fathers, according to the order of their birth.
One who raises his hand [to strike] shall pay ten kārṣāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.60)
With one foot, twenty [times]. Viṣṇu 5.61.
For striking with a piece of wood, the first amercement shall be imposed.
With a stone, the middling [fine]. Viṣṇu 5.63.
By means of a weapon, it is the highest [merit]. (Viṣṇu 5.64)
For plucking at the feet, hair, garment, or hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.65)
One who causes pain without drawing blood shall pay a fine of thirty-two paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.66)
Along with blood, [one commits] sixty-four [offenses]. (Viṣṇu 5.67)
In the case of breaking a hand, foot, or tooth, or in the case of cutting off an ear or nose, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
Viṣṇu 5.69: [The same penance applies] for restraining movement, food, or speech, and for dealing a blow.
And in the case of a fracture of the eyes, neck, arms, thighs, or shoulders, it is the highest [punishment]. (Viṣṇu 5.70)
Viṣṇu 5.71: A king shall not release from bondage one who pierces both eyes for as long as he lives.
Or one should make it exactly like that, according to Viṣṇu 5.72.
Viṣṇu 5.73: When many people strike one person, the punishment for each shall be double that which has been prescribed for a single offender.
[The same applies] to those standing near him who do not run toward one crying out, and to those passing by. (Viṣṇu 5.74)
And all those who cause injury to a person shall pay the expenses incurred for his recovery.
And those who cause suffering to domestic animals [are liable to the same fine]. Viṣṇu 5.76.
One who steals a cow, a horse, a camel, or an elephant shall have one hand and one foot amputated.
Viṣṇu 5.78: He is unborn, unchanging, incapable of being stolen, and the sole agent.
One who steals grain shall be fined eleven times its value. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.79)
And one who steals grain [is also liable]. Viṣṇu 5.80.
Viṣṇu 5.81: One who steals more than fifty [units] of gold, silver, or clothing shall be punished with mutilation (vikara).
Viṣṇu 5.82: He shall be fined eleven times the value of that which was deficient.

Viṣṇu 5.83: One who steals articles made of thread, cotton, cow-dung, molasses, curds, milk, buttermilk, grass, salt, clay, ashes, birds, fish, ghee, oil, meat, honey, split pulses, bamboo, earthenware, or metal vessels shall be fined three times their value.
And [the same applies] to cooked foods, according to Viṣṇu 5.84.
For the theft of flowers, green shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or leaves, the fine is five kṛṣṇalas.
And [the same applies] to leafy vegetables, roots, and fruits, according to Viṣṇu 5.86.
One who steals a jewel shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who steals articles not specifically mentioned [in the preceding rules] shall pay a fine equal to their value. (Viṣṇu 5.88)
Viṣṇu 5.89: Thieves shall be made to pay the owner the full value of everything that has been stolen.
Viṣṇu 5.90: Thereafter, the application of the prescribed punishment for them [shall take place].
Viṣṇu 5.91: He who gives the wrong path to those for whom the right path must be given shall be fined twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who does not offer a seat to one worthy of a seat [incurs a fault]. (Viṣṇu 5.92)
And not worshipping one who is worthy of worship—Viṣṇu 5.93.
And [the same applies] to the transgression of failing to invite a neighboring Brāhmaṇa, Viṣṇu 5.94.
And those who, having invited [others], do not provide them with food (Viṣṇu 5.95).
Having been invited and having replied "So be it," one who does not eat [the meal] [should give] a gold *māṣaka*.
And for one who provides a dwelling, double the amount of food [is required].
One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall pay sixteen suvarṇas.
For one who causes another to lose their caste, the penance lasts for a hundred years.
According to Viṣṇu 5.100, one is liable to capital punishment for drinking liquor.
For one who defames a Kṣatriya, the fine is half of that. Viṣṇu 5.101.
For defiling a Vaiśya, the fine is half of that as well—Viṣṇu 5.102.
For one who defames a Śūdra, the first amercement is prescribed. (Viṣṇu 5.103)
If one who is untouchable touches a member of the three higher castes who is touchable by his own will, he shall be put to death.
Viṣṇu 5.105: One should strike a woman in her menses with whips.
One who commits an act of impurity even near a path, a garden, or water shall be fined one hundred paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.106)
And one should abandon that as well. (Viṣṇu 5.107)
One who breaks a house, the ground, a wall, or similar structures shall be fined the middle amercement.
And one should apply that [mantra] as well. (Viṣṇu 5.109)
One who throws an object that causes distress into another's house shall pay one hundred paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.110)
And one who denies what is common property, Viṣṇu 5.111.
And one who does not give what has been sent [to him], according to Viṣṇu 5.112.
And one who abandons a father, son, teacher, sacrificial client, or officiating priest, provided they have not fallen from their status, is also [an offender]. (Viṣṇu 5.113)
And one should not abandon them. (Viṣṇu 5.114)
Viṣṇu 5.115: And those who feed Śūdras and wandering mendicants at rites for the gods or the ancestors [are also excluded].
And one who performs unsuitable actions. (Viṣṇu 5.116a)
And one who breaks into the houses of those living by the sea. (Viṣṇu 5.117)
One who administers an oath when not authorized [by the court] is liable for a fine. (Viṣṇu 5.118a)
Viṣṇu 5.119: One who causes the destruction of the virility of animals.
Viṣṇu 5.120: In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses is ten paṇas.
And for one who would act in the interval between those two, the punishment shall be the highest amercement.
And for one who practices fraud regarding weights and measures, [the same punishment applies]. (Viṣṇu 5.122)
Viṣṇu 5.123: And also for one who speaks falsely regarding what is not a fraud.
And for one who sells counterfeit goods, [the fine is] as prescribed by Viṣṇu 5.124.
Viṣṇu 5.125: [The king shall punish] merchants who, having banded together, withhold their merchandise at an unfair price.
And for those who sell [the property] individually, [the same penalty applies], according to Viṣṇu 5.126.
If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be compelled to pay it along with the profit.
And the king shall fine him one hundred paṇas.
Whatever loss occurs to one who purchases what has been sold without payment shall belong to the purchaser alone. (Viṣṇu 5.129)
Viṣṇu 5.130: For one who sells what is prohibited for a king, there shall be the forfeiture of that [article].
A ferryman who collects a land toll shall be fined ten paṇas.

Viṣṇu 5.132: A boatman, a customs officer, and one who collects tolls [are liable for the sin] of one who follows a student, a forest-dweller, a mendicant, a pregnant woman, or a person visiting a sacred ford.
And he should give that to them. (Viṣṇu 5.133)
Viṣṇu 5.134: In gambling, those who play with false dice shall have their hands cut off.
For those who gamble with fraudulent devices, the thumb and forefinger shall be cut off.
And [the same applies] to those who break open knots, Viṣṇu 5.136.
And for those who commit acts of abduction, the hands shall be cut off. (Viṣṇu 5.137)
Viṣṇu 5.138: If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman is not present, the fault lies with the herdsman.
And he shall pay the value of the lost animal to its owner. (Viṣṇu 5.139)
One who milks a cow without permission shall pay twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
If a buffalo should cause the destruction of crops, its keeper shall be fined eight *māṣas*.
The owner of a cow that has no keeper [is liable for its loss]. (Viṣṇu 5.142a)
But a horse, a camel, or a donkey [is the vehicle for a Brāhmaṇa]. Viṣṇu 5.143a: A horse, a camel, or a donkey.
If it is a cow, then half of that [penance].
Half of that [is the fine for] goats and sheep. (Viṣṇu 5.145)
Viṣṇu 5.146: If they sit down after having already eaten, the fine is double.
Viṣṇu 5.147: In all cases, the owner [of the field] shall also receive the value of the crop that has been destroyed.
On a path, in a village, or at the edge of a pasture, there is no offense. (Viṣṇu 5.148)
And [the same applies] when it is not enclosed, according to Viṣṇu 5.149.
Viṣṇu 5.150: For a short time.
And [the same applies] to the milk of cows that have calved after being set free [as a rite], Viṣṇu 5.151.
He who employs members of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who has abandoned the life of a renunciant shall perform service for the king. (Viṣṇu 5.153)
And a hired servant who abandons his service before the full term has expired shall pay the entire amount of the wages.
And according to Viṣṇu 5.155, he shall pay one hundred paṇas.
Viṣṇu 5.156: Whatever is destroyed through his fault shall belong to the owner.
Except in the case of an act of God. (Viṣṇu 5.157)
Viṣṇu 5.158: If the master should dismiss the hired servant before the term is completed, he must pay him his full wages.
And one hundred paṇas to the king. (Viṣṇu 5.159)
According to Viṣṇu 5.160, this is except in the case of a hired servant.
Viṣṇu 5.161: He who gives a girl, already betrothed to another, to someone else, shall be punished like a thief.
Viṣṇu 5.162: Except for the fault of bestowing a boon.
Viṣṇu 5.163: By abandoning one who is faultless.
And [he should avoid] his wife, Viṣṇu 5.164.
If one who is unaware openly purchases another's property, he is not at fault in that matter. (Viṣṇu 5.165)
The owner shall receive the property. (Viṣṇu 5.166)
Viṣṇu 5.167: If one should purchase [an article] that is unmanifested [in its true nature] and of low value, then both the buyer and the seller are to be punished like thieves.
One who misappropriates the property of a corporate body shall be banished.
And whoever should violate that agreement with him—Viṣṇu 5.169.
Viṣṇu 5.170: [The judge] shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay the wealth to the creditor together with the interest.
And he shall be punished by the king like a thief; Viṣṇu 5.171.
And he who says that something was deposited when it was not deposited; Viṣṇu 5.172.
Having punished the violator of a boundary with the highest amercement, the king shall have the boundary re-established.
One who eats forbidden food that causes loss of caste shall be banished. (Viṣṇu 5.174)
One who sells what is unfit for consumption or what is not to be sold, as well as one who breaks an image of a deity, shall be punished with the highest amercement.
A physician who practices deceitfully toward persons of the highest status [shall be punished].
Viṣṇu 5.177: For those of middling [strength], the middling [penance].
Among animals, it is first [to be performed]. (Viṣṇu 5.178)
One who fails to give what has been promised shall be compelled to pay it and be fined the first amercement. (Viṣṇu 5.179)
Viṣṇu 5.180: For those who give false testimony, the confiscation of all their property shall be carried out.
Viṣṇu 5.181: [The same penalty applies] to members of the court who subsist on bribes.
He who, without having released from one person land measuring at least a *go-carma* that has been mortgaged to him, should bestow it upon another, is to be put to death.
If [the weight] is less than sixteen suvarṇas, he shall be fined. (Viṣṇu 5.183)
If a man were to eat for a year whatever fruit he could obtain alone,
that earth— whether it be small or vast— would be no more than the size of a cow-hide.
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them,
he whose possession is accompanied by its fruit prevails, provided it was established without force.
But when property has been enjoyed for a long time with a clear title and through possession, the original acquirer obtains it there;
it can never be taken away from him.

Whatever property has been enjoyed by the father in accordance with the custom of possession and according to dharma, when he has died, he [the son] need not be questioned regarding it; for that which was acquired through possession belongs to him.
But land that has been enjoyed by three persons in due order,
even in the absence of a written document, may be acquired there by a fourth person.
In the case of killing clawed animals, horned animals, fanged animals,
or assassins (ātatāyins), as well as elephants, horses, and other such creatures, the killer incurs no guilt.
Whether it be a teacher, or a child, or an elder, or even a Brāhmaṇa deeply learned in the scriptures—
if he approaches as an *ātatāyin* (an assassin), one must indeed slay him without hesitation.
In the killing of an *ātatāyin* (one who seeks to kill), no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer;
whether done openly or in secret, it is simply fury recoiling upon fury.
One who raises a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who raises his hand to utter a curse;
one who kills by means of the Atharvan [mantras]; and a slanderer among kings—[these are to be avoided].
One should know that one who violates the wife [of another] is one of the seven assassins;
others say that those who seize fame and wealth, as well as those who take away dharma and artha, are also such.
O Earth, I have described to you in brief the procedure for punishment for all offenses; it would be excessively prolix were it to be detailed at length.
In other offenses as well, having ascertained the caste, wealth, and age [of the offender],
the king shall determine the punishment after consulting with Brāhmaṇas.

One who releases a person liable to punishment from that punishment shall incur double the penalty. And a man appointed [to oversee justice] who inflicts punishment on those not liable to it is the lowest of men.
In whose city there is no thief, no one who covets another's wife, and no one of wicked speech—[that king is equal to Brahmā].
That king who does not inflict punishment for violence nor kill those deserving of death shares in the world of Śakra.
Viṣṇu 6.01: Now, a creditor of superior rank shall receive from a debtor of inferior rank the amount of wealth as it was given.
Two, three, four, five, and a hundred [days] per month, according to the sequence of the social classes.
Or all castes may pay the interest as it was agreed upon by themselves. (Viṣṇu 6.03)
Even for one who has not performed [the rite], it is as prescribed when the year has elapsed.
Viṣṇu 6.05: There is no interest on the use of a pledge for personal enjoyment.
Except in the case of destruction caused by the king or by fate, the debtor of the highest grade shall pay back the lost pledge.
Viṣṇu 6.07: Even when the night has entered its final increase.
An immovable pledge [may not be alienated] except by a specific agreement.
Whatever immovable property has been given solely for the purpose of settling the money received, that shall be returned once the money received has been settled.
Viṣṇu 6.10: Interest on a loan that has been advanced ceases to accrue from that point forward if the creditor does not accept the repayment of the principal.
According to Viṣṇu 6.11, the maximum interest on gold is double the principal.
For grain, the interest is threefold.
For cloth, it is fourfold. (Viṣṇu 6.13)
The eight qualities of taste are described in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.14.
VI.15: The offspring belongs to the woman and the animals.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.16: [The gift of] fermenting agents, cotton thread, leather, weapons, bricks, and charcoal is inexhaustible.
For those not specifically mentioned, the fine is double.
One who accomplishes a matter entrusted to him by any means whatsoever should not be censured by the king. (Viṣṇu 6.18)
If one who is being prosecuted approaches the king, he shall be fined an amount equal to that [of the plaintiff].
If the debtor of the superior kind approaches the king, then the debtor of the inferior kind, having been proven by him, shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the amount of the debt.
And one who has obtained wealth and is thus released from the highest debt shall pay a twentieth part.
Viṣṇu 6.22: Even if the entire [debt] is denied but a portion is admitted, one must pay the whole.
And for that [debt], there are three means of proof: a written document, witnesses, and a formal agreement.
What has been received in the presence of witnesses should be returned in the very same manner, in the presence of witnesses.
When the defendant has entered the court for the purpose of the written document, the judge shall cause the document to be read aloud.
In the case of a partial payment or when the document is not present, the debtor who owes the highest amount shall provide his own written acknowledgment.
Viṣṇu 6.27: If the deceased was a debtor, or if he has gone forth as a wandering ascetic, or if he has been away on a journey for twenty years, his wealth must be paid by his sons or grandsons.
Viṣṇu 6.28: There is nothing higher than this for those who are free from desire.
Whether he has sons or is sonless, the inheritor of the estate shall pay the debt. (Viṣṇu 6.29)
Viṣṇu 6.30: One who seizes the wife of a man destitute of wealth [is a thief].
Viṣṇu 6.31: A woman does not incur [the debt] created by her husband or her son.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.32: Neither a wife nor sons [are entitled to inherit] what has been made over by a woman to her husband.
Viṣṇu 6.33: [An expiation] performed by a son does not [apply to] the father.
He who remains after a debt has been incurred by undivided family members shall pay it.
Viṣṇu 6.35: And the paternal debt belongs to brothers who have not divided [the inheritance].
And they shall be divided into shares according to their respective inheritance.
According to Viṣṇu 6.37, the husband of women belonging to the classes of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, hunters, or prostitutes shall pay the fine.
That which has been promised by word of mouth must not be withheld from anyone.
And that which is done for the sake of one's family (Viṣṇu 6.39).

Viṣṇu 6.40a-c: He who, having received a loan in its entirety, promises "I shall pay it tomorrow" in a peaceful manner, but later does not give it out of greed, shall likewise incur interest on that amount.
Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for trust, and for payment;
however, if the first two fail, the debt must be paid by them, and in the case of the latter, even their sons may be liable.

If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to their respective agreements; however, if no specific distinction has been made regarding the amount, the payment shall be made according to the will of the creditor.
Whatever amount the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
the debtor ought to pay that same amount doubled to the surety.
Viṣṇu 7.01 Now, documentary evidence is of three kinds.
Viṣṇu 7.02: [Evidence] is of three kinds: witnessed by the king, witnessed by witnesses, and without witnesses.
Viṣṇu 7.03: In the royal court, a document executed by a *kāyastha* appointed thereto, bearing the seal of its superintendent, and witnessed by the king, is valid.
Viṣṇu 7.04: Wherever, by whomever, and in whatever manner a document has been written, provided it is marked with the signatures of the witnesses and contains witnesses themselves.
A document written by one's own hand is valid even without witnesses. (Viṣṇu 7.05)
That which is caused by force is invalid, according to Viṣṇu 7.06.
Viṣṇu 7.07: All those [deeds] performed through fraud are likewise [invalid].
Even a case supported by witnesses is [rejected] if it is tainted by corrupted actions or marked by corrupt witnesses. (Viṣṇu 7.08)
And it was written by a scribe of such a kind [as previously described]. (Viṣṇu 7.09)
Viṣṇu 7.10: And [an act] committed by a woman, a child, one who is not independent, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one who is terrified, or one who has been beaten.
Viṣṇu 7.11: That which is not contrary to local custom, whose subject matter and defining characteristics are clear, and whose sequence and syllables are unimpaired, is authoritative.

One should establish a doubtful document by means of the castes [of the signatories], the marks made by them, the leaves [used], and logical arguments, as well as by means of evidence corresponding to those circumstances.
Viṣṇu 7.13: Wherever a debtor, a creditor, a witness, or even a scribe dies, one should validate that document by means of their own handwriting.
Viṣṇu 8.01 Now, those who are not witnesses.

Viṣṇu 8.02: Nor [should one eat] from a king, a learned brahmin (śrotriya), a renunciant, a gambler, a thief, one dependent on another, a woman, a child, a violent person, one who is very old, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one who is accused of a crime, an outcast, or one afflicted by hunger, thirst, calamity, vice, or passion.
And [the spies] who are connected with enemies, friends, or those involved in wealth, as well as those who have witnessed misconduct and those who possess capable assistants.
But one who, though not appointed as a witness, comes forward and speaks [is also considered a witness]. (Viṣṇu 8.04a)
And a single person is not a witness. (Viṣṇu 8.05)
Viṣṇu 8.06: In cases of theft, violence, verbal or physical assault, and adultery, witnesses need not be examined.
Now, concerning witnesses. (Viṣṇu 8.07)

Viṣṇu 8.08: Those born of noble families, endowed with good conduct and wealth, performers of sacrifices, ascetics, possessed of sons, knowers of dharma, students of the Vedas, truthful, and advanced in the three branches of knowledge.
One who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities and is approved by both parties, even if he is alone.
Viṣṇu 8.10: When two parties are disputing, the witnesses of the one who has the prior claim are to be questioned.
Viṣṇu 8.11: Where, due to the requirements of the case, the burden of proof falls upon the plaintiff, there it also falls upon the defendant.
Viṣṇu 8.12: If the designated witness has died or has gone to another country, those who have heard what was stated by him are the authority.
A witness is one who has seen [the matter] with his own eyes or heard it from others. (Viṣṇu 8.13)
And witnesses are purified by truth. (Viṣṇu 8.14)
Viṣṇu 8.15: Where there is the killing of those belonging to the [four] orders, there it is [expiated] by a false statement.
To purify himself from that, a twice-born man should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the Kūśmāṇḍī verses.
A Śūdra should give a single day’s portion of fodder for ten cows.
Viṣṇu 8.18: One should recognize a false witness by a change in natural disposition, a loss of facial color, and incoherent speech.
And having summoned witnesses at sunrise, he should question them after they have taken their oaths.
One should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak," according to Viṣṇu 8.20.
"Speak the truth," [he says] to a Kshatriya. *Viṣṇu* 8.21.
A Vaiśya [is purified] by means of cows, seeds, or gold.
But for a Śūdra who has committed all the great mortal sins (mahāpātaka), [the penance is as follows]. Viṣṇu 8.23.
And he should cause the witnesses to hear [the following]: Viṣṇu 8.24.
Those worlds which belong to the perpetrators of great sins and those which belong to the perpetrators of minor sins, these also belong to false witnesses.
And between birth and death, there is the loss of whatever good deeds have been performed. (Viṣṇu 8.26)
By truth the sun gives heat. (Viṣṇu 8.27)
By truth the moon shines. (Viṣṇu 8.28)
By truth the wind blows. (Viṣṇu 8.29)
By truth, the earth supports [beings]. (Viṣṇu 8.30)
By truth, the waters stand firm. (Viṣṇu 8.31)
By truth, Agni [is established]. Viṣṇu 8.32.
And the ether [is established] by truth. Viṣṇu 8.33.
By truth, the gods [are pleased]. Viṣṇu 8.34.
Through truth, sacrifices [are established]. (Viṣṇu 8.35)
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
For those who, though knowing the facts, remain silent and indifferent when called upon to give testimony,
they are equal to false witnesses in their sin and also in their punishment.
Thus indeed the king shall question the witnesses according to the order of their castes. He whose claim the witnesses declare to be true shall be the victor;
he who speaks otherwise shall certainly suffer defeat.

In a conflict between witnesses, O lord of men, the king should accept the majority; when they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their qualities; and when there is a conflict between those with qualities, he should accept the best among the twice-born.
In whatever legal dispute a false witness should speak untruth, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been executed, it shall be as if undone.
Viṣṇu 9.01 Now, the performance of the seasonal rites.
In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [the punishment shall be] according to his will.
In cases of deposits and theft, the value of the object shall be the standard of measure.
Viṣṇu 9.04: In all matters concerning property, one should calculate the value in gold.
In that case, if the amount is less than one *kṛṣṇala*, he should cause a Śūdra to swear by holding blades of *dūrvā* grass.
A handful of sesame seeds deficient by two kṛṣṇalas [is the fine].
If it is deficient by three kṛṣṇalas, he shall pay a fine of silver.
If it is less than four kṛṣṇalas, the fine shall be one suvarṇa.
Viṣṇu 9.09: [I bow to Him] who holds the plow that raised up the earth when it was burdened by the five Kṛṣṇas.
In the case of a Śūdra, a fine of half a suvarṇa less than one gold coin (suvarṇa) shall be imposed.
Thereafter, according to the requirements of the case, one of the following—[the ordeal by] the balance, fire, water, or poison—should be administered.
When the profit is twofold, the contractual arrangements for a Vaiśya are as previously described.
For a Kṣatriya, [the punishment] is threefold. (Viṣṇu 9.13)
For a Brāhmaṇa, [the interest] shall be fourfold, excluding the case of a pledge.
One should not administer an ordeal to a Brāhmaṇa. (Viṣṇu 9.15)
Viṣṇu 9.16: [This applies] except for an action bound to a future time or occasion.
In the case of a treasury, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa who has taken earth from a furrowed ploughed field to swear an oath.
Viṣṇu 9.18: Even when the offense previously observed is slight and the matter is minor, one should administer one of the divine ordeals.
The virtuous do not disclose the conduct of the virtuous, even when it concerns a matter of great importance.
The plaintiff shall proceed with the case by presenting his head.
And one who is accused shall undergo the ordeal.
Viṣṇu 9.22: In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [punishment may be imposed] even without the cutting off of the head.
Viṣṇu 9.23: A scale ordeal should be administered to women, Brāhmaṇas, the deformed, the infirm, and the sick.
And that [fragrance] does not waft when there is no wind.
Viṣṇu 9.25: Fire must not be given to lepers, the infirm, or blacksmiths.
And [the same applies] during the autumn and summer seasons. (Viṣṇu 9.26)
Viṣṇu 9.27: Poison must not be administered to lepers, those suffering from bile disorders, or Brāhmaṇas.
And during the rainy season, Viṣṇu 9.28.
Viṣṇu 9.29: Water [is forbidden] for those afflicted by phlegm or disease, for the timid, for those suffering from asthma or coughing, and for those who live by water.
And during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, [one should perform the rites] as prescribed by Viṣṇu 9.30.
Viṣṇu 9.31: A treasury must not be given to atheists.
Nor in a region afflicted by disease or pestilence (Viṣṇu 9.32).
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on,
he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the gods and the Brahmins.
Viṣṇu 10.01 Now, the ordeal by balance (dhaṭa).
Viṣṇu is four cubits in height and two cubits in width.
There, a balance made from a strong tree, five cubits in length and with scales on both ends, [should be placed].
And she shall be maintained by one among the following: a goldsmith, a worker in bronze, or a smith.
And there, one should place a man who has performed the divine rite in one scale-bowl, and a counterweight such as a stone in the second.
Having made two persons of equal weight well-marked—one as Viṣṇu and the other as the person—he should cause the [suspected] person to descend.
And one should take up the ordeal by balance according to the established rule.
And [he saw] Tulādhāra, the tenth incarnation of Viṣṇu.
Those worlds that are ordained for the slayers of Brahmins, and those worlds for false witnesses— those same worlds belong to the one who handles the scales dishonestly while weighing falsely.
O Viṣṇu, you are designated as the *dhaṭa* by words that are synonyms for Dharma. O *dhaṭa*, you alone know those things which human beings do not perceive.
"O Viṣṇu, this man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed upon you;
therefore, you ought to protect him from this doubt in accordance with dharma."
Then, however, he should place that man once again on the scale;
if, when weighed, he increases in weight, then he is pure according to the law.
In the case of the breaking of the suspension cord or the snapping of the axle, one should again mount the man [on the scale].
For in this way, there arises a certain knowledge from which a definitive conclusion follows.
Viṣṇu 11.01 Now, concerning the fire.
One should draw seven circles with an interval of sixteen finger-breadths each.
Then, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hands of Viṣṇu, who is facing eastward with both arms extended.
And one should wrap those two hands, together with the thread, with a cord.
Then, he should place there an iron ball weighing fifty palas, heated to the color of fire, and of uniform shape.
Taking him up, he should proceed, placing his feet in rhythmic circles, neither too quickly nor too slowly.
Then, having passed through the seventh circle, he should drop a lump of iron upon the ground.
Viṣṇu 11.08a: One whose hands are burnt anywhere [during the ordeal] should be declared impure. Viṣṇu 11.08c: But that man who is not burnt at all shall be considered pure.
But he who causes [the accused] to fall out of fear, or who is not perceived as burnt,
shall have the iron brought back again because the ordeal has not been cleared of doubt.
Viṣṇu 11.10a: At the very beginning, one should examine his hands for signs of having crushed grains of rice.
Viṣṇu 11.10c: Having consecrated two lumps of iron with mantras, one should then place them in his hands.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
O Agni, you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
"Viṣṇu 11.12a: This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification.
Viṣṇu 11.12c: Therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Viṣṇu 12.01 Now, regarding water.
In water that is free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like—Viṣṇu 12.02.
Viṣṇu 12.03: There, having grasped the knees of another person who is submerged up to the navel and is free from disease and malice, one should enter the consecrated water.
At that same moment, another man should discharge an arrow with a bow that is neither too fierce nor too soft.
And another man would swiftly bring that arrow back.
Among them, he who is not seen is proclaimed pure;
otherwise, he would be impure even if only a single limb were visible.
O Viṣṇu, you move within the waters of all beings like a witness;
you alone know those waters which human beings do not know.
"O Viṣṇu, this man, accused in a legal dispute, is sinking into you."
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, you ought to protect him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
Viṣṇu 13.01 Now, poison.
All kinds of poisons are not to be given away.
Except for the Śārṅga bow produced from the Himālaya mountains.
And one should give seven barley grains soaked in clarified butter to the person accused.
If the poison is digested easily, free from the distress of its onset,
then knowing him to be pure, one should release him at the end of the day.
O Poison, because of your nature as poison and your treacherous character, you are cruel toward all embodied beings;
O Poison, you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, seeks purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Viṣṇu 14.01 Now, the treasury.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should drink three handfuls of water from their ritual bathing.
Saying, "This was not done by me," he faces the installed deity.
Within fourteen days, or even within twenty-one days,
he shall see either disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, or perhaps a royal calamity.
One should know him to be impure; conversely, one is pure in the opposite case. And the righteous king should honor a man who has been proven pure in an ordeal.
Viṣṇu 15.01 Now, there are twelve kinds of sons.
Viṣṇu 15.02: The first is the legitimate son of the body (aurasa), begotten by oneself upon one's own wedded wife.
A son begotten by a man of the highest caste upon a wife who has been duly authorized by her sapinda is the second type, known as the *kṣetraja* (field-born).
Viṣṇu 15.04: The son of a daughter (putrikā-putra) is the third.
She who is given by her father with the stipulation, "The son whom she bears shall be my son," is a putrikā.
According to Viṣṇu 15.06, even one bestowed according to the procedure for an appointed daughter (*putrikā-vidhi*) is indeed an appointed daughter if she is without a brother.
The fourth is the paunarbhava (the son of a remarried woman).
A woman who has been consecrated again with the *akṣata* rite is called a *punarbhū*.
Moreover, even one who has previously belonged to another man is not [considered] unrefined [if she has been married].
The fifth is the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), according to Viṣṇu 15.10.
Viṣṇu 15.11: He who was begotten by one who had not been consecrated while still in her father's house.
And he [is the master] of the one who has taken her hand in marriage.
And the one born in secret within the house is the sixth.
Viṣṇu 15.14: He belongs to the one from whose bed he was born.
The son born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍha) is the seventh.
Viṣṇu 15.16: The son of a woman who undergoes the sacramental rites while pregnant belongs to her [biological father].
And he [is the witness] of the one who takes her hand.
And Dattaka is the eighth. (Viṣṇu 15.18)
And he belongs to those by whom he was given to his mother and father. (Viṣṇu 15.19)
And the ninth is the purchased [slave]. Viṣṇu 15.20.
And he belongs to the one by whom he was purchased. (Viṣṇu 15.21)
The tenth [type] is that which comes of its own accord; this is Viṣṇu 15.22.
And he belongs to whichever [deity] he has approached.
The eleventh, however, is the *apaviddha*.
Viṣṇu 15.25: One who has been abandoned by his father and mother.
And he [is the one] by whom that [debt] was taken.
And wherever he was produced, he became the twelfth. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 15.27)
Among these, each preceding one is superior to the next.
He alone is the heir to the inheritance. (Viṣṇu 15.29)
And he should also support others. (Viṣṇu 15.30)
Viṣṇu 15.31: For those who have not been married, one should perform the sacramental rites according to the extent of one's own wealth.
Those who have fallen from caste, eunuchs, those with incurable diseases, and the physically deformed do not receive a share of the inheritance.
Viṣṇu 15.33: They must be maintained by those who inherit their property.
And their legitimate sons (aurasa) shall be the heirs to their shares.
But not for one who has fallen [from his caste]. (Viṣṇu 15.35)
Viṣṇu 15.36: But when an act leading to loss of caste has been committed, those born subsequently [to the offender] are excluded from inheritance.
And those born of women in the inverse order of castes have no share in the inheritance. (Viṣṇu 15.37)
His sons [acted] even regarding their grandfather’s property. (Viṣṇu 15.38)
Those who take portions [of the property] must be supported by them.
And he who takes the wealth shall also be the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Viṣṇu 15.41: Even among those married to different women, the son of one is indeed the son of all.
And [the same applies] to brothers born of the same father. (Viṣṇu 15.42)
Viṣṇu 15.43: Even if he has not obtained his father’s wealth, a son should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself.
In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality,
provided he beholds the face of the born son while it is still living.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through a great-grandson, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Viṣṇu 15.47: In this world, no distinction is found between a grandson and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son delivers a man who has no son, just like a grandson.
Viṣṇu 16.01: Sons born of women of the same caste as their father are of the same caste.
Viṣṇu 16.02: From women of the same varṇa as their mothers, when married in the direct order of castes (anuloma), [sons] are of the same varṇa as their mothers.
Those born from women in the inverse order of castes are despised by the noble.
Therein, the son of a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra man is an Āyogava.
Viṣṇu 16.05: The Pulkasa and the Māgadha are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman by Vaiśya and Śūdra fathers, respectively.
And the Caṇḍāla, Vaidehaka, and Sūta are the sons of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and a Kṣatriya, respectively.
And the mixtures of mixtures are innumerable.
Viṣṇu 16.08: The descent into the arena for the Āyogavas.
The state of being a hunter belongs to the Pulkasas.
Viṣṇu 16.10: The act of praising is that of the Māgadhas.
And for the Caṇḍālas, their occupation is the execution of those condemned to death.
The protection of women and their livelihoods are the duties of the Vaidehakas.
Viṣṇu 16.13: For charioteers, the management of horses and chariots.
Viṣṇu 16.14: For Caṇḍālas, the specific rules are dwelling outside the village and wearing the clothes of the dead.
And for all [these], marriage shall be with those of the same caste.
And the embezzlement of one's father's wealth (Viṣṇu 16.16).
Viṣṇu 16.17: These castes born of intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own respective occupations.
The self-sacrifice of the body for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of cows, performed without worldly motive,
as well as [dying] in the protection of women, children, and others, is a cause of liberation even for those outside [the fold].
Viṣṇu 17.01: If a father divides his property among his sons, he has full freedom of will regarding wealth acquired by himself.
But regarding property inherited from a grandfather, the ownership of both father and son is equal.
Viṣṇu 17.03: Those who have divided the paternal estate shall give a share to one born after the partition.
Viṣṇu 17.04: The property of one who dies without a son goes to his wife.
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the daughter, according to Viṣṇu 17.05.
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the paternal ancestors.
In the absence of that [son], it goes to the mother (Viṣṇu 17.07).
In the absence of that [son], it goes to the brother (Viṣṇu 17.08).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the brother's son (Viṣṇu 17.09).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the kinsman (Viṣṇu 17.10).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to a kinsman (sakulya).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to one who studied together with him.
Viṣṇu 17.13: In the absence of those [heirs], the property goes to the king, with the exception of the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 17.14: For the sake of the Brahmins, [one should act] for the Brahmins.
The teacher shall take the property of a forest hermit. (Viṣṇu 17.15)
Or a disciple, according to Viṣṇu 17.16.
But a reunited co-heir shall take the share of one who was reunited, and a uterine brother that of a uterine brother;
he shall give and he shall take the share of one who has been born or one who has died.

Viṣṇu 17.18: What is given by the father, the mother, the son, or the brother; what is received at the nuptial fire; what is given upon supersession; what is given by a kinsman; the bride-price; and the subsequent gift—these constitute the woman’s property.
In the case of the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, when she has died childless, [the property] belongs to her husband.
And in the remaining cases, the father shall take [the property].
Viṣṇu 17.21: Whatever wealth belongs to all [the brothers] when a daughter has been born goes to the daughter.
If ornaments have been worn by women while their husband is still living, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their caste.
But for those who have many fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father;
whatever paternal inheritance belongs to a person, he shall take that, and no other.
Viṣṇu 18.01: If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons from wives of the four castes, they shall divide the paternal inheritance into ten parts.
In that case, the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares.
A son of a Kṣatriya woman [from a Brāhmaṇa father] inherits three shares. (Viṣṇu 18.03)
The son of a Vaiśya woman has two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.04)
But the son of a Śūdra woman inherits one share, according to Viṣṇu 18.05.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have three sons, excluding a Śūdra, they should then divide that wealth into nine parts.
Viṣṇu 18.07: According to the order of their castes, they shall take portions divided into four, three, and two parts respectively.
Viṣṇu 18.08: Dividing [the estate] into eight parts, excluding the Vaiśya, they shall take four, three, and one [shares] respectively.
Viṣṇu 18.09: [The earth] was divided into seven parts, excluding the Kṣatriyas—[namely] four, two, and one.
Viṣṇu 18.10: Excluding the Brāhmaṇas, [the other castes] are divided into six groups: three, two, and one.
Viṣṇu 18.11: Among the sons of a Kṣatriya by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra wife, this same division [of the estate] applies.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, then from the wealth divided into seven parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares.
A member of the royal caste [should recite] three [verses]. (Viṣṇu 18.13)
Now, if there is a Brāhmaṇa [husband] and two wives, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya, then from the estate divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares.
A Vaiśya has two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.15)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into five parts.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, may take four shares. (Viṣṇu 18.17)
A Śūdra [may marry] one [woman]. (Viṣṇu 18.18)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons who are a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, then they should divide that wealth into five parts.
A Kṣatriya, however, may take three shares. (Viṣṇu 18.20)
A Vaiśya has two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.21)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons who are a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into four parts.
A Kṣatriya, however, may take three shares. (Viṣṇu 18.23)
Viṣṇu 18.24: A Śūdra [shall pay] one [paṇa].
Viṣṇu 18.25: Now, if a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya should have two sons who are a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into three parts.
A Vaiśya may take two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.26)
Viṣṇu 18.27: A Śūdra [should offer] one.
Now, the sons of a Brāhmaṇa born of a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā—provided they are the only son—are entitled to inherit the entire estate. (Viṣṇu 18.28)
Viṣṇu 18.29: For a Kṣatriya, they are a Rājanya and a Vaiśya.
Viṣṇu 18.30: For a Vaiśya, [the witness] must be a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra [is the heir] of a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 18.31)
Among the twice-born, however, a Śūdra son alone shall take half the inheritance.
Whatever destiny belongs to the inheritance of one who dies without a son, that same destiny applies here to the second half [of the estate].
The mothers take away their shares according to the portion belonging to their sons. (Viṣṇu 18.34)
And unmarried daughters [are entitled to a share]. (Viṣṇu 18.35)
Sons of the same caste shall take equal shares. (Viṣṇu 18.36)
Viṣṇu 18.37: They should give the eldest an extra share of the best property.

Viṣṇu 18.38: If there should be two sons of a Brāhmaṇī and one son of a Śūdrā, then of the wealth divided into nine parts, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇī shall take eight shares and the son of the Śūdrā shall take one.

Now, if there should be two sons of a Śūdra woman and one son of a Brāhmaṇa woman, then the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares of the property divided into six parts, and the two Śūdra sons shall take two shares.
By this sequence, the allotment of portions occurs elsewhere as well.
If those who have been partitioned while living together should divide again, the division there shall be equal; in that case, seniority does not apply.
Whatever one acquires by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, that which is obtained through one's own effort, he is not obliged to give away unless he so desires.
But when one recovers ancestral property that had not been obtained, he shall not share it with his sons; likewise, he need not share what he has acquired by himself against his will.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession, pasture land, and books are not to be divided.
Viṣṇu 19.01: One should not have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra.
Viṣṇu 19.02: A twice-born man shall not [study] with a Śūdra.
Viṣṇu 19.03: Sons shall carry out the funeral rites for their father and mother.
Śūdras shall not [serve] a Brāhmaṇa, even if he be their father. (Viṣṇu 19.04)
Those Brahmins who carry out the funeral rites for a Brahmin who is without a protector partake in the world of heaven.

Having carried away the deceased relative and performed the cremation rites, they should approach the funeral pyre in a counter-clockwise direction and immerse themselves in water along with their clothes.
Having performed the offering of water for the deceased, they should offer a single funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass.
Having changed their garments and bitten neem leaves, they should place their foot on a stone at the doorway and then enter the house.
And they should throw unbroken grains of rice into the fire.
On the fourth day, they should perform the collection of the bones.
Viṣṇu 19.11: Their [bones] shall be cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
For as many thousands of years as the bones of a person remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that long he dwells in the heavenly world.
Viṣṇu 19.13: For as long as the period of impurity lasts, they should offer water and one funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the deceased.
And they should subsist on food that has been purchased or obtained [as alms].
And they abstain from eating meat. (Viṣṇu 19.15)
Viṣṇu 19.16: Those who sleep on the bare ground.
And those who sleep separately [from their wives]. Viṣṇu 19.17.

Having departed from the village at the end of the period of impurity, and having had their beards shaved, they should enter their home after bathing with a paste of sesame or mustard seeds and changing their clothes.
Having performed the rite of pacification there, they should also perform the worship of the Brahmins.
Viṣṇu 19.20: The gods are the invisible gods; the Brāhmaṇas are the visible gods.
The worlds are sustained by the brahmins. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 19.21)
By the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, the deities abide in heaven;
a word spoken by a Brāhmaṇa never becomes false anywhere.

Whatever the Brāhmaṇas, being most highly pleased, declare, that the deities welcome with approval. When those whose gods are visible are constantly satisfied, the gods whose gods are invisible become likewise satisfied.
Those of undaunted spirit should offer consolation to those afflicted by grief who have lost their kinsmen;
O Earth, delighter of the mind, I shall now declare to you those words with which they should do so.
That which is the northern course of the sun is the day of the gods.
The southern solstice is night for Viṣṇu.
A year is a day and night for Viṣṇu.
Thirty of those [fortnights] make a month.
Twelve months constitute a year. Viṣṇu 20.05.
The Kali Yuga consists of twelve hundred divine years.
The Dvāpara age consists of twice that number [of years].
The Tretā age consists of three such triple-units.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four such [units]. Viṣṇu 20.09.
Twelve thousand divine years constitute a cycle of four yugas.
Seventy-one cycles of four yugas constitute a manvantara.
And a thousand cycles of the four yugas constitute a kalpa.
And that [period] is one day of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
And his night is of the same duration.
By this reckoning of months and years, with such a day and night, the lifespan of the entire Brahmā is one hundred years.
And a day of Puruṣa is delimited by the lifespan of Brahmā.
At the end of that [day], there is a great kalpa.
His night is of exactly the same duration.
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 20.19: There is simply no reckoning of the number of human days and nights that have already passed.
And not for those yet to come. (Viṣṇu 20.20)
Because time has neither beginning nor end. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 20.21)
Thus, in this supportless time that is ever-flowing,
I do not perceive any being whose stability could be permanent.
The grains of sand in the Gaṅgā and the drops of rain when Indra pours down may be counted in this world,
but the deceased ancestors cannot be counted.
In every kalpa, fourteen lords of the gods perish,
as do the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of Daityas have been destroyed here by Time; what then can be said of human beings?
Many royal sages, endowed with all virtues,
as well as gods and celestial seers, have likewise met their end through the power of time.
Those who are capable in this world of being the cause of creation and destruction—
even they are led away by Time, for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having been overtaken by time, every living being is led to the next world; since a creature is subject to the bonds of its own actions, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no companionship in this world.
Since people grieving here do not benefit the deceased, one should therefore not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
For one who departs with both his good deeds and his evil deeds as his two companions,
what need has he for kinsmen, whether they grieve or not?
While there is impurity among his kinsmen, the deceased finds no stability;
therefore, he goes back to those very ones who offer the funeral cakes and water.
One who has died remains a *preta* until the performance of the *sapindīkaraṇa* rite;
to him who has gone to the world of the *pretas*, one should offer food together with a water-pot.
Having gone to the world of the ancestors, one eats at a śrāddha meal food equal to the svadhā offering;
therefore, offer the śrāddha for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
Whether in the state of a god, in a place of torment, in the womb of an animal,
or likewise in the human state, one receives the śrāddha offered by one's own kinsmen.
When a śrāddha has been performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer of the śrāddha is certain.
Therefore, having abandoned useless grief, the śrāddha should always be performed.
Only this much should always be performed for the deceased by his kinsmen;
a man should not seek to benefit the deceased by grieving, for it benefits neither him nor himself.
"Seeing the world without refuge and kinsmen dying,
O men, always choose Dharma alone as your companion."
Even when dead, a kinsman is unable to follow a deceased man;
for, with the exception of the wife, the path to Yama is closed to everyone else.
"Virtue alone follows him wherever he goes;
indeed, in this worthless world of men, practice virtue without delay."
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's task is finished or unfinished.
Death seizes and departs with one who is attached to fields, shops, or houses, yet whose mind is elsewhere,
just as a she-wolf seizes a lamb.
Time has no one dear to it, nor is there anyone who is its enemy;
when the lifespan resulting from one's actions is exhausted, Time forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings,
nor even recitations can save a human being who is overtaken by death or even by old age.
For even with hundreds of precautions, one is not able to ward off an impending calamity;
what lamentation can there be in that regard?
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does the deed performed in the past unfailingly find its doer.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, and indeed unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age within this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
Just as a person here takes up a new garment after discarding one previously worn, so too does the embodied soul take up a new body bound by its past actions.
Weapons do not cut him; fire does not burn him;
water does not moisten him; and the wind does not dry him up.
This [Self] is incapable of being cut, incapable of being burnt, incapable of being moistened, and indeed incapable of being dried up;
it is eternal, ever-moving, fixed, immovable, and ancient.
"He is called unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable;
therefore, knowing him thus, you ought not to grieve."

Viṣṇu 21.01 Now, upon the passing of the period of impurity, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as he is able, facing northward, after honoring them with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and other such items.
Viṣṇu 21.02: One should modify the mantras in the singular when only one person is intended.
In the vicinity of the leavings, he should offer one funeral cake (piṇḍa) alone, addressed by that person’s name and lineage.

When the Brahmins have finished eating and have been honored with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should offer inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) by means of the name and lineage (gotra) of the deceased, and then prepare three furrows (karṣū): four finger-breadths wide, that deep, and that long, dug at a distance of one span apart.
