And having established three fires near the trench (karṣū) and strewn grass around them, he should offer three oblations into each one of them.
To Soma, who honors the ancestors, Svadhā! Homage!
To Agni Kavyavāhana, Svadhā! Salutation! (Viṣṇu 21.07)
To Yama, to Aṅgiras, svadhā, obeisance! Viṣṇu 21.08.
And at the three places, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) as before.
Having filled three trenches with rice, curd, ghee, honey, and meat, one should mutter the mantra "etad te" (this for you).
In this manner, one should perform [the rites] every month on the anniversary of the death.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, preceded by the gods, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
Viṣṇu 21.13: At this point, one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and the offering of water for the feet (pādya).
Viṣṇu 21.14: He should join [the water] from the vessel for the guest's feet into the three vessels for the ancestors' feet with the mantra: "May the Earth unite with you."
Viṣṇu 21.15: One should offer four rice-balls (piṇḍas) in the vicinity of the remnants of the meal.
And having followed the Brahmins who have finished their meal and been given their sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them.
Then, one should place the *piṇḍa* for the deceased (*preta*) among the three *piṇḍas*, just like the water from the vessel used for washing the feet.
Viṣṇu 21.18: Even when in close proximity to the three trenches, it is exactly the same.

Having performed the Śrāddha for twelve days, including the Piṇḍīkaraṇa along with the monthly rites, one should perform it either on the thirteenth day; or, having performed the Śrāddha for twelve days like the monthly rites, one should perform it on the thirteenth day.
For Śūdras, however, [the rite] takes place on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras.
If an intercalary month (adhimāsa) should occur within the course of a year, then one should add one day for the purpose of the monthly rite.
The *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for women should be performed in the same manner;
likewise, one should perform the *śrāddha* every year as long as one lives.
For one whose sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for a year.
Viṣṇu 22.01: For a Brāhmaṇa, there is ten days of impurity (*āśauca*) upon the birth or death of those who share the funeral rice-ball (*sapinda*).
For a Kṣatriya, it lasts twelve days.
For a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days. (Viṣṇu 22.03)
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] for one month.
And the sharing of the funeral rice-ball (sapindata) ceases with the seventh person.
Viṣṇu 22.06: During a period of impurity, fire-offerings, giving, receiving, and one's own Vedic study are suspended.
Viṣṇu 22.07: During a period of impurity, one should not eat the food of anyone.
If one eats food even once from those who are in a state of impurity, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, his own period of impurity lasts for as long as theirs.
Viṣṇu 22.09: Upon the removal of impurity, one should perform an expiation.

Viṣṇu 22.10: Having eaten during the period of impurity of a person of his own caste, a twice-born man should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
Viṣṇu 22.11: But a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted during the period of impurity caused by the death of a Kṣatriya, becomes pure after performing this very [rite].
And a Kṣatriya [is impure] during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya. (Viṣṇu 22.12)
In the case of impurity due to the death of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.

Viṣṇu 22.14: During the period of impurity for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and during the period of impurity for a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya shall go to a flowing river and mutter the Gāyatrī five hundred times.
And a Vaiśya, during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a Śūdra shall perform a bath during the period of impurity of the twice-born.
A Śūdra, having bathed during the period of impurity caused by a Śūdra's death, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Viṣṁu 22.19: For wives and slaves, the period of impurity is equal to that of their master, according to the order of their castes.
When the master has died, [the property] belongs to oneself. (Viṣṇu 22.20)
Viṣṇu 22.21: For those of lower caste who have sapinda-relationship with persons of higher caste, purification occurs at the end of that [latter's] period of impurity.
For a Brāhmaṇa, in the case of sapinda relations who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods of impurity are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively.
For a Kṣatriya [impurity] regarding a Vaiśya or a Śūdra lasts for six nights and three nights respectively.
For a Vaiśya among Śūdras, purification occurs after six nights.
In the case of a miscarriage, [the penance lasts] for as many days and nights as there were months [of pregnancy]. (Viṣṇu 22.25)
If a child is born dead, or if it dies shortly after birth, there is immediate purification for the family.
In the case of a child who dies before the eruption of teeth, the impurity lasts for only that very day.
Viṣṇu 22.28: For him there is no consecration by fire, nor the rite of water-libation.
But if a tooth has emerged, yet the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) has not been performed, [the impurity lasts] for a day and a night. (Viṣṇu 22.29)
But for one whose tonsure ceremony has been performed yet who has not undergone other purificatory rites, purification occurs after three nights.
Thereafter, at the time as previously stated.
Viṣṇu 22.32: Marriage is the sacramental rite for women.
Viṣṇu 22.33: Among consecrated women, there is no period of impurity for the paternal kin.
Viṣṇu 22.34: If her birth or death should occur while she is in her father’s house, then there shall be impurity for one night and three nights respectively.
Viṣṇu 22.35: If another birth-impurity should occur during the midst of a birth-impurity, then purification occurs upon the conclusion of the first impurity.
Viṣṇu 22.36: [If it occurs] at the end of the night, [the period of impurity lasts for] two days.
Viṣṇu 22.37: [If performed] at dawn, [the result is attained] in three days.
Viṣṇu 22.38: Even if a death among one's own kin occurs during the period of impurity due to another death, the procedure is the same.
Having heard [of the death] while staying in another country, one becomes pure by means of the remainder of the period of impurity following birth or death. (Viṣṇu 22.39)
Viṣṇu 22.40: When the period of impurity has passed, [the purification] at the end of a year occurs after one night.
After that, by means of bathing. (Viṣṇu 22.41)
When the preceptor and the maternal grandfather have passed away, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
Viṣṇu 22.43a: When sons other than the legitimate son of the body have been born or have died;
Viṣṇu 22.43c: and when wives who had previously been married to another have given birth or have died.
Viṣṇu 22.44: Upon the death of the wife of a teacher, a son, a sub-teacher, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a fellow student, or a pupil, one becomes pure after one night.
And [one should not eat] when the king of one's own country is present. (Viṣṇu 22.45)
And also when someone who is not a sapinda dies in one's own house. (Viṣṇu 22.46)
There is no period of impurity for those killed by Bhṛgu, fire, fasting, water, in battle, by lightning, or by a king. (Viṣṇu 22.47)
For kings, there is no [impurity] regarding the performance of their royal duties.
Not [is there any fault] for those observing vows while they are engaged in their vow. (Viṣṇu 22.49)
Nor [should one study] during the sacrificial session of those performing a long-term sacrifice (sattra).
Viṣṇu 22.51: Not [the sin of killing] regarding the work of artisans performed by artisans.
Viṣṇu 22.52: [There is no fault] for those who carry out the king's orders, acting according to his will.
Viṣṇu 22.53: [The impurity does not apply] in the case of the consecration of a deity or a marriage, provided the preparations have already been made.
Viṣṇu 22.54: Not during a disturbance of the country.
And even in times of dire distress, Viṣṇu 22.55.
Those who commit suicide and those who are outcasts do not partake in the impurity rites or the water libations.
On the day of death, the female slave of one who has fallen [from caste] should cast away a jar of water with her foot.
He who cuts the noose of one who has died by hanging is purified by the *tapta-kṛcchra* penance. (Viṣṇu 22.58)
And one who performs the funeral rites for those who have committed suicide [is also excluded]. (Viṣṇu 22.59)
And one who causes the shedding of those tears [is also guilty]. (Viṣṇu 22.60)
Viṣṇu 22.61: For every deceased person, [the purification is attained] by the relatives after they have shed tears together and performed a ritual bath.
If the collection of bones has not yet been performed, [one becomes pure] by bathing with one's clothes on.

Having followed the funeral procession of a Śūdra corpse, a twice-born man should go to a river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
For the funeral rites of a deceased twice-born man, one hundred and eight [oblations] are prescribed.
A Śūdra, having followed a deceased person, should perform a ritual bath.
Upon inhaling the smoke from a funeral pyre, all social classes (varṇas) should perform a ritual bath.
Viṣṇu 22.67: [One should not recite the Veda] during sexual intercourse, after a bad dream, when blood is in the throat, or after vomiting and purging.
And also when the act of shaving the beard has been performed. (Viṣṇu 22.68)
And having touched one who has touched a corpse, or a menstruating woman, a Caṇḍāla, or a sacrificial post; Viṣṇu 22.69.
Except for what is fit to be eaten, one should avoid the carcass of five-toed animals, as well as their bones and fat.
In all these baths, one should not wear a garment that has not been washed.
A woman in her menses becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
If a woman who is menstruating touches another woman who is menstruating and of a lower caste, she shall not eat until she has become purified.
Having touched a woman of the same caste or of a higher caste, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or being desirous of eating or studying; having drunk, bathed, spat, or put on a garment; having stepped onto a road, or having voided urine or feces; and having touched the bone of a five-clawed animal that is not fatty—one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
And [the same applies] when conversing with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas (Viṣṇu 22.76).
Viṣṇu 22.77: One who has been defiled by bodily impurities below the navel or on the arms, or by liquor or wines, shall become pure by washing that limb with earth and water.
If one is struck elsewhere, one should wash that limb with earth and water and then perform a ritual bath.
But one who has been defiled by [food from] a mouth [of an outcaste] should fast and bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And one who is struck by the lips [of another]. Viṣṇu 22.80.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax,
sweat, nails, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
Gauḍī, mādhvī, and paiṣṭī are to be known as the three kinds of liquor;
just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the twice-born.
Viṣṇu 22.83a: Mādhūka, aikṣava, ṭāṅka, kaula, khārjūra, and pānasa;
Viṣṇu 22.83c: mṛdvīkā-rasa, mādhvīka, maireya, and that which is produced from the coconut.
"These ten kinds of liquor are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them."
A disciple, however, performing the ancestral rite (pitṛmedha) for his deceased teacher,
becomes pure there after ten nights together with those who partake of the funeral food.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, one who is under a vow is not deprived of his vow.
One who has been assigned a penance shall not perform the water-libation until the completion of the vow;
but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water,
smearing with cow-dung, wind, ritual action, the sun, and time— these are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Among all forms of purity, the purity of food is declared to be supreme;
for he who is pure regarding food is truly pure, not he who is merely pure by means of earth and water.
The learned are purified by forbearance; those who have committed forbidden acts are purified by giving gifts;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by the recitation of prayers; and those most proficient in the Vedas are purified by austerity.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
Viṣṇu 22.93a: This determination regarding bodily purification has been declared to you.
Viṣṇu 22.93c: Now hear the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.
Viṣṇu 23.01: That which is defiled by bodily impurities, by spirituous liquors, or by intoxicants is considered "extremely defiled."
Viṣṇu 23.02: All metal vessels that have been excessively defiled shall be purified by being cast into fire.
Viṣṇu 23.03: A vessel made of jewels, one made of stone, or a lotus-shaped vessel [is purified] by burying it in the earth for seven nights.
Viṣṇu 23.04: [An image] made of horn, ivory, or bone [is purified] by planing.
One should discard [an image] made of wood or clay. Viṣṇu 23.05.
If a garment that has been excessively soiled becomes clean after being washed, one should cut it away.
The purification of golden, silver, lotus-shaped, and gem-studded vessels that are not stained is by means of water.
Viṣṇu 23.08: [The purification] of cups made of stone, as well as of the *graha* vessels.
Viṣṇu 23.09: [The purification] of the *caru* vessel, the *sruk*, and the *sruva* ladles is performed with hot water.
Viṣṇu 23.10: By wiping the sacrificial vessels with the hand during the performance of a sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 23.11: [Purification] of the wooden sword (sphya), winnowing basket (śūrpa), cart (śakaṭa), pestle (musala), and mortar (ulūkhala) is by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
And [the same applies] to beds, vehicles, and seats. Viṣṇu 23.12.
And [the same applies] to many [offenses]. (Viṣṇu 23.13)
And [the same rule applies] to grain, skins, ropes, woven goods, wickerwork, thread, and cotton cloth. (Viṣṇu 23.14)
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, fruits, and flowers. (Viṣṇu 23.15)
And [the same applies to] grass, wood, and dry leaves. (Viṣṇu 23.16)
Viṣṇu 23.17: By washing these [limbs].
And [the same applies] to small quantities. (Viṣṇu 23.18)
Silk and woolen cloth [should be purified] with alkaline salts.
Viṣṇu 23.20: [The purification] of woollen blankets is by means of ariṣṭaka fruits.
Viṣṇu 23.21: [The purification] of silk cloths is by means of *śrī-phala* fruits.
For linen garments, [the purification is] with white mustard seeds; (Viṣṇu 23.22).
And [the same applies] to objects made of horn, bone, or ivory. (Viṣṇu 23.23)
Viṣṇu 23.24: [The price] of deer-skin rugs is determined by lotus-like eyes.
For those made of copper, brass, tin, and lead, [purification is] with acidic water.
One should purify bell-metal and iron with ashes. (Viṣṇu 23.26)
Viṣṇu 23.27: [The purification] of wooden objects is by planing.
[The purification] of things produced from fruit [is performed] with cow-hair. Viṣṇu 23.28.
According to Viṣṇu 23.29, purification by sprinkling is for things that are heaped together.
For liquids, purification is by means of straining.
Regarding Viṣṇu 23.31: by means of providing water and fire for the abundant products of sugarcane, such as molasses and the like, which have been stored in the house.
And [the same applies] to all types of salt, Viṣṇu 23.32.
According to Viṣṇu 23.33, earthen vessels [are purified] by firing again.
Viṣṇu 23.34: By re-consecrating images of deities that have been purified like material objects.
Regarding food that has not been rendered impure, one should discard only that portion which is defiled and perform the threshing and washing of the remainder.
Viṣṇu 23.36: Food prepared in an amount exceeding one droṇa does not become defiled even if it is contaminated.
Having removed only that which has been defiled from it, one should pour gold-infused water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra into it, and one should show it to a goat and to fire.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed over,
and that which is defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impure matter do not depart from an object,
so long must earth and water be applied in all cases of purification of substances.
A goat and a horse are pure by their very mouths; likewise, the impurities of cows and humans are not [inherently defiling]. Roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.
Roads, mud, and water touched by outcasts, dogs, or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of burnt bricks.
Now, for all living beings, one should effect purification with earth and water;
and for those who are extremely defiled, purification must always be performed without negligence.
Water on the ground is meritorious where a cow would satisfy her thirst;
likewise, water on a stone is pure provided it is not contaminated by impurities.
From a well in which a five-toed animal has died, or which is otherwise utterly defiled,
one should draw out all the water and purify the remainder with a cloth.
One should perform the kindling of the fire in a well that has been lined with baked bricks;
subsequently, one should pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into a well newly filled with water.
O Earth, in the case of small and stagnant reservoirs of water, purification is declared to be the same as for a well; however, in large bodies of water, there is no defilement.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by word.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
so too is almsfood received through a Brāhmaṇa intermediary, and all mines whatsoever.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
The meat of an animal killed by dogs is declared to be pure;
likewise is the meat of one killed by carnivorous beasts, or by others such as Caṇḍālas and robbers.
Viṣṇu 23.51a: One should declare those apertures which are above the navel to be pure; Viṣṇu 23.51c: those which are below are impure, as are the excretions that have fallen from the body.
Flies, droplets, shadows, a cow, an elephant, a horse,
sunbeams, dust, the earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure.
The primary drops that fall upon the limbs do not make one impure;
nor do those that enter the mouth via the beard, nor those caught between the teeth. (Viṣṇu 23.53)
The drops that touch the feet of one who is providing water for others to sip are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
If one who has food in his hand is somehow touched by someone who is impure from remnants of food,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without even setting that object down.
A house is purified by sweeping and smearing; a book, by sprinkling;
and [the ground] by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and scraping.
The purification of the ground is achieved either by burning it or by the dwelling of cows upon it. Cows are purifying and auspicious; in cows, all worlds are established.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all sins.
Cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and gorocanā [are likewise sacred].
This water from the horns of cows is a supreme limb [of the ritual], most auspicious and preeminent among the products of cows; it is meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
Scratching the bodies of cows indeed destroys all impurities;
by giving morsels of food to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
For the Gaṅgā dwells here in the footprint of cows, and nourishment is increased in their dust;
Lakṣmī resides in their dung, and Dharma in bowing to them; therefore, one should always perform prostration to them.
Viṣṇu 24.01 Now, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives according to the sequence of the castes.
For a Kṣatriya, there are three [wives]. (Viṣṇu 24.02)
For a Vaiśya, there are two [months]. Viṣṇu 24.03.
Viṣṇu 24.04: One [wife] for a Śūdra.
Viṣṇu 24.05: Among those [wives], the hand should be taken in marriage according to the order of their respective castes.
According to Viṣṇu 24.06, a Kṣatriya maiden may shoot an arrow at one who makes a proposal to her when he is not of her own caste.
Viṣṇu 24.07: A goad [is the gift] for a daughter of a Vaiśya.
Viṣṇu 24.08: [The penance for one who wears] the hem of a garment belonging to a Śūdra woman.
One should not take as a wife a woman who belongs to the same *gotra* or who has the same *ṛṣi*-lineage (*pravara*).
Viṣṇu 24.10: [A bride] from the mother’s side up to the fifth generation, and from the father’s side up to the seventh generation; Viṣṇu 24.11: nor one who is not of good family.
Nor one who is diseased. (Viṣṇu 24.12)
Nor one with an extra limb. Viṣṇu 24.13.
Nor one who has a missing limb. (Viṣṇu 24.14)
Nor one who is excessively tawny. Viṣṇu 24.15.
Nor one who is garrulous. Viṣṇu 24.16.
Now, there are eight forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca [are the eight forms of marriage].
Viṣṇu 24.19: Having invited [the groom], the giving of a daughter to one who possesses virtuous qualities is the Brāhma [form of marriage].
The offering made to a priest presiding at a sacrifice is for the gods (daiva).
By the mention of "a pair of cows," the [verse] belongs to the Ṛṣis (the Ārṣa marriage).
The Prajāpatya [gift] consists in the giving of what has been requested. (Viṣṇu 24.22)
Viṣṇu 24.23: The Gāndharva form of marriage is the union of two people who desire each other, in the absence of their mother and father.
Through purchase, one becomes an Asura. (Viṣṇu 24.24)
Viṣṇu 24.25: By seizing [the enemy] in battle, one becomes a Rākṣasa.
Viṣṇu 24.26: From approaching [a woman] while she is asleep or intoxicated, the Paiśāca form [of marriage arises].
Viṣṇu 24.27: Among these, the first four are lawful (dharmya).
Even the Gāndharva marriage is permitted for Kṣatriyas, according to Viṣṇu 24.28.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman purifies twenty-one generations of men.
The son of Daivī was Caturdaśa. Viṣṇu 24.30.
And there are seven sons of Ārṣī, according to Viṣṇu 24.31.
The Prājāpatya penance lasts for four days.
Viṣṇu 24.33: By giving a daughter in the Brāhma form of marriage, one causes her to go to the world of Brahmā.
By means of divine [action], one attains heaven. (Viṣṇu 24.34)
The Vaiṣṇava [sacrifice] is performed according to the Ṛṣi [tradition]. Viṣṇu 24.35.
By the Prājāpatya penance, one reaches the world of the gods.
By the Gāndharva rite, one goes to the world of the Gandharvas. (Viṣṇu 24.37)
The father, the grandfather, a brother, a paternal relative, the maternal grandfather, and the mother—these are the givers of a daughter in marriage.
In the absence of the former, the subsequent one remains in its own nature; thus [the sequence] is "the other, the other. (Viṣṇu 24.39)
A maiden, having waited through three menstrual seasons, may choose her own husband;
but once three seasons have passed, she always has the power over herself.

A maiden who sees her menses while still in her father’s house and remains unconsecrated by marriage is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; one who carries her away does not incur guilt for taking a learned woman.
Viṣṇu 25.01 Now, the duties of women.
Viṣṇu 25.02: [The wife] shall practice the same vows and conduct as her husband.
Viṣṇu 25.03: Worshiping one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, teachers, deities, and guests.
Viṣṇu 25.04: The state of having well-refined utensils.
Viṣṇu 25.05: Not having an open hand (generosity).
Viṣṇu 25.06: The state of having well-concealed vessels.
Viṣṇu 25.07: Lack of interest in fundamental duties.
Viṣṇu 25.08: Devotion to auspicious conduct.
When the husband has gone abroad, she should not perform acts of personal adornment. (Viṣṇu 25.09)
Viṣṇu 25.10: Not entering the houses of others.
Viṣṇu 25.11: One should not remain standing at the doorway, nor near the cattle, nor at the windows.
Viṣṇu 25.12: Lack of independence in all actions.
In childhood, youth, and old age alike, there is dependence upon the father, the husband, and the son.
When her husband has died, she shall observe lifelong celibacy or ascend the funeral pyre after him.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even a fast;
by serving her husband, however, she is exalted in heaven.
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still alive,
she takes away his lifespan and goes to hell.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those lifelong students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins).
Viṣṇu 26.01: When there are many wives of the same caste, he should perform religious duties together with the eldest.
Viṣṇu 26.02: And when they are of mixed castes, he may do so even with one of the same caste who is the youngest.
In the absence of a woman of the same caste, however, one may take a woman of the next lower caste, even in times of distress.
But a twice-born man must never [beget a son] by means of a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra wife of a twice-born man can never serve the purpose of dharma;
she is declared to exist for the sake of pleasure alone for him who is blinded by passion.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry a woman of inferior caste,
quickly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and Atharvans are dominated by that [impurity], neither the ancestors nor the gods eat; he does not go to heaven.
Viṣṇu 27.01: When the presence of the embryo is clearly discerned, the rite of impregnation (niṣeka) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.02: Before the fetus begins to move, the Puṃsavana rite [should be performed].
Viṣṇu 27.03: In the sixth or eighth month, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.04: And when a son is born, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.05: At the end of the period of impurity, the naming ceremony (nāmadheya) should take place.
The auspicious [mark] belongs to the Brāhmaṇa. (Viṣṇu 27.06)
For a Kṣatriya, [the fine] is twenty-seven times the strength [of the offense].
For a Vaiśya, it should be provided with wealth. (Viṣṇu 27.08)
Viṣṇu 27.09: [The food] of a Śūdra is contemptible.
In the fourth month, the ceremony of showing the sun takes place.
Viṣṇu 27.11: In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.
Viṣṇu 27.12: In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.13: These same rites for women are performed without mantras.
Their marriage is performed with the recitation of mantras.
Viṣṇu 27.15: For a Brāhmaṇa, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) takes place in the eighth year from conception.
According to Viṣṇu 27.16, [the initiation] for a king is in the eleventh year from conception.
Viṣṇu 27.17: For Vaiśyas, [initiation] occurs in the twelfth year from conception.
Viṣṇu 27.18: Their girdles (mauñjya) are made of muñja grass, bowstring, or balbaja grass.
The sacred threads and garments made of cotton, hemp, and wool; Viṣṇu 27.19.
Viṣṇu 27.20: Deer-skins, tiger-skins, and goat-skins.
The staffs are made of palāśa, khadira, or udumbara wood. (Viṣṇu 27.21)
Viṣṇu 27.22: The hairline, the forehead, and the region of the nose are equal [in measure].
Or rather, all [of them] indeed [are entitled]. (Viṣṇu 27.23)
They are not crooked and possess their bark. Viṣṇu 27.24a.
Wandering for alms, he perceives that which begins with you, that which is in the midst of you, and that which ends with you.
The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
From this point forward, if these three [classes] likewise remain uninitiated at the proper time,
they become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vrātyas, and are censured by the Āryas.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, and girdle are prescribed for him, whatever staff and whatever garment [are prescribed], those same items shall also be used during his religious observances (vrata).
Having cast his girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are ruined, he should take others while reciting the mantras.
Viṣṇu 28.01 Now follows the residence in the teacher’s family for those practicing the vow of studentship (brahmacārins).
Viṣṇu 28.02: The worship of the two twilights (saṃdhyā).
Viṣṇu 28.03: One should recite the morning twilight prayer while standing, and the evening twilight prayer while seated.
Viṣṇu 28.04: At two times of the day, one should perform the ritual of ablution and the rites pertaining to the sacred fire.
Viṣṇu 28.05: Submerging in water like a staff.
Viṣṇu 28.06: Studying when summoned.
Viṣṇu 28.07: Performing what is pleasing and beneficial for the guru.
Viṣṇu 28.08: Wearing a girdle, a staff, a deerskin, and the sacred thread.
Viṣṇu 28.09: Except for the family of one's teacher, he should wander for alms among those who possess virtuous qualities.
Viṣṇu 28.10: Eating almsfood authorized by one's guru.

Viṣṇu 28.11: One should avoid salt, fermented liquids, stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, the remnants of others' food, injury to living beings, and vulgar speech during the performance of a śrāddha.
Viṣṇu 28.12: Sleeping on the ground.
Viṣṇu 28.13: One should rise before one's teacher and go to sleep after him.
Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), he should perform the salutation to his teacher (gurv-abhivādana).
And with his hands crossed, he should touch his feet.
Viṣṇu 28.16: [One should touch] the right [foot] with the right [hand], and the other [foot] with the other [hand].
And at the conclusion of the salutation, he should announce his own name, ending with the word "bhoḥ."
Whether standing, sitting, lying down, eating, or facing away, one should not engage him in conversation.
Standing, one should serve him who is seated; approaching, him who is walking; going forward to meet him, him who is coming toward oneself; and running after him, him who is running away.
Facing one who has turned his face away. (Viṣṇu 28.20)
Having approached the presence of one who is standing at a distance.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu as he lies asleep, [one should recite] 28.22.
And he should not sit at his ease within the range of that person's sight.
And one should not utter his name alone.
One should not imitate his gait, gestures, speech, and so forth. (Viṣṇu 28.25)
Wherever there may be censure or slander of him, he should not remain there.
Viṣṇu 28.27: He should not sit on the same seat as him.
Except for traveling by stone, wooden plank, or boat. (Viṣṇu 28.28)
Viṣṇu 28.29: When the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher.
And one who has not been instructed by his teacher should not salute his own elders.
Viṣṇu 28.31: Toward a child, one of equal age, a teacher, or the son of a teacher, one should behave as toward a guru.
One should not wash his feet. (Viṣṇu 28.32)
One should not eat what is left over as leavings. (Viṣṇu 28.33)
In this manner, one should acquire the Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas.
Then, from Viṣṇu 28.35, the Vedāṅgas.
But he who, having not studied the Veda, exerts himself in other matters, goes to the state of a Śūdra along with his progeny.
Viṣṇu 28.37: The first birth is from the mother; the second is the binding of the girdle of muñja grass.
In that regard, Sāvitrī becomes his mother and the teacher (ācārya) becomes his father. By this very fact, they attain the status of the twice-born.
Viṣṇu 28.40: Prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, a twice-born man is equal to a Śūdra.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) should remain either shaven-headed or with matted hair.
After completing the study of the Veda, having been permitted by his teacher and having given him a gift, he should perform the ceremonial bath.
Then, one should spend the remainder of one's life in the family of the guru alone.
In that case, when the teacher has passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher himself.
Viṣṇu 28.45: [The same penance applies] for approaching the wives of one's guru or women of one's own caste.
In the absence of that [marriage], he should become a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*) devoted to the service of the sacred fire.
The Brahmin who thus practices the vow of celibacy without sloth goes to the highest station and is not born here again.
Viṣṇu 28.48a: [The penance for] the intentional emission of semen by a twice-born man who is observing a vow.
Those who know the Dharma say that for a religious student (brahmacārin), this constitutes a transgression of his vow.
When this sin has been incurred, having donned the skin of a donkey,
he should go about for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them and eating only once a day,
and performing ablutions three times a day, he becomes purified in one year.
If a twice-born student (*brahmacārī*) should involuntarily emit semen during sleep,
he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the *ṛc* verse beginning with "punar mām."
If, while not being ill, he fails to go for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for an *avakīrṇin*.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware, he shall fast for the day while reciting [the sacred prayers].
Viṣṇu 29.01: One should know him as an *ācārya* who, having performed the initiation and the instruction in the vows, teaches the Veda.
But he who should teach this for a fee, him one shall treat as a mere sub-teacher (upādhyāya) or as a teacher of only a single portion.
Viṣṇu 29.03: One should know that he who performs another's sacrificial rites is his officiating priest (ṛtvij).
One should not employ anyone who has not been examined.
One should not teach [the Veda] during these times.
One should not initiate him [into the Vedic studies]. Viṣṇu 29.06.
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two dies or incurs enmity.
Where neither virtue nor wealth exists, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge must not be imparted, just as one would not sow auspicious seed in barren soil.
"Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.'"
O Viṣṇu, do not speak of me to one who is envious, dishonest, or crooked; thus may I remain possessed of power.

"O Brahmin, you should teach me to that person whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy; to one who would never deceive you and who would never say anything unkind—teach me to such a guardian of the treasure."
Having performed the ritual commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the Vedic meters on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, one should study for four and a half months.
Then, one should perform their dismissal outside.
Between the Utsarjana and Upākarma rites, one should engage in the study of the Vedāṅgas.
One should not study for a day and a night on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
Viṣṇu 30.05: Nor during the impurity caused by the birth of a child or the death of a relative, nor during the period of another season or the occurrence of an eclipse.
Viṣṇu 30.06: Not during the departure of Indra.
And [one should not study] when a violent wind is blowing.
Viṣṇu 30.08: [One should not study] during unseasonable rain, lightning, or thunder.
Viṣṇu 30.09: [One should not study] during earthquakes, the falling of meteors, or when the quarters of the sky appear to be on fire.
Viṣṇu 30.10: Nor in a village where a corpse lies inside.
Not during a conflict of scriptural authorities. (Viṣṇu 30.11)
Nor [should one study] amidst the barking of dogs, the howling of jackals, or the braying of donkeys. (Viṣṇu 30.12)
Nor when there is the sound of musical instruments. (Viṣṇu 30.13)
One should not [recite] in the presence of a Śūdra or an outcaste.
Nor [should one urinate] in a temple, a cremation ground, at a crossroads, or on a main road. (Viṣṇu 30.15)
Viṣṇu 30.16: Nor [should one enter] the water's edge.
One should not sit with the feet placed upon a seat.
Viṣṇu 30.18: Not on vehicles drawn by elephants, horses, camels, boats, or oxen.
Viṣṇu 30.19: Nor one who has vomited.
Viṣṇu 30.20: Nor one who has been purged.
Viṣṇu 30.21: One who has not digested [his food] should not eat.
Viṣṇu 30.22: [There is no penance] for passing between five-clawed animals.
Nor [should one recite] during the calamities of a king, a Vedic scholar, a cow, or a Brāhmaṇa. (Viṣṇu 30.23)
Nor at the ceremony for the commencement of Vedic study (anupākarmaṇi).
Viṣṇu 30.25: Not during the act of evacuation.
In the sound of the Sāman, the Ṛc and Yajus do not exist.
One should not go to sleep after studying during the final watch of the night.
Even when engaged in study, one should avoid reciting during the periods when study is prohibited.
Viṣṇu 30.29: Because that which is studied during a time unfit for study yields no fruit either in this world or in the next.
Viṣṇu 30.30: By the study of that [text], there is a depletion of the lifespan of both the teacher and the pupil.
Therefore, with the exception of the days when study is forbidden, one who desires the world of Brahmā should sow knowledge in the fields of worthy disciples by means of the teacher.
Viṣṇu 30.32: At the beginning and at the conclusion of the study of the Veda, the pupil must perform the clasping of the teacher’s feet.
And the Praṇava should be uttered. (Viṣṇu 30.33)
And in that regard, whatever *ṛc* verses he recites, by means of those, there comes to be satisfaction for his ancestors through the clarified butter (*ājya*).
By that honey, [he attained] the Yajus formulas. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 30.35)
Viṣṇu 30.36: That which is the Sāman chants, by that milk.
Viṣṇu 30.37: With that which is Atharvaṇic, [one should offer] with that meat.
Viṣṇu 30.38: By him who studies the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and Dharmaśāstras, it is as if he has eaten his food.
And he who, having acquired knowledge in this world, should live by it, that [knowledge] shall not yield fruit for him in the next world.
And he who destroys the reputation of others by means of his own learning.
And one should not acquire knowledge from others who are studying without having been granted permission.
The theft of that [Veda] from him constitutes the stealing of Brahman, which leads to hell.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge,
one should never bear malice toward the person from whom that knowledge is received.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world.
Viṣṇu 30.45: One should understand that birth to be his which his mother and father produce for him through their union, when he is born here from a womb.
But that caste which his preceptor, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is true, and it is free from old age and death.

He who fills one's ears with that which is not false, bringing about freedom from suffering and bestowing immortality—he should be regarded as both father and mother; knowing what he has done for him, one should never bear him malice.
Viṣṇu 31.01: There are three things that are extremely heavy for a man.
Viṣṇu 31.02: The mother, the father, and the teacher.
Viṣṇu 31.03: One must always be intent on serving them.
Whatever they may tell you, that you should do.
One should act for their pleasure and welfare. (Viṣṇu 31.05)
Without being permitted by them, one should not do anything at all.
These three are indeed the Vedas; these three are indeed the gods;
these three are indeed the worlds; and these three are indeed the sacred fires.
Viṣṇu 31.08: The father is the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire.
All duties are honored by him who honors these three;
but for him who disregards them, all ritual acts are fruitless.
By devotion to his mother he attains this world; by devotion to his father, the middle world;
and indeed, through service to his teacher, he reaches the world of Brahmā.

Viṣṇu 32.01: A king, an officiating priest, a learned Vedic scholar, one who prohibits unrighteousness, a teacher, a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, an elder brother, and a relative are to be treated like an Ācārya.
Viṣṇu 32.02: Their wives are of the same caste (savarṇā).
Viṣṇu 32.03: A mother’s sister, a father’s sister, and an elder sister.
Viṣṇu 32.04: For one's father-in-law, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, and officiating priest who are younger than oneself, rising to meet them is itself the salutation.
Viṣṇu 32.05: For women of lower castes who are the wives of one's gurus, one should perform a salutation from a distance, but not the touching of their feet.
Viṣṇu 32.06: One should not perform the uprooting of hair, the application of collyrium, the binding of the hair, the washing of the feet, and so forth for the wives of one's teachers.
Even if she is not a relative, another's wife should be addressed as "sister," "daughter," or "mother. (Viṣṇu 32.07)
And one should not address one's teachers by the pronoun "you."
If he transgresses that [rule], he should remain without food and, having propitiated him at the end of the day, eat.
And one should not engage in contentious discussions with one's teacher.
And he should certainly not engage in the censure of this [text].
And it is not unintended. (Viṣṇu 32.12)
A young wife of one's teacher, however, should not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world by a man who has completed twenty years of age and is capable of discerning virtues and faults.
However, on this earth, a young man may at his pleasure perform a formal salutation according to the rule for the wives of his teachers who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey, one should clasp the feet of the teacher's wives every day and offer salutations,
remembering the dharma of the virtuous.
Wealth, kinship, age, action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is more weighty than the preceding.
A ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa and a hundred-year-old king—one should recognize these two as father and son; however, of the two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.
Among Brahmins, seniority is determined by knowledge; among Kṣatriyas, by valor;
among Vaiśyas, by grain and wealth; and among Śūdras, solely by birth. (Viṣṇu 32.18) [End of Part 1] (Viṣṇu 33)
Now, for a person, there exist three most terrible enemies known as desire, anger, and greed.
33.02 Through attachment to possessions, especially for those in the householder stage of life, [this arises].
Therefore, being overcome by this, he engages in minor offenses, great sins, secondary sins, and minor transgressions.
In cases that cause loss of caste, those that cause mixture of castes, and those that render one unworthy of receiving gifts.
Viṣṇu 33.05: And for miscellaneous minor offenses that bring about impurity.
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to the destruction of the self—
namely desire, anger, and greed— one should therefore conquer these three.
Viṣṇu 34.01: Sexual intercourse with one’s mother, sexual intercourse with one’s daughter, and sexual intercourse with one’s daughter-in-law are the most heinous crimes (atipātaka).
But those who have committed these most heinous sins (atipātakin) should enter the fire;
for indeed, no other expiation for them exists in any way whatsoever.
Viṣṇu 35.01: Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and violating the teacher’s wife—these are the great sins (mahāpātakas).
And their conjunction [is also a cause]. Viṣṇu 35.02.
One falls by associating with an outcast for a year.
Viṣṇu 35.04: By means of a single vehicle, food, eating, and sleeping.
But through connections such as those by marriage, by the sacrificial ladle, or primarily by blood, [the impurity ceases] immediately.
Those who have committed great sins may be purified by the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha),
as well as by visiting all the sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth.

Viṣṇu 36.01: For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, for a woman in her menses, for a pregnant woman, for a woman of the Atri lineage, for an embryo of unknown sex, and for one who has come for refuge—killing any of these is equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
False testimony and the murder of a friend—these two are equal to the drinking of liquor.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the seizure of land and the theft of a deposit are equal to the theft of gold.
Viṣṇu 36.04: Sexual intercourse with the wives of a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, or a king is equal to violating the bed of one's guru.

And approaching the father’s sister, the mother’s sister, or one’s own sister [is a mortal sin].* *Note: This verse is part of a section on *mahāpātaka* (mortal sins) according to the legal tradition of Viṣṇu.*
And sexual intercourse with the wives of a learned Vedic scholar, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a friend.

Viṣṇu 36.07: [One incurs sin by approaching] one’s own sister, a female friend, a girl of the same lineage, a woman of the highest caste, a maiden, a woman born of the lowest caste, a menstruating woman, one who has sought refuge, a female ascetic (*pravrajitā*), or one who has been entrusted [to another].

Viṣṇu 36.08a–c: These are secondary sinners (*anupātakin*), just like those who commit the great sins (*mahāpātakinaḥ*). They are purified by the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Viṣṇu 37.01: Speaking falsehood for the purpose of self-exaltation.
Slander directed against the king is a transgression punishable by death.
And [the sin of] obstinately persisting in falsehood toward one's teacher is equal to that of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu 37.04: Censuring the Vedas.
And the abandonment of what has been studied [is a cause for loss of caste]. Viṣṇu 37.05.
And [the same applies] to the fire, the ancestors, the mother, the son, and the wife.
Viṣṇu 37.07: Eating food that should not be eaten or consuming what is unfit for consumption.
Viṣṇu 37.08: Stealing the property of others.
Viṣṇu 37.09: Approaching the wives of others.
Viṣṇu 37.10: Officiating at the sacrifice of one for whom it is forbidden to sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 37.11: Living by means of improper action.
And accepting gifts from the wicked. (Viṣṇu 37.12)
The killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a cow.
Viṣṇu 37.14: Selling what should not be sold.
Viṣṇu 37.15: The state of being a *parivitti* (one whose younger brother marries before him) occurs when the elder brother [marries after his younger brother].
Viṣṇu 37.16: [The penance for] marrying before an elder brother.
And he should give him his daughter in marriage. (Viṣṇu 37.17)
And officiating at sacrifices for others (Viṣṇu 37.18).
Viṣṇu 37.19: The state of being a Vrātya.
Teaching for a fee (Viṣṇu 37.20).
And receiving instruction from a hired teacher [is a cause for loss of caste]. (Viṣṇu 37.21)
Viṣṇu 37.22: He has authority over all mines.
Viṣṇu 37.23: The setting in motion of the great machine.
Viṣṇu 37.24: Indeed, [this includes] the injury of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and medicinal herbs.
Viṣṇu 37.25: The livelihood of a woman.
And there is engagement in acts of sorcery and rites for the sake of power. (Viṣṇu 37.26)
Viṣṇu 37.27: Undertaking actions for one's own sake.
Not maintaining the sacred fires. (Viṣṇu 37.28)
Viṣṇu 37.29: The non-discharge of debts owed to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
Viṣṇu 37.30: Studying false scriptures.
Viṣṇu 37.31: Atheism.
Viṣṇu 37.32: [The same applies] to one who is like a bard (kuśīlava).
Viṣṇu 37.33: Drinking intoxicants and consorting with women [inappropriately].
Thus end the minor offenses (upapātakas), according to Viṣṇu 37.34.
But these men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, they should perform the Parāka penance or sacrifice with the Go-sava rite.
Viṣṇu 38.01 Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 38.02: Smelling that which should not be smelled or intoxicating liquor.
Deceit. Viṣṇu 38.03.
Viṣṇu 38.04: Engaging in sexual intercourse with animals.
And [the suffix *viṣṇu*] is used in the masculine sense.
Thus end the acts that cause loss of caste, according to Viṣṇu 38.06.
Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance;
if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
Viṣṇu 39.01: The killing of domestic or wild animals is an act that causes the confusion of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
Having committed an act that causes mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), one should eat barley-gruel for a month,
or else one should perform the *kṛcchra* or *atikṛcchra* penance as an expiation.
Viṣṇu 40.01: Accepting wealth from those who are censured, trade, living by usury, speaking untruths, and serving Śūdras—these are acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts.
Having rendered someone unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), one is purified by the Tapta-kṛcchra penance,
or by the Śīta-kṛcchra, or again by the Mahāsāṃtapana.
Viṣṇu 41.01: The killing of birds, of aquatic animals, and of creatures born in water.
And [the same applies] to worms and insects. (Viṣṇu 41.02)
Viṣṇu 41.03: Eating after having followed [the guest] halfway.
Thus, according to Viṣṇu 41.04, these [acts] bring about impurity.
For acts that cause defilement, the *taptakṛcchra* is the means of purification;
or else, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* is the purifying expiation.
Viṣṇu 42.01: That which has not been mentioned is miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka).
Having ascertained the gravity or lightness of a miscellaneous offense,
a wise man shall perform the penance with the approval of Brāhmaṇas, as appropriate.
Viṣṇu 43.01 Now, the hells.
Viṣṇu 43.02 Tāmisra.
Viṣṇu 43.03: Andhatāmisra (the darkness of blindness).
Viṣṇu 43.04: Raurava.
Viṣṇu 43.05: [The hell named] Mahāraurava.
Viṣṇu 43.06: Kālasūtra.
Viṣṇu 43.07: Mahānaraka.
Viṣṇu 43.08: The means of restoration to life.
Viṣṇu 43.09: Avīci.
Viṣṇu 43.10: Tapanam (The Burning).
Viṣṇu 43.11: Saṃpratāpana (the "Scorching" hell).
Viṣṇu 43.12: Saṃghātakam.
Viṣṇu 43.13: The kākola.
Viṣṇu 43.14: A bud.
Viṣṇu 43.15: [It is] putrid earth.
Viṣṇu 43.16: An iron spike.
Viṣṇu 43.17: Ṛbīsa.
Viṣṇu 43.18: A path that is uneven.
Viṣṇu 43.19: The thorny silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*).
Viṣṇu 43.20: Dīpanadī.
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 43.21: The Forest of Sword-Leaves.
Viṣṇu 43.22: "The iron prison."
Viṣṇu 43.23: Those who have committed heinous sins (atipātakin) and have not performed expiation for them are cooked in these hells, one after another, for the duration of a kalpa.
Viṣṇu 43.24: Those who have committed great sins [remain so] for the duration of a Manvantara.
And those who have committed secondary sins (anupātakin). Viṣṇu 43.25.
Those who have committed minor offenses [must remain outside] for the duration of four yugas.
And those who have performed acts that cause the mixture of castes must remain so for a thousand years.
And those who have committed acts that cause the loss of caste. (Viṣṇu 43.28)
And those who have been rendered unworthy through the *apātrīkaraṇa* rites (Viṣṇu 43.29).
And those who have committed acts that cause impurity. Viṣṇu 43.30. And those who have performed acts that cause defilement.
And those who have committed miscellaneous sins [remain so] for many series of years.
Viṣṇu 43.32: Sinful men who have committed offenses, immediately after giving up their life-breaths, reach the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering.
Just as they are dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama,
being led away with great difficulty and distress.
Being devoured by dogs, jackals, and flesh-eaters, as well as by crows, herons, cranes, and the like,
and likewise by fire-mouthed serpents and scorpions.
Being burned by fire, pierced by thorns,
split apart by saws, and tormented by thirst.
Tormented by hunger and likewise by packs of fierce tigers,
they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
Desiring the food and drink of others,
they are beaten by the servants with faces resembling those of terrifying crows, herons, cranes, and other such birds.
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places they are beaten with pestles;
and in some places they are crushed upon iron hammers and likewise upon stone slabs.
In some places they eat vomit, in some pus and blood;
in some places feces, and in others flesh, which is most dreadful with the stench of pus.
In some places they remain in dreadful darkness,
being devoured by worms with most terrible fire-like beaks.
In some places they are afflicted by cold, and in others they dwell in the midst of impurity;
furthermore, in some places those most dreadful ghosts devour one another.
In some places they are struck by living beings while hanging there;
in some places they are hurled about by showers of arrows, and in others they are cut to pieces.
With their feet placed upon necks and entwined by the coils of serpents,
they are likewise tormented by mechanical devices and dragged along by their knees.
With their backs, heads, and necks broken, with needle-like throats, and most dreadful,
they possess bodies as large as houses, yet incapable of enduring torture.
Thus, having experienced their sin as suffering sinners, they become deeply distressed; they enter the wombs of animals and undergo various miseries.
Viṣṇu 44.01 Now, for those of sinful nature who have experienced suffering in the hells, there are rebirths in the animal wombs.
Viṣṇu 44.02: For those who have committed extreme crimes, there is a succession through all the stationary wombs.
And for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), there are births as worms.
For those who have committed minor offenses, the wombs of birds [are the result]. —Viṣṇu 44.04
Viṣṇu 44.05: Those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) are born from aquatic wombs.
For those who have committed acts that cause the loss of their caste, there are births among the species of aquatic creatures.
Those who have performed acts that cause the mixture of castes enter the wombs of animals. (Viṣṇu 44.07)
For those who have performed the act of making themselves unworthy of receiving gifts, there are rebirths as animals. (Viṣṇu 44.08)
Among humans, those who have performed acts that cause impurity are born into untouchable wombs.
Viṣṇu 44.10: Among the miscellaneous [offenses], those who are scattered [in their conduct] indeed become violent eaters of raw flesh.
One who eats food that is unfit to be eaten or consumed becomes a worm.
Viṣṇu 44.12: A thief becomes a hawk.
Viṣṇu 44.13: A hole-dweller that steals away the excellent path.
A mouse that steals grain [is the expiation]. Viṣṇu 44.14.
Viṣṇu 44.15: A swan is one who steals bell-metal.
Viṣṇu 44.16: One who carries water [in a vessel] on the heart, and one who immerses oneself in water.
Viṣṇu 44.17: A honey-gatherer.
Viṣṇu 44.18: Milk is for the crow.
A dog [perceives] taste. Viṣṇu 44.19.
Viṣṇu 44.20: A mongoose [is the deity of] ghee.
A vulture [eats] flesh. Viṣṇu 44.21.
The water-fowl [attains] fat. Viṣṇu 44.22.
Viṣṇu 44.23: One who drinks oil becomes oil itself.
Viṣṇu 44.24: "Lavaṇa" means "one who speaks ill."
In the case of curd, the punishment is a fine of one hundred and forty-four paṇas.
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge.
Dardura [became] a linen garment. Viṣṇu 44.27.
A Krauñca bird [kills] one who wears clothing made of cotton. Viṣṇu 44.28.
Viṣṇu 44.29: A lizard [is the portion] of a cow.
Viṣṇu 44.30: A vālguda is molasses.
The muskrat [is the presiding deity] of odors. Viṣṇu 44.31.
Viṣṇu 44.32: A peacock [is the deity of] leafy vegetables.
Viṣṇu 44.33: Sedhā is one who has prepared food.
A scorpion [is produced] from food that has not been offered.
Viṣṇu 44.35: Agni [was born] from Baka.
Viṣṇu 44.36: Household utensils.
Red garments belong to Jīvajīvaka; Viṣṇu 44.37.
The tortoise [supports] the elephant. Viṣṇu 44.38.
A tiger [kills] a horse. (Viṣṇu 44.39)
A monkey [eats] fruit or a flower. (Viṣṇu 44.40)
A bear [kills] a woman. Viṣṇu 44.41.
For a Vaiśya, the vehicle is a camel. (Viṣṇu 44.42)
A vulture [devours] animals. Viṣṇu 44.43.
Having forcibly seized any property whatsoever belonging to another, or having consumed an offering that has not been consecrated by sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
Women also, by stealing according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives of those very creatures [whom they have stolen].
Viṣṇu 45.01: For those who have been overcome by the sufferings of hell and have emerged from the state of animals, these marks appear among human beings.
One who suffers from leprosy is a perpetrator of a most heinous sin.
A killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with consumption.
A drinker of liquor becomes one with blackened teeth.
A stealer of gold becomes one with deformed nails.
One who fails to repay his teacher’s fee becomes one with bad skin. Viṣṇu 45.06. One who fails to repay his teacher’s fee becomes one with bad skin.
Viṣṇu 45.07: A slanderer has a putrid nose.
One with a foul-smelling mouth is a slanderer. (Viṣṇu 45.08)
A thief of grain becomes deficient in limbs. (Viṣṇu 45.09)
A thief who has stolen mixed goods has an extra limb.
One who steals food will suffer from chronic illness.
One who steals speech becomes mute. (Viṣṇu 45.12)
One who steals clothing becomes afflicted with vitiligo.
One who steals a horse becomes lame.
One who reviles gods or Brahmins becomes mute.
One with a flickering tongue is a poisoner. (Viṣṇu 45.16)
One who sets fire [to another's property] shall become insane, according to Viṣṇu 45.17.
One who acts in opposition to the guru becomes afflicted with epilepsy. (Viṣṇu 45.18)
But one who kills a cow becomes blind.
And one who steals a lamp [is reborn as a moth]. Viṣṇu 45.20.
And one who extinguishes a lamp becomes one-eyed. (Viṣṇu 45.21)
A washerman is one who sells tin, chowries, and lead. (Viṣṇu 45.22)
A seller of one-hoofed animals is a hunter of wild beasts. (Viṣṇu 45.23)
One who eats from a sacrificial pit has a vulva for a mouth. (Viṣṇu 45.24)
A bell-ringer is a thief. (Viṣṇu 45.25)
A usurer is a bhrāmarī.
One who eats only refined food becomes solitary and suffers from abdominal tumors caused by wind.
One who violates an agreement becomes a bald-headed man. Viṣṇu 45.28.
A man with elephantiasis and one who has violated his vow of celibacy.
One who destroys the livelihood of others becomes poor. (Viṣṇu 45.30)
One who causes suffering to others becomes afflicted with a chronic disease.
Thus, by virtue of specific past actions, they are born endowed with particular marks:
afflicted by diseases, as well as blind, humpbacked, lame, or one-eyed.
Dwarfs, the deaf, the mute, and others who are likewise weak—
therefore, one should perform expiation with every possible effort.
Viṣṇu 46.01 Now, the kṛcchra penances follow.
One should not eat for three days. (Viṣṇu 46.02)
And one should perform the ritual bath three times every day—at dawn, noon, and sunset.
Viṣṇu 46.04: Immersing oneself in water three times during each bath.
Having immersed himself in water, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while focused on Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu 46.06: Standing during the day, he should remain standing.
Viṣṇu 46.07: At night, he should remain seated.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
"Viṣṇu, 46.09"—thus is the Aghamarṣaṇa [hymn].
One should eat in the evening for three days, in the morning for three days, and eat food obtained unasked for three days; this is the Prājāpatya penance.
For three days one should drink warm water, for three days warm ghee, for three days warm milk, and for three days one should not eat at all; this is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
With these very same [substances] when cold, it is the *śītakṛcchra*.
The *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk alone for twenty-one days.
The *udaka-kṛcchra* consists of consuming barley-meal with water for one month.
By subsisting on lotus stalks, there is the Mūla-kṛcchra penance.
The Śrīphala-kṛcchra consists of subsisting on bilva fruits. (Viṣṇu 46.16)
Or with lotus-seeds, according to Viṣṇu 46.17.
For one who abstains from food, the *parāka* penance is completed in twelve days.
Viṣṇu 46.19: One should eat cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass for one day; on the second day, one should fast. This is the *sāṃtapana* penance.
The Mahāsāṃtapana penance consists of the daily practice of consuming cow urine and other substances.
And the *atisāṃtapana* consists of [the same] practiced for three days. (Viṣṇu 46.21)
Viṣṇu 46.22: The consumption of oil-cake, rice-scum, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, with an interval of fasting between each, constitutes the Tulāpuruṣa penance.
The *parṇakṛcchra* consists of drinking water boiled with the leaves of each of the following: *kuśa*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *padma*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vaṭa*, *brāhmī*, and *suvarcalā*.
Having undergone a shave, he should perform all these *kṛcchra* penances,
bathing daily at the three sessions of the day, sleeping on the ground, and having his senses subdued.
One should avoid excessive conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts; one should constantly recite purifying prayers and offer oblations according to one's ability.
Viṣṇu 47.01 Now follows the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should eat forty-seven mouthfuls of food that does not cause transformation.

Viṣṇu 47.03: One should increase those [meals] during the waxing of the moon's digits and decrease them during its waning; on the new moon day, one should not eat at all. This is the Cāndrāyaṇa penance known as "Barley-shaped" (yava-madhya).
Or it may be like an ant in the middle [thinner in the center].
That [lunar month] in which the new moon occurs at the middle [of the month] is called *pipīlikā-madhya* ("ant-middle").
That [lunar month] whose full moon day falls on the middle of the month is called *yavamadhyama*.
If one eats eight morsels every day for a month, that is the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*.
Eating four mouthfuls in the evening and four in the morning constitutes the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one should eat in any manner whatsoever three hundred meals minus sixty within a month, that is the common *cāndrāyaṇa*.
O Earth, in former times, the stainless Seven Sages,
as well as Brahmā and Rudra, having performed this vow, attained the supreme abode.
Viṣṇu 48.01: Now, if one should consider oneself heavy with sins committed by one's own actions, one should cook a *prasṛti* measure of barley-gruel for one's own sake.
Viṣṇu 48.02: One should not offer oblations into the fire after that [time].
And there is no offering of oblations (bali) here.
Viṣṇu 48.04: One should consecrate with mantras the uncooked, the being cooked, and the cooked [food].
While it is being cooked, one should perform the protection rite.

Viṣṇu is the path of the gods, the leader of poets, the seer of the wise, the buffalo of wild beasts, the hawk of vultures, and the axe of the forests; as Soma, he passes through the filter, chanting aloud.
"Viṣṇu 48.06"—with these words, he binds the darbha grass.
And one should eat that [milk-rice] after it has been boiled and poured into a vessel.

"O gods born of the mind, who delight in the mind, who are highly skillful and whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us; may they aid us; obeisance to them! To them, Svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer oblation into oneself.
Then, having finished eating, he should touch his navel.

"O Waters, having been bathed in you, may you become drinkable; O Yavas, dwell within our bellies! May they be for us free from disease, free from consumption, and free from sin—divine, immortal, and increasers of cosmic order. Thus [he says].
One who desires intelligence should [fast] for three nights. Viṣṇu 48.11.
One who commits a sin [becomes purified] after six nights.
Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself from any one of the great sins.
By a twelve-night fast, one burns away even the sin committed by one's ancestors.
Having drunk [it] for a month, all sins are [purified].
And for twenty-one nights, [the penance is] barley grains from which the husks have been removed by cows.
"You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey. You are the cleanser of all sins, a purifier held sacred by the seers."
Ghee is barley, honey is barley, and water is barley—the nectar of immortality.
May all of these purify whatever sin or evil deed I have committed.
O barley grains, destroy the misfortune and the ill-fortune known as Kālakarṇī— whatever has been done by speech, whatever deed has been committed, and whatever evil has been conceived by the mind.
O Yavas, purify for me that which has been licked by a dog or a pig, that which is defiled by food-leavings,
and the failure to serve my mother and father.
The food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or one in a state of birth-impurity,
the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral— purify these for me with barley.

O barley grains, purify for me the deceit of children, unrighteousness, and whatever is committed at the king's gate; the theft of gold, the state of being a *vrātya*, the officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice, and the reviling of Brahmins.
Viṣṇu 49.01: Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva on the twelfth day.
Viṣṇu 49.02: [One should worship] with flowers, incense, unguents, lamps, and food offerings, as well as by gratifying the fire and the Brāhmaṇas.
Having performed this vow for one year, O Viṣṇu, one becomes purified from sins.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, one attains Śvetadvīpa.
By performing this on the twelfth days of both fortnights for one year, one attains the heavenly world.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, [one attains] the world of Viṣṇu.
In this very same way, it is also [to be understood] regarding the fifteenth days.
By attending upon Keśava, who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day, and who has become Yoga, one shall attain the Great.
That full moon day in which the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky is declared to be the "Great Full Moon" (mahatī pūrṇamāsī) within the year.
On that day, acts such as giving gifts and fasting are proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
likewise, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) which falls on a Sunday (śukla) and is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism [is also so].
Having constructed a leaf-hut in the forest, he should dwell there.
Viṣṇu 50.02: He should bathe three times a day.
And proclaiming his own deed, he should practice begging for alms from village to village.
And he should sleep on a bed of grass.
This is the great vow (mahā-vrata). Viṣṇu 50.05.
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform [expiation] for twelve years.
Viṣṇu 50.07: A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 50.08: Nor one who is pregnant or in her menses.
Or a woman of the Atri lineage, O Viṣṇu.
Or a friend, according to Viṣṇu (50.10).
In the case of killing a king, one should perform the Mahāvrata twice over.
In the case of killing a Kṣatriya, the penance is one-quarter less than that for a Brāhmaṇa.
For killing a Vaiśya, the penance is half [of that prescribed for a Kṣatriya].
Half of that [penance] is for killing a Śūdra.
In all [these cases], according to Viṣṇu 50.15, he shall have a corpse's head as his banner.
For one month, having shaved his head, he should follow after cows.
While they are seated, he should sit.
And he should remain standing when they are standing. Viṣṇu 50.18.
And he should rescue those who are sinking.
And Viṣṇu shall protect [us] from fears.
Without providing protection for them from cold and other such elements, one should not provide it for oneself. (Viṣṇu 50.21)
One should bathe with cow urine.
And he should subsist on cow-products.
Viṣṇu 50.24: One should perform this cow-vow in the event of killing a cow.
Having killed an elephant, one should give five dark-blue bulls as a gift.
Viṣṇu 50.26: A horse or a garment.
For killing a donkey, one should give a one-year-old ox as a gift.
And for the killing of rams and goats, [the penance is] that of Viṣṇu (50.28).
For killing a camel, the fine is one *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala*.
Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights.

Having killed any one of a mouse, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a water-snake, or a python, and having fasted and fed a Brāhmaṇa with *kṛsara*, one should give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
For killing a monitor lizard, an owl, a crow, or a fish, one should fast for three nights.
Having killed any one of the following—a swan, a crane, a balākā bird, a water-fowl, a monkey, a hawk, a vulture, or a ruddy goose—one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a snake, one should give a spade made of black iron.
Having killed a eunuch, one [is purified] by [carrying] a load of straw.
Having killed a boar, [one obtains] a jar of ghee. (Viṣṇu 50.36)
Viṣṇu 50.37: A partridge [is purified] by a droṇa of sesame seeds.
A parrot two years old, like a calf. Viṣṇu 50.38.
A three-year-old krauñca bird [is the sacrificial fee]. Viṣṇu 50.39.
For killing a carnivorous beast, one should give a milch cow.
For killing a carnivorous wild animal, [one should give] a heifer.
In the case of killing an animal not specifically mentioned, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon killing a bird, one should eat only at night.
Or he should give a silver māṣa.
Having killed an aquatic creature, one should fast.
But for the killing of a thousand creatures possessing bones,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra.
But for the killing of animals possessing bones, one should give even a small gift to a Brahmin;
for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses are to be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food,
those born from fluids, and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛta) is the complete purification.
For the unauthorized taking of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
A drinker of spirituous liquor, excluded from all ritual acts, shall subsist on grains for a year.
Upon consuming any one of the impure liquors or intoxicants, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And [the same penance applies] for eating garlic, onions, leeks, anything having a similar odor, village pigs, village cocks, monkeys, or the flesh of cows—Viṣṇu 51.03.
Viṣṇu 51.04: In all these cases, at the conclusion of the penance, one should perform the sacramental rite (saṃskāra) for the twice-born once again.
Shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows are to be avoided in the rite of re-consecration (punar-saṃskāra).
If one eats the meat of five-toed animals, excluding the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one should fast for seven nights.
Having eaten the food of a member of a religious order, a prostitute, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights.
Viṣṇu 51.08: [The food] of a Takṣaka and of a leather-worker.
And [the food] of usurers, misers, those initiated for sacrifice, those bound in fetters, those accused of crimes, and eunuchs [is forbidden]. (Viṣṇu 51.09)
And [the food] of unchaste women, hypocrites, physicians, hunters, the cruel, the fierce, and those who eat the remnants of others [is forbidden].
Viṣṇu 51.11: [The food] of a woman whose husband is not a hero, of a goldsmith, of one whose husband has fallen from his caste, and so forth, [is forbidden].
And for those who speak slanderously or falsely, who have violated their dharma, and who sell the essence of the self, [the same applies].
And [the food] of actors, weavers, ungrateful persons, and washermen [is forbidden].
And [the food] of a blacksmith, a Niṣāda, a stage-player, a fisherman, and a seller of weapons is forbidden.
And [the food] of dog-cookers, vintners, oil-pressers, weavers, and washermen [is forbidden]. Viṣṇu 51.15.
And [the same applies to] those who dwell in the house of a menstruating woman together with her paramour.
Viṣṇu 51.17: [Food] looked upon by one who has killed an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, pecked at by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow.
If [the food] has been intentionally touched with the foot or sneezed upon (Viṣṇu 51.18).
And [the time] for those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted, according to Viṣṇu 51.19.
Viṣṇu 51.20: [One should not eat] meat that has not been offered in sacrifice or meat obtained for no purpose.
Regarding the consumption of the meat of all fish, with the exception of the *pāṭhīna*, *rohita*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* species, one should fast for three nights.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of any water-born creature, Viṣṇu 51.22.
Having drunk water contained in a vessel that held liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights.
And those who have stayed in a vessel that held liquor [become pure] after five nights.
One who drinks Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor, should immerse himself in water, mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and then consume clarified butter.
For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten unknown meat from a slaughterhouse and dried meat, [one should fast for three days]. (Viṣṇu 51.27)
For eating the flesh of carnivorous beasts or birds, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

If one eats the flesh of the kalaviṅka, the plava, the cakravāka, the haṃsa, the rajjudāla, the sārasa, the dātyūha, the parrot, the sārikā, the crane, the balākā, the cuckoo, or the khañjarīṭa, one should fast for three nights.
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of one-hoofed animals and those with two rows of teeth.
Viṣṇu 51.31: And for eating the meat of any bird, except for the partridge, the kapiñjala, the quail, the vartikā, and the peacock, [one must fast] for a day and a night.
One who eats insects for one day should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
And [the same penance applies] for eating the flesh of dogs. (Viṣṇu 51.33)
For eating mushrooms or *kavaka* fungi, one must perform the *sāṃtapana* penance.
Having avoided preparations of barley, wheat, and milk, as well as those treated with fats, fermented acids, and *khāṇḍava* sweets, one should fast after consuming whatever has become stale.
And those tree-exudations that arise from incisions or from impure substances, as well as those that are red.
Viṣṇu 51.37: Lotus roots, food prepared with water, kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, fried pastries, food offered to the gods, and sacrificial oblations.
And all kinds of milk, with the exception of that from cows, goats, and buffaloes. (Viṣṇu 51.38)
Viṣṇu 51.39: Those [days] which are less than ten days [are also considered impure].
And the milk of a cow that is dripping, one that has recently calved, or one whose calf is absent. (Viṣṇu 51.40)
And those who eat impure food [are also excluded]. Viṣṇu 51.41.
And those things that have turned sour, with the exception of curd.
One who belongs to the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya-āśramin) shall fast for three nights after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha).
And he should dwell in water for one day.
For eating honey or meat, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance. (Viṣṇu 51.45)
If one eats the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
Having eaten the leavings of a dog, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For eating food containing five-clawed animals, excrement, or urine, [one must observe penance] for seven nights.
If one eats at an *āma-śrāddha*, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall undergo this for seven nights.
For eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, one must observe the five-night penance.
For eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, one must observe a fast for three nights.
But for eating the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa's meal, the penance is one day.
A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra must fast for five nights.
One who eats the leavings of a Vaiśya shall fast for three nights.
A Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra [is likewise excluded].
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights.
Having eaten prepared food [from such a person], one must perform the Parāka penance.
A Brahmin, adhering to the eternal rule, must never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, he may eat those consecrated with mantras, established in the perpetual ordinance.
"For as many hairs as there are on the animal,
so many times does the one who kills an animal in vain incur death here and, after passing away, suffer the lack of atonement."
Cattle were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
for sacrifice is the source of prosperity for all, therefore killing in a sacrifice is not killing.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as the sin that accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain.
Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states of existence once again.
