In the honey-mixture offering, in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—
it is only in these cases that animals may be slain, and never otherwise.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, by killing animals for the sake of sacrifice,
leads both himself and the animals to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Vedas, even in times of distress.
Whatever injury to the moving and unmoving world is ordained by the Veda, one should know that as non-injury alone; for from the Veda, dharma shone forth.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor when dead.
He who does not desire to inflict the sufferings of bondage or death upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one performs, and toward whatever one forms an attachment—
that very thing one obtains without effort, provided that one does not harm anything whatsoever.
Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having thoroughly reflected upon the origin of meat and the killing and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat like a Piśāca, disregarding the prescribed rule,
becomes beloved in this world and is not afflicted by diseases.
The one who consents, the one who dissects, the one who kills, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat,
the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— all these are considered slayers.
"He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another,
without having first worshipped the ancestors and the gods— there is no doer of more unmeritorious deeds than he."
He who should perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by eating divine fruits and roots, nor by consuming the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He shall devour me in the hereafter, whose flesh I eat in this world"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "meat" (māṃsa).
One who has stolen gold, having confessed his deed to the king, shall hand over a wooden pestle.
Through the slaying or the abandonment of Viṣṇu, one becomes purified.
One should perform the Mahāvrata for twelve years, or [for a shorter duration] up to Viṣṇu (52.03).
And one who misappropriates a deposit is [guilty of the same]. Viṣṇu 52.04.
And one who steals grain or wealth shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
For the theft of a human being, a woman, a well, a field, or a pond, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed.
Viṣṇu 52.07: For substances of little value, the Sāṃtapana penance is prescribed.

Viṣṇu 52.08: For one who consumes food, drink, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, or fruits [that have been touched by a dog], the penance is the drinking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Viṣṇu 52.09: For stealing grass, wood, trees, dry food, molasses, clothing, leather, or meat, one shall fast for three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one shall eat small grains for twelve days.
Viṣṇu 52.11: For stealing cotton, silk from worms, wool, and the like, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Viṣṇu 52.12: For stealing animals with cloven hooves or solid-hoofed animals, one should fast for two nights.
In the case of stealing birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or articles made of split bamboo, one shall fast for a day.
Having recovered by any means the stolen property from the creditor,
one should then perform an expiation for the removal of that taint.
Whatever a man who is unrestrained may take from others,
by that very thing he shall be deprived when he is born again in whatever state of existence.
Since life, virtue, and desire are all established upon wealth,
one should therefore avoid the destruction of wealth through every possible effort.
But he who is intent on harming living beings, as well as he who is intent on harming wealth— of these two,
the one intent on harming wealth attains great suffering.

Viṣṇu 53.01 Now, regarding sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, one shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for a year in the forest, wearing rags, according to the procedure for the Mahāvrata.
And for approaching the wife of another, Viṣṇu 53.02.
Viṣṇu 53.03: And the cow-vow (go-vrata) applies when one has sexual intercourse with a cow.

Viṣṇu 53.04: In the case of discharging semen in a male, in a non-vaginal opening, in the air, in water, during the daytime, or while riding in a vehicle drawn by oxen, one should perform a bath along with one's clothes.
And by approaching a Caṇḍālī woman, one attains equality with her—thus says Viṣṇu (53.05).
If done through ignorance, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (Viṣṇu 53.06)
And for approaching a cow or a prostitute, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a woman who has once been unfaithful to her husband shall perform that same vow which is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years.
Viṣṇu 54.01: Whosoever is a sinful soul, with whomsoever he associates, he shall perform the very same expiation as that person.
Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-clawed animal or from one that is extremely defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
A Kṣatriya [shall fast] for two days. (Viṣṇu 54.03)
Viṣṇu 54.04: For one day, a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra [should eat] at night. (Viṣṇu 54.05)
And at the conclusion of the vow, all should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A Śūdra shall drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while a Brāhmaṇa shall drink liquor;
both of them go to the hell known as Mahāraurava.
If a man approaches his wife during her season except on the forbidden days, he shall fast for three nights.
A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 54.10: For voiding urine or excrement without water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One who has been released from the rising of the sun should bathe with his clothes on and recite the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
One who has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, a village pig, a donkey, a monkey, a crow, or an unchaste woman should go to a river and perform sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
One who has extinguished the sacred fires or neglected the Vedas shall bathe at the three daily sessions, sleep on the ground, and subsist for one year by begging alms only once a day.
For falsely exaggerating one's own qualities, for persistent falsehood toward a teacher, and for reviling him, one should subsist on milk alone for one month.
An atheist, one who lives as an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa—these shall subsist on alms for one year.
The one superseded in marriage, the one who supersedes, she by whom he is superseded, the giver, and the officiating priest—all these should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells living beings, land, merit, or Soma shall perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.

One who sells fresh herbs, perfumes, flowers, fruits, roots, skins, cane, split bamboo, chaff, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, cow's milk, oil-cake, sesame seeds, or sesame oil must perform the Prājāpatya penance. (Viṣṇu 54.18)

One who sells items made of phlegm-like substances, lac, honey, beeswax, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, tin, lead, black iron, copper, bronze, or swords, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Viṣṇu 54.19)
One who sells dyed cloth, dyes, gems, perfumes, molasses, honey, liquids, or wool shall fast for three nights.
One who sells meat, salt, lac, or milk shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And he should bring him back again.
Having traveled on a camel or a donkey, or having bathed naked, slept, or eaten, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Viṣṇu 54.23.
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month while staying in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

Having performed sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, having performed funeral rites for others, and having performed malevolent magic or a deficient sacrifice, one removes that sin by means of three *kṛcchra* penances.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
But for those twice-born men who, having engaged in improper acts, desire to perform penance and have been abandoned by the Brāhmaṇas,
one should likewise prescribe this same [penance].
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation,
they are purified by relinquishing it, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and by austerity.
Upon the omission of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.
Having threatened [to strike], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance;

for actually striking, the Atikṛcchra. One should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra for causing blood to flow from a Brāhmaṇa. One should not have any dealings with those who have been purified of their sins.
And one who knows the Dharma should not feel contempt for these [outcastes] once they have performed the ritual purification.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful— even if they are pure according to dharma— nor with those who kill those who have sought refuge, nor with those who kill women.
One who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen,
as well as women and the sick, deserve half of the prescribed penance.
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been specifically stated,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
Viṣṇu 55.01 Now, the secret penances follow.

Having reached the river Viṣṇu, one who bathes daily, performs sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the prescribed rules, and eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) once a day, becomes purified from the murder of a Brahmin within a month.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
Viṣṇu 55.04: By means of this vow and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, even a drinker of spirituous liquor becomes purified.
By reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one who has committed the theft of gold [is purified].
One who has violated the teacher's bed is purified by fasting for three nights and performing the recitation and fire-oblation of the Puruṣasūkta.
Just as the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha), the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
A twice-born man should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
indeed, all the sins of a twice-born man are consumed by breath control.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath;
that is called Prāṇāyāma.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out one quarter from each;
that is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, reciting this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
Having repeated this triad one thousand times outside [the village],
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
A Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who is devoid of these three— right time, proper action, and his own duty— incurs censure among the virtuous.
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) preceded by the syllable Om,
together with the three-footed Gāyatrī, should be known as the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness attains the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath-control is the supreme austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic acts of offering oblations and performing sacrifices flow away;
however, that which is imperishable should be known as the Imperishable, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.

The sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual (vidhi-yajña). That which is whispered (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundredfold more effective, and that which is mental (mānasa) is a thousandfold.
Those four types of *pākayajñas* which are accompanied by the *vidhiyajñas*—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*).
A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through the mere recitation [of sacred texts]; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, he who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, furthermore, these are the purifiers of all the Vedas.
Viṣṇu 56.02: By means of the recitation of these and by burnt offerings, the twice-born are purified from their sins.
Viṣṇu 56.03: The Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Viṣṇu 56.04: [This is] composed by Deva.
Viṣṇu 56.05: The Śuddhavatī verses.
Viṣṇu 56.06: [The hymn] beginning with "taratsamandīya."
Viṣṇu 56.07: The Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.
Viṣṇu 56.08: The Pāvamānī verses.
Viṣṇu 56.09 Durgā-Sāvitrī.
Viṣṇu 56.10: [The hymns] beginning with *atīṣaṅga*.
Viṣṇu 56.11: Verses in the *padastoma* meter.
The Vyāhṛtis are equal [in length] to the Viṣṇus.
Viṣṇu 56.13: The Bhāruṇḍas.
Viṣṇu 56.14: Candra-sāman.
The two *sāmans* are the Puruṣavrata and the Sāman.
Viṣṇu 56.16: [The verse beginning with] "ab-liṅgam" //
Viṣṇu 56.17: [This verse] belongs to Bṛhaspati.
Viṣṇu 56.18: The Gō-sūkta (Hymn to the Cow).
Viṣṇu 56.19: The Hymn to the Horse (Aśvasūkta)
And the two Sāmans, namely the Candra-sūkta.
Viṣṇu 56.21: The Śatarudriya.
Viṣṇu 56.22: The Atharvaśiras.
Viṣṇu 56.23: The Tri-suparṇa.
Viṣṇu 56.24: The Great Vow (mahā-vrata).
Viṣṇu 56.25: The Nārāyaṇīya.
And the Puruṣasūkta, [Viṣṇu 56.26].
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these, when sung, purify living beings, provided they desire to attain the memory of their past births.
Viṣṇu 57.01 Now follow those who are to be avoided.
Viṣṇu 57.02: The Vrātyas.
Viṣṇu 57.03: They have fallen.
Viṣṇu 57.04: Those who are impure for three generations on both the mother’s and the father’s side [are excluded from inheritance].
Viṣṇu 57.05: All such persons are indeed unfit to be fed and unfit to receive gifts from.
And one should avoid the habit of accepting gifts from those whose gifts are not to be accepted.
Through the acceptance of gifts, the Vedic splendor of Brahmins perishes.
He who accepts gifts from material objects without knowing the rules for acceptance sinks down together with the giver.
And he who, though capable of receiving gifts, should avoid receiving them, attains the world of the givers.
One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection from fear, meat, honey, a bed, a seat, a house, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered. (Viṣṇu 57.10)
Prajāpati has declared that alms offered spontaneously upon being invited, and not previously solicited, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years of him who treats with contempt that [cow],
nor does the fire carry his sacrificial oblation.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, or wishing to honor the ancestors and the gods, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself should not find satisfaction in that.
Even in these matters, though he may be capable of accepting gifts from them,
he should not take [gifts] from unchaste women, eunuchs, outcasts, or enemies.
But when his teachers have passed away, or if he lives at home without them,
seeking his own livelihood, he should always accept [gifts] from virtuous persons.
A partner in a business venture, a family friend, a slave, a cowherd,
and a barber— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Viṣṇu 58.01 Now, for one in the householder stage of life, there are three kinds of wealth.
Viṣṇu is white, brindled, and black.
When one performs funeral rites for the deceased with white wealth, by that he attains divinity.
That which was performed by Śabala was human.
Viṣṇu 58.05: That which was done by Kṛṣṇa resulted in his birth as an animal.
According to Viṣṇu (58.06), that which is acquired by one's own occupation is "white" for all.
Viṣṇu 58.07: That which is acquired through subsequent activity is variegated (śabala).
And Viṣṇu (58.08) [states that] Kṛṣṇa is obtained through a function separated by one [letter].
That which has come down by succession, that which is given as a gift out of affection, and that which is acquired together with the wife—
all such wealth is declared to be "white" (śukla) for all heirs without distinction.
That which is obtained through bribery or a fee, the sale of what should not be sold, and that which is received as a favor for a service rendered— this is declared to be "stained" (śabala) wealth.
That which is acquired through backbiting, gambling, theft, receiving gifts from improper persons, violence,
and fraud is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa) wealth.
Whatever a man performs with whatever kind of material substance, he obtains a corresponding fruit both after death and in this world.
A householder in the stage of the domestic life shall perform the *pākayajñas* in the nuptial fire.
Viṣṇu 59.02: And the Agnihotra sacrifice is performed in the evening and in the morning.
One should offer oblations to the deities.
One should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices at the times of the conjunction and opposition of the moon and the sun.
Viṣṇu 59.05: [The expiation] for a transgression is by means of an animal sacrifice.
And during the autumn and summer, one should perform the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice.
Or, according to Viṣṇu (59.07), it is when rice and barley have been cooked.
Viṣṇu 59.08: [Wealth] exceeding that which is sufficient for three years.
Viṣṇu 59.09: Every year, [one should perform the sacrifice] with Soma.
In the absence of wealth, one should perform the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice.
One should bestow in its entirety all the wealth obtained by begging for the sake of a sacrifice.
One should offer the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice every evening and every morning.
And one should give alms to the mendicant.
By giving alms that have been honored, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
In the absence of a mendicant, one should give at least a mouthful of food to cows.
Or one should cast it into the fire. (Viṣṇu 59.16)
Even when food is already being eaten, one should not turn away a beggar.
The mortar and pestle, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and household utensils—these are the five slaughter-houses of the householder.
And for the sake of expiating that [sin], one should perform sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the spirits, the ancestors, and human beings.
Viṣṇu 59.20: The study of one's own [Vedic] texts is the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña).
Viṣṇu 59.21: The oblation offered to the gods is the *daiva* [rite].
The libation for the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa) belongs to the Pitṛs. (Viṣṇu 59.22)
Viṣṇu 59.23: Bali is a Bhūta.
And the sacrifice to men consists in the honoring of guests. (Viṣṇu 59.24)
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— though he breathes, he does not truly live.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts. Therefore, the one in the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, all living beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
Having constantly practiced the pursuit of the three aims of life, the giving of food, the worship of the gods, the honoring of Brahmins, the study of one's own Veda,
and the libations to the ancestors, a householder goes to the station of Śakra.
Viṣṇu 60.01: Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should void urine and feces.
Viṣṇu 60.02: At night one should face south, during the day one should face north, and at the two twilights one should face both ways.
Viṣṇu 60.03: Not on ground that has not been covered.
Nor on ground ploughed by a plow. (Viṣṇu 60.04)
Nor in the shade. (Viṣṇu 60.05)
And not on saline soil.
Not on grassy ground. (Viṣṇu 60.07)
Viṣṇu 60.08: Not [in a place] containing living beings.
Not in a pit, [O Viṣṇu].
Nor on an anthill. (Viṣṇu 60.10)
Viṣṇu 60.11: Not on a path.
Viṣṇu 60.12: Not on a carriage road.
Viṣṇu 60.13: Nor [should one eat] when another person is impure.
Not in a garden. (Viṣṇu 60.14)
Nor near a garden or water. (Viṣṇu 60.15)
Not on ashes. (Viṣṇu 60.16)
Not on glowing coals. (Viṣṇu 60.17)
Not on cow dung. (Viṣṇu 60.18)
Nor in a cow-pen (Viṣṇu 60.19).
Nor in the sky. (Viṣṇu 60.20)
Not in water. (Viṣṇu 60.21)
One should not look directly at the wind, fire, the moon, the sun, a woman, a teacher, or a Brahmin.
One should not have one's head uncovered. (Viṣṇu 60.23)

Viṣṇu 60.24: Having wiped the anus with a clod of earth or a brick and having taken hold of the penis, one should rise and perform purification with water and earth drawn from [clean ground] until the odor and the coating are removed.
One application of clay should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten to one hand,
seven to both hands, and three to the feet.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Viṣṇu 61.01 Now, one should not eat a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood.
Nor [should one use] that which comes from the śleṣmātaka, ariṣṭa, vibhītaka, dhava, or dhanvana trees.
Nor [should one use] that which is produced from the bandhūka, nirguṇḍī, śigru, tilva, or tinduka trees.
And [the fire] produced from *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, *pippala*, *iṅguda*, or *guggulu* wood is not [to be used].
Viṣṇu 61.05: Not [the fibers] produced from the pāribhadraka, amlikā, mocaka, śālmalī, or śaṇa plants.
Viṣṇu 61.06: Not sweet.
Viṣṇu 61.07: Nor [should one eat] sour [food].
Nor [should one eat] that which is dried out from the top.
Viṣṇu 61.09: Nor one that is perforated.
One should not smell a putrid odor. (Viṣṇu 61.10)
Viṣṇu 61.11: Nor [should one eat] that which is slimy.
One should not face south or west [while eating]. Viṣṇu 61.12.
And he should eat facing either northward or eastward. (Viṣṇu 61.13)
Of the *vaṭa*, *asana*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *badara*, *sarja*, *nimba*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *kakubha*, and *bilva*—any one of these [should be used].
Astringent, bitter, and pungent [tastes]. Viṣṇu 61.15.

Having become pure in the morning and restrained in speech, one should consume a tooth-cleansing twig that is twelve finger-breadths long, as thick as the tip of the little finger, and provided with a brush-like end.
Having washed it and broken it, one should carefully discard it in a clean place. On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should never eat a tooth-stick at any time.
Viṣṇu 62.01 Now, at the base of the pupils of the twice-born, there is a sacred site named Prājāpatya.
At the base of the thumb is the region of Brahmā.
The divine [sacrifice] is performed at the tips of the fingers; thus says Viṣṇu (62.03).
At the base of the index finger is the region of the ancestors (pitrya).

Viṣṇu 62.05: Seated in a clean place, with his knees apart, facing either east or north, with his mind fixed on that [act] and with a cheerful disposition, he should sip water that is not hot from a fire, not frothy, not poured by a Śūdra using only one hand, and not alkaline.
One should sip water three times with the Brāhma-tīrtha.
One should wipe it twice. (Viṣṇu 62.07)
Viṣṇu 62.08: One should touch the cavities, the head, and the heart with water.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified by water that has merely touched the lips once.
Viṣṇu 63.01 Now, for the sake of acquisition and preservation, one should approach the Lord.
One should not set out upon a journey alone.
One should not [dwell] together with those who are unrighteous.
Nor with outcastes (vṛṣala). Viṣṇu 63.04.
Not with enemies. (Viṣṇu 63.05)
Not too early at dawn.
Not too late in the evening. (Viṣṇu 63.07)
Not during the two twilights.
Viṣṇu 63.09: Not at midday.
Viṣṇu 63.10: [A place] where water is not readily available.
Not too quickly. (Viṣṇu 63.11)
Viṣṇu 63.12: Nor with vehicles constantly occupied by children, the sick, or those in distress.
Nor with those who have missing limbs. (Viṣṇu 63.13)
Not with those who are dejected. (Viṣṇu 63.14)
Viṣṇu 63.15: Not with cows.
Not with those who are unsubdued. (Viṣṇu 63.16)
Viṣṇu 63.17: Without first giving fodder and water to his draft animals, one should not satisfy one's own hunger and thirst.
One should not stand upon a crossroads.
Nor at night at the foot of a tree. (Viṣṇu 63.19)
One should not [enter] an empty dwelling. (Viṣṇu 63.20)
Viṣṇu 63.21: Not even a blade of grass.
One should not [enter] a pen for tethering cattle. (Viṣṇu 63.22)
One should not look at hair, chaff, a skull, bone, ashes, or charcoal. (Viṣṇu 63.23)
Viṣṇu 63.24: Not the core of cotton.
One should circumambulate the crossroads.
And [he should perform] the worship of the deity Viṣṇu (Viṣṇu 63.26).
And the well-known trees. Viṣṇu 63.27.
And [he sees] fire, a Brahmin, a group of women, a full water-jar, a mirror, an umbrella, a banner, a flag, the śrīvṛkṣa tree, the vardhamāna, and the nandyāvarta.
A palm-leaf fan, a fly-whisk, a horse, an elephant, a goat, a cow, curd, milk, honey, and white mustard seeds.
And [he should offer] a lute, sandalwood, weapons, fresh cow dung, fruits, flowers, fresh vegetables, gorocanā, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
And [he gives] turbans, ornaments, jewels, gold, silver, garments, seats, vehicles, and material offerings.
Having seen a golden pitcher, a field of fertile soil, a bound animal, a young maiden, and fish, one should set forth—so says Viṣṇu (63.32).
Now, having seen those who are intoxicated, insane, or deformed, one should turn back.
And those who have vomited or purged, those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and dwarfs.
And those who are clad in saffron robes, who have gone forth as renunciants, and who are soiled.
And [he should avoid] oil, molasses, dried cow-dung, fuel, grass, palāśa leaves, ashes, and charcoal. (Viṣṇu 63.36)
And those who are salt-makers, eunuchs, liquor-distillers, hermaphrodites, cotton-growers, rope-makers, those bound in fetters, and those with disheveled hair.
At the time of departure, one should offer salutations to a lute, sandalwood, fresh vegetables, a turban, ornaments, and a young maiden. (Viṣṇu 63.38)
One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a Brahmin, a teacher, a tawny cow, or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
And the water used for bathing after spitting, vomiting, or voiding blood, feces, and urine. (Viṣṇu 63.40)
One should not step over a calf's tethering rope.
One should not run while it is raining heavily.
One should not cross a river in vain.
One should not [eat] without having offered water to the deities and the ancestors.
Not with the two arms. (Viṣṇu 63.45)
Nor with a leaking boat. Viṣṇu 63.46.
One should not stand upon a riverbank.
One should not look down into a well. (Viṣṇu 63.48)
One should not transgress [this]. Viṣṇu 63.49.

Way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed ritual ablutions, women, the sick, bridegrooms, and those in chariots; and among these, O Lord of the Earth, the king is superior, as is one who has performed ritual ablutions to the king.
One should not perform a ritual bath at water-reservoirs belonging to others.
Viṣṇu 64.02: In times of distress, one may perform the rite by extracting five lumps of earth and using that water.
Viṣṇu 64.03: Not when there is indigestion.
Nor one who is afflicted by illness. (Viṣṇu 64.04)
One should not [bathe] naked. Viṣṇu 64.05.
Not at night. (Viṣṇu 64.06)
Viṣṇu 64.07: Except for the sight of Rāhu.
Not during the two twilights.
Viṣṇu 64.09: One who is habituated to the morning bath should bathe after beholding the eastern quarter, which is copper-red like the dawn.
Having bathed, one should not shake one's head. (Viṣṇu 64.10)
One should not draw up water from one's limbs.
One should not touch [it] as one would oil, O Viṣṇu.
One should not wear a garment previously worn that has not been washed first.
Having bathed, he should wear two washed garments along with a turban.
One should not engage in conversation with Mlecchas, outcastes, or those who have fallen from their caste.
One should bathe in natural springs, divine pools, and excellent lakes.

Water on the ground that has been drawn up from a well is meritorious; water flowing from a stationary source is more so; therefore, it should not be taken [from there]; even more so, that which is collected by the virtuous; but water from the Gaṅgā is meritorious in every respect.

Having removed impurities with clay and water, and having immersed himself in the waters and sat down, he should consecrate the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*.
Then, submerged in water, he should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Or [he may recite]: "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (Viṣṇu 64.20).
The *drupadā* and the *sāvitrī*. Viṣṇu 64.21.
Or one may recite the section beginning with "yuñjate manaḥ" (Viṣṇu 64.22).
Or the Puruṣasūkta (Viṣṇu 64.23).
Having bathed and while still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libations to the gods and ancestors while remaining in the water.
If one has changed one's clothes, one should do so after crossing over to the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Without having performed the libations to the gods and ancestors, one should not wring out the bathing cloth.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the ritual touching (upaspṛśet).
With the Puruṣasūkta, one should offer flowers to the Puruṣa verse by verse.
And [he should offer] handfuls of water, Viṣṇu 64.29.
At the very beginning, one should perform the libation for the gods with the "divine" (daiva) tīrtha.
Immediately after that, one should offer to the ancestors with the ancestral rite (pitrya).
There, first of all, one should perform the libation for those belonging to one's own lineage.
Then [he should offer it] to the relatives and kinsmen. (Viṣṇu 64.33)
Then, [he spoke] to his friends. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 64.34)
Thus, one should be a regular daily bather.
And having bathed, one should recite the purificatory mantras according to one's ability.
Especially [the recitation of] the Sāvitrī. (Viṣṇu 64.37)
And the Puruṣasūkta, Viṣṇu 64.38.
There is nothing superior to these two.
One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors,
as well as for the recitation of purificatory texts and for giving gifts as prescribed by the rules.
Misfortune, Kālakarṇī, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—these perish for one consecrated with merely water; such is the established doctrine.
For one who bathes daily does not behold the suffering of the torments of Yama;
by daily bathing, even those men who have committed sins are purified.

Viṣṇu 65.01 Now, therefore, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should worship the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, either in the image of a deity or on a consecrated spot.

Having given the "taking of life" (jīvādāna) with the mantra "Of the two Aśvins, [you are] the breath; they are yours," and having performed the invocation with the anuvāka beginning with "They yoke the mind" (yuñjate manaḥ), he should perform prostration with his knees, hands, and head.
One should present the *arghya* offering with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Viṣṇu 65.04: The water for washing the feet [is offered] with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ."
"May the waters of the desert be auspicious to us"—with these words, the water for sipping is offered.
"O Waters, carry away this [sin]," with these words, the bathing water is used.
Viṣṇu 65.07: "On the chariot, on the axles, on the bull, on the prize"—with these [mantras], the anointing and the ornaments [are performed].
"Viṣṇu 65.08: 'yuvā suvāsāḥ'—with this [verse], the garment."
Regarding "Viṣṇu 65.09 puṣpāvatīḥ," it means flowers.
"Thou art the yoke; drive away [evil]"—with these words, he offers incense.
For the lamp, [he recites] "Thou art splendor, thou art semen" (Viṣṇu 65.11).
With the verse "dadhi-krāvṇa," [he offers] the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should offer the food oblation with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha."
The fly-whisk, the fan, the measure, the umbrella, as well as the vehicle and the seat—
all that he should offer to the God with the Sāvitra mantra alone.
Having thus worshipped him, one should then recite the Puruṣa-sūkta;
with that very [sūkta], one should offer oblations of clarified butter if one desires the eternal state.
Viṣṇu 66.01: One should not perform rites for the gods or the ancestors with water that has been drawn at night.
Viṣṇu 66.02: One should not offer an ointment that is devoid of sandalwood, musk, wood, camphor, saffron, and nutmeg.
Nor [should one wear] clothing dyed with indigo.
Viṣṇu 66.04: An ornament that is a counterfeit of gems or gold [is not permitted].
Viṣṇu 66.05: Nor one who has a foul odor.
Viṣṇu 66.06: It should not have a foul odor.
Nor that which is produced from thorns. Viṣṇu 66.07.
One should offer even that which grows on thorns, provided it is white and fragrant.
One should also offer red saffron and lotuses.
One should not use any living being for the purpose of incense.
66.11 Nothing at all [should be used] for the purpose of a lamp except ghee or oil.
Viṣṇu 66.12: Nothing that is unfit to be eaten [should be offered] for the purpose of a food offering (naivedya).
Viṣṇu 66.13: Nor even in the milk of goats or buffaloes, even if it is fit for consumption.
And the flesh of five-clawed animals, fish, and boars [is forbidden].
Being self-restrained and pure, one should offer everything; with the mind fixed on Him and being well-disposed, one should be free from haste and anger.

Viṣṇu 67.01: Then, having swept around the fire, sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, and poured water around it, one should take the first portion from all sides of the cooked food and offer it as an oblation.
To Viṣṇu, to Vāsudeva, to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, to Puruṣa, to Satya, to Acyuta, to Vāsudeva.
Then [offerings] to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Indra and Agni, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, Anumati, Dhanvantari, Vāstoṣpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then, O Viṣṇu, one should offer the bali-oblation with the remainder of the food.
Viṣṇu 67.05: [The same applies] to food and secondary food.
Viṣṇu 67.06: On all sides, to the east of the fire.
"Thou art named Ambā," "Thou art named Dulā," "Thou art named Nitantī," "Thou art named Cupuṇīkā"—thus for all [the waters].
"O Nandinī, O Subhagā, O Sumaṅgalī, O Bhadraṅkarī!"—thus he circumambulated his own cows, keeping them to his right.
To Viṣṇu at the pillar, to Dhruvā, to Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī, and to the Lords of the Forest.
Viṣṇu 67.10: At the gateway between dharma and adharma, and unto death.
To Varuṇa at the water-reservoir.
"O Viṣṇus," [he says] over the mortar.
"Viṣṇu 67.13: With the words 'To the Maruts,' [he offers] on the lower grinding stone."
Above, in the shelter, [one should offer] to King Vaiśravaṇa and to the spirits (bhūtas).
"To Indra and to Indra's men"—thus [one offers] in the eastern half.
"To Yama and to the servants of Yama," [he offers] in the southern half.
"To Viṣṇu" and "to the attendants of Varuṇa"—thus [he offers] in the western half.
"To Soma, to the Soma-persons"—thus [he offers] in the northern half.
"To Brahmā and to the attendants of Brahmā," [he says] in the middle.
To Ākāśa, above, [Viṣṇu 67.20].
On a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should offer oblations during the day with the words, "To the beings who roam by day."
"From the night-walkers" means at night.

Viṣṇu 67.23: Then, upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing south, he should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa) for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, as well as for the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, by means of their names and lineages (gotra).
Viṣṇu 67.24: And he should present to the rice-balls unguents, flowers, incense, food offerings (naivedya), and so forth.
Having placed a water-pitcher nearby, one should cause the recitation of a benediction.
One should offer [the food] on the ground for dogs, crows, and outcaste dog-cookers.
And one should give alms. (Viṣṇu 67.27)
And one should exert the greatest effort in honoring guests. (Viṣṇu 67.28)
One should diligently honor a guest who arrives in the evening.
One should not allow an uninvited guest to stay in one's house without having been fed.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes and as the husband is the lord of women, so is the guest the lord of the householder. (Viṣṇu 67.31)
By worshipping him, one attains heaven. (Viṣṇu 67.32)
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he takes away that person's merit and bestows his own demerit upon him.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest;
because he stays for an indefinite period, he is therefore called an *atithi*.
One should not consider a Brahmin who is a resident of the same village, nor one who is merely an acquaintance,
to be a guest when he has arrived at the house, whether it be where the wife resides or where the sacred fires are maintained.
But if a Kṣatriya has come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may,
if desired, be fed even after the Brahmins have finished eating.
Even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who have arrived at the household as guests should be fed along with the servants, while practicing compassion toward them.
Viṣṇu 67.38a: Other guests as well, such as friends and so forth, who have come to his house out of affection; Viṣṇu 67.38c: he should feed with his wife ordinary food according to his ability.
One should feed those living in one's own household— a maiden, a sick woman, and likewise a pregnant woman— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that foolish man who, without having first given to these,
eats for himself, does not realize that while eating he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, as well as his own servants, have finished eating,
the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the ancestors, human beings, his dependents, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains.
He who cooks for his own sake alone eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice.
A householder does not attain such worlds through his own Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, or asceticism as he does through the honoring of guests.
In the evening and in the morning, one should offer a seat and water to a guest,
as well as food according to one's ability, having honored them in accordance with the prescribed rule.
By the gift of each of these— a shelter, a bed, an oil massage for the feet, and a lamp— one obtains a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.
Viṣṇu 68.01: During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat.
Having bathed, one should eat from two vessels that have been released [from the ritual].
When the two [suns] have set without having been released, one should bathe and, on the following day, behold [the deity].
One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, nor during an eclipse of a cow or a Brahmin.
Nor during the king's misfortune, according to Viṣṇu 68.05.
When one who has been away from home considers the Agnihotra sacrifice to have been performed, then he may eat. (Viṣṇu 68.06)
When one considers that the Vaiśvadeva offering has indeed been performed, [then one may eat]. (Viṣṇu 68.07)
And when one considers that a festival day has occurred on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Viṣṇu.
And one should not eat while what has been previously consumed is undigested.
Viṣṇu 68.10: Not at midnight.
Viṣṇu 68.11: Not at midday.
Viṣṇu 68.12: Not during the two twilights.
One should not [recite] while wearing wet clothes. *Viṣṇu* 68.13.
Viṣṇu 68.14: He shall not wear only a single garment.
Viṣṇu 68.15: Not naked.
Not in water. (Viṣṇu 68.16)
One should not sit in a squatting posture.
One should not [recite] while seated on a broken seat. (Viṣṇu 68.18)
Nor [should one study] while lying on a bed. (Viṣṇu 68.19)
Viṣṇu 68.20: Nor at a meal where the food is divided.
Viṣṇu 68.21: Not on one's lap.
Not on earth, Viṣṇu 68.22.
Not on the hand. (Viṣṇu 68.23)
And where one might offer salt, that one should not eat.
One should not revile children.
Viṣṇu 68.26: One person alone does not eat the refined food.
Viṣṇu 68.27: [One should not eat] oil that has not been removed.
One should not eat parched grain during the day. (Viṣṇu 68.28)
Viṣṇu 68.29: One should not [perform] any activity involving sesame seeds at night.
Viṣṇu 68.30: Nor barley-meal mixed with curds.
Viṣṇu 68.31: [One should not eat] the kovidāra, the vaṭa, the pippala, śāṇa, or śāka.
Viṣṇu 68.32: Not having given [it].
Viṣṇu 68.33: Not without having offered oblations.
One should not [enter] with unwet feet. (Viṣṇu 68.34)
And neither his hands nor his face shall be moist. (Viṣṇu 68.35)
And one who has not yet cleansed himself after eating should not take up clarified butter.
One should not look at the moon, the sun, or the stars.
One should not touch the head. (Viṣṇu 68.38)
One should not recite the Veda.
One should eat facing the east. (Viṣṇu 68.40)
Or he may face the south. Viṣṇu 68.41.
Having honored Viṣṇu with food.
Viṣ�cheṣṇu 68.43: He should be of cheerful mind, wearing a garland, and anointed with unguents.
Viṣṇu 68.44: One should not consume [the remainder] until it is completely finished.
Except for curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain flour, and sweetmeat balls.

One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor likewise while standing; nor should many eat together while being watched by many, nor should many eat together in a single place.
One should never drink water from one's cupped hands (añjali) in an empty house, a fire-sanctuary, or a temple; nor should one practice over-satiation.
One should not eat a third meal, nor anything unwholesome under any circumstances; one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat in the morning.
One should not eat food that is corrupted by intention, nor from a vessel defiled by intention;
nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth between the knees.
Viṣṇu 69.01: On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, one should not approach a woman.
One should not eat after having partaken of a śrāddha meal.
Viṣṇu 69.03: Not having given [it].
Viṣṇu 69.04: One should not be invited to a śrāddha ceremony [if one is] not [properly] invited.
Viṣṇu 69.05: One who is under a vow must not [be so].
Viṣṇu 69.06: One who has not been initiated [should not perform these rites].
One should not [sit] in temples of the gods, cremation grounds, or deserted dwellings. (Viṣṇu 69.07)
Nor at the roots of trees. (Viṣṇu 69.08)
Not during the day, O Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu 69.10: Not during the two twilights.
Viṣṇu 69.11: Nor [should one eat] from a defiled [vessel].
Viṣṇu 69.12: He is not defiled.
Nor one who has anointed herself with oil. (Viṣṇu 69.13)
Viṣṇu 69.14: Nor [should one eat] when one has anointed oneself with oil.
Nor one afflicted by disease. (Viṣṇu 69.15)
One who is afflicted by disease [is not eligible]. (Viṣṇu 69.16)
One who desires to live a long life should not approach a woman who is deficient in limbs, nor one with extra limbs, nor likewise one who is older in age,
nor a pregnant woman.
Viṣṇu 70.01: One should not sleep with wet feet.
Viṣṇu 70.02: Nor with the head toward the north-west.
One should not [bathe] naked. (Viṣṇu 70.03)
Viṣṇu 70.04: Not in accordance with the lineage.
Not in the sky. Viṣṇu 70.05.
One should not sleep on a bed made of Palāśa wood.
Nor [should one worship] in an image made of five kinds of wood.
Viṣṇu 70.08: Not for the purpose of breaking an elephant.
Viṣṇu 70.09: Not for one killed by lightning.
Viṣṇu 70.10: Not when it is broken.
Nor on the back of a fire, O Viṣṇu.
Nor [should one eat] from that which grows on a tree watered by a jar (Viṣṇu 70.12).
One should not [recite] in cremation grounds, deserted dwellings, or temples of deities.
Nor in the midst of the fickle. (Viṣṇu 70.14)
Not in the midst of women. (Viṣṇu 70.15)
Nor [should one step] over grain, cattle, a guru, fire, or the gods.
One should not sleep while impure from food remnants, nor during the day, nor during the two twilights, nor on ashes;
nor in an unclean place, nor on moist ground, nor on a mountain peak.
Viṣṇu 71.01 Now, one should not hold anyone in contempt.
And one should not mock those with deficient or extra limbs, the foolish, or those destitute of wealth.
One should not serve those who are inferior. (Viṣṇu 71.03)
One should not perform any action that contradicts one's own study of the Vedas.
Viṣṇu 71.05: One should adopt an attire appropriate to one's age.
Of learning, noble lineage, wealth, and country—Viṣṇu 71.06.
Viṣṇu 71.07: He should not be arrogant.
Viṣṇu 71.08: He should constantly examine the scriptures and other such sources.
When one has the means, one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (Viṣṇu 71.09)
One should not say, "It does not exist. (Viṣṇu 71.10)
One should not wear a garland that is scentless, foul-smelling, or red. (Viṣṇu 71.11)
One should wear even a red lotus. (Viṣṇu 71.12)
And a bamboo staff. Viṣṇu 71.13.
And a water-pot containing water. (Viṣṇu 71.14)
Viṣṇu 71.15: The sacred thread shall be made of cotton.
And two earrings made of gold. Viṣṇu 71.16.
One should not look at the rising sun. (Viṣṇu 71.17)
One should not look at the sun as it is setting. (Viṣṇu 71.18)
Nor [should one eat] what is covered by a garment. (Viṣṇu 71.19)
Nor [should one look at one's reflection] situated in a mirror or in the midst of water.
Viṣṇu 71.21: Not at midday.
One should not look at the face of an angry teacher. (Viṣṇu 71.22)
Viṣṇu 71.23: Nor one's own reflection in oil or water.
Not in a mirror that is dirty. *Viṣṇu* 71.24.
Viṣṇu 71.25: [One should not touch] one's wife at the time of eating.
One should not look at a naked woman. (Viṣṇu 71.26)
One should not look at anyone while they are urinating. (Viṣṇu 71.27)
And one should not look at an elephant that has broken loose from its tethering post.
And one who is situated in an unfavorable position should not engage in a fight with a bull or similar animals.
Nor one who is insane. (Viṣṇu 71.30)
Viṣṇu 71.31: Not from one who is intoxicated.
One should not throw impure substances into the fire.
Viṣṇu 71.33: Not blood.
Viṣṇu 71.34: Not poison.
Viṣṇu 71.35: Also [the same applies] to water.
One should not step over fire.
One should not warm one's feet [over a fire]. Viṣṇu 71.37.
One should not wipe oneself on *kuśa* grass.
One should not wash [the teeth] in a bronze vessel.
One should not place one foot upon the other.
One should not draw the earth.
One should not crush clods of earth. (Viṣṇu 71.42)
One should not be a cutter of grass. (Viṣṇu 71.43)
One should not cut one's nails or hair with the teeth.
And one should avoid gambling. (Viṣṇu 71.45)
Like the service of the morning sun. Viṣṇu 71.46.
Viṣṇu 71.47: One should not wear garments, sandals, garlands, or sacred threads that have been worn by another.
One should not impart sacred knowledge to a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 71.48)
Viṣṇu 71.49: Neither leavings nor sacrificial offerings [should be given to a Śūdra].
Viṣṇu 71.50: Nor sesame seeds.
And one should not teach him the Dharma.
Viṣṇu 71.52: It is not a vow.
One should not scratch one's head or belly with both hands joined together.
One should not refuse curd or flowers.
One should not pull at one's own garland.
One should not awaken one who is asleep. (Viṣṇu 71.56)
One should not cause one who is impassioned to become dispassionate.
One should not speak to a woman in her courses.
Viṣṇu 71.59: Nor [should one eat] those born of Mlecchas or outcastes.
In the presence of the god Agni and a Brahmin, one should raise the right hand.
One should not point out a cow grazing in another's field. (Viṣṇu 71.61)
One should not drink while the calf is drinking. (Viṣṇu 71.62)
One should not cause those who are not haughty to exult.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 71.64)
Not in a place crowded with unrighteous people. (Viṣṇu 71.65)
One should not dwell with one who is devoid of medical knowledge.
Viṣṇu 71.67: Not when [the victim] has been struck down.
And not for long on a mountain—Viṣṇu 71.68.
One should not engage in useless exertion. (Viṣṇu 71.69)
Viṣṇu 71.70: Nor [should one eat] while dancing or singing.
One should not snap one's fingers. (Viṣṇu 71.71)
One should not utter anything vulgar. (Viṣṇu 71.72)
Viṣṇu 71.73: Not untruth.
Viṣṇu 71.74: Not what is unpleasant.
One should not strike anyone in a vital spot.
One who desires to live a long life should not despise oneself.
One should perform the twilight worship for a long time. (Viṣṇu 71.77)
One should not play with snakes or weapons. (Viṣṇu 71.78)
One should not touch the bodily apertures without a specific cause. (Viṣṇu 71.79)
One should not raise a rod against another.
One should strike one who is to be punished for the purpose of correction.
One should strike him on the back with a bamboo leaf or with a rope. (Viṣṇu 71.82)
One should avoid disparaging gods, brahmins, the scriptures, and those of great soul.
And wealth and pleasure that are contrary to righteousness [should not be pursued]. (Viṣṇu 71.84)
And even a dharma that is loathed by the world [should not be practiced]. (Viṣṇu 71.85)
And on the festival days (parvan), one should perform propitiatory fire-offerings (śānti-homa).
One should not cut even a blade of grass.
And he should remain adorned.
Thus one should be a practitioner of right conduct. *Viṣṇu* 71.89.

One who desires righteousness and has conquered his senses should practice that conduct which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, which is consistent with Dharma, and which is practiced by the virtuous.
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, the desired goal;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and through right conduct, one destroys inauspicious marks.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is endowed with faith, and is free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
One should abide with self-restraint and discipline.
And self-restraint of the senses is proclaimed as Viṣṇu.
For one who is self-controlled, this world and the next belong.
Viṣṇu 72.04: No ritual action whatsoever succeeds for one who is not self-controlled.
Self-restraint is the supreme purifier; self-restraint is the supreme auspiciousness. Through self-restraint, one obtains everything that one desires in the mind.
If the horses do not carry away that chariot which travels with five [horses] yoked together, moving at the speed of thought along the noble path,
then the enemies shall likewise not overcome him who has thus departed.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
Viṣṇu 73.01 Now, one who desires to perform a śrāddha should invite the Brāhmaṇas on the day before.

On the second day, during the forenoon of the bright fortnight or the afternoon of the dark fortnight, he should cause the Brahmins—well-bathed and having sipped water—to sit upon seats covered with Kuśa grass, arranged in order of their seniority according to age.
Two [brāhmaṇas] for the rite to the gods, facing east, and three for the rite to the ancestors, facing north.
Viṣṇu (73.04): One [offering] for each [deity], or one for both.
In the case of *āma-śrāddhas* and those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one should offer oblations into the fire using the first five [verses] of the Viṣṇusūkta.
In the animal *śrāddhas*, [the offering is made] with the middle pentad of Viṣṇu.
On the new moon days, [one should worship] with the excellent group of five, according to Viṣṇu 73.07.
After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, during the Kṛṣṇa-aṣṭakās, one should proceed respectively with the first, middle, and highest groups of five [days].
And on each successive Aṣṭakā day, Viṣṇu 73.09.
Then, having been authorized by the Brahmins, he should invoke the ancestors.
Having performed the dismissal of the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds while reciting the two verses beginning with "Viṣṇu" and "Apayantu asurāḥ," [he should proceed].

"O Viṣṇu, 73.12: Having performed the invocation with the mantra, 'Come hither, O all you ancestors; may they come to me first; this is for you, O ancestors,' and having offered water for washing the feet (*pādya*) mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds, using fragrant water with the mantras 'Those who stand immortal' (*yās tiṣṭhanty amṛtāḥ*) and 'What my mother [did]' (*yan me mātā*), and having prepared and offered the respectful oblation (*arghya*), and having applied unguents, he should worship the Brahmins according to his ability with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, garments, flowers, ornaments, incense, and lamps. Then, taking food soaked in ghee, [he addresses them as] the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus."
Having observed thus and said, "I shall perform [the oblation] in the fire," and having been told by the Brahmins, "Do so," he should offer three oblations.

Having performed the consecration of the oblation with the mantras, "Those who are my fathers," and "This, O fathers, is for you, this sacrifice," he should first present food to the two facing east with the mantra, "Salutation to all the gods (viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ)," placing it in whatever vessels are available, especially those made of silver.
Viṣṇu 73.14: [One should offer] to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather by means of their names and lineages (nāma-gotra) to those facing north.
While the Brahmins are eating that [food], he should mutter: "Whatever [fault] I have committed through excess day and night, O you who devour raw flesh. (Viṣṇu 73.15)
And the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras—thus [it is said]. (Viṣṇu 73.16)

Viṣṇu 73.17: Near the remains of the food, upon *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing southward, he should place one rice-ball for the father, reciting: "The earth is the sacrificial ladle; it is imperishable."
"Antarikṣaṃ darvir akṣitā" (The atmosphere is the imperishable ladle)—with these words, he offers the second pinda to the grandfather.
"dyaur darvir akṣitā" (the sky is the imperishable ladle)—with this as the third [verse], [he offers] to the great-grandfather.
Viṣṇu 73.20: "To those ancestors who have passed away here," thus [saying], a garment should be given.
"O Fathers, provide us with heroic food"—with these words, he offers the food.
"O ancestors, rejoice here according to your respective portions"—with these words, one rubs the hands on the roots of the *darbha* grass.

With the verse "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," having performed the scattering of water around the rice balls (piṇḍas) in a clockwise direction, one should present the arghya, flowers, incense, ointments, food, and other kinds of eatables and edibles.
And a water-vessel joined with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds. (Viṣṇu 73.24)

When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, [the host] should sprinkle food along with grass with the words, "May it not fail me," and place the scattered remnants of food before the leavings. Having asked, "Are you satisfied? and "Is it well-prepared?", he should first give water for sipping (ācamana) to those facing north, then to those facing east. Then, having sprinkled the site of the Śrāddha with the words "Well-sprinkled," he—holding Darbha grass in his hand—should perform everything else.

Then, having circumambulated [the deity] from the front while facing east, saying "O Rāma, whatever belongs to me," and having returned, he should honor them with sacrificial fees according to his ability; then, having said, "May you be pleased," and when they have replied, "We are pleased," he should mutter the mantra, "The gods and the ancestors."

Having offered water for the inexhaustible [libation] by means of the names and lineages, saying "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should then, with palms joined and mind fixed on that, request [the blessing] from those facing east with a well-disposed mind.
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
"Let it be so," they should say. (Viṣṇu 73.29)
"May our food be abundant, and may we receive guests;
may there be those who ask of us, and may we never have to ask anyone."
Having received these blessings with the two verses beginning with "Viṣṇu" (73.31).
Then, with the mantra "vāje vāje," he should dismiss the Brāhmaṇas,
having honored them according to the rule, followed them, and saluted them.

Viṣṇu 74.01: Having performed the *śrāddha* on the *aṣṭakā* days according to the divine (*daiva*) rite with vegetables, meat, and cakes, and having offered oblations into the fire on the subsequent *aṣṭakās* (the *anvaṣṭakās*) as on the *aṣṭakās*, he should likewise feed the Brahmins first for the sake of the mother, the paternal grandmother, and the paternal great-grandmother; then, having honored them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he should follow them as they depart and bid them farewell.
Then, one should construct trenches.
At its base, having performed the kindling of the fire in the east, north, and southeast, he should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
At the base of the three furrows for the men; at the base of the three furrows for the women.
Viṣṇu 74.05: One should fill the three pits for the person with water mixed with food.
Viṣṇu 74.06: [One should offer] three furrows for women with food and milk.
With curd, meat, and milk, [he should fill] three trenches respectively.
Having filled [the vessel], one should recite this: "May this be inexhaustible for you, O venerable ones, and for you, O venerable ladies."
Viṣṇu 75.01: If one should perform a śrāddha while his father is still living, he should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it.
O Viṣṇu, those whose grandfather is living while both their father and paternal grandfather are still alive [should perform the rite].
Viṣṇu 75.03: While one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are living, one must not perform [the Śrāddha] at all.
Viṣṇu 75.04: He whose father is deceased should, having offered a rice-ball (piṇḍa) to his father, offer to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather.
Viṣṇu 75.05: He whose father and grandfather are deceased should offer two rice-balls to them and then offer one to his great-grandfather.
If one's grandfather has become a *preta*, he should place a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for him and then offer two rice-balls beyond the great-grandfather.
In the same manner, a wise man should perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers;
he should do so according to the rule by adapting the mantras, while for the remaining ancestors it should be performed without mantras.

Viṣṇu 76.01: The three new-moon days, the three Aṣṭakās, the three Anvaṣṭakās, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following [the latter], and the times of the ripening of rice and barley.
Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha to be obligatory;
indeed, one who does not perform the Śrāddha on these occasions falls into hell.
Viṣṇu 77: The Transit of the Sun.
Viṣṇu 77.02: The two equinoxes.
Viṣṇu [is especially worshipped] during the two solstices.
Viṣṇu 77.04: Vyatīpāta.
The birth constellation of Viṣṇu is Śravaṇā.
And there is prosperity, O Viṣṇu.
Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha to be those for optional rites;
whatever Śrāddha is offered on these occasions conduces to infinity.
A wise person should certainly not perform a Śrāddha during the two twilights or at night; however, it may be performed even during those times if there is an eclipse of the moon or sun.
For a Śrāddha offered at the time of the appearance of Rāhu remains as long as the moon and stars;
endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills all their desires.
Viṣṇu 78.01: By constantly performing a śrāddha on a Sunday, one obtains good health.
Good fortune is attained in the lunar mansion of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā), and good fortune in the lunar mansion of Candra (Mṛgaśiras).
On a Tuesday, one should worship Viṣṇu for victory in battle.
Viṣṇu 78.04: All desires [are fulfilled] on a Thursday.
Viṣṇu 78.05: [One obtains] the desired knowledge in the Jaiva [mantra].
In the case of Venus, there is wealth.
O Viṣṇu, life [is attained] when Saturn is in the seventh house.
Viṣṇu 78.08: [One who dies] under Kṛttikā goes to heaven.
Viṣṇu 78.09: Offspring [is obtained] through the Rohiṇīs.
In the north, [the offering] leads to spiritual luster. Viṣṇu 78.10.
Viṣṇu 78.11: Success in action [is attained] in the Raudra [mudrā].
Viṣṇu 78.12: [One should give] land under Punarvasu.
One should perform the rite for nourishment under the Puṣya asterism.
Viṣṇu 78.14: [One should worship] Śrī on the serpent.
Viṣṇu 78.15: All desires [are fulfilled] at the rite for the ancestors.
In the *Bhāgya* [chapter], there is good fortune (*saubhāgya*). (Viṣṇu 78.16)
Viṣṇu 78.17: [The word] *dhanam* [is used] in the sense of "bringing in" (income).
Viṣṇu 78.18: Preeminence among kinsmen is [granted] in the hand.
In the [chapter] on Tvaṣṭṛ, regarding the sons of Rūpavatī, [it says]: Viṣṇu 78.19.
Success in trade [is attained] under Svāti, according to the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 78.20.
Gold [is auspicious] under the asterism Viśākhā.
Viṣṇu 78.22: Friends [should be honored] with friendliness.
Viṣṇu 78.23: Sovereignty [is attained] in the realm of Śakra.
Viṣṇu 78.24: [One should perform] agriculture at the root.
Success in sea travel is attained when [the Moon] is in Aquarius.
Viṣṇu 78.26: "In the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one obtains all desires."
Viṣṇu 78.27: Preeminence results from the Abhijit [nakṣatra].
Viṣṇu 78.28: All desires [are fulfilled] by listening.
Or salt in the presence of Indra. (Viṣṇu 78.29)
In the western quarter, there is health. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 78.30)
Viṣṇu 78.31: [The fine for] base metal is one ājā.
Viṣṇu 78.32: A snake in the house is a source of misfortune.
One should give cows under the asterism of Puṣya.
Viṣṇu 78.34: [One should offer] horses in the month of Āśvina.
In the south, [the deity] Jīvita [is worshipped]. Viṣṇu 78.35.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), beautiful women [enter] the house; thus says Viṣṇu 78.36.
On the second lunar day, one should worship the maiden Varadā, who grants boons.
Viṣṇu 78.38: On the third lunar day, one obtains all desires.
On the fourth day, one should offer animals to Viṣṇu.
On the fifth [lunar day], one obtains handsome sons. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 78.40)
On the sixth day, there is victory in gambling. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 78.41)
Viṣṇu 78.42: [One should undertake] agriculture on the seventh lunar day.
Trade on the eighth day [is forbidden], according to Viṣṇu 78.43.
On the ninth [lunar day], one should offer animals to Viṣṇu.
On the tenth day, the Vājina [oblation]. (Viṣṇu 78.45)
On the eleventh day, one obtains sons endowed with Vedic splendor (brahmavarcasvin). —Viṣṇu Purāṇa 78.46.
Viṣṇu 78.47: [One should give] gold and silver on the twelfth day.
On the thirteenth lunar day, one attains good fortune. (Viṣṇu 78.48)
Viṣṇu 78.49: All desires [are fulfilled] on the fifteenth day.
For those slain by weapons, the fourteenth day is prescribed for the performance of the śrāddha rite.
Furthermore, there are two verses sung by the ancestors: Viṣṇu 78.51: "There are also two verses sung by the ancestors."
"May there arise in our lineage some preeminent man who,
with a concentrated mind, [performs this] on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight during the rainy season."
He who performs a śrāddha with honey-sweetened milk-rice throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or during the time of the elephant’s shadow; Viṣṇu 78.53.
Viṣṇu 79.01 Now, one should not perform a śrāddha with water taken at night.
In the absence of *kuśa* grass, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* grass in place of the *kuśa*.
For the purpose of clothing, thread made from cotton is used.
One should discard the [old] state even if it consists of unwashed cloth. (Viṣṇu 79.04)
Viṣṇu 79.05: Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, and those produced from thorny plants [are not to be used].
One should offer white, fragrant flowers—even those grown on thorny plants—as well as red ones that grow in water.
One should not offer fat or marrow for the purpose of a lamp.
One should offer either clarified butter or oil. (Viṣṇu 79.08)
One should not offer anything produced from living beings for the purpose of incense.
One should offer guggulu mixed with honey and clarified butter.
Viṣṇu 79.11: Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka are for the purpose of unguents.
One should not give salt that has been directly perceived [as impure].
And with his hand, [he offered] ghee, side-dishes, and so forth. (Viṣṇu 79.13)
One should give vessels made of metal.
Especially those made of silver, O Viṣṇu. (Viṣṇu 79.15)
Viṣṇu 79.16: One should place a sword, a razor, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and unbroken grains—these are purifying and destructive of demons.

Viṣṇu 79.17: One should avoid long pepper, mukundaka, bhūstṛṇa, drumstick tree, mustard, surasā, sarjaka, suvarcala, pumpkin, bottle gourd, eggplant, pālakyā, upodakī, taṇḍulīyaka, safflower, piṇḍāluka, and buffalo milk.
Viṣṇu 79.18: And black gram, lentils, food that has stood overnight, and prepared salt.
One should avoid anger. (Viṣṇu 79.19)
One should not shed tears.
One should not act with haste. (Viṣṇu 79.21)
Viṣṇu 79.22: For the gift of ghee and other substances, vessels made of precious metals, swords as vessels, and even inferior vessels are recommended.
And on this point, there is a verse: Viṣṇu 79.23.
A gift given with vessels made of gold or silver, or with a sword, or with one made of udumbara wood, or even with a vessel of phalgu wood, attains imperishability.
Viṣṇu 80.01: With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, śyāmāka grain, priyaṅgu, nīvāra, mung beans, and wheat, [the ancestors] are gratified for one month.
For two months, [one should subsist] on fish meat.
Viṣṇu 80.03: [One should offer] three [oblations] with the meat of a deer.
And one who has stolen four [animals] is purified by the sacrifice of a ram.
Viṣṇu 80.05: [The rite] with the five [offerings] is performed with the Śākuna [Sāman].
With a goat, [one attains] sixfold [merit].
Viṣṇu 80.07: [The same duration] with the Raurava hell.
Viṣṇu 80.08: Eight [elephants] with spotted sides.
Viṣṇu 80.09: [The penance] with nine cows.
Viṣṇu 80.10: Ten [cows] for one who has killed a buffalo.
Viṣṇu 80.11: But with a hornless goat, [the sacrifice is] elevenfold.
For one year, [he should subsist] on cow's milk or its derivatives.
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors: Viṣṇu 80.13.
Kālaśāka, mahāśalka, and the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa;
as well as rhinoceroses, excluding those with horns—we shall eat these until the sun's end.
One should not place food upon a seat.
One should not touch Viṣṇu with one's foot.
One should not sneeze upon Viṣṇu.
One should drive away the malevolent spirits (yātudhānas) with sesame seeds or mustard seeds.
And when it has been covered, one should perform the śrāddha.
One should not look at a woman in her menses.
Nor a dog, O Viṣṇu.
Not a village pig (Viṣṇu 81.08).
Nor a village cock (Viṣṇu 81.09).
One should diligently cause the Śrāddha for the Unborn (Ajasya) to be presented.
And the Brahmins, restrained in speech, should eat.
Not [should one eat] with the head wrapped [in a cloth]. (Viṣṇu 81.12)
One should not [enter] wearing sandals. (Viṣṇu 81.13)
Viṣṇu 81.14: [The feet of the image] shall not rest upon a pedestal.
Neither those with missing limbs nor those with extra limbs should look upon the śrāddha.
Śūdras [are not entitled to this], Viṣṇu 81.16.
Viṣṇu 81.17: They are not outcasts.
Not for those who are chronically ill. (Viṣṇu 81.18)
At that time, he should honor a Brāhmaṇa with the consent of the Brāhmaṇas, or a mendicant.
O Viṣṇu, when asked by the donor, the Brāhmaṇas should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
As long as there is steam from the food, as long as they eat in silence,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described, so long do the ancestors eat.
Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
one should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have finished eating.
For those who have died without the sacraments, for those who have abandoned their families, and for women of the household,
the portion of the leavings and whatever food is scattered upon the *darbha* grass shall be their share.

The remnants of food that have fallen upon the ground at a funeral rite for the ancestors are declared to be the allotted share for the group of slaves, provided they are neither crooked nor deceitful.
Viṣṇu 82.01: In a rite dedicated to the gods, one should not examine a Brāhmaṇa.
One should examine [the recipient] with great care at a rite for the ancestors.
One should avoid those who have missing or extra limbs. (Viṣṇu 82.03)
And those who persist in improper actions.
[Viṣṇu 82.05] Those who observe the "cat-vow" (baiḍāla-vratika).
Viṣṇu 82.06: Those who wear the sectarian marks in vain.
Viṣṇu 82.07: Those who subsist by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra).
And [he should avoid] those who serve the gods for a livelihood.
Viṣṇu 82.09: [He should avoid] physicians.
The sons of unmarried women, Viṣṇu 82.10.
Viṣṇu 82.11: His sons.
Viṣṇu 82.12: [Those who perform] many sacrifices.
Viṣṇu 82.13: Those who perform sacrifices for an entire village.
Viṣṇu 82.14: Those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
Viṣṇu 82.15: [The sin of] one who performs sacrifices for those for whom it is forbidden to sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 82.16: [The penance for] those who have fallen from their caste (vrātyas).
Viṣṇu 82.17: [The same applies] to those who sacrifice for them.
Viṣṇu 82.18: [He should punish] those who cause harm at the beginning of a festival.
Viṣṇu 82.19: [He should punish] informers.
Those who teach for a wage (Viṣṇu 82.20).
Those taught by hired teachers (Viṣṇu 82.21).
Those nourished by the food of a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 82.22)
Viṣṇu 82.23: [One becomes fallen] through association with those who have fallen.
Those who do not study [the Vedas]. (Viṣṇu 82.24)
Those who have fallen away from the worship of the twilights (Viṣṇu 82.25).
Viṣṇu 82.26 [concerning] the king's servants.
Viṣṇu 82.27: [One should not look at] those who are naked.
Viṣṇu 82.28: [Those] who are disputing with their father.
And those who abandon their father, mother, teacher, the sacred fire, or their own Vedic study (Viṣṇu 82.29).
For these are declared to be outcasts among Brahmins, defilers of the assembly;
a wise man should carefully avoid them at the performance of a śrāddha rite.
Viṣṇu 83.01 Now, those who purify the company at a meal (paṅktipāvanas).
Viṣṇu 83.02: One who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 83.03: [The practitioner] maintains the five fires.
Viṣṇu 83.04: One who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
Viṣṇu, who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Viṣṇu 83.06: He was also one who had reached the further shore of even a single limb of the Veda.
Viṣṇu was one who had reached the further shore of the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and Grammar.
He was also one who had reached the further shore of a single treatise on dharma.
Viṣṇu, purified by the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Viṣṇu 83.10: Purified by sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 83.11: Purified by austerity.
Viṣṇu 83.12: Purified by truth.
Viṣṇu 83.13: Purified by mantras.
Viṣṇu 83.14: Devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Viṣṇu 83.15: The lineage of that which has been given as a brahmadeya.
Viṣṇu 83.16: The Trisuparṇa.
Viṣṇu 83.17: A son-in-law.
And a daughter’s son is also a worthy recipient.
And especially so for yogins. (Viṣṇu 83.19)
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors: Viṣṇu 83.20.
"May he also be born in our lineage who would diligently feed a yogi—
a brahmin at a *śrāddha*— by which we ourselves may be satisfied."
Viṣṇu 84.01: One should not perform a śrāddha in a region inhabited by mlecchas.
Viṣṇu 84.02: One should not go to a country of the Mlecchas.
"Having drunk water at the drinking-troughs of others, one attains equality with them," so says Viṣṇu (84.03).
That region in which the established order of the four castes does not exist should be known as a Mleccha country; beyond that is Āryāvarta.
Viṣṇu 85.01 Now, at Puṣkara, the śrāddha is inexhaustible.
Viṣṇu 85.02: And [the practice of] recitation, burnt offerings, and austerities.
Viṣṇu 85.03: By merely bathing at Puṣkara, one becomes purified from all sins.
In this very same way, it is at Gayāśīrṣa.
Viṣṇu 85.05: At the banyan tree.
Viṣṇu 85.06: On the Amarakaṇṭaka mountain.
Viṣṇu is at Varāhaparvata.
Viṣṇu 85.08: anywhere whatsoever on the bank of the Narmadā.
Viṣṇu 85.09: On the bank of the Yamunā.
Especially at the Gaṅgā, [as stated in] Viṣṇu 85.10.
Viṣṇu 85.11 at Kuśāvarta.
Viṣṇu 85.12: [The mantra] is in the *bindu*.
Viṣṇu 85.13: On the Nīla mountain.
Viṣṇu 85.14: At Kanakhala.
Viṣṇu 85.15: At Kubjāmra.
Viṣṇu 85.16: At Bhṛgutuṅga.
Viṣṇu 85.17: At Kedāra.
Viṣṇu 85.18: At Mahālaya.
Viṣṇu 85.19: At Naḍantikā.
Viṣṇu 85.20: [The rite] in Sugandhā.
Viṣṇu 85.21: [The Lord is] at Śākambharī.
Viṣṇu 85.22: At Phalgutīrtha.
In the Mahāgaṅgā [at the place] of Viṣṇu (85.23).
In the village of Trihalikā, [Viṣṇu] 85.24.
Viṣṇu 85.25: At Kumāradhārā.
Viṣṇu 85.26: At Prabhāsa.
"Wherever [one may be] along the Sarasvatī, and especially so."
Viṣṇu 85.28: [The merit is] at Gaṅgādvāra.
And at Prayāga, Viṣṇu 85.29.
Viṣṇu 85.30: At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Viṣṇu 85.31: [He dwelt] constantly in the Naimiṣa forest.
Especially at Vārāṇasī, [this applies] to Viṣṇu, 85.32.
Viṣṇu 85.33: At the hermitage of Agastya.
In the hermitage of Kaṇva, Viṣṇu 85.34.
In Kauśikī, [as stated in] Viṣṇu 85.35.
On the bank of the Sarayū, Viṣṇu 85.36.
At the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotiṣā, [Viṣṇu]. (Viṣṇu 85.37)
Viṣṇu 85.38: At Śrīparvata.
Viṣṇu 85.39: at Kālodaka.
Viṣṇu 85.40: At Uttaramānasa.
Viṣṇu 85.41: [The same applies] in the case of a mare.
Viṣṇu 85.42: [The merit gained] at Mataṅgavāpī.
In the case of the seven sages (the Great Bear), [the calculation is] according to Viṣṇu 85.43.
In the footstep of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇupada).
Viṣṇu 85.45: [He dwells] at the station of the path to heaven.
Viṣṇu 85.46: [The merit is] at the Godāvarī.
Viṣṇu 85.47: At the Gomatī.
Viṣṇu 85.48: [He is present] at the Vetravatī river.
At the Vipāśā [river], Viṣṇu 85.49.
Viṣṇu 85.50: [The measurement] on the Vitastā river.
On the bank of the Śatadrū, Viṣṇu 85.51.
Viṣṇu 85.52: [The tīrtha] on the Candrabhāgā river.
In the Irāvatī [river], Viṣṇu 85.53.
On the bank of the Sindhu river, [at] Viṣṇu 85.54.
Viṣṇu 85.55: [He is] in the south at Pañcanada.
Viṣṇu 85.56 enjoins:
In these and other such sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as in others... [Viṣṇu 85.57]
In the best of rivers, [O] Viṣṇu, 85.58.
Viṣṇu 85.59: Even in all their own natures.
On the sandy banks, Viṣṇu 85.60.
Viṣṇu 85.61: [One should bathe] at the Prasravaṇa springs.
Viṣṇu 85.62: On mountains.
In the groves, Viṣṇu 85.63.
In the forests, [he is] Viṣṇu, 85.64.
In the groves, Viṣṇu 85.65.
In houses smeared with cow dung, Viṣṇu 85.66.
Viṣṇu 85.67: [One should not look] at beautiful things.
And on this point, there are these verses sung by the ancestors:
"May that person be born in our family who shall offer us handfuls of water,
especially in rivers containing abundant cool water."
"May there arise in our lineage some preeminent man who,
with a concentrated mind, shall perform for us the śrāddha ceremony at the banyan tree of Gayāśīrṣa."
Viṣṇu 85.71a: One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā;
Viṣṇu 85.71c: Or he may perform the horse sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull.
Viṣṇu 86.01 Now follows the rite of the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga).
Viṣṇu 86.02: On the full moon day of either Kārttika or Āśvayuja.
In that regard, at the very outset, one should examine the bull.
Viṣṇu 86.04: [The gift] of the son of a cow that has a living calf and yields milk.
Viṣṇu 86.05: Endowed with all auspicious marks.
Viṣṇu 86.06: Blue.
Or one that is reddish-brown, with the face, tail, feet, and horns being white.
Viṣṇu is the one who covers the herd.

Then, in the midst of the cows, having strewn grass around a well-kindled fire and having cooked a *caru* offering for Pūṣan with milk, and having offered it while reciting, "May Pūṣan follow the cows; may our delight be here," the iron-smith shall brand the bull.
On one side with a discus, and on the other side with a trident.
And one should bathe Viṣṇu with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā" and with the verse "śaṃ no devīḥ."

Having brought [the sacrificer], who has bathed and is adorned, together with four heifers that have likewise bathed and are adorned, one should mutter the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.
One should recite "O bull, you are the father of calves" into the right ear of the bull.
And this [verse] from Viṣṇu 86.14:
For the Blessed Lord Dharma is proclaimed to have four feet;
I choose him with devotion—may he protect me in every way.
