"O Viṣṇu, I give this young man to you as a husband; sport and move about with him, your beloved. May we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies; O King Soma, may we not fall into the power of the enemy."
One should have a bull yoked with a heifer placed in the northeastern direction;
one should give the officiating priest (hotṛ) a pair of garments, as well as gold and bell-metal.
To the iron-smith, a wage desired by his mind should be given;
one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas here with food containing abundant ghee.
In whatever reservoir of water a bull that has been released drinks,
that entire reservoir of water attends upon his ancestors.
Wherever a proud bull scratches the earth with its horn,
an abundant supply of food and drink for the ancestors is thereby presented.

Viṣṇu 87.01 Now, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should prepare a black antelope skin with its hooves and horns— its horns adorned with gold and its hooves with silver, and its tail decorated with pearls— and spread it upon a woolen cloth.
Then, one should cover it with sesame seeds.
And one should fashion Viṣṇu with a golden navel.
One should cover [the image] with a pair of unwashed garments.
One should have it adorned with all kinds of perfumes and jewels. (Viṣṇu 87.05)

Having visualized four radiant vessels filled with milk, curd, honey, and ghee in the four directions, he should give them to a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, who has been adorned and covered with a pair of garments.
And on this point, there are these verses: // Viṣṇu 87.07 //
But he who gives a black antelope skin, complete with its hooves and horns, covered with sesame seeds and garments, and adorned with all kinds of jewels; [attains the highest world].
By him, the earth—along with its oceans and caves, its mountains, forests, and groves, extending to the four quarters—would be considered given; of this there is no doubt.
He who places sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter,
and gives them to a Brahmin, overcomes all evil deeds.
Now, when a cow is giving birth, she becomes the earth.
By giving that adorned woman to a Brahmin, one obtains the fruit of the gift of the earth.
Regarding this, there is a verse: Viṣṇu 88.03.
Having given a cow with her calf that has a mouth on both sides, one who is faithful and composed attains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on the bodies of the two.
The month of Kārttika has Agni as its presiding deity.
And Agni is the mouth of all the gods.

Therefore, by bathing outdoors during the month of Kārttika, being devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) even once, one becomes purified from the sins committed throughout a year.
He who bathes daily throughout the entire month of Kārttika, having conquered his senses, reciting prayers,
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and remaining self-controlled, is liberated from all sins.

Viṣṇu 90.01: On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when it is joined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should cause a brāhmaṇa to receive at moonrise one prastha of powdered salt with a golden center.
By this rite, one is born endowed with beauty and good fortune.

If the full moon day of Pauṣa should coincide with the Puṣya asterism, on that day one whose body has been rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds, who has been consecrated by sprinkling from a jar filled with cow’s ghee, and who has bathed with all medicinal herbs, all perfumes, and all seeds— having bathed the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva with ghee, having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, and having offered oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava, Śākra, and Bārhaspatya mantras— should cause the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce auspicious blessings with ghee mixed with gold.
One should give a pair of garments to the maker.
By this action, Viṣṇu is nourished.
If the full moon of Māgha is joined with the Maghā constellation, one becomes purified by performing a Śrāddha ceremony with sesame seeds on that day.

If the ninth lunar day of Phālguna is joined with the Phalgunī constellation, by offering a well-prepared and well-spread bed to a Brāhmaṇa on that day, one obtains a charming wife who is beautiful and wealthy.
Even a woman [should not abandon] her husband. Viṣṇu 90.08.
If the Caitrī full moon is conjoined with the Citrā asterism, one attains good fortune by the gift of variegated garments on that day.

If the Vaiśākhī full moon is conjoined with the Viśākhā nakṣatra, by satiating seven Brahmins with sesame seeds mixed with honey on that day and thereby pleasing Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from sins.
If the full moon of Jyeṣṭha should coincide with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, by the gift of an umbrella and sandals on that day, one attains lordship over cattle.
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, when it is conjoined with the Āṣāḍhā nakṣatra, by the gift of food and drink, one obtains that very same [merit] in an inexhaustible manner.
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa joined with the asterism Śravaṇā, by giving a water-cow together with food, covered with a pair of garments, one attains heaven.
On the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, when it is joined with the Proṣṭhapadā constellation, one becomes completely liberated from all sins by the gift of a cow.
In the month of Āśvayuja, when the moon has entered the asterism Aśvinī, by giving a vessel filled with ghee along with gold to a Brahmin, one becomes possessed of a radiant fire.

If the full moon day of Kārttika should coincide with the Kṛttikā constellation, one who, at the rising of the moon, gives to a Brāhmaṇa a white bull or one of another color, provided with all kinds of grain, jewels, and perfumes, in the midst of lamps, shall not experience fear in the wilderness.

On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one who has fasted, having worshipped Śrī Vāsudeva with unbroken grains (akṣata), and having offered oblations of those same grains and given them as gifts, becomes purified from all sins.
And whatever one gives on that day, that attains imperishability.

When the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa has passed, one who has fasted, bathed with sesame seeds, offered a libation of sesame, worshipped Vāsudeva with sesame, offered oblations of those same sesame seeds, and given and eaten [sesame], becomes purified from sins.

When the full moon of Māgha has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who has observed a fast should, upon reaching the Śravaṇa asterism, offer two lamps with two large wicks before Śrī Vāsudeva.
Viṣṇu 90.21: On the right side, having given a full garment dyed with safflower along with a balance of ghee weighing eight [units] more; //
On the left side, having offered eight [offerings] together with sesame oil, covered entirely with a white cloth.
Having performed this, in whatever kingdom, in whatever region, or in whatever family one is born, one becomes radiant there.
Having offered clarified butter daily to Brahmins throughout the entire month of Āśvina and thereby gratified the two Aśvins, one becomes possessed of beauty.
In that very month, by feeding Brahmins daily with products of the cow, one becomes a possessor of a kingdom.

Viṣṇu 90.26: Every month, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Revatī, one who feeds Brahmins with the supreme food—rice-porridge mixed with honey and ghee—for the sake of pleasing Revatī, and thereby gratifies Revatī, becomes a partaker of beauty.
In the month of Māgha, having offered oblations of sesame seeds into the fire every day and having fed Brahmins with boiled grain mixed with ghee, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire.
Viṣṇu 90.28: Having bathed in river water on every fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) and having worshipped the King of Dharma (Dharmarāja), one becomes purified from all sins.
If one desires abundant enjoyments that reach even to the moon and the sun,
one should always bathe in the morning during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna.
Viṣṇu 91.01 Now, when water begins to flow from a well dug by someone, half of that person's evil deeds is destroyed.
The maker of a pond, being eternally satisfied, attains the world of Varuṇa.
One who gives water becomes eternally satisfied. Viṣṇu 91.03.
For one who plants trees, those trees become sons in the next world.
Viṣṇu 91.05: One who gives trees gratifies the gods with the flowers of those trees.
And [he should honor] guests with fruits. (Viṣṇu 91.06)
And with his shadow, he protects those who have approached him.
When the god rains water, [he satisfies] the ancestors.
One who builds a bridge attains heaven. Viṣṇu 91.09.
Viṣṇu 91.10: One who builds a temple for a deity attains the very world of that deity for whom he constructs the temple.
Having sprinkled it with nectar, Viṣṇu shines with glory.
Having performed the *vicitra* [rite], one attains the world of the Gandharvas.
By the offering of flowers, one becomes possessed of splendor.
By the offering of unguents, one becomes possessed of fame. (Viṣṇu 91.14)
By the offering of a lamp, one becomes possessed of keen vision and radiant everywhere.
By the gift of food, one becomes strong. (Viṣṇu 91.16)
By removing the remains of offerings made to the gods, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.

[One attains merit] from sweeping the temple of a god, from smearing it [with cow dung], from cleaning the remnants of a Brahmin's meal, from washing the feet [of a guest], and from attending to the sick.
In the case of wells, groves, tanks, and temples of the deities,
the one who performs the restoration obtains the original merit.
Viṣṇu 92.01: The granting of fearlessness is superior to all other forms of giving.
By the gift of that [image], one attains the desired world.
And by the gift of land, O Viṣṇu.
By giving away even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide, one becomes purified from all sins.
By the gift of a cow, one attains the heavenly world.
One who gives ten cows [attains] the worlds of the cows (Go-loka).
One who gives a hundred cows [attains] the worlds of Brahmā.

Having given a cow with golden horns, silver hooves, a pearl-tipped tail, a bronze milking vessel, and a cloth as an upper garment, one attains the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on that cow's body.
Especially so, O Viṣṇu, in the case of a tawny cow.
By giving a tamed bull capable of bearing the yoke, one becomes the donor of ten cows.
The giver of a horse attains the same world as the Sun.
One who gives clothing attains the same world as Candra (the Moon).
By the gift of gold, one attains residence in the same world as Agni.
Through the gift of silver, one obtains beauty.
By the gift of vessels made of refined metal (taijasa), one becomes a recipient of all desires.
Through the gift of ghee, honey, and oil, one attains health. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 92.16)
Viṣṇu 92.17: [One attains this] by the gift of medicine.
And by the gift of salt, one gains beauty.
Through the gift of grain, Viṣṇu [attains] satisfaction. (Viṣṇu 92.19)
And by the gift of grain, [one attains] Viṣṇu. 92.20.
Viṣṇu 92.21: The giver of food obtains everything.
Through the gift of grain, one attains good fortune.
One who gives sesame seeds obtains desired offspring. (Viṣṇu 92.23)
Through the offering of fuel, the fire becomes blazing. (Viṣṇu 92.24)
And in battle, one attains complete victory.
By the gift of a seat, one gains a place [in heaven]. Viṣṇu 92.26.
By the gift of a bed, one obtains a wife. (Viṣṇu 92.27)
By the gift of sandals, one obtains a chariot yoked with mules. (Viṣṇu 92.28)
By the gift of an umbrella, one attains heaven. (Viṣṇu 92.29)
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan and a fly-whisk, one attains comfort on the road.
By the gift of a site, one attains lordship over a city.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is held dear in the home,
that very thing should be given to one possessed of good qualities by him who desires that it be imperishable.
Viṣṇu 93.01: What is given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa yields an equal reward in the world beyond.
For one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, [the fine] is double that of Viṣṇu.
One who has studied the Vedas obtains a thousandfold more than Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu is infinite, having reached the further shore of the Vedas.
But the domestic priest is the vessel for himself alone.
Viṣṇu 93.06: [The same applies to] one's sister, daughter, and son-in-law.
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who follows the "cat-vow," nor to one who follows the "heron-vow," nor to a sinner, nor to one who does not know the Veda.
One who makes righteousness his banner, yet is ever greedy, deceitful, and a hypocrite toward the world;
such a person, who is injurious and seeks to deceive everyone, should be known as one who observes the "cat-vow" (baiḍālavratika).
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on accomplishing his own ends,
crafty, and falsely humble, is one devoted to the "heron-vow" (baka-vrata).
Those in the world who follow the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception toward women and Śūdras.
Such a Brahmin, both in this world and after death, is censured by those who discourse on the Veda; and whatever vow is performed through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas.
He who, not being a bearer of the marks, lives by subsisting on the guise of one who bears the marks,
takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal.

One should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor to one who has done a favor; it is certain that gifts should not be given to those habituated to dancing and singing even for the sake of dharma.
Viṣṇu 94.01: Upon seeing wrinkles and grey hair, a householder should take refuge in the forest.
And [the same applies] when one sees the offspring of one's own offspring, according to Viṣṇu 94.02.
Or, having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may go followed by her.
There too, one should tend the sacred fires.
Viṣṇu 94.05: One should not neglect the five sacrifices with food that has not been produced by the plow.
And one should not abandon one's own daily study.
Viṣṇu 94.07: He should observe celibacy.
Viṣṇu 94.08: He should be clothed in skins or bark garments.
Viṣṇu 94.09: And he should wear his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails [long].
One should bathe at the three sessions of the day.
One who lives by the pigeon-observance may store provisions for a month or for a year.
One who has accumulated [grain] over the course of a year should discard what was previously stored on the full moon day of Āśvayuja.
Or, dwelling in the forest, he may eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from a village,
using either a cup made of a *palāśa* leaf, his hand, or a wooden bowl.
Viṣṇu 95.01: A forest-dweller should wither his body through austerity.
In the summer, one should practice the penance of the five fires.
Viṣṇu lies in the sky during the rainy season.
Viṣṇu 95.04: During the winter, one should wear wet clothes.
Viṣṇu 95.05: He should eat only at night.
Viṣṇu 95.06: Or he may be one who eats at intervals of one day, two days, or three days.
Viṣṇu 95.07: One who subsists on flowers.
Viṣṇu 95.08: One who eats only fruit.
Viṣṇu 95.09: One who eats only vegetables.
Or he may subsist on leaves. (Viṣṇu 95.10)
Or, at the two ends of the fortnights, one should eat barley-food only once.
Or he may subsist by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Viṣṇu 95.13: [He shall be] one who grinds with a stone.
Or he may use his teeth as a mortar.
This entire world of gods and humans has austerity as its root;
austerity is its middle and its end, and it is likewise sustained by austerity.

Whatever is difficult to practice, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is distant, and whatever is difficult to perform— all that can be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed invincible.

Viṣṇu 96.01 Now, having ripened his passions within the three stages of life, one who has performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice and given away all his possessions as the sacrificial fee may depart for the stage of the wandering mendicant.
Having internalized the sacred fires within himself, Viṣṇu should go to the village for the purpose of begging alms.
Viṣṇu 96.03: He should practice alms-gathering from seven households.
If he does not obtain [them], he should not be distressed.
One should not beg from a mendicant.
When people have finished eating and the collection of bowls has passed by, he should collect alms.
Viṣṇu 96.07: [One should eat] from a vessel made of clay, a wooden bowl, or a gourd.
And their purification shall be by means of its water.
One should be wary of gains obtained through excessive honor.
Viṣṇu 96.10: He should have his dwelling in an empty house.
Or he may have his dwelling at the foot of a tree.
One should not stay for a second night in a village.
Viṣṇu 96.13: He should take only as much clothing as is necessary to cover his private parts.
One should place one's foot purified by the gaze.
One should take water that has been purified by a cloth.
One should speak words purified by truth.
One should perform actions purified by the mind.
One should desire neither death nor life.
One should endure harsh words. (Viṣṇu 96.19)
One should not despise anyone whatsoever.
One should be free from expectations. (Viṣṇu 96.21)
Viṣṇu 96.22: One who does not offer salutations.
Whether one person cuts off his arm with an axe or another anoints his other arm with sandalwood paste,
he should think neither ill of the former nor well of the latter.
One should be constant in breath control, concentration, and meditation. (Viṣṇu 96.24)
Viṣṇu 96.25: One should perceive the impermanence of saṃsāra.
The impurity of the body, Viṣṇu 96.26.
By old age, there is a transformation of form. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 96.27)
And suffering from bodily, mental, and external diseases. (Viṣṇu 96.28)
And with those born together, Viṣṇu 96.29.
[He experiences] dwelling in the womb in perpetual darkness. (Viṣṇu 96.30)
And [one should not eat] in the midst of urine and excrement. (Viṣṇu 96.31)
And there, one experiences the suffering of cold and heat. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 96.32)
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 96.33: At the time of birth, there is the experience of great suffering due to emerging from the narrowness of the womb.
In childhood, there is delusion and subjection to teachers and others.
From study [comes] manifold suffering; (Viṣṇu 96.35)
Viṣṇu 96.36: In youth, failing to attain the objects of the senses, or attaining them by improper means, one falls into hell due to the indulgence in those objects.
Dwelling with those who are unpleasant and separation from those who are dear.
And in hell, there is very great suffering.
In the wandering through saṃsāra and within the wombs of animals.
Thus, in this ever-moving cycle of existence, there is no happiness whatsoever.
Furthermore, whatever is designated as pleasure merely in comparison to the absence of suffering, that too is impermanent.
Viṣṇu 96.42: If one lacks the capacity for that service, or if it cannot be obtained, there is great suffering.
And one should view this body as consisting of the seven constituent elements (dhātus).
Viṣṇu 96.44 consists of fat, blood, flesh, marrow, bone, pith, and semen.
Viṣṇu 96.45: Covered with skin.
And it is foul-smelling. (Viṣṇu 96.46)
Viṣṇu 96.47: [The body is] an abode of impurity.
Even when surrounded by hundreds of pleasures, it is subject to transformation.
Even if held with great effort, it is subject to destruction.
Viṣṇu 96.50: It is the abode of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy.
Viṣṇu 96.51: [The body] consists of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
Viṣṇu 96.52: [The body] is composed of bones, veins, arteries, and sinews.
Viṣṇu 96.53: [One should not eat food] that is dusty.
Viṣṇu 96.54: [The gift of] six types of bark.
It is supported by three hundred and sixty bones.
Viṣṇu 96.56: Their division [of inheritance].
Including the small teeth, there are sixty-four teeth.
There are twenty nails. Viṣṇu 96.58.
And the rods for his hands and feet. (Viṣṇu 96.59)
There are sixty joints of the fingers.
Viṣṇu 96.61: Two on the two heels.
Viṣṇu 96.62: [One should place] four [mudrās] on the ankles.
Viṣṇu 96.63: Four [finger-breadths] on the two forearms.
Viṣṇu 96.64: Four [finger-breadths] in the two shanks.
Two each on the knees and the cheeks (Viṣṇu 96.65).
Viṣṇu 96.66: [The marks] on the thighs and shoulders.
Viṣṇu 96.67: [The bones are] in the eyeballs, the palate, the hips, and the flat bones of the pelvis.
Viṣṇu 96.68: One bone of the female organ.
The backbone consists of forty-five parts.
Viṣṇu 96.70: The neck consists of fifteen bones.
Viṣṇu 96.71: One joint of the collarbone.
Likewise, the jaw [is formed] by Viṣṇu. (Viṣṇu 96.72)
And at its base, there are two [deities].
The two [teeth] are on the forehead, the eye, and the cheek.
The nose consists of solid bone.
Along with the Arbudas and Sthālakas, there are seventy-two Pārśvakas.
The chest consists of seventeen [ribs]. Viṣṇu 96.77.
Viṣṇu 96.78: Two conch shells.
And there are four skull-fragments of the head, so it is said in Viṣṇu 96.79.
In this body, there are seven hundred vessels (sirās).
There are nine hundred sinews.
Viṣṇu 96.82: Two hundred vessels (dhamanīs).
Viṣṇu 96.83: Five hundred peśīs.
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 96.84: There are twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred and fifty-six minor vessels (dhamanīs).
There are three hundred thousand pores for the beard and hair.
Viṣṇu 96.86: There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas).
Viṣṇu 96.87: Two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores and sixty-seven lakhs of body hairs.
Viṣṇu 96.89: The navel, the king of the anus, semen, blood, the two temples, the head, the throat, and the heart—these are the seats of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
The two arms, the two shanks, the waist, and the head—these are the six limbs.

Fat, omentum, the place of slaughter, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the kidneys, the bladder, the receptacle of feces, the stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the rectum, the abdomen, and the pelvic cavity.

Viṣṇu 96.92: The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-cavities, the two ears, the two cheeks, the two eyebrows, the two temples, the two gums, the two lips, the two groins, the two testicles, the two kidneys, the two phlegm-glands, the two breasts, the uvula, the two buttocks, the two arms, the two calves, the two thighs, the two shanks, the palate, the belly, the two heads of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, and the nape of the neck—these are the locations in this body.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects of the senses.
The nose, eyes, skin, tongue, and ears are the organs of perception (buddhīndriyas). Viṣṇu 96.94.
The hands, feet, anus, genitals, and tongue are the organs of action (karmendriyas).
The mind, the intellect, the self, and the unmanifest—these are beyond the senses.
"O Earth, this body is designated as the 'field' (kṣetra).
Those who know this declare that he who understands it is the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña)."
"Know me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in all fields, O lady;
the discernment of the field and the knower of the field is that which must be known eternally by one who seeks liberation."

With his feet placed upward upon his thighs, having laid his left hand upon his right, with his tongue motionless against the palate, not touching his teeth with his teeth, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the quarters of space, free from fear and with a tranquil self, he should contemplate that which transcends the twenty-four principles.
Viṣṇu is eternally beyond the senses, devoid of qualities, transcending sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, omniscient, and infinitely vast.
Viṣṇu is all-pervading and exceedingly subtle.
Viṣṇu has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and the power of all sense organs everywhere.
One should meditate on Viṣṇu in this manner.
And for one who is intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu, the manifestation of yoga occurs within a year.

Now, if one is unable to fix the mark upon the formless, then, having meditated first on each preceding one among earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, self, the unmanifest, and the puruṣa, and having attained the mark therein, one should abandon that and meditate on the next following one.
Thus one should begin the meditation on the Puruṣa.
If he is still unable even in that, he should meditate on the Person like a lamp in the center of his own heart-lotus, which is turned downwards.

If one is unable even for that, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with armlets, marked with the Śrīvatsa, his chest decorated with a forest garland, possessing a gentle form, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with the earth situated between his feet.
"Whatever one meditates upon, that one attains"—this is the secret of meditation (dhyāna).
Therefore, having abandoned everything that is perishable, one should meditate upon the imperishable alone.
And there is not even a single syllable that exists apart from Puruṣa.
Having reached him, one becomes liberated.
Because the Great Lord, having pervaded the entire city [of the body], lies within it,
he is therefore called "Puruṣa" by those who contemplate reality.
During the first and last watches of the night, the yogin should always remain unwearied.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu as the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle, who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Viṣṇu is the self of reality, unapproachable, and devoid of all categories of existence;
he is incapable [of action], yet the sustainer of all, free from qualities, and the enjoyer of qualities.
Viṣṇu is both outside and within all beings; he is the unmoving and indeed the moving. Because of his subtlety, he is unknowable; yet he is far away and also near at hand.
He is undivided, yet he exists as if divided by the elements;
he is the form of the past, the future, and the present; he is the devourer and the progenitor.
He is the light of even the luminaries; he is said to be beyond darkness.
He is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attained through knowledge; he is established in the hearts of all.
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief.
Having understood this, my devotee attains to my own state of being.
Viṣṇu 98.01: Having been addressed in this manner, Vasumatī, having prostrated herself with her knees and head, spoke.

"O Blessed One, these four elements always have their abodes near you: space in the form of the conch, wind in the form of the discus, fire in the form of the mace, and water in the form of the lotus. I too wish to remain revolving between the feet of the Blessed One in this very form."
Having been addressed in this way, the Blessed One said, "So be it."

Viṣṇu is the supreme refuge of the world.
"Obeisance, obeisance," [said] Viṣṇu (98.101).
Having thus praised him with a tranquil mind,
the goddess Earth, her desire attained, then spoke face-to-face to the deity.
Having seen Śrī, who had taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, blazing with ascetic power and possessing the lovely hue of well-refined gold,
the goddess Earth, filled with joy, questioned her.
O Viṣṇu, whose excellent hands are as beautiful as blooming red lotuses, whose feet are held by a navel like a blooming red lotus,
who always resides in a dwelling like a blooming red lotus, and whose complexion is equal to the center of a blooming red lotus!
O Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like blue lotuses, whose complexion is like refined gold, who wears white garments and has limbs adorned with jewels;
O moon-faced one, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, endowed with great majesty, the foremost in the world!
You alone are the sleep of the world, the primary source, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, Virati, and Jayā;
you are Kānti, Prabhā, Kīrti, Vibhūti, Sarasvatī, Vāk, and Pāvanī.
Viṣṇu 99.05a: Svadhā, Titikṣā, Vasudhā, Pratiṣṭhā, Sthiti, Sudīkṣā, and likewise Sunīti; Viṣṇu 99.05c: Khyāti, Viśālā, as well as Anasūyā, Svāhā, Medhā, and likewise Buddhi.

O dark-eyed one, just as this best of gods stands having pervaded the entire three worlds, so too do you stand, O giver of boons; nevertheless, O powerful one, I ask you about the abode of your majesty.
Having been addressed in this way, Lakṣmī, standing then before the best of gods, spoke to the Earth:
"I am always stationed at the side of the god Madhusūdana, O you of golden hue."
"O Sustainer of the World, listen: by his command, the virtuous declare that I am he whom I remember in my mind, endowed with Śrī; and hear also where I always abide when he is being remembered."
Moreover, O Viṣṇu, I dwell in the sun, in the moon, and in the cloudless sky rich with hosts of stars.
Likewise, O Earth, upon pure gold and stainless silver, on gems and spotless garments, on rows of white palaces, and in temples adorned with banners; Viṣṇu 99.10.
Viṣṇu 99.11a: Immediately [one becomes pure] upon seeing fresh cow-dung, or a rutting lordly elephant, or a joyful horse;
Viṣṇu 99.11c: likewise upon seeing a bull endowed with pride, or a Brāhmaṇa engaged in Vedic study.
I am established upon the lion-throne, the *āmalaka* fruit, the *bilva* fruit, the umbrella, the conch, and likewise the lotus;
in the blazing sacrificial fire, in the stainless sword, and in the reflection of the mirror.
I stood upon soft ground that had been freshly turned up, amidst decorated jars filled with water, accompanied by fly-whisks and palm-leaf fans,
and beside charming golden water-pots.
Likewise in milk, clarified butter, fresh grass, honey, and curd;
in the body of a virtuous woman, in the body of a maiden, and in the bodies of the gods, ascetics, and those who have offered oblations at sacrifice.

When an arrow has been discharged in battle, when one stands [in readiness], when one has died and departed to dwell in heaven, when there is the sound of the Vedas, or the sound of a conch, or the utterance of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, or the sound of musical instruments; in these cases, [one may eat].
At the consecration of a kingdom, as well as at a wedding, a sacrifice, or when one has bathed one's head;
likewise among white flowers, on mountains, among delightful fruits, and by the best of rivers.
In full lakes as well as in waters, on ground covered with grassy meadows and clusters of lotuses;
in a forest, in a calf, in a joyful infant, and in a virtuous man devoted to righteousness.
One who follows established conduct, is constantly devoted to the scriptures, modestly dressed, and likewise well-attired;
Viṣṇu 99.19a: [One should not enter] a house where the husband is content with his own wife, devoted to dharma, intent on righteousness, and free from overeating;
99.19c: nor one that is always adorned with flowers, whose limbs are fragrant, which is smeared with perfumes, and well-decorated.

When [the king] abides in truth, is intent on the welfare of all beings, endowed with forbearance, free from anger, skilled in his own affairs as well as those of others, possesses a virtuous mind, and is always humble; Viṣṇu 99.20.

Among women who are always well-adorned, devoted to their husbands, speaking kindly, not wasteful of their resources, blessed with sons, careful in guarding their household goods, and fond of making offerings; Viṣṇu 99.21.

I am ever established in those women whose dwellings are well-cleaned, who have conquered their senses, who are free from strife, who are not covetous, who have regard for righteousness, who are endowed with compassion, and who are devoted to the Slayer of Madhu.
"Without the Supreme Person, I shall never remain even for the duration of a single blink of an eye.
(End of half-verse) This preeminent treatise on Dharma was spoken by the Lord himself.
Those twice-born who shall uphold [this], their destination shall be the highest heaven.
This is purifying, auspicious, conducive to heaven, and indeed life-prolonging;
it bestows knowledge, fame, and increases wealth and good fortune.
It should be studied, retained, recited, and heard;
it should always be made to be heard at śrāddha ceremonies by men desiring prosperity.
O Earth, this supreme secret has been told to you; the man who, desiring prosperity, always recites this daily, [attains his goal].
Out of grace, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I have bestowed this supreme, glorious, and auspicious work;
it is the destroyer of evil dreams, endowed with great merit, the abode of Śiva, and the eternal scripture of Dharma. [End of Part 2 = End of Viṣṇu-smṛti] EOF

Having honored Yājñavalkya, the Lord of Yogins, the sages said:
"Tell us in their entirety the duties of those belonging to the castes and stages of life, as well as those who are outside them."
Remaining in Mithilā, that lord of yogis, having meditated for a moment, spoke to the sages:
"In whatever region there is a black antelope, in that place you should learn the laws of dharma."
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) mixed together with the Vedas—
these are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, and Aṅgiras;
Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, and Likhita; Dakṣa and Gautama; Śātātapa and Vasiṣṭha—these are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
When a gift is given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time, with the right means and accompanied by faith— that is the complete definition of dharma.
Revelation (śruti), tradition (smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), and what is pleasing to oneself—desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma.
Among the acts of sacrifice, right conduct, self-control, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts, this indeed is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga.
An assembly (*parṣat*) consists of four persons who know the Vedas and the Dharma, or even those who possess the threefold knowledge (*traividya*);
whatever that assembly declares shall be the Dharma, or a single person who is the most eminent among those who know the supreme self (*adhyātma*).
[2. The Section on the Religious Student] (p. 5) Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.10: The castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with the funeral rite are performed with sacred mantras.

The conception rite (garbhādhāna) is performed during the fertile period; the quickening rite (pumsavana) before the fetus moves; the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) in the sixth or eighth month; and these, along with the birth rite (jātakarman), are to be performed upon the child's birth.
On the eleventh day, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) is performed; in the fourth month, the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*);
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*); and the tonsure (*cūḍā*) should be performed according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb is pacified;
these rites for women are performed silently, but their marriage is accompanied by mantras.
The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth];
for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh; for Vaiśyas, according to some, in the same [eleventh], and for others, according to family custom.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should teach him the Veda preceded by the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis),
and he should also instruct him in the rules of purification and proper conduct.

During the day and at the twilights, one should perform the voiding of urine and feces with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) placed over the ear and facing north; if it be at night, one should face south.
Having risen with his penis still held [in hand], he should, using earth and water drawn up from the ground,
untiringly perform purification until the odor and the stain are removed.
With his knees between his hands, seated in a clean place facing north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The base of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand,
are respectively the tirthas of Prajāpati, the ancestors, Brahmā, and the gods.
Having sipped water three times and wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the cavities of the head with water—
water that is natural, free from foam and bubbles.
The twice-born classes are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate, respectively;
women and Śūdras are purified when the water merely touches the lips.
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the waters, sprinkling [the body] with water, restraint of the breath,
worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head and preceded by the Vyāhṛtis, joined with the Praṇava at each beginning; this threefold repetition is the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma).
Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water while reciting the three verses dedicated to the waters,
he should sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the stars appear in the west.
One should perform the morning twilight ritual in this manner before sunrise, remaining standing until the sun is seen;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-rite during both twilights.
Then he should salute his elders, saying, "I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study.
When summoned, he should study; whatever he has obtained, he should report it to him.
He should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body.

Those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, virtuous, and respectful; who are good, capable, trustworthy, and givers of knowledge and wealth—these should be taught the Dharma according to the law.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, and a sacred thread, as well as a girdle.
He should go about for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own subsistence.
The practice of begging alms for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is characterized by the word "bhavat" at the beginning, middle, and end, respectively.
Having performed the fire-rites, he should eat with speech restrained, at the permission of his teacher,
after performing the *āpośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it.
Remaining in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should not eat food from a single source except in times of distress.
A Brāhmaṇa may, at his pleasure, eat at a *śrāddha* feast, provided he does not violate his vow.
One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, sour substances, women, and the harming of living beings; as well as gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and so forth.
He is a *guru* who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him; he who, having initiated him, gives him the Veda is designated an *ācārya*.

The teacher who imparts even a single portion [of knowledge] is called an *upādhyāya*, and the one who performs the sacrifice is called an *ṛtvij*. These are to be honored according to their seniority; yet among them all, the mother is the most venerable.
For each Veda, the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) is twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until the Veda has been mastered, while others say it ends at the sixteenth year with the tonsure ceremony (*keśānta*).
Until the sixteenth year for Brāhmaṇas, until the twenty-second for Kṣatriyas, and until the twenty-fourth year for Vaiśyas, is the final time for the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
From this point forward, these fall [from their caste] and are excluded from all religious duties;
they are *vrātyas* who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*, except for the *Vrātyastoma* sacrifice.
Since Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are born once from their mother and a second time from the binding of the girdle of Muñja grass, they are therefore remembered as "twice-born" (dvija).
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means of attaining the highest good, surpassing sacrifices, austerities, and even auspicious ritual acts.
The twice-born who studies the Rigveda daily satisfies the gods with honey and milk,
and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
He who studies the Yajus formulas daily according to his ability satisfies the gods with clarified butter and nectar,
and likewise the ancestors with ghee and honey.
He who recites [this] daily shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and by means of the Sāman chants, he shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and ghee.
Reciting the Atharvāṅgirasaḥ, the twice-born man should satisfy the gods with fat,
and the ancestors daily with honey and clarified butter, according to his ability.
He who studies daily, according to his ability, the dialogues, the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsīs, the Gāthās, the Itihāsas, and likewise the sciences (vidyās).
It provides satisfaction to the dwellers of heaven with meat, milk, boiled rice, and honey;
and one should likewise provide satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
When they are satisfied, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires; and whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain the fruit of each one of them.

A twice-born man who constantly engages in the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) here in this world enjoys three times the fruit of gifting the earth filled with wealth, as well as the fruit of supreme austerity.
But a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher; in the absence of the teacher, with the teacher's son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire.
By means of this procedure, one who has conquered his senses, casting off the body, attains the world of Brahman and is not born here again. [3.
Section on Marriage]
Having given a gift to the teacher, or with his permission, he may perform the ceremonial bath;
for he should either have brought the Veda to completion, or the vows, or indeed both.
Having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should marry a woman who possesses auspicious marks—
one who has never belonged to another, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.
One who is free from disease, has brothers, and is not born of the same *ārṣa* lineage or *gotra*;
likewise, she who is beyond the fifth on the mother’s side and the seventh on the father’s side;
and she who comes from a great family of *śrotriyas* renowned for ten generations.
Nor from one who, though prosperous, is afflicted with the defect of a contagious disease.

(Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.54c) One who possesses these very same qualities, who is of the same caste (*savarṇa*), learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), carefully examined for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people, is the preferred [bridegroom]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.55a–c)
As for that which is said— that the taking of a Śūdra woman as a wife by the twice-born—
is not my opinion, because in such a case, he himself is born [from her].

Three wives are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya respectively, according to the order of the castes; likewise, one wife is prescribed for one born as a Śūdra. Among these, the wife of her own caste is the primary one for each.
In the Brāhma marriage, having invited [the groom], the girl is given adorned according to one's ability;
the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides.
The *daiva* form consists of giving [the bride] to the officiating priest at a sacrifice; the *ārṣa* form consists of taking two cows.
The son born of the first [form] purifies fourteen generations, and the son born of the latter [form] purifies six.
Having said this, "May she who is given to a suitor practice dharma together with him"—
that body, when born from her, purifies six generations on each side along with herself.
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden.

The hand should be taken [as the marriage token] for women of the same caste; a Kṣatriya woman should take an arrow, and a Vaiśya woman should take a goad at the wedding of one born of the first-born caste.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a sapinda relative, and likewise the mother;
in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the maiden, provided they are of sound mind.

If he does not give her away, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo at every menstrual period. However, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among those who are suitable.

A maiden is given only once; he who carries her away [after she has been given] incurs the punishment for theft. Even if she has been given, one may take her back from the previous husband if a more excellent suitor arrives.
One who gives a gift without declaring its defect shall be punished with the highest amercement;
but one who abandons a faultless gift, or falsely accuses it of being defective, shall be fined one hundred [paṇas].
A woman who has not been deflowered and one who has been deflowered are both called *punarbhū* when she undergoes the sacramental rite again;
likewise, a *svairiṇī* is she who, having abandoned her husband, out of desire resorts to a man of equal caste.
A brother-in-law, with the permission of his elder, or a sapinda or a sagotra, being anointed with clarified butter, may approach a childless woman during her season with the desire for a son.
He may go [to the husband] from the time of conception; otherwise, he would become an outcast. A son born according to this rule becomes his "soil-born" (kṣetraja) son.
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, defiled, subsisting on mere food, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
Soma gave them purity, and Gandharva gave them beautiful speech; Pāvaka gave them fitness for all sacrificial rites, for women are indeed pure.

Purification from sexual intercourse during the fertile period is prescribed; however, abandonment is ordained if a pregnancy results, as well as in cases such as killing the fetus or the husband, and likewise for other great sins.

A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, a rogue, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly, one who gives birth only to daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband— such a wife may be superseded.
A superseded wife must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue. Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish.
Whether her husband be dead or living, she who does not approach another man attains fame in this world and rejoices together with him in the hereafter.

If he abandons a wife who obeys his commands, is skillful, bears him heroic sons, and speaks kindly, he should be made to pay her a third share of his property; if he possesses no property, he must provide for her maintenance.
Wives must carry out the word of their husbands; this is the highest duty of a woman. For one defiled by a mortal sin is to be awaited until purification.
Since the infinity of worlds and the attainment of heaven through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons depend upon them,
therefore women should be cherished and well protected.

Women have sixteen nights [of fertility] during their season; among these, he should approach her on the even nights. He should remain as one practicing celibacy (*brahmacārī*) and avoid the forbidden days (*parvaṇi*) as well as the first four nights.
Proceeding in this manner, he should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the Maghā and Mūla constellations;
when the moon is in its full strength, a man may once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks.
Or he may act according to his desire, remembering the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for women are declared to be worthy of protection.
Wives are to be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, paternal kinsmen,
mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and other relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Keeping the household utensils well-ordered, being skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure,
she should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law, being entirely devoted to her husband.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey should abandon play, bodily adornment, attendance at social gatherings and festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others.
The father shall protect the maiden; once she is married, the husband; and in old age, the sons.
In the absence of these, her paternal kinsmen shall protect her; a woman never possesses independence.
She should not be superseded by her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles;
she should not be inferior [to them], for without her husband, she would otherwise become censurable.
Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, conducting herself according to her own proper discipline, and having conquered her senses,
she attains fame in this world and the highest state after death.

If there is another wife of the same caste, he should not have religious duties performed by her; among wives of the same caste, according to the rule of dharma, no other wife may be employed without the eldest.
Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband shall, without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule. [End of Chapter 4:
The Distinction of Classes and Castes]
From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage; through blameless marriages, these sons increase the progeny.
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is born the Mūrdhāvasikta; from the same father and a Vaiśya woman, the Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra woman, the Niṣāda or the Pāraśava is born.
From a Kṣatriya man, sons known as the Māhiṣya and the Ugra are born of Vaiśya and Śūdra women respectively;
from a Vaiśya man, a Karaṇa is born of a Śūdra woman. This is the rule declared for wives who have been duly married.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
and from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Māgadha is born; from a Śūdra father, a Kṣattṛ is born.
And from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother, a Vaiśya woman indeed gave birth to an Āyogava son.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
these and others are to be known as those born in the inverse and natural orders.
The elevation of caste is to be known as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation;
upon the reversal of occupations, there is equality, and the status of higher and lower is as previously described.
A householder should perform every day the *smārta* rites in the marriage fire,
or those performed at the time of inheritance, or the *śrauta* rites in the *vaitānika* fires.
Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the prescribed rules of purification,
the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion (*prātaḥ-sandhyā*), preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Having offered oblations into the fires dedicated to Sūrya, he should, with a concentrated mind, mutter the mantras;
and he should master the meanings of the Vedas as well as various treatises.
And he should approach the Lord for the sake of accomplishing his goals regarding acquisition and preservation;
having bathed, he should likewise offer libations to and worship the gods and the ancestors.

For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*), one should, according to one's ability, recite the Vedas, the *Atharvaveda*, the *Purāṇas* along with the *Itihāsas*, as well as spiritual knowledge (*vidyā*) concerning the self.

The offering of the *bali*, the *svadhā* oblation, the fire sacrifice (*homa*), the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), and the hospitable reception of guests constitute the great sacrifices to the beings,
the ancestors, the gods, Brahman, and human beings.
From the food remaining after the oblation has been offered to the gods, he should present the *bhūtabali* (offering to the spirits).
He should place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows.
Food should be given to the ancestors and to men, as well as water every day;
one should constantly perform the private recitation of the Veda, and one should not cook food for oneself alone.
Having fed the children, those living in their father's house, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick,
young girls, guests, and servants, the husband and wife may eat the remainder.
By sipping water at the beginning and likewise at the end while eating,
a twice-born man should ensure that his food is neither naked nor immortal.
To the various social classes, one should give according to one's ability and in due order by virtue of their status as guests;
a guest must not be turned away in the evening, even if offered only words, a place to lie down, grass, and water.
Having honored the mendicant, alms should be given to him who observes his vows;
and one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time.
Or he should provide for a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) a large bull or a large goat, along with hospitable treatment,
a seat, delicious food, and pleasant speech.
But every year, the Snātaka, the teacher, the king, a dear friend, one for whom one has performed a marriage, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice, are worthy of the Arghya offering.

A traveler on the road who is a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) and has mastered the Vedas is to be known as a guest (*atithi*). These two are to be honored by the householder who desires the world of Brahman.
One should not have a taste for food prepared by others, except when invited by those who are blameless; one should also avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating.
He should follow the guest—a learned Vedic scholar who has been satisfied—until he reaches the boundary of his village;
for the remainder of the day, he should sit together with cultured men, beloved friends, and kinsmen.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions, having offered oblations into those fires and attended upon them,
and having eaten with his dependents to the point of moderate satisfaction, he should then go to bed.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā, he should reflect upon his own welfare;
he should not neglect virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times, according to his ability.
They are to be honored according to their sequence by virtue of learning, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth.
Even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves honor in his old age.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, bath-graduates, women, the sick, bridegrooms, and those in chariots; among these, the king is to be honored by them, and the bath-graduate is to be honored by the king.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are the duties of the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
for the Brāhmaṇa, however, there are additionally the receiving of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
for a Vaiśya, moneylending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are prescribed.
The service of the twice-born is the duty of a Śūdra; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while acting for the benefit of the twice-born.
Delighting in his wife, pure, supporting his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites,
he should not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses;
generosity, self-control, compassion, and patience—these are the means for accomplishing the dharma for all.
One should likewise adopt a conduct that is consistent with one's age, intelligence, wealth, speech, dress, learning, lineage, and actions— conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit.
A twice-born man who possesses more than three years' worth of grain may indeed drink Soma;
he whose food supply lasts for one year may perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice.
Every year, the Soma sacrifice, the animal sacrifice, and likewise the Pratyayana;
the Āgrayaṇa-iṣṭi must also be performed, as well as the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
In the absence of these [materials], a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a deficient rite when the necessary materials for one that yields fruit are available.
By performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra, one is born as a Cāṇḍāla;
by not giving what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one becomes a vulture or even a crow.
Or he may possess grain sufficient for a granary or a jar; or he may have enough for three days, or even not enough for the morrow.
Or he may live by gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains; among these, each subsequent mode is superior. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.128)
One should not seek wealth that conflicts with Vedic study from whatever source it may come;
nor should one always indulge in forbidden pursuits, but remain contented.
If, while living with them, he should desire wealth due to hunger, he may seek it from a king, a pupil, or a patron;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who argue for the sake of debate, heretics, and those who act like herons.
Wearing white garments, with his hair, beard, and nails clipped short, and being pure,
he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is false, nor should one be a thief or a usurer.
Wearing a girdle of muñja grass, the sacred thread, carrying a bamboo staff and a water-pot,
he should circumambulate deities, clay mounds, cows, Brahmins, and trees, keeping them to his right.
But one should not urinate in a river, in shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one face the fire, the sun, a cow, the moon, the twilight, water, a woman, or a twice-born man.
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one look at urine, feces, impure things, or the stars Rāhu.
One should recite the entire mantra thus: "This is my thunderbolt.
While it is raining, one should go about uncovered; nor should one sleep with the head toward the west.
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it.
One should not drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one awaken a sleeping person.
One should not play with dice or with those who destroy dharma, nor should one lie down to sleep with those who are diseased.
One should avoid performing actions that are prohibited, crossing a river while facing the smoke of a funeral pyre,
and standing upon hair, ashes, chaff, charcoal, or a skull.
One should not announce a cow suckling her calf; one should never enter through any opening other than the door;
and one should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures.
In the matter of receiving gifts, the outcaste, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the king are defective;
each of these is ten times more blameworthy than the one preceding it, respectively.
The commencement of the study of the Vedas (*upākarma*) for the chapters [of the Veda] takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa,
or under the asterism Hasta when the herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal ritual of the dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarga) outside, at the edge of the water, according to the prescribed rule.
There is a suspension of study for three days when one's pupil, officiating priest, teacher, or kinsman has died;
likewise upon the commencement (upākarmaṇi) and the conclusion (utsarge) of the Vedic term, and when a master of one’s own Vedic branch (śākhā) has passed away.
[In the case of a Vedic scholar of one's own branch: Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.145:
Upon the thundering of clouds at twilight, a thunderclap, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor;
and having completed the Veda, as well as having studied the *Āraṇyaka*, one should remain for a day and a night.

On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during an eclipse, at the junctions of the seasons, or after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha) or accepting a gift from such a feast; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.146.
When [the sacrificial fire] is touched by a domestic animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a mouse, there is a fast for one day and night;
likewise when lightning strikes or when [the sacrificial post] is erected.
When there is the barking of a dog, the howling of a jackal, the braying of a donkey, the hooting of an owl, or the sound of a lute, an arrow, or one who is distressed;
or when one is near impure substances, a corpse, a Śūdra, an outcaste (antya), a cremation ground, or a person who has fallen from his caste.

In an impure place, when one is personally impure, during a downpour of lightning and thunder, after eating while the hands are still wet, inside water, at midnight, or during a violent wind; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.149.
During a shower of dust, a conflagration of the quarters, at the twilights, in mist, or when there is fear;
while running, when there is a foul odor, or when a learned man has arrived at the house.

Upon the mounting of a donkey, a camel, a carriage, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; or upon climbing a tree, a barren spot, or a mountain—these they know to be thirty-seven temporary interruptions of study.
One should not step upon the shadow of a deity, an officiating priest, a bath-graduate, a teacher, or a king, nor that of another's wife,
nor blood, feces, urine, spittle, ointments for the body, and the like.
The Brahmin, the snake, and the Kṣatriya—these should never be treated with contempt.
Until death one should desire prosperity; one should not touch anyone on their vital spot.
One should discard remnants of food, excrement, urine, and water from a distance;
one should always practice the conduct of right behavior as fully declared in the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
One who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food, nor should he touch them with his foot;
he should not engage in reviling or beating others, though he may strike his son or pupil [for correction].

One should diligently practice dharma through action, mind, and speech; however, one should not practice even that which is technically dharma if it fails to lead to heaven or is loathed by the world.
With mother, father, guests, brothers, paternal kin, maternal relatives, and maternal uncles;
with the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and kinsmen.
By avoiding disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, children, wives, slaves, and blood relatives, a householder shall conquer all the worlds.
One should not bathe in the waters belonging to others without first taking up five lumps [of earth];
however, one may bathe in rivers, natural reservoirs of the gods, lakes, and springs.

One should avoid the beds, seats, gardens, houses, and vehicles of another that have not been given; likewise, one should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress.
Of the miserly, the bound, and thieves; of eunuchs, actors, and wrestlers;
of flute-players, the accused, usurers, prostitutes, and those initiated for a group sacrifice.
[The food] of physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and those who bear enmity;
and [the food] of the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātya, the hypocritical, and those who eat the remnants of others.

[The food] of a woman without a male relative, a goldsmith’s wife, a woman conquered by her husband, a village-priest, a seller of weapons, a blacksmith, a weaver, and one who subsists by keeping dogs [is forbidden].
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.164: [The impurity lasts for one day] in the case of those who kill the cruel, a king, a washerman, an ungrateful person, or one who lives by slaughter;
and in the case of a laundryman, a liquor-seller, and those who live in the same house as a paramour.
The food of slanderers and liars, as well as that of jugglers and bards,
and likewise that of those who sell *soma*, must not be eaten.

Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend, a sharecropper, and a barber may be eaten; as may the food of one who has offered himself [as a servant]. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.166] (Section 7:
On Edible and Non-edible Food)

Meat that has not been honored, meat prepared in vain, that which contains hair or insects, that which is sour, stale, or the leavings of another, that which has been touched by a dog, or that which has been looked upon by an outcast— [these should be avoided].
One should avoid food that has been touched by a menstruating woman, food that has been publicly proclaimed for sale, and food that has been passed around;
as well as food smelled by a cow, the leavings of a bird, or food intentionally touched with the foot.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil or fat.
One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days,
a camel, animals with uncloven hooves, those belonging to females, wild animals, and sheep.
One should avoid sacrificial oblations intended for the gods, the śigru plant, red exudations from incisions,
meat not consecrated by ritual invocation, things produced from excrement, and mushrooms.
Carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, parrots, peckers, ṭiṭṭibhas, cranes, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all those dwelling in villages; (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.172).
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakrāhva, balākā, baka, and viṣkira birds;
and kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī prepared for no sacred purpose.
The kalaviṅka, the crow, the osprey, the rajjudālaka, web-footed birds, the khanjarīṭa, and wild animals or birds that are unknown.
Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, the flesh of a dog, dried meat, or fish, one should dwell for three days observing a fast.
Having eaten onions, village pigs, mushrooms, village cocks,
garlic, and leeks, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the pangolin, and the hare are edible;
and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita are indeed edible.
Likewise, the *pāṭhīna*, the *rājīva*, and the *saśalka* fish may be eaten by the twice-born. Therefore, listen to the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
In a life-threatening situation, at a śrāddha ceremony, when meat has been consecrated by sprinkling, or when eating at the request of a twice-born,
one who eats meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors incurs no fault.
That person of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the bodies of those animals.
A Brahmin who abstains from meat, even while living at home, obtains all his desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice; he becomes a sage. [End of Chapter 8:
The Section on the Purification of Substances]
Of gold, silver, and lotuses; of vessels with upward openings, water-jars, and stones; of vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and skins.
The purification of drinking vessels and cups is prescribed to be by means of water;
however, the caru-pot, the large and small sacrificial ladles, and vessels containing oily substances are purified with hot water.

The sprinkling with water (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed for the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the skin (ajina), and grains; for the pestle (musala), the mortar (ulūkhala), and the cart (anaḥ); and for many objects that are joined together, such as grain and garments.
The cleaning of wooden, horn, or bone [vessels], and of those made from fruit-shells, is by means of cow-hair;
the cleaning of sacrificial vessels during a ritual act is with the hand.
Woolen cloth and silk are purified by saline earth, water, and cow urine; likewise, fine cotton cloth is purified with bilva fruit, and woolen blankets from Kambhoja with ariṣṭa fruit.
Silk is purified by white mustard seeds, and earthenware by re-firing;
the hand of an artisan, food obtained as alms, and the mouth of a woman are likewise pure.
The purification of ground is achieved through sweeping, burning, the passage of time, and the treading of cows;
likewise, a house is purified by sprinkling, scraping, smearing, and by sweeping and plastering.
When food has been smelled by a cow, or likewise defiled by hair, flies, or insects,
water, ashes, or even earth should be thrown into it for the sake of purification.
Tin, lead, and copper are purified by alkaline substances, acids, water, and cow-urine;
bell-metal and iron are purified with ashes and water; and for liquids, purification consists of floating them [in water].
That which is smeared with impure substances is purified by earth and water through the removal of odor and the like;
that which is commended by word, washed with water, and that which is unknown are always pure.
Water that is naturally pure, which has reached the earth and is sufficient to satisfy a cow, is clean;
likewise is meat that has been brought down by dogs, Caṇḍālas, carnivorous beasts, and the like.
A ray of light, fire, dust, shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth,
the wind, droplets, flies, a calf, and [the sun] at dawn are pure to the touch.
The mouth of a goat and a horse is pure, but not that of a cow; nor are impurities originating from humans [pure].
And roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.

Droplets from the mouth are pure, as are the drops from sipping water; likewise, the beard and what is stuck between the teeth are pure once they have been removed from the mouth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.195)
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and having put on a different garment, one who has already sipped water should sip water again.
Roads, mud, and water touched by outcastes, dogs,
or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built with baked bricks.
Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas,
for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of Dharma.
Brahmins who are devoted to learning and study are the source of all;
among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and even more excellent than they are those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self.
Neither by learning alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient;
rather, that person in whom both of these, as well as good conduct, reside is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given by a wise man desiring his own welfare to an unworthy recipient.
A gift should not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
for by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward.
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on specific occasions;
even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith.
A milch cow with horns tipped in gold and hooves in silver, well-tempered, provided with a cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee, should be given away.
The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is tawny (kapilā), she delivers his lineage even unto the seventh generation.
The giver of a cow with a calf that has hair equal in number to the years of both ends [of the Manvantara],
giving her according to the previously mentioned rite, attains heaven.
As long as both the feet and the face of the calf are visible within the womb,
for that long the cow should be considered as the entire earth, until she releases the fetus.
By giving a cow, whether it be a milch-cow or even one that is not, in whatever manner possible—
provided it is healthy and free from affliction— the donor is glorified in heaven.
Massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshipping the gods,
washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away their remnants are equal to the gift of a cow.
By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a house, gold, and draft animals, one is glorified in heaven. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.210)
By giving a house, grain, protection from fear, shoes, an umbrella, garlands, ointments, a vehicle, a tree, a favorite object, or a bed, one becomes exceedingly happy.
Since Brahman, which consists of all dharmas, is superior to all gifts,
one who gives it attains the imperishable world of Brahman.
Even though he is capable of receiving gifts, he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds that belong to those whose nature is to give.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, fragrant substances, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these should not be refused.
Food brought unsolicited may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds,
except in the case of unchaste women, eunuchs, outcasts, and enemies.
For the sake of honoring gods and guests, for the sake of his teacher and dependents, or indeed for his own subsistence, he may accept gifts from anyone at all. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.216)
The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, a time of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices,
the availability of materials, the presence of worthy Brahmins, the equinox, and the sun's transit.
Vyatīpāta, gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and one’s own inclination toward performing a śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the proper times for a śrāddha.

One who is foremost among all the Vedas, a learned scholar of the Veda (*śrotriya*), a knower of Brahman, and young; one who knows the meaning of the Veda, a master of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, and one who knows the *Trimadhu* and *Tri-suparṇa* hymns.

A sister’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, one who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.220–221a.

Those who are devoted to ritual action, those devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five sacred fires, those who are lifelong students, and those who are dedicated to their fathers and mothers— these are the Brahmins who constitute the perfection of a Śrāddha.

One who is diseased, one with missing or redundant limbs, one who is blind in one eye, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken the vow of chastity, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* sons, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth.

One who teaches for a fee, a eunuch, one who defiles a maiden, one accused of a grave crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.223.

One who abandons his mother, father, or guru; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala* (a Śūdra woman); the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.
On the day before [the ceremony], the self-possessed and pure host should invite the Brāhmaṇas;
they too must remain restrained in their actions of mind, speech, and body.
In the afternoon, having honored those who have arrived with a welcome, he—
holding purifying grass in his hand and after they have sipped water— should cause them to sit upon their seats.
One should invite an even number of guests for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors;
this should be done in a purified place that is well-spread out and sloping toward the south.
Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each;
the same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common offering.
Having given water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for seats, he should,
being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O All-Gods" (*viśve devāsaḥ*).
Then, having scattered barley grains into a vessel provided with a strainer,
he pours water while reciting "śam no devīr" and likewise barley grains while reciting "yavo 'si."
With the mantra "yā divyā," he should pour the *arghya* water into their hands;
having given water, fragrance, garlands, incense, and a lamp,
as well as a gift of clothing and water for the purpose of washing the hands.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should perform the circumambulation of the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grass blades while reciting the verse "oṣaṃs tvā" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.233ab), he should invoke the ancestors;
then, permitted by them, he should mutter the verse "āyantu naḥ" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.233cd).

Having scattered sesame seeds all around with the mantra "apahatāḥ" (they are struck away), one should perform the rites for which barley is intended using sesame seeds; one should offer the *arghya* and other offerings as before.
Having offered the *arghya* water for them and having placed the remaining drops into a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down with the formula, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors."

Intending to offer [the oblation] into the fire, he takes up food soaked in clarified butter and asks, "Shall I sacrifice? Having been authorized with the reply, "Do so," he offers it into the fire as in the Pitṛyajña.
With a concentrated mind, he should offer the remains of the oblation into vessels as they are available,
especially those made of silver.

Having offered the food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra "The earth is the vessel" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.238a). Then, having recited "Idam Viṣṇuḥ" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.238c), one should cause the thumb of the twice-born guest to enter the food.
