Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyāhṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," they should eat while remaining silent, provided that [the recitation] has been performed comfortably.
One should give food that is desirable and fit for oblation, free from anger and without haste;
one should continue until satisfied, reciting purifying mantras as well as the previously mentioned prayers.
Having taken food [and asked], "Are you satisfied? and having obtained permission regarding the remainder, one should scatter that food on the ground and offer water once for each [guest].
Having taken all the food together with sesame seeds, facing the south,
he should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
In the same manner, one should likewise offer water for sipping to the maternal grandfathers;
thereafter, one should cause the benediction "svasti" to be recited and also offer the water for imperishability (*akṣayya-udaka*).
Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being authorized with the words "Let it be spoken," he should say to those present, "Let the *svadhā* be uttered."
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," one should then pour water on the ground;
and when the *Viśvedevas* have been gratified, one should mutter this [verse] as uttered by the Brahmins.
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having spoken these kind words and having prostrated,
he should dismiss them with the words "vāje vāje," while being pleased, performing the dismissal starting with the ancestors.
But that vessel for the ancestors into which the previous remnants had first been poured— having turned that ancestral vessel face upwards, one should dismiss the Brahmins.
Having circumambulated [the place] clockwise, he should eat what was consumed by the ancestors;
on that night, however, he should remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) together with the Brahmins.
Thus, performing the circumambulation in a clockwise direction, one should sacrifice to the Nāndīmukha ancestors on the occasion of prosperity;
the offerings should consist of balls of food mixed with curd and jujube fruits, performed with barley.

The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of offerings to the gods; it has a single *arghya* offering and a single *pavitraka*; indeed, it is performed without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa*, and with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
At the dismissal of the Brahmins, in place of the word "akṣayya" (imperishable), he should say, "May [the ancestors] be gratified";
they should then reply, "We are gratified."
One should prepare four vessels containing fragrant water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
One should perform the remainder as before with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ";
this is the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, which for a woman is performed as a single-recipient offering (eka-uddiṣṭa).
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has taken place before the completion of a year,
one should provide food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year.
On the anniversary of the day of death, the rite should be performed every month for a year;
likewise, the annual rite is to be performed, with the first one taking place on the eleventh day.
One should give the rice-balls to a cow, a goat, or a Brahmin, or else cast them into fire or water;
provided that Brahmins are present, one should not wipe away the remnants of the twice-born.
One may indeed [satisfy the ancestors] for a month with sacrificial food (haviṣya), but for a year with milk-rice (pāyasa);
likewise with the meat of fish, deer, wild boar, birds, goat, or spotted deer.
By offering the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively,
the ancestors are satisfied for increasing periods of one month each in this world.
The meat of the rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, honey, or the food of ascetics;
the meat of the iron-eater (iron-ore), large-leaved vegetables, and the flesh of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane.
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
A maiden, those who recognize maidens, cattle, and even virtuous sons;
gambling, agriculture, trade, as well as animals with cloven and uncloven hooves.
One who always performs the Śrāddha obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desires. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.263)
On the days beginning with the first lunar day, excluding the fourteenth,
that [offering] is given there for those who have been slain by weapons.
For one obtains heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength,
as well as a preeminent son, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, and auspiciousness.
He attains the status of one whose wheel of sovereignty rolls unimpeded, as well as success in trade and other such pursuits;
he gains freedom from disease, renown, freedom from sorrow, and the highest goal.
He who duly bestows wealth, the Vedas, medical success, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life at a Śrāddha;
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, one who is an adherent of the doctrine of the afterlife, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires.
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the Śrāddha;
when satisfied by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
The ancestors, when pleased, bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.270)
Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā for the purpose of obstructing the accomplishment of actions and for the lordship over the Gaṇas.
Learn now the characteristics of one who is possessed by that [demon]:
in his dreams he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men.
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he stands together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels in one place.
Even while walking, he perceives himself as being followed by others;
dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he desponds without any apparent cause.
Afflicted by that [demon], a prince does not obtain a kingdom;
a maiden does not find a husband; and a woman does not conceive offspring or a fetus.

The teacher does not obtain the status of a teacher, nor does the Vedic scholar obtain a student; likewise, the student does not obtain the study [of the Vedas]; the merchant does not obtain profit, and the farmer does not obtain the fruits of agriculture.
On an auspicious day, his ceremonial bath (snāna) should be performed according to the prescribed rules;
he should be anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.

Likewise, for one whose head has been anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, the auspicious twice-born ones should be requested to recite the benediction (*svasti*).
From a horse stable, an elephant stable, an anthill, a confluence,
and a lake, one should take earth, yellow pigment, fragrant substances, and bdellium, and cast them into the waters.
Then, water that has been drawn from a lake by four persons of the same caste in four jars should be placed upon a red bull-hide, and thereupon the auspicious seat (bhadra-āsana) is to be set.
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, purified by the seers—by that I sprinkle you; may the *pāvamānī* verses purify you.
"May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune; and may the seven Ṛṣis grant you fortune."
Whatever ill fortune is in your hair, whatever is in your parting, and whatever is in your head; whatever is in your forehead, your ears, and your eyes—may the waters destroy that forever.
Having bathed, he should offer mustard oil from a ladle made of Udumbara wood into his own head,
while grasping Kuśa grass with his left hand.
*Mita* and *sammita*, as well as *śāla* and *kaṭaṅkaṭa*,
*kūśmāṇḍa* and *rājaputra*— at the end [of these names], they are accompanied by the word *svāhā*.

Having spread *kuśa* grass on all sides upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, he should offer [the oblation] with their names and with *bali*-mantras accompanied by the word "namas," using both husked and unhusked rice grains as well as rice mixed with sesame paste.
Likewise, cooked fish and raw fish are considered meat; the measure is exactly this much.
Variegated and fragrant flowers, the three kinds of liquor, radishes, *pūrikā* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, and likewise garlands of *uṇḍeraka* flowers.
Having collected all these— curd, rice, milk-rice, flour mixed with jaggery, and sweetmeats— and having placed them on the ground, he should then place his head [there].
Then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka, by offering a full añjali of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers as an arghya oblation, [reciting]:
"Grant me beauty; grant me fame; grant me fortune, O Bhavānī."
"Give me sons, give me wealth, and grant me all my desires."
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
he should feed the Brāhmaṇas and also give a pair of garments to his Guru.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By always performing worship of Āditya, as well as the *tilaka* of the Lord (Śiva),
and likewise that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain success.
One who desires prosperity, one who desires peace, one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, or likewise one performing malevolent rites, should perform the sacrifice to the planets.
The Sun, the Moon, the Son of the Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), Śanaiścara (Saturn), Rāhu, and Ketu— these are remembered as the planets.
The planetary images should be made, respectively, from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead,
and bell-metal.
Or they may be drawn by members of their own respective castes on a cloth, or with fragrant pastes in mandalas;
likewise, garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors.
Fragrances, offerings, and incense—specifically guggulu—should be presented; and oblations accompanied by mantras must be performed for each respective deity.
The verses "ākṛṣṇena," "imam devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed to be used in their respective order.
"O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the noble ones, likewise from the flowing liquor;
'May the goddesses be auspicious to us,' likewise from the stalk; 'making this our banner' likewise."
The *arka*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, and *pippala*;
the *udumbara*, *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and *kuśa* grasses are the sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) in their respective order.
For each [deity], however, one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations should be offered,
mixed with honey and clarified butter, or with curd and milk.
Jaggery with rice, milk-rice, sacrificial food consisting of *ṣaṣṭika* rice cooked in milk,
rice with curd, sacrificial flour-cake, meat, and various kinds of fine food.
The wise man should thus provide food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets,
according to his capacity or as it may be obtained, having honored them with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rules.
A milch cow, a conch shell, likewise a bull, gold, a garment, a horse in sequence;
a black cow, iron, and a goat—these indeed are recorded as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Whoever is in distress at any time should honor that person with effort;
for Brahmā has granted them this boon: "When you are honored, you shall honor [others] in return."
The rises and falls of lords of men depend upon the planets; likewise, the existence and non-existence of the world depend on them. Therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
[1.308Aa] One should offer this hospitality to the planets even after a year;
[1.308Ac] endowed with health and strength, he shall live for a hundred autumns. [13.
Section on the Duties of Kings] (p. 107)
One who possesses great energy, is liberal in giving, grateful, a servant of the elderly,
humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure.
One who is not prolix in his deliberations, possessed of memory, not mean-spirited, nor harsh, likewise righteous,
free from vices, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.

The lord of men should be trained in the protection of his own vulnerabilities, as well as in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) and the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise in the science of livelihood (vārtā) and the triple Veda (trayī).
He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure; with them, and then with a Brahmin, he should deliberate upon the affairs of the kingdom, and thereafter he himself.
He should appoint as his domestic priest one who is well-born on both sides, skilled in astrology,
proficient in the science of statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*), and likewise versed in the *Atharvāṅgiras* [mantras].
For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, he should indeed choose officiating priests (ṛtvij),
and he should also perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should give enjoyments and various kinds of wealth to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings.
O Brahmin, that which is offered into the fire by means of the sacred fires— being unspilled, undisturbed, and untainted by expiatory rites— is declared here to be the most excellent.
What has not been acquired should be sought through righteous means; what has been acquired should be protected with effort;
what has been protected should be increased through prudent policy; and what has been increased should be bestowed upon worthy recipients.
Having granted land or having established a permanent endowment (*nibandha*),
the king should cause a written deed to be executed for the information of future benevolent rulers.
Having inscribed upon a cloth or a copper plate his own lineage and himself, marked with his own seal, the lord of the earth [should grant it].
He should cause a durable edict to be made, which includes the measurement of the land received, a description of the boundaries of the gift,
and is completed with his own hand and the date.

He should settle in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, productive, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the protection of his people, his treasury, and himself.
In each of those matters, he should appoint supervisors who are proficient, skillful, pure,
and diligent in the affairs of income, production, and expenditure.
There is no higher duty for kings than this:
that wealth acquired in battle is always given to the Brahmins and security is granted to the subjects.
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land,
without turning their backs and with weapons not used deceitfully, go to heaven like yogins.

The king takes away the merit of those who do not retreat when their ranks are broken, as well as that of those who are slain while fleeing from the battle. These steps [of the army] are equal to sacrificial rites.
One should not kill one who says "I am yours," a eunuch, one who is unarmed, one who has surrendered to another, one who has desisted from combat, or one who is watching the battle as a spectator.
Having ensured protection, he should rise and personally inspect his income and expenditures;
then, having attended to legal affairs and bathed, he may eat according to his desire.
He should deposit gold brought by messengers in the treasuries;
then, having consulted with his ministers, he should inspect the spies and dispatch envoys.
Thereafter, he may move about at his own pleasure, or remain in the company of his ministers;
having inspected the troops, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he should enjoy himself with songs and dances, and likewise recite his private Vedic study.
One should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise wake up with that same sound;
one should reflect upon the scriptures with the intellect, as well as upon all duties to be performed.
Then, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and others;
and he should be greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers.
Having seen [the results], he should give cows, gold, and land to those who know the celestial bodies and to physicians;
furthermore, he should give houses and dwellings to those learned in the Vedas.
Toward Brahmins he should be patient; toward his affectionate kin, straightforward; toward his enemies, wrathful;
and toward his circle of servants and subjects, he should be like a father.
By protecting [his subjects] according to the law, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for the protection of his subjects is superior to all other forms of giving.
He shall protect the subjects who are being oppressed by rogues, thieves, evildoers, perpetrators of great violence, and the like— and especially by scribes.
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not being protected,
half of that belongs to the king, because he receives taxes from them.
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed over the kingdom,
the king should honor the virtuous and put to death those who are the opposite.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
he should always cause those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) to dwell [in his realm], providing them with constant gifts, honors, and hospitality.
That king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means shall, before long, lose his royal fortune and perish along with his kinsmen.
The fire produced from the suffering and distress of the subjects does not cease until it has consumed the king’s lineage, his fortune, and his very life.
Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,
that very same dharma he obtains in its entirety when bringing another's kingdom under his control.
In whatever country a particular custom, legal practice, or family tradition exists,
that very same one must be maintained when it has come under one's control.
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, he should therefore keep his counsel well-guarded,
so that others do not know it until the results of his actions have come to fruition.
The enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, and the one beyond him—
this circle [of kings] should be considered in due order through the employment of conciliation and other strategic means.
The means are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise force;
when properly employed, these may succeed, but force is the last resort when no other way remains.
He should properly determine these strategic qualities: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and the double policy.
When the enemy kingdom is endowed with the excellence of crops, then he should march;
provided that the enemy is weakened while his own army and men are joyful and well-supplied with mounts.
The accomplishment of action is established in both destiny and human effort;
therein, destiny is manifested as the human effort performed in a previous body.

Some wise thinkers maintain that the fruit [of action] arises from destiny, others from inherent nature, some from time, and others from human effort, while still others hold it to arise from a combination of these.
For just as a chariot cannot move with only a single wheel,
so too destiny does not succeed without human effort.
Since the acquisition of friends is superior to the acquisition of gold and land,
one should therefore strive to obtain them, remaining composed and guarding one's truthfulness.
The sovereign, the ministers, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Having obtained that [kingly power], the king should inflict punishment upon those of evil conduct;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times.
He cannot be led away by right means by one who is greedy, of unrefined intellect, lacking in truthfulness, impure, or devoid of good companions, even if he be wise.
When employed according to the scriptures, it shall gladden the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it would provoke its wrath.
Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
but for a king, proper punishment brings about heaven, fame, and victory.
Even a brother, a son, a worthy guest, a father-in-law, or a maternal uncle— there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king.
That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and duly executes those deserving of death has performed sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial fees.
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine lawsuits day by day, each yielding fruit equal to that of a sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.360)
The king, having disciplined those who have strayed from their own duties— whether they be families, castes, guilds, or even local assemblies— should establish them on the right path.
A particle of dust moving in a sunbeam through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three *gaura* make one *yava*; three of those middle-sized *yavas* make one *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.
Four or even five suvarṇas are proclaimed to be one pala;
two kṛṣṇalas make a silver māṣa, and sixteen of those make a dharaṇa.
Ten *dharaṇas* make one *śatamāna*, and ten [of those] make one *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *niṣka*; a copper coin weighing one *kārṣika* is called a *paṇa*.
A fine of eighty thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa);
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that is recorded as the lowest.
The punishment of reproach, the punishment of speech, the punishment of fine, and likewise the punishment of death—
these should be applied either individually or collectively, according to the nature of the offense.
Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength, as well as the age,
the action, and the wealth, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
[End of the Chapter on Conduct]
[II. Chapter on Legal Procedure] [1.
Section on the General Matrix of Legal Procedure] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.1a: The king shall examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
In accordance with the treatises on Dharma, he should be free from anger and greed.
The king should appoint members of the court who are accomplished in sacred learning and study, who know the dharma, who speak the truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend.
But when, due to the demands of business, the king is unable to oversee legal proceedings himself,
he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws to act together with the members of the court.
Those members of the court who act contrary to the legal codes out of passion, greed, or fear shall each be punished with a fine double that of the amount in dispute.
When one, having been oppressed by others through a path deviating from the Smṛtis and established custom,
makes a complaint to the king, that indeed constitutes a ground for legal action.
In the presence of the defendant, the plaintiff shall cause a document to be written down exactly as it was stated,
marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other identifying characteristics.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.7: The defendant shall provide an answer in the presence of the plaintiff who has stated his case;
thereafter, the plaintiff shall immediately cause to be written the proof for the matter he has asserted.
When that is established, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
This four-footed judicial procedure has been demonstrated in legal disputes.
[2. Chapter on the Special Categories of Legal Procedure] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.9: Without having fully resolved the initial charge, one should not bring a counter-charge against the opponent;
nor should one, by means of another matter, cause a person already charged to deviate from what has been stated.
In cases of assault and acts of violence, one may bring a counter-charge;
in such instances, a surety capable of resolving the matter must be accepted from both parties.
If he denies it and is subsequently proven guilty, he shall pay the debt to the king and an equal amount as a fine;
one who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim.

In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations regarding a cow, or the violation of a woman, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately; in other matters, the time for litigation is said to depend on the will of the parties.
He moves from one place to another,
licks the corners of his mouth, his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale.

When his speech becomes parched and faltering, when he speaks much that is contradictory, when he does not honor [the witness] with his voice or eyes, and when he also distorts his lips; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.14.
He who undergoes a change from his natural state through the actions of mind, speech, or body—
whether in a formal accusation or in giving testimony— is proclaimed to be corrupt.
He who, being independent, attempts to prove a doubtful matter; he who departs [from court];
and he who, though summoned, says nothing—all such a person is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment.
When there are witnesses for both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff;
when the plaintiff's case has been refuted, they belong to the defendant.
If a dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the defeated party to pay the fine,
his own wager, and the debt itself to the creditor.
Having set aside frivolous pleas, the king should conduct legal proceedings on the basis of the truth;
for even the truth, if not presented, is lost in a lawsuit.

If a defendant denies a written document but is proven in even one part of it, he must be made by the king to pay the entire amount; however, that which was not previously declared shall not be accepted [as evidence].
When there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, however, reason prevails in legal proceedings;
it is established that the Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative than the Arthaśāstra.
It is declared that documentary evidence, possession, and witnesses are the means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
In all disputes regarding property, the subsequent legal action is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior action is more powerful.
Loss of land occurs after twenty years for one who sees it being enjoyed by another but does not speak out; loss of wealth occurs after ten years.
Except for property consisting of pledges, boundary marks, deposits, and the wealth of the mentally incapacitated or minors;
likewise, except for the property of sealed deposits, the king, women, and Vedic scholars.
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates deposits and other such items to pay the debt to the creditor,
and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity.
Title-deed is superior to possession, except in the case of possession inherited through prior succession;
even a title-deed has no force at all where there is not even a slight amount of possession.
But he by whom the title-deed was executed shall, when sued, produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more weighty.
If one who has been accused is proven to have come from another [source], his heir shall recover that property;
in such a case, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of legal title.
Those authorized by the king— whether guilds, corporations, or families—
each preceding one among them is to be understood as more authoritative than the following in legal proceedings concerning men.
One should set aside legal proceedings brought about by force or intimidation,
as well as those conducted by women, at night, inside a house, outside, or by enemies.
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified,
as well as one conducted by an incompetent person, is not valid.
Lost property that has been found must be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by characteristic marks, he deserves a fine equal to its value.
Upon finding a treasure-trove, the king shall give half to the twice-born;
however, a learned twice-born man may take the whole, since he is the master of all.
When a treasure is found by someone other than the rightful owner, the king shall take a sixth part;
however, if it is discovered without having been reported, he shall be made to pay that [sixth part] as well as a fine.
Property stolen by thieves must be restored by the king to the subject;
for if he does not restore it, he incurs the guilt of the one to whom it belongs.
[3. Chapter on the Taking of Loans] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.37: With a pledge, the interest shall be one-eightieth part each month;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred.
Those traveling through wildernesses shall pay ten percent, those traveling by sea twenty percent, or one hundred percent;
or they may all pay interest as agreed upon by themselves, regardless of their respective castes.
The maximum interest on livestock and female animals is eightfold; on liquids, it is eightfold; and on clothes, grain, and gold, it is fourfold, threefold, and twofold respectively.
One who, having approached [the court], pursues his claim should not be censured by the king.
But one who, while his case is being adjudicated, goes to the king [himself] shall be punished and made to pay that debt.
A debtor to creditors shall be made to pay according to the order in which the claims were received; however, after that, he must first pay the king and then to a Brāhmaṇa.
The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount recovered;
and the creditor who has obtained his due shall be made to pay five percent.
One may compel a man of low caste who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income.
If one does not accept one's own wealth when it is being offered, having been lent out,
once it has been deposited with a neutral third party, it shall not increase beyond that point.
If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided,
the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad.
A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, his son, or by his son;
likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, except when it was contracted for the sake of the family.

A son shall not pay, on behalf of his father, debts incurred through drinking liquor, gambling, or dicing; nor the remainder of fines or customs duties; nor gifts made for no purpose; nor such debts as are not ancestral.
The husband shall pay the debt of the wives of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, and hunters,
because their livelihood depends upon him.
A woman shall pay a debt that was contracted by her with her husband's consent, or one that she herself incurred; she is not otherwise liable to pay any other debt.
When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; however, if it is denied, it is established by witnesses.

The inheritor of the estate shall be made to pay the debt, as shall the one who takes the wife; likewise, the son whose property has not been alienated to others shall pay for his father who leaves no heir.
Furthermore, among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son,
suretyship, debt, and witness testimony are traditionally held not to apply when they have not yet divided their inheritance.
Suretyship (*prātibhāvya*) is prescribed for the purpose of appearance, for confidence, and for payment.
However, if the first two [types] fail, the debt must be paid; in the case of the other, even the sons are liable.

Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, they must pay if they were established for the purpose of giving.
If there are many sureties who pay the debt with their own shares,
they should do so among those who have relied on a single liability, according to the creditor's preference.
But whatever wealth a surety is compelled to pay publicly to the creditor,
that shall be doubled and must be repaid by the debtors to him.
Interest on female slaves and cattle is simply the offspring; on grain, it is threefold;
clothing is declared to be fourfold, and liquids likewise eightfold.
A pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, provided it is not redeemed;
a pledge for use is forfeited at the appointed time, but one that yields fruit is never forfeited.
In the case of using a pledge that was meant only for custody, there is no interest; likewise if it is damaged or lost.
It must be restored if it is destroyed or ruined, except when the loss is caused by fate or the king.
The validity of a pledge is established through its acceptance; even if it is being protected, it may reach a state of worthlessness.
If that occurs, another pledge must be provided, or the creditor shall become a sharer in the debtor's wealth.
He shall cause [the debtor] to pay the money with interest for that which was made by means of a pledge based on good conduct (*caritra-bandhaka*);
he shall cause the value of the object made by way of a true-bond (*satyaṃkāra*) to be paid back as double.
When the debtor has arrived [to redeem it], the pledge must be released; otherwise, he would become a thief.
If the creditor is absent, he may obtain the pledge after depositing the money with a local family.
Or, having been valued at the time [of the loan], it may remain there without interest;
or, even without the presence of the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses.

But when the debt has become doubled on the pledge, then indeed the pledge must be released once the money derived from it has entered into the creditor's possession and reached the amount of double the original debt.
(Chapter 4: On Deposits)

When an object placed in a container is handed over into the hand of another without being described, that object is termed *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit); it must be returned in exactly the same condition.
He shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves;
however, if it is not recovered despite being sought, he shall be made to pay the value and a fine equal to that amount.
If one makes a living by his own will [using another's property], he shall be punished and made to pay that [property] along with its interest.
This same rule applies to items borrowed, entrusted for delivery, deposits, and pledges.
[Chapter 5: On Witnesses]
Those who practice austerity, are disposed toward giving, are of noble birth, speak the truth,
are devoted to dharma, are upright, have sons, and are endowed with wealth.

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; they are traditionally held to be either of the same caste and class as the litigants, or all may serve for all.
Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, those accused of crimes, performers on stage, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired senses; (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.70).
An outcaste, a relative, one interested in the matter, a partisan, an enemy, a thief,
one who commits violence, and one whose fault has been observed— these, beginning with the "expelled," are not to be admitted as witnesses.
Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is approved by both parties.
In cases of adultery, theft, verbal abuse, and violence, everyone may be a witness.
He should cause the witnesses to hear [the following] in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant:
"Those worlds which are for those who commit minor sins, as well as for those who commit great sins;
those worlds which belong to arsonists, and those which belong to the slayers of women and children."
He who gives false testimony incurs all of those [sins].
Whatever merit has been performed by you throughout hundreds of previous births,
know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood.
For if men fail to give testimony, the king shall cause them to pay the debt along with a fine of ten percent on the forty-sixth day.
For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the facts],
he is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment.
In a conflict between two witnesses, the testimony of the majority prevails; likewise, when the numbers are equal, the testimony of those possessing superior qualities prevails.
But when there is a conflict even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who possess the highest degree of excellence should be accepted.
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
he who asserts otherwise is certainly defeated.
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if other witnesses who are more virtuous,
or twice as numerous, should state otherwise, the former witnesses are considered perjured.
The forger and the false witnesses shall each be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, while a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished.
He who, having been made to hear the testimony by others, denies it, being enveloped by darkness—him he shall cause to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, he shall banish.
In cases where the death of members of the [four] castes would otherwise occur, one may speak untruth as a witness;
to purify oneself from that sin, the twice-born should offer a *sārasvata* oblation of boiled rice (*caru*).
(Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.83) [Section on Written Documents] (pp. 190–191)
Whatever matter has been settled between two parties by their own mutual consent,
a written document should be executed for that purpose, provided it contains witnesses and begins with the name of the creditor.

[The name] should be marked by the year, month, half-month, day, [the mother's] name, caste, one's own *gotra*, the status of being a student (*brahmacārin*), one's own name, and the names of one's father and so forth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.85)
When the matter is concluded, the debtor should write with his own hand:
"What is written above is my assent, [the signature] of the son of so-and-so."
The witnesses, moreover, should write with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers, as follows: "I, so-and-so, am a witness here"—thus they should all write. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.87)
"Requested by both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so, by such-and-such a person"—
thus the scribe should write at the end.
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is declared to be valid evidence, provided it was not executed through force or fraud.
A debt contracted by means of a written document is to be paid by only three generations of persons;
however, a pledge is enjoyed only so long as that debt has not been repaid.
If a document is located in another country, is illegible, lost, erased, stolen,
broken, burnt, or torn, one should have another document executed.
The purification of a doubtful document may be established by means of a signature in one's own hand and so forth,
as well as by reason, probability, performance, marks, connection, and title.
The debtor, having paid the money, should write on the back of the document;
or the creditor, upon receiving it, should provide a receipt marked with his own hand.

Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or else have another document executed for the sake of clearing the obligation; or whatever debt was recorded with witnesses must be paid in the presence of witnesses. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.94) [7.
Section on Ordeals]
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the ordeal by sacred libation—these are the divine ordeals for the purpose of purification in this world;
they are employed in cases of grave accusation when the accuser is prepared to undergo the penalty himself.
Or, by mutual consent, one may act as the debtor and the other as the creditor;
even without a formal promissory note, one may do so in cases of treason against the king or for a mortal sin.
Having summoned him who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on,
the king should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of Brahmins.
The balance is for women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick;
fire or water is for the Śūdra, or seven barley-grains for the ordeal by poison.
One should not employ a plowshare, nor poison, nor a scale for less than a thousand [paṇas].

In matters concerning the king and in cases of formal accusation, these should always be used by those who are pure. One who is accused should resort to the scale, held by experts in the art of weighing.
Having become level with the counterweight, it was lowered after a mark had been made.
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the balance.
Having observed that the two hands have crushed grains of rice,
one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread.
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
O Sage, like a witness, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins.
When he has spoken thus, [the judge] shall place a smooth iron ball, weighing fifty palas and glowing with fire, upon both of his hands.
Taking that [fire], he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles;
each circle should be known to be sixteen finger-breadths in diameter, with an equal interval between them.
Having released the fire, one whose rice-grains have been crushed but not burnt shall attain purification.
If the ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, he should take it up again.
Having sworn an oath over water, saying, "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth," [he should drink].
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should enter the water after grasping the thighs.

If another swift man, having brought back an arrow shot simultaneously [with the defendant], should see the defendant with his limbs submerged when that [arrow] has passed, he shall attain purification. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.109) "O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and dharma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.110)
"Protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me."
Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison produced from the snowy mountains;
if it is digested without its characteristic effects manifesting, one should declare that person to be pure.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take the water from their ablution;
having poured it out, one should then cause [the person] to drink three handfuls of that water.
If a terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate occurs for anyone within fourteen days [of the ordeal], he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.113)

[8. Chapter on the Division of Inheritance] (p.216) Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114: If the father should make a division, he may divide the sons according to his will; or he may give the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. (p.220) Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114c: Or all may be equal sharers.

If [the father] should make equal shares, the wives must be made sharers equally, provided that no woman's property has been given to them by her husband or by her father-in-law. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.115)
If one who is capable does not exert himself, a separate partition may be made after giving him something;
for those whose shares were divided unequally, the partition made by the father is declared to be lawful.
After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.

The daughters shall take the remainder of the mother's estate after the debts; in their absence, the lineage [inherits]. Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal property [is one's own].
That which is given out of friendship or for the sake of marriage shall not belong to the heirs.
If one recovers property that had been stolen but which has come into his possession by succession, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what is obtained through learning.
When property is acquired for the common benefit, the division is ordained to be equal;
however, for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is determined according to the fathers.
Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, or a leasehold, or even property itself—
in those cases, the ownership of the father and the son is indeed equal.
A son born after the partition of the estate from a wife of the same caste is entitled to a share;
or rather, his share shall be determined from the visible assets, after deducting the income and expenses.
Whatever has been given by both parents belongs to that [child] alone;
when the sons divide the inheritance after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share.
But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own share.
The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, shall receive four, three, two, and one shares;
those born of a Kṣatriya shall receive three, two, and one shares; but those born of a Vaiśya shall receive two and one shares.
If any property that was mutually misappropriated is discovered after the partition has been made, they shall divide it again in equal shares; such is the settled rule.
A son begotten by means of *niyoga* upon the wife of another by a man who has no son is,
according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both [the biological father and the husband].

The legitimate son (aurasa) is born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-suta). The son of the field (kṣetraja), however, is one begotten upon the wife by a man of the same lineage or another.
A son born secretly in the house is known as a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born);
one born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather.
A son born to a woman who has been previously married—whether she was a virgin or not—is a *paunarbhava* son;
he whom the mother or the father gives away becomes an adopted (*dattaka*) son.
One who is purchased from those two is a "purchased" son; one who is made by himself is an "artificial" son (kṛtrima).
One who gives himself away is a "self-given" son; one conceived in the womb and brought forth together with the bride is a "son born of a remarried woman" (sahoḍha).
He who is taken up after having been abandoned is an *apaviddha* son;
among these [types of sons], each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of each preceding one.

I have declared this rule regarding sons of the same caste; however, even one born of a Śūdra woman through a Śūdra by his own desire shall be a sharer of the inheritance. When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share.
A man who has no brothers shall take the entire inheritance, except for the son of a daughter.
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, their sons, the agnates (gotrajas), the kinsmen, the disciples, and those who have lived as religious students (sabrahmacārins).
In the absence of these, each succeeding one among them becomes the heir to the wealth of the deceased.
For this rule applies to all castes in the case of one who has died without a son.

The heirs of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and students (*brahmacārin*) are, in order: the teacher (*ācārya*), the virtuous pupil (*sat-śiṣya*), the spiritual brother (*dharma-bhrātṛ*), and those who share the same sacred ford (*eka-tīrthin*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.137)

But a reunited coparcener shall take the share of a reunited coparcener, and a uterine brother that of a uterine brother; he shall give and receive the share for one who is born and for one who has died.
But a son born of a different womb who is reunited with the estate shall take the wealth, not one who is not reunited;
even one who is not reunited may take it, but one who is reunited and born of a different mother shall not.

A eunuch, one who has fallen from caste, his offspring, a cripple, one who is insane, one who is mentally dull, and one who is blind— these, as well as those afflicted by incurable diseases and the like, should be maintained [by the family], but they shall receive no share of the inheritance.
Among these, the legitimate sons (*aurasa*) and those born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), being free from defects, are entitled to inherit their shares;
and their daughters must be maintained until they are provided with husbands.
The childless wives of these [deceased brothers] who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
likewise, those who are unchaste or hostile may be banished.
That which is given by the father, the mother, the husband, or a brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire;
and that which is given on account of supersession—these are declared to be the woman’s property.
Likewise, property given by a relative, a nuptial gift (śulka), and even a subsequent gift (anvādheya)—
if she dies without offspring, her kinsmen shall obtain that.
The property of a woman who dies without offspring belongs to her husband even in the case of the four [marriages] beginning with the Brāhma;
however, among the remaining [marriages], if she has borne children, it goes to her daughters, and in the absence of daughters, it goes to her father.
Having given away a girl, one who takes her back shall be fined and shall also pay the expenses along with interest.
If she has died, he may take back what was given after deducting both types of expenses.
In times of famine, for religious duties, during illness, or when there is imprisonment,
the husband is not required to return the woman's property that he has taken from her.

One should give an equal amount as an *ādhivedanika* fee to a wife who has been superseded by another; however, if no such property was previously given to her, one should provide half of that amount once it has been given.

In a dispute regarding the concealment of a partition, the determination of the partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, written records, and separate houses and fields. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.149) [9.
Section on Disputes Concerning Boundaries] (p. 255)
In a dispute concerning a boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders and others, the cowherds, the farmers who work the boundary, and all those who frequent the forest shall be witnesses.
They should establish the boundary, marked by mounds, charcoal, husks, and trees,
as well as by irrigation channels, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines, and the like.
Or four, eight, or even ten neighboring villagers from the same village,
wearing red garlands and garments, shall carry the boundary markers while supporting the earth.
But for false testimony, they shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement.
In the absence of cognizors and boundary marks, the king is the establisher of the boundary.
In the case of groves, temples, villages, water-stations, gardens, and houses, this same rule is to be understood as applicable; likewise in the case of rainwater, flowing streams, and the like.
In the case of breaking a boundary mark, likewise for crossing a boundary,
and for the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middle.
A dam that causes little harm but brings about beneficial results should not be prohibited.
A well that occupies another's land is permissible if it yields much water for one's own small field.
If one should construct an irrigation channel on a field without having informed the owner, the benefit of the produce belongs to the owner; in his absence, it belongs to the king.

If a person neither cultivates nor causes to be cultivated a field that has been struck by the plough, he shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation and have the field cultivated by another. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.158) [Section on Disputes between Owner and Herdsman] (p. 261)
A female buffalo that destroys crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow shall be fined half of that, and a goat or sheep half of that again.
If those who have eaten sit down [to sleep], the fine is double that which has been stated;
this same rule applies even in a pasture, as does the penalty for a female donkey, a camel, or a buffalo.
As long as the crop perishes, so long shall the fruit belong to the owner of the field;
the cowherd is to be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine.
There is no offense in a field located on a path or at the edge of a village pasture; however, if one acts intentionally, he deserves punishment like that of a thief.
Large bulls, animals let loose for sacrifice, those that have recently calved, those that are traveling, and so forth—
those for which there is no keeper are not to be claimed [as lost], even if they are overwhelmed by divine or royal power.
Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening,
so too a hired laborer must make good those that have died or been lost through negligence.
But when destruction occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, as well as the value of the property itself for the owner.
Cattle may graze according to the will of the village folk or by the authority of the king;
furthermore, a twice-born man may take grass, firewood, and flowers from anywhere at all times.
The distance between fields in a village should be one hundred bows in circumference;
for a market town it should be two hundred, and for a city four hundred. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.167) [Chapter 11: Sale Without Ownership] (p. 265)
One may recover one's own property sold by another; however, the purchaser is at fault if the sale was not publicly announced.
One who buys from a low person in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time, is a thief.
Having discovered what has been lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
and if there is a lapse in time or place, one should seize the person oneself and hand him over.
Purification [from the sin] comes from the production of the seller; the owner recovers the property, and the king receives a fine.
The buyer recovers the price from him who was the seller of that [stolen article].
A lost property may be recovered through legal title or through possession; otherwise, if it is not proven by the claimant, he shall pay a fine of five times its value to the king.
He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*.
If property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officials or guards of the station, the owner may take it back within one year; after that, the king shall take it.
For a single-hoofed animal, one should pay four *paṇas*; for a human, five;
for buffaloes, camels, and cattle, two each; and for goats and sheep, one-quarter each. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.174)

One's own property may be given away without detriment to one's family, except for one's wife and sons; nor may one's entire estate be given while there are descendants, nor that which has been promised to another.
The acceptance of a gift should be public, especially in the case of immovable property. What has been promised as a gift, once given, must not be taken back again. [13.
Section on Regret over Purchases]
The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men should take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, three months, three days, and half a month, respectively.
Gold is not diminished when melted in fire; silver [loses] two palas per hundred;
tin and lead [lose] eight [palas], and copper [loses] five, while iron [loses] ten.
For woolen, cotton, and silk threads, the interest on a hundred [karṣas] is ten palas;
for medium quality, the interest is five palas, while for fine quality, it is considered to be three palas.
In the case of manufactured cloth and woven woolen cloth, a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized;
however, there is neither loss nor increase in the case of silk and bark garments.

Having ascertained the place, the time, and the possession, as well as the strength and weakness in the case of a lost property, those who are experts shall declare what must be paid without doubt. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.181] [Chapter 14:
On Failure to Serve after Having Agreed]

One who has been made a slave by force, or even one sold by thieves, is released [from slavery] by saving his master's life, by abandoning his food, or by the payment of his ransom. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.182)

One who has abandoned the life of a wandering ascetic becomes a slave of the king until death. Slavery among the social classes occurs through the natural order (ānulomya), not against it (pratiloma).
Even one who has mastered his craft shall reside in the house of the teacher for the prescribed period as a resident pupil (*antevāsī*);
he shall receive his food from the teacher and deliver to him the fruits of his labor. [15.
Section on the Breach of Agreement]
Having established a residence in the city and appointed Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide those learned in the three Vedas with a livelihood and say: "Let your own dharma be protected."
But that which is established by convention (*samayika*) provided it does not conflict with one's own duty (*nijadharma*),
as well as that which is ordained by the king— both of these must be protected with effort.
But he who misappropriates the property of a corporation, or whoever violates an agreement,
the king shall confiscate all his possessions and banish him from the realm.
The command of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be obeyed by all;
whoever therein acts contrarily shall be fined the first amercement.

The lord of the earth, having honored them with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality, should dismiss those who have assembled for the business of the assembly once their task is accomplished. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.340)
One sent on a mission for the sake of a collective undertaking shall deliver whatever he may obtain;
if he does not deliver it himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value.
Those who know the Dharma, who are pure and free from greed, shall be the deliberators on affairs; their word, when they speak for the welfare of the community, must be carried out.
This same rule applies to guilds, merchants, heretics, and assemblies;
the king should protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional customs. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.192) [Section on the Payment of Wages] (p. 278)
A laborer who has received wages but abandons his work shall pay double;
if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount, and the tools must be protected by the employer.
But he who employs laborers without having fixed their wages shall be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle,
or crops.

If one should miss the proper place and time, or should effect a profit in a manner other than prescribed, in that case it shall be at the will of the owner; if more has been done, an additional amount should be paid.
Whatever amount of work one performs, that much shall be his wages.
If the task is impossible for both [master and laborer] to accomplish, it is so; but if it is possible, he shall perform it according to the agreement.
If goods are lost due to causes other than the king or an act of God, the carrier shall be made to pay for them;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages.
If he abandons a servant who has set out on a journey, he must pay him a seventh part of the wages;
if he abandons him on the way, a fourth part; and if he abandons him halfway, he must pay the full wages, as must the one who causes him to be abandoned.
(Chapter 17: On Gambling and Betting)
In a gambling match where the interest on the stake is one hundredfold,
the keeper of the gaming house shall take five percent from a dishonest gambler and ten percent from any other.
Having been properly protected, he shall give the king the share as previously determined.
He shall cause the winner to take possession of what was won and, being patient, shall give the truthful word to the victor.

When the king has received his established share and the circle of gamblers is well-known, he should cause the winner to pay the stake at a place where the assembly is present; otherwise, he should not do so.
For they alone are the observers of legal proceedings and the witnesses;
therefore, those who play with false dice or by deceitful means should be banished by the king along with their gaming equipment.
Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the purpose of identifying thieves; this same rule is to be understood as applicable to betting with living creatures and to challenging matches.
[18. Section on Verbal Abuse]
If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, senses, or afflicted by disease by means of praise that is true, false, or otherwise,
he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas.
If one swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king should compel that person to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas].
In cases of unrighteous acts, the fine shall be half; it shall be double for women of other men and for those of the highest castes.
Punishment must be administered according to the relative superiority or inferiority of the social class and birth.
In cases of defamation involving the inverse order of castes, the fines shall be double and triple respectively;
for the castes in the natural order, they shall be reduced by half and half again from that amount.
In cases of verbal threats regarding the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine shall be one hundred [paṇas];
for those regarding the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it shall be half of that.
But one who is unable [to provide security] and speaks thus shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
Likewise, one who is able shall be made to provide a surety for his safety.
For an insult involving a crime causing loss of caste, the punishment is the middle amercement;
but for one involving a minor offense, he should be made to pay the first amercement.

Insulting those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity is the highest amercement; insulting a caste or a guild is the middle amercement; and insulting a village or a district is the first amercement. (Chapter 19: On Assault)
In a case where a killing has occurred without witnesses, the legal proceeding must be examined through physical marks, circumstantial reasoning, and documentary evidence,
for there may be a danger of false marks being fabricated out of fear.
A fine of ten paṇas is prescribed for touching ashes, mud, or dust;
for touching impure matter, the heel, or spittle, the fine is double that amount.
In the case of women of equal status, the punishment is the same; against those of higher status, it is double;
against those of lower status, it is half the penalty. However, there is no punishment for acts committed through delusion, intoxication, and the like.
But in the case of a non-Brāhmaṇa, a limb that causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa shall be cut off;
however, if he merely raises his hand, the first amercement is the punishment, and if he actually touches him, half of that.
If one merely brandishes a hand or a foot, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively;
however, if all of them use a weapon against one another, the middle amercement shall apply.
For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing the hands, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for causing pain, tearing the garment, wrapping the feet, or stepping upon them, the fine is one hundred.
A man who causes pain with wood or other implements without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine shall be double.
In the case of breaking a hand or a foot, or cutting off the ear or the nose, the middle amercement is the punishment;
likewise for causing a wound that breaks the skin, or for striking one who is nearly dead.
In cases of obstructing movement, eating, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
For many people who kill a single person, the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed.
That which was stolen during a quarrel must be restored, and the fine shall be double that amount.
He who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its removal,
as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel.
In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to collapse,
one should be made to pay five, ten, or twenty *paṇas*, as well as the cost of repair.
One who throws into a house property that causes pain, or likewise something life-threatening,
shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* for the first offense, and for the second, the middle amercement.
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise severing a limb or a member,
the fine for small animals shall start from two paṇas and increase in sequence.
For cutting off the sexual organ or causing death, the middle amercement shall be imposed, as well as the price of the animal;
for large animals, the fine in these cases is double.
For cutting branches,
trunks, or the entire body of trees that bear shoots or have spreading branches, and for trees that provide livelihood, the fine is double that of twenty [paṇas].
In the case of trees growing near a shrine, a cremation ground, a boundary, a sacred site, or a temple,
as well as for a tree of renown, the fine is double.
For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines, the fine shall be half of that prescribed previously for the places mentioned above.
[End of Chapter 20: On Violence]
The forcible seizure of common property is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence).
The fine for this is twice the value of that property; however, if there was a denial [of ownership], it is fourfold.
He who causes another to commit *sāhasa* shall be made to pay double the fine.
And he who, having spoken thus, "I am the giver," should cause [the gift] to be performed, shall incur a fourfold [penalty].

One who rejects or transgresses the guest-offering (arghya), one who strikes his brother’s wife, one who fails to give what has been promised, and one who breaks a house by digging a tunnel into the sea; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.232.
For one who commits an injury against neighbors, guild members, and others,
a fine of fifty paṇas is the settled rule for these cases.
One who approaches a widow against her will,
one who does not come to the rescue when a cry for help is raised, one who raises a false alarm, and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the highest castes— [these shall be punished].
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at a rite for the gods or the ancestors is unfit;
likewise, one who administers an improper oath or performs the duties of an unworthy person is unfit.
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small livestock,
one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant’s pregnancy [are liable for the same fine].
Father, son, sister, brother, husband and wife, and teacher and pupil— among these, one who abandons another who has not fallen from caste shall be liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
A laundryman who wears another's garment shall be fined three *paṇas*;
however, for selling, hiring out, pledging, or borrowing it, he shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses shall be three paṇas;
and for whoever stands between them, the fine shall be eightfold.
One who forges scales, edicts, measures, or coins,
as well as anyone who transacts business with these [forged items], shall be made to pay the highest fine.
He who declares a counterfeit coin to be genuine, or a genuine coin to be counterfeit—
that examiner of coins shall be made to pay the highest fine.
A physician who practices deceitfully shall be punished with the first amercement for treating animals,
the middle amercement for humans, and the highest amercement for royal officers.
He who binds one who should not be bound, he who releases one who is bound,
and he who [binds] one who has not yet attained legal capacity, shall be made to pay the highest fine.

Whoever should take even an eighth part [of the value] by means of a measure or a scale, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas], as determined according to the increase or decrease [in the value].
In the case of commodities such as medicine, oil, salt, perfumes, grain, molasses, and the like,
one who adulterates them with inferior substances shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas.
For making what is not a genus appear as a genus by means of clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth,
the fine for selling such items is eightfold.
For one who brings for deposit or sale goods that are wrapped in a casket, counterfeit goods,
or artificial items, a punishment shall be prescribed.
If a commodity worth five *paṇas* is damaged, the fine is fifty; if it is worth ten *paṇas*, the fine is said to be one hundred.
For an item worth twenty *paṇas*, the fine is two hundred; and as the value increases, the fine increases accordingly.
For those artisans and craftsmen who, acting in concert, fix a price that is too high,
or who knowingly cause a decrease or an increase in the price, the highest fine shall be imposed.
For merchants who, acting in concert, obstruct the sale of merchandise by fixing an improper price,
or for those who sell it [in such a manner], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement.
The price established by the king every day shall be the basis for sale or purchase;
from that [established price] comes the profit for merchants, which is declared to be their legitimate earnings.
A merchant dealing in local goods may take five percent profit;
however, he who buys and sells foreign goods immediately may take ten percent.

Having established the expenses arising from the merchandise upon the price of the goods, a sale price that provides favor for both the buyer and the seller should be fixed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.253) [Chapter 21:
The Section on Non-Delivery after Sale] (p. 298)

If a seller does not deliver the merchandise for which the price has been received to the buyer, he shall be made to pay that price along with the interest, or the profit realized from the direction from which the goods were obtained, if they have arrived from abroad.
Even if it has been sold, the article may be resold if the previous buyer does not take delivery;
for if the loss results from the fault of the buyer, that loss shall belong to the buyer alone.
If a commodity becomes damaged due to an injury caused by the king or by fate,
that loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, does not deliver it.
If one sells an item in the hand of another, or sells what is defective as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be double the value of the item.
If a merchant, unaware of the loss or profit of his merchandise, has no right of repentance after having purchased it; yet if he exercises such a right, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth.
[Chapter on Joint Undertakings] (p. 300)
When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership,
the profit and loss shall be according to their respective capital, or as determined by their agreement.
If a deposit is lost through negligence—whether it was forbidden [to use] or not specifically authorized—the owner shall pay for it;
furthermore, he who protects the deposit from loss is entitled to a tenth part as his reward.
The king shall take a twentieth part as a toll from the offering of goods for sale;
however, that which is sold while being obstructed by royal officials, or that which is fit for the king's use, shall go to the king.
One who falsely declares the quantity [of goods], one who evades the customs station,
and one who buys or sells with fraudulent intent, shall be made to pay eight times [the value].
A ferryman who takes toll for goods transported by land shall be made to pay ten *paṇas*;
this same penalty applies for failing to invite Brahmins and neighbors [to a feast].
When a man has died while traveling in another country, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives shall take his property; if they do not arrive, the king shall take it.
They should abandon one who acts deviously or one who yields no profit; if unable to do so, he should have the work performed by another.
By this rule, the procedure for officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers has been declared. [23.
Steya-prakaraṇam] (p. 303)
A thief is apprehended by pursuers either through stolen property or by his tracks;
likewise, one who has committed a prior offense and one who wears unclean clothing [is apprehended].
Others also are to be apprehended on suspicion, such as those who conceal their caste, name, and so forth;
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and drink, and those whose faces and voices are parched and altered.

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet possess great expenditures, and those who sell goods that do not exist— these are [to be suspected as spies].
If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft does not clear himself,
the king, having caused the stolen property to be restored, shall punish him with the penalty prescribed for a thief.
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, the king shall have him executed by various forms of capital punishment;
however, if he is a Brāhmaṇa, he should be branded with a mark and banished from his own kingdom.
If cattle are killed or stolen, the blame falls on the village headman if they have not left the village;
but on the headman of the pasture if it happens on the road, and on the one who guards the herd if it happens outside the pasture.
The village itself shall provide [the boundary] within its own limits, or at the point where it extends;
or else, five villages beyond a *krośa*, or even ten villages.
Men who capture bards, those who carry off horses and elephants,
and those who kill by force, he shall cause to be impaled upon stakes.
Those who commit robbery by breaking into a house or those who cut open a knot (to steal goods) shall have a hand and a thumb cut off;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot.
In cases of seizing property that is small, middling, or large, the punishment shall be determined according to its value;
in the administration of punishment, one must carefully consider the place, time, age, and capacity [of the offender].

Having provided food, shelter, fire, water, sacred mantras, and the expenses for implements to a thief or a murderer who knows [the victim], the highest fine shall be imposed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.276)
In the case of causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed;
likewise, for the killing of a man or a woman, the highest or the lowest fine may be imposed.
Furthermore, a woman who has committed a grave offense, one who has killed a man, or one who has destroyed a dam— provided she is not pregnant—
one should cause her to be cast into water after having bound a stone to her.
One who administers poison or fire, or one who causes the death of her husband, her teacher, or her own child,
should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be caused to die by cows.
In the case of one killed whose identity is unknown, the sons and kinsmen should immediately be questioned, as well as his women who were devoted to other men, each separately.
Or, desiring her property or her livelihood, with whom has she departed? One should also slowly question people near the place of death.
Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the king’s wife, shall be burned on a pyre of straw.
In the case of adultery with another's wife, a man shall be seized by the hair-to-hair;
or immediately by the marks born of passion, provided there is mutual acknowledgment by both parties.
Touching the knot of the lower garment, the breasts, the covering [of the body], the thighs, or the hair;
conversing at an improper place or time; and sitting together on the same seat.
In the case of a prohibition, a woman shall pay one hundred [paṇas], while a man shall pay two hundred as a fine;
if they both persist in the act despite the prohibition, their punishment shall be the same as that for adultery.
In the case of a man of the same caste, the highest fine is prescribed; in the case of a lower caste, the middle fine;
in the case of a higher caste, the death penalty for the man, and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the woman.

If one carries off an adorned maiden, he shall pay the highest fine; otherwise, the lowest. In the case of women of his own caste, he shall pay a fine, but in the case of those of higher castes, death is ordained by law.
There is no offense in approaching women of lower castes who are willing; otherwise, there is punishment.
But in the case of defilement, the hand shall be cut off; and in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there is likewise death.
For defiling a woman, one shall pay a hundred [paṇas]; for making a false accusation, two hundred.
