For having intercourse with cattle, one shall be made to pay a hundred; for having intercourse with a low-caste woman or a cow, the middle amercement.
A man who has sexual intercourse with female slaves kept in the household, or likewise with female servants,
even though they are women with whom one may lawfully go, shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.291ab: (In the case of approaching a female slave by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.291cd: If she is unwilling and he approaches many men, the fine for each is twenty-four [paṇas].

A prostitute who has accepted her fee shall not, if she is unwilling, pay double; if the fee was not accepted, she should be made to pay an equal amount. A man likewise should be treated in exactly the same manner.
For one who approaches a woman in a non-vaginal opening, or urinates facing a man,
as well as for one who has sexual intercourse with a female ascetic, the fine is twenty-four *paṇas*.
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, he should be branded with the mark of a eunuch and banished;

likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the lowest caste shall become one of the lowest caste himself, while for a man of the highest caste approaching a woman of the lowest caste, the punishment is death.
[Section 25: Miscellaneous Matters]
He who writes a royal edict that is either deficient or excessive,
or he who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment.
One who defiles a twice-born man with forbidden food shall be punished with the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that.
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall have three limbs mutilated and be made to pay the highest fine.
A fault committed by a four-footed animal is not [attributed to its owner] if it cries out "Move away! while doing so;
the same applies to damage caused by wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, arms, or draft animals.
If damage is caused by a vehicle with a broken nose-rope, or one with a broken yoke and so forth,
or if it moves backward while retreating, the owner does not incur guilt.

Even if capable of doing so, an owner who does not rescue [his livestock] from fanged or horned animals shall pay the first amercement; likewise, if a cry for help has been raised, he shall pay double.
If one addresses a paramour as a "thief," he shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;
likewise, one who abandons wealth after having lived off it shall be made to pay that same amount increased eightfold.
Having cut off the tongue of one who speaks what is displeasing to the king, of one who reviles him, or of one who divulges his secret counsel, he shall banish him.
For one who sells a limb from a dead body, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the vehicle or the seat of the king, the punishment is the highest fine (uttamasāhasa).
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king,
and likewise for a Śūdra living by means of the status of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine is eight hundred [paṇas].
But if the judges have wrongly decided legal cases,
they shall be fined by the king twice the amount of the dispute, along with their fellow members.
If one who has been defeated even by a legal process should think, "I am not defeated," then,
having won him again when he returns, the king shall cause him to pay double the fine.
Whatever fine has been unjustly taken by a king, he should report that to Varuṇa and personally give it to Brahmins increased thirtyfold. [End of the Chapter on Legal Procedure]
[III. Chapter on Expiation] [1.
Section on Impurity] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.1a: One who is less than two years old should be buried; one should not perform the water-libation for such a child thereafter.
The other [the student], followed by his kinsmen, should follow him as far as the cremation ground.
If he has passed away having entered the sacred fires, he should be cremated with the worldly fire by those reciting the *Yamasūkta* and the *Gāthās*,
provided that the purpose of the ritual for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) has been fulfilled.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.3: Within seven or even ten days, the kinsmen approach the water, facing the direction of the ancestors, [saying]: "May our sin be cleansed by this water."
In this same manner, the water-rite (udaka-kriyā) is performed for maternal grandfathers, teachers, and deceased persons;
however, the offering of water is optional for friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests.

Restraining their speech, they pour out water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage; those who are students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) shall not perform the water-libation, nor likewise those who have fallen from their status (*patita*).

Heretics, those who have no protector, thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who act according to lust, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide— these are not entitled to the period of impurity nor to the water libation.
When they have performed the water-libations, emerged from the water, and are standing upon soft grassy ground,
having bathed, one should address them with ancient historical narratives.
He who seeks a core in human existence— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on the water— is utterly deluded.
If this body, composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state,
what cause for lamentation is there, since it was brought about by the actions arising from one's own body?
The earth, which supports all beings, will go to destruction, as will the oceans and the gods;
how then will the mortal world, which is like foam, not go to destruction?
Since the deceased helplessly consumes the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should therefore not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability.
Having thus made their agreement, they should go home preceded by a child;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water, they should enter while touching fire and other [sacred objects], water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds;
and having anointed themselves, they should step slowly onto a stone.

The rites beginning with the entry [into the house] must also be performed for those who have touched a corpse; however, for others who desire it, purification occurs instantly through bathing and self-restraint.
Having carried out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or preceptor, one who is under a vow remains under that vow;
he should not eat food from a restricted source, nor should he dwell together with them.

Eating food that has been purchased or obtained, they should sleep separately on the ground; for three days, food should be offered to the deceased according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña.
Water and milk should be placed in an earthen vessel for one day in the open air.
The Vaitāna and Aupāsana sacrifices, as well as other rites, must be performed according to the injunctions of the Śruti.
Impurity due to death (śāva-āśauca) is prescribed to last for either three nights or ten nights.
In the case of a child less than two years old, the period of impurity (sūtaka) for both parents belongs to the mother alone.
Regarding the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) of the parents, it certainly belongs to the mother because of the manifestation of that [menstrual] blood;
on that day, there is no defilement for the ancestors, because of the cause of their own birth.

In the interval between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days [of the period of impurity]. In the case of a miscarriage, nights equal in number to the months [of gestation] are the cause of purification.
For those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for those who commit suicide, [the impurity lasts] as long as the corpse is visible.
If he has gone abroad, the period remaining shall apply; once that period is completed, he becomes pure after offering water libations.
For a Kṣatriya, the period is twelve days; for a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days;
for a Śūdra, it is thirty days, or half of that (fifteen days) if he lives according to the law.
Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is prescribed as one night;
until the initiation into the vows (vratādeśa), it is three nights; and beyond that, ten nights.

But for those who have not taken a maiden as a wife, for children, for the teacher’s pupil, for one who has studied the Vedas, for a maternal uncle, for a Śrotriya, for sons other than the legitimate son of the body, and for wives who have gone to another man, purification takes one day (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.24–25).
When the king who provided residence has died, that very day is the cause for purification.
A Brāhmaṇa must never follow after a Śūdra or another twice-born person. Having followed them, he becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
There is no period of impurity for kings slain by lightning,
nor for those killed in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whomever the king so desires.

For officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), and those performing sacrificial rites; likewise for those observing the vows of a *sattra*, celibate students (*brahmacārin*), donors, and those who know the Veda (*brahmavid*).
In giving a gift, in marriage, in a sacrifice, in battle, during a calamity befalling the country,
and even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained.

If one is touched by a woman in her courses or by those who are impure, one should bathe; if touched by them, one should perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśet). Furthermore, one should mutter the non-Vedic mantras (ab-lingāni) and recite the Gāyatrī once mentally.
Time, fire, ritual action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water,
subsequent remorse, and fasting— all these are causes of purification.
For those who have committed forbidden acts, giving gifts, the current of a river, earth, and water purify; indeed, for the twice-born, renunciation is also a means of purification.
For those who know the Vedas, austerity is the highest; for the wise, patience; for the tall, water;
for those whose sins are concealed, the silent recitation of prayers; and truth is said to be the highest for the mind.

Austerity and knowledge are the purifiers of the elemental self (bhūtātman); wisdom is the purifier of the intellect; and the supreme purification of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is held to arise from the knowledge of the Lord (Īśvara). [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.34] (Chapter 2: On Duties in Times of Adversity, p. 356)
A twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, or even by that of a Vaiśya in times of distress;
having emerged from that distress and having purified himself, he should then establish himself on the [proper] path.
Fruit, stone, linen, soma, humans, cakes, and climbing plants;
sesame, boiled rice, juice, alkaline substances, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.36)
Weapons, liquor, honey-remnants, honey, lac, and sacrificial grass;
clay, leather, flowers, blankets, hair, buttermilk, poison, and earth.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, lead, Śaka, fresh herbs, oil-cakes, and likewise the scents of animals; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.38.
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one should never sell sesame seeds; for the sake of dharma, they may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
Lac, salt, and meat are causes for falling [from caste] if sold;
however, milk, curd, and liquor cause one to become of a lower caste.
A Brahmin who, having fallen into distress, accepts or consumes food from any source whatsoever, is not tainted by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.

Agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, trade by cart, mountain-mining, service to others, and begging from those of similar status— these are the means of livelihood in times of distress.
If one who is hungry remains for three days and takes grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa,
having received it, he must report that according to the law when questioned.
Having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, Vedic study, austerity, and family, the king shall provide him with a righteous means of livelihood.
[3. Chapter on the Duties of the Forest-Dweller] (p.

360) Having entrusted his wife to his son, or accompanied by her, the forest-dweller, remaining celibate, shall go to the forest together with his sacred fires and his domestic hearth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.45)

One who maintains a beard, matted locks, and body hair, being self-possessed, should satisfy the fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents with food grown without the use of the plow.
One should accumulate wealth for the sake of a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been acquired, one should relinquish it in the month of Āśvayuja.
Self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts,
devoted to Vedic study, inclined toward giving, and intent on the welfare of all living beings.

He may use his teeth as a mortar, eat only what is ripened by time, or grind with a stone; likewise, he should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as other ritual acts, using fruits and oils.
One should always pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts or spend it with Kṛcchra penances;
or one may eat when a fortnight has passed, or when a month has passed, or even when a day has passed.

One should sleep on the ground at night, being pure; during the day, one should pass the time by standing on tiptoe, or likewise by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or by the practice of yoga.
In the summer, he should stand in the midst of five fires; during the rainy season, he should sleep on the bare ground;
and in the winter, he should wear wet clothes—or perform penance according to his capacity.
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood paste—
toward both of them alike, one should be neither angry nor pleased.
Or, having consigned the sacred fires to himself, dwelling among trees and eating moderately,
he should beg for alms solely from the houses of forest-dwellers for the sake of sustenance.
Or, having brought eight morsels from a village, he should eat them while restraining his speech;
or, subsisting on air, he should walk toward the north-east until his body collapses. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.55) [Chapter on the Duties of Ascetics] (p. 365)
Having performed from the forest or from the house an *iṣṭi* sacrifice in which the entire property is given as the sacrificial fee (*sārvavedasadakṣiṇā*),
and having at its conclusion internalized those fires within himself according to the *prājāpatya* rite;
One who has studied the Vedas, performed silent recitation, fathered a son, given food, maintained the sacred fires,
and offered sacrifices according to his ability— such a person may direct his mind toward liberation, and not otherwise.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, tranquil, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot,
and dwelling alone in solitude, he should wander as a mendicant and resort to a village only for the sake of alms.
Being vigilant, he should go about for alms in the evening, unobserved;
in a village secluded from other mendicants, he should seek only as much as is necessary for sustenance, free from greed.
The vessels of an ascetic are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear toward all beings, the twice-born becomes immortal.
A mendicant, however, must especially purify his inner disposition,
because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence.
One should contemplate the dwellings in the womb and the various states of existence born of karma,
as well as mental anxieties, physical diseases, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of form.

Through the yoga of meditation, one who is subtle and established in the self should perceive the occurrence of the reversal of the pleasant and unpleasant throughout thousands of births. Indeed, the stage of life (*āśrama*) is not the cause of *dharma*; rather, it becomes so when it is practiced [in accordance with *dharma*].
Therefore, one should not do to others that which is unwholesome for oneself.
Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint,
control of the senses, and learning— all these are declared to be dharma.
"Just as sparks fly forth from a heated mass of iron,
even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the Supreme Self."
In that regard, the self itself performs some action by its own nature,
and some [action] through habituation— [an action] consisting of both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
The cause, the imperishable, the agent, the knower, the possessor of qualities,
and the controller— though unborn, it is proclaimed to be "born" due to the assumption of a body.
Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, wind, light, water, and earth—
each possessing one additional quality— so too, while coming into being, he takes them back again.
Through the oblation the sun is nourished; from the sun comes rain, and from that the plants. That food, in the form of essence, attains the state of semen.
But when there is union between a woman and a man, and the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord himself, as the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements.
The senses, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude,
retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Effort, form, color, accentuation, aversion, existence, and non-existence—
all this is born of that [Self] as it desires a beginning for itself, though it is without beginning.
In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, coagulated with the bodily elements;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; and in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs.
From ether [come] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, strength, and so forth;
and from air [come] the sense of touch, movement, expansion, and even dryness.
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, color, and luminosity;
from phlegm (rasa), however, come the sense of taste, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness.
In the third [state], the immutable Self grasps the smell of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form; thereafter, it vibrates.
By failing to grant her pregnancy-longing, the fetus may incur deformity or even death; therefore, one should fulfill whatever is dear to the woman.
In the fourth month, there is the stabilization of the limbs; in the fifth, the emergence of blood;
and in the sixth, the development of strength, complexion, nails, and hair.
In the seventh and eighth [weeks], it is endowed with consciousness and mind, possessed of channels, sinews, and vessels, and also possesses skin, flesh, and memory.
Again, the *dhātrī* (nurse), again the *gharma* (heat), and his vital energy (*ojas*) flow away;
therefore, the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of life.
In the ninth or even the tenth month, by powerful birth-winds,
he is expelled like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish pain.
Its bodies are sixfold, and it possesses six skins;
likewise, its limbs are six, and its bones amount to three hundred and sixty.
Together with the sockets, there are sixty-four teeth; the nails are twenty;
and the fingers and toes constitute four locations for them.
There are sixty finger-breadths (aṅgulis) in the two heels; four in the ankles;
four bones in the forearms (aratnis); and exactly that many in the two shanks (jaṅghās).
One should point out that there are two each produced at the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, the shoulder-blades,
the collarbones, the palate, and the hip-blades.
The hip consists of one bone; likewise, there are forty-five bones in the back.
The neck consists of fifteen bones; each clavicle is a single bone, as is the jaw.
At its base are two [bones], the forehead, the eyes, and the cheeks; the nose consists of solid bone;
the ribs together with the costal cartilages and the *arbuda* bones are seventy-two.
The two temples, the four skull-bones, and likewise the chest consisting of seventeen bones—this is the collection of bones in a human being. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.90)
Smell, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects of the senses;
and the nose, the eyes, the tongue, the skin, and the ear are the sense organs.
One should know that the two hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the two feet are indeed the five organs of action; and the mind is of the nature of both.
The navel, the vital energy (ojas), the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples,
as well as the head, the shoulders, the throat, and the heart— these are the seats of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The omentum, the fat, the slaughter-wound, the navel, the *kloman*, the liver, the spleen;
the small intestine, the two kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces;
then the stomach, the heart, the large intestine, and the rectum.
The abdomen and the two pelvic cavities—this is declared to be the width.
The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-flaps,
the two ears, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins.
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, the breasts (which arise from a mass of phlegm),
the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the calves and thighs— these are the swellings.
The palate, the stomach, the top of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, and the navel—
these are the locations within this body.
The two eyes, the two ears, the two feet, the hands, and the heart—
these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
There are exactly seven hundred channels (śirā), nine hundred ligaments (snāyu),
two hundred arteries (dhamanī), and five hundred muscles (peśī).
Know that there are twenty-nine lakhs,
nine hundred and fifty-six vessels known as *dhamanīs*.
Three hundred thousand hairs, including the beard and head hair, are to be known as belonging to embodied beings;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (*marmāṇi*) and two hundred joints (*sandhayaḥ*).
There are fifty-four crores,
sixty-seven lakhs, and fifty thousand pores of the hair, along with the sweat-exits.
Even if one were to follow and understand each individual atom as it is divided by the winds, one would still not comprehend the entire arrangement of these elemental constituents.
Nine añjalis of liquid are to be known [as the measure for a month], ten for water,
seven for feces, and eight for blood are proclaimed.
Phlegm is six [parts], bile five, and urine four;
muscle-fat three, fat two, marrow one, and half of that is in the head.
"The phlegm has such-and-such strength, the vital energy (ojas) has such-and-such strength, and the semen has such-and-such strength"—
he who possesses this unstable body should strive for liberation.
Seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) issue forth from the heart;
among them, in the center, is that which has the luster of the moon, known as hitā and ahitā.
The Self, situated in the center of that orb, is motionless like a lamp;
it is to be known, and having known it here, one is not born again.
And that Āraṇyaka which I obtained from the Sun should be known; likewise, the Yoga-śāstra proclaimed by me should be studied by one who desires Yoga.
Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses focused on no other object,
the Self who resides here in the heart like a lamp should be meditated upon as the Lord.
By reciting the Sāman chants according to the prescribed rules, without error and with focused attention,
one attains the supreme Brahman through that practice.
The *ullopya*, *madraka*, *prakarī*, *apara-antaka*, *auveṇaka*, *saro-bindu*, and the *uttara* songs; these are the musical compositions (*gītakas*).
The *ṛk-gāthā*, the *pāṇikā*, the *dakṣavihitā*, and the *brahmagītikā*—this is what should be sung; through the practice of these, it is designated as "liberation."
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, who is proficient in the *śrutis* and *jātis*,
and who understands the rhythmic beats (*tāla*), attains the path to liberation without effort.
If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through yoga,
he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.
The self is said to be beginningless, while its beginning is the body;
indeed, the entire universe originates from the self, and the self arises from the universe.
"How is this world—including its gods, asuras, and humans—produced? And how is the Self [situated] within it? Tell us this, for we are utterly bewildered."
Indeed, that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion has a thousand hands, feet, and eyes;
he possesses a thousand [rays] and has the brilliance of the sun.
He is the Self, the sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) of universal form;
as Virāj, he attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food.
That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substances and deities,
having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit.
Having joined the Soma with the wind, it is then led upward by the rays;
having been brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, it is led further on.
From the orb of the sky, that Sun emits the supreme nectar,
from which all beings— whether they are eaters or non-eaters— are born.
From that food, again comes sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again sacrifice. In this way, this wheel revolves without beginning or end.
The self is beginningless; there is no origination of the inner self.
However, the person is a composite entity born of delusion, desire, aversion, and action.
That primordial deity, who has been described by me as having a thousandfold self—
his social classes (varṇas) are, respectively, those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet.
From his feet the earth was born; from his head the sky arose;
from his nostrils the vital breaths, from his ears the directions, from his touch the wind, and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun;
from his loins arose the intermediate space and the world of moving and non-moving beings.
O Brahmin, if this is so, how is it that he is born into sinful wombs?
How does that Lord become joined with undesirable states of being?
And how is it that there was no prior cognition even for one endowed with the instruments [of perception]?
Why does the omnipresent one not perceive the sensation, even though he too is omnipresent?
Through defects born of actions of mind, speech, and body, this living soul attains the state of lower animals, birds, and immobile beings, as well as existence within hundreds of wombs.
Just as the states of embodied beings within their bodies are infinite,
so too are the forms of those possessing bodies here in all wombs.
The ripening of some karmas occurs after death, while for others it occurs in this life;
for yet others, it occurs both here and there—the state of being [the result] therein is the purpose.
Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable,
and being intent on false beliefs, one is born in other wombs.
A man who speaks untruth, a slanderer, one who utters harsh words,
and one who engages in idle chatter is born among wild animals and birds.

One who delights in taking what is not given, one who violates another’s wife, and one who causes injury to stationary beings (plants and trees) contrary to the prescribed rules, is born among stationary beings. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.136)
One who knows the self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses, performs dharma, and is learned in Vedic knowledge— such a person of sattvic nature attains birth among the gods.
One who delights in improper actions, who is undisciplined, enterprising, and sensual—
that person of rajasic nature, upon dying among men, attains another birth.
One who is prone to sleep, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct— such a person characterized by *tamas* is born among the animals.
Thus, possessed by passion and darkness,
wandering here and joined with undesirable states of being, he enters the cycle of transmigration.
For just as a soiled mirror is incapable of reflecting a form,
so too is the intellect (*karaṇa*) that has not been ripened incapable of self-knowledge.
Just as in an unripe mango, even though a sweet taste exists, it is not perceived; so too, when the instruments [of cognition] are unrefined, knowledge is not attained within the self.
The embodied soul experiences all sensations based within its own body;
yet the yogi who is liberated does not experience any of these sensations.
Just as the single ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels,
so too the one Self appears as many, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.
Brahman, ether, air, fire, water, and earth are the primary elements;
from these [arise] these worlds, this self, and all that is moving and unmoving.
Just as a potter makes a jar through the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood; so too [does the agent produce effects].
Just as a goldsmith takes mere gold and,
through contact with his own saliva, produces a vessel, or as a silkworm produces a cocoon [from its own secretions].
Having thus taken up the instruments [of action], the Self creates itself and, coming together with the instruments, casts itself into various wombs here in this world.
The great elements are real, and the self is likewise indeed so;
for who, having seen with one eye, sees with the other otherwise?
Who indeed understands speech once it has been heard again after being heard?
Whose is the memory of a past object, and who is the creator of a dream?
One who is made arrogant by birth, form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth,
exerts himself toward the objects of the senses, such as sound, through action, mind, and speech.
With a mind clouded by doubt as to whether the fruit of action exists or not, he is deluded;
for even though he has not attained perfection, he considers himself to have attained it.
"My wife, son, and ministers; I am theirs"—such is his fixed conviction.
He always possesses a perverted mind regarding matters that are beneficial or harmful.
One who makes no distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower, or between the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikāra),
and one who attempts suicide by fasting, fire, weapons, water, or by throwing oneself down [from a precipice].
One who behaves in this manner, whose self is undisciplined, and who possesses false attachments,
is bound by action through hatred, delusion, and desire.
Service to the teacher, discernment regarding the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras,
the performance of those prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech.
Avoiding the sight of women and touching them, perceiving all beings as one's own self,
renouncing possessions, and wearing a worn-out saffron robe.
The restraint of the senses from their objects, the avoidance of sloth and laziness, the thorough examination of the body, and the perception of evil in worldly activities.
Purity of the *sattva* quality consists in being free from passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), as well as desirelessness and tranquility.
One who is thoroughly purified by these means becomes fit for the *sattva* and attains immortality.

Through the recollection of reality, through the presence [of the mind], through the application of the inner being (*sattva*), through the complete exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, the yoga of the good proceeds.
He whose mind, upon the dissolution of the body, is established in the Lord and grounded in *sattva*,
with an undeluded intellect, shall properly attain the recollection of his former births.
Just as Bharata colors his own body with various pigments,
creating diverse forms, so too does the Self assume bodies born of karma.

The deformity of the embryo at birth—such as being deficient in limbs—is seen to result from defects in time, karma, the self, and the seed, as well as from those of the mother. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.163)
This self has never before been liberated from egoism, the mind, the sense of movement, the fruit of action, and the body in any way whatsoever.
Just as the continued existence of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the vessel,
and the oil, so too is the destruction of life observed to occur prematurely through such a transformation.
His rays are infinite, situated in the heart like a lamp;
they are white, black, variegated in form, tawny, blue, and red.
Among them, he who stands alone above, having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, attains through him the supreme goal.
That other hundred rays of his which are situated upwards— by means of them,
he attains the celestial bodies together with their abodes.
And those rays of his which are of many forms below and possess a mild luster—
with them he wanders helplessly in this world for the experience of the fruits of his actions.
By means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge; by birth and by death;
likewise by affliction, by going, and by not going; and indeed by truth and by falsehood—Yājñavalkya 3.170a-c.
Through superior happiness and suffering, through auspicious and inauspicious actions,
and through the fruits arising from the knowledge of omens, the cries of birds, and the conjunctions of the planets.
Through the movements of the stars and constellations, through waking states and those born of sleep,
and likewise through space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness.
Through the Manvantaras, through the attainment of the Yugas, and even through mantras, medicinal herbs, and fruits—
one should know the Self as the cause of the world.
Egoism, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude,
the transition between the various sense organs, desire, retention, and life— these [are the functions of the mind].
Heaven, dreaming, the impelling of entities, the movement of the mind,
the winking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and grasping— these consist of the five elements.
Since these signs of the supreme Self are observed,
therefore there exists a Self beyond the body, all-pervading and sovereign.

The organs of perception together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action, as well as the ego-sense, the intellect, and the elements beginning with earth; indeed, these are [the constituents].
The unmanifest Self is declared to be the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) of this field; it is the Lord dwelling within all beings, who is both existent and non-existent, being and non-being.
From the unmanifest (avyakta) arises the intellect (buddhi); from that, the emergence of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
and from the ego-sense arise the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the rest, each possessing one additional quality [than its predecessor].
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever among these has emerged from which [element], that dissolves back into that very same one.
Just as the Self creates itself, so has it been described by me to you;
though he is the Lord, he does so through the ripening of the three kinds of karma.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed proclaimed to be its very qualities;
for when possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel.
He alone is the Supreme Person, both without beginning and yet possessing a beginning;
he is declared to be subject to transformation, with a form perceivable by the subtle senses (*liṅgindriya*).
By that path which lies between the Pitṛyāna, the Ajavīthī, and Agastya,
those who maintain the sacred fire and desire heaven go toward the celestial realm.
And those who are devoted to giving, properly endowed with the eight qualities,
and dedicated to the vow of truth— they too proceed by that very same path.
Therein, eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders were subject to rebirth; they served as the seed and the promoters of Dharma.
Residing in the world of the gods between the Seven Sages (the Great Bear) and the path of the Nagas,
there are an equal number of sages who have abandoned all undertakings.
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings.
From which [the Veda] come the Vedas, the Purāṇas, as well as the sciences and the Upaniṣads;
the verses, the aphorisms, the commentaries, and whatever else consists of speech.
The recitation of the Veda, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint,
faith, fasting, and independence are the causes for the knowledge of the Self.
For he is indeed to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
moreover, he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard from by the twice-born.
Those twice-born who, having resorted to the forest, know him thus, and who worship the Truth endowed with supreme faith; Yājñavalkya 3.192.
In due order, they arise from him: the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, and likewise the northern solstice, the world of the gods, the sun, and the lightning.
Then a person born of the mind (mānasa), having approached them, makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahman (brahmalaukika);
for them, there is no return here again.
For those men who have conquered heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[they travel] by way of smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice.
The world of the ancestors, the moon, the wind, rain, water, and the earth—
they enter these in succession here, and from there they return once again.
That self-possessed man who does not understand these two paths shall become either a venomous snake, a moth, an insect, or a worm.
With his feet placed on his thighs and palms turned upward, having placed his left hand upon his right,
he should slightly lift his face with the palms upward and steady it against his chest.
With eyes closed, established in *sattva*, not touching the teeth with the teeth,
the tongue motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly still.
Having restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should undertake breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) twice or even thrice.
Then the wise man, maintaining *dhāraṇā*, should fix his self upon that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp.
Invisibility, the power of recollection, radiance, the faculty of sight, as well as the faculty of hearing,
and likewise the ability to enter the bodies of others after casting off one's own body.
The creation of objects at will is indeed the mark of perfection in yoga;
for one who has attained perfection in yoga, by casting off the body, he is fit for immortality.
Alternatively, even one who has renounced ritual acts and dwells in the forest, studying the Veda,
eating moderately and subsisting on alms not solicited, shall attain the highest perfection.

One who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is kind to guests, who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth— even such a householder is indeed liberated. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.205)
Having experienced the terrible and horrific hells born of great sins,
those who have committed great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma.
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of deer, horses, boars, and camels;
the drinker of spirituous liquor enters the wombs of donkeys, Pukkasas, and Venas—of this there is no doubt.
The stealer of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a winged insect; and the violator of the Guru’s bed shall gradually become a grass, a shrub, or a creeper.

A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from a wasting disease; a drinker of spirituous liquor, from black teeth; a stealer of gold, from deformed nails; and one who violates the bed of his teacher, from skin disease.
Whosoever among these associates with another, he is reborn bearing the characteristics of that person:
a stealer of food shall suffer from indigestion, and a stealer of speech shall be mute.
One who adulterates grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a putrid nose;
one who steals oil shall be a drinker of oil; and a backbiter shall have a foul-smelling mouth.
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest.
One who steals the jewels of another is born into a low caste; by killing a peacock one becomes a parrot, and by stealing auspicious perfumes one becomes a muskrat.
A mouse [is the thief] of grain; a camel [the thief] of a vehicle; a monkey [the thief] of fruit;
a water-fowl [the thief] of water; a crow [the thief] of milk; and a house-builder [the thief] of household utensils.
A gadfly [destroys] honey, a vulture [destroys] meat, a monitor lizard [destroys] a cow,
a crane [destroys] fire, a leper [destroys] clothing, a dog [destroys] flavor, and a cricket [destroys] salt.
This has been stated by me for the purpose of illustration regarding the act of theft;
for the various kinds of objects are indeed equal to the various species of living beings.
Having obtained the fruit according to their actions, through the lapse of time they attain the state of animals;
being deprived of auspicious marks, they are born as the lowest of men, impoverished.
Then, having become free from stain, they are born into a great family as enjoyers of life,
endowed with learning and possessed of wealth and grain.
By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the practice of what is censured,
and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man falls into ruin.
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become propitiated.
Men who are devoted to sinful deeds and do not perform penance, being remorseless,
go to terrible and dreadful hells.
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka.
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃprapātanam, Mahānaraka, Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Mahāpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka; Asipatravana and Tāpana as the twenty-first.

Those lowest of men who have not performed expiation remain afflicted by the terrible sins arising from mortal transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) as well as those arising from minor transgressions (*upapātaka*).
Through penances, the sin committed through ignorance departs;
however, one who acts out of desire becomes subject to legal proceedings here [only] by virtue of a specific scriptural statement.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru’s bed—
these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*), as is he who associates with them.

Excessive reviling of gurus, reviling the Vedas, the killing of a friend, and the destruction of what has been studied—these should be known as equal to the murder of a Brahmin. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.228)
Eating forbidden food, dishonesty, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation,
and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The theft of a horse, a gem, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow,
as well as the misappropriation of a deposit, is indeed equal to the theft of gold.

Sexual intercourse with the wife of a friend, virgins, women of one's own womb (uterine sisters), women of the lowest castes, women of the same lineage (gotra), and women closely related by marriage is declared to be equal to violating the teacher’s bed.
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, and also a daughter-in-law;
likewise, the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and the teacher’s daughter.
He who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the Guru’s bed; his penis shall be cut off and he shall be put to death, as shall the woman if she was willing.
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling goods that should not be sold, and gambling; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.234.
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a salary, adultery, marrying a woman previously married by another, usury, and the manufacture of salt; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.235.
The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censurable wealth; atheism; the neglect of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.
Stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; abandoning one's father, mother, or son; and selling a tank or a grove.

Defiling a maiden, officiating at the marriage of one who has already married a sister (parivindaka), giving a daughter in marriage to such a person, dishonesty, and the violation of a vow; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.238.

Undertaking ritual actions for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning sacred study, the sacred fire, and one's offspring, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.239.
Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, injuring women, living by the sale of medicinal herbs, constructing murderous traps, and the sale of oneself— these are vices.
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
Studying false scriptures, engaging in mining operations,
and the sale of one's own wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).
Carrying a skull as his banner, subsisting on alms, and proclaiming his deed,
the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall attain purification after twelve years of eating measured food.
By rescuing a Brāhmaṇa or twelve cows,
or likewise by bathing in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, one attains purification.
Having seen on the road a Brāhmaṇa or even a cow afflicted by a long-lasting or severe illness, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by setting them free from danger.
If one has brought back all the property of a Brahmin that was stolen, or if he has caused the thief to be killed,
or if he has been wounded by weapons for that purpose, he is purified even while still alive.
With the mantra "Svāhā to the body hairs," one should indeed offer the body starting from the hair down to the marrow, using these mantras in their proper sequence.
Or, having been made a target in battle, he may attain purification if slain;
even if still living, he is purified if he is near death, afflicted by a mortal wound.
Or, being self-restrained, having recited the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times in the forest while eating moderately, he would be purified by following the Sarasvatī river against its current.
Or, by giving sufficient wealth to a worthy recipient, one may attain purification;
for the sake of the purifier's own purification as well, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is prescribed by tradition.

One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the penance prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa; likewise shall one who destroys an embryo, and one who slays an Ātreyī woman, according to their respective castes.

One should perform the penance even if one has not actually killed [the victim], provided one approached with the intent to kill; however, if the Brāhmaṇa was engaged in a Soma sacrifice, one should prescribe double the penance.
Having drunk any one of these— liquor, water, clarified butter, cow urine, or milk— that is as hot as fire,
the drinker of liquor attains purification through death.
Clad in animal hair or wearing matted locks, he shall perform the penance for killing a Brahmin;
or he may eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for three years.

But having unintentionally drunk *surā* liquor, or [consumed] semen, feces, or urine, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.255)
That Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband;
in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, and a sow.
But the thief of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold must offer a mace to the king, explaining his own deed; whether slain by it or released, he remains impure.
Yājñavalkya 3.258ab: Without reporting it to the king, one who performs the penance for drinking liquor shall become pure.
Yājñavalkya 3.258cd: Or he may give gold equal to his own weight, or do what pleases the Brahmins.
He shall lie upon a bed of heated iron together with an iron woman;
having seized and cut off his testicles, he shall cast away his body toward the region of Nirṛti.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year,
or he may recite the Vedic Saṃhitā for three months while observing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
But he who associates with these for a year becomes equal to them.
He may marry a maiden from among them who is fasting and possesses no property.
However, having slain all those of low caste, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A Śūdra, even though deprived of the right [to perform Vedic rites], becomes pure through this same period of time.
The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month, remaining self-restrained;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following after cows, he is purified by the gift of a cow.
Or, being composed in mind, he should perform either the Kṛcchra or the Atikṛcchra penance;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and one bull as a gift.
Purification for minor offenses (upapātaka) may be achieved in this manner by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
or else by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance.
For killing a Kṣatriya, a man should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh,
or he may perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years.
A killer of a Vaiśya shall perform this penance for one year, or give one hundred and one cows;
a killer of a Śūdra shall perform this for six months, or else give ten cows.
Having caused the death of women who are of ill-conduct among Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Śūdras, one should give,
respectively, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep for the sake of purification.
Having killed a woman who has not committed a grave offense, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra;
likewise, for killing a thousand vertebrate animals, or an equal number of invertebrates.
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or birds,
one should drink milk for three days or perform the *kṛcchra* penance consisting of one-quarter of its requirements.
For an elephant, five dark-blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and rams, a bull; and for a crane, a three-year-old bull should be given.
Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous animal, a water-bird, a land-fowl, or a peacock, one should give a cow; but for killing a non-carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
For killing snakes, an iron rod [is the fine]; for a eunuch, tin and lead; for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; and for a horse, a piece of fine cloth.

But for those beginning with the elephant, if one is unable to give a drona of sesame seeds as a gift for each [killing] of a partridge, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for the purification of each individual case. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.274)

For killing a living being produced from fruit, flower, food, or sap, one must eat ghee; for killing something with bones, something small should be given as a gift, but for something boneless, one must perform a breath-control exercise (*prāṇāyāma*). For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc* verses should be recited.
For the useless cutting of medicinal herbs, one should follow a cow for a day while subsisting on milk alone.
One who has been bitten by a promiscuous woman, a monkey, a donkey, a dog, a camel, or the like, or by a crow,
becomes purified by performing breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) in water and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
With the two verses beginning "That semen of mine today" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.278ab), he should consecrate the spilled semen;
with that [semen], he should touch the space between the breasts and the middle of the eyebrows using the ring finger.
Having seen one's own reflection in water, one should mutter "May splendor be in me";
likewise, when impurity is seen, or in cases of fickleness and even falsehood, one should recite the Sāvitrī.
A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) who, having approached a woman, becomes an *avakīrṇin*,
is purified by sacrificing a donkey as an animal dedicated to Nirṛti.
Having neglected the begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill,
one who has violated his vow through lust should offer two oblations with these two [verses].
Then he should perform the propitiatory rite with the mantra "sam mā siñcantu"; however, for eating honey or meat, an *kṛcchra* penance and the remaining vows must be performed.
Having acted in opposition to his guru, one becomes purified only after propitiating him;
if the guru dies while being dispatched [on a mission], the [offender] should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. However, if a Brahmin dies while a service is being performed for him, there is no sin.
In the case of the digestion of bulls' meat, or in the administration of medicines and fire-rites,
the guilt of one who makes a false accusation is double that of one who speaks the truth.
He who speaks falsely incurs the guilt of one who has been falsely accused;
he who falsely charges another with a great sin or a minor offense shall subsist on water for a month, reciting sacred prayers with his senses restrained.
One who has been falsely accused should perform the Kṛcchra penance or the Āgneya penance;
alternatively, he should offer a Puroḍāśa cake to Vāyu or even a sacrificial animal to Vāyu.
If one approaches his brother’s wife without being authorized, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having approached a woman in her courses, he becomes purified by consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights.
One who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy of them (vrātyas), even if performing malevolent rites, shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances;
likewise, one who has caused the Veda to be forgotten shall subsist on barley for a year after abandoning one who has sought refuge.
A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) who dwells for one month in a cow-pen,
subsisting on milk and devoted to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts.
Having bathed in water, one should perform breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) after riding a donkey-cart or a camel-cart;
likewise, after bathing naked, eating, or having gone to a woman during the day.
Having addressed a guru as "thou," or having defeated a Brahmin in debate,
or having bound him with a garment, one must immediately appease him and fast for one day.
If one raises a staff against a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if one strikes him down, it is an *atikṛcchra*.
If blood flows, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; if the blood is internal, it is a *kṛcchra*.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin,
an expiation should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been stated.
The kinsmen of the outcast should carry a pot of water outside the village;
they should exclude him from all social functions.
When he has returned after having observed his vow, they should cause him to pour out a new jar of water; they should not despise him, nor should they live with him in any way whatsoever.
This same rule for those who have fallen from their caste is proclaimed for women as well:
they should be given clothing at the edge of the house, along with food and protection.
Approaching a man of low caste, causing an abortion, and harming her husband—
these also certainly constitute specific causes for the loss of status for women.
One should not dwell with those who harm one who has come for refuge, children, or women—
even if they have performed their penances— nor with those who are ungrateful.
When the water-pot has been discarded, he who stands in the midst of his kinsmen should provide fodder for the cows;
for this is the first act of hospitality shown to one who has been honored by the cows.
One whose offense is publicly known should perform a vow approved by an assembly;
however, one whose offense is not publicly known should perform a secret vow.
Having fasted for three nights and recited the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn while submerged in water, a killer of a Brahmin is purified by giving a milch cow.
Or else, subsisting on air for a day, he should stand in water and offer forty oblations of clarified butter while reciting, "Svāhā to the body hairs. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.302)
Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses, one becomes pure;
but a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, remaining in water while reciting the *rudra*, is purified.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated by reciting the *sahasra-śīrṣā* hymn.
At the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow should be given by each of these separately.
One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins,
as well as for those born from minor offenses (upapātaka) and for that which has not been specifically prescribed.
Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink purifying water consecrated by the syllable *oṃ*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.306)
Whether it be committed at night or even during the day, whatever has been done through ignorance—
all that perishes by performing the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) at the three periods of the day.
The recitation of the Śukriya and Āraṇyaka texts, and especially that of the Gāyatrī—
these, as well as the Rudra-ekādaśinī, are indeed removers of all sins.
Wherever a twice-born man perceives himself to be defiled,
in each such case there shall be an oblation with sesame seeds and likewise the recitation of the Gāyatrī.

Sinful acts, even those arising from the great crimes (mahāpātaka), do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Veda, who is patient, and who is intent upon the performance of the five sacrifices.
Subsisting on air while standing during the day and spending the night within water while gazing at the sun,
one who has recited the Gāyatrī a thousand times shall be purified— except for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity, truthfulness, sincerity,
non-violence, abstention from theft, gentleness, and self-restraint— these are declared in the Smṛti to be the *yamas*.
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, Vedic study, restraint of the sexual organ,
service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas).
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
one should fast on the following day and perform the *sāntapana* penance.
For six days, one should consume the substances of the Sāntapana penance separately, followed by a day of fasting;
this seven-day rite is known as the Mahāsāntapana Kṛcchra.
When one drinks the decoctions of *parṇa*, *udumbara*, *rājīva*, *bilva* leaves, and *kuśa* grass,
each separately, every day, it is declared to be the *parṇakṛcchra*.
One should drink each of these—boiled milk, ghee, and water—daily for one day, followed by a fast for one night; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for,
and fasting— this is proclaimed as the Pādakṛcchra penance.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold [fast] is called the *prājāpatya*.
This very same [practice], when one eats only as much food as fills the palm of the hand, becomes the *atikṛcchra*.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days.
A fast for twelve days is proclaimed as the *parāka*.
Eating oil-cake, water from rinsed rice, buttermilk, water, and barley meal on successive days,
followed by a fast for one night, is called the *saumya-kṛcchra*.
By practicing each of these in succession for three nights,
this is to be known as the "Weighing against a Man" (tulāpuruṣa), which lasts for fifteen days.
While performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should eat morsels of food the size of a peacock’s egg, increasing them according to the increase of the lunar days during the bright fortnight,
and decreasing them one by one during the dark fortnight.
Alternatively, one may consume two hundred and forty morsels of food in any manner whatsoever during the course of a month; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who bathes at the three daily sessions should perform the Kṛcchra or likewise the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
one should mutter purificatory prayers and consecrate the morsels of food with the Gāyatrī mantra.
For sins not specifically prescribed [by penance], purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon.
One who performs the *kṛcchra* penance while desiring righteousness shall obtain great prosperity;
with a well-concentrated mind, he attains the fruit of a great sacrifice.
Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya,
the sages spoke thus to that great-souled lord of yogis, who possessed immeasurable splendor:
Those who, unwearied, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and go to the third heaven.
One desiring knowledge shall obtain knowledge; likewise, one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
similarly, one desiring long life shall obtain long life, and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity.

For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a *śrāddha* ceremony from this [work], the satisfaction of the ancestors for him shall be inexhaustible; there is no doubt in this matter.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious,
and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth, by the retention of this scripture.
"O Bhagavān, please grant your approval for the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice to belong to that wise man who causes this [text] to be heard by the twice-born on every sacred festival day (parvan)."
Having heard this speech of the Sage, Yājñavalkya, his soul filled with joy, said,
"So be it," after having paid homage to the Self-Existent One.
[End of the Chapter on Expiation]
The *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* is completed.

www.sub.uni-goettingen.de/ebene_1/fiindolo/gretil/gretdias.pdf [Ācārādhyāya] [1. Upodghātaprakaraṇam]
Having honored Yājñavalkya, the lord of yogis, the sages said:
"Tell us in their entirety the duties of those belonging to the castes, the stages of life, and others."
Remaining in Mithilā, that lord of yogis, having meditated for a moment, said to the sages:
"In whatever region there is a black antelope, learn the duties in that place. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.2)
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) are the Vedas;
these are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of Dharma.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time through the right means— that possesses the complete characteristics of dharma.
Revelation, tradition, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma.
Of the acts of sacrifice, ritual conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the study of scripture, this indeed is the supreme duty: the perception of the Self through yoga.

An assembly of four who know the Veda and the Dharma, or even one consisting of those learned in the three Vedas—whatever they declare shall be the Dharma; or else a single person who is most excellent among those who know the inner self.
[2. The Section on the Religious Student (Brahmacārin)] The castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with those at the cemetery are indeed performed with sacred formulas.

The rite of conception (garbhādhāna) occurs during the fertile period; the rite for ensuring a male child (pumsavana) before the fetus moves; the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) in the sixth or eighth month; and these [rites], along with the birth ceremony (jātakarman), are performed at the time of birth.
On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month, the first outing;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be performed according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb is pacified;
these rites for women are performed silently, but the marriage ceremony is accompanied by mantras.

The initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth]; for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh year plus one; and for Vaiśyas, in the twelfth year, or according to family custom.
Having initiated the pupil with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) at the beginning,
the teacher should teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purification and proper conduct.
During the day and at the twilights, one should void urine and feces facing north with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) placed over the ear; if it is at night, one should face south.
Having risen with his penis still held [in the hand],
he should, without sloth, perform purification that removes odor and residue, using earth and water drawn from [the well].
Seated with his knees together in a clean place, facing either north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The bases of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand,
are respectively the *prājāpatya*, *pitrya*, *brāhma*, and *daiva* tīrthas.
Having sipped water three times and wiped his mouth twice,
he should touch the cavities of his head with water that is in its natural state and free from foam and bubbles.
The twice-born classes are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively;
a woman and a Śūdra are purified when it has merely touched the lips.
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the water-deities, sprinkling [water] over oneself, restraint of the breath,
worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head (śiras) preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and joined with each Praṇava;
this is the threefold restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama).
Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water consecrated by the three verses addressed to the waters,
he shall sit reciting the Sāvitrī until the appearance of the stars in the west.
One should thus stand during the morning twilight until the sun appears;
likewise, one should perform the fire-rite during both twilights.
Then he should salute his elders, saying,
"I am so-and-so," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the purpose of Vedic study.
When summoned, he should study; whatever he has obtained, he should offer to him;
and he should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body.

Those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, virtuous, and free from envy; who are capable, have obtained knowledge from a worthy teacher, and provide wealth; such good people should be taught the Dharma according to the law.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, a sacred thread, and a girdle;
he should go about begging alms from blameless Brahmins for his own sustenance.
The practice of wandering for alms among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas— in that order— is characterized by the word "bhava" at its beginning, middle, and end.

Having performed his fire-ritual, he should eat while maintaining silence, with the permission of his teacher, preceded by the *āpośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.31)
Established in the life of a student (brahmacarya), a Brāhmaṇa shall not eat food from a single person except in times of distress;
however, he may at will eat at a funeral feast (śrāddha), provided he does not violate his vow.
One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, fermented gruel, women, injury to living beings, gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and the like.
He who, having performed the [initiatory] rites, imparts the Veda to him is a Guru;
he who, having initiated him, gives him the Veda is declared to be an Ācārya.

The teacher, the officiating priest, and the performer of sacrifices are said to occupy a single portion [of respect]. These are to be honored according to their precedence, yet among them, the mother is the most venerable.
For each Veda, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall be twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until the Veda has been mastered, and the tonsure ceremony (keśānta) takes place in the sixteenth year.
The time for the initiation ceremony for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is up to the sixteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-fourth year respectively; beyond these, it is no longer permissible.
Henceforth, these persons, excluded from all religious duties, have fallen from the Sāvitrī; they are outcasts (vrātyas), except for the Vrātyastoma sacrifice.
Since Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are born once from their mothers and a second time from the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, they are therefore remembered as "twice-born."
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for achieving the highest good through sacrifices, austerities, and auspicious deeds.
The twice-born who studies the Rigvedic verses every day shall satisfy the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
He who daily studies the Yajus formulas according to his ability satisfies the gods with ghee and nectar,
as well as the ancestors with clarified butter and honey.
He who recites [these] every day shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and he shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and ghee through the Sāman chants.
Reciting the Atharva-Angiras hymns, the twice-born man should daily gratify the gods with fat and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter, according to his ability.
He who studies daily, according to his ability, the dialogues (vākovākya), the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsī verses, the Gāthās, the Itihāsas, and the sciences (vidyās); // Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.45 //
He provides satisfaction for the gods with an offering of meat, milk-rice, and honey;
and he should provide satisfaction for the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
Satiated themselves, they satisfy him with the auspicious fruits of all his desires;
whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain the fruit of each one.
The twice-born who is constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) enjoys here the fruit of three earths filled with wealth, as well as that of supreme austerity.
But a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher;
in his absence, he may dwell with the teacher's son, his wife, or even in the sacred fire.
Wearing away the body by this method, with his senses conquered,
he attains the world of Brahmā and is not born again in this world.
[3. Chapter on Marriage] Having given a gift to the teacher, he should perform the ceremonial bath, or do so with his permission;
having mastered the Veda, or the vows, or indeed both.
Having remained firm in his vow of celibacy, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—
one who has belonged to no other man before, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.
One should marry a woman who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same ṛṣi-lineage or gotra as oneself,
beyond the fifth degree on the mother’s side and likewise beyond the seventh degree on the father’s side.
From a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations,
even if it be prosperous, yet not afflicted by the defect of hereditary diseases.
A bridegroom of the same caste who possesses these very qualities, is learned in the Vedas,
has been carefully tested for virility, is young, wise, and beloved by the people, is the most excellent.
As for what is said regarding the taking of a Śūdra wife by those of the twice-born castes—this is not my opinion, because in that case, he himself is born [from her]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.56)
Three wives in the order of the castes, two likewise, and one respectively, are the lawful wives for the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; for one born as a Śūdra, she alone is his own.
The Brāhma marriage consists of giving away a girl, adorned according to one's means, after inviting her [to the ceremony];
the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides.
In the Daiva marriage, the bridegroom gives a cow and a bull to the officiating priest at the sacrifice; in the Ārṣa, he gives two cows.
The son born of the first [marriage] purifies fourteen generations, and the son born of the latter [the Ārṣa] purifies six.
Having said this, that body which is given to a seeker by one practicing dharma together with her purifies six ancestors on each side, along with herself. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.60)
The Āsura [form] is from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva is from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa is from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca is from the deception of the maiden. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.61)

The hand should be taken in marriage from women of the same caste; however, for the marriage of a twice-born man, a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, and a Vaiśya woman should take up a goad.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a sapinda relative, and likewise the mother— each subsequent one among these,
provided he is of sound mind, gives the girl in marriage upon the failure of each preceding one.
By not giving her away at each fertile season, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo;
however, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among those who are eligible.
A maiden is given only once; he who carries her off incurs the punishment of a thief.
Even if she has been given away, one may take her back from the previous husband if a more excellent suitor arrives.
One who gives a girl in marriage without disclosing her defects shall be punished with the highest fine;
but one who abandons a girl who is faultless, or falsely accuses her of a defect, shall be fined one hundred panas.
The *akṣatā* (unviolated) and the *kṣatā* (violated), as well as the *punarbhū* (one remarried after being consecrated again),
and the *svairiṇī* (self-willed woman) who, having abandoned her husband, resorts out of desire to a man of her own caste.

If she is childless, the husband's younger brother, with the permission of his elder, or a sapinda or a sagotra, having anointed himself with clarified butter and desiring a son, may approach her during her season.
He may go until conception occurs; otherwise, he would become fallen. Born according to this rule, he becomes his son as a *kṣetraja*.
One should cause an unfaithful wife to live deprived of her authority, in a state of impurity, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
Soma gave them purity, and the Gandharva gave them beautiful speech;
Agni gave them complete fitness for sacrifice; therefore, women are indeed fit for sacrifice.
Purification after menstruation is prescribed for sexual intercourse during the fertile period;
however, abandonment is ordained in cases of pregnancy, the killing of the husband, and likewise for other grave sins.
A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, one who is deceitful, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly,
one who bears only daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband, may be superseded by another wife.
A wife who has been formally accepted must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish.
Whether her husband is dead or alive, she who does not approach another man attains renown in this world and rejoices with him in the hereafter.

If he abandons a wife who is obedient, capable, the mother of his sons, and speaks kindly, he shall be made to pay a third part of his property; if he possesses no wealth, he must provide maintenance for her.
Wives must carry out the word of their husbands; this is the highest duty of a woman.
For one who is defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) is to be awaited until purification.
Because of this, women should be enjoyed and should be well protected, for through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons one attains infinity in this world and reaches heaven.
The nights of women during their fertile period are sixteen; among these, he should approach his wife on the even nights.
He should remain as one observing celibacy, avoiding the sacred festival days (parvan) and the first four nights.
Proceeding in this manner, a man should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla;
when the moon is in its full strength, he shall once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks.
Or he may act according to his desire, mindful of the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for women are declared to be worthy of protection.
Women should be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, paternal kinsmen, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and other relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Keeping the household utensils well-ordered, being skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure,
she, devoted to her husband, should perform the salutation of the feet of both parents-in-law.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey should renounce play, the adornment of her body, attendance at social gatherings and festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others.
The father shall protect the maiden; her husband, when she is married; and her sons in old age.
In their absence, her kinsmen shall protect her; a woman never has independence.
