She should not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles;
otherwise, she would be blameworthy in the absence of her husband.
Devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to their master, well-conducted, and having conquered their senses,
they obtain fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death.
If another wife of the same caste exists, he shall not have religious duties performed by her;
among wives of the same caste, according to the rule of dharma, no other may act except with the eldest.
Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband shall,
without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule.

[4. Chapter on the Distinction of Color and Birth] From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage; through blameless marriages, sons are born who increase the progeny. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.90)
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born; from a Vaiśya mother, an Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra mother, a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava.

From a Kṣatriya father and Vaiśya or Śūdra mothers, the sons Māhiṣya and Ugra are declared; from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, the son is Karaṇa. This is the rule prescribed for women who have been wedded.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
and from a Śūdra, one born [on a Brāhmaṇa woman] is a Caṇḍāla, excluded from all religious duties.
A Vaiśya woman bore to a Kṣatriya a Māgadha, and a Śūdra woman bore a Kṣattṛ;
furthermore, a Vaiśya woman begot a son, an Āyogava, from a Śūdra.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
these, born from inverse and natural orders, are to be known as both "untrue" (asat) and "true" (sat).
The excellence of caste is to be known as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation;
upon the reversal of actions, there is equality, and as before, there is the distinction of higher and lower.

[5. Chapter on the Duties of the Householder] A householder should perform the *smārta* rites daily in the nuptial fire, or in the fire brought at the time of inheritance; he should perform the *śrauta* rites in the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.97)
Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rites of purification,
the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsaṃdhyā), preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Having offered oblations into the fires dedicated to the Sun, he should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras,
master the meaning of the Vedas, and study various treatises.
And he should approach a lord for the sake of achieving security and prosperity;
having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship the gods and the ancestors.

To the best of one's ability, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite the Vedas, the Atharvaveda, the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, and spiritual knowledge (adhyātmavidyā).
The Bali-offering, the Svadhā-oblation, Vedic study, and the hospitable reception of guests are the great sacrifices for the spirits,
the ancestors, the gods, Brahman, and human beings.
From the remnants of the food offered to the gods, he should present the *bali* offering to the spirits;
he should also place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows.
Food should be given daily to the ancestors and to men, as well as water;
one should constantly perform the private recitation of the Veda, and one should not cook food for oneself alone.
Having first fed the children, the daughters living in the household, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick,
young girls, guests, and servants, the husband and wife may eat the remainder.
A twice-born person eating food should likewise perform the *āpośana* rite both before and after; thus the food should be made as if not naked and as if it were nectar.
One should give to the castes according to their status as guests, according to one's ability and in due order.
A guest must not be turned away even in the evening, even if only with words, a place to sit, grass, or water.
O monks, alms should be given with respect to one who observes his vows;
and one should feed friends, relations, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time.
One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya),
along with hospitable treatment, a seat, delicious food, and pleasant, truthful speech.

However, every year the following are worthy of the guest-offering (arghya): a Snātaka, a teacher, a king, a dear friend, one for whom one’s daughter is being wed, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.110)
A traveler and a learned Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas should be known as guests;
these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahmā.
One should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by those whose conduct is blameless; one should avoid restlessness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating.
He should follow the guest—a learned *śrotriya* who has been satisfied—until the boundary of his village;
he should spend the remainder of the day with disciplined men, beloved friends, and kinsmen.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions, having offered oblations into those fires and worshipped them,
and having eaten with his dependents to a degree that is not excessive, he should then go to rest.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, he should contemplate what is beneficial for himself;
he should not neglect virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times, according to his ability.
They are to be honored according to their sequence by virtue of knowledge, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves honor on account of his advanced age.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath after Vedic study, women, the sick, ascetics, and holders of the discus; among these, O King, the one who has performed the ritual bath is to be honored even by the king.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are the duties of the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
for the Brāhmaṇa, however, there are the additional duties of receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and teaching.
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
for a Vaiśya, it is traditionally held to be moneylending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born.
Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites,
he shall not neglect the five great sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses,
charity, self-control, compassion, and patience are the means for the practice of Dharma for all.
One should likewise adopt a conduct that is consistent with one's age, intelligence, wealth, speech, appearance, learning, lineage, and actions— conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit.
A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may indeed drink the Soma;
he whose food supply lasts for one year may perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice.
Every year the Soma sacrifice is to be performed, as well as the animal sacrifice at each solstice;
likewise, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be observed.
In the absence of these, a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a rite with deficient procedures when the necessary materials are available, for it would fail to yield its fruit.
By performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra, one is born as a Cāṇḍāla;
by not giving what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one becomes a vulture or even a crow.

Or he may possess grain sufficient for a granary or a jar; or he may live on what is gathered three days at a time, or even on what is sufficient for a single day; or he may subsist by gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains—among these, each subsequent mode is superior.
[6. Section on the Duties of a Snātaka] He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with his Vedic study, nor from improper sources;
he should never indulge in forbidden things, and he should always be contented. *Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra* 1.129.

If he suffers from hunger, he may seek wealth from kings, pupils, and patrons for whom he performs sacrifices; however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who rely on mere reasoning, heretics, and those who act like herons.
Wearing white garments, with his hair, beard, and nails kept short, and being pure,
he shall not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is untrue, nor should one be a thief or a usurer.
Wearing the sacred thread of a Dakṣāyaṇī, carrying a bamboo staff and a water-pot,
he should circumambulate clockwise the gods, clods of earth, cows, Brahmins, and trees.
But one should not urinate in a river, in shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one face fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or the twice-born.
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one, while impure, look at urine, feces, or the stars during an eclipse.
One should recite every mantra with the thought, "This is my vajra.
One may go about unsheltered during rain, and one should not sleep with the head facing west.
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
nor should one warm one's feet over fire, nor step over it.
One should not drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one awaken a sleeping person.
One should not play with dice or with those who destroy dharma, nor should one lie down to sleep with those who are diseased.
One should avoid forbidden actions, the smoke from a funeral pyre, crossing a river [by swimming],
and staying upon hair, ashes, chaff, charcoal, or a skull.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter a place by any way other than the gate;
nor should one accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures.
In the matter of receiving gifts, the butcher, the wheel-maker, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the king are wicked;
each of these is ten times more blameworthy than the one preceding it in order.
The ritual for commencing the study of the chapters (of the Vedas) is performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa,
or under the asterism Hasta when the medicinal herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedic texts (chandas) outside, near water, according to the prescribed rule.
There is a suspension of study for three days in the event of a death among pupils, officiating priests, teachers, or kinsmen;
likewise at the commencement (upākarmaṇi) and conclusion (utsarge) of the Vedic term, and when one who has mastered one's own Vedic branch (svaśākhā-śrotriya) dies.
Upon the thundering of clouds at twilight, a hurricane, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors;
and having completed the Veda, one should study the *Āraṇyaka* for a full day and night.
On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, or the eighth lunar day; during an eclipse of Rāhu; at the transitions of the seasons; or after eating, or having accepted food offered at a Śrāddha ceremony.

If an animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a mouse passes between [the teacher and pupil], there shall be a fast of one day and night; the same applies when the banner of Indra (the *śakradhvaja*) is lowered or raised.
When there is the sound of a dog, a jackal, a donkey, an owl, a *sāman* chant, or an arrow;
or when one is near impurity, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste (*antyaja*), a cremation ground, or a fallen person.
In an impure place, when one is personally impure, during a thunderstorm with lightning,
after eating while the hands are still wet, inside water, at midnight, or in a violent wind— one should not study.

During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mists, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at the house—one should run [to meet him]. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.150 //

When there is the sound of a donkey, a camel, a vehicle, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; or when trees grow on a barren field—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary prohibitions for study.
One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a sacrificial priest, a snātaka, a teacher, or a king, nor that of another's wife;
nor should one step on blood, feces, urine, spittle, ointments for the body, and the like.
Brahmins and those whose nature is that of Kṣatriyas must never be treated with contempt.
Until death one should desire prosperity; one should not touch anyone in their vital parts.
One should discard remnants of food, excrement, urine, and foot-wash water at a distance;
one should always properly practice the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
One who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food with his foot;
he should not revile or strike them, though he may strike his son or pupil.
One should practice dharma with effort through deed, mind, and speech;
however, one should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it leads away from heaven or is loathed by the world.
With mother, father, guests, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, maternal uncles, the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and relatives; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.157 //
By avoiding disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, children, wives, slaves, and kinsmen, a householder shall conquer all the worlds.
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first removing five lumps [of earth];
one may, however, bathe in rivers, natural reservoirs, lakes, and springs.
One should avoid another's bed, seat, garden, house, and vehicle;
and one should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress.

[The food] of misers, of bound thieves, of eunuchs, of actors, of flute-players, of those accused of crimes, of usurers, of courtesans, and of those initiated into a guild; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.161 //
[One should not eat the food] of physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and enemies;
nor of the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātyas, the hypocritical, and those who eat the remnants of others.
[One should not eat the food] of a woman without a husband, a goldsmith, a woman who has conquered her village [by charms], a sacrificer for a village,
a seller of weapons, a blacksmith, a weaver, or one who lives by dogs.
[One should avoid the food] of a cruel man, a king, a washerman, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter,
a laundryman, a professional wrestler, and those who live in the house of a paramour.
One must not eat the food of the slanderer and the liar, nor that of those who subsist by playing the wheel or by singing, nor likewise that of those who sell Soma.
Among Śūdras, those who are slaves, cowherds, family friends, and those who till half the field [in partnership],
as well as barbers and he who offers himself [as a servant], are those whose food may be eaten.

[7. Section on Edible and Non-edible Food] Food that is not honored, meat not intended for sacrifice, food containing hair or insects, what has turned sour, stale food, leavings, food touched by a dog, or food looked upon by an outcaste; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.167 //

One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food announced [beforehand], and food that has been passed around; as well as food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, and food intentionally touched with the foot.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations made from wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil or fat.

One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, of one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or of a barren cow; likewise, the milk of camels, of single-hoofed animals, of women, of wild animals, and of sheep.
One should avoid sacrificial offerings intended for the gods, the śigru plant, red exudations from incisions,
meat that has not been consecrated with ritual formulas, substances produced from dung, and mushrooms.
Flesh-eating birds, the dātyūha, parrots, peckers, ṭiṭṭibhas, cranes, one-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.172 //
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, and baka birds, as well as grain-scatterers;
and rice-milk preparations, barley-meal cakes, wheat-cakes, milk-porridge, and fried cakes, when prepared for no sacred purpose.
The kalaviṅka, the kākola, the kurara, the rajjudālaka,
web-footed birds, the khañjarīṭa, and wild animals and birds that are not [otherwise] known.
Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, dog meat, dried meat, or fish, one should dwell for three days observing a fast.
Having eaten onion, village-pig, mushroom, village-cock,
garlic, or leek, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the pangolin, and the hare may be eaten;
and among fish, those with the mouths of lions and the rohita fish may be eaten.
Likewise, the pāṭhīna, rājīva, and scaled fish may be eaten by the twice-born;
therefore, hear now the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.

In a life-threatening emergency, at a śrāddha ceremony, when it has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the request of a twice-born, one who eats meat after having worshipped the gods and ancestors incurs no fault. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.179)
That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.180)
By abstaining from meat, a Brahmin who is a sage, even while dwelling at home, attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice.

[8. Chapter on the Purification of Substances] For objects made of gold, silver, or lotus; for upper vessels, water-drawers, and stones; and for vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and hides.
The purification of bowls and cups is held to be by means of water;
however, vessels for the *caru* oblation, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and those containing oily substances are purified with hot water.
The sprinkling of the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the hide (ajina), the grain, the pestle (musala), the mortar (ulūkhala), and the fire-wood;
and the sprinkling of many grains and garments when they are gathered together.

The purification of sacrificial vessels made of wood, horn, or bone is by scraping; for those produced from fruit, it is by wiping with cow-hair; and during the performance of a sacrifice, it is by the hand.
Woolen cloth and silk are purified with alkaline water, cow's urine, and wood-apple (śrīphala); likewise, aśu-paṭṭa and kutapa are purified with ariṣṭa.
Linen cloth purified by being boiled with white mustard seeds; earthenware by being fired again;
the hand of an artisan; merchandise; alms-food; and likewise the mouth of a woman.
The purification of the ground is achieved by sweeping, burning, the passage of time, or the treading of cows;
likewise, a house is purified by sprinkling, scraping, and smearing, as well as by sweeping and smearing.
When food has been smelled by a cow, or when it is defiled by hair, flies, or insects,
water, ashes, or even earth must be thrown into it for the sake of purification.
The purification of tin, lead, and copper is by means of alkaline substances, acids, water, and earth;
that of bell-metal and iron is by ashes and water; and the purification of liquids is by immersion.
The purification of that which is smeared with impurities is by means of earth and water, through the removal of odor and the like;
what is commended by word, what is washed with water, and what is unknown [to be defiled] are always pure.
Water on the ground that is naturally pure and sufficient for one's thirst is clean;
likewise is meat fallen from the mouth of a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, a carnivorous beast, or the like.
A ray of light, fire, dust, shade, a cow, a horse, the earth, and the wind;
droplets and flies are pure when touched; and a calf is pure when discharging its milk.
The mouths of goats and horses are pure, but those of cows and humans are not;
roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.
Droplets from the mouth are pure, as are drops from the water used for sipping;
likewise, the beard that has entered the mouth is pure, and once one has removed what is stuck between the teeth, one becomes pure.
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and after changing one's garment, one who has already sipped water (ācamana) should sip water again.
The mud and water in a street that have been touched by outcastes, dogs,
or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks.

[9. Chapter on Giving] Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the preservation of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the protection of Dharma. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.198)
The Brahmins who are devoted to sacred learning and study are the source of all;
among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and even more excellent than they are those who possess the highest knowledge of the supreme self.
Neither by knowledge alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient;
that in which both conduct and these two [knowledge and austerity] reside is indeed proclaimed to be a worthy recipient.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
a wise man who desires his own welfare should not give anything whatsoever to an unworthy recipient.
A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
for by accepting it, he leads both the donor and himself downward.
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions;
even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, of good disposition, covered with cloth,
accompanied by a bronze vessel and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given away.
The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is tawny (kapilā), she further delivers his lineage up to the seventh generation.
By giving a cow with her calf and facing both ways, according to the previously mentioned rite, the giver attains heaven for as many *yugas* as there are hairs on the bodies of the two.
As long as both the feet and the face of the calf are visible within the womb,
for that long the cow is to be known as the Earth, until she releases her embryo.
Having given a cow, whether it be a milch-cow or even one that is not,
provided it is healthy and free from affliction, the donor is glorified in heaven.
Massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods,
washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away their leavings are equal to the gift of a cow.
By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter,
a dwelling, gold, and draft animals, one is glorified in heaven.
By giving a house, grain, safety, sandals, an umbrella, a garland, ointment, a vehicle, a tree, a favorite thing, or a bed, one becomes supremely happy.
Since Brahman consists of all dharmas and is superior to all gifts,
one who gives that [the Veda] attains the imperishable world of Brahman.
Even if he is capable of receiving gifts,
he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds which belong to those whose nature is to give.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers,
curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these may or may not be refused when offered.
One may accept food brought unasked even from a person of evil deeds,
except from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy.
For the sake of honoring the gods and guests, or for the purpose of supporting his teacher and dependents,
or indeed for his own subsistence, he may accept gifts from anyone.
[10. Chapter on the Faithful] The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, a time of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices,
the presence of suitable materials and Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign.
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the proper times for a Śrāddha.

One who is preeminent among all the Vedas, a learned scholar of the Veda (*śrotriya*), a knower of Brahman, young, one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, and one who knows the *Trimadhu* and *Trisuparṇa* hymns.

A sister’s son, a sacrificial priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, one who has kindled the Triṇāciketa fire, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.220.

Those Brahmins who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong students, and those devoted to their fathers and mothers, are the ones who bring perfection to the Śrāddha.

One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, a *kuṇḍa* or a *gola*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; YDh_1.222.

One who teaches for a fee, a eunuch, one who defiles a maiden, one accused of a heinous crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.223.

One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala*; the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.
On the day before [the ceremony], the self-possessed and pure host should invite the Brahmins;
they too must remain restrained in their thoughts, words, and physical actions.
Having honored those who have arrived with a welcome in the afternoon, he—
holding the *pavitra* grass in his hand and having himself sipped water for purification— should cause them to sit upon their seats.
One should invite an even number of Brahmins for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors;
this should be done in a clean place that has been strewn [with grass] and slopes toward the south.
Two [seats] are for the gods, facing east; three for the ancestors, facing north; or even one for each.
The same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common procedure (tantra) for all.
Having provided water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for seats, he should, being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (RV 7.35.1).
Then, having scattered barley grains over a vessel containing a purifier (pavitra),
he should pour water with the verse "May the divine waters be auspicious to us" (śaṃ no devīr) and likewise scatter barley grains with the formula "Thou art barley" (yavo 'si).
With the mantra "yā divyā," he should pour the *arghya* water into their hands;
having given water, he should offer perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps.
Likewise, he should give a garment and water for the purpose of washing the hands;
then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should perform the rite for the ancestors (pitṛs) in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having offered double-folded kuśa grass and having invoked the ancestors with the verse "uṣantas tvā," he should, being permitted by them, recite the mantra "āyantu naḥ" thereafter.
Having scattered sesame seeds all around with the mantra "apahatāḥ," one should perform the functions of barley using sesame seeds, and offer the *arghya* and other honors as before.
Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down below with the words, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors."
Intending to offer it into the fire, he takes up food soaked in clarified butter and asks, "Shall I proceed?
Having been authorized with the words, "Do so," he offers it into the fire as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
With a concentrated mind, he should present the remains of the oblation in vessels,
using whatever are available, and especially those made of silver.
Having given the food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra "The earth is the vessel";
then, having recited "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should cause the thumb of the twice-born guest to rest upon the food.
Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyahṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as necessary for comfort.
Free from anger and without haste, he should give food that is desirable and fit for oblation;
and until [the guests] are satisfied, he should mutter purificatory texts as well as the previously mentioned prayers.
Having taken food and being satisfied, and having obtained permission regarding the remainder,
one should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once for each [guest].
Taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing the south,
he should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).
In the same manner, one should likewise offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the maternal grandfathers;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the Svasti formula and the offering of the inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka).

Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word "svadhā. Being authorized with the words "Let it be spoken," he should say to the invited guests, "Let the svadhā be uttered for the ancestors."
When they have said, "Let there be *svadhā*," he should then pour water on the ground;
and when the Brahmins have said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," he should mutter this: Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.245.
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.246)
Having spoken thus and having uttered pleasant words, he should bow down and dismiss them with the words "vāja vāja," being joyful, while performing the dismissal beginning with the ancestors.
But having turned face upwards that vessel for the ancestors into which the remnants were previously placed in the *arghya* vessel, one should dismiss the Brahmins.
Having circumambulated [the vessel] from left to right, he should eat what has been served to the ancestors;
he should observe celibacy for that night together with the Brahmins.
Thus, proceeding in a clockwise direction during a rite for prosperity, one should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors with offerings;
the ritual acts are performed with barley, and the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) are mixed with curd and jujube fruits.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of the gods, with only one offering of water (*arghya*) and one purifying blade of grass (*pavitraka*);
it is indeed performed without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
At the dismissal of the Brahmins, he should say "May you be satisfied" at the place where the offerings are inexhaustible;
they should reply, "We are satisfied."
One should prepare four vessels containing scented water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," he should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is also performed for a woman as an Ekoddiṣṭa.
For one whose *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite occurs before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year.
On the anniversary of the day of death, the rite should be performed every month for a year;
likewise, it should be performed annually, while the first rite is performed on the eleventh day.
One should give the morsels of food to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else throw them into fire or water;
while Brahmins are present, one must not clear away the remnants of the twice-born's meal.
Indeed, by means of sacrificial food (haviṣya) one satisfies [the ancestors] for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
likewise by fish, deer, antelope, bird, goat, and spotted deer meat.
The ancestors, when offerings are made here, are satisfied for increasing periods of one month each by the meat of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively.
The meat of the rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, honey, or the food of sages;
the meat of iron-colored fish, large leafy vegetables, and the flesh of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane.
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
A daughter, those who seek a daughter in marriage, cattle, virtuous sons,
as well as gambling, agriculture, trade, and animals with cloven and uncloven hooves.
The giver of a Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desired objects. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.263)
On the days beginning with the first lunar day, excluding the fourteenth,
food is offered there for those who have been slain by weapons.
For one obtains heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength, as well as a preeminent son, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, and auspiciousness. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.265)
As well as the turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], success in trade and other such pursuits,
freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly bestows the Śrāddha offering obtains wealth, the Vedas, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī,
he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires.
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the Śrāddha;
when satiated by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
When pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.270)

[11. The Section on the Ritual for Gaṇapati] Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā for the purpose of accomplishing the success of ritual actions and for the lordship over the hosts (gaṇas). Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.271.
Learn now the characteristics of one who is afflicted by that [demon]:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men.
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he dwells together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels.
Even while walking, he imagines himself followed by others;
dejected and with his undertakings frustrated, he sinks down without apparent cause.
Afflicted by that [evil eye], the prince does not obtain a kingdom;
the maiden does not find a husband, and the woman does not obtain offspring from her womb.

The teacher does not attain the status of an ācārya, nor does the learned one [attain] discipleship; likewise, the student does not obtain his studies, the merchant does not gain profit, and the farmer does not succeed in his cultivation.
On an auspicious day, his ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed according to the prescribed rules,
after he has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.

Likewise, for one whose head is anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, virtuous Brahmins should pronounce the benediction of *svasti*.

One should throw into the water earth from a horse stable, from an elephant stable, from an anthill, from a confluence, and from a lake, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), fragrant substances, and guggulu resin.
Having brought water from a lake in four jars of a single color,
one should then place the auspicious seat upon a red bull-hide.
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, purified by the seers—I sprinkle you with it; may the *pāvamānī* verses purify you.
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the Seven Seers grant you fortune.
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, at the parting of your hair, or on your head; whatever is in your forehead, your ears, or your eyes—may the waters destroy it forever.
Having bathed, he should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of Udumbara wood into his head, while holding Kuśa grass with his left hand.
And with [the names] Mita, Sammita, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa,
Kūśmāṇḍa, and Rājaputra, [one should offer oblations] at the end accompanied by the word "svāhā."
Having spread *kuśa* grass on all sides upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, he should offer [the oblation] with their names and with *bali*-mantras accompanied by salutations.
Rice grains both prepared and unprepared, as well as rice mixed with minced meat, cooked fish and likewise raw fish, and meat—only these [are permitted]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.287)
Variegated and fragrant flowers, as well as the three kinds of spirituous liquor, radishes, fried cakes, sweetmeats, and garlands of *uṇḍeraka*— these he should offer.
Having collected all these— curd-rice, milk-rice, and flour-cakes with molasses and water— and having placed them upon the ground, he should then place his head there.
Then he should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka,
by offering a full añjali as an arghya consisting of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers.
Grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me fortune;
grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires.
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
he should feed the Brahmins and also give a pair of garments to his preceptor.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By constantly performing the worship of the Sun, as well as the tilaka of his Lord and that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain success.

The Section on the Pacification of Planets] One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, and nourishment, or likewise one performing malevolent rites, should perform the sacrifice to the planets.
The Sun, the Moon, the Son of the Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu are known as the planets.
The planets should be fashioned in order from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal.
They should be depicted on a cloth with their respective colors, or in mandalas using fragrant pigments;
garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors.
Fragrances, offerings, and incense of guggulu should be presented;
and sacrificial oblations (caru) accompanied by mantras must be prepared for each respective deity.
The verses "ākṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed to be used according to their respective order.
"Bṛhaspate ati yat aryaḥ," likewise "annāt parisrutaḥ";
"śaṃ no devīḥ," likewise "kāṇḍāt"; and "ketuṃ kṛṇvan" for these [verses].
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, then pippala,
udumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in their respective order.
For each [deity], however, one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations should be offered,
combined with honey and clarified butter, or with curd and milk.
Rice with molasses, milk-rice, sacrificial food, rice mixed with milk,
rice with curd, clarified butter, flour-meal, meat, and variegated rice.
In this manner, a wise man should provide food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets,
honoring them with due ceremony and according to his ability or as it may be obtained, in accordance with the prescribed rule.
A cow, a conch shell, a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, a black cow, iron, and a goat— these are indeed remembered as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) in their respective order.
And whoever is in distress at any time should honor him with effort;
for Brahmā has granted this boon to them: "When you are honored, you shall honor [others] in return."
The rise and fall of kings, as well as the existence and non-existence of the world, are dependent upon the planets; therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
One should perform this hospitality for the planets even once a year;
endowed with health and strength, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
[13. Chapter on the Duties of Kings] One who possesses great energy, is liberal, grateful, and serves the elders;
who is humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.309 //
One who is not dilatory, possessed of mindfulness, noble-minded, and likewise not harsh;
righteous, free from vices, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.

Furthermore, that lord of men was disciplined in the protection of his own weak points through the science of metaphysics (ānvīkṣikī) and likewise through the science of government (daṇḍanīti), as well as in the science of economics (vārtā) and the triple Vedas (trayī).
He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure;
with them he should deliberate on the kingdom, and thereafter with a Brahmin, and finally by himself.
He should appoint as his domestic priest (purohita) one who is renowned for his learning, skilled in astrology,
proficient in the science of government (daṇḍanīti), and likewise versed in the Atharvāṅgiras [Veda].
For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
he should indeed choose officiating priests and should likewise perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
And he should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings.

An oblation offered into the fire of a Brahmin from the presence of a [common] fire— one that is not spilled, not disturbed, and not defiled by expiatory rites— is declared here to be the most excellent.
One should seek what has not been obtained through righteous means; what has been obtained, one should protect with effort;
what has been protected, one should increase through prudent policy; and what has been increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients.
Having granted land or established a fixed endowment,
the king should cause a deed to be executed for the information of future benevolent rulers.
On a cloth or on a copper plate, the lord of the earth, having inscribed his own lineage and himself, marked with his own seal; YDh_1.319.
One should cause a firm edict to be issued, specifying the extent of the land received, describing the boundaries of the gift,
and completed with one's own hand and the date.

He should dwell in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the protection of his people, his treasury, and himself.
In each of those matters, he should appoint supervisors who are proficient, skillful, pure,
and diligent in the affairs of revenue and expenditure.
There is no duty for kings higher than this: that wealth acquired in battle is given to the Brahmins, and constant fearlessness is granted to the subjects.
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land,
without turning their backs and with weapons used without deceit, go to heaven like yogis.
When those who do not retreat have been broken, the king takes the merit of their steps, which are equal to a sacrificial rite; but he takes the evil deed of those who are slain while fleeing.
One should not strike one who proclaims "I am yours," a eunuch, one who is unarmed, one who has joined another's side, one who has retreated, or one who is merely looking on at the battle.
Having performed his protective rites and arisen, he should personally inspect income and expenditure;
then, having attended to legal affairs, he should bathe and eat according to his desire.
Gold brought by the attendants he should deposit in the treasuries;
thereafter, having consulted with his ministers, he should review the secret agents and dispatch messengers.
Then he may roam at his own pleasure, or, having met with his ministers and inspected his forces, he should deliberate together with the commander-in-chief.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret reports of his spies;
he may enjoy himself with songs and dances, and he should likewise recite his sacred study.
He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise wake up to that same sound;
he should contemplate the scriptures with his intellect, as well as all his duties.
Then, having been greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers, he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and among others.
Having seen [the results], he should give cows, gold, and land to astrologers and physicians;
furthermore, he should give dwellings and houses to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).

A king should be patient toward Brahmins, straightforward toward those who are affectionate, and wrathful toward his enemies; toward his circle of servants and his subjects, he should be like a father.
Protecting his subjects according to the law, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for the protection of subjects is superior to all other forms of giving.
He shall protect the subjects from being oppressed by flatterers, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like, and especially from the scribes.
Whatever offense the subjects commit when they are not protected,
half of that belongs to the king, since he receives taxes from them.
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed to govern the realm,
the king should honor the virtuous and put to death those who act contrarily.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
he should always cause those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) to dwell [in his realm], honoring them with gifts, respect, and hospitality.
A king who increases his own treasury from the kingdom by unjust means shall, before long, lose his royal fortune and meet with destruction along with his kinsmen.
The fire born from the suffering and oppression of the subjects does not cease until it has consumed the king’s lineage, his fortune, and his very life.
Whatever duty belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,
that very same duty he attains in its entirety while bringing another's kingdom under his control.
In whatever country there is a particular custom, legal practice, or family tradition,
that very same thing must be maintained when one has come under its influence.
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, he should keep his counsel well-guarded so that others do not know it until the results of his actions have come to fruition.

The enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, the one beyond him, and the one beyond that— this circle [of states] should be considered in due order, employing the strategic means beginning with conciliation (sāman).
The means—conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise punishment—may succeed when properly employed; yet punishment is the last resort when no other way remains.
He should properly deliberate upon these six political expedients: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and duplicity.
When the enemy kingdom is endowed with the qualities of abundant crops, while he himself is weak and his own mounts and men are joyful and vigorous, then he should march forth.
The accomplishment of action is established upon both destiny and human effort;
therein, destiny is that which was manifested through human effort in a previous body.

Some of those possessed of wise intellects maintain that the fruit [of action] arises from destiny, others from inherent nature, some from time, some from human effort, and others from a combination of these.
For just as a chariot cannot move with only one wheel,
so destiny does not succeed without human effort.
Since the acquisition of a friend is superior to the acquisition of gold or land, one should strive to obtain such a friend and, with a concentrated mind, protect the truth.
The sovereign, the ministers, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Having obtained that [kingly power], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times.
He cannot be led away by right means by one who is greedy, of unrefined intellect, untruthful to his word, impure, lacking good companions, or lacking wisdom. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.355 //
When applied according to the scriptures, it shall bring joy to the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it will provoke their wrath.
Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
however, proper punishment brings a king heaven, fame, and victory.
Whether it be a brother, a son worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle— there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king.
That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and causes those deserving of death to be executed properly,
has performed sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial fees.
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine legal cases every day, each yielding a fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.

Having disciplined those who have deviated from their own duty— whether they belong to families, castes, guilds, corporations, or even rural districts— the king shall establish them on the right path.
A mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three *gaura* seeds are one *yava*; three *yava* are one middle-sized *kṛṣṇala*;
five *kṛṣṇala* are one *māṣa*; and sixteen *māṣa* are one *suvarṇa*.
Four or five suvarṇas are proclaimed to be one pala;
two kṛṣṇalas make one silver māṣa, and sixteen of those make a dharaṇa.
Ten *dharaṇas* make a *śatamāna*, and ten [of those] make a *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* make a *niṣka*; a *kārṣika* is a copper coin known as a *paṇa*.
A fine of eighty-one thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement;
half of that is declared the middle, and half of that again is recorded as the lowest.
The punishment of reproach, the punishment of words, the punishment of fines, and likewise corporal punishment—
these should be applied either individually or collectively, according to the nature of the offense.
Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength,
as well as the age, the action, and the wealth [of the offender], he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
[End of the Ācārādhyāya] [II. Vyavahārādhyāya] [1. Sādhāraṇavyavahāramātṛkāprakaraṇam] (The General Section on the Framework of Legal Procedure)
Free from anger and greed, the king should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the treatises on Dharma.
The king should appoint as members of his council those who are accomplished in learning and study, who know the Dharma, who speak the truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend.
If, however, due to the demands of business, the king is unable to personally oversee legal proceedings,
he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa learned in all the Dharmas to preside over them together with the court members.

Whether out of passion, greed, or even fear, those members of the court who act contrary to the law or fail in their mindfulness shall each be fined double the amount of the fine imposed on the litigant.
When one who has not been overcome by others through a path deviating from the conduct prescribed by tradition brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a ground for legal procedure.
The defendant must write down in his presence that which has been stated by the plaintiff,
marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other such identifying characteristics.
The answer to the matter heard [by the court] shall be written down in the presence of the plaintiff;
thereafter, the defendant shall immediately set forth the proof for the matter he has asserted.
Upon the establishment of that [evidence], one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
This fourfold judicial procedure has been set forth for use in legal disputes.
[2. Chapter on the Special Categories of Legal Procedure] One should not bring a counter-charge against someone without having first resolved one's own accusation;
nor should one, by means of another, alter what has been stated by a defendant who has been formally charged.
In cases of mutual assault and in matters of violence, one may bring a counter-charge;
a surety capable of seeing the case through to its conclusion must be accepted from both parties.
If he denies it, the defendant shall pay that amount to the king as well;
one who makes a false accusation shall pay double the value of the claim.

In cases of violence, theft, verbal abuse, false accusations regarding a cow, or a woman, one should initiate a lawsuit immediately; in other matters, the time is prescribed according to one's own discretion.
He moves from one place to another, licks the corners of his mouth,
his forehead perspires, and his face becomes discolored.
With words faltering as they grow parched, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor speech or sight, and he even distorts his lips.
He who undergoes a change from his natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body—
whether in a legal proceeding or as a witness— is proclaimed to be wicked.
He who, having initiated a suit on a doubtful matter, fails to prove his case independently, or he who absconds,
or he who says nothing when summoned— he is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment.
When witnesses exist on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff;
but when the initial claim is refuted, they belong to the defendant.
If the dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine,
his own wager, and the debt to the creditor.
Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the facts;
for even a fact, if not presented [in court], is lost in a legal proceeding.

If a defendant denies a written document, but is proved in one part of it, he shall be made by the king to pay the entire debt; however, that which was not declared [in court] shall not be accepted [as evidence].
When there is a conflict between two Smṛti texts, the principle that prevails in practice is this:
the Dharmaśāstra is more authoritative than the Arthaśāstra. This is the established rule.
Written documents, possession, and witnesses are declared to be the means of proof;
in the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
In all disputes concerning property, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful.
For land that is being enjoyed by another, the loss to one who sees it but does not speak out occurs after twenty years;
for property [other than land], the loss occurs after ten years.

Except for property placed under a boundary, deposits, and the wealth of the mentally disabled or children, as well as the wealth of sealed deposits, the king’s women, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 2.25 //
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates deposits and other such items to pay the wealth to the owner,
and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity.
Title-deed is superior to possession, except in the case of property inherited through prior succession;
even if there is a title-deed, it has no force at all where there is not even a small amount of possession.
But he by whom the title-deed was executed, being summoned, must produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more authoritative.
If one who was accused should have died, his heir shall clear him [of the debt];
in that case, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of a legal title.
Guilds appointed by the king, then trade associations, and finally families—
each preceding one among these is to be understood as more authoritative than the following in the legal procedure for men.
One should set aside legal transactions brought about by force or fraud, as well as those conducted by women, at night, inside a house, outside [the village], or by enemies. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.31)
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, in distress, a child, or terrified,
as well as one that is incoherent, is not valid.
Property lost and then recovered must be returned by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to the value of that property.
Having found a treasure-trove, the king shall give half to the twice-born;
the learned twice-born, however, may take it all, since he is the master of everything.
When another person has found a treasure, the king shall take a sixth part of it;
if he is discovered without having reported it, he shall be made to pay that [treasure] as well as a fine.
The king must restore property stolen by thieves to the inhabitant of the realm;
for by not restoring it, he incurs the same guilt as the thief.
[3. Chapter on the Non-payment of Debt] Interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month when there is collateral;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per month. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.37)
But those who travel through forests shall pay ten percent, and those who travel by sea a hundred percent;
or all may pay interest as agreed upon by themselves, regardless of their respective castes.
The maximum interest on the offspring of cattle and women is eightfold;
that on clothes, grain, and gold is fourfold, threefold, and twofold respectively.
One who, having approached [the court], is proving his case shall not be censured by the king;
but one who, while being tried, goes to the king [to complain against the judge], shall be punished and made to pay that wealth.
A debtor shall be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they presented their claims;
however, after having paid the Brāhmaṇas, he shall pay the king immediately thereafter.
The king shall compel the debtor to pay ten percent of the amount proved due;
and the creditor, having recovered his wealth, shall be made to pay five percent.
One may compel a person of low birth who has become impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his means.
If one does not accept one's own loaned wealth when it is being offered,
provided that it has been deposited with a neutral intermediary, it shall not increase beyond that point.
Whatever debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who are undivided,
the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad.
A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife or son, nor one contracted by a son;
likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, except for the sake of the family.

A son shall not pay, on behalf of his father, debts incurred through liquor, passion, gambling, fines, or taxes, nor those remaining from such obligations, nor any gift made for no purpose. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.47)
The husband shall pay the debt of a cowherd, a liquor-seller, an actor, a washerman, or a hunter's wife,
because their livelihood depends upon him.
A woman shall pay a debt incurred by her husband, or one contracted jointly with him; or she may pay a debt contracted by herself. She is not liable for any other debt.
Whether the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons; if it is denied, it is established by witnesses.

The heir to the estate shall be made to pay the debt, as shall the husband who takes the widow; likewise, the son whose property is not dependent on others shall pay for one who dies without a son and leaves no heirs.
Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son,
standing as a surety, contracting debt, or acting as a witness is not permitted before partition.
Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment;
however, in the case of the first two types failing, the debt must be paid by the sons as well.

Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stood as sureties for payment (*dāna*) shall pay it.
If there are many guarantors who would each pay the debt with their own shares,
then among those who share a single liability, the creditor may proceed as he pleases.
But whatever wealth a surety is compelled to pay publicly to the creditor,
that shall be twice as much when it is to be repaid by the debtor.
In the case of offspring and livestock, the interest is indeed threefold;
grain is said to be fourfold, and likewise, liquids are eightfold.
A pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, provided it is not redeemed;
however, a pledge for use (kālakṛta) is forfeited with the lapse of time, whereas a pledge to be enjoyed for its produce (phalabhogya) is never forfeited.
No interest accrues on a pledge when it has been used by the creditor; nor does it accrue when a pledge that yields a benefit is lost.
If the pledge is destroyed or ruined, except through an act of God or the king, it must be restored.
If, after the pledge has been accepted, it becomes worthless even while being preserved,
another object may be pledged in its stead, or the creditor may take his share of the debt from the debtor's wealth.
He shall cause the debtor to pay back with interest the money borrowed on the security of character;
however, he shall cause the payment of double the amount for goods received as a pledge under a formal agreement (satyaṃkāra).
When the debtor has arrived, the pledge must be released; otherwise, he would become a thief.
If the creditor is absent, the debtor, having deposited the money with a member of the creditor's family, may take back his pledge.
Or it may remain there at its value fixed at that time, without interest;
or, with the consent of the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
But when the debt has become doubled,
then indeed the pledge must be released once the money produced from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and reached the amount of double the original debt.

The Section on Deposits] When an object is placed in another's hand without being described and while remaining in its original state, that is a sealed deposit (*aupanidhika*); it must be returned exactly as it was.
However, he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate (natural calamities), or by thieves;
but if it is not returned when sought, he shall be made to pay the value and a fine equal to that amount.
One who lives by his own will [on another's property] shall be punished and made to pay that [property] along with interest;
this same rule applies to goods borrowed, pledged, deposited, or entrusted as a deposit.
[5. Chapter on Witnesses] Those who are ascetic, charitable by nature, of noble birth, speakers of truth,
devoted primarily to dharma, upright, having sons, and endowed with wealth.

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of Vedic (śrauta) and Smārta rites; they are prescribed to be of the same caste and class as the parties, or all may serve for all.
Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused, performers on stage, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired faculties; YDh 2.70.
An outcast, a relative, one interested in the matter, an associate, an enemy, a thief,
one who commits violence, and one whose fault has been observed— these, beginning with the "expelled," are not to be admitted as witnesses.
Even a single person who knows the law may serve as a witness if he is approved by both parties;
however, in cases of adultery, theft, verbal assault, and violent crime, everyone is eligible to be a witness.
He should cause the witnesses, who are present near the plaintiff and the defendant, to hear [the following]:
"Those worlds which are for those who commit sins, as well as for those who commit mortal sins (mahāpātakin)," Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.73.
And those worlds which belong to those who set fire to dwellings, and those which belong to the slayers of women and children—
he who gives false testimony attains them all.
Whatever merit you have performed throughout hundreds of previous births,
know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood.
For if men fail to give testimony regarding a debt secured by a pledge,
the king shall cause them to pay the entire amount on the forty-sixth day.
For that lowest of men who does not give testimony even though he knows [the facts], is indeed equal to false witnesses in his sin and also in his punishment. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.77)
In a case of division, the testimony of the majority is to be accepted; likewise, when the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities.
But when there is a division even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most excellent in virtue should be adopted.
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
for him who asserts otherwise, defeat is certain.
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous,
or twice as numerous, should state it otherwise, the former witnesses shall be considered false.
The forger and the witnesses shall each be punished separately;
the punishment is twice the amount of the disputed sum, and it is ordained that a Brāhmaṇa shall be banished.
He who, having been made to hear the testimony from others, conceals it, being shrouded in darkness, shall be made to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, he shall banish.
Where the execution of those belonging to the [four] castes would otherwise occur, there one may speak untruth as testimony;
to purify that act, the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī.
Section on Documents] Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement, a document with witnesses should be executed; in that case, the creditor’s name must be mentioned first.
It shall be marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, one's own lineage (gotra),
fellow-student status, and the names of one's father and so forth.
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall write his own name by his own hand:
"What is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so."
And those witnesses, being equal in status, shall each write by their own hand, preceded by the name of their father, "I, so-and-so, am a witness here. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.87)
Then, at the end, the scribe shall write: "This has been written by me, [Name], the son of [Name], at the request of both parties. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.88)
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is considered valid evidence, except when it was produced by force or fraud. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.89)
A debt recorded in writing must be paid by only three generations of persons;
however, the pledge is enjoyed as long as that debt has not been repaid.
If a document is located in another country, is difficult to read, lost, rubbed out, stolen, torn, burnt,
or otherwise destroyed, one should have another document executed.
The validity of a doubtful document may be established by means of a handwriting sample written by the party's own hand and other such evidence,
as well as through reasoning, the acquisition of what was due, performance of the act, distinctive marks, connection, and the cause of its arrival.
The debtor, having paid the money, should write on the back of the document;
or the creditor, having received the payment, should provide a receipt marked with his own hand.
Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or else have another executed for the sake of clarity;
or whatever document there may be that is accompanied by witnesses, that must be delivered in the presence of witnesses.
Chapter on Ordeals] The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals used here for the sake of purification;
these are employed in cases of grave accusation when the accuser has placed his head upon the stake. *Yājñavalkya Smṛti* 2.95.
Or, by mutual consent, one may perform the work while the other supervises the head;
or even without the head-fee, one may perform it in cases of treason against the king or for a mortal sin.
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on,
he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas.
For women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brahmins, and the sick, the ordeal shall be by balance;
for a Śūdra, by fire or water; or seven barley grains by poison.
One should not carry a ploughshare, nor poison, nor a scale for less than a thousand [palas];
however, for the sake of the king or in cases of formal accusation, they may be carried, provided one is always pure.
The accused, having mounted the scale, shall be attended by experts skilled in weighing;
once balanced with the counterweight, a mark shall be made, and he shall then be lowered from it.
O Tula, you were created by the gods of old as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the balance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.102)
Then, having observed that his hands have been rubbed with rice grains,
he should place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread for that same duration.
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins.
When he has spoken thus, one should place upon both his hands a smooth iron ball weighing fifty palas and heated to the color of fire.
Taking it up, he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles;
each circle should be known as sixteen finger-breadths in width, with the same interval between them.
Having released the fire, if he has crushed the grains but they are not burnt, he attains purity;
if the rice-ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, he should take it up again.
Having sworn an oath over water with the words, "O Varuṇa,
protect me by truth," one should seize the knees of a person standing in water reaching up to the navel and cause him to drink the water.
If another swift man, having brought back the arrow released at that same moment,
should see the man's body submerged when he has departed, he shall obtain purification.
O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in the dharma of truth;
protect me from this curse, and by virtue of that truth, become nectar for me.
Having spoken thus, he should consume the Śārṅga poison born of the snowy mountains;
if it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare him pure.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having poured it out, one should then make him drink three handfuls of that water.
If a terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone before the fourteenth day, he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt.

[8. Chapter on the Division of Inheritance] If the father should make a division, he may divide the sons according to his will; either by giving the best share to the eldest, or all may be equal sharers. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114)

If he should divide [the estate] into equal shares, the wives whose property (*strīdhana*) has not been given by their husband or by their father-in-law must be made equal sharers. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.115)
If a capable father, though not desiring it, makes a separate allotment by giving something to some sons,
that distribution among those who are otherwise divided unequally is declared to be lawful, as it was made by the father.
After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally;
the daughters shall take the remainder of the mother's estate after the debt has been cleared, and in their absence, the [mother's] lineage [shall inherit].
Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without using the paternal estate,
as well as what is obtained through friendship or received at marriage, shall not belong to the heirs.
If one recovers property that was taken away but had come to him by succession, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning.
When the property arises as a common whole, however, the division is traditionally held to be equal;
but for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father.
Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, or a hereditary grant, or even movable property, the ownership therein is indeed equal for both the father and the son. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.121)
A son born after the partition of the estate from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share;
or that share may be determined from the visible assets, after deducting the income and expenses.
Whatever has been given to him by his parents shall be his property alone;
when they divide the estate after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share.
But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own shares, [should be so consecrated].
The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, shall receive four, three, two, and one shares;
those born of a Kṣatriya, three, two, and one shares; and those born of a Vaiśya, two and one shares.
If any property that was taken from one another is discovered after the partition has been made, they shall divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule.
A son begotten by appointment upon the wife of a man who has no son is,
according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral oblation for both fathers.
The legitimate son is one born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra).
The son of the soil (kṣetraja) is one begotten upon the wife by a kinsman of the same lineage or by another.
A son born secretly in the house is known as the "secret-born" (gūḍhaja);
one born of an unmarried girl is considered the "maiden-born" (kānīna), the son of his maternal grandfather.
A son born of a woman who has been previously married, whether she was previously intact or not, is a *paunarbhava*.
A son whom either the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* (given) son.
One who is purchased by both [parents] is a "purchased" son; one who is sold is a "sold" son; one who is made so by himself is a "self-made" son;
one who gives himself is a "self-given" son; and one conceived in the womb and born together [with the bride] is a "son received with the bride" (sahoḍhaja).
But he who is taken up after having been abandoned becomes an *apaviddha* son;
among these, each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of each preceding one.
This rule has been declared by me regarding sons born of wives of the same caste;
however, even one born of a Śūdra woman through a Śūdra father out of desire shall be a sharer of the inheritance.
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him (the son of a remarried woman) a recipient of half a share;
one who has no brothers shall take the whole, except for the sons of the daughters.
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers,
as well as their sons, the agnates (gotrajas), the relatives (bandhus), the disciples, and those who have studied under the same teacher (sabrahmacārins).
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them is the heir to the wealth of the deceased who died without a son; this rule applies to all social classes.
The heirs of forest-dwellers, ascetics, and lifelong students are, in order: the teacher, a virtuous pupil, a spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred site (tīrtha).
But a reunited coparcener shall give, and a uterine brother shall take, the share of one who has been reunited or of one who has died; and [the same applies to] one who is born [after reunion].
But a uterine brother who is a reunited coparcener shall take the wealth, not a non-uterine brother;
even one who is not reunited may take it, but one who is reunited and born of a different mother shall not.
A eunuch, an outcast, one born of such [an outcast], a cripple, one who is insane,
one who is mentally dull, a blind person, and those afflicted with incurable diseases and the like, should be maintained by the family but are entitled to no share of the inheritance.
However, among these, the legitimate sons (aurasa) and those born of the wife (kṣetraja), being free from defects, are entitled to inherit;
their daughters, moreover, must be maintained until they are given away in marriage.
The childless wives among them who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
however, those who are unfaithful or likewise hostile shall be banished.
