What is given by her father, mother, husband, or brothers; what she receives at the nuptial fire; and what is received as a gift upon supersession—this is proclaimed to be a woman’s property (strīdhana).
Likewise, the property given by a kinsman, the nuptial fee (śulka), and the after-acquired property (anvādheya)—
if she dies childless, her kinsmen shall obtain that.
The property of a woman who dies childless belongs to her husband even in the case of the four [marriages] beginning with the Brāhma;
however, if she has daughters, it goes to them; in the remaining [marriages], it goes to the father.
Having given away his daughter, he who takes her back shall be punished and shall pay the expenses along with interest;
if she has died, he may take back what was given after deducting the expenses incurred by both parties.
In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction [to travel],
a husband is not required to return to his wife the property she received from him.
One should give an equal amount as an "inducement for supersession" (ādhivedanika) to a wife who has been superseded;
however, if no separate property (strīdhana) was given to her, one should assign half of that amount.
When a partition has been concealed, the determination of a partition should be understood to arise from kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, written documents,
and separate houses and fields belonging to each individual.

[9. Section on Disputes Concerning Boundaries] In a dispute over the boundary of a field, the neighbors, the elders and others, the cowherds, those who cultivate the borderlands, and all those who frequent the forests [shall be consulted]. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 2.150.
They should demarcate the boundary, characterized by landmarks such as mounds, charcoal, husks, trees,
embankments, anthills, hollows, bones, and shrines.
Or the neighboring villagers from all four directions— four, eight, or even ten—
bearing earth and wearing red garlands and garments, shall lead the boundary line.
But those who speak falsely shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement.
In the absence of witnesses or signs, the king is the establisher of the boundary.
This same rule is to be understood as applying to groves, temples, villages, watering places, gardens, and houses, as well as to rainwater, flowing streams, and the like.
In cases of breaking a boundary, likewise in crossing a limit,
and in the seizure of a field, the punishments are low, high, and middling respectively.
However, a dam that causes little harm and brings about welfare is not to be prohibited;
nor is a well that takes water from another's land if it provides much water for one's own small field.
If one constructs an irrigation channel on a field without having informed the owner, the produce belongs to the owner;
in his absence, it belongs to the king.
If a person neither cultivates a field that has been ploughed nor causes it to be cultivated, he shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation;
another shall cause the field to be cultivated.
[10. The Section on Disputes between Owners and Herdsmen] A buffalo that causes damage to the crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow, half of that; and a goat or sheep, half of that again.
For those who sit down after having eaten [the fodder], the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed;
for these same persons, the fine is the same even in the case of a pasture-land, and for donkeys, camels, and buffaloes, it is equal to that for a cow.
As long as the crop is destroyed, so long shall the fruit belong to the owner of the field;
the cowherd is to be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine.
There is no offense in [grazing] on a path, at the edge of a village pasture, or in a field, provided it is unintentional;
but if done intentionally, one deserves punishment like that of a thief.

Large bulls, animals that have been set free, those born from a cow in labor, newcomers, and others for which there is no keeper— these must not be claimed [as lost], even when overwhelmed by divine calamities or royal authority.
Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening,
so too must he who has received wages be made to pay for those that have died or been lost through negligence.
But when damage occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner.
The grazing of cattle may take place according to the will of the villagers or by the authority of the king;
furthermore, a twice-born man may gather grass, firewood, and flowers from anywhere and at all times.
The distance between fields within a village shall be one hundred bow-lengths;
for a market town (kharvaṭa) it shall be two hundred, and for a city (nagara) four hundred.
[11. Chapter on Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner] One may recover one's own property sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the sale was not publicly announced.
In a secret transaction from a person of inferior status, for an inferior price, or at an improper time, the purchaser is a thief.
Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
and in cases where there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize the offender oneself and hand him over.

Purification comes from seeing the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the buyer recovers his price from whoever was the seller of that [stolen] item. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.170)
What is lost must be recovered through legal title or possession;
otherwise, it is subject to a fine of five times its value, which must be paid to the king if it is not proven [to belong to the claimant].
He who recovers property that has been stolen or lost from the hand of another,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas.
If property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officials or local guardians, the owner may reclaim it within one year; after that period, the king shall take it.
One should pay one paṇa for a single-hoofed animal, four or five for a human,
two each for a buffalo, a camel, or a cow, and a quarter-paṇa each for goats and sheep.

[12. Section on Non-delivery of Gifts] One's own property may be given away without detriment to one's family, except for one's wife and sons; nor may one's entire estate be given while there are descendants, nor that which has already been promised to another. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.175)
The acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property;
and what has been promised as a gift must be given, and once given, one must not take it back again.

[13. Section on Rescission of Purchase] The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and male slaves shall take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month respectively. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 2.177 //
Gold is not diminished when placed in fire; silver loses two palas per hundred;
tin and lead lose eight palas per hundred; and copper loses five palas per hundred, as does iron.
In a hundred [palas] of wool, cotton, or silk thread, the increase is ten palas;
in medium quality, the increase is five palas; but in fine quality, it is considered to be three palas.
In woven cloth and in hair-cloth, a loss of one-thirtieth is considered [to occur];
however, there is neither loss nor increase in silk or in garments made of bark-fiber.

Having ascertained the place, the time, and the nature of the object, as well as the strength and weakness of the parties involved when [the property] has been lost, those who are skilled in the matter should declare what must be paid; that shall be given without doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.181)

[14. Section on Failure to Serve after Having Accepted Service] One who has been forcibly made a slave by thieves, or even one who has been sold, is released from slavery by saving the life of his master, by abandoning his food, or by the payment of his ransom. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.182)
One who has been expelled from the order of renunciation becomes the king's slave for life;
among the social classes, slavery may occur through the natural order, but never in the inverse order.
Even when he has mastered the craft, the apprentice shall continue to reside in the teacher's house for a fixed period;
subsisting on food provided by the teacher, he yields the fruit of his labor to him.

[15. Chapter on the Breach of Agreements] Having established his residence in the city and appointed Brāhmaṇas there, the king should tell those learned in the three Vedas who receive a livelihood: "Let your own duty be protected. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.185)
But that which is established by convention, provided it does not conflict with one's own dharma,
as well as any law enacted by the king, must also be protected with effort.
But he who misappropriates the property of the community, or whoever violates a formal agreement,
the king shall confiscate all his possessions and banish him from the realm.
The advice of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all;
whoever acts contrary to that shall be fined the first amercement.

The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the assembly with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business has been accomplished.
One who has been dispatched for the business of a collective shall hand over whatever he may obtain;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times that amount.
Those who know the Dharma, who are pure and free from greed, should be the ones to deliberate on affairs;
the word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out.
This same rule applies to guilds, merchant communities, heretical sects, and corporations;
the king shall protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional way of life.
[16. The Section on Non-payment of Wages] One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double;
if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount. The implements must be protected by the servants.
But he who employs laborers without having fixed their wages shall be made by the king to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, or crops.

If one should violate the place or the time, or should effect a gain in a manner other than prescribed, in that case it shall be at the pleasure of the owner; if more has been done, more should be given.
Whatever amount of work one performs, that much shall be his wages;
if the task is impossible for both to accomplish, they may perform it as prescribed if it is possible.
The carrier shall be made to pay for any goods lost that were not destroyed by the king or by fate;
likewise, one who causes an obstacle to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
If he abandons him on the way after he has set out, he must pay one-seventh of the fee;
if he abandons him at the halfway point, he must pay the entire fee; and the same applies to the one who causes him to be abandoned.
[17. Chapter on Gambling and Betting] When the stake involves interest of one hundred, the keeper of the gambling house shall take five percent from a rogue gambler,
but ten percent from any other.
Having protected it properly, he should give the king the share as prescribed;
he should cause the winner to take what was won and give it to the victor, speaking the truth and remaining patient.

When the king has received his established share and the assembly of gamblers is well-known, he shall cause the winner to pay the stake in a place where the court is present; otherwise, he shall not do so.

For they alone are the observers of legal proceedings and the witnesses; therefore, those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception should be banished by the king along with their implements.
Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the purpose of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applying to betting on living creatures and to challenges to combat.

[18. Section on Verbal Abuse] If one insults those who are deficient in limbs, senses, or afflicted by disease by means of praise that is true, false, or otherwise, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.204)
If a man swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king should compel him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas].

The infliction of punishment should be carried out by considering the higher or lower status of the castes and classes involved: half the penalty for offenses against those of low standing, double for offenses against women of others, and likewise for offenses against those of superior rank.
In cases of defamation involving the reverse order of castes, the fines shall be double and triple;
for the castes in the natural order, they decrease by half and half from that amount.
For verbal threats of injury to the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred;
for such threats regarding the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that.
But one who is unable [to pay] and speaks thus should be fined ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is able should be made to provide a surety for his security.
For an accusation made regarding an offense causing loss of caste (pātaniya), the punishment is the middle amercement;
but for one involving a minor offense (upapātaka), he shall be made to pay the first amercement.

The fine for insulting those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity is the highest amercement; that for insulting a guild or association is the middle amercement; and that for insulting a village or a district is the lowest amercement.
[19. Section on Assault] When a person has been killed without witnesses, the legal case must be investigated by means of physical marks, circumstantial reasoning, and testimony,
for [an assailant] might create false marks out of fear.
A fine of ten paṇas is prescribed for touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust;
for touching [another] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, the fine is double that amount.
In the case of other men's wives who are of equal status, the punishment is the same; for those of superior status, it is double;
for those of inferior status, it is half a fine; and there is no punishment when the act is committed through delusion, intoxication, and the like.
But for one who is not a Brahmin, that limb which causes injury to a Brahmin shall be cut off;
if he merely raised his hand, the first amercement is the punishment, but if he actually touched him, it is half of that.
If the hand or foot is raised [in a threatening manner], the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively;
but for all [such acts] against one another with a weapon, the middle amercement applies.
For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a cloth, or stepping upon [the feet], the punishment is one hundred.
A man who inflicts pain with wood or other implements without shedding blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine shall be double.

For the breaking or cutting off of a hand, a foot, or a tooth, or for the cutting off of the ears or the nose, the middle amercement is the punishment; likewise for causing a wound that results in death or for striking someone so severely they are as good as dead.
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
For many who strike one person, the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed;
for property taken during a quarrel, it must be restored, and the fine shall be double that amount.
But he who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its removal,
as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel.
In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to collapse,
one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of the damage.
One who throws into a house property that causes suffering or is life-threatening shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas for the first offense and the middle amercement for the second.
In cases of causing pain, drawing blood, or cutting off a limb or member,
the fine for small animals shall be two paṇas and so forth, in successive order.
In the case of cutting off the male organ or killing [the animal], the middle amercement shall be imposed, as well as its value;
for these great cattle, the fine in these instances is double.
For cutting all the branches and trunks of trees that are capable of sprouting and growing,
as well as for destroying twenty trees that provide livelihood, the fine shall be double.

In the case of trees growing near a shrine, a cremation ground, a boundary, a sacred site, or a temple, as well as for a tree renowned [for its sanctity], the fine is double. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.228)
For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs,
and climbing vines in the aforementioned locations, the fine shall be half of that prescribed for the previous [trees].
Section on Violence] Violence (*sāhasa*) is defined as the forcible seizure of common property;
the fine for this is twice its value, but if there is denial, it is fourfold. *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* 2.230.
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times the amount.

One who neglects the offering of the *arghya* water, one who strikes his brother's wife, one who fails to deliver a entrusted message, and one who breaks down a house situated by the sea; // Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.232 //
For those who cause harm to neighbors, guild members, and others,
the settled rule is that their fine shall be fifty paṇas.

One who approaches a widow of her own accord, one who does not run to help when a cry for aid is raised, one who raises a false alarm, and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the higher castes; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 2.234 //
One who feeds those among Śūdras who have renounced the world at rites for the gods or the ancestors;
one who makes an improper oath; and one who performs the duties of an unworthy person—these are excluded.
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus; YDh_2.236.
A father, son, sister, brother, husband and wife, or teacher and pupil— whoever abandons any of these when they have not fallen from their caste— shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
A washerman who wears another's garment shall be fined three paṇas;
however, for selling, exchanging, pledging, or borrowing it, he shall be fined ten paṇas.
In a dispute between father and son, however, the witnesses shall be fined three paṇas;
and for anyone who stands as an intermediary between them, the fine shall be eightfold.
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins,
as well as anyone who deals with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
He who declares a counterfeit coin to be genuine, or a genuine coin to be counterfeit—
that examiner of currency shall be made to pay the highest fine.
A physician who practices falsely shall be punished with the first amercement for treating animals,
the middle amercement for humans, and the highest amercement for royal officers.
He who binds one who should not be bound, he who releases one who has been bound,
and he who obstructs legal proceedings, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
He who takes even an eighth part [of the value] by means of a false measure or scale shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this is ordained for both increase and decrease.
If one adulterates medicinal herbs, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses,
and other such commodities with inferior substances, he shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen *paṇas*.
For one who attributes a higher quality to clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark,
or cloth when they do not possess that quality, the fine shall be eight times the value of the article for sale.
For one who brings for deposit or sale a casket containing precious goods that are counterfeit,
a punishment shall be prescribed.
For damage of one paṇa, the fine is fifty; for five paṇas, it is said to be one hundred;
for two paṇas, the fine is two hundred; and as the value increases, the fine increases accordingly.
For artisans and craftsmen who, having banded together,
fix the price of their goods while knowing whether that price ought to decrease or increase, there shall be the highest fine.
For merchants who, having banded together,
withhold their merchandise at an improper price or sell it [at such a price], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement.
Whatever price is fixed for a commodity by the king, by that price its sale or purchase should be conducted;
the surplus obtained from this is recorded as the profit of the merchants.
A merchant who buys and sells immediately may take five percent on goods from his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land.
Having deducted from the value of the merchandise the expenses incurred in producing it,
the price should be fixed so as to grant favor to both the buyer and the seller.
[21. Section on Non-delivery after Sale] He who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, shall be made to pay it with interest;
or, if the buyer has come from another region, he shall be made to pay the profit derived from that region.
Even if an item has been sold, it may be resold if the previous buyer does not accept it;
however, if the loss occurs due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed fall upon the buyer alone.
If a commodity becomes defective due to an injury caused by the king or fate,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, does not deliver it.
If one sells an item into the hand of another, or sells what is defective as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be double the value of the price.
A merchant who, unaware of the depreciation or appreciation of his merchandise, has no right to rescind a purchase; if he does so, he shall be liable for a fine of one-sixth [of the value].
[Chapter 22: On Joint Undertakings] When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership,
the profit and loss shall be according to their respective capital, or as determined by their agreement.
If a deposit is lost through negligence—whether it was forbidden [to use] or not specifically instructed [how to handle it]—the bailee must restore it;
furthermore, he shall receive a tenth part as his fee for having guarded it against loss.
The king shall take a twentieth part as tax from the offering of *arghya*;
however, that which is established as a monopoly (*vyāsiddha*), what is fit for the king, or what has been sold [as such], belongs to the king.
One who speaks falsely regarding the quantity [of goods] while departing from a customs station,
as well as one who engages in fraudulent buying and selling, shall be made to pay eight times the amount.
A ferryman who collects a land toll shall be made to pay ten paṇas;
this same penalty applies to Brāhmaṇas and neighbors for failing to invite one another [to a feast].
When a deceased person has gone to another country, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives who have arrived there shall take his property; in their absence, the king shall take it.
One should abandon work that is sluggish or yields no profit; if one is unable, one may have it performed by another.
By this rule, the duty of officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers is declared.
[Chapter 23: On Theft] A thief is apprehended by pursuers either by means of the stolen property or by his footprints;
likewise, one who has committed a prior offense, as well as one who resides in an impure dwelling.
Others also should be apprehended with suspicion on account of their concealing their caste, name, and so forth,
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and liquor, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered.

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet incur expenses, and those who sell goods that do not belong to them; // Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.268 //
If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft does not clear himself,
he shall be made to restore the stolen property and be punished with the penalty prescribed for a thief.
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, the king shall execute him by various means of death;
however, having branded a Brāhmaṇa with a mark, he shall banish him from his own kingdom.
If cattle are killed or stolen, the fault lies with the village headman if they have not yet left the village;
however, on the road, it lies with the superintendent of the pasture, and outside the pasture, with the one who protects against thieves.
One should give as much land as can be traversed on foot by a village boundary, or five villages outside the *krośa*, or even ten villages. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.272)
Those who seize bandits, those who carry off horses and elephants,
and those who commit violent assaults, the king shall cause such men to be impaled upon stakes.
For the offenses of one who causes a monk to leave the order and one who breaks a sealed knot, the hands and nose shall be cut off;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot.
For the theft of small, medium, or large property, the punishment shall be proportional to its value;
in the administration of punishment, one must carefully consider the place, time, age, and capacity [of the offender].
If one knowingly provides a thief or a murderer with food, shelter, fire, water, mantras, or the means for their sustenance, the highest fine shall be imposed.
For causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed;
likewise for the killing of a man or a woman, either the highest or the lowest fine applies.
A woman who has committed a heinous crime, one who has killed her husband, one who is not pregnant, or one who destroys a dam—
he shall cause her to be cast into water after being bound with stones.
One who administers poison or sets fire, or one who causes the death of her husband, her teacher, or her own child,
should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by oxen.
The sons and kinsmen of one who has been killed while unrecognizable must quickly investigate,
as well as his women who were devoted to other men, each separately.
Or, desiring [to know about] his wife, property, or livelihood, he should ask people near the place of death slowly: "With whom did this man depart? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.281).
Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of the king, shall be burned in a fire of straw mats.
[Chapter 24: On Adultery] A man shall be apprehended for adultery with another's wife by seizing her by the hair,
or immediately by signs born of passion, or likewise when both parties confess it.
Touching the knot of the lower garment, the breasts, the covering [of the body], the thighs, or the hair;
conversing in an improper place or time; and sitting together on the same seat.
In the case of a prohibition against a woman, she shall pay one hundred [paṇas], while a man shall pay two hundred as a fine;
in the case of a prohibition against both, their punishment shall be the same as that for adultery (saṃgrahaṇa).

In the case of those of the same caste, the highest fine shall be imposed; in the case of a woman of a lower caste, the middle fine; but in the case of a man of a higher caste, death, and for a woman of a higher caste, the cutting off of the ears and other such limbs.
For abducting an adorned maiden, the king shall impose the highest fine; otherwise, for other maidens, the lowest fine.
In cases involving women of his own caste, he shall impose the prescribed fine; however, for abduction from a higher caste, death is ordained by tradition.
There is no offense if she consents and is of a compatible class; otherwise, there shall be punishment.
But for defilement, the hand shall be cut off; likewise, in the case of a woman of the highest caste, there shall be death.
One should be made to pay one hundred for defiling a woman; two hundred for making a false accusation;
for having intercourse with a female animal, he should be made to pay one hundred; and for approaching a low-caste woman or a cow, the middle amercement.
In the case of female slaves, whether they are kept in the household or are otherwise dependent, even if they are women with whom intercourse is permissible,
a man shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas.
If one approaches a slave woman by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
if she is unwilling and there are many men involved, the fine is twenty-four paṇas for each individual.

A prostitute who has accepted her fee shall not, if she does not wish to comply, be made to pay double; if the fee was not accepted, she should be made to pay an equal amount. A man likewise should be treated in exactly the same manner.
For one who has sexual intercourse with a woman in an improper place, or who urinates upon a man, the fine is twenty-four paṇas; the same applies for approaching a female ascetic.
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a male organ and banish him;
likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the lowest caste shall become a member of that very caste, while for a man of the highest caste approaching a woman of the lowest caste, there is death.
[Chapter 25: Miscellaneous Matters] He who writes a royal edict deficient or even excessive,
or he who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment.
One who defiles a twice-born man with forbidden food shall be punished with the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that.
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall be deprived of three limbs and made to pay the highest fine.
The same fault incurred by using a four-legged animal applies to one who calls out,
"Do not avoid it," as well as to one who uses wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, arms, or a pair of yokes.
If injury occurs by means of a vehicle with a broken nose-rope, or one with a broken yoke and so forth,
or if it moves backward, the owner is not liable for the offense.

Even if capable of doing so, a master who fails to rescue [his dependents] from fanged or horned animals shall pay the first amercement; likewise, if they have cried out for help, he shall pay double.
One who calls his paramour a "thief" shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;
but if he releases him after having lived off his wealth, he shall be made to pay eight times that amount.
Having cut out the tongue of one who speaks what is disagreeable to the king, of one who reviles him, or of one who divulges his secret counsel, he should banish him.
The punishment for one who sells the limbs of a corpse, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the vehicle or the seat of a king, is the highest amercement.
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who acts against the king's commands,
and likewise for a Śūdra living by the profession of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.
But having seen legal proceedings wrongly decided by the king,
the members of the court, together with the victor, shall be fined double the amount of the dispute.
If one who thinks "I am not defeated" is in fact defeated according to the law,
he shall be defeated again upon his return and made to pay double the fine.
Whatever fine has been unjustly taken by the king, he should present it to Varuṇa and himself give it to Brahmins increased thirtyfold.
[End of the Vyavahārādhyāya] [III. Prāyaścittādhyāya] [1. Āśaucaprakaraṇam]
One should bury a child less than two years of age and must not offer water for them thereafter;
others, surrounded by their kinsmen, should follow [the corpse] as far as the cremation ground.

If he has been initiated, he should be cremated with the worldly fire while those chanting the *Yamasūkta* and the *Gāthās* perform the rites according to the procedure for one who maintained the sacred fires, as if they were effective.

On the seventh or even the tenth day, the relatives go toward the waters facing the direction of the ancestors, reciting: "May the evil be burnt away from us; may the waters purify our sin. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.3)
In this manner, the water-rite for maternal grandfathers and teachers is performed;
however, the offering of water out of affection is for friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests.
Restraining their speech, they should pour out water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage;
however, those practicing celibacy and likewise those who are outcasts should not perform the water libation.

Heretics, those who have no protector, thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who go after their own lusts, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide— these are not entitled to the period of impurity nor to the water-offering.
When they have finished the water libations, emerged from the water, and are seated upon soft,
grassy ground after their bath, one should instruct them with ancient historical narratives (itihāsas).
He who seeks a core in human existence— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on water— is utterly deluded.
If the body, which was composed of five elements,
has returned to its fivefold state through the actions arising from its own body, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
The earth, which supports all beings, goes to destruction; so do the oceans and the gods.
How then will the world of mortals, which resembles foam, not go to destruction? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.10)
Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should therefore not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability.
Having heard this, they should go home preceded by a child;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of their house.
Having sipped water and touched fire and other elements, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds,
they should enter [the house], having anointed themselves and placing their feet slowly upon a stone.
Even for those who have touched a corpse, the rites beginning with entry [into the village] are performed;
for those who desire it, purification occurs at that very moment through bathing and self-restraint, as well as for others.
Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or preceptor, one who observes a vow remains a vow-observer;
he should not eat food from a person in distress, nor should he dwell with such people.
Eating food that has been purchased or obtained, they should sleep separately on the ground;
for three days, food should be offered to the deceased according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña.
Water and milk should be kept for one day in an earthen vessel;
furthermore, the sacrificial rites (vaitāna) and the domestic rites (aupāsana) must be performed because of the injunctions of the Śruti.
Impurity due to death (śāva) is prescribed for three nights or ten nights;
however, in the case of a child under two years of age, impurity due to birth (sūtaka) belongs to both parents, yet it belongs to the mother alone.
Regarding the birth-impurity (sūtaka) of the parents, it certainly belongs to the mother because of the appearance of her blood;
on that day, however, there is no defilement for the ancestors, because it was their cause of birth.
In the interval between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days;
however, in the case of a miscarriage, nights equal in number to the months [of gestation] are the cause of purification.
In the case of those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for those who commit suicide, purification occurs immediately;
if they have been away on a journey, purification occurs at the end of the remaining period; and when that period is complete, one becomes pure after offering water libations.
For a Kṣatriya, the period is twelve days; for a Vaiśya, it is fifteen;
for a Śūdra, it is thirty days, or half of that for one who conducts himself righteously.
For those from birth until the cutting of the teeth, impurity is declared to last for one night;
until the initiation (vratādeśa), it lasts for three nights; and beyond that, for ten nights.

But for approaching unmarried girls, children, a teacher’s pupil, one who has studied the Vedas, or a maternal uncle who is a Śrotriya, the purification is the same as for an Adultery (ahsa). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.24)
In the case of sons other than those born of one's own body, of wives who have gone to another man,
and when the king by whom one resides has died— that very day is the cause for purification.
A Brahmin should never follow after a Śūdra or another twice-born person;
having followed them, he becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
There is no period of impurity for kings, nor for those killed by lightning,
nor for one who dies in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or if the ruler of the earth so desires.

Likewise for officiating priests, those initiated for sacrifice, and those performing sacrificial rites; as well as for those observing the vow of the *sattra* sacrifice, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman.
In matters of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, and the calamity of a country,
as well as in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained.

If he is touched by those who are menstruating or impure, he should bathe; if he is touched by them [in turn], he should sip water for purification. He should also mutter verses containing the word "water" (abliṅga) and recite the Gāyatrī mantra once mentally.
Time, fire, ritual action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water,
subsequent remorse, and fasting— all these are causes of purification.
For those who have committed forbidden acts, giving gifts effects purification; for a river, its current does so;
for that which is to be cleansed, earth and water do so; and for the twice-born, renunciation indeed effects purification.
Austerity is said to be the strength of those who know the Vedas, forbearance that of the wise, water that of the body,
silent recitation that of those whose sins are concealed, and truth that of the mind.
For the elemental self (bhūtātman), austerity and knowledge are the means of purification; for the intellect (buddhi), it is wisdom (jñāna);
and for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), purification is considered supreme through the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara).
[2. The Section on Duties in Times of Distress] In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even that of a Vaiśya;
having emerged from that distress and having purified himself, he should return to his own path.
Fruits, stones, linen, Soma, humans, cakes, creepers, sesame, boiled rice, meat broth, alkaline substances, curd, milk, ghee, and water. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.36 //
Weapons, liquor, beeswax, honey, lac, and the stalks of sacrificial grass;
earth, leather, flowers, blankets made of goat hair, hair, buttermilk, poison, and soil. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.37 //
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, lead, Śakas, Ārdra, medicinal herbs, oil-cakes, livestock, and perfumes; likewise, [these are forbidden].
Even when living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one should never sell sesame seeds;
for the sake of dharma, they may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
Lac, salt, and meat are causes for falling [from caste] if sold;
whereas milk, curd, and liquor cause one to become of a lower caste.
Whether receiving or eating from anyone whatsoever when fallen into distress,
a Brahmin is not defiled by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.

Agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, trade by cart, mountain-mining, service to others, marsh-land cultivation, the king, and begging— these are the means of livelihood in times of distress.
Having remained hungry for three days, one may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa;
having received it, the person so engaged must report it according to the law.
Having ascertained his conduct, lineage, character, learning, study, austerity, and family, the king shall provide him with a righteous means of livelihood.
Chapter on the Duties of the Forest-Dweller] Having entrusted his wife to his sons, or accompanied by her,
he should go to the forest as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), observing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), maintaining the sacred fires (*sāgni*) and the domestic fire (*sopāsana*).
Self-controlled, wearing a beard, matted locks, and body hair, he should satisfy with food grown without the plow the sacred fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents.
One should accumulate wealth for the sake of a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been accumulated, one should relinquish it in the month of Āśvayuja.

Self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts, devoted to Vedic study, habitually generous, and intent on the welfare of all beings; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.48.
Using his teeth as a mortar, eating only what is ripened by time, or using a stone for grinding,
he should perform the rites and activities prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis with fruits and oils.
One should pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇa fasts or always subsist on Kṛcchra penances;
or one may eat once a fortnight, or once a month, or even once a day has passed.
Being pure, he should sleep on the ground at night; during the day, he should pass the time by standing, sitting, walking about, or likewise by the practice of yoga.
In summer he should stand amidst five fires; in the rainy season he should sleep on the bare ground;
and in winter he should wear wet clothes, or otherwise perform penance according to his ability.
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood paste— toward both of them,
he is without anger and without satisfaction, remaining equal toward all.
Or, having internalized the sacred fires within himself, dwelling among trees and restricting his food,
he should beg for alms only for the sake of sustenance at the dwellings of forest-dwellers.
Or, having brought eight morsels from a village, he should eat them while restraining his speech;
or, subsisting on air, he should walk toward the northeast until his body is worn away.

[4. The Section on the Duties of the Ascetic (Yatidharma)] Having performed the *prājāpatyā* sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), either from the forest or from the home, and having at its conclusion internalized those sacred fires within oneself; YDh 3.56.

Having studied the Vedas, performed recitations, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires, and offered sacrifices according to his ability, he should then set his mind on liberation; it cannot be otherwise.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, peaceful, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot,
delighting in solitude, he should wander forth as a mendicant and resort to a village for the sake of alms.
Vigilant and unobserved, he should wander for alms in the evening in a village free from other mendicants, seeking only enough for his sustenance and remaining free from greed.
The vessels of ascetics are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
Having fully restrained the collection of senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear toward all beings, the twice-born becomes immortal.
But a mendicant, in particular, must purify his intention for action,
because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence.
One should contemplate dwelling in the womb, as well as the various states of existence born of karma,
mental anxieties, physical ailments, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of physical form.
Through the yoga of meditation, one may perceive within the self the subtle Self, situated in the self, as well as the reversal of the pleasant and unpleasant throughout thousands of births.
The stage of life is not the cause of dharma, for dharma is that which, when practiced, leads to well-being.
Therefore, one should not do to others that which is unwholesome for oneself.
Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint,
control of the senses, and learning— all this is declared to be Dharma.
Just as sparks fly forth from a heated mass of iron,
even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the Self.
In this regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some by its own nature, and some through habituation; it consists of both dharma and adharma.
The signless, imperishable, the agent, the knower, the possessor of qualities, and the controller—though unborn, he is proclaimed "born" due to the assumption of a body. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.69)
Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, air, light, water, and earth—
each possessing one more quality than the preceding— so too does he take them back while coming into being.
By the oblation the sun is nourished; from the sun comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen.
But when a man and a woman unite, and the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord himself, as the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements.
The sense organs, mind, vital breath, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.73 //
Effort, form, color, likes and dislikes, existence and non-existence—
all this is born of that beginningless one who desires a beginning.
In the first month, it becomes a state of moisture, a coagulation of the elements;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; and in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs.
From space [he obtains] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, strength, and so forth;
and from wind, the sense of touch, movement, expansion, and even dryness.
From bile (pitta), however, come vision, digestion, heat, form, and luminosity;
from rasa (nutritive essence), however, come the sense of taste, coolness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness.
In the third month, the unborn self perceives the smell of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and form; thereafter, it begins to move.
By not granting her pregnancy-longings, the fetus may incur defects, deformity, or even death; therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the woman.
In the fourth month there is the stabilization of the limbs; in the fifth, the production of blood;
and in the sixth, the emergence of strength, complexion, nails, and hair.
Endowed with mind and consciousness, joined with channels, sinews, and arteries,
he also possesses skin, flesh, and memory in the seventh and eighth [weeks].
Furthermore, his nourishment, heat, and vital energy (ojas) waste away;
thus, in the eighth month, the fetus born is deprived of life.
In the ninth or even the tenth month, he is expelled by the powerful winds of birth,
like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by distress.
His body is sixfold; it possesses six layers of skin, six limbs, and three hundred and sixty bones.
Together with the sockets, there are sixty-four teeth; the nails are twenty;
and the digits of the hands and feet—these constitute their four locations.
There are sixty bones in the fingers; two in the heels and four in the ankles;
there are four bones in the forearms, and exactly that many in the shanks.
One should designate two each as arising from the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, the shoulders,
the palms, the soles, and the two buttocks.
There is one bone in the pubic region, forty-five in the back,
fifteen bones in the neck, one in each clavicle, and likewise one in the jaw.
At its base are two [bones], the forehead-eye and the two cheeks; the nose consists of solid bone;
and the ribs, together with the sockets and the tubercles, number seventy-two.
There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise seventeen bones in the chest; such is the collection of bones in a person.
Smell, form, taste, touch, and sound are known as the objects;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ear are the sense organs.
One should know that the hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the feet are indeed the five organs of action; and the mind is of a dual nature.
The navel, the vital energy (ojas), the anus, the semen, the blood, the two temples,
as well as the head, the shoulders, the throat, and the heart— these are the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The omentum, the fat, the slaughter-wound, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen, the small intestine, the two kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of feces; Yajurveda 3.94.
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the anus, the abdomen,
and the two internal organs of the rectum— this is declared to be the extent [of the torso].
The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two auditory canals,
the two ears, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins.
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, and the two breasts are produced from the accumulation of phlegm;
likewise are the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the calves, thighs, and the muscles of the shanks.
The belly, the bladder-head, the chin, the two tonsils, and the nape of the neck—
these are the locations in this body.
The two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the anus,
and the genitals— these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
There are exactly seven hundred vessels (śirā), nine hundred ligaments (snāyu),
two hundred arteries (dhamanī), and five hundred muscles (peśī).
Know that there are twenty-nine hundred thousand, nine hundred,
and fifty-six vessels known as *sirās* and *dhamanīs*.
It should be known that embodied beings possess three hundred thousand hairs on their beard and head;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (marmans) and two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores,
sixty-seven lakhs, and half a lakh of hair-pores, along with the openings for sweat.
The atoms, divided and counted by means of the winds, are such that even a single person may understand their nature and their arrangement. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.104)
Nine añjalis of rasa (chyle) are to be known, ten of water,
seven of feces, and eight of blood are proclaimed.
Phlegm consists of six parts, bile five, urine four, muscle fat three, and fat two; marrow is one part, while the brain is situated above it.
"The vital essence of phlegm is just this much, and the semen is just this much"—this body is so unstable; he for whom it exists must strive for liberation.
Seventy-two thousand channels named Hitā and Ahitā issue forth from the heart; in their midst is that which has the luster of the moon.
The self situated in the center of that maṇḍala is immovable like a lamp;
it is to be known, and having known it here, one is not born again.
And that which I obtained from the Sun, the Āraṇyaka,
as well as the Yogaśāstra proclaimed by me, should be known by one who desires to attain Yoga.
Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses focused on no other object,
one should meditate upon that Lord who dwells as the Self within the heart like a lamp.
By reciting the *Sāmaveda* chant without error according to the prescribed rules,
one who is attentive attains the Supreme Brahman through that practice.
The Aparāntaka, Ullopya, Madraka,
Prakarī, Auveṇaka, Sarobindu, and Uttara are the types of songs.
The *ṛggāthā*, the *pāṇikā*, those composed by Dakṣa, and the *brahmagītikā*—this is what is called *geya*; through the practice of these, it is designated as "liberation."
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, is proficient in the musical scales and modes,
and understands rhythm, attains the path to liberation without effort.
If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through yoga,
he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.
The self is said to be beginningless, yet its beginning is the body;
the entire world originates from the self, and the self originates from the world.
How are we, along with the world of gods, asuras, and humans, bewildered by this?
Tell us how the universe arose and how the Self exists within it.
Indeed, that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion has a thousand arms, eyes, and feet; he possesses the radiance of the sun and has a thousand heads.
He is indeed the Self, the sacrifice, the omniform Prajāpati;
as Virāj, he attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food.
That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substance and deity,
having gratified the gods, [gratifies] the sacrificer with its fruit.
Then, having been joined with the wind, the Soma is led by its rays;
it is brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
From the orb of the sun, that sun emits the supreme nectar,
which is the source of birth for all beings, whether they are of the nature of eaters or non-eaters.
From that food, again comes sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again the ritual.
In this manner, this wheel, without beginning or end, revolves perpetually.
The self is beginningless; no origination exists for the inner self.
However, the person (puruṣa) is a composite entity born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma.
The primordial deity whom I have described to you as the thousandfold self— his social classes emerged from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, respectively.
From his feet the earth was born, and from his head the sky arose;
from his nose the vital breaths, from his ear the quarters of space, from his touch the wind, and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun;
from his loins came the intermediate space and the entire world with its moving and unmoving beings.
If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born in sinful wombs?
How can he, who is the Lord, be joined with undesirable states of being?
And why is there no prior cognition even for one endowed with the instruments [of perception]?
Why does the all-pervading [Self], though itself omnipresent, not perceive the sensation [of another]? (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.130)
Through the defects born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, this living soul undergoes existence among hundreds of wombs, reaching the state of the lowest animals and stationary beings.
And just as the states of beings within their bodies are infinite,
so too are the forms of embodied beings here in all wombs.
The ripening of karmas for some occurs after death, while for others it arises in this life;
for yet others it occurs both here and in the next world—such is the nature of things, and therein lies the purpose.
Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable,
and being intent on what is false, one is born into other wombs.
A man who speaks falsehood, who is slanderous, harsh,
or a speaker of idle gossip, is born among beasts and birds.
One who delights in taking what is not given, who consorts with the wives of others,
and who is a violent injurer of immobile beings by improper means, is born among stationary things.

One who knows the self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered the senses, performs dharma, and is learned in the Vedic sciences— such a person of sattvic nature attains birth among the gods.
One who delights in the non-existence of the effect [in the cause], who is unsteady, enterprising, and sensual—
that person of rajasic nature, having died among men, attains another birth.
One who is drowsy, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct, being characterized by tamas, shall be born among the animals.
Thus, possessed by passion and darkness,
wandering here and joined with undesirable states, he enters the cycle of worldly existence.
For just as a dirty mirror is incapable of reflecting forms,
so too one whose faculties are unripened is incapable of self-knowledge.
Just as the sweet taste, though present, cannot be perceived in two unripe mangoes,
so too knowledge is not attained within the self when the faculties are unripened.
An embodied being experiences all sensations within his own body;
however, the yogi who is liberated does not experience any of them.
Just as the single space appears distinct within jars and other vessels,
so too the one Self appears as many, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.
Ether, air, fire, water, and earth are the constituent elements;
from these come these worlds, this Self, and all that is moving and unmoving.
Just as a potter makes a jar from the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, clay, and wood; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.146 //

Just as a goldsmith [fashions] a form by taking only gold, or as a silkworm [produces] a cocoon through the union with its own saliva, so too does one [construct the body]. // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.147 //
Having thus taken up these causes, the Self, having come together with the instruments, creates itself within those various wombs here.
The great elements are real, and the self is indeed just like them;
for who, having seen with one eye, can see again with the other? (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.149)
Who indeed recognizes speech when it is heard again and again?
To whom does the memory of past objects belong, and who is the creator of dreams? (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.150)
Proud on account of birth, physical form, age, conduct, learning, and so forth,
he exerts himself toward objects such as sound through action, mind, and speech.
With a mind full of doubt as to whether the fruit of action exists or not, he is deluded; for even though he is unaccomplished, he considers himself accomplished. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.152)
"My wife, my sons, and my ministers; I belong to them"—such is his fixed notion, and he always possesses a perverted mind regarding things that are beneficial or harmful.
He regards the object of knowledge, the knower, primordial nature, and its transformations as indistinguishable;
he exerts himself in fasting, fire, blows, and leaping into water.
One who behaves in this manner, being undisciplined in self and possessed of false attachments,
is bound by action, as well as by hatred, delusion, and desire.
Service to the teacher, discernment regarding the meanings of the Vedas and the scriptures,
the performance of those prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech.
Abstinence from looking at or touching women, perceiving the Self in all beings,
renouncing possessions, and wearing worn-out saffron-colored garments.
The restraint of the senses from their objects, the avoidance of drowsiness and laziness,
the thorough examination of the body, and the perception of evil in worldly activities.

Through these means— purity of the *sattva* quality by being free from *rajas* and *tamas*, freedom from desire, and tranquility— one who is thoroughly purified becomes fit for *sattva* and attains immortality.
Through the establishment of mindfulness of reality, through the application of being, through the exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, the yoga of the good proceeds.
He whose mind, at the dissolution of the body, is firmly established in the Lord with a steady intellect, shall attain the recollection of his former births.
For just as Bharata colors his own body with pigments,
creating various forms, so too does the Self [assume] bodies born of karma.
The deformity of the fetus at birth— such as being deficient in limbs— is seen to result from defects in time, karma, the self, and the seed, as well as from those of the mother.
This self has never at any time been liberated from egoism, the mind, the sense of motion, the fruit of karma, and the body.
Just as the stability of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the vessel, and the oil, so too is its alteration observed; likewise, the premature exhaustion of the life-force occurs.
Infinite are the rays of him who abides in the heart like a lamp—
white, black, variegated in form, tawny, blue, and red.
One among them stands above; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, by that [path] one goes to the supreme goal.
That other hundred of its rays which are situated upwards,
by means of them he reaches the bodies of the gods together with their abodes.
Those multiform rays of his that shine below with gentle luster—
by means of them, he wanders helplessly in this world for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his karma.
By means of the Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge; by birth and by death;
likewise by affliction, by going, and by coming; indeed, by truth and by falsehood.
[He should not be led astray] by prosperity or by pleasure and pain, nor by auspicious or inauspicious actions,
nor by the results arising from the knowledge of omens, birds, or the conjunctions of planets.
By the movements of the stars and constellations, by waking states as well as those born of dreams, and likewise by space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness; // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.172 //
Through the succession of Manvantaras, the arrival of the Yugas, and even by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, and fruits,
one perceives the Self as the wealth and the cause of the world.

Ego-consciousness, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, happiness, fortitude, the transition between the various senses, desire, retention, and life—these [are the marks of the self]. (Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.174)
Heaven, dreaming, the impelling of entities, the movement of the mind, the winking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and the grasping of the five elements; 3.175.
Since these marks of the Supreme Self are observed,
therefore there exists beyond the body the all-pervading Lord, the Self.
The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action,
as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the elements beginning with earth.
The Unmanifest is called the Self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this field;
it is the Lord dwelling within all beings, who is both being and non-being, and that which is both existent and non-existent.
The arising of the intellect (buddhi) is from the unmanifest (avyakta); from that, the emergence of the ego (ahaṃkāra);
and from the ego, the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the rest, each possessing one additional quality.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever of these has emerged from which [element] dissolves back into that very same one.
I have explained to you how the Self creates itself,
even though it is the Lord, through the ripening of the three kinds of karma.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed proclaimed to be its very qualities;
for when possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel.
He alone is the supreme Puruṣa, both beginningless and yet possessing a beginning;
he is described as having a form perceivable by the subtle body (liṅga) and the senses, along with its modifications.
Between the path of the fathers (pitṛyāna) and the path of the constellations (ajavīthī), and between that and the region of Agastya,
by that way those who maintain the sacred fire and desire heaven proceed toward the celestial realm.
And those who are devoted to giving and endowed with the eight qualities correctly,
they too, being dedicated to the vow of truth, proceed by that very same path.
Among them, eighty-eight thousand sages were householders;
they were subject to rebirth, served as the seeds [of future lineages], and were propagators of the Dharma.
Between the Seven Sages and the Nāgavīthī, there dwell those who have taken refuge in the world of the gods;
there are just as many sages, entirely free from all worldly undertakings.
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings.
For from it come the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the sciences,
the Upaniṣads, as well as the verses, the aphorisms, the commentaries, and whatever else consists of speech.
The recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint,
faith, fasting, and independence are the causes for the knowledge of the Self.
For he is to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
moreover, he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
Those twice-born ones who, having resorted to the forest hermitage, find Him thus and worship the Truth with supreme faith— Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.192.
In due order, they pass through the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, and likewise the northern solstice,
the world of the gods, the sun, and that which possesses lightning.
Then a person born of the mind approaches them and makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahmā;
for them, there is no return here again.
For those men who have conquered heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[the path leads] through smoke, the night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice.
They arise here in succession— the world of the ancestors, the moon, the wind, rain, water, and the earth— and they go back again in the same order.
The self-possessed man who does not understand these two paths shall become either a venomous serpent, a moth, an insect, or a worm.
With his feet placed flat upon his thighs and his right hand resting on the left,
he should slightly lift his face upward and steady it with his chest.
With eyes closed, established in *sattva*, not touching the teeth with the teeth,
the tongue fixed motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly still.
Having restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
he should undertake breath control (prāṇāyāma) twice or even thrice.
Then the wise man, maintaining concentration, should fix his self upon that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp and is to be meditated upon there.
Invisibility, memory, luster, vision, as well as the power of hearing,
and the ability to enter the bodies of others after casting off one's own body.
The creation of objects at will is indeed the mark of perfection in yoga;
when yoga is perfected, one who casts off the body is fit for immortality.
Alternatively, even one who has renounced ritual acts and dwells in the forest, studying the Veda,
eating only what is unasked for and being moderate in diet, shall attain supreme perfection.

For even a householder is liberated if he has acquired wealth by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites, and speaks the truth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.205)

[5. The Section on Expiation] Having experienced the terrible and dreadful hells born of mortal sins (mahāpātaka), those who have committed such great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.206)
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a deer, a horse, a pig, or a camel;
the drinker of spirituous liquor [enters] the womb of a donkey, a Pulkasa, or a Venā—of this there is no doubt.
A stealer of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a moth;
and one who violates the teacher’s bed shall gradually become grass, a shrub, or a creeper.

The killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; the drinker of spirituous liquor shall have black teeth; the stealer of gold shall have deformed nails; and the violator of the Guru’s bed shall have a skin disease.
Whosoever among these lives with another, he is born bearing the characteristics of that person:
a stealer of food shall be afflicted by disease, and a stealer of speech shall be mute.
One who steals grain shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a foul-smelling nose;
one who steals oil, a habit of drinking oil; and a backbiter, a foul-smelling mouth.
Having abducted another's wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region of the forest.
One who steals the jewels of others will be born into a low caste;
by killing a peacock one becomes a leaf-eating bird, and by stealing fragrant substances one becomes a musk-rat.
A mouse shall be the stealer of grain; a camel the vehicle; a monkey the fruit;
a water-fowl the water; a crow the milk; and a house-builder (the white ant) the household utensils.

A stealer of honey becomes a gadfly; a stealer of meat, a vulture; a stealer of a cow, an iguana; likewise, a stealer of fire, a crane; a stealer of clothing, one afflicted with leucoderma; a stealer of liquids, a dog; and a stealer of salt, a cricket.
This has been stated by me for the sake of illustration regarding the act of theft;
for just as there are various kinds of objects, so too are there various classes of living beings.
Having obtained the fruit according to their karma, through the passage of time, they are born as animals;
then, having lost their auspicious marks, they become impoverished and the lowest of men.
Then, having become free from stain, they are born into great families as enjoyers of life,
endowed with learning and possessed of wealth and grain.
Through the non-performance of what is prescribed, through the practice of what is censured,
and through the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall.
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become propitiated.
Men who do not perform penance for their sins, being devoted to evil deeds and devoid of remorse,
go to terrible and agonizing hells.
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka.
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃprapātana,
the great Naraka Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Mahāpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka,
as well as Asipatravana and Tāpana— the twenty-first.
Worst of men who have not performed expiation go forth accompanied by the terrible consequences arising from mortal sins (mahāpātaka) as well as those arising from minor offenses (upapātaka).
Sin committed unintentionally is removed by penances;
however, one who acts intentionally becomes fit for social intercourse here only by virtue of a scriptural declaration.
The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief, and likewise the violator of the Guru's bed—
these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is he who dwells together with them.
Exceedingly severe abuse of gurus, reviling the Vedas, killing a friend,
and the wasting of what has been studied should be known as equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Eating forbidden food, crookedness, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation,
and tasting the mouth of a woman in her courses are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The theft of a horse, a jewel, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow,
as well as the misappropriation of a deposit, is indeed equal to the theft of gold.
Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, with virgins, with women of one's own uterine kin, with women of the lowest castes,
with women of the same lineage (sagotra), or with the daughters of one's pupils is declared to be equal to violating the bed of a guru.
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, the daughter-in-law, the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter; ||| Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.232 |||
But he who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed;
his penis shall be cut off and he shall be put to death, as shall the woman if she was willing.
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling merchandise unfit for sale, and gambling; YDh 3.234.
Taking instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, causing a younger brother to marry before the elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt; YDh 3.235.
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of reprehensible wealth;
atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.
Stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice;
abandoning one's father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove.

Defiling a maiden, officiating at the sacrifice of one who marries before his elder brother, giving a daughter in marriage to such a man, crookedness, and the breaking of a vow; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.238.

Engaging in undertakings for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning the study of the Vedas, the sacred fires, and one's sons, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen; YDh 3.239.

Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, killing women, living by the sale of medicinal herbs, the construction of injurious machines, vices, and the selling of oneself— these are [grounds for loss of caste].
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
Studying false scriptures, having authority over mines,
and the sale of one's wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).
Carrying a skull as his bowl, bearing a banner, subsisting on alms, and making his deed known,
the slayer of a Brahmin shall attain purification by living on moderate food for twelve years.
One may attain purification by rescuing a Brāhmaṇa, or by saving twelve cows,
or likewise by bathing at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having seen on the road a Brahmin or even a cow afflicted by a long-lasting and severe disease, the slayer of a Brahmin becomes pure by restoring them to health.
If he has been brought before the court, or if all his property has been confiscated, or if he has been killed,
or if he is wounded by weapons for that purpose, he is purified even while still alive.
Saying "Svāhā to the body hairs," he should likewise offer his body, beginning with the hair and ending with the marrow, with these mantras in the proper sequence.
Or, being made a target and slain in battle, he attains purification;
even while living, one who is nearly dead and afflicted by wounds becomes purified.
Having recited the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times in the forest with self-restraint, he shall be purified; or by eating sparingly while traveling upstream along the Sarasvatī.
Or, by giving sufficient wealth into the vessel, one may attain purification;
for the sake of the purifier's own purification, the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice is prescribed as an offering.

One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the penance prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; likewise, one who destroys an embryo or one who kills an Ātreyī woman shall perform the same penance according to the respective caste.

One should observe the vow even if one does not kill, provided one has come together for the purpose of killing; however, if a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a Soma sacrifice is killed, one should prescribe a double vow.
Having drunk any one of liquor, water, ghee, cow urine, or milk that has been heated until it resembles fire,
a drinker of liquor attains purification through death.
Either clothed in hair or wearing matted locks, he shall perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin;
or he shall eat oil-cake or grain-particles at night for three years.
But having drunk liquor, or [consumed] semen, feces, or urine through ignorance,
the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again.
That Brāhmaṇa woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of the ancestors;
even in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, or a sow.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold must present a club to the king, declaring his own deed; whether he is killed by it or released, he remains impure.
Having reported it to the king, one who has performed the penance for drinking liquor becomes purified;
or he may give gold equal to his own weight, or do whatever brings satisfaction to a Brahmin.
He shall lie upon a heated iron bed together with an iron woman;
having had his testicles cut off, he shall cast away his body in the direction of Nirṛti.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for three years,
or he may practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months while reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā.
Whoever indeed lives together with these for a year becomes equal to them;
he may marry a maiden from among them who is fasting and possesses nothing.
Having killed all those who have fallen from their caste,
even a Śūdra, though lacking the right to perform Vedic rites, becomes purified by this very penance of Cāndrāyaṇa over time.

The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for one month, remaining self-controlled, sleeping in a cow-pen, and following after the cows; he is purified by the gift of a cow.
Or, being composed in mind, he may perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give ten cows and one bull.
Purification for a minor offense (upapātaka) may likewise be achieved by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
or by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance.
For killing a Kṣatriya, a man should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh,
or else he should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years.
A killer of a Vaiśya shall perform this penance for one year or give one hundred cows;
even a killer of a Śūdra shall do this for six months, or else give ten milch-cows.
Having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly,
one should give, for the sake of purification, in order, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, and a sheep.
Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the vow prescribed for killing a Śūdra;
likewise for a thousand vertebrate animals, or a cartload of those without bones.
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance.
For an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and sheep, a bull should be given; and for a crane, a three-year-old [bull].
Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous animal, or a peacock that frequents water or land, one should give a cow; but for killing a non-carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
