For killing snakes, an iron staff must be given; for a eunuch, tin and lead; for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a guñjā seed; and for a horse, a fine cloth.

But one who is unable to give the gift of a drona of sesame seeds for each of the [animals] beginning with the elephant, such as the partridge, shall perform a Kṛcchra penance for the purification of each individual case.
For killing a living being produced from fruit, flowers, food, or sap, one should consume clarified butter;
for killing something with bones, something small should be given as a gift; but for killing something boneless, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc* verses should be recited;
for cutting medicinal herbs in vain, one should subsist on milk and follow cows for a day.
One who has been bitten by a harlot, a monkey, a donkey, a camel, or the like, or by a crow,
becomes pure by performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in water and consuming clarified butter.
With the two verses beginning "That semen of mine today," one should consecrate the spilled semen;
with the ring finger, one should touch the space between the breasts and the middle of the eyebrows.
Seeing one's own reflection in water, one should mutter "Maya tejaḥ";
and when one has seen something impure, or acted with fickleness, or even spoken an untruth, one should mutter the Sāvitrī.
A student of sacred knowledge who, having gone to a woman, becomes one who has broken his vow,
is purified by sacrificing an ass as an animal dedicated to Nirṛti.
But having neglected the begging for alms and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill,
one should offer two oblations with the two verses beginning "kāmāvakīrṇaḥ."
Then one should perform the ritual attendance, saying, "May they sprinkle me with this.
For eating honey or meat, a *kṛcchra* penance must be performed, as well as the remaining vows.
Having acted contrary to the teacher's will, one becomes pure only after propitiating him;
however, if the teacher is sent on a mission and dies, the pupil must perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
But there is no sin if a Brahmin dies while assistance is being rendered;
nor is there sin when bulls are in the process of digestion, or during the administration of medicine or fire-rites.
The guilt of one who brings a false accusation is twice as great as that of one who speaks the truth;
furthermore, by speaking falsely, he takes upon himself the guilt of the person falsely accused.
He who falsely accuses another of a great sin or a minor sin shall subsist on water for a month, reciting prayers with his senses restrained.
One who has been falsely accused should perform a difficult penance (kṛcchra), or specifically the Agneya penance;
he should offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to Vāyu, or indeed a victim animal to Vāyu.
One who approaches his brother's wife without being authorized should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
by approaching a woman in her courses, he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights.

One who performs sacrifices for those excluded from the community (vrātya-yājaka), even if performing malevolent rites (abhicaraṇa), as well as one who has forgotten the Veda (vedaplāvī) or abandoned one who has sought refuge, shall perform three kṛcchra penances and subsist on barley for a year.
Dwelling in a cow-pen for one month as a celibate student, subsisting on a milk-vow and devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, he is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts.

One who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma) after bathing in water, one who has traveled in a vehicle drawn by a donkey or a camel, one who bathes naked, and one who eats or has sexual intercourse with a woman during the day— [these must perform penance].
Having addressed a guru with "huṃ" or "thou," or having defeated a Brahmin in debate,
or having bound him with a garment, one must quickly propitiate him and fast for a day.
If one raises a staff to strike another, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if he strikes him down, it is an *atikṛcchra*;
if blood flows, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and if the blood is internal, it is a *kṛcchra*.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the sin,
an expiation should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been stated.
His own relatives should have a slave-girl carry a pitcher outside the village;
they should exclude him from all social functions. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.294)
When he has returned after completing his vow, they should offer him a new water-jar;
they should not despise him, nor should they live with him in every respect [as before].
This same rule is proclaimed for women who have fallen from their caste:
they should be given a dwelling at the edge of the house, food, clothing, and protection.
Approaching a low-caste man, causing an abortion, and harming one's husband—these also certainly constitute specific acts leading to the loss of caste for women. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.297)
One should not live together with those who harm one who has sought refuge, children, women,
or ascetics— even if they have fulfilled their vows— nor with those who are ungrateful.
When the water-pot has been set aside, he who stands in the midst of his kinsmen should first offer fodder to the cows;
for this is the true honoring of one who has already been honored by the cows.
One whose fault is publicly known should perform a vow approved by an assembly;
however, one whose fault is not publicly known should perform a secret vow. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.300) [Secret Expiation]
Having fasted for three nights and recited the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn while submerged in water, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa is purified by giving a milch cow.
Saying "Svāhā to the body hairs," or else, subsisting on air for a day,
he should stand in water and offer forty oblations of clarified butter.
Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa hymns, one who is pure is purified;
but a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, standing in water, is purified by reciting the Rudra-hymns.
One who recites the *Sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn] is released from the sin of violating the Guru’s bed;
at the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow must be given separately by each of these [offenders].
One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) should be performed for the removal of all sins,
indeed for the various minor offenses (upapātaka) and for those not specifically prescribed.
Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink purifying Soma-water consecrated with the syllable *oṃ*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.306)
Whatever may have been done out of ignorance, whether by night or by day,
all that perishes through the performance of the twilight devotions at the three times of the day.
The recitation of the Śukriya and the Āraṇyaka, and especially that of the Gāyatrī—
these, as well as the Rudraikādaśinī, are indeed removers of all sins.
And wherever a twice-born man considers himself defiled,
in each such case there shall be an oblation of sesame seeds and likewise the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Sins, even those arising from the great crimes (mahāpātaka), do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and who is intent upon the performance of the five sacrifices.
Subsisting on air, standing during the day and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun,
one is purified from all sins except the killing of a Brahmin by reciting the Gāyatrī a thousand times.
Celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity,
truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, refraining from theft, gentleness, and self-control are known as the *yamas*.

Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas). // Yājñavalkya-smṛti 3.313 //
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, one should fast on the following day; thus one performs the *Sāntapana* penance.
When one observes a fast for six days while consuming the various substances of the *sāntapana* penance separately,
this seven-day rite is known as the *mahāsāntapana*.
When the leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, lotus, and *bilva* trees, along with *kuśa* grass water,
are drunk individually every day, it is declared to be the *parṇakṛcchra*.
One should drink hot milk, hot ghee, and hot water, each for one day respectively, followed by a fast for one night;
this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and fasting— this is proclaimed as the Pādakṛcchra penance.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold rite is called the *prājāpatya*;
this same rite becomes an *atikṛcchra* when one eats only as much food as fills the palm of the hand.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days;
the *parāka* is proclaimed to consist of fasting for twelve days.
The daily consumption of oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, and barley-meal,
followed by a fast for one night, is called the Saumya Kṛcchra.
By practicing each of these for three nights in succession,
this is to be known as the "tulāpuruṣa" (weighing-person) penance, lasting fifteen days.
While performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should take rice-balls the size of a peacock's egg, increasing them by one each day during the bright fortnight,
and decreasing them by one each day during the dark fortnight.
Alternatively, one may consume exactly two hundred and forty morsels of food within a single month; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who bathes at the three periods of the day should likewise perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
he should recite purificatory mantras and consecrate the morsels of food with the Gāyatrī.
Purification for unspecified sins is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon.
One who performs the Kṛcchra penance while desiring righteousness shall attain great prosperity;
being well-concentrated, he obtains the fruit of a major sacrifice.
Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya,
the ṛṣis spoke thus to that high-souled lord of yogins, who possessed immeasurable splendor:
Those who, unwearied, shall uphold this treatise on Dharma will attain fame in this world and go to the third heaven.
A seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and likewise one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
similarly, one desiring long life shall obtain long life, and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity.
For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a śrāddha ceremony, there shall be inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
By the retention of this scripture, a Brāhmaṇa attains the state of being a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth.
May you grant your approval for the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice that belongs to that wise man who causes this to be heard by the twice-born on every sacred festival day.
Having heard this speech of the sages, Yājñavalkya, with a joyful heart,
said, "So be it," after having paid homage to the Self-existent One.
